https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Fiona the hippo’s death was tragic. But blaming a ‘bad mom’ is absurd | Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
“Do they know the identity of the mother of the boy with the hat Fiona swallowed??” asks one Facebook post with thousands of likes. “She should be charged!!”
Spend a few minutes scrolling social media, and you will find endless variations of this statement. On Thursday, Fiona, a beloved hippo, died after eating a hat that had fallen into her enclosure at the Cincinnati zoo. Now a lot of angry people are out for blood.
By all accounts, Fiona’s death was a freak accident. A visitor, thought to be a small child, tossed a hat into the air. It was caught by a ceiling fan which launched it in just the right direction through a 1ft opening in the hippo’s viewing windows. Fiona ingested the hat, causing fatal medical complications that won’t be entirely clear until a post-mortem.
“We probably couldn’t make [it] happen again if we tried,” a zoo spokesperson, Michelle Curley, said in a statement to Axios about this unfortunate sequence of events.
But while Fiona’s death may have been a tragic accident, social media mobs are desperate to find someone to blame. And the obvious scapegoat is the mother. She should have disciplined her bratty child! She should have taken the hat away from the kid! She should have been a better parent!
We’ve seen almost this exact story play out before.
Ten years ago, authorities killed a 17-year-old gorilla called Harambe after a three-year-old boy crawled into the enclosure at Cincinnati Zoo. The child’s mother, who had her hands full with three other kids when the incident occurred, was identified by name and immediately became the target of an online witch-hunt. More than 500,000 people signed a petition asking for her to be held accountable, and she was mercilessly harassed. Nobody seemed to ask where the father was.
Harambe’s death was a slightly different set of circumstances from Fiona’s. Nevertheless, the reaction demonstrates a social impulse to blame mothers for anything and everything involving their children.
“Blaming mothers is automatic, almost instinctive,” the legal scholar Linda Fentiman wrote of the Harambe case at the time. “The tendency to blame mothers for all potential and actual harm to their children is deeply imbedded in our psyche, our culture, and our legal system.”
Mothers are held to impossibly high standards and: “When any mortal mom is compared to the perfect mother, she is likely to be found wanting, and thus, potentially negligent.”
Fentiman added that there is a “growing trend in American society to seek a legal remedy for many accidents or unfortunate incidents which previously would have been viewed simply as bad luck”. It’s more comforting, after all, to have someone to blame than to face the fact that life can be random and cruel.
And mother-blaming goes well beyond fatal zoo incidents. From the 1950s to the 1970s, autism was blamed on “refrigerator mothers” who were emotionally cold and distant from their child. Now that’s been discredited, but there’s plenty more junk science out there. Last year, the Trump administration distorted scientific studies to claim that there was a link between women using Tylenol while pregnant and autism in children.
Mother-blaming is also deeply embedded in legal systems around the world. A report published this year analyzed 91 published family law judgments in England and Wales and found “mothers’ behaviour [was] scrutinised intensely while the fathers’ conduct was contextualised or minimised”.
None of this, to be clear, is to say that mothers, and parents more generally, shouldn’t ever be held accountable for their offspring’s actions.
As anyone who has set foot in a public space recently can confirm, there are a lot of parents out there who seem unwilling to set any boundaries for their children. I, for one, will never forget being trapped on a transatlantic flight with a child who would not stop playing their screechy recorder.
Forget everything I’ve said about institutionalized misogyny in the legal system: straight to jail for that mother.
Elon Musk says he’s not Maga and feels foolish about midterm spending
Regrets: Elon Musk has a few. The world’s richest person denied being Maga this week, adding: “I’m not sure what Maga means.” I’m pretty sure it means wearing a custom Maga hat, aligning yourself with Donald Trump’s Maga policies, accompanying the president on state trips, and spending obscene amounts of money propping up Maga candidates.
Why don’t we hear of the ‘epidemic’ of women’s loneliness?
“We’re living through a global crisis of loneliness, with the World Health Organization declaring it a priority for public health, but it’s hard to miss that the coverage and conversation has been overwhelmingly focused on men,” writes Elle Hunt.
Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya minority
The international court of justice (ICJ) found that the 2016-2017 military campaign by Myanmar targeting its Rohingya minority amounted to genocide in a landmark ruling. “Legal experts see Thursday’s judgment as a key test for sexual violence in genocide assessments, as the convention says the crime can include acts with the intent to ‘prevent births’,” the Guardian reports. “Investigators have said gang-rapes and soldiers’ mutilation of women’s genitals were carried out intentionally and systematically to stop reproduction.”
Seventy–two-year-old Palestinian woman killed by Israeli militants
Fadha Wadha was standing outside her home in the occupied West Bank when she shot in the head after Israeli settler militants fired towards Palestinian houses.
One in four women globally unable to refuse sex within marriage
Forty-five percent of women in west and Central Africa have no power of consent, according to a new report by the UN Population Fund (UNFPA). In east and southern Africa and in Arab states, 33% of women are also unable to say no to their partner.
Nearly one in four children now live in conflict zones
A new report by Save the Children found the highest number of children living in conflict zones since records began in 1990. Africa is home to 44% of the global total, a nearly 20% increase from 2024. The report found the fastest-growing grave violation against children is the denial of humanitarian aid. More than 70% of all verified aid denial last year took place against Palestinian children.
Melania Trump has a new docuseries out
“Calling Melania thin gruel would be an insult to the gruel industry,” writes Stuart Heritage who bravely endured the entire documentary. “There are times when even the interviewer palpably gives up.”
Joe Biden told Netanyahu he loved and admired him in final call from White House
The Jerusalem Post reported that it obtained a transcript of Biden’s last conversation with accused war criminal Benhamin Netanyahu. “I can’t tell you how much I appreciate you and what you’ve been through,” Biden said. “I admire you. It took a lot of courage to do what you did.” Want to spell out exactly what Netanyahu did, Joe? He has the blood of tens of thousands of dead Palestinian kids on his hands. Dropping 2,000lb bombs on tent camps full of starving people isn’t exactly how I’d define “courage”.
‘Parents are up in arms over school photos that look like mug shots’
So says the Wall Street Journal, which reports: “We’re in the midst of a no-smile epidemic” amongst school-age children. While I’d take all this with a pinch of imported German rock salt, there are some fun nuggets here about how social media trends are impacting school photos. “[M]ale students are tilting their head backwards,” one staff photographer told the WSJ. “They tell me they are ‘aura farming.’ I had to look it up.” I had to look it up too.
- Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US pursuit of ‘Trump-class’ warships has blown cost of new fleet by billions, report warns
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ben Doherty in New York
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
The US navy’s commitment to the new Trump-class battleships has blown out the cost of its new fleet by billions of dollars, a report to the US Congress has found, as the acting secretary of the navy conceded this week the Iran war was “stretching” the fleet’s capacity.
The challenges facing the world’s biggest naval force were highlighted this week, when the return of the USS George Washington from the Middle East on Wednesday ended a rare three-month period when the US had no aircraft carrier across all of the Pacific. Deployments have been regularly running beyond 300 days, with the maintenance and repair of ships deferred so they can stay at sea longer.
Outpaced in shipbuilding by China, the US navy wants to increase its fleet from 286 battle force ships to 381 over the next 30 years.
But the congressional budget office’s analysis of the navy’s 2027 shipbuilding plan states the navy’s projections have underestimated the costs of its new fleet by billions because some ships’ designs have proven more complicated than expected, and the “estimated costs of some ships were unrealistically low in earlier shipbuilding plans”.
Total shipbuilding costs would average $54bn annually (in 2026 dollars) over the next 30 years, the CBO found, about 18% more than navy estimates.
“Much of the additional costs in the 2027 plan stem from the navy’s decision to purchase 15 large, heavily armed battleships, which would concentrate firepower in a few large ships and thus would be at odds with the navy’s stated goal of distributing it among a greater number of ships or vessels.”
The 15 new battleships are the proposed “Trump-class” warships, which the president has said will be 100-times more powerful than any previous warship in a US fleet, and will “inspire fear in America’s enemies all over the world”. Senate appropriators this week proposed cutting to zero the $1bn the navy sought in advanced procurement this fiscal year for the Trump-class ships.
On Wednesday, the acting secretary of the navy, Hung Cao, conceded before a Senate confirmation hearing that the Iran war was “stretching” the fleet’s capacity.
“This war, again, I know it’s a strain on our navy,” he told senators.
His term as acting secretary – he requires a special waiver to be permanently appointed because of his recent active service – was criticised by Democratic senators. “The world is less safe as a result of the Iran war,” Richard Blumenthal told Cao.
“We’ve seen costs soar, lives lost, casualties. Our relationships with allies deteriorate as a result of this war. In fact, the navy has been stretched beyond sustainable limits under your watch, and the fleet is in worse condition than it was when you took office along with this president.”
The conflict in Iran is estimated to have cost the US $260bn, Michigan senator Elissa Slotkin told the committee hearing.
“Yet we do not have the same freedom of navigation that we had a year ago.”
For all of the effort and resourcing of the world’s most powerful bluewater navy to keep the strait of Hormuz open, passage across the contested waters remains at barely more than a third of pre-war levels.
Shipping traffic remains approximately 65% below the rate before the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran on 28 February, according to the latest weekly report from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations.
A year ago, the cost to insure a commercial ship for a single passage through the Strait of Hormuz was $54,000, Cao told the Senate: “Today it’s $64m just to get across.”
The additional cost of every passage is borne by consumers all around the world, in higher prices for fuel, fertilizer, and food.
US navy ships are also consistently running longer and longer deployments. Since the start of the Iran war, ships have been deployed for 10 to 11 months, far beyond the standard seven months, and sailors have been told to expect extended deployments will remain standard for a number of years.
Several ships have spent beyond 300 days on deployment since the war began. The USS Abraham Lincoln went 265 days at sea, the longest a navy ship has gone without visiting a port.
Challenged about a “mental health crisis” onboard the Lincoln, Cao insisted eight reported suicide attempts on board were instead “suicide mitigations”.
He dismissed concerns that sailors onboard US ships were going hungry. In response to testimony before the Senate committee that one sailor had reported losing 45lbs (20.4kg) in six months on deployment “because of a lack of food”, Cao put it down to fussiness, likening it to “my kids opening up the refrigerator door and saying: there’s nothing to eat in here”.
For only the second time in two decades, the US navy had no aircraft carrier group in the Pacific between August and November. The Washington has returned to to the control of the US Pacific fleet “conducting routine operations” in the Asia-Pacific region.
Prof Kevin Rowlands, journal editor at the Royal United Services Institute, told the Guardian the “overstretch” facing the US navy was “critical but manageable – for now”.
He said: “The real problems will arise further down the line if the war continues. Every long deployment will have a knock on effect for maintenance and people in future.”
Naval planners work on a broad ‘rule of threes’: to have a single platform permanently available for deployment, a navy needs three.
“When one ship is deployed, another is preparing and training to replace it, and another is in maintenance, recovering having just come back. Effectively you need at least three to maintain one on station permanently. So, when something ‘new’ comes along, such as the war against Iran, it affects planning and allocation everywhere else.”
The US has, for decades, enjoyed an unrivalled naval pre-eminence, able to project power across the world. But China is rapidly catching up. US naval intelligence estimates China’s overall shipbuilding capacity is roughly 232 times greater than that of the US. Chinese shipyards delivered more than twice the naval tonnage as US yards across 2024 and 2025, according to the World Defense Shipbuilding report.
US allies, such as the nations of the first island chain off the Chinese mainland, and Pacific allies such as Australia “will always want US ships to be available in their region”.
“But, in return, the US would like its allies to share some of the burden it currently carries… the projection of naval power becomes a diplomatic negotiation, especially when the US sees the world through a transactional lens.”
“With Aukus, and the commitments to the Indo-Pacific, and commitments to Nato, and now the Middle East, the US can just about manage but there is zero spare capacity. That’s why one thing going wrong has negative impact everywhere. That, in essence, is the overstretch.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Brazil’s Jair Bolsonaro in intensive care with bowel obstruction
The former president, serving a sentence for plotting a coup, is stable and breathing on his own, the hospital says.
Brazil’s former President Jair Bolsonaro is in intensive care after being diagnosed with an acute bowel obstruction, according to the DF Star hospital where he is being treated.
Bolsonaro, 71, was admitted on Friday with abdominal pain. In a bulletin on Saturday, the hospital said doctors have started giving him fluids and nutritional support, and inserted a tube into his stomach.
It said the former president is clinically stable and conscious, although they said there was no projected date for his discharge.
“There is hope that his condition will improve,” his son, Senator-elect Carlos Bolsonaro, wrote on X on Saturday afternoon. “He is being closely monitored and is fighting to get his bowels working again, with his usual grit and focus.”
In the early hours of Saturday morning, he described his father’s difficult night of treatment, where food residue was removed from his stomach using a tube inserted into his nose, and bouts of nausea.
“I’m not a doctor, but I’ve never seen him like this,” he wrote, suggesting that his father might need another surgery, which would be his 10th in less than eight years.
“All this is happening to a man sentenced to 27 years in prison without having committed any crime, while criminals do whatever they want with what’s left of this country,” the younger Bolsonaro continued.
Bolsonaro has been serving a 27-year sentence since last year for an attempted coup after losing the 2022 election to current President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva. Bolsonaro has denied the charges.
He has been hospitalised repeatedly and has had to undergo surgeries after being stabbed in 2018 during a campaign event.
He was transferred in March to house arrest after spending several months in jail because of his health issues.
Next month, Brazil’s Supreme Court is set to consider the constitutionality of a law that changes how sentences are calculated, which could shorten his sentence and those of others convicted in the 2022 coup plot.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Cavaliers’ James Harden rolls back years with ‘vintage’ 51-point explosion to pass Kobe Bryant
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
James Harden’s game has evolved over the past couple of seasons, with the Cleveland Cavaliers guard now counted on more to create open shots for teammates than to be the prolific scorer he was during his first 12 years in the league.
On Friday night, though, Harden showed he can still produce the kind of performance that leaves fans and teammates in awe.
Harden scored 51 points and passed Kobe Bryant for the third-most 50-point games in NBA history as the Cavaliers defeated the Indiana Pacers 128-119 in an NBA Cup game.
“It’s a different role for me. My usage rate isn’t extremely high every game. We have somebody for that. So mine is kind of scoring when I need to, but then distributing the ball,” Harden said. “My number is called and you need to go out there and put the shots up. OK, I can still do it. I knew I can do it, but it’s just when you don’t do something consistently and then it goes away a little bit or you just don’t know if you got it or not.”
Harden now has 26 career 50-point games after being tied with Bryant for nearly a year. His previous 50-point game came nearly a year ago with the Los Angeles Clippers, when he scored 55 against Charlotte on 22 November 2025.
Michael Jordan is second with 31, while Wilt Chamberlain is the runaway leader with 118.
“When you talk about just basketball, obviously Wilt was elite, but you got Mike and Kobe, shooting guard position, the best to ever do it. So just to be in that conversation, it’s very humbling and it’s definitely special,” Harden said.
The performance was reminiscent of the kind of games the 18-year veteran produced during his run with the Houston Rockets, when he was named NBA MVP for the 2017-18 season and had three straight seasons averaging at least 30 points a game.
Harden played a season-high 40 minutes and shot 15 of 26 from the field, including seven of 11 from three-point range. He also made all 14 of his free throws and had six rebounds and six assists for the Cavaliers, who have won three of four but are only 9-8 after reaching the Eastern Conference finals last season.
“Nights like that are so special. The crowd appreciated that performance. That wasn’t like we’re 10 games above .500 and everything’s peachy. So it was a clutch performance. We needed that tonight,” Cavaliers coach Kenny Atkinson said.
Harden, who turned 37 in August, also became the sixth NBA player aged 37 or older to have a 50-point game, joining Bryant, Jordan, LeBron James, Jamal Crawford and Stephen Curry.
Harden said he felt it was going to be a big night from the opening tip. He scored 15 in the first quarter and had 24 by halftime.
“That was vintage where really you can’t do anything if you’re the opposing coach. Especially when he’s getting by you like that, when they started taking away a step back and one or two crosses and he’s in the lane, then there’s just no stopping him,” Atkinson said. “There’s really nothing you can do. So vintage, very reminiscent of his Houston days.”
Harden had 42 points after three quarters, when the Cavaliers led 103-82. Indiana rallied to get within six with two minutes remaining before Harden made one final push. A three-pointer from the top of the key with 57.9 seconds left extended Cleveland’s lead to 124-113 before he made a pair of free throws to reach 51 points 15 seconds later.
“I think what excites me a lot is even being in my 18th year learning how to still be impactful. It’s easy when you’re young, 23, 24, you run around, you jump high and can move fast and get by,” he said. “Now it’s like, you’re not as fast. Can you still get by people or how can you get by somebody? That’s the evolution of James Harden and figuring that out. Tonight was a confidence booster that I can do it at a high level still.”
Harden also became the sixth player in Cavaliers history to have a 50-point game, and the first since Donovan Mitchell’s 71-point outing against Chicago on 2 January 2023.
“I think I can speak for every hooper, especially when you’re at that level. Sometimes you just need that. Sometimes you need to just remind yourself just because you’re in such a rare era doesn’t mean you’re not human. And I think for him to tell you guys that, I’m glad he said that because that shows the human side that we all see of him,” Mitchell said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Iran says held talks with Qatari mediators, urges US to accept conditions
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Iran says held talks with Qatari mediators, urges US to accept conditions
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says reopening the strait is ‘not difficult’ if the US accepts reasonable conditions.
Iran says Qatari mediators have travelled to Tehran as the country’s foreign minister urges the United States to accept Iranian conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
News of the talks came as the commander of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) toured an underground missile facility on Saturday and the country’s president said Iran is facing a “silent economic war”.
A Qatari delegation visited Tehran on Friday night and held two hours of talks with Iranian officials, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said, according to Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency.
“We are in contact with mediators, including the Qataris, both in person and virtually, and are holding the necessary discussions to see whether another opportunity can be given to diplomacy,” he said on Saturday.
The US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28, prompting Tehran to launch strikes against Israel and Gulf states hosting US military bases. The conflict has drawn in countries across the region, disrupted shipping and pushed up global energy prices.
Gharibabadi said the talks have not yet become formal negotiations. If they do, the technical details of Iran’s nuclear programme would be discussed, he added, but Iran’s position is that its enriched uranium must not leave the country.
He also said Iran regards the US economic blockade as an act of war and will “take any action necessary” to break it.
For his part, US President Donald Trump told Fox News on Saturday that he wants a “permanent” deal that stops Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. He said Iranian officials are “very, very difficult”.
“We make a deal, and then they break the deal the next day,” he added.
Reopening Hormuz ‘not difficult’
The ongoing talks in the region “must be given a chance, and the blockade must be lifted rationally,” Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday, according to state television.
“Our position is clear: as long as Iran’s demands are not met, the discussion on the Strait of Hormuz and its opening is pointless,” he said.
“At the same time, we have always affirmed our readiness for dialogue, just as we are ready to defend ourselves.”
Iran’s conditions have included ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the US counter-blockade of Iranian ports.
Araghchi also said reopening the strait is “not difficult”, and requires the US only to “accept reasonable conditions that are in accordance with international law”, Tasnim reported.
The minister said there is “no solution” unless Washington acknowledges its mistakes and fulfils its previous commitments.
Iran has restricted shipping through the strait, which normally carried about a fifth of the world’s oil, since the war began. The US has imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports in response.
‘Silent economic war’
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Saturday that his country is facing a “silent economic war” that is “tougher than a war with missiles”, according to the state news agency IRNA.
Pezeshkian told a meeting of investors and producers that “a group of bullies, oppressors, and coercers sought to bring down our country”, but that Iranian businesses had managed market conditions well.
He said the government was working to avoid power cuts over the winter.
Meanwhile, IRGC commander Major-General Ahmad Vahidi toured an underground missile facility, accompanied by Brigadier General Majid Mousavi, who heads the IRGC Aerospace Force, Tasnim reported.
Vahidi was briefed on the force’s readiness and recent developments in its missile programme.
The visit follows the Aerospace Force’s unveiling of a new underground facility earlier this month, where it displayed ballistic and cruise missiles and their launchers, Tasnim said.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Fair-weather Silicon Valley pivots away from the right after blue wave: ‘I’m not Maga’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Johana Bhuiyan
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
A short two years ago, Elon Musk stood before an audience of tens of thousands of people in New York City and proudly told them: “I’m not just Maga. I’m dark, gothic Maga.”
On Wednesday, Musk spoke with much less conviction. “I’m not Maga,” he said. “Well, at least I’m not sure what Maga means.” The richest person in the world added he felt “foolish” for spending some $500m to elect Republicans in the midterms. “If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money,” he said at the New York Times’ DealBook conference, adding that he did not have “some sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican party”.
Silicon Valley’s tycoons made a hard-right pivot during Donald Trump’s second term, courting the president both on X and in private meetings, donating millions to his inauguration and, later, to his pet project, the White House ballroom. Musk himself spent more than $200m through his political action committee, America Pac, to help elect Trump in 2024. The attempts to cozy up to the president appeared to work. Trump took office in January 2025 flanked by some of the very executives who once banned him from their platforms in 2021. Musk, for his part, was installed as the head of the so-called “department of government efficiency”, a newly conceived and temporary federal initiative.
After Democrats’ decisive triumph in the US midterm elections, though, many of the tech barons are retreating.
The CEO of Palantir, Alex Karp, was among the first to attempt a pivot, softening his previously hardline stance on immigration a week before Musk in an interview with Politico. The animated leader of the tech firm that has powered Trump’s deportation apparatus said that the president mishandled immigration enforcement.
“I was really happy to hear the president be honest that – you know, his words, I believe, were something like: ‘Yeah, we kinda went too far,’” Karp told Politico. “And I’m glad he’s saying in public now what I’ve been saying in private.”
Karp, who once described the company as “anti-woke”, broadened his retreat from immigration to right-leaning politics in general.
“I’ve been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far-left environment. I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir – all of our products are essentially progressive,” he said.
Karp’s latest comments stand in stark contrast with Palantir’s work with the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE), functioning, according to Lesley Nash, a staff attorney at immigration defense organization Just Futures Law, as the “corporate and data analytics backbone of ICE”.
“Look, we power ICE,” Karp said in an earnings call in November 2025. “We power efforts to defend America and Ukraine. And with allies. We’re on the frontline of all adversaries, including vis-a-vis China. And we support ICE, and we’ve supported Israel. I don’t know why this is all controversial, but many people find that controversial.”
“Our ability to win while sticking by what we believe is important for the world,” he added in the call.
Other Silicon Valley leaders had also changed their tones in the immediate aftermath of the midterms.
Mark Zuckerberg, the CEO of Meta, is reportedly showing signs of shifting left. After the company bid farewell to Joel Kaplan, its president of global affairs and former adviser to George Bush, Meta recruited and promoted a more bipartisan slate of executives, according to Axios. Kaplan, who has been at Meta for 15 years, was promoted at the start of the Trump administration and was known for his ties to the the Republican party.
Following the political winds
Many Silicon Valley CEOs have helmed their companies for years, and it’s not their first time maneuvering the changing tides of American politics .
Though a self-described moderate, Musk previously donated to the Democratic national committee as well as Barack Obama’s re-election campaign in 2012. In 2018, he celebrated Tesla achieving a perfect score on an index of LGBTQ+ equality in the workplace for a fourth year in a row.
“Don’t buy our car if that’s a problem. People should be free to live their lives where their heart takes them ❤️🧡💛💚💙💜🖤💖🌈,” he wrote.
Eight years later, having moved from California to Texas and donated hundreds of millions of dollars to Republican candidates, Musk struck the opposite tone. He fear-mongered about the Democratic candidate for Senate in Texas, by tweeting that James Talarico “will trans your kids”.
After a blue wave swept over the US, though, he seems to again be shifting his stance. Responding to a question Wednesday about Texas’s Democratic governor-elect, Musk said, “I don’t think she’s sort of a far-left governor, and based on everything I’ve heard about her, I think everything will be fine in Texas with Gina [Hinojosa] as governor.”
He described her as “quite moderate” and characterized his own politics the same way.
At Meta, Kaplan helped Zuckerberg ingratiate the firm with the Trump administration over the last two years, completing its transformation away from the once proudly left-leaning company it had claimed to be. Kaplan replaced Nick Clegg, who, as a former deputy prime minister in the UK, had taken a more global approach. When Meta was just called Facebook, the company had championed diversity, with a goal of ensuring half its workforce was from underrepresented backgrounds. Zuckerberg and other leaders started a group to help immigrants. The company also temporarily banned Trump’s Facebook account after the January 6 insurrection.
While Silicon Valley firms regularly sway with the political winds, few companies have done so while being as deeply embedded in controversial government policies as Palantir.
Palantir has a long history of working with the US Department of Homeland Security, first winning a contract with ICE’s investigative arm in 2011 under Barack Obama. In the ensuing decade and a half, it has cast itself as a friend to whichever party is in power while maintaining that business.
Under the first Trump administration, Palantir worked closely with ICE’s investigative unit, developing software that helped the agency investigate and arrest people using a searchable super-network of government and private databases.
As the first Trump administration came to a close, Palantir attempted to distance itself from the president’s aggressive immigration policies. In September 2020, just a few months before Joe Biden was elected to be president, the company called Trump’s zero-tolerance immigration policy that led to family separations “abhorrent” and said that it violated “basic human decency and human rights standards”.
Five years later, under the second Trump administration, the company was awarded a $30m contract to develop a software platform called Immigration OS for DHS that would “streamline” the identification and deportation of immigrants. The company’s products were “integral to ICE’s draconian immigration enforcement and deportation abuses”, said Nash, of Just Futures Law.
Juan Sebastián Pinto, a former content strategist at Palantir, now speaks out against the company’s defense and immigration enforcement work. He spent his time at the company crafting the language to market Palantir to government and commercial customers. He said the company and Karp have historically used public statements to appeal to whoever has power over government contracts. The company will have to work overtime to glaze over its involvement with the second Trump administration, said Pinto. The company’s tools have been used by ICE and in the Iran war and “really challenged our democracy, our fourth amendment, our perception of safety”, he said.
“Palantir’s priority right now is to shape the narrative as much as it can to avoid responsibility because it’s going to be facing a lot of questions from the incoming Democratic administration,” he said.
Neutral tools?
Palantir describes the tools it builds in a way many tech companies do: as neutral platforms that bend to the wills of the people that use them.
As Palantir decried Trump’s family separation policy in 2020, Palantir’s then director of privacy and civil liberties, Courtney Bowman, said that, though the company accepted the “moral implications” of working with ICE, its technology was politically agnostic and “serves the core institutional missions of our partners, not any political or ideological agenda or individual elected official”.
Among those customers is ICE, tasked with deporting all undocumented immigrants in the US. For Palantir, that meant working with and optimizing the work of a government entity that the company once expressed concern about, over the “potential serious human rights violations” the agency was committing.
Nash at Just Futures Law said that Karp’s purported concern over Trump’s immigration enforcement tactics fall flat.
“Palantir’s CEO may now express that he had doubts about the very immigration system his company enabled, but private expressions of concern will not mitigate or alleviate the harm that this system has and continues to cause,” Nash said. “Companies like Palantir must take a hard look at corporate accountability and complicity with the worst abuses of the Trump administration.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Thousands protest across Europe over living costs and housing
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Thousands protest across Europe over living costs and housing
Demonstrations in France and Portugal follow youth-led protests over education and economic hardship across Europe.
Thousands of people have taken to the streets across Europe to protest against rising living costs, unaffordable housing and cuts to public services, as students and workers demand action from their governments.
Demonstrators marched across France and Portugal on Saturday, following youth-led protests in several European countries on Friday.
The gatherings reflect overlapping concerns about economic insecurity, education and future opportunities, although their demands and scale differ considerably between countries.
In France, the Ministry of Interior said 82,500 people joined demonstrations nationwide on Saturday, including 21,500 in Paris, down from 106,000 the previous weekend. Organisers estimated a higher turnout of 150,000.
The protests, now in their sixth consecutive weekend, began in September with students demanding better schools before expanding to include trade unions and the Yellow Vests, a movement that emerged in 2018 over rising fuel prices and living costs.
Demonstrators have also criticised police violence and a new law strengthening protections for officers who use firearms.
Portugal protests
In Portugal, thousands marched through Lisbon despite heavy rain, calling for higher wages, affordable housing and relief from rising prices.
The demonstration was organised by CGTP, the country’s largest trade union federation, which also demanded higher pensions and cheaper essential goods.
Portugal’s housing pressures have intensified as property prices have more than doubled since 2017.
Average annual earnings in 2025 were 37 percent below the European Union average, according to the EU’s statistics agency, Eurostat.
The weekend’s demonstrations followed Friday’s youth protests in Germany and Sweden.
About 4,000 people gathered in Berlin, while police reported roughly 200 participants at a Saturday march in Helsinki organised by left-wing and student groups.
Organisers of an international youth strike said demonstrations were planned in at least 25 countries, with demands ranging from greater education funding and climate action to opposition to compulsory military service.
In Germany, the youth campaign Gen Z regelt, meaning “Generation Z takes charge”, announced demonstrations in 73 locations.
In Italy, a nationwide strike organised by the CGIL, one of the country’s main trade union confederations, disrupted transport, schools and some healthcare services on Friday.
Demonstrations took place in more than 100 cities, with union leader Maurizio Landini claiming more than one million participants nationwide.
While some protests were linked through the international youth initiative, others grew out of established national campaigns, bringing different groups onto the streets over concerns about living standards and government spending.
Separately, thousands protested in the Croatian capital, Zagreb, on Saturday over the death of a man at a psychiatric hospital.
Four medical technicians are under investigation on suspicion of aggravated murder.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Did Democrats fail Florida? Angie Nixon on ‘missed opportunity’ in midterms
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: David Smith in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
To call it a blue wave, said the Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, would be an epic understatement. The midterm elections were “the political equivalent of a meteor strike”. But one state, DeSantis added with pride, was able to “hold the line”. And that state was Florida.
On a night when almost everything else went right for Democrats, David Jolly fell short by 1.3 percentage points against Republican Byron Donalds, who will become Florida’s first Black governor, while Angie Nixon, bidding to become the state’s first Black senator, lost by 2.9 percentage points to Republican Ashley Moody.
Even the losses, however, were remarkable performances in a state that has shifted right in recent years and become the adopted home of Donald Trump, and where two years ago he defeated Kamala Harris by 13 percentage points. In an election where Democrats were winning in Kansas, Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas, Nixon was left asking: did Florida Democrats lose because the party didn’t support them?
“It was a missed opportunity,” the 42-year-old said pointedly. “I’m going to work to bring everybody together so that we don’t miss opportunities like that anymore.”
Democratic party leaders and major national donors made calculated investments in key battlegrounds elsewhere, producing stunning victories in unexpected places. Yet that generosity came at the expense of southern states like Florida and Louisiana, where local candidates were largely left to fend for themselves.
Was that because too many people had written Florida off as a red state? “Folks often write the south off. Now we’ve shown that Florida is in play, the south is in play, and I’m hoping that through my advocacy and me being so vocal that people will take note and will listen and donate to more candidates in the south,” Nixon said.
With nearly 24 million people, Florida is the third most populous state in the US. Covering its vast geographical expanse requires a huge war chest and saturation TV strategy. Nixon had neither. “I would say we were out-fundraised and Florida’s a very big state,” was her simple diagnosis.
Moody had raised $14.5m compared to Nixon’s $11.3m, according to the Federal Election Commission, while outside groups spent $10.4m opposing Nixon versus $3.6m spent opposing Moody.
Without the funds to buy airtime across Florida’s multiple expensive media markets – from Miami and Orlando to Tampa and Jacksonville – Nixon found herself overwhelmed by negative advertising from Moody and her allied political committees. “They hit me hard on it, and we didn’t have enough money to push back until it was too late.”
While conservative groups sought to depict Nixon as a far left extremist (“Angie Nixon is actually a socialist,” said one), she believes it was a more traditional attack that hurt her the most. “Those didn’t necessarily work. What we saw worked was when they were trying to say that I was raising taxes on people.”
By the time Nixon’s campaign could afford to explain her economic platform, the ads had done their damage. Nixon believes that “of course” national Democrats should have intervened sooner. But she is careful not to dwell too long on the blame game.
“I wish more people gave me money, period. I’m going to work to move forward and work to organise and create an environment where, despite whatever the conditions of that year are, that we’ll still be able to win.”
Nixon’s optimism is bolstered by what transpired on election night in other southern contests, where underfunded candidates demonstrated that progressive, community centred campaigns can break through longstanding conservative strongholds.
She points to Scott Colom, the progressive prosecutor who became the first Black senator elected in Mississippi since the Reconstruction era. The lesson of those races, for Nixon, is that no red state is a monolith and no southern state is permanently out of reach if the party is willing to contest it.
Even with more money, however, any Democrat running in Florida faces a structural barrier erected over successive legislative sessions: the deliberate erosion of voting rights. Nixon points the finger at DeSantis. “That man has done so much as it relates to voter suppression. He’s done so much to suppress voters. Every single year they have attacked voting rights and the election laws and so now we’re dealing with that.”
While turnout rates among registered Democrats remained high, the overall playing field has been warped by the fact Florida now has 1.5 million more registered Republicans than Democrats, a huge reversal after Democrats held the advantage for decades.
Nixon argues that this gap did not emerge organically but was engineered by targeted legislation designed to debilitate voter registration drives. In recent years, Florida’s Republican supermajorities have enacted onerous penalties and strict restrictions on grassroots civic organisations.
She continued: “That gap is there because they made it harder for third-party organisations to be able to register voters. Historically, those third-party groups registered more people of colour. That was intentional to make it harder.”
In a state where vote-by-mail (VBM) had long been a secure and convenient staple used by voters of all political stripes, Republicans also changed the rules to require voters to renew their requests for mail ballots after every general election cycle.
Nixon added: “It was also intentional to change up the vote-by-mail laws because again, low-income working families and people of colour vote by mail more often because they’re working.
“They made it hard for that to happen and so we saw a huge drop. Thousands upon thousands of folks who would normally get VBMs did not get them because they didn’t know about the new law.”
In short, does Nixon believe she would have won on a level playing field? “Oh, absolutely, yes,” she replied without hesitation. “I do.”
It follows that Nixon refuses to accept that Florida, once a quintessential swing state but where Democrats have not won a Senate race since 2012, is now a lost cause. “We need to work to close the voter registration gap. We need to continue to organise and go meet people where they are.”
Nixon joined the Democratic Socialists of America over the summer, though she acknowledged some disagreements with the organisation. During her campaign she shared stages with the progressive stars senator Bernie Sanders and congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
But Nixon continues to resist easy categorisation. “I’m not interested in labels,” she said. “I’m interested in working with whoever wants to work to advance the agenda for working families.”
That agenda, she believes, is where Democrats can rebuild a working-class coalition that cuts across traditional partisan lines. When asked what the incoming Democratic majorities in Congress should prioritise in Washington, Nixon reels off an ambitious populist legislative platform centred on basic economic security.
“They need to pass comprehensive healthcare: push for Medicare for All. They need to increase the minimum wage. They need to push for comprehensive and compassionate immigration reform. They also need to hold Donald Trump and his people accountable.”
Does the Democratic party possess a coherent, compelling vision for the future? “We need more diverse voices in the conversation for us to get there,” Nixon said candidly. “I don’t think we’re there yet.”
Whether Nixon herself will launch another bid for elected office remains an open question. For now, her focus is on launching a political action committee, Never Scared, so that whoever steps onto the ballot in the future will not face the same structural headwinds she encountered.
“I am deciding right now. What I am doing is working to create the conditions, create the environment where folks will win whether or not the south gets funded by more historical donors.”

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.title: ‘Shakespearean tale of ego, greed and ambition’: the scandalous story of televangelism
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Andrew Lawrence
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
For three decades, film-maker Joe Berlinger has gripped true-crime buffs with his deep dives into small-town murders and infamous serial killers. His Netflix explorations of John Wayne Gacy and Jeffrey Dahmer helped flip documentary storytelling from viewer homework to a welcome distraction.
After dedicating so much time to the life of Jeffrey Epstein, the kidnapping of JonBenét Ramsey and other unsolved mysteries, Berlinger thought Primetime Preacher$, his new Netflix documentary on America’s televangelist boom, would offer a break. But it turns out that’s a pretty juicy crime story too, about the religious right’s bank job on American politics. “The deeper resonance for me came when I realized that the global televangelism rise actually mirrors the rise of the religious right,” he says. “Religion and politics, from Reagan on, has really changed politics for the worse in my opinion. This was the birth of that.”
In the early 1970s, roughly a quarter of US adults identified as evangelical Christians. As televangelism expanded, so too did the appeal of the prosperity gospel – this notion that personal prosperity was an indicator of divine favor. It encouraged the faithful not only to tithe generously to God’s work, but also to the ministers ostensibly chosen to carry out His will.
Primetime Preacher$ focuses on three: Jerry Falwell, Jimmy Swaggart and Jim Bakker – pillars of the movement who paved the way for Joel Osteen, TD Jakes and other modern contemporaries while establishing the comedic archetype of the greedy pulpit huckster, played by everyone from Steve Martin to Druski. Americans who lived through this period will remember these pioneering holy men well – Falwell, the befrocked Lee Iacocca clone who steered the “moral majority” and Liberty University; Swaggart, the fire-and-brimstone Pentecostal who rivaled cousin Jerry Lee Lewis for theatrics; and Bakker, the Mr Rogers type who famously lost his TV megachurch after an extramarital affair and a federal fraud scandal brought down PTL ministry (short for Praise the Lord, obviously).
What my young mind couldn’t appreciate at the time from scanning grocery aisle tabloid covers, eavesdropping on the TV news and observing the disgraced PTL first lady on the RuPaul Show was how tightly the three men were intertwined. “It’s a fun little Shakespearean tale of ego, greed and ambition,” Berlinger says. “A clash of these three men and this bizarre era in history.”
Bakker anchors the 114-minute film. Through archival video and interviews with close associates and the Pulitzer prize-winning Charlotte Observer team that uncovered the scandal, Berlinger shows how the genial former puppeteer won followers with folksy charm and Tonight Show-style productions that sold a more compassionate version of Christianity to a satellite audience of more than 13 million people. Behind the scenes, Jim and Tammy Faye carved out a life of luxury on the church’s dime, with homes (including an air-conditioned doghouse), a private jet and a pair of facelifts for Jim.
Swaggart took deep offense at Bakker’s PTL, however. He delivered over-the-top sermons to steer his flock away from football games and movies, while disparaging Bakker as a false prophet who was leading a double life. On CNN, he called Bakker “a cancer on the body of Christ”.
It all came to a head in the late 1980s, when Jessica Hahn, a former church secretary, publicly accused Bakker of rape and it emerged that she had received $265,000 in exchange for her silence. (Hahn, who endured a level of public scorn that seems unthinkable in the current post-#MeToo era, declined Berlinger’s sit-down invitation.) IRS auditors later concluded that $1.3m in ministry funds had been spent for the Bakkers’ personal benefit.
Bakker resigned from PTL and brought in Falwell to keep donations flowing and manage the crisis, thinking his friend would hold down the fort long enough for him to make a triumphant comeback. “I think he was genuinely interested in not having a massive embarrassment for Christianity,” Berlinger says. “There was a lot of good that PTL was doing that he thought was worth preserving. But did he think he could also expand his reach? Yes, but I don’t think he wanted to expand his reach to personally enrich himself.”
Falwell, the canniest operator, wound up burying his biggest competition. He went public with details of more of PTL’s financial improprieties, the Bakkers’ handwritten severance wishlist (“$300,000 for life to Jim … a maid and a secretary for one year”) and rumors that Bakker may have engaged in homosexual relationships. Ultimately, Falwell walked away from a business that was more than $65m in the hole. Swaggart, though, was in no position to gloat. After fiercely proclaiming that he had never had sex outside of marriage, much less disrobed for another woman, Swaggart was snapped during a tryst with a sex worker in New Orleans.
The film takes obvious satisfaction in the hypocrisy on display, not least Swaggart’s insistence on cutting a hole in his pants to maintain the, um, spirit of the truth. “Swaggart was telling people how to live,” Berlinger says. Swaggart’s melodramatic apology – “I have sinned against you, my Lord!” – became fodder for Jim Carrey and others keen to send up similar figures. And the laughing only got louder when Swaggart was caught soliciting again three years later.
Primetime Preacher$ shows how trouble beyond the pulpit drove a broader political conversion. When Bakker, who served almost five years in prison on federal fraud and conspiracy charges, ran into questions from Jimmy Carter’s Federal Communications Commission over PTL’s fundraising practices, he lent his considerable platform to Ronald Reagan, midwifing the California governor’s makeover from divorced Hollywood B-lister into the cowboy conservative who spoke of a “city upon a hill” that “hungers for a spiritual revival”.
In the nearly half century since, a movement that once warned against worldly entanglements has become a cornerstone of the GOP coalition, helping elect every Republican president since Reagan. That includes Donald Trump. His standing with evangelicals was shaky, to say the least, until a timely blessing from Jerry Falwell Jr – who extends the movement’s legacy of scandal (grist for its own documentary as well). Falwell Jr also appears in the film, explicitly invoking his father – who, before his death in 2007, declared the scandals of those bygone decades had “strengthened broadcast evangelism and made Christianity stronger, more mature and more committed”. That the Christian right remains a powerful political force, despite the recent blue wave, strengthens his claim.
Only Tammy Faye Bakker emerges from this story as something close to a redeemable character. She at least appeared genuinely committed to meeting faith-seekers where they were. While Jim sought to grow PTL into the Disney of Christianity, Tammy Faye aspired to be more of a Dolly Parton-style entertainer who led with humor – and suffered endless jokes about her caked-on makeup – while giving a platform to gay faith leaders whom other Christians had pushed aside and condemned to hell.
After divorcing Jim, Tammy Faye had a glorious second act as a kitschy B-lister and unabashed LGBTQ+ ally before dying from cancer in 2007. Jay Bakker, who followed his parents into ministry, does his mother proud by wrapping himself in a progressive theology that embraces LGBTQ+ rights – a position that opened a rift between him and his father that did not close with Jim’s death last month. “I found him to be extremely sympathetic as a person and as a character,” Berlinger says. “It also speaks so loudly to Jim Bakker’s character that he rejected Jay Bakker when he became LGBTQ-affirming.”
And yet: the biggest irony in Primetime Preacher$ isn’t Jim Bakker pivoting from come-to-Jesus telethons to hawking doomsday prepper kits. It’s him essentially showing the televangelists who followed him how not to get caught. Today’s TV megapastors don’t cloak their avarice in the faith and good works of the church. They just come right out, ask for the jet and claim it’s God’s will. “It’s amazing people give under those circumstances,” Berlinger says. “But people want to believe, you know?”
- Primetime Preacher$ is now available on Netflix

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Did you come down with GTA flu? I won’t judge – I may even join you in Vice City | Imogen West-Knights
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Imogen West-Knights
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
If there were an unusual number of people missing from your workplace at the back end of this week, they may have come down with GTA flu. You don’t need to be a video game person to have heard that there’s a new instalment of Grand Theft Auto, the enormously popular series in which you drive around sprawling American cities committing crimes. It has been all over the news. And if you are not a video game person, maybe that seems baffling. Why is this game such a big deal?
Let me assure you that this is no ordinary video game release. The last GTA instalment, GTA V, came out in 2013, so fans have waited 13 years for this game. On Wednesday, before the game had even been released in the US, PlayStation Network experienced widespread disruption attributed to an overload of people trying to download an update needed for the game. After its first day of sales, it was already thought to be the biggest entertainment launch of all time, having made $2.36bn (£1.8bn) – nearly as much as the latest Spider-Man film over its entire run.
In terms of the sheer number of people excited about it, it’s a cultural moment that might rank alongside something like a football World Cup. And so it has spawned something being called the GTA flu: millions of people around the world pulled sickies in order to devote the day of release to cracking incalculable numbers of beers and playing until their eyes go funny. This isn’t the first time GTA flu has swept the world: it happened back in 2013 for GTA V’s release, too. There is, alas, still no cure.
I asked around, and plenty of my friends and acquaintances admitted to being among the GTA bunkers, although most had booked the day off rather than feigning a cough to get their gaming hours in. One friend reported that every single man on her team had requested leave on Thursday, and I heard about another person who went a step further and timed quitting his job in order for his unemployment to coincide with this momentous week. On Thursday, I went to visit a friend, a man who had booked annual leave weeks in advance for the release of GTA VI, to see what the fuss was about.
When I arrived, he was at a quayside bar called the Rusty Anchor, losing a game of pool to a man in wraparound shades. We spent an hour or so driving around so he could give me a sense of the world he was just starting to discover – gorgeously rendered sunsets over the sea, rundown liquor stores and truck stops fringed with Florida-esque plantlife creeping through the concrete. The map for this game is huge – twice as big as it was in the last instalment and nearly as big as the real city of Miami – and getting to know all its corners will involve many, many hours of adventuring for its players.
Something else caught my eye in the news reports about GTA mania, though. I came across a post on a website describing an event being planned by players of GTA V, the 2013 instalment. Gamers would gather inside the online, collaborative version of the game and take a final, ceremonial drive through the game’s city, Los Santos. No reckless driving, no running down pedestrians, just a stately procession to say farewell to the world they had loved, before embarking on GTA VI. They were calling this “the last ride”.
I was never a GTA person. Not for any moral handwringing reasons (and look, yes, this is a game where you can and do kill people), but just because I was always more drawn to colourful platform games in my youth, or glorious time-sinks such as The Sims. But I am very much an open-world video game person. The rolling grasslands of Red Dead Redemption 2, the twinkling forests of The Legend of Zelda games, the bamboo groves of Ghost of Tsushima: all of these are places I have spent a lot of my life. Several times in any given week I think longingly about Zelda’s Kingdom of Hyrule in particular, knowing that I can just boot up the game and go there, but now that I’ve finished the main story, and practically all of the side adventures, it feels like a place I can’t quite go back to.
I miss it there. Anywhere you spend a lot of time accrues meaning, and modern video games create vast, richly detailed places to become attached to. That last ride through Los Santos makes sense to me. What my friend who I played some GTA with on Thursday was excited about mostly wasn’t firing a gun, or driving a really sick whip. It was getting to know the world.
It might seem sort of silly for people to get excited enough about a video game to risk pissing off their employers by pretending to be sick. I wouldn’t say that I approve, necessarily, of people bunking off school and work. Certainly not in a national newspaper. But I do understand. For millions of players, this week is their first introduction to a world where they will spend hours upon hours, exploring, marvelling, discovering. And, yes, sometimes shooting drug dealers.
- Imogen West-Knights is a writer and journalist

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Bruce Schneier
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.
The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.
None of them should surprise, though. Our computerized infrastructure is both vulnerable and fragile.
Much of it is old and has been incrementally patched and upgraded over the decades. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. There often aren’t good backup systems. And more and more of it is centralized, meaning that individual failures have cascading consequences across many different aspects of our lives and society.
A lot of our tech infrastructure just barely works. And when it fails, it can fail badly. It’s the very opposite of resilience.
There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream from the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system – and that’s where the core problems lie.
Security, safety, resilience, redundancy and recoverability are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs. More importantly, they are costs that don’t generate near-term profits.
Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, prioritizes near-term profits over everything else. This squeezes all apparent inefficiencies – and, additionally, all other positive intangibles – out of a company in pursuit of those profits.
Market competition, essential for the forces that nudge companies to provide better services, is another perceived inefficiency. Monopolization removes it in pursuit of near-term profits.
From the perspective of a quarterly budget, spending on reliability measures is an inefficiency. They’re expenses that don’t generate revenue. They feel wasteful … until something bad happens.
But, if you’re lucky, you can push the costs of failure on to society, further increasing profits. So, we get stranded in airports when planes don’t fly, or have to deal with the fallout when we can’t withdraw money from our bank accounts.
The effects of those economic pressures are brittle systems, with single points of failure and cascading failure modes. They’re more susceptible to cyber-attack – both human and AI-fueled – and more susceptible to random mistakes.
The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures.
Upgrading our computerized systems, increasing their reliability, removing single points of failure, and making them more resilient are all technical problems. But they won’t happen until we fix the political and economic ones.
We need to change the economic incentives that make it profitable to operate these systems just at the edge of functionality, and to push the costs of failure on to all of us. Fixing that requires regulation – with enforcement and meaningful fines – and stringent antitrust enforcement.
But while that’s all easy to say, it’s much harder to implement – especially in the US where monied interests have such a tight hold on the legislative agenda. Until this changes, we should expect lots more of these sorts of failures in the future.
- Bruce Schneier is a security technologist who teaches at the Harvard Kennedy School at Harvard University and the University of Toronto’s Munk School
