https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Why Somalia’s president turned against his former ally, the UAE
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Why Somalia’s president turned against his former ally, the UAE
Behind Somalia’s break with the UAE lies a domestic power struggle with regional leaders close to Abu Dhabi.
Three years ago, at a town hall meeting in Mogadishu, Somali President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud defended one of his country’s most controversial foreign partnerships.
The United Arab Emirates, he declared, was “one of the greatest pillars” of Somalia’s war against the al-Qaeda-linked armed group al-Shabab. He praised Abu Dhabi’s support for the country’s armed forces despite longstanding concerns about its political influence.
Having returned to power in 2022, Mohamud sought to repair relations with the Gulf state after a period of strained ties under his predecessor, while reassuring a sceptical Somali public that the UAE’s involvement was a boon rather than a hindrance.
This year, that relationship unravelled spectacularly.
On November 19, Somalia ordered the Emirati ambassador to leave the country and recalled its own envoy from Abu Dhabi, marking the sharpest rupture yet in a relationship that had shifted from close security cooperation and deep commercial ties to open hostility.
The UAE said it had already withdrawn its diplomatic staff from Mogadishu in January.
The decision came 10 months after Somalia annulled several commercial, defence and security agreements with the UAE, accusing its former ally of undermining its sovereignty.
In a sharp public rebuke two days before the expulsion order, Mohamud accused the UAE of heightening political divisions, financing rival regional administrations and supporting armed actors operating beyond the federal government’s control.
“A brother does not burn your house. A brother does not buy your property without your knowledge. A brother does not divide your family,” he said.
“After years of diplomatic engagement, the Federal Government assesses that UAE policies threaten Somalia’s national security,” Awes Hagi Yusuf Ahmed, Somalia’s national security adviser (NSA), said in a post on X.
The UAE hit back, accusing Mogadishu of allowing its internal political disputes to strain bilateral ties, in an apparent reference to the president’s contentious relations with some of Somalia’s semi-autonomous regional administrations, which maintain close ties with Abu Dhabi.
Anwar Gargash, a senior Emirati official, said the UAE’s ties with Somalia would “remain deeper and stronger” despite the president’s criticism.
The diplomatic rupture comes amid an escalating domestic power struggle between Mohamud and regional leaders resisting his efforts to reassert federal authority, several of whom have cultivated close ties with Abu Dhabi.
It also marks a striking reversal for a president during whose first term the UAE significantly expanded its foothold in Somalia and who later emerged as one of Abu Dhabi’s strongest defenders.
Somalia divided
Somalia’s efforts to rebuild national institutions since the establishment of a permanent federal government in 2012 have unfolded alongside the consolidation of regional administrations that retain considerable autonomy and political power.
Abu Dhabi’s ties with Mogadishu deepened during Mohamud’s first presidency, from 2012 to 2017.
The UAE reopened its embassy in the capital in 2014, and Mohamud inaugurated a UAE-funded military training centre for Somali forces the following year.
At the same time, the Gulf state cultivated commercial, security and diplomatic ties with regional administrations, including Puntland and Jubbaland, as well as Somaliland, which declared independence from Somalia in 1991.
The UAE is also one of Somalia’s most important trading partners, serving as an important source of imports and a hub for Somali businesses trading in international markets.
But its influence extends well beyond trade, with big investments in infrastructure and security concentrated in Somaliland, Puntland and Jubbaland.
Among the most visible of these investments is Berbera port in Somaliland, where Dubai’s state-owned port operator DP World has invested heavily in expanding the facility and developing a trade corridor connecting it to Ethiopia and the wider region.
Through its subsidiary P&O Ports, the company also operates Bosaso port in Puntland, with both ports providing crucial sources of revenue for their respective administrations.
Somaliland’s Foreign Minister Abdirahman Dahir Adam said the UAE treated it as an independent state, making it an attractive partner, while Emirati investments had created jobs and improved regional connectivity.
“The UAE saw Somaliland’s potential early and backed that view with real investment,” Adam told Al Jazeera.
“The impact on our economy has been significant. DP World’s development of Berbera Port and the Berbera Corridor has turned Berbera into a serious regional gateway,” he added.
Their strategic location along the Gulf of Aden also gives Somaliland and Puntland considerable leverage, making them attractive partners for foreign powers seeking a foothold along one of the world’s busiest shipping routes.
The UAE has developed military facilities near both ports, while in Puntland it helped establish and fund the Puntland Maritime Police Force (PMPF), initially an antipiracy unit that has since become an important counterterrorism force.
More recently, it has supported Puntland’s campaign against ISIL (ISIS) in Somalia with drone attacks and carried out a strike this year against al-Shabab in support of Puntland’s forces, a security official in the region told Al Jazeera.
Abu Dhabi maintains similar commercial and security ties with Jubbaland, which borders Kenya, although the extent of its involvement there is less publicly documented.
A senior Puntland official speaking anonymously told Al Jazeera the UAE’s interventions had helped regional states consolidate their authority, with no equivalent assistance coming from the federal government. “It is obvious why on that level the UAE is a more important partner,” the official said.
Aweis Ahmed, a Somalia expert at Chatham House, told Al Jazeera that while Emirati support had brought tangible benefits to Somalia’s regional states, it had also strengthened their position against the federal government, undermining Mogadishu’s efforts to assert its authority.
“They view these things differently. On the one hand, it helps the peripheries, whilst it undermines the centre,” Ahmed said.
Different priorities and interests
That partnership suffered a setback after Mohamud left office in 2017, when his successor, Mohamed Abdullahi, also known as Farmaajo, refused to take sides in a diplomatic dispute between the UAE and Saudi Arabia on one side and Qatar on the other.
Relations improved after Mohamud returned to power in 2022, but tensions persisted over Abu Dhabi’s increasingly independent dealings with regional administrations, often bypassing the federal government entirely.
Abdinor Dahir, director of the Somalia-based Adkaysi Institute for Research, Peace and Inclusive Resilience, told Al Jazeera that the UAE’s relationships with regional states had deepened disagreements over who had the authority to conclude agreements with foreign partners.
“Overall, the regional states’ external relationship with the UAE and the resulting disputes weaken federal authority, undermine counterterrorism cooperation, and risk turning foreign policy into a permanent source of internal conflict,” Dahir said.
The dispute came to a head in January, when Mogadishu annulled its agreements with Abu Dhabi, accusing the UAE of secretly transporting an Emirati-backed Yemeni separatist leader through Somaliland without authorisation.
Somaliland, Puntland and Jubbaland rejected the announcement, insisting their agreements with Abu Dhabi, particularly over ports, would remain in force.
NSA Yusuf Ahmed accused the regional administrations of compromising national security through their independent dealings with Abu Dhabi.
“Port agreements for Berbera, Bosaso and Kismayo, concluded outside federal authority, take strategic infrastructure out of national control,” he said in a post on X. “That is a security question, not a political one.”
President’s contentious agenda
But the dispute with the UAE has also become entangled with a wider struggle over political power within Somalia, as Mohamud’s efforts to strengthen the central government through constitutional and electoral changes have met resistance from regional leaders.
Puntland and Jubbaland, both federal member states, have opposed changes they say would weaken their autonomy, while functionally independent Somaliland has long rejected Mogadishu’s authority.
Somali officials have also accused the UAE of backing the deposed leader of Southwest State, Abdiaziz Hassan Laftagareen, who has fought to retake several towns around the regional capital, Baidoa, in recent months.
Laftagareen told Al Jazeera that he would remove Mohamud’s ally, who took power following a contested election in Baidoa.
Aweis Ahmed, the Chatham House expert, told Al Jazeera the UAE’s support for Mohamud’s domestic opponents had helped them thwart his efforts to push through contentious constitutional and electoral changes.
“This issue with the UAE is more about the local dynamics than some big question about sovereignty for Hassan Sheikh,” he said.
“A direct line to Abu Dhabi gives these sub-national leaders more room to pursue their own priorities when relations with Mogadishu are difficult,” Dahir said.
Importing UAE’s rivalries
However, Aweis Ahmed warned that the UAE’s involvement, along with that of other powers from the Middle East, was deepening domestic divisions while drawing Somali actors into wider regional disputes.
“They have made important contributions, but overall their involvement is exacerbating Somalia’s internal and external issues,” he said.
The federal government has aligned itself closely with Turkiye, Qatar and Egypt, while some regional administrations have cultivated ties with the UAE and Ethiopia, and Somaliland has drawn closer to Israel.
“These countries have their own issues, and they’re overlapping with Somalia’s internal rivalries,” Aweis Ahmed said.
At home, Mogadishu has increasingly deployed its growing military strength, including Turkish-trained troops, against UAE-aligned rivals opposed to Mohamud’s constitutional and electoral agenda.
Turkish-trained federal forces helped remove Southwest State leader Abdiaziz Hassan Laftagareen from power, while a similar attempt to dislodge Jubbaland’s Ahmed Mohamed Islam, also known as Madobe, following his disputed re-election in 2024 failed.
In Puntland, tensions with Mogadishu prompted regional forces to seize several federal military bases and expel federal institutions.
Beyond Somalia, Sudan has complained to Mogadishu about the UAE’s alleged use of facilities in the port cities of Bosaso and Berbera to supply the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the paramilitary group fighting the Sudanese army.
A Somali source told Al Jazeera that Sudan’s intelligence chief raised the issue during a visit to Mogadishu in 2025, pressing Somali officials to at least publicly condemn the alleged supply operations if they were unable to stop them.
In early November, Yassir al-Atta, the Sudanese army chief of staff, went further, alleging that fighters from northern Somalia had taken part in the conflict alongside the RSF.
The passage of Abu Dhabi-backed Yemeni separatist leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi through Somali territory has similarly drawn Mogadishu into tensions between the UAE and Saudi Arabia over Yemen.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Max Verstappen touches perfection in dramatic Las Vegas Grand Prix win
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Giles Richards in Las Vegas
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Max Verstappen won the Las Vegas Grand Prix with a remarkable, determined drive for Red Bull having done battle in a thrilling contest where the lead changed 35 times but the Dutchman remained absolutely indomitable, his skill and racecraft unmatched. His margin at the flag was just six-tenths of a second over the second -placed McLaren of Lando Norris, with his teammate Oscar Piastri finishing in third.
World Champion Kimi Antonelli who was in the fight was fourth and Alpine’s Pierre Gasly in fifth. George Russell, who vied for almost the entire race for the lead, was unlucky in running over debris at the death causing him to lock up and drop to ninth.
However once more there was a disaster for Ferrari as Charles Leclerc went to pass Hamilton at turn seven and the pair struck one another on lap 38. Hamilton went into a spin losing places and dropping to tenth. The incident was investigated by the stewards and Leclerc was given a 10-second penalty for causing a collision.
The somewhat fractious relationship taking another blow just after the pair had been given a dressing down by team principal Fred Vasseur for clashing in Mexico but it will also increase pressure on the Frenchman, with Hamilton having already insisted the team institute some form of rules of engagement between them. Another long and urgent debrief awaits, with Vasseur likely to once more be furious. Hamilton finished in seventh with Leclerc in 10th.
For Verstappen this was a masterclass, the new regulations and conditions on the streets of Las Vegas meant the race was one of classic old-school slipstreaming, the field bunched up with seconds of one another, nose to tail and with no driver able to break away. Once Verstappen held the lead from the off he was hunted to the flag but no one could break his grip for more than a few corners.
The pattern was established in the early laps. By lap two, with the tyres coming up to temperature, Russell closed on Verstappen and swept past on the Strip but Verstappen immediately came back at him at turn 17, the final corner to retake the lead.
A dance they would repeat time and time again as a great train of cars trailed behind them clustered together, the top ten all within five seconds as Verstappen defended his place, with no little vigour. Russell took another shot on lap 14 and made it past but yet again with the slipstream now in his favour the Dutchman again pounced back at turn 17.
Isack Hadjar joined the fray too before he had a front wing failure and the fact that the cars were still so close that Norris, who had been all but out of it in the first stint on the soft tyre, suddenly found real pace on the mediums and he was back in it from nowhere as was Piastri, who had started in 17th.
Antonelli also joined the fun taking second from his teammate, with the Italian then passing Verstappen for the lead but once more with Verstappen coming back.
The final lap then was vital, Verstappen entered it in the lead and he pushed hard even as Antonelli, who was losing power at the crucial moment, was passed by both McLarens but they were not close enough to challenge the Dutchman. It was decisive as he took the flag by just six-tenths of a second, a bigger lead than he might have imagined he would have for most of the 50 laps in Las Vegas, with the top five all within three-seconds.

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: The European revolt may be coming to the UK
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
The European revolt may be coming to the UK
There is enough justified anger among the British youth to spark a wave of mass protests.
The protests engulfing Europe represent a new level of popular mobilisation quite unlike any historical precedent. In France, Spain, Italy, Serbia, Germany and other countries across the continent, mass movements are challenging austerity and government failures.
On Friday, the United Kingdom saw what is likely to be the beginning of its own wave of youth-driven demonstrations. Thousands of students walked out of hundreds of schools and universities around the country, from Aberdeen to Brighton, Swansea to Nottingham, making it one of the largest student mobilisations since the tripling of tuition fees back in 2010.
The protests were called by organisations involved in the International Conference Against War, a pan-European initiative aimed at coordinating the movements against militarism. The University and College Union (UCU) was the first union to back the initiative with a National Day of Action, urging members across the university sector to hold protests and rallies alongside students.
That major unions followed UCU in supporting the walkouts, including Unison, Unite, the National Education Union (NEU), GMB and the Educational Institute of Scotland (EIS), speaks to the potential of union support.
In London, demonstrations from universities and colleges converged on Trafalgar Square to chants of “fight for our future, not their wars” before moving to Downing Street to hear student activists and trade union leaders berate the government for prioritising defence spending over education and public services.
There is indeed much for British youth to be angry about. Like in the rest of Europe, young people in the UK are facing a convergence of high inflation, unemployment, economic stagnation, the gutting of public services and deteriorating living standards, including a housing crisis stoked by property speculation. Combined with police brutality over solidarity with Palestine, unrestrained racism and sexism and expectations of environmental and climate catastrophe, mass protest is rather predictable.
According to government estimates, close to one million people between 16 and 24 years of age are “Neets” – not in education, employment or training; this is more than 13 percent of that age group. Young people make up more than 40 percent of the unemployed in the country. Apart from a tough job market, there is also a rampant mental health epidemic and an education system that few can afford.
Here we have the makings of a social and economic crisis waiting to happen, and yet the government response has been to seek more austerity.
It is a wonder that Alan Milburn, former Labour minister responsible for introducing private finance into the NHS in the late 1990s, was commissioned to write the controversial report on Neets for the government. Why bother to provide welfare when the private sector can solve the crisis? Unsurprisingly, Milburn’s recommendations are market-focused and include cutting certain benefits for youth, including for those with disabilities.
This comes on top of years of austerity in the higher education sector. Job cuts and course closures have become standard responses from university management dealing with the lack of direct government funding. Many describe it as academic vandalism. What funding cuts have produced is extreme dysfunction, chaos and mismanagement: Faustian bargains with banks, management consultants and corporate outsourcing that serve efficiency and profit over quality provision.
While education and civilian job openings are dwindling, British youth are offered more opportunities in the army, which is now promoting a fully paid 18-month “foundation scheme”.
Military training, bolstered by a public campaign around “warfighting readiness” as part of last year’s Strategic Defence Review, was the brainchild of ministers under Keir Starmer, one of the most unpopular prime ministers in British history. True to form, Starmer pushed through an additional 15 billion pounds ($19.6bn) towards defence immediately before leaving office, for a total of 298 billion pounds ($389.8bn) over four years.
This is a worrying trend across Europe: While there are diminishing funds for public services, military spending is shooting up. This fact has not been lost on young people.
But what is driving this rearmament frenzy is that the European project is increasingly being bound together by NATO, along with Trump’s insistence that the EU should pay its fair share in maintaining the alliance. Support for Ukraine against Russia is at the centre of that project.
If youth mobilisation in the UK reaches the same level as in France, for example, this could be the first major test of Andy Burnham’s government. The French revolt was started over education – not the first strikes in French history over education, considering the origins of the 1968 uprisings. Still, France spends 5.1 percent of GDP on education.
The UK spends 4.1 percent of GDP on education, and even part of this budget has been diverted to defence, with less funding for schools in the coming years.
The UK has had seven prime ministers in the past decade, each one unable to deliver desperately needed income and wealth redistribution. A decade of Tory prime ministers allowed the rich to get very rich. Starmer continued the tradition. He was hammered by Reform and the Greens in the last local elections, firstly because he was unable to come through on the social democratic promises that many were hoping a Labour government would provide.
But second, he failed to recognise the genuine anger over British complicity in the Palestinian genocide, and then responded to mass protest with punitive legislation. Notwithstanding the Burnham bounce, the sitting prime minister has stuck to the same tack as his predecessor. His new foreign secretary has admitted that the government got it wrong over Palestine, but this needs to be backed up by action.
As Burnham faces growing protest, a heavy-handed approach will not work. Nor will more neoliberal reforms. A half-century of privatisation, deregulation and cuts to social welfare has produced the current malaise, and the crisis is only deepening.
The youth and the rest of European society are demanding change – real, lasting change in the political and economic spheres.
The revolutions that convulsed Europe in 1848 were a response to severe economic crisis, unemployment and bad harvests that caused famine. The European protests today unfold under comparable conditions. The task of those who want to see change is an internationalism that can generalise grievances, coordinate the movements and deliver concrete solidarity against austerity and war.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: My husband has such bad breath we haven’t kissed in years – but he won’t see a dentist | Ask Annalisa Barbieri
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Annalisa Barbieri
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
I’ve got a very upsetting problem in my marriage: my husband has extremely bad breath. We have been together for 20 years and it has always been noticeable, but has got worse in recent years. Recently, he lost a tooth, which he said he knocked out, but I’m pretty certain it fell out due to gum disease.
I have spoken to him about this issue in the past, and even managed to get him to the dentist once, but he became so frightened that he ran out of the surgery. Since then, whenever I mention his breath or the dentist, he becomes very defensive.
I feel embarrassed when he is talking to other people because I know they can smell it too.
We haven’t kissed in years as the thought of kissing makes me feel sick. He often complains that I don’t initiate sex, and asks why I’m not more affectionate towards him. The truth is that his breath puts me off. I don’t want to hurt him by saying this, but it is becoming increasingly difficult for me to feel physically close to him.
I know his fear of the dentist is real. I don’t want to shame him or make him feel unattractive. But I also feel frustrated because I have tried to help him and he simply won’t address it.
How can I talk to him about this?
It’s going to be difficult to talk about this in a way that won’t upset him, but it’s about minimising the impact and, crucially, getting his teeth and gums seen to. I went to two specialists this week, psychotherapist Chris Mills and “gentle” dentist Dr Neera Maini, who works with nervous patients.
Mills was unequivocal: “You are the one person in the world who can and must tell him his breath smells, and it’s also worrying in terms of what it signals about his health. He needs to hear it’s intolerable for you and that for him to dismiss this as irrelevant is wholly unacceptable.” Mills even suggested telling him his breath repels you. I think that’s strong, but as he said, “It leaves no room for doubt.”
“Your husband’s terror is making victims of both of you,” said Mills. “You clearly love him, but do you love yourself enough to no longer let him get away with this?” Mills suggested starting the conversation with something like: “There’s something I need to say to you that I don’t think you’re going to want to hear. It’s important, so please hear me out before you respond. You have bad breath and I need you to see a dentist in order to assess what’s wrong. I know that scares you, and I will support you however I can. Your breath is preventing me from being intimate with you, and that’s a terrible loss. Plus, I’m worried what it might indicate about your health.”
Maini explained: “It takes effort to get a tooth out, so for it to just fall out like that suggests really advanced gum disease.” She also said certain medical conditions and medications can cause a dry mouth and bad breath, but in the first instance “a trip to the dentist is called for”.
To find a gentle dentist near you, do a Google search for “gentle dentists for nervous patients + your area”. Such a practice would make a longer than usual appointment, everything would be done at the patient’s pace and you can sometimes visit the surgery beforehand to get acquainted with the environment if that helps. Then there’s sedation, which isn’t a general anaesthetic, to calm the patient.
I’m afraid there’s no way around this other than you saying something. I wish he hadn’t left it to you to do, but here we are.
Every week, Annalisa Barbieri addresses a personal problem sent in by a reader. If you would like advice from Annalisa, please send your problem to ask.annalisa@theguardian.com. Annalisa regrets she cannot enter into personal correspondence. Submissions are subject to our terms and conditions. The latest series of Annalisa’s podcast is available here.

World Central Kitchen founder says three killed in Gaza strike 'not part of our team'
The founder of the World Central Kitchen, Jose Andres, has said that the three people killed in an Israeli strike on a vehicle delivering food aid in Gaza, did not belong the organisation, nor did the vehicle.
In a post on X, Andres said, "Early reports linked them to World Central Kitchen. They were not part of our team, and it was not our vehicle. That's all we know."
"But here is what I do know. More than a year into a ceasefire, people in Gaza are still dying. Families are facing a fourth winter in tents," he added.
The Israeli army had earlier claimed in a post on X that it targeted three “Islamic Jihad terrorists” in a vehicle used to transport food and supplies to other group operatives in Gaza.
Andres added that a "ceasefire is not peace", calling upon leaders to work towards ending the conflict.
"To every leader with the power to change this, on every side: finish the work. End this war for good, so Palestinians and Israelis can live in safety, and so the people of Gaza can start to rebuild their homes, their schools, their kitchens," he said.
"Our teams, Gazans feeding Gazans, were cooking again today. They will be there tomorrow. A plate of food is hope. But it is not a future. Peace is."

Kansas City Current defeat Washington Spirit 2-1 to lift first NWSL title
Trinity Rodman left in tears after scoring Spirit’s only goal as DiBernardo and Debinha give Current closely-fought win.
Kansas City Current have defeated the Washington Spirit in a closely-contested final to be crowned the NWSL champions for the first time as Trinity Rodman’s bid to avoid a third consecutive final defeat ended in bitter disappointment in Washington, DC.
Vanessa DiBernardo curled in a goal direct from a corner and Brazilian international Debinha added a second in stoppage time to set up Kansas City’s 2-1 victory at Audi Field on Saturday.
Rodman headed in a 98th-minute goal to pull one back for Spirit, but Kansas City held on to win.
“We knew it was going to be a battle; we felt good coming out of the first half,” said DiBernardo, who was named the championship MVP months after returning to professional football following the birth of her daughter.
“We just had to be patient and finish off the game.”
It was another crushing loss for United States star Rodman and her Spirit teammates, who were also beaten in the final in 2025 and 2024.
Rodman, who was in tears at the final whistle, was knocked out of her stride earlier in the game.
The 24-year-old was on the receiving end of a rugged aerial challenge from Kansas City’s Laney Rouse after just five minutes and needed treatment on the sidelines.
Rodman returned to the field grimacing in pain and clutching her shoulder but completed the game.
The opening goal came early in the second half, with DiBernardo’s in-swinging corner looping into the net after Kansas City’s Kayla Sharples cleverly blocked Washington goalkeeper Sandy MacIver.
Deep in stoppage time, Debinha added Current’s second after a sweeping counterattack, before Rodman’s header was too little, too late.
The victory was Kansas City’s first NWSL title after losing in the championship game to the Portland Thorns in 2022.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: ‘Serious error of judgment’: outrage over military AI event at Berlin arts complex
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Philip Oltermann European culture editor
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
With their cavernous post-industrial venues, teeth-grinding four-by-four beats and bouncers that look like Blade Runner extras, Berlin’s nightclubs trade on a reputation for bleakness. A recent event at one of the city’s most legendary clubland institutions, however, has proven too dystopian even for seasoned techno-heads.
On 11 November, the Kraftwerk Berlin arts complex had its central hall transformed into what visitors described as something resembling a war room, with maps and aerial footage projected on to concrete walls, drones hanging from the ceiling, and guards in flak jackets patrolling the premises with sniffer dogs.
Those who flocked to the venue – which hosts the experimental music festival Atonal and is part of the same complex as the techno club Tresor – had come for the launch of Clarity, an AI targeting system developed by the German arms startup Helsing.
Kraftwerk Berlin this week apologised for a “serious error of judgment” and vowed to revise its commercial rental department’s booking policy, after outrage over the event rippled through Berlin’s music scene. The row has raised uncomfortable questions about the commercialisation of the German capital’s famed nightlife, and the culture sector’s traditional pacifism at a time of growing security threats.
The Munich-based Helsing was founded in 2021 and counts the Swedish tech entrepreneur and Spotify co-founder Daniel Ek among its investors and board co-chairs. On its website, it describes Clarity as an agentic intelligence platform designed to use drone, satellite and sensor data to lock on to targets.
It claims that human operators remain responsible for approving any strikes.
Helsing says Clarity is “developed and built in Europe under European control”. The market leader for battlefield software is Palantir’s Maven, the system that has powered US military strikes on Iran this year. European governments have been scrambling for alternatives to US-developed systems. France’s domestic intelligence service has already announced it is dropping Palantir for a homegrown rival.
But European governments’ boosting of their arms industries is also clashing with an anti-militaristic cultural consensus – nowhere more so than in the former cold war pressure cooker of Berlin, where nightclubs became spaces to dance away the anxieties of the arms race.
“The fact there is a war in Europe and that Ukraine needs German support should not mean that we switch off all our critical faculties,” said Michail Stangl, a Berlin-based music curator and DJ. “We are already seeing how AI-driven targeting systems are being used in Gaza, and it’s hard to imagine that once a company like Helsing develops a successful arms system, it would not sell it on to authoritarian regimes, domestic police, or organisations like Frontex to be used against migrants.”
Speaking to the German broadcaster RBB at its launch event, a Helsing spokesperson said none of its military systems were designed to identify persons, and that Clarity was built to seek out objects such as radar systems, launch pads and ships.
It also said Clarity’s agents specialised in “looking for patterns of behaviour”, which could be interpreted as relating to human activity. Helsing did not respond to a request for comment.
The Clarity launch event was condemned in the strongest terms by Tresor, a nightclub and record label that acted as a bridge between post-Wall Berlin and Detroit’s electronic music scene in the 1990s. “It has no place in the spaces our community has built,” it said in a statement.
Tresor’s founder, the Berlin nightlife entrepreneur Dietmar-Maria “Dimitri” Hegemann, is also the managing director of Kraftwerk Berlin. Hegemann has called the booking “unacceptable”, saying it was done by “a staff member at the company responsible for Kraftwerk’s commercial rental business”, without him being consulted. Given his central role at the arts complex, and the level of planning usually required for such a high-security event, this has surprised some Berlin clubland insiders.
That Berlin’s former underground music venues are rented out for commercial purposes is no longer a deviation from the norm. As recently as 19 October, Kraftwerk Berlin hosted an investment summit organised by the German government and featuring a podium discussion between the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, and the chip manufacturer Nvidia’s then chief executive, Jensen Huang.
In a Q&A released after the Clarity row, Kraftwerk Berlin said it had declined a proposed Palantir-sponsored event in 2022 after consulting its cultural teams.
Defenders of such commercial usages point out that many of Berlin’s nightclubs are struggling with rising rents and plummeting bar revenues. Kraftwerk Berlin may not be one of them, however. The total assets of its operating company, Schaltraum Berlin, were reported in June as having a value of €4.3m (£3.6m).

https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.title: What Sandpapergate reveals about Australian cricket
https://www.aljazeera.com/opinions/2026/.text:
What Sandpapergate reveals about Australian cricket
A toxic culture of winning at any cost has been hiding behind the myth of ‘mateship’.
“I knew it was wrong. I knew that using sandpaper was not simply pushing the boundaries of the laws of cricket. It was cheating,” former Australian Test cricketer Cameron Bancroft wrote in a 4,000-word expose.
His frank admission that he knowingly cheated and then lied to investigators and the Australian public was raw.
The footage of Bancroft shoving sandpaper down the front of his trousers, in an attempt to hide his illegal ball tampering during the 2018 Test series between South Africa and Australia, has been seen all over the world; the act of cheating has never been in question.
But the fallout, eight years in the making, no longer centres on a square of sandpaper. It revolves around a culture that placed winning above sound ethics. It created such deep-seated fear that lying – both directly and by omission – became a means to survive, and ultimately exposed the national belief that Australian men’s cricket was underpinned by a sacred sense of “mateship” – standing above self-interest – as a myth.
The basic facts of Australia’s ball-tampering scandal have long been established. Bancroft, with the tacit encouragement of teammate David Warner and under then-captain Steve Smith, who elected to look the other way, executed a premeditated plan to alter the ball’s surface during the third Test in Cape Town, in order to promote reverse swing.
Once he was caught, the public outrage and revulsion were overwhelming. Cricket Australia, the national cricket governing body, rushed through an inadequate investigation, omitting many of the touring party, and concluding that knowledge of the plan was confined to Bancroft, Warner and Smith. It imposed draconian penalties: yearlong bans for Smith and Warner, nine months for Bancroft.
Coach Darren Lehmann eventually stood down, followed out the door by several support staff, administrators and board members.
The cone of silence surrounding the affair cracked open with the release of Usman Khawaja’s autobiography, Sabr, in which he alleged everyone in the dressing room was in on the plan. Players and coaching staff came out publicly to either back Khawaja’s story or reject his version of events.
Current team captain Pat Cummins, who was also part of the team in 2018, publicly insisted that he did not know about the use of sandpaper. This was reportedly the final straw for Bancroft: “It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone,” he wrote.
For eight years he had borne the brunt of being labelled a cheat and watched his former teammates carry on with their Test careers – including Smith and Warner, after serving their bans.
Within hours of Cricket Australia’s announcement of an independent “truth forum” that would provide a “safe place” for discussion – a belated effort to stem the tide of damaging public confessions – Bancroft’s self-penned expose was published in The West Australian newspaper.
Not only did he insist that everyone was in on the scheme, but it was not an isolated occurrence, as the investigation had concluded; he had also used sandpaper in the second Test in Gqeberha that year.
“I made a terrible decision because I wanted to belong in the Australian team,” Bancroft wrote.
The context of his choice shouldn’t be overlooked. He was a 24-year-old adult, yet a junior member of the side playing in his seventh Test, and he desperately wanted to fit in.
The years leading up to the South Africa tour were defined by an increasingly toxic culture in which the boundaries of sportsmanship were tested, stretched and treated as pliable when convenient.
The Australian men’s team were the self-appointed guardians of “the line”, their own behaviour consistently justified as being on the right side of what was acceptable under the mantra of playing “hard but fair”. There was a lack of strong and ethical leadership in the dressing room, from the coaching staff all the way up to the Cricket Australia boardroom.
An independent, wide-ranging review by ethics nonprofit organisation The Ethics Centre, conducted in the aftermath of the affair, exposed a culture of “winning without counting the costs” that seeped throughout Cricket Australia. It was a culture in which staff and players feared the consequences of speaking honestly. It is no wonder that silence and dishonesty flourished in order to protect the brand and ensure self-preservation.
“We were frightened,” Bancroft wrote. “We were under pressure. We were trying to manage a situation that was rapidly getting away from us.”
While the on-field reputation of the Australian Test team has improved since 2018, fronted by captains Tim Paine and then Cummins, the blackened seeds sown were nourished by years of resentment and grievance, and have now emerged fully grown in blighted and twisted ugliness.
The complexity and nuance of ball-tampering have been overtaken by accusations of who knew what and a tug-of-war over who owns the truth – not to mention an administration that desperately hoped a web of half-truths and omissions would hold.
It has held a confronting mirror to the wider public’s veneration of “mateship”, the close bond of brotherhood that Australians have long held as core to their national identity. The baggy green cap worn by the country’s Test cricketers has been its unofficial symbol. Friendship may be universal, but mateship – that’s unique to Australia. The cap looks increasingly frayed with every public disclosure.
For Australians to accept that a young player would consider cheating, and then lie about cheating, as the best way of fitting in with his “mates”, it would mean questioning this idea of national exceptionalism. It would mean accepting that self-interest would trump the sacrosanct bonds of selfless “mateship”.
There have been widespread calls for Australian cricket to move on and a growing collective weariness that this unseemly and unflattering saga continues to dominate the news landscape. Perhaps the reflection in the mirror is simply too confronting to sustain the gaze.
There is an alternate universe in which Cricket Australia, in the aftermath of Newlands, could have stood the three central players down for the final Test, pending a full and thorough investigation that would have included all members of the touring party, rather than a select few. The players could have been supported and could have had the moral fortitude to be completely honest. An open and mature public conversation could have taken place about the nature of ball-tampering and any disciplinary action better reflected the nature of the “crime”. Responsibility could have been shared and Cricket Australia could have accepted its full portion.
It wouldn’t have been easy; it would still have been controversial, but it would likely not have been what is now: an omnishambles of human and reputational wreckage that may yet prematurely end careers.
In 2018, Bancroft thought the Australian team “were down the rabbit hole so far”.
Eight years later, Australian cricket has yet to reckon with its own shortcomings, still stuck in a hole of its own making.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Pro-Israel Hakeem Jeffries says he will push legislation targeting settler violence
Pro-Israel US Democratic leader, Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become the first Black speaker of the House of Representatives next year, has pledged to advance legislation targeting Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank within the first 100 days of the new Congress.
In an interview with The New York Times, Jeffries said the West Bank Settler Violence Protection and Prevention Act should be among the early legislative priorities, adding that he expected strong support for it within the House Democratic Caucus.
Jeffries also described the devastation inflicted on Palestinian civilians in Gaza as “unacceptable, unsustainable and un-American”, calling for increased humanitarian assistance, medical aid, housing support and access to clean water and air.
Asked whether he supported the proposed Block the Bombs and Stop the Settlements bills, which call for restricting arms sale to Israel and broader sanctions on settlement expansion, Jeffries said he had not taken a position.
On calls to halt US weapons exports used in regional conflicts, he said the current approach was “not sustainable” and needed to change.
More than a million people have signed a petition urging Democrats to reject Hakeem Jeffries as the next Speaker of the US House of Representative. An Economist/YouGov poll published last month found that Jeffries had just a 26 percent approval rating among registered voters.
Critics say that one reason Jeffries' popularity has taken a hit is that he is an avid supporter of Israel.
The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (Aipac) ranks among his top campaign-financing contributors.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Kenya’s internet metering bill raises privacy and affordability concerns
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Kenya’s internet metering bill raises privacy and affordability concerns
Kenya’s proposed internet metering law has prompted concerns over privacy, surveillance and rising connectivity costs.
Nairobi, Kenya – A proposed law requiring internet service providers in Kenya to monitor subscribers’ data consumption and introduce identifiable meter numbers has drawn opposition from industry and civil society groups, amid concerns about affordability, privacy and the handling of personal information.
The Kenya Information and Communications (Amendment) Bill, 2025, sponsored by Aldai MP Marianne Jebet Kitany, seeks to make consumption-based internet billing mandatory. It would require providers to assign each customer a unique meter number, monitor usage, convert it into readable details and issue invoices based on consumption.
The Bill’s stated objective is to protect consumers from unfair billing and ensure they pay for the internet they use. But the Communications Authority of Kenya (CA), telecommunications companies and civil society organisations have questioned whether mandatory metering is necessary and whether the proposed framework provides adequate safeguards for subscribers’ information.
The debate has intensified as the National Assembly’s Departmental Committee on Communication, Information and Innovation considers the legislation. The regulator has urged legislators not to make metered billing compulsory, while Telkom Kenya has warned of potential consequences for privacy, affordability and investment.
Privacy at risk
The Bill would require internet service providers to operate systems that monitor customer usage, convert consumption into readable details and generate invoices. Providers would also have to submit information about their billing systems, including subscriber meter numbers, to the regulator at least once every financial year.
The proposed provisions do not expressly require providers to record the content of private messages or the websites subscribers visit. However, civil society organisations have questioned what usage information would be collected and how identifiable records would be stored, accessed and shared.
The International Commission of Jurists (ICJ) Kenya has questioned the necessity of mandatory metering, arguing that the regulator already has powers to address billing complaints and protect consumers.
Demas Kiprono of ICJ Kenya has argued that the proposed system raises questions about whether the collection of identifiable usage information is necessary and proportionate to the Bill’s stated consumer-protection objective.
The concerns relate to the potential consequences of linking individual subscribers to records of their internet use. Critics say the legislation should specify who could access such information, how long it could be retained and the circumstances in which it could be disclosed.
Kenya’s Data Protection Act, 2019, already provides a framework for processing personal information. Opponents of the Bill say Parliament should make clear how those protections would apply to the proposed metering system.
The Mokaya case
Questions about telecommunications data have also featured in court proceedings involving university student David Ooga Mokaya.
He was arrested in November 2024 over a social media post concerning President William Ruto and charged with publishing false information. On February 19 this year, Senior Principal Magistrate Caroline Nyaguthii acquitted him under Section 215 of the Criminal Procedure Code, finding that the prosecution had not proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.
After his acquittal, Mokaya filed a petition at the High Court seeking protection of his personal information. He argued that information, including call data records, subscriber details, location data and metadata had been supplied to investigators without his consent. The allegations form part of the separate civil proceedings and should not be treated as a final judicial finding.
On February 25, Justice Bahati Mwamuye issued interim conservatory orders restraining the respondents and interested parties from transferring, sharing or disclosing Mokaya’s personal data without his written consent, a valid court order or an express provision of written law permitting disclosure.
The orders were issued pending further proceedings in the case. They do not establish that the proposed internet metering system would be used for surveillance. They do, however, illustrate the legal questions that can arise over the collection and disclosure of telecoms data.
The cost of data
Privacy is not the only concern. Mandatory consumption-based billing could also affect how households and businesses budget for connectivity.
In a submission to parliament on November 3, the Communications Authority cautioned against making metered billing compulsory across the sector. It said the approach could have unintended consequences for affordability, digital inclusion and consumer choice, particularly among low-income households, students, small businesses and communities in underserved areas.
The regulator noted that background applications, software updates, streaming and cloud services can consume data without users closely monitoring their usage.
Instead of prescribing one billing model, the Authority proposed usage alerts when subscribers reach 50, 80 and 100 percent of their data allowance, free real-time usage dashboards and monthly spending caps. It also recommended independent certification and periodic audits of metering systems, clearer itemised bills and stronger procedures for resolving billing disputes.
The Authority’s position is that consumer protection can be strengthened through regulations and licensing requirements without requiring every provider to adopt consumption-based pricing.
The financial impact of a change would depend on providers’ pricing and individual patterns of internet use. Customers who consume relatively little data could benefit from paying according to usage, while those who rely on large or continuous data allowances could face different costs. The Bill does not set the retail prices providers would charge.
Business concerns
Telecommunications companies have questioned whether the proposed changes could impose additional costs on providers and affect investment in broadband services.
Telkom Kenya Chief Executive Officer Mugo Kibati told the parliamentary committee on November 10 that mobile internet accounts for about 96 percent of data subscriptions and is already billed by volume. The proposed changes would therefore mainly affect fixed broadband services, which account for the remaining share, he said.
According to the Kenya News Agency’s report of the hearing, Telkom argued that a uniform metering framework could increase compliance costs and create risks for subscriber privacy and investment.
The company proposed that providers disclose their billing models, charges and fair-use policies before customers subscribe. It also called for free access to consumption information, itemised bills on request, effective dispute-resolution mechanisms and independent audits where billing accuracy is questioned.
Telkom further urged legislators to protect unlimited and speed-based internet packages, allow providers at least 18 months to comply with any new requirements and require aggregated rather than individually identifiable subscriber information to be submitted to the regulator.
Carole Kairuki, chief executive of the Kenya Private Sector Alliance, also raised concerns about the potential effect of mandatory metering on businesses. In an interview with Al Jazeera, she said changes to internet billing could increase compliance costs and make connectivity expenses less predictable for businesses, particularly smaller enterprises.
A wider debate
The Bill’s memorandum says the proposed amendments are intended to protect consumers from exploitation and secure their economic interests under Article 46 of the Constitution. It also states that the legislation does not limit fundamental rights and freedoms.
The disagreement is over whether mandatory metering is the most effective way to achieve that objective and whether the proposed provisions offer sufficient protection for subscribers’ information.
The debate comes amid wider public scrutiny of digital rights and the handling of online activity in Kenya, particularly following the 2024 protests against the Finance Bill. Kelvin Kubai, an Advocate of the High Court of Kenya, told Al Jazeera that internet access is important to young people’s civic participation and their ability to hold public officials accountable. He argued that any new regulatory framework should take those uses into account.
Parliament must weigh the Bill’s consumer-protection objective against concerns raised by the regulator, internet providers and civil society groups. The Communications Authority has proposed greater billing transparency, usage alerts and independent audits as alternatives to compulsory consumption-based billing.
Telkom CEO Kibati warned politicians against imposing obligations that could undermine a developing sector.
“Sometimes you can go overboard in trying to protect consumers that you actually kill a nascent, growing sector,” he told the parliamentary committee.

https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.title: Displaced Darfur families face volatile winter as Sudan aid cuts bite
https://www.aljazeera.com/features/2026/.text:
Displaced Darfur families face volatile winter as Sudan aid cuts bite
Sudan’s displacement crisis could worsen with winter approaching.
Omdurman, Sudan – When Fatima Mohamed Haroun was displaced from West Darfur state at the start of Sudan’s war in 2023, she never imagined she would find herself caring for four of her grandchildren far from her home.
Haroun, who believes she is aged about 60, said her son went missing a year ago. His wife died after giving birth, leaving Haroun as the sole guardian of her four grandchildren.
Now living in a crumbling mudbrick building in al-Ghadir, north of Omdurman, in Khartoum state, she has received no humanitarian assistance since her displacement.
Without an income, it is only the goodwill of her neighbours that prevents Haroun and her grandchildren from starving. But every day is a battle to find food, water or medicine, and with winter fast approaching, proper shelter, warm clothes, and blankets for the children are another priority.
“I cannot work or earn money, so we depend on neighbours who occasionally give us food. But even our neighbours sometimes have nothing to eat. When they have no food, my grandchildren and I go to bed hungry,” she told Al Jazeera.
“We have no supplies to help us cope with the cold, not even blankets to keep us warm. We sleep on the ground with only the sky above us. The cold is severe, and the children are suffering. We appeal to the government and humanitarian organisations to provide food, blankets, covers and other basic necessities to help us endure the cold and protect our children.”
Temperatures can drop significantly in Omdurman during the winter, and at night al-Ghadir can be particularly cold due to its location close to mountainous areas. Displaced families living in temporary shelters here are especially vulnerable because they lack blankets, winter clothing and heating facilities.
The war in Sudan, which broke out between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary in April 2023, has led to one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.
Khartoum state, which was initially one of the epicentres of the war but is now relatively more stable, continues to host large numbers of people forced to flee their homes, particularly from southern and western Sudan where fighting is ongoing. Millions of people in areas such as Darfur have experienced or are at risk of horrific violence, forcing them to flee to other parts of Sudan or neighbouring countries where they live in horrendous conditions.
As of July 30, Khartoum state was hosting 414,252 internally displaced people, according to data from the International Organization for Migration’s (IOM) Displacement Tracking Matrix (DTM).
Winter is expected to worsen conditions for families living in temporary shelters or unfinished buildings without adequate blankets and warm clothing.
Sudan has more than 8.5 million internally displaced people, according to DTM Sudan, with the IOM and the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) warning that millions are still without a roof over their heads and risk losing access to emergency shelters due to funding shortages.
About 15.4 million people in Sudan need emergency shelter and basic household items. The agencies said funding shortages mean humanitarian organisations can prioritise assistance for only 10 percent of those in need, leaving millions without support.
Fighting, general insecurity, drone attacks on civilian infrastructure and camps, as well as other logistical challenges were all obstructing aid deliveries, the agencies said. Less than half of the funding for Sudan’s 2026 Humanitarian Response Plan, which requires $2.9bn to assist 20.4 million people in need, had been received, forcing humanitarian agencies to scale back some services.
Abdelaziz Suleiman Ori, director of culture and information for the Darfur regional government, said his administration was monitoring the conditions for displaced people in host states, including Khartoum, and coordinating humanitarian assistance.
The regional government has drawn up a winter plan that includes blankets, clothing and food to respond to the impending crisis, but Ori acknowledged that available resources were so far insufficient.
“Since the outbreak of the war on April 15, Governor Minni Arko Minawi has dispatched humanitarian convoys from Port Sudan to el-Fasher, passing through Madani, Kosti and El Obeid. We are also in contact with international organisations and UN agencies to monitor the situation of displaced people in different states,” Ori told Al Jazeera.
“Our winter plan includes blankets, clothing, food and children’s necessities. But our resources are not enough to meet the needs of the large number of displaced people. We appeal to humanitarian partners to provide more support.”
Ori said that only a collective response – involving regional government, host states, local authorities and NGOs – can properly respond to the crisis.
“Responsibility for displaced people is shared between the regional government, host states, local communities and humanitarian organisations,” he said.
“We coordinate efforts, seek relief assistance and monitor their conditions with local authorities. We bear part of the responsibility, but need greater cooperation to ease their suffering.”
Kheira Matar Hassan, a resident of Darfur, passed through Renk, Rabak and Khartoum at the start of the war before settling in al-Ghadir camp in 2023. She became separated from her husband when he went looking for work in a gold mining area in Chad at the same time.
She has received no word from him since he disappeared and has been left alone to support their seven children. They live in a dilapidated home built of bricks and mud bricks with damaged areas covered with cloth and plastic sheeting.
Hassan said she has received no support from the government or NGOs, and to support her children, she washes and irons clothes for families in the area, earning just enough money to buy food.
But her income is irregular, and if she has no customers, her family goes hungry. Lacking blankets or adequate shelter, she fears the impact that falling winter temperatures will have on her children. It stands in stark contrast to their former life, when her father worked as a farmer, and the family had enough food to eat.
“We are just here, trying to get by. Our circumstances are extremely difficult; we are really struggling here,” she told Al Jazeera.
“We came from an area where we were not poor. We had our land, cultivated it and lived off what it produced. But the war brought us here. Please look at us and consider our circumstances. We are really suffering.”

Turkey says Israel could use Druze support to launch Syria operation
Israeli could use its support of the Druze to launch an operation in Syria, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said, warning that such an attack could lead to a wider conflict in the region.
In an interview with Turkish media, Fidan said Israel is providing military equipment and support to a Druze tribe in Syria, and may use that support to provoke the Syrian army and launch an attack.
Fidan said Turkey has discussed such the possibility of this operation with European and American officials.
The violence last year in Druze-majority Sweida - which began with clashes between Druze factions and Bedouin fighters in the southern province - left more than 2,000 people dead, including 789 Druze civilians, according to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights.
The Sweida violence also saw Israel launching air strikes in the province as well as in the capital Damascus, nominally in support of the Druze minority. In August, it struck a Syrian airbase where it said Turkey was planning to deploy forces.

Turkish foreign minister says Iran war fallout threatening global markets
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan has said the economic burden brought by the US-Israel war is getting harder for many countries, while emphasising a ceasefire was needed to reverse global financial crises.
Speaking to Turkish broadcaster TGRT Haber on Saturday, Fidan warned that the fallout from the conflict is threatening international markets.
“It is heading toward having very destructive effects,” he said.
Fidan said diplomatic efforts to re-open the Strait of Hormuz remain active, even though the process appears to be deadlocked, citing his recent discussion with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani.
He also said that Ankara was keeping the humanitarian crisis in Gaza on the global radar permanently despite other international crises.
"In every speech, every initiative, and every platform wherever it may be, the Gaza issue is one we have not, and will not, allow to be forgotten," Fidan said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Fossil fuel impasse pushes COP31 climate talks into second day of overtime
COP31 President Murat Kurum asks negotiators to consider a last-minute proposal in attempt to reach an agreement.
Turkish officials have asked negotiators at the COP31 climate summit to consider a last-minute proposal as talks stretched into a second day of overtime over the fossil fuels issue.
“We believe that we have put forward a text which all the parties can agree upon,” COP31 President Murat Kurum told a late-night plenary session on Saturday.
Kurum, who is also Turkiye’s environment minister, said the conference would reconvene later on Sunday morning to approve the deal.
The latest text was not immediately made public, and it was unclear if negotiators had received the wording overnight, which would give nations only a few hours to submit objections and changes.
An earlier draft had drawn strong condemnation for failing to mention fossil fuels, the largest contributors to climate change.
Kurum said he believed concerns around fossil fuels had been addressed, as had those around helping developing countries finance their adaptations to climate change.
The new text followed intensive consultations between Australia, which is leading the talks; Turkiye, which is hosting the meeting; and nearly 200 delegations from many of the world’s richest, poorest, largest and smallest nations.
Delegations had until 03:00 GMT on Sunday to raise any objections to the deal, with a session scheduled at 06:00 GMT to begin approving it.
The summit’s agreement is meant to address how the world will deal with climate change, which drives heatwaves, floods and other disasters.
An opening draft from Australia on Monday called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels. A slimmer version on Thursday removed every mention of them after Saudi Arabia and other major oil and gas producers objected.
Key issues that slowed down the agreement included how much effort countries should make to wean themselves off fossil fuels, such as coal, oil and gas.
Other issues included whether to encourage industrial carbon capture and storage of pollutants, as well as whether ramping up electricity should only be done with renewables, such as wind and solar, or also involve other sources like natural gas and coal.
To avert the most catastrophic effects of warming, experts said the world needs to urgently and drastically cut fossil fuel emissions.
The two-week talks in the Turkish city of Antalya were due to end on Friday.
In a letter sent on Saturday to this year’s cohosts, Turkiye and Australia, 100 civil society groups warned that they were “on course to preside over one of the most disappointing COPs” the UN has ever held.
The letter stated there were only hours left “to save this COP from becoming a low point of three decades of climate negotiations”.
In the lead-up to these talks, the United Nations said the world would likely blow past the 2015 Paris Agreement goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.

Israeli occupation, Iranian interference threat to Lebanese sovereignty, Aoun says
Lebanese President Joseph Aoun has accused Iran of meddling in Lebanon's affairs through Hezbollah's weapons and also demanded Israel withdraw from the country's south.
In a speech on the eve of Lebanon's 83rd independence anniversary, Aoun vowed to press ahead with plans to bring all weapons under state control.
Lebanon's sovereignty still faces two threats, he said: "The Israeli occupation of parts of our territory" and foreign interference from "influential elements within the Iranian regime" through weapons and decisions outside the authority of the Lebanese state.
On Israel, Aoun stressed Lebanon's message was clear and direct: "Withdraw from every inch of Lebanese territory. Stop your attacks."
There would be "no occupation ever again", he said. "And no weapons outside the state that... serve the interests of, foreign powers," he added, without naming a specific group.
Such weapons may once have served a purpose, he said, but later imposed a high cost on Lebanon when they came to serve causes beyond its borders.
"You must hand over your weapons," Aoun said.
The Lebanese government has committed to disarming Hezbollah, whose arsenal has long outstripped that of the national army and which has justified its weapons as necessary to resist Israel.
In June, Lebanon and Israel signed a framework agreement that included the disarmament of Hezbollah, a gradual Israeli withdrawal from territories it occupies in the south and the deployment of the Lebanese army to the area.
But implementation has stalled and Hezbollah has refused to surrender its weapons.
Israel's army still carries out strikes, shelling and detonations in the south, where its forces are operating in a self-declared "security zone" running around 10 kilometres.

- A Russian cargo ship was hit by a Ukrainian drone and caught fire in the Baltic Sea on Saturday, as Finland’s prime minister said Kyiv had the right to hit back against its “aggressor”. The Finnish prime minister, Petteri Orpo, suggested the incident in the Gulf of Finland had to do with Russia’s war in Ukraine. “War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity,” Orpo said on X. “Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor.”
- Hours later, a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating Finnish airspace, according to the Finnish defence minister, who drew a possible link between the two incidents. “The suspected airspace violation may be linked to rescue or monitoring operations involving a cargo ship that was damaged in the Gulf of Finland,” Antti Hakkanen said on X.
- Petteri Blomvall, an officer at the Finnish Border Guard, said: “I can confirm that a Ukrainian drone strike hit the ship in the morning that caused the fire … The crew from the ship has been evacuated, the ship is anchored and the firefighting is ongoing.”
- The Finnish Defence Forces identified the ship as the Sparta II, which is under Ukrainian and US sanctions, according to the site Opensanctions. The website said the ship was suspected of transporting weapons from Syria to Russia. The MarineTraffic maritime monitoring website said the Sparta II had departed St Petersburg around 11pm and was bound for the port of Baltiysk, in the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad.
- Finland’s defence ministry said it had immediately informed Nato of the drone strike. It also said temporary restrictions were being enforced in the airspace and maritime area of the eastern part of the Gulf. Rattled by Russia’s invasion, Finland joined Nato in 2023, dropping decades of military non-alignment. The Gulf of Finland is a key maritime passage for Russia, leading to the former capital St Petersburg.
- “I can guarantee that Nato will defend every inch of Polish territory,” Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, said in Warsaw on Saturday, after two Russian missiles and a drone crashed in its territory on Friday. Poland accused the Kremlin of “intentional provocation” after the incident, as it occurred near where thousands of European troops allied with Ukraine were holding training exercises.
- A meeting of Nato’s North Atlantic Council will be held in Brussels on Monday to discuss the violation of Polish airspace by Russian missiles. “In the near future, we will receive strong support from our NATO allies to bolster the protection of our eastern border,” Polish defence minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz wrote on X on Saturday.
- In Kyiv, residents say they are unbothered by Russian attacks on the city’s bridges, as Moscow tries to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, Dan Sabbagh reports. Alongside its attacks on the capital’s electricity, heating and water systems, Russia has been attacking Kyiv’s bridges since early October, trying to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, home to about a third of its population. Moscow struck the bridges twice again this week, first on Tuesday – overshadowed by Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch road bridge to Crimea. Then again during a noisy Thursday night, hours after Vladimir Putin promised there would be a “far more painful” response to the demolition of his pet project.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Eleven killed in burst of violence during Mexican cartel leader’s capture
Seven alleged cartel gunmen and four soldiers were killed in the operation to arrest Fausto Isidro Meza Flores.
The operation to capture Mexican cartel boss Fausto Isidro Meza Flores in the country’s Sinaloa state has left at least 11 people dead.
Mexico’s Defence Ministry said on Saturday that seven alleged cartel gunmen and four Mexican soldiers were killed in the overnight operation.
Meza Flores, known as “El Chapo Isidro”, was captured on Friday and flown to Mexico City on Saturday after hours-long violence involving a firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen overnight, roadblocks and burning trucks in the city of Guasave.
Two other men were also captured and flown to Mexico City. The ministry identified them as German N, known as “Serafin”, the group’s alleged second-in-command, and Jose N, an alleged financial operator of the cartel. Both were also flown to Mexico City and handed over to prosecutors.
Meza Flores, one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, climbed the ranks to lead the Beltrán Leyva cartel and later became the boss of his own group, the Meza-Flores transnational criminal organisation.
He was also a key ally to “Los Mayos”, a faction of the Sinaloa Cartel, which the United States designated as a “foreign terrorist organization” last year.
The US wanted Meza Flores for trafficking drugs to the country and offered a $5m reward for information leading to his arrest.
Residents terrified
The firefight in Guasave broke out about 7pm on Friday (02:00 GMT on Saturday), according to residents. Military helicopters and drones were soon flying overhead, with helicopters opening fire on key locations across the city.
Videos show screaming civilians fleeing gunfire at a baseball game, burning cars and businesses, and circling helicopters shooting at people below.
Because of the violence, the Mexican army and National Guard special forces were unable to extract Meza Flores from Guasave until 4am (11:00 GMT) on Saturday, said a federal official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorised to discuss the case.
While a tense calm has settled over Guasave since the operation, experts warned that picking off cartel bosses could set off more waves of violence in a region already caught up in a power struggle between warring factions.
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has been under pressure from US President Donald Trump to crack down on cartels and has gone after illegal groups more aggressively than her predecessors. Homicides have dipped significantly in her two years in office.
The US Drug Enforcement Administration commended Mexican authorities, as did Washington’s ambassador to Mexico.
“Results like these don’t happen overnight. They are built on sustained cooperation and trust. This is what partners can accomplish together,” US Ambassador Ronald Johnson said in an X post.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: California train burglars carefully executed heists for ‘staggering’ $22m haul
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Fourteen people in southern California have been accused of burglarizing more than $22m worth of goods from moving freight trains, in a plot reminiscent of the US old west, when outlaws and bandits wreaked havoc on the nascent railroad industry.
The justice department has brought railroad theft charges against the group for raiding at least 36 trains and selling thousands of stolen Nike sneakers, among other products, on the black market.
“The scale of the theft is staggering,” first assistant US attorney Bill Essayli said.
Nathan Daniel Angel, 21, was the alleged ringleader for the so-called “Los Trenes” (“the trains”) scheme, which spanned 2024 through 2026. Court documents did not list an attorney for Angel or the other charged individuals.
Each robbery took a similar form.
Angel’s associates, including his father and two uncles, stowed away on moving freight trains, according to a grand jury indictment.
With some of the men on board serving as lookouts, the others would slash the train’s air hose, causing a sudden loss of air pressure and forcing an emergency stop of the entire vehicle. The maneuver is perilous given the risks of derailment.
Once the train was disabled, the rest of the Los Trenes crew would swoop in to load up the stolen goods and stash the loot at houses across southern California, prosecutors say.
Angel posed for a selfie, where he threw up the peace sign, in front of several boxes containing Nike merchandise, in a February 2024 photograph, attached to court documents.
The next burglary would come months later.
In October 2024, Donta Hedgeman, 27, sawed through the lock of a container on a moving Nike train, according to video evidence.
The heists ramped up in 2025, even as signs emerged that law enforcement was catching on to the alleged thefts.
An unidentified “co-conspirator” texted 23-year-old Carlos Luis Fernando Martinez on 17 April 2025 to say he had been arrested for receiving stolen property.
“They want me to tell them who did I get them from and who had the other pairs,” the person wrote.
Martinez responded, instructing the person to contact him over Signal, an app with encrypted messaging.
Twelve days later, the crew made off with 1,170 tools and 17,000 parts from Milwaukee Tool.
Police officers appeared to sniff around an unnamed company, which purchased a slew of stolen products from the crew in the fall of 2025.
A different “co-conspirator” speculated on their fate. “Good luck with them wires/if they go deep in the case/You’re cooked,” they wrote to Martinez.
Then, on 16 January 2026, Angel and 25-year-old Fredy Marquina referenced a partner being intercepted by police: “They just got Jorge for buying and receiving/stolen property.”
Once again, faced with the mounting risk of being caught, the men proceeded with further heists in the summer of 2026.
In July 2026, Angel Sanchez, 24, shared an AI-generated image that appeared to glamorize their robbery spree.
Masked men tossed Nike sneakers off a Burlington Northern Santa Fe Railway (BNSR) train into luxury cars inscribed with the words “Los Trenes”.
In the image, a helicopter circled above, shining a searchlight.
If convicted of the conspiracy charge, the men face at least five years in prison. The theft of interstate railroad charge has a maximum penalty of 10 years in prison.
A conviction for violence against railroad carriers would carry the most severe punishment with a possibility of life in prison.
Prosecutors described this week’s sweeping indictment as the culmination of a 14-month-long investigation.
“We are determined to protect this vital supply chain and ensure that goods reach their intended destinations, not the black market,” said Nathan Hochman, the Los Angeles county district attorney.

Overturned boat carrying mourners to funeral kills at least 24 in Nigeria
Police say the boat driver fled and the vessel’s manager was taken into custody.
A boat believed to be carrying hundreds of attendees to a funeral has overturned in southern Nigeria, killing at least 24 people, according to authorities.
The overcrowded vessel capsized on Friday in Bayelsa State after a mechanical failure while travelling from the communities of Ayama to Ukubie, according to police.
“So far, 24 bodies have been recovered from the scene of the incident, while search and rescue operations are ongoing,” Manzo Ezekiel, a spokesman for the National Emergency Management Agency, said on Saturday.
Rescue and search operations were continuing, he added.
Two children were among the four bodies initially recovered from the water on Friday, police said at the time, adding that 24 people were rescued, with 19 treated at a local clinic and five taken to hospital in the state capital.
Police did not say how many people were on board, but some residents told the Reuters news agency there were at least 300.
Police said the driver fled and the vessel’s manager was taken into custody.
According to a statement from the Bayelsa State Police Command, the accident occurred at the river junction between the Oweikorogha and Otuan communities, in the state’s Southern Ijaw district.
The boat that capsized was travelling “for a burial ceremony”, the statement also said, adding that police are “coordinating efforts with local divers and other responders”.
Such boat accidents are common on Nigeria’s busy rivers and waterways, often caused by overloaded vessels, poor maintenance, or failure to comply with safety regulations.
A similar incident occurred in August, when at least 51 people died after a boat sank in northwest Nigeria’s Sokoto State. In another incident, in January, at least 26 people drowned after a boat ferrying people from Jigawa to Yobe State capsized.
