Les sondages faussent ils l’élection présidentielle ? | AUX URNES ETC.
Publié le 22 novembre 2026
De la présidentielle française de 2022 aux législatives de 2024, en passant par le fiasco du sondage Selzer aux États-Unis ou les élections au Brésil, les instituts de sondage se trompent régulièrement. Pourtant, ils dictent le rythme médiatique, créent des dynamiques artificielles, influencent le vote utile et déterminent même le temps de parole des partis politiques. Comment sont fabriqués ces sondages ? Qui les possède et qui les commande ? Plongée dans les coulisses d'une industrie qui façonne la vie politique.
Premier épisode d'AUX URNES ETC., notre nouvelle émission politique mensuelle qui décrypte la fabrique du vote, avec Émilio Meslet et Christophe Deroubaix

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Europe is entering a ‘supercycle’ of national elections. Their outcomes could shake the EU’s foundations
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Jon Henley Europe correspondent
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
In late 1998, Tony Blair was prime minister of Britain, Lionel Jospin was prime minister of France, and Gerhard Schröder had just been elected chancellor of Germany. The EU had 15 member states and pro-European, centre-left parties were in power – either alone or in coalitions – in all but two of them.
Brisk economic growth was lifting living standards. Eastward enlargement was under way. In Washington, Bill Clinton was pursuing the same brand of “third way” centrism as a middle path between free-market capitalism and traditional socialism. The EU felt like it had the tide of history behind it.
Not quite three decades later, the continent’s politics once again seem to be tilting in a single direction – except this time, the momentum appears to belong to the nationalist far right, and could bring a significant unpicking of the postwar European consensus that built the EU.
Between the end of this month and the end of next year, an extraordinary electoral sequence will sweep the bloc. Voters in four of the EU’s five biggest member states, by population and economy, head to the polls, with parliamentary elections also due in Estonia, Finland, Greece and Slovakia, and regional ballots in Germany.
Spain kicks off the cycle with a snap general election on 29 November, with prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s socialist coalition facing probable defeat to rightwing parties in the shape of the conservative People’s party (PP) and far-right Vox, which already govern together in some Spanish regions.
Next come presidential and parliamentary elections in France in the spring. The clear frontrunner in the presidential race is Marine Le Pen of far-right the National Rally (RN), well ahead of the far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon and a hopelessly divided mainstream opposition.
When Poland votes later next year, nationalist parties that between them command nearly half the national vote could well unseat the liberal coalition of prime minister, Donald Tusk, despite recent splits. And in Italy, Giorgia Meloni, whose Brothers of Italy party has far-right roots, hopes to secure a second term in elections due before the end of 2027 – while facing pressure on her right flank from the upstart National Future party.
Paradoxically, this nationalist surge arrives amid strong public support for the EU. Shocked by the chaos of Brexit and seeking reassurance in an increasingly alarming world, a record 74% of Europeans say their country benefits from membership, and very few Eurosceptic parties now advocate leaving outright.
The Eurosceptics and nationalists do, however, still view the bloc as a top-down project that undermines national sovereignty, and aim to transform it into an altogether looser association of sovereign nation-states. In the words of the Italian political scientist Natalie Tocci, that means this coming electoral supercycle could “dramatically change the face of Europe” – triggering not simply “a slow erosion of the European project but a hollowing out, if not an outright implosion”.
All elections differ and national specifics loom large. But analysts agree the underlying forces at work here are connected: sluggish growth, ageing populations, strained public finances and a spiralling cost of living have chipped away at support for Europe’s traditional catch-all centre-left and centre-right parties. The wave of youth-led protests sweeping Europe is only the most visible sign of deep voter discontent.
Meanwhile, nationalist parties have become increasingly adept at conjuring and exploiting an ever-evolving list of supposed threats and crises, from migration and vaccines to the green transition, support for Ukraine, globalisation, international elites and supranational institutions – narratives bolstered by Russian disinformation and overt backing for “patriotic” parties from Donald Trump’s White House. As a result, politics has fragmented, and polarised: nearly one in four voters now backs far-right parties – a share that has grown almost fivefold since the mid-1990s.
The rise has not been linear: over the past year or so, while the far-right Alternative für Deutschland scored a historic regional election victory in eastern Germany, in the Netherlands Geert Wilders’s Freedom party lost nearly a third of its seats, Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz was soundly beaten in Hungary and the far-right Sweden Democrats shed support for the first time in 16 years.
But the underlying upward trend appears clear – fuelled above all, political scientists argue, by media normalisation and mainstreaming of far-right ideas, most notably on immigration. Centre-right parties are gradually dismantling “firewalls” that once barred cooperation with the radical right. At the European level, the centre-right European People’s party has increasingly turned to farther-right groups to roll back parts of the European green deal and tighten migration rules.
For the EU, the biggest impact of this election supercycle could be in the European Council of national leaders, which now features just three centre-left heads of government out of 27. If Eurosceptic leaders in France, Spain and Poland join those of Czechia, Italy, Romania, Slovakia and Slovenia by the end of 2027, they would not have the numbers to rewrite EU law – but they would constitute a formidable blocking minority.
EU budget negotiations, future enlargement, aid to Ukraine and deeper integration in essential fields such as defence, energy, finance and technology could all face paralysis, analysts warn.
Safety in numbers, notes Tocci, could change current leaders’ behaviour in the council. Meloni’s relative restraint has been dictated, in part, by her relative isolation among mainstream peers such as Tusk, Sánchez and France’s Emmanuel Macron (alongside Rome’s reliance on €200bn in EU recovery funds).
If she were instead sitting down with the likes of Le Pen, Poland’s far-right Law and Justice (PiS) leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, and a Vox-backed Spanish government, with National Future’s hardline Roberto Vannacci breathing down her neck at home and those EU funds winding down, she might have less incentive to play pro-EU ball.
Analysts agree, though, that the decisive battleground is France. Le Pen’s election platform sets her on a collision course with Brussels: she aims to cut €11bn from France’s EU budget contribution, hold a constitutional referendum to proclaim the supremacy of French over European law, and breach various single-market rules.
And France “carries very significant influence over the EU”, said Mujtaba Rahman of the Eurasia Group consultancy. Compared with Orbán, he notes, a president Le Pen would have “far more leverage to carry out the far-right playbook of subverting the EU’s law-based, supranational architecture”.
Until now, Brussels has contained disruptors such as Orbán largely because there were rarely more than two or three round the table. A cohesive Eurosceptic bloc would leave the EU unable to enforce rule-of-law standards, further integrate economic and security policies or, indeed, agree on anything much at all. The first victim would very probably be Ukraine, with Le Pen leading a blocking caucus against further aid.
Three decades on from 1998, Europe’s coming elections, concluded Stefan Lehne of the Carnegie Europe thinktank, could well turn into “key tests of the EU’s resilience”. The threat to the bloc might not be immediate or existential, he said, but the medium-term risks were significant.
“A stronger role for the radical right may be unlikely to dismantle the EU as it exists today,” Lehne said, but could “prevent it from becoming what it needs to be to deal with the challenges of the future”. And gradually but inevitably, prolonged failure to act collectively as and where needed would lead a “loss of relevance”.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/liv.title: Hull City v Brighton: Premier League – live
https://www.theguardian.com/football/liv.author: Dominic Booth
https://www.theguardian.com/football/liv.text:
73 mins: Yeah, Brighton haven’t really found their rhythm since making the triple change. Kostoulas is making the runs in behind, he just needs to be found.
- Premier League updates from the 2pm GMT kick-off
- Live scores | Table | Follow on TikTok | And mail Dom
Sun 22 Nov 2026 10.35 EST
First published on Sun 22 Nov 2026 08.00 EST
Sun 22 Nov 2026 10.35 EST
First published on Sun 22 Nov 2026 08.00 EST
72 mins: It’s become a bit scrappy, which suits Hull just fine, with the hosts still looking pretty sharp and organised in defence, leaping onto the loose balls. A 0-0 would be frustrating in some ways, given how often they draw at home, but it would also represent a solid point against a good team.
Hull have a corner here. Can they produce something unexpected?
69 mins: Coyle makes a HUGE interception as Costinha looked to play in Minteh, who was in acres of space.
Brighton settle for a corner, then, as De Cuyper takes a low kick which rolls out pretty harmlessly in the end.
Hull have made a double swap, with Matt Crooks and Elliot Stroud taken off by Sergej Jakirovic.
Ryan Giles and Hjerto-Dahl have come on.
67 mins: Brighton are indeed making some subs: Hinshelwood, Minteh and Kostoulas are ON.
Ayari, Rutter and Boscagli are all replaced.
Thanks for listening, Fabian.
Oh my goodness I thought Belloumi had scored! He travelled with the ball so far, carrying it deep into the Brighton box, then cutting inside on his left foot and somehow sliding it way of the near post. He holds his head in his hands.
64 mins: For me, Brighton lack a bit of thrust in the final third so I’d be sending on Minteh and Kostoulas. But that’s just me. And I eat Pringles and watch games from my upstairs spare room, while Hürzeler, who is my age, manages Brighton.
63 mins: That’s canny play from Thomas, tracking back to nick the ball off Costinha and then forcing the Brighton right-back to foul him. It’s a yellow card for Costinha too.
There’s very little respite for Hull, though; even when they get the ball forward, it’s coming back just as quickly.
61 mins: Rutter teases Coyle on the Brighton left before flashing one across the face of goal. Pretty harmless actually, that one, and the Frenchman cuts a frustrated figure.
60 mins: Rutter volleys over after Brighton keep it alive following Gross’s free-kick. A very difficult one for the former Leeds forward.
59 mins: Brighton have put in countless low crosses today. None of them have really worked; it’s been clearance after clearance from Ajayi and Mendy in the Hull backline.
Gourna-Douath goes into the book for a cynical tackle.
58 mins: The longer this remains goalless, the more you think Hull might fancy nicking all three points. Belloumi does well to dart inside off the right and arrow goalwards, but Verbruggen is equal to the shot.
56 mins: Thomas sends in a decent cross from the left, but Brighton clear and quickly counter … and Rutter decides to pass rather than shoot at the crucial moment.
Probably a case of overplaying it, there, as Gross also tried to lay it off and Hull scrambled it away.
55 mins: The Sky Sports commentators are already joking about Tzolakis being awarded the player of the match prize. There’s still a LONG time remaining for Brighton to find a way past him, guys …
53 mins: 12 shots, six on target, no goals. Hull’s goal is living a charmed existence this afternoon.
Another big chance missed by Gomez! This is really, really close. He brought it down so nicely with a cushioned touch, then from an acute angle he fired inches wide.
How many opportunities do Brighton actually need to score?
51 mins: What Hull have been able to do in this game is keep Pascal Gross quiet, largely nullifying his threat, keeping him closely marked … as I say that the German is able to unleash a left-footed shot, but it’s a fairly routine save from Tzolakis.
50 mins: Dunk strides forward into midfield and his deflected through-ball almost spun kindly for Rutter.
Then, Gomez continues to find space on the Brighton right but his cross is missed completely by the onrushing Ayari. A complete air shot.
48 mins: Brighton opted not to make a change at half-time, but I wonder how long it will be before Hürzeler calls upon the likes of Hinshelwood, Minteh and Kostoulas from his bench, which is pretty stacked talent-wise.
46 mins: And Thomas is straight into the action, pressing Costinha and winning Hull a throw-in.
Daniel Sturridge has just described modern day shin-pads as “sim card sized” on Sky Sports, which is phenomenal I must say. Sorba Thomas is sporting a super-small pair on his legs.
Back under way for the second half! Let’s have some goals, please …
Sorba Thomas is on for Hull, replacing Mohamed-Ali Cho, so a like-for-like change out wide by Sergej Jakirović.
Hull at home in the Premier League this season:
- Hull 2-0 Manchester United
- Hull 0-0 Aston Villa
- Hull 2-2 Everton
- Hull 1-1 Brentford
- Hull 2-2 Ipswich
- Hull 0-0 Brighton (HT)
“Drawn with the Tigers, you’re getting drawn by … “
Not everyone is enjoy this game as much as me, it appears.
Mary Waltz emails in: “Dom, greetings from California. It’s still dark here and the early start was not a problem. But I am struggling to stay awake watching this match.”
It does need a goal, Mary, I will admit that.
Konstantinos Tzolakis was no doubt the hero of that half for Hull. The data tells us that Brighton fashioned chances worth 1.75 expected goals across 10 shots, five of which were on target.
Fabian Hürzeler will scarcely believe his team haven’t scored, yet he and his staff must find answers after the break.
Time for me to grap a cuppa and some more Pringles (other oddly-shaped crisps are available).
HT: Hull 0-0 Brighton
Brighton should be 1-0 up at half-time – and they carved out possibly their best and clearest chance on the brink of the whistle. Gomez ran onto the cross from the left, drilling low and hard, but somehow Konstantinos Tzolakis got something in the way of it and it deflected out for a corner.
Pascal Gross thinks he was fouled in the buildup to that chance, but both Peter Bankes and VAR have dismissed his appeals. Phew … what a flurry of activity just before the break. After all that it’s finished goalless after the first 45 minutes.
45 mins +2: One underrated and less heralded aspect of Brighton’s game in how aggressive and physical they are. I feel like they have stood up to the physical challenge posed by Hull and imposed themselves on the game, before getting on the ball to strut their stuff.
The Seagulls are trying to fashion a chance late in the first half, right now …
Three added minutes. Brighton would love a breakthrough here.
44 mins: I say it’s been a gruelling half for Hull … but the home fans will be delighted with their team’s commitment and focus.
There’s a blow here for them, though. Tim Iroegbunam is going to be forced off with an injury. A replay of the challenge that caused the problem is quite tough to watch, a really nasty one as Iroegbunam clashed with Chema Andres.
Gourna-Douath is going to come on, he’s receiving instructions now.
I cannot see a foul in that melee – play on. Hull certainly are making the most of the set-piece opportunities they are getting, though. McBurnie is doing a great job drawing fouls from Vuskovic and Lewis Dunk.
41 mins: Verbruggen sprawls across his goal to make sure Belloumi’s free-kick does not sneak in. Hull then have a couple of crossing opportunities and start to get physical, amid halfhearted appeals for a home penalty.
Some positive moments for the Tigers towards the end of a gruelling half.
39 mins: Brighton could and possibly should have scored two or three already.
Hull will not care one bit. McBurnie has won another free-kick from the frustrated Vuskovic. The young Seagulls centre-back is getting a different kind of challenge at the MKM Stadium today.
Off the woodwork from Ayari! He met Gomez’s cutback with a sweet right-footed shot … and then Rutter is denied by another Tzolakis save from close range. A really big double chance for Brighton. Tzolakis and the frame of the goal are both proving hard to get past.
36 mins: McBurnie makes a nuisance of himself to win a corner for Hull and the crowd respond to his efforts with a roar.
It’s a damp squib in the end, however, as Verbruggen gets some catching practice from the resulting kick.
34 mins: It’s (more) bad news for my FPL team as Vuskovic kicks the ball away after fouling Cho and gets a booking for his troubles.
33 mins: Rutter isn’t a regular starter for Brighton, especially not in the No 9 position and I wonder whether the Seagulls are missing having an out-and-out striker. Rutter, Gomez, Gross and Ayari … they all kind of prefer playing in the pocket. Maybe a focal point would benefit Brighton instead.
32 mins: Cho gets a rare opportunity to run at Costinha and gets in a cross with his left foot, which Matt Crooks tries to flick from behind him. Unfortunately for Hull, Crooks cannot get any power on the flick and it’s straight at Verbruggen.
Tzolakis parries from Rutter at the other end, another smart save from the Hull stopper.
30 mins: Hull really aren’t having much of the ball. Even when they do, it’s pumped long quite swiftly.
28 mins: A well co-ordinated press from Hull has Verbruggen and his defenders worrying for a moment, hurriedly squirrelling the ball into touch, which allows another long throw from the hosts. Mendy hooks it tamely at the Brighton goal, and Verbruggen collects.
26 mins: If Hull versus Brighton feels strange as a top flight game, that’s because this is the first time they’ve ever met in the Premier League.
Fabian Hürzeler will not be panicking on the touchline, despite the goalless scoreline. His team’s general dominance will be his overriding thought.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/liv.title: Liverpool v Manchester United: Premier League – live
https://www.theguardian.com/football/liv.author: Rob Smyth
https://www.theguardian.com/football/liv.text:
Mauricio Pochettino has called on Manchester United to have “no fear” when they travel to Anfield for his first game. The Argentinian does not want his players to take a backward step as he targets a fast start.
United are 19th in the Premier League and Liverpool fifth but the head coach will not accept any self-doubt. Pochettino is known for being attack-minded and is keen to instil those ideals, but will have had only three days with the players since replacing Michael Carrick.
“We are going to Anfield with the idea to win and be brave and to be Manchester United,” Pochettino told the club’s website. “The history talks for us, and what we need to expect. We need to be sure that we are brave and we are protagonists and go there with no fears and challenge a very good team like Liverpool.”
No big surprises in Mauricio Pochettino’s first Man Utd XI. The most notable selection is probably the centre-back pairing of Matthijs de Ligt (starting his first Premier League game since November 2025) and Lisandro Martinez.
There are three changes from the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa in Michael Carrick’s final game: De Ligt, Martinez and Patrick Dorgu replace Noussair Mazraoui, Harry Maguire and Amad Diallo.
Liverpool bring in Rio Ngumoha for Cody Gakpo, the only change from their win at Crystal Palace before the international break.
The first day in a new job is supposed to be gentle and relaxed: small talk, smaller admin, a few bits of work and some lamentably awkward handshakes. Mauricio Pochettino’s first day* as Manchester United manager is the polar opposite. Liverpool away, the ultimate domestic challenge for any United manager.
This quirk of employment opportunity and fixture list might be a good thing for Pochettino. It’s a free hit, with nobody of sound mind expecting his brave new world to begin until he has had months on the training ground. And if United do win, it’ll increase the length of the free pass that every new manager receives.
Andoni Iraola only joined Liverpool in June, yet he’s already their 11th longest-serving manager. Iraola has made a promising start, including some rousing victories in Europe in particular.
In the Premier League, Liverpool’s main problem has been their home form. They’ve taken five points from five games, but it’s a bit early to lament the demise of Fortress Anfield. Three of those five matches were against the top three of Manchester City, Arsenal and Brighton.
Today, almost unbelievably, Liverpool are playing the team in 19th place: Mauricio Pochettino’s Manchester United.
Kick off 4.30pm.
* Yes, yes, I know this isn’t actually his first day in the job, but you know exactly what I mean so let’s not allow semantics to undermine a perfectly half-arsed preamble.

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.title: Cop31 live: EU and others reject deal as longest climate summit ever faces collapse
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.author: Bibi van der Zee
https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text:
Cop31 climate talks set to end in deep division as key deal rejected
The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey.
The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”
Our colleagues in Antalya, Fiona Harvey and Graham Readfearn, have written about the outcome here.
He is followed onto the dais by the UNFCCC chief Simon Stiell, who spoke to reporters outside shortly before.
Stiell tells the plenary: “I share the disappoinment of many. Cop31 has been unable to agreee on both preseidency led decisions." Once again he emphasised where there has been progress. But, he said, “climate impacts are rising the world over. Fossil fuel costs are driving inflation the world over.”
“We’ve brought almost 200 countries together over two decades which have delivered results: climate targets, new goal and a goal on adaption.
“But there are lessons that must be learned… Consensus works best from ground up, with full transparency, taking time to listen to all views and building on what came before. There is clearly scope to improve, modernise and reform, not only because of what happend here but also because we must evolve.”
“This process has suffered setbacks before and come back stronger, it must do so again. Humanity can not afford anything else.”
The Cop president Murat Kurum has now resumed the plenary, opening it with a very sincere apology to the Ghana delegation who accused him of cutting them off earlier.
“Ghana is our friendly and brotherly country. I would like to ask their excellencies; such an attitude is by no means our attitude towards ghana and I have explained this to her. Again I’d like to apologise for the misunderstanding.”
The consensus system fell short today, concedes UNFCCC chief
Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of the UNFCCC, has just held a short press conference, where he emphasised that there had been many good outcomes of the conference but also acknowledged the issues.
Asked whether the consensus based system which broke down today when several countries refused to endorse the cover decision, he said: “That is the process we have, that is the process that got us through Paris and the progress made since, so it has worked.”
However, pressed further by a reporter who said that it may have worked in the past, but clearly did not work here, he conceded: “It certainly fell short today, but there are two stories to be told here.” He reminded reporters that this was a technical cop, and a significant number of the 160 agenda items were passed.
However, he said: “In terms of reform there has been a lot of discussion over the last couple years over the process … The conversation about how the process is to evolve moving forward is a live conversation.” And he said that he was engaging with parties around those challenging questions.
Lord Nicholas Stern, who wrote a landmark economic review of the impact of climate change for the UK government back in 2006, is searching for the positives. He points out that there were also positive developments in Turkey and says:
“We should now focus on the year ahead and work to strengthen shared commitment and to re-establish confidence in the multilateral process. We should remember that a valuable agreement was reached at the COP16 summit in Cancun, Mexico, in 2010 a year after disagreement in Copenhagen at COP15.
“The COP32 summit in Addis Ababa will provide a significant opportunity for the world to come together again to chart a new pathway for economic development and growth, particularly in Africa.”
Reaction to the failed cover decision and other key agenda points continues to pour in.
Ann Harrison, climate justice policy advisor at Amnesty International, said:
Countries from across regions were right to reject the colossal betrayal that the COP31 co-presidencies tried to pass off as climate action. They resisted a polluters’ charter designed to protect corporate profits while sacrificing people and the planet. They refused to accept a deeply unjust text that failed even to name fossil fuels while opening the door to risky technologies that could prolong their use.”
Mark Watts, executive director of C40 Cities, said:
This is one of the darkest hours in the history of climate negotiations and Cops cannot go on like this. The world needs braver leadership and urgent action. The era of overshoot has no room for failed climate diplomacy anymore. Every Cop must deliver collective action to accelerate the transition away from fossil fuels and address the most severe impacts of climate breakdown.
Today the Cop of Antalya failed to do that. The lack of courage by too many at Cop31 is not only undermining multilateralism, but, in the face of Super El Niño and worsening long-term climate conditions, it is costing lives.”
Teresa Anderson, the global lead on climate justice at ActionAid International, said:
Temperatures are rising, impacts are rising, but support for climate-hit countries is shrinking. The EU’s refusal to allow real progress on adaptation finance means that harvests will fail when they might have thrived. Buildings will collapse that could have withstood storms. People will drown because they didn’t get a flood alert. Millions of people will be left to deal with hunger, destruction and death that could have been avoided if rich countries cared about humanity’s future.
While the EU’s standing up to a text weak on fossil fuels has helped its reputation in this space, its self-appointed crown of climate leadership sits crookedly. The success of climate negotiations cannot be judged on carbon dioxide alone. Until wealthy polluting countries can stop seeing climate finance as a zero-sum game, climate talks will fail in their job of keeping humanity safe from rising temperatures.”
Reaction is also coming in from scientists based in the UK.
Prof Martin Siegert, University of Exeter, said:
“This could be, strangely, good news for the climate process. A line has been drawn, where international agreement can only proceed if there is clear agreement that fossil fuels need to be transitioned away from as soon as possible. The science, which is so obvious, demands this. To agree to anything less would be more of a disaster than the failings of COP31. It doesn’t mean the end of the COP process - but a resetting is needed so that it focuses on firm action to reduce global emissions, to transition to renewable energy and electrification, and to do all this urgently within a fair and just framework.”
Prof Mark Maslin, Professor of Climatology, UCL, said:
“This is probably the worst COP ever - all because fossil fuel producing countries refuse to allow the fundamental cause of climate change - namely fossil fuels – to be mentioned in the final agreement. Fossil fuels were first mentioned in COP26 in Glasgow and at COP 28 in Dubai the agreement stressed the need to transition away from the using fossil fuels. But since then, Saudi Arabia and Russia with occasional support from India, China and USA have watered down or blocked ever attempt to get global agreements on how to decarbonize the world economy. This is geopolitics playing with the lives off millions of people and the fate of the global environment.”
Prof Ali Mashayek, Department of Earth Sciences, University of Cambridge, said:
“The collapse of COP31 reflects a rift that has been widening for years. One side holds that fossil fuels are a given and we should simply get on with renewables and adaptation. The other insists we must confront decarbonisation head-on, however painful. That rift was bound to surface, and forcing an agreement nobody believes in would not have helped. You cannot solve a problem without naming its root cause. Climate impacts are already here and worsening fast. We can no longer afford flimsy, non-binding deals produced by exhausting annual marathons. COPs have achieved a great deal, but we now need serious, efficient action and honest messaging. This failure could be the precursor to exactly that.”
'Australia left nothing on the field,' says Cop co-president Chris Bowen
Graham Readfearn
Australia’s climate change minister, Chris Bowen, has just spoken to reporters outside the plenary room. He says he hasn’t slept for three days.
“Unfortunately we were unable to reach agreement on a cover decision and that’s very disappointing,” he said.
“Ultimately looking back many parties who are people of good faith had very strong red lines on a couple of key issues and despite many many attempts on reflection those red lines were not able to be met.”
He thanked his staff for their efforts. “Australia left nothing on the field,” he said, but the red lines they had tried to negotiate were “unbridgeable”.
He said one key red line was the language around the transition away from fossil fuels.
“Some parties insisted if it was mentioned, they would veto,” he said.
“Fossil fuels – we tried to strike a balance,” he said. “In the end it wasn’t enough... I would have been happy with transition away from fossil fuels being in the text, but that was not going to get support from parties. Given it’s the existing position of [previous] Cops... parties couldn’t live with that.”
He said “in the real world” the transition away from fossil fuels was inevitable and was irreversible, and happening at speed.
The electrification target, which was in the unadopted Antalya Pact, had a lot of support, he said, and it was not a deal breaker.
The UN secretary-general Antonio Guterres – right at the end of his term of office, has sent out a statement on the conference:
“I am deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome. I share the very profound frustration of all those who expected governments to rise to the moment the climate crisis demands.”
He doesn’t comment on the decision by countries to reject the text, but does say: “At COP28 in Dubai, all countries agreed to transition away from fossil fuels in a just, orderly and equitable manner. The task now is to accelerate that transition, finance and deliver it.
“I welcome countries coming forward with concrete plans to do so.’
Guterres has many times singled out fossil fuels for their role in the climate crisis.
Mohamed Adow, director of the thinktank Power Shift Africa, says,
“This has been the worst ever COP and its collapse needs to be a wake up call for the world.
Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed and expecting a carefully worded declaration to get them off the hook.
COP31 was a ghost COP, and its lack of progress will haunt the climate vulnerable.
Despite progress in recent years agreeing to transition away from fossil fuels in 2023 and a promise to triple adaptation finance in 2025, this year everything ground to a halt. At a time when climate breakdown is only getting worse, this is unforgiveable.
Previous COP achievements show that the multilateral process is not to blame, it is the countries blocking progress on finance to accelerate climate action which that are ultimately responsible.”
Jasper Inventor, head of COP31 Greenpeace Delegation, says:
“We came to COP31 to end fossil fuels, not promote them and extend their lifeline. It’s bitterly disappointing to leave without a clear outcome or a credible pathway to end fossil fuels. We stopped a bad deal that favours fossil fuels, but leaving without a deal is still a failure for communities on the climate frontlines. As always, it is the world’s most vulnerable communities who bear the consequences of this failure. We’ve run out of time to avoid overshoot, but we can still keep 1.5°C alive.”
Tuvalu’s climate minister, Maina Talia, is now speaking. “There is significant work ahead of us”, he says, adding that we must transition away from fossil fuels in a way that is just. “Tuvalu cannot do this alone.”
China experts were critical of the approach taken by the presidency, and suggested that China could have been allowed to play a larger role.
Li Shuo, Director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute, said: “COP31 should have advanced global climate cooperation despite an increasingly difficult geopolitical landscape. Instead, Antalya represents a major setback for multilateral climate diplomacy — the most significant failure since Copenhagen.
“China may have seemed a quiet player at COP31, but its presence is increasingly self-assured and influential. As the global climate agenda faces mounting geopolitical and economic headwinds, Beijing is providing continuity and stability within the multilateral system. Unfortunately, the COP31 Presidency did not effectively deploy China’s discreet power in the chaotic final stages of the negotiations.”
Kate Logan, Director of China Climate Hub and Climate Diplomacy at the Asia Society Policy Institute, said: “COP31 suffered in the hands of a disorganized presidency and stark geopolitical divides. With the US still sitting out and the EU facing down populism, China emphasized managing expectations and upholding multilateralism. While Beijing’s unique positioning enables it to forge alignment where few others can, China remained hesitant to step into a higher-profile role as consensus started to crumble.
“As the world’s dominant producer of clean technologies, China’s economic interests are increasingly intertwined with the objectives of climate talks. Officials highlighted how Chinese clean technologies are reducing emissions globally but trade protections raise costs and slow implementation, reflecting Beijing’s persistent frustration with tariffs that inhibit the free flow of clean tech. China’s $15 billion renewable energy deal with host Türkiye on the sidelines of COP31 shows how Beijing is advancing progress in the real economy, even if not necessarily captured by formal negotiations.”
Reaction to the breakdown of the talks, and the rejection of the key text, are flowing in from NGOs and campaigners.
Asad Rehman, chief executive of Friends of the Earth, said:
“After decades of broken pledges and hollow commitments, an agreement built on yet more empty promises would have been unforgivable and no substitute for the transformative action we urgently need. So the dramatic rejection of the Presidency’s final text by some, though underscoring the lack of consensus that’s been reached, restores some level of faith in its recognition that a deal of this calibre is no deal at all.”
He added:
“What matters now is not when governments reconvene, it’s how they do so. The world doesn’t need more meetings with wooly commitments. We need global governments, including the UK, to come back to the negotiating table ready to deliver. That means cutting emissions fairly at home, transitioning our economies in a way that leaves no one behind, and providing the public climate finance so desperately needed to protect people, livelihoods and our planet from unimaginable harm.”
Ani Dasguputa, president and CEO of the World Resources Institute, said:
“The hollow outcome at COP31 was a failure of political leadership, not a failure of the Paris Agreement. When narrow national interests override collective responsibility to confront the climate crisis, the entire world pays the price. Climate summits are not stages for posturing; they require every country to roll up their sleeves and do the hard work of finding ambitious common ground.
At a time when the science could not be clearer, it is indefensible that countries could not agree on even mentioning fossil fuels, the primary driver of climate change. The science has long settled this question – it’s time for the politics to catch up.”
Countries are still taking it in turns to speak in the plenary room. Despite a lack of consensus over the cover decision, Canada and others such as Fiji have said they want to continue discussions about oceans and strengthening the Cop process itself.
Canada concluded its statement saying “multilateralism is essential”.
Cop31 climate talks set to end in deep division as key deal rejected
The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey.
The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”
Our colleagues in Antalya, Fiona Harvey and Graham Readfearn, have written about the outcome here.
Although parties are still speaking in the plenary hall, discussion is now swirling around the final outcome of the talks. The presidency has headed out to the hall to speak to the press, and has confirmed that there will be no new draft cover decision. There is a lot of confusion about the next steps here.
The talks have now all but collapsed. A number of side deals will be passed, but the number of rejections of the core deal continue to mount.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Netanyahu rival condemns settler arson attacks on Palestinian villages in West Bank
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Lorenzo Tondo in Jerusalem and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Arson attacks by militant Israeli settlers on Palestinian villages in the occupied West Bank have caused a political row in Israel, drawing condemnation from Gadi Eisenkot, the opposition leader, who described them as “Jewish terrorism”.
Dozens of settlers raided Palestinian communities overnight on Saturday, setting fire to about a dozen vehicles and several homes and scrawling racist graffiti. At least four communities were attacked. Israeli police said they had launched an investigation with forensic teams.
Photographs from Kafr Malik, near Ramallah, showed one slogan written in Hebrew that read: “This is the first revenge.” Several vehicles and homes were set alight in the village.
Images from nearby Deir al-Sudan showed vehicles on fire. Palestinian reports said an agricultural building had been set ablaze in Deir Ballut and cars were torched in Deir Abu Mashal.
An inconclusive election last month stripped Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli prime minister, of his majority. Eisenkot has been asked to form a government, though his prospects seem little better.
“Last night’s arson attacks in Judea and Samaria were acts of Jewish terrorism, in every sense of the term,” Eisenkot said, using the biblical name for the West Bank. “Extremist groups that set fire to vehicles and homes are undermining regional stability, putting lives at risk and doing grave damage to Israel’s national security and foreign relations.”
Referring to Itamar Ben-Gvir, Israel’s national security minister, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister, he added: “The actions led by Ben-Gvir and Smotrich in the West Bank have brought the area to the brink of unchecked anarchy.”
Eisenkot, who has been given 28 days to form a government by President Isaac Herzog, with a possible 14-day extension, urged the Israeli government and security establishment to “use every tool at their disposal – including administrative detention and targeted operations by the Shin Bet – to stop the rioters and impose harsh sanctions on them”.
In an unprecedented rebuke on Sunday, several other members of the Israeli parliament criticised Netanyahu over escalating violence by militant settlers against Palestinians.
Yair Lapid, the leader of Yesh Atid, held Netanyahu’s government responsible for encouraging the attacks. “Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence by the Israeli government,” he said on X, adding that ministers were deliberately encouraging the militant settlers’ violence “through their silence”.
Yair Golan, the leader of the Democrats party, warned of the possibility of a third intifada, and described the West Bank as “on the brink of an explosion”.
“Anyone who wants to prevent a third intifada must replace the current government, which provides cover and support for Jewish terrorism and abandons security,” Golan said on X. “Jewish terrorism harms innocent Palestinians and Israeli army soldiers, and pushes Israel toward unprecedented international isolation.”
Noam Tibon, a retired army major general and Knesset member, gave a similar warning. “If Israel does not eliminate Jewish terrorism in the West Bank, it will destroy Israel,” he wrote.
Netanyahu has not yet responded to the accusations.
Australia announced sanctions on Wednesday against three people and four Israeli entities, including a construction company, over their role in the expansion of illegal settlements and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
A day earlier the UK imposed sanctions on eight Israeli construction companies involved in building illegal settlements in the West Bank, which the UN regards as Palestinian territory under Israeli occupation since 1967.
Since the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attacks on Israel, there has been a surge of Israeli settlement expansion and violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers.
On Tuesday, a 72-year-old Palestinian woman was shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli militant settlers in a village near Jericho, where the group has recently moved in after taking over several Palestinian homes.
Reuters contributed to this report

https://www.humanite.fr/environnement/co.title: « Pris en otage par des États pétroliers », « retour en arrière »… On vous explique ce qui bloque à la COP31
https://www.humanite.fr/environnement/co.author: La rédaction avec AFP
https://www.humanite.fr/environnement/co.text:
La COP31, plus longue conférence de l’ONU sur le climat de l’histoire, a échoué en Turquie, ce dimanche 22 novembre, à adopter un projet de décision finale qui omettait les énergies fossiles, après son rejet par l’Union européenne et d’autres pays.
« Nous n’approuverons pas une décision (…) ne mentionnant même pas les combustibles fossiles, qui sont le principal moteur du changement climatique », a annoncé le ministre irlandais du Climat Darragh O’Brien, dont le pays assure actuellement la présidence de l’UE, en séance plénière. La représentante du Panama a ensuite indiqué que son pays s’opposerait aussi formellement à l’adoption du texte, suivie par les îles Marshall, le Vanuatu ou Belize.
Le président turc de la COP31 a été contraint de reconnaître son échec à faire adopter la proposition de déclaration politique qu’il avait préparée avec la présidence australienne des négociations, et qui devait faire office de principal résultat de la conférence.
« Il semble que certaines parties s’opposent à ce texte » et, en l’absence de consensus, les « décisions n’ont pas été adoptées », a admis Murat Kurum lors d’une séance plénière.
La Turquie et l’Australie, aux commandes en vertu d’un partage des tâches inédit, avaient publié dimanche un nouveau projet de décision finale ne mentionnant toujours pas explicitement les énergies fossiles mais contenant un appel à l’électrification.
Une ultime version, contenant des changements cosmétiques, a été publiée à la dernière minute avant la réunion des pays en plénière.
La COP31 en Turquie est déjà devenue la plus longue COP Climat de l’Histoire, battant le record précédent de la COP25 à Madrid en 2019. Les décisions doivent être prises par consensus de quelque 200 pays à la COP, si bien que l’opposition formelle d’un seul d’entre eux peut bloquer une décision.
« Prise en otage par des États pétroliers »
Le texte proposé « nous ramène en arrière », avait dénoncé la ministre française de la Transition écologique Monique Barbut. Ce projet d’accord est « inacceptable », avait aussi averti son homologue allemand Carsten Schneider.
Le texte ne contenait toujours pas d’appel explicite à sortir du charbon, du pétrole ou du gaz fossile, dont l’utilisation est la principale cause du changement climatique.
Il se contente d’une discrète allusion au résultat de la COP28 de Dubaï, qui avait pour la première fois appelé en 2023 les pays du monde à une transition afin de sortir des énergies fossiles.
Des nations du Pacifique, d’Europe ou d’Amérique latine n’ont cessé de réclamer ces derniers jours une mention explicite des énergies fossiles dans le texte final. Mais les producteurs d’hydrocarbures, Arabie saoudite en tête, s’y opposent.
La COP31 « a été prise en otage par des États pétroliers », a dit à l’AFP Darragh O’Brien. Au coeur de la discorde également, le texte demande d’accélérer le recours aux technologies de captation, utilisation et stockage du carbone (CCUS), promues par les entreprises pétro-gazières.
« Le changement climatique nécessite toutes les solutions sur la table », a défendu le représentant saoudien, Mohammad Ayoub.
« Piège »
Le projet de décision contenait en revanche l’objectif, porté par la Turquie, d’augmenter « la part de l’électricité dans la consommation finale totale d’énergie à 35 % à l’échelle mondiale d’ici 2035 », associé à des efforts pour accroître le recours à une « énergie propre ».
Les attentes étaient limitées avant ce grand rendez-vous onusien, mais la Turquie espérait le conclure avec des avancées face à l’urgence climatique, la planète subissant toujours davantage les effets du réchauffement d’origine humaine.
Un accord substantiel est rendu difficile par le contexte géopolitique, marqué par la flambée des prix de l’énergie liée à la guerre au Moyen-Orient. Et en l’absence, une nouvelle fois, des États-Unis.
Autre question âprement débattue : les financements que les pays développés, historiquement responsables de la plupart des émissions, se sont engagés à verser aux pays en développement pour les aider à lutter contre les effets du changement climatique.
Les Européens avaient prévenu avant la COP qu’ils n’avaient aucunement l’intention d’apporter des financements supplémentaires, mais simplement d’assurer des engagements passés.
Le projet de compromis de dimanche évoquait enfin la question, également disputée, du calendrier de publication des prochains rapports du Giec, le groupe de scientifiques travaillant sous l’égide de l’ONU.
Le texte souligne « l’importance » de ces rapports pour le prochain « bilan mondial » des efforts des pays pour limiter leurs émissions de gaz à effet de serre, prévu en 2028. L’Inde et l’Arabie saoudite préfèrent attendre 2029 pour ces rapports.
Le projet d’accord insistait aussi sur l’importance de plafonner le réchauffement climatique à 1,5°C par rapport à la période 1850-1900, une demande majeure des petites îles menacées par la montée des eaux.
La Terre de nos batailles
La justice climatique, c’est notre bataille. Celle qui relie luttes environnementales et sociales pour contrer un système capitaliste faisant ventre de tout. Du vivant, de la planète, de notre humanité.
Il n’y a pas de fatalité.
- Nous démasquons les manipulations des lobbies.
- Nous battons en brèche les dénis climatiques mortifères.
- Nous mettons en valeur les initiatives visant à réduire les inégalités environnementales et les fractures sociales.
Soutenez-nous.
Je veux en savoir plus

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: How did Republicans lose so badly in North Carolina?
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Ariana Baio
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Republicans suffered sweeping losses across the country in the midterm elections, but perhaps nowhere as large as North Carolina.
Democrats flipped a US Senate seat for the first time since 2008, as well as five House seats, one of which Cook Political Report had rated “solid” Republican, and four others considered “likely” Republican. Democrats also held power in the state’s first district, which Republicans had targeted in a redistricting effort.
One of the seats Democrats flipped belonged to Richard Hudson, a representative who led House Republicans’ re-election efforts as the head of the National Republican Congressional Committee. It was the first time an NRCC chair had ever lost a general election.
As of Monday, the Associated Press hadn’t called four of the House races, but two were leaning in favor of Democrats.
North Carolina’s statehouse flipped for Democrats for the first time in more than a decade and Republicans are holding onto the state senate by a one-seat margin – which is currently headed to a recount.
This was all in a state that had only voted for one Democratic presidential candidate since 1980, and hadn’t elected a Democrat to the Senate in almost 20 years. So how did Republicans lose so badly in North Carolina?
“They took voters for granted,” said Anderson Clayton, the 28-year-old chair of the North Carolina Democratic party.
“They thought they could gerrymander themselves into having a seat and not actually have to go out and fight for it, and I think voters looked at them and said: ‘That’s not how we roll. That’s not how it works in North Carolina.’”
Clayton, who has been working to flip North Carolina blue since she was elected in 2023, points to multiple factors this election cycle: Trump’s unpopularity fueling North Carolinians’ frustrations with the current status quo, and a fleet of younger candidates running for office.
But she emphasized Republicans’ failure to address issues affecting voters, especially in North Carolina’s rural districts, as one of the top reasons.
As an example, she pointed to a recent quote from Donny Lambeth, a seven-term Republican state representative, who lost by eight percentage points.
Lambeth told the New York Times that he mistakenly listened to members of his caucus who told him he was in a “safe district” and did not need to spend “any money”. In 2024, Lambeth had won by approximately 14 percentage points.
“I was like: ‘Well, did you go out and talk to any of your voters?’” Clayton said in response to Lambeth’s admission. “‘Like, did you actually speak to somebody on the ground in your district?’”
Felice Pete, an RNC committee member from North Carolina and longtime Republican activist, acknowledged Republicans’ shortcomings.
“You have places where we didn’t think we’re going to lose, like Virginia Foxx, and looking back, people took it for granted. These were safe, red counties. And it’s just getting out the vote effort,” Pete said.
The Associated Press has not called Foxx’s race in North Carolina’s fifth congressional district because of an ongoing recount, but her Democratic opponent, Chuck Hubbard, is ahead by a thin but likely insurmountable margin.
“The 2024 win for Republicans was not done with traditional Republicans,” Pete said. “They were first-time voters, they were independents, there were a lot of young minority men, a lot of young college-aged men.”
“I just think, with redistricting, we just did not have the effort focused with getting out the votes,” Pete said.
Republicans had invested time, money and energy into maintaining their majority through redistricting, under pressure from the US president. They redrew lines to try to flip the first congressional district, but it didn’t work; the incumbent Democrat, Don Davis, held onto his seat.
Clayton accused Republicans of getting “elitist” in the midterms and relying too heavily on consultants – a criticism Democrats often face.
“Instead, you had real grassroots energy from Democrats that won seats that honestly, they shouldn’t have, in some ways, on Tuesday night,” Clayton said.
In parts of the state that are comfortably red, such as Davidson county, located in central North Carolina, the electorate moved 16 percentage points in favor of Democrats compared with 2024, according to NBC’s decision desk.
Christopher Jessup, the chair of the Davidson county Republican party and a longtime Republican advocate, said he wasn’t sure why that happened but attributed it to “probably some voter turnout”.
Jessup highlighted that his county still overwhelmingly voted for the Republican candidates in the midterms, and praised the work his colleagues and teams did. Despite that, the sixth congressional district, where Davidson county is located, flipped for Democrats.
When asked what the top issue for voters in the county was, Jessup said “a very negative view of Roy Cooper”.
Cooper, the former governor of North Carolina, defeated Michael Whatley, the former head of the Republican National Committee and chosen directly by Trump, by nearly 20 percentage points.
Republicans had anticipated Cooper’s win. By October, the top Super Pac for Senate Republicans cancelled remaining ads that it had booked in the state.
Like many Republicans, Pete is still dissecting why messaging that won over North Carolinians in 2024 didn’t resonate in 2026. But she has some theories, starting with the fact that Trump 2024 voters felt “betrayed”.
“The word that I hear over and over is betrayal,” Pete said. “Many of those people felt like voting did not matter because they felt like 2024 was their last hope to have this correction, and then they go, and here we are.”
Pete pointed to Trump’s campaign promise not to start more wars, which he failed to deliver on when he started a conflict with Iran in February. That conflict, which Congress never formally approved, has pushed gas and diesel prices up, causing a chain reaction that has affected other everyday costs, such as groceries.
She added that messaging that won voters over in 2024 “started to shift” or wasn’t being communicated well from “some higher-ups, or even our administration”. That includes mass deportations; during his campaign, Trump promised to target every undocumented immigrant, but administration officials now claim they target undocumented immigrants with violent criminal histories.
Citing a personal example, Pete said the young men that she gathered to go out door-knocking in 2024 did not want to work for the 2026 midterms; she called the experience “a microcosm of what happened”.
“We have to have an honest assessment of that and just the detriment of not fulfilling, or seemingly fulfilling, the promises you make,” Pete said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Iran unveils dual-missile launcher, new ‘missile city’: What to know
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Iran unveils dual-missile launcher, new ‘missile city’: What to know
Military officials tour underground facility in show of military capabilities despite US attacks.
Iran is putting its upgraded missile systems and underground military facilities on display, delivering a defiant message that it still has significant military capabilities despite US-Israeli attacks.
The latest showcase included a dual-missile launcher capable of firing two liquid-fuelled missiles simultaneously, according to state media broadcasting footage of military commanders touring an underground missile facility.
Officials insisted Iran has strengthened its missile and air-defence capabilities since previous rounds of fighting, including the launch of the US-Israel war in late February. Still, Iran is under mounting economic pressure from a naval blockade imposed by the United States that has disrupted its oil exports.
Here’s everything to know about the new dual-missile launcher and Iran’s “missile city”:
What is the new launcher?
Iran has developed a range of ballistic and cruise missiles over the past three decades.
The new dual-missile launcher was unveiled as Major-General Ahmad Vahidi, commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), toured the underground facility on Saturday.
The IRGC aerospace force flaunted its range of upgraded missiles and military equipment, including the launcher, which is designed to carry and fire two liquid-fuelled missiles simultaneously, according to state broadcaster IRIB.
Liquid-fuelled missiles are launched vertically and offer speed-control capabilities, which can aid in overcoming air defence systems, IRIB reported.
State media said the latest generations of Iranian missiles have improved in range, accuracy and guidance capabilities independent of the US Global Positioning System (GPS).
What is known about the underground ‘missile city’?
Vahidi’s tour followed the IRGC aerospace force’s announcement of a new underground facility on November 10, according to the semiofficial Tasnim News Agency.
Tasnim said Iran is constructing underground military complexes able to continue weapons production and storage even under heavy bombardment.
The IRGC has said it transferred its missile and drone production lines from the surface to underground facilities to allow it continuing missile production.
Footage broadcast by IRIB on Saturday showed kilometres of tunnels and hundreds of missiles and launchers, including double launchers, among other systems.
Reporting from Tehran, Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar said it was not clear when the state broadcaster’s footage of the underground site was filmed.
“The IRGC are trying to send a message to the outside world that they are not short of ammunition; they have enough missiles and enough launchers,” he said.
“If the war resumes again, they are going to deploy these capabilities,” he added. “It is a part of their propaganda, but also, Iran is flexing its muscles and trying to restore deterrence.”
Rami Khouri, a public policy fellow at the American University of Beirut, said Iran can safely store spare parts, raw materials and chemicals needed for creating missiles and drones at its underground sites in addition to storing finished missiles and drones.
Iran has been planning for such a scenario for decades, he said. “So there’s no doubt that Iran has stored an enormous amount of all of this,” Khouri, who is also a nonresident senior fellow at the Arab Center Washington DC, told Al Jazeera.
“They’ve shown … they’re prepared to stand sanctions and keep fighting.”
What is Iran trying to achieve by showcasing its defence capabilities?
Rob Geist Pinfold, a lecturer in international security at King’s College London, said Iran is now more emboldened than ever to assert its military capabilities due to the outcome of the US midterm elections, in which President Donald Trump’s Republican Party suffered sweeping losses.
The rising cost of living as a result of the war on Iran was a major factor in how people in the US voted in the elections, which saw Democrats winning control of both chambers of Congress.
“So [Trump] looks more like the boy who cried wolf,” Pinfold told Al Jazeera. “There seems to be a feeling that the US has been deterred or disincentivised from escalating the conflict.”
Khouri said Iran has taken a gradual approach to showing its technical and military capabilities as well as its political will to strike back.
“[This is] all designed to show the US and Israel … [that] Iran has very sophisticated capabilities that can both evade the Western defence forces and defence systems … and at the same time reach targets that it wants to hit in the countries that it decides to attack,” he said.
At the same time, Iran is suffering under the US naval blockade of its southern ports, so it feels the need to escalate because it feels backed into a corner, Pinfold noted.
He added that Iran’s economy is already in recession and there are growing fears it could suffer an even bigger hit.
“Very little if any oil is coming out of Iran at the moment,” Pinfold said.

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/amnesty-in.title: « Pourquoi la France bloque-t-elle l’aide financière ? » : la question qui a valu à la militante Mariam Touré d’être exclue de la COP31
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/amnesty-in.author: Hayet Kechit
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/amnesty-in.text:
Mariam Touré, une jeune militante pour la défense des droits humains, s’est vu retirer son accréditation à la COP31 au sein de la délégation française après avoir demandé des comptes à la ministre de la Transition écologique dans un échange filmé en marge des débats le 20 novembre. Amnesty International dénonce la « pente glissante » empruntée par la France.
La ministre de la Transition écologique n’aime visiblement pas qu’on lui réclame des comptes. « Pourquoi la France bloque-t-elle les avancées sur l’aide financière pour l’adaptation à la crise climatique ? ».
Cette question posée par Mariam Touré – une conseillère jeunesse des Nations unies (ONU) accréditée par la France – à Monique Barbut au détour d’un couloir lors de la COP31 a valu à la première de se retrouver sans badge, dès le lendemain, à la porte des négociations du centre de conférences d’Antalya, en Turquie.
Signalement à l’ONU
La vidéo de ce bref échange, interdite de diffusion mais visionnée par des journalistes de RFI qui ont révélé l’affaire le 20 novembre, montrerait une ministre particulièrement agacée. La question, posée de façon courtoise, assure Le Monde, qui a également consulté la vidéo, a été « perçue comme agressive » par le cabinet de la ministre.
Les représailles n’ont pas traîné : en plus de son exclusion, la jeune militante s’est vue faire l’objet d’un signalement à l’ONU pour cette infraction à « la charte de bonne conduite des membres de la délégation ». En cause : l’enregistrement de cet échange « réalisé sans le consentement de la ministre ».
Ann Harrisson d’Amnesty International, qui a fourni un nouveau badge à Mariam Touré, a pour sa part dénoncé des mesures d’intimidation, révélatrices « d’une pente glissante » et prévient : « J’espère que cela ne signifie pas que la France prend le chemin autoritaire qu’on a vu dans d’autres pays. »
La Terre de nos batailles
La justice climatique, c’est notre bataille. Celle qui relie luttes environnementales et sociales pour contrer un système capitaliste faisant ventre de tout. Du vivant, de la planète, de notre humanité.
Il n’y a pas de fatalité.
- Nous démasquons les manipulations des lobbies.
- Nous battons en brèche les dénis climatiques mortifères.
- Nous mettons en valeur les initiatives visant à réduire les inégalités environnementales et les fractures sociales.
Soutenez-nous.
Je veux en savoir plus

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: What next for Iraq’s push against militias following Jurf al-Sakhar deal?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
What next for Iraq’s push against militias following Jurf al-Sakhar deal?
Thursday’s Iran-brokered compromise may bode poorly for Baghdad’s attempt to curb militia influence.
The entry of Iraqi government forces into Jurf al-Sakhar, a town 60km (37 miles) southwest of Baghdad long held by the Iran-backed armed group Kataib Hezbollah, has raised questions about the future of Iraqi militias in the country.
A deal reached between Iraqi authorities and Kataib Hezbollah about control of Jurf al-Sakhar, where oil smuggling was allegedly taking place, staved off a potential confrontation between the two sides.
It is the latest episode in Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s push to assert federal government control over the country and crack down on corruption, which is allegedly funding pro-Iran militias.
So how does Thursday’s compromise bode for the Iraqi state’s mission to rein in militias and weapons outside its control?
What happened at Jurf al-Sakhar?
Kataib Hezbollah seized Jurf al-Sakhar from ISIL (ISIS) in 2014, renaming it Jurf al-Nasr (“victory”). For the 12 years since then, it has prevented state authorities from re-establishing control and allegedly siphoned oil from local pipelines.
After an intelligence report was released this week about oil smuggling in Jurf al-Sakhar, the government formed a high-level committee to investigate the issue.
After an anti-corruption crackdown was announced, al-Zaidi then gave Kataib Hezbollah until Friday to withdraw from the town. A compromise deal was reached a day before the due date, with government forces entering Jurf al-Sakhar and establishing a joint operations centre in the town. This should see the gradual withdrawal of Kataib Hezbollah units and the phased deployment of an army brigade, a federal police brigade, an energy police regiment and two brigades from the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF) to the town.
The compromise reportedly came after direct Iranian intervention brokered by Esmail Qaani, head of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) elite Quds Force, which once joined the PMF on the front lines against ISIL and maintains deep ties with several of Iraq’s militias.
Why is Baghdad moving against militias?
PM al-Zaidi, a businessman with a Shia background, took power in May, vowing to end corruption and the fragmentation of the country’s security landscape.
Initially, he set a deadline of September 30 for militias to place their weapons under state control, coinciding with the withdrawal of US and allied forces from Iraq. While US forces withdrew, the militias refused to comply, and the deadline was pushed to June 2027.
Of major concern to Baghdad is the use of Iraq by armed groups to launch unauthorised attacks at Iran’s behest. Since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran, several Iraqi militias have pledged to support Iran’s war effort. Baghdad has acknowledged that attacks targeting neighbours have been launched from its territory and has vowed to put an end to them.
Akeel Abbas, an expert in Iraqi affairs, said Baghdad was the reason for the government’s intervention in Jurf al-Sakhar, not the issue of oil smuggling.
“This area, which the state could not enter since 2014, did actually participate in Iran’s war effort, bombing Gulf countries, bombing US interests in Iraq,” he told Al Jazeera.
“There are other areas, but this one is the strongest, most fortified, and the best weaponry is stored there.”
In July, after Iran-aligned militias attacked Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline, the United States and Saudi Arabia launched retaliatory strikes against PMF targets across Iraq, killing at least 20 personnel and drawing condemnation from Baghdad.
By establishing a presence in Jurf al-Sakhr, once the site of former President Saddam Hussein’s military-industrial complex, Baghdad signalled to the US that it was removing it as a potential target.
What next?
Zeidon Alkinani, founding director of the Doha-based Arab Perspectives Institute, said the deal over Jurf al-Sakhar was a positive step, especially as it was secured through negotiation and not armed confrontation.
“The remaining questions are how long this will take and what the armed groups will want in return,” he told Al Jazeera. Kataib Hezbollah may also retain its influence in the area through PMF units, with the process of deployment likely to take weeks to complete.
“How the next phases go will determine whether this becomes a real return of state authority or just a rearrangement of who controls the area,” Alkinani said.
Tallha Abdulrazaq, an Iraq expert and strategy and security consultant, said that the deal was compromised by the presence of militia and pro-militia personnel in the security contingent sent by Baghdad.
“Effectively, we’re changing Shia militias for Shia militias, but in uniform,” he said. “There has been no announcement about them being disarmed and their missile and drone manufacturing facilities set up with Iranian expertise being dismantled.”
Where did Iraq’s militias come from?
Iran-backed armed groups have become some of the most powerful actors in Iraq since the US-led invasion of Iraq overthrew President Saddam Hussein’s government in 2003.
Some of Iraq’s most influential militias – like Kataib Hezbollah and Asa’ib Ahl al-Haq – found their genesis in the resistance to US occupation, many with the alleged support of Iran.
Others were formed in response to the threat posed by ISIL after a fatwa was issued by leading Iraqi Shia cleric Ali al-Sistani, fighting under the banner of the PMF.
The PMF are a recognised component of Iraq’s security forces, granting the militias semiofficial status. However, some Iraqi militias, such as Kataib Hezbollah, still operate outside the framework of the state and have been accused of undermining the government’s legitimacy.
There have also been frequent accusations that militias operate corrupt patronage networks to finance themselves, and that their close relationship with Tehran has frustrated the Iraqi government’s efforts to govern the country.

https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.title: NFL’s Jaylen Harrell hospitalised and investigated for assault in car crash
https://www.aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11.text:
NFL’s Jaylen Harrell hospitalised and investigated for assault in car crash
Police in United States investigating whether Tennessee Titans defensive end assaulted a rideshare driver before collision.
Tennessee Titans defensive end Jaylen Harrell has been hospitalised in Florida after being involved as a passenger in a rideshare car in what the team have called a “serious” accident.
The Tampa Police Department said in a preliminary report that Harrell was riding about 8:45am (13:45 GMT) on Friday in the back seat when “he reportedly assaulted the driver while the vehicle was in motion.”
The driver of the Kia Sorento then swerved, struck a Toyota Highlander and collided with a utility pole, the police report said.
Police investigation under way
Harrell, 24, was thrown from the backseat, hit the windshield and lost consciousness, according to the police report.
Harrell was hospitalised with serious injuries while the rideshare driver, identified as a man in his mid-30s, sustained “minor injuries” and was treated at the scene, according to police. The driver of the Highlander was not injured, the police said.
Detectives are working through the timeline of events in investigating the crash, according to the preliminary report.
The Titans issued a statement on Saturday but did not disclose Harrell’s condition or the injuries he had suffered nor did they mention the assault accusation.
Harrell has not played this season after tearing an ACL in August during the preseason and being placed on the injured reserve list.
“We have been in constant communication with Jaylen’s family and are still working to gather more information,” the team said in its statement.
“At this time, Jaylen remains in the hospital and continues to receive care. We ask that Jaylen and his family’s privacy be respected at this time. We will provide an update when appropriate.”
The accident occurred in Tampa, Harrell’s hometown.
The Titans selected the University of Michigan alumnus in the seventh round of the 2024 NFL Draft. He has appeared in 34 games (two starts) and has 38 tackles, seven tackles for a loss and 4.5 sacks.

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/data-cente.title: Finlande : coup d’arrêt pour le data center de Google… après que la firme a rasé illégalement 400 000 arbres
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/data-cente.author: Lina Sankari
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/data-cente.text:
Sans attendre l’étude d’impact environnemental, Google a déboisé depuis mars 400 000 arbres des forêts finlandaises pour ériger ses centres de données. Le tollé a entraîné l’arrêt du projet en septembre 2026, mais a aussi mis en lumière la collusion du gouvernement de droite.
C’est l’histoire d’une affaire qui a mal tourné. Sur le papier, le placement le plus juteux de l’histoire de la Finlande : 13 milliards d’euros. Tout le monde est gagnant. Google d’abord, qui a vu dans la Finlande un pays de cocagne au climat suffisamment froid pour rafraîchir les quatre centres de données qu’il entendait ériger, au cœur d’espaces naturels à perte de vue. A priori, aucun humain à la ronde pour mener la fronde. Avec son électricité décarbonée à bas coût, le territoire avait même tout pour plaire.
Côté finlandais, on se réjouit également de la contrepartie : une rénovation de la centrale nucléaire de Loviisa, vouée à la fermeture d’ici à 2030 pour les deux unités qui la composent. Son exploitation peut désormais courir jusqu’en 2050....

https://www.humanite.fr/societe/sante/rh.title: Rhume, maux de gorge, toux : pourquoi il faut éviter certains médicaments en vente libre
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/sante/rh.author: Marc Hénée
https://www.humanite.fr/societe/sante/rh.text:
L’avancée des déserts médicaux, le manque d’accès aux soins et la baisse des prises en charge poussent près de neuf Français sur dix a avoir recours à l’automédication. Mais derrière la facilité d’accès aux médicaments sans ordonnance se cachent des risques parfois méconnus. Certains traitements courants sont même à proscrire.
Près de neuf Français sur dix pratiquent l’automédication. Le recours à des médicaments en vente libre permet au marché de l’automédication, dont la valeur est estimée à 3,7 milliards d’euros, d’enregistrer une croissance annuelle de 7,1 %. Pourtant, vente libre n’est pas synonyme d’innocuité, et le réflexe consistant à stopper net des symptômes n’est pas forcément une bonne idée.
