https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120405.title: Die Linke | Nahost in Brandenburg nicht weit weg
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120405.author: Andreas Fritsche
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120405.text:
- Berlin
- Die Linke
Nahost in Brandenburg nicht weit weg
Linke-Landesverband plant Gespräche über Israel und Palästina. Der Antisemitismusbeauftragte begrüßt sachliche Debatten, aber davon hält er wenig.
Staaten haben kein Existenzrecht, aber Menschen. Unter anderem diese Aussage von Vanessa Emde zu Israel und Gaza wurde als Provokation verstanden. Über einen Antrag, Emde aus der Linksfraktion im Berliner Abgeordnetenhaus auszuschließen, soll voraussichtlich diesen Dienstag abgestimmt werden.
Aber haben Parteien ein Existenzrecht? Die in der Geschichte der Bundesrepublik einst so bedeutsame FDP scheint ihres inzwischen verwirkt zu haben. In Brandenburg scheiterte Die Linke bei Landtagswahlen an der Fünf-Prozent-Hürde, in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern die CDU. Das eine war in Ostdeutschland unerhört, das andere insgesamt.
Mittlerweile winken Brandenburgs Sozialisten in den Meinungsumfragen zwar wieder neun Prozent. Dennoch stehen bis zur nächsten Landtagswahl 2029 noch eine lange Durststrecke und ein hartes Stück Arbeit vor ihnen. Wie will der Landesverband beweisen, dass er gebraucht wird?
Zumindest in einer Frage wird ein falscher Weg eingeschlagen, findet die Ex-Landtagsabgeordnete Andrea Johlige. Es sollen nämlich unter Einbeziehung jüdischer und palästinensischer Organisationen Nahostgespräche etabliert werden. »Ich halte es für wenig zielführend, ausgerechnet zu einem Thema, das geeignet ist, die Partei zu zerlegen und das gleichzeitig in der Brandenburger Bevölkerung kaum jemanden interessiert, einen aufwendigen Prozess zu starten und die wenigen Ressourcen der Partei dafür zu verschwenden«, sagt Johlige.
»Der Faschismus steht mit einem Bein schon in der Tür, in diesem Land findet gerade der größte Sozialabbau seit Bestehen der Bundesrepublik statt, die Menschen ächzen unter steigenden Lebenshaltungskosten und die Mieten explodieren, aber Die Linke in Brandenburg beschäftigt sich mit einem Konflikt am anderen Ende der Welt, den sie eh nicht lösen kann.« So was könne man machen, »wenn man zu viel Zeit und Kraft hat«, schimpft Johlige. Aber nicht in einer Zeit, in der der Landesverband am Boden liege und für die Brandenburger Bevölkerung in relevanten Fragen nicht mehr wahrnehmbar sei.
Der scheidende Landesgeschäftsführer Stefan Wollenberg bestätigt, dass es bei der hiesigen Linken anders als in Berlin keine großen Auseinandersetzungen zu Israel und Palästina gebe. Konsens sei die Beschlusslage der Bundespartei: »Unsere Solidarität gilt der Zivilbevölkerung.« Aber: »Ein Diskussionsangebot wollen wir dennoch entwickeln.«
Der neue Landesvorstand, der bei einem Parteitag am 28. und 29. November in Blankenfelde-Mahlow gewählt wird, soll dazu innerhalb von sechs Monaten ein Konzept entwickeln und auch schon erste Veranstaltungen durchführen. So sieht es ein Antrag vor, über den der Parteitag abzustimmen hat. Eingereicht wurde dieser Antrag von Stefan Wollenberg selbst und von Julia Wollenberg, die bisher noch stellvertretende Landesvorsitzende ist, außerdem von Sibylle Wallat-Schwarz, die sich als Vizelandesvorsitzende bewirbt – sowie von Patricia Usée und Rolf Niebel-Dietrich von der Landesarbeitsgemeinschaft Palästinasolidarität.
Diese Landesarbeitsgemeinschaft (LAG) ist in Brandenburg noch relativ neu. Sie hat sich im Frühjahr gegründet und ist seit einigen Monaten offiziell anerkannt. Knapp 50 der rund 5400 Genossen in Brandenburg haben sich bisher angeschlossen. Anders als auf Bundesebene und in Berlin gibt es hier keine israelsolidarische Arbeitsgemeinschaft Schalom. Da es aber darum gehe, miteinander ins Gespräch zu kommen, hofft Usée inständig, dass sich an den geplanten Diskussionen auch Parteimitglieder beteiligen, die der Bundesarbeitsgemeinschaft Schalom nahestehen. Sonst könnte sie ja einfach zu Veranstaltungen der Palästinasolidarität einladen, sagt sie. Man wolle aber diese Debatte bewusst »in die Mitte der Partei rücken« und »Platz für vertrauensvolle Gespräche schaffen«.
»Der Krieg im Nahen Osten zählt zu den großen Themen unserer Zeit«, sagt Usée. »Deshalb halte ich es für ein wichtiges Zeichen, dass wir uns nicht wegducken vor schwierigen Themen, vor Antisemitismusvorwürfen oder Diffamierungskampagnen.«
In der Begründung des Antrags für den Parteitag steht: »Wir gehen auch schwierige Auseinandersetzungen offensiv an. Dafür braucht es Räume für politische Verständigung, gegenseitiges Zuhören und fundierte Auseinandersetzung mit der Geschichte und Gegenwart Israels und Palästinas.« Ansatzpunkt sollen die bereits gestarteten Nahost-Fachgespräche der Bundespartei sein. Ein vergleichbares Format in Brandenburg könne dazu beitragen, »innerparteiliche Diskussionen zu versachlichen, Wissen zu vertiefen und eine gemeinsame Grundlage für unsere politische Arbeit zu schaffen«.
Brandenburgs Antisemitismusbeauftragter Andreas Büttner begrüßt »jeden ernsthaften Versuch, die Nahost-Debatte zu versachlichen und mit den jüdischen Gemeinden in Brandenburg ins Gespräch zu kommen«. Es sei richtig, dass der Antrag Gesprächsregeln vorsehe und es ablehne, Jüdinnen und Juden für das Handeln Israels in Haftung zu nehmen. Sinnvoll sei der Vorstoß in dieser Form trotzdem nicht, kritisiert Büttner. Denn der Landesverband solle auf einen Bundesparteitagsbeschluss verpflichtet werden, der Israel des Völkermords bezichtige und zu allem schweige, worauf es ankomme: zum Massaker vom 7. Oktober 2023, zur palästinensischen Terrororganisation Hamas, »zum Existenzrecht Israels und zum israelbezogenen Antisemitismus, auch in den eigenen Reihen«. Wer Antisemitismus nur noch in einer Aufzählung mit anderen Formen der Menschenfeindlichkeit nenne, bekämpfe ihn nicht, sondern lasse ihn darin verschwinden.
Dialog brauche eine Grundlage, sagt Büttner. Dazu gehöre eine klare Definition von Antisemitismus, die Zusammenarbeit mit den jüdischen Gemeinden und eine eindeutige Abgrenzung von Demonstrationen, auf denen Israel das Existenzrecht abgesprochen werde. »Solange das fehlt, ist der Antrag ein Verfahren ohne Haltung.« Andreas Büttner war von 2009 bis 2014 FDP-Landtagsabgeordneter und gehörte von 2019 bis 2024 der Linksfraktion an. 2015 ist er aus der FDP ausgetreten, 2026 aus der Linken.
In Deutschland leben schätzungsweise 200.000 Menschen mit palästinensischen Wurzeln, davon 40.000 in Berlin. Belastbare Zahlen für Brandenburg gibt es nicht. Bekannt ist jedoch, dass in Brandenburg gerade einmal 35.000 Muslime wohnen, ein Großteil von ihnen Syrer und Afghanen. Der Anteil der Palästinenser dürfte verschwindend gering sein. Die Zahl von Menschen jüdischen Glaubens beläuft sich auf rund 2000. Anders als in Berlin leben in Brandenburg fast keine Israelis und auch dort sind es nur ein paar Tausend. Dabei ist allerdings zu berücksichtigen, dass die Statistik sie bei doppelter Staatsbürgerschaft nur als Deutsche erfasst.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120404.title: Fußball | Austria Wien stellt beim 0:4 gegen Bayern Zuschauerrekord auf
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120404.author: René Hamann, Wien
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120404.text:
- Sport
- Fußball
Austria Wien stellt beim 0:4 gegen Bayern Zuschauerrekord auf
Champions League: 9124 Fans sehen die Niederlage gegen die deutschen Meisterinnen. München hofft weiter auf den Direkteinzug ins Viertelfinale.
Die entscheidende Szene im Champions-League-Spiel am Donnerstagabend zwischen den Gastgeberinnen Austria Wien und dem FC Bayern München spielte sich in der 52. Minute ab. Da verkündete der Stadionsprecher, wie viele Fans ins Franz-Horr-Stadion im Wiener Arbeiterbezirk Favoriten gekommen waren. 9124 – österreichischer Rekord im Frauenfußball, zumindest für ein Klubspiel. Bei Frauenländerspielen heißt das Stadion Viola Park. Als Österreich dort am 26. September 2023 gegen Frankreich spielte, kamen sogar 10 051 Fans.
Auf die Zahl 8500 hatte man hingearbeitet, gar hingefiebert, jetzt waren über 600 Menschen mehr gekommen. Jubel brandete auf. Ansonsten gab es für die Einheimischen an diesem novemberkalten, nieselverregneten Abend nicht viel zu jubeln: Die Bayern fertigten die Austria souverän mit 4:0 (2:0) ab; sie brauchten dafür nur eine eher durchschnittliche Leistung.
Aber die Bayern spielen auch bei den Frauen inzwischen in einer eigenen Liga. Sie werden in dieser Saison wohl ihren neunten Meisterinnentitel holen. Auch in der Champions League rechnen sich die Münchnerinnen diesmal Chancen auf den Titel aus – und das zu Recht. Vor dem letzten Spieltag liegen sie auf Platz drei. Die ersten vier der 18 Teams ziehen direkt ins Viertelfinale ein. Ob sich die Bayern den Umweg über die Playoffs sparen, entscheidet sich am 16. Dezember im Heimspiel gegen den FC Barcelona. Der Titelverteidiger führt auch diesmal die Tabelle an.
Für die wackere Austria, die Ende Mai ihren ersten Meistertitel feierte, ist das Abenteuer Europa nach der Klatsche am Donnerstag fast schon beendet. Einen mageren Punkt konnten die »Veilchen« im Heimspiel beim 1:1 gegen Inter Mailand in ihrer Debütsaison einheimsen: Immerhin, sagt man hier in Wien.
Österreichs Frauenfußball hat noch Rückstand auf die europäische Spitze; in der obersten Spielklasse, ebenso Bundesliga genannt, spielen nur zehn Teams, darunter zwei Spielgemeinschaften. Die allgemeine Entwicklung ist vergleichbar: Reine Frauenvereine werden sukzessive nach unten durchgereicht; oben spielen die Abteilungen der Profiklubs, die man von den Männern kennt. Also spielen neben der Austria auch der Linzer ASK, Sturm Graz und RB Salzburg oben mit; in diesem Jahr hat es endlich auch Rapid Wien, der große Erzrivale der Austria, ins Oberhaus geschafft. Fürs nächste Derby im April wird denn auch der nächste Zuschauerrekord angepeilt.
Die Offensive macht den Unterschied
Und klar, die besten Österreicherinnen spielen im Ausland, die meisten immer noch in der deutschen Bundesliga, auch beim FC Bayern standen drei von ihnen am Donnerstag im Kader. Aufgelaufen ist davon letztlich nur Sarah Zadrazil; die österreichischen »Starspielerinnen« Katharina Naschenweng und Barbara Dunst haben es gerade nicht leicht in München. Relativ zeitnahe Rückkehr nach Österreich nicht ausgeschlossen.
Die Tore für die Bayern schossen eh andere – die Offensive machte im Franz-Horr-Stadion den Unterschied. Austria versuchte es mit Kompaktheit und schnellem Umschaltspiel, doch ihre Konter wurden von der Bayern-Verteidigung gut abgelaufen. Und vorne wurde rasch ersichtlich, dass die Bayern das bessere Offensivspiel hatten und einfach zielstrebiger auftraten. Nach dem 1:0 durch Nationalspielerin Klara Bühl (27.) und dem 2:0 durch Pernille Harder in der Nachspielzeit der ersten Halbzeit übernahmen die Bayerinnen die Spielkontrolle; das Spiel war gelaufen. Mit Alara Şehitler (75.) und Sophie Proost (90.+2) war es jungen Ergänzungsspielerinnen vorbehalten, für den Endstand zu sorgen.
Es hätten auch mehr Tore für den FCB rausspringen können. Auf Wiener Seite freute man sich über die vollen Ränge. Ex-Bayern-Spielerin Carina Wenninger fasste es so zusammen: »Es war einfach richtig, richtig cool, auf dem Feld zu stehen.«
Abschied in Manchester
Die Austria darf sich jetzt noch auf ein Gastspiel beim englischen Meister Manchester City freuen. Danach gilt das Hauptaugenmerk der Titelverteidigung in der heimischen Liga – was angesichts der Konkurrenz schwer genug werden wird. In der Bundesliga liegt die Austria auf Rang drei, hat allerdings zwei Spiele weniger absolviert als Tabellenführer St. Pölten, der frühere Dauermeister.
Ansonsten stehen für das österreichische Nationalteam die schweren Playoff-Spiele gegen die Schweiz auf dem Programm. Das Ziel ist die WM im Sommer 2027 in Brasilien. Nach dem Hinspiel am 1. Dezember steht das Rückspiel am 5. Dezember an, wieder im Stadion der Austria. Der nächste Rekord kann also kommen.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120405.title: Gedenkstätte Ravensbrück | Das Männerlager des Frauen-KZ
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120405.author: Andreas Fritsche
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120405.text:
- Berlin
- Gedenkstätte Ravensbrück
Das Männerlager des Frauen-KZ
Online-Ausstellung der Gedenkstätte Ravensbrück schildert fast vergessene Schicksale von 30 Häftlingen.
Insgesamt 132.000 Frauen und Kinder litten in den Jahren 1939 bis 1945 im Konzentrationslager Ravensbrück, aber in einem angeschlossenen Männerlager gab es auch 20.000 männliche Häftlinge. Im September 1959 wurde die Mahn- und Gedenkstätte Ravensbrück eröffnet.
»Es ist nun ein Frauentreffen geworden und das Männerlager ist gänzlich in den Hintergrund geschoben worden«, bedauerte Józef Kwietniewski zwei Monate später im November 1959. Es sei ihm erklärlich, »denn Ravensbrück ist nun mal als ausgesprochenes Frauenlager bekannt«, bekannte Kwietniewski in einem Brief an Karl Gerber. »Wir müssen jedoch auch an unsere Kameraden denken. Es waren viele prächtige Kerle, und unsere Toten dürfen auch nicht vergessen werden.«
Der polnische Pfadfinder Kwietniewski und der deutsche Kommunist Gerber waren beide Häftlinge des Männerlagers. Kwietniewski arbeitete dort als Schreiber und nahm heimlich Nummernbücher mit auf den Todesmarsch. In die Bücher waren Namen und Häftlingsnummern eingetragen. Kwietniewski versuchte auch, die Häftlingskartei zu retten – als Beweismaterial für die von der SS begangenen Verbrechen. Doch diese Dokumente sind überwiegend vernichtet. Drei Nummernbücher aber, die sich heute in Warschau befinden und in Kopien in Ravensbrück, sind eine wichtige Quelle zur Geschichte des Männerlagers.
Unter anderem Auszüge aus diesen Nummernbüchern zeigt die neue Online-Ausstellung »Einige Baracken weiter«, mit der die Gedenkstätte Ravensbrück über das Männerlager informiert. »Mehr als 80 Jahre nach der Befreiung ist das Männerlager Ravensbrück in der öffentlichen Erinnerung noch immer wenig präsent«, weiß Gedenkstättenleiterin Andrea Genest. Mit dieser Ausstellung wolle man das ändern.
Vorgestellt werden die Schicksale von 30 Personen, darunter auch das von Józef Kwietniewski. Er starb 1969. In Bytom und Umgebung sind eine Straße, eine Schule und mehrere Pfadfindergruppen nach ihm benannt. In dieser Stadt in Polen hatte der Pädagoge Kwietniewski schon am polnischen Gymnasium unterrichtet, als die Kommune in Oberschlesien noch Beuthen hieß und zu Deutschland gehörte. Nach seiner Befreiung kehrte er dorthin zurück.
Józef Kwietniewski kam 1903 in Lünen bei Dortmund zur Welt. Sein Vater war wie damals so viele polnische Bergarbeiter ins Ruhrgebiet gezogen. Józef Kwietniewski leitete ab 1927 den Verband polnischer Pfadfinder in Deutschland. 1939 verhaftet, kam er zunächst ins KZ Buchenwald und dann nach Ravensbrück. Nach der Befreiung war Kwietniewski von 1947 bis 1950 stellvertretender Bürgermeister von Bytom und saß von 1961 bis 1969 als Abgeordneter der Polnischen Vereinigten Arbeiterpartei im Sejm, dem Parlament der Volksrepublik Polen.
Niemals im Männerlager von Ravensbrück war der sowjetische Jagdflieger Michail Dewjatajew. Im Juni 1944 bei Lwiw abgeschossen, versuchte er, aus dem Kriegsgefangenenlager zu flüchten, wurde erwischt und ins KZ Sachsenhausen gebracht. Von dort schaffte ihn die SS im Oktober 1944 in das dem KZ Ravensbrück zugeordnete Außenlager Karlshagen auf der Insel Usedom. Dort musste Dewjatajew auf dem Flugplatz Peenemünde arbeiten. Im Februar 1945 töteten er und neun weitere Häftlinge einen Wachmann und entkamen mit einem Bomber vom Typ Heinkel He111. Nach ihrer Notlandung hinter der Frontlinie geriet die Gruppe allerdings in den Verdacht, mit dem Feind kollaboriert zu haben. Dewjatajew saß bis September 1945 in Untersuchungshaft und wurde auch nach seiner Entlassung immer wieder verhört. Er lebte bis 1957 zurückgezogen, wurde erst dann rehabilitiert und als Held der Sowjetunion ausgezeichnet. Dewjatajew lebte noch bis 2002. Auch seinen Lebensweg schildert die Online-Ausstellung.
Männliche Häftlinge waren zunächst ab 1938 beim Bau des Frauen-KZ eingesetzt und später viele in der Rüstungsindustrie. Der 1932 geborene jüdische Junge Otto Kallus ist 1944 aus den Niederlanden nach Ravensbrück deportiert worden. Hier trennte ihn die SS im Oktober von seiner Mutter und seinen Geschwistern und steckte ihn ins Männerlager. »Einige Baracken weiter, sonst nichts. Aber es war eine ganz andere Welt«, erinnerte sich Kallus später. »Im alten Lager, wie schwer es auch war, hatten wir einen Ort, wo man sich um uns kümmerte, auch wenn man uns nicht helfen konnte.«
28.000 Männer, Frauen und Kinder haben Ravensbrück nicht überlebt. Aber Kallus starb erst 2018. Seine Worte »einige Baracken weiter« gab der neuen Ausstellung ihren Namen. Sie zeigt Fotos und Dokumente. 2027 soll eine Begleitpublikation erscheinen.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: ‘GO NAVY’ becomes ‘GO ARMY’ after overnight prank at Navy football stadium
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Guardian sport and agencies
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
The large letters that spell “GO NAVY” in the upper seating level of the Naval Academy’s football stadium were changed to “GO ARMY” in an elaborate overnight prank before the Midshipmen hosted No 24 Memphis on Saturday.
The stunt involved rearranging the blue and yellow seat backs at Navy-Marine Corps Memorial Stadium in Annapolis, Maryland, a task made considerably more complicated by the fact that the seats are bolted into place.
The letters were back to normal well before the noon kickoff. A Navy spokesperson said security footage showed uniformed Army cadets in the stadium between 1am and 4am.
According to the Athletic, stadium workers began restoring the original message at 6am, completing the job before the gates opened to spectators four hours later. Navy reportedly regarded the operation as a successful rivalry prank and did not expect any legal repercussions.
A member of ESPN’s TV broadcast team posted a picture on social media at 10.19am with the explanation: “Not AI ... 20 staff members have been working for the last couple of hours to fix the seat backs. Army Navy rivalry heating up already.”
The stunt was the latest chapter in a decades-long tradition of elaborate practical jokes between the two military academies, known as “spirit missions”, which have frequently involved the theft of each other’s mascots.
In 1991, Navy midshipmen made off with four of Army’s mule mascots, while Army cadets have repeatedly targeted Navy’s goat, Bill. A 2021 raid famously resulted in the wrong goat being taken. The academies signed an agreement in 1992 intended to put an end to mascot thefts, although the tradition has proved difficult to stamp out.
In 2022, Navy personnel flew three small aircraft over the West Point campus, scattering ping-pong balls bearing pro-Navy slogans along with leaflets.
The overnight incursion did little to spoil Navy’s Saturday. The Midshipmen upset Memphis 38-34, improving to 4-6 after entering the game with just three victories in nine outings.
Navy face Army on 12 December in East Rutherford, New Jersey.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Champion’s corner: KC Current win first NWSL Championship with 2-1 stunner over Spirit
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Pablo Iglesias Maurer at Audi Field
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
It took five years, 90 minutes and a goal for the ages, but the Kansas City Current have their first-ever NWSL championship.
Riding a wave of momentum created by a 54th-minute Olimpico from midfielder Vanessa DiBernardo, and capping it off with an all-important breakaway winner from Debinha, the Current silenced the partisan, sellout crowd at the heavily-favored Washington Spirit’s home ground with a 2-1 victory on Saturday.
The Spirit, heartbroken at the final whistle, have now lost three consecutive NWSL Championships.
“Obviously this one hates way worse than any of the other ones,” forward Trinity Rodman said afterward. “I don’t even think you have words in this moment — it is too fresh.”
DiBernardo’s goal was stunning, a driven, bent corner kick played to the far post that eluded Spirit goalkeeper Sandy MacIver, her defenders and Current forward Haley Hopkins, potentially DiBernardo’s intended target. The Spirit’s players and fans alike pleaded with center referee Joshua Encarnación, suggesting he examine the play on VAR for obstruction, as MacIver had potentially been screened. The review never came.
Whether played directly on goal intentionally or otherwise, the effort will go down as one of the most memorable in NWSL Championship history. At 34, DiBernardo becomes the oldest player in league history to score in a final, and was later named the match’s MVP.
“I’ve been to the game a few times and haven’t won, but this one just felt a little lighter,” said DiBernardo, who gave birth to Charlie, her first child, in January and took time off before returning to the Current in March. “I think just having Charlie, it just brings a different perspective on life. I knew the game was big and it was a big moment, but just kinda having her, just spending the day with her, it just felt really special.”
The game’s early phases were forgettable save for one incident which would go on to affect the remainder of the match: a bruising, high-speed tackle on Rodman by Current defender Laney Rouse in the fifth minute. The challenge sent Rodman flying and appeared to injure her left elbow; the Spirit forward, nearing tears, spent much of the first half in visible pain and seemingly never fully recovered. Rouse was not cautioned for the challenge.
“[It helped set the tone] in the sense that it hurt really bad, yes,” Rodman said. “As a team, you always want to put the first hit in. You’re taught to do that. Credit to them. I wish I was the one who put her on the ground. They did a really good job at setting the tone and controlling the first half.”
It was far from the game’s only physical moment. Neither team managed to settle into any meaningful rhythm during an opening 45 that felt at times more like a title fight than a title match. Encarnación, involved in his first NWSL final, called a very tight match and the near-constant stoppages in play were the defining characteristic of a sometimes ugly opening phase. In many ways it was not entirely his fault: the message-sending start from KC and the Spirit’s subsequent response often compelled him to act. The 19 combined first-half fouls between both sides were the most in any half of any NWSL title match in league history.
“It felt like we couldn’t play more than two minutes without a whistle,” Rodman said. “We were fouling, they were true calls for sure — but I think you lose control of the game really quickly that way ... It definitely messed with our rhythm a little bit.”
Paradoxically, though, the match was won with speed. Deep into second-half stoppage time, the Current found their eventual match-winner on a breakaway. After doggedly winning back possession after a Spirit free kick late on, Kansas City forward Debinha streaked upfield from just beyond the center stripe, looking off a wide-open Temwa Chawinga and rounding MacIver who looked on hopelessly as the Brazilian slotted it home.
Moments later, Rodman – somehow still in the match after not only the early challenge but a later high-speed collision with Current goalkeeper Lorena – pulled one back for the Spirit. Falling away from goal 10 yards out, Rodman got her head on the end of a Tara Rudd cross, placing it perfectly over Lorena’s outstretched arms and into the far-side netting. The ensuing five minutes – the game ended in the 102nd – were chaotic but the Spirit couldn’t quite find the equalizer.
After a slow start, the Current were well-managed by former Major League Soccer and US national team member Chris Armas. Armas was widely considered a controversial selection at the time of his appointment but proceeded to lead the club to their first championship in his first season, doing so by beating Gotham FC and now the Spirit, two sides picked by many as potential league-winners.
“I think from the front to the back we made it a point that every person on this team defends and if somebody is going to make a mistake the other person is going to have their back,” Current defender Izzy Rodriguez said. “We try and turn every 1v1 situation into a 1v2 for us, and I think that showed up today. We were winning our duels and second balls and those are things that win games.”
For the Spirit, the loss is devastating. They become the first American professional club – men’s or women’s – to lose three consecutive finals since the New England Revolution of Major League Soccer, who did so in the mid 2000s. In their five Championship appearances, the Spirit have won just one time, in 2021.

https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.title: Lionel Messi at center of red-card controversy as Inter Miami face early MLS playoff exit
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.author: Guardian Staff
https://www.theguardian.com/football/202.text:
Columbus Crew coach Laurent Courtois said Lionel Messi should have been sent off after throwing a ball into an opponent’s face as Inter Miami crashed to a 3-0 defeat in the MLS Cup playoffs on Saturday.
Messi’s frustration boiled over on the stroke of half-time when he hurled a throw-in into the face of Columbus forward Gonzalo Tapia, with 10-man Miami trailing 1-0 at the time.
Messi and Tapia were both shown yellow cards for the incident by referee Allen Chapman, but Courtois said afterwards that the Argentina superstar should have been given a red card.
“Everybody knows that he deserved more than a yellow card,” Courtois said at a post-game press conference when asked about the incident. “It’s just really sad.”
Chapman later defended his decision to show Messi only a yellow card.
“The force used was negligible and the offense did not reach the level of violent conduct,” Chapman told a pool reporter.
Miami had already been reduced to 10 men when the incident occurred and were trailing 1-0 after an early penalty from the Chile international Tapia.
The reigning MLS champions went on to suffer a 3-0 defeat, with Taha Habroune doubling Columbus’s lead shortly after half-time before Tapia added his second at Miami’s Nu Stadium.
The result means seventh-seeded Columbus, the 2023 champions, can eliminate Messi and Miami from the playoffs with a victory in Game 2 of the best-of-three series in Ohio next Friday.
“It was a game where nothing went right for us, and we effectively created their chances for them,” Miami coach Kily González said afterwards.
“We didn’t produce the great performance we had hoped for. Everything went wrong, but we have to learn from it because next time, if we don’t win, we’re out.
“There’s no better challenge for us as a team than this. It’s a test of character, and I know my team has that character.”
FC Dallas 3-0 Portland Timbers
Joaquín Valiente scored twice in the space of two minutes as FC Dallas beat the Portland Timbers 3-0 in the opening game of their best-of-three Western Conference first-round series.
The 25-year-old Uruguayan midfielder broke the deadlock in the 53rd minute, volleying home a rebound after Daniel Job’s shot was parried by Portland goalkeeper James Pantemis.
Valiente doubled the lead two minutes later, timing his run to meet another pass from Job before redirecting the ball between Pantemis’s legs.
Samuel Sarver completed the scoring in the fourth minute of stoppage time, finishing a cross from Logan Farrington on the counterattack.
Dallas goalkeeper Daniel de Sousa Britto, known simply as Daniel, made four saves, while Pantemis finished with five for Portland.
The Timbers also lost Ariel Lassiter to an apparent injury in the 33rd minute.
Second-seeded Dallas can advance to the Western Conference semi-finals with a victory in Portland next Saturday.
New England Revolution 2-0 Philadelphia Union
Teenager Peyton Miller scored one goal and helped create another as the New England Revolution beat the Philadelphia Union 2-0 in the opening game of their Eastern Conference first-round series.
The 19-year-old Miller became the fifth-youngest goalscorer in MLS Cup playoffs history when he volleyed home a cross from Jack Harrison in the 73rd minute, his effort bouncing off the crossbar and into the net.
New England had taken the lead in the 10th minute when Miller’s shot from the edge of the penalty area deflected off Philadelphia defender Nathan Harriel for an own goal.
Harrison, who came on as a substitute in the 62nd minute, was making his first appearance since 9 September after missing more than two months with a quadriceps injury.
Philadelphia nearly equalized in the 37th minute when Cavan Sullivan turned and fired a shot from outside the penalty area that struck the left post.
The Union fielded the youngest starting lineup in MLS Cup playoffs history, with an average age of 23 years and 207 days, breaking the record set by the New York Red Bulls in 2022.
Matt Turner made two saves to preserve the shutout for New England, who can advance to the Eastern Conference semi-finals with a victory in Philadelphia next Saturday.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/Why-T.title: Why is Turkey warning of an Israeli military operation in Syria?
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/Why-T.author: Reem Aouir
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/Why-T.text:
Why is Turkey warning of an Israeli military operation in Syria?
Turkey's foreign minister has warned that Israel could launch a military operation in Syria, accusing it of backing a faction within the country's Druze community in an attempt to provoke the Syrian army and create a pretext for intervention.
Hakan Fidan made the remarks in a televised interview with Turkish broadcaster TGRT Haber on Saturday, saying Ankara had raised the possibility with regional allies, as well as US and European officials.
"There is a scenario in which the Israeli army uses this as a pretext to launch an operation against Syria," Fidan said.
The Turkish foreign minister also alleged that Israel was supporting one of three major factions within Syria's Druze community, supplying it with weapons and ammunition by helicopter on a weekly basis.
“In southern Syria, as you know, there are Druze. These Druze are divided into three major tribes within Syria. Two of these are genuinely on the side of the Syrian government and are anti-Israel. But one of them is supported by Israel.”

Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
He claimed the faction was seeking to provoke Syrian government forces, potentially giving Israel justification to intervene militarily.
Omer Ozkizilcik, a non-resident senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, described Ankara’s warning as a precautionary move.
“Turkey's public warning aims at preventing Israel from doing something stupid in southern Syria before Israel actually does it,” he told Middle East Eye.
Fidan’s warning comes amid continued Israeli military activity in southern Syria and unresolved tensions between Damascus and Druze armed groups in the southern province of Sweida.
Sweida, the Druze-majority province in southern Syria, has been run as a de facto area under the spiritual leader Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, who has publicly aligned himself with Israel.
Most of its armed factions are grouped under the Sweida National Guard, a coalition of Druze militias backed by Israel and allied with al-Hijri.
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan says Israel is supplying a Druze faction in southern Syria with weapons and ammunition by helicopter every week, seeking to provoke the Syrian army. Fidan warned that Israel intends to use these provocations as a pretext to launch a military operation and push further into Syrian territory. He said two of Syria’s three major Druze tribal groups support the Syrian government and oppose Israel, while the third is backed by Tel Aviv.
— Middle East Eye (@MiddleEastEye) November 22, 2026
In July, al-Hijri suggested that Sweida could be integrated into Israel to preserve its autonomy.
Last month, The National reported, citing unnamed sources, that Israeli helicopters had dropped surveillance, radar and other equipment inside Sweida.
Flying over the Yarmouk River basin and villages in Deraa on the way to Sweida, sniper rifles and night-vision systems had also reached the National Guard.
A senior Syrian government official also told The Jerusalem Post in October that an Israeli helicopter had landed in Sweida and delivered significant quantities of weapons and ammunition.
Ozkizilcik also pointed to reports of Israeli helicopters arriving in Sweida and senior Israeli Druze military commanders visiting the province and meeting relatives, describing them as indications that tensions could be building.
"There is something potentially growing, but it's too early to clearly assess," he said.
'Destabilising neighbours'
Last week, the UN's deputy special envoy for Syria, Claudio Cordone, told the Security Council that Damascus had deployed additional forces to Sweida amid reports of continued Israeli support for local armed actors.
He said the province "remains in a tense security and political stalemate".
Fidan's remarks came days after he hosted his Syrian counterpart, Asaad al-Shaibani, in Ankara, where he called on Israel to halt its attacks in southern Syria and base its security arrangements on the 1974 Disengagement of Forces Agreement.
"The security of any state cannot be built upon the destabilisation of its neighbours," Fidan said at the joint press conference on Tuesday.
Ozkizilcik described Ankara's warning as a precautionary move intended to deter Israel from launching an operation in southern Syria.
"Turkey is trying to raise awareness and prevent it from happening," he said.
Ankara is a close ally of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa's government.
In August, Israel struck the Abu al-Duhur airbase, about 70km from the Turkish border, later saying Damascus had been preparing to let Turkey deploy radar and air-defence systems operated by Turkish personnel there.
US envoy Tom Barrack later said the strike had been intended to bait Ankara.
“If Israel launched a major military ground offensive in southern Syria, this would open Pandora’s box for all kinds of military escalation,” Ozkizilcik told MEE.
He said such an offensive could turn into a wider confrontation involving Turkey, even if Ankara was reluctant to deploy its own troops directly.
"I do not see a scenario in which Turkey would not be involved in a military escalation against Israel," he said.
He added that Ankara would likely support the Syrian army and coordinate with Arab allies.
“It would be a disaster for Israel militarily, and also politically and diplomatically,” he said.
Ozkizilcik said the risk of Israeli escalation in Syria should also be viewed against the backdrop of Benjamin Netanyahu’s domestic political uncertainty, arguing that the Israeli prime minister had previously used military action to improve his electoral prospects.
“If he cannot go to war again against Iran due to American obstacles, the most likely area for him to launch a new war might be Syria,” he said.
In April, Fidan also stated that Israel was holding back from some actions in Syria because of the war on Iran, but had not abandoned them.
"Later, when the time comes, it may want to act," he said at the time.
'Israel first' vs 'America first'
During the interview, Fidan also shed light on Gaza and accused Israel of blocking thousands of container homes that Turkey had prepared for Gaza.
He said Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan had ordered that the units, which Turkey used to house survivors of the 2023 earthquakes, be sent to the enclave.
"Israel is not allowing the containers to enter Gaza on the grounds that they are made of metal," Fidan said.
Israel claimed Hamas could use the metal to manufacture weapons, he added.
Fidan also described an ongoing "hidden struggle" in the United States between forces that put "Israel first" and those that put "America first".
He said US policy in the Middle East had for decades often served Israeli interests more than American ones, and that Netanyahu's policies had harmed Trump.
"Trump, who boasted of being a man who makes peace, seemed to have become a president who enters wars instead of achieving peace, and who fights on behalf of Israel," Fidan said.
He added that a growing current in the US was rejecting military intervention, and that public hostility towards Israel was rising.
Fidan also defended Turkey's role in the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan in August, which commits each member to treat an attack on one as an attack on all three.
He said Ankara was giving Riyadh the defence support it needed, but accused critics in Turkey of exaggerating the pact.
He dismissed warnings in Turkey that soldiers would die in Yemen's desert, saying that unlike a century ago, when Yemen was Ottoman territory, it was now an independent state.
He also noted that Turkey had sent troops to Afghanistan as part of Nato without facing similar criticism.
"Why was there no problem when it concerned Nato, while there is a problem when it concerns a regional defence alliance in an Islamic region?" he said.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Drone attacks kill four near Sudan’s capital, damage UN building
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Drone attacks kill four near Sudan’s capital, damage UN building
The Rapid Support Forces are blamed as drones reportedly hit United Nations and government buildings, as well as Khartoum’s airport.
Drone attacks blamed on Sudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) have killed four people in and around the capital, Khartoum, and damaged a United Nations building, according to local reports and UN officials.
The attacks early on Sunday struck residential areas as Sudanese air defences responded to drones reportedly targeting government buildings and Khartoum’s airport.
The strikes have raised fresh concerns about the growing danger to civilians and aid workers as Sudan‘s war increasingly relies on drones.
Explosions were heard across the capital between approximately 2am (00:00 GMT) and 4:30am (02:30 GMT), according to witnesses cited by the AFP news agency, as the army attempted to intercept the drones.
Al Jazeera’s AlMigdad Alruhaid reported from the city of Omdurman, across the Nile from Khartoum, that three people were killed and nine wounded when a drone struck a home in northern Omdurman.
A child was also killed in a separate attack south of the capital.
In the village of Jebel Aulia, about 45km (28 miles) south of Khartoum, a witness told AFP that a drone hit the home of a mosque official who calls worshippers to prayer. Residents searched the wreckage for trapped relatives.
The UN’s humanitarian coordinator in Sudan, Denise Brown, said on Sunday that one of its buildings had been damaged while staff were inside.
The UN’s humanitarian office, which coordinates emergency relief, condemned the danger to its personnel in a civilian neighbourhood, calling it “unacceptable”.
A Sudanese army source told AFP on Sunday that the drones had been launched from neighbouring Ethiopia’s Bahir Dar airport. The allegation could not be independently verified.
Ethiopia has previously denied Sudanese accusations that it allows the RSF to carry out attacks from its territory.
Sudan has also lodged complaints with the UN Security Council, the body responsible for international peace and security, and the African Union, a continental organisation, over alleged drone operations originating in Ethiopia.
Soldiers executed
Separately on Sunday, Sudan’s government accused RSF fighters of executing captured soldiers in southeastern Blue Nile state, near the Ethiopian border.
The government condemned the alleged killings as violations of international humanitarian law. The accusation has not been independently verified.
Both the RSF and the Sudanese army are relying more frequently on drones to hit enemy targets. More than 1,100 were killed by drones in the first half of this year, according to the United Nations.
The UN Children’s Fund (UNICEF) has said that drone attacks account for about two-thirds of children killed or injured in Sudan from the period of January to September.
The war in Sudan between the army and the RSF began in April 2023. It has led to one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, with 13 million people displaced and some regions facing famine.

This is an entry from: Live: IRGC claims attacks on two US bases in Bahrain
Israel: Eisenkot and Netanyahu parties meet again for unity government talks
22 November 2026 14:19 GMT
Representatives from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party and the party of his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar, met on Sunday to discuss forming a unity government, Haaretz is reporting.
The meeting follows earlier talks last Sunday after nearly a month of deadlock in the Israeli Knesset since October's election, which saw no party gain an overall majority. Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot have so far failed to negotiate a viable coalition government alongside smaller parties.
Absent from Sunday's meeting were representatives of Naftali Bennett's Together party, which received the third-largest vote share and attended the previous round of talks.

https://www.aljazeera.com/video/featured.title: The Drugs Don’t Work
https://www.aljazeera.com/video/featured.text:
Featured Documentaries
The Drugs Don’t Work
A look at how antibiotic overuse could fuel superbugs, killing eight million people annually by 2050.
The challenges posed by antimicrobial resistance show where its impact is most acutely and tragically manifested: infant mortality in the developing world, specifically in sub-Saharan Africa. This film shows what these bland statistics mean in real terms to the health workers and families affected, following them as they struggle to fight this battle with low-tech solutions.
The Drugs Don’t Work follows the battle to the United Kingdom and examines how and why penicillin, the world’s most successful antibiotic, was invented. It then examines why pharmaceutical companies like GlaxoSmithKline are struggling to produce novel solutions to the problem of antimicrobial resistance (AMR).
The film also explores the cutting edge of academic research at British universities and hospitals supported by the power of the UK-based tech company DeepMind, and features academics and advocates who are devoting their lives to solving the problem. Returning to Africa, it shows how local innovation and the tools offered by the developed world are now saving lives and contributing to the global battle against AMR – an effort that could ultimately save millions of lives.

Saudi Arabia, Qatar join condemnation of Iran attack on Bahrain
Saudi Arabia and Qatar have joined the UAE in condemning Iran's attack on Bahrain earlier on Sunday.
In a statement posted on X, Qatar's foreign ministry expressed its "categorical rejection of attacks on economic facilities, civilian objects and civilians, and affirms that the continuation of these attacks represents a dangerous escalation that threatens the region’s security and stability”.
Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, said it "affirms its full solidarity with Bahrain in all measures it takes to protect its security and stability", accusing Tehran of "undermining regional security and stability”.
Iran attacked US military bases in both Qatar and Saudi Arabia, along with Bahrain, Kuwait, the UAE, Oman, Iraq and Jordan throughout the first months of the war, which began in late February. But such attacks have lulled since April amid ceasefire negotiations between Washington and Tehran.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Zelenskyy urges US to release Patriot missiles as Russia kills 3 in Ukraine
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Zelenskyy urges US to release Patriot missiles as Russia kills 3 in Ukraine
A Russian drone attack kills at least two people near Kyiv as Russian shelling kills one in Zaporizhzhia.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has urged the United States to approve the delivery of Patriot interceptor missiles after a week of Russian attacks across 20 regions of the country with the latest ones killing three near Kyiv and in Zaporizhzhia.
In a post on Telegram on Sunday, Zelenskyy said Russia launched about 2,700 attack drones, nearly 1,460 guided aerial bombs and 165 missiles over the past week. A significant share of the missiles were ballistic, he said, including some supplied by North Korea.
“Against this backdrop, it is particularly difficult to understand the delays in the delivery of antiballistic systems to Ukraine,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine is short of US-made Patriot interceptors, which can shoot down ballistic missiles.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine’s partners had already paid for the missiles through a NATO-coordinated programme that funds purchases of US weapons for Kyiv. However, their delivery is still awaiting Washington’s approval.
Rescuers search rubble near Kyiv
One of the latest Russian attacks hit a five-storey apartment building early on Sunday in the village of Dymer, north of Kyiv, causing part of it to collapse.
Zelenskyy initially said nine people had been evacuated and 14 were unaccounted for.
Rescuers later recovered two bodies as emergency crews searched for 11 people, including two children, who were missing, according to Russia’s Interfax news agency, citing Radio Liberty.
Mykhailo Semikin, the acting head of the Zaporizhia regional military administration, also said a man was killed in Russian shelling in the city of Zaporizhzhia.
Moscow says it hits cargo ship and power facilities
Also on Sunday, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said its forces struck a cargo ship northeast of Ukraine’s Black Sea port city of Odesa overnight.
The ministry said Russian drones struck the Pravoberezhna electricity facility in Zaporizhzhia, which it said supplied power to Ukrainian arms manufacturers. It reported further strikes on an oil refinery, electrical substations and a data centre operated by MKM Telecom.
In its battlefield update, the ministry claimed Russian forces had taken control of the Ukrainian village of Sosnovyi Bir in the northeastern Kharkiv region and destroyed a launcher for Ukraine’s Neptune coastal missile system.
It also said it struck energy and transport facilities it described as serving Ukraine’s military. The Russian claims could not be independently verified.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.title: Cop31 ends in failure as countries reject climate deal over fossil fuels
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Daniel Tester
https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.text:
Cop31 ends in failure as countries reject climate deal over fossil fuels
The United Nations climate summit in Turkey became the longest-ever UN climate conference on Sunday as negotiations over a final agreement descended into deadlock, with the European Union and several other countries formally rejecting the proposed text.
The talks in Antalya, known as Cop31, continued more than 44 hours beyond their scheduled Friday conclusion, surpassing the previous record set by Cop25 in Madrid in 2019.
The latest draft, presented by the Turkish and Australian presidencies in an attempt to bridge divisions between countries, failed to secure consensus over its omission of explicit references to fossil fuels and disagreements over climate finance.
At the closing plenary, Cop31 President Murat Kurum acknowledged that countries had failed to agree on the proposed document.
“We have done our utmost. Ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” Kurum said.
This is a developing story. We'll bring more updates shortly.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Why Bangladesh descended into violence ahead of Hasina’s planned return
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Why Bangladesh descended into violence ahead of Hasina’s planned return
Supporters of the ousted PM, who lives in self-imposed exile in India, have protested against rejection of her return.
Bangladesh has deployed paramilitary troops to help contain a wave of violence that erupted after supporters of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina staged protests against the government’s rejection of the ousted leader’s planned return to the country.
At least four people have been killed and police stations, banks and even the ancestral home of the former interim leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner, Muhammad Yunus, have been attacked in a week of violence.
Violence erupted after supporters of Hasina’s now-banned Awami League party took to the streets as part of weeklong protests that overlapped with the anniversary of the former leader’s death sentence last year. Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal sentenced Hasina to death in absentia for crimes against humanity related to the 2024 student-led protests.
Earlier this month, Hasina requested a new passport and identity card to allow her to return to Bangladesh. She has been living in self-imposed exile in India after fleeing the country in the wake of the July 2024 student-led uprising.
But the Bangladesh government, led by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, says she is a convicted criminal, and she can only return under the extradition treaty with India.
Rahman has blamed India for the unrest. “It is not only that; they have not looked at the interests of Bangladesh and its people. At the same time, the country across the border, where they have fled to, is their master… To satisfy those masters, they have again started conspiring against Bangladesh and its people,” Rahman said in parliament on Friday.
So why does Hasina still want to return to the country, and are the recent protests spontaneous or orchestrated?
Here’s what we know:
What do we know about the deadly protests?
Since mid-November, arson attacks and violence have been reported across 28 districts of Bangladesh.
At least four people have been killed in the political violence since November 14, including three political activists and a bus worker who died when his vehicle was torched, according to local media reports.
Two men from the ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) were killed in the Narail district, according to the AFP news agency. In retaliation, BNP supporters set ablaze more than a dozen homes belonging to Awami League supporters in the district.
A Narail resident, who asked not to be identified for fear of reprisals, said as many as 50 houses had been damaged in the district.
“We are terrified by the clashes,” he told AFP. “We have asked our women and children to stay inside unless it is absolutely necessary.”
Late Wednesday, police said the ancestral home of Yunus was set on fire in the port city of Chittagong. It was not immediately clear who was behind the blaze.
“Criminals set fire to the eastern side of the house. The area was being used as a storeroom,” Chittagong Metropolitan Police spokesman Aminur Rashid said, adding there were no casualties.
Yunus, who was targeted by Hasina during her term in power, has faced hostility from her supporters. Grameen Bank, set up by Yunus, said 22 of its branches were subject to arson attacks.
State news agency BSS reported that 90 additional platoons of the paramilitary Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) had been deployed nationwide.
National police chief Md Ali Hossain Fakir told BSS that security had been restored in Gopalganj, Hasina’s hometown and a longstanding stronghold of her party.
“I urge the peace-loving people of this area to stand against those involved in sabotage and disorder,” he added.
Khandakar Tahmid Rejwan, lecturer of global studies and governance at the Independent University, Bangladesh (IUB) and contributing analyst at the United States defence think tank Jamestown Foundation, told Al Jazeera that the protests do not appear to be entirely spontaneous in nature.
“If they were genuinely organic and spontaneous, one would arguably expect to see broader public mobilisation and participation across different parts of the country. Instead, what we are witnessing is a concentration of protest activity in areas such as Gopalganj, Faridpur, and Madaripur, which have traditionally served as strongholds of the Awami League’s support base,” he said.
He noted that while sporadic protests and demonstrations have also been reported in other parts of the country, their scale and geographical spread, at least so far, suggest localised unrest rather than a nationwide mobilisation.
“Although these incidents are concerning from the perspective of public order and political stability, the available pattern of mobilisation does not, at this stage, indicate a level of nationwide momentum that could fundamentally challenge the incumbent government’s position,” he added.
What triggered the violence?
The recent protests began soon after the government rejected Hasina’s request for her passport and identity card on November 9. Hasina served as prime minister from 1996 to 2001, and again from 2009 to 2024, but her nearly 15 years of iron-fist rule have been slammed by human rights organisations.
She was sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against humanity over her deadly crackdown on the student-led protests in 2024. As many as 1,400 people may have been killed in the violence, according to United Nations estimates.
Hasina has, however, denied these charges and told the Reuters news agency on November 9 that she intended to return to Bangladesh and surrender before a court. Her aides added the date would be announced once various formalities were completed.
But her request has been denied by the current government.
“Bangladesh does not give passports to terrorists who kill thousands of people and flee. It will work under the current extradition arrangements with India to pursue and get the terrorist Hasina handed over,” State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir said earlier this month.
The Bangladeshi prosecutor Md Aminul Islam, who secured the death sentence for Hasina at the Dhaka-based International Crimes Tribunal, said she will be executed if she returns home.
“Sheikh Hasina has no option but to face the execution of the verdict,” Islam told reporters.
Protesters have also been calling for the ban on Hasina’s party to be lifted and detained leaders and supporters of the party to be released from prison.
Why does Hasina want to return to Bangladesh?
Hasina still enjoys support among a section of the population, while many others want to see her hanged.
Her return could also worsen political tensions as Prime Minister Rahman’s government tries to restore stability two years on from the 2024 uprising.
But her game plan behind why she wants to return is unclear.
Some analysts have questioned whether Hasina genuinely intends to return to face the law.
Others have questioned whether she is using the promise to revive her political fortunes from self-imposed exile in India. New Delhi, her close ally for decades, has sheltered her since she fled Dhaka in August 2024. But her continued presence has become a point of contention between the two countries.
Rejwan believes there are several interconnected factors behind Hasina’s renewed emphasis on returning to Bangladesh.
“First, there is the domestic political context. It has been nearly 10 months since the incumbent government assumed power, and during this period, it has faced a number of challenges, including inflationary pressures, economic stagnation and a fuel crisis. While these difficulties are not entirely homegrown and are, to a considerable extent, linked to broader geopolitical and global economic developments, it remains difficult to communicate these complexities to the general public. Their everyday consequences inevitably affect public morale and confidence in the government,” he said.
“Secondly, there is the ongoing political debate surrounding whether the Awami League should remain proscribed or be allowed to resume its political activities,” he added.
He noted that several international actors and civil society voices have advocated lifting the temporary ban and allowing the party to return to mainstream political activities, potentially following the prosecution and sentencing of those responsible for the atrocities committed during the July 2024 uprising.
“Thirdly, there is India’s role, which cannot be entirely overlooked. Sheikh Hasina and several Awami League leaders and activists who fled Bangladesh following the collapse of her government in August 2024 have reportedly continued to receive varying degrees of support from India. There have also been discussions and speculation about whether New Delhi has been exploring possibilities for negotiating her safe return to Bangladesh, potentially under arrangements that would ensure her security, including protection under the custody of the Bangladesh Army,” he added.
Mushfiqul Fazal Ansarey, a senior Bangladeshi diplomat, said that Hasina does not intend to return to face her sentence. “In my assessment, her talk of a comeback is intended to rally supporters and destabilise Bangladesh,” he told Al Jazeera.
The violence, Ansarey said, has extended abroad, with Awami League supporters reportedly attacking Nahid Islam’s entourage in Romford, east London. Islam, who was part of the student-led uprising, is a member of parliament.
“Arson, killings and intimidation cannot be presented as political protest. The neighbouring country should ensure that its territory is not used to organise or incite violence against Bangladesh.”
What are the political ramifications of the Awami League protests?
Besides deploying police forces to contain the protests, in an effort to build unity, Prime Minister Rahman has held talks with Shafiqur Rahman, the leader of the opposition party Jamaat-e-Islami.
The Jamaat’s Secretary-General Mia Golam Porwar told the Bangladeshi newspaper The Daily Star that the two leaders viewed the meeting positively and hoped it would strengthen democracy in the country.
“If this initiative is taken with the intention of moving forward with everyone on board, it will be good. We want to view it positively. If the initiative genuinely has good intentions, we want it to succeed,” he said on Sunday.
Rejwan, from the Independent University of Bangladesh, said that from the Awami League’s perspective, one of the most unfavourable political developments would be the possible convergence of political interests between the BNP and Jamaat-e-Islami, particularly if their existing political differences were set aside in the interest of preventing the Awami League from regaining political ground.
“Beyond the Awami League, Jamaat-e-Islami remains one of the few political organisations in Bangladesh with an established grassroots organisational structure, a relatively disciplined cadre base, and extensive networks of political mobilisation. This gives the party a significant organisational capacity to counter the Awami League’s own entrenched political networks and grassroots mobilisation,” he said.
He highlighted that another crucial variable is the extent of residual popular support for the Awami League.
“If Sheikh Hasina were to return to Bangladesh, how would the politically dormant but ideologically sympathetic sections of the population respond? Would her return reactivate sections of the Awami League’s grassroots support base, or would the party’s political isolation and organisational setbacks limit its ability to mobilise them?” he said.
“Ultimately, the sustainability and effectiveness of any BNP–Jamaat political understanding aimed at containing the Awami League’s political resurgence would depend not merely on elite-level negotiations but also on the ability of both parties to manage their competing political interests and respond to the evolving sentiments of the wider electorate,” he said.

'Deserved to fail': Cop31 ends in failure as countries reject deal over fossil fuels
The Cop31 climate summit in Turkey ended without agreement after the European Union and several countries rejected a proposed deal that failed to explicitly address fossil fuels and provide stronger financial support to developing nations.
Cop31 President Murat Kurum said that the negotiations had failed to secure consensus, adding that the proposed decisions had not been adopted.
"It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted," he told the closing plenary.
"We have done our utmost. Ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum such as a 'take it or leave it' demand."
The European Union, the Marshall Islands, Panama, Norway and Vanuatu were among those that formally objected to the proposed Antalya Pact.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
The talks had been scheduled to end on Friday but continued until Sunday, as negotiators tried to resolve disagreements over the proposed agreement.
The breakdown followed more than two weeks of negotiations, making the summit the longest in the history of the UN climate conference process.
Ireland's Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, formally rejected the Antalya Pact, saying it failed to meet the urgency of the climate crisis.
"We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science, and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required… that does not even mention fossil fuels," he said.
The dispute centred on the omission of an explicit reference to transitioning away from coal, oil and gas, despite the commitment made by countries at Cop28 in Dubai in 2023.
The latest draft referred to earlier decisions, including the Dubai agreement, but did not explicitly mention fossil fuels.
It also retained provisions on carbon capture and storage, a technology promoted by some oil-producing countries but criticised by environmental groups as a potential means of prolonging fossil fuel production.
'Moves us backwards'
The United Kingdom criticised the proposed agreement. Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said the summit had failed to build the consensus required for meaningful climate action.
"This Cop sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with ever more urgency to address it.
"The moment required bold ambition, and we have been working tirelessly to try to build consensus. It is immensely disappointing we have been unable to do so," she said.
The UK described the text as a setback, saying: "It moves us backwards; it is the lowest common denominator when it should have been uniting us in action."
Panama also formally rejected the agreement, saying the text failed to address its demands.
"What we cannot accept is that we are asked to drop our stance because the atmosphere does not negotiate, the planet does not negotiate," the representative said.
The Republic of the Marshall Islands also rejected the proposed agreement, warning that it threatened the security of vulnerable island nations.
"We will not be forced to accept false solutions. We will not accept an outcome that undermines our security," its representative said.
"Our needs are so great, but the gap keeps growing. People are dying, the seas are rising."
Norway also joined the objections, while Germany had earlier indicated that it would not accept the draft in its existing form.
'Deserved to fail'
Harjeet Singh, strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative, told Middle East Eye that the proposed agreement had failed on four critical fronts: fossil fuels, climate finance, adaptation and loss and damage.
Singh said a reference to the Cop28 outcome was insufficient, arguing that the Dubai agreement had gone further by calling for a transition away from fossil fuels.
“A mere reference to the Cop28 outcome was never going to be enough. Three years ago in Dubai, we got a far better text that called for a transition away from fossil fuels. This rejection shows the world will not accept going backwards," he said.
Singh, who is a global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign, accused wealthy countries of resisting efforts to establish measurable financial commitments under the Paris Agreement.
“Rich countries were reminded of the Paris Agreement provision that says they must pay, but they forced the deletion of every number that would show whether they have.
"They even erased the word 'debt' from a finance decision, while countries across Asia and Africa spend more on debt repayments than on protecting their people. That is why this text deserved to fail,” he told MEE.
Singh said the proposed outcome also failed to provide adequate support for adaptation, which he described as a matter of survival for vulnerable communities.
“The Adaptation Fund, which delivers money directly to frontline communities, raised barely $50m here against a target of $300m a year. The text's response was to 'encourage contributions', with no amount, no deadline and no country named," he said.
"With the $120bn figure deleted and the tripling pathway pushed to 2027, the message to the world's most vulnerable was clear: you're on your own."

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
How El Chapo Isidro, alleged Mexican cartel leader, was captured
Operation in Sinaloa state resulted in deadly heavy battles between members of security forces and gunmen.
After weeks of careful and detailed planning, Mexican special forces have captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as El Chapo Isidro, a notorious alleged cartel leader on the FBI’s 10 most-wanted list.
Authorities said on Saturday Meza Flores was arrested at a compound in Guasave, in the northwestern state of Sinaloa, following a stealth operation that left four members of the security forces and seven suspected gunmen dead.
The capture highlighted the “unwavering determination to curb organised crime activities to protect and safeguard the public’s peace and security”, the Mexican Secretariat of National Defence said in a statement.
Here’s what we know about how the operation went down:
Who is Meza Flores?
Meza Flores, 44, is believed to be the leader of the Los Mazatlecos gang, based in Guasave, an agricultural area in Sinaloa.
The group was formerly part of the now-extinct Beltran Leyva Cartel but has operated independently since 2013. Meza Flores had long been subject to arrest in Mexico on charges of organised crime.
He also faces criminal charges in the United States, which had offered a reward of up to $5m for information leading to his capture.
If he is convicted, he could face the death penalty or life in prison.
How did security forces plan the raid?
The operation to capture Meza Flores took place on Friday, but preparations for it began way before.
The Mexican military said the raid, which came after two previous attempts to detain him, was conducted “following coordination” with US intelligence in the “framework of bilateral cooperation”.
Mexico’s Special Forces of the National Guard, the National Army and US intelligence agencies all collaborated on the massive raid operation, according to authorities.
Mexican officials said they had given US intelligence agencies information to locate Meza Flores weeks ahead.
US officials flew reconnaissance drones over the area where he was believed to be holed up, according to The New York Times. Using live video information from the drones, Mexican military analysts were then able to determine the cartel boss’s daily routines.
They also intercepted his communications, including text messages with his mother, wife and sister, to confirm events and meetings he planned to attend, The Times reported.
On Friday, Meza Flores was tracked to a home in Guasave, thanks to phone and radio communications, as well as drone surveillance. Mexican special forces used his voice, build and how he walked to confirm it was him before moving in.
What happened at the raid?
Prior to targeting the home in Guasave, officials first planned two other diversions in Los Mochis, another city in Sinaloa’s northwest.
As the raids distracted cartel members who exchanged fire with the security forces, more than two dozen undercover soldiers from the Joint Special Force elite army unit stormed Meza Flores’s location, The Times reported. They were covered by a ring of dozens of other soldiers, as well as two Mexican Black Hawk helicopters that engaged cartel members positioned in armoured, mounted pick-up trucks in a firefight.
The operation sparked panic across the surrounding area, with gunfire forcing the suspension of a professional baseball game in Guasave, according to local media. Television footage showed players running off the field as loud bangs were heard.
The heavy gun battles between security forces and cartel members left the streets of Guasave smouldering with burned-out cars and destroyed structures.
How was the cartel leader transported?
After the special forces managed to subdue Meza Flores, the tricky issue of exiting Guasave and Sinaloa remained.
That’s where another distraction measure kicked in: two helicopters hovered over the house and then headed in the direction of Los Mochis, creating the impression that Meza Flores was being transported there.
A third stayed back and continued to engage the gunmen.
Amid the chaos, the special forces bundled Meza Flores into an armoured vehicle and drove out of Guasave.
Footage released on social media showed special forces leading a cuffed Meza Flores onto a military transport plane. Early on Saturday morning, the alleged cartel boss arrived in Mexico City, the Mexican defence ministry said in a statement.
In addition to the seven suspected gunmen killed, another eight suspected to be cartel members were arrested, the ministry said, including a man identified as Meza Flores’s cousin and second in command. Another high-ranking member of the gang was identified as the cartel leader’s brother-in-law and the group’s financial operative.
Several weapons and munitions were also seized.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/live-blog/.author: Daniel Tester

'Jewish terrorism in every sense': Eisenkot blames Smotrich and Ben Gvir for settler attacks
Israeli politician Gadi Eisenkot has condemned a series of arson attacks by settlers in the occupied West Bank as "Jewish terrorism", accusing far-right ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben Gvir of fuelling violence against Palestinians.
Settlers attacked the villages of Deir al-Sudan, Deir Abu Mashal and Kafr Malik, near Ramallah, overnight between Saturday and Sunday, setting fire to Palestinian-owned vehicles and spraying racist graffiti on homes, according to Palestinian media reports.
Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, described the attacks as "Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word" and called on the government and security establishment to take tougher action against violent settlers.
"The acts of sabotage carried out by extremist groups setting fire to vehicles and homes undermine regional stability, endanger lives and seriously harm Israel's national security and foreign relations," he wrote on X.
Eisenkot was tasked with forming Israel's next government on 8 November by President Isaac Herzog.
He accused National Security Minister Ben Gvir and Finance Minister Smotrich of bringing the West Bank "to the brink of unchecked anarchy".
"This reality is not inevitable," he said, describing it as the consequence of poor leadership.
He said authorities should use all available measures, including administrative detention and targeted operations by the Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, to stop the perpetrators.

'Jewish terrorism in every sense': Eisenkot blames Smotrich and Ben Gvir for settler attacks
Israeli politician Gadi Eisenkot has condemned a series of arson attacks by settlers in the occupied West Bank as "Jewish terrorism", accusing far-right ministers Bezalel Smotrich and Itamar Ben Gvir of fuelling violence against Palestinians.
Settlers attacked the villages of Deir al-Sudan, Deir Abu Mashal and Kafr Malik, near Ramallah, overnight between Saturday and Sunday, setting fire to Palestinian-owned vehicles and spraying racist graffiti on homes, according to Palestinian media reports.
Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, described the attacks as "Jewish terrorism in every sense of the word" and called on the government and security establishment to take tougher action against violent settlers.
"The acts of sabotage carried out by extremist groups setting fire to vehicles and homes undermine regional stability, endanger lives and seriously harm Israel's national security and foreign relations," he wrote on X.
Eisenkot was tasked with forming Israel's next government on 8 November by President Isaac Herzog.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
He accused National Security Minister Ben Gvir and Finance Minister Smotrich of bringing the West Bank "to the brink of unchecked anarchy".
"This reality is not inevitable," he said, describing it as the consequence of poor leadership.
He said authorities should use all available measures, including administrative detention and targeted operations by the Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, to stop the perpetrators.
Yair Lapid, another opposition politician, also condemned the attacks, describing them as "terrorism" resulting from government negligence.
"Jewish terrorism is the product of criminal negligence on the part of the Israeli government," Lapid said.
"By remaining silent, government ministers are deliberately encouraging these pogroms," he added.
"When we form a government, we will tackle this terrorism and restore governance, law and order."
The Palestinian news agency Wafa reported that 12 vehicles were set on fire across the three Palestinian villages.
Israeli police said they had opened investigations into arson, vandalism and property damage.
Settler violence displacing Palestinians
The latest attacks come amid a sustained escalation in settler violence across the occupied West Bank, where Palestinian communities have faced assaults, arson, property destruction, restrictions on access to farmland and the expansion of settlement outposts.
The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (Ocha) recorded 40 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage across 30 Palestinian communities between 10 and 16 November.
The attacks left 38 Palestinians injured and displaced 68 people, including 31 children.
Ocha also recorded 428 settler attacks resulting in casualties or property damage during the 2026 olive harvest season between 1 September and 16 November.
The incidents have disrupted farmers' access to their land and damaged agricultural property and livelihoods.
In October, the UN agency recorded 467 settler attacks, the highest monthly figure since it began documenting such incidents in 2006.
Ocha said settler violence and access restrictions had displaced about 6,800 Palestinians, including more than 3,200 children, across 137 communities since January 2023.
In 2026 alone, 2,894 Palestinians had been displaced by such violence. The attacks have also been linked to the expansion of settlement outposts and the gradual loss of Palestinian access to land.
According to Israeli settlement watchdog Peace Now, settlers had taken control of more than 100,000 dunams (10,000 hectares) of land in Areas A and B, with violence and threats used to restrict Palestinian access and, in some cases, pressure families to leave their homes.
