https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Kim Hew-Low
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
My Journey Through San Francisco’s Internet Archive
To most people, the archive is just a portal on their computer. But it’s also a physical space made by a person who has never cared more about the preservation of digital history.
I was in San Francisco late this summer, against my will. My husband has family there, and when we visit, we stay at the townhouse in Inner Richmond where his mother, her mother, and her mother before her all grew up. His great-great-grandmother, Carolina, sailed from Genoa to New York in early 1889, and, for whatever reason, continued west—perhaps to farm or to reunite with relatives, though the family only speculates, since the details went unrecorded.
But evidence of her existence is sprinkled all over the townhouse. I am told by my mother-in-law that the interior looks the same as always: the parquet floors and pink-tiled bathroom are a portal to Carolina’s time. There is a metal chute in the kitchen for disposing of gas-stove matches, and a fold-out booth in the hall where you can sit to make telephone calls. We use a plastic lighter these days, and the landline is disconnected, but my mother-in-law ensures that the chute and the booth remain. She lives in Michigan now and becomes more wistful in San Francisco, as if everything there is asking her to remember a time before. In the morning, she asks us over coffee if we heard the foghorns last night: As a child, she had kept her windows open to hear them boom out as she fell asleep.
I love staying there, in that apartment. But I do not love staying in that city. People say that, because I’m Australian, I should like the eucalyptus and the swell from the Pacific. But there are the Teslas and the Waymos and the coolers with blinking faces delivering food that was probably 3D-printed in an automated ghost kitchen. I saw a billboard walking down Geary for a start-up that said “THAT’S SO AGENTIC.” Their CEO had recently posted a selfie with Benjamin Netanyahu on X, while opining about how artificial intelligence is enhancing Israel’s defense forces.
Near the billboard were clusters of people milling about the Safeway parking lot, people in vans with the engines running, and people counting change at the Chinese butcher. I wondered what they thought about being “agentic,” or about self-driving cars and coolers with pixelated heart eyes. I wondered, in other words, how a handful of nerds had terraformed the city, and what their despotic ambitions mean for everyone else. I can ignore that thinking more easily once I am out of San Francisco; it helps to live in a place like Brooklyn, and to work with people who are obsessed with books—people who, I imagine, would also treasure match chutes and telephone booths.
And yet: Just the other day I was chatting with my neighbor, who happened to share that they worked as a programmer at an AI start-up called “Writer.” I did not care to reciprocate what I do for work in response. As we spoke, the precious binary I had constructed between San Francisco and New York began to fray. I had to acknowledge what I already knew: Geographical distance from Silicon Valley is increasingly irrelevant as its political economy widens. But if there are AI people in Brooklyn, there must be people who still read and write books in San Francisco, too, I thought. Which is why I decided, when I was there, to visit the Internet Archive.
The Internet Archive, a digital library website, began 30 years ago in San Francisco. But in other, less obvious ways, it does not belong to its city of origin. A portion of its servers are housed in a Greek Revival building, formerly a Christian Science church, whose crowning acroteria break with the rows of pastel townhouses. The site was chosen as Archive headquarters for its vast Corinthian columns, which lend it a resemblance to the Library of Alexandria: fated real estate for a nonprofit striving for “Universal Access to All Knowledge,” which its founder, Brewster Kahle, calls “Alexandria 2.0.” When I enter through the iron doors for a tour one Friday afternoon, Kahle welcomes me in belted khakis and thick-soled tennis shoes. He is a bespectacled, ruddy-faced figure, whose general vigor—and frizzy tonsure of gray hair—suggests that he has been electrocuted in a minor, even pleasant way. He remarks, while rising to his tiptoes, that our group is filling out the foyer.
I have technically visited the Archive several times before. On my laptop, I frequently use the Wayback Machine in the process of my research to view old websites and books and magazines. A good portion of the group here, I learn, has also visited the Archive online. So why have all of us pilgrimaged here—some of us for the second time—in real life? Kahle begins the tour by playing an obsolete record on a gramophone; then he shows us, across the foyer, a 1980s arcade game called Prince of Persia. I find myself, improbably, next to a family from Australia, who tell me they planned their visit around a week-long computer programming conference. “What a name,” says their mother, “Brewster Kahle. It’s almost mythical, don’t you think?”
Kahle summons us, like disciples, to ascend to the building’s former nave: a grand rotunda that slopes toward an altar bathed in stained-glass-filtered light. I slot into a pew behind some incoming Berkeley freshmen, who are taking a summer English class titled “Language, Culture, and the Media.” Their teacher has assigned them a list of media-literacy terms to consider: things like “bias” and “deepfakes” and “truth” and further down the page, “power and control.” Kahle walks up to the altar to introduce the Wayback Machine, a software robot that crawls the Internet taking snapshots of what it finds for posterity. Some of its 1 trillion archived Web pages are stored on the servers arranged behind us, black towers that flicker blue whenever someone, from anywhere in the world, is accessing those archives from their device. Kahle loads the machine from his computer and projects his view on a screen that spans the altar. It lights up with scrollable thumbnails—a small sample of the million archived webpages—from which he chooses, at random, the homepage for a wildcat conservation organization in the Netherlands.
Kahle shares that he named the Wayback Machine after a segment of Rocky and Bullwinkle that he watched while growing up in Scarsdale in the early 1960s. In “Peabody’s Improbable History,” Mr. Peabody, a polymath Harvard graduate—and, it bears clarifying, a bowtie-wearing beagle—introduces his human, Sherman, to a gizmo-laden portal. “Open the door and there we are—or were, really,” he explains, walking on all fours through the WABAC Machine into an Ancient Grecian agora. At the Archive, our own Peabody scrolls back in time on his computer, raising bygone versions of the leopard conservation homepage: a streamlined menu followed by a photo of a leopard followed by blocks of black text on a solid white screen. “Here we are,” he says, “a good 1990s look,” as if we followed him through the portal. “The idea is to help people see what the world really looked like in the past.”
In the 1990s, Kahle was in the midst of moving from Cambridge, Massachusetts, to Menlo Park. He had studied at MIT and was working at Thinking Machines Corporation, where he spent the ’80s devising a system to connect their supercomputers to one another in an “interconnected network”—literally an early version of the Internet. With Wide Area Information Servers, or WAIS, you could search through text that was indexed on that network, and receive a list of documents ranked according to how they matched. By the end of that decade, Kahle was looking to California, with intentions to take his system to the market.
Then Tim Berners-Lee, a British computer scientist, came along with a protocol called the World Wide Web. The Web supplanted WAIS partly because of its streamlined design, which enabled the routine ease with which we continue to browse: URLs offer users a standardized language for describing where files live, and when you visit a file’s address, embedded hyperlinks lead you to others. It’s a system that prevails for good reasons, though it made some real trade-offs, too. WAIS, which became obsolete, was underpinned by a time axis: this enabled “version control,” which recalled past versions of a page. Berners-Lee had at one point considered something similar for his Web. It was ultimately not a priority, as users seemed more excited to access up-to-date information.
Berners-Lee and other scientists have grown more concerned about digital transience, or the way that things on the Internet frequently disappear for good. But Kahle belongs to a group for whom that has always been a priority. He started the Archive from his attic in 1996, a year before Terry Kuny, an information and communication specialist, published an academic article on the possibility of a “digital dark age”—the idea that a lack of information could seriously compromise the historical record. By and large, however, most people were just acquainting themselves with the Internet rather than thinking of how to preserve it, and were thrilled with the prospect of life online as we know it: a place that pulses along in the present without much regard for the past.
Kahle describes these conditions as akin to “standing on shifting sand.” At the altar, he points to the shelves that once displayed numbers of hymns: 314, 404, and 451, for the kind of congregation that gathers these days. Most of our group gets 314: pi. Fewer of us get 404: the code for link rot, which is when a web page no longer lives at the address that is linked in a URL. Kahle says that the lifespan of a Web page is, on average, 100 days. But the fact of its expiration is only stated when the cause of death is rot, which produces the explicit, if enigmatic message “Page Not Found.” It is far more common, instead, for a page to be simply overwritten, which bears no similar indication that the original page is lost. In these cases, the grain of sand is buried, disappearing permanently without a trace.
As someone who has plastered images of their life all over MySpace and Facebook and Instagram, this comes as a surprising and in some ways welcome fact: Nothing on the web lasts forever—not braces or ex-boyfriends or overpenciled eyebrows. Though I am privy, too, to the ways in which this generates other problems. I edited at The Believer shortly after it had been sold, first to an Internet marketing company, then back to the publisher McSweeney’s: Its online archive contained the essays that lit up my interest, as a teen, in magazines, but during my time on staff were replaced by listicles of sex toys (the marketing company kept contractual rights to the domain). Web pages are, in this way, frequent collateral to commerce. Mountains of data were lost when MySpace, Friendster, and Tumblr reconfigured. I only grasped the implications, however, as magazines moved from print to online, and parts of Hairpin, Catapult, Gawker, and Curbed went dark. These do not include the conscious deletions made at Buzzfeed in 2014, when four thousand older posts were judged to conflict with new editorial standards.
No one from our tour group correctly guesses 451: the specific kind of rot that occurs when a page is removed for legal reasons. Downstairs, where the tour concludes over tubs of ice cream from Mitchell’s, I find Kahle savoring a cone of his favorite Macapuno. I introduce myself as a reporter from New York. “Fuck The New York Times!” he blurts out.“Sorry, I mean, I love journalists. But seriously, fuck those guys.”
The outburst seems to reveal the cumulative stress that various media and publishing conglomerates have wrought for the Archive in recent years: it was brought to court for alleged copyright violations, first by Hachette in 2020, then by UMG Recordings last year. The Archive settled with UMG but lost to Hachette in a costly appeal that threatened to bankrupt the organization. Now, news outlets like the Times—and the Financial Times and The Guardian—have limited the Archive from accessing their content. They have argued that the Wayback Machine allows their archive to be mined for LLM training. But Kahle refuses to take this on face value. “Copyright is about fair pay,” he says. “But they don’t care about paying their people. They only care about paying themselves.” Last year, to his point, Reddit gave the familiar reasons when it decided to limit the Wayback Machine from crawling its web pages—all while licensing that content to Google, as data sets, for tens of millions of dollars.
But undermining the Archive at this moment might be especially debilitating to the historical record. While it is typical for new governments to make changes to federal websites, the scope and pace of deleted government data has been unprecedented under Trump. In his first week back in office, more than eight thousand web pages vanished: guidelines for overdose prevention; statistics on hate crimes; research on experimental medicines and vaccines. Analysts observed that the deletions may have been triggered by certain terms: this might account for the wholesale purge of pages about the Enola Gay, the aircraft that dropped the atomic bomb on Hiroshima in WWII. The Wayback Machine was able to catalog most of these otherwise defunct details; it remains the only place where the public can access a detailed timeline of January 6, produced by the Congressional Committee that reviewed the attack on the Capitol.
This is compounded by the ease with which the government has deputized Big Tech. Shortly after the United States sanctioned three Palestinian human rights groups last year, YouTube deleted the accounts that belonged to them, adding to censorship by Meta of thousands of posts of the atrocities in Gaza. Meta was later found to have also complied with the Israeli government, which requested that it censor posts that opposed its involvement in the conflict in Iran. Domestically, Google Maps has deleted reviews of ICE detention centers. Every day provides more reasons, in Kahle’s mind, for news outlets to work with the Wayback Machine: Restricting the public record further undercuts their own goal to distribute information. He reminds me that 451 is also the number of degrees, in Fahrenheit, at which paper is said to ignite automatically—made famous by the Ray Bradbury novel about a government that burns books.
At the end of Fahrenheit 451, a group of exiled “Book People” make their return to a bombed-out city. They are led by a former government fireman. When he makes a fire at their campsite for the night, he considers how those flames will be used for warmth instead of destruction. I had walked into the Archive with a narrow idea of who constitutes “Book People.” As it turns out, many technologists study the Internet because they were captivated, first, by books. Right before the Internet Archive was founded, about an hour away at Stanford, two doctoral students in computer science dreamed of a digital library project. Larry Page and Sergey Brin later founded the company Google. In 2002 they started scanning books under the codename Project Ocean.
Kahle was a vocal opponent of this project, which we know now as Google Books—in short because it was billed as a library while largely privatizing potential public resources. I realize, after we talk, that I cannot simply look for people in this new era of technology who work with books: Sometimes people with books still want to burn libraries down (or in Anthropic’s case, shred them en masse with hydraulic guillotines). The “Book People” I am looking for are preoccupied specifically with libraries, which is another way of saying that they are devoted to the past and to the public—to ensuring that everyone can access the archive. I assumed that most of these “Book People” worked in publishing or media and lived in New York. But I learn in San Francisco that they might look different to how I’d imagined them: They might be engineers or even programmers, more fluent in code than in Classics, but just as committed to the project of preserving history.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Jack Cushman, for example, taught himself programming at 13. (He bought C Programming for Dummies and a computer from Sears on an installment plan.) But he has worked for over a decade at the Berkman Klein Center at Harvard, one of several library institutes that works in tandem with the Internet Archive.
I initially came to Cushman through the Public Data Project, which he established just over a year ago to catalog disappearing government data. Cushman formerly worked as a lawyer, which he went to school for in 2005, driven in part by what was happening at Google Books. “It started to seem like law as much as code controlled what was possible in the world,” he told me over the phone. “They were like: We have all the books of the world and we can’t show them to you because that would be against the law. I remember thinking that was not how that was supposed to go.” A decade later, in 2016, Cushman’s instincts were confirmed: Google won a copyright legal battle in which the courts upheld their right to scan millions of books.
After working for a time in appellate courts—the branch of law that depends, in particular, on referencing what came before—Cushman went to work in libraries, where he continues to use technology for preserving public knowledge. I expected that most of our call would be devoted to the Public Data Project—how much data is missing, and what kind. But Cushman instead gently steers me to think beyond the scope of those deletions. He tells me that the problem goes beyond one administration; It is that we have built, both through code and through the courts, a highly privatized Internet, which conflicts with the very notion of a functional public memory, one that enables future generations to retrieve the information they need.
If the architects of the Internet dreamed of a network of interconnected servers, then “Book People,” like Cushman, are dreaming up a network of interconnected archives: where institutions all over the world work to preserve some slice of history, such that the endangerment of one could be protected by the others. The design problem, in his mind, is not technological in nature. It is how to get working people the resources to continue library work, broadly defined. “It’s not about what kind of hard drive we need to buy for storage,” he says. “It’s about what people need so that they can keep these institutions going.” Berkman Klein is university-funded, and independent donors have enabled Internet Archives to open in Canada and Amsterdam. But the private sector, historically backed by the courts—and in collusion with the Trump administration—requires that funding, and protection from litigation, is pursued through multiple governmental channels. (Places like France and Sweden have already sponsored library projects.)
Cushman thinks that we should start looking in places like these to house more archives, where governments are resilient and interested in thinking, not unlike my mother-in-law, about how to preserve the past and pass it down the generations. Though he also thinks the United States should act as a cautionary tale, a reminder about what can happen when administrations change. A truly resilient network of libraries relies on more than one place or a single group of people: beyond San Francisco or New York or even a handful of countries alone. “Of course. there are other places that won’t feel like natural homes,” he says. “But I think it’s still important for us to keep trying, to keep looking everywhere.”

https://www.propublica.org/article/alaba.title: A Cop Was Charged With Causing His Wife’s Miscarriage. Alabama’s Laws Came Down Harder on Pregnant Women Who Used Drugs.
https://www.propublica.org/article/alaba.author: Amy Yurkanin
https://www.propublica.org/article/alaba.text:
Reporting Highlights
- A Brutal Attack: A rookie cop in rural Alabama told his colleague he had hit his pregnant wife in the stomach and choked her before she started to miscarry.
- Laws for the Unborn: Under Alabama law, fetuses have equal protections. But those laws are limited in how they punish people who abuse their pregnant partners.
- Unequal Outcomes: Women accused of drug use during pregnancy face far more legal scrutiny, even when their babies are healthy.
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
On the night of Feb. 15, 2022, Robert Maddox Jr., a rookie cop in a small Alabama town, called his colleague in a panic. His wife was about three months pregnant and bleeding heavily. They needed someone to watch their two sleeping children while they went to the hospital.
Headland police Officer James “Bo” Knight arrived with his wife. He had been serving as a mentor of sorts to Robert, who had just recently joined the department, and had urged him to reach out if he ever needed help.
The situation Knight encountered was a heavy one. Robert had something in a plastic bag that looked to Knight like fetal remains. His wife stood by silently. Robert said he’d be back as soon as possible, that he was taking both his wife and the bag to the hospital.
When the couple returned three hours later, Robert was holding a white container.
“They put my fucking baby in a box,” he said.
Investigators soon began building a case that it was Robert who caused the miscarriage. About six weeks after she lost the pregnancy, Brittany Maddox reported her husband for assaulting her before and after she went to the hospital. She first went to an abuse-prevention organization, which connected her to the police and helped her get a protective order from the court. She provided the Houston County judge with a description of how Robert choked and beat her in front of their 1- and 2-year-old children just before the miscarriage, as well as pictures taken starting the following week of marks on her neck. She handed over text messages from Robert in which he promised not to hurt her again and begged her to consider how his imprisonment would hurt their family.
“Being honest is going to get us both screwed,” he wrote. “The truth is going to give me locked up.”
Then, the Headland Police Department colleague who had offered to help Robert stepped forward. Knight gave a sworn statement to investigators in Dothan, the nearby city where the young couple rented an apartment. He recounted how, weeks after the incident, Robert confided in him that he had hit Brittany in the stomach, choked her and pushed her to the ground.
“I asked him how many times he has done this,” Knight said in his statement. “He stated many.”
According to the statement, Knight asked when he had last hurt her — and Robert responded “the night before you kept my kids.”
In Alabama, the legal implications of causing a miscarriage are severe. Politicians and prosecutors have long proclaimed their mission to defend the unborn. The state has gone further than almost every other to embrace “fetal personhood” — the legal concept that embryos and fetuses deserve the same rights and protections as children. The result is that people charged in Alabama with harming a fetus face especially lengthy prison sentences.
The authorities came down hard on Robert, at least at first. He was charged with murder.
But in the years that followed, Houston County’s criminal justice system would prove lenient for him. Robert was released on bond about five weeks after his arrest and never again saw the inside of a jail or prison cell.
His case stands in stark contrast to dozens of other fetal personhood prosecutions in Houston County, which sits in the corner of the state near the borders of Florida and Georgia. Those defendants were pregnant women. They were charged not for actually harming their unborn babies but for potentially endangering them — not by violence but by using drugs.
In all but one of those cases, which date back nearly two decades, their babies survived. Some of the women spent months in jail and even went to prison.
A former nurse, who had been battling a meth addiction for years, was arrested in 2018 after she tested positive for drug use while in labor and wound up spending nearly 10 months in prison. Another woman, who also tested positive at the hospital where she gave birth, ended up in jail for four months in 2024 — and said many fellow inmates were women who’d been arrested for using drugs while pregnant.
Houston County District Attorney Russ Goodman, who took office in January 2023, said in an email that his office has made efforts to help the women by recommending addiction treatment as part of their sentences. He also said some were rearrested and imprisoned for violating probation — or never completed the treatment offered by the court.
“During my term it is rare that we would sentence a defendant in these types of cases to a straight prison sentence,” Goodman said, “unless of course there were other extenuating circumstances, such as prior criminal history.”
As for Robert Maddox, Goodman said that the evidence against him was inconclusive, and he questioned the prior district attorney’s decision to seek an indictment. “It pained me as a prosecutor that I was not to be able to seek justice in this case,” he said.
Robert declined an interview but said in an email, “I was made out to be someone I wasn’t.” He did not respond when pressed to elaborate. ProPublica later sent him a detailed list of the allegations against him. He replied, “That is not what happened.” In response to a follow-up email, he said his wife had no bruising or marks at the hospital.
“If I was abusive and abused her then took her to the hospital they would have saw the marks and not let me leave with her,” he wrote in an email.
Lourdes Rivera, president of the advocacy group Pregnancy Justice, said her organization has identified 2,298 cases of women arrested since 2006 on charges related to their pregnancy. Most of those were for drug use and are concentrated in Oklahoma, South Carolina and Alabama. Rivera said the numbers of women prosecuted for pregnancy loss appear to be on the rise compared with the years before the U.S. Supreme Court overturned the right to an abortion.
“Law enforcement is using laws that were never intended to apply to pregnancy to investigate, arrest and punish women,” Rivera said. “And it’s only getting worse.”
Robert’s promise not to hurt Brittany again after the miscarriage lasted about a week, she said. She would later tell a judge that he began hitting and choking her again, and photos from that time show bruising on her neck and eye. In that time, something shifted.
“I started hating him when I saw my baby dead,” she wrote in response to ProPublica’s questions.
She said it took her several weeks to come forward because she had to work through complicated feelings about the loss of both her pregnancy and a husband she still loved despite the hatred that was building. She also wasn’t sure if she and her daughters could safely leave him.
About a week before she went to the authorities, she got a text from her husband asking if she’d give him one more chance. “I can’t give you your baby back,” he wrote. “That’s something I’m always going to live with knowing I did that.”
Asked about the text, Robert wrote to ProPublica, “I was referring to having to pull my kid out a toilet I couldn’t believe I had to do that. It was painful emotionally.”
Robert had started working as an officer at the Headland Police Department about four months earlier. Brittany worried the other officers would side with her husband, but she quashed her fears and reached out on social media to several of them anyway. She said Robert went into her account and deleted the messages she’d sent. But it was too late.
Knight, one of the officers she messaged, confronted Robert, who admitted that he had hit Brittany in the stomach before the miscarriage, the officer later told the Dothan police. Robert furiously messaged Brittany.
“If you want me to go to jail keep accusing me of it,” he wrote. “Just know I love you and it will never happen again but I think I’m getting fired.”
Domestic abuse is a leading killer of pregnant women. And for every fatal case, there are an estimated 70 nonfatal ones. Researchers have found that almost 13% of women surveyed experienced domestic violence during pregnancy.
Nonfatal cases usually go unreported, according to Maeve Wallace, an expert on domestic violence at the University of Arizona. The same goes for miscarriages, which often happen at home and may leave no medical record. That can make it difficult to determine how often abuse causes miscarriage, she said.
Brittany said her relationship with Robert had been turbulent from the start. She was still in high school when they started dating, and she uprooted her life to relocate to his hometown of Dothan. She said he started physically hurting her months into the relationship and that it escalated after the move. Brittany found herself isolated in Alabama, where life revolved almost entirely around her husband, two young children and the couple’s car-detailing business.
“Robert would also hurt me if things weren’t done perfectly or if any issues happened,” Brittany wrote.
Unlike many other victims of domestic violence, she hounded the police and prosecutors to take her case seriously after the miscarriage.
Cases against abusers accused of causing pregnancy loss can be tricky to prove, often requiring evidence that the abuser intentionally struck the victim in the stomach and testimony from a forensic pathologist linking the violence to the pregnancy loss. In one strange turn, a grand jury in a city outside of Birmingham indicted a woman for starting a fight that led to her being shot in the stomach and suffering a miscarriage.
It’s easier and more common to pursue charges against defendants when they are accused of killing both a pregnant woman and her fetus.
Laws don’t provide an easy path for punishing abusers of pregnant women, especially when the baby survives, according to law professor Mary Ziegler, who teaches at the University of California, Davis. But laws do make prosecution of pregnant women who use drugs astonishingly easy. Those cases come to light almost automatically — and there is little opportunity to challenge them. Hospitals frequently administer drug tests to pregnant women and notify child protective services of positive results. Those agencies often turn over that information to police in Alabama, where drug use is not grounds just for a child welfare investigation but for a felony charge.
The women are prosecuted under Alabama’s chemical endangerment law, which makes it illegal to expose children to drugs. Although the 2006 law initially was designed to address the dangers of home-based meth labs, prosecutors almost immediately began using it against pregnant women.
ProPublica identified more than 40 pregnant women arrested in Houston County since 2009 on chemical endangerment charges after testing positive for drugs. An analysis of court data also found that the county prosecuted women for chemical endangerment at one of the highest rates in the state, though the data doesn’t specify whether the cases involved pregnancies.
In one case, a 24-year-old whose newborn tested positive for methadone and marijuana received a five-year prison sentence in 2009. Another woman, who’d been convicted for exposing her fetus to THC in 2013, had her probation revoked for possessing synthetic marijuana and spent about nine months in prison.
Pat Jones, who was Houston County’s district attorney at the time of these cases, did not respond to a request for comment.
According to Ziegler, there is a pronounced unevenness in who gets punished under statutes that protect fetuses.
“The versions of personhood that are enshrined in our laws have tended to focus on the conduct of women,” she said.
Courtney Haney grew up in Dothan but left at age 18 to join a high-pressure sales crew that traveled across the country, selling boxes of frozen meat door-to-door. The work was stressful, and it attracted misfits and risk-takers. Several of her colleagues used drugs, but Haney became pregnant unexpectedly and stayed clean.
Her daughter was born healthy, arriving exactly on her due date. But soon, cracks appeared in her relationship with the father, and he split, taking the baby with him. When her colleagues moved on to other cities, Haney remained in Denver to look for her child. She had no family there and no friends. Her despair became overwhelming. She turned to drugs and became homeless, eventually losing custody.
Almost a year later, Haney found out she was pregnant again and returned to Dothan in 2020 with a full-blown addiction to heroin. She went to the hospital with contractions the week before she gave birth and knew she would test positive for drugs. She also said no one offered her options for drug treatment, even after she asked for help. Instead, hospital staff stabilized and discharged her. She kept using until she returned to give birth, when she was drug-tested again.
“I was holding my daughter in my hands and the police walked in,” Haney said.
They asked her questions, and she hoped they might show mercy and allow her to go home with her child. After they told her she might be charged with a felony for exposing her fetus to drugs, she burst into tears.
“I answered honestly, thinking that if I’ve answered honestly they wouldn’t press charges,” she said. “And that was pointless.”
She was arrested for chemical endangerment three months later.
For women struggling with addiction during pregnancy, a chemical endangerment arrest can initiate a cycle of devastating court fees, imprisonment on probation violations and even additional charges. And the separation from their newborns and other children can drive them deeper into addiction. Unlike in many other counties, Houston County does not offer a drug court program, which allows defendants to get substance-abuse treatment instead of prison time and avoid a felony on their record.
A woman who was about seven months’ pregnant was arrested in Houston County the very same day as Robert Maddox, in 2022. She was briefly jailed for violating probation stemming from a past chemical endangerment conviction. She then faced additional felony charges when, weeks later, she tested positive for cocaine at the hospital where she gave birth. She later received a five-year sentence and wound up at Tutwiler Prison for Women.
Her release date is right before Christmas in 2028.
Haney had no felony convictions, but a sentencing report recommended against straight probation due to charges in other states that had been dismissed. Ultimately, the Houston County district attorney’s office offered a plea deal for a lesser charge and just over a year of probation.
Haney struggled to abide by the conditions of her sentence. She did not complete court-ordered drug treatment and failed to report to her probation officer several times. As a result, she was jailed for a total of four months.
Many of the other women jailed with her also had been arrested on charges of chemical endangerment as a result of failing drug tests during childbirth.
“Whenever I went to jail, that’s where I met most of them,” Haney said. “There’s a whole lot of them in Houston County.”
Haney became pregnant two more times while she was addicted. For her third child, she traveled to nearby Georgia to give birth, and then to Florida for her fourth. Neither state arrests women for prenatal drug use at the same high rate as Alabama.
Xaviera Smith, a former nurse and mother of three from Tennessee, said she knew she would be arrested before she even gave birth in Houston County to her youngest son in 2018. Smith couldn’t deny the results of the drug test that had been administered while she was in labor. She had been battling a meth addiction for years.
She said that, fortunately, her baby was born healthy and did not need to go to the neonatal intensive care unit for drug withdrawal.
Smith had a court-appointed attorney who negotiated a deal on her chemical endangerment charge. She was sentenced to 10 years but could avoid prison by serving time through the local work-release program.
“I just went to court and took what they gave me,” Smith said. ”There’s nothing I really could do.”
After violating the terms of work release, she ended up in prison for nearly a year.
Brittany Maddox believed the case against her husband was a straightforward one. She felt there was solid evidence that the abuse caused her miscarriage. But the effort proved to be harder than she anticipated.
A few months after his arrest, the grand jury declined to indict him for murder, opting instead for a lesser charge of manslaughter.
The indictment alleged that Robert had “recklessly” caused the death of his wife’s fetus by “punching her in the stomach with a closed fist.” The maximum punishment would be 20 years in prison.
As Robert waited for his day in court, he asked the judge to relax some of the conditions of his bond. He had lost his job with the Headland police because of his wife’s claims of abuse and had started washing cars again. He wanted the court to remove the ankle monitor so he could more easily travel to work in Florida, which is near Dothan.
From her home out of state, Brittany had been calling the district attorney’s office once or twice a month to ensure authorities kept an eye on her estranged husband’s whereabouts. She was shocked to learn of his out-of-state travel request — not from prosecutors but from a news story. For the first time since his arrest, she felt unsafe.
A judge denied his motion to remove the ankle monitor but granted his request to commute to north Florida.
Brittany stayed in touch with prosecutors and began to mentally prepare for trial. She said that as months stretched into years, the conversations with them began to shift. They asked her how she felt about a plea deal, and she said she would be open to it, as long as the charge related to her miscarriage wasn’t dropped completely.
“I told them I could push through a trial emotionally,” Brittany wrote.
Finally, almost four years after Robert was arrested, his attorney brokered a plea deal with prosecutors. He would plead guilty to domestic violence, and the prosecution would recommend the manslaughter charge be dismissed.
Goodman, the district attorney, told ProPublica that he would not have been able to prove at trial that Robert committed manslaughter. “There was never any evidence that tied the actions of the defendant to the death of the baby,” he said, adding that “no expert could tie a causal connection.”
He also said he explained to Brittany that “we would not have moved forward on the manslaughter case” had he been in office when his predecessor chose to seek an indictment against Robert.
Brittany said if Goodman believed the charge should be dropped, he should have done it sooner, instead of having her spend years preparing for trial.
“The charge being dropped four years after he was arrested as part of a plea deal makes no sense to me,” she said. “That wrecked me in a lot of ways, more than the times I laid in bed for days after he hurt me.”
On May 18, 2026, Robert appeared before a judge in a Houston County courtroom. Brittany attended the hearing as well. She had traveled to Alabama for all of the hearings, even though she still feared being in the same room with Robert.
After all that waiting, the sentencing felt surprisingly short to her. When the judge moved to dismiss the most serious charge, he didn’t say the word manslaughter or mention the miscarriage. Brittany said she tried to ask questions about the deal, but she wasn’t sworn in, and the judge quickly moved on.
“The victim and the defendant were in a verbal dispute whereas the defendant was alleged to throw the victim down and choke her,” the judge said. “The state alleges that this occurred in front of their minor children as well.”
The judge went on to say that the presence of the children might have increased Robert’s punishment to a minimum six months’ imprisonment. But because he was a first-time offender, that minimum didn’t apply.
The judge sentenced him to five years’ probation and fined him about $3,000, which he could pay off at $50 a month. Then the judge added one more thing: anger management classes, to be completed through the court referral office.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Black People Have Every Reason to Doubt Official Narratives About a Recent Spate of Hangings
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Kali Holloway
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Black People Have Every Reason to Doubt Official Narratives About a Recent Spate of Hangings
Prematurely ascribing deaths to suicide does away with questions that deserve real answers.
Since September 2025, at least 10 Black people have been found hanged in public outdoor spaces across the country. Among the first institutions to sound the alarm was the Legal Defense Fund, an outgrowth of the NAACP, an organization founded nearly 120 years ago to resist anti-Black violence, particularly lynchings. Citing “the well-documented legacy of racial terror against Black people in the United States,” the group sent letters to Congress and the United Nations in August calling for “a rigorous inquiry to ensure that our past history of widespread targeted Black killings is not recurring.” The following month, Representative Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts and 59 other House Democrats wrote to the Justice Department and the FBI demanding a “comprehensive federal investigation into every hanging death of a Black individual.” Also in September, the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation’s 55th annual conference convened a panel discussion titled “Stop the Lynchings.”
I do not pretend to know that every Black person found hanged over roughly the last year was the victim of a lynching. As the civil rights lawyers, forensics experts, and mental-health scholars on the CBCF panel emphasized, Black American suicide rates have increased 53 percent over just the last decade; for Black adolescents, the rates skyrocketed 144 percent between 2007 and 2020. In some of these cases, authorities have offered evidence that rules out foul play or suggests that the death wasn’t motivated by racial hatred. A publicly unidentified Black man found hanged this September in Maryland was reportedly shown on security footage carrying a rope. After Tasia Fortune was found hanging in Mississippi, three Black men were charged with murder, and police concluded that the scene was “staged” postmortem to look like a lynching. But clearance statistics prove that police put in less work to solve homicides, or any violent crime, when the victims are Black. Prematurely ascribing deaths to suicide—as too many families contend the police have in these cases—does away with the pesky questions that deserve real answers.
As in the case of Juliana Nzita, a 16-year-old found hanged from a tree in May at a North Carolina church she did not attend, whose death was ruled a suicide within three days. A Charlotte Observer investigation found that police hadn’t ordered an autopsy, recovered her cell phone, or interviewed the man who found her body. The aunt of Justice “Kai” James, found hanging in Albany, Georgia, told the local outlet WALB that police claimed surveillance footage existed but then refused to let her see it. When the Atlanta Black Star asked a Michigan State Police officer why Jerard “Jay” Jackson’s death in Roxbury, Michigan, was ruled a suicide, he stated, “It looked like that, so that’s why I said it appeared to be a suicide.”
Yet as these cases have gained attention, a familiar strain of disparaging commentary has followed. Syndicated columnist Rich Lowry called questions about whether the hangings might be lynchings symptomatic of a “profound and disturbing racial paranoia.” More than one outlet mocked Pressley’s description of the deaths as a “national crisis.” In the National Review, Black conservative writer Wilfred Reilly pronounced fears of resurgent racial terror a “fake lynching scandal.” In seeking to understand the causes of these deaths, it is certainly fair to think critically. But the notion that Black folks’ distrust of law enforcement and other government officials is a kind of hysteria—instead of a logical response to US history—is a familiar way of waving off Black pain to avoid reckoning with its underlying causes.
There were nearly 6,500 extrajudicial lynchings between the end of the Civil War and 1950, according to the Equal Justice Initiative. The law didn’t simply fail Black Americans; the institutions supposedly tasked with enforcing it regularly abetted, covered up, or sanctioned bloody violence against them. Sheriffs and deputies facilitated or even participated directly in the violence, and coroners, prosecutors, juries, and politicians helped the perpetrators avoid punishment. Though the heyday of white racial terror arguably ended with the demise of Jim Crow, the federal government only passed the Emmett Till Anti-Lynching Act in 2022—after 200 similar bills had failed.
In its 1951 petition to the UN, the Civil Rights Congress wrote that lynchings were intended as “a powerful source of constant terror…to the whole Negro people.” That terror created trauma that was passed down through generations. Reilly snarks at the idea that “simply seeing a picture of a rope tied in a hangman’s knot can allegedly invoke this pain,” as if Black folks don’t deserve to still be hurt by the imagery of racial terror. Such dismissiveness is galling in a country where Black life has been so indelibly shaped by lynching. Many members of Black communities in the North and West can trace their family’s Southern origins back along the railroad lines that carried 6 million Black refugees away from Jim Crow racial terror. Places that once had the most lynchings now have the lowest Black voter registration and Black economic mobility, as well as the highest numbers of Black folks imprisoned or shot dead by police. Montgomery, Alabama, is home to an entire museum devoted to lynching and the scars it has left on this country.
After police declared the 2018 hanging death of Willie Andrew Jones Jr. a suicide, the civil rights lawyer Jill Collen Jefferson conducted her own investigation, turning up evidence the police had missed. Those findings helped Jones’s family win an $11 million wrongful-death settlement. In February, Jefferson’s human-rights nonprofit, Julian, released a study cataloging more than 70 deaths of Black people between 2000 and 2025 that she describes as “modern-day lynchings” by hanging or other violent means.
The history of racial terror does not answer what happened in any of the cases now under scrutiny. But it does explain why Black people’s fears are rational, their questions justified, and why “Just trust the authorities” is an absurd demand to make of them.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Frieze Artist Award reimagines endangered Lebanese site
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Kabir Jhala
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
One of Lebanon’s most intriguing archaeological sites is the inspiration behind the inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi Artist Award, given to the fast-rising Lebanese artist Dala Nasser to create her installation Qubbat Duris. The work takes its name from a 13th-century Muslim shrine near Baalbek, northeast of Beirut, which is composed from the ruins of two separate ancient Roman sites: granite columns from Baalbek’s Temple of Jupiter hold up limestone sarcophagi from a necropolis.
Placed in the atrium of the fair, the work will comprise a timber frame evoking Qubbat Duris’s structure, with fabrics covered in charcoal rubbings of the remaining ruins and painted with ash, raw clay and terracotta draped over it.
Nasser is best known for her archaeological frottage paintings—made using the surfaces of endangered historical sites—which consider the artist’s role in reproducing, and bearing witness to, history and landscape.
Though Nasser is not the first artist to engage with Qubbat Duris, she points out, many of her antecedents are problematic. “The site has already been extensively imagined and reimagined in art historical painting,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “From Orientalist depictions to the backdrop to one of Gertrude Bell’s most circulated photographs, taken in costume on horseback.”
Similar works of Nasser’s—such as Adonis River (2023) and Wedding at Qana (2024)—have also taken as their subjects “landscapes that loom large in historical painting but look nothing like the landscape itself in Western Asia, either overwhelmed by Orientalist tropes or painted as scenes of European countryside, betraying the artists’ lack of knowledge and limits of imagination”, she says. “I am trying to make paintings that are truthful to the landscape.”
The question of “truth” pertains to Qubbat Duris’s position as a site that reflects the layered cultural histories and religions of Lebanon. “It exists as a palimpsest from the second century AD until today, carrying all of the traces in between,” Nasser says.
Meanwhile, the role of evidence and recording in Nasser’s practice also considers the risks of erasure faced by much of Lebanon’s cultural artefacts, particularly from Israel’s longstanding and continued occupation of the country. On 15 October 2024, Qubbat Duris sustained slight damage from Israeli airstrikes; previously during the 2006 Israel-Lebanon war, an Israeli airstrike dislodged one of the shrine’s stones. “I’m interested in how a place like Qubbat Duris carries physical evidence of everything it’s endured, including scars of damage,” Nasser says.
• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November

https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.title: The Uncanny Choreography of Trisha Brown
https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.author: Gillian Jakab
https://www.thenation.com/article/cultur.text:
Uncanny Correspondences
The radical choreography of Trisha Brown
The Uncanny Choreography of Trisha Brown
After a career spanning five decades, and 10 years after her passing, the choreographer and dancer is having a moment.
In 1982, the dancer Trisha Brown started an unorthodox correspondence with the musician and performance artist Laurie Anderson. Anderson’s debut studio album, Big Science, had just been released, and Brown, emerging as one of the leading dance artists of her generation, had choreographed a 10-minute duet to the song “Sweaters.” She sent it to Anderson by videotape without sound. Anderson then composed a new score for Brown’s dance and mailed back a cassette with the music. And with that, Brown set in motion the latest in a series of multimedia collaborations, not just with Anderson but with the artist Robert Rauschenberg, that would result in her masterwork, Set and Reset.
In October 1983, Set and Reset premiered at the Brooklyn Academy of Music’s Next Wave festival. The dance opens on Rauschenberg’s sculptural set Elastic Carrier (Shiner), a rectangular prism flanked by two pyramids. The first movements are projections of newsreel-style found footage—traffic, baseball, a monkey—shifting onto the fabric forms that rise to make way for the performers as they appear. Two stagehands enter holding a dancer horizontally overhead, charting the stage perimeter as she walks on a wall that isn’t there. It’s a witty quotation of one of her earlier works, 1971’s Walking on the Wall. Meanwhile, Anderson’s score—part sci-fi, part groovy rhythm—keeps the dancers in motion. They break away in different directions, each doing a variation of the piece’s basic movement phrases. Straight limbs slice the air, punctuating slinky hip swivels with geometric precision. Individuals relate to one another like a Fibonacci sequence in nature, in mathematical patterns so seamless that one doesn’t register the equation behind the pine cone’s spiral. This cascading energy, simultaneously fluid and structured, epitomizes Brown’s movement language.
This past February, the Trisha Brown Dance Company performed Set and Reset on the BAM stage of its premiere—a reprise that marked a major stop in the company’s ongoing “Dancing With Bob” tour celebrating Rauschenberg’s centennial. The double bill includes Merce Cunningham’s Travelogue and is taking Brown’s dance company all over the world, from Beverly Hills to Chicago, Vienna to Paris.
Much has changed since Set and Reset’s debut four decades ago. In the early 1980s, Brown benefited from substantial federal funding. In 2025, as part of the Trump administration’s attack on cultural institutions, the National Endowment for the Arts revoked a major grant intended for the tour. Now her company must lean more heavily on private funds, such as from the French jewelry company Van Cleef and Arpels. But so deep-seated is Brown’s choreography in the postmodern canon that watching the piece today, one can sense its constancy, as though Brown were in the translucent wings of Rauschenberg’s set directing it. When Anderson’s voice proclaims “Long time no see” over her electronic score, it is now a greeting to these old friends. No worries that neither Brown nor Rauschenberg are alive; Set and Reset reaches them as a séance of sorts, made easier by the staying power of their legacies.
Born in 1936 in Aberdeen, Washington, Trisha Brown graduated from Mills College in 1958 with a degree in dance. She learned improvisation techniques from Anna Halprin in San Francisco before making the inevitable crossing to New York City. When she arrived in the early 1960s, Brown took classes at the Merce Cunningham studio and worked answering phones there. That’s how she met Rauschenberg: “This man used to call named Bob Rauschenberg, and I had the greatest conversations with him,” she told David Sears in a 1982 interview for Ballet Review. It would be another decade before they officially collaborated, but Brown admired Rauschenberg’s dynamic stage designs for Cunningham and others, as well as his exhibitions pushing the limits of sculpture and painting. (“I was bowled over that anyone would put a bed on the wall and put some paint on it,” she said of one of the artist’s early “combines,” Bed.)
Brown eventually graduated from Cunningham’s reception desk and matriculated into the street school broadly referred to as New York’s downtown art scene. She was a founding member of the Judson Dance Theater—the now-legendary avant-garde collective that rejected the drama of early modern dance and championed a democratic, pedestrian form of movement. Under the roof of Judson Memorial Church, Brown trail-blazed what we now refer to as postmodern dance along with people like Yvonne Rainer, Steve Paxton, and Simone Forti. By the 1970s, Brown wasn’t under the roof so much as outside or even on top of it. Her 1971 Roof Piece and her “equipment pieces,” such as Man Walking Down the Side of a Building (1970), liberated dance from theaters and set it loose in galleries, lofts, parks, and in front of buildings. When Brown’s Walking on the Wall was performed on the exterior of the Whitney, it was Rauschenberg who supplied the equipment.
As the 1980s approached, Brown’s work began to change. A transition from site-specific dances to a cycle of proscenium pieces posed new questions of perspective and audience. While Brown’s dances were welcomed by mainstream concert venues like BAM and backed by conventional art-funding sources, they retained their experimental edge. It was in this era that Brown opened her company to men and began documenting not just her finished pieces but her creative process on video. It was also in this period that she developed Set and Reset.
At once wild and precise, playful and deadpan, Set and Reset respects the choreographic categories that came before it even as it defies them. The veteran critic Deborah Jowitt once noted that “it’s always been one of the high aspirations of modern dance not to move like the person you started with.” Martha Graham broke away from her teachers at the Denishawn school in the 1920s. Graham’s disciples—the generation of Merce Cunningham and Paul Taylor—then distinguished themselves in turn against their inherited gospel. In Set and Reset, as the name implies, Brown marked herself out as one of the true innovators of dance movement in the 20th century. By that point, it seemed like her movement came, as Brown once put it, from “Heaven.”
The heaven that Brown may have had in mind, as Susan Rosenberg expertly shows in her book Trisha Brown: Choreography as Visual Art, was her childhood in the rural beauty of Washington State. Of course, the inspiration might have come from somewhere else, too. But Brown’s work was, as Rauschenberg once noted, “just about as personal” as one can get: “She’s right on the edge—I mean if she weren’t so eccentric, it would be too autobiographical, but she is such an unpredictable person, actually, that even if it is autobiographical, it looks abstract.”
It’s this personal quality that fed Brown’s artistic relationships, including in the making of Set and Reset. Despite privileging structure, logic, and mathematical precision, her principles of motion had at their core a collaborative element—one born out of her interactions with others. The paradigmatic example is what Brown called “memorized improvisation,” which she used to create Set and Reset. Generating spontaneous building blocks of movement from her body and engineering them into a choreographic flow, she then had her dancers execute the material in the studio, down to the last square inch, before encouraging them to improvise from it—“play with visibility and invisibility”—over and over until a new set of movements emerged. “Brown felt that instinctual behavior brought up tenderness and sort of a sabotage aspect to the work. You get all kinds of things happening outside the confines of the original, rigorously organized material. [Set and Reset] was really one of the first times that humor was an element of the work—high jinks, exuberance all showed up and were then committed [to the choreography],” recalled Carolyn Lucas, a former dancer with the company and its current associate artistic director. “She said at one point of the dancers, ‘I couldn’t keep them out of the work.’”
With her outside collaborators, Brown also cultivated equally intimate exchanges, such as her VHS-for-cassette-tape dialogue with Anderson that prompted the making of Set and Reset. The composer dubbed it “electronic closeness,” a kind of Snapchat ahead of its time. Brown got just as close with others, like Rauschenberg, but each time through different means. In Brown’s own words: “In Set and Reset, the communication between [Bob and me] was direct, almost as if he lived inside of me, or me inside of him. There were correspondences that were uncanny.” Brown was not just aware that her collaborative demands ran deep; it was her consciously imposed condition, her sine qua non of the artistic relationship. “One factor in all of my collaborations is that I work with friends of mine,” Brown told The Brooklyn Rail in 2005. “You need to know if they’re going to go ballistic at the drop of a hat or not. You have to know if they’ll be able to deal with it.”
Brown did not completely blur the borders of music, visual art, and dance in her work. Nor did she insist on the complete autonomy of each of these art forms the way Cunningham, Cage, and Rauschenberg had done. What she did do was bring each discipline into a quasi-familial relationship characterized by both proximity and distance. In Set and Reset, Brown would send Anderson weekly videos of new movement phrases as Anderson worked on the score. Rauschenberg labored over the set and costumes at a greater distance from the other two, insisting that “the sturdiest kind of collaboration happens when you allow all the participants as much freedom as they can absorb.” Out of this practice came Elastic Carrier (Shiner) and his silk-screened city images on the dancers’ costumes. Grayscale, they are in contrast with Rauschenberg’s projected moving images, forming the kind of two-way flow that characterized Brown’s practice.
After a career spanning five decades, and 10 years after her passing, Trisha Brown is having a moment. The reprise of Set and Reset, in a tour honoring one of her closest artistic partners, stands as a testament to her legacy, not by imparting it to those around her but by pulling them into it. Her work is powerful enough to jump generations. Her set of movements are still in motion, and her collaborators—some alive, others now dead—span nearly half a century of American art, music, and dance. Some of her collaborators will need to be reached by séance; others are immediately accessible. But their sheer number is both the proof of Brown’s achievement as a choreographer and the reason why Set and Reset feels as fresh today as it did back in 1983.
