https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Seven shows to see in the UAE during Frieze Abu Dhabi
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Razmig Bedirian
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Reem Al Mubarak: What We Left in the Sandbox
Rizq Art Initiative, Abu Dhabi, 6 November-10 January 2027
In What We Left in the Sandbox, Reem Al Mubarak’s solo exhibition at Rizq Art Initiative, the Emirati artist explores how child’s play can be a powerful medium of creativity and memory. Through a series of sculptural works, etchings and drawings, Al Mubarak strives to recall specific places and objects from her own childhood, embracing the distortions of memory. A monumental sandcastle evokes a child’s perspective of space, while bubble wrap that has been compulsively popped or left intact is cast in resin, turning a disposable material into an enduring sculptural form.
The exhibition is curated by the architect and researcher Azza Aboualam, who was the curator of the UAE’s national pavilion during the 2025 Venice Architecture Biennale.
Shaikha Al Mazrou
Cultural Foundation, Abu Dhabi, 12 November-15 March 2027
In 2022, Shaikha Al Mazrou presented her large-scale work Red Stack as part of Frieze Sculpture in London’s Regent’s Park. The work exemplifies her deft approach to defying perceptions through her choice of materials. It features a pile of red cushions constructed from fibreglass and resin on a metal framework. Despite the hardness of the materials, the creased and pillowy cushions evoke a sense of softness.
She receives her strongest spotlight to date with her solo exhibition at the Abu Dhabi’s Cultural Foundation. It will feature past work alongside new commissions created specifically for the venue’s atrium. Al Mazrou’s work is also on view at Frieze Abu Dhabi with Lawrie Shabibi.
All Manner of Experiments
NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery, Abu Dhabi, until 3 January 2027
In 1951, Jewad Selim and Shakir Hassan Al Said established a movement that sought to express Modernist art principles through a uniquely Iraqi perspective. It would prove to be one of the most defining moments of Arab art.
All Manner of Experiments is perhaps the most comprehensive survey of the Baghdad Modern Art Group. It presents seminal works from the period as well as contemporary pieces that highlight the ongoing legacies of the group.
The exhibition at the New York University (NYU) Abu Dhabi Art Gallery brings together works from 1946 to 2023, from private and institutional collections. Selim’s experiments with abstraction are represented, as well as Al Said’s figurative expressions and his latter work that employed Arabic letters to convey an inner dimension. Key works by Dia al-Azzawi, Madiha Umar and Khalid al-Rahal are also presented, with the exhibition concluding with contemporary pieces by Mahmoud Obaidi, Walid Siti and Rand Abdul Jabbar, among others.
A key point of departure in this show is Selim’s Freedom Monument, a 50m-long sculpture in Tahrir Square that was commissioned just after the 1958 military coup that overthrew the Hashemite monarchy and established the Iraqi Republic. Though Selim died in 1961 before the sculpture fully materialised, it is considered to be one of his most enduring works, potent with the sensibilities that inspired the Baghdad Modern Art Group. Read from right to left—like an Arabic text—the monument tells the story of the revolution. Its bronze figures draw from Sumerian motifs while also employing Modernist aesthetics.
Spices and Wonders: Sailing the Indian Ocean
Louvre Abu Dhabi, until 14 February 2027
The Indian Ocean has been a pivotal node of cultural exchange for centuries, and an exhibition at the Louvre Abu Dhabi unravels the ancient maritime connections that linked Europe, Africa and the Middle East to South and Southeast Asia. Held in collaboration with the Guimet Museum in Paris, the exhibition charts these links through artefacts, textiles, ceramics and spices.
This investigation extends to Art Here—a staple show in Louvre Abu Dhabi’s calendar, presenting works shortlisted for the annual Richard Mille Art Prize. This year’s exhibition, exploring the theme of “Confluences” is curated by Kamini Sawhney (until 28 February 2027).
Serendipitously, the theme of Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi also looks towards the Indian Ocean, presenting artefacts, maps and rare books. Presentations at Frieze will contribute to research into an understudied historical topic with implications for the modern era.
Vantage Point 13
Photography Gallery, Sharjah, until 29 November
The 13th edition of Vantage Point takes place at the Photography Gallery in Sharjah, a venue that opened in November 2025. The exhibition, an annual fixture in Sharjah’s arts programme since 2013, is being held in an overhauled format. Each year, dozens of international artists have taken part in the exhibition, which celebrates photographic works across genres, from photojournalism to more experimental compositions. Vantage Point has now been pared down, exhibiting commissioned works by six photographers, and it will also be a biennial event moving forward.
Sathish Kumar presents a series of images that focus on his brother, an oil worker in Abu Dhabi. Photographs of Kumar’s family in the industrial city compound in Al Ruwais are juxtaposed with those taken in Bengaluru in southern India. Much of the latter centre around the construction site of the family home. The series, titled Bond, alludes to the fraught experiences of many South Asian labourers who travel to the Gulf with the aim of financially supporting their parents and families back home.
The other works featured in the exhibition are equally evocative and personal. Latifa AlBokhari presents tender images that mark key moments in a woman’s life in the Gulf, from henna traditions to wedding preparations. Guanyu Xu shows life-sized images of domestic interiors that offer clues to the personalities of the people that inhabit them. Luisa Dörr documents with painterly sensibilities a female-focused equestrian school in Mexico. Maheder Haileselassie spotlights archival images of Arbegnoch fighters, who resisted the Italian occupation of Ethiopia between 1936 and 1941. Finally, Adam Rouhana presents larger-than-life portraits of Palestinians from the West Bank, whom he photographed in a travelling studio.
Artist’s Rooms: Walid Siti; Shezad Dawood; Lulua Alyahya; Afrah Shafiq; Bani Abidi
Jameel Arts Centre, Dubai
The Jameel Arts Centre has given five artists each a dedicated space within the institution.
One room charts four decades of Walid Siti's practice. Sketches of dark, spiralling towers embody the human pathology of scaling literal and proverbial heights. Sculptures and acrylic paintings of mountains, meanwhile, beckon to the peaks of his native Iraqi Kurdistan. A commissioned large-scale sculpture is the centrepiece of the exhibition. It outlines a mountain in stacked polystyrene, with writing on its underside that reflects on the turbulent history of Kurdistan.
Bahraini painter Lulua Alyahya presents the urban and natural environments of the Gulf with diffused brushstrokes. Her work often teeters on the absurd, with lions scowling from computer screens and chickens hatching eggs that fry on the pavement.
Afrah Shafiq is showing Nobody Knows For Certain, an interactive video game work that drawns on a lesser-known but rich period of cultural exchange between India and the Soviet Union that took place between the 1950s and 80s.
New Dream Machine Project, a three-metre-high installation by Shezad Dawood, is a gyrating tower pulsing with light. Inspired by Brion Gysin’s Dreamachine, which the artist devised after his time in Tangier and after “experimenting with altered states of being” with members of the Beat Generation. The installation was prototyped by artisans in Fes, Morocco, with the final version engineered in Slough, England.
Trembling Hands (2024) by Bani Abidi gathers the artist's portraits of artists, journalists and politicians who spoke out against the genocide of Palestinians, some of whom faced backlash, censorship or repression as a result.
The sky held it, the earth remembered
Ishara Art Foundation, Dubai, until 15 December
The sky held it, the earth remembered presents the work of Pakistani artist Shahana Rajani, Indian artist Rohini Devasher and Bangladeshi artist Sarker Protick, all of whom consider how memory and history are preserved and transmitted.
In Rajani’s three-channel video Lines that World a River, a woman paints a house along the banks of a river. The scene is vibrant with its textured blues and chalky greens. Rajani zooms in on the woman’s fingers. Her nails are streaked with the white of the paint she uses to draw the river’s foam. The drawing is of the woman’s ancestral village along the Indus River Delta—now submerged after the construction of hydraulic dams and barrages.
The work—a new iteration of Rajani’s Four Acts of Recovery, which won the Han Nefkens Foundation’s inaugural South Asian Video Art Production Grant in 2023—shows how displaced communities in the Indus region have developed mural painting practices to remember their lost homes.
Devasher’s Latent Fields comprises three sprawling silk panels that hang from the ceiling. Their dots and patterns allude to sunspots and other solar events, coming together as a monumental record of celestial time.
In Dhaka 1217, meanwhile, Protick presents 135 photographs that capture the transformation of the neighbourhood where the artist was born and continues to live.

https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.title: Three of the Financial Sins That Left Chicago $55 Billion in Debt — and Counting
https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.author: Heather Cherone
https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.text:
Chicago’s finances have long been strained by soaring pension expenses, spiraling personnel costs and a massive amount of debt. Budget deficits and financial crises now arrive with regularity, as city leaders face crucial decisions on how to dig out of this financial mess.
The track record of decision-making within City Hall suggests that avoiding hard choices for expediency leads to trouble.
The city must spend billions every year from its main account — known as its corporate fund — to keep current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its pension funds. The debt consists of $19 billion in loan payments that must be repaid by revenue from property and sales taxes as well as $36 billion to ensure former employees get retirement benefits. The city also borrows money to make improvements to its water and sewer systems and to fund operations at its airports, but that debt is repaid with fees, not money from the corporate fund.
Here are three of the big decisions Chicago officials have made over the years that dug the city into such a massive financial hole.
Pension Holiday Snowballs Into Peril
In 2000, the city’s pensions were 85% funded, which meant the funds could easily pay benefits to employees as they retired, records show. But a series of decisions in both Chicago and the Illinois capital of Springfield unraveled that strong position, leading to the current mountain of $36.4 billion in pension debt.
First, the twin blows of the “dot-com” bubble bursting in 2000 and the Great Recession in 2007 wiped out nearly $16 billion from those funds.
Around the same time came a self-inflicted blow. In 2005, the state legislature, at the request of then Chicago Mayor Richard M. Daley, passed legislation allowing the city to contribute less every year than what was actually needed to pay retirees.
As a result, in 2006 and 2007, Daley was able to stop making annual contributions to four pension funds for police officers, firefighters, laborers and municipal employees. He received near-unanimous support from the Chicago City Council. Daley, who was mayor from 1989 through 2011, declined to comment for this story.
Daley’s “pension holiday” meant the city could balance its budget without a politically perilous property tax hike. But that maneuver laid the foundation of the current pension crisis facing the city.
In 2010, having seen the financial fallout from the pension legislation, state legislators passed a law that banned city officials from taking another pension holiday by setting a firm schedule for the city to pay back its skipped payments — no excuses allowed.
Two of Chicago’s pension funds must be funded at a 90% level by 2055, with the other two hitting that mark by 2058, according to state law. This requirement caused a spike in the city’s annual payments.
Trying to ease Chicago’s snowballing pension burdens, lawmakers passed a new measure reducing the retirement benefits offered to state employees who began work on or after January 1, 2011.
But that revised law touched off a new set of problems. The well-intentioned effort to reduce costs actually reduced pension benefits too drastically. Under federal law, public sector pension funds must pay workers no less than what they would have earned if they paid into Social Security.
In 2021 and 2025, lawmakers agreed to change the law and ensure that first responders — police and firefighters — in Illinois are paid at least the minimum required by law.
Fixing those funds will cost Chicago an additional $11 billion to get to the 90% funded level required by state law over the next three decades, according to city projections. Gov. JB Pritzker signed the legislation over the objections of city officials.
Long-Term Lease, Long-Lasting Regrets
Facing big deficits in 2008 in the wake of the Great Recession, Daley and the City Council found what they thought was a creative solution to the city’s financial woes.
They would lease the city’s parking meters to a conglomerate of investment funds for 75 years in return for $1.5 billion up front. That massive influx of cash meant no one had to make any hard decisions to fill the city’s budget gap and avoid a politically unpopular property tax increase.
But the deal ended up a loser both politically and financially.
The new owners of the meters immediately jacked up the cost to park, infuriating residents. In a matter of months, members of the City Council began regretting their votes, and Daley announced he would not run for reelection.
By 2025, the city’s meters generated $2.2 billion in revenue for the investors, with another 58 years still left on the lease.
The city considered buying the parking meters back this year, but Mayor Brandon Johnson told reporters “the final purchase price was far too high.” The city would have had to borrow billions to finance the $3.2 billion purchase.
Elected officials across the political spectrum agree that the city would have been much better off raising property taxes instead of leasing the parking meters in 2008.
But even as the gap between the city’s revenues and its expenses continues to widen, property tax hikes remain the third rail of Chicago politics.
Chicagoans’ property taxes last jumped in 2021, when former Mayor Lori Lightfoot raised them by $93.9 million and passed a budget that automatically hiked property taxes to keep pace with inflation.
Johnson campaigned against those automatic property tax increases, forcing Lightfoot to drop a proposal to hike taxes by $42.7 million in 2023, just months before she lost her bid for reelection.
The automatic property tax hike was eliminated, even though it could have prevented the city’s credit rating from being downgraded repeatedly and significantly reduced the annual budget gaps.
In a postscript to the parking meter debacle, Chicago Parking Meters LLC sold the meters contract earlier this year to an investment firm, triggering a one-time payment to the city of $75 million. The City Council and Johnson then battled over how best to use that money for pension costs, creating a temporary hole in the 2027 city budget.
The Financial Toll of Police Misconduct
The 2014 police murder of 17-year-old Laquan McDonald changed nearly every aspect of City Hall politics around policing. Despite decades of scandals, misconduct and brutality, the Police Department had managed to fend off reform. But that ended with McDonald’s death, even as city leaders continued to fear a backlash from residents concerned about crime rates and a politically powerful police union.
After a massive outcry greeted footage of McDonald getting shot 16 times while he walked away from officers, the federal government launched a probe that in 2017 found ample evidence that the department routinely violated the constitutional rights of Black and Latino Chicagoans.
In 2019, the Chicago Police Department agreed — under the oversight of a federal judge — to change the way officers are trained, supervised and disciplined. In taking so long to address a pernicious problem, a succession of city leaders set up Chicago for a huge financial hit.
The true scope of police misconduct and what it will cost the city is only now becoming clear.
From 2019 to 2025, as the city scrambled to fill budget holes, it agreed to pay nearly $730 million to resolve lawsuits alleging officers committed a wide range of misconduct, according to a WTTW News analysis of city records. The most expensive cases involve wrongful convictions that sent Chicagoans now declared innocent to prison for decades, as well as botched raids and police pursuits that violated CPD policy and led to injuries, according to that analysis.
In 2026 alone, Chicago has spent more than $277 million to resolve lawsuits alleging police misconduct, records show. That includes nearly $100 million to resolve 90 lawsuits filed by people who allege they were wrongfully implicated based on evidence gathered by former Sgt. Ronald Watts, who was convicted in 2013 of taking bribes. He has denied wrongdoing.
Johnson has urged the City Council to borrow an additional $481 million to cover the costs of resolving more lawsuits, with $260.8 million earmarked for 17 people wrongfully convicted based on evidence developed by former Chicago police Detective Reynaldo Guevara. A judge determined Guevara told “bald-faced lies” while under oath in 2017, a fact that will be presented to any jury asked to determine whether the city should be held accountable for claims of misconduct. He has repeatedly invoked his Fifth Amendment right not to incriminate himself when pressed to testify in civil cases.
Another 25 lawsuits naming Guevara remain pending.
Guevara is now one of the most notorious members of the Chicago Police Department, costing taxpayers more than any other officer, including former Cmdr. Jon Burge, who tortured and beat more than 100 Black men from the 1970s to the 1990s, city officials have acknowledged.
Records show that Guevara, who retired from CPD in 2005 and lives in Texas, collects an annual payout of $91,000 from the city’s depleted police pension fund.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Nomad art and design fair lands at Abu Dhabi’s Modernist former airport terminal
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Aimee Dawson
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The UAE is home to a trove of Modernist building designs thanks to the country’s founding in 1971 and the ensuing construction boom. One such building is the decommissioned Terminal 1 of Zayed International Airport, which was designed by the French architect Paul Andreu and opened in 1982. Now a designated heritage site, it is the unique venue for the Abu Dhabi edition of the itinerant art and design fair Nomad (18-22 November), which returns to the city for a second time in partnership with Abu Dhabi’s Department of Culture and Tourism.
“Architecture has always been fundamental to Nomad,” says the fair’s founder and director, Nicolas Bellavance‑Lecompte. “[Terminal 1] has a very particular architecture, but also a history as a place of movement and exchange. Rather than placing conventional booths inside it, we wanted to work with the building as we found it—its terminals, corridors, scale and different spatial conditions—and allow those qualities to become part of how the works are experienced.”
This year, the fair is expanding that mission with ambitious site-specific takeovers of four of the airport’s private terminals by Nilufar gallery, Gallery Fumi, Galerie Gastou and the jewellery advisory firm A2Z. There are 50 exhibitors taking part this year (compared with 40 last year) including local returning participants such as Leila Heller Gallery and the A/P Room as well as international spaces like Paris-based Galerie BSL, Milan’s Galleria Rossana Orlandi and Carpenters Workshop Gallery from London.
Highlights at the fair will include Maison Intègre’s bronze objects made using the ancient technique of lost wax, cast from recycled metal at its foundry in Burkina Faso; Seoul-based gallery Vein’s pairing of contemporary Korean practices with traditions including ottchil lacquer and mother-of-pearl inlay; and Polish design from Craftica Gallery.
Bellavance‑Lecompte says that jewellery will also be in the spotlight—as well as the 450 sq. m exhibition by A2Z, there will be presentations from the designers Studio Renn, Mattar jewellers and the gallery and advisory Ars Belga/Matthu-Boghossian. The Belgian jewellers Levuma will collaborate with the London gallery JCRD Design to bring together fine jewellery, diamonds and Brazilian design.
Another important development for Nomad this year is its expanded roster of institutions and non-profit initiatives on show in the old airport’s departure hall. Joining Irthi Contemporary Crafts Council—a Sharjah-based organisation that works with female artisans from the UAE and the wider Middle East, North Africa, South and Southeast Asia regions—which returns for this edition, is the recently established Design Commission Abu Dhabi and a collaborative presentation from the Institut du Monde Arabe (IMA) in Paris and House of Artisans, a cultural centre in Abu Dhabi that preserves traditional Emirati crafts. The project will bring together the French Sudanese fashion designer Abdel El Tayeb, who won the Confirmed Talent category of IMA’s 2024 Design Prize, and Emirati artisans to create a site-specific installation. “[This project] speaks to an idea at the heart of this edition: craft is a living practice, and something new can emerge when makers from different places work together,” Bellavance‑Lecompte says.
For Nomad’s inaugural Abu Dhabi edition, galleries reported sales exceeding $20m and many are “returning this year with more ambitious projects”, Bellavance‑Lecompte says. He expects that Abu Dhabi’s expanding cultural calendar and soon-to-open Guggenheim museum will bring more international collectors, curators and attention to the city and to Nomad. “Last year showed us that there is serious interest in collectable design, and this year we can build on those relationships,” he says.
• Nomad Abu Dhabi, Old Abu Dhabi Airport, 18-22 November

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Chuck Schumer Is Yesterday’s Man
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Jeet Heer
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Chuck Schumer Is Yesterday’s Man
The Senate Democratic leader just keeps showing why he needs to be replaced.
If you want to ruin a boisterous celebration, just hand over a microphone to Chuck Schumer. The Senate Democratic leader is the ultimate buzzkill, adept at deploying a droning voice that can turn giddy jubilation into existential dread.
November 3 was one of the happiest nights Democrats have known in decades, as the sheer size of the party’s victory in the midterm elections became apparent. After a decade of Trump dominating public life as standard-bearer of the Republican Party, here at last was proof that the public, even in red states such as Texas and South Carolina, were fed up. Beaten down as they were by frustration at the GOP pushing a hard-right agenda, Democrats could finally entertain the hopes of a better future.
But the brief remarks Schumer delivered that night were a reminder that Trump and the Republicans were only part of the problem the country faces. There’s also the disheartening fact that the Democrats are led by political dinosaurs who have no understanding of the urgency of the current moment.
Schumer is now facing a challenge for the post of Senate majority leader from Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen. Schumer’s election night speech offers clear evidence as to why Van Hollen deserves to win.
Schumer started with a question: “How did he win?” His answer: “First and foremost, we focused on American families and their pain and their needs, their suffering. They are not having a good life, and they are worried about the future for themselves and their children.” Schumer summed up the election as being about three issues: costs, chaos, and corruption.
What’s notable among this vague litany of complaints are all the issues left out that produced heated debate and no shortage of voter anger: the Iran War and its role in destabilizing the world economy, US support of Israel as a factor in the war, the rise of AI and data centers, and the outsize roles of tech plutocrats like Elon Musk in corrupting the political system.
Schumer expressed surprise that the Republicans “embraced Trump” and “followed Trump over the cliff as some of the time he talked about extraneous things that were ridiculous but much of the time he implemented things that raised their costs.” For most people, talking about “extraneous things” would not make the list of Trump’s thousand worst offenses, so it was puzzling why Schumer felt it necessary to highlight in a short victory speech.
Schumer ended his peroration with a puzzling metaphor: “The American people reduced the red brick wall to a pile of bricks.” As commentators such as Jon Stewart and Sam Seder pointed out, these words were more likely to generate confusion than inspiration. What exactly is the “red brick wall”? Further, walls are usually reduced to rubble, not a pile of bricks. If the bricks still exist, then the red wall can be rebuilt.
Seder rightly noted the absurdity of Schumer’s amazement at congressional Republicans’ loyalty to Trump, given that anyone who has been sentient for the last decade should have noticed that Trump easily won the GOP presidential nomination three times in a row and turned the party into his personal cult. There are few facts more obvious in American public life than that the Republican Party is completely subservient to Trump. But it’s a fact that Schumer still has a hard time accepting or acknowledging.
Partly, this is because Schumer is deeply committed to ancien régime restoration. He still seems to see Trump as a regrettable anomaly who will one day disappear and allow those most mythical creatures, the “reasonable Republicans,” to return. In this worldview, Democrats such as Schumer have to keep signaling they are ready to work with Republicans in order to hasten the return of normal politics. This is why Schumer can only talk about politics in the most abstract of terms (costs, chaos, and corruption) rather than specifying real areas of disagreement.
Schumer has been quite candid about this strategy. In March 2025, he caved in to Republicans during budget negotiations, making concessions that angered his fellow Democrats. Explaining his thinking in an interview with The New York Times, Schumer said his goal was to wait till Trump’s approval ratings have dropped below 40 percent:
And when he went below 40 percent in the polls, the Republican legislators started working with us. He was at 51. He’s now at 48. We’re gonna keep at it until he goes below 40. Look, I talk to a lot of these Republican legislators. I’ve worked with them. Some of them are Trump devotees. But many of them don’t like him, don’t respect him and worry about what he’s doing to our country. Right now he’s so popular they can’t resist him. I mean, so many of them came to me and said: “I don’t think Hegseth should be defense secretary or R.F.K. should be H.H.S. But Trump wants him. He won.” The Republicans would like to have some freedom from Trump, but they won’t until we bring him down in popularity. That happened with Bush in 2005. It happened with Trump in 2017. When it happens, I am hopeful that our Republican colleagues will resume working with us. And I talk to them. One of the places is in the gym. When you’re on that bike in your shorts, panting away next to a Republican, a lot of the inhibitions come off.
This theory of latent Republican moderation rests on nothing more than locker-room conviviality—hardly the basis for a meaningful political agenda. We will now have an empirical test to see if Schumer’s theory is correct. Trump’s approval ratings went below 40 percent in April and have generally stayed well under that threshold. The Republicans suffered a wipeout in the midterms. Yet there is no evidence that the GOP is moderating. In the wake of the midterm trouncing, House Republicans picked Jim Jordan, a hard-right Trump loyalist, as their new leader. The House held a vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who brought the motion to the floor, was the only Republican to vote for it. That near-total GOP opposition, and the fact that 11 Democrats failed to show up for the vote, was enough to kill the effort. Massie himself had been defeated earlier this year in the Republican primary and is leaving Congress.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Like many centrists, Schumer fashions himself as a realist. In truth, he’s a fantasist whose theory of politics rests on a world that no longer exists, if it ever did.
Beyond his fetishization of bipartisanship, Schumer’s substantive political commitments are also out of tune with the current urgent moment in politics. In an interview with The Nation, Senator Bernie Sanders listed three areas where Schumer is out of touch: Israel/Palestine, taxing the wealthy, and AI. Sanders described Schumer as someone who “a guy who wants to tinker around the edges” rather than fight for systematic change. In other words, Schumer is yesterday’s man, which is reason enough to support Chris Van Hollen as a replacement.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Has the couple in Jan van Eyck’s ‘Arnolfini Portrait’ been misidentified?
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: J.S. Marcus
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Jan van Eyck’s Arnolfini Portrait (1434) has been a signature work in London’s National Gallery since it arrived at the museum in 1842. A few key facts about the dual portrait, showing a youngish man and his idealised wife, could be gleaned just by looking at the work’s prominent Latin inscription, which translates as “Jan van Eyck was here 1434”. Over the years, just about everything else associated with the painting, from its mysterious room to the obscure occasion, has been open to debate, other than the surname of the man—Arnolfini, connected to an extended family of wealthy merchants from Lucca active in 15th-century Bruges, where Van Eyck had his studio.
Now, on the occasion of the National Gallery’s exhibition Van Eyck: The Portraits (21 November-11 April 2027), which brings together all nine of the artist’s surviving panel portraits, the Berlin-based curator Stephan Kemperdick, writing in a catalogue essay, has planted a possible bombshell by suggesting that the man in the Arnolfini Portrait is Van Eyck himself, and that the woman standing next to him is the artist’s wife Margaret, the sitter in another Van Eyck portrait from 1439, which is on loan to the show from Bruges.
Kemperdick’s theory, presented in recent talks but published now for the first time, is not an entirely new one. In the late 1840s, the National Gallery’s future first director Charles Eastlake contended that the artist’s inscription, which he thought could be translated as “Jan van Eyck was this [one]”, meant that the painting was also a dual portrait of the artist and his wife. But in the early 1860s, the British art historian W. H. James Weale interpreted a reference in a 16th-century inventory to a certain “hernoul le fin” in the painting, which he regarded as the French version of the Italian surname Arnolfini. The connection between the couple and that family was thus set in stone, though scholars disagree, often vehemently, about which particular member of the Arnolfini clan is shown.
Kemperdick has revisited the inscription, which is unusually large and conspicuously places the artist’s name next to the male figure’s head. He argues this indicates a direct connection between Van Eyck and the man. He has also reconsidered the association between the “hernoul le fin” reference and the surname Arnolfini. Citing the early-modern categorisation of the late-medieval work as not a portrait at all, but rather a lewd genre painting, Kemperdick suggests that “hernoul le fin” is not the correct surname of the sitter, but a subsequent and mocking moniker used by later generations to misidentify the man as a “a deceived cheat”. Kemperdick also suggests that a reference to St Margaret in the bedstead statue near the woman’s head serves to identify her as Van Eyck’s wife.
Multiple Arnolfini portraits
Kemperdick is the curator of German, Netherlandish and French Paintings before 1600 at the Berlin Gemäldegalerie, which is noted for its Early Netherlandish holdings and has in its own collection a Van Eyck portrait (around 1435-38) of the very same man who appears in the National Gallery’s Arnolfini Portrait. The two will be shown together in the London exhibition.
Nicholas Flory, the co-curator of Van Eyck: The Portraits along with Emma Capron, the National Gallery’s curator of early Netherlandish and German painting, says that he and Capron find Kemperdick’s theory “interesting” but “speculative”, citing, among other reasons, that the woman in the Bruges portrait, whom we know to be Margaret based on the inscription, has greyish-blue eyes while the woman in the Arnolfini Portrait has brown eyes.
Other leading Van Eyck scholars also have their doubts. The German art historian Till-Holger Borchert—now the director of the Suermondt-
Ludwig-Museum in Aachen and the former director of Musea Brugge in Bruges—is familiar with Kemperdick’s theory. “I’m not entirely sure I can concur,” he says. He thinks the early-16th-century inventory reference—associated with the painting’s owner at the time, Margaret of Austria, the governor of the Habsburg Netherlands—is a near iron-clad reference to the Arnolfinis. The Ghent University art historian Maximiliaan Martens, who has been involved in the lengthy restoration of Van Eyck’s Ghent Altarpiece, also “doesn’t see any reason to doubt” that the inventory reference is to the Arnolfinis.
The implications of Kemperdick’s theory are far-reaching. Another Van Eyck portrait at the National Gallery, from 1433, showing a much older man than the figure in the Arnolfini Portrait, is now tentatively identified by the London museum as a self-portrait. This, however, cannot be the case if Kemperdick’s theory is correct.
The exhibition Van Eyck: The Portraits will label the Berlin work with its previous and longstanding reference to the Arnolfinis, while the Gemäldegalerie, under Kemperick’s guidance, has recently renamed it Portrait of a Man with a Red Chaperon. And the debate about the couple promises to continue long after the show closes in April.
“I have thought for 30 years about this,” Martens says of the figures in the Arnolfini Portrait. He says he is still not sure if the man is Giovanni di Arrigo Arnolfini (who was apparently not married at the time the painting was made) or his cousin, Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini (whose wife had died before the painting was made).
Other aspects of the dual portrait that scholars continue to debate include whether the heavy-bellied woman is actually pregnant (Kemperdick and Martens think that may be possible, while Flory and Capron think she is just gathering up her heavy skirts), and whether the room itself is a real space or an imagined one (imagined, say Flory and Capron; real, says Martens).
Beyond who made it and when, the Arnolfini Portrait remains a mystery, which is in keeping for an artist whose date and place of birth, among other foundational knowledge, is also speculation. Asked to comment on the enigma associated with the Arnolfini Portrait, Borchert says: “Can you tell me anything about Van Eyck that isn’t enigmatic?”

https://citylimits.org/nueva-norma-feder.title: Nueva norma federal pone en peligro vivienda de miles de familias neoyorquinas con situaciones migratorias mixtas
https://citylimits.org/nueva-norma-feder.author: Daniel Parra
https://citylimits.org/nueva-norma-feder.text:
Share This Article
Los defensores de la vivienda afirman que tienen la intención de oponerse a la aplicación de la normativa del Departamento de Vivienda y Desarrollo Urbano de Estados Unidos (HUD por sus siglas en inglés), que, según ellos, podría obligar a unos 2.500 hogares neoyorquinos a renunciar a las ayudas federales para la vivienda o a separarse de sus familias.
Este artículo se publicó originalmente en inglés el 16 de noviembre. Traducido por Daniel Parra. Read the English version here.
El 10 de noviembre, el Departamento de Vivienda y Desarrollo Urbano de los Estados Unidos (HUD por sus siglas en inglés) publicó una norma que exige a los hogares que residen en viviendas públicas financiadas con fondos federales que acrediten su ciudadanía, lo que podría afectar a miles de familias con situaciones migratorias mixtas.
La nueva norma, que se propuso a principios de este año y entraría en vigor el 14 de diciembre, endurece los requisitos de acceso a las ayudas federales para el alquiler, especialmente para los inmigrantes.
Actualmente, los inmigrantes indocumentados no pueden optar a las ayudas federales para la vivienda. Sin embargo, se les permite vivir en viviendas subvencionadas con fondos federales —como los edificios de la Autoridad de Vivienda de la Ciudad de Nueva York (NYCHA por sus siglas en inglés)— junto con otros miembros de la familia que cumplan los requisitos, en lo que se denomina hogares de “estatus mixto”.
Estos hogares pagan un porcentaje más alto del alquiler para compensar la presencia del miembro de la familia que no cumple los requisitos, y reciben lo que se conoce como “una tarifa prorrateada” (prorated assistance).
Según la nueva normativa, todos los miembros de un hogar que reciba ayudas federales para el alquiler —incluidos aquellos con vales de la Sección 8 o que vivan en viviendas públicas de la Sección 9— deberán probar su ciudadanía o un estatus migratorio que les dé derecho a recibir subvenciones federales, tal y como se establece en la normativa federal denominada Sección 214.
Incluso los inmigrantes que se encuentran legalmente en Estados Unidos podrían verse afectados por ese requisito, según los expertos.
“Las personas pueden estar en Estados Unidos de forma legal, pero no por ello tienen necesariamente derecho a la ayuda para el alquiler en virtud de la Sección 214”, explicó Lucy Newman, abogada supervisora de la unidad de vivienda pública de Legal Aid Society, y añadió: “esa es una parte realmente importante de todo esto”.
Entre los estatus migratorios que dan derecho a recibir ayudas federales para la vivienda se incluyen los residentes permanentes, asilados o refugiados, supervivientes de la trata de personas, solicitantes en virtud de la Ley contra la Violencia hacia las Mujeres e inmigrantes admitidos para recibir asistencia temporal legal, entre otros.
Entre los estatus migratorios que no dan derecho a estas ayudas se incluyen los titulares de visas U, beneficiarios del programa DACA, TPS e inmigrantes indocumentados.
Newman explicó que en promedio tres de cada cuatro miembros de los hogares de estatus mixto de la ciudad de Nueva York tienen un estatus migratorio que les da derecho a recibir ayuda federal, y advirtió que la nueva norma podría provocar que esos miembros con derecho a la ayuda se muden o les obligue a separarse de sus seres queridos.
Una coalición de 22 fiscales generales estatales, entre ellos el de Nueva York, envió en abril una carta al secretario del HUD, Scott Turner, oponiéndose al cambio normativo que afectaría a 2.500 hogares con estatus mixto en Nueva York.
“Nosotros y otros activistas estamos trabajando para retrasar o detener la aplicación de esta medida, lo que incluye plantearnos emprender acciones legales”, afirmó Newman.
Los comentarios públicos presentados en contra de la norma argumentaban que es innecesaria porque los miembros del hogar que no cumplen los requisitos no reciben subsidios federales, y que desplazaría a algunos hogares sin liberar ayudas para otros.
“En realidad, resulta más caro financiar a los hogares que cumplen todos los requisitos, ya que la ayuda tiene que cubrir a todas las personas de ese hogar”, explicó Newman. “Si esta norma entra en vigor, la situación general será que se acabará ayudando a menos personas porque el programa costará más”.
“En realidad, resulta más caro subvencionar a los hogares que cumplen todos los requisitos, ya que la ayuda tiene que cubrir a todas las personas de ese hogar”, explicó Newman. “Si esta norma entra en vigor, la situación general es que acabarán ayudando a menos personas porque el programa costará más”.
Según el Center for Budget and Policy Priorities, un grupo de análisis político no partidista, casi 80,000 personas de 20,000 hogares de todo el país podrían correr el riesgo de perder sus viviendas; el 96 por ciento son personas de color, de las cuales el 86 por ciento son latinas.
Después de California y Texas, el estado de Nueva York es el tercero con mayor número de hogares de estatus mixto en viviendas públicas.
NYCHA, que gestiona un programa de la Sección 8, así como conjuntos de vivienda pública de la Sección 9, no respondió de inmediato a una solicitud de comentarios sobre el cambio normativo. El Departamento de Conservación y Desarrollo de la Vivienda de la ciudad, que también gestiona la Sección 8 a nivel local, remitió las preguntas a la oficina del alcalde.
En una declaración a City Limits, el alcalde Zohran Mamdani expresó su oposición a la norma, al tiempo que tranquilizó a los neoyorquinos que reciben ayudas federales para la vivienda asegurándoles que el anuncio de la semana pasada no supondrá un cambio inmediato en su subsidio.
“En la ciudad de Nueva York, creemos que todo el mundo merece un lugar seguro y asequible al que llamar hogar, independientemente de dónde haya nacido o de su situación migratoria”, afirmó Mamdani. “La ciudad está evaluando todas las opciones disponibles para defender a los neoyorquinos y proteger su acceso a la vivienda. Porque nadie debería vivir con el miedo de perder su hogar por el lugar de donde proviene”.
La División de Vivienda y Renovación Comunitaria del estado de Nueva York (DHCR por sus siglas en inglés), que forma parte del Departamento de Vivienda y Renovación Comunitaria de Nueva York y supervisa algunos programas de la Sección 8, afirmó que “seguirá analizando el posible impacto de estos cambios propuestos”.
En una entrevista con FOX, el secretario del HUD, Turner, se refirió a la norma como el cierre de una “brecha legal que llevaba décadas existiendo”.
“Estamos poniendo fin a las subvenciones destinadas a las fronteras abiertas de Biden, defendiendo el estado de derecho, cerrando la brecha legal de décadas de antigüedad relativa a los ‘compañeros de piso con estatus mixto’ y protegiendo el dinero de los contribuyentes estadounidenses”, declaró un portavoz del HUD en un comunicado a City Limits, señalando que el cambio liberará $218 millones en subvenciones para “hogares estadounidenses que cumplan todos los requisitos”.
Sin embargo, los defensores de la vivienda señalan que, en la actualidad, no se ofrecen ayudas a las personas que no cumplen los requisitos para acceder al programa.
“Las familias con estatus mixto subvencionan las viviendas del HUD para el resto de personas”, afirmó Marie Claire Tran-Leung, directora del Proyecto de Iniciativa contra los Desahucios y abogada responsable del Proyecto Nacional de Derecho de la Vivienda.
«Si estas familias se ven obligadas a marcharse, habrá menos fondos disponibles para las viviendas subvencionadas por el HUD, lo que reducirá la oferta de viviendas y agravará la crisis de la vivienda para todos”, añadió Tran-Leung. “Esto es especialmente importante en un lugar como Nueva York, donde existe sin duda una escasez de viviendas y, sobre todo, una escasez de viviendas asequibles”.
No obstante, tanto ella como otros defensores de la vivienda instan a la gente a tener paciencia y a mantener la calma.
“Existe el riesgo de que las familias se autoexpulsen en este momento, a pesar de que tienen derecho a quedarse donde están”, subrayó Tran-Leung. “Aún no tienen que marcharse hasta que esta norma entre en vigor, y los defensores están tratando de idear o impulsar diferentes vías para bloquear o retrasar esa fecha de entrada en vigor”.
Los abogados en vivienda explicaron que, a partir del 14 de diciembre, en caso de que la norma entre en vigor, los inquilinos dispondrían de 90 días para demostrar su situación migratoria. Incluso si una autoridad de vivienda decide que alguien no cumple los requisitos, subrayaron los defensores, los residentes siguen teniendo derecho a un debido proceso con las garantías debidas.
“Eso es otra cosa que queremos destacar: se supone que debe haber un proceso, por lo que no debería ser algo que ocurra de la noche a la mañana”, explicó Tran-Leung.
Los defensores relacionaron el cambio normativo con la agresiva campaña de la administración Trump contra la inmigración. El HUD intentó impulsar una política similar en 2019, durante el primer mandato del presidente Donald Trump, pero el presidente Joe Biden la retiró posteriormente.
“Lo que vemos es cómo Trump y el HUD se aprovechan de las crisis económicas para destruir los programas federales de vivienda, sembrando la división y convirtiendo a los inmigrantes en chivos expiatorios”, afirmó Tran-Leung.
Otra consecuencia de la norma, explicó Newman, es una menor estabilidad para los inmigrantes que están a punto de obtener la regularización.
“Hemos tenido clientes que, tras un periodo de 18 meses, ahora son titulares de la tarjeta verde”, señaló. “Hay muchas personas que viven en esos hogares y que podrían regularizar su situación migratoria en un futuro próximo”.
Por ahora, sin embargo, según Newman, “la gente debe saber que, hasta que entre en vigor, nada ha cambiado. No deben mudarse ni ser desahuciados por miedo”.

https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-is-fed-.title: New York Is Fed Up With Chuck Schumer
https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-is-fed-.author: Holly Pretsky
https://hellgatenyc.com/new-york-is-fed-.text:
When did New York voters begin to turn on their five-term U.S. Senator Chuck Schumer? 
Was it when he squandered Democratic leverage to hash out a deal to avoid a government shutdown last year? (Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez called that move a "betrayal.")
Or perhaps it was his April vote, along with just six other Democrats, to continue sending military bulldozers to Israel, at a moment when Americans are increasingly fed up with Israel's war in Gaza.
Maybe they thought Schumer had lost touch with reality when he refused to endorse Zohran Mamdani last year, a decision that was echoed in his failure to recognize other progressive juggernauts across the country before the 2026 midterms.
Or perhaps Schumer's appeal has been steadily ebbing for years, as his longstanding coziness with Wall Street feels wildly out of step at a time of surging economic populism and anger at a "rigged system." Schumer's daughters' employment at Facebook, Amazon, and, no kidding, OpenAI, certainly looks corrupt.
Whatever love we once felt for the avuncular retail politician known for his annual visits to each of New York's 62 counties, his high school graduation speeches, and his parade grand marshaling, New York is over it. 
In his home state, his job approval rating bottomed out at 27 percent in February, according to Marist. A more recent Quinnipiac survey had him at 36 percent, but still underwater with 54 percent of New Yorkers polled disapproving of the job he's doing. "Poll after poll suggests that the American people want real change," Senator Bernie Sanders said at a recent press conference with Senator Elissa Slotkin as they called for new Senate leadership. We reached out to Schumer's team to run all this by them, and we'll update this story if they respond.

https://hellgatenyc.com/menin-speech-con.title: This Wasn't on Julie Menin's Public Schedule
https://hellgatenyc.com/menin-speech-con.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/menin-speech-con.text:
When bigots began making Islamophobic demands that Mayor Zohran Mamdani stay away from the 9/11 commemoration events, City Council Speaker Julie Menin rose to his defense, calling the insults "absolutely inappropriate." And when Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu accused the mayor of being an antisemite who supports terrorists, Menin suggested Netanyahu's rhetoric was dangerous: "This idea of what the prime minister said can really incite violence. We cannot have this."
But on Monday afternoon, Speaker Menin lent her credibility to a forum that was honoring people who have spent the last several years trading in Islamophobia and anti-Palestinian rhetoric. The event was not included on Menin's public schedule emailed to the City Hall press corps.
Speaker Menin was given headliner treatment at Touro University's annual antisemitism symposium, alongside actor Debra Messing, who said she didn't vote for Zohran Mamdani in the 2025 mayoral primary because he "celebrated 9/11" and who spent Election Day 2025 re-sharing numerous Islamophobic memes that referred to Mamdani as an "actual communist jihadist" and stated that Muslims are "commanded to lie if it means spreading Islam." Messing spoke towards the end of the event, and also received an award. (As did singer and MAGA donor Gloria Gaynor.)
Another speaker at this year's symposium: Mort Klein, the national president of the Zionist Organization of America, who has proudly used the slur "filthy Arab," praised President Donald Trump's plans to level Gaza, and called Mamdani a "Jew-hater."
While New York City's political leaders who marched in this year's Israel Day Parade—including Speaker Menin—rushed to condemn the presence of Israeli finance minister Bezalel Smotrich, Klein defended him. Smotrich has called for the "total annihilation" of Palestinian cities in Gaza.

https://citylimits.org/federal-cuts-coul.title: Federal Cuts Could Threaten HIV Prevention, as Latinos Make Up 41% of New Diagnoses in NYC
https://citylimits.org/federal-cuts-coul.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/federal-cuts-coul.text:
Share This Article
“We are invisible when it comes to understanding the challenges related to many health issues. And when we talk about HIV, it is even more alarming,” said Guillermo Chacón, president of the Latino Commission on AIDS.
Funding cuts to HIV prevention programs could make it harder for Latino New Yorkers—who are already disproportionately impacted by the virus—to access testing, treatment and other essential health services, health advocates warn.
The concerns were raised at a press conference last month ahead of National Latino AIDS Awareness Day. This year’s theme, “Knowing Your HIV Status Is a Good Place to Start,” focused on the importance of testing as the first step toward prevention, treatment and care.
Attendees—a mix of elected officials, public health advocates and Latino leaders—also called for greater access to health services and efforts to reduce the stigma that prevents people from seeking care.
“There has been so much stigma in our communities,” City Councilmember Alexa Aviles, who represents Brooklyn’s Sunset Park, said during the event. “This is an epidemic that we have made so much progress in, and yet still Latinos are disproportionately impacted.”
According to the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene’s 2024 HIV Surveillance Report, released in December 2025, the city recorded 1,791 new HIV diagnoses in 2024—up 5.4 percent from the year prior.
Latino residents accounted for 41 percent of those cases, despite making up approximately 30 percent of the city’s population.
For Guillermo Chacón, president of the Latino Commission on AIDS, the numbers reflect deeper structural problems in how public health institutions address the needs of Latino communities.
“We are invisible when it comes to understanding the challenges related to many health issues. And when we talk about HIV, it is even more alarming,” he told City Limits.
Chacón, who has worked with the organization for 32 years, said one of the main challenges is that public health systems often approach health disparities through racial categories, overlooking the specific needs of Latino communities.
He also pointed to barriers affecting immigrants who may struggle to navigate the U.S. health care system, particularly when it comes to sexual health education and access to prevention tools such as pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, which helps prevent HIV infection.
He described how even a negative interaction with clinic staff can discourage someone from returning for care. Limited operating hours can create another barrier for people who work during the day. “If people are working Monday through Friday, it is not going to work. You have to offer services at night and on weekends,” he said.
Those challenges are unfolding as federal funding for HIV prevention faces potential reductions.
Congress funded the Centers for Disease Control’s domestic HIV prevention program at $755.6 million for fiscal year 2026, according to the HIV Medicine Association. The Trump administration’s 2027 budget request would eliminate that core funding, keeping only $220 million for the Ending the HIV Epidemic initiative, and the House Appropriations Committee’s spending bill includes no money for the account.
Fiscal year 2027 began Oct. 1, but Congress has not passed a full-year health spending bill. A stopgap measure signed Sept. 2 keeps funding at 2026 levels through Dec. 11, and the Senate has yet to act. Meanwhile, the Kaiser Family Foundation reports the CDC is ending its direct, five-year grants to community-based organizations—$239.3 million nationwide—and sending supplemental money to health departments instead.
Chacón pointed to a recent three-year contract renewal for the Latino Commission on AIDS’ religious leadership program, which works with churches to provide health education and connect congregations with testing and other resources. Despite securing the contract, the organization faced a 60 percent funding reduction.
New York City’s Health Department warned last year that cuts to Medicaid, and stricter eligibility rules for Medicaid recipients that take effect in January, further threaten the city’s prevention progress. Medicaid is the largest source of insurance coverage for people with HIV in the country, according to the Kaiser Family Foundation.
On the local level, the Health Department says a new program aims to widen access.
“Hook Up and Bridge,” which began this fall, funds 26 clinical and community organizations to provide HIV and sexual health services directly or through referrals.
“Latino communities are among the most affected by HIV in New York City,” Sarah Braunstein, assistant commissioner of the department’s Bureau of Hepatitis, HIV and STIs, told City Limits.
Many groups funded through the new initiative have long served Latino New Yorkers by offering Spanish-speaking staff who are “trusted messengers.” Specific outreach plans are still being developed, she said.
Beyond testing and treatment, the initiative is meant to be a touchpoint for broader needs, according to the department. Braunstein said the program is open about sexual health, with providers trained to take sexual histories in an “affirming, open, stigma-free” way.
For Chacón, addressing the epidemic requires stronger partnerships among government agencies, nonprofits and communities, as well as confronting the stigma that keeps people away from care.
“The stigma, for me, is the fundamental obstacle to making a difference,” he said.

https://hellgatenyc.com/bk-dems-chair-ti.title: No One—Not Even the Judge—Knows Who Runs the Brooklyn Dems Right Now
https://hellgatenyc.com/bk-dems-chair-ti.author: Jessy Edwards
https://hellgatenyc.com/bk-dems-chair-ti.text:
After a series of unfavorable court rulings for the Brooklyn Democratic Party's old guard that found their various attempts to cling to power were unlawful, certain members may have wished they could turn back the hands of time.
In retrospect, perhaps they wouldn't have invited people who lost their elections to vote on their "power-grab" rule changes—a move the court deemed illegal. Maybe they wouldn't have held a Sunday night Zoom meeting to "elect" Assemblymember Nikki Lucas as party chair—a move the court deemed illegal. And maybe they wouldn't have made the fatal error of accidentally leaving a candidate for county committee chair off their slate—allowing their sworn enemy, Congressmember Nydia Velázquez, to lead the party as interim chair. 
But just as party reformists thought they were moving forward towards electing district leader Julio Peña III as their new chosen chair, a time portal has indeed opened—not from the driver's seat of a DeLorean, but rather through a peculiarity in Brooklyn Supreme Court Judge Peter Sweeney's most recent ruling.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: A TikTok superstar bares all: Siorna Ashby’s best shot
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Interview by Imogen Tilden
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
I met Meg at a nude life-drawing class. I was struck by how free she seemed and how powerfully that came through in her modelling. I asked if I could photograph her for my project Body Like Mine. This series explores the difference between how our bodies are perceived externally and how we experience them ourselves. We see a body and we bring our own judgments and assumptions on to it, but the lived experience is very different.
Rather than portraying an idealised body, the project aims to explore what it feels like to inhabit your own body, and to see it as worthy of attention without asking it to become anything else first.
My photography is collaborative. I brought some visual ideas to the shoot, and Meg brought her own ways of moving and expressing herself. The photograph developed between us. I took references from art history: Jenny Saville’s nudes and Lucian Freud’s work have inspired me, along with the sense of flesh and physical presence in Rubens’ paintings.
I lit her in a painterly way and used a canvas backdrop. As I was photographing her, I found myself getting lower down. I wanted the body to have a real presence in the photograph, to become the portrait itself. It was Meg’s idea to scrunch her belly in that way. I asked her to look away so that her face wouldn’t be the first place your eye went. I love how fleshy the image feels. Portraits often rely on the face and eyes to communicate who someone is. Here, I wanted to explore how much of Meg’s presence and personality could come through her body and gesture.
Meg loved it and was delighted when the image was selected to be displayed in the National Portrait Gallery. Her nude modelling is only a small part of what she does – most of her time and energies go into raising awareness about overconsumption and the “tat” that fills our lives and ends up in landfill. She’s a superstar on TikTok!
“Fat women’s femininity is [often] stripped from them and … I am masculinised and called brave for just existing in this body. When I am life modelling, I feel the most feminine and deeply in touch with myself. I am proud to take up space and represent people who often are not,” she says.
My commissioned work specialises in boudoir and nude photography. Coming to this has been a personal journey. I was very critical of my body – I was one of those women who couldn’t look in a mirror. For me, being behind the camera was also a way of avoiding being in photographs. I liked having that control. I started out doing headshots, but when you run your own business, you need to be visible. I became frustrated with all the negative feelings I had about myself, and one day I stripped off and I took my own photographs of my nude body. And when I looked over the images I was shocked to realise that I didn’t hate them. In fact I thought they were beautiful.
And then I noticed a change in myself. I was walking down the street taller. I wasn’t wearing cardigans to hide my arms. And I realised that maybe I can help others. I don’t think a photograph can resolve someone’s relationship with their body, but it can be one part of seeing themselves differently, feeling more connected to their body, or recognising that they are worthy of being seen.
But there is a tension in my work between beauty standards and how women want to be seen. Much of the boudoir photography I do sits in that culture that shapes how women think they should look and what makes a body beautiful or desirable. But who decides what makes a body either of these things? Women’s bodies don’t exist to meet someone else’s expectations of beauty or desirability, which change over time. There is room for wanting to feel sexy, but whose idea of sexy are we working towards?
When I make or look at a nude photograph, I ask what the pose, light, colour and composition are communicating. Whose perspective is shaping the image, and how much say does the person being photographed have in how they are seen?
With Body Like Mine, I want to give more space to people’s own accounts of living in their bodies, particularly where those experiences differ from what others assume when they look at them. The next person I’m photographing lives with endometriosis, and another participant is experiencing memory loss. I want us to explore how those experiences might be expressed in a photograph, guided by what each person wants to share.
Before we photograph, I ask each person to choose a few words that describe what they would like us to express together. Those words give us a starting point for the images. Meg’s were “real”, “joyful” and “free”.
Body Like Mine is part of the Winston Taylor photo portrait prize exhibition at the National Portrait Gallery, London, until 17 January. siornaphotography.com; @siornaphotography
Siorna Ashby CV
Born: Blackpool, 1983
 
High point: Having my photograph of Meg Foster, Body Like Mine, selected for the National Portrait Gallery’s Winston Taylor photo portrait prize 2026 exhibition.
 
Top tip: Talk through boundaries before artistic nude or boudoir photoshoots, and keep checking in as you work. Make it easy for someone to change their mind, and be ready to adapt a pose, change direction or put the camera down.

https://gothamist.com/news/owner-of-pean.title: Owner of Peanut, scandalously slain NY squirrel, charged with upstate mortgage fraud
https://gothamist.com/news/owner-of-pean.author: Jon Campbell
https://gothamist.com/news/owner-of-pean.text:
The outspoken owner of an internet-famous squirrel was arrested Wednesday on fraud charges connected to the animal sanctuary he founded and named after his pet before it was euthanized by New York officials.
Mark Longo, 36, who gained notoriety for his viral videos with the squirrel, Peanut, was arraigned on charges including residential mortgage fraud and second-degree grand larceny in the Southport Town Court near the Pennsylvania border. He pleaded not guilty, according to New York State Police.
Longo built up a following of hundreds of thousands of social-media users by documenting Peanut’s wacky antics. In the closing days of the 2024 presidential race, New York authorities obtained a warrant to seize the critter and a raccoon, which are considered wildlife that can’t legally be kept as pets. The squirrel then bit an officer — and protocol called for it to be euthanized, decapitated and tested for rabies, which came back negative.
The episode became a cause célèbre for JD Vance, Elon Musk and other MAGA supporters while causing an outcry and a wave of violent threats that sent shockwaves through the state Department of Environmental Conservation, Gothamist previously reported.
At the time, state authorities said Longo did not have the proper license to care for a squirrel and a raccoon. Longo was not charged in connection with the incident.
But in recent weeks, Longo and his wife, Daniela Bittner, have both found themselves accused of being on the wrong side of the law.
Along with Longo’s arrest Wednesday, Bittner — who is originally from Germany — was detained by federal immigration authorities in mid-October and is facing possible deportation, according to the Associated Press. Longo has blamed her detention on a paperwork snafu.
On Wednesday, state police accused Longo of using fake pay stubs, letters and application documents to get a $720,000 mortgage. That amount matches the mortgage Longo and two associates received in 2023 for a Chemung County property that became the 311-acre P’Nut’s Freedom Farm Animal Sanctuary.
Longo did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Peanut’s death led to hundreds of threats against the state DEC and its top officials, with at least 10 buildings temporarily closing down due to bomb threats.
Among those who left violent voicemails, one man said he wanted to see DEC agents “laying dead in the f—ing street.” Another called for the agents involved in the search to be executed on live television.
As a result, the DEC’s entire workforce of about 3,000 employees was permitted to work remotely for a few days. The agency also pulled back on certain public-facing operations, including so-called deer checks along major thoroughfares to weed out poachers, Gothamist reported last year.
State police say they began their fraud investigation of Longo in December 2024, not long after Peanut’s seizure. The agency says it “received information about financial irregularities involving Longo” then, according to a news release.
In all, Longo faces 14 criminal counts ranging from mortgage fraud and grand larceny — both Class C felonies — to falsifying business records, a lower class E felony. He was released on his own recognizance and is scheduled to return to court in February, police said.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: MTA Drivers Taking 50 Sick Days a Year May Be to Blame For Your Canceled Bus
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Jose Martinez
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Close to 1,000 bus operators call out sick in excess of 50 days a year, MTA officials said Wednesday, charging that no-show “bad apples” have left riders hanging on nearly 120,000 trips this year alone.
“Don’t milk the city and state and regional taxpayer so you can sit at home or go to Florida or whatever,” Janno Lieber, MTA chairperson and chief executive, said in response to a question from The City Reporter.
The striking numbers surfaced during a budget presentation at the transportation authority’s monthly board meeting, with Lieber challenging what he described as a “small outlier” of absentee employees to “go find another job.”
Just under one in 10 bus operators take more than 50 paid sick days a year — with limited consequences because of a difficult disciplinary process, Lieber said.
Those days add up to a lot of cancelled trips — and taxpayer money. The MTA said it loses $20 million for every day in lost productivity across its entire workforce.
MTA Chief Financial Officer Jai Patel outlined how most employees are expected to be available for service 227 days a year out of 261 potential workdays.
“In reality, the latest data puts us at about 201 days, with about 19 sick days taken and another seven for workers’ comp and other reasons,” she said.
MTA data shows that as recently as 2013, the number of productive days per employee had climbed as high as 207. That number plummeted to 193 during the COVID-scarred year of 2020, when transit ridership plummeted during the pandemic even as workers kept the subways and buses running.
Officials said the frequent use of sick days comes with a high cost for commuters and the MTA’s finances, citing how the transportation authority has to rely on overtime and reserve bus operators to fill shifts.
But Patel said that some bus operators are “basically whole again” by taking an overtime shift that makes up for sick days.
“We’ve seen that persistently in sort of the bad actors in that sick-leave policy,” she said.
The absentee issue is especially acute among the MTA’s nearly 13,000 bus operators, who make up the largest single group of workers at the transit agency.
“Many of them are doing the right thing and showing up to work day in and day out,” Lieber said. “But about a thousand of the operators are taking a significant number of sick days, over 50 days per year.”
That has amounted to 118,000 canceled trips so far this year, he added, because “there was no bus operator available to drive the bus.”
“It burns everybody else who’s showing up to work,” Lieber said.
Transport Workers Union Local 100, which represents the largest number of MTA bus drivers, declined to comment through a spokesperson. The union is in the midst of contract negotiations with the MTA.
“We are working hard to get the TWU contract settled,” Lieber said. “I think we are making progress and I’m not ready to say anything more specific than that, but that is very much a priority.”
The grumbling over canceled bus trips came after the MTA had to contend in recent years with hundreds of operator vacancies that stemmed from retirements, a pre-pandemic hiring freeze and worker deaths. To fill the shortfall, the transportation authority in 2021 began a hiring spree.
MTA Board Member Marc Herbst said he was “shocked” by the high sick-leave numbers.
“If I had a job where I only had to show up four days a week and not even include vacation and personal time, that’s unbelievable,” he said.
The head of an organization that advocates for MTA express bus riders said those who travel between the boroughs and Manhattan are subjected to more crowded carriages and getting pinched in the wallet as a result of driver absences.
“Some people work at odd hours when the express bus may run only hourly,” said Vittorio Bugatti, founder of the Express Bus Advocacy Group. “For those people working at night and heading to Manhattan, they may be forced to take an expensive Uber if they live somewhere where there literally is no alternative like a subway.”
Lieber said it’s very difficult to discipline or fire workers who frequently call out sick. He blamed “too many roadblocks” in the disciplinary process against absentee bus drivers for the low worker-availability rates, saying it’s “really hard to get those people out the door.”
“We need to cut through all that and have a short, predictable disciplinary process,” he said. “It will be fair for them because they will hopefully get the message and come to work.”
“Or they can go get work at another place, they’re not ready to work at the MTA,” Lieber added. “Go find another job.”

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/18/s.title: Sean Duffy’s DOT Pitches Congestion Pricing Grants While Trying to Kill Congestion Pricing
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/18/s.author: Dave Colon
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/18/s.text:
So now U.S. DOT Secretary Sean Duffy says congestion pricing is just fine, a complete 180 from what the Trump administration had been saying for more than six years. The Streetsblog Photoshop Desk
President Trump and Secretary Sean Duffy’s Department of Transportation, which has spent two years trying to kill New York City’s congestion pricing program, has exciting news for cities across America: They can apply for grants to launch their own congestion pricing programs.
A triumphant press release from the Federal Highway Administration on Wednesday announced that cities can apply for $100 million in grants for a number of programs that reduce congestion including “HOV toll lanes, as well as congestion, cordon, and parking pricing programs” (emphasis added).
Trump and Duffy have famously warred with the MTA and the Empire State over New York City’s congestion pricing program, which has reduced the number of vehicles in the Manhattan core and provided a reliable revenue stream to fund capital work on the city’s mass transit system.
The federal agency’s reversal clearly surprised MTA Chairman and CEO Janno Lieber. On Wednesday, he interrupted an ongoing press conference after his agency’s monthly board meeting to acknowledge the email and wonder aloud why the FHWA wants more congestion pricing programs around the country.
“Either they’ve been hacked, or Sean Duffy’s been reading the press on this subject, but either way, that’s a pretty remarkable about-face,” said Lieber. “I think it really speaks to the fact that this program has not only survived legally but has been such a success in its implementation.”
The MTA boss was magnanimous in the face of the somewhat maddening news that the proudly anti-congestion pricing administration is now promoting congestion pricing, even as the MTA continues to defend the toll in court from Duffy’s and the president’s campaign to kill it for good.
“In the long run, the fact that the program has been successfully implemented, and the legal fight about it, has been part of making sure the world understands how successful and effective it has been, is actually a net benefit to those of us who believe this kind of initiative is worth the candle,” he said.
After cutting vehicle entries into Manhattan south of 60th Street by 11 percent in its first year, the toll has continued to reduce vehicle entries into Manhattan’s central business district. In 2026, fewer than 500,000 vehicles on average entered lower Manhattan during every month but October, compared to five months that averaged more than 500,000 daily vehicle entries into the Manhattan CBD in 2025.
New York City’s economy has not fallen apart. Furthermore, the MTA has successfully defended the traffic toll in six separate federal lawsuits in the Southern District of New York, two in New Jersey and one state-level lawsuit in New York.
Of course, U.S. DOT is bound by law to offer states and cities the chance to apply for projects to reduce congestion through congestion pricing or cordon pricing. But the law does require Duffy and his agency to award grants for traffic tolls. He and U.S. DOT are free to spend all of their time and money on the other traffic-reduction strategies mentioned in the press release, such as traffic monitoring and on-demand micro-transit.
Still, as long as the federal transportation agency is mentioning cordon pricing, it is as good time as any to remind longtime readers that Duffy pronounces the word “cordon” in a weird way — as cor-DON — which really set off this reporter in early 2025.
Dave Colon is a reporter from Long Beach, a barrier island off of the coast of Long Island that you can bike to from the city. It’s a real nice ride. He’s previously been the editor of Brokelyn, a reporter at Gothamist, a freelance reporter and delivered freshly baked bread by bike.
"The NYPD will be able to continue to use bicycles as a form of transit," Mamdani said at a press conference about his disbanding of the NYPD's Strategic Response Group. "And what we’ve made very clear is a limitation on the use of bicycles as a weapon or form of aggression.”

Art Bridges has announced that it will give $9.5 million to extend its Access For All Initiative, which has helped 64 museums across the US to offer free admission and community-based programming. The original funding happened over the course of a three-year evaluation period. The evaluation was a success: Art Bridges found that museums were able to attract a “more local, loyal and diverse visitor community,” according to a press release. The support will help 61 of the original 64 museums and will fund the program through 2029.
Attendance at Access for All programs grew by more than a tenth of a percent from the first year to the second, according to the evaluation. Museums that moved towards a free admission model saw a 22% increase on average in attendance. Surveyed program attendees reported declines in barriers to visiting. Lack of time fell from 46% in Year 1 to 27% in Year 3; financial barriers from 28% to 12%; and lack of awareness from 27% to 11%. The Whitney Museum, one of the participants in the initiative, had 67,000 visitors last year for its free Second Sundays, more than double the museum’s usual Sunday attendance.
The Access For All Initiative began in 2024, with $40 million towards museums in 36 states and Puerto Rico. “The strategy behind the second tranche of funding was to give our organizations an off-ramp, so that they could sustain this beyond Art Bridges’s support,” Art Bridges CEO Anne Kraybill said in an interview with ARTnews, adding that “anytime you take something away, it can be hard for the community to understand why. Our initial three-year investment was the proof of concept that a lot of these organizations needed for their local philanthropists to come along.”

https://gothamist.com/news/city-to-demol.title: City to demolish Brooklyn building damaged in deadly Flatbush collapse
https://gothamist.com/news/city-to-demol.author: Phil Corso
https://gothamist.com/news/city-to-demol.text:
New York City officials say they will demolish a Brooklyn apartment building that was severely damaged in last week's collapse of a neighboring building that killed eight people.
The Department of Buildings announced on Wednesday that engineers determined the building at 1323 Flatbush Ave. is too unstable to repair safely. The building was heavily damaged when the apartment building next door, 1321 Flatbush Ave., collapsed into an adjacent construction site on Wednesday, Nov. 11.
“Given the dangerous condition of the building and the imperative to make sure no one else gets hurt, ordering for the controlled safe demolition of the building is the only available option,” Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said in a statement.
The department said the building's condition has continued to deteriorate since the collapse, leaving its interior exposed to the elements. Engineers determined that allowing workers inside to install supports would put them at risk.
Officials said tenants also cannot return to retrieve their belongings because of unstable floors and asbestos contamination.
The city has since established a fenced-off safety zone around the building and plans to reinforce the neighboring property at 1325 Flatbush Ave. before demolition begins, officials said.
The cause of the deadly collapse remains under investigation, authorities said.
The Department of Buildings is also inspecting more than 160 construction sites associated with companies and individuals involved in the adjacent development project.
City officials said displaced tenants are receiving hotel accommodations through the American Red Cross through at least the end of November.
