https://jacobin.com/2026/11/jeffries-hou.title: Hakeem Jeffries Aside, Congress’s Left Is Well Positioned
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/jeffries-hou.author: Branko Marcetic
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/jeffries-hou.text:
Hakeem Jeffries Aside, Congress’s Left Is Well Positioned
Hakeem Jeffries will be the next House speaker, a depressing fact for many angry at the Democratic Party status quo. But there is a strong case that the Left is well positioned for fights with Jeffries and the party establishment in the near future.
In a bitter disappointment for the Left, Hakeem Jeffries — the vehemently pro-Israel Wall Street darling who once, bizarrely, did a version of George Wallace’s infamous “segregation forever” speech, only subbing in “Israel” for “segregation” — will be the next speaker of the House of Representatives. The vote wasn’t even close: 251–11, with two members abstaining, something Jeffries’s allies are already celebrating as a sign of his domination of the Democratic caucus.
Going into this election, the members of the expanded Squad — the twenty or so progressives and socialists elected to Congress who may or may not now be known as “The Bloc” — viewed the two years between now and 2028 as a vital, possibly final, chance for Democrats to deliver some actual results for working people and avert future political disaster. Jeffries’s ascension to the speaker’s gavel drastically reduces the chances of that happening.
That’s the pessimistic way to look at it, at least. There is also a rosier perspective.
But to start with, there’s a lot to be pessimistic about. Hakeem Jeffries is a champion of political and economic elites. He and the rest of the House leadership are largely funded by the exact industries — finance, defense, health insurers and pharmaceuticals, the crypto industry, and firms like Palantir — that are militantly against the kind of change that people voted his party into power to see.
His ambitious agenda if Democrats won was to reverse a handful of policies Donald Trump had enacted last year, including ending the Iran war, and simply bring us back to the intolerable status quo ante that produced Trump’s election in the first place. Jeffries is already punting on the budding plan to end the war by defunding it. He has refused to commit to even holding a vote on US aid to Israel, putting him at odds with not just a large supermajority of his party’s own voters but most of the American public.
Jeffries is, in other words, an embodiment of everything people do not like about the Democratic Party, which is more or less what incoming Ohio Rep. Don Leonard told him in a closed-door meeting, a sentiment Jeffries apparently gets. Upon telling the speaker-to-be to his face that his name was “synonymous” with the “low quality” of today’s Democratic Party brand, Jeffries, according to Leonard, nodded.
Socialists and progressives did not even try to mount a challenge to Jeffries, seemingly confirming fears that the blowout margin of the Democrats’ midterm win would, paradoxically, produce a more conservative outcome by shrinking the Left’s leverage. The party’s left-populist wing made the calculation that Jeffries simply had unassailable numbers, thanks in no small part to his lockstep support from the powerful Congressional Black Caucus (CBC), which views the history-making aspect of the first black House speaker as critically important, regardless of that speaker’s actual politics.
Some progressives have also pointed to the lack of viable (or really, any) challenger to Jeffries to explain the failure to move against him, which is partially true. They still could have tried to muster enough members to oppose him that it would make his eventual path to the speakership (for which the actual, full House vote will take place next year) more difficult and eventually wring concessions out of him, as the GOP’s Freedom Caucus did to Kevin McCarthy three years ago.
The counterargument to this is that Republicans in 2023 had a far slimmer majority than the Democrats will have — just nine seats, compared to the Democrats’ eighty-five seats and counting next year — and that they did this on the back of a GOP midterm performance widely viewed as a flop compared to the Democrats’ historic overperformance this year, which Jeffries’s allies like the CBC wasted no time in crediting him personally with.
In any case, the party’s left bloc — which, of course, is still getting its bearings and hasn’t even been sworn in yet in Congress — decided the slim chances of rolling Jeffries wasn’t worth the risk of drawing his ire. The strongest, “steel man” argument for this is that they have done something similar to Zohran Mamdani in New York, who likewise calculated that, given his relatively weak position as a newly elected insurgent mayor, there was no plausible pathway to challenging centrist Democrats in New York, and he would be more successful if he avoided spending political capital on what he viewed as a suicide mission.
That decision saw Mamdani effectively quash a Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) primary endorsement against Jeffries last year, both to keep the powerful Democratic leader out of his hair as he got his nascent mayoralty going and because he assessed that such a challenge could not win, and ally himself with centrist governor Kathy Hochul, betting he could accomplish the kinds of legislative victories he needed to succeed as mayor by cozying up to the governor (who holds significantly more power across multiple fronts) than by antagonizing her. Both of those proved to be successful bets for Mamdani.
We’ve gotten some idea of what the consequences for crossing Jeffries could look like from Leonard, who last week revealed party leadership had threatened to make him lose reelection in two years time if he didn’t get behind the Brooklyn Democrat. Other than Leonard, from what we know so far, the others who voted against Jeffries were almost all socialist freshmen in safe blue districts — or, in the case of incoming Reps. Frederick Haynes III and Adam Hamawy, Medicare for All–supporting progressives in safe blue districts.
In other words, the votes against Jeffries are from members who have nothing to lose and in fact could benefit politically in the long run from going on the record opposing someone expected to be a disappointing speaker.
By one view, this failure to block Jeffries will be fatal to the party and to any hope of it pursuing a pro-working-class agenda. Shortly after the result, Corbin Trent, cofounder of Justice Democrats and former staffer to both the Bernie Sanders presidential campaigns and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, had told me his fears that the Democrats would fail “if the same people who drove this bus of the party into the hands of Donald Trump twice” stayed in place, meaning Jeffries and his Senate counterpart, Chuck Schumer. Trent has spread that message elsewhere, including on Fox News, where he appeared to not-so-subtly prod his former boss, Ocasio-Cortez, to be more outspoken in this fight, saying that anyone planning to run for president in 2028 “should be voicing up now.”
As a number of incumbent and incoming left-insurgent lawmakers told me in the process of reporting a forthcoming In These Times piece on the midterm result, a Democratic failure to deliver results, or even to appear to be trying to deliver them, could spark another Obama era–like mass disillusionment that could end up empowering someone much worse than Trump not far down the line. According to the pessimistic view of where things currently stand, we are well on the way to that future right now.
But again, that’s not the only way to assess what happened here.
Jeffries Isn’t Out of the Woods
There is good reason not to swallow wholesale the corporate center’s triumphalism over the vote margin, which the corruption-tainted Rep. Henry Cuellar gloated showed the opposition to Jeffries is just “a small number of votes that are marginalized” and that “this small little group cannot tell the caucus where we need to be at.” Those reasons go beyond the fact that some version of this line is what this crowd has constantly been telling themselves as their grip on the party has slowly faded the past ten years.
In advance of the vote, Jeffries had already moved on his initial, tepid program of Trump reversals by publicly endorsing Bernie Sanders’s Medicare expansion plan over the weekend. Sanders’s proposal — lowering the Medicare eligibility age to fifty-five, including dental, vision, and hearing in the program, and covering all children with it until they turn nineteen — was not something any Democrat brought up or ran on during the midterms. Yet Jeffries’s adoption of it means it’s quickly becoming a consensus position among both the Democrats’ populist and corporate wings since the Vermont senator first brought it up two days after the election.
This would not be a minor reform. It would extend free public health insurance to 3.45 million adults and anywhere from four–seven million kids, depending on exactly how many children are thrown off health insurance in the years ahead by Trump’s Medicaid cuts. It would go much further than the Medicare-related parts of Joe Biden’s popular but never-passed Build Back Better bill, which merely added hearing to the program’s coverage, and would go a long way toward alleviating voters’ cost-of-living concerns, since health care is one of the biggest, most stress-inducing, and sometimes life-ruining costs anyone can deal with in today’s United States.
Left-insurgent lawmakers view the next two years as a unique opportunity: either they pass something that Trump actually ends up signing into law, making good on their election promises and tangibly making voters’ lives better, or Trump vetoes a bunch of things they pass, letting them make the argument to voters in 2028 that they need a Democratic president in the White House. If Jeffries’s movement on this matter holds, it will put socialists and progressives in a decent position to actually pursue this strategy.
Meanwhile, the fact that Jeffries has moved suggests he’s more vulnerable than the numbers today make it seem. Jeffries has, incredibly, a worse approval rating than outgoing Republican House speaker Mike Johnson, and while he at least gets overall positive marks from Kamala Harris voters, liberals, and Democrats — three of the paltry four groups he’s not underwater with — he gets them just barely, unable to muster majority support from any of those three.
More worrying for Jeffries, his congressional district, New York’s 8th, where he will have to contest a primary election in just two years’ time, is deep in DSA territory, in a state and city where the socialist organization has emerged over the past year as a leading political power.
To its immediate north is the 7th district, where DSA member and Mamdani ally Claire Valdez (who just voted against Jeffries) easily bested the Brooklyn borough president for the seat, and at whose watch party DSA members chanted “You’re next!” when Jeffries came on the screen. Bordering its panhandle to the west is the heavily Jewish 10th district, where another Mamdani ally, Brad Lander, comfortably ousted one of the Democrats’ most well-financed and most ardently pro-Israel members of Congress by taking direct aim at his unconditional support for Israel’s genocide. A little further up, and you get to the kingdom of another Mamdani ally and DSA member, Ocasio-Cortez, who eight years ago made her 14th district the final resting place for the career of a different corporate Democrat once tipped to be a future speaker.
In other words, for the sake of his career, Jeffries has to watch his left flank for the next couple years. A misstep, or a series of them, where he ends up looking like the singular roadblock to Democrats’ progressive ambitions, will be a weakness that a future primary challenger will eagerly exploit.
Piling on the pressure is the fact that next year’s Democrat-led Senate is now looking like a far more progressive chamber than usual. Besides Sanders, the country’s most prominent and well-liked socialist, it will feature three of his endorsees (Abdul El-Sayed, Troy Jackson, and Peggy Flanagan), all of whom campaigned on Medicare for All, and sixteen others who — however disingenuously — endorsed Sanders’s legislation on the program last year, as well as one other — Ron Wyden — who has come around to the idea in the past year, and vowed to use his coming chairmanship of the Senate Finance Committee to push through an expansion of the program.
It’s notable that the bold idea to risk a government shutdown in order to force Trump to end the Iran war originated from the Senate, and so far has the sign-on of not just Sanders and Chris Van Hollen — who has spent the past twenty-two months courting progressive support for a potential 2028 run — but centrists Michael Bennet and Tammy Duckworth. It’s notable, too, that Jeffries felt he had to go along with the Medicare expansion proposal, another progressive idea that came out of the Senate.
What happens in the Senate majority leadership race could intensify this dynamic. If Schumer — who is more vulnerable than Jeffries and underwater with the left-leaning demographics that still give the future speaker a slim positive approval rating — really is replaced by the more progressive Van Hollen, it may add further pressure on Jeffries, given that he can’t politically afford to look like he’s stymieing the party’s agenda or undermining its resistance to Trump.
None of this is guaranteed, and it’s possible in a few months to a year, this will all read as wildly overoptimistic.
But the opposite, pessimistic case isn’t guaranteed either, and there are reasons to think that the Democrats’ populist wing of socialists and progressives has cards it’s yet to play, as it once more thanklessly drags the party into saving itself. Jeffries’s victory yesterday is certainly a blow for the Left. But it’s not out of the question that in hindsight, it looks more like losing a battle while winning the war.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: These singles gathered in Central Park to swap their exes’ stuff
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: James Ramsay
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
This column originally appeared in the Looped In NYC newsletter. Sign up here.
One of the hardest parts of breaking up, especially in this town, is dealing with your ex’s stuff. Most newly-eligible New Yorkers simply don’t have the space for it — in their apartments nor in their hearts.
But of course, one person’s baggage can be another’s treasure, so the upstart dating network Park Bench recently hosted “The Ex-Change,” a mixer of sorts for people to swap mementos.
“The singles that we've talked to are always looking for ways to meet other singles, but in a not explicitly singles-coded way,” said Kasey Luo, a co-founder of Park Bench. This idea had a convenient value proposition: Whether or not you came away with a phone number, you wouldn’t leave empty-handed.
“New Yorkers love free stuff,” Luo said.
Arihant Barajatya — who, for what it’s worth, was one of the few male attendees and the only one game enough to talk to us — was giving away a pair of unisex sweatpants he’d shared with his ex.
“ I don't want anything that reminds me of her now,” he said.
While everything was gratis, the few dozen items people brought, laid out on picnic blankets, covered a range of monetary values. A paperback copy of “2666.” A pack of Marlboro Golds. A navy blue Burberry raincoat with the tags still on.
“I got this Le Labo clutch,” said Brianne Adiola, who was parting with some denim outfits. “I honestly only picked it up because I know Le Labo's expensive.”
But for the people discarding some of these big-ticket items, the benefits were clearly priceless.
When I asked Eliwa Onanga why she was parting with a chic pair of saddle shoes, she said they had nothing to do with an ex and everything to do with her own personal growth.
“ I think there was a time where I felt like I really had to show up super ‘professionally’ at work,” she said. “And I don't necessarily feel that way anymore.”
Margo Hera, who’d recently broken up with her partner of eight years, was giving away a steel sword from the series “One Piece” that could likely fetch three figures.
“ I bought [my ex] this as a present, and she left it,” she said. “It's an anime thing. I've never watched anime. I watched two episodes of the live action with her and I couldn't get into it.”
Read into this what you will, but that wasn’t the only sword-as-a-gift on offer.
“He told me he wanted dangly earrings, so I actually bought these for him,” said Julia Cooper, holding up a pair of sword earrings. “Then he never wore them, and he kinda, like, gifted them back, and I just decided I didn't want anything that reminded me of him at all.”
And that wasn’t the only thing Cooper was giving away for free — she also had some dating advice to offer: “ If you're feeling any sort of negative type of feelings, just break up. If you're spending more of your days unhappy with someone, it's not gonna get better, and the relief that you feel, it's really great.”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Paved-Over Black Cemetery Could Qualify as Landmark, Commission Says
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Greg B. Smith
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Researchers at the city’s Landmarks Preservation Commission have determined that an African burial ground in Elmhurst, Queens, that currently sits under an illegal parking lot is likely eligible for landmark status.
“We believe the former cemetery has cultural and historic significance related to the 19th Century Black and abolitionist history of New York City,” Margaret Herman, the commission’s director of research, wrote last month. “Research staff finds that the former cemetery may merit consideration for designation as a landmark.”
The finding is a preliminary step that could help transform a cemetery underneath an empty parking lot into a memorial for the upwards of 300 free-born and formerly enslaved Black New Yorkers buried there.
After The City Reporter revealed that tow trucks hired by the NYPD to remove abandoned vehicles from the streets were dropping cars and trucks there, a host of elected officials called on the administration of Mayor Zohran Mamdani to purchase the site and turn it into a memorial. The lot was soon shut down by the Buildings Department.
In August the Elmhurst History and Cemetery Preservation Society filed a request with Landmarks after the revelation about the parking lot’s use. Herman responded to the group’s president, Mariaelena Giampino, in October revealing that the commission’s research unit agreed the site was likely eligible to be landmarked.
The cemetery was formed in the early 19th century by the founders of what would become the St. Mark African Methodist and Episcopal Church. The church and its burial ground were sold in the 1930s and St. Mark moved a mile away to Jackson Heights. The church continues to serve as steward of the cemetery site and under state law can play a role in determining its ultimate fate. The Rev. Kimberly Detherage of St. Mark’s has called for the city to buy it.
Mamdani Administration Cool to City Purchase
The site is currently controlled by a limited liability corporation that bought the loan of the previous owner after they defaulted on their mortgage when plans to build a luxury co-op building stalled. Over the summer Queens Borough President Donovan Richards Jr. called for the city to step in, and in September pushed the Mamdani administration to protect the site.
On Thursday, Matthew Rauschenbach, a spokesperson for the mayor, said the city has no current plans to purchase the burial ground. He declined to comment on the Landmarks letter. All of the commission’s 10 members are mayoral appointees.
In September, state Attorney General Letitia James also got involved, filing a motion in a pending foreclosure lawsuit demanding that, whatever happens to the burial ground, the bodies be treated respectfully under the state’s Unmarked Burial Site Protection Act.
“The New Yorkers laid to rest at this historic burial ground worked to build this city even while it denied them their freedom,” James said in a statement Wednesday. “Their final resting place deserves respect. I welcome any effort to offer these souls the permanent protection they are owed, including this first step toward landmark designation.”
In her letter, Herman cited that law in noting that the fate of the lot will likely be complicated.
Landmark status, she wrote, “may not be the only or most appropriate tool to achieve that community’s goals.” Landmarked burial sites are usually either on public land or are privately-owned cemeteries that are still in use. She said that moving the remains to another site “would not typically be considered appropriate.”
Herman noted that the Unmarked Burial Site law provides for the involvement of the state’s archaeologist in consultation with the church about “appropriate next steps.”
A spokesperson for the state archaeologist on Wednesday did not respond to a request for comment.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-phill.title: Rejecting Equality Is a Long-Standing American Tradition
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-phill.author: Robbie Nelson
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-phill.text:
Rejecting Equality Is a Long-Standing American Tradition
The current version of explicitly anti-egalitarian politics adopted by today’s economic and political elites is only the latest in a long tradition of American reactionary thought that insists that all men and women are not, in fact, created equal.
Living in a country whose residents include both the world’s first trillionaire and 1.5 million homeless schoolchildren, the fact of American inequality is hard to miss. Such a reality produces countless justifications, explanations, and plans for ameliorating its worst impacts across the political spectrum. But at its sharpest edge, it also produces a coterie of intellectuals, pseudo-intellectuals, tycoons, activists, and posters who don’t merely attempt to explain or excuse inequality but rather celebrate its fruits and try to consolidate its bases.
Silicon Valley today plays host to the most prominent nest of techno-fascists, neoreactionaries, transhumanists, and “effective altruists” whose obscene wealth allows them to shape political discourse far beyond the strengths of their ideas or their personal charms, such as they are.
But as Kim Phillips-Fein demonstrates in her new book Country of Lords, the current version of explicitly anti-egalitarian politics adopted by today’s economic and political elites is merely the latest in a long tradition of American reactionary thought. Aimed squarely against the premise announced in the Declaration of Independence that “all men are created equal,” this intellectual and political lineage has been carried forward by the lawyers, business moguls, charlatans, and academics who form the primary figures of Phillips-Fein’s sweeping tour of American political history.
Country of Lords is a highly readable book, filled with a cast of colorful characters both well-known and more obscure. It sets forth a counter-history to the sunny, West Wing–style liberal narrative in which the inevitable march of American progress toward equal inclusion only faces obstacles thrown up by the dead weight of tradition or ignorance. Instead, building upon her previous work about the role of right-wing businessmen in fighting against the New Deal, Phillips-Fein shows the strenuous and continuous efforts of reactionary figures not merely to conserve some traditional order but to transform and reestablish new hierarchies in the face of technological, social, and political change.
Action and Reaction
The book is organized into six primary chapters, arranged chronologically and each anchored around a few historical figures and their connected sets of ideas. The New England statesman John Adams and the racist pro-slavery theorist George Fitzhugh might seem an odd pairing, but Phillips-Fein links their attempts to define the roles of their respective political and racial “aristocracies” in the early decades of American Republic. Likewise with the Yale professor William Graham Sumner and industrialist Andrew Carnegie enunciating their own versions of “survival of the fittest” in the context of Gilded Age industrial society.
Next are the “utilitarian racists,” anchored by Lothrop Stoddard and his infamous 1920 book, The Rising Tide of Color Against White World-Supremacy, a deeply racist cri de coeur (beloved by The Great Gatsby character Tom Buchanan) that identified World War I and the Bolshevik revolution as the tipping points against European colonial power. The interwar period ushered in the age of Henry Ford and his “Gospel of Production,” a corporatist vision of American society in which the unequal unity of proprietors and their loyal workers could box out both the (Jewish-coded) union Reds and the (Jewish-coded) financiers.
The book’s fifth chapter, perhaps its most interesting and certainly its most expansive, takes a broader view of postwar liberalism’s discontents. Particularly potent are the various debates around the rise of intelligence quotient (IQ) tests, standardized college admissions exams like the SAT, and ideas about “equality of opportunity” in the midst of the legal changes called forth by the civil rights movements of the 1950s and ’60s. The author eventually hones in on the scientist-turned-racist-crank William Shockley and the Harvard psychologist Richard Herrnstein, two figures associated with the thesis that IQ is heritable and racially differentiated. Phillips-Fein pairs the race-and-IQ crowd with the libertarians and monetarists represented by the likes of Ayn Rand and Milton Friedman. What united these seemingly disparate figures was their belief that purportedly “neutral” mechanisms (standardized intelligence tests and free-market competition) could separate the “natural elite” from those meant to be ruled. The book ends with an investigation of the antidemocratic strains within Silicon Valley that provide a surprising intellectual continuity between the countercultural 1960s to the corporate consolidation of the 1980s and ’90s to the emergence of hard-right tech anti-humanists that dominate the scene today.
Each chapter could stand on its own, a mini-history of a particular moment and the multiple strands of anti-egalitarian politics that attended it. But, taken together, they paint a larger picture. By fleshing out both the continuities and similarities between inegalitarian ideas across time, some crucial patterns emerge. Idiosyncratic though they may be, these anti-egalitarian thinkers did not develop their ideas in a vacuum. Rather, their politics are deeply responsive to the emerging shape of struggle from below. In other words, reactionary thinkers are always reactive to historically particular assertions of political power from the lower orders.
Although each chapter focuses primarily on conservative ideologues, their antagonists make consistent appearances. In each successive historical moment, new rounds of egalitarian struggle imperiled the ruling order. In response, new reactionary ideologies emerged that sought to both enshrine and update the ideological map of inequality.
The story lurking beneath The Country of Lords is that of an episodic but relatively cohesive American egalitarian tradition. From radical Enlightenment thinkers and indebted Revolutionary War veterans to abolitionists, Knights of Labor to the Socialist Party of Eugene V. Debs, garment workers on the Lower East Side to the NAACP of W. E. B Du Bois, United Auto Workers organizers to civil rights activists and beyond, American history has churned out ceaseless waves of agitators and movements seeking to overturn the social, economic, and political order and establish a more equal future.
The task of the modern reactionary, then, has not been to simply assert the God-given superiority of certain aristocratic families, but rather to counter each successive challenge with an updated and reorganized hierarchy that fits the changing social, technological, and economic landscapes that they encounter. Henry Ford’s worldview was not atavistic but distinctly modern and technologically driven, in the spirit of his age. His model of American corporatism incorporated not only the revolutionary technologies of internal combustion and the assembly line, but also cutting-edge social-scientific research into managing his workers’ lives and bodies on and off the factory floor.
Richard Herrnstein likewise did not subscribe to George Wallace–style Southern segregationism, but rather employed advanced (though subsequently debunked) statistical methods to make his arguments about race and IQ, being careful not to deny the possibility of individual black success stories. In other words, the realities of social mobility, new institutions, and new social attitudes pressurized the shape of these anti-egalitarian ideas.
Almost all of these anti-egalitatarian figures relied heavily on the discursive power of science and technology in both their explanations of inequality and their visions of how that inequality could be leveraged for social good. As the primary modern schema for adjudicating differences between things and producing causal explanations for social phenomena, the natural and social sciences loom large in the reactionary imagination as both threats and resources.
It is telling that almost all of this book’s subjects were not, themselves, born into high privilege. They ranged from working-class immigrants who worked their way up through industry or academia (Carnegie, Herrnstein, Friedman) to the children of middling farmers (Ford, Adams, Sumner) to the children of moderately successful provincial professionals (Fitzhugh, Stoddard). Interestingly, two of the techno-racists (Shockley and Peter Thiel) are the children of prosperous but highly peripatetic mining engineers.
Having gained a vantage point on American society from both outside and inside the elite, these up-and-comers were often able to craft and mobilize ideological concepts that went beyond mere defense of status quo elite configurations. Because of their personal prominence in the American economic or intellectual scene, these individuals had deep investment in both upholding the legitimacy of the system as well as opening that system up to the fresh perspectives of those coming from outside the blue-blood northeastern elite. Potential for upward social mobility of one kind or another is a load-bearing feature of most modern reactionary ideologies, because it both serves to justify the merited existence of a ruling class while also leaving open the possibility of entry. The replenishment of the upper classes and the defanging of disruptive movements from below are the dual goals of these political movements.
Constructing Equality
Because of its particular focus on the history of anti-egalitarian ideas in the United States as well as its slim profile, Country of Lords does not spend much time building up a competing, left-wing account of and response to inequality. While the Left’s primary political task is countering actual inequality in the workplace, social relations, and the state, we also have to develop our own story about the nature of inequality in order to counter some of the key arguments of the reactionaries and their liberal fellow travelers.
There are both empirical observations and normative claims at the heart of this story. First, human beings are not “equal” or equivalent in terms of our physical capacities, desires, and talents. We inhabit different bodies and life experiences. But we assert that human beings do have equal dignity and worth and thus should be given, to the greatest extent possible, equal power to determine our own lives and to participate in decision-making that shapes our societies. The question at play in modern progressive politics is determining which institutions and historical processes can cultivate flourishing egalitarian societies in the context of human diversity and nonequivalency.
Historically speaking, unequal social classes are a pretty recent human social phenomenon, only emerging around twelve thousand years ago during the Neolithic revolution. During this era, the advent of agriculture, livestock domestication, sedentary urbanism, and the complex social division of labor fed into the generation of social surplus. In other words, these societies were able to produce and store more food than was necessary to meet their populations’ immediate needs.
New elites emerged and solidified their ability to command others’ labor, coordinate production and exchange, and make decisions about how to mobilize that social surplus. These new practices enabled the development of larger human populations, more advanced technology, and greater complexity in social, cultural, and economic life.
This rough historical sketch, viewed in a certain way, lends credence to anti-egalitarian arguments: human societies, since the birth of agriculture, have depended in fundamental ways on social hierarchy. In this telling, hierarchical divisions of labor were necessary to produce the technological advancements that have propelled humanity from living as small bands of hunter-gatherers to becoming geo-engineers and star-travelers.
However, the anti-egalitarians err in misidentifying the historically functional inequality of class society as an intrinsic inequality. Unequal power over the social surplus was provisionally necessary for the class system as it has emerged, but, empirically speaking, the actual people in those dominant positions over the course of history have not shared any intrinsic biological, moral, or technical superiority over those they have dominated.
The socialist movement has thus set for itself the most ambitious task imaginable: the construction of systems that sustain a complex divisions of labor necessary for a technologically advanced mass society — which is comprised of individuals who each have unique capacities and desires — while maintaining roughly equal access to social income and roughly equal decision-making power about the production and distribution of social surplus. An equal future cannot simply be wished or asserted: it needs to be built.
Despite Karl Marx’s famous injunction against “writing recipes for the cookshops of the future,” there has been a rash of recent English-language writing attempting to sketch the contours of a socialist future. While each example deserves its own complex treatment — and there are tensions between different visions — the ideas and institutions of democracy lie at the heart of each one.
The particular combination and format of representative and direct democratic decision-making is up for contestation, as is the precise role of markets in economic life. But democratic decision-making is the key mechanism for synthesizing the reality of individual difference with the need for collective deliberation and rough equality of political power. In a socialist future characterized by social complexity, division of labor, technological advancement, civil liberties, rough equality of social income, and rough equality of political capacity, democracy is the indispensable technology.

https://gothamist.com/news/incoming-ny-r.title: Incoming NY Rep. Constantino isn’t looking to make friends. What are Republicans to do?
https://gothamist.com/news/incoming-ny-r.author: Jon Campbell
https://gothamist.com/news/incoming-ny-r.text:
This column originally appeared in The Politics Brief, our weekly newsletter on the people, power and policies that shape New Yorkers' lives.
Sign up to get the full version where you can ask questions, share news tips and weigh in on the conversation. Hits inboxes on Wednesdays.
Anthony Constantino has an — ahem — unusual approach to politics.
The Republican businessman who owns Sticker Mule, an online printing company, will represent New York’s 21st Congressional District next year, after eking out a win to succeed Rep. Elise Stefanik in the state’s North Country. He didn’t get there by playing it safe.
You might’ve seen his rap video baselessly accusing New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani of associating with terrorists, or his full album honoring President Donald Trump. Perhaps you saw a clip of his election night victory speech, where he cursed at “evil” reporters and called for Diddy’s release. Or maybe you keep up with his very active X account, where he’s settling scores with GOP leaders who failed to back him in a contentious primary and trying to convince Nvidia to reinstate its embattled ex-CEO.
Now, Constantino is trying to put his mark on the state Republican Party before officially joining New York’s congressional delegation in January. It’s left Republican leaders grappling with the same question: What do we do with this guy?
Liz Joy, the Republican Party’s regional chair for New York’s North Country, has clashed with Constantino for more than a year. The feud has spilled out into the open since the election, with Constantino calling her a “stone cold loser and quite evil” and Joy saying Constantino is "mentally unfit for office."
Joy said Republican leaders have already been discussing potential opponents for Constantino in a 2028 Republican primary.
”The conversations about a primary were already taking place before the election,” said Joy.
Constantino didn’t have the backing of the state Republican Party and most GOP leaders in the 21st District during his bruising primary battle with state Assemblymember Robert Smullen in June. But he did have the support of a far more influential Republican in his red-leaning district: Trump, whose endorsement helped propel Constantino to a primary victory.
Constantino was able to survive the blue wave that overtook much of the country — but just barely. The latest count had Constantino up by 1.6 percentage points over Democrat Blake Gendebien. Stefanik won the same district by 24 points two years ago.
“I think that the election results in NY-21 clearly show that the Republican Party has not embraced Anthony Constantino's style of erratic and bombastic behavior and language,” Joy said.
On X, Constantino said he “banned [Joy] from my race” and won. “All Party Bosses who elevated her should be ashamed of themselves,” he wrote.
Other Republicans say Constantino’s win in the midst of a blue wave is reason enough to give him a seat at the table as the party tries to rebuild.
Former Rep. Marc Molinaro, a Republican who previously ran for governor and won a seat in the state Assembly this year, said voters “desperately want authenticity.”
“[Constantino] does speak to a segment of voters — by the way, not all Republicans — who want people to take on the elites, who want candidates who speak and talk and feel the way they do,” Molinaro said. "And is that the orthodox, traditional candidate for office? No. But there are lessons to be learned there.”
Constantino’s camp didn’t respond to requests for comment. But the congressmember-elect has been outspoken on social media about Republican leaders — including state GOP Chair Ed Cox, who’s led the state party since 2023 and, before that, from 2009 to 2019.
After Constantino declared victory on election night, he took to X at 3:15 a.m. to call Cox “dumb as rocks.”
“I am with the people and insist we rebuild the Party,” Constantino posted. “Fire Ed Cox!”
Cox hasn’t addressed Constantino’s criticism directly, at least in public. But he issued a statement following Election Day calling on the party to “regroup,” saying that now is “not the time for accusations or a circular firing squad.”
The Republican chair’s term runs through September. He’s given no indication he intends to step down before then.
Last week, the party held a virtual meeting with county chairs across the state to shift the focus to the 2027 elections — when Republicans are bracing for a possible ballot measure that, if approved, could clear the way for Democrats in Albany to redraw the state’s congressional map.
On Wednesday, Constantino again took to X to call out “haters” who have underestimated him and are now “doubting if I’ll perform in Congress for my district and get things done.”
“What will it take for my haters to get tired of being wrong and looking stupid?”
We want to hear from you
House Democrats have officially nominated Hakeem Jeffries to become speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives. What issues should he focus on first when he takes the speaker’s gavel in January?
We'll share responses in next week's newsletter. (Sign up!)
This week in New York politics
- New York City will offer career training and medallion buybacks for horse carriage drivers as part of Mayor Mamdani's plan to wind down the carriage horse industry.
- New York City buildings inspectors have halted construction completely or in part for at least five projects tied to a pair of engineers in the wake of a fatal Brooklyn building collapse, a Gothamist analysis shows.
- Mayor Mamdani declined to endorse Brooklyn native U.S. Sen. Chuck Schumer as the next Senate majority leader.
- The City Council passed a bill banning surveillance pricing, which charges different prices based on algorithms or shoppers’ personal data.
- Gov. Kathy Hochul called on U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy to resign or be fired after a communications failure grounded all flights across the country last Friday.
- A bill in the City Council would force companies like Amazon to hire its delivery workers directly, pitting them against the Teamsters union, which supports the bill.
- Mayor Mamdani selected Eric Thor, who recently served as co-chair of New York City’s chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America, to lead the Office of Nightlife.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/le-pen-far-r.title: The Violent Far-Right Response to France’s Protests
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/le-pen-far-r.author: Olly Haynes
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/le-pen-far-r.text:
The Violent Far-Right Response to France’s Protests
In recent weeks, French far-right militants have carried out several violent attacks. While media focus on young rioters breaking shop windows, they ignore the reactionaries who use deadly force against minorities and left-wingers.
For France’s media-political classes, the recent student movement has prompted a series of searching questions about violence and who has the right to use it. Debates often center on the alleged closeness of protesters to La France Insoumise, implying that Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s left-wing party is somehow responsible for vandalism by protesters and marginal acts of violence by students. Less remarked upon however, is that a wave of violence coming from the far right has also marked the protests and the presidential election campaign. Nor has it been much noted that this violence has killed already, and that Marine Le Pen’s Rassemblement National (RN) is alarmingly close to the violent groupuscules involved.
Already on October 24, far-right militants attacked trade unionists and protesters in Rouen, Nice, and Montpellier. In a video taken by a bystander in Rouen, Normandy, members of local identitarian movement Les Normaux can be seen throwing a man to the pavement before kicking him. None of the men were arrested by the police, although officers were present on the scene. The identitarians attempted to intimidate protesters by yelling far-right slogans such as “Rouen, Rouen is nationalist” and “the street and France belongs to us.”
The group had launched similar attacks on protesters the week before, beating two people to the ground and leaving them bloody. In a video taken before the incident, a man can be seen at the head of their march, a leather belt wrapped around his fist, metal buckle in hand like a makeshift knuckle-duster. Street Press, a news website that closely monitors far-right activity, identified the man as Mathieu Balavoine, who runs a production company that was hired by the Rassemblement National in 2024, and that last year earned over €100,000 for a contract making videos for the party’s group in the European Parliament.
The far right’s propensity for lethal violence has also been demonstrated elsewhere in recent weeks. On October 23, Kevin Tessier, a coked-up fascist armed with an automatic weapon, fired 128 bullets at black and Arab people in the city of Trappes, killing one person and injuring four. Trappes had repeatedly been the subject of a media moral panic about “territories lost to the Republic” because of their large minority populations. Le Pen contributed to this over the years, tweeting in 2018 following a stabbing in the city, that Trappes is “the symbol of those cities and neighborhoods where the French Republic has retreated, making way for communalism and Islamism.” Tessier’s motives were undeniably racist. Whether he was influenced directly by Le Pen’s words is unknown, but stickers found in his house suggest that he was at least a party sympathizer. Among a copy of Adolf Hitler’s Mein Kampf and other items indicative of his far-right ideology, were thirty stickers bearing the words “Long Live France, the RN, proud to be French.”
These were just the most recent instances of a longer story of far-right violence in France. In 2022 Argentine rugby player Federico Martín Aramburú was gunned down in the street by two former members of the Groupe Union Défense (GUD), a fascist youth circle with close ties to the RN. In 2023, a wave of far-right violence was unleashed in reaction to the Nahel Merzouk riots, which followed the police killing of a seventeen-year-old. That year, France became the only European country to see a major increase in the number of violent attacks by far-right groups compared to the 2010–2022 national average, according to a study by the Center for Research on Extremism. Since then, acts of violence by such groups targeting ethnic minorities and political opponents have become increasingly common. According to daily Libération, there was an average of one far-right attack per week in 2025.
The groups perpetrating these attacks — the formations that emerged following the self-dissolution of the GUD and the mandatory dissolution of Génération Identitaire — are alarmingly close to the RN.
According to Thomas Portes, who is president of the National Observatory of the Far Right, and France Insoumise MP for Saint-Denis, “There has been no break between the parliamentary far right and the groupuscules.”
[In France] we have an annual mobilization by the May 9 Committee; it’s a Nazi demonstration in homage to a fascist activist who died. It was banned this year, but two years ago, the paperwork for the demonstration was filed by a parliamentary attaché for the RN, called Maylis de Cibon. There was a parliamentary assistant called Raphaël Ayma, who spoke at a conference of the friends of Léon Degrelle, a Belgian Nazi figure [before Ayma was expelled from the RN]. There is the press secretary of the RN group, Elise Laplace, who has just married a neofascist activist that arranged an attack on a political meeting in Bordeaux that was organized by my fellow [France Insoumise] MPs Louis Boyard and Carlos Martens Bilongo.
“It goes beyond the assistants,” Portes tells Jacobin, pointing to the case of Tiffany Joncour, an RN MP whose husband, a hooligan with a background in the identitarian movement, beat up her parliamentary assistant whom he suspected of having an affair with her.
Portes’s list continues, telling Jacobin about four further examples. Even this list is not exhaustive. While researching another article, in the Eurocom forum that the group organizes through, I found an account of the Save Europe Act, an organization linking identitarian movements across Europe, which includes several groupuscules accused of violence. The account bore the name and location of Philippe Eymery, an RN regional counselor whose party branch was exposed in 2018 for employing Génération Identitaire activists. Eymery recently appeared on a radio show alongside various extreme-right groups that are members of the Eurocom group, promoting remigration. (He did not respond to my message requests on Twitter attempting to confirm if he was the owner of the account with his name.)
At France Insoumise’s own summer university in August, the party’s parliamentary chief Mathilde Panot told journalists that this would be an unusual presidential election campaign because of the level of violence that she and her colleagues expected. Her assessment has already proved prescient, though France Insoumise has in fact long been a target for far-right violence. The Trappes killer had a list suggesting he was intending to target France Insoumise MPs David Guiraud and Aymeric Caron, as well as anti-police-violence campaigner Assa Traoré and Green MP Sandrine Rousseau. France Insoumise canvassers and parliamentary assistants have been beaten up while campaigning for Mélenchon, and even the Quentin Deranque affair, which ended with a neo-Nazi activist dying from injuries sustained in a street fight by antifascist activists, began with fascist activists ambushing the antifascist activists outside a France Insoumise meeting in Lyon.
According to Portes, there is an “operation to reverse society’s moral compass based on falsehoods, which is targeted against us. For example, yesterday the minister of education tried to claim that it was France Insoumise, our activists and officials, who brought fireworks to high school students to allow them to fire them at school buildings. The interior minister was forced to deny it today. . . . As for the far right, we represent everything that they hate. That is to say the imaginary of an anti-racist, anti-colonial, antifascist, egalitarian, New France.”
Part of Marine Le Pen’s strategy of detoxification has been to expel party members associated with openly extreme or violent groups in French politics. However, they only seem to be expelled when the press gets wind of it, and even then those close to the leader can escape unscathed. The Rassemblement National in parliament with the “shirts and ties” is just “decor” and “window dressing” says Portes. “When you look at the list of people who are elected officials for the RN, or their assistants, it’s a nursery of neo-Nazi, nationalist, royalist, and identitarian activists.”
Le Pen may have successfully detoxified the party brand. That doesn’t, however, mean that it has actually changed.

https://gothamist.com/news/mayor-mamdani.title: Mayor Mamdani signs NYC's carriage horse ban after decades of animal rights activism
https://gothamist.com/news/mayor-mamdani.author: Liam Quigley
https://gothamist.com/news/mayor-mamdani.text:
Animal rights activists who fought for decades to ban the city’s 160-year-old horse-drawn carriage industry were handed a major victory on Thursday when Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed a bill banning the practice.
A turning point in the push to ban the industry came over the summer when an 18-year-old visiting from India with his family was thrown from a carriage in Central Park after its driver lost control of the animal. Romanch Mahajan was killed in the crash, which left the smashed-up carriage in the middle of the park’s drive. The horse was uninjured. But other horses have died on the streets of the city, their deaths captured in gruesome viral videos that were fodder for animal rights groups.
The bill to ban the industry passed the City Council last month.
The carriage horse industry maintains that the animals are well cared for and beloved by the 200 or so people who drive and care for them. Drivers now face an uncertain future with their careers set to come to an end by June 2028, when the law requires the industry to be banished from the park.
Carriage owners have city-issued medallions to operate, much like taxi drivers.
The city plans to buy back medallions from the carriage owners and launch a training program for the drivers and stable hands. Details on the buybacks and job training aren't due until April 2027.
“As New York City moves to bring the horse-drawn carriage industry to a close, we have a responsibility to the workers who have built careers in this industry,” the mayor wrote in a statement accompanying a Tuesday announcement. “This administration will not leave them behind.”
The Transport Workers Union has bitterly fought the move to ban the industry. They argue the city’s promises are unfunded and have vowed to file a lawsuit the moment the mayor signed the law.
The union's president, John Samuelesen, said in a statement that the law is unconstitutional.
“The City Council passed a horrifically flawed and unconstitutional anti-worker bill that abolishes an entire industry without any funding, mandates, or guarantees,” he wrote. He added that if the city faces a fiscal crisis, the whole plan could easily be abandoned.
“That would leave hundreds of horse-carriage workers, owners, and family members on the curb with nothing at all.”

https://gothamist.com/news/builder-facin.title: Builder facing bankruptcy will lead environmental review of controversial NJ ICE warehouse
https://gothamist.com/news/builder-facin.author: Mike Hayes
https://gothamist.com/news/builder-facin.text:
Residents of Roxbury, New Jersey, have expressed alarm because the Trump administration selected a company run by a Boston real estate developer with a troubled financial record to lead a court-ordered environmental review of plans to convert a local warehouse into one of the country's largest immigration detention facilities.
Gothamist confirmed that developer James Grossmann’s company Rudiarius, Inc. has been subcontracted to conduct the environmental review, according to a company spokesperson. The firm’s selection has not been previously reported and may indicate that the White House remains committed to opening the facility, despite Republican losses in this month’s midterm elections and a lawsuit from New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill to stop it.
The Trump administration agreed earlier this year to conduct the environmental review before moving ahead with its plans. In May, a federal judge ordered the project put on hold pending the completed review.
Grossmann ran a separate development company in Boston, Rise Construction Management, that is currently facing a $27 million bankruptcy and several lawsuits claiming he failed to pay development partners and subcontractors.
Rudiarius is a partner firm of Nashville, Tennessee-based SK2, LLC, which received a $31.8 million contract to convert the warehouse into an ICE detention facility if the environmental assessment clears the path for the project to proceed, according to USAspending.gov, posing a potential conflict of interest.
Grossmann managed at least one other environmental assessment for the Department of Homeland Security at a similar warehouse in Surprise, Arizona, that ICE plans to use as a detention facility. The review found that the facility would have no significant impact on the surrounding area. Critics called the review lax and said it ignored serious environmental concerns. Local lawmakers have also pushed back against the plan.
Brian Kiernan, a Roxbury resident, said he feared the environmental review would not be done properly because of the connections between Rudiarius and SK2.
“Is the study going to be a true study, or is it going to be lip service to get the results that his client desires and to get a fee?” he said.
David Broderick, an attorney representing Project No ICE North Jersey Alliance, a local activist group formed last year to oppose the Roxbury project, said he’s concerned about Grossmann’s financial troubles.
“It sounds like [DHS officials] have picked someone and a company which is uniquely unqualified to perform this,” Broderick said.
In an interview, Rudiarius’ spokesperson Jessica Tocco defended Grossmann’s track record and Rise Construction’s bankruptcy proceedings. She said the company is a “completely different LLC” from Rudiarius.
“Some businesses work, and some don't,” she said, adding that the environmental review in Roxbury is “not officially underway.” She did not provide a timeline for the review to start.
In a House Homeland Security Committee hearing Wednesday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin also said he could not provide a timeline for the environmental review or the administration’s plans to begin construction work at the Roxbury site.
SK2’s representatives did not respond to multiple requests to be interviewed or provide comment on its connection to Grossmann and Rudiarius.
In a court filing Tuesday, the New Jersey attorney general’s office said that after “repeated requests over 11 days,” DHS provided it with a copy of the $31.8 million contract with SK2, LLC. Attorney General Jennifer Davenport said in the filing that she “continues to be concerned” that DHS is violating the judge’s court order by “pressing ahead with steps” to convert the warehouse.
A copy of the contract with SK2 does not mention Rudiarius or any other subcontractors. It states that DHS intends to spend $650,000 on the environmental review.
Roxbury Township Mayor Shawn Potillo said in an emailed statement that the township council plans to contact Roxbury’s legal counsel, the New Jersey attorney general’s office, and their federal representatives about the selection of Rudiarius to manage the environmental review.
“The Township has no authority or involvement in the federal government's decisions regarding the qualifications or suitability of contractors retained to perform federal work,” the statement said. “Regardless of those decisions or the contractors involved, our position remains unchanged; Roxbury Township opposes the proposed ICE facility.”
$27 million in bankruptcy debt
By his own account, Grossmann rose through the ranks at nationally renowned Suffolk Construction for more than two decades before starting his own company, Rise Construction Management, in 2019.
Court records show the company became mired in legal disputes within two years of being founded.
In 2020, Parks Plus, Inc., a New Jersey-based company that specializes in manufacturing and installing elevated parking systems, entered into a nearly $1 million contract at a new condo development under construction by Grossmann’s company in the Brighton section of Boston, according to Parks Plus’ Senior Vice President Ryan Astrup.
He said Rise Construction was “difficult from the get go” and failed to pay more than $50,000 it owed Parks Plus.
“It kind of fizzled out from there. We made several attempts to collect, and they went unanswered,” Astrup told Gothamist.
His company is one of more than 50 firms with debt claims against Rise Construction, according to an August 2026 Chapter 7 bankruptcy filing. According to the filing, several claims — including the one from Parks Plus — are in dispute due to litigation.
Two developers who worked on projects with Rise Construction are suing the company for more than $2 million. Each claims that Rise failed to pay subcontractors. The Lever previously reported Grossmann’s financial troubles.
Tocco said Rise and Grossmann’s troubles can be attributed to market headwinds and a “very tough time for developers.”
“He's doing the right thing,” she said. “He's closing that company with his partners through a legal bankruptcy process.” She added that Rise is one of “dozens” of companies that Grossmann has started during his career in the construction industry.
“To be out there for thirty years and have as many businesses as he had and had one not work out, that's a pretty good track record,” she said.
‘Uniquely unqualified’
News that the federal government signed the $31.8 million contract with SK2 to renovate the warehouse has sowed confusion about the project’s status.
Kiernan, the Roxbury resident, and his wife live about a three-minute drive from the warehouse site off Route 46 in the Ledgewood section of the township. He said he had not gotten clarity from his local elected officials on whether the project is still on hold as the court ordered. And he said he was alarmed that Grossmann’s company would conduct the environmental review.
“This is the individual through a new company who's supposedly going to perform this environmental study, that raises real concern,” he said.
Rudiarius’ environmental assessment of the proposed ICE facility in Arizona has also faced local scrutiny. DHS released the report on November 9.
The environmental group, Partner Engineering and Science, Inc., which conducted the study on Rudiarius' behalf, found that the facility would not have a significant impact on the surrounding area. As in New Jersey, Arizona’s attorney general sued the Trump administration over the conversion project. Local officials and activists have lashed out at the review’s findings.
Brent Peak of Northwest Valley Indivisible, a local grassroots political organization opposed to the facility, criticized the 81-page report for only briefly mentioning a nearby warehouse storing hazardous materials.
“It is completely ridiculous, negligent and derelict that this is one of the primary concerns brought up in the attorney general’s lawsuit,” Peak told AZFamily.com. “And they give it one paragraph out of those 81 pages.”

https://hyperallergic.com/drawing-center.title: Drawing Center's Laura Hoptman Wins Curatorial Excellence Award
https://hyperallergic.com/drawing-center.author: Valentina Di Liscia
https://hyperallergic.com/drawing-center.text:
Drawing Center's Laura Hoptman Wins Curatorial Excellence Award
Plus: Joyce Awards winners announced, Agnes Gund's gift to art in schools, and Derrick Adams and LEGO make a splash in Miami.
Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.
Laura Hoptman Wins CCS Bard Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence
The Center for Curatorial Studies at Bard College announced Laura Hoptman, executive director of the Drawing Center in New York, as the recipient of the 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence, a $25,000 prize. Hoptman's curriculum vitae reads like a roll call of NYC's major institutions: She started out as an assistant curator at the Bronx Museum in the 1980s and later held curatorial roles at the Museum of Modern Art and the New Museum.
So it is no surprise that, when asked what this recognition signified for her, Hoptman chose to invoke the network and community that her career has grown alongside.
“The best kind of professional recognition comes from one's peers, and this is one of the many reasons why this award is so meaningful to me,” Hoptman told Hyperallergic in an email. “It also reminds me how damn lucky I have been to have spent the last 30 years around art and artists in one of the greatest cultural hubs in the world. After all this time, my vocation still fills me with joy.”

Art Basel Miami Beach is set to open on December 4, but the collective Artists 4 Artists Miami has launched a campaign to boycott the fair, inviting local artists, curators, gallerists, collectors, and residents to abstain from participating and to consider long-term alternatives to the commercial juggernaut.
According to the Art Newspaper, Artists 4 Artists Miami announced plans for a boycott at a protest outside the Miami Beach Convention Center at the end of last year’s edition. Of primary concern is the extent to which the economic activity at the fair actually concerns the city’s artists and residents (as opposed to visitors), particularly as it becomes increasingly expensive to live and work in Miami. Organizers also question the associations between some of the fair’s partners and investors and various political and corporate influences.
Signatories to the boycott must pledge not to attend Art Basel Miami Beach, not to exhibit work at the fair, not to exhibit during Miami Art Week, or to withhold their labor from the fair. They can also choose alternatives to these options, which allows participants to assess what is realistic for their situation.
As economically significant as the fair is for the city—generating nearly $60m for the city of Miami Beach and $570m for Miami-Dade County in 2025, according to local officials—some desire more robust local support year-round. Ariel Lynch, an artist and educator who has lived in the city for four years and who signed the pledge, told The Art Newspaper, “Miami deserves more than institutions like Art Basel Miami Beach.”
Artists 4 Artists Miami organizers are contacting local cultural and political organizations for endorsements and partnerships. misael soto, an artist and founder of Artists 4 Artists Miami, said, “We realize that in order to refuse to take part in something as intertwined and culturally impactful as Art Basel, you really have to start building an alternative.”
