https://hyperallergic.com/rare-hilma-af-.title: Rare Hilma af Klint Painting Sells for Staggering $12.7M
https://hyperallergic.com/rare-hilma-af-.author: Anna Lee
https://hyperallergic.com/rare-hilma-af-.text:
Rare Hilma af Klint Painting Sells for Staggering $12.7M
The 1920 painting smashed its original sale estimate and the previous benchmark for a work by the Swedish forebearer of abstraction.
Hilma af Klint's painting “Ser III No. 5” (1920) sold for a record $12.7 million (SEK 128.9 million) at Bukowskis's modern art and design auction in Stockholm today, November 19, fetching over 16 times the upper end of its estimated price.
The first abstract painting by the Swedish artist and "mother of abstraction" to appear on the open market in 30 years, "Ser III No. 5" was one of the 85 geometric paintings the artist produced during a fervent months-long process in 1920. Theosophical symbols, triangles, and circles in "Ser III No. 5" provide insight into af Klint's last engagement with geometric abstraction before she turned to more naturalist watercolors in the last years of her life.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/anthropic-ai.title: Anthropic Is Already Part of the Security Establishment
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/anthropic-ai.author: Jacob Davis
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/anthropic-ai.text:
Anthropic Is Already Part of the Security Establishment
Four trustees elect most of Anthropic’s board, and one of them runs a leading national security think tank. The establishment didn’t have to buy Anthropic to get a seat at the table.
Anthropic, which priced its initial public offering (IPO) last night and began trading on the Nasdaq today, published an S-1, the corporate prospectus for the offering. The document, which extends over five hundred pages, is intended to provide potential investors with an outline of its corporate structure, business model, and financial situation. Much of the document is, accordingly, dedicated to mundane legal minutiae: long lists of hypothetical events that might adversely affect investments, specific provisions for investment to comply with foreign nations’ securities law, etc.
Some points, however, are quite instructive. As the filing explains, large-scale corporate decisions are overseen by a “long-term benefit trust” (LTBT): a five-person body responsible for appointing a majority of Anthropic’s board and entitled to a special class of corporate stock. Unlike most benefit trusts, the LTBT is a “‘purpose trust’ that is managed for the achievement of a purpose rather than for the benefit of a particular set of beneficiaries.”
While the LTBT itself has received mainstream attention, less notice has been given to the identity of the trustees. Of the four currently appointed, one is Ben Bernanke — infamous as the architect of the Obama-era Wall St bailouts. And one is Richard Fontaine, chief executive officer of the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) and North American executive director of the Trilateral Commission. The latter appointment is especially noteworthy, for it speaks to an increasing coalescence of Anthropic, effective altruism, and the US national security establishment.
Company Purpose
The LTBT is something of a novelty in corporate structure. It is a fine-tuning of the usual public benefit corporation (PBC) — a form of corporate governance that allows the company to balance other stated interests against the pecuniary interests of its shareholders. Anthropic’s innovation is to hand over much of the responsibility of enforcing these competing interests to the LTBT, which will eventually appoint a majority of the board of directors. The company is also unusual in the sweeping humanitarian nature of its “company purpose,” against which shareholder returns are to be balanced: “the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.”
The LTBT is an important indicator of Anthropic’s ethical self-understanding. According to the S-1, it “is intended to operate as an independent body of Trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise.” These experts are selected for their perceived competence in promoting the humanitarian company purpose and “the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct” — a class which, given Anthropic’s stated beliefs about its potential impact, includes all living humans. In addition to vesting them with material power, therefore, Anthropic’s choice of LTBT members says something about what the company understands those humanitarian interests to be.
A Greater Degree of Moderation in Democracy
Both CNAS and the Trilateral Commission enjoy a dark reputation among critics of the US-aligned international security community. The commission is especially notorious, and has long starred as the villain in a number of conspiracy theories of varying levels of plausibility. CNAS, however, may yet be the more influential of the two, and is to all appearances more bound up with the emerging hybrid of corporate AI, effective altruism, and the security establishment.
The Trilateral Commission is a private, international membership organization intended “to discuss and propose solutions to some of the world’s toughest problems.” Members include various senior government officials, business executives, and academics. They are drawn primarily from the commission’s eponymous three regional groups: Europe (mainly Western), East Asia (mainly Japan), and North America (mainly the United States). Their official 2025 leadership list, which names Fontaine as executive director of the North American group, mourns the passing of two founders: David Rockefeller and Dr Henry Kissinger. The commission’s operations are famously clandestine, which together with the elite status of many of its members has contributed to its perennial mystique.
Among leftists, it may be best known for its 1975 report (one of only a handful available to the public), “The Crisis of Democracy” — which was prominently criticized at the time by Noam Chomsky. The report’s section on the United States, authored by conservative intellectual Samuel P. Huntington, ascribes the preceding decade’s social turmoil to an “excess of democracy” — to be counteracted by “a greater degree of moderation in democracy.” Included in this excess were protest movements opposed to the Vietnam War and in support of racial justice. These movements helped dangerously integrate hitherto marginal populations, like black Americans, into the political process. “This marginality on the part of some groups [ . . . has] been one of the factors which has enabled democracy to function effectively.”
Half a century later, a similar attitude toward protest survives in Anthropic’s commercial and political activities. As Daniel Boguslaw details in The American Prospect, the company has been explicit about its plans to deploy AI to surveil, predict, and stifle protest activism. These plans include collaboration with law enforcement, and fit well with historical calls for digital surveillance from AI safety lobbyists at organizations with ties to Anthropic. Fontaine, who has served as the commission’s North American executive director since 2019, was appointed to Anthropic’s LTBT in 2025.
The Revolving Door
CNAS, on the other hand, is a Washington-based national security think tank with extensive ties to both Republican and Democratic White House administrations. Joe Biden and Donald Trump staffers with CNAS ties include senior figures like Avery Alpha, who occupied high-level roles at the Central Intelligence Agency and Department of Homeland Security from 2017 to 2025 before turning to consultancy work. The organization has traditionally pursued a broadly neoconservative line on foreign policy. Fontaine was elevated as president in 2012, only to be promoted again to CEO in 2019 — five months before his Trilateral Commission executive appointment.
CNAS also has an exceptional history of conflicts of interest and likely illicit influence. Several of these came to light in a 2021 bombshell report by the Revolving Door Project, which also helped expose CNAS members’ deep presence in the Biden and Trump administrations. The center has repeatedly championed private sector industries, international organizations, and foreign governments from whom it has received funding — often without explicit acknowledgement in the course of their advocacy.
Fontaine himself has taken direct part in these ethically suspect lobbying campaigns. In 2009, for example, he coauthored a policy paper defending the use of private military contractors in the war on terror — without any explicit acknowledgement of CNAS’s funding from several military contractor firms. He also did not acknowledge the $25,000–$50,000 funding the think tank had received from the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, during an event to promote NATO in 2019 at the Truman Library.
Anthropic is now itself among the beneficiaries of this conflict-ridden advocacy. On November 3, CNAS published a report advocating a suite of policy recommendations to protect against autonomous AI agents. The proposed policies align largely with Anthropic’s own stated regulatory agenda. And, conspicuously, certain of the policies clearly serve Anthropic’s commercial interests — especially against Chinese competitors. These include crackdowns on potential avenues of model distillation by foreign entities as well as diplomacy to erect barriers to powerful open-weights models. Model distillation by Chinese competitors has long been a sore point for Anthropic, and these competitors overwhelmingly favor open-weights licensing. At no point does the report mention Fontaine’s ties to Anthropic.
This hidden connection is just one part of a broader integration of CNAS, Anthropic, and affiliated organizations. CNAS affiliates now include major figures at Anthropic, like the center’s adjunct senior fellow, Michael Sellitto. Sellitto, who served on the National Security Council during the Obama and first Trump administrations and currently serves on the Council for Foreign Relations, is head of Anthropic’s Global Affairs team. The team is associated with Anthropic’s known surveillance activities and advocacy.
Effective Altruists and New Cold Warriors
CNAS has also maintained a partnership with the Center for Security and Emerging Technology (CSET) — an Anthropic-linked AI safety lobbying organization with deep ties in Washington. In 2025, for example, CSET announced its new advisory board, including CNAS member Michael Brown. It has also collaborated on several policy documents and research projects, particularly on combating Chinese AI development.
CSET enjoys extensive connections with Anthropic. These include personal overlaps, like Anthropic adviser and CSET Senior Fellow Ben Buchanan, or Anthropic policy executive and CSET advisory board member Joel Meyer. The two organizations have collaborated on the CHIPS Act and export controls against China, and are generally united under the ideological banner of effective altruism and AI safety.
In addition to personnel, CSET, CNAS, and Anthropic are linked financially through Coefficient Giving, the premier effective altruist donor body. Since its founding in 2019, CSET has received over $100 million from Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy), most of it in advance of its collaboration with CNAS. CNAS, too, has received funding directly from Coefficient Giving, albeit in smaller quantities. The bulk of this transfer was conducted in 2022 and 2025, when it received grants of a bit over $5 million and $8 million, respectively, for work in AI governance and security. These larger grants built on a series of smaller ones (from around $24,000 to $260,000) starting in 2017.
Anthropic enjoys deep ideological and personal ties with Coefficient Giving. Both emerged from the effective altruist and AI safety movements, which continue to shape their rhetoric and policy directions. Holden Karnofsky, cofounder of Coefficient Giving’s precursor GiveWell, is married to Anthropic board member Daniela Amodei, herself the sister of Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. Neil Shah, another LTBT member, served as managing director of Givewell until 2022. And Joe Carlsmith formerly led the AI-focussed “Worldview Investigations” team at Coefficient Giving (then Open Philanthropy). Now, he heads the “character” team at Anthropic, which is devoted to tailoring the values and personality of the company’s “Claude” assistants.
In the coming years and months, we are likely to witness a new influx of Anthropic money into Coefficient Giving and similar funding organizations — and thereby to more distant beneficiaries like CSET and CNAS. Many employees and executives have announced their intention to donate large portions of their wealth to charity, sometimes up to 80 percent. Coefficient Giving, itself a tax-deductible 501(c)3 nonprofit, has been recognized as a “favorite” of Anthropic executives, whose personal net worths extend into the tens of billions. In addition to laundering the donors’ reputations, these wealth transfers thus promise to further entrench the financial and organizational ties between Anthropic on the one hand and the Washington security establishment on the other.
Entanglement
The foregoing connections only scratch the surface of Anthropic’s ever-deepening entanglement with the security state. Beyond Fontaine, for example, the LTBT includes Harvard physicist Christopher Stubbs — who in addition to his academic appointments serves as a member of the independent scientific advisory group JASON. JASON’s work (much of it classified) largely concentrates on defense and nuclear strategy, including “studies under contract to the Department of Defense, the Department of Energy, the National Nuclear Security Administration, the U.S. Intelligence Community, and the FBI.” Most notoriously, it collaborated with military leadership during the Vietnam War, as revealed by Freedom of Information Act disclosures in 2002.
These connections do not merely speak to the increasing influence of the security establishment over Anthropic (and vice versa). They are also a clue as to the meaning of the company’s professed concern for human welfare and survival. Together with statements from company leadership, they paint a picture of long-term human interests deeply inflected by interventionist, antidemocratic, and anti-privacy strains in modern American foreign policy. Those who distrust such strains would do well to regard Anthropic, or any company with similar entanglements, with serious apprehension.

Vincent van Gogh’s 1890 Châtaigniers en fleurs (Blossoming Chestnut Trees) sold for $190.4 million at Sotheby’s in New York last night, smashing the artist’s auction record and blowing past the $180 million it had been expected to command. Previously, the most paid at auction for the Dutch master’s work was $117.2 million for his 1888 Verger avec cyprès (Orchard with Cypresses), at Christie’s in 2022. The New York Times identified the buyer as New York gallerist William Acquavella.
The painting also achieved the second-highest price of any work ever sold by Sotheby’s, surpassed only by Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer, 1914–16, which hammered for $236.4 million last year.
The sale capped a tumultuous week for the painting, which nearly didn’t make it to the auction block after the heirs of German Jewish publisher Samuel Fischer challenged the sale—by members of the Blaquier-Arrieta family, which had purchased the painting in 1975—saying that the family had sold it under duress in Amsterdam while escaping Nazi Berlin in 1936. Sotheby’s pushed back, pointing out that the work had fetched 68,000 Swiss francs (about $22,000 at the time), which it said was market rate for the era.
At the eleventh hour, with the sale fast approaching, Sotheby’s announced that Fischer’s descendants had reached an agreement with the Blaquier-Arrieta family.
“In recognition of the painting’s complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust,” Sotheby’s said in a statement, “the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement.”
The terms of the agreement were not disclosed; whether Fischer’s heirs will reap any financial reward from the work’s sale is unclear.

https://hyperallergic.com/the-ebullient-.title: The Ebullient Ecofeminism of Carolina Caycedo
https://hyperallergic.com/the-ebullient-.author: Eileen G’Sell
https://hyperallergic.com/the-ebullient-.text:
The Ebullient Ecofeminism of Carolina Caycedo
Her candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy.
ST LOUIS, MO — A pink lake under an avalanche of digital detritus; a neon rainbow behind a man in a hazmat suit; a gilt sky above a lone wind turbine. These are among the surreal, meticulously rendered scenes in Carolina Caycedo’s series Mineral Intensive (2023–ongoing).
Caycedo’s candy-colored drawings lure the eye only to disquiet the mind, exposing the contradictions of so-called clean energy, whose production often depends on environmentally destructive mineral extraction.
Such visual beguilement — and ecological exigency — anchors Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots, an exhibition of sculpture, video, printmaking, and drawing that explores the joyous, multisensory dimensions of the artist’s activism.
Born and raised in Bogotá, Colombia, the Los Angeles-based artist devoted two years to collaborative research with botanists, plant taxonomists, and Native elders, informing her rendering of prairie and botanical life across the Mississippi River watershed. By turns bright and delicate, Caycedo’s Plant Portraits series (2021–ongoing) lends an ecofeminist bent to the larger show, merging feminine anatomy with botanical illustration.
Like a heavenly necklace, “Celestial Autonomy, the Dance of Big Dipper and North Star” (2023) dangles in the center of the gallery. Constructed of Alaskan nets, buoys, and other fishing equipment — its title honors the indigenous communities in the region.
Across the Mississippi River, another sculptural installation, “Fiesta de la Raíces” (2026), vivifies the National Building Arts Center in Sauget, Illinois. A three-dimensional “portrait” of the area’s root systems, the sculpture resembles a shaggy chandelier of rope, beads, and natural fibers — beckoning admirers to bask in its festive opulence.
At a time when ecological disaster feels ever imminent, art attuned to earthly precarity can often feel didactic or downright drab. Caycedo insists on an alternate vision: Humanity in sync with a resplendent planet — the ground beneath us trembling with riches, the sky adorned with unseen stars.
Carolina Caycedo: Growing Deep Roots continues at the Kemper Art Museum at Washington University in St. Louis (One Brookings Drive, St. Louis, Missouri) through January 4, and at the National Building Arts Center (NBAC) (2300 Falling Springs Road, Sauget, Illinois) through December 12. The exhibition was curated by Meredith Malone and James McAnally.

The city of Sydney has launched its “artist living grants” program, where 40 artists are given $25,000, about $16,650 USD, no strings attached. The program is based on an income for artists grant that was introduced in Ireland three years ago. It was just made permanent this past winter, giving 2,000 creatives €325 a week.
The program is the first of its kind in Australia and is open to artists of all disciplines in Sydney. There are no limits on how the grant is spent, and the money can be used for anything, including living expenses and producing new work. “There are no specific requirements to ‘create’, or restrictions on other work, meaning the money can be spent on… whatever the artist needs,” said City of Sydney Greens councillor Sylvie Ellsmore in a statement given to the Guardian. The flexibility of the grant recognizes that artists spend hours outside of the studio to support their practice—applying to grants, working part-time, or freelancing.
For the 2021-2022 fiscal year, the average income of a professional artist in Australia was $54,500 ($36,308 USD). Like many metropolitan areas, artists are unable to keep up with the cost of living and move away. “We don’t want our city to lose its local storytellers and creative soul,” said Clover Moore, Sydney’s lord mayor. “While it’s not a cure all, these grants will boost 40 Sydney artists working across a range of artforms at different points in their careers, with many from under-represented communities.”
Ellsmore added: “Basic income models are how we should be funding the arts – with money going directly to artists, musicians, writers and creators, no strings attached.”

https://hyperallergic.com/laia-abril-pho.title: Laia Abril Photographs the Instruments of Rape Culture
https://hyperallergic.com/laia-abril-pho.author: Alina Cohen
https://hyperallergic.com/laia-abril-pho.text:
Laia Abril Photographs the Instruments of Rape Culture
In her latest show, garments and other objects serve as stand-ins for the systems that allow sexual assault to persist.
Editor’s Note: The following story contains mentions of sexual assault and harassment. To reach the National Sexual Assault Hotline, call 1-800-656-HOPE (4673) or visit online.rainn.org.
Some institutional rape cases create a glut of content. Recent allegations against Cornell students led to the publication of the accused’s portraits, images of their text messages, and videos of their fraternity house. Tweets and articles flooded the internet, while a journalist’s attempt to identify Jane Doe launched an entire Instagram campaign: Users posted their own pictures with the hashtag #iamjanedoe to help shield the victim. On the other side of the spectrum, reported rapes in the military, the Catholic Church, and less wealthy communities around the world may be met with silence, handled privately, or otherwise fail to galvanize the digital realm.
Spanish photographer Laia Abril — whose larger project “A History of Misogyny” has also tackled feminicide, abortion, and endometriosis — faces a tricky mandate as she created On Rape and Institutional Failure, first shown in 2020 and now on view at the International Center for Photography. Her images have to be compelling without embracing spectacle, specific while addressing an enormous, global theme.
The artist makes two key choices, one conceptual and one formal: She shoots objects instead of people, all in black-and-white. Honing in on her palette, Abril gets at the seemingly eternal nature of misogyny; her distilled images stoke a similarly condensed rage.

The Stedelijk Museum Amsterdam has announced Krist Gruijthuijsen as its new director. Gruijthuijsen arrives to the institution from Finland’s EMMA – Espoo Museum of Modern Art, where he has served as director since 2025, and from Kunsthaus Zürich, where he is curator at large. He will succeed Rein Wolfs, who has led the museum since late 2019. Gruijthuijsen will take up his new post in July 2027.
“The Supervisory Board is convinced Krist Gruijthuijsen is the right person to succeed Rein Wolfs,” said board chair Annelies van der Pauw in a statement. “We are confident that his energy and vision will help shape the museum’s future in an inspiring way, and that he will make a compelling case for the importance of modern and contemporary art and design.”
The Netherlands-born Gruijthuijsen brings two decades of experience to his role. Before joining EMMA, he was director of Berlin’s KW Institute for Contemporary Art from 2016 to 2024. Among the exhibitions he organized were solo shows by Willem de Rooij, Beatriz González, Leonilson, Hassan Sharif, and David Wojnarowicz. He was previously director of Grazer Kunstverein in Graz, Austria, from 2012 to 2016; concurrently, he helmed the Fine Arts Department at the Sandberg Instituut in Amsterdam, beginning in 2011. With Maxine Kopsa, he cofounded Kunstverein Amsterdam in 2009, spending four years as its director.
“The museum has long held a special place in my personal and professional life, as it does in the history of modern and contemporary art and design,” said Gruijthuijsen in a statement. “An essential part of my role will be to deepen the museum’s relationship with Amsterdam: to make it ever more open, engaged, and connected to the city and its communities. I want the Stedelijk not only to reflect the world we live in, but also to actively contribute to shaping its future.”

https://gothamist.com/news/family-of-wom.title: Family of woman killed in wrong-way crash files wrongful death lawsuit against NYC, DOT
https://gothamist.com/news/family-of-wom.author: Brittany Kriegstein
https://gothamist.com/news/family-of-wom.text:
The family of a young woman who was struck and killed by an SUV driver in Manhattan last year has filed a wrongful death lawsuit, alleging widespread negligence by the city, the Department of Transportation, the driver and the car rental company he worked for.
Valerie Schoeck, 27, was fatally hit while crossing Morton Street and 7th Avenue in the West Village last November, according to the NYPD. Gary Levinson, 62, was behind the wheel of the van that struck her, and police said he was going the wrong way. He was arrested months later and charged with criminally negligent homicide and reckless driving.
In their lawsuit filed Wednesday, Schoeck’s family alleges that the city’s Department of Transportation did not have a “One Way” sign on Morton Street and failed to install other warning signs and traffic control devices while they repaved and redesigned the roadway.
They also allege negligence on the part of Courier Car Rental and Bero Parking Corp., which both operate on the corner where Schoeck was killed, for not putting up adequate signage to keep pedestrians safe. Levinson was driving one of Courier Car Rental's vehicles at the time of the crash, the lawsuit states.
“The simplest of acts by each defendant could have prevented this unspeakable tragedy. Their failure to do so requires accountability and each defendant must answer to the law,” wrote Imran H. Ansari, the attorney representing the family, in a statement.
Schoeck’s family said she was engaged to be married and building a successful career in public relations when she died.
“Valerie’s death has left our family wrapped in silence and emptiness that no words can ever fill,” they wrote in a statement, “But, we will carry her memory with tenderness and strength, refusing to let the light she brought into our lives grow dim. We will keep seeking the truth, accountability and justice she deserves.”
In May, Levinson pleaded guilty to criminally negligent homicide and was sentenced to a five-year revocation of his professional license. He was placed on a three-year conditional discharge, meaning he does not have to serve time in prison but has to follow several court-mandated requirements, including community service, which Levinson’s attorney said he completed last year.
The city’s Department of Transportation did not immediately respond to an inquiry about the lawsuit. A representative of Courier Car Rental declined to comment, and contact information for Bero Parking Corp. was not immediately available.
The lawsuit said the family is seeking damages in “an amount that exceeds the jurisdictional limits of the lower Courts” but did not specify further.

https://gothamist.com/news/polluting-tra.title: Polluting trailers at Hunts Point market would be banned under new NYC Council bill
https://gothamist.com/news/polluting-tra.author: Elizabeth Kim
https://gothamist.com/news/polluting-tra.text:
A new City Council bill would ban idling diesel-powered refrigerated trailers in New York City warehouses, targeting a major polluter in the South Bronx: Hunts Point Produce Market.
The measure, which will be introduced Thursday by City Councilmember Justin Sanchez of the Bronx, seeks to force an end to the trailers that have long been a symbol of the environmental injustice that helped the South Bronx earn the nickname “asthma alley.” Gothamist reported in September that a $650 million deal to redevelop Hunts Point — and eliminate the need for the trailers — had collapsed amid concerns from the co-op of produce operators at the market, which supplies as much as 60% of the city’s produce.
The market, which sits on city-owned land, has for years relied on transport refrigeration units, also known as TRUs, to store produce because the facility’s 1960s-era warehouses are at capacity. The rumbling trailers are known for operating 24/7 at the site. Each trailer produces emissions equivalent to 330 truck trips on the Cross Bronx Expressway every day, according to the governor’s office.
In his final days in office, previous Mayor Eric Adams announced the plan to modernize the Hunts Point market facility. But the deal fell apart this summer under Mayor Zohran Mamdani after market operators raised questions about whether the project might disrupt their operations.
Sanchez’s bill applies to all stationary diesel-powered transport refrigeration units in large warehouses, food distribution centers, marine terminals and railyards across the city. Violators would face fines of up to $5,000.
“There is no reason why Hunts Point needs to suffer at the behest of being the food distribution hub of the city,” Sanchez said. The neighborhood, which is heavily trafficked by trucks, has some of the highest asthma rates in the country.
Joel Fireman, a third-generation Hunts Point produce operator and co-president of the co-op, disputed the extent of the pollution and said the bill would only wind up hurting a major employer in the Bronx. He said the site currently has around 800 trailers, many of which run on both diesel and electric.
But he said the market’s old infrastructure prevents operators from accessing more electricity. That is one of the major reasons city officials have encouraged the co-op to redevelop the facility.
“Environmentally we’re all in favor of cleaning up the market,” Fireman said. “Don’t put obstacles in our way. Come up with a solution.”
The bill comes ahead of a Dec.16 City Council hearing, when members are expected to grill administration officials on why the Hunts Point deal collapsed.
Mamdani has blamed his predecessor Eric Adams for rushing a deal before all parties agreed to the terms. He said the city is looking to “create a new path forward” but has not said whether the city can salvage the funding, which included $370 million in federal loans and grants.
Officials, including city Comptroller Mark Levine, have urged City Hall to try to resurrect the project, saying, “We cannot let this fail.”
Sanchez said his proposed legislation is intended to put pressure on everyone at the bargaining table. “We're not going to just let folks pollute our air indefinitely,” he said.
The current lease between the city and Hunts Point co-op operators expires in 2039. If passed, the legislation would take effect two years after it becomes law.
Sanchez said other U.S. municipalities have passed similar legislation. He said he is currently recruiting other council members to co-sponsor the bill.
Cassio Mendoza, a spokesperson for Mamdani, said the mayor’s office would review the legislation.
“The Mamdani administration remains committed to working with local stakeholders to identify solutions that reduce harmful emissions and improve the quality of life for Hunts Point residents,” he added in a statement.
A spokesperson for Council Speaker Julie Menin’s office said she will review the bill once it is introduced.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-looks-to-.title: NYC looks to close a 'loophole' in sanctuary protection for immigrants
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-looks-to-.author: Arya Sundaram
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-looks-to-.text:
The New York City Council's immigration committee is considering a set of bills that meant to close a “loophole” in the city’s sanctuary laws, which limit local officials' cooperation with federal immigration authorities.
A bill introduced by Councilmember Elsie Encarnación, the immigration committee chair, would explicitly prohibit city jail officials from notifying federal immigration agents of a detainee’s release unless provided with a judicial warrant.
A similar bill, also introduced by Encarnación and set for review during a Council hearing on Friday, would establish similar restrictions for the NYPD.
Under the city’s sanctuary protections, an immigrant detainee must have been convicted of a serious or violent crime, or come up as a possible match on a terrorist screening database, to warrant being turned over to federal immigration officials. The law also requires that federal officials provide a warrant from a judge.
But city jails have transferred dozens of people to federal immigration authorities in recent years, without receipt of a judicial warrant, jail officials have repeatedly testified in the City Council. From July 1, 2025, to June 30 this year, the city's Department of Correction transferred 24 people to federal immigration authorities, and 19 people during the year prior, according to agency data.
James Conroy, the Department of Correction’s chief lawyer, justified these transfers in a March Council hearing, citing another section of the city’s sanctuary laws. Those provisions under certain circumstances allow jail officials to share information with federal authorities even without a judicial warrant, he said.
The proposed revisions in Encarnación’s bills would remove any ambiguity and make plain that a judicial warrant was required under almost all circumstances.
Rosa Cohen-Cruz, director of immigration policy at the Bronx Defenders, who helped draft and lobby for the bills, said they are important measures for ensuring due process for immigrant detainees and preventing individuals from ending up in the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which she called a “rogue, violent, dangerous organization.”
“ We should be protecting all New Yorkers,” Cohen-Cruz said in an interview. “We should not be funneling any New Yorkers into that system, regardless of their criminal legal system contact.”
The Department of Correction did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for the NYPD said the Council’s bill is already the law, and that the NYPD can’t transfer a detainee into ICE custody without a judicial warrant, and hasn’t transferred someone into ICE custody in about a decade.
The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not respond to requests for comment.
New York City agreed in December 2024 to pay up to $92.5 million to settle claims it unlawfully detained more than 20,000 undocumented immigrants beyond their scheduled release from city jails, to allow for their transfer into federal immigration custody.
The hearing at 10 a.m. on Friday will also include an update on the current state of immigration enforcement in the city.

https://gothamist.com/news/black-and-his.title: Black and Hispanic Staten Islanders get nearly half of obscure pedestrian law tickets
https://gothamist.com/news/black-and-his.author: Ben Feuerherd
https://gothamist.com/news/black-and-his.text:
NYPD officers don’t issue many “pedestrians on roadways” criminal tickets. Most New Yorkers probably don’t even know that offense exists.
It criminalizes walking in the street when a sidewalk is available – an offense that sounds similar to jaywalking, which was legalized in the city in 2024 in part because lawmakers said its enforcement disproportionately targeted Black and Hispanic residents.
So far this year, officers have issued 68 criminal summonses for pedestrians on roadways, according to researchers at John Jay College of Criminal Justice. Of those, officers wrote 30 in the 120th precinct on Staten Island, all but one to Black and Hispanic people, the researchers found. The disparity has caused residents, researchers and attorneys to question if those groups are being unfairly targeted.
Gothamist has previously reported that police have disproportionately targeted residents of some city neighborhoods as part of a quality of life crackdown. Some residents and police reform advocates have criticized the NYPD and Mayor Zohran Mamdani for prioritizing such enforcement, saying it’s a waste of resources and disproportionately affects low-income people of color. Prior to his election, Mamdani campaigned on moving police away from low-level enforcement so officers are more able to focus on solving larger crimes. Earlier this month, the department issued guidance to officers instructing them not to enforce offenses including spitting and engine idling in certain circumstances.
“ That reminds me of stop and frisks,” said Asar Glenn, 45, a Staten Island resident of the sprawling Park Hill Apartments, near where officers have issued six pedestrian tickets so far this year. “ I think they just want to get IDs off of people that they stop, see if they got a record or whatever. It's like fishing.”
NYPD spokesperson Brad Weekes defended the ticketing in a statement and said the offense being enforced is not the same as jaywalking.
"These summonses were not connected to jaywalking and were the result of legitimate law enforcement activity," Weekes said.
Officers from the 120th precinct, which covers Staten Island neighborhoods including Tompkinsville, New Brighton and Stapleton, have written more than 44% of the pedestrians on roadways tickets citywide, according to the analysis by researchers at John Jay College. Of those ticketed for the offense in the precinct, 26 were Black, three were Hispanic and one person was white, the researchers said.
Officers in the precinct with the second highest number of such tickets — the 33rd precinct in Washington Heights — have issued a total of five tickets for the offense so far this year. In all of 2025, officers from the 120th precinct issued 11 of the summonses.
‘Hot Spots’
Matthew Weiss, a New York attorney who has specialized in traffic infractions for decades, said in the 30 years he has practiced law, he’s never defended a client against a pedestrians on roadways ticket.
Under the law, if a sidewalk is available, pedestrians are required to walk on it and not walk in the roadway, Weiss said. If there is no sidewalk, pedestrians are required to walk as far left as possible on the road or on the shoulder facing oncoming traffic.
“Pedestrians that receive such a ticket should argue for dismissal … if in fact they're just crossing the street, not walking along on the street,” Weiss said. “If they go to court and make that legal argument it has strong potential for being successful in my opinion.”
Michael Rempel, a researcher who worked to compile the summons analysis at John Jay College, said the infraction is strikingly similar to jaywalking.
Rempel noted that he and the other researchers identified “hot spots” within the 120th precinct where police officers wrote a disproportionate number of tickets for the offense. They include intersections near large housing complexes, including the Stapleton Houses, a NYCHA development, the Park Hill Apartments, and intersections near single-level attached homes along Jersey Street on the border of the St. George and New Brighton neighborhoods.
“They are all in urban places,” Rempel said. “It confirms that we're not dealing with really fast roads where someone walking in the road is creating a public safety danger to themselves.”
‘Tension’
The North Shore of Staten Island, a large slice of which is patrolled by officers from the 120th precinct, is a racially diverse set of neighborhoods that feature a mix of large apartment buildings, bustling urban blocks, as well as streets dotted with large Victorian homes in what can feel like a suburban setting.
Criticism of how police respond to low-level offenses in this section of Staten Island is not new. The issue exploded more than a decade ago when an NYPD officer killed 43-year-old Eric Garner with a chokehold after stopping him for apparently selling loose cigarettes.
White residents make up the largest racial group on Staten Island’s North Shore, and nearly a quarter of residents identify as Black. Asian residents and residents of other races make up another 27% of the population, according to numbers released by the State Comptroller’s Office in 2024.
The New York Civil Liberties Union, a legal nonprofit that has previously challenged NYPD officers disproportionately stopping Black and Hispanic residents, said in a statement the fact that officers are writing a disproportionate amount of the pedestrian tickets in this area is disconcerting.
“Time and time again, we’ve seen the NYPD disproportionately target Black, brown, and low-income people with low level enforcement under the guise of quality-of-life policing,” said Daniel Lambright, director of Criminal Justice Litigation at the NYCLU. “Mayor Mamdani must act now to bring an end to these racist broken windows policing tactics.”
Residents who spoke to Gothamist near the streets where the tickets were issued had a mix of opinions about the cluster of pedestrians in roadways tickets that were issued in their neighborhood.
On a recent afternoon, Mildred Cosme was walking down Jersey Street near where police officers have issued six of the pedestrian tickets so far this year.
She said seeing police makes her feel safer when she is running errands at a nearby Family Dollar or when she’s heading to the laundromat.
“I don't like to walk here around certain hours,” she said. “It concerns safety.”
Across the street from the Stapleton Houses, Steven Velez, 36, said he wished police would focus on larger crimes in the neighborhood, noting the number of walls around the NYCHA development that are covered in memorial murals in honor of residents killed in the neighborhood.
Velez recalled that police officers stopped one of his coworkers and accused him of trespassing as the man was leaving Velez’s building recently.
“You over here stopping a guy from trespassing when he wasn't trespassing,” he said. “ It's kind of stupid to be honest with you.”
Outside of the Park Hill Apartments, Glenn added that he’s concerned for young people in the neighborhood who may be stopped by police for low-level offenses.
“ There's always going to be tension between the community and the police,” he said. “The older residents might feel a little comfortable 'cause they don't come outside, they don't get hassled as much, but the younger people, they always going to feel it.”

https://hyperallergic.com/hilma-af-klint.text:
Hilma af Klint Is Rolling in Her Grave
The Swedish artist’s painting went under the hammer for an obscene amount of money. Plus: Lowery Stokes Sims reviews Richard Powell’s new book on pigment, Blackness, and paint.
Nothing in visual culture is neutral, least of all the color wheel itself. Scholar Richard Powell explores this deceptively simple truth in his new book, tackling the theoretical entanglement of race and pigment and how Black painters have used color over time. Trailblazing art historian Lowery Stokes Sims, formerly a curator at the Met Museum and director of the Studio Museum in Harlem, parses his richly layered essays today, linking the critical theory of Josef Albers and Darby English to the practices of artists like Jacob Lawrence and Alma Thomas. The book, Sims writes, shifted the way she’ll look at art moving forward.
Meanwhile, on the other end of the spectrum: News broke that a 1920 painting by Hilma af Klint sold for $12.7 million. Yes, the same Hilma af Klint who described herself less as an artist and more as a channel for a higher power, who followed the guidance of spirits that took physical form through her paintings. But hey, at least the painting’s owner has a new addition to their investment portfolio?
In reviews, Alina Cohen spends time with the poignant, impactful photographs by Laia Abril, who evokes the systems of patriarchy and sexual violence through the quietly haunting garments and objects in their wake. As the Cornell 7 case continues and convicted abusers sit in office, Abril’s photographs “reject both the invisibility of some crimes and the all-too-visible nature of others.” More, as always, below.
—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books
Richard Powell Unsettles Race and Color Theory
I was aware of the place of color theory in the practice of art and knew the names of important theorists, from Johann Wolfgang von Goethe to Johannes Itten to Josef Albers. But otherwise, I presumed artists’ palettes were the result of personal predilection, technical explorations (i.e., the opening up of brushstrokes and form in the 19th century and the introduction of a wall of color in the 20th century), or cultural orientation. So it was therefore with great interest that I approached reading Richard Powell’s latest publication, Colorstruck!: Painting, Pigment, Affect (2026). | Lowery Stokes Sims
