https://www.artnews.com/list/art-news/ma.title: The 16 Most Expensive Artworks Ever Sold at Auction
https://www.artnews.com/list/art-news/ma.author: Daniel Cassady
https://www.artnews.com/list/art-news/ma.text:
Auction records make for great headlines, like the 2026 banner sale of Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16), which topped $236.4 million at Sotheby’s. There’s a thrill in watching numbers climb into the stratosphere, each sale another reminder that, in the art market, money has a way of bending reality. But the price of a painting has never been the most interesting thing about it.
Look at the list of the most expensive artworks ever sold at auction, and you’ll see more than just a parade of billionaires with good taste (or at least expensive taste). You’ll see a history of ideas—what mattered to the artists who made them, what obsessed the collectors who chased them, and how we decide, decades or centuries later, which works still hold power.
Yes, Salvator Mundi sold for $450 million, but is it really a Leonardo? Picasso’s Women of Algiers, Pollock’s Number 7A, 1948, and Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn all shattered records, with the Pollock work shooting far beyond its $100 million estimate when it came to auction at Christie’s in May 2026 in a sale of works from the S. I. Newhouse collection. But these works’ real value has nothing to do with what someone was willing to pay on a given evening at Christie’s. The best art—the kind that shifts culture, lingers in your mind, and changes how you see the world—exists in a space money can’t touch.
But of course, once a work crosses a threshold, there’s something almost inevitable about the price spiral. With each record-breaking sale, the bar gets set higher, the stakes get sharper, and the frenzy deepens. The game has changed, but in a way, the auction houses are just as much a stage for the spectacle as for the art itself. Every price tag opens the door to another possibility. If one work can sell for $450 million, what’s to stop the next from reaching half a billion—or more? With so many players in the game, all vying for the ultimate cultural trophy, the numbers have a way of multiplying faster than the logic behind them.
And yet, the more those numbers rise, the further they drift from the essential thing that makes art so valuable: the art itself. High prices can make us think we’re in the presence of something transcendent, but it’s the work that holds the power, not the price. So, here’s the list. The numbers are staggering, but don’t get too caught up in them. The real story is in the art itself.
A version of this article was first published on November 19, 2025. It was last updated on November 20, 2026.
- Edvard Munch, The Scream, 1895 Sold for $119.9 million at Sotheby’s New York in May 2012 When it sold for $107 million at Sotheby’s New York, Munch’s pastel The Scream (1895), one of the four versions—two painted and two in pastel—that he made of the same subject, became the most expensive work ever to be sold at a public auction, stealing the trophy from Picasso’s 1932 Nude, Green Leaves and Bust, which sold at Christie’s in 2010 for $106.5 million. At the time, it was the only version of The Scream still in private hands; its seller was Petter Olsen, a Norwegian businessman whose father, Thomas, was Munch’s friend and patron. The picture, which opened at $40 million, sparked a 12-minute bidding war, with wide-eyed potential buyers both in the salesroom and on the phones. According to the Wall Street Journal, its buyer was investor Leon Black, a trustee at the Museum of Modern Art, where The Scream later went on view. After the sale Olsen, described by Art in America as “the wild-haired and bespectacled seller,” read a statement that tied the work to climate change and global warming: “The Scream for me shows the horrifying moment when man realizes his impact on nature and the irreversible changes that he has initiated, making the planet increasingly uninhabitable. . . . More death, less life. And very few lifeboats left as we go down.”
- René Magritte, Empire of Light, 1954 Sold for $121 million at Christie’s New York in November 2024 The “crown jewel” of the auction market in 2024 (as Christie’s so humbly put it) was perhaps the finest example of a subject that Magritte revisited more than 25 times throughout his career: an otherworldly scene showing a house on tree-lined street at night. But instead being enveloped in darkness, the sky above the trees is impossibly blue, with big, cottony clouds floating by. This 1954 version of Empire of Light, which sold for $121 million and came from the collection of designer and philanthropist Mica Ertegun, set a new record for Magritte’s work at auction. After the sale, Christie’s chairman of 20th and 21st century art Alex Rotter said the house that evening had adopted a “masterpiece approach” to this sale. “In a market that is not so easy to maneuver, we thought that if we present the greatest works we can get … these are the best examples,” Rotter said, admitting that the auction had its share of lots that didn’t catch collectors’ attention. But “the works that we put all the emphasis behind really proved us right. They had multiple bidders and showed that a market based on individual taste is on the rise.”
- Paul Cézanne, Mont Sainte-Victoire, 1888–90 Sold for $137.7 million at Christie’s New York in November 2022 Cézanne’s deliciously rich landscape of the French countryside and his beloved Mont Sainte-Victoire is the second of five works from the Paul Allen sale at Christie’s to make this list. When the hammer fell, Mont Sainte-Victoire (1888–90) doubled Cézanne’s previous auction high of $60.5 million, for a still life from the collection of John Hay Whitney. Like Cézanne’s best works, Mont Sainte-Victoire breaks aspects of the world—in this case, a French mountain—into shapes shaded with color, as though they were three-dimensional geometrical forms. In that way, Cézanne paved the way for Cubist artists such as Pablo Picasso and George Braque, who would push his innovations even further toward abstraction.
- Pablo Picasso, Woman with a Watch, 1932 Sold for $139.3 million at Sotheby’s New York in November 2023 Woman with a Watch (1932), one of Picasso’s many paintings of his mistress Marie-Thérèse Walter, became the second most expensive work by the artist ever sold at auction when it fetched $139 million at Sotheby’s in 2023. The canvas, from the collection of late philanthropist Emily Fisher Landau, drew intense bidding before selling to a phone bidder represented by Sotheby’s head of global fine art, Brooke Lampley. Woman with a Watch had a rarefied provenance, changing hands just a few times since Picasso painted it in 1932. It was acquired by Landau in 1968 from Pace Gallery, which had purchased it from Switzerland’s Galerie Beyeler two years earlier. Pictures of Walter typically go for top dollar. In 2010, Nude, Green Leaves and Bust—also painted in 1932—broke records at $106.5 million. Still, the most expensive Picasso of all time is a work that does not depict Walter. But more on that in a bit.
- Qi Baishi, Twelve Screens of Landscapes, 1925 Sold for $140.8 million at Poly International Auction Co., Ltd., Beijing in December 2017 Qi Baishi’s Twelve Screens of Landscapes (1925) shattered records in 2017, selling for RMB 931.5 million ($140.8 million) at Beijing Poly Auction and making it the most expensive Chinese artwork ever sold at auction. The bidding war lasted over 20 minutes, with more than 60 bid increments before a Chinese collector secured the 12-panel piece. Each 70-inch panel captures a sweeping vista from Qi’s travels across China. Originally displayed at his solo exhibition in 1954 and later featured in a memorial show in 1958, the set of panels was kept by Qi’s pupil, Xiuyi Guo, before resurfacing at auction. A similar version of Twelve Screens of Landscapes, painted around 1932 as a gift to Kuomintang general Wang Zuanxu, resides in the Chongqing Museum. The set sold in 2017 was the only one in private hands at the time, making it a rarity.
- Alberto Giacometti, Pointing Man, 1947 Sold for $141.3 million at Christie’s New York in May 2015 Alberto Giacometti’s Pointing Man (1947) became the most expensive sculpture ever sold at auction when it fetched $141.3 million at Christie’s New York in May 2015. The life-size bronze, standing at more than five and a half feet tall, was sold by real estate magnate Sheldon Solow, surpassing Giacometti’s previous auction record of $104.3 million, which was set at Sotheby’s London five years earlier by Walking Man I (1960). One of six casts made by the artist (not counting an additional artist’s proof), this particular Pointing Man had been held privately for 45 years before the sale. Four of those casts reside in major museums, including the Museum of Modern Art in New York and the Tate in London, which made this auction a prime opportunity for collectors. Similar sculptures by Giacometti depicting skeletal, elongated figures have likewise sold for big sums. At the time, Christie’s head Pylkkänen called the piece “one of the finest works of art I have had the honor to handle.” Whoever bought the piece clearly agreed about its quality.
- Francis Bacon, Three Studies of Lucian Freud, 1969 Sold for $142.4 million at Christie’s New York in November 2013 Francis Bacon’s Three Studies of Lucian Freud (1969) briefly became the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction when it sold for $142.4 million at Christie’s New York in November 2013. The triptych surpassed the previous record, held by Edvard Munch’s pastel The Scream, which sold for $119.9 million at Sotheby’s in 2012 (and which also appears on this list, above). Bacon’s three-panel portrait—each part stands six and a half feet tall—depicts Bacon’s longtime friend and artistic rival, Lucian Freud, in a series of contorted poses. The piece had an unusual history: its panels were separated by a dealer in the 1970s and remained apart for 15 years before being reunited by a collector in 1989. The work was expected to sell for over $85 million, but after a five-minute bidding war, it was secured by New York’s Acquavella Galleries. In a strategic move, Christie’s shifted the Bacon painting to the ninth lot of the evening to allow unsuccessful bidders a chance at other works—an approach that proved successful, contributing to the auction house’s record-breaking $691.6 million total for the night. Shortly after the sale, the anonymous buyer lent the triptych to the Portland Art Museum for public viewing from December 2013 to March 2014.
- Georges Seurat, Models (Small Version), 1888 Sold for $149 million at Christie’s New York in November 2022 In November 2022, an early 20th-century masterpiece by Georges Seurat, Models (Small Version) (1888), sold for a staggering $149 million at Christie’s New York. The painting, depicting three nude figures in Seurat’s signature pointillist style, was one of the rarest privately-owned works by the artist. It came from the collection of Microsoft co-founder Paul Allen and was expected to surpass $100 million at auction. The bidding opened at $75 million, drawing competition from four bidders, including specialists representing clients in New York and Asia. After several minutes of heated back-and-forth, the work hammered at $130 million, with Christie’s Asia chairman securing the piece for a final total of $149 million, including fees. The sale set a new auction record for Seurat, shattering his previous high of $34 million, achieved in 2018 for The Harbor at Grandcamp(1885). The last time Models (Small Version) appeared on the market was in 1970, when it fetched just over $1 million at Christie’s. Prior to Allen’s ownership, it had belonged to the influential collector John Quinn, a champion of modernist artists in the early 20th century.
- Amedeo Modigliani, Reclining Nude (on Her Left Side), 1917 Sold for $157.2 million at Sotheby’s New York in May 2018 Amedeo Modigliani’s Reclining Nude (on Her Left Side) (1917), one of the artist’s most celebrated nudes, sold for $157.2 million at Sotheby’s New York in 2018. The total price, including the buyer’s premium, followed a hammer bid of $139 million, which fell just short of its undisclosed estimate of $150 million. Despite this, the sale set a record for the most expensive artwork ever sold at Sotheby’s at the time. The large-scale canvas—depicting a nude woman gazing over her shoulder at the viewer—was the star lot of the auction house’s Impressionist and Modern art sale. Bidding opened at $125 million with auctioneer Helena Newman presiding over the room. The winning bid came from a client on the phone with Simon Shaw, Sotheby’s co-head of Impressionist and Modern art worldwide, after a subdued and measured exchange. The work belongs to Modigliani’s groundbreaking series of reclining nudes, painted between 1916 and 1919. When first exhibited in 1917 at Parisian dealer Berthe Weill’s gallery, these erotic paintings caused such a scandal that police shut down the show after just two days. At the time, only two drawings were sold. While the sale price was extraordinary, it did not surpass Modigliani’s auction record, which remains with Reclining Nude (1917–18), sold at Christie’s in 2015 for $170.4 million to Chinese collector Liu Yiqian. Sotheby’s, however, positioned Reclining Nude (on Her Left Side) as a transformative work, with Simon Shaw stating, “There is the nude before Modigliani, and there is the nude after Modigliani.”
- Amedeo Modigliani, Nu couché, 1917–18 Sold for $170.4 million at Christie’s New York in November 2015 Amedeo Modigliani’s Reclining Nude (1917–18) shattered expectations at Christie’s New York in 2015, selling for $170.4 million, more than doubling the artist’s previous auction record of $70.7 million. The work, which carried an on-request estimate of over $100 million, became the second-most expensive painting ever sold at auction at the time. The sale took place during Christie’s curated evening auction, “The Artist’s Muse,” which aimed to build buzz around 20th-century masterpieces. Despite a mixed night—with several major lots, including works by Willem de Kooning and Lucian Freud, failing to sell—the Modigliani nude electrified the room. Bidding was fierce, ultimately concluding with a Chinese collector securing the work via telephone, as revealed by Pylkkänen after the sale. (The collector was later revealed to be Chinese billionaire businessman Liu Yiqian.) Reclining Nude is part of Modigliani’s celebrated series of reclining nudes, painted between 1916 and 1919. These works, revolutionary in their sensuality and bold in their approach to form, scandalized Paris when first exhibited at Berthe Weill’s gallery in 1917, leading to the show’s abrupt closure by police. Today, they are considered among the most important contributions to the modern nude tradition. The sale of Reclining Nude was a high point in an otherwise uneven auction, which totaled $491.4 million—above its $440 million low estimate but falling far short of the $705.8 million brought in by a similar sale earlier that year. While other records were set that night—including for works by Gustave Courbet, Balthus, and Roy Lichtenstein—the Modigliani painting stood out as the undeniable star of the evening, solidifying the artist’s status as one of the most sought-after names in the art market.
- Pablo Picasso, Women of Algiers (Version ‘O’), 1955 Sold for $179.4 million at Christie’s New York in May 2015 Pablo Picasso’s Women of Algiers (Version ‘O’) (1955) set a new auction record in 2015 when it sold for $179.4 million at Christie’s New York, becoming the most expensive painting ever sold at auction at the time. The painting, the final and most intricate piece in Picasso’s 15-work “Women of Algiers” series (1954–55), had an on-request estimate of around $140 million but soared past that figure after deep bidding. The competition for the masterpiece played out entirely over the phone, with then-Christie’s executives Loic Gouzer and Brett Gorvy representing rival bidders. Pylkkänen, serving as auctioneer, declared “Still many people in the game” as bidding climbed past $140 million. Eventually, Gorvy’s bidder emerged victorious with a hammer price of $160 million, drawing cheers from the audience. The “Women of Algiers” series was inspired by Eugène Delacroix’s 1834 masterpiece of the same name. Created in response to the Nationalist uprising in Algeria against French colonial rule, the series reflects Picasso’s fascination with both European Orientalist art and the evolving political landscape of the time. The version here is considered the most elaborate and fully realized of the set. The painting had a notable provenance, originally acquired by New York collectors Victor and Sally Ganz directly from legendary dealer Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler in 1956. It first appeared at auction in 1997, when it sold for $31.9 million—meaning its value increased nearly sixfold in less than two decades. While Christie’s maintained confidentiality regarding the winning bidder, reports later suggested that the buyer was former Qatari Prime Minister Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber Al Thani. The sale reinforced Picasso’s dominance in the art market, cementing Women of Algiers (Version ‘O’) as one of the defining auction moments of the decade.
- Jackson Pollock, Number 7A, 1948, 1948 Sold for $181.2 million at Christie’s New York in May 2026 This 11-foot-wide painting by Jackson Pollock came to auction at Christie’s with both a first-class provenance and remarkable historical cachet. Pollock painted the work in 1948, the year after he first devised his drip painting technique, in which the artist flung his paint at the canvas rather than applying it directly using his brush. The technique distanced Pollock’s hand from his painting, leaving the application of his paint to chance. Before he owned Sotheby’s, businessman A. Alfred Taubman owned the painting, selling it to publishing magnate S. I. Newhouse in 2000. In 2026, nearly a decade after Newhouse’s death, the painting headed to sale at Christie’s with a $100 million estimate, poising it to break Pollock’s record. At the time of the Christie’s auction, the painting hadn’t been seen publicly since 1977. The work ended up shooting far beyond its estimate and becoming one of the most expensive paintings ever sold. Bidding opened at $80 million, and following 60 bids, the painting hammered at $157 million. With fees, the total rose to $181.2 million.
- Vincent van Gogh, Blossoming Chestnut Trees, 1888 Sold for: $190.4 million On November 18, 2026, Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), a picture of sunlit trees set against oncoming storm clouds, sold for $190.4 million (including fees) at Sotheby’s. The cover lot for the auction house’s Blaquier-Arrieta collection sale, which the house had billed as “legendary,” it set a new auction record for the Dutch painter. The reported buyer was dealer William Acquavella. The artist’s previous record of $117.2 million was set at Christie’s in November 2022 when Orchard with Cypresses (1888), a landscape from the collection of Microsoft cofounder Paul Allen, sold for $102 million. The new result beat that by $73.2 million, a jump of 62.4 percent in just four years. That the sale happened at all was a victory for Sotheby’s. Just days before the auction, descendants of Samuel Fischer, the German Jewish publisher who once owned the painting, challenged its sale, arguing that their family had been forced to part with it in Amsterdam in 1936 because of Nazi persecution. Sotheby’s disputed the claim, pointing to archival records showing the painting had sold for 68,000 Swiss francs, around $22,000 at the time, which it considered a fair market price. After several days of talks, the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the Fischer heirs reached an agreement, clearing the painting’s title. Painted shortly after Van Gogh arrived at Auvers-sur-Oise in May 1890, Blossoming Chestnut Trees is among the 70-plus paintings (and more than 50 drawings) that the artist made there before taking his own life only two months later. It was also one of only eight Auvers landscapes still in private hands, according to research cited by the Art Newspaper. The electric scene, with its thick brushwork, also hadn’t been seen in decades. It was last exhibited at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in 1964 before Argentine collectors Carlos Pedro and Nelly Arrieta Blaquier, bought it in 1975—the kind of provenance and scarcity that fuels record-breaking prices like this one.—Daniel Cassady
- Andy Warhol, Shot Sage Blue Marilyn, 1964 Sold for $195 million at Christie’s New York in May 2022 Andy Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn, one of the most iconic images in modern art, became the most expensive 20th-century artwork ever sold at auction when it fetched $195 million at Christie’s New York in 2022. The silkscreen portrait, based on a publicity still of Marilyn Monroe from the 1953 film Niagara, is part of Warhol’s famous “Shot Marilyn” series—named after a 1964 incident when performance artist Dorothy Podber fired a gun at a stack of Warhol’s canvases. The work was the star lot of the evening, drawing competition from four bidders, including three on the phone and one in the room. Art dealer Larry Gagosian, bidding in person, ultimately secured the painting with a hammer price of $170 million, well below its $200 million estimate. The “Shot Marilyn” works are among Warhol’s most coveted pieces, with only five versions in existence. This particular portrait had been in a private collection for five decades, coming from the estate of Swiss dealers Thomas and Doris Ammann. With no financial guarantee, its sale marked a major moment for both the Warhol market and the broader contemporary art market. In surpassing the $179.4 million record set by Picasso’s Women of Algiers (Version ‘O’) (1955) in 2015, Shot Sage Blue Marilyn reaffirmed Warhol’s place at the pinnacle of modern art valuations. While some experts saw the sale as a watershed moment, others noted that privately brokered transactions for blue-chip artworks have long exceeded the $200 million mark.
- Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer, 1914–16 Sold for: $236.4 million Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1914–16) became the second-most expensive artwork ever sold at auction when it achieved $236.4 million at Sotheby’s in November 2025, surpassing Klimt’s previous records and setting a new high for any work of modern art. The full-length portrait, one of only two named Klimt commissions in private hands, was the undisputed centerpiece of the sale of the Leonard A. Lauder Collection. Bidding opened at $130 million and unfolded over 20 tense minutes, narrowing to two phone bidders represented by Sotheby’s specialists David Galperin and Julian Dawes. Dawes’s bidder ultimately won with a hammer price of $205 million, prompting applause in the salesroom and marking the most expensive lot ever handled by Sotheby’s. The result vaulted past Picasso’s Les Femmes d’Alger (Version ‘O’), which had held the record for a modern artwork at $179.4 million since 2015. Andy Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn, meanwhile, made global headlines when it skirted the $200 million mark in 2022. The painting was commissioned by one of Klimt’s most important patron families, survived wartime confiscation, and was restituted in 1948 before entering Lauder’s collection in the 1980s. Estimated in excess of $150 million, it had been widely expected to challenge the artist’s previous high. Instead, it rewrote the record books—cementing Klimt as one of the few early-modern painters consistently capable of commanding nine-figure prices in today’s market, and potentially opening the door for even more masterpieces to break the $200 million barrier.
- Leonardo da Vinci, Salvator Mundi (Savior of the World), c. 1500 Sold for $450.3 million at Christie’s New York in November 2017 In a landmark moment in the art world, Leonardo da Vinci’s Salvator Mundi (c. 1500) set a new record for the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction, fetching an astonishing $450.3 million at Christie’s in New York in November 2017. The sale, which took place in a packed salesroom at Christie’s Rockefeller Center headquarters, was driven by an intense 19-minute bidding war. Bidding began in earnest at $100 million—which was also the guarantee—and escalated rapidly from there, with cheers and applause breaking out as the painting crossed the $200 million threshold. Pylkkanen, again serving as auctioneer, skillfully kept the crowd engaged as bids climbed incrementally in the final moments. At one point, the bidding reached $350 million, before finally settling at $400 million, with an additional $50 million in fees for the buyer. The Salvator Mundi’s journey to the auction block was filled with intrigue, including debates over its authenticity and a controversial restoration by conservator Dianne Modestini. Despite these uncertainties, the painting’s remarkable backstory and its connection to Leonardo da Vinci—whether authentic or not—captivated buyers. The work had once sold for just $1,175 in 2005, when it was attributed to a follower of Leonardo, but was later restored and re-attributed to the master himself. The sale marked a culmination of a carefully orchestrated marketing campaign by Christie’s, which included a global tour and celebrity endorsements, such as Patti Smith and Leonardo DiCaprio. The Salvator Mundi’s new auction price far eclipsed the previous record-holder, Pablo Picasso’s Women of Algiers (Version O) (1955), which had sold for $179 million earlier that year. This sale marked not only a record-breaking moment for the auction house but also highlighted the increasingly influential role of market value in the art world, where the price tag may overshadow the painting’s historical and artistic significance. The buyer of Salvator Mundi was revealed a month after to the sale to be Saudi Arabian crown prince Mohammed Bin Salman, with quiet plans for it to eventually go on view in Riyadh.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/el.title: El Greco Masterpiece Gets Its Colors Back After More Than 400 Years
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/el.author: Daniel Cassady
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/el.text:
King Philip II of Spain wasn’t particularly impressed with El Greco‘s The Martyrdom of Saint Maurice and the Theban Legion when he first saw it. The following four centuries of dirt, varnish, and enthusiastic repainting hadn’t done the picture any favors, either.
A painstaking nine-month restoration, recently finished, has found the monumental painting looking considerably more like the one El Greco envisioned. The muddy browns and sickly greens that had dulled the picture for generations are gone. In their place are brilliant blues, reds, yellows, and purples, along with a newfound depth that had been buried beneath grime.
The restoration was conducted at Madrid’s Royal Collections Gallery, under the supervision of Rafael Alonso, an 81-year-old former Prado Museum restorer, who has spent decades working on El Greco’s paintings. The project was supported by the Fundacion Callia in partnership with Spain’s Patrimonio Nacional, which oversees the country’s royal collections.
The results were reported in detail by El País, whose writer followed the restoration from the painting’s removal from El Escorial in February through its finished restoration in October. And what a job it was.
Alonso had initially expected the restoration to take about four months. But once he and fellow restorer Adela Murgui began cleaning the enormous canvas, which measures nearly 15 feet high and 10 feet wide, they discovered that its condition was far worse than even feared.
“When I put the cotton to the painting, my heart sank,” Alonso told El País. Centuries of varnish and repainting had darkened the colors and flattened the composition. In the 19th century, he explained, painters had simply painted over damaged areas, often adding their own interpretations of what El Greco intended.
The restorers spent months carefully stripping away those additions, revealing the original paint beneath. Afterward, the repaired the damaged areas using soluble materials, taking pains not to add anything that couldn’t be removed later.
The restoration is particularly striking given the painting’s rather unhappy beginnings.
El Greco painted The Martyrdom between 1580 and 1582 for the basilica at El Escorial, Philip II’s vast monastery and palace outside Madrid. The king wanted a powerful statement of Catholic faith, while the artist hoped the commission might secure him a permanent position as a court painter.
Neither’s wish was totally granted.
Rather than concentrate on the grisly execution of Saint Maurice and his fellow Christian soldiers, El Greco pushed the violence into the background. Up front, he placed a group of handsome soldiers in brightly colored clothing, their elongated bodies and theatrical poses exemplary of the skills he had learned in Venice and Rome.
Philip II apparently admired the painting’s quality, paying the artist a substantial sum of 800 ducats, but felt it wasn’t right for its intended religious setting. The work was relegated to another room, and El Greco never clinched the royal appointment he’d hoped for.
The painting stayed there for most of the next 444 years, apart from a trip to Madrid for an exhibition in 1999, all the while gradually losing most of its remarkable color and atmosphere.
The restoration also marks another achievement for the Fundacion Callia, founded by Carmen Reviriego, which has helped restore works by Zurbarán, Rubens, Brueghel the Elder, Velázquez, and others through its partnership with Madrid’s Royal Academy of Fine Arts of San Fernando. According to El País, the foundation has helped mobilize €5 million for the preservation of artworks.
When ARTnews spoke with Reviriego in March, she described Callia as an “incubator of patrons,” bringing together collectors and philanthropists from Spain, Latin America, and beyond. Her goal is to encourage a stronger culture of private support for the arts in a country that has traditionally relied heavily on public funding.
Reviriego had specifically mentioned The Martyrdom during that interview as an example of the work the foundation hoped to support. “El Greco was the Jeff Koons or Damien Hirst of his day,” she told ARTnews this week, “and Phillip II was the most power man and greatest patron of the 16th century.”
There’s a nice historical symmetry here. Reviriego argued that great works of art are rarely the achievement of an artist alone. Without patrons, many wouldn’t exist at all. She pointed to the Royal Collections themselves, built in part through the patronage of Philip II, the very king who commissioned The Martyrdom more than four centuries ago. Now, private patronage has helped give that painting a new life.
For Alonso, meanwhile, the completed restoration marks something of a farewell. After decades spent working on El Greco’s paintings, he told El País that The Martyrdom was the last of the artist’s great masterpieces still awaiting restoration.
The newly restored painting is expected to go on temporary display at Madrid’s Royal Collections Gallery before returning to El Escorial. This time, visitors will get a much better idea of what Philip II saw more than four centuries ago.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/gr.title: Grand Theft Auto VI ’s Vice City Pays Homage to the Bass, Among More Art Easter Eggs
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/gr.author: Tessa Solomon
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/gr.text:
The new Grand Theft Auto arrived this week, the messianic reward after 13 long years, offering the best-rendered version of the series’ standing promise: anything, within the scope of its metropolis and the player’s imagination. I watched my cousin paint a house for his avatar’s girlfriend, then hop in a car and drive to the Bass Museum. Or rather, to the Vice City Museum of Art, the faithful replica of it in Vice City, the game’s fictional Miami.
Rockstar teased that Grand Theft Auto VI would boast the franchise’s sharpest graphics yet, and the claim was not exaggerated. The Vice Museum of Art captures the Bass’s signature civic Art Deco style: a pale limestone facade (the real stuff was quarried in the Florida Keys) and, as far as I could tell, even the carved decorative relief around the entry. It’s a far cry from the series’ earliest entries, when a building like this would have been a smooth beige box; here, the facade looks textured. We parked and admired its public art: a riff on Miami Mountain, a tower of boulders by Ugo Rondinone permanently installed in Collins Park, outside the Bass. Part of Rondinone’s “Mountain” series, it’s made of garishly clashing fluorescent rocks stacked high and probably visible from space. The Vice City version has swapped stone for emojis: winking, crying, smiling.
Vice City may be hiding another Easter egg for art heads. Months ago, a screenshot circulated online from an expansion for Grand Theft Auto Online, showing a new character in a shirt with an “Art Oregano” logo. It’s a safe bet that it’s a nod to Art Basel Miami Beach, held at the Miami Beach Convention Center, since it’s set in the same font as the fair’s. The herby homage was well received. “I hope he’ll be in GTA 6 having his own little art studio or something,” wrote one Reddit user. Another added, “I can’t wait to wear this shirt to Art Basel this year, if I can pull myself away from GTA6.”
Art Basel Miami Beach runs December 4-6; keep an eye out for Art Oregano shirts. And, perhaps, as players make it further into the notoriously long game, a new version of Art Oregano may appear.
I couldn’t personally verify whether the game includes a replica of the fair, with NPCs entering and exiting, as the Vice Museum did. We’d spent the momentous night mundanely, mostly comparing paint swatches. All of it in line with what viral clips suggest: the game’s characters can do drugs and rob banks—chaos, generally speaking—but we’d rather have time to drive with no destination in mind.
Before I left, my cousin regretfully canceled our plans to visit the Guggenheim on Saturday. He has to work.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/bi.title: Judge Allows Lawsuit Over Allegedly Stolen Fra Angelico to Move Forward
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/bi.author: Daniel Cassady
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/bi.text:
A New York judge has refused to throw out a lawsuit over a 15th-century Fra Angelico painting that the heirs to the Bic pen fortune say was stolen by their family chauffeur and later sold by the late art dealer Richard Feigen.
In a decision dated October 26 and filed on November 16, New York Supreme Court Justice James G. Clynes rejected an attempt by Feigen’s estate and associated businesses to get the case dismissed. Their main argument? The family had waited too long to sue.
“No family should lose a treasured work of art simply because the people who handled this stolen property were sophisticated dealmakers,” Luke Nikas, a lawyer for the Bich family, told ARTnews. The Bich family is determined to recover what belongs to them, and today’s decision is an important step toward achieving that result.” The ruling is good news for the Bich heirs, though there’s still a long way to go. The judge hasn’t decided who owns the painting, or even whether it was stolen.
As ARTnews reported in April, the dispute centers on Saint Sixtus (ca. 1453–55), a painting by the Italian Renaissance master that Baron Marcel Bich, the founder of Bic, bought at Sotheby’s in 1972 for £130,000. The painting eventually passed to his son Bruno, who kept it in his Fifth Avenue apartment in Manhattan. Then, around 2006, it disappeared.
According to a lawsuit filed in March by Bruno’s three sons, Gonzalve, Charles, and Guillaume, the family’s chauffeur, Roy Morrow, stole the painting and sold it to Feigen for $3 million. The family says Morrow had no paperwork proving the painting was his, but Feigen bought it anyway and promptly insured it for $8.5 million, nearly three times what he’d paid.
Feigen, one of New York’s best-known Old Master dealers before his death in 2021, later consigned the painting to Christie’s. In 2018, it was sold for $5.4 million to Chilean billionaire Álvaro Saieh and his wife, Ana Guzmán.
The Bich brothers say they didn’t learn where the painting ended up until 2023. They asked for it back the following year, but Saieh and Guzmán refused. So the brothers sued, demanding the painting’s return, along with damages and money from its sale.
Feigen’s representatives tell a different story. In March, lawyers for his estate told Reuters that Morrow had signed a bill of sale saying he owned the painting. The Saiehs, meanwhile, have said they bought it in good faith, relying on Christie’s research.
Which brings us to the latest ruling.
Feigen’s lawyers argued that the family had simply waited too long to bring its claims. After all, Feigen bought the painting in 2006 and sold it in 2018. The brothers didn’t file their lawsuit until March 2026.
But stolen art can be a tricky business under New York law. Generally, when someone buys a stolen artwork in good faith, the clock doesn’t start ticking on a claim for its return until the rightful owner demands it back and the buyer refuses.
Things get more complicated when someone is accused of knowingly dealing in stolen property. The clock can start earlier, and Clynes said there were too many unanswered questions about Feigen’s purchase to settle the issue now.
The judge also rejected, for now, an argument that the family had dragged its feet for so long that allowing the case to continue would be unfair. Lawyers call that laches. Both arguments can come up again later.
Feigen’s side did score one win. The judge dismissed claims against his revocable trust and its trustees because the family hadn’t shown enough to connect the trust to the money from the painting’s sale. The brothers can bring those claims again if they find more evidence.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/da.title: How do Artworks Acquire Value? New York Art Dealers David Nolan and Anton Svyatsky Weigh In.
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/da.author: Lmiller
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/da.text:
How do artworks acquire value? I discussed this complex question with two New York art dealers during Art Week NYC, a citywide festival organized by ARTnews, Artforum, and Art in America.
David Nolan, whose eponymous gallery has been open since 1987, gave the view of an art world veteran; Anton Svyatsky, who opened Management in 2023, provided a newer perspective. 
	Along the way, we discussed the role of the collector in sustaining value, the challenges of pricing artworks by emerging artists, the ways in which influence and market value have become decoupled, the casino that is the auction house and the zoo that is the art fair.
At our talk on Friday, November 13 at the PMC Studio in Midtown Manhattan, Svyatsky insisted that collectors need to see themselves as responsible for an artist’s value, rather than depend on dealers and institutions for that function. This shift in perspective, and a return to collecting artists in depth, may well be the key to ridding the art world of speculators. Nolan recalled the immense changes that took place during the 1980s, and the increasing attention paid to artworks’ financial value.
Speaking of casinos, a flask emerged at the mention of the new partnership between Artnet and Kalshi—you can catch that moment and other choice ones in the video of the talk above.

https://hyperallergic.com/the-real-miami.title: The Real Miami Museums and Artists Behind GTA VI’s Vice City
https://hyperallergic.com/the-real-miami.author: Rhea Nayyar
https://hyperallergic.com/the-real-miami.text:
The Real Miami Museums and Artists Behind GTA VI’s Vice City
From The Bass in Miami Beach to the murals of Wynwood, the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is heavily inspired by the local arts scene.
After 13 agonizing years of waiting for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6), gamers worldwide wasted no time tearing up the streets of the game's fictional state of Leonida after it was released yesterday, November 19. The South Florida-inspired game environment is heavily influenced by the culture, environment, and architecture of Miami — from its Art Deco resorts, white-sand beaches, Cuban quarter, and strip clubs, right down to its museums and arts venues.
As fans embed themselves in GTA 6's immersive landscape, many have recognized real-life locations across South Florida making unexpected cameos. One such case is the Vice Museum of Art, which Rockstar Games confirmed is modeled after the Bass Museum of Art in Miami Beach.
“It was totally unexpected to see Grand Theft Auto VI reimagine The Bass as the ‘Vice City Museum of Art,’” said Silvia Karman Cubiñá, executive director of the Bass Museum of Art, in an email to Hyperallergic.
“It’s a wonderful reminder of how art and architecture can become part of popular culture,” she continued. “Now, I’m just curious: will the Vice City Museum of Art get more visitors than we do?!”
While not listed as a landmark like the Vice Museum of Art, another building in Downtown Vice City appears to be directly modeled after the Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM). Situated near the Vice City Arts Center, which is heavily based on Miami's Adrienne Arsht Center for Performing Arts, the PAMM-inspired building sits right on the water's edge just as the museum does in real life.
“We were as delighted as anyone else to find PAMM in what feels like the biggest video game of all time,” said Alexa Ferra, PAMM's senior director of marketing and communications, in an email to Hyperallergic.
Ferra attached a photo someone sent her from the game showing the PAMM dupe and some gummy bear-inspired sculptures installed in the shallow water.
“It's a testament to our stunning Herzog & de Meuron building, and goes to show if you stick around long enough, you'll pop up in the unlikeliest — but inevitable — of places.” Ferra added.
Other references to Miami's arts and culture scene include Leonida's Stockyard neighborhood, which directly channels the street murals and warehouse-lined roads of the Wynwood Arts District. It was reported earlier this summer that Rockstar Games had hired over 50 real street artists to design the in-game murals across Stockyard. Users shared they've spotted the works of street artist Ahol Sniffs Glue (David Anasagasti), among others.
Miami-raised contemporary photographer Josh Aronson also took notice of GTA 6's inclusion of his installation at the Catalina Hotel & Beach Club in Miami Beach during Miami Art Week 2024, which Rockstar Games incorporated in Vice City's own Catalina Hotel. From Aronson's Florida Boys (2020–) photo series, the photo “Spring” (2024) was made into an enormous sublimated fabric print that hung from the second-story window of the hotel.
The same printed photo, which features a group of cheerful young men photographed from above while floating in water, is shown at Vice City's Catalina Hotel.
“Florida Boys is my own imagined version of Florida, so I love that it gets to live on in another imagined Florida,” Aronson told Hyperallergic. “The installation at the Catalina was temporary, but in Vice City, someone might stumble upon it years from now. It’s a reminder of the wild ways we encounter art today, and how a work can find new life long after it comes down.”
GTA6's pre-holiday release comes just before Miami Art Week begins early next month. Those dropping in can find some of Aronson's installations on view beyond Vice City at the Vizcaya Museum and Gardens and the Museum of Contemporary Art, North Miami, and also pay homage to the cultural venues and districts that inspired Leonida.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/wo.title: Working Mothers Face Pervasive Discrimination in London Art World, Study Finds
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/wo.author: Anne Doran
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/wo.text:
Despite the contemporary art world’s increased attention to women’s experiences and the politics of care in its public-facing programming, working mothers employed by London’s galleries and auction houses face widespread discrimination, according to a new study. As reported by the Art Newspaper today, a survey of 50 employees working in the UK capital’s commercial art sector has found that, for many, having children comes at considerable professional cost.
The study, conducted by Kate McMillan and Cleo Roberts-Komireddi and published today in the European Journal of Cultural Studies, looked at the extent to which pregnancy and maternity affected career progression among art world workers. Moving beyond previous studies centered on fine artists or senior directors, it focused on lower-paid, non-artist roles such as sales, administration, and marketing.
Roberts-Komireddi and McMillan’s research, which also included 12 in-depth interviews, reveals an industry “marred by implicit and explicit expectations that often result in workers needing to choose between their careers and being parents,” they write. Three quarters of respondents felt that motherhood had impeded career advancement, while 20 percent said they had been explicitly denied promotion.
The authors found poor and sometimes illegal practices across the industry, including employees being “managed” out of their roles while on maternity leave. Such practices, they note, are made possible by a lack of formal human resource structures—only half of the respondence worked for organizations with dedicated HR staff, and just 60 percent said their workplace had a specific parental leave policy. They additionally blamed the art market’s pervasive culture of secrecy.
Class and wealth also play a role in shaping employee experience, the study suggests. For junior employees on modest salaries, the cost of childcare can make travel and attendance at evening events difficult and increase the likelihood of discrimination on the job. At the same time, a lack of resources makes challenging such discrimination daunting, with many women instead choosing to take a less senior position, move into freelance work, or leave the art world.
Roberts-Komireddi and McMillan’s study spanned small galleries to multinational auction houses and found problems across the board. As they say in their report, “A lack of accountability pervades the sector.”

https://hyperallergic.com/a-view-from-th.title: A View From the Easel: Rei Xiao
https://hyperallergic.com/a-view-from-th.author: Lakshmi Rivera Amin
https://hyperallergic.com/a-view-from-th.text:
A View From the Easel: Rei Xiao
“I love that my roommate’s cat, Astrid, whom I appointed as my studio assistant, can always come and join me when I am painting.”
Welcome to the 364th installment of A View From the Easel, a series in which artists reflect on their workspace. This week, Rei Xiao paints a world of surreal, feline figuration into being while navigating the artist visa system and managing their studio assistant (a dignified cat named Astrid).
Want to take part? Check out our submission guidelines and share a bit about your studio with us through this form! All mediums and workspaces are welcome, including your home studio.
Rei Xiao, Brooklyn, New York
How long have you been working in this space?
Two years.
Describe an average day in your studio.
I work from my apartment. The most predictable parts of my studio day start with putting on my sunscreen and painting clothes. It’s a very small space that I paint in, so I usually have to push stuff aside when I start, like my painting cart, stool, and trash bin. 
I, then, turn on my air purifier, open the lids of my palettes, scrape paints from the previous session, and play either TV shows I’m familiar with or podcasts hosted by comedians in the background. The day usually ends with my cleaning the palette, emptying and wiping my brush cleaning tank, and diligently washing my brushes. Then I wash my face and go to sleep.

https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/a.title: Maren Hassinger Won’t Be Weighed Down
https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/a.author: Emily Watlington
https://www.artnews.com/art-in-america/a.text:
Maren Hassinger’s retrospective at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA) has a radiant warmth about it—surprisingly so, given that it’s a show made mostly of gray metal sculptures whose edges could prick you raw. This warmth owes a lot to the photographs, printed mural-sized and filling vitrines, taken by her long-term collaborator Adam Avila. Scattered throughout, they show Hassinger dancing, beaming, and/or hamming it up for the camera, often mirroring her sculpture’s forms with her body. But it owes, too, to the ways she rose to meet her career’s surprising twists and turns.
Rejected in college from Bennington’s dance department in the 1960s, Hassinger was pushed toward sculpture by a teacher who noticed her gift. “My love of motion,” she says in the catalog, carried her from one to the other. Clement Greenberg was a guest at her senior thesis critique: He had “the gift of gab, but was a bit of a bully” she remembers with accurate alliterations. He would not be her last mean man.
In graduate school, at UCLA, Hassinger was rerouted once again after finding the sculpture program to be a boys’ club. As she remembers it, not one single woman was enrolled. So she found a home in fiber, a typical tale, and made it work: “Truthfully,” she admits in the catalog, “I was just trying to get a degree so I could teach and make art.” But she found herself too impatient for the loom and uninterested in making fabric. So she gathered fibers out in the world, chancing upon a weighty rope in a shipyard. It was made of blonde hemp but discolored by oil. Playing around, she eventually unraveled some of its strands before tying segments into a series of loose, giant macrame knots that greet visitors to BAMPFA, where they lie on the ground as if waiting to be pulled tight.
Hassinger would marry craft techniques with industrial materials henceforth—a revealing portrait of women’s changing work in her time. She became such a regular at one LA wire shop that they featured her on the cover of their trade magazine. Soon, she was incorporating elevator cables—effectively wire ropes, their cords twisted together—into what would become her best known works. Leaning (1980) sees cables with frayed ends bundled in some two dozen bouquets. Only the central arrangement has a flat bottom and sits sturdily; the rest are free to lean.
Fiber meets metal in River, a 2,000-pound rope-chain Hassinger made as an ambitious graduate student in 1972. But where was a student to store such a behemoth? Recognition would not come until much later—as the title of her work Wallflower series (1975) attests—so she let River go, then finally remade it in 2011 for a Studio Museum acquisition. (Good thing she had so many photographs). A few other works at BAMPFA are recreations, too, but after school, she mainly made sculptures that could be coiled up and made compact: a resourceful response to the realities of real estate.
To see Hassinger’s work is to think about the act of making it. It shows you: Knots are blown up big so that you can see each twist and turn. Her titles are often verbs, as with Whirling (1978), Walking (1978), and Leaning (1980). “When she talks about the work, she moves” explained Margot Norton, who co-curated the show with Anthony Graham.
Hassinger met the obstacles that came her way, as a Black woman born in 1947, with poetry and practicality in equal measure. Of her turn to newspaper, which she twisted and knotted for a cascading 2008 installation, she explains that the material “is very handy and cheap [laughs].” But it also must have been cathartic to rip the headlines into strips. Her resourcefulness and resilience define the show, which sees her rethink sculpture without storage, fiber without fabric, choreography without corporeality.
Hassinger hardly did it alone. “Working alone is so antisocial” as she quips in the catalog. When Senga Nengudi first saw Hassinger’s work in 1975, she was thrilled to see another Black woman working with sculpture and performance, then looked her up. They became fast friends. With David Hammons, Nengudi then suggested that Linda Goode-Bryant show Hassinger at her gallery, Just Above Midtown (JAM). That show’s main work, Beach (1980), is installed at BAMPFA, too.
When Hassinger’s cohort of Black LA artists—known as Studio Z—lacked opportunities, they invented their own, as when Hassinger, Nengudi, Ulysses Jenkins, and others performed at the 1982 opening of “Afro-American Abstractions.” They had neither hung work on the walls nor been included in the checklist, but they did call up the Los Angeles Municipal Art Gallery to accept a nonexistent invitation: “We are so thrilled to be doing the opening performance!” they informed whoever answered the phone.
In the 1990s, Hassinger found herself without a studio. Starved for space, she turned to video. Birthright (2005) is nothing like her sculptures, but it will forever change how you see them. Onscreen, the artist interviews her uncle about her family tree. She learns that her grandmother, Puddin, had been the product both of incest and an interracial affair. Puddin’s parents hadn’t known that they were nephew and aunt, because Puddin’s father was born out of wedlock to his lover’s father who had a secret Native mistress.
Once the affair was discovered, Puddin was given away to a plantation caretaker who had been enslaved, and her father was lynched by a white mob. Puddin’s son—Hassinger’s dad—never talked about any of this: He was abandoned too by Puddin, then struggled to relate to women, cutting Hassinger out of the will and passing down patterns. “My legacy was to feel unloved,” the artist concludes in the video. But then the show keeps going.
Right next to Birthright, the curators installed Love (2008/2026), and it is here—halfway through the retrospective—that galleries of gray give way to hot pink. Plastic shopping bags filled with human breath and love notes cover the walls. Her lightness beams off the building, but look closely and you’ll find a sense of play throughout the show.
Thinking about familial lineages, Hassinger’s knots and ropes start to feel like umbilical cords severed and frayed. History is hefty, but it never weighs the work down in any sense of the word. “I always felt so good when I danced,” the artist explains, “lighter, faster.” It is easy to imagine her dancing in her studio while walking around BAMPFA, where one gets a sense of heaviness made to look light. Untitled (1972/2020) sees ropes with looped ends, noose-like, but instead of being tied into knots, strands are undone and then woven back together seamlessly. In the galleries, the ropes dangle gracefully from the ceiling and weigh heavy on the floor.
Hassinger is an artist who sees things soberly as they are and imaginatively as they might be—a gift that enables her to turn junkyard findings into elegant arrays and litter into love.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120404.title: Neues Nachrichtendienstrecht | Deutsche Geheimdienste haben jetzt Zugriff auf Sensoren in Autos
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120404.author: Matthias Monroy
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120404.text:
- Politik
- Neues Nachrichtendienstrecht
Deutsche Geheimdienste haben jetzt Zugriff auf Sensoren in Autos
Werkstätten, Speditionen und Autovermieter sollen nach einem neuen Gesetz Fahrzeugdaten an BND und Verfassungsschutz liefern – und darüber schweigen.
Am 13. November hat der Bundestag das Gesetz zur Reform des Nachrichtendienstrechts verabschiedet. Der Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) und das Bundesamt für Verfassungsschutz können auf dieser Grundlage auch private Firmen zur Herausgabe von Fahrzeugdaten verpflichten. Diese müssen ohne Verzug und lückenlos antworten und dürfen die Öffentlichkeit oder Betroffene nicht darüber informieren.
Auf die neue Pflicht im Gesetzestext hat der Experte für Überwachungstechnik Erich Möchel im IT-Fachportal Golem aufmerksam gemacht. Sie trifft Autohersteller und Werkstätten, Vermietungen, Carsharing-Anbieter und Speditionen, außerdem Betreiber von Reservierungs- und Vertriebssystemen im Reiseverkehr. Zu den begehrten Informationen zählt das Gesetz unter anderem die Fahrgestellnummer, Standortdaten aus der Satellitenortung, Fahrstrecken und Parkpositionen. Dazu kommen Messwerte aus der Fahrzeugsensorik: Tempo, Kilometerstand, Tankfüllstand, die Belegung der Sitze und sogar das Straffen der Sicherheitsgurte.
Abgefragt werden können außerdem die Zahl der zurückgelegten Fahrten und die Zahl der Personen, die ein Auto fahren. Laut Begründung erlauben solche Statusdaten Rückschlüsse auf das Nutzungsprofil und auf Aktivitäten der Beteiligten. Der Tankfüllstand verrate die Reichweite und sei deshalb »für die operative Arbeit nutzbar«.
Standard liegt schon vor
Möchel wies bei »Golem« auf eine Norm hin, an der sich die Behörden orientieren können. Diese wurde vom Europäischen Institut für Telekommunikationsnormen (ETSI) im Frühjahr 2024 veröffentlicht und beschreibt, wie Polizei und Geheimdienste Fahrzeugdaten bei Herstellern oder deren Dienstleistern anfordern können.
Die Norm sieht auch eine Zuordnung zwischen Mobilfunk- und Fahrzeugdaten vor. Dazu gehören die Teilnehmerkennung der SIM-Karte (IMSI), die Gerätekennung (IMEI) und die Teilnehmerkennung im 5G-Netz (SUPI), außerdem die Hardwareadressen des Bluetooth- und des Ortungsmoduls. Behörden sollen so Informationen aus der Mobilfunküberwachung einem bestimmten Fahrzeug zuordnen können.
Möchel zufolge lässt sich ein Auto über die Schnittstellen der Netzbetreiber dann sogar in Echtzeit verfolgen. Das betrifft auch Mobiltelefone, die einmal mit dem Bordsystem gekoppelt waren: Wer also sein Handy in einem Mietwagen oder Carsharing-Auto verbindet, hinterlässt für die Geheimdienste eine verfolgbare Spur.
Werden Bild- oder Sprachdaten übermittelt?
Moderne Fahrzeuge sind innen oder außen mit Mikrofonen, Kameras und weiterer Sensorik ausgestattet. Nach Darstellung von »netzpolitik.org« könnten daher auch Videoaufnahmen oder Sprachdaten an Geheimdienste übermittelt werden – sofern ein Fahrzeug diese speichert.
Die ETSI-Norm erklärt sich für andere Fahrzeugdaten als die Mobilfunkkennungen nicht zuständig, diese liegen in den Systemen der Hersteller. Möchel bezweifelt in »Golem«, dass globale Konzerne wie Tesla oder Stellantis den Diensten bereitwillig Auskunft geben. Er liest die Gesetzesbegründung so, dass auch deren Verfasser*innen damit nicht rechnen.
Möchel erwartet eher, dass Vertragswerkstätten herangezogen werden, weil sie auf Herstellerdatenbanken zugreifen können. Sie sind meist mittelständisch, haben kaum juristische Abteilungen und unterstehen direkt deutschem Recht.
Branche verlangt Klarheit
Wer im zuständigen ETSI-Komitee sitzt und dort die Normen mitentwirft, wird nicht veröffentlicht. Laut Möchel sind das Bundeskriminalamt, mehrere Landeskriminalämter und der Verfassungsschutz vertreten, der BND vermutlich über Verbindungspersonen der Polizei. Der Verband der Automobilindustrie sagte »netzpolitik.org«, er sei an der Normung nicht beteiligt.
Der Zentralverband Deutsches Kraftfahrzeuggewerbe hatte den Entwurf zur Nachrichtendienstreform mit den enthaltenen Pflichten für die Automobilindustrie bereits als unverhältnismäßig und kaum umsetzbar kritisiert. Weil die Datenstrukturen je nach Hersteller abwichen, müsse genau festgelegt sein, was herauszugeben sei. Bußgelder könnten Betriebe in ihrer Existenz gefährden.
Der Bundesverband Spedition und Logistik fordert gegenüber netzpolitik.org ebenfalls rechtssichere Vorgaben und mahnt Datenschutz, Verhältnismäßigkeit und Zweckbindung an. Er sieht seine Branche aber nicht als »verlängerten Arm der Geheimdienste«.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.

https://taz.de/Neuer-Roman-von-Daniel-Ke.title: Neuer Roman von Daniel Kehlmann: Diesseits von Afrika
https://taz.de/Neuer-Roman-von-Daniel-Ke.author: Dirk Knipphals
https://taz.de/Neuer-Roman-von-Daniel-Ke.text:
Neuer Roman von Daniel Kehlmann: Diesseits von Afrika
In „Afrika“ sublimiert Daniel Kehlmann die Empörung über den Kolonialismus und mokiert sich über Preußen. Außerdem bringt er einen zum Lachen.
Berlin im Winter – als Herz der Finsternis. Obdachlose wärmen sich an Feuern. Im Grunewald schießen sich Männer bei Duellen tot. Künstler malen auf großen Ölschinken Menschen, „die sich im Gleichschritt bewegten“. In den Cafés sehen die Kellner wie Soldaten aus. Alle benehmen sich zu zackig. Mittendrin: ein „gräuliches germanisches Prunktor“.
Daniel Kehlmann verwendet in seinem neuen Roman „Afrika“ einigen erzählerischen Ehrgeiz darauf darzustellen, wie unzivilisiert Berlin im ausgehenden 19. Jahrhundert gewesen ist. Berliner Aufklärung, Humboldt, Schinkel – in diesem Roman wie nie da gewesen. Die etwas vordergründige, aber im Romanzusammenhang funktionierende Pointe dabei: Zugleich maßt man sich hier an, die „Zivilisierung“ der „Wilden“ Afrikas zu verhandeln, was als Kongokonferenz 1884 ja tatsächlich stattgefunden hat. Eine postkolonial informierte, erzählerisch ins Satirische sublimierte Empörung darüber ist in dem Roman deutlich spürbar.
Bismarck hatte die europäischen Großmächte zusammengerufen, um die Bedingungen zu klären, unter denen der ganze afrikanische Kontinent kolonisiert werden sollte. Dem belgischen König wurden große Teile des Kongo als private Kolonie zugestanden. In ihr agierten die Kolonisatoren mit unglaublichen Grausamkeiten, die etwa Joseph Conrad zu seiner Erzählung „Herz der Finsternis“ bewogen.
Der Roman
Daniel Kehlmann: „Afrika“. Rowohlt, Hamburg 2026. 256 Seiten, 24 Euro
In der berühmten Schlusswendung richtet Conrad die Perspektive zurück auf die Metropolen Europas, die das eigentliche Herz der Finsternis beherbergen, weil in ihnen die Kolonialisierung organisiert wurde. Unter diesem Aspekt lässt sich Kehlmanns Roman unter seiner komödienhaften Oberfläche als ein stellenweise groteskes Prequel von Joseph Conrad lesen.
Klischees über „nackte Wilde“
Blackfacing, Exotisierung, Klischees über „nackte Wilde“ ohne Ende: Den alltäglichen Rassismus der Zeit stellt Kehlmann immer wieder direkt aus. Ihre weltpolitische Ignoranz auch: „Grenzen im Urwald! Flaggen zwischen Elefanten und Tigern. Dort wohnt eh niemand, also was soll’s!“ Doch der inzwischen 51-Jährige wäre nicht der Erzähler, der er ist, wenn der ernste Hintergrund nicht mit einem höheren literarischen Spiel verbunden wäre.
Es besteht darin, in diesem historischen Setting die tragikomische Geschichte einer Jedermannsfigur zu erzählen. Gustav „Gustl“ Strinetzky heißt sie, ein österreichischer Legationsrat, der sich durch Unterschlagungen in einen „Schlamassel“ hineinmanövriert hat. Unvorbereitet stolpert er in die Kongokonferenz und wird dort – man fühlt sich szenenweise an die Coen-Brüder erinnert – durch allerlei Missverständnisse als gewiefter Strippenzieher wahrgenommen.
Etwas knarzt hier die Dramaturgie, doch, Bereitschaft mitzuspielen seitens des Lesers vorausgesetzt, funktioniert sie ganz gut. Vor allem aber baut Kehlmann die sich ergebenden Begegnungen seiner Hauptfigur zu funkelnd bösen Porträts aus. Bismarck ein selbstverliebtes Denkmal seiner selbst. Henry Morton Stanley ein Lügner und Schlächter. Am schlechtesten kommt der belgische König weg, Kehlmann stellt ihn als obszönen, geldgierigen, sadistischen Giftzwerg dar.
Sehr hübsch dagegen die Szenen in der österreichischen Botschaft. Einem Legationsassessor rutscht heraus, dass – Kehlmann mischt fröhlich marxistisches Vokabular unter – die Welt sich am „Übergang zur modernen kapitalistischen Produktionsweise befindet“, später muss er sich für seine Hellsicht entschuldigen. Man nimmt mit: In der K.-u.-k.-Monarchie ist Klugheit nicht der Karriere förderlich.
Je näher die Figuren der Macht stehen, desto kaputter zeichnet Daniel Kehlmann sie. Mit keiner Figur des Romans kann man sich identifizieren. Dafür bringt einen das Buch – bei dem Setting ein Kunststück für sich – zwischendurch immer wieder zum Lachen, so hanebüchen sind die Wendungen, so slapstickartig die Dialoge. An Vergangenheitsverklärung erweist sich dieser Erzähler stabil uninteressiert.
Präfeministische Anwandlung
Statur nimmt bei alledem zunehmend die Frau des Legationsrats Strinetzky an, die sich auf einem Ball im Kronprinzenpalais in präfeministischer Anwandlung fragt, „wieso Frauen sich so bereitwillig in ihr verordnetes Schicksal der Dummheit“ fügen.
Im letzten Drittel gesteht Kehlmann dann auch seinem Jedermann Strinetzky – streckenweise in virtuos gehandhabter erlebter Rede – echte Tragik zu. Es geht hier um verpasste Fluchtmöglichkeiten, aber auch darum, im entscheidenden Moment als Paar seine sozialen Rollen nicht hinter sich lassen zu können. Die Finsternis der Welt ließe sich erst dann aufhellen, wenn sich die Finsternis in den sozialen und Geschlechtsbeziehungen aufhellt. Was aber, diesen Stachel bohrt einem der Schluss tief ins Herz, erst einmal nicht der Fall ist. Schon ein gutes Buch.
Gemeinsam für freie Presse
Die taz gehört zu 100 Prozent ihren Leser:innen und ist damit nicht nur konzernfrei, sondern auch kostenfrei zugänglich. Alle Artikel stellen wir frei zur Verfügung, ohne Paywall. Gerade in diesen Zeiten müssen Einordnungen und Informationen allen zugänglich sein. Unsere Leser:innen müssen nichts bezahlen, wissen aber, dass kritischer, unabhängiger Journalismus nicht aus dem Nichts entsteht. Dafür sind wir sehr dankbar. Damit wir auch morgen noch unseren Journalismus machen können, brauchen wir mehr Unterstützung für taz zahl ich. Dank Ihnen haben wir nun die 50.000 erreicht. So viele unterstützen freiwillig und regelmäßig. Noch nicht dabei? Werden Sie jetzt Teil der Community! Jetzt unterstützen

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120406.title: Skispringen | Warum Norwegens Dominanz in Lillehammer Misstrauen weckt
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120406.author: Lars Becker
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120406.text:
- Sport
- Skispringen
Warum Norwegens Dominanz in Lillehammer Misstrauen weckt
Die Gastgeberinnen belegen die ersten fünf Plätze. Für Severin Freund springt die Erinnerung an die manipulierten Anzüge des Männerteams in Trondheim mit.
Die Sonne ging unter über dem Mjosa-See, es war eine malerische Kulisse beim ersten Einzel-Weltcup der Skispringerinnen in diesem Winter in Lillehammer. So richtig genießen konnten das Deutschlands Fliegerinnen aber am Samstagnachmittag nicht. Podestplätze hatten sie als Ziel für diesen Winter ausgegeben, doch zum Auftakt reichte es für Selina Freitag und Agnes Reisch mit haushohen Rückständen zu den überragenden Norwegerinnen nur für die Plätze acht und zehn.
Das Gastgeber-Team feierte einen historischen Fünffachsieg und untermauerte am Tag nach dem souveränen Triumph im Mixed-Wettbewerb seine Dominanz. Was mit Blick auf den Anzug-Skandal um die norwegischen Skispringer bei der Nordischen Ski-WM vor zwei Jahren in Trondheim auch für Misstrauen in der Skisprungszene sorgte.
»Sie fliegen wahnsinnig gut – das kann viele Ursachen haben. Wenn man so dominant ist und es diese Vergangenheit gibt, denkt man auch daran«, erklärte Olympiasieger und Weltmeister Severin Freund als Experte im ZDF. Bei der WM vor zwei Jahren hatten Norwegens Skisprung-Männer um Weltmeister Marius Lindvik mit einem steifen Band im Anzug betrogen und waren disqualifiziert worden. Es folgten massive Regeländerungen im Skispringen.
Spektakuläre Überlegenheit
Zu Beginn dieses Winters sind Frauen und Männer aus dem norwegischen Fliegerteam wieder so überlegen vorn. »Das ist schon spektakulär«, kommentierte Freund. Selina Freitag hatte als beste Deutsche stolze 63 Punkte Rückstand auf die norwegische Siegerin Eirin Maria Kvandal – das sind umgerechnet 35 Meter. »Der zweite Sprung macht Hoffnung, da bin ich mit mehr Schmackes gesprungen«, meinte die zweimalige Weltmeisterin Freitag.
Bundestrainer Heinz Kuttin war nicht zufrieden: »Unser Anspruch ist, dass wir ganz vorne mitspringen wollen. Es ist positiv, dass wir fünf Springerinnen im Finaldurchgang hatten. Es sind noch kleine Baustellen drin bei den Sprüngen. Geschmeidigkeit und Selbstvertrauen fehlen noch. Wir haben schon noch Luft nach oben.«
Auch im Mixed nur Fünfte
Ein ähnliches Fazit hatte das deutsche Team schon nach dem enttäuschenden fünften Platz im Mixed-Springen am Freitag ziehen müssen. Das deutsche Quartett mit Agnes Reisch, Philipp Raimund, Selina Freitag und Pius Paschke hatte unglaubliche 190,7 Punkte Rückstand auf Sieger Norwegen, auch der anvisierte Podestplatz war von Anfang bis Ende außer Reichweite.
Ein missglücktes Debüt auch für den neuen Männer-Bundestrainer Andreas Mitter, der die Nachfolge des zuvor sieben Jahre amtierenden Cheftrainers Stefan Horngacher angetreten hat. »Das war sicher nicht der Einstieg, den wir uns erwartet haben«, erklärte Mitter. Tiefpunkt für die deutschen Männer war der 55. Platz von Andreas Wellinger in der Qualifikation, womit der zweimalige Olympiasieger die Qualifikation für das erste Einzelspringen der Saison am Samstagabend verpasste. Auch der Rest des deutschen Teams um Olympiasieger Philipp Raimund flog im Schatten der überlegenen norwegischen Männer weit hinter der Weltspitze hinterher.
Eine gute Nachricht gab es an diesem Samstag aber doch noch aus deutscher Sicht im ersten Springen nach dem Rücktritt von Rekord-Weltmeisterin Katharina Schmid. Luisa Görlich feierte mit Platz 25 ein erfolgreiches Comeback nach ihrem dritten Kreuzbandriss. »Ich habe mich sehr gefreut, die Schanze ist schön, in Lillehammer passt einfach alles. Nach drei Jahren wieder hier, nach zwei Jahren zurück im Weltcup – ich bin einfach glücklich. Ich habe heute den ersten Schritt zurück mit ein paar Weltcuppunkten gemacht«, erklärte Görlich mit einem Lächeln im Gesicht: »Ich hatte wirklich viel Spaß.« Noch mehr davon hatten die dominanten Norwegerinnen.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/so.title: Art Advisor Sophia Cohen on How the Next Generation of Collectors Is Approaching the Art Market
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/so.author: Lmiller
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/so.text:
During during Art Week NYC, a citywide festival organized by ARTnews, Artforum, and Art in America, I was joined by art advisor Sophia Cohen to explore one of the hottest topics in the art market today: the next generation of collectors.
Cohen is the founder of Siren, an art advisory and curatorial consultancy. She started her career working for dealer Gavin Brown, who, Cohen explains, taught her about the importance of being with artists of your own generation and how an art dealer can function as an important steward for the artists they represent. When Brown’s gallery closed in 2020, Cohen pivoted to Gagosian (“the exact opposite,” in her words), where she spent six years, eventually becoming an associate director. Cohen is also one of four co-chairs leading the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Vanguard Council, an invite-only group of next-generation patrons.
At our talk on Friday, November 13, at the PMC Studio in Midtown Manhattan, Cohen spoke about the advice she gives to young collectors about when and how to buy, and why it’s sometimes important to make mistakes. She also gave insight into her own collecting, and discussed how today’s patrons are structuring their giving. Watch the video above to see the whole conversation.
	
.

https://taz.de/Tatort-Schauspielerin-Mel.title: Tatort-Schauspielerin Melika Foroutan: „Wir können nicht immer nur empört sein, wir müssen handeln“
https://taz.de/Tatort-Schauspielerin-Mel.author: Jîyan Battal
https://taz.de/Tatort-Schauspielerin-Mel.text:
Tatort-Schauspielerin Melika Foroutan: „Wir können nicht immer nur empört sein, wir müssen handeln“
Die Deutsch-Iranerin Melika Foroutan spielt die Ermittlerin im Frankfurt-Tatort. Abseits ihrer Rollen setzt sie sich für die Menschen im Iran und in Palästina ein – ein Gespräch.
Ein Notruf führt die Tatort-Ermittler Maryam Azadi (Melika Foroutan) und Hamza Kulina (Edin Hasanović) zu einem Fall von 1999: Eine ehemalige Kellnerin glaubt, den seit einem Bombenanschlag im Café Hajduk verschollenen Navid Hosseini wiedergesehen zu haben. Dahinter steckt ein politisches Attentat auf die iranische Opposition.
Die beiden Ermittler arbeiten an Cold Cases, die aufgerollt werden, sobald neue Indizien oder Zeugen auftauchen. „Unser Fokus liegt dabei oft auf den Hinterbliebenen der Opfer, Menschen, die nie erfahren haben, wer das Verbrechen an ihren Liebsten begangen hat und die durch unsere Ermittlungsarbeit von der Qual der Ungewissheit befreit werden“, sagt die Schauspielerin Foroutan im Interview der taz. Sie findet es reizvoll, dass ihre Rolle analytisch, empathisch und klug ist.
Am 22. November erscheint eine neue Folge des Frankfurt-Tatorts, bei der es um eine sehr persönliche Geschichte der Ermittlerin Azadi geht. Der Plot bahnte sich schon in der ersten Folge „Dunkelheit“ an, als Azadi bereits inoffiziell ermittelt.
ist Schauspielerin und lebt in Berlin. Bekannt ist sie vor allem für ihre Rollen im Frankfurter Tatort und in der Netflix-Serie „Die Kaiserin“. 2026 erhielt sie den Grimme-Preis für „Tatort – Dunkelheit“.
„Unser Wunsch war es, einen politischen Thriller zu machen. Da Maryam Iranerin ist, lag es nahe, die Geschichte mit ihrer Biografie und ihrer Herkunft zu verknüpfen. So kam die Idee zu Mykonos auf, ein bitterer Fall aus der Realität“, sagt Foroutan im Gespräch mit der taz über die Entstehung der Folge. Im Jahr 1992 wurden in Berlin im Auftrag des iranischen Geheimdienstes vier kurdische und iranische Exilpolitiker erschossen, die sich im Restaurant Mykonos verabredet hatten.
Entscheidend ist die Straflosigkeit
Der Anschlag wurde damals aufgeklärt und ist deshalb streng genommen kein Cold Case. „Aber er zeigt deutlich, dass die Repressionen des Regimes nicht an den Grenzen des Iran enden. Seine Gegner werden hier wie dort immer noch unter Druck gesetzt, bedroht und getötet, und das seit Jahrzehnten“, so Foroutan.
Entscheidend sei für sie die Straflosigkeit: „Die Tatsache, dass über einen so langen Zeitraum schwere Menschenrechtsverbrechen begangen werden, ohne dass die Verantwortlichen zur Rechenschaft gezogen werden, ist ein zentraler Grund dafür, dass sich die Gewalt immer wieder fortsetzt, und das zeigen wir auch in unserem Tatort.“ Foroutan hat die Dialoge für den Tatort maßgeblich entwickelt, sie habe etwa darauf geachtet, dass sie zeitgemäß klingen.
Das brauche es, auch weil sich der Iran verändert habe, sagt die Schauspielerin und Aktivistin. „Die Machthaber und Unterdrücker haben sich ein neues Gewand angelegt, sie sehen nicht mehr so aus und sprechen auch nicht mehr so, wie wir es aus amerikanischen Filmen der 90er Jahre kennen. Für eine moderne Erzählung dürfe man das nicht übersehen, damit man nicht in Klischees verfällt“.
Azadis Gerechtigkeitssinn prägt die Handlung. Im Film erinnert eine Psychologin sie daran, dass sie als Polizistin den Staat vertritt. „In der Szene sagt Maryam, dass eben dieser Staat verantwortlich war für die Vertuschung am Mord von sechs Menschen.“ Die Ermittlerin will das nicht hinnehmen und wird aktiv: Sie nutzt die Mittel und Zugänge des Systems, das Unrecht begangen hat, um Gerechtigkeit zu erreichen.
Auch Gaza und Sudan sollten behandelt werden
Gerechtigkeit, ist das nicht zu idealistisch? Foroutan entgegnet: „Artikel 1 des Grundgesetzes sagt, dass die Würde des Menschen unantastbar ist.“ Aber die Gegenwart zeige laut der Schauspielerin etwas anderes: „Wir leben in einer Demokratie, und trotzdem erleben wir in Deutschland Polizeimaßnahmen, die einem rechtsstaatlichen Verständnis nicht standhalten, etwa bei palästinasolidarischen Demonstrationen oder bei Protesten der Klimaaktivisten. Ich finde, nichts rechtfertigt das brutale Zusammenknüppeln von Menschen, die für ihre politische Haltung demonstrieren. Was soll damit bezweckt werden?“
Ihr Engagement geht außerhalb des Sets weiter. „Die ‚Frau-Leben-Freiheit‘-Bewegung wurde so groß, weil ein riesiger Teil der Bevölkerung auf die Straße ging, um das Regime zu stürzen“, sagt Foroutan. Mittlerweile ist dieser Kampf aber aus dem Blick geraten. „Weil so viel gleichzeitig passiert, wir haben keine unendliche Kapazität alles aufzunehmen, es ist ein Kampf um Aufmerksamkeit, und dieser Kampf ist ungerecht“.
Auch deshalb ist für sie das Krimiformat, das jeden Sonntag immer noch Millionen Menschen anschauen, eine Möglichkeit, eine politische Geschichte zu Iran zu erzählen, ohne dass sich jemand daran reibt. Sie wünscht sich in Bezug auf viele Konflikte, wie aktuell in Gaza oder Sudan, dass die Empathie nicht selektiv ist, sondern universell: „Ich wünsche mir, dass auch palästinensischen Kolleg*innen die Möglichkeit gegeben wird, in prominenten Formaten ihre Geschichte zu erzählen, sei es im Tatort oder in einem anderen Format.“
Vorsicht, kleiner Spoiler: Im Tatort kommt heraus, dass die Behörden bei dem Attentat im Café Hajduk davon gewusst haben, dass das iranische Regime dahinter steht. Sie haben es trotzdem als organisierte Kriminalität eingestuft, nicht als politisch motiviertes Attentat.
„Tatort: 4 Finger“
So., 22. November, 20.15, ARD, und in der Mediathek
Foroutan hat mit dem Ende gehadert: „Ich habe mit unserem Autor Constantin Lieb und unserem Regisseur Andreas Prochaska ausführlich darüber gesprochen. Ich wollte, dass der Attentäter geschnappt und bestraft wird. Was soll ich sagen, es hätte mir Genugtuung verschafft.“ Am Ende habe sie den realistischeren Schluss akzeptiert, zumindest für das Fernsehprogramm.
Engagements jenseits des Filmsets
Ihr Engagement für die Menschen im Iran geht jedoch weit über ihre Rolle im Film hinaus: „Ich habe mich mit dem Europäischen Zentrum für Menschenrechte ECCHR und iranischen politischen Akteur*innen zusammengeschlossen und dem Generalbundesanwalt geschrieben. Wir haben ihn aufgefordert, angesichts der schweren Menschenrechtsverbrechen im Iran tätig zu werden.“
Als Grundlage verweist sie auf die Amnesty-Dokumentation „Architects of Atrocities. Er dokumentiert Verbrechen gegen die Menschlichkeit während der „Frau, Leben, Freiheit“-Proteste 2022, darunter rechtswidrige Tötungen, Folter und sexualisierte Gewalt, und zeichnet die Befehlsketten dahinter nach.
„Die Verbrechen werden begangen, es gibt Verantwortliche, und es gibt Zeugen. Wir können nicht immer nur empört sein, wir müssen handeln,“ sagt sie und führt fort: „Wenn der Generalbundesanwalt aktiv wird, wer weiß, vielleicht hat der nächste Film über die Strafverfolgung iranischer Verbrecher dann ein glücklicheres Ende.“
