https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Conservative media weighs its future as cracks emerge in Trump’s movement
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Jeremy Barr in Washington
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
As a so-called “blue wave” crashed across the country on the night of 3 November, conservative hosts and commentators on Fox News displayed an almost virtuosic ability to avoid directly blaming Donald Trump for the Republican party’s defeat, instead pinning the blame on impertinent voters who didn’t grasp the strength of the economy.
“In some sense, Mr Trump was too successful in the first year and didn’t sell it enough in the second year,” said Larry Kudlow, a Fox Business Network host who served as the president’s director of the National Economic Council during his first administration.
But two weeks on, Trump’s electoral wipeout is facilitating difficult conversations about the future of the conservative media ecosystem – and whether outlets that target a Republican-voting audience need to create some distance from an unpopular president. Some other outlets, like the Maga-aligned Real America’s Voice News network, are planning to go the other direction and double down on Trump.
“The whole landscape can now be reordered, and I think it will be,” said Steve Bannon, a former chief strategist to Trump during his first administration who now hosts a show for Real America’s Voice.
Several conservative media personalities pinned the blame on Fox News for leading the party – and Trump – astray, with former host Tucker Carlson saying that the results signaled the end of “the Fox News era”. (Carlson didn’t respond to a message seeking comment.)
Bannon, who contends that Rupert Murdoch has long “hated Trump”, predicted that the network will utilize the party’s recent “rejection” at the polls to move away from Trump and embrace more traditional, George W Bush-era Republican priorities.
“They’re going to try to kick Trump into the dustbin,” he said. “They clearly have moved beyond Trump and they want to move beyond Trumpism … What they’re going to do is, with a thousand cuts, convince their ageing audience that Maga and what Maga stands for is too extreme.”
In contrast, Bannon said he expects Real America’s Voice and other outlets to “triple down” on the Maga movement and “populist nationalism.”
Bannon is not alone in his criticism of Murdoch’s media empire. Conservative commentator Ann Coulter said that she views the channel and its sister outlet, the New York Post, as “90% responsible for the GOP wipeout in the midterm elections”, blaming voices in the Murdoch media empire for encouraging Trump to launch – and sustain – an unpopular war against Iran.
Atlanta-based conservative radio host Erick Erickson said a realignment away from Trump will probably start in his medium before it carries over to conservative television – though he said it will take time, and will depend on how important access is for certain personalities.
“The more often you spend time at Mar-a-Lago, the less likely you are to distance yourself from Trump, because you still want in,” said Erickson, who vocally opposed Trump in 2016 before coming around ahead of his 2020 re-election bid.
Charlie Sykes, a former conservative radio host who also opposed Trump from the beginning, said the election has shown “cracks in that alternative reality silo” on Trump-aligned channels and platforms.
“In general, I think the scope of the blowout was just so great that even deep in the rightwing media ecosystem, they had to feel the tremors of it,” said Sykes, a former MS Now commentator who now writes on Substack. “And so that has been kind of interesting, this sense of like, ‘OK, we need to really come to grips with this and maybe figure out a way to move on.’”
Trump’s decision to attack Iran in February fomented division within the conservative media ecosystem, with many commentators viewing it as an abdication of his promise to abstain from foreign wars and focus on the US.
“I think those divisions are just going to widen,” Sykes said.
The Daily Caller, which was co-founded by Carlson in 2010 as something of a conservative alternative to the New York Times, made waves ahead of the midterms for calling out Trump’s war against Iran – and the high prices that have come out of it. “The Daily Caller is clearly positioning itself for a landscape not just post-midterms but post-Trump, and for a bitter and intensifying intraparty media battle,” the digital publication Semafor wrote on 1 November.
In an interview, Daily Caller editor-in-chief Amber Duke said the publication is more focused on reflecting the mood of the American people – particularly younger people affected by a challenging economy – than boosting Trump and the Maga movement.
“I think what we are doing is so unique that we are really setting ourselves apart,” she said. “We view ourselves as a principled, America-first outlet. I think there’s a difference between Maga and America-first.”
Duke also acknowledged the economic opportunities that drive support for the president. “Trump is a content goldmine. He drives a lot of traffic, a lot of clicks,” she said. “That content mine is eventually going to dry up. I would definitely be concerned if I had my entire business model tied around this uniquely celebrity-oriented newsmaker. How am I going to continue to stay in business after that? For us, it’s: Let’s just tell the truth to the American people, and that truth is not going to be dependent on any one person or political party.”
Some conservative outlets that are closely tied to Trump, however, don’t see any reason to do anything differently.
“Nothing changes with us,” Newsmax chief executive Christopher Ruddy said. “We’re going to continue reporting on the administration and we will continue to cover the Congress. We make a very concerted effort to always get both sides on our reports and in our TV opinion segments.”
Charles Herring, president of the far-right One America News Network, echoed that sentiment: “Our reporting doesn’t change based on the political pendulum or who resides in the White House. We are working hard every day to further enhance our coverage for our viewers.”
Still, there are limits to how far some conservative media organizations can stray from the president, considering the economic imperative to retain a pro-Trump audience. “The thing to understand about conservative media is that it’s not necessarily always top down,” Sykes said. “It’s often: What will the audience tolerate? … Nobody wants to get too crosswise with their audience.”
But the vast majority of conservative news sites have already seen declines in online traffic in recent months, according to industry tracker Howard Polskin, an early warning sign for the party’s midterm chances. “Audiences are not buying what Maga media is selling anymore,” he said.
“My prediction would be that in the next two years, rightwing media will become fractured with more infighting, breaking into two camps: pro-Maga/Trump and anti-Maga/Trump,” Polskin added. “Traffic to rightwing websites will continue to nose dive, much more so than mainstream media.”
Several conservative media veterans who spoke with the Guardian said the selection of a 2028 Republican presidential nominee will probably be a defining moment for the sector, and one that could split conservative media into different camps.
On the notion that vice-president JD Vance will be Trump’s heir apparent, Erickson said: “I actually am kind of encouraged by the level of pushback after the election that maybe this isn’t a good idea.” Brian Kilmeade, the co-host of the influential Fox News morning show Fox & Friends, has been particularly critical of Vance for seeming to distance himself from Trump’s decision-making on Iran. On his radio show this past week, Kilmeade said that Vance “never should have been vice-president” and that he’s “amazed that President Trump puts up with it”.
Over the next two years, conservative media personalities will have to put their chips down on a candidate. The challenge, Sykes said, is “figuring out where the audience is going, and getting there first”. He also expects conservative media outlets to prioritize attacking Democrats and undermining their control of Congress.
“It’s no longer about defense of Trump,” he added. “It’s like: What’s next? And everybody’s got to make that pivot.”

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: UE rejeita acordo final da COP31 por falta de menção a impactos de combustíveis fósseis
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A União Europeia (UE) anunciou neste domingo (22) que não aceitará o texto final da COP31, realizada em Antália, na Turquia. O motivo é a retirada de qualquer menção explícita aos combustíveis fósseis do documento, após pressão da Arábia Saudita e de outros países produtores de petróleo. A posição foi anunciada pelo ministro irlandês do Clima e da Energia, Darragh O’Brien, representante da presidência rotativa do bloco. Para ele, é inadmissível aprovar uma decisão que não reconheça os combustíveis fósseis como principal motor das mudanças climáticas.
A recusa europeia, entretanto, evidencia uma contradição na atuação do bloco durante as negociações. Embora defenda maior ambição no enfrentamento à crise climática e rejeite um acordo que não estabeleça referências à transição para longe do petróleo, do carvão e do gás, a UE resistiu à ampliação dos recursos financeiros destinados aos países em desenvolvimento. Na quinta-feira (19), uma das versões da minuta deixou de incluir a previsão de US$ 120 bilhões anuais, a partir de 2035, para financiar medidas de adaptação climática nos países mais vulneráveis. A retirada ocorreu em meio à posição europeia de não ampliar suas contribuições públicas, limitando-se aos compromissos financeiros já assumidos.
A postura foi criticada pelo climatologista e ativista Harjeet Singh, que reconheceu a importância de rejeitar um acordo sem referências aos combustíveis fósseis, mas apontou a incoerência da União Europeia ao cobrar maior ambição dos países em desenvolvimento sem garantir os recursos necessários para viabilizar a transição energética. “Não se pode exigir ambição dos países em desenvolvimento e se recusar a financiar essa transformação”, afirmou Singh. O climatologista também criticou o bloqueio europeu a um mecanismo efetivo de transição justa e à continuidade da expansão de infraestruturas fósseis no próprio continente.
Para o também membro do Grupo Técnico de Especialistas em Gestão Abrangente de Riscos, no âmbito do Mecanismo Internacional de Varsóvia para Perdas e Danos das Nações Unidas, não é possível exigir compromissos mais ambiciosos dos países em desenvolvimento enquanto os países ricos se recusam a financiar essa transformação. A justiça climática, argumenta, precisa estar baseada em compromissos concretos, financiamento adequado e uma transição energética efetiva.
O impasse também ameaça os avanços obtidos na COP30, realizada em Belém, em 2025. A proposta brasileira de construir roteiros para orientar o afastamento dos combustíveis fósseis e o combate ao desmatamento perdeu espaço nas negociações da COP31. Além disso, a retirada da meta de US$ 120 bilhões anuais para adaptação climática representa um recuo no compromisso de ampliar o financiamento aos países vulneráveis. Enquanto países produtores de petróleo resistem a compromissos concretos de transição energética e nações ricas limitam sua disposição de financiar a adaptação, os países do Sul Global continuam pressionando por medidas que enfrentem tanto as causas quanto os impactos da crise climática.
Com informações AFP.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Trump criticises Schumer amid push for new Democrat leadership in US Senate
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Trump criticises Schumer amid push for new Democrat leadership in US Senate
Schumer, who has led the Democratic caucus since 2017, faces a challenge from Chris Van Hollen in his bid to be the next Senate majority leader.
Chuck Schumer, the top Democrat in the United States Senate, is facing backlash against his bid to serve as Senate majority leader in the incoming Congress.
On Sunday, President Donald Trump added to the ongoing criticism of Schumer’s leadership, signalling there would be tension with the White House if Schumer were picked again to lead the Democratic caucus.
“It is going to be very hard for me to work with Chuck Schumer should he become Senate Majority Leader,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
“He failed badly as ‘Leader’ once before, one of the worst in history, and I have little doubt that he will fail again.”
The debate over Schumer’s leadership has underscored divides within the Democratic Party, particularly in the wake of the November 3 midterm elections.
Following a historic set of victories, Democrats are set to take control of both chambers of Congress in January.
Schumer, who leads the Democratic Senate minority, is hoping to retain his leadership position. A closed-door, secret-ballot vote is scheduled for December 1 to decide the majority leader.
A senator representing New York since 1999, Schumer has expressed confidence in his odds, saying he has the necessary votes to stay in charge.
“I will be elected majority leader,” Schumer told reporters last week.
But critics say Schumer, who will turn 76 on Monday, is ill-suited to lead a Senate Democratic caucus increasingly shaped by younger, anti-establishment lawmakers.
Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen, backed by progressives, has mounted a campaign to challenge Schumer for the majority leader role.
Van Hollen told NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday that he, too, was confident of winning.
“If you look at our caucus, you can see a huge appetite for change. They are seeing the American people and the Democratic Party calling for change. They also want to change the way we do business in the United States Democratic caucus and the United States Senate,” he said.
Schumer has also seen falling public approval ratings. In mid-November, a poll by the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos found that 34 percent of self-identified Democrats viewed Schumer favourably. That percentage was down from 38 percent in February.
November’s poll also suggested that 43 percent of Democrats held an unfavourable view of Schumer, who has led Senate Democrats since 2017.
The Senate Democratic leader is the only unresolved role among Congress’s top four positions.
House Democrats last week nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be speaker in the next Congress.
Meanwhile, John Thune will continue to lead Senate Republicans, and Representative Jim Jordan will succeed Speaker Mike Johnson as the top House Republican.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Why I won’t leave mathematics, despite AI solving centuries-old problems | Ken Ono
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Ken Ono
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Last year, I nearly quit mathematics. On 20 November, Levent Alpöge announced that, working with Claude, he had proved the Riemann hypothesis, a 167-year-old problem about the distribution of prime numbers. The Lean and Mathlib communities have since certified the formal proof. We are only beginning to understand the argument. What kind of future awaits someone beginning a life in mathematics?
In May 2025, I led the number theory team for Epoch AI’s FrontierMath project. We wrote difficult problems to test large language models. I watched an unreleased ChatGPT model compute all the moments of Tamagawa numbers of elliptic curves, drawing on work by Manjul Bhargava and Roger Heath-Brown, and on papers my father wrote in the 1960s. I was stunned.
I earned my PhD in 1993 and built a life around research, teaching, and mentoring. I’d love to prove that Ramanujan’s tau function never vanishes, or that half of the partition numbers are even. My 25-year-old self would have been crushed by what we are witnessing today. Nothing I write can reassure someone just starting a career. I can explain why I stayed.
My father, a number theorist, died in January. As a boy, I learned from him about Ramanujan, whose notebooks have occupied mathematicians for generations. Ramanujan believed a Hindu goddess gave him mathematical formulas in his dreams. When I considered working on AI, I feared my father would see it as abandoning mathematics. Instead, he told me AI reminded him of Ramanujan: discoveries from an unexpected source might leave us much to understand. I do not take that comparison literally. Ramanujan was a human with an extraordinary imagination and life. My father’s response brought me to tears. It gave me permission to keep being a mathematician in a way I had not anticipated.
Today, I am on leave from the University of Virginia and work as Founding Mathematician at Axiom Math. We use AI to formalize, verify and extend mathematical proofs in Lean, a language in which a small checking program verifies each step. This work can expose gaps and make proofs inspectable and reusable. Human judgment remains essential: we must check that the formal statement says what we intended.
We released the first complete Lean formalization of the classification of finite simple groups, one of mathematics’ largest proofs. Announced in 1983, the classification required decades of work by many mathematicians; a major gap was filled in 2004. Our AI helped produce 43.1 million lines of Lean code. In the process, we found a problem in a published route to a key theorem and supplied an alternative argument. Lean’s kernel checks the resulting formal proof. The mathematics belongs to the generations who developed it. Our formalizations of the classification and other bodies of math are already helping us build and check further mathematics.
After 24 days of work, I watched the final milestones land on my laptop. I cried. I thought about the people who had made the classification possible, and about the father I could no longer tell. But I am 58. I’ve advised 35 PhD students, 17 postdocs, and hundreds of undergraduates. I’ve had opportunities young mathematicians cannot assume. I cannot ask a graduate student to regard uncertainty as an adventure because I have found rewarding work within it.
At a Berkeley colloquium two days after OpenAI announced its Navier–Stokes solution, a scheduled lecture became a town hall lasting almost two and a half hours. Students asked about credit, transparency, hiring, and how mathematicians whose work came first were treated. Some asked me what I would do to help them. Campus security was locking the building as we left.
The declaration A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics, signed by Terry Tao and other Fields Medalists, warns about rushed announcements, inadequate attribution and the loss of mathematical understanding. I share those concerns. At a National Academies meeting, I put my position this way: hope is not a plan, and nostalgia is not mentoring.
Universities, journals, employers and funding agencies must decide what they support and reward. Students and younger colleagues should have a voice while those decisions are still open, as should mathematicians who choose to work without AI. In the discussions where I have a voice, I will argue for that participation.
Students need room to struggle with mathematics and learn to question the tools they use. In my advising, I will ask what a young mathematician understood, originated, or made possible. Access to a powerful system is no substitute for those contributions. For work I help publish, readers should know what has been proved, what remains assumed, and who contributed the ideas.
I want my students, and their students, to develop ideas that are genuinely their own. I want them to have colleagues who listen and the material support to pursue a mathematical life. My work at Axiom is one part of how I am trying to contribute. It does not replace my obligations as a teacher and mentor. I may be wrong about how this will unfold. I am still learning what it means to be a mathematician.
- Ken Ono is a number theorist and professor of mathematics at the University of Virginia, currently on leave as founding mathematician at Axiom Math. A former vice-president of the American Mathematical Society, he is known for his work on Ramanujan and integer partitions.
- These views do not necessarily reflect those of Axiom Math, the University of Virginia, the National Academies, or any other institution with which I am affiliated.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: CNJ cria regra para corrigir registros por mortes em ações policiais
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Ana Cristina Campos
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Resolução recente do Conselho Nacional de Justiça (CNJ) que determinou a inclusão da informação de que a morte ocorreu em decorrência de intervenção policial na certidão de óbito é vista como um avanço pelo professor do Departamento de Sociologia da Universidade Estadual do Rio de Janeiro (Uerj) e pesquisador do Laboratório de Análise da Violência, Ignácio Cano.
Ele explica que o país tem duas fontes de informação sobre mortalidade violenta: os dados da polícia e os da saúde. Estes são baseados nas certidões de óbito. Segundo ele, a informação de que a morte ocorreu em decorrência de intervenção policial raramente aparecia nesses documentos. Cano acredita que essa determinação ajudará a diminuir a brecha entre os dados da polícia e os do sistema de saúde.
“Isso se enquadra dentro de uma tentativa mais ampla de fiscalização e monitoramento da violência policial, que, no Brasil, corre solta, com mais de 6 mil pessoas mortas por intervenção policial. É um número elevadíssimo sem que haja investigações aprofundadas, sem que haja um controle sobre isso”, diz o especialista.
A mudança também permitirá que famílias solicitem a correção de documentos antigos que não registram essas circunstâncias. A medida é adotada em um país que registrou 6.602 mortes decorrentes de intervenções policiais em 2025, uma média de 18 pessoas por dia, segundo o 20º Anuário Brasileiro de Segurança Pública.
Antes, os registros de óbito de pessoas mortas em intervenções policiais costumavam apresentar apenas a causa médica do falecimento, sem identificar as circunstâncias em que ele ocorreu. Com a nova regulamentação, os cartórios de registro civil terão procedimentos padronizados para acrescentar essa informação, mediante apresentação da documentação exigida.
A resolução estabelece uma redação padronizada: “Morte não natural, violenta, ocorrida em decorrência ou no contexto de intervenção de órgão de segurança pública, nos termos do título apresentado”. A norma também proíbe expressões consideradas estigmatizantes, como “auto de resistência”, “resistência seguida de morte” e “confronto”, nos registros e certidões abrangidos pela regulamentação.
Segundo o Fórum Brasileiro de Segurança Pública, as mortes decorrentes de intervenções policiais representaram 16,2% das 40.775 mortes violentas intencionais registradas no país em 2025, aproximadamente uma em cada seis vítimas. A Bahia concentrou o maior número absoluto, com 1.570 mortes, enquanto o Amapá apresentou a maior taxa proporcional, com 17,1 vítimas por 100 mil habitantes.
Correção de registros antigos
Uma das principais novidades é a possibilidade de corrigir registros antigos. Familiares poderão procurar o Cartório de Registro Civil competente para solicitar a inclusão das circunstâncias da morte, mediante apresentação de documentos previstos pela norma, como decisões judiciais definitivas, relatórios finais de comissões da verdade oficialmente constituídas e atos formais de reparação que identifiquem individualmente a vítima e o contexto do falecimento.
Quando a família já tiver documentação suficiente, o procedimento poderá ser realizado diretamente no cartório, sem necessidade de nova autorização judicial. Caso contrário, será possível solicitar o reconhecimento judicial das circunstâncias da morte, inclusive com base em indícios como boletins de ocorrência, laudos periciais, depoimentos de testemunhas e relatórios de organismos de direitos humanos. O Ministério Público e a Defensoria Pública também poderão requerer a abertura do procedimento, especialmente em situações de vulnerabilidade.
A medida alcança ainda casos de morte presumida, quando uma pessoa desapareceu em decorrência ou no contexto de intervenção de órgãos de segurança pública e teve sua morte judicialmente declarada. Nessas situações, a informação sobre o contexto será incluída no campo relativo à causa da morte.
Secretário-geral da Associação Nacional dos Registradores de Pessoas Naturais (Arpen-Brasil), Gustavo Renato Fiscarelli, diz que uma certidão de óbito não é apenas um documento que formaliza uma morte. Ela também preserva a história daquela pessoa e permite que sua família exerça direitos.
“Ao incorporar informações oficialmente reconhecidas sobre as circunstâncias do falecimento, o Registro Civil contribui para que esses documentos sejam mais completos, respeitem a memória das vítimas e evitem que os familiares precisem comprovar repetidamente fatos já reconhecidos”, afirma.
Além da mudança nas certidões, o Registro Civil contribuirá para a produção de dados nacionais sobre essas ocorrências. O Operador Nacional do Registro Civil de Pessoas Naturais (ON-RCPN) terá 90 dias, contados da publicação da resolução, para criar um campo específico na Central de Informações do Registro Civil (CRC). Os cartórios comunicarão os registros e retificações realizados, permitindo a consolidação de estatísticas em um painel público nacional.
Segundo a Arpen-Brasil, a iniciativa também está relacionada a decisões da Corte Interamericana de Direitos Humanos envolvendo o Brasil e busca assegurar os direitos à memória e à verdade.
“O reconhecimento do contexto da morte no Registro Civil, entretanto, não significa automaticamente a responsabilização civil, administrativa ou criminal de agentes públicos, nem gera, por si só, direito à indenização”, diz a associação.
Como solicitar a inclusão da informação
Familiares de pessoas mortas em decorrência de intervenções de órgãos de segurança pública poderão apresentar ao Cartório de Registro Civil competente a documentação que reconheça as circunstâncias do falecimento. Com documentação suficiente, a retificação poderá ser realizada sem nova autorização judicial. Na ausência dos documentos, será necessário obter o reconhecimento judicial do contexto da morte.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Trump to host private dinner for largest owners of his meme coin
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Trump to host private dinner for largest owners of his meme coin
Sunday’s dinner is the third private event for top holders of the $Trump meme coin, launched shortly before his second inauguration.
United States President Donald Trump will host a third private dinner for top investors in his meme coin $TRUMP, reigniting questions about potential conflicts of interest with his cryptocurrency ventures.
Sunday’s gala will take place at the Trump National Golf Club outside Washington, DC.
According to the dinner’s official website, the top 185 meme-coin holders will be invited to a gala dinner, where guests will include businessman Kevin O’Leary and boxer Floyd Mayweather.
The top 29 holders, meanwhile, will be given special access to a VIP reception where Trump will reportedly be present.
“There will be no private meetings with The President. No gifts will be accepted,” the website said of the VIP reception.
The event has been billed as “a once-in-a-lifetime experience — an evening you will talk about forever”.
But Democrats have accused the Republican leader of leveraging his public office for profit in violation of federal law. They see such dinners as an opportunity for private interests to pay for access to the president.
“Trump is continuing to exploit the presidency for his personal gain,” Kendall Witmer, the deputy communications director for the Democratic National Committee, said in a statement.
In October, shortly after the gala was announced, eight Democratic senators issued an open letter promising to investigate any conflicts of interest such an event might raise.
“President Trump’s continued monetization of his name and likeness once again raises serious ethical concerns, necessitating this request for a robust inquiry into the President’s financial entanglements and personal profiteering,” the letter said.
The Democratic Party has since won majorities in both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm race, paving the way for possible inquiries and subpoenas when the new members are sworn in next year.
Trump’s White House has dismissed the criticism, calling the dinner a “private event, not a government function”. It has also emphasised that “there is no promise of official government action in exchange for attending”.
Trump has also argued that many of his assets are held in a trust while he is in office, though that trust is largely run by his family members.
The president is a stakeholder in cryptocurrency firms like World Liberty Financial, and has made promoting cryptocurrency a central part of his second term.
Under his leadership, the US Treasury established a reserve of digital currency assets, as part of Trump’s effort to make the US the “crypto capital of the world”.
Sunday’s gala is believed to be the third such dinner for top $Trump meme coin holders.
Meme coins trade on a popular likeness from the internet. Trump launched his on January 17, 2025, days before the start of his second term.
To encourage meme-coin purchases, Trump and his business partners held private events on May 22, 2025, and again on April 25, 2026, for top holders of the cryptocurrency.
The first was held at the same Trump golf club outside Washington, DC, and the second took place at Mar-a-Lago, Trump’s Florida resort.
The May 2025 dinner reportedly required a minimum of $55,000 in $Trump coins to attend.
At the time, Chinese crypto investor Justin Sun was declared the winner of a “contest” for who held the most $TRUMP coins. Sun held about $18m of the coin in 2025, as well as tokens from World Liberty Financial.
Earlier this year, Sun sued World Liberty Financial, saying it had frozen his access to the assets he owned with it, making it impossible for him to sell them.
Trump’s inauguration in January 2025 proved a major boost for his coin, pushing its value to $74.
The $Trump coin has since lost value. On the eve of the gala dinner, it is worth about $0.88.
According to financial disclosure forms released earlier this year, Trump earned more than $2.2bn in 2025, the first year of his second term.
Much of that wealth came from meme coins, tokens and other digital assets. Some $636m came from $Trump meme coin sales.

https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.title: ‘Harsh to be under her thumb’: Pitchfork’s Ryan Schreiber on selling to Condé Nast and Anna Wintour
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.author: Owen Myers
https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/n.text:
On the early November day that I met Pitchfork founder Ryan Schreiber in New York City, the website he created is all that anyone on my timeline can talk about, again. Today, it’s thanks to a freshly dug-up tweet from Jon Ossoff, the newly re-elected Georgia senator, who sincerely wrote in 2012: “Looking forward to your writeup of the new @imaginedragons album.”
It’s an all-timer, up there with Phoebe Bridgers saying that she thinks about the site’s review of Jet’s second album (a video of a monkey pissing in its own mouth) once a day, and Halsey wishing that the Pitchfork office, which is on the site of the 9/11 attacks in New York, would “collapse already”. The joke in Ossoff’s case is that Pitchfork would not be caught dead praising the purveyors of stomp clap radio rock; a 2021 review characterized the band’s music as “emotions fired out of a T-shirt cannon”.
Since Schreiber founded the site in 1995, Pitchfork has become as synonymous with a roving sense of new music discovery as it has with sharp and often barbed criticism. While Spin and Rolling Stone were still focused on monthly print issues, the site met the speed of music consumption in the Napster age, publishing reviews when albums leaked online rather than waiting for CD drop dates, and helped to break a wave of, broadly, left-field white artists that included Arcade Fire, Fleet Foxes, Interpol, Sufjan Stevens and Grimes. By the time Schreiber sold the website to Condé Nast in 2015, the site was the most influential publication in music. He resigned three years later. (A disclosure: I have written for Pitchfork since 2018.)
Schreiber is in a jocular mood when I meet him, which might have something to do with the “blue tsunami” sweeping the country in the aftermath of the US midterm elections. If he’s nervous about the release of his dishy upcoming memoir, he doesn’t show it. Titled Weird Era: How Pitchfork Changed Music Forever, the book finds Schreiber opening up about the site’s rapid rise and its sale to Condé Nast for the first time since he quit in 2018, as well as his own story of coming out as gay in his 40s. He is often unsparing when describing what he sees as his failings. “One of the most rewarding things has been able to be able to go on record and take accountability,” he tells me, sitting on a cafe terrace in the last of the fall sun. “To be like, ‘This is why it happened the way it did’, or ‘This was a mistake.’”
Growing up in a blue-collar Minneapolis suburb, Schreiber was a loner kid who was relentlessly bullied. Music was his escape: first Prince and Janet Jackson, and later Nirvana and riot grrrl, the feminist punk subculture that was born from Olympia, Washington. He clicked with a sentiment espoused by Kurt Cobain on a T-shirt he wore on the cover of Rolling Stone that read “Corporate magazines still suck.” Schreiber was instead drawn to the DIY spirit and humor of Cake, a pop culture zine, as well as the righteous snark of British publications like Melody Maker and NME. “Zine culture made me feel that I could do this in a way that doesn’t have to be from a formally educated, journalism degree background,” he says. “When I got online, I was like, ‘I could literally just start doing this by myself.’”
Launched in 1995 as Turntable and renamed Pitchfork a year later, the early site’s reviews were scrappy and irreverent, but full of distinctive voice. Schreiber didn’t know anything about how the music industry worked but was ballsy enough to cold-call record labels, and ended up scoring interviews with alt-rockers like Low, Kelley Deal and Modest Mouse. “I’d grown enough of a thick skin in school, being bullied,” he says. “But my mom and dad were very nurturing. So despite the fact that I was up against it at school, and there was no way for me to be liked as a person, I didn’t give a shit what anybody thought of me.”
Early Pitchfork was anti-canon, unafraid to tear down rock legends like the Pixies’ Frank Black, Metallica and Sonic Youth, whose 2000 album NYC Ghosts & Flowers was compared to an open mic night in hell. At times, they took it too far. When Schreiber’s beloved shit-kicking alt rock hero Liz Phair went pop and teamed up with Avril Lavigne’s producers, the album was given a rare 0.0 rating. In Weird Era, Schreiber writes: “Looking back now, it’s the single best example ever set for how not to employ the 0.0 rating: as petty personal retribution.”
Some of Weird Era’s inside baseball may be lost on generalists, but longtime Pitchfork readers will probably pore over the nerdier details, like when Schreiber and his team debate whether Arcade Fire’s Funeral was a perfect 10 (it was awarded 9.7) or the now quaint-feeling controversy that greeted the site’s first pop-leaning tracks of the year list in 2003, which featured Outkast, Beyoncé and Justin Timberlake in podium positions. “It was a groundbreaking time for pop music and for R&B and hip-hop especially,” he tells me. “I’m probably 24 at that time, and I couldn’t not just have my mind blown by this incredible sound design. The fact that these songs are dominating pop radio was like, ‘Oh, the world is waking up to more experimental and adventurous sounds.’”
I venture that perhaps it was less that the world was waking up to Black pop and hip-hop innovators than that the white critical establishment was finally beginning to take them seriously. “You’re right,” Schreiber says. “Part of it was me moving away from lily-white Minneapolis to Chicago,” he says. “The culture around me changed very much as well.” He was also impacted by critic Kelefa Sanneh’s argument in his well-known 2004 essay The Rap Against Rockism about the deeper prejudices that might inform a music snob’s disdain for pop and R&B. Once I read that, I was like: “Oh, shit. There’s really something deeper at play here that I need to re-evaluate my entire stance on.”
In the early 2010s, Pitchfork expanded into video, launched a short-lived film vertical called The Dissolve and a blog section called The Pitch. “I think I would have slowed down a little bit,” Schreiber says. Moving with more caution may have helped avoid a notorious incident in 2012 when Pitchfork filmed a video interview with Chicago rapper Chief Keef at a shooting range, unaware that the then 17-year-old rapper was on parole and legally banned from handling firearms. After Keef’s rival Lil Jojo was shot dead later that year, Pitchfork was suddenly at the center of a police investigation and was subpoenaed by Illinois prosecutors, who used the site’s audio and video records as evidence to send Keef to juvenile detention.
Schreiber says he was devastated by the series of events. “It was a learning moment where we started to realize we need more checks and balances here, and maybe a little bit more of a diverse makeup of our team,” he says. “This was well overdue, and it was time to put resources into this as company policy.” He adds that the diversity of the team “absolutely” changed after that.
After leaving Pitchfork, Schreiber came out as gay. He says that the experiences that followed the end of his two-decade heterosexual marriage were among the most challenging of the book’s passages to write about. “I’m quite guarded in some ways,” he says. “I’m conscientious of what feels like a TMI moment.” The closest that the very tactful Weird Era comes to that is a passage where he talks about a (failed) hookup through an unnamed dating app which is almost certainly Grindr. Did he have to write it through gritted teeth? “Yes,” he says, laughing. “Oh god, yeah.”
It took him back to the painful memory of being discovered fooling around with another boy at age 13 and the grilling from his parents that followed. It sounds horrifying – any closeted teenager’s nightmare. “It buried that side of my sexuality,” he says. After his mother read an advance copy of Weird Era this summer, he talked to her about the episode for the first time in decades. “She was very regretful about how the situation was handled,” Schreiber says. “But I also understood it from her standpoint as I was writing it, and I was trying to step into her shoes. In the late 80s, Aids was perceived as such a death sentence in pop culture.”
In the book he writes: “It wasn’t until I was out of the spotlight and no longer the public face of the company that I began to question how much of my identity I’d engineered to lead the business and how much I’d suppressed because it didn’t fit the image I felt I had to project.”
I’m curious why Schreiber thought that being Mr Pitchfork was incompatible with being an out gay man. Put simply, he was afraid. “I did feel like, moving to New York, that this personality of who people understood me to be was already established,” he says. “There was an element where I was like, ‘beginning to experiment with my sexuality in any open way would lead to speculation and questions and confusion. I had worked so hard to build this reputation.’”
The idea that telling the truth could risk losing everything you’ve built will be familiar to many who have been in the closet. “I had not really ever given myself permission to explore it,” Schreiber says.
By the mid-2010s, Pitchfork was in trouble, with dwindling ad revenue and a staff of 50 to support. Condé Nast had been circling for a while, and Schreiber met with executives in 2015 to discuss an acquisition. “What if selling out could save us?” he writes.
Condé promised to get Pitchfork out of its financial hole and put its corporate bigwigs on its business operations. “Like the indie band signing a deal with a major, part of me knew the promises weren’t true,” he writes. “But I still hoped Pitchfork might be the rare exception – the outlier that conquers the mainstream while retaining total creative control.”
His skepticism was not unfounded. The acquisition was announced in a press release in which a Condé executive said: “Pitchfork brings a very passionate audience of millennial males into our roster.” The internet had a field day, with Jezebel writing a story titled Bro, Condé Nast Bought Pitchfork! That Is Fucked News For Us Men.
Schreiber soon soured on Pitchfork’s new home thanks to an ad team who were laughably ill-suited to manage site partnerships (among their proposed brand deals were with Topgolf complexes and Dave Matthews’ wine company), as well as the mean girl energy of Condé HQ. In one memorable passage from Weird Era, Schreiber recounts how, after then-incumbent Vanity Fair editor Radhika Jones showed up to an interview with Anna Wintour wearing tights printed with a fox illustration, Wintour was so tickled by this fashion faux pas that she gifted all editors with fox-patterned stockings and socks for the holidays.
“Seeing it at hand was as ugly, if not maybe a little bit uglier than I anticipated,” he says of Wintour’s behavior, adding that he believes she has “a callous disregard for any empathy” and sees Condé Nast employees as “just a cog in a broader machine”.
“I think she sort of likes the villain reputation,” he goes on. “But it was a very harsh reality to be under her thumb, and at the same time disregarded and ignored. There was no warmth whatsoever.”
Schreiber remembers his final day at Pitchfork as “one of the worst days”. He wipes moisture from his right eye. “In the time since, I’ve looked back and gone, ‘What if we’d held on? What if we tried to make some of these difficult decisions ourselves that were ultimately made for us?’” Has revisiting the time made him regret any of his decisions? “I wouldn’t say that there’s anything that writing the book has made me regretful of”, he says. “It’s just helping to process things.”
Many felt that Condé showed their true colors in 2024 when they canned the majority of the site’s staff in a move that also laid off Puja Patel, Schreiber’s successor as editor-in-chief. (Wintour, one staffer reported, declined to remove her sunglasses while telling employees they had got the chop.) The site is now edited by Mano Sundaresan, founder of the No Bells music blog. “The new guard is killing it,” says Schreiber, adding that he is friendly with Sundaresan.
Today, Pitchfork remains one of the few publications whose opinion you can trust about music at all in the wake of the erosion of alt weeklies, the blogosphere and just about every legacy music publication out there (those that are clinging on are either on life support or hailing latter-day Taylor Swift albums as instant classics on release). You might often disagree with Pitchfork scores, ruthlessly graded on a 10-point scale from 0.0 to 10.0, but the site is still the only publication out there that can get an entire friend group riled up over a decimal point.
Since selling Pitchfork, Schreiber has bounced between gigs, dabbled in advisory and management for new artists, DJed at art openings and curated a monthly playlist called What’s Good. Recently, he’s been experimenting with filming commentaries on front-facing video, TikTok style. “There’s a sense of freedom in reinvention,” Schreiber says. “I still quite enjoy writing as well. At the core, I’m still a critic, listener and pundit. It’s something I can’t turn off: I’m obsessed with music.”
- Weird Era: How Pitchfork Changed Music Forever: A Memoir is out on 1 December in the US, with UK and Australia release dates to be announced

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Pernambucano eleito nos EUA admira Lula e defende governo com mais políticas sociais
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Vinicius Sobreira
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A vitória do Partido Democrata nas eleições parlamentares e de governadores dos Estados Unidos, no início de novembro, levou para as câmaras estaduais alguns brasileiros, entre os quais o pernambucano Danillo Sena, ou “Dan Sena”, de 40 anos. Natural de Timbaúba, ele vive na cidade de Acton, a 34 quilômetros de Boston, ambas no estado de Massachusetts, na costa leste do país. Com o sotaque preservado e memórias do São João, o parlamentar conversou com o Brasil de Fato sobre sua trajetória e posições políticas.
Filho de uma professora e de um proprietário rural, Danillo teve uma infância entre o campo e a cidade no município de 54 mil habitantes (em 2022) localizado na zona da mata norte de Pernambuco, próximo à fronteira com a Paraíba. Suas memórias mais antigas da política remetem ao início dos anos 2000, quando seu tio Zé Canela foi vereador pelo MDB. “Lembro da maneira como a política era feita lá [em Timbaúba], os trios elétricos, palanques. Mas eu achava interessante as pessoas abordarem ele na rua. Eu entendi que os políticos são pessoas que podem aprovar leis para beneficiar a sociedade”, pontua.
Ao resgatar o Danillo criança e adolescente, o deputado diz que percebeu cedo as desigualdades socioeconômicas. “Era muito consciente dessas diferenças entre ricos e pobres. Isso me influenciou muito desde criança”, afirma. Mas foi adolescente, já nos EUA, estudante do ensino médio, que ele se tornou politicamente ativo. “Fui a Washington D. C. [capital do país] lutar por direitos dos imigrantes e aqui na State House [sede do governo de Massachusetts] fui várias vezes”, recorda, mencionando a luta para que imigrantes pudessem pagar o mesmo que os estadunidenses nas mensalidades das universidades locais. “Mas nunca pensei em ser deputado. Parecia um sonho distante”, pontua Sena.
Na universidade, chegou a cursar dois anos de engenharia, mas logo mudou de ideia. “Eu gostava mesmo era de sociologia e história. Então fui fazer ciência política”, explica. Após se formar, em 2013, foi trabalhar com o senador estadual James Eldridge, que Sena conhecia dos tempos de ativismo estudantil — nos EUA, o poder legislativo a nível estadual também é bicameral, como o nacional, com câmara de deputados e senado. Danillo foi diretor distrital de Eldridge por seis anos (2014-2020), sendo responsável pela agenda do senador no distrito e mediando as demandas locais e o representante. “Passei a entender como o governo funcionava”, diz o pernambucano.
O deputado estadual
Em 2020, a deputada estadual Jen Benson abriu mão do mandato restando seis meses para a conclusão, o que levou a uma eleição especial na qual Danillo se candidatou e venceu para representar a população do 37º distrito de Middlesex, com apoio e mentoria de Eldridge. “Foi um sonho que se realizou, apesar de eu não ter planejado isso. Profissionalmente eu já me sentia completo trabalhando para o senador. Hoje faço um trabalho parecido com o que eu fazia, mas podendo produzir ainda mais projetos de lei para atender a população”, comemora Sena. “Projetos que eu debati [como estudante] com o senador há 15 anos, hoje eu voto para aprová-los. É muito gratificante. Me sinto privilegiado”, resume.
Após cumprir os seis meses do “mandato-tampão”, o pernambucano enfrentou uma segunda eleição no mesmo ano, sendo reeleito, o que se repetiu em 2022, 2024 e agora em 2026, já que os mandatos de deputados nos EUA duram apenas dois anos. Nesta campanha para o 5º mandato, suas pautas principais foram a ampliação do acesso à saúde, às universidades e também a construção de novas creches, além de debater caminhos para conter a subida de preços de moradia em Massachusetts.
O estado, cuja capital é Boston, vota majoritariamente com os Democratas. A governadora Maura Healy (Democratas) foi reeleita com 1,7 milhão de votos (62,3%), assim como o senador Edward J. Markey (Democratas). Os nove deputados federais eleitos por Massachusetts também são democratas. Mas a “onda azul” alcançou até estados tradicionalmente Republicanos, como o Texas, que elegeu a democrata Gina Hinojosa após 36 anos do Partido Republicano no poder local.
A “onda azul” democrata
Questionado sobre as causas para esse movimento político, Sena cita a inflação, relacionada à guerra iniciada por Israel contra o Irã, com apoio direto dos Estados Unidos a Israel nesse conflito. “A gasolina e a comida estão mais cara. nós estamos sentindo no bolso esse conflito que está acontecendo [no Irã]”, diz ele. Já sobre a migração de voto do “eleitorado latino”, que votou em Trump em 2024 e agora elege parlamentares democratas, o brasileiro cita o impacto negativo da política de perseguição à população estrangeira nos Estados Unidos, agravada pela forma como ela tem sido executada.
“Na campanha, Trump disse que deportaria ‘os criminosos’, mas vimos que a grande maioria das pessoas detidas não tinham registros criminais ou tinham pequenas coisas. E eu acho que houve um grande abuso de poder dos agentes federais do ICE, até com mortes”, recorda Danillo Sena, citando vídeos que viralizaram com agentes mascarados realizando abordagens truculentas, quebrando janelas de carros para remover o condutor imigrante. “A maioria do povo americano discorda dessa maneira de fazer. E isso causou muita revolta”, avalia.
Questionado sobre o momento de ressurgimento da extrema-direita no mundo, Danillo evitou caracterizá-los como fascistas ou radicais. “A sua experiência de vida te torna mais conservador ou mais liberal. Tenho todo respeito com ambos os lados”, pontuou, avaliando o momento como “muito polarizado”. “Mas estou muito feliz com a vitória de Lula no Brasil e espero que aqui nos Estados Unidos a gente continue esse movimento, saindo do lado mais extremo da direita e indo para o centro, elegendo futuramente um presidente democrata”.
O pernambucano se coloca como centro-esquerda e defende que o poder público assuma mais responsabilidades na garantia de direitos da população. “As políticas sociais da esquerda ou do Partido Democrata são muito importantes para um governo. Quando vejo essa direita que quer tirar o governo do caminho, a gente acaba perdendo o controle e algumas empresas cometem abusos contra seus funcionários, por exemplo”, conclui.
Ted Kennedy, Lula, futebol e São João
Perguntado sobre figuras políticas que o inspiram, Danillo cita “a história e trajetória de Lula”; a admiração pelo tio e ex-vereador timbaubense Zé Canela, que Sena descreve como alguém comprometido com a população; mas sua principal referência política é Ted Kennedy, que foi senador de Massachusetts e faleceu em 2009. “A oratória dele, os discursos em defesa dos imigrantes e pessoas mais vulneráveis, isso me tocou muito. Eu olhava para ele com muito respeito”, lembra Sena.
Irmão do ex-presidente John F. Kennedy, Ted era católico, mas defensor do direito ao aborto, do casamento entre pessoas do mesmo sexo, dos direitos dos imigrantes nos EUA e de um maior controle sobre a venda e posse de armas no país. Também atuou para que os EUA parassem de vender armas para a ditadura de Pinochet no Chile e que impusesse sanções à África do Sul pelo seu regime de Apartheid.
A cada biênio ou triênio, Danillo Sena volta a Pernambuco para visitar a família em Timbaúba, vive novamente a dinâmica da cidade, onde ele já se tornou conhecido das lideranças políticas locais. Casado com a imigrante cambojana Melinda Yim e pai de três crianças (de cinco, sete e doze anos), Sena também aproveita a viagem para passear no Recife e levar a família para tomar banho nas praias pernambucanas e paraibanas, onde a temperatura do Atlântico é mais convidativa.
As vindas a Pernambuco não foram o suficiente para ele ter um time do coração. “Não torço para nenhum, mas já me disseram que se eu sou de Pernambuco, deveria torcer pelo Sport”, afirma, entre risos, citando ainda uma viagem de avião em que encontrou atletas do Náutico e “tietou” os alvirrubros. Danillo joga futebol com amigos nos Estados Unidos, “mas só no verão”, diz ele, destacando que não encara a brincadeira no frio do inverno.
O pernambucano não tem memórias de brincar Carnaval, mas diz ter “boas recordações do São João. Brinquei muito. É o meu feriado brasileiro favorito”. Em alguns anos a igreja da comunidade em que ele reside promove uma festa junina, que o ajuda a manter as memórias vivas, tanto quanto o sotaque pernambucano. “Isso não sai. Mas tenho orgulho do meu sotaque, porque ele mostra de onde eu sou”, diz ele.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 with North Carolina seat
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Democrats win largest House majority since 1992 with North Carolina seat
At least 258 US House seats are now under Democratic control, with four more midterm races yet to be decided.
The Democratic Party has won at least 258 seats in the United States House of Representatives, its highest total since 1992.
On Sunday, a congressional race in North Carolina was decided after a recount, giving Democrats their 258th House seat, as a handful of races in the 2026 midterm elections are still being counted.
The race for North Carolina’s 5th congressional district saw Democrat Chuck Hubbard defeat Republican incumbent Virginia Foxx, who has served 11 terms in Congress.
The win was symbolic of a larger political shift in North Carolina and elsewhere, as longtime Republican strongholds flipped to Democratic hands, sometimes for the first time in decades.
Foxx was first elected in 2004, and in recent years, she was the chair of the House Rules Committee. According to The Associated Press news agency, only 330 votes separated Hubbard and Foxx as of Sunday, when the race was called in the Democrat’s favour.
Four House races have yet to be called, meaning Democrats may still expand their already sizeable majority in the 435-member House.
The party has now picked up about 47 House seats. Currently, in the outgoing Congress, Democrats hold 214 seats.
But the House was not the only congressional chamber to flip in this year’s midterm elections.
In the 120th Congress, set to be sworn in on January 3, Democrats will also hold 56 seats in the US Senate, its largest majority in more than a decade.
Those majorities give the Democratic Party significant power over legislation, although President Donald Trump, a Republican, has already pledged to veto bills the party puts forward.
Experts say the Republican Party’s drubbing in the midterm elections was driven by voter frustration with issues like the cost of living, the US-Israel war on Iran, corruption and immigration raids.
It was also widely interpreted as a referendum on Trump’s second term, which began in 2025.
As of November, only 32 percent of Americans approved of Trump’s job performance, according to a poll by the news agency Reuters and the research firm Ipsos.
Democrats have framed their electoral victory as a unique opportunity to shape the final two years of Trump’s presidency.
Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a progressive who won her re-election bid in New York’s 14th congressional district, called the political shift a “mandate for change”.
“This is a historic moment for our country. This is one of the largest classes we have seen,” Ocasio-Cortez said at the US Capitol.
The party’s majority in the House will be larger than any since Democrat Bill Clinton was first elected president in 1992 with a 258-seat majority for his party.
It is also just above the 257 seats held by Democrats when Barack Obama was elected in 2008.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Câmara abre semana com previsão de votação do ajuste fiscal e negociações sobre Orçamento
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A Câmara dos Deputados inicia a semana com a previsão de votar, já na segunda-feira (23), o pacote de ajuste fiscal aprovado pelo Senado. O presidente da Casa, Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), convocou uma sessão extraordinária para discutir o Projeto de Lei Complementar (PLP) 299/2026, que reúne medidas de contenção de despesas e ampliação da arrecadação federal. A votação dependerá da conclusão da fase de discussão da proposta e da aprovação de um requerimento de urgência.
O pacote prevê mudanças nas regras de execução do Orçamento, ampliação dos instrumentos de bloqueio de despesas, revisão de benefícios tributários e alterações nos repasses da União a estados e municípios. Segundo estimativas apresentadas pelo governo, as medidas devem contribuir para uma economia de R$ 56 bilhões e o cumprimento da meta de superávit primário de R$ 18,7 bilhões em 2027.
O texto-base foi aprovado pelo Senado no dia 12 de novembro, por 45 votos a 31. Na quarta-feira (18), os senadores concluíram a análise dos destaques e encaminharam a proposta à Câmara. O relator, Eduardo Braga (MDB-AM), negociou alterações com representantes do governo e da oposição, incluindo mudanças nas compensações previstas na Lei Kandir, que trata da desoneração das exportações.
O texto original reduzia as transferências da União a estados e municípios, que servem para compensar perdas de ICMS sobre exportações, de R$ 4 bilhões para R$ 1 bilhão por ano entre 2027 e 2030. Após acordo entre Eduardo Braga e a oposição, o piso anual de 2027 a 2030 subiu de R$ 1 bilhão para R$ 2 bilhões.
Na Câmara, o presidente, deputado federal Hugo Motta (Republicanos-PB), defende a apreciação da proposta, enquanto o relator, Mauro Benevides Filho (União Brasil-CE), apresentou parecer preservando o conteúdo central aprovado pelo Senado. Por se tratar de um projeto de lei complementar, a aprovação exige o voto favorável de pelo menos 257 dos 513 deputados.
Orçamento de 2027 terá novas etapas de votação
A Comissão Mista de Orçamento (CMO) também terá uma semana de atividades importantes para a tramitação da proposta orçamentária de 2027. O cronograma prevê a votação do relatório da receita na quarta-feira (25) e do relatório preliminar na quinta-feira (26).
O relatório da receita analisa as estimativas de arrecadação que servirão de base para a elaboração do orçamento. Já o relatório preliminar estabelece regras e parâmetros para a distribuição dos recursos, incluindo os limites e as condições de atendimento das emendas parlamentares. A aprovação desses documentos antecede a análise detalhada das despesas previstas para o próximo ano.
Na última semana, 16 comissões do Senado e do Congresso aprovaram 96 propostas de emendas ao Orçamento de 2027, que somam R$ 85,9 bilhões em pedidos de recursos para áreas como saúde, educação, segurança pública, infraestrutura e meio ambiente. Os valores ainda dependem da análise da Comissão Mista de Orçamento e não representam despesas já aprovadas.
Entre as propostas estão R$ 14,5 bilhões em emendas da Comissão de Assuntos Sociais, destinadas a iniciativas de saúde e assistência social, e R$ 6,9 bilhões da Comissão de Educação, incluindo recursos para a educação básica, universidades federais e o programa Pé-de-Meia. A Comissão de Meio Ambiente apresentou propostas que somam R$ 2 bilhões, voltadas, entre outras ações, à política climática e ao combate ao desmatamento.
Pelo calendário apresentado pela CMO, a votação do relatório geral está prevista para 16 de dezembro, com análise pelo plenário do Congresso no dia seguinte.
Tributação, trabalho intermitente e maioridade penal
Na terça-feira (24), a Comissão de Finanças e Tributação da Câmara tem audiência pública prevista para discutir a alíquota-base de 11,3% da Contribuição sobre Bens e Serviços (CBS), tributo criado pela reforma tributária. O percentual foi calculado pelo Tribunal de Contas da União (TCU) para 2027, e os deputados deverão discutir os critérios utilizados e os impactos econômicos da cobrança.
Também na terça-feira, uma comissão especial da Câmara poderá votar o parecer sobre o projeto que amplia o limite anual de faturamento dos microempreendedores individuais (MEI), atualmente fixado em R$ 81 mil. A proposta, já aprovada pelo Senado, eleva o teto para R$ 130 mil e permite a contratação de até dois empregados. A reunião está prevista para as 15h30, com relatoria de Jorge Goetten (Republicanos-SC).
A Comissão da Amazônia e dos Povos Originários e Tradicionais da Câmara realiza, ainda na terça, audiência pública sobre a criação da Comissão Nacional Indígena da Verdade. O debate abordará a investigação de violações de direitos contra povos indígenas e a formulação de políticas de memória, justiça e reparação.
No Senado, a Comissão de Direitos Humanos tem na pauta de quarta-feira (25) uma proposta de autoria de Paulo Paim (PT-RS) para revogar o trabalho intermitente, modalidade de contratação introduzida pela reforma trabalhista de 2017. O modelo permite a prestação de serviços em períodos alternados de trabalho e inatividade, com remuneração correspondente às horas ou aos dias efetivamente trabalhados.
Também na quarta, a comissão especial da Câmara que analisa a redução da maioridade penal de 18 para 16 anos vai realizar uma nova audiência pública. O relator da proposta, Mendonça Filho (PL-PE), indicou a possibilidade de votação do parecer no início de dezembro. A medida é alvo de questionamentos de organizações de defesa dos direitos de crianças e adolescentes, que contestam sua eficácia no enfrentamento da violência.
