https://www.theguardian.com/football/liv.text:
Brentford, though, what a piece of work. You get the sense every single person in that club is excelling and they’re improving a some rate. I’d like to see them properly attack the Cup this season, because in a one-off game, they can beat anyone.
I couldn’t manage to indoctrinate football into my daughter, but she did come to Wembley for the women’s Euro final and absolutely loved it. Not a chance she’d have felt that way watching the men.
David Moyes shakes Keith Andrews’ hand even before the whistle goes. A fantastic performance from Brentford, who move sixth, a point behind Bournemouth in fifth; Everton stay ninth.
90+3 min The home fans sing “England’s No 4” at Jordan Pickford, who I don’t think could’ve done much about any of the goals. And it’s great to see the near-post corner working well; made famous by Anders Limpar and Steve Bould at Arsenal, when executed properly, it’s almost undefendable. I don’t get why more teas don’t use it.
90+1 min We’ll have three additional minutes, but VAR wants' a look; was Carvalho offside? No he wasn’t, and he has his goal – a nice moment, given his injury woes.
And you can’t say Brentford – and Everton – don’t deserve this. A near-post corner attacked by Ajer, who I think gets a flick and, as the ball speeds into the six-yard box, Carvalho extends a reflex knee to divert it into the net from three yards.
89 min Brentford’s next three fixtures: Man United (a), Arsenal (h), Man City (h). I’m looking forward to those, and I’d back them to get six points minimum.
87 min A ball into Wilson, who’s been a decent focal point, and Carvalho picks up the set-back, opening his body to pass a shot … that’s blocked by a flying body.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Federal appeals court hands Trump way out of conviction for hush-money payment
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Associated Press
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
A federal appeals court on Monday gave Donald Trump a new pathway to erasing his hush money criminal conviction, moving the case to a federal court where he could seek to have it dismissed on immunity grounds.
A three-judge panel of the second US circuit court of appeals reversed a lower court decision that had kept the case in state court in New York, where Trump was tried and convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records to obscure a $130,000 payment to adult-film performer Stormy Daniels.
The panel ordered a lower court to promptly issue a decision on whether the case should remain in federal court. If that happens, Trump could then argue that verdict should be discarded because of presidential immunity.
The decision also set in motion a halt to proceedings in Trump’s simultaneous state court appeal. Trump denies wrongdoing and was given no punishment in the case, which made him the first US president convicted of a crime.
In a two-page order, the second circuit panel said it disagreed with the late US district judge Alvin Hellerstein’s earlier denial of Trump’s request to move the historic case from state court to federal court, a process known as removal.

https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.title: US states sue SpaceX over Grok AI’s creation of child sexual abuse material
https://www.aljazeera.com/economy/2026/1.text:
US states sue SpaceX over Grok AI’s creation of child sexual abuse material
Virginia and Oregon filed separate lawsuits on Monday, accusing the company of promoting Grok’s ‘spicy mode’.
The US states of Virginia and Oregon have sued Elon Musk’s SpaceX, saying the business harmed consumers by avoiding safeguards when it designed and launched an artificial intelligence chatbot capable of creating sexualised images.
The attorneys general of both states filed complaints in separate lawsuits on Monday.
Several states had announced investigations into Grok over similar claims in recent months, but Virginia and Oregon are the first states to sue.
The lawsuits filed in state courts accuse SpaceX of misleading consumers about Grok’s safety and failing to put adequate safeguards in place while promoting its “spicy mode”. The feature allows users to take an existing photograph of a person and generate a sexual or nude image or video, according to the lawsuits.
The company prioritised its business model over the safety of millions of people, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones said in his state’s lawsuit.
“To push its lagging product, Grok, to tens of millions of new users, it stripped out industry-standard safeguards and marketed a ‘spicy mode’ built to produce nudity,” Jones said in the lawsuit. “For these Defendants, weak safeguards were not a failure but a feature.”
Virginia and Oregon accused SpaceX of violating their respective consumer protection laws. They are seeking damages, penalties and court orders forcing the company to stop violating state law.
SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Grok is available to users of X, the social media platform that is a subsidiary of SpaceX.
In a statement posted on X on Monday that did not directly address the lawsuits, the platform’s safety team said it had taken action to block prompts that could generate sexualised or nude imagery and worked with law enforcement to pursue people who use the platform to make it.
“The people who tried to use Grok Imagine to generate this material did so by deliberately violating our Terms of Service and working aggressively to circumvent our safeguards,” the company posted.
Virginia’s lawsuit cites data from a study by the Center for Countering Digital Hate, which estimated that between December 2025 and January 2026, Grok generated and posted millions of sexualised images on X, including more than 20,000 depicting children.
Investigators from the attorney general’s office in Virginia found that Grok’s image moderation was inconsistent, and that the bot would advise users on how to circumvent the moderation measures by avoiding words that triggered it, according to the lawsuit.
Beginning in January, Grok told users that its image generation features were only for paying subscribers, which did not stop the images’ creation but allowed the company to profit from them, the lawsuit said.
SpaceX is facing more than a dozen lawsuits brought by individuals who say nonconsensual sexual images of them as minors or adults were generated by Grok.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: US drug prices leave patients facing impossible choices
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
US drug prices leave patients facing impossible choices
Despite working and having health insurance, some of the country’s sickest patients have trouble affording the medicines they need.
Sarah Wisniewski and her sister were once contemplating an extraordinary arrangement to manage their shared multiple sclerosis (MS) diagnoses: alternating months taking a life-changing medication.
The drug, which Wisniewski says costs thousands of dollars a month without insurance coverage, was so expensive that the sisters considered rationing their treatment rather than going without it entirely.
“It’s a weird thing to have to think about,” the 45-year-old told Al Jazeera. “You go to college, you get insurance, you get a good job, you pay your bills, you do everything right and, still, you’re having to ration your medication.”
Wisniewski is one of more than four in 10 adults in the United States who did not take medication as prescribed last year because of the cost, estimates KFF, an independent health policy research organisation.
Her experience highlights the growing financial pressures facing some of the nation’s sickest patients, who have trouble affording costly prescription medications, despite having jobs and private health insurance.
‘Every spare dime’ needed for medications
Wisniewski was diagnosed with MS in 2017 after experiencing increasingly debilitating symptoms, including difficulties with her vision, mobility and breathing.
She became one of the nearly eight in 10 American adults who are living with at least one chronic condition, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
In the summer of 2024, her neurologist prescribed Kesimpta, a medication that, she says, dramatically improved her condition. But her insurance company, Blue Cross Blue Shield, notified her it would not cover the treatment.
Wisniewski appealed three times before requesting a hearing in her state of Maryland. Only weeks before that hearing was due to take place did her insurer agree to cover the medication.
Without that intervention, Wisniewski said, she would have faced a monthly bill of approximately $10,000.
The impact of obtaining treatment has been significant on her life.
“I went from barely being able to walk … Now, I walk my dog every morning, a mile-and-a-half to two miles,” she said.
Wisniewski has also been able to maintain her federal contracting job, which she described as highly technical and demanding.
But the financial burden remains substantial. Even with the help of insurance, Wisniewski estimates she spends between $800 and $900 each month on medication.
“Almost every spare dime I get is going to just keeping me healthy, so I can make it to work the next day,” she said.
‘A uniquely American problem’
Unlike many countries, particularly wealthier ones, the US allows pharmaceutical companies significantly more latitude to set their own prices.
According to the Patients For Affordable Drugs Now patient-advocacy organisation, current laws give manufacturers “unilateral power to set launch prices in the US and the ability to raise prices at will”.
“I believe this is a uniquely American problem, ”Wisniewski said. “Other countries are … able to provide for their citizens these drugs, if not for free, at an affordable level.”
The monthly cost of her medication in Canada is 2,333 Canadian dollars ($1,623). It’s even lower in Australia at 41 Australian dollars ($27) or 6.60 Australian dollars ($4.37) with a concession card, which allows eligible residents in the country to receive discounts on healthcare and prescription medicines.
The Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA), a consortium that represents US drug companies, argues that a complicated network of third-party middlemen, known as pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs), and insurance companies are to blame for the country’s high drug prices.
“PBMs and insurers control benefits through processes like prior authorisation, embedded step therapy, and formulary controls that may allow PBMs and insurers to deny coverage or push patients to alternative treatments from the initially prescribed medicine,” PhRMA’s website said. The organisation did not reply to a request for comment.
A study by the nonpartisan RAND organisation, released in 2024, found that US prescription drug prices were substantially higher than those in other wealthy countries, particularly for name-brand medications.
Using 2022 data, RAND’s researchers found that US manufacturers’ gross prices across all prescription drugs were 278 percent higher than the average prices in 33 other high-income countries. For brand-name drugs, US prices were more than four times the comparison-country average.
But the consequences of the current US system can extend far beyond the cost of individual prescriptions.
Wisniewski said the money she spends maintaining access to medication is money she cannot put toward local businesses, transportation or investments in her community.
“I really think that a lot of people, at an abstract level, understand that this could happen to anybody at any point in time,” she said. “But I don’t think that it really hits home to folks that you are legitimately one bad phone call away from losing everything.”
What can be done?
After this month’s historic midterm elections in the US, where Democrats won control of both chambers in the US Congress by wide margins, there will be few areas of agreement with Democrats’ Republican counterparts – and President Donald Trump.
But targeted reforms that address the high cost of prescriptions could be an area where both parties find common ground.
A survey conducted by Fabrizio Ward in March 2025 found more than three in four voters – including 70 percent of Trump supporters – wanted Congress to take action on reducing drug prices.
The issue was the focus of a US Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on Tuesday of last week, when lawmakers and healthcare experts examined how pharmaceutical companies and insurers influence pricing and access to medication.
At that November 17 hearing, witnesses highlighted several factors contributing to high prescription drug costs, including pharmaceutical patent protections and the role of PBMs.
Merith Basey, chief executive officer of Patients For Affordable Drugs Now, argued that pharmaceutical companies exploit the patent system to delay competition from cheaper alternatives.
One of those practices, known as patent thicketing, involves companies securing multiple patents covering different aspects of a medication or its delivery device, potentially making it more difficult for competitors to introduce generic alternatives.
Basey told lawmakers the introduction of generic competition could substantially reduce prices, arguing a single generic competitor can lower a drug’s price by 39 percent, while six or more competitors can reduce prices by as much as 95 percent.
But other witnesses pointed to PBMs, claiming their involvement in distributing drugs can influence pricing.
The Senate panel has advanced a number of proposals to tackle the high cost of prescription drugs in the US. One of those is the bipartisan Eliminating Thickets to Improve Competition (ETHIC) Act, which would limit the practice of patent thickening, making it easier for generic drugs to enter the US market and lower costs.
“Big Pharma knows exactly what it’s doing in monopolising the US patent system: driving up drug costs for Americans while preventing generic-drug manufacturers from getting their foot in the market,” Republican Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri, one of the bill’s sponsors, said in a statement.
Wisniewski noted that while the ETHIC Act wouldn’t make her prescription “cheap”, it would be “astronomically better than what we have now”.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Iran flogs singer Parastoo Ahmadi for performing without headscarf
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Iran flogs singer Parastoo Ahmadi for performing without headscarf
Ahmadi and four production team members also face two-year bans on travel and artistic activity.
Iran has flogged a singer and her production team after they were convicted of “offending public decency”, according to local media.
The sentence of 74 lashes handed down to Parastoo Ahmadi and four members of her team was carried out in the city of Qom on Monday, the singer’s lawyer Mostafa Nili told the Emtedad news website.
A court in the city had sentenced the quintet in June. They were convicted of “producing and publishing obscene and immoral content online” over a video showing Ahmadi performing without wearing the mandatory hijab alongside male musicians.
The video was posted on YouTube in December 2024. In addition to the flogging, the five were banned for two years from taking part in artistic and musical activities and leaving Iran.
Western governments and human rights groups have condemned flogging as a form of torture that violates international law.
Iran rejects criticism of its human rights record and says Western countries should address abuses of their own.
Iran’s mandatory hijab rules became a focal point of protests in 2022 after Mahsa Amini, a Kurdish Iranian woman, died in custody following her arrest for allegedly violating the dress code.
More women have since defied the rules in Tehran and elsewhere in Iran, while authorities have enforced them more selectively.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: The life, death and improbable rebirth of LA’s most beloved diner
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Andrew Gumbel in Los Angeles
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Sometimes, an old-school American diner is just a diner. And sometimes, like the Original Pantry in downtown Los Angeles, it feels like the heart and soul of a city, a bellwether of good times and bad.
For decades it was famous for never closing. Located in a low-slung shotgun building on a busy corner, it fed politicians, movie stars, students, criminals and street bums around the clock, seven days a week. The doors had no locks, because the place had no need for them. The portions were huge, the prices dirt cheap, and many of the servers, in bow ties and white shirts, looked like extras from a Harold Lloyd two-reeler.
The diner survived speculative booms, depressions, an emergency relocation due to freeway construction, periods when downtown seemed to roll up its sidewalks at the end of the business day, and epidemics of homelessness, drug abuse and crime.
Long after the Pantry started to feel like a time capsule from another era – its Depression-era menu of pancakes, omelettes and steaks making no attempt to keep up with the evolving tastes of a global culinary capital – it clung on thanks to the determination of its businessman owner, Richard Riordan, who bought it during the Reagan era and went on to serve two terms as LA’s mayor.
Riordan wasn’t daunted when a 37-storey financial services tower sprang up on the next-door lot, or when a large corporate event space, LA Live, ate up much of the vacant land to the south and east. When the county health department forced the Pantry’s first closure in 1997 after finding dozens of minor food safety infractions, Riordan rushed over from city hall and worked the phones himself until his beloved restaurant, now dwarfed by skyscrapers, was back open.
Still, the restaurant could not stave off decline forever. When Riordan died in 2023, the business was in a post-Covid funk it couldn’t shake, the staff was in an uproar over unpaid back wages and – the ultimate indignity – the kitchen had started making its once-fabled pancakes from a packaged mix.
It wasn’t long before Riordan’s heirs put padlocks on the door and had the police escort out the last of the workers, many of whom had worked there for decades. The local papers wrote obituaries, and Los Angeles plunged into mourning for another historical landmark run over by the relentless march of history.
And yet, this week, the Pantry has made the most improbable of comebacks.
It is no longer open around the clock. The hash browns no longer look like bricks that could feed a family for a week. But it is open once more, under new ownership and with a new mission as a nonprofit devoted to helping LA’s large homeless population. A dozen of its former workers have put their uniforms back on, giving the place much of its old flavor even as it seeks to define itself as something new.
“What I see,” LA’s mayor-elect, Nithya Raman, said at a raucous, packed opening ceremony on a rain-swept Thursday morning, “is a room full of people who never gave up hope.” Since the Pantry has no liquor license, everyone raised coffee mugs instead.
To the many fans who either attended with an invitation or stood in line in the pouring rain for a chance to be among the first ordinary diners to place their orders, the Pantry’s reopening carries symbolic weight for the city as a whole. Restaurant union leader Kurt Peterson called it “one of the great Los Angeles love stories” – the romantic notion that in one spot, at least, all distinctions between the city’s haves and have-nots melt away like butter in a pan.
The turnaround at the Pantry comes after a painful couple of years in which two foothill neighborhoods were wrecked by wildfires, the cost of living has soared, thousands remain homeless, immigration raids have torn apart families and communities, and retail businesses – including restaurants – have shuttered faster than new ones have been able to take their place.
“Hopefully, this is a sign that the doom loop is finally reversing,” said the Pantry’s new owner, Ukrainian American businessman Leo Pustilnikov.
Such optimism might have been less warranted if Pustilnikov had wanted to run the Pantry as a conventional business. Instead, he decided the only money-making part of the venture would be a digital billboard on the roof. For the restaurant itself, he turned to a local homelessness services provider called Hope the Mission and offered a roughly 50% break on the rent if in exchange they would bring the Pantry back and commit to ploughing any profits into helping homeless people get back on their feet.
It was not a difficult sell. “Pancakes with a purpose,” was how Hope The Mission’s founder, Ken Craft, saw the concept, and he set about raising more than $1m to replace the Pantry’s ageing kitchen equipment, update the tables and chairs so they would no longer be sticky with chewing gum and bacon grease, replace the black-and-white checkered floor, and rethink the menu for a city more cosmopolitan and eclectic than it was on opening day in 1924.
The Pantry still looks like its old self, with pictures of Marilyn Monroe and Humphrey Bogart on the wall, an old taxi phone, and a cashier’s cage taking up pride of place near the front door, even though the restaurant mostly uses hand-held credit card machines. The new operators have also left an area in front of the cage, an archeological showcase of sorts, where customers over the decades wore through 12 layers of flooring.
The eggs and hash browns no longer land like bowling balls in the diners’ stomachs but come gently crisped on the edges. In a nod to LA’s multiculturalism, there are poblano chilis in the Denver omelette and Korean pickles in the coleslaw. For the first time, the Pantry now has an in-house baker producing a vanilla-bean cheesecake and a chocolate crunch cake that taste refreshingly light.
Unlike many American cities, which have slowly lost their fabled delis and diners, LA has a track record of putting up a fight whenever its culinary history is on the line. A similarly storied establishment, Cole’s, which once played host to Hollywood’s most notorious gangster, Mickey Cohen, and claims to be the home of an LA special, the French dip sandwich, had its own reopening after a threatened closure earlier in the week.
Langer’s Deli, the only fully unionized restaurant in town aside from the Pantry, has been making noises about giving up because of drug and crime problems around its MacArthur Park home, but its customers have so far successfully pleaded to keep the doors open.
For Raman, who is eager to turn the page on Karen Bass’s unpopular single term as mayor and prove, once she takes office next month, that she can enact tangible change, the Pantry is a feelgood story too good not to latch on to. During her election campaign she visited twice and promised, if elected, to issue an executive order declaring that the Pantry serves “the best damned pancakes” in town.
Hope the Mission’s staff tried to hold her to that on Thursday – she smiled and shrugged when it came up – but her presence alone was a gift to a restaurant seeking to put itself back on the map. Along with Raman, the festivities attracted the city council member for downtown, a county supervisor and a former mayor.
“Our city is crying out for a comeback story,” said Rowan Vansleve, Craft’s deputy at Hope The Mission. And he made a vow of his own: that the Pantry, if successful, would go back to opening around the clock.
“If people can come back in the wee hours and have a slice,” he said, pointing to the chocolate cake, “LA will be back.”

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: US releases files on suspected Bigfoot sightings in Montana and Oregon
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Eric Berger
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
Bigfoot has quietly appeared again.
Well, not Sasquatch directly, but new files about the cryptid.
In a public archive, the US Forest Service recently added reports concerning suspected encounters with Bigfoot – or its remnants in Montana and Oregon.
A newly released 1982 report showed how a wildlife biologist investigated peculiar tracks in north-east Oregon.
The additional documents also included a 2003 Montana newspaper story about a reported sighting of Bigfoot tracks and a testimonial about the history of a creek area in Montana where people spotted what they thought was “a very large bear, except bears don’t walk on their hind legs only for short distances”.
The recent release of the files by the US Forest Service comes months after residents in rural Ontario, Canada, reported encounters with massive figures that matched the description of Bigfoot.
Collectively, they add to a long history of suspected sightings of Bigfoot or markings from the bipedal ape whose existence has not been confirmed by science. The Bigfoot Mapping Project contains more than 16,000 reports on the cryptid, a term referring to an animal or creature whose existence has not been proven.
Carleton University philosophy professor Josh Redstone previously told the Guardian that Bigfoot is a prime example of how fascinating the unverified can be for humans.
“For people who believe in Sasquatch, there’s an excitement around the possibility of discovering something new,” Redstone said.
In the 1982 report, the biologist, Rodney Johnson, investigated tracks at three locations in the Umatilla National Forest in north-east Oregon. To determine their origin, Johnson – or a fellow investigator – made plaster casts of two of the tracks.
Johnson gave eight reasons why he did not think the tracks belonged to Sasquatch, including:
- “The stride of the tracks did not change with slope.”
- “The tracks at both sites were not to the ‘bottom’ of the mud.
- “The small toes lack a definite ‘pad’ at the tips as would be expected.”
Still, Johnson did not entirely dismiss the Bigfoot theory.
“If the tracks were faked, someone went to a great deal of trouble and detail,” Johnson wrote. “The ‘print’ marks on the foot would have to be very hard to duplicate. They appear very natural. I would almost suspect a cast made of an actual foot would have had to be used to make the ‘fake’ feet. If this were the case though, the other creases in the foot should have shown.”
In a subsequent report from the forest service, the investigator stated that the tracks “were a very clever attempt to perpetrate a hoax”.
“Trusting that this memo will suffice to close this ‘Bigfoot’ case,” the report stated.
That case might have been closed – but there were others.
In the 1980 testimonial, which reads like a novel, Leo Kinney in Montana wrote: “Now to tell some of the things that made history.”
He and three others entered the woods to retrieve an elk carcass, he wrote. But he said they instead spotted “another type creature that walked on its hind legs that altho [sic] there wasn’t actual sightings, tracks, a strong odor and a gruntling sound were observed”.
After determining that the creature had supposedly picked up the elk and dragged it, “we held a conference and decided that we were not particularly anxious to catch up to whatever it was and tho [sic] we didn’t confess it at this time, in later conversations we found out that we all had a very uneasy feeling and could feel chills running up and down our backs.”
The journalist who produced the 2003 Clark Fork Valley Press story wrote that a group in Montana found hundreds of “strange footprints”.
“I didn’t believe it until I saw the tracks,” one woman said.
Residents in rural Ontario in June reported seeing two creatures scavenging through garbage.
“One big, one not so big,” an account stated. “The cinnamon was prominent on the smaller one.”
All who believe they have spotted a trace of Bigfoot submit a report to the Bigfoot Mapping Project.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/demo.title: The Future Is Bright for the Democrats, as Long as They Don’t Have to Interact With the Public
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/demo.author: Noah Hurowitz
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/demo.text:
Clutching a Shake Shack bag in the Denver airport Saturday, Lis Smith held forth on her “do’s and don’ts” for the Democrats. Do: Focus on cost of living and accountability for the excesses of the Trump administration. Don’t: Prioritize revenge on Trump before hitting your affordability goals.
“The voters who helped us get this majority were voters that said we want you to lower our costs, we want you to listen to us, we want you to root out corruption,” said Smith, a prominent strategist for the centrist wing of the Democratic Party. “We’re living in the middle of a cost-of-living-crisis, and if you’re not talking to voters about that issue, not meeting them where they are in terms of their anger at the system, at both the economic and political system, like, you’re doing it wrong.”
Smith was among the flotsam and jetsam of exhausted Democratic politicos swirling about Denver International Airport in a surreal coda to a gathering she’d helped organize: a two-day conference of moderate and center-left Democrats exploring the future of the party, aptly dubbed “What’s Next.”
It was organized by the self-styled pragmatists of Majority Democrats, a hybrid political action committee and super PAC bankrolled by the hedge fund tycoon Stephen Mandel and his wife, Sue, and co-signed by the Searchlight Institute, a centrist think tank launched by former staffers of John Fetterman who have sought to quash the party’s focus on more left-leaning policy. The conference was seen as a practice ground for stump speeches from potential 2028 presidential candidates, heavy on party unity and light on ideological debate.
Within the confines of the Mission Ballroom complex in Denver’s River North neighborhood, it was a safe space for hopefuls like former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, Sen. Ruben Gallego of Texas, Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, and Sen. Corey Booker of New Jersey to test out their lines for next cycle — before they have to go in front of the public.
But now, it was stuck.
On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop order, throwing the nation’s airports into chaos and canceling thousands of flights. As the situation was unfolding, Buttigieg joked onstage that he’d be available to help anyone looking to rebook their flight. On Saturday, 24 hours later, that joke might have been less funny to the likes of Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, who told The Intercept he had been unceremoniously deplaned from a flight canceled at the last minute.
Despite the airline chaos, Smith was feeling good. To her, the attendees represent the future in a post-Blue Tsunami landscape — and you better not call them the establishment.
“Majority Democrats does not consider itself a centrist organization,” said Smith, who worked on Buttigieg’s 2020 presidential run, former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo’s 2018 reelection campaign, and Cuomo’s 2021 response to sexual harassment allegations. “So we want to be an alternative to the stale establishment that puts up candidates like Joe Biden or like Andrew Cuomo for mayor.”
Smith said she welcomed it when “What’s Next” became the scene of early shots in a battle over Democratic leadership in the Senate. On Thursday, the first night of the conference, at about 7 p.m. Mountain time, news broke that Sen. Chris Van Hollen — a Maryland Democrat, conference invitee, and rumored 2028 hopeful — planned to mount a challenge to Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for party leadership.
“I think a little democracy in the United States Senate caucus is a good thing,” he said at his first press conference on the matter on Friday. “I think it’s important that we give Senate Democrats a choice. We gave voters all over the country a choice, and they chose change.”
Van Hollen, who has differentiated himself from Schumer with his critical stance on Israel, told reporters he had decided to abandon a go for the White House in 2028 in favor of shaking up the party’s presence in the Senate.
It was a slight departure from the celebratory mood in Denver, where the words “big tent” were frequently bandied about. At the airport, Smith told The Intercept she and other organizers were as surprised as anyone by Van Hollen’s announcement. “We invited Van Hollen just as we invited anyone who was on the list of potential 2028ers,” she said. “But what better place to do it, I guess!”
Aside from Van Hollen positioning himself as a progressive challenger to Schumer, there was a noted absence of the party’s left flank. The progressives who did make the invite list stayed on message with the “takes all kinds” approach to Democratic victory.
“It’s a really good time to be a Democrat right now,” said Morris Katz, a campaign adviser to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and, later, to Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner. “I think if you look at the historic wins that we had across the country and the way those candidates spoke, they sound a lot more like Bernie Sanders in 2016 than Hillary Clinton in 2016.”
But not everyone was feeling the love. Shelby Green, an organizer for a campaign in Florida to turn the state’s bankrupt Brightline railroad service into a public asset, criticized the conference organizers for having few Black women speakers on the main stage. She spoke bitterly of what she described as the party’s failure to properly support Angie Nixon, a Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidate who narrowly lost her contest for Senate in Florida.
“They waited until just weeks before the election to do a get-out-the-vote push, when they should have been doing voter registration,” Green said. “I think there should have been a space to apologize to Angie Nixon and to apologize to the South and say, ‘I’m sorry we underinvested, what can we do to make sure we don’t miss the ball next time?’”
Perhaps the most heated moments came when the conference attendees were forced to interact with members of the public — particularly those who disagreed with them.
On Friday morning, moments into a sit-down interview on the main stage between Jessica Tarlov, a token Democrat on Fox News, and New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, heir apparent to the Democratic leadership in the House, a small group of protesters stood up and started to shout for some of the left-wing policies that had gone largely unmentioned inside the conference.
“When is it time for Medicare for all?” one protester called out, prompting boos and jeers from the crowd. “When is it time for an arms embargo?”
As the protesters were ushered out, Jeffries began to speak of the honor he felt at “the trust placed in us by the American people.”
“Nobody trusts you!” another protester called out.
The conference shielded its attendees from most of the dissent. On the drive into the city on Thursday morning, The Intercept spotted a gaggle of protesters from the group Indivisible hoisting a huge banner on a highway overpass declaring “No Schumer Coronation,” objecting to the New York Democrat’s presumed rise as Senate majority leader. The group reappeared outside the convention center on Friday morning alongside protesters from Sunrise Movement demanding a Green New Deal, while police in riot gear milled around an armored vehicle looking bored and over-equipped. Onboard a shuttle bus ferrying conference-goers from their hotels to the convention center, one battle-hardened Democratic operative derided the protesters as “wacktivists,” expressing a distaste for the so-called “groups” blamed by many in the Democratic establishment for dragging the party left on social issues, to its detriment in 2024.
On the street corner on Friday morning, Tammy Butters, a retired teacher, told The Intercept that she was merely there to encourage those inside to not “chicken out” of holding the Trump administration accountable.
“There’s all this talk of compromise and talking to the other side, and I get that,” Butters said. “But I think we the people are screaming for accountability, and accountability and affordability are not separate issues. We are capable of doing both.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://www.propublica.org/article/trump.title: Corporations Are Using Trump’s Tariff Refunds on Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing Consumers
https://www.propublica.org/article/trump.author: Robert Faturechi, Nick McMillan
https://www.propublica.org/article/trump.text:
When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world’s largest tool companies, got hit with President Donald Trump’s tariffs last year, the firm made clear that it would be sharing the pain with its customers.
The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports.
Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients:
Its own leaders.
The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis of thousands of securities filings and earnings calls for publicly traded companies.
Other recognizable companies include the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls and the golf equipment brand Titleist.
Dozens of other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money other than to characterize the windfall as the kind of earnings they use to determine executive bonuses.
The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting the roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they’ve asked for, and it has denied ProPublica’s requests for this information. But reporters found some of these details while reviewing the disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies.
Some have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for example, “returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing,” though they generally don’t say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future increases. Others are paying back businesses they sold products to because they had itemized receipts that detailed the tariff markups.
But consumers hoping for refunds appear to be largely out of luck. With the help of artificial intelligence, ProPublica identified companies that said they planned to refund customers with their tariff windfalls. Almost all of them deal with other businesses, not consumers.
“Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money because it wasn’t anything the executives did that they should be rewarded for. It was a government mistake that resulted in a refund,” said Gregory Germain, a corporate law professor at Syracuse University. “It really explains why it’s so important for the government, when they’re doing something like this, to think it through to make sure consumers don’t pay extra money and not get it back.”
The chain reaction that led to these bonuses began in the first months of Trump’s second term. In February 2025, Trump declared a national emergency over illegal drugs coming in across the border and unilaterally announced new tariffs on goods from the countries he deemed responsible: Canada, Mexico and China.
Then, in April, he declared a second national emergency, this one over the U.S. trade deficit — the fact that the U.S. was importing more than it exported. Declaring it “Liberation Day,” Trump unveiled a poster in the Rose Garden detailing his most sweeping tariffs yet on goods from more than 100 countries.
Those tariffs remained in place, with some tweaks, until earlier this year when the Supreme Court struck them down, ruling that Trump had needed congressional approval to impose them.
That left the federal government scrambling to figure out how to refund billions in duties it had collected over the prior year on more than 53 million imported shipments. U.S. Customs and Border Protection set up an online application system. But only the direct payers of the tariffs — called the “importers of record” — are eligible to apply, not the businesses and consumers who took a hit downstream.
The New York Federal Reserve Bank, which analyzed the prices of a broad swath of goods, found that 26% of the tariff costs were eaten by American customers; a study from Harvard Business School put the estimate at 43%. One study estimated that Trump’s tariffs cost typical American households about $1,000 last year.
The administration and Congress have not placed constraints on how companies use the tariff refunds, though there have been calls to do so. After the Supreme Court ruling, a group of Democratic senators wrote to the president, asking if he would require companies to pass along part of their payments to consumers and assign penalties to those that did not. Doing otherwise, said Sens. Elizabeth Warren, Cory Booker and Peter Welch, would render the refunds “a giveaway to giant corporations that amounts to theft from the middle class.”
Though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has denied that the tariffs resulted in significantly higher prices, he has acknowledged the fundamental unfairness of only importers of record getting the refund. “I got a feeling the American people won’t see it,” he said in February at an Economic Club of Dallas event.
Bessent has made the argument that it’s the Democrats who challenged the tariffs in court, not the administration that imposed the tariffs, who are responsible for the transfer of wealth from American consumers to companies.
“The Democratic attorney generals who filed a ridiculous lawsuit against this administration wanted the money to go back to the payer of record,” he said at a press conference. “If I hear another Democratic legislator make the inane remark, ‘The American people should get the money’ — the American people had the money in the U.S. Treasury and we were forced to give it back.”
In some cases, companies have said that they will be splitting at least some of their refund checks with their customers. ProPublica’s analysis shows these companies’ customers are generally other businesses, not average consumers. Among them is Varex Imaging Corp. in Utah, which sells X-ray imaging components for medical businesses and cargo screeners. Varex and firms like it have not elaborated on why they are passing along refunds, but trade experts suspect these business-to-business vendors have detailed contracts that itemize tariff costs.
Shipping companies, like UPS and FedEx, have set up online portals for customers seeking refunds. Though the firms are technically importers of record, they imported goods on behalf of businesses and individuals that paid them to ship products. The companies are itemizing how much customers paid in tariffs and reimbursing them.
A series of lawsuits are attempting to force companies that sell directly to consumers to share some of their refunds. Dozens of firms have been sued, including big-box stores Walmart and Target and apparel companies such as Nike and Lululemon. Apparel and leather costs were some of the hardest hit by Trump’s tariffs. Legal analysts have cast doubt on whether these lawsuits will succeed, though some trade experts have speculated that businesses that used the tariffs as cover to raise prices more than they needed to might settle to avoid embarrassing disclosures.
One of the companies facing a lawsuit is Stanley Black & Decker, the toolmaker that ProPublica found was using some of its refund on bonuses. The named plaintiff is a Wisconsin resident who bought a handheld blower, an impact wrench, a hedge trimmer and other tools from the company last year, but the lawsuit seeks to represent thousands of other customers as well.
“Unless restrained by this Court,” the complaint reads, the company “stands to recover the same tariff payments twice — once from consumers through tariff-inflated prices and again from the federal government through tariff refunds.”
On multiple occasions, the company has acknowledged publicly that it was raising prices because of the tariffs.
The month before the November 2024 election, as Trump was campaigning on dramatic new tariffs, the toolmaker’s then-CEO, Donald Allan Jr., told shareholders that Stanley Black & Decker was preparing for the possibility. “Obviously, coming out of the gate, there would be price increases associated with tariffs that we put into the market,” he said during an earnings call. Then, a few months after Trump unveiled his tariffs, Allan said his team was “remaining focused on executing our robust plan designed to mitigate tariffs” that he said included “targeted pricing actions to improve our gross margin.” Later that year, his successor as chief executive, Chris Nelson, described more price hikes: “We are implementing a second price increase during the fourth quarter to maintain our innovation and brand investments, given the pressures resulting from tariff-related cost increases.”
In its more recent disclosures, the company has been vague about how much of its refund was going to executives, simply saying that some of that gain “was partially offset by directly attributable costs for variable incentive compensation.” “Incentive compensation” is a term the toolmaker uses to describe bonuses.
The company has not responded to the allegations in the lawsuit brought by the Wisconsin resident and did not answer ProPublica’s questions about who is getting paid the bonuses, how much they’re worth and whether customers should be reimbursed.
Securities experts who reviewed the disclosures for ProPublica said it appeared the windfall boosted the company’s profits, which factor into formulas that help determine bonus pay for executives and other employees.
“It wasn’t the executive that triggered that extra profit, so why should their compensation go up?” Germain, the corporate law professor said. “This is one of many examples where these formulas don’t do what they should do.”
The company’s leaders, securities experts said, could have given money back to consumers or lowered prices. Retail giant Burlington Stores, formerly known as Burlington Coat Factory, appears to have done just that.
CEO Michael O’Sullivan recently said the company got $55 million in tariff refunds and “rather than taking a one-time boost to earnings” the company plans “to deliver even sharper values to our shoppers,”
“Over the last few years, the rising cost of living has made life difficult for many customers,” O’Sullivan said, adding that the coming discounts meant investors should expect the “direct impact of tariff refunds to be neutral.”
A company spokesperson confirmed to ProPublica that none of its tariff refund will be going to bonuses.
Not so for other companies.
Acushnet, the Massachusetts golf equipment company that includes the brand Titleist, disclosed an “incentive compensation expense of approximately $12.0 million” out of its refund. Acushnet declined to respond to questions from ProPublica.
TJX, the Massachusetts parent company of TJ Maxx and Marshalls, said it got back $331 million, but as a result, it “accrued incremental expenses of $112 million for year-end incentive compensation and discretionary bonuses for eligible Associates globally.”
The company declined to answer questions from ProPublica about how far down the chain of command the bonuses would go and how much of them would be reserved for top managers. “Given that this is an accrual, and we have not reached the end of our current fiscal year, we have not disclosed any breakout beyond this,” a spokesperson said. The company also declined to say whether it would lower prices or pay back customers with the rest of its refund, saying only that “the remaining amount will be used to support our future growth.”
ProPublica’s examination of tariff refunds was limited to publicly traded companies, which are required to disclose detailed financial information. None of the companies that said they are using the money for bonuses have ever said they planned to refund customers. How private companies are using their refunds is unclear because they aren’t normally required to disclose such information.
Nick Guest, an accounting professor at Cornell University who has studied executive compensation, said the argument for granting leaders bonuses based on the tariff refunds could go both ways.
“If they were penalized for something out of their control,” he said, referring to earnings hits caused by Trump’s tariffs last year, rewarding them now “seems reasonable.”
“But you could say the same thing about customers. If they were penalized, then is it reasonable that they’re not getting rewarded now?” Guest asked. The companies, he said, are “not obligated to give refunds or reduce prices, but doing so could certainly build goodwill with customers.”

https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.title: Chicago Is $55 Billion in Debt, With No End in Sight. It’s a Threat to City Services.
https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.author: Heather Cherone, Jared Rutecki, Vernal Coleman
https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.text:
Reporting Highlights
- Crushing Debt: Chicago’s mismanagement of pensions and heavy reliance on borrowing over decades have created an unrelenting financial burden.
- Vicious Cycle: To solve its annual budget crunch, more borrowing is used to fill in holes, including back pay for firefighters and payouts for police misconduct.
- Strained Services: Solutions to crises involving public health lack the funding that can improve the lives of Chicagoans, and basic inspections for sidewalks and restaurants fall short.
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
When the city of Chicago eventually finishes its spending plan for 2027, $3.9 billion will come right off the top.
Taxpayers will have nothing to show for it. Not a single cent of that money will be used to fill a pothole, pick up a can of garbage, pay a firefighter to respond to an emergency or address lead poisoning in children.
Strapped into a straitjacket made up of the city’s debt, there is nothing Chicago’s mayor or City Council can do about it, forced to spend billions every year simply to stay current on the $55 billion it owes to banks and its pension funds.
No other big city will pay more toward its debt this year or next, according to an analysis by WTTW News and ProPublica. This year, $3.6 billion out of a $16.6 billion budget was consumed by debt.
New York City, with a population three times the size of Chicago’s and a budget more than seven times as big, has $47 billion in debt backed by tax revenues. Los Angeles, which has approximately 1 million more residents than Chicago but a smaller budget, has $1 billion in debt set to be paid back with taxes, records show.
According to all four of the major Wall Street credit-rating agencies, New York’s and Los Angeles’ fiscal health make them much better choices for investors. Chicago’s history of questionable borrowing and budgeting — it chose to either ignore or short its pension payments for years — has undermined its credibility.
Its credit rating now sits just two or three levels above junk status, making the cost of borrowing even more onerous. And the city’s chief financial officer, tasked with managing city debt and relationships with credit agencies, resigned last week in stunning fashion, saying she no longer could continue in the role because it would compromise her “integrity and professional obligations.” She had come from Fitch Ratings, a credit agency, and had been on the job for only three months.
Chicago’s Pension Systems Are Less than 50% Funded
The city is an outlier among other large cities, where most pensions are at least 75% funded.
Options for a financial rescue are limited or unpalatable. Pension obligations, locked in by law and political realities, remain untouchable. There is little public or political appetite to raise property taxes or cut city jobs, particularly among the ranks of police, the city’s largest workforce. A windfall from the city’s still-under-construction casino grows more unlikely than ever.
The office of Mayor Brandon Johnson, who is finishing up his first term in office, blames “reckless financing methods” from past administrations for the city’s financial bind.
“Savings and efficiencies alone cannot solve the city’s persistent structural gap,” the city’s Office of Budget and Management wrote to WTTW and ProPublica in response to questions for this story. In searching for revenue streams, Johnson has sought to impose new taxes on the city’s biggest corporations — an effort that has met stiff resistance.
Tackling the pension crisis, the city since 2023 has paid an additional $1 billion into its four pension funds above what is required by state law, records show, an infusion that the city touts as a stabilizing force.
But, like his predecessors, Johnson continues to rely on borrowing. Since taking office in 2023, Johnson has added $1.9 billion to the city’s debt obligations, according to city data.
That borrowing has “advanced desperately needed investment in economic development and affordable housing in historically underserved communities on the South and West sides,” according to Johnson’s spokesperson.
It also has been used to keep the city functioning. In 2026, for example, Chicago borrowed $166 million to pay firefighters what they were owed for working without a contract — and annual raises — for four years. Officials acknowledged they failed to set enough cash aside annually to cover those widely anticipated costs. The city borrowed an additional $267 million to cover the soaring cost of lawsuits alleging Chicago police officers committed a wide range of misconduct.
In some cases, the Johnson administration has negotiated agreements with its lenders that allow the city to pay only interest for several years, backloading its debt burden.
Chicago’s Debt Payments Were the Largest Category of the City’s Budget in 2026
With so much of the city budget dedicated to debt and pensions — and more cordoned off by federal and state laws that mandate spending for specific purposes, such as transportation — Chicago officials get to decide how to spend just one-third of its annual budget, records show.
The result for residents: Restaurant inspections are lagging. Complaints about crumbling sidewalks and injuries from those hazards pile up, without timely repairs. The city’s Public Health Department doesn’t have enough caseworkers to handle the intensive intervention needed for children suffering from lead poisoning.
The budget pressures are unrelenting. In August, Johnson announced another borrowing plan to fix a budget shortfall that emerged midyear. He blamed the City Council for overestimating the impact of new revenue streams while his council foes accused him of continuing a pattern of questionable borrowing habits.
Amid the finger-pointing, Johnson acknowledged the bind facing his administration and the city as a whole. “We cannot continue to budget by searching for loose change in the couch,” he said.
Watching the annual struggles of city officials to climb out of its money pit leaves many residents feeling more than a little uneasy about what comes next.
“It is the feeling that people get when they max out their credit card and they’re barely paying the minimum,” said Alderperson Andre Vasquez, who represents the 40th Ward and speaks often of growing up in a family that struggled to pay the rent every month. “You’re behind on your utilities. So you get mail every month, letting you know you’re behind.
“And at some point, you’re not even gonna open the envelope anymore, because the feeling of dread, even trying to see it, is a challenging one. That’s how people in Chicago feel.”
Unhealthy Fallout
When Johnson ran for mayor in 2023, he repeatedly emphasized his commitment to invest in the city’s neighborhoods in order to build a healthier city. Central to his message was a pledge to reopen six mental health clinics closed by former Mayor Rahm Emanuel when he faced his own budget pressures in 2011.
Those closures fueled a terrible cycle, Johnson has said. Chicagoans in desperate need of counseling and medication instead found themselves in crisis, forced to call 911 for help or struggle alone.
But during Johnson’s time in office, the city has reopened just two clinics. The city’s lack of capacity has forced nonprofit organizations to pick up the slack, despite their own funding woes and staffing challenges.
Johnson, who has touted his record of investing in “historically underserved communities,” is promising to open another clinic in 2027. But fulfilling that promise hinges on the outcome of a court fight over whether Chicago can levy taxes on social media companies like Facebook and YouTube.
“The need is big and growing,” said Mark Ishaug, CEO of Thresholds, a nonprofit group that specializes in community care. “We don’t have enough money, and what we do have is being threatened.”
Hemmed in by the city’s budget, Johnson has worked to expand mental health services outside the traditional clinic setting by offering counseling at libraries across the city several times a week and launching a “street psychiatry” program focused on unhoused Chicagoans.
Chicago’s wide range of public health needs often have solutions that require money the city lacks.
In recent years, for example, the Public Health Department’s food safety programs have been “not in substantial compliance,” according to a 2025 state audit. The department has had to prioritize restaurants and other eateries that are considered high risk while lower-risk establishments are inspected less frequently. But even that effort falls short. State law requires three inspections a year for high-priority eateries, yet that happens at only 15% of those, records show.
Inspections also were at the center of a 2023 City Council proposal to prevent lead poisoning, especially among the city’s vulnerable children living in aging or neglected housing. More than 600,000 houses and apartments, the majority of the city’s homes, were built before 1978, when lead paint was banned by the federal government. Lead paint poses a hazard in 99% of homes built before 1978, officials have said.
One solution suggested by an alderperson would’ve mandated that the city inspect every Chicago home or apartment every five years for lead paint and other health hazards. But the proposal would have required the Public Health Department to hire 600 new inspectors, more than doubling its total workforce — and its budget. Ultimately, not a single hearing was held on the idea.
This March, the issue came up again, when the City Council created a working group to develop a plan to proactively inspect all Chicago homes offered for rent. The first step would be a study and recommendations within six months. But that deadline passed without any public progress, despite several community meetings.
The department’s current efforts to address child lead poisoning underscore the impact of budget pressures.
The department receives more than 1,000 notifications each year about children with lead poisoning. Each report kicks off a complicated remediation process, involving multiple city departments, designed to identify and remove the lead source from the child’s home. Health department nurses work with the families to monitor their children’s health and assess whether the city’s abatement efforts are working.
Public health records provide a snapshot of workloads for caseworkers during the first quarter of the year, with several handling more than 200 cases at a time. “Concerns remain for case managers with persistently high caseloads,” wrote a supervising nurse in an April email to department leaders.
A department spokesperson said it reaches out to all families in these situations, “providing at minimum direct outreach and educational materials.” More than 96% of families that are contacted get a home visit from department staff. The spokesperson did not say what percentage of families the city is able to reach.
In the coming months, Public Health will have to do even more with its limited budget. The state of Illinois has lowered the threshold for elevated levels of lead in the blood, which will lead to increases in positive tests.
Coupled with the city’s efforts to expand blood tests for children in areas on the South and West sides, even more families are expected to enter the queue for case management.
Patchwork Solutions
Felicia Nalls-Bradley just wanted to get to work. It was her first week on the job.
But she tripped over an uneven sidewalk on the South Side in 2022. As she fell, she struck a fence and suffered injuries to her head, neck, shoulders, hands and back that required surgery and almost a week in the hospital. Records describe the path as “unreasonably hazardous,” with a 2-inch difference in elevation between two portions of the walkway.
She sued the city for negligence and settled for $400,000 last year. It was one of more than 350 sidewalk-related cases the city has settled since 2010, records show. The city has paid at least $16.1 million to resolve such claims during that period.
Records and deposition testimony from those cases describe a largely reactive maintenance system that relies heavily on residents to report problems.
A city engineer testified in a sidewalk-injury deposition in 2024 that Chicago does not routinely inspect its sidewalks. He also said that employees investigating a complaint are not expected to identify other hazards nearby.
In separate testimony in 2017, another engineer said the city responded to about 13,000 sidewalk maintenance requests annually but had only a handful of crews rotating across Chicago to make repairs.
The engineer’s testimony in another case contrasted his professional desires with the limitations of his resources. “In a perfect world I would like to do that, yes,” he said about inspecting every sidewalk complaint.
He then added a caveat: “This is the real world.”
Injuries — and lawsuits — are not the only consequence of poor sidewalk maintenance. Iliana Haven, who uses a power wheelchair and scooter because of a neuromuscular condition, said they regularly encounter obstacles as they struggle to get around.
A thwarted trip to the Puerto Rican People’s Day Parade exemplified their problems as they encountered broken and uneven sidewalks on their scooter. After being unable to find a passable route, Haven called family for help.
It took about 30 minutes for relatives to find Haven. Family members returned home to get a motorized wheelchair, which could more easily carry Haven to the event. But it had nearly concluded by the time everybody got through the entrance gate. Haven appreciated the help and took it with good humor, but the ordeal highlighted a lesson.
“It is a rule of mine to never leave anywhere by myself if I can help it,” Haven said.
They also understand the frustration of others challenged by sidewalks. The lack of access impacts businesses in the end, they said.
“There’s a huge number of disabled people in the city of Chicago. We would love to go and spend our money,” Haven said. “We can only do that if we can leave our house.”
The Debt Burden
After declaring that he would run again for mayor in next year’s election, Johnson gathered the media in early October to tout what his administration called a success story, a concrete example of his commitment to building up neglected areas of the city.
Under bright skies, he cut the ribbon on seven new two-flats in North Lawndale, a West Side neighborhood that has seen its population dwindle and its crime rate remain stubbornly high. The only way to reverse those entrenched trends, he said, is to create safe, affordable new homes that will allow Chicagoans to “put down roots and build wealth.”
The homes were built on city-owned vacant land; they also were built on more city debt. The Johnson administration used $5.4 million from the $1.25 billion Johnson borrowed in 2025 to fund housing and economic development projects across the city.
The debate over that borrowing crystalized Chicago’s current governing dilemma: Should it reduce its dependence on debt or address crucial needs for Chicagoans? And is it possible to do both?
Some alderpersons warned the city could not afford to borrow another $1.25 billion and questioned the wisdom of a payment schedule that avoids paying any principal until 2028. If that debt is not retired until 2055, as scheduled, taxpayers will have paid more than $98.9 million in interest costs alone, records show.
That borrowing is at the heart of Johnson’s attempt to expand the city’s economic capacity and invest in neighborhoods that have long been ignored by City Hall. His administration defends the borrowing by saying there is a plan to pay it back with a new approach that doesn’t affect taxpayers. Nearly four dozen tax-increment financing districts are set to expire by 2039, allowing more than $2 billion to flow back to the city, Chicago Public Schools and other taxing districts in coming years, records show.
Some alderpersons remain skeptical of Johnson’s budget strategy, and his overall financial stewardship was dealt a significant setback when Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch resigned Friday. She described a deep rift with the administration over how to portray the city’s finances.
“The Chief Financial Officer’s statements about the City’s finances are relied upon by investors, rating agencies, City Council, and taxpayers, and they must be complete and accurate,” she wrote to Johnson. “I am not able to fulfill those obligations under the conditions in which I have been asked to serve.”
The city responded by criticizing her job performance, saying she had been “largely absent” as Johnson’s team worked on its 2027 budget.
In the aftermath, alderpersons are seeking an audit of city finances. A majority already have been sparring with Johnson over borrowing.
They moved in September to make it harder to take on new debt by requiring the votes of at least 30 alderpersons, not just a simple majority from the panel of 50. Johnson blasted that change, saying it would stop investment flowing to neighborhoods like North Lawndale, and vetoed it.
Justin Marlowe, a professor at the University of Chicago Harris School of Public Policy and the director of the Center for Municipal Finance, said Johnson faces hard choices as he tries to implement his agenda.
“I give the mayor credit for having aspirations to make housing more affordable and to expand behavioral and mental health care,” Marlowe said. “These are all noble goals. But the city can’t afford it.”
Less than two weeks later, Johnson was back at City Hall, giving his 2027 budget address and outlining his plans to fill yet another large gap. Among his solutions again was a corporate tax, which once again was deemed dead-on-arrival by key alderpersons. But the City Council may have no choice but to go along with Johnson’s plan for more borrowing.
He proposed borrowing $481 million in 2027 to cover the cost of resolving lawsuits alleging that police misconduct led to wrongful convictions and deadly pursuits. If approved by the council, it would mark the second straight year that the city has borrowed to cover its bills, a move that financial experts consider a sign of worsening financial distress.
Marlowe said the city has no choice but to borrow to cover those costs, calling it the “least bad option” available to the city.
But Joseph Ferguson, who heads the Civic Federation, a nonpartisan budget watchdog group, was unimpressed by Johnson’s presentation. He’s seen a pattern over decades in which city officials plan to make it through the next election cycle or the next budget fight without looking toward lasting solutions.
Johnson’s plan, Ferguson said, shifts costs onto future taxpayers and only manages to “dig the city deeper into a financial hole.”
