https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Jared Abbott, Frederick DeVeaux
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Democrats Finally Ran as Economic Populists—Thanks to Newcomers
We analyzed 16 years of Democratic campaigns. The 2026 surge in attacks on billionaires and corruption came from newcomers, not party leaders, and they’re about to remake the caucus.
Ten years after Bernie Sanders’s first presidential run, the left’s argument that economic populism is the way to win back working-class voters has gone mainstream. Within days of the November 3 midterms, a consensus had formed that economic populism was why Democrats won. “The simplest summary,” the New York Times editorial board wrote on November 9, “is that they ran as economic populists and cultural moderates.” The board granted that Trump’s unpopularity was “the main engine” of Democrats’ victories, but in the Times’ telling it was the populist message that allowed Democrats in places like Kansas and Texas to “persuade many voters who previously considered their party unacceptable,” which made their campaigns “a road map” for Democrats.
Along similar lines, Data for Progress titled its postelection memo “How Democrats Rode Economic Populism to Landslide Victory,” concluding that “candidates who ran on bold, economic populist agendas won competitive races.” Senator Elizabeth Warren wrote in Time that Democrats won as “populist economic fighters” who called out the corrupt politicians and corporate interests that had rigged the system.
At the Center for Working-Class Politics, we have spent years urging Democrats to make exactly this turn toward economic populism, ideally delivered by working-class candidates. Economic populism starts with basic economic concerns like affordability, but it does not stop there. It also speaks to the sense that government serves a wealthy few rather than ordinary people. By blaming economic elites and the politicians who serve them, economic populism connects pocketbook concerns with anger about corruption and political unresponsiveness, and promises to take them on.
A 2021 survey we conducted found that economically populist messages did better with working-class voters than the Democratic establishment’s usual fare, and a 2023 follow-up found that “economic populism can help progressives win more working-class voters,” including in Trump country. After the 2024 election, we argued that Kamala Harris had turned away from economic populism to her peril. Last fall, our survey of voters in four Rust Belt states found that economic populism had broad appeal, especially when it named corporate greed and mass layoffs. And this year, an enormous survey experiment we conducted found that Democrats who placed themselves on the side of working people and took on corporate and political elites won more working-class support than Democrats who stuck to more traditional Democratic messaging.
But is it really true that Democrats of all stripes at last took our advice and turned to economic populism in 2026? And if they did, was it incumbents who changed their tune, or a new wave of challengers committed to a break with the party’s past messaging failures? To find out, we measured the populist content of Democratic campaigns going back to 2010.
What we found runs against much of the postelection conventional wisdom. Democrats really did run as economic populists in 2026, a major shift from previous years. But that shift came largely from a new class of candidates, not from incumbents or party leaders like Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer, whom the Washington Monthly’s Bill Scher credited with “colossal midterm victories.”
Still, it is much harder to say how much economic populism helped Democrats win in a year when all Democratic candidates rode the same wave. Candidates who ran more populist campaigns do not appear to have performed better than those who ran less populist ones. If economic populism mattered electorally, beyond what might mostly have been a national backlash against Trump, it may have worked by shifting the party’s brand as a whole rather than by boosting individual candidates. What is clear is that the candidates driving this populist shift were disproportionately newcomers, including many who won and will now pull the Democratic caucus in a direction that sounds much more like Bernie Sanders than like Chuck Schumer.
Democrats Turned Up the Economic Populist Dial Dramatically in 2026
To see just how differently Democrats campaigned in 2026 compared with past cycles, we scraped and analyzed the campaign websites of more than 6,000 Democratic candidates who ran for Congress between 2010 and 2026. Campaign websites are one place where nearly every candidate lays out what they stand for in their own words, which lets us compare the whole field of Democratic candidates from one cycle to the next.
The chart below shows a striking shift from 2024 to 2026. The share of Democrats who mentioned billionaires more than tripled, from 12 percent to 40 percent. Mentions of corruption rose from 18 to 39 percent, corporate PACs from 10 to 25 percent, monopolies from 6 to 19 percent, and working people and families from 43 to 68 percent. Democrats also talked much more about affordability, tariffs, Medicaid, and other economic issues, while abortion, climate change, and several cultural issues appeared less often.
But more talk about the economy does not necessarily mean more economic populism. Economic populist messages also blame economic elites for making ordinary people’s lives harder. So we built a model to identify anti-elite sentences that specifically blamed economic elites, rather than simply attacking Trump or Republicans.
That measure shows an even clearer break in 2026, as well as which candidates drove the surge in economic populism. Among Democrats who won House and Senate seats, newcomers used about 93 anti-elite sentences per 1,000 sentences on their campaign websites, compared with about 36 for incumbents. Incumbents changed relatively little. The big jump came almost entirely from candidates who were not already in office.
Breaking the pattern down by issue tells the same story. Among Democrats elected in 2026, newcomers were much more likely than incumbents to talk about billionaires, corruption, working people, large corporations, corporate PACs, monopolies, wealthy donors, and corporate greed. This difference appears on almost every economic populist theme we measured.
The sharpest populist shift came from newcomers. Sitting Democrats did not suddenly remake themselves in the image of Sanders. Instead, a new class of Democrats brought a much more anti-elite message with them and will now make up a substantial part of the Democratic congressional caucus.
To be clear, campaign websites do not capture everything candidates do or say, and candidates may strategically emphasize certain issues or types of language on websites that they wouldn’t foreground in higher-stakes settings like paid media. So we also collected a much broader set of campaign materials for the 56 Democrats in the most competitive House and Senate races, including ads, debates, press releases, and social-media posts.
In that fuller record, anti-elite rhetoric was widespread: Virtually every candidate used economic populist language at least to some degree; 43 percent of the roughly 400 ads we analyzed attacked economic elites specifically, and at least 44 of the 56 candidates ran at least one ad attacking elites of one kind or another. The populist turn was broader than the website data alone suggest. But the websites still show who leaned into it most heavily and made it central to their campaigns: overwhelmingly, the newcomers.
The Most Populist Candidates Did No Better Than Other Democrats
A thornier question, however, is whether individual candidates were rewarded for leaning furthest into economic populism. Much of the postelection commentary assumes they were. The Times editorial board held up candidates like Josh Turek, who won Iowa’s open Senate seat as a self-described “common-sense prairie populist,” and Bobby Pulido, who flipped Texas’s 15th Congressional District after telling voters that “the people in office have sold us out,” as models for the party. Data for Progress went further, concluding in its postelection memo that candidates with bold economic populist agendas had won competitive races.
That is a much harder claim to test. Congressional races differ in all kinds of ways, and in 2026 Democrats everywhere benefited from the same national swing. So we cannot cleanly say how much any one message caused a candidate to do better. But we can ask a simpler question: Did the Democrats who leaned hardest into economic populism clearly outperform those who leaned into it less?
Our own research gave us reason to expect a mixed answer. In the large survey experiment we fielded this year, Democrats who put themselves on the side of ordinary people did better with working-class voters than Democrats who used conventional, technocratic language. But once they had done that, adding sharper attacks on economic elites barely pushed voters’ support up any further.
We see something similar in the election results. We sorted nearly all Democratic House and Senate nominees into thirds based on how much of their campaign website attacked economic elites. If turning up the populist dial gave candidates an extra boost, the most populist third should have gained more ground over Harris’s 2024 margin than the least populist third. They did not. All three groups ran about 14 to 15 points ahead of Harris, almost exactly the same improvement. Adjusting for incumbency gives the same result.
In the chart below, we also highlight candidates with working-class backgrounds, shown in green. Democrats elected more working-class candidates in 2026 than in any recent cycle, and our past research finds that working-class voters tend to prefer candidates with working-class backgrounds because they see them as more likely to understand voters’ everyday problems. But here too, there is no obvious electoral bonus. Working-class candidates, while running more economic populist campaigns than the typical Democrat, performed neither better nor worse than expected.
We then looked more closely at the 56 most competitive House and Senate races, where we had much richer data. Here we could also compare each result with what a typical Democrat would have been expected to do in the same race, given the district, incumbency, and the national political environment.
Again, there was essentially no relationship between how populist a candidate sounded and how far they ran ahead of or behind expectations. Our sentence-level measures of anti-elite rhetoric told the same story. Some of the biggest over-performers, including Henry Cuellar in South Texas, were among the least populist candidates in the group, while some of the most populist ran behind expectations.
None of this shows that economic populism hurt Democrats, or even that it did not help them. The comparisons are too noisy for that. But they do show that the candidates who leaned into economic populism most heavily did not clearly separate themselves from the rest of the Democratic field. Whatever economic populism did for Democrats in 2026, it does not look like individual candidates could simply ratchet up their economic populist messaging to win more votes.
Voters Knew Which Candidates Were Working-Class Populists, but Partisanship Drove Their Support
If voters had never noticed which candidates were running as economic populists, it would be no surprise that the populists did no better than other candidates. But our tracker surveys show that many voters did notice.
To see this up close, we tracked four races through the fall with The Nation and the polling firm Nira Data, interviewing likely voters each month from August through October. Dan Osborn, an independent running for Senate in Nebraska, Brian Poindexter in Ohio, Bob Brooks in Pennsylvania, and Rebecca Cooke in Wisconsin were chosen because each candidate paired a working-class biography with a campaign built around economic populism. We asked voters whether each candidate was more or less on the side of working people, and of corporations and the wealthy, than most Democrats, and what kind of work they had done before politics.
We found that the candidates’ populist messages and their working-class biographies both registered with the electorate: Voters were much more likely to say each candidate was more on the side of working people than most Democrats and less on the side of corporations and the wealthy.
Many voters also recognized the candidates’ working-class backgrounds, though far from all did. In Nebraska, 58 percent said Osborn had done working-class work before politics, compared with 7 percent for Republican Pete Ricketts, and Brooks and Poindexter opened smaller but still sizable gaps over their opponents. The exception was Wisconsin, where Republican Derrick Van Orden, a retired Navy SEAL, was about as likely as Cooke to be seen as working class.
Yet when we asked voters in their own words what they liked or disliked about these candidates, few talked about economic populism or working-class backgrounds. Across the four races, 35 percent mentioned the candidate’s party, Trump, or the Republican opponent, compared with 18 percent who mentioned the candidate’s background or economic populist messaging.
So these candidates’ economic populist messaging did reach voters; many saw these candidates as more pro-worker, less corporate, and more working-class than the typical Democrat. But those perceptions rarely seemed to be the driving force behind voters’ support for candidates. Party labels, Trump, and the candidates’ Republican opponents mattered more.
These results fit a broader story about the election. Trump was deeply unpopular, and much of the Democratic wave was plainly a backlash against him and the Republican Party. CNN’s postelection analysis found that more than three-quarters of voters who backed Harris in 2024 said they used their House vote to express opposition to Trump, while only about a third of Trump’s own 2024 voters said they used their 2026 vote to show support for the president.
When the national political environment is so strongly tilted against the party in power, there is less room for differences between individual Democratic candidates to matter. So the fact that the most populist candidates did not clearly outperform the rest does not mean economic populism was irrelevant. It may simply mean that, in 2026, voters were responding more to the parties as a whole than to which Democrats leaned the hardest into economic populist messaging.
Economic Populism Won Inside the Democratic Party
While it is hard to say how much economic populism helped Democrats win in 2026, it clearly changed the Democratic Party itself.

Voters seem to have noticed the shift at the party level. In Data for Progress’s survey of likely voters in the last days of the campaign, the populist lines Democrats used reached far more voters than their moderate ones, and they did so across party lines.
Seventy-eight percent said they had heard Democratic candidates say billionaires and the wealthy should pay more in taxes, and 71 percent had heard them say big corporations were raising prices to boost their profits. Fewer than half had heard Democrats call for an all-of-the-above energy policy (49 percent) or talk about securing the border (42 percent), and only 37 percent remembered hearing Democratic candidates promise to work with Republicans.
And the messaging shift voters heard showed up in whom Democrats sent to Congress. The chart below compares the Democrats serving in Congress after the 2016 and 2026 elections. In 2016, only about 10 percent had mentioned billionaires in their campaigns. Sanders was one of them. By 2026, that share had tripled to 33 percent, with newcomers accounting for much of the growth. Attacking billionaires and corporate power once marked a Democrat as a Sanders insurgent. In 2026, it was something Roy Cooper’s, Chris Pappas’s, and Josh Turek’s campaigns had in common with Dan Osborn’s.
Moving economic populism to the center of the Democratic Party did not happen by accident. Sanders and the movement around him spent years pushing Democrats toward economic populism, as did researchers and organizations like ours. The evidence from 2026 suggests that this effort succeeded in changing how much of the party talks and how Democrats are perceived by voters.
The Sanders wing is no longer a lonely corner of the Democratic Party. It is growing. Many of its newest candidates are winning, and its language is increasingly the party’s language. The next question is what Democrats do with that victory.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Frieze Abu Dhabi’s Global Futures section to reflect the 'turbulence and violence of our times'
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Razmig Bedirian
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Abdullah Al Saadi devises an alphabet from sweet potatoes; Ala Younis’s mosaics make monuments from old, nondescript buildings; Mohammed Joha assembles cardboard and textiles as collages addressing displacement.
Disparate as these works seem, they are being shown in dialogue with one another in the Global Futures section at Frieze Abu Dhabi, where they will be presented as unique systems of knowledge that preserve memory and lived experience.
Curated by Tarini Malik, the section features solo presentations by artists from a range of artistic and cultural backgrounds. In some ways, the section builds upon conversations from other parts of the fair. Frieze Masters Abu Dhabi, for instance, will investigate historic routes of migration, trade and cultural exchange across the Indian Ocean. Global Futures appears to attempt this within a contemporary context.
Organic process
“The process of putting together Global Futures actually came together quite beautifully and organically,” Malik says. “We started with a number of proposals, looking at projects that felt so apt to this moment. We thought about what it means to have a fair, what it means to have this international constellation of galleries at this moment in Abu Dhabi. What are the conversations happening within the cultural sphere that are prevalent to this moment?”
With Taymour Grahne Projects, the Kuwaiti artist Ala Younis will present 11 works from her Climate Conditions series. The mosaic panels, crafted out of hand-cut stones and mounted on metal frames, depict old office buildings, municipal structures and other places in Abu Dhabi that are often overlooked. Younis first unveiled the series in her 2025 solo exhibition at the NYU Abu Dhabi Art Gallery. The project materialised after a three-year stay in the Emirati capital. Knowing the city’s propensity for rapid change, she sought to document and commemorate the structures as she saw them. In rendering their likeness in mosaics, Younis alludes to the Roman tiles that have outlasted the structures they once decorated. The title of the project refers to how the structures interact with the environment—their wood and metal bits expanding and contracting to changes in humidity and temperature.
The Mexican artist Tania Candiani, on the other hand, looks underground for a more sprawling and rhizomatic type of structure. Her Root Systems, presented by Galeria Vermelho, charts networks of plant roots in embroidery, unearthing a subterranean language with its own systems of exchange and communication.
Complementary projects
“These projects established two very different but sort of complementary points of departure,” Malik says. “They look at these ideas of migration, of ecology, of transformation—shared across different temporalities and across different structures.”
These themes, Malik says, resonate across the other presentations in Global Futures.
Through his Naked Sweet Potato series, Abdullah Al Saadi transcribes his personal engagement with the landscape of his native Khor Fakkan. Studying the different shapes and textures of sweet potatoes, the Emirati artist renders a language from the vegetable. He makes jewellery from it and he uses it to revisit his childhood, to transcribe his excursions to the UAE countryside. Where Candiani lays bare the universal language of roots, Al Saadi’s Naked Sweet Potato introduces an idiosyncratic and deeply personal lexicon to the conversation. The series includes drawings, paintings, sculptures and engravings, as well as collected materials. First shown at the UAE National Pavilion during the 2011 edition of the Venice Biennale, Naked Sweet Potato will be presented at Global Futures by Aisha Alabbar Gallery.
Reconstruction from ruin
With Zawyeh Gallery, the Palestinian artist Mohammed Joha will exhibit No Shelter, building upon the series he is presenting at this year’s Venice Biennale (until 22 November). His canvases feature stratified layers of discarded textiles, paper and cardboard that come together as vibrant, abstracted landscapes.
The artist, who is based in France, began the series as he watched the destruction of his native Gaza from afar. His work comes as a poignant expression of heartache, the shredded materials evoking the devastation of Gaza and the forced displacement of its population. The way they come together in colourful compositions, however, simultaneously stands up against the violence, insisting on reconstruction in the face of ruin.
“I looked at projects that reflected the turbulence of our times, the violence of our times,” Malik says. “Things can feel unsettled and art opens up a dialogue for us to understand one another.”
The Indian-born artist Arshi Irshad Ahmadzai, showing at Global Futures with the Mumbai-based gallery Chatterjee & Lal, will be showing her series Azal se Abad tak, which includes drawings and paintings on cloth. The works investigate how different cultures have articulated the concept of eternity.
The Ghanaian artist Godfried Donkor will present paintings, collages and embroidery with Gallery 1957. He draws from an eclectic range of inspirations for his works, including comic book superheroes, boxing athletes as well as mythological figures.
Post-conflict narratives
Finally, Marfa’ Projects will exhibit works by the Lebanese artist Seta Manoukian. A celebrated figure of the late 1960s Beirut art scene, Manoukian’s paintings are a stunning, often otherwordly depiction of life during the Lebanese Civil War. The works Manoukian produced after emigrating to Los Angeles in the late 1980s can be regarded as attempts at establishing stability and certainty in the aftermath of the conflict. These include works from her T-Shape series, which will be exhibited at the fair.
“We have work from her Rose series to her Rock series, as well as one of her early more figurative paintings,” Malik says. “In a constellation of around five or six works, we’re trying to build something that feels like a journey through the life of a really iconic artist.”
All in all, the Global Futures section, Malik says, seeks to draw connections between the exhibiting artists in a way that does not reduce the “specificity of where these artists are from and what they’re talking about”.
“I think we’ve chosen works together that really represent [a given] body of work by that artist in the best way possible,” Malik says. “It was really about building shared connections […] while also thinking about how they intersect in the UAE and in this rapidly transforming city.”
• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Sean Duffy and the Perils of Trump's Made-for-TV Cabinet
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: John Nichols
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Sean Duffy and the Perils of Trump’s Made-for-TV Cabinet
The secretary of transportation was a reality-TV “star” and a Fox Business cable host. But when the American aviation system was grounded, he lost it.
Twenty years ago, Sean Duffy was a washed-up reality-TV personality competing in lumberjack contests and making ends meet as a small-town district attorney in northern Wisconsin. Then, the 2010 Tea Party election wave swept him into Congress. But Duffy wasn’t exactly satisfied with the new gig. He grumbled about the pay—$174,000 annually—and, in 2019, he quit to become a lobbyist and the cohost of a cable show on the Fox Business channel.
This turned out to be an unexpectedly shrewd choice. Duffy was glib, good-looking, and on cable news, and that was enough to convince Donald Trump—who, as we all know, thinks that being glib, good-looking, and on cable news automatically qualifies you to run essential sections of the federal government—to nominate the Wisconsinite as the nation’s 20th secretary of transportation. Unfortunately, like so many of the score of Fox hosts who have gotten Trump administration gigs as cabinet secretaries, czars, ambassadors, and Justice Department hangers-on, Duffy was woefully unprepared to do the job.
That was abundantly clear last Friday, when Duffy was called upon to explain the FAA’s decision to bring the nation’s aviation system to a halt. In the same week that another Fox alum, “War Secretary” Pete Hegseth, narrowly escaped impeachment, Duffy was thrust into the limelight as a bumbling sidekick for Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, himself a former mixed martial arts prizefighter. At a moment of national anxiety, Duffy defaulted to the talking-head formula, which imagines that any crisis—no matter how serious—can be addressed with a word salad of implication, insinuation and invective.
Duffy’s performance was so miserable that it provoked an immediate demand for his removal from New York Governor Kathy Hochul, who called to mind the cabinet secretary’s former career as a “star” of MTV’s The Real World: Boston and his recently launched reality travel series The Great American Road Trip. “Through it all, he’s been more focused on starring in his own reality show than addressing the crisis at his agency,” said Hochul, adding, “From chronic air traffic controller shortages to repeated communications breakdowns, serious lapses in our aviation system have become a pattern on Sean Duffy’s watch.” Richard Clarke, a former counterterrorism official in Republican administrations, labeled Duffy and Mullin’s double act “perhaps the worst crisis communications press conference I’ve ever seen.”
Facing questions about whether the grounding of 14,000 flights and the disruption of travel plans for millions of Americans might have resulted from software problems, cyberattacks, or rogue AI agents, Mullin mused about how “you just can’t rule out anything at this point” and complimented his absent boss. “This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like,” he declared. “He puts leaders in place, and he allows them to lead.”
That pronouncement provoked major head-scratching when Mullin turned the microphone over to Duffy, whose performance reminded everyone that “the leadership of President Trump” involves installing Fox hosts in positions where they inevitably get in over their talking heads. In no time, they are mismanaging wars and national emergencies with the sort of deer-in-the-headlights desperation that inspires confusion rather than confidence.
On Friday, and then again in a follow-up press conference on Saturday, Duffy made excuses, muddled explanations, and griped about how he didn’t have enough money to do his job—even though he’s a Republican cabinet member in a Republican administration with perhaps the most subservient Republican Congress in US history at his disposal.
On this weekend’s Saturday Night Live, “Weekend Update” anchor Colin Jost reflected on how “the FAA suddenly and mysteriously grounded all US flights yesterday” and then—barely containing his laughter—explained, “The scary thing by far about all these flights getting grounded was the messaging from the normally dependable Trump administration. First, they said it was a telecommunications outage as of now. Why add ‘as of now’? No one wants to hear, ‘Your child is safe—as of now.’ Then Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said the whole situation was the result of a contractor upgrading copper wire to fiber optic cable. So, one guy switched out one wire and took out all planes? I think that’s literally a scene from the movie Airplane!”
Just as jarring was Duffy’s wild-eyed ranting about how Congress was not providing sufficient funding to upgrade communications systems and airports. During the Friday night press briefing, Duffy repeatedly demanded $50 billion in new money—even though he had a hard time explaining precisely what he’d done with the $12.5 billion his department got last year for air traffic control improvements, and even though Duffy had been asking just a day earlier for a mere $30.1 billion for aviation upgrades.
Instead of making a compelling case for necessary infrastructure investment, Duffy appeared to be grabbing numbers out of the sky. CNN headlined a report: “Messaging failures worsened the air traffic freeze and sowed distrust in government.” When Duffy attempted to hold another briefing on Saturday, microphone feedback created such a mess that the Irish Star newspaper declared, “Sean Duffy forced to halt ‘clown show’ press conference due to technical glitch.”
On a more serious note, newly elected US Representative Fred Wellman (D-MO) announced, “I’m calling for a full investigation of this failure and the resignation of Secretary Duffy. We will find out the damage that his incompetent leadership has done to our air traffic system. Instead of filming reality TV shows he should have been ensuring the safety of Americans.”
The calls for accountability will keep coming. No one seriously doubts that America has underfunded infrastructure projects that must be addressed—on the ground and in the air. But everyone who is serious about these issues is entertaining fresh doubts about whether Sean Duffy’s TV experience has prepared him for this reality.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: 'It is an unusual model, but I am an unusual person': Shafeena Yusuff Ali on her Abu Dhabi foundation and gallery
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Kabir Jhala
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
If the art world is an orchestra of players, Shafeena Yusuff Ali is attempting a one-woman band. Born in Abu Dhabi to the Keralan billionaire M.A. Yusuff Ali, whose Indian-Emirati conglomerate LuLu Group spans retail, hospitality and real estate, she considers among her roles: collector, dealer, art historian, writer, entrepreneur and adviser to corporate and private collections.
It was upon acquiring work for her family’s London hotel that Yusuff Ali began envisioning a career within art. A trio of successive master’s degrees in art history, business administration and social impact led her to establish Rizq Art Initiative in 2023, an Abu Dhabi-based organisation that includes a commercial gallery, an artist and curator residency, an education platform, an off-site exhibitions programme and an advisory. The organisation is presently in the process of separating into a for-profit commercial gallery and a non-profit foundation.
“It is an unusual model, but I think I am an unusual person,” she says. “Not
many gallerists have three postgraduate degrees, and carry both business and academic backgrounds. I understand how industries work and I have also written an art historical paper on each work in my collection”.
Rizq, which in Arabic means “provision” or “sustenance”, was established to kickstart a nascent scene by plugging overlooked gaps in the local art ecosystem. “The biggest challenge facing the Abu Dhabi art scene is a lack of nuanced peripheral actors,” Yusuff Ali says. “Critics, fabricators, experimental spaces, warehousing and storage. For an art ecosystem to work you need all these elements to work in coherence.”
Informed by Yusuff Ali’s ties to both India and the UAE, Rizq focuses on artists from the Global South, including young Emiratis Shamsa Almansoori and Reem Al Mubarak, and the Keralan watercolourist Anupama Alias Ani. Of just five commercial galleries in Abu Dhabi “we are the only one focusing on artists from the global majority”, she says.“This is important in a city where most inhabitants are from regions the art world doesn’t necessarily cater to.” During Frieze Abu Dhabi (18-22 November), the gallery is staging a solo show by Al Mubarak.
Beyond its Abu Dhabi gallery, Rizq also programmes offsite exhibitions, including a satellite show for the sixth edition of the Kochi Biennale in Kerala, contributing to a growing dialogue between the art worlds of South Asia and the Gulf.
Yussuf Ali's heritage also informs what she buys: areas of interest include lesser-known South Asian Modernists, such as the Keralan painter K.C.S. Paniker, as well as pioneering artists of the UAE like Hassan Sharif. Perhaps the artist whose work she has collected most widely is Vivek Vilasini, the only Indian member of the Flying House, a 2000s experimental art collective in Dubai that has hugely influenced today’s contemporary art scene in the UAE. “Vivek is a friend,” Yusuff Ali says. “It is remarkable that an Indian artist in the UAE has played such a central role in defining the nation’s art history.”
As for Abu Dhabi, Yusuff Ali believes in the long term, and understands that the local market is “only just beginning to grow”. Presently her private funds keep Rizq’s gallery afloat, but she is quick to point out that she speaks the language of business alongside art. “I have established a proof of concept and spent the past three years demonstrating measurable impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. “I am confident that the next time we speak, we will have brought enough patrons on board to become profitable.”
The Art Newspaper: What was the first work you bought?
Shafeena Yusuff Ali: The first significant work was a Mona Saudi sculpture, Mother and Child (1981), before she passed away. I bought it when I was pregnant—and at a generationally different price. When I was buying it I fully realised it was special.
And the most recent?
A painting by one of the forgotten masters of Kerala, N.K.P. Muthukoya.
If you could own any work from a museum what would it be?
I’d like to hang a work by Amrita Sher-Gil alongside one by Princess Fahrelnissa Zeid. My life bridges South Asia and the Middle East and these two women are strikingly similar in how they lived painful but luxurious lives.
Where do you like to eat in Abu Dhabi?
My favorite shawarma place is Al Akkawi.
What do you recommend doing outside the fair?
November is perfect biking weather. Walk around the city—don’t drive. And get a boat to one of the outer islands. They can be really magical.
What is your least favourite thing about art fairs?
Sometimes it gets too homogenous—the same seven galleries showing the same seven artists.
What should people know before coming to Frieze Abu Dhabi?
The culture here is quite shy, and highly relationship based. Newcomers might struggle if they lack patience.
• Frieze Abu Dhabi, Manarat Al Saadiyat, 19-22 November

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Parthenon’s east pediment, ‘the most famous image of antiquity’, recreated in Frankfurt exhibition
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Catherine Hickley
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Vinzenz Brinkmann’s quest to solve the mysteries of the destroyed east pediment of the Parthenon, which depicted the birth of Athena, dates back 40 years.
In 1986, he scaled ancient Greece’s most famous temple at night by rope to examine the base of the east pediment under special lamps that function only without ambient light, hoping to find traces left by 39 lost sculpted figures over the main gate.
“Nothing came of that,” says Brinkmann, who is now the head of antiquities at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt—except, he adds, rumours about ghosts on the Acropolis that flew around Athens.
But now, Brinkmann says his team has solved a riddle akin to “putting together a jigsaw puzzle without having all the pieces”. The results of decades of research will go on show in an exhibition, Athena, the Stage is Yours: the Parthenon Puzzle, opening at the Liebieghaus on 18 November.
Long a flashpoint in Greek-British relations, the politics of the Parthenon surfaced in the run-up to the opening. The exhibition was to include marble fragments from both the British Museum in London and the Acropolis Museum in Athens. But, as The Art Newspaper reported last month, the Greek government withdrew its loan of nine fragments: according to Greek media reports, the request was rejected by Greece’s Central Archaeological Council on the grounds that they would be shown alongside British Museum pieces removed from the Acropolis by Lord Elgin. The Greek ministry of culture’s press office did not respond to emailed requests for comment and confirmation.
Elgin Marbles row makes ripples
Greece has for decades demanded the return of the Parthenon Marbles taken by Elgin, which have been housed in the British Museum since 1817. The Liebieghaus has, however, secured a rare loan of two fragments from the British Museum. After the Greek government’s withdrawal, a British Museum spokesperson confirmed that the museum “will still be loaning”.
“The cancellation of the loans from Greece does not detract from the exhibition’s concept, or its scholarly significance,” declares Elisabeth Pallentin, a spokesperson for the Liebieghaus. “The exhibition is based primarily on new findings resulting from many years of research at the Liebieghaus.”
The east pediment is probably “the most famous image of antiquity”, Brinkmann says, with the centre of the sculpted ensemble composed of 3.5m-tall figures. The pediment was destroyed at some point between the fifth century AD and 1670—it is not known when or why, though there are plenty of theories—and 80% of it is still missing.
The rest is in fragments in museums around the world. Until now, no one had succeeded in fully reconstructing the central figures, Brinkmann says. “In the last 200 years, there have been a lot of proposals, but we saw that there were always gaps.”
The most serious work on the east pediment had been undertaken more than a century ago by a British Museum curator, Arthur Hamilton Smith, Brinkmann says. Smith partially recreated the east pediment using plaster casts from the British Museum and cooperated with colleagues in Athens to obtain more casts; his reconstruction went on display in the museum in 1908.
“He did a fantastic job in preparing the way,” Brinkmann says. “That was our basis.”
Although the Liebieghaus team recreated these fragments using scans and a 3D printer, the majority of the pediment was still missing. A breakthrough came when the team began investigating reliefs from the lids of Roman sarcophagi, which proved the key to unlocking the mystery.
“It was really a chance discovery,” Brinkmann says. “During a visit to the Hermitage in St Petersburg in 2014, we noticed a figural relief on the lid of a sarcophagus that was clearly closely related to the composition of the east pediment. It refers to the few surviving figures from the corners of the pediment, such as Helios and Selene with their chariots, but also to figures that have repeatedly been proposed as having belonged to the east pediment, such as the Horae/Moirai.”
They discovered nine sarcophagi in total with relevant reliefs. Most were in the Vatican Museums and elsewhere in Rome. “They had been overlooked,” Brinkmann says. “But the Romans copied everything the Greeks did.”
None of these reliefs showed the entire east pediment ensemble; each depicted a different subset of the 39 figures. But with the aid of computer technology, the team established that the remaining fragments of the east pediment and the depictions on the reliefs were a 100% match.
The team’s research has yielded some surprises. It was not previously known, for instance, that the Dioscuri, the twin horsemen known as Castor and Pollux to the Romans, were portrayed on the pediment. The figures served as models for the giant figures on the Quirinale in Rome, which are almost identical and date from antiquity, Brinkmann says. The twins are portrayed standing next to their bucking horses with anxious expressions, straining at the reins in an effort to control them.
This portrayal of the Dioscuri makes sense only in the context of the birth of the goddess, Brinkmann says. In mythology, Athena burst forth from her father Zeus’s forehead after he had swallowed her mother. Her birth is described in the Homeric hymns as causing Mount Olympus to shake, the earth to shriek, and the sea to swell and rage.
“The Dioscuri are heroic horsemen in mythology,” Brinkmann says. “They don’t lose control of their horses. But the birth of Athena was a primordial cosmic event that unleashed a natural disaster. What we see are the consequences.” Other figures in the recreated ensemble are also responding to the cataclysm: Hermes, for instance, is depicted holding onto his hat.
Brinkmann is known internationally for his research into polychromy in ancient Greek and Roman sculpture. An exhibition he curated, Gods in Color—Painted Sculpture of Classical Antiquity, has travelled the world, having been shown in several US locations, Athens, Oxford, Istanbul, the Vatican Museums and elsewhere.
It is possible that the new Liebieghaus exhibition will travel too, Brinkmann says. But not, it seems, with marbles from the Athens collections, with recent developments giving little room to hope that a lasting settlement between Greece and the British Museum is on the horizon.
• Athena, the Stage is Yours, Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection, Frankfurt, 18 November-25 July 2027

https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: Critical Condition: What Are We Doing About Nuclear War?
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: Matt Bivens
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
Critical Condition: What Are We Doing About Nuclear War?
Doctors are calling for verifiable, deadline-driven agreement to eliminate all nuclear weapons. The flourishing—and even the survival—of the human species is at stake.
What will it take to get us all to think in a new way?
Someone (the artistic wife of a Manhattan Project scientist, actually) came up with the idea for a clock, its hands ticking ever closer to that sinister midnight. Dentists collected more than 320,000 baby teeth to show how radioactive strontium-90 accumulated in the mouths of our children after all of the hydrogen bomb tests.
Moviemakers offered dramatizations. Think of actor John Lithgow in the closing moments of The Day After, broadcasting via shortwave radio from postapocalyptic Kansas City: “Hello? Is anybody there? Anybody at all?” Or actor Slim Pickens straddling a missile like a mechanical bull, waving his cowboy hat and whooping as he rides a nuke down to blow us all up.
Our most famous thinkers tried logic and eloquence. Physicist Albert Einstein, mathematician Bertrand Russell, chemist Linus Pauling, and other great minds begged us in a famous and beautiful letter: “Remember your humanity, and forget the rest.” It’s been an exhortation cited ever since, blazoned across T-shirts and saluted by a Nobel Prize. The Rev. Martin Luther King Jr., another giant of American moral life, repeatedly pointed out that the civil rights movement couldn’t succeed if the world were annihilated by nuclear war. “It is a wonderful thing to work to integrate lunch counters, public accommodations, and schools,” King observed. “But it would be rather absurd to work to get schools and lunch counters integrated and not be concerned with the survival of a world in which to integrate.”
Others buttressed logic and eloquence by sharing tragic personal experience. The child survivors of the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings, now all quite elderly, travel the world to testify about a horrible tragedy from the quaint old days, back when the world knew of only two small (15-kiloton) nuclear weapons. It can be startling to remember this: These weapons have only been around for less than a single human lifespan. We have very little actual experience with them.
More than 1 million people gathered in New York’s Central Park in 1982 to insist something be done, in the largest political demonstration in American history. Catholic popes repeatedly called for nuclear disarmament. Nuns and priests went to jail, often for years, for the crime of sneaking onto military bases and hammering symbolically upon the ICBMs there, as per Isaiah 2:4: “They shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.”
In fact, every major religion has condemned nuclear weapons. Of course they have; these weapons are utterly immoral.
Monks in traditional Buddhist robes once walked 1,600 miles across America to make this point, carrying burning embers lit by a fire associated with the Hiroshima bombing.
Quakers in the 1950s sailed into closed military zones to disrupt nuclear tests, and the Golden Rule Peace Boat sails again today for nuclear disarmament, thanks to a salvage and restoration by Veterans for Peace.
Muslim leaders who have publicly opposed nuclear weapons on moral grounds include Iran’s Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed at age 86 by the Trump administration. Khamenei was killed—alongside his daughter, his toddler granddaughter, and other family members—at the opening of a war the White House says is about preventing Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons.
How many ways can a message be shared?
Dramatic clocks, heroic sailboats, radioactive baby teeth, nuns going to jail for hammering on a missile, Buddhist monks walking hundreds of miles across America with fire from Hiroshima, the wisdom of Einstein and King and the child survivors of Nagasaki, a million people crowded into Central Park… How many different ways can the great danger to human survival be risen up against, revealed, explained?
To the long list of those efforts we can now add an editorial published this week simultaneously in more than 100 medical journals around the world, ranging from The Lancet and the British Medical Journal of the United Kingdom to the Nigerian Journal of Paediatrics and the Medical Journal of Australia. (Disclosure: I am one of the coauthors.)
From Switzerland to Nepal and from Croatia to Colombia, across general journals and specialty journals, the world’s physicians (and medical students, dentists, nurses, and even veterinarians) will share the same message with one another.
It will be published by and for the geriatricians of Germany in Zeitschrift für Gerontologie und Geriatrie; by and for the doctors of North Africa in La Tunisie Médicale; and by and for the medical educators of Central America in Revista Médica Hondureña. It will be offered in the British Journal of Cancer, the African Journal of Reproductive Health, the International Nursing Review, the Philippine Journal of Otolaryngology Head and Neck Surgery, and many other niche publications. Along the way, it has been actively supported by national medical societies, including those of France, Norway, Denmark, and others.
And it will be read. We know this from the two prior times (in 2023 and 2025) that International Physicians for the Prevention of Nuclear War has pulled off this feat of a simultaneous worldwide medical journal publication.
“As a project, this is not merely a broad communications effort, it is a real game-changer,” says editorial coauthor Chris Zielinski, a past president of the World Association of Medical Editors. “Normally, medical journals go to great lengths to ensure that the material they publish has not appeared in any other medical journals. The fear of plagiarism is extreme.”
But species-level threats to humanity have motivated scientific journal editors around the world to set aside business as usual. (There have also been simultaneous worldwide editorials in 2021, 2022, and 2023 about the dangers of climate change.)
“The international network has been used to raise information literacy in a way which is both refreshingly new, and yet extremely traditional,” Zielinski says. “There has never been anything remotely like it in the health sector—or, for that matter, in any other sector.”
Will it matter? Will it help?
It’s certainly not more eloquent than Russell-Einstein or Martin Luther King. Or the author Jonathan Schell, a former peace correspondent for The Nation, who in The Fate of the Earth warned how easy it is to slip into denial about the nuclear bomb—that “while it relentlessly came to threaten the existence of everything, it physically touched nothing, and thus left people free not to think about it.”
It was not unless one lifted one’s gaze from all the allegedly normal events occurring before one’s eyes and looked at the executioner’s sword hanging over everyone’s head that the normality was revealed as a sort of mass insanity. This was an insanity that consisted not in screaming and making a commotion but precisely in not doing these things in the face of overwhelming danger, as though everyone had been sedated.
Passengers on a ship who are eating, sunning themselves, playing shuffleboard, and engaging in all the usual shipboard activities appear perfectly normal as long as their ship is sailing safely in quiet seas, but these same passengers doing these same things appear deranged if in full view of them all their ship is caught in a vortex that may shortly drag it and them to destruction. Then their placidity has the appearance of an unnatural loss of normal human responses—of a pathetic and sickening acquiescence in their own slaughter.
No editorial published simultaneously in Farm Animal Health and Nutrition, the European Journal of Nuclear Medicine and Molecular Imaging, and Supportive Care in Cancer is going to rival that kind of passionate prose.
All we can do is lay out the scientific facts.
§ Nine nations hold more than 12,000 nuclear weapons—most of them so massive that a Hiroshima A-bomb is tiny in comparison (and in fact, a Hiroshima-sized bomb often literally acts as the blasting cap to detonate the larger bomb).
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
§ There are enough nuclear bombs to torch the cities, wreck the climate, and kill every human being many, many times over. (In fact, as recounted in The Nation not long ago, a “minor” nuclear war between far-off India and Pakistan would so disrupt world agriculture that, over the next two years, it could kill two out of three Americans. From hunger!)
§ Yet the plan is to keep these weapons on hair-trigger alert—ready for accidental or intentional launch in a matter of minutes—and to sink billions of dollars into building more.
§ All of the US-Russian arms control agreements have been rescinded or have expired. As the US, Russian, and Chinese presidents meet this week in China, Donald Trump says he wants to talk about a major new arms control agreement involving all three nations. But expectations for success are exceedingly low.
§ The majority—the majority!—of the world’s nations have voted emphatically to do away with these ridiculous and morally offensive explosive devices. The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons was passed easily by the United Nations and has been gathering ratification by national parliaments around the planet. That said, the ban treaty has been ignored by many nations, including every nuclear-armed nation: America, Russia, China, Israel, North Korea, Britain, France, India, and Pakistan.
Hello? Is anybody there? Anybody at all?

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: MCA Chicago receives gift of 65 works, most of them by women and artists of colour
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Ruth Lopez
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
A recent gift of 65 works to the Museum of Contemporary Art (MCA) Chicago honours the institution's upcoming 60th anniversary and its outgoing director, Madeleine Grynsztejn.
The philanthropists Jack and Sandy Guthman worked with the MCA’s curatorial team, poring through the couple’s extensive collection to choose the pieces. Grynsztejn got the selection down to 65, then hit a wall. Paring it down to 60, as originally intended, became an excruciating process. The Guthmans, champions of the MCA for decades, did not force the museum to choose just 60.
Grynsztejn considers this an extraordinary model for what can happen when a museum and philanthropists are in alignment. To date, the Guthmans have donated 130 works to the MCA—the largest donor gift in the museum’s history.
For Grynsztejn, building a great museum collection takes not only visionary leadership but visionary philanthropy. “The Guthmans have invested in Chicago artists, making their gift one that also has a civic impact,” she tells The Art Newspaper. Included in the gift is work by Amanda Williams, Dawoud Bey and Rashid Johnson.
The Guthmans have spent decades supporting Chicago’s civic and cultural institutions. As a real estate lawyer, Jack started out by providing pro bono services. Meanwhile, Sandy directed her family’s foundation Polk Bros. Jack was elected as a trustee of the MCA in 1989 and currently serves on its board. For the MCA’s 50th anniversary, the couple donated 50 photographs by women artists.
The current gift includes 23 pieces by artists of colour and 19 by women. Thirteen artists are new to the MCA’s collection, including Mohamed Bourouissa, James Casebere, Julia Fish, Christian Marclay, Adrian Paci, Elle Perez and Shinique Smith. Other gifts, like photographs by Bey, deepen the MCA’s holdings.
“In some cases, we are adding an entirely new collection,” Grynsztejn says, referring to Bey’s early photography in Harlem, “and in some cases, we are gaining an icon, as in Christopher Wool’s Untitled (1995-96).”
The MCA began as a kunsthalle in 1967. It started receiving gifts, so in 1974 it formalised its collection. Despite the fact that the very first piece to enter the MCA’s collection was by Marisol, it eventually began to reflect the usual gender and racial biases.
During her tenure, Grynsztejn has sought to change that by establishing the Women Artists Initiative, inspired by the experience of many colleagues who have found it more challenging to fundraise for exhibitions by women artists. The museum’s proof-of-concept came with the success of exhibitions by Faith Ringgold, followed by a traveling Yoko Ono retrospective. The MCA has added women artists to the collection at four times the national average. Recently, the initiative has been renamed the Madeleine Fund for Women Artists and now has a $5m endowment.
Since Grynsztejn’s arrival at the museum in 2008, the MCA’s collection has grown from approximately 1,300 to 3,800 works. At least half of the acquisitions under her leadership have been by women and artists of colour. “This is not woke or [diversity, equity and inclusion],” she says. “It’s good business and good culture. Because if you are a public trust, you are in service to your public.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Victoria Law
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
What Gavin Newsom’s Commutations Mean for the Future of the Death Penalty
Officials in some states continue to seek the death penalty while others, like Newsom, have vowed to bring the sentences to a halt.
June Oceans was returning to her dorm from a tutoring session when she learned she was no longer sentenced to execution.
“Congrats, did you hear?” the other woman asked. Oceans had no idea what she was talking about.
Her friend had been listening to the news at her prison job and heard that California Governor Gavin Newsom had commuted the sentences of every single person sentenced to death in the state.
“I was shocked,” Oceans, who had been sentenced to death in 1994, told The Nation. Watching the news later, she was filled with excitement. But it was a cautious excitement. “I needed to know some details before I could feel relief,” she added.
On November 5, two days after Election Day, Newsom commuted the sentences of the 548 people on death row to life without parole. Newsom’s action is the largest death sentence commutation in recent US history.
California has more people on death row than any other state. Its last execution was in 2006. In 2019, Newsom issued a moratorium on executions, stating that the death penalty is “unfair, unjust, wasteful, protracted and does not make our state safer.”
“I will not oversee execution of any person while Governor,” he stated in that executive order.
“Newsom’s decision is huge,” Sandra Babcock, founder of the Cornell Center on the Death Penalty Worldwide, told The Nation. “California was the behemoth of the death penalty because of the sheer number of people on death row.”
Under California law, the governor can unilaterally grant clemency to people with one felony conviction, which is 166 people on death row. The only requirement is notifying prosecutors and victims’ families.
For the other 382 people, who have a felony conviction unrelated to their death penalty case, they must wait for the California Supreme Court to rule on the governor’s mass clemency. “The court is not reviewing cases one by one,” clarified Natasha Minsker, director of the California Anti-Death Penalty Coalition, which had called on Newsom to grant this mass commutation. “The issue has been presented to the court as: Can the governor commute all death sentences because they are death sentences? Can he choose life over death in all cases at once? And that’s the question they’re going to answer.”
If the court does not approve the commutations before Newsom leaves office in January, they would expire, leaving the death sentences in place. But, notes Minsker, final briefs are due December 4, signaling that the court intends to resolve the issue before Newsom leaves office.
Before Newsom, the largest mass commutation happened in 2003 when the then–governor of Illinois, George Ryan, nullified death sentences for 167 people shortly before leaving office.
Newsom’s action doesn’t abolish the death penalty in the state. Only voters can do that via a ballot referendum, and they failed to do so in 2012 and again in 2016. Incoming Governor Xavier Becerra has vowed to continue the moratorium on executions.
Nonetheless, some prosecutors have pledged to continue seeking the death penalty. “I’m going to continue to seek it when appropriate,” Michael Hestrin, the Riverside County district attorney, told The New York Times. His county has sent more people to death row than any other in recent years, and its prosecutors are currently seeking capital punishment in 20 cases. In Kern County, 179 miles north, prosecutors are seeking the death penalty in 13 cases.
They are in the minority. Across California’s 58 counties, only 12 continue to pursue death sentences. “In California, the death penalty is dying on the vine,” said Minsker. “The vast majority of prosecutors understand this is a false promise and a waste of public safety resources.”
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
It seems to be dying nationwide as well. In 1991, a Gallup poll found that 76 percent of US adults were in favor of the death penalty. The next year, Bill Clinton made a point of leaving the presidential campaign trail to attend the execution of Ricky Rector, a man with mental disabilities so pronounced that he saved the dessert from his last meal “for later.” Two years later, in 1994, approval of the death penalty rose to 80 percent. Support has been waning ever since thanks to decades of organizing against the death penalty by advocates and family members of those behind bars. This past October, a Gallup poll conducted in the weeks after Christa Pike’s horrifically botched execution in Tennessee found that 49 percent of US adults were in favor, the first time approval has dipped below 50 percent since 1971.
Still, on the same day as Newsom’s announcement, Florida, Alabama and Indiana each executed a person via lethal injection. But, noted Babcock, only a small percentage of jurisdictions within death penalty states still seek executions. In Texas, for instance, only two of its 254 counties pursued a new death sentence in 2025.
“Newsom’s decision to commute death sentences is an incredibly important act of moral courage and leadership,” said Minsker. “He is showing leaders that we can have safety without sacrificing our shared humanity.”
Noting that California holds one-quarter of all death sentences in the country, she added, “For Governor Newsom to commute one-quarter of the death sentences, the largest death row in the Western Hemisphere, it’s the most significant blow to the death penalty in decades.”
She hopes that his action will push other governors to follow suit, such as Ohio’s Mike Dewine, who has publicly called for an end to the death penalty, or incoming Governor Amy Acton, who has vowed to continue Dewine’s moratorium.
Not only does Newsom’s action clear the way for them to do the same, but the sheer size of California’s death row means that mass commutations elsewhere will seem less extreme. For Ohio, that would mean 112 sentences, or for Pennsylvania that would mean 103 sentences, said Babcock, noting that any other mass commutation would be much smaller.
Oceans turns 58 next month. She was 25 years old when she was sentenced to death. During her years on death row, she was incarcerated in a men’s prison before her transition. There, she watched some of her peers, including those who mentored her, be taken away for execution.
“Shakespeare wrote, ‘When sorrows come, they come not by single spies, but in battalions,’” Oceans, now at the Central California Women’s Facility, reflected. “It’s a difficult situation to be isolated and realize that every good inspiration [including the men who befriended and mentored her] you ever had is no longer here. And then you have to wrestle with the reality that that is the exact process they [the state] intend[s] to exercise on me.”
For over a decade, Oceans was left in legal limbo after voters passed Proposition 66 in 2016. Intended to speed up legal proceedings before execution, it did the opposite: The new law required that state habeas cases (in which people who are incarcerated can challenge their sentence of execution) begin at the lower courts but did not provide a method to pay for counsel, leaving Oceans and many others without representation.
“Now everything seems bright,” she said.
