https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Do art fairs care about non-VIP visitors?
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Scott Reyburn
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
October’s Paris art week had become the must-attend fixture of the international art market calendar, particularly for wealthy Americans. No other city could match the range and quality of the French capital’s art fairs and exhibitions, both at public museums and private foundations. And what about all those charming restaurants, cafes and shops?
“It’s important to be in Paris,” said Chris Sharp, the Los Angeles gallerist and founder of Post-Fair, a boutique California-based event that held its first edition in the French capital this October. “Paris is the undisputed capital of the art world—once a year,” Sharp added, speaking at Post-Fair’s preview on 19 October, in the chic Marais district. Nearby, someone had sprayed “mort aux riches” across the window of a bank.
The previous weekend, Paris had been rocked by mass demonstrations that in some areas had escalated into riots and looting. Further demonstrations, highlighting the neglected state of France’s secondary schools, the ever-rising cost of living and other grievances, had been planned in Paris and other French cities on the afternoon of Saturday 24 October. Unemployment in France for those aged 15 to 24 currently stands at 21.5%, almost three times the rate in neighbouring Germany.
On Tuesday 20 October, the day of the ultra-exclusive Avant-Première pre-preview of Art Basel Paris in the Grand Palais, the French activist collective Pillage de Classe (class plunder) posted a message on Instagram exhorting protesters to “take back” the famous Belle Époque exhibition hall on Saturday, the penultimate day of the week’s flagship fair.
Of course, the Grand Palais was not stormed, Bastille-style. In the highly unlikely event of protesters managing to “take back” the building, they would have been disappointed, just as revolutionaries had been in 1789, when they discovered the prison they had liberated contained just seven detainees. Art Basel Paris, taking no risks, had closed the event two days early on Friday evening (after an excoriating letter from France's gallery association to fair director Karim Crippa, Art Basel recompensed exhibitors 20% of their stand fees).
The mega-gallery Hauser & Wirth took even fewer risks, emptying its stand the day before, leaving three paintings by the local artist Hélène Delprat. The fair had been shortened to three VIP preview days plus just one day for the general public. Satellite fairs, like Paris Internationale and Post-Fair, closed at lunchtime on Saturday.
That Saturday afternoon, more than 100,000 people duly turned out to demonstrate. However, these proved predominantly peaceful and were confined by the police to the outskirts of the city.
The disruption in Paris had surely been a momentary blip. And Art Basel’s ultra-wealthy invitees, which the top end of the international art trade likes to call the “right kind of people”, had already been and gone. But what about the reputational impact?
Luxury playground?
“The collateral damage is substantial considering the whole point of being in Paris is to let yourself surrender to its myriad charms,” said Andrew Terner, a New York-based private dealer and collector, speaking in the immediate aftermath of the early closure.
The French authorities blamed “ultra-left radical groups” for the violence that had marred weeks of otherwise peaceful protests, begun in September by discontented teenage lycée students. Pillage de Classe is certainly a left-wing radical group; it views Art Basel Paris as a luxury playground in which art is used by the ultra-wealthy to protect their capital from taxation.
But maybe (leaving aside its desire to take the Grand Palais by storm) Pillage de Classe has a point, at least with regard to the fair’s top French clients. In France, the net worth of the country’s 500 wealthiest individuals has ballooned from 6% of the country’s GDP in 1996 to 42% in 2024, according to a much-cited article in the French business magazine Challenges. Tax reforms introduced by President Macron in 2017 excluded stocks, financial assets (including art) and corporate investments from wealth tax calculations.
Tax breaks
Moreover, in 2003 the French government had granted tax breaks of up to 75% for private individuals and 60% for corporations that supported the arts. This encouraged investment in glitzy private foundations, such as the Fondation Louis Vuitton, François Pinault’s Bourse de Commerce, the Fondation Cartier and the newly opened Île Seguin luxury hotel and Large art centre, which have become such an alluring feature of the Paris art scene for international visitors. According to research by Apollo magazine, Bernard Arnault’s LVMH luxury group received an aggregate tax break of €518.1m between 2007 and 2017 to set against the €790m the corporation spent building the Frank Gehry-designed Fondation Louis Vuitton.
The ultra-wealthy have also grown a lot wealthier in the US in recent years. The share of the nation’s wealth held by the richest 0.0001% (around 200 individuals) is now more than seven times what it was in 1980, according to a November Substack posted by the Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman.
Today’s art market is dominated by the world’s wealthiest people buying the world’s most expensive art. Most of these people are pretty old. This is not a good look now that the Democrats have won a landslide victory in the US midterm elections, driven by a massive turnout of young voters. Authoritarian rulers like Viktor Orbán in Hungary and Aleksandar Vučić in Serbia have been voted out of office. Young people have been protesting en masse about their diminished life chances in France and more than a dozen other countries across the world.
Suddenly, ordinary people matter again. The young matter. But do they matter at art fairs?
Young people priced out
Take ticket-pricing. In October, the general public were charged £48 each to attend Frieze London, with students being asked to pay £32. Does Frieze, which is owned by the billionaire Ari Emanuel, the former chief executive of the US entertainment conglomerate Endeavor, want to actively discourage young people from visiting? Or is that ticket price an acknowledgement that pretty much the only students who can now afford to attend the UK’s art colleges come from more affluent backgrounds?
The following week, Art Basel Paris, part of James Murdoch’s Lupa Systems investment portfolio, was charging €47 for a standard day pass and €30 for a student ticket. “The galleries pay for the fair. Visitors are a side business,” says Magnus Resch, a New York-based author and art market entrepreneur. According to Resch’s back-of-an-envelope calculations, stand fees generate at least €15m, while tickets bring in less than €3m. “Charging the public €47 isn’t about the money. It’s about keeping the fair exclusive.” (Art Basel does not reveal detailed breakdowns of its revenue streams.)
“It is important for the public to visit an art fair,” says Guillaume Sultana, whose contemporary art gallery exhibited on the upper level of Art Basel Paris, where footfall is slower than down on the ground floor among the mega-galleries. “But a lot of general visitors on the weekend are a bit frustrated because public tickets are very expensive.”
The main business is done during the very first days of an art fair, always
Sultana acknowledges that “the main business is done during the very first days of an art fair, always”. Despite the fair being truncated, Sultana describes the experience as “very good”, having sold a painting by the young Syrian artist Osama Al Rayyan during the preview for €15,000, among other works.
In the funfair-mirror optics of the international art market, €15,000 might appear a relatively “affordable” price point. But traditionally, sensible collectors have been advised to spend no more than 5% of their available wealth on art. So, whoever bought that Al Rayan painting, should, theoretically, have had €300,000 of spare cash available. For would-be younger collectors in today’s tough economic conditions, these are intimidating figures, unless they can call on the bank of mum and dad.
Collecting art is in serious danger of being perceived as something that old, rich people do. With so many established collectors ageing and selling, rather than buying, and a democratic wave pushing back against oligarchical wealth, this might be a good moment for the art market to think more about inclusivity than exclusivity, to take a broader view of who might be the “right kind” of people.
After all, who wants “death to the rich” sprayed across their gallery window?

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Want to Upend “Citizens United”?
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: David Moore
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Want to Upend Citizens United?
Check out the Montana Plan.
Want to Upend “Citizens United”?
Check out the Montana Plan.
On November 3, two-thirds of Montana voters approved a measure that strips corporations of the power to spend money on elections, striking a blow against corporate political cash in a state that went for Donald Trump by 20 points in 2024.
Initiative 194, known as the “Montana Plan,” is a first-of-its-kind ballot measure that rewrites state law so that “artificial persons”—such as corporations, nonprofits, unions, and trade associations—are no longer allowed to spend on candidates, PACs, or ballot measures. Advocates hail the plan as a novel legal strategy to bar corporate and dark money from influencing elections, and say that versions are being pursued in more than 30 states.
The measure passed by 66 to 34 percent, making Montana the second state, after Hawaii, to use its power over corporate charters to sidestep the US Supreme Court’s 2010 decision in Citizens United v. FEC. The ruling, which held that the First Amendment prohibits the government from restricting independent political spending by corporations and unions, relied on the claim that spending not coordinated with a candidate cannot corrupt; now candidates are permitted by the Federal Election Commission to raise money for their allied super PACs, and in practice frequently coordinate with them. Over 465,000 Montana voters voted on the initiative, which was greeted with a lawsuit from the Montana Republican Party and conservative groups on election night, before the race was called.
The initiative’s approval came as the 2026 elections smashed spending records. AdImpact tallied $11.9 billion in media spending nationwide, making this the most expensive election on record for political advertising. Outside spending on federal races, by groups like super PACs that pay for things like ads and mailers, was projected by OpenSecrets to reach $3.9 billion, a record for a midterm. The nonprofit also calculated that dark money flowing into federal races surpassed $1.5 billion, more than in the 2024 presidential cycle.
Voters this year noticed. An AP poll of midterm voters found that government corruption was the factor most mentioned in the survey as “crucial” in their choice for Congress, followed by the cost of living. More than half of midterm voters pointed to corruption as a main concern in the poll, conducted by the nonpartisan SSRS.
The Montana Plan redefines the powers the state grants to artificial persons, like corporations and nonprofits, to no longer include spending in elections—harnessing the legal distinction between constitutional rights and charter powers that are issued by states. Rather than restricting corporate speech rights, which Citizens United protects, the statutory Initiative 194 changes Montana’s code so that the state no longer grants artificial persons the power to spend on politics. Corporations and covered entities would no longer be allowed to contribute to any candidate, political party, or political committee in an election in Montana, including state and local ballot initiatives. Backers say that corporations remain free to advocate for candidates without giving money.
The measure applies to companies chartered in the state as well as out-of-state companies and nonprofits, so a Delaware corporation or a Washington, DC, nonprofit will be barred from unloading cash in a Montana election. Political committees, including super PACs, can still spend in the state, and individuals can still give to them—but corporations, nonprofits, and other artificial persons can no longer contribute to those committees. The new law does not apply to individuals, government bodies, or the distribution of news or commentary, unless the outlet is controlled by a party, PAC, or candidate.
A company, nonprofit, union, or other group found to be in violation would forfeit its charter privileges, including limited liability, and would be required to pay back its spending, regardless of whether it won or lost in the contest. The legal theory behind the plan, dubbed the Corporate Power Reset, was developed by Tom Moore, senior fellow at the Center for American Progress, who compiled a tracker of ballot initiatives and state bills introduced or being considered. Montana supporters say that once the law is in effect, disclosures listing the donors behind spending groups in the state will be names of real people, not corporations or dark-money groups.
The law is set to take effect on January 1, 2027, and legal challenges are underway that could be bound for the US Supreme Court, where the case would pit long-standing legal precedent for states’ authority to define corporate powers against the ruling in Citizens United. The Montana lawsuit, filed by the Institute for Free Speech on behalf of the state GOP and conservative groups, argues that the law violates the First Amendment by barring them from spending to communicate about candidates and ballot measures.
The nonprofit behind the initiative, the Transparent Election Initiative (TEI), says it anticipated the legal challenge and is prepared to defend the plan while helping other states advance their own versions.
“What I’ve been saying to folks for two years now is, there is a solution,” said Jeff Mangan, a former state legislator and Montana commissioner of political practices who is TEI’s founder and president, of the flood of corporate and dark money in elections.
“I started at the beginning of 2025, doing a listening session across the state, just asking folks about how they felt about money in politics, and if they’re ready for a change,” Mangan said. “I always led with the same question: Do you believe there’s too much money in politics? Everyone said yes.”
Since Citizens United, he said, people had been told that “there’s nothing you can do unless you have an amendment to the Constitution or the Supreme Court overturns it.” When he outlined the plan building on the state’s authority over corporations “to change the way corporations spend in elections, which will affect dark money and the amount of money going into our politics,” he said, “people got excited about it and wanted to collect signatures.”
TEI’s all-volunteer signature drive collected more than 50,000 signatures from all 56 Montana counties, above the 30,121 valid signatures required, with more than 600 volunteers helping the initiative qualify for the ballot. Mangan said TEI aimed to show the measure could make the ballot without the paid signature gatherers that have become commonplace for campaigns.
He pointed to the surge of corporate money this cycle. “The amount of money this year alone is staggering,” he said. Public Citizen recently found that 40 percent of the $1.8 billion that corporations have spent since the Citizens United ruling came in the 2026 midterms. The scale of the spending was inescapable, Mangan said, in recent Montana races like the 2024 Senate contest between Democrat Jon Tester and now-Senator Tim Sheehy, which set a national record for per-voter spending. He points out that billionaires are free to form PACs, just with their names attached. “They choose to spend anonymously through C4s or keep it dark for a reason,” he said, referring to 501(c)4 nonprofits.
A 2018 documentary about secret spending in Montana politics, Dark Money, was a regular feature of the signature drive. TEI showed the movie about a dozen times around the state, Mangan said, including a screening in Helena with remarks from the filmmaker, Kimberly Reed, who is from there.
Volunteers from other groups joined to put the Montana Plan in front of voters. The League of Women Voters of Montana’s members gathered signatures and hosted voter education events around the state, said Bonnie Lorenzen, the group’s president.
“The League of Women Voters of Montana chose early on to endorse the Montana Plan because it aligned perfectly with the League’s goal to ensure that our government serves the people, not wealthy special interests,” Lorenzen told The Nation. “We believe this is best attained by promoting transparency in government and eliminating dark money, which is what the Montana Plan aims to do.”
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
“Our elected officials need to be responsive to their constituents who elect them, not to corporate entities financing their campaigns,” Lorenzen said.
Former Republican governor Marc Racicot endorsed the Montana Plan, calling it “a brilliant idea,” along with Tester and Gary Buchanan, a former independent candidate for Congress. Groups applauding the plan included the cross-partisan Issue One, Free Speech for People, and Craig Holman, government affairs lobbyist for Public Citizen. Opposition to the ballot initiative came from groups including the Montana Chamber of Commerce, the Montana Mining Association, and the Montana Petroleum Association, as well as the state GOP. In April, the Montana Supreme Court unanimously dismissed a challenge from business groups that would have barred I-194 from the ballot, ruling that citizens have a right to go through the initiative process.
In May, Hawaii became the first state to enact a law based on the Corporate Power Reset framework, when Act 11, passed with near-unanimous support in the state House and Senate, was signed by Governor Josh Green. The law takes effect July 1, 2027, though it faces two federal lawsuits: one from the free-market think tank Grassroot Institute of Hawaii, and a second from the massive dark-money lobby the US Chamber of Commerce.
Bills based on the Corporate Power Reset were introduced in nearly 20 states this year, after New York was the first to introduce the legislation in late 2025. The New York Assembly bill was sponsored by Assemblyman Micah Lasher, now a US representative-elect, and the Senate bill by Senator Kristen Gonzalez; both bills were left in committee.
“We’ve always said it has to be a local solution, it has to be a state-by-state solution,” Mangan said of others seeking to pass the plan, whether through ballot initiatives or state legislatures. The measure’s spread across the map, he said, shows it has been “embraced by folks across the political spectrum.” After the plan’s resounding passage in Montana, he sees people thinking, “Oh, we can actually do something, rather than just saying we can do something.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Yayoi Kusama sets $15m record as Sotheby’s opens New York mega-sales
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Carlie Porterfield
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Just months after her death, a work by Yayoi Kusama set a new auction record at Sotheby’s in New York, as the auction house kicked off the marquee November sales on Monday night with back-to-back auctions that brought in $378.7m (with fees). The evening also saw records for Sam Francis, Jonas Wood, Firelei Báez and Tomma Abts. Not a bad start to a week in which auction houses expect to sell as much as $2.4bn in art.
Kusama’s No. 3P.B. (1960) fetched $12.5m ($15m with fees), against an estimate of $10m to $15m, setting a new auction record for the Japanese artist who died in August. One of Kusama's earliest landmark Infinity Nets series, the painting was included in a 1961 exhibition at the Whitney Museum of American Art, among the artist's earliest inclusions in an American institutional show. The work was the fifth most expensive lot in Sotheby’s The Now and Contemporary Evening auction, which brought in $224.78m ($268.7m with fees).
The 53-lot sale, which carried a pre-sale estimate of $226.2m to $323.1m—the highest since May 2024, according to Sotheby’s—saw two works withdrawn and five unsold, including works by Ellsworth Kelly, Kerry James Marshall, Roy Lichtenstein and Keith Haring, as well as Ayrton Senna's Formula 1 car inexplicably included in the sale. While around 45% of lots hammered within their estimates, bidding was uneven.
Roy Lichtenstein’s Reflections on “Painter and Model” (1990) led the sale in terms of value, hammering for $22m ($24.6m with fees) against an estimate of $20m to $30m. It was followed by Willem de Kooning’s Water...Soft Banks and a Window (Untitled VIII) (1975), which fell short of its $20m low estimate, hammering for $17.1m ($20.3m with fees). Andy Warhol’s Flowers (1964) fetched $15.2m ($18.2m with fees), just above its $15m high estimate.
Sam Francis’s Towards Disappearance I (1958) sold for $15m ($17.1m with fees), at the low end of its $15m to $20m estimate, setting a new auction record for the artist. It was a case of déjà vu: the same painting had previously set Francis’s auction record when it sold in 1999.
One of the most exciting moments of the evening came when five bidders battled for six minutes over Jeff Koons’s Bob-Tail (1991), a depiction of an Old English Sheepdog. The work ultimately hammered for $9m to a roar of applause.
Another standout result was Salman Toor’s Lavender Boy (2019), which went for $340,000 ($435,200 with fees), more than four times its $80,000 high estimate even without buyer's premium being factored in.
The evening kicked off with the single-owner sale of the collection of cable television magnate Theodore Baum and his wife Ruth. The 24-lot auction generated $90.8m ($109.9m with fees), comfortably within its $74.4m to $109m pre-sale estimate, with a 100% sell-through rate. However, one-third of the lots hammered below their low estimates, while just one-quarter exceeded their high estimates.
The top lot was Joan Mitchell’s Green Book of Barbara Guest (1965-68), which hammered for $16.2m ($19.3m with fees), among the highest results for the artist at auction, against an estimate of $12m to $18m. The Baums acquired the work in 1986 for just $65,000; including Sotheby’s fees, the winning bidder paid almost 300 times that amount.
It was followed by an untitled 1998 Mark Rothko painting, which fetched $15.5m ($17.7m with fees), surpassing its $10m to $15m estimate. The Baums purchased the work for $115,000 in 1983, according to Sotheby’s, meaning Monday’s buyer paid more than 150 times that amount, including fees. The third most valuable lot was Andy Warhol’s The Scream (After Munch) (1984), sold for $6.8m ($7.9m with fees) against an estimate of $4m to $6m. Together, the three works accounted for around 42% of the sale’s $91.4m hammer total.
Not every work met expectations. Franz Kline’s Figure (1955) recorded the largest shortfall in dollar terms, hammering for $1.8m ($2.3m with fees), against an estimate of $4m to $6m—55% below its low estimate.
After the sale, Sotheby’s said works from single-owner collections achieved $239m (with fees), making up almost 60% of the evening’s total earnings.
“When your sale is the opener for a major season like this, there’s always a sense of heightened anticipation," Lucius Elliott, Sotheby's head of contemporary art marquee sales, said following the auction. "I think this evening’s sale did what everyone hoped it would—signaled that the market is in a great place and demand is strong. We saw real competition for coveted works, with a keen focus both on works from admired collections and for the works we specifically sought out for this sale to meet the demand we knew was there. The evening’s final tally—double that of the equivalent evening last season—says it all.”
On Tuesday night, the New York art world's eyes will turn toward rival auction house Christie's for the 20th century auction, led by paintings with eight-figure estimates by Wassily Kandinsky, Gustav Klimt and Pablo Picasso.

“It is time to start thinking outside the box/apartment and offer a solution to homeless victims of domestic violence.”
Today, more than 16,000 families, including 28,000 children, are living in New York City’s shelter system.
Unfortunately the number one reason is domestic violence, accounting for 20 percent of entries into the family shelter system. This incredible and sad statistic greatly out weighs traditional factors, such as overcrowding (11 percent) and eviction (also 11 percent). It is estimated that one third of all the families in the system are families suffering from domestic violence, and the city’s 54 domestic violence family shelters are insufficient.
As a result, city shelters designated for domestic violence are saturated, and many families are directed to the regular shelter system. By not being in a DV shelter, these families are not receiving the support that they and their children need to deal with this trauma, and the help needed to obtain permanent housing.
Perhaps even more disturbing is the fact that 40 percent of felony assault cases in the city since the COVID-19 pandemic are related to domestic violence. This has resulted in nearly 20 percent of all new intake at the family shelter system being related to domestic violence.
The quick release of defendants—whether through automatic bail schedules, rapid pretrial release, or early prison discharge—exposes domestic violence victims to immediate physical danger, psychological trauma, and coercion. Because domestic abuse is uniquely characterized by ongoing power dynamics and escalating patterns of control, rapid release often strips away the critical time window victims need to secure safety.
As a former deputy commissioner at the New York City Department of Homeless Services and a vice president for supportive housing at Women in Need, I believe the key to reducing this trend in domestic violence is to greatly increase the amount of supportive housing for DV victims.
There are presently over 6,000 vacant apartments in the New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA), and I believe that DV victims should be given priority in filling them.
In addition, a novel ideal would be to create a program to match DV families with NYCHA residents who have several bedrooms, but now live alone. In this way the DV families could help pay the rent for the single, often elderly person, who has more than enough space at this point in their lives.
We could call this program Adopt a Family. This would be a win/win situation for all those involved. A prior report from the Independent Budget Office estimated that nearly one third of NYCHA’s nearly 180,000 apartments, or 57,000 units, are under occupied. Of those under occupied apartments, half were headed by a senior citizen.
It is time to start thinking outside the box/apartment and offer a solution to homeless victims of domestic violence.
Robert Mascali is a former deputy commissioner at the New York City Department of Homeless Services and a vice president for supportive housing at Women in Need.

https://hellgatenyc.com/vanity-fair-timo.title: The Timothée Chalamet Vanity Fair Profile Makes Me Sick
https://hellgatenyc.com/vanity-fair-timo.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/vanity-fair-timo.text:
It's Wednesday, you deserve a treat, like an episode of the Hell Gate Podcast! Listen here or watch here.
The cover story of Vanity Fair's Holiday Issue, a profile of Timothée Chalamet, is excruciating.
I can sympathize with its writer, Vanity Fair's "senior editorial director," (whatever that means) Mark Guiducci. An A-list celeb like Chalamet has little incentive to do anything the broke, failing media wants these days. He calls the shots, even to a legendary magazine like VF. Like an emailed excuse to a college professor, Guiducci drops a few references to the constraints he's working with: He's only got 90 minutes before Chalamet heads to Yankee Stadium to watch them get creamed by the Tampa Bay Rays, and he uses a few of them to eat a Lenwich; Chalamet is rigorously media-trained, and he and his publicists have dictated several "no-go zones" in advance, including his relationship with Kylie Jenner; the photoshoot in Iceland has already occurred.
And so, Guiducci begins the piece with expectation-setting: Nothing noteworthy will happen, because "it's dangerous business for a movie star to open his mouth these days." There especially will not be a gaffe like the one made earlier this year during the Oscar campaign for "Marty Supreme," where Chalamet (arguably correctly) noted opera and ballet as mediums with waning mainstream appeal. That actually caused discourse, and who wants that? And anyway, that was said in a videotaped interview with another actor (obviously). This is a magazine profile.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Hundreds of NYC Students Still Without School Bus Transportation, Officials Say
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Samantha Olander, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters.
Hundreds of New York City students still lack assigned school bus transportation more than two months into the academic year, education officials told City Council members Wednesday.
Roughly 2,000 students started the school year without bus service, and 467 remained without assigned transportation as of Wednesday, officials said at an oversight hearing. Most of the students initially affected have individualized education programs, or IEPs, that require transportation to and from school.
The figures point to persistent problems in a system that carries about 150,000 students daily, even as officials pour more money into busing. The city spent $2.1 billion on student transportation in fiscal year 2026, up from $1.46 billion five years earlier, and has budgeted $2.28 billion for fiscal year 2027. City officials had warned of potential bus shortages before classes began in September.
Kevin Moran, the Education Department’s deputy chancellor for school operations, acknowledged that “too many families have experienced delays, route changes, staffing shortages or gaps in service.” He attributed some gaps to transportation requests submitted after an Aug. 6 registration deadline, including for students who moved, changed schools or had their transportation needs updated.
Before the hearing, dozens of parents, students, advocates and elected officials rallied on the steps of City Hall to demand better bus service. The gathering, organized by the Road to Better Busing Coalition and ARISE Coalition, featured signs reading “NYC needs better busing” and “Late bus = lost learning.”
Parents described how transportation problems have disrupted their children’s education. Divya Mathew said the bus for her 7-year-old daughter, who attends a private school for students with disabilities, routinely arrived 30 minutes to more than an hour late at the start of the year. The delays threatened her daughter’s speech and occupational therapy services, Mathew said, so she began driving her daughter to school. Mathew said she filed nearly 25 complaints to the Education Department’s Office of Pupil Transportation before the problem was resolved.
At the hearing, Councilmember Eric Dinowitz, who chairs the Education Committee, called unreliable bus service a “perennial issue.” He described a student whose bus arrives an hour before school ends, forcing the family to choose between missed instruction and paying for private transportation.
“It is heartbreaking and unconscionable to receive emails and phone calls that a child didn’t get on the bus because it never came,” Dinowitz said.
Moran said every route that lacked a driver on the first day of school now has one, and the city has offered temporary rideshare transportation to some families awaiting bus assignments. He cited a parent survey showing nearly 90% satisfaction with transportation during the 2025-26 school year.
But staffing gaps remain for students who need additional support. More than 350 students are still waiting for the paraprofessionals their IEPs require to accompany them on the bus, officials said. Paraprofessional shortages have previously left students with disabilities unable to attend school.
Students with assigned routes face problems, too. Councilmember Lincoln Restler said nearly 90,000 bus routes were delayed last school year, about 500 per school day, and said 56,000 students experienced delays of more than an hour.
Restler and Dinowitz are sponsoring legislation requiring the Education Department to publish monthly data on early, late and missed pickups and drop-offs on a public dashboard. The data would go beyond the department’s existing vendor report cards, which initially lacked on-time performance figures. Education Department officials said they support the bill’s intent and want to work with the council on a feasible reporting timeline. Council members discussed the measure Wednesday without taking a vote.
Lawmakers Scrutinize NYC School Bus Oversight
In 2019, the city contracted with Via Transportation to modernize its school bus system, including tracking buses and students and developing more efficient routes. The contract is now valued at $51.7 million, but the promised route optimization software remains unfinished years after its original deadline. Asked why the city still uses older routing software, education officials said the COVID-19 pandemic interrupted development and the department had not been ready to integrate some features into its systems.
Contractor oversight has also drawn scrutiny. A December 2025 comptroller audit found the department failed to consistently use available data to identify problem routes and hold bus companies accountable. The city could have assessed $44.3 million in penalties for violations of GPS tracking requirements during the 2024-25 school year, the audit found, but assessed just $1.7 million.
Drivers must log into the city’s tracking app, which launched in 2024, so families can locate their children’s buses. Moran said officials initially held off on penalizing some bus companies for GPS tracking violations because of technical problems and training needs. The department has since assessed about $270,000 in tracking penalties, he said, and drivers now log in about 93% of the time.
That scrutiny could shape the city’s next round of bus contracts. Last November, the Panel for Educational Policy approved three-year contract extensions after a dispute that threatened to disrupt bus service. The agreements expire in 2028, and City Council members have called for new contracts with companies committed to improving service.
Samantha Olander writes about Newark and New York schools.

https://gothamist.com/news/ny-to-pay-12m.title: NY to pay $1.2M to a woman who accused ex-Manhattan corrections officer of sexual assault
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-to-pay-12m.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/ny-to-pay-12m.text:
New York will pay $1.2 million to a woman who sued the state after she accused a former corrections officer of repeatedly sexually assaulting her at a women’s prison in Manhattan, according to lawyers.
The settlement is the first case that closed after the three-year look back period of the Adult Survivors Act ended, lawyers said. The New York law, signed by Gov. Kathy Hochul in 2022, allowed alleged victims of sexual assault to file lawsuits after the statue of limitations had expired.
The ASA established a one-year period for these lawsuits to be filed from Nov. 24, 2022 to Nov. 24, 2023.
The lawsuit accused Corrections Officer Leslie Dawkins of sexually abusing the inmate in her prison cell more than 20 times between August 2010 and January 2011, according to lawyers.
Dawkins has also been named in more than 15 other ASA suits, with prison records revealing that the state corrections department had received several complaints from other incarcerated women about the former corrections officer, according to Slater Slater Schulman LLP, the law firm that represented the woman in this case.
The law firm also said that other prison staff and an internal investigation had warned the state about the sexual abuse that occurred at the now-shuttered Bayview Correctional Facility in Chelsea for decades, and that the state failed to address the issue.
“Three years after New York’s Adult Survivors Act lookback window closed, survivors are only now having their day in court after years of unnecessary delays that only serve to retraumatize our clients,” said Adam Slater, a founding and managing partner at the firm. “This outcome shows the State is prepared to accept responsibility and be held accountable for the harm it caused generations of women.”
The law firm said that it is representing 1,200 of an estimated 1,600 people who have filed lawsuits using the ASA after claiming sexual abuse in New York state prisons.
“New York passed the Adult Survivors Act to help survivors of sexual abuse and assault seek justice,” New York Attorney General Letitia James said in a statement. “In every matter, the Office of the Attorney General is committed to following the facts and the law where they lead. In this case, the evidence led to conceding the state’s liability and agreeing on compensation.”
Attorney information for Dawkins was not made immediately available.
The story was updated with a statement from the attorney general.

The New Museum has announced a multiyear partnership with the Toronto-based Vega Foundation, an organization dedicated to commissioning and supporting video art. It was launched by Elisa Nuyten, a New Museum board member.
The Vega foundation primarily provides opportunities to emerging and mid-career artists who work in film and video. Recent artists who have received Vega commissions include Ali Cherri, Diego Marcon, Martine Syms, and Yuyan Wang. The foundation started in 2022, and has primarily collaborated with Canadian institutions.
Vega’s first commission associated with its New Museum partnership will be a solo show at the institution by the Thai artist Korakrit Arunanondchai, set to open in February. The subject of his exhibition will be the phenomenon of post-Vietnam War-era ghost cinemas in Thailand—venues where monks staged screenings via portable projectors in otherwise dilapidated architecture. The show will take the form of a video installation that includes fog, light, and a soil floor, and will also feature a performance series by Tosh Basco.
“For Vega, supporting artists also means thinking about how their work continues to reach new audiences and find new contexts over time,” said Nuyten in an email to ARTnews, “That’s something I’d really like to see come out of this partnership.”
Massimiliano Gioni, director of the New Museum, said that “Vega’s work creating a network of possibilities for works that might otherwise never be realized is perfectly aligned with what the New Museum was founded to do nearly fifty years ago, giving artists the freedom and resources to take risks, experiment, and pursue ideas that might initially seem strange or even impossible. To me, that is precisely what contemporary art needs.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/jeffries-con.title: Don’t Mourn Hakeem Jeffries’s Speakership. Organize.
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/jeffries-con.author: Austin Warrington
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/jeffries-con.text:
Don’t Mourn Hakeem Jeffries’s Speakership. Organize.
Hakeem Jeffries was elected the next Speaker of the House because the Left simply does not currently have the power to elect a speaker who reflects the progressive mandate we saw in the midterms. Changing that reality, however, is possible.
In the wake of the midterms, the entirety of left-liberal America was jubilant. Democrats won majorities in the House and Senate, outperforming even the most idealistic predictions. But it was not only the Democratic victories that shocked observers — it was the kind of candidates who won. Democratic socialists had their strongest showing of any election in recent history, winning 169 endorsed ballot measures and seats at the local, state, and federal levels — their strongest showing of any general election in recent history. And the wins by nonsocialist progressives and even many centrists affirmed an agenda championed by democratic socialists, centering economic populism, wealth redistribution, and universal health care.
But then a harsh reality set in: the near inevitability of Rep. Hakeem Jeffries as the next Speaker of the House, a result that seemed to fly in the face of the progressive results we’d just seen. On Wednesday, just eleven Democrats voted against Jeffries in an internal nonbinding vote, including a bloc of five newly elected democratic socialists, joined by two additional Democrats. In a statement on their decision, the no voters cited ongoing negotiations around “Medicare for All, stopping [Immigration and Customs Enforcment (ICE)] terror, getting money out of politics, [and] ending the genocide in Gaza.” Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez notably did not join the no votes.
Jeffries is decidedly not a leftist nor a progressive. He is a pro-corporate Democrat who defends Israel and readily takes American Israel Public Affairs Committee money and corporate money. How, in the face of such a resounding progressive message from voters, could there be no clear alternative?
It’s understandable that some on the Left might feel deflated by this outcome. But we can also see the speaker conundrum as exposing an organizing void in Congress, one that the broadly left-leaning forces that felt so heartened by the midterm results have to confront soberly: we simply do not currently have the power, leverage, or internal relationships to elect a speaker that reflects the mandate we just witnessed. Changing that reality will need to start with an honest evaluation of the conditions surrounding the speakership race.
Jeffries has spent years building up to this moment. The relationships he’s nurtured with his careful, deliberate style and results he’s delivered to the Democratic caucus — negotiating important earmarks for Democrats in a Republican-controlled House, leading a multistate campaign to neutralize Republicans’ gerrymandering efforts, and steering increasingly large fundraising hauls to the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee — were all leading to this moment. Any challenger, particularly one from a rising Left that is at its very beginnings in the halls of power, would be at a massive disadvantage.
Not only that, but any defectors willing to stick their necks out to back an alternative would be putting a target on their back, as Jeffries plays a key role in committee assignments and setting the agenda for the floor. Asking our electeds to risk their ability to successfully carry out their jobs and advance our priorities would be irresponsible without a viable path to success.
Socialists grappling with increasing power in government have to think long-term about how to create the conditions where a majority of House Democrats can back a socialist speaker. The time to start building toward that outcome is now, in Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) working groups and organizing committees across the country. Our bench of socialist electeds needs to be deeper in a way that can build buy-in for our goals among the general public, and we need to continue the work of relationship-building with our existing socialist electeds.
Deepening our bench of electeds happens at every level of government and requires a clear-eyed assessment of what it takes to win races, which usually centers on an ambitious fundraising plan. Designated candidate recruitment organizers can begin by identifying prospective candidates and taking meetings now in anticipation of 2028; ideal candidates have preexisting ties to DSA or a labor union, direct organizing experience, a demonstrated commitment to advancing socialist policies, and a willingness to work collaboratively and meet regularly with chapter leaders once elected.
Creating buy-in and demonstrating the popularity of our agenda among the public requires frequent and honest communication with the public. Rep. Ocasio-Cortez excels at this, making the often opaque operations of Congress accessible to millions through social media. To elect a socialist speaker, we would need to launch a campaign early, educating the public on the mechanisms as well as the stakes of the speaker’s race and building consensus around a candidate. A successful campaign will put us in a strong position when it is time for members to vote, where we can flex our organizing muscle to exert pressure using all of the support we’ve built throughout the course of the campaign.
Most importantly, we will need to continue the work of building relationships with our bloc of socialist electeds across the country. This work is carried out by trusted organizing leaders in regularly scheduled group meetings. It necessitates strong interpersonal skills on both ends, including the ability to manage conflict healthily and negotiate. Chapters with maturing socialist coalitions should connect with the architects of more established programs to take some of the many lessons that have emerged over the years.
What distinguishes democratic socialists from other politicians is that strategizing and organizing don’t stop after election day. The project of building power is year-round and relies on the active participation of skilled organizers working with elected officials. In the past two weeks, Representatives-elect Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier have organized canvasses of their constituents, asking them directly what they should prioritize in Congress and who they should back as speaker. This ongoing dialogue with constituents represents a new kind of strategy — one in which elected officials meet people where they’re at to continue the work of organizing outside of an electoral context, facilitating dialogue at the doors and creating trust and buy-in.
This is only a small piece of what it will take to win our agenda, but it is an important and meaningful step toward the kind of politics we should always be practicing: one that centers the needs of working people and ensures their voices echo in the halls of power.

https://gothamist.com/news/hudson-valley.title: Hudson Valley duck farm suing over NYC foie gras ban destroyed in fire
https://gothamist.com/news/hudson-valley.author: Walter Wuthmann
https://gothamist.com/news/hudson-valley.text:
A Hudson Valley duck farm at the center of a high-profile lawsuit challenging New York City’s foie gras ban was destroyed in a fire early Thursday morning, according to Sullivan County fire officials.
Hudson Valley Foie Gras is one of only two remaining foie gras farms in the entire country, alongside La Belle Farms, which is also in Sullivan County. The two farms are asking the New York Court of Appeals to overturn the city’s ban on the fatty delicacy made from the livers of force-fed ducks and geese.
County officials said they received a 911 call from Hudson Valley Foie Gras’ facility in Bethel at 1:10 a.m. Thursday. By the time firefighters from the Smallwood-Mongaup Valley Fire Department arrived on scene the largest building was already fully engulfed, with the fire spreading rapidly through other wood-framed structures.
“The fire took off so fast, there was no way to get inside,” said Smallwood-Mongaup Valley Fire Chief Charlie Kalinowski. More than two dozen nearby fire departments responded to the blaze.
Kalinowski said most of the buildings at the Hudson Valley Foie Gras property were completely destroyed. Fire officials said “some” of the ducks and geese were rescued, including hundreds of hatchlings, but others were killed by the flames.
It’s not clear how many ducks and geese were on site. Hudson Valley Foie Gras Manager Marcus Henley told a Gothamist reporter at a previous visit to the farm’s nearby Ferndale facility that they process about 6,000 ducks a week. Reached by phone Thursday, Henley declined an interview but said no employees or first responders were injured.
Henley told Radio Catskill Thursday that the fire is suspected to have started due to an electrical malfunction. The Sullivan County Fire Investigation Team said its investigation is ongoing and no cause has been determined.
Henley’s farm is at the center of an ongoing legal battle pitting the New York City Council, which banned the sale of foie gras in 2019, against the farms and the New York Department of Agriculture, which argue the local measure violates state agricultural policy. Animal rights activists say the process of making foie gras amounts to animal cruelty.
Radio Catskill’s Kimberly Izar contributed to this report.

https://gothamist.com/news/85k-watch-tak.title: $85K watch taken from man who blacked out in woman’s SUV in NYC, NYPD says
https://gothamist.com/news/85k-watch-tak.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/85k-watch-tak.text:
A man who agreed to hang out with a stranger in her SUV in Chelsea earlier this month lost consciousness after imbibing a drink and woke up to find his $85,000 watch gone from his wrist, police said Thursday.
The 40-year-old man was near West 15th Street and 10th Avenue after 2 a.m. on Sunday, Nov. 1, when a woman in a white Kia Sportage struck up a conversation and invited him to hang out, according to the NYPD. He agreed and got into the car, police said.
As they drove around, she offered him a cocktail, which a police spokesperson said held an unknown substance. At some point, he lost consciousness, police said.
When he came to a dozen blocks away, the watch, an Audemars Piguet Royal Oak, was gone from his wrist, according to police. He woke up on the street at West 24th Street and Seventh Avenue, police said.
The NYPD released images of the woman it's seeking and a white SUV on Thursday, and asked the public for help.
Police described the woman as wearing a black and white top, blue jeans and black sneakers. The department is investigating the theft as a grand larceny and said no injuries were reported.
Authorities are asking anyone with information to call Crime Stoppers.

https://gothamist.com/news/watch-mta-bus.title: Watch: MTA bus video captures moment of deadly Brooklyn building collapse
https://gothamist.com/news/watch-mta-bus.author: Charles Lane
https://gothamist.com/news/watch-mta-bus.text:
A new video released by the MTA provides a rare look at the moment of last week's building collapse in Brooklyn, which killed eight people and injured 18 others.
The 45-second clip was recorded by an MTA bus on the B103 route as it headed south on Flatbush Avenue just around 4 p.m. on Nov. 11. It shows the front of a three-story Flatbush apartment building splitting down the middle and dropping into a neighboring construction site, as people on the sidewalk scatter.
In the video, the building’s northeast corner tips into the excavation site next door, shearing the front of the building in two. It takes about seven seconds for the building to fall.
Gothamist reported this week the city had shut down at least five projects tied to a pair of engineers in the wake of the collapse and is inspecting more than 160 construction sites tied to companies and people involved in the development project. At least one tenant is suing the landlord of the building, after reporting cracks in the building’s foundation that the owner never addressed.
But more than a week after the collapse, officials have not said exactly what caused the building to fall.
The Department of Buildings and law enforcement are investigating, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani has said the Brooklyn district attorney’s office is also involved.
Workers had been excavating the empty lot at 2625 Bedford Ave. for a new apartment building earlier that day, officials said.
The Department of Buildings had issued a stop work order at the lot in March, and an inspector found a month later that the owners had kept up demolition work in violation of it, a department spokesperson said.
On Wednesday, the Department of Buildings said it will demolish 1323 Flatbush Ave., a neighboring building damaged in the collapse, after engineers determined it is too unstable to repair safely.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: These are New Yorkers' favorite books of 2026
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Hannah Frishberg
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
The New York Public Library has released its annual Best Books list based on New Yorkers’ favorites, a reliably diverse array of titles.
This year has proven no exception: A press release from the library describes the list, chosen by librarians and other NYPL staffers, as “uniquely informed by the literary interests of actual New Yorkers.” It includes 260 books that range from bestsellers to foreign translations to sleeper hits across genres.
Highlights from the roundup’s three age-based sublists (adults, teens and kids, plus 25 Spanish children’s book titles) include Emily St. John Mandel’s future-set novel “Exit Party,” Joshua Jelly-Schapiro’s Harry Belafonte biography “Daylight Come” and, in the Kids category, Georgina Chadderton’s graphic memoir “Oh Brother.”
NYPL also released a list of the year’s Notable Audiobooks.
Library officials described the list as an annual "love letter" to New Yorkers and other readers, curated by real New Yorkers with genre expertise and community connections.
Many of the list’s top titles that had lengthy wait times for checkout even ahead of the list's release are now available via no-wait digital access to anyone with a library card. All items on the Notable Audiobooks list are also available for no-wait digital access through year’s end.
NYPL is hosting two free author talks next month: Some of the year’s buzziest fiction authors (Valeria Luiselli, Douglas Stuart and Vincent Yu) are at the Stavros Niarchos Foundation Library on Dec. 3. Then, at Staten Island’s Stapleton Library branch on Dec. 9, will be an author discussion of the year’s best mysteries and thrillers.

https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-socialist.title: NYC socialists want to be AOC's 'foot soldiers' in 2028. Moderates fear a backlash.
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-socialist.author: Brigid Bergin
https://gothamist.com/news/nyc-socialist.text:
New York City’s Democratic Socialists of America, emboldened by Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s popularity and a wave of democratic socialist victories, want to send Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to the White House in 2028. And that’s sparking pushback from mainstream Democrats, who caution the socialist label could prove to be more of a liability than an asset.
The local chapter of the DSA adopted a resolution at its convention in Manhattan last weekend, voting 291-193 to encourage Ocasio-Cortez to run for president.
“ We are excited to be the backbone and foot soldiers of her race,” said NYC DSA co-chair Grace Mausser. “And we want her to know that it's absolutely necessary that a left wing, that a progressive — ideally a socialist — run for president.”
The city’s DSA chapter has built a formidable reputation for its canvassing operation, driving up voter turnout in competitive primary and general election contests in 2025 and 2026.
While not a formal endorsement, the resolution sent a strong message following the recent political triumphs of other democratic socialists like Mamdani, Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, as well as a total of 16 state legislators including a pickup of seven new seats for socialists in office.
New York City’s local DSA chapter also joins 18 others including Los Angeles, Chicago, Boston, Atlanta, San Antonio, Milwaukee and Wichita, which already adopted the Ocasio-Cortez 2028 resolution.
But Democrats are split on whether the socialist label helps or hurts Ocasio-Cortez’s potential candidacy.
One operative in the second camp is Tré Easton, vice president of public affairs at the Searchlight Institute, a Washington, D.C.-based think tank that is working to expand where Democrats can win nationally.
“ My honest opinion is if Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is serious about wanting to be president either in 2028 or in the future, the best thing that she could do for herself politically would be to let her DSA membership lapse,” Easton said.
He said there are organizational benefits to having DSA in your corner, with strong voter education and turnout operations, especially in a blue state like New York, “but the brand is not good nationally.”
Easton cited the recent experience of Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan, whose association with the DSA through endorsements from prominent DSA members like Ocasio-Cortez, Mamdani and Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders – even though El-Sayed is not a DSA member – was seen as a liability.
Roughly a week before Election Day, El-Sayed was still facing questions lumping him in with his democratic socialist allies. “I’m just not a socialist,” El-Sayed said. “I believe in capitalism.”
Ocasio-Cortez – who is weighing a presidential bid, a Senate run or remaining in the House – had hinted the results in Michigan would inform her thinking.
“If Abdul can win in Michigan, anybody can win anywhere,” the New York Times reported she told attendees at a fundraiser for El-Sayed in New York City last month. El-Sayed won by 7 points, which was a smaller margin than his 11-point lead in pre-election polls.
Just ahead of the midterm elections, Ocasio-Cortez’s congressional campaign issued a memo that detailed how she has successfully campaigned for candidates in “rural districts and battleground seats.”
In addition to her support of El-Sayed, the memo cited Ocasio-Cortez’s work on behalf of Sam Forstag, a Montana smokejumper and labor union leader who was trailing in his bid for the House by 20 points before AOC’s endorsement. Forstag ultimately won his Democratic primary by 4 points and went on to flip the Republican-held House seat earlier this month.
The five-page memo described her as a champion for all “working people,” but notably did not use the word socialist.
Kendall Scudder, head of the Texas Democratic Party that successfully helped elect James Talarico to the U.S. Senate and Gina Hinojosa as governor along with flipping the Texas state house, said there is risk for a DSA candidate in a presidential primary when so many of the other candidates are likely to be moderates.
“ What I fear is that if we do end up in a situation where we have a DSA candidate running for president, all the nominees are gonna campaign on the DSA person being bad instead of campaigning on what solutions are you offering and bringing to the table to make people's lives better?” Scudder said.
But he said this is also where Ocasio-Cortez can distinguish herself from the pack. He said voters want to know how candidates are going to make their lives more affordable, whether that’s helping to pay for their kids' soccer cleats or giving them a pathway to buy a home someday.
Scudder argued labels are the currency of party insiders and that voters care more about robust party primaries that show what different solutions candidates have to offer them. He spoke from experience, after facing blowback “because I didn’t muscle our own primary” between Talarico and former House Rep. Jasmine Crockett earlier in the year.
He said competitive, high-energy contests actually have the effect of engaging more voters.
“ If Congresswoman Ocasio-Cortez feels like she has something to offer the country, she should run and let the voters sort that out,” Scudder said. “ Anyone who wants to run should do that, and we should have a knock-down, drag-out primary where people are forced to put organizations together and forced to earn people's votes.”
“ It'll make us a stronger party, 'cause we're gonna talk about issues in ways we wouldn't have otherwise,” he added.
Alyssa Cass of Slingshot Strategies, who worked on the successful campaigns of Rep. Pat Ryan, a moderate Democrat in the Hudson Valley, said the message that unites Democrats now is one focused on economic populism.
When Ryan and Ocasio-Cortez first campaigned together in 2024, they took a boat ride on the Hudson River and framed their commitment to cleaning the waterway as a fight against big business.
This year, Ryan and Ocasio-Cortez campaigned together again multiple times, and jointly appeared with Gov. Kathy Hochul in support of her one-year data center moratorium, another fight that frames the government working on behalf of local communities against big tech giants.
Cass said the only people who care about the “socialist” label are in the political class.
“I don't doubt that people will try to tag her as ‘DSA’ and make that a thing,” said Cass. “I think that it hurts all of us in the political class who will be subjected to infinity hours of online discourse by Twitter warriors, but it hurts her with voters very little because… it feels like a lazy, and at this point, boring attack line.”
Mausser, the NYC DSA co-chair, said consultants who continue to fear the “socialist” label are missing the point of the “blue tsunami” in the most recent election.
“Of course, not everyone in that tsunami identified as a socialist, but the top line of all Democratic messaging was about affordability, which is something that Zohran put into the zeitgeist,” she said. “And if people can't update their expectations about what that means, I think they may not be successful political consultants for much longer.”

https://gothamist.com/news/federal-gover.title: Federal government claims control of Newark Housing Authority
https://gothamist.com/news/federal-gover.author: Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/federal-gover.text:
The Trump administration has taken over the Newark Housing Authority, according to a letter posted to the homepage of the authority’s website and later confirmed by its executive director.
The letter posted by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development said the largest public housing authority in the state had failed to “attain specific occupancy targets” and to “improve financial performance,” but provided no further specifics as to how the authority fell short.
There was no public announcement of the move outside of the letter and federal officials did not respond to questions Thursday night.
The Newark Housing Authority operates 44 housing developments around the city.
According to the letter dated Thursday from HUD Assistant Secretary Benjamin Hobbs to the leaders of the Newark Housing Authority, federal authorities had issued a final determination of substantial default for breaching the terms of a 2024 agreement between HUD and the authority.
HUD wrote that it warned the authority of its findings in two separate letters, dated Sept. 22 and Nov 5. While the local authority responded, the federal agency said the responses were insufficient.
“NHA has not taken good faith efforts to substantially improve,” Hobbs wrote in Thursday’s letter. “HUD considered NHA's reported progress and claimed corrective efforts before determining whether further action is warranted. Those efforts do not outweigh the continued failure to meet benchmarks that NHA itself agreed to over two years ago.”
Neither HUD nor Mayor Ras Baraka’s office immediately responded to requests for comment.
As part of the takeover, HUD dismissed the authority's entire board of commissioners. The Newark Housing Authority’s website had been updated on Thursday night to show that responsibilities of the board had been transferred to two officials in HUD’s Office of Public and Indian Housing: Deputy Assistant Secretary Shylon Ferry and Associate Deputy Assistant Secretary Daniel Sherrod.
A Newark Housing Authority board meeting scheduled for Friday has been cancelled, according to a notice posted on the authority’s website.
“NHA's day-to-day operations and resident services will continue as usual under HUD oversight,” the notice read.
