https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: Take me to the fatberg! The £437m new Museum of London is an astonishing sight
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Oliver Wainwright
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
‘All the grit and the glitters,” trumpets a big illuminated sign on the roof of the old Smithfield general market, beaming out as if advertising a raunchy burlesque show. It is the jazzy tagline of the new-look London Museum, which has gone from being marooned on a roundabout in an armpit of the City to taking over this prime Victorian market complex, following an arduous decade-long transformation.
The slogan is fitting for a museum that displays everything from priceless Tudor jewels to a lump of congealed fat and rags dredged from a Whitechapel sewer. Just as the colossal fatberg was scraped from the murky depths, so has the former market hall (and its extensive warren of basement vaults) been meticulously scoured and scrubbed up. London’s centre of butchery for 800 years, which Charles Dickens found “all asmear with filth and fat and blood and foam”, has been lavished with a £437m glow-up, reborn to tell the story of the capital in all its gritty, glittery glory. And the finished result is an astonishing sight.
It may be hard to remember now just how off-putting the museum’s previous home was. Since 1976, it had been imprisoned in a windowless brick bastion, throttled by traffic and accessed by a couple of elevated bridges, like a fortified keep. “We still got 700,000 visitors a year,” says Alec Shaw, director of transformation. “But they wouldn’t come back.” It was a dingy ordeal, somewhere you went because your school dragged you there, not for the active pleasure of spending time.
Now it is hoped people will drift in off the street, possibly without even knowing they’re entering a museum. “We’re essentially wrapped with 250 metres of high street,” says Asif Khan, one of the architects involved, alongside Stanton Williams and conservation specialists, Julian Harrap Architects. The 44 shop units that used to ring the market, where grocers and butchers hawked their wares to the street, have been converted into 12 outward-facing “houses” for the museum and its partner organisations, “making it more like a coral reef than a singular organism”, says Khan. Encrusted with these retail barnacles, which will range from cafes and pubs to galleries and shops, the museum hopes to lure in passersby who might never have thought of going.
Inside, they will find a place that is light years from the city museum stereotype of a dusty, fusty repository. Opened in 1883, the general market was the last of Smithfield’s three market halls designed by City architect Horace Jones, also the author of Tower Bridge. Jones concocted a dazzling cathedral of commerce: a majestic dome rises above the vast former market hall, where decorative iron “phoenix columns” support a lattice of trusses that hold up a roof of vaulted skylights.
Around the edges, dilapidated shops have been stripped away to reveal the building’s raw brick shell, with iron fireplaces left hanging surreally halfway up the walls. The former shop of James Burden Ltd, purveyors of premium meat, now houses a stepped theatre for educational programmes. Another unit has become the museum store, where the wares of London artisans will be on sale.
In every nook, historic architectural details have been lovingly preserved, making the building itself, and its accrued layers of history, a prime exhibit. Bucketloads of fragments in the museum’s collection – known as “bulk archaeology” – have even been cast into the polished concrete floor, forming a sort of archaeological terrazzo from bits of old pots, pipes and tiles. “It’s a gesture to our primordial reflex to dig, to find,” says Paul Williams, co-founder of Stanton Williams. Kids will love searching for curious fragments.
 
Thirteen displays are scattered around the perimeter of the main hall, loosely themed around “Our Time”. Topics range from greyhound racing – there’s a rotating “totalisator” contraption used to calculate betting odds at Harringay Stadium – to an altar of shop signs, where the likes of Morley’s fried chicken and Topshop glow like neon relics of the British high street. A stack of hefty speakers teeters in one corner, dedicated to carnival sound system culture. Shaw promises the space will come alive with DJs on Friday and Saturday nights, when the museum will open until midnight.
In tune with the neighbourhood’s 24-hour culture, it will open again at 7am with a ring of the last bell to be cast in the Whitechapel foundry , just as the meat market traders clock off next door, and revellers stagger out of Fabric night club, perhaps accidentally stumbling into the museum on their way home.
“We will be flowing out on to the streets and going right into the night,” says museum director Sharon Ament, who wants it to retain the energy and bustle of a market. With at least four entrances and no ticketing or bag checks, it is aiming to redefine how a museum meets the surrounding city, as a truly porous public place. “You might even slip on a piece of old chicken skin on the way,” she adds, “and we love that.”
 
The main former market hall feels quite sparse (left empty with corporate hire in mind) but its sheer scale means that pleasingly chunky objects can be displayed. Syd’s coffee stall, a century-old east London institution run by three generations, stands on one side, near an Italian knife-grinding van parked precipitously up on a mezzanine balcony. Syd’s, which will serve tea on Tuesday afternoons, was donated by the family on the proviso that it wouldn’t be used to serve “posh coffee”. It makes a refreshingly earthy foil to Clerk’s House, the museum’s restaurant, where you can dine on a Smithfield chop for £34.
The hall feels as if it will be a lively place to loiter, with the energy of a station concourse, but the main event is buried underground. A cut in the floor leads visitors down, past theatrical layers of pigmented concrete suggesting sedimentary earth, to the stygian realm of “Past Time”. Here, in the atmospheric former goods depot, the museum’s trove of 5,000 objects are displayed in five loosely chronological chapters, charting London’s 2,000 year history from Roman Londinium to the fatberg.
Designed by Atelier Brückner, it is a well-paced romp through neolithic axes, medieval glassware, royal robes and rock guitars, culminating in the museum’s most startling feature. At the far end of the vaults, a big picture window opens on to a tunnel where you can marvel at the Thameslink trains swooshing by. Few museums have ever managed to convey the thrill of infrastructure quite so viscerally. Delight in the startled shock of commuters as they see your ghostly face peering back at them from the shadows.
It goes on and on. (Shaw estimates it would take eight hours to see everything.) A series of side rooms, like chapels along a nave, contain displays dedicated to Roman mosaics, the Great Fire, women’s suffrage, and the Cheapside Hoard, a bounty of Elizabethan and Jacobean jewellery discovered in 1912.
Along the way, the museum made some momentous discoveries of its own. A set of vaulted chambers was uncovered, which will become an additional exhibition space set to open next year with items from the Bloomberg collection, which were found during construction of the megalithic media company’s HQ. Back upstairs, one of the shop units was revealed to contain a miraculously intact tiled interior of Lockhart’s Cocoa Rooms, a temperance movement cafe from 1875. It will operate as another living exhibit, serving hot chocolate late into the night – a touch of Victorian abstinence fitting for gen Z’s sober social habits.
These discoveries, along with Covid and inflation, are part of the reason the project budget rocketed from an initial £150m, as the scope grew ever larger. A second phase is now under way, due in 2028, which will see the neighbouring 1960s poultry market transformed with conservation labs, open collection storage and a large temporary exhibition space beneath Ove Arup’s soaring concrete dome. As Williams notes, wholesale markets make ideal venues for museums: “Where else in London could you find a world-class exhibition space,” he asks, “with a loading bay purpose-made for articulated lorries?”
The project is one of the most accomplished and complex transformations of an existing building the capital has seen, but it almost didn’t happen – twice. Behind all the grit and glitter is the fact that this magisterial complex almost became a soulless office development, as so tragically happened to the bulk of Spitalfields market in the early 2000s at the hands of Norman Foster. Save Britain’s Heritage (SBH) fought two public inquiries, with English Heritage in 2007 and the Victorian Society in 2014, against the City of London Corporation, which would have happily seen most of the market bulldozed for offices in the name of growth.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Mexico to try ‘El Chapo Isidro’ despite US extradition request
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Mexico to try ‘El Chapo Isidro’ despite US extradition request
Fausto Meza Flores faces drug trafficking and weapons charges after his capture in a violent Sinaloa operation.
Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, an alleged cartel leader known as “El Chapo Isidro”, will be tried in Mexico despite an extradition request by the US, in a move that could worsen already-strained relations between the two countries.
Attorney General Ernestina Godoy told reporters on Monday that Mexican authorities “are going to put him on trial in this country”.
Meza Flores, one of the FBI’s 10 most wanted fugitives, was captured after an hours-long firefight between Mexican forces and cartel gunmen on Friday at a compound in Guasave, in the northwestern state of Sinaloa. He was flown to Mexico City the following day.
He faces local charges for weapons offences and methamphetamine possession with intent to sell.
US involvement
Earlier on Monday, Security Minister Omar Garcia Harfuch said Washington had requested Meza Flores’s extradition after his capture in the northern state of Sinaloa.
President Claudia Sheinbaum said US authorities provided intelligence support but did not participate directly on the ground.
US surveillance drones were authorised to help track Meza Flores before the raid, authorities added, despite sensitivities over US anti-drug operations in the country in recent months.
Four Mexican soldiers and 16 alleged cartel gunmen were killed in the overnight operation, according to the Mexican Secretariat of National Defence.
Meza Flores is accused by US authorities of leading a major trafficking network that moved heroin, cocaine, methamphetamine, marijuana and fentanyl across the border.
The US Department of Justice said he faces six charges in the US that include running a continuing criminal enterprise, narcoterrorism, money laundering conspiracy and weapons offences.
His arrest is the latest in a series of high-profile anti-cartel operations by Mexico, including the February killing of Nemesio “El Mencho” Oseguera, as US President Donald ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌Trump presses ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌the Sheinbaum government to crack down on organised crime.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120407.title: Antifaschismus | Brandanschlag und Grablichter
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120407.author: Andreas Fritsche
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120407.text:
- Berlin
- Antifaschismus
Brandanschlag und Grablichter
Brandenburger Aktionsbündnis gegen Gewalt, Rechtsextremismus und Rassismus veröffentlicht Broschüre »Rechtsextrem, mittendrin«.
In Alt Zauche-Wußwerk bei Lübben hat es in der Nacht zum Sonntag gebrannt. Offenbar nicht zufällig hat es den Verein Freiwald getroffen, denn die Feuerwehr geht von Brandstiftung aus. Wie die Initiative Sichere Orte Südbrandenburg am Montag mitteilte, bemerkte Vereinsgeschäftsführerin Shan Metz die Flammen gegen 19 Uhr und konnte diese mit zwei beherzt helfenden Passanten bis zum Eintreffen der Feuerwehr in Schach halten. So hält sich der Schaden glücklicherweise in Grenzen. »Nur der Vorrat an Brennholz ist ausgerechnet jetzt, wo die kalte Jahreszeit vor der Tür steht, verbrannt oder klitschnass«, erklärt der Verein. Außerdem musste Metz, die als Antifaschistin bekannt ist, wegen eingeatmeter Rauchgase in der Notaufnahme behandelt werden.
Dem mutmaßlichen Brandanschlag soll eine verbale Auseinandersetzung mit jugendlichen AfD-Anhängern auf Instagram vorausgegangen sein. »Ein Zusammenhang ist naheliegend, aber zurzeit noch nicht nachgewiesen«, heißt es. Der Verein, der sich für den klimagerechten Waldumbau einsetzt, will sich nicht einschüchtern lassen. »Wir pflanzen weiter.«
»Rechtsextremismus ist eines der drängendsten Probleme in Brandenburg«, sagt Thomas Wisch. Er ist Vorsitzender des brandenburgischen Aktionsbündnisses gegen Gewalt, Rechtsextremismus und Rassismus. Regelmäßig gebe es antidemokratische Stimmungsmache und populistische Lügenkampagnen auf der Straße, im Internet und im Parlament, sagt Wisch. »Und es bleibt nicht bei Worten. Seit Jahren nimmt die Zahl rechtsextremer Gewalttaten in Brandenburg zu.« Fast täglich komme es zu einem Angriff.
So schildert Wisch die Lage im Vorwort der neuen Broschüre »Rechtsaußen, mittendrin«, in der sein Aktionsbündnis darüber aufklärt, was hinter Kampagnen von Rechtsextremisten steckt. »Ehrenamtliche Initiativen und professionelle Verbände sind zum Ziel verleumderischer parlamentarischer Anfragen geworden«, schreibt Wisch. »Einzelne Aktive werden sogar persönlich bedroht.«
Wisch erläutert, dass rechte Strategien nicht zufällig entstehen. Er spricht von erprobten Methoden, demokratische Strukturen anzugreifen, Menschen einzuschüchtern und gesellschaftliche Konflikte zu verschärfen. »Wenn wir uns diese Vorgehensweisen vor Augen führen, können wir die dahinterliegenden Absichten früher erkennen und ihnen gezielt entgegentreten. Dazu soll unsere Broschüre einen Beitrag leisten.«
Ein Kapitel ist dem Friedhof in Halbe gewidmet. Dort sind fast 30.000 Soldaten und Zivilisten beigesetzt, die kurz vor Ende des Zweiten Weltkriegs in einer Kesselschlacht vor den Toren Berlins ums Leben kamen. Seit 1991 erlebte der Ort im Landkreis Dahme-Spreewald Aufmärsche von Neonazis, die zum sogenannten Heldengedenken kamen. Später gründete sich ein Aktionsbündnis Halbe, das dagegenhielt. Auch änderte das Land Brandenburg 2006 extra sein Versammlungsgesetz. So konnten große Aufmärsche am Soldatenfriedhof nicht mehr stattfinden.
Zum Jahreswechsel 2024/2025 sind dann aber unzählige Grablichter aufgestellt worden. Allerdings konnte diese Aktion nach einer Änderung der Friedhofsordnung ein Jahr später nicht wiederholt werden. Dennoch ist Arnold Mosshammer vom Aktionsbündnis Halbe überzeugt, dass der Soldatenfriedhof künftig wieder verstärkt in den Fokus der extremen Rechten rücken werde. Die Broschüre zitiert Mosshammer: »Die AfD agiert geschickter als frühere Parteien wie NPD und DVU.«
Ein anderes Kapitel befasst sich mit einem Bürgerbegehren gegen ein Asylheim in Prenzlau, maßgeblich vorangetrieben von dem AfD-Landtagsabgeordneten Felix Teichner. Thema sind außerdem Neonazis, die gegen den Christopher Street Day in Bernau mobil machten, und anderes mehr. So findet auch die Initiative Sichere Orte Südbrandenburg Erwähnung, die sich nach einer Serie von Anschlägen in Cottbus und Umgebung gebildet hat.
Sich Räume nicht nehmen lassen und Haltung zeigen, empfiehlt das Aktionsbündnis gegen Gewalt, Rechtsextremismus und Rassismus. Es gebe nicht die eine perfekte Strategie. »Wichtig ist, Konzepte auszuprobieren und auch gelegentliche Misserfolge in Kauf zu nehmen, solange man aktiv bleibt und aus Erfahrungen lernt.«
Die Broschüre »Rechtsaußen, mittendrin« kann im Internet kostenlos heruntergeladen werden: www.aktionsbuendnis-brandenburg.de/produkt/rechtsaussen-mittendrin
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Butt of the joke: Trump impersonator mocks president at Canada press dinner
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Leyland Cecco in Toronto
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, was joined on stage in Ottawa by a Donald Trump impersonator who mocked the US president to raucous laughter from a crowd of politicians and journalists at a parliamentary press gallery dinner on Saturday.
With coiffed hair and an ill-fitting suit, comedian Mark Critch – who portrays the president on the sketch show This Hour Has 22 Minutes – danced on to the stage and lampooned the trade war Trump started as well as the president’s threats to annex Canada.
“We’re going to have a great deal,” Critch said, channeling Trump’s distinct mannerisms. “There’s only one thing standing in the way: me, because I’m crazy.”
The fake Trump continued that he was “so popular we just had a big, blue wave”, a reference to the Democratic rout of Republicans in this month’s US midterm elections.
He also mocked Trump’s frequent mentions of other men’s physiques, saying of the comedian Mark McKinney, who was portraying Carney, that he had “a great ass – doesn’t he? What a beautiful ass, he’s got such an incredible ass.”
He earned the most laughter of his short appearance for saying of Carney: “I don’t call him the governor to his face, because I’m a coward”. The real Trump has frequently attempted to insult Canada’s leaders by calling them governor, not prime minister, suggesting Canada is a US state.
The annual dinner, attended by media, political leaders and lobbyists, is often defined by carefully written jokes by the staff of party leaders.
Throughout his own 16-minute set, Carney poked fun at his political rivals, the media and the US president.
At one point, he remarked: “Damn, this is a tough room, and I’ve been in the Oval Office. Alone. With its new interior decorator.”
Clips of the dinner, including the crowd laughing at the president, have circulated widely on US media.
The newly appointed governor general, Louise Arbour, also gave a speech, including a nod to the prime minister’s decision to travel extensively around the globe.
“Our prime minister is already getting a lot of attention. Actually, I heard a guy the other day compare him to God. Now seriously, do you know the difference between God and Mark Carney? God is everywhere, and Mark Carney is everywhere except in Ottawa where he’s supposed to be,” she said.
The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, also used the evening to poke fun at his own reputation.
“Some say that Mark has a controlling leadership style. There’s been reports that he yells and micromanages his staff. He acts like a miserable prick to journalists,” he said. “And when I hear things like that, I say once again, he’s stealing all my ideas.”
He attracted a stunned silence, however, for alluding to Justin Trudeau’s relationship with Katy Perry, saying, “Trudeau is running around the world doing to a faded pop princess what he did to Canada” while prime minister, a remark that was widely criticised as demeaning to the pop star.
The New Democratic party leader, Avi Lewis, who has not yet won a seat in parliament, took a shot at Carney’s early exit from the event, as well his own party’s dismal standings. “I do not have a seat in the House of Commons, but when I am given one at dinner, I stay there all night long,” he said.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120407.title: Bildungspolitik | Neue GEW-Chefin: »Mit einer AfD-Regierung käme viel obendrauf«
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120407.author: Hendrik Lasch
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120407.text:
- Politik
- Bildungspolitik
Neue GEW-Chefin: »Mit einer AfD-Regierung käme viel obendrauf«
Die linke Ex-Abgeordnete Kristin Heiß führt die Bildungsgewerkschaft in Sachsen-Anhalt, wo an den Schulen ein tiefgreifender Umbruch droht.
Kristin Heiß ist die vierte Landesvorsitzende der GEW in Sachsen-Anhalt seit 1990, und vieles spricht dafür, dass sie diejenige ist, auf die der schwierigste Job wartet. »Mit einer möglichen AfD-Regierung käme auf die vielen Themen, die uns als Bildungsgewerkschaft beschäftigen, ordentlich was obendrauf«, sagt die 43-Jährige, die bei einer Landesdelegiertenversammlung am Wochenende mit einer klaren Mehrheit von 90 Prozent zur Nachfolgerin von Eva Gerth gewählt wurde. Diese hatte den Landesvorsitz zehn Jahre lang inne. Bis März wird sie noch unterstützend an der Seite der neuen Vorsitzenden stehen, um einen nahtlosen Übergang zu gewährleisten.
Heiß ist die erste GEW-Landeschefin, die nicht zuvor als Lehrerin gearbeitet hat. Sie kehre mit der Wahl allerdings gewissermaßen »zu meinen Wurzeln zurück«, sagt sie. Nach dem Studium in Politikwissenschaften und Soziologie war sie ab 2009 drei Jahre lang Organisationssekretärin bei der GEW, bevor sie zunächst als Referentin im SPD-geführten Ministerium für Arbeit und Soziales arbeitete und später in den Landtag wechselte. Dort gehörte sie von 2016 bis 2021 und dann wieder ab 2024 bis zur Wahl im September der Linksfraktion an und profilierte sich als deren Expertin für Finanzen. Während der zweijährigen Unterbrechung war sie im Bildungsministerium tätig. Jetzt geht sie quasi den umgekehrten Weg ihres Vor-Vorgängers: Thomas Lippmann war von 1998 bis 2016 GEW-Chef, bevor er für die Linke in den Landtag einzog und dort zeitweise auch die Fraktion führte; Heiß kommt von der Linken auf den Chefposten der Gewerkschaft.
Dieser ist auch in anderen Bundesländern anspruchsvoll. »Es gibt unzählige Themen, die gar nichts mit der AfD zu tun haben«, sagt Heiß und zählt auf: Lehrermangel und Debatten um die Arbeitszeiten an Schulen; die Frage, wie in den Kitas auch angesichts sinkender Kinderzahlen ein Personalabbau vermieden werden könnte; befristete und prekäre Arbeitsverhältnisse in der Wissenschaft und die Novellierung des Bafög; eine mangelhafte Ausstattung der Jugendhilfe.
Dazu kämen freilich viele weitere Baustellen, sollte die AfD ab Dezember in dem Bundesland erstmals den Ministerpräsidenten stellen und eine Landesregierung bilden können. Die als gesichert rechtsextrem eingestufte Partei hat in ihrem »Regierungsprogramm« einen grundlegenden Umbau des Schulwesens angekündigt. Geplant ist etwa ein Angriff auf die Mitbestimmung. Schule sei neben Militär und Wirtschaft einer der Bereiche, wo »demokratische Mitbestimmung fehl am Platz« sei, heißt es in dem Programm. Auch bei den Unterrichtsmethoden droht ein konservativer Rollback. Der Inklusion wurde der Kampf angesagt. Das Programm »Schule gegen Rassismus« soll abgeschafft, stattdessen vor Schulen die Bundesflagge aufgezogen und bei Veranstaltungen die Nationalhymne gesungen werden.
Zu den Kernanliegen der AfD gehört es, politische Meinungsäußerungen von Lehrkräften zu unterbinden. Sie will das im Beutelsbacher Konsens verankerte Indoktrinationsverbot durch ein »politisches Neutralitätsgebot« ersetzen, mit dem es Lehrern untersagt würde, sich mit einer eigenen Position an politischen Diskussionen zu beteiligen. Die Debatte läuft im Land bereits. Unlängst hatte ein Fall aus der Altmark für bundesweite Schlagzeilen gesorgt. Dort hatte ein Lehrer im Zusammenhang mit Äußerungen über die AfD vom Landesschulamt eine Abmahnung erhalten. Kurz vor einem Gerichtstermin wurde diese indes aus der Personalakte entfernt.
Heiß bedauert das: »Wir hätten uns eine gerichtliche Klärung gewünscht, um Sicherheit für die Kolleginnen und Kollegen zu bekommen.« Generell sei die Verunsicherung in der Lehrerschaft nicht nur bei diesem Thema groß. »Wir verzeichnen eine Rekordzahl von Anfragen bei der GEW-Rechtsberatung«, sagt Heiß. Um diese bewältigen zu können, wird die Stelle mit Unterstützung des Bundesvorstands um einen Juristen und einen Sachbearbeiter aufgestockt – womöglich auch in der Erwartung, dass viele der Konflikte früher oder später auch in anderen Bundesländern drohen. »Wir sind wohl leider negative Spitzenreiter«, sagt die neue GEW-Landeschefin.
Die Gewerkschaft sucht die Lehrkräfte in Sachsen-Anhalt dafür bestmöglich zu wappnen. Kürzlich wurde eine »Überlebensfibel« aufgelegt. Sie solle, erklärt die GEW, »Klarheit schaffen, wo Verunsicherung durch politische Ankündigungen, Ministeriumserlasse oder dienstliche Weisungen entsteht«. Die Broschüre, die stark nachgefragt wird, gibt Antworten auf 40 Fragen, von Meinungsfreiheit bis zu politisch motivierten Sanktionen, und nennt mögliche Gegenmaßnahmen.
In vorderster Reihe führen müssen wird die Auseinandersetzungen die neue GEW-Landeschefin. Inzwischen gibt es auch Spekulationen darüber, wer ihr direkter Gegenüber in der Landesregierung sein könnte. Nach Informationen von Table Briefings will die AfD ihren Landeschef Martin Reichhardt zum Kultusminister machen. Er hatte bis 1996 ein Pädagogik-Studium an der Bundeswehruniversität absolviert, war dann Offizier und sitzt derzeit im Bundestag.
Reichardt gehört zu den besonders radikalen Vertretern in der AfD und sorgte zuletzt nicht nur durch ein Foto für Aufsehen, das ihn mit einer Geste zeigt, die als Hitlergruß zu deuten ist. Er fällt auch immer wieder durch verbale Entgleisungen auf. Zuletzt beschimpfte er die Presse als »Propagandaknechte« und die Muttersprache als »aufgedunsenes, intersektional-feministisches Flittchen«. Derlei Wortwahl finde sie befremdlich, sagt GEW-Chefin Kristin Heiß, die generell erwartet, mit Reichardt als Minister »werden wir uns festhalten müssen«.
Bangemachen allerdings gilt nicht. In der Gewerkschaft selbst registriert Heiß sogar »Aufbruchstimmung«. Die aktuelle politische Entwicklung führe zwar dazu, dass für progressive Positionen »das Feld enger wird«, bewirke aber auch, dass sich mehr Menschen engagieren wollten. Dabei gehe es um Widerstand gegen den Rechtsruck, aber nicht nur, betont die Gewerkschafterin. »Wir drehen uns nicht die ganze Zeit um die AfD.«
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.title: We vetted thousands of early Black Friday deals to find 42 worth pouncing on
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.author: Filter Writers

It’s almost Thanksgiving. That means early Black Friday deals are already here, a consolation prize for the full price you probably paid for your flight home.
 
With thousands of new sales popping up every day, our pro product testers are already hard at work combing through them to find the true deals actually worth your time.
 
Here are our favorite sales that you can buy before the Macy’s parade, across categories from tech to beauty.
 
To stay up to date on new deals, bookmark this page, as we’ll add new Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales throughout the next week.
- Visit our ultimate guide to Black Friday for more deals, carefully vetted and curated by Filter US editors
   
Kitchen
Magnifique Glass Air Fryer
In our review of Magnifique’s combo air fryer, we loved its glass construction, which does away with the usual nonstick-coated basket. This handsome standalone air fryer uses the same appealing materials, and at $128, it’s enjoying its biggest sale since launch. Karen Yuan
Stasher Reusable Stretch Lids
Our editors love these stretchy silicone lids for covering everything from bowls of soup and salad to opened drink cans. They’re durable, safe to pop in the dishwasher and endlessly useful. At 35% off, now’s a great time to stock up (right before the holiday leftover crush). Karen Yuan
 
  
The Pink Stuff Miracle Cleaning Paste 
 
This cult-favorite pink paste is a superhero for tackling stubborn kitchen grime, from greasy stovetops to stained sinks. It’ll get at your bathroom grout, too. At just $4, it’s a satisfyingly cheap cleaning upgrade. Karen Yuan
Le Creuset Signature Round Wide Dutch Oven
We love a Le Creuset deal, especially when it involves this gorgeous lavender-hued Dutch oven. It’s perfect for searing, braising and simmering, and Sur La Table’s exclusive Provence shade is particularly pretty. It makes a great gift, too. Karen Yuan
Anyday Anydeli Mixed Set
We’re huge fans of Anyday’s colorful, leak-resistant silicone containers, which make storing and reheating leftovers a breeze. They’re microwave-, freezer- and dishwasher-safe, and this six-pack is now at its lowest price ever. Read our full rave review. Karen Yuan
Sleep
Mzoo Sleep Mask
This Mzoo is the top pick in our Best Sleep Masks guide. Filter reviewer Juno DeMelo called it “the Goldilocks of masks,” noting it effectively blocked light without slipping throughout the night. Lauren Gould
Loop Quiet 2 Earplugs
$20 $25 at Amazon, Loop (with code PROMO-26VIP)
These earplugs were one of our top recommendations for achieving a better night’s rest. We love their comfortable fit and that they come in four sizes to accommodate multiple ear shapes. Lauren Gould
Cozy Earth Bamboo Pajamas

Reviewer Juno DeMelo slept with four popular models in our Best Bluetooth Sleep Masks guide and left impressed by the Manta’s design. “Slidable tabs on either side of the strap make it easy to adjust the position of the speakers, and you can also adjust the position of the eye cups,” she wrote. Lauren Gould
Coop Adjustable Pillow

It comes with memory foam cubes to adjust to your liking, and its medium firmness will suit most sleepers. It’s also beloved by our writer, Kori Perten, who remained loyal to Coop’s adjustable model after testing other options from Coop. Lauren Gould
Home
Dyson V15 Detect cordless vacuum
$600 $850 at Amazon, Walmart, Dyson
How do you know when you’ve missed a spot? The Dyson V15 Detect uses an angled green laser that illuminates fine dust and dirt on hardwood floors. A swappable battery eliminates a common point of failure for many cordless vacuums. Filter US editor Jeffrey Van Camp has had his for two years and swears by it. $600 is about the floor for its pricing over the past few years. Jon Chan
Bissell Little Green Mini portable carpet cleaner
This small but mighty carpet cleaner has a cult following, and after using it, we can see why. It’s powerful for its exceptionally compact size, and easy to use. When you’re done the hose wraps around the Little Green’s body, and it stands just over 12 inches tall, making it easy to store in the back of a closet, under a sink or even in a car trunk. Jon Chan
 
  
Samsung Bespoke French door fridge
This capacious French door fridge is perfect for anyone who loves hosting. The FlexZone drawer is a separate area with independent temperature controls that can be set to anywhere from extra cold for additional freezer space to just chilly enough for a refreshing drink. Speaking of drinks, it can also produce spherical ice, ideal for keeping cocktails cold without watering them down, and a built-in water pitcher that refills itself with filtered water. Jon Chan
Frontgate Resort Collection bath towels
Everyone owns towels, but these exceptionally plush ones are a great way to add a little luxury to your daily routine. When I tested 16 different models to find the Best Bath Towels, I praised these for their lightweight feel and high absorbency. Giving them as a gift? They come in 28 different colors, and for $16, you can personalize them with a monogram. Jon Chan
Adjustable heavy-duty metal shelving unit
Stop putting off organizing your garage or basement with this exceptionally low price on heavy-duty steel shelving from Lowe’s. Powder coating and smooth, machined edges prevent the unit from rusting and from scratching boxes (or your hands). In our experience, a boltless design translates to a quick assembly and allows you to adjust the height of all five shelves without much hassle. Jon Chan

Travel

Whenever I’m asked about the Best Carry-On Suitcases, I always recommend the Away Bigger Carry-On Flex, particularly for overpackers. It’s roomy, durable, and always passes the sit-and-zip test whenever I’ve gone overboard with clothes. Go for the bright colorways and you’ll never lose it in a crowd. While I’d happily pay full price for this specific carry-on, it’s currently 25% off, which saves you nearly $100. Lydia Mansel
Trtl Pillow Plus
I’ve been on eight flights more than 15 hours long this year alone, so I know a thing or two about in-flight essentials. The Trtl Pillow Plus is, hands down, my must-have for any red-eye. The adjustable built-in neck support system means I wake up pain-free, even after nodding off for a full eight hours of sleep. Lydia Mansel
Bellroy Lite Travel Pack 30L Carry-On Travel Backpack
Named one of the best personal-item backpacks by The Filter US team, the Bellroy Lite Travel Pack 30L Carry-On Travel Backpack is the definition of a frequent-flier essential. It may be compact, but it doesn’t skimp on function, with loads of exterior and interior pockets, built-in packing cells, and a separate pocket that fits a 16-inch laptop. Lydia Mansel

Compression socks are another accessory I won’t hop on a long-haul flight without. While I was skeptical of them at first, my legs and feet feel infinitely fresher after I get off the plane, and I don’t feel as restless while I’m in my seat. These Comrad compression socks, which provide 15-20 mmHg compression, were named the best compression socks for travel by The Filter US — so grab them while they’re on sale. Lydia Mansel

AirTags are the perfect gift for the traveler in your life, but I’d also snag a few for yourself while this four-pack is $20 off. Put one in your suitcase, your wallet, and your purse. The next time your luggage goes missing, or you misplace your wallet, all you have to do is open up the Find My app on your iPhone. You’ll be able to instantly track down their respective locations. Lydia Mansel

The Guardian’s tech editor Samuel Gibbs called these the “best-sounding Beats yet” in his four-star review, and this is the lowest price we’ve ever seen for them. They last up to 40 hours per charge, and offer premium features like lossless USB-C audio, plus Apple perks like one-touch pairing and built-in Find My feature. Quentyn Kennemer

A full Sonos wireless speaker system can cost thousands, but the Sonos Ray is an affordable starter with many of the same perks. Our Guardian reviewer gave it five stars, and said it delivers “top-quality audio for a serious TV sound upgrade” and it’s satisfyingly loud for its compact size. This is the lowest price we’ve seen it, matching its 2025 holiday discount. Quentyn Kennemer
Life360 Tile Bluetooth tracker (4-pack)
Apple AirTags only work with Apple devices, but our tech experts say “Tile trackers are the next best thing” for Android users who need help locating everyday items. These let you view their last known location on your phone and can make a sound within a reasonable distance. Each tracker has a key ring for attaching to your bag. If you use iPhone, AirTags are also $23 on Amazon, about as cheap as they’ve ever been. Quentyn Kennemer
Amazon Kindle Scribe, 32GB
It’s pricey even with this historically low discount, but the Scribe should last many years. It holds thousands of ebooks, Kindle or otherwise, and lets you write notes within those books or on empty pages in a digital notebooks. “The writing experience on the Scribe is shockingly good,” wrote the Guardian’s tech editor Samuel Gibbs in our Kindle Scribe review. To him, it felt like the closest thing to writing on actual paper. To learn about e-readers, check out our Best ebook readers guide. Quentyn Kennemer
Blink Outdoor 4 (2 Cameras with Doorbell 2K+)
This home security starter kit (a favorite of Filter US tech writer Adam Doud) is back down to an all-time low price. It includes two battery-powered Blink Outdoor 4 security cameras, plus a video doorbell that can detect people, packages and vehicles. (Some features require an optional subscription.) Each camera records up to 2K resolution, can survive in various weather conditions and lasts months on standard AA batteries. Quentyn Kennemer
Outdoors
Kelty Love Seat camping chair
This roomy two-person camp chair got a shout out in our list of thoughtful wedding gifts.. Filter US Reviewer Paige Triola likes this Kelty bestseller for marshmallow roasting by the campfire and backyard get-togethers. If you’re a fan of the brand, there are many other Kelty products discounted this week. For more chair ideas, we also have a Best camping chairs guide (we may add this model in a future update). Paige Triola.
Merach T12 Foldable Treadmill
Filter US reviewer Paige Triola says this compact, reasonably priced treadmill is a gamechanger for her home gym setup: “Owning a treadmill felt like an unattainable dream because of the size and cost – this model solves both of those problems.” The running platform folds up when not in use, making it ideal for small spaces. Paige Triola
BucketGolf 9 Hole Family Bundle
$170 $210 at BucketGolf, $169 200 at Amazon
This outdoor game is a fun alternative to standard lawn games like cornhole or horseshoes. Filter US Reviewer Paige Triola gifted it to her mother-in-law, an avid golfer, and found it to be a family-friendly activity that gets everyone out of the house. This is the lowest price it will be during the holidays. Paige Triola
Osprey Daylite Wheeled Duffel 115 bag
$243 $325 at Amazon, $243 $325 at Osprey
In our gift ideas for skiers guide, Filter US Reviewer Paige Triola liked the Daylite 26+6 backpack for holding extra gear, but she also uses the matching Daylite Wheeled Duffel for adventure travel. Lightweight and sturdy, this rolling duffel is collapsible, allowing it to be easily stored when not in use. This discount started in September, but it’s still a remarkably good deal for a bag that was $325 all year before that, and $295 last year. Paige Triola
Novaa Light Pad red LED light therapy pad
As noted in our Essential exercise products guide, this red light pad uses 216 medical-grade LEDs to aid your workout recovery. I reported noticeably less aches and inflammation when doing 20-minute Novaa Light Pad sessions after exercise. This is the lowest price we’ve seen on it this year. To learn more about red light therapy, read our red light explainer. Paige Triola
Beauty
 
***
 
MediHeal Hyaluronic Acid sheet mask 10-pack
I’ve never met a MediHeal sheet mask I didn’t like, and this simple moisturizing hyaluronic acid one is a good place to start. I keep these sheet masks in my fridge to de-puff, and they give my skin the perfect smooth base for my makeup. Carolin Lehmann
Farmacy Green Clean cleansing balm
This is probably my favorite makeup remover. It melts off makeup incredibly well (no raccoon eyes) and doesn’t glob onto my contact lenses as some other cleansing balms do. It’s also great for melting off stubborn sunscreen. You can get 25% off all orders, and 30% off orders of $100 and more, at Farmacy through November 28. Carolin Lehmann
NuFace Trinity+ starter kit
It’s almost spooky how this FDA-cleared microcurrent facial sculpting device instantly lifts your face. I’ve had it used on me during a facial, and I came out looking good as new. Through 2 December, you can enjoy 30% off sitewide, 40% off $500 and more and 50% off $750 and more at NuFace. Carolin Lehmann
Kosas Air Brow
Kosas already has its Black Friday sale going on with 25% off site-wide. If you don’t know where to start with the brand, may I suggest the Air Brow? Tinted brow gels are so hard to get right, and this one is my favorite. It doesn’t over-deposit product, and it holds your brows in place. When I’m in a rush, this is all I’ll use on my brows. Carolin Lehmann
Fashion
Blank NYC Feeling Pretty floral quilted jacket
I own this adorable jacket, and it’s not only 50% off, but also part of Lulus’ buy one get one free sale. Blank NYC makes the most fun, high-quality coats, and this quilted fall option comes in a pretty vintage-inspired cream floral. Carolin Lehmann
Vici Chill Whispers contrast trim shearling jacket
This great sand colored zip-up is 30% off at Vici right now. Its contrast faux leather stitching looks super chic, and it’s been ideal for me to pop on during fall’s in-between weather. Carolin Lehmann
Paige Ronan top and Leenah wide-leg jean
Top: $168 $239 at Paige, Jean: $190 $269 at Paige
I received tons of compliments on this denim Paige set, which I wore on my birthday. It’s so flattering, and a matching set always makes you look like you have it all together. The jeans are great because they come in two lengths, plus they’re super soft and comfortable. Carolin Lehmann
FarmRio Coast Stars mini dress
This cheery 100% linen mini has teeny fish hanging off its ties and stunning embroidered scallops along the neckline. As the proud owner of this dress in another print, I can attest that Farm Rio never fails to overdeliver with the fun attention to detail. Carolin Lehmann
Ugg Classic Ultra Mini stitched boot
My Ugg minis are the classic version, but this on-sale stitched alternative is even cuter. These are so easy to throw on with any style of pants in the colder months, whether you’re running to Pilates or walking in snowy conditions. Carolin Lehmann
Retailer sale pages
If you want to browse more Black Friday 2026 deals yourself, the links below lead directly to each major retailer’s holiday deals homepage. Check out our many buying guides and holiday gift guides for more ideas.
How we choose the deals in this guide
We work for our readers, rather than the brands we write about. Every item we recommend is something a Filter editor or contributor has personally tested and can vouch for unless stated otherwise. On occasion, we may present a close substitute from the same brand and explain any differences from the original.
We scour competing retailers for the lowest prices on any item, and we use price-tracking tools such as Camelcamelcamel to check price history and ensure the discounts are truly good value, rather than a faux markdown. (So while we love sharing good deals, we also aren’t afraid to call out the unimpressive ones.)
Our mission at the Filter US
Our mission is to help you filter out junk products and buy fewer, better things.
At the Filter US, we test the products we recommend ourselves and never take your trust for granted. We also consider possible impacts on your health or the environment in our coverage and companies cannot purchase a spot in our product rankings because we are here to serve you, not corporations.
Our dedicated testing, editing and production teams are based across the United States and Canada. We are a part of the Guardian’s US editorial team and our journalists follow its strict ethical standards. Learn more about us here.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/pro-.title: The Year of the Pro-Palestine Super PAC
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/pro-.author: Akela Lacy
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/pro-.text:
The recent midterm election cycle marked by historic levels of pro-Israel spending saw an emerging trend that aimed to counter their influence: a new crop of pro-Palestine PACs.
Led by American Priorities PAC, which formed in January as part of an effort by donors, including supporters of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who opposed U.S. military support for Israel, a cadre of pro-Palestine organizations spent more than $14.4 million on races this cycle. Almost all of their candidates won.
“In the midst of the genocide, we felt compelled to push every lever and engage in every way possible to push candidates and the [Democratic] party to catch up to its base,” said Margaret DeReus, who leads the Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project and the Peace, Accountability, and Leadership political action committee, or PAL PAC. Both groups spent on pro-Palestine ads for the first time this cycle.
As DeReus and other leaders of the emergent pro-Palestine lobby told The Intercept, voters, especially Democratic ones, have become increasingly disillusioned with Israel and frustrated with politicians who support unchecked military aid to the country. “I don’t think there is an issue that I can think of where the party position, the mainstream party position, is so out of step with the base,” DeReus said.
The new pro-Palestine spending is a drop in the bucket compared to the more than $84 million the pro-Israel lobby poured into elections this cycle. AIPAC’s super PAC outspent pro-Palestine groups almost 6 to 1 — and that doesn’t include the more than $50 million AIPAC funneled directly to candidates. The pro-Palestine side may never match their opponents dollar for dollar.
“The point is, nobody has to outspend AIPAC,” said Beth Miller, political director at the advocacy group Jewish Voice for Peace Action. Her group doesn’t spend directly on elections and instead focuses on mobilizing anti-Zionist Jewish voters. “AIPAC is spending this much money because the message they are trying to force down voters’ throats is unpopular.”
The pro-Israel lobby long dominated the discourse on Israel policy before its flagship group, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, started spending directly on elections for the first time in the 2022 cycle. But as AIPAC and other pro-Israel groups find their brand growing increasingly toxic amid public outcry over U.S. military support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza, pro-Palestine money is shifting the terrain when it comes to election spending.
Simply put, Miller said, “Their message goes further because it’s popular.”
Whether the spending is for or against the pro-Israel lobby, it’s rare to see political ads that directly address U.S. policy toward Israel. For one thing, the topic can be controversial — even if the controversy is manufactured.
When Rebellion PAC, a committee founded to back the 2020 congressional campaign of left-wing commentator Cenk Uygur, ran an ad supporting Abdul El-Sayed and connecting high grocery prices to U.S. support for Israel, the fallout threatened to upend the Michigan Senate race. Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., called the ad antisemitic and took it as an opportunity to air her grievances with her former primary opponent, eventually switching her endorsement to Republican Mike Rogers. The PAC originally ran a version of the ad during Uygur’s short-lived 2024 presidential bid.
Voters didn’t seem to be swayed by the controversy, and El-Sayed beat Rogers by a comfortable 7 percentage points. “The drama comes from a handful of elected officials and an establishment that, at best, takes an outdated view of how Israel and AIPAC operate,” said Greg Krieg, spokesperson for American Priorities, which was not affiliated with the Rebellion PAC ad but did produce other ad spots that criticized the U.S. relationship with Israel.
“Not every ad we ran was about Israel, obviously, but the topic came up often because it united Democrats across the party’s ideological spectrum,” Krieg said. “This is not a controversial issue at a grassroots level.”
That new, vocally pro-Palestine PACs are backing successful candidates alongside veteran left organizations is a sign of health for a nascent effort, Miller said.
The midterms were “a test case of: Will this message resonate with voters? And the answer overwhelmingly was yes,” Miller said. “This is a sign of the increasing power and mobilization of the Palestinian rights movement in the political and electoral space.”
Groups like American Priorities and PAL PAC often endorsed the same candidates as progressive bench-builders like Justice Democrats and the Working Families Party. In some cases, the Palestine solidarity movement seemed to breathe a much-needed new life into the electoral left.
The pro-Israel lobby doled out bruising defeats last cycle, after making a promise to unleash its full arsenal to oust critics of Israel from Congress. AIPAC’s super PAC spent more than $25 million to unseat then-Reps. Cori Bush, D-Mo., and Jamaal Bowman, D-N.Y. — a quarter of the $100 million it spent on primaries in 2024.
Reeling from those losses, progressive and Democratic strategists went back to the drawing board. Alone, they could never hope to have the same infrastructure or wield the same influence as a group like AIPAC. But together, they could more effectively pool their resources to tap into public opinion shifting further each year in their favor.
One of the new pro-Palestine groups, American Priorities, was born out of a desire to leverage that shifting public opinion against U.S. support for Israel into electoral wins. As the first truly pro-Palestine super PAC, the group spent $8.15 million backing 15 candidates this cycle, 13 of whom won. (The group also considered spending for Angie Nixon, a Florida democratic socialist who narrowly lost her bid for U.S. Senate, but ended up putting the money into another race.)
Twelve of the 20 candidates backed by PAL PAC won their races, including El-Sayed and Donavan McKinney in Michigan, Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York, Adam Hamawy in New Jersey, Melat Kiros in Colorado, and Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania.
The growing networks allowed groups like Justice Democrats to get involved in more races. It came back from its losses and had its most successful cycle yet, electing eight of the 15 candidates it endorsed, four of whom unseated Democratic incumbents. The group spent $5.5 million in total this cycle, including $4.6 million on ads across all its races. And it went much further: Last cycle, Justice Democrats spent a combined $3.3 million alone backing Bush and Bowman before they lost.
Together, IMEU Policy Project and PAL PAC spent $2.15 million on ads and bundling for candidates. “We ran on proud anti-genocide and pro-freedom platforms,” DeReus said. “We knew that this was a cycle where that platform could win, and we wanted to be a part of making that happen.”
Meanwhile, AIPAC and other pro-Israel groups saw diminishing returns on election spending this cycle, as they battled waning public opinion and increasingly concealed their spending in races.
“Their names often tell you very little about who’s behind them or what they’re actually trying to do — and their ads almost never mention Israel,” Krieg said. “Everybody is looking at the same polling. We have voters who agree with us, so we’re willing to say plainly what we stand for and put our names on it. When you’re pushing a position that voters don’t support, you’re naturally going to be a lot less transparent about what you’re doing.”
The general public had a greater knowledge of AIPAC’s brand and its role in maintaining a pro-Israel U.S. policy this time around, said Justice Democrats spokesperson Usamah Andrabi. This cycle also saw more candidates willing to translate public agitation against U.S. support for Israel into campaigns, he said, pointing to other efforts he said helped voters understand AIPAC’s role in elections from groups like TrackAIPAC.
“Voters’ awareness and opposition to Israel’s genocide and apartheid was raised so much higher due to grassroots movements and groups that organized against it,” Andrabi said. “We were able to — across every single one of our campaigns — talk about AIPAC as AIPAC, and talk about the genocide as something we wanted to end, and connect the dots for people.”
It’s a stark contrast to 2024, when Justice Democrats met with candidates whose top concerns were avoiding AIPAC’s wrath, Andrabi said. “Even then, in 2024, we were telling these campaigns, ‘Look, there’s no going under, around, behind, over AIPAC. The only way to defeat this lobby is to go right through them,” he said. “The political courage amongst a lot of Democratic candidates and a lot of people within the Democratic Party was just not there in 2024.”
As the 2028 presidential race begins to take shape, the same pro-Palestine groups are preparing to push candidates to meet voters where they are on Israel policy.
“Particularly with Abdul’s victory in Michigan, that win capped off a year that has really proved that Palestinian rights is an asset, not just in safe blue districts, but in the most critical of swing states,” DeReus said. Even President Donald Trump knows how much of a liability being pro-Israel has become, she added, pointing to his late-breaking claim on Election Day that the U.S. would end military support to Israel.
Potential Democratic contenders in 2028 would do well to take that lesson to heart, DeReus said, as groups like hers gear up to push candidates to support an arms embargo, sanction Israel, and recognize the genocide. She said the group hopes to see someone like Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., enter the race, but that it would also support Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., should she decide to run.
In DeReus’s view, “2024 was the last presidential election we will see where Palestinian rights were disregarded.”

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/ice-.title: ICE Shot Pepper Spray Into a Car in a Traffic Stop, Then Broke a Detainee’s Collarbone
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/ice-.author: Jessica Washington
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/16/ice-.text:
Jose Rosito Roca Estrada and his friends were on their way to work in a van on June 27, when a car in front of them slammed on its brakes, forcing them to crash into it and ricochet backward on the busy highway.
Three more cars surrounded theirs, and an estimated 10 to 12 officers poured out. The agents screamed at the men to get out of the vehicle despite traffic whipping by, Roca Estrada and fellow passenger Elvis Manuel Mejia told The Intercept. The stalemate ended with the sound of shattering glass and an asphyxiating cloud of chemicals flooding the car.
According to a new federal lawsuit and photos from the scene shared with The Intercept, federal agents smashed the car’s back windows and “sprayed the occupants with pepper spray through the lowered side windows.”
Officers then dragged a scared and temporarily blinded Roca Estrada from the car. “I was afraid they might be robbing me,” 24-year-old Roca Estrada told The Intercept through a translator. “They did not identify themselves. I was worried they were kidnapping me because they were asking very personal questions.”
The June attack is one of six stories described in a lawsuit brought by several groups — including the American Civil Liberties Union of Virginia, the Washington Lawyers Committee for Civil Rights and Urban Affairs, the Legal Aid Justice Center, and multiple law firms — alleging widespread “unlawful and dangerous” warrantless arrests by immigration officials in Virginia.
On behalf of Roca Estrada and other plaintiffs, the groups are suing the Department of Homeland Security, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Acting Director of ICE David Venturella, and ICE D.C. Field Office Director Robert Guadian. They’re asking the court in the Eastern District of Virginia to force DHS to comply with congressional limits on warrantless immigration arrests and prohibit the agency from making immigration arrests without legally required individual assessments.
“They have a mandate from the Trump administration … to get creative and make arrests, however they see fit,” said Sophia Gregg, an immigrants’ rights attorney at the ACLU of Virginia. “The agents are ill-trained, and even when they do violate the law, there are no consequences.”
Roca Estrada said that the officers demanded to search his pockets, and when he declined, an agent threw him to the ground headfirst and dug his knees into his upper back. He remembered screaming as pain began to radiate through his collarbone. An X-ray reviewed by The Intercept would later confirm it was broken.
According to Roca Estrada and the lawsuit, officers began to punch and hit him in the back, eventually twisting his arm to place him in handcuffs and into the vehicle. Roca Estrada said that nurses who examined him after the alleged assault told him that blood had filled his lungs, and the lawsuit notes he was diagnosed with a broken clavicle and a lung injury. At no point, the lawsuit alleges, did officers ask the necessary questions to determine whether Roca Estrada was deportable or whether he was a flight risk.
Immigration officers are only supposed to make warrantless immigration arrests if they have determined “probable cause” to believe a person is unlawfully present likely to escape before a warrant can be obtained. But in an effort to meet the Trump administration’s nationwide quota of 3,000 immigration arrests per day, the lawsuit alleges, the Department of Homeland Security has chosen to pursue an unlawful policy and practice of “arrest-first, investigate-later” — leaving a trail of traumatized victims who should have never been arrested in the first place.
In the first year of the Trump administration, immigration arrests drastically increased in Virginia. According to the lawsuit, in 2025, ICE made “970 arrests each month in Virginia and Washington, D.C. — nearly five times the average monthly arrest volume in 2024.”
Reached by The Intercept, a DHS spokesperson said that agency had “arrested Jose Rosito Roca Estrada, an illegal alien from Guatemala,” using Roca Estrada’s full name even though The Intercept had not provided it, but denied that its officers “fractured a detainee’s collarbone.” The spokesperson did not deny that officials had deployed chemical weapons, saying, “staff relied on their training to gain compliance.”
“Claims that agents did not properly identify themselves are FALSE. When our heroic law enforcement officers conduct operations, they clearly identify themselves as law enforcement,” wrote the spokesperson. “At NO time were any of the detainees thrown to the ground during the arrest. Allegations that our officers fractured a detainee’s collarbone during the arrest are FALSE.”
Six weeks after Roca Estrada’s arrest, 18-year-old Britney Ramirez Corona was home caring for her 4-year-old sister in Norfolk, Virginia, when she found out ICE had detained her fiancé, his brother, and his brother-in-law.
It was another traffic stop, and Ramirez Corona, a U.S. citizen and recent high school graduate, had to go pick up their abandoned car. There, according to the lawsuit, an ICE officer demanded her identification, refused to let her get her wallet, and accused her of lying about who owned the vehicle. They handcuffed and pinned her, the lawsuit alleges — leaving her little sister to cry and wander into a busy road.
Eventually, ICE allowed another sister, 15, to come pick up the 4-year-old, then took Ramirez Corona into custody. She sat in “handcuffs, ankle shackles and a waist chain” for hours, according to the lawsuit, until her 15-year-old sister was able to bring her birth certificate — showing she was a natural-born U.S. citizen.
The lawsuit argues that Ramirez Corona’s arrest exemplifies an out-of-control trend of warrantless and often nonsensical arrests. Stephen Miller, then homeland security adviser and now the White House chief of staff, directed agents to “just go out there and arrest,” and the department seems to have complied.
“More than half of all the people ICE arrested in July 2026 did not have a criminal record,” the plaintiffs note. “And more than 500 people detained by ICE since January 2025 are U.S. citizens — another likely undercount — like Ms. Ramirez Corona.”
The same month that Roca Estrada says that federal agents temporarily blinded him, broke his collarbone, and beat him until his lungs filled with blood, Congress approved another $72 billion in funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Immigrant advocacy groups warned ahead of the funding vote that additional money for ICE and President Donald Trump’s brutal immigration crackdown would mean more people would suffer a fate like Roca Estrada’s — or worse. The next month, ICE agents fatally shot Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Texas and Joan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Maine, both in their cars.
Physicians for Human Rights and the UC Berkeley Human Rights Center documented over 412 incidents of misuse of force by law enforcement agents at immigration protests from June 2025 to May 2026, including the use of chemical irritants like pepper balls and pepper spray — the same family of weapons Roca Estrada and Mejia suspect was set off in their car.
In ICE custody, 52 people have died during the first 500 days of the second Trump administration, according to Human Rights Watch, while use-of-force by guards remains largely unknown.
“We have received many more reports of violent use of force against people,” said Jeff Migliozzi, the communications director for Freedom for Immigrants, which runs the National Immigration Detention Hotline, referencing hotline numbers from June and July. “The overwhelming forces of intimidation and fear and retaliation, the M.O. of ICE has not changed. But certainly, as more people are detained, there’s more incidents [of violence].”
The DHS spokesperson claimed that Roca Estrada and everyone arrested along with him were offered medical care but declined, adding that “one of the detainees indicated that he had a prior shoulder injury.”
Roca Estrada tells a very different story.
He says he spent the next month tossed between detention centers in Virginia and West Virginia. Because he was not given a sling, Roca Estrada fashioned one for his broken collarbone out of bedsheets. He said he largely went without medical care despite agonizing pain that prevented him from laying down at night.
Roca Estrada said it got so bad he nearly fainted, at which point he was taken to a hospital.
“After medical personnel offered to document his injuries and consult a forensic physician, officers abruptly removed him from the hospital and returned him to detention,” the lawsuit alleges. “For weeks thereafter, Defendants failed to provide the promised follow-up care.”
According to the lawsuit, none of this should have happened because Roca Estrada never should have been detained in the first place.
The suit alleges that immigration officers never asked the 24-year-old “about his immigration history, whether he possessed lawful status, where he worked, how long he had lived in Virginia, whom he lived with, whether he had family or community ties in the United States, or similar questions to assess whether he was likely to escape before a warrant could be obtained.”
Other stories in the lawsuit follow a similar pattern. Catarina Rebeca Us Lopez, a 24-year-old woman from Guatemala, was detained in Centreville, Virginia, during a traffic stop around 6:00 a.m. with her husband. She alleges that masked officers blocked her car at a traffic light and forced her and her husband from the vehicle.
The officers falsely claimed that her husband had a deportation order, according to the lawsuit. But when her husband asked questions about the stop, Us Lopez alleges an agent pepper-sprayed him in the face and threatened to draw their weapons.
According to Us Lopez, officers did not “inquire about her immigration status, ask where she lived, inquire about her family, ask about her ties to the community, or otherwise conduct any individualized investigation concerning whether she was lawfully present in the United States or likely to escape before a warrant could be obtained.”
Instead, she claims that officers ignored her as she explained that she had work authorization and did not have a deportation order in place, and allegedly mocked her requests for answers and legal assistance.
For Roca Estrada, his physical injuries and trauma left him unable to work for a month. While he was detained, he also lost his apartment and had his personal belongings sent back to Guatemala without his consent, according to the lawsuit.
“The way that I was arrested … and the immense pain that I had to go through during this whole experience,” said Roca Estrada. “What happened to me was not just.”
