Yemeni government forces say they carried out 697 strikes targeting the Iran-aligned Houthis over the past few hours, the army’s spokesperson Majed al-Nuzaili said.
Al-Nuzaili said in a post on X that the attacks included 17 air strikes, 32 drone attacks, 28 rocket attacks and 620 artillery attacks targeting Houthi positions, gatherings, vehicles and weapons depots.
These strikes killed 97 Houthi commanders and fighters and destroyed or damaged 76 vehicles and combat assets, he said.
The government forces and their allies continue to repel Houthi attacks in Taiz amid ongoing clashes on the Marib and al Jawf fronts, he added.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Climate scientists urge US lawmakers to vote no on sweeping permitting bill
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Oliver Milman
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
A group of more than 120 climate scientists have urged US lawmakers to not pass contentious legislation to speed up the building of energy projects, datacenters and other infrastructure, amid a growing backlash to the sweeping permitting bill.
In an open letter to members of the House of Representatives, the collection of Earth and social sciences researchers expressed “deep concern” that the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (or Baaja) weakens environmental laws, locks in new fossil fuel projects without recourse and delivers only minor cuts to planet-heating emissions.
“We understand the need for trade-offs and compromise when passing bipartisan legislation,” they wrote. “But as scientists we feel strongly that the costs of this bill to the climate are too high.”
Last week, the US Senate rapidly passed Baaja, a bill co-written by two Democratic and two Republican senators but one that has bitterly divided Democrats and environmentalists. The House is set to vote on the bill next week, where it will be signed by Donald Trump into law if passed.
Michael Mann, a climate scientist who helped arrange the open letter, said that he did so because Baaja is a “deeply problematic bill” that is “backed by a veritable who’s who of bad fossil fuel and dark money actors”.
Mann said that Democrats, who take control of Congress in January, should “scrap Baaja, which in the end only takes us further down the dangerous fossil fuel pathway, and put a sensible, popular datacenter bill on Trump’s desk and force him to veto it. And force Republicans to defend sustaining that veto.”
Timmons Roberts, a Brown University academic and letter co-signatory, said the bill is “very worrisome, it has felt very rushed and there is grave potential for damage that can’t be undone any time soon”.
“We are in a broken system, and it’s hard to build anything, but there has to be a better way to do this,” Roberts added. “In some ways it feels like we are being held hostage. If you want more renewables you have to also see the lock-in of fossil fuels and the devastating gutting of core legislation that has allowed the US to improve its natural environment.”
Mann said that Sheldon Whitehouse, the Democratic senator and longtime champion of climate action who has co-sponsored Baaja, has “long been one of my heroes, and nothing pains me to find him not only in support of the bill but in fact one of its principal backers”.
Asked for his response to the letter, Whitehouse said: “I have great respect for these climate scientists, and I am sorry to disagree with them here. The important takeaways about this bill are the gigaton-scale emissions reductions, the freed-up clean power, the $10bn in annual consumer electricity savings, and the $35bn whack at datacenters.”
Supporters of Baaja, who include some Democrats, a minority of green groups and other climate scientists, point to the laborious, sometimes terminal wait for clean energy projects to be approved and come online, as well as the lack of integrated power lines to take solar or wind-generated electrons to where it is needed.
Baaja would slash the barriers to new transmission lines and shrink the role of statutes such as the Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act in scrutinizing various projects, aiding their rapid approval and making them virtually immune from being overturned by any future administration or the courts.
This should unleash much of the clean energy waiting to be connected to the grid but will also sideline legal challenges to new oil pipelines, datacenters and other infrastructure, such as ICE detention centers. This has raised alarm over a potential surge in fossil fuel activity and datacenters sited on public lands, with little community or tribal input.
“Congress must reject Baaja in its entirety,” the National Congress of American Indians said in a statement. “Native sovereignty, sacred places, and cultural heritage are not negotiable.”
The varied coalition of opponents, including former vice-president Al Gore, also argue that Trump will not faithfully execute the law. The president, a major backer of the artificial intelligence industry, has said Baaja result in a “tremendous amounts of new building” for dat centers but has insisted that he will still not allow the permitting of new wind power, which he has called a “major loser”.
“Democrats, what is the matter with you? Don’t you know better than to trust Trump?” the actor Mark Ruffalo, an environmental advocate, said in a widely-viewed social media post.
Unusually for a major, 500-page piece of legislation, Baaja has been pushed through Congress without a hearing. The pace of its ascension increases its chance of getting needed Republican support, including Trump’s, to pass, with no guarantee of such backing should Democrats write their own, revised version from January.
Faced with this dilemma, some Democrats in the House opposed to Baaja have set about trying to amend it rather than immediately kill it. This may succeed given that Republicans’ already slender hold on the House has been largely erased, with many Republicans now not in Washington for the lame-duck session after losing in the midterm elections.
“There are amendments to fix this bil that would hacve broad bipartisan support but we are about to find out if this is a ‘take it or leave it’ jam job,” Jared Huffman, a California Democrat, told the Guardian. “The Republicans will push for Democrats to abstain or not show up, that power play will come next week.”
Huffman, who is set to chair the House’s natural resources committee when Democrats take control of the chamber, has proposed five amendments to Baaja. These include more consultation with tribes and legal recourse for communities, as well as full reviews fore data centers and ending the “forever permit” provisions that ensure projects can continue even if they are shown to be destructive or unlawful.
“Look how thrilled the White House, the fossil fuel industry and big AI and datacenter interests are with this bill. They want what it gives and they aren’t going to stop wanting that six weeks from now,” Huffman said.
“We will be able to cut a deal on better terms then; we need to be better negotiators. This episode shows the dangers of not acting because you get something like Baaja, which is extremely destructive. If we go the next two to four years without legislating on a permitting deal, then shame on us.”

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Rebel group retreats in DR Congo after heavy clashes with government forces
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Rebel group retreats in DR Congo after heavy clashes with government forces
CRP halts advance towards Bunia, citing commitments made during Ugandan-mediated talks with the government.
The rebel group led by convicted war criminal Thomas Lubanga has withdrawn from areas recently seized in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) after days of heavy fighting with government forces.
The Convention for the Popular Revolution (CRP) announced on Tuesday that it had decided to halt an advance towards the town of Bunia, the capital of Ituri province in northeast DRC.
In a statement, the group cited a commitment made in talks with the Congolese government, mediated by Uganda’s President Yoweri Museveni, as one of the reasons for its withdrawal.
The CRP’s decision came one day after the group seized the Iga-Barriere, a strategic area about 25km north of Bunia, forcing government troops to withdraw towards the provincial capital.
Lubanga, a former leader of the Union of Congolese Patriots, was convicted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) in 2012 on charges of recruiting and using child soldiers.
He was sentenced to 14 years in prison and released in March 2020 after completing his sentence. Lubanga remains sanctioned by the United Nations.
Lubanga announced the formation of the CRP in 2025, opening another front against the DRC’s President Felix Tshisekedi.
The group said the decision to withdraw troops was made “out of respect for the commitments made at the State House” by the Congolese government and the CRP, referring to an October 9 meeting hosted by Uganda between Lubanga and a delegation of senior government and military officials.
Disrupting Ebola response
On Sunday, the World ‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌‌Health Organization said fighting near a hospital in the Ituri province, north of Bunia, forced the evacuation of health workers and aid partners, disrupting Ebola response efforts.
The DRC is experiencing its largest and deadliest Ebola outbreak, which has spread across the country’s east and northeast. Ituri remains one of the most affected provinces.
Thousands of civilians have reportedly been displaced towards Bunia since the weekend due to renewed fighting between rebel fighters and government forces, according to local media reports.

https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/does-.title: Who wins from Baghdad's move to clip Kurdish autonomy - the US or Iran?
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/does-.author: Sean Mathews
https://www.middleeasteye.net/news/does-.text:
Who wins from Baghdad's move to clip Kurdish autonomy - the US or Iran?
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has said Baghdad will take over all of Kurdistan's border crossings and several oil fields that the autonomous region controls, in a move that was widely condemned by the region’s leaders as a step to clip their autonomy.
Baghdad’s decision comes at a time of internal division in the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) and as the Middle East braces for a potential new US-Israeli attack on Iran.
Under American pressure, Zaidi recently attempted to crack down on Kataib Hezbollah, a powerful Shia militia in Iraq aligned with Iran, which officials in Baghdad say has earned hundreds of millions of dollars from smuggling oil.
Zaidi's spokesperson Sabah al-Numan said on Tuesday that, based on those findings, Baghad would take control of "all border crossings in the Kurdistan Region".
He added that Zaidi directed the oil ministry "to manage all oil fields" that are under Kurdish "security authority" despite lying outside the Kurdistan Region, in the provinces of Diyala, Kirkuk, Salaheddine and Nineveh. Zaidi also ordered the Kurdistan government not to approve oil exports except through the federal oil ministry.

Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
The KRG is guaranteed some autonomy under Iraq’s 2005 constitution, but its control of border crossings has been a longstanding issue of dispute, as have energy resources.
Does Iran or the US benefit?
The move by Baghdad’s central government to wrest control of the posts alongside energy facilities comes as it tries to seal new energy deals with Turkey and looks to pipelines through the region to bypass the Strait of Hormuz.
The KRG region has been a close US security partner for decades, but the last US troops left Erbil, the region's capital, in September, completing a full US withdrawal from Iraq. The region faced hundreds of Iranian missile and drone strikes during this year's war.
Experts debated whether Baghdad's decision was made with the agreement of Iran, which has called on the KRG to rein in Kurdish opposition groups, or the US which has lobbied regional states to consolidate federal power.
Tom Barrack, the US ambassador to Turkey and Middle East envoy, has been the main proponent of this view.
Yesar Al-Maleki, a Gulf analyst at the Middle East Economic Survey, said Zaidi was taking advantage of a shift in the US.
“Washington, has clearly shifted its Iraq policy toward greater centralisation; the PUK and KDP are no longer presenting a united front in Iraqi politics; and the US military withdrawal has given Baghdad greater security bandwidth,” he wrote on X.
'Tehran fears an uprising'
But Fabrice Balanche, a Kurdish expert, said Baghdad’s move would benefit Iran as well, given its suspicion of the US and Israel using the region as a base to attack it.
“Iraq’s determination to dismantle the KRG by depriving it of its economic resources must be seen in the context of the conflict between the US and Iran,” he wrote in an essay.
“Tehran fears that Iraqi Kurdistan could serve as a rear base for an uprising in Iranian Kurdistan,” he added.
The KRG is at its weakest in years. The region is dominated by two family dynasties, the Barzani family in Erbil, which leads the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP), and the Talabani family in Sulaymaniyah, which leads the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK).
The PUK withdrew from the region's parliament in November and its leader, Bafel Talabani, said the region was already living "the reality of two governments and two administrations".
Kurdistan Region Prime Minister Masrour Barzani said his government was "surprised" by Zaidi's decisions, calling them "completely unacceptable".
But both parties put aside their differences to issue a relatively mild censure of Baghdad’s decision.
“The Kurdistan Region has never sought anything beyond the rights guaranteed to it under the Iraqi Constitution. However, its constitutional rights have been violated over the years,” the statement said.
“We stress that all parties must abide by the Constitution and that, should any dispute arise between the Kurdistan Region and the Federal Government, the Constitution must serve as the ultimate point of reference,” the statement added.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Canada says it ‘does not report to the US’ after Pentagon memo criticizing military spending
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Leyland Cecco in Toronto
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
Canada is a “sovereign nation” that does not “report” to the United States, the country’s defense minister said after the Pentagon released a scathing memo that criticized the supposedly “atrophied” defence capabilities of its northern neighbour.
The document, released Tuesday, said Canada had “yet to make the hard decisions and tradeoffs” necessary to meet previous defence spending pledges and become a “credible partner in the defense of our shared continent”.
The Pentagon memo said it took Canada nearly two decades to finally reach spending promises made in 2006 “despite Canada’s role as a major G7 economy as well as one of the largest and wealthiest members of the NATO alliance”.
Historically, Nato members have fallen short of meeting the security organization’s funding goals. When Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, only three Nato members – the US, the UK and Greece – were meeting the alliance’s guideline of spending 2% of GDP on defence. By 2025, all 31 members with armed forces, including Canada, had reached the goal.
The document also suggested Canada faces significant operational hurdles in its air, land and sea operations, blaming political leaders for pursuing “parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization”.
The Pentagon document said the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, was “laser focused” on modernizing Canada’s military, suggesting American taxpayers had been “footing the bill for its defense” for decades.
The defense minister, David McGuinty, told reporters he could not “divine” the thinking behind the Pentagon’s decision to criticise Canada’s defence spending now.
“The amount of co-operation we are pushing under NORAD [North American Aerospace Defense Command] has not changed. What we’re doing together at Nato has not changed. Our military-to-military co-operation has not changed. Our work on integrated air missile defence has not changed,” he said.
McGuinty also bristled at the suggestion from a reporter that the memo implied Canada required approval from the US when it came to its spending plans.
“Canada is a sovereign nation. I’ll be very direct. We don’t report to the United States,” he said.
The memo came as a Canadian official travelled to Europe to pitch a new defence bank championed by the prime minister, Mark Carney.
Isabelle Hudon, Canada’s lead negotiator for establishing the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, is looking to cajole more countries into joining a global initiative that would lend to governments and contractors at low cost to support defense projects.
Ten countries have pledged their support but no others from the G7 have done so yet, with both the UK and Germany so far declining to join. Hudon says the €4bn in commitments secured so far is enough to start the bank up but she is aiming for up to €100bn.
Carney has made significantly increased spending commitments in defence. The country spent $63.4bn on national defence in 2025, meeting its Nato pledge to spend 2% of gross domestic product for the first time.
Last year, Nato members agreed to raise the goal to the equivalent of 5% of GDP by 2035.
Canada’s federal budget this month laid out a plan to spend about 4% of Canada’s GDP on defence and security annually by the end of the decade, and 5% by 2035, including the purchase of submarines and early warning aircraft.
Canada’s air power is a key point of friction with Washington. Carney’s government has yet to make a final decision on its order of F-35 fighter jets from the US firm Lockheed Martin and is weighing the possibility of purchasing Swedish-made Gripen aircraft instead. The multibillion-dollar purchase has been the subject of a political review for more than a year. The Pentagon memo warned that operating a “mixed fleet” of aircraft would “compound existing personnel shortfalls”.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/17/van-.title: Chris Van Hollen’s Evolution on Israel and Palestine
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/17/van-.author: Jonah Valdez
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/17/van-.text:
When Chris Van Hollen first ran for Senate in 2016, he was considered the pro-Israel, Democratic establishment pick with the backing of AIPAC-aligned donors. He was a U.S. representative who regularly voted to approve military aid to Israel; his opponent, Rep. Donna Edwards, was an outspoken critic of the Israeli government and the pro-Israel lobby. He outspent her 3 to 1 and won the Maryland Democratic primary by about 130,000 votes.
A decade later, Van Hollen has evolved into one of the harshest critics of Israel in the Senate. He’s staked his criticism of Israel’s genocide in Gaza and apartheid rule of Palestinians as a key argument behind his run against staunch Israel-defending Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for Senate majority leader.
Politicians often update their stances with the times, leaving voters to sort out what’s a genuine change of heart and what’s opportunism. In Van Hollen’s case, advocates for Palestine who seek to end U.S. military support for Israel told The Intercept that his evolution is a sign that he can be pushed by public pressure.
“Before this evolution, Van Hollen had looked a lot more like a mainstream Democrat on Israel,” said Yousef Munayyer, a senior fellow at the Arab Center Washington D.C. and a longtime advocate for Palestinian rights. “Times have changed in a lot of ways, where the Democratic base has changed in a lot of ways, and he has changed along with it — I don’t know that the same can be said for a lot of other folks, like Chuck Schumer.”
Van Hollen was elected to the House in 2002, in the feverish early years of the war on terror, and joined the vast majority of his colleagues from both parties in unconditionally supporting arms transfers to Israel. In 2010 and 2012, he co-sponsored the initial round of funding for U.S. support of Israel’s Iron Dome missile defense systems and called for additional cooperation between Israel and the Pentagon for weapons development, such as enhancing Israel’s F-35 fighter jet program. In 2016, the year he was elected to the Senate, he co-sponsored a House resolution affirming a 10-year memorandum of understanding between the U.S. and Israel to continue providing State Department funds for Israel to buy weapons. The MOU, inked by President Barack Obama, was widely seen by observers as a concession to Israel to alleviate pressure over his Iran nuclear agreement — which Van Hollen supported and Schumer famously opposed.
Van Hollen’s Maryland House district had a large pro-Israel voter base, Munayyer pointed out, and some of his pro-Israel stances may have been the product of being responsive to his constituents. But in the Senate, Van Hollen continued to support Israel, backing a 2018 bill that authorized extending military aid to the country until at least 2028, as well as guarantees to loans and access to U.S. military stockpiles until 2023.
His most notable shift has followed the October 7, 2023, attacks. While that year, Van Hollen supported a resolution that “reaffirms Israel’s right to self-defense” and promised military equipment resupply, he has since co-sponsored resolutions and bills that invoked the use of Biden-era sanctions against Israeli settlers in the West Bank, voted several times to block the sale of some weapons to Israel, and is leading an effort to strip a Pentagon spending bill of its provisions that more closely tie the U.S. and Israeli militaries. He also introduced a resolution demanding a State Department report on Israeli detention of Palestinian children and Israeli military and settler killings of American citizens in the West Bank.
Margaret DeReus, executive director of the pro-Palestine lobbying group Institute for Middle East Understanding Policy Project, which collaborated with Van Hollen on the recent State Department resolution, said she is supporting his run for majority leader, arguing that he would help rein in some of the least popular excesses of the Trump administration.
“Senate Democrats should be led by a Majority Leader who is committed to fighting the Trump Administration on the Iran war, stopping the lawless ICE raids on American cities, and ending US aid to Israel,” she told The Intercept in a statement. “Senator Van Hollen is a leader in the Senate for enforcing US laws around military assistance to countries committing human rights violations, including in Palestine and Sudan, and for ending this illegal war.”
And unlike Schumer, Van Hollen’s past support for Israel was not unequivocal.
During Israel’s war on Lebanon in 2006, he wrote a letter to then-Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice criticizing the Bush administration’s decision not to push for an end to Israel’s bombing of civilians, which drew backlash from supporters of Israel. In 2019, Van Hollen took to the Senate floor to blast then-Sen. Marco Rubio’s bill to crack down on the Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions movement in the U.S., saying he disagreed with the boycott but wanted to uphold constitutional rights. The following year, he gave a floor speech to oppose Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s plan to unilaterally annex parts of the West Bank, and he introduced a 2021 Pentagon-spending amendment that would have prohibited Israel from using U.S. aid for its annexation efforts. After Israeli forces killed Palestinian American journalist Shireen Abu Akleh, he pushed the Biden administration to seek accountability.
This marks a contrast with Schumer, DeReus said. She said the current minority leader has a “long record of paving the way for this disastrous war [on Iran] as the only current Senate Democrat who voted against Obama’s JCPOA,” which placed agreed-upon restraints on Iran’s nuclear development. And he has continued to support military assistance to Israel.
During recent resolutions to block sales of certain weapons to Israel, Schumer was among the minority of Senate Democrats who voted against it.
Schumer and Van Hollen’s offices did not respond to The Intercept’s requests for comment.
On a press tour over the weekend after announcing his run for the leadership position, Van Hollen differentiated himself from Schumer on Israel and Palestine, criticizing Schumer for siding with the pro-Israel lobby against progressive Senate candidates in the Democratic midterm primaries and speaking against “a blank check” to the Israeli government.
“We’re seeing violent settlers push Palestinians off their land with the complicity of the Israeli government,” Van Hollen said Sunday on Fox News. “I don’t think American taxpayer dollars should be going to that purpose.”
While Van Hollen’s strong stand against Israel appears to be, in part, motivated by personal moral conviction and a desire to “look yourself in the mirror at the end of the day,” whether or not he continues to push for Palestinian rights if elected leader will depend on how much Palestine remains a litmus test in the Democratic Party, said Tariq Kenney-Shawa, an associate fellow at Palestinian think tank Al-Shabaka.
“I really think it’ll come down to whether and how [Van Hollen] continues to be pressured by the movement and the Democratic base,” Kenney-Shawa said.
Munayyer also credits the gains made in Congress to a global organizing movement against Israel’s genocide and apartheid rule, which he said has made the issue into something beyond even Palestine and Israel.
“It’s seen as a proxy for authenticity,” he said. “And if you say that you’re going to do something on this issue, then you back away from it, it looks like you just don’t have the integrity to do the things that you need to do.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://apache.be/2026/11/06/onderzoeksr.title: Onderzoeksrechters worden pion van beleid in nieuwe wet op woonstbetredingen
https://apache.be/2026/11/06/onderzoeksr.author: Walter De Smedt
https://apache.be/2026/11/06/onderzoeksr.text:
De voormalige voorzitter van de vereniging van onderzoeksrechters, Walter De Smedt, maakt brandhout van de net gestemde wet over woonstbetreding. Die wet, met als enige doel het verwijderen van mensen zonder papieren, gaat volledig voorbij aan de kerntaak van een onderzoeksrechter: onafhankelijk onderzoeken en voorlopige maatregelen nemen.
In de twaalfde eeuw maakte de Luikse prins-bisschop Albert de Cuyck een charter. De voornaamste regel daarin, “Pauvre homme en sa maison est roi”, heeft de geschiedenis − inclusief twee wereldoorlogen − overleefd.
Daar is nu verandering in gekomen. Mensen zonder papieren die een uitvoerbare verwijderingsmaatregel hebben, die weigeren mee te werken én door hun gedrag een gevaar vormen voor de openbare orde of nationale veiligheid moeten kunnen worden aangehouden, zelfs indien daarvoor de woning moet worden betreden. Daarvoor is de tussenkomst van een onderzoeksrechter voorzien. Die kan een “machtiging” verlenen en de modaliteiten ervan bepalen. Ongeacht of deze ingreep nodig en grondwettelijk is, moet de vraag gesteld worden wat een onderzoeksrechter in deze “politiek-bestuurlijke” procedure komt doen.
Advocaten en onderzoeksrechters tegen
Een onderzoeksrechter is een rechter die in het kader van een strikte procedure even strikt omschreven opdrachten heeft. Hij treedt enkel op in een voorlopig strafonderzoek, een onderzoek naar mogelijke gepleegde strafbare feiten. Het is zijn opdracht alle maatregelen te nemen die de rechtscolleges in staat moeten stellen met kennis van zaken te oordelen. Daartoe kan hij ook, met aanhaling van de redenen, grondwettelijk beschermde rechten schenden, een aanhoudings- of een huiszoekingsbevel verlenen.
Deze maatregelen zijn enkel voorlopig. Vrijheidsberoving wordt door de onderzoeksgerechten, de raadkamer en de kamer van inbeschuldigingstelling, beoordeeld. Alles moet nadien door de strafrechter worden overgedaan in een openbare en tegensprekelijke procedure waartegen ook de rechtsmiddelen van verzet, beroep en cassatie openstaan. Geen wonder dat de onderzoeksrechters én de twee advocatenordes een negatief advies gaven.
In voorliggend wetsvoorstel gaat het niet om een strafonderzoek. Het gaat evenmin om een voorlopig vooronderzoek dat onder toezicht van de onderzoeksgerechten staat en evenmin wordt overgedaan in een openbare en tegensprekelijke procedure. Het enige doel is de verwijdering van mensen zonder papieren. Het gaat hierin ook niet om een rechterlijk bevel maar om een rechterlijke “machtiging”. De onderzoeksrechter kan weigeren en de modaliteiten bepalen. Toch is het duidelijk dat hier beroep gedaan wordt op een rechter omdat het niet anders kan, maar dat die daarvoor uit zijn eigen procedure en de daarin voorziene waarborgen moet treden. De essentie van zijn opdracht, zelf onderzoeken en voorlopige maatregelen nemen ontbreekt. Ook het toezicht van de onderzoeksgerechten en van de strafrechter in een openbare en tegensprekelijke behandeling ontbreekt.
“Verkrachters, drugsdelinquenten en haatpredikers”
Even opmerkelijk als de vorige bezwaren is het echte doel van de wet. Volgens de minister van Asiel en Migratie Anneleen Van Bossuyt (N-VA) gaat het om “verkrachters, drugsdelinquenten en haatpredikers” die uit het land moeten worden gezet. “Die mensen zullen zich nu niet langer achter een voordeur kunnen verschuilen”, zegt ze aan VRT.
De vraag is hoe er voor deze opvatting een meerderheid kon worden gevonden. Zelfs de beweerde liberalen van Anders stemden mee. Als het om de uitzetting van verkrachters, drugsdelinquenten en haatpredikers gaat is de wet de meest grove miskenning van de rechtsstaat. Voor dergelijke misdrijven is er immers een strafprocedure met een vooronderzoek, een tegensprekelijk en openbaar onderzoek ter zitting waarin de rechten van de verdediging moeten worden gerespecteerd.
Buiten de reguliere rechtspraak
In 1933 vaardigde Duits president Paul von Hindenburg de Rijksdagbrandverordening uit over de brand van de Reichstag, het Duitse parlementsgebouw, op 27 februari 1933. Door deze Schutzhaft (“beschermende bewaring”) konden de Gestapo (Geheime Staatspolizei), de SA (Sturmabteilung – de milities van de nazipartij) en de SS (Schutzstaffel – de lijfwacht van Hitler) volledig buiten de reguliere rechtspraak om burgers willekeurig en voor onbepaalde tijd opsluiten.
Deze Schutzhäftlinge kwamen niet in reguliere gevangenissen terecht maar werden direct naar concentratiekampen gestuurd. In het begin ging het om communisten, sociaaldemocraten, vakbondsleiders en tegenstanders van het regime. Daarna werden Joden, Roma en Sinti, Jehova’s getuigen en homoseksuelen opgepakt. Later ondergingen daklozen, bedelaars, sekswerkers en langdurig werklozen hetzelfde lot. Onder de benaming Sicherheitshaft werden tijdens de bezetting van België burgers en verzetsstrijders door de Sicherheitspolizei (Sipo-SD) opgepakt en naar het Fort van Breendonk gebracht en vandaar naar de concentratiekampen.
Machtiging
Het voorstel van de woonstbetredingen staat niet alleen. Ook bij de toepassing van de afkoopwet werd het rechterlijke bevel omgezet in een rechterlijke “machtiging”. Dat is een bevestiging van de toegenomen opdrachten en bevoegdheden van het openbaar ministerie als ambtenaar van het door slechts één minister bepaald strafrechtelijk beleid. Ook de afhandeling van het strafproces neigt steeds meer naar een enkele “machtiging” van de openbare vordering.
Vraag is natuurlijk wat de onderzoeksrechters er van gaan maken. Dat heeft het voorstel echter reeds voorzien. Als de éne weigert kan een andere worden aangesproken. Dat was onder de Sicherheitshaft evenzo: de onwillige rechters werden ook afgevoerd.
