https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Ten essential artworks to see in Budapest
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: J.S. Marcus
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
In April, Hungarians shook off 16 years of right-wing populist rule when they voted overwhelmingly against prime minister Victor Orbán and his Fidesz party. With Orbán’s culturally regressive movement in tatters, Budapest is now reclaiming its status as one of Europe’s most important artistic capitals, and experiencing a wave of visitors newly drawn to the city in the wake of the country’s political about-face.
Hungarians trace their history back to around 900 AD, when nomadic Magyar tribes arrived in Europe’s Carpathian basin, but their capital city and their national identity are really 19th century inventions. The sprawling, multi-ethnic Kingdom of Hungary, which once stretched from the Mediterranean to what is now southwestern Ukraine, rebelled against Hapsburg dominance in the mid-19th century. That break culminated in 1866, when Austria and Hungary became constituent parts of a new dual monarchy, spurring on the 1873 union of the separate towns of Buda and Pest, reconstituted as a Belle-Époque boomtown.
Hungary’s best-known art institution, the Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest (MFAB), first opened in 1906 on the Pest side of the Danube, though it has roots in an earlier collecting spree of the Esterházy family, the highest of Hungary’s high nobility. The museum’s broad range of Old Master paintings and its world-class prints and drawings collection arguably make it the most important museum of its kind between Vienna and St. Petersburg. In 1957, the bulk of its Hungarian holdings were separated into a new institution, the Hungarian National Gallery, which eventually moved over to the Buda side of the city, into the onetime Habsburg Royal Palace. Though the Orbán regime had planned to rehouse it again, it remains in situ for the time being, and its collections of Hungarian art, spanning centuries, testifies to a rich and varied artistic tradition almost entirely unknown outside the country. Back over in Pest, a new cultural development, Müpa Budapest, opened in 2005, providing a home to the city’s Ludwig Museum, with a collection of contemporary art from national and international figures.
Raphael's Esterházy Madonna (around 1508)
Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest
Heroes’ Square
Tiny and technically unfinished, with the Virgin’s face and the figures of the Christ child and St. John the Baptist mere underdrawings, this tempera-and-oil on panel work has a grace and graphic quality that have helped make it the best-known Renaissance work in the country.
Produced at the end of Raphael’s Florentine period, when his output still reflects a youthful interest in Leonard da Vinci, the painting apparently first made its way north of the Alps in the early 18th century during the papacy of Clement XI, landing in the Esterházy collection by 1812. Stolen in 1983, along with the museum’s prized Giorgione portrait and other works, it was recovered the following year in a Greek monastery.
Mihály Munkácsy's The Last Day of Condemned Man (1870)
Hungarian National Gallery
Szent György tér
In Hungary’s heyday before the First World War, when Budapest began to compete with Vienna, painter Mihály Munkácsy was a national hero. Born in what is now Ukraine, then educated at the art academies of Vienna, Munich and Düsseldorf, he eventually settled in Paris, with a base of collectors stretching from Central Europe to the American Midwest. His Budapest funeral procession, in spring 1900, was witnessed by hundreds of thousands people and remains a unique event in the history of the country.
Working in a number of established genres, from history painting to portraiture, he went on to decorate both Vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum and Budapest’s new Parliament building. But this breakthrough work—which scarcely gives a clue whether the condemned man in question is a criminal or a victim of injustice—remains his best known. Winning a gold medal at the 1870 Paris Salon, it was a main topic of conversation in the French capital during the final days of the doomed Second Empire.
Leonardo da Vinci's Study for the Head of a Soldier in the Battle of Anghiari (around 1504–05)
Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest
Heroes’ Square
The MFAB's prints and drawings collection has legendary status among scholars in the field, with key works stretching from Renaissance Italy to early 20th-century Vienna, leading up to the present day. This exquisite Leonardo drawing—one of three in the collection—is a preparatory work associated with a planned mural in Florence’s Palazzo Vecchio meant to commemorate the Florentine Republic’s victory over the Duchy of Milan in 1440.
Left unfinished in 1506, when Leonardo himself left for Milan, the partial mural, made using an unstable oil-based technique, was nonetheless one of Cinquecento Florence’s star attractions, until its degraded version fell victim to a 1560s renovation. This red-chalk drawing of a Florentine captain, produced using a live model, is known for its depiction of intense emotion.
The Holy Crown of Hungary (around 12th century)
Hungarian Parliament
Kossuth Lajos tér
The Kingdom of Hungary—defeated in the First World War, then dismantled, degraded and now disappeared—lives on in this mysterious and glorious object. One of Europe’s oldest surviving crowns, with a lower section of enamel imagery dating all the way back to medieval Byzantium, it likely took on its present appearance in the 12th century. Containing both Latin and Greek inscriptions, and bejeweled with sapphires, garnets and amethysts, the elaborate golden crown had mystical status. It was not only a symbol, but treated as the actual incarnation of the Hungarian state, and sovereigns were not regarded as rulers until it was placed on their heads.
A miraculous survivor of Hungary’s cataclysmic 20th century, it was brought back into use in 1990 following the collapse of communism. Placed on Hungary’s newly devised coat of arms, it has been on display in the national parliament since 2000.
Lili Ország’s Wall of Icons II (Blue) (1969)
Hungarian National Gallery
Szent György tér
Now regarded as one of the most important artists to emerge in Hungary after the Second World War, Ország, born into a Hungarian Jewish family in what is now Ukraine, barely escaped being deported to Auschwitz and later survived the war as a Christian convert.
Judaism, Christianity, and her own biography fuse together in her mature paintings, whose religious elements were in defiance of official communist policies. This late piece, showing a repeating Madonna-and-Child motif, is part of a series of oil-on-fiberboard works. Invoking her longstanding interest in Orthodox Christian imagery, it also alludes to her own trauma at not having had a child.
Francisco de Goya’s The Water Carrier (1808 – 12)
Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest
Heroes’ Square
Goya’s transition from a designer of Rococo tapestries to the great harbinger of Modernism is on view in this legendary painting, made during the dark years of Napoleonic Spain's Peninsular War, a guerrilla conflict that foreshadowed the atrocities of the 20th century.
An apparent genre scene showing a rustic girl carrying food and water, the painting is in fact a wartime vision of desperate heroism. The late art critic Robert Hughes was fascinated by the work, which he regarded as an “emblem of resistance.” He writes, in his 2003 biography of the artist: “You would be very grateful to see her if you were crouched stiffly behind a rock in the parching autumn sun of Aragón, breathing hot dust with the ricochets whining above.”
Can Togay and Gyula Pauer’s Shoes on the Danube Bank (2005)
Id. Antall József rkp
In the years after the collapse of communism in 1989, the newly open societies of Central and Eastern Europe revisited the horrors of their 20th century in a number of commemorative works. This installation on the banks of the Danube, which memorialises the victims of the predominantly anti-Semitic massacres by Hungary’s fascist militias in 1944-45, is now considered one of the most artistically successful.
Comprising 60 pairs of rusty iron shoes, it was devised by Togay, a filmmaker, and executed together with Pauer, a performance artist and sculptor. Fixed in concrete but eerily scattered, the shoes—in women’s, men’s, and children’s sizes and styles—recall the militia's orders of its victims to remove their shoes before shooting them into the river.
Victor Vasarely's Zebras (1939)
Vasarely Museum Budapest
Szentlélek tér
For the first few decades of the 20th century, Budapest was a hothouse of the avant-garde, nurturing the likes of Modernist painter László Moholy-Nagy; Bauhaus architect Marcel Breuer; and the supreme chronicler of 1930s Paris, photographer Gyula Halász, otherwise known as Brassaï. Their work is hard to find back in Budapest, but their near contemporary, Victor Vasarely, the great pioneer of Op Art, has his own museum here.
Schooled in Modernist trends in a Budapest private art academy, Vasarely decamped for Paris in 1930, and his experiments there in the late 1930s anticipated Op Art’s illusions and manipulations by some three decades. This tempera-on-paper work was a stand-out at this year's survey of the artist, Vasarely 120, held at MFAB. It is considered a great forerunner of the movement, which Vasarely went on to promote, often in ever-larger formats, until his death in 1997, aged 90.
Pieter Bruegel the Elder's The Preaching of St. John the Baptist (1566)
Museum of Fine Arts, Budapest
Heroes’ Square
Hungary’s longtime Habsburg rulers, residing up the Danube in Vienna, began amassing their unique collection of works by Pieter Bruegel the Elder within decades of his death in 1569. But this late work somehow got past them, ending up in the Hungarian collection of the noble Batthyány family.
A vast social panorama, with a solemnity largely missing from the artist’s more raucous works, the painting depicts nobles and soldiers, burghers and peasants, Jews and Turks, the healthy and the infirm. Nearly all are transfixed and transformed by the teachings of Christ, as spoken by St. John the Baptist, who is illuminated by little more than the attention of the crowd.
Dóra Maurer's Bent Plane with Wings (1996)
Ludwig Museum
Komor Marcell utca
During the Orbán years, Budapest’s large national art institutions took on a retrograde atmosphere, with leading artists, like their emerging counterparts, often resorting to alternative or municipal venues. Paradoxically, it coincided with an international breakthrough of some cutting-edge figures, like Maurer, who had a 2019 survey at London’s Tate Modern.
A trained graphic artist, Maurer was eventually drawn to geometric abstraction and witty illusionism. This mature acrylic-on-wood piece, acquired by the Ludwig Museum in 1998, uses lines on an apparently curved surface to create a near-sculptural, if resolutely two-dimensional piece.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Della Robbia relief at the Frick Collection gets a crucial upgrade
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: J.S. Marcus
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
For a good part of the 15th and 16th centuries, Florentine sculptors named Della Robbia were making glazed terracotta works of great renown. But not all Della Robbias were created equal. Scholars and collectors have long given strong preference to Luca della Robbia (1399/1400-1482), the founder of the dynasty, and his nephew Andrea della Robbia (1435-1525). Similar works by later Della Robbias and those produced by the workshop can come in a very distant third. For decades, New York’s Frick Collection believed it owned a relief by the family workshop, dated no earlier than the 16th century. But now, after technical analysis and consultation with experts in the field, the museum has updated its Virgin and Child to a 15th-century original, likely from the 1470s or 80s.
“We’re suggesting it’s by Andrea,” says Greta Llanes Serrano, a conservation fellow at the Frick who worked on the recent treatment that helped pinpoint the new attribution.
The framed relief depicts a veiled Madonna holding a Christ child, attended by cherubs. Fashioned out of buff-coloured earthenware, it has the Della Robbia clan’s distinctive white and blue glazes, with, in this case, traces of gilding. The work was first acquired by Helen Clay Frick, Henry’s daughter, in 1922 and spent most of the last century stashed outside the main reading room of the Frick Art Research Library.
Llanes Serrano says the road to the new attribution was filled with twists and turns, and an outright gap or two.
The early American luminary in Della Robbia studies was the Princeton University art historian Allan Marquand (1853-1924). Llanes Serrano says that in a 1906 publication Marquand identified the work, then in the possession of a private German collector, as being by either Luca or “very early Andrea”. Then, in 1914, he decided “that it had to be Andrea”. After it landed in the Frick family collection and found its way to the library entrance, it went from being a Della Robbia, generally, she says, to a work by Andrea—a decision, she notes, recorded by a librarian, though who actually made the decision is not known. Later, it was outright demoted to “school of Della Robbia” and has had that lower-rung status since at least 2008.
Julia Day, who was appointed last year as the Frick’s new chief conservator, thought it was time to take a new look at the work after attending a Della Robbia conference in spring 2025. “I just thought that we have this piece, and nobody’s really spent time looking at it,” Day says.
Llanes Serrano, who analysed the relief over the last year in the Frick’s new conservation studio, says XRF analysisallowed her to move back the dating and place it closer to Andrea himself. “I took multiple readings on different spots on the back and front,” she says, of the non-invasive technique.
The process revealed the elements present in the glaze, and then she compared her results with other analyses of autograph Della Robbia works. This helped her to place it in the new 1470s-80s time frame, when the older Luca was giving way to the younger Andrea. Meanwhile, another clue was plainly visible: “The Christ Child is clothed,” she says. In later versions of the motif made by the sculptors and their workshop, she adds, it was more common to show him unclothed.
A few weeks ago, the museum moved the work away from the library, where it was out of view from the general public, and installed it in a damask-lined spot in the mansion’s first-floor Octagon Room, fresh from its makeover during the Frick’s recent renovation.
Day says this kind of conservation-guided upgrade is a rarity at the Frick, happening perhaps once a decade. The Virgin and Child is the only Della Robbia piece in the museum's collection, she adds.

https://hellgatenyc.com/azar-williamsbur.title: Tuck Into Some Crazy Delicious Persian Dishes in Williamsburg
https://hellgatenyc.com/azar-williamsbur.author: Scott Lynch
https://hellgatenyc.com/azar-williamsbur.text:
Soroosh Golbabae's journey began back in Tehran, where he was born, raised, and, thanks to his mother, first realized that he wanted to spend his life in the kitchen. "Growing up around my mom's cooking played a big role in getting me excited and engaged with food in the first place," he told Hell Gate.
In 2015, Golbabae went all in on his dream, enrolling in the Culinary Institute of America and moving to Bed-Stuy. "It was such an amazing opportunity, coming here," Golbabae said. "So many different chefs, so many different types of food, so much to learn. I wished only that I had more time in the day, to work a triple shift, to learn even more. That's the energy of this city when you first get here."
Like many CIA students, Golbabae was initially drawn into the fine-dining scene, working at heavy hitters like Gramercy Tavern, Sofreh, Eyval, and Sawa, throwing various solo pop-ups along the way that reflected his desire "to elevate Persian cuisine, but keep its soul, its authenticity." But for his first restaurant, Golbabae and his business partner Fardad Zabetian wanted to bring something even more accessible, and more affordable, to his community.
The result isĀzar, which serves a tight menu of loghmeh—Persian for "morsels," though everything here is actually pretty hearty—in a casual, cool-looking setting. Basically, Golbabae takes Persian classics, inspired by comfort- and street-food favorites from Tehran, prepares them with skill and intention, puts them on top of housemade flatbread (it's a kind of a hybrid between lavash and taftoon), and creates these killer, four-bite, handheld delights.

https://hellgatenyc.com/a-barnes-noble-s.title: A Barnes & Noble—Sans Bathroom—Hits the East Village
https://hellgatenyc.com/a-barnes-noble-s.author: Christopher Robbins
https://hellgatenyc.com/a-barnes-noble-s.text:
Inside the brand-new East Village Barnes & Noble on Wednesday, Booker Prize-winning author Douglas Stewart signed copies of his latest novel to celebrate the grand opening of the corporate chain's newest location.
Outside on the sidewalk along Avenue A, a group of independent booksellers spread out their wares in defiance. Usually the group, called Armageddon Time, spends their Sundays selling books outside Tompkins Square Park, though they also have day jobs at bookstores around town. Wednesday's gathering was a kind of protest—a "Barnes & Ignoble Book Fair."
"Someone said to me, like, 'It's good because people are turning away from Amazon and going to Barnes & Noble.' What a pathetic fucking choice!" Szczypka said, in between drags of a rolled cigarette. "All of these bookstores have been carrying this flame because there's like, legitimate interest. It's like a community, like a trade, through ups and downs. And then Barnes & Noble comes in like, right at the end, after BookTok and everything else. And their windows are full of commercial literature."

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: E-Bike Battery Safety Bill Heads to Trump After Bipartisan Senate Approval
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Greg B. Smith
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
The Senate on Thursday unanimously approved a bill sponsored by New York Sens. Chuck Schumer and Kirsten Gillibrand that aims to stem the sale of unsafe e-bike batteries that have ignited hundreds of fires across the city this year.
The bill has twice passed the House and now heads to President Donald Trump’s desk. It requires the Consumer Product Safety Commission to set safety standards for the lithium-ion batteries that power e-bikes and e-scooters and gives the agency the power to halt the sale, distribution and importation of non-compliant batteries.
Batteries that are not safety certified are susceptible to bursting into flame, a phenomenon that’s resulted in 406 fires and nine deaths in New York City so far this year. The City Reporter has been reporting on this problem since 2022.
The bill passed in the House in 2024 and 2025 where it was sponsored by Rep. Ritchie Torres (D-Bronx). But it never made it to the Senate floor because Sen. Rand Paul, R-Kentucky, blocked it via a tactic known as a “hold” that allows a single senator to stymie consideration of proposed legislation.
On Thursday Sen. Gillibrand, the bill’s lead sponsor in the Senate, requested a bipartisan unanimous consent on bringing it to the floor for a vote. The bill then passed with support from both Democrats and Republicans.
“We have lost far too many New Yorkers due to underregulated lithium-ion batteries,” she said. “Passing this bill is an important step in preventing future fires. I urge the president to immediately sign this bill into law and for CPSC to meet its requirements.”
Sen. Schumer said the bill’s passage “brings us one step closer to protecting the public and firefighters from the growing hazards of these low-quality and dangerous batteries.”
As the proliferation of e-mobility devices took off with the growth of delivery drivers during the pandemic, the danger of unsafe batteries increased annually. Since 2019, more than 1,600 e-bike battery fires have resulted in 46 deaths and 628 injuries in the five boroughs.
The Fire Department has repeatedly issued warnings about the dangers uncertified batteries pose and has urged the owners of e-bikes, e-scooters and other e-mobility devices to rely only on safety certified batteries.
In 2023, after an alarming wave of battery fires, the city passed a law barring the sale of uncertified batteries. But since then, enforcement of this law has wavered, records obtained by The City Reporter have shown.
Last month a battery fire at a public housing development in The Bronx resulted in four deaths. Then earlier this month a fire in a Sunset Park apartment building resulted in six fatalities, including an 11-year-old boy. The cause of that fire has not yet been announced but fire officials confirmed two charred e-bikes were removed from the building following the blaze.
The deadly role unsafe batteries play in these fires took center stage in the tragic 2023 death of journalist Fazil Kahn when a raging fire erupted in an apartment below him where tenants were charging multiple batteries. Weeks earlier 311 callers had warned the city about this, but there was no response.

https://hellgatenyc.com/make-me-drain-ca.title: I Hereby Volunteer for the Drain Captain Program That I Am Urging the City to Institute
https://hellgatenyc.com/make-me-drain-ca.author: Max Rivlin-Nadler
https://hellgatenyc.com/make-me-drain-ca.text:
When there's a big rainstorm coming, the City sometimes sends its residents a warning text: "Help prevent street flooding by clearing leaves and debris from catch basins near your home if it is safe to do so. If you're cleaning catch basin grates, be sure to wear gloves & watch out for traffic."
As the text indicates, the city wasn't built for the type of storms we've gotten in the Anthropocene, the imposing churlish thunderheads that absolutely drench, flooding streets and snarling commutes. The sewer system and its network of thousands of storm drains quickly get clogged with street debris, especially during autumn.  
But for most people, the emergency text is puzzling: Catch basins? Gloves? Traffic? Plus, it's November, the peak of the fallen leaf season. Seems like a lot of work for one person!
But what if the city had a volunteer army ready to clear the city's storm drains, sparing their neighbors from flooding, making sure water doesn't run into basements, pool at bus stops, and make crosswalks unsafe? Call them "The Drain Captains."

https://www.artforum.com/news/san-diego-.author: Samuel Wilken
https://www.artforum.com/news/san-diego-.text:

San Diego is getting a new contemporary art museum. The 12,000-square-foot space, called the Strauss Family Gallery, will open next spring. The museum will be free and open to the public. It will host a variety of exhibitions, residencies, and public programs. The museum will be part of the University of California, San Diego.
Museums in San Diego have struggled in the past few years. The Institute of Contemporary Art San Diego laid off almost half of its staff this summer due to financial concerns. In an interview with the Art Newspaper, UC San Diego’s chief campus curator, Jessica Berlanga Taylor, said that the institution has considered these challenges and hopes that the Strauss will be a valuable resource for the city.
The Strauss will be the first “ground-up” museum at the university. UC San Diego already has some infrastructure for the arts on campus. It has the nearly sixty-year-old Mandeville Art Gallery, the Stuart Collection, and a black-box theater. The Strauss will encompass gallery spaces and a black-box theater as well. It also will bring important opportunities for new curatorial research and commissions. The goal for the Strauss, said Berlanga Taylor, is to engage San Diego community members through new public programs and to work with emerging and established artists.
“We’re connecting art inside with art outside now with the Strauss and the Stuart Collection, but we also want to distinguish very clearly what Stuart is about and what the Strauss will achieve,” said Berlanga Taylor. “The Strauss is very much about perception and experience, but it’s also about expanding our ways of knowing and presenting different forms of knowledge that you wouldn’t necessarily encounter in the classroom.”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Where Enrollment Fell in NYC Public Schools This Year
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Michael Elsen-Rooney, Chalkbeat
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
This story was originally published by Chalkbeat. Sign up for their newsletters at ckbe.at/newsletters.
Nearly two-thirds of New York City public schools lost enrollment over the past year, according to newly released school level numbers.
The school-by-school data offers the most granular look yet at how kindergarten to 12th grade enrollment in the nation’s largest school system dropped by 23,000 this year — the largest year-over-year drop since the COVID-19 pandemic. Nearly 1,100 of the city’s roughly 1,600 schools have fewer students than last year, a Chalkbeat analysis found. (Scroll to the bottom of the story to look up how each school’s enrollment changed over the past year.)
The new numbers are a snapshot from Oct. 31 and are only preliminary, officials said. They could change by next summer, when the city usually releases final enrollment figures.
Ongoing enrollment losses have left the city with a growing number of tiny schools, which are more expensive to operate and often can’t provide students the academic and extracurricular options they need. There are 240 schools with 200 or fewer students this year, up from 219 such schools last year, according to the new data. The Education Department has already made five proposals to close and merge schools this year, with more likely to come.
The data underscores the stakes of a decision now facing Mayor Zohran Mamdani: whether to keep budgets steady at schools where enrollment is lower than projected. Typically, the Education Department claws back money from those schools midyear. But since the pandemic, the city has mostly refrained from cutting those schools’ budgets — at a cost of hundreds of millions of dollars a year.
Chalkbeat found that more than 800 schools have fewer students than projected, meaning the city will once again have to spend a hefty sum in order to keep those schools’ budgets steady. Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels has said a decision will come soon about whether school budgets will be slashed midyear.
Several factors are driving the more than decadelong enrollment decline in New York City, including a decrease in the number of children born each year and an exodus of families with young children from the city.
President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown starting in 2025 reduced border crossings and brought an immigration-fueled enrollment boom in many New York City schools to a halt. That pattern appeared to continue this school year, with some of the steepest enrollment losses coming in schools and districts that enroll a high percentage of immigrant students.
The two geographic districts with the largest share of students learning English — District 32 in Bushwick, Brooklyn, and District 24 in Corona and Elmhurst in Queens — were the two districts that saw the steepest K-12 enrollment losses, Chalkbeat found. (Preschool enrollment was not counted in district totals because full data isn’t yet available.)
Queens’ ATLAS, formerly known as Newcomers High School — the city’s largest school for newly arrived immigrant students — has fewer than 600 students this year, down 26% from last year and more than 50% from its peak of 1,428 students in the 2023-24 school year, when the immigration influx was at its height.
Manhattan Comprehensive Night and Day School, which serves many older immigrant students, is down 20% to 548 students, from 687 last year.
The Internationals Network, a group of public high schools designed for newly arrived immigrant students, is down about 6% overall in enrollment — double the city’s average rate — said executive director Lara Evangelista.
“In comparison to where our schools typically are, they’re below projections because you don’t have new arrivals,” she said.
Beyond the steeper losses in immigrant-heavy schools and neighborhoods, the enrollment declines were widespread: All but one of the city’s 32 geographic districts lost students. The exception was District 23 in Ocean Hill/Brownsville, which gained nine students.
District 75, which encompasses schools across the city geared toward students with complex disabilities, also grew, continuing a yearslong trend.
Michael Elsen-Rooney is a reporter for Chalkbeat New York, covering NYC public schools. Contact Michael at melsen-rooney@chalkbeat.org

https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-tears.title: Mamdani tears Achilles in soccer match against NYC press corps, will be out for the season
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-tears.author: Elizabeth Kim, Clayton Guse
https://gothamist.com/news/mamdani-tears.text:
Mayor Zohran Mamdani tore his Achilles tendon during a soccer game between his staffers and members of the city’s press corps Thursday night.
The mayor was brought out in a wheelchair Friday morning into the City Hall rotunda for a press conference, wearing a medical boot on his right leg. He used crutches to walk to the podium and confirmed the injury when asked by a reporter who played at the game.
Mamdani arrived late to the 7 p.m. game at an indoor soccer field in the Financial District. He said he did not stretch before playing.
“I forgot that I was 35,” he said.
It’s a season-ending injury. He said he’ll be in a boot for six to eight weeks and won’t be able to play soccer again for nine months. Dora Pekec, a mayoral spokesperson, said it was “TBD” whether Mamdani would require surgery.
Mamdani — who was the captain of his high school soccer team during his senior year at Bronx Science — scored a goal shortly after entering the game. He logged an extended amount of minutes, while the members of the press team, which included multiple Gothamist journalists, adopted a strategy of frequent player substitution. The game was seven-against-seven on a short field.
It was a non-contact injury. Mamdani, a midfielder, raced after a ball and landed awkwardly on his right leg. He was helped off the field by his press secretary, Joe Calvello, and Gothamist reporter David Brand.
The mayor’s office won the game, but the final score is disputed. Mamdani said his team beat the press group — called “The Kickers” — 10 to 5. Some members of the press on Friday insisted the final score was 8 to 4, while others said it was 8 to 5.
Brand netted a goal during the match. Gothamist transportation and infrastructure editor Clayton Guse tallied an assist on The Kickers’ first goal in a pass to Crain's reporter Jack Grieve. Guse said the assist was the product of “grit, but more importantly gumption.”
Gothamist reporters Liam Quigley and Walter Wuthmann also played valiantly. Wuthmann saved a goal with a header when his team’s keeper was out of the net.
It’s unclear how the injury will affect the mayor, who is known for his youthful energy and social media videos. He has often been seen criss-crossing around the city on a bicycle and getting into pick-up basketball games.
The mayor’s injury was a slight distraction during his Friday morning press conference, which was convened to unveil his plan to close Rikers Island in 2032, five years after the legal mandate. The announcement brought a parade of elected officials and advocates at the more than one-hour event. In the moments where he did not have to stand at the podium, the mayor rested on a stool.
Many of the speakers wished the mayor a speedy recovery.
“I want to assure everyone it is not because of a budget fight with the Council,” joked City Council Speaker Julie Menin. “We really, really hope that you feel better.”

https://hellgatenyc.com/mamdani-soccer-a.title: How Mamdani Tore His Achilles
https://hellgatenyc.com/mamdani-soccer-a.author: Hell Gate
https://hellgatenyc.com/mamdani-soccer-a.text:
On Thursday night, around two dozen members of the New York City press corps gathered in a subterranean soccer field near City Hall for a friendly match against the mayor's press office and the footballer-in-chief, Mayor Zohran Mamdani. It ended with a resounding victory for the mayor's office, and the mayor in a wheelchair.
"I scored a goal soon after getting on the pitch, and I forgot that I was 35," Mamdani said at a press conference Friday morning, next to a pair of crutches. "I tore my Achilles, and I will be in a boot for six to eight weeks, and I will play soccer in about nine months."
The energy going into the contest was a bit frenzied. For one, the venue was a harshly-lit, windowless box with unforgiving turf and walls like a hockey rink—the refuge for white-collar athletes who need to blow off steam following a 10-hour day of staring at a screen. 
And while the match was in good fun, the fourth estate and the mayor's press team frequently have an adversarial relationship over emails and phone calls and texts. Now, they'd get a chance to channel that energy into bragging rights.
Then there was the question of the mayor's talents: Sure, he played soccer as a kid. But was he any good? If a reporter tackled him hard…what would happen?
The press corps was jumpy. They warmed up amid shouts of "let's hear it for the First Amendment!" and "Box out with your ass! Stick your ass out!"
The mayor's press team was smaller in number, and didn't have the jumpy energy that radiated from the journalists.

A woman was found dead in a Lower Manhattan building on Friday afternoon, according to police.
The NYPD said officers responded to a call at 27 Catherine St. at around 3:22 p.m.
Police said they found an unconscious and unresponsive woman at the scene, with signs of trauma to her neck.
The woman — whose identity has yet to be released — was pronounced dead at the scene.
Police said no one has been taken into custody and the investigation is ongoing.
