https://gothamist.com/news/princeton-phd.title: Princeton doctoral student from China detained by ICE in Washington, DC
https://gothamist.com/news/princeton-phd.author: Arya Sundaram
https://gothamist.com/news/princeton-phd.text:
A Princeton University doctoral student was detained by federal immigration agents at Reagan National Airport in Washington, D.C., on her way home from presenting research at a neuroscience conference, according to university officials and her colleagues.
Rodney D. Priestley, dean of Princeton’s Graduate School, said the university was arranging legal counsel for the student, Eva Yi Xie.
“News of Eva's detention is distressing for me and many members of the Princeton University community,” Priestley said in a statement. “We hope Eva will soon be able to resume her studies at Princeton.”
Xie is a third-year neuroscience doctoral student, according to her website. She graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in May 2024. She emigrated from China in 2016, according to the Daily Princetonian, the university’s student newspaper, which first reported the news of Xie’s arrest.
The Brody Lab at Princeton, which studies cancer immunotherapies, said in a social media post that Xie was being held at a detention center in Chantilly, Virginia.
“She went to a conference to present her work, and now she’s in a detention center,” the Brody Lab wrote on X. “She should be home.”
The lab wrote that Xie sent a "call for help" to her labmates on Slack on Thursday, then they lost contact with her. She had attended the Society for Neuroscience conference in Washington, D.C., earlier in the week, and presented her research on Wednesday, according to her LinkedIn.
The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

https://gothamist.com/news/mta-chair-ske.title: MTA chair skeptical of Amtrak's big idea to unify Penn Station's railroads
https://gothamist.com/news/mta-chair-ske.author: Clayton Guse
https://gothamist.com/news/mta-chair-ske.text:
This column originally appeared in On The Way, a weekly newsletter covering everything you need to know about NYC-area transportation.
Sign up to get the full version, which includes answers to reader questions, trivia, service changes and more, in your inbox every Thursday.
Amtrak has floated a “through-running” system at Penn Station where commuters can ride a single train between New Jersey and Long Island without transferring, but MTA Chair Janno Lieber gave the idea a reality check this week.
I interviewed Lieber live on stage at WNYC’s The Greene Space on Tuesday, and the conversation unsurprisingly turned to plans to improve Penn Station, including a plan to have LIRR trains travel into New Jersey and allow NJ Transit trains to continue to Long Island. Lieber said he fears the construction needed to implement the plan would be too disruptive to service at the Midtown train hub.
For starters, crews would need to remove columns and tracks to put in a wider platform that allows riders to quickly get on and off trains to speed up service. That all spells major disruptions for the 600,000 daily subway and train riders at Penn Station, Lieber noted.
“You can't just focus on Penn Station and start tearing apart the tracks,” Lieber said. “That’s like we’re going to have to kill the village to save it.”
Lieber also noted that NJ Transit’s infrastructure and trains are far older and less reliable than the Long Island Rail Road’s. He questioned whether there’s even room to run trains from New Jersey to Long Island through Amtrak’s East River tunnels, which the MTA plans to soon use for Metro-North trains into Penn Station through its Penn Access project.
He said he was open to the idea of through-running as a larger transportation concept for New York City’s terminal stations.
“Just talking about tearing up Penn Station to make wider platforms because somebody might want to go from Secaucus to Sunnyside is not the way to answer that question,” he said. “If you want a real through-running system, let's talk about all of the issues and do it in a systematic way.”
As Amtrak pushed ahead on its plans to rebuild Penn Station earlier this year, the federal railroad released a study showing through-running could be a way to expand service at the hub without expanding its footprint. A second report from Amtrak on regional train service in and out of Penn is in the works. That report likely will include further examination of through running.
The idea has been posed as a way to handle more trains at Penn Station when the new Gateway tunnels double rail capacity between New Jersey and Midtown. Gov. Kathy Hochul has said she’s against a separate Amtrak proposal to increase service at Penn by expanding the station south by razing a block south of West 31st Street.
Through-running is an idea that’s been on transit planners’ minds for decades. The Regional Plan Association has been pushing an idea called the “Trans-Regional Express” that would consolidate parts of the MTA and NJ Transit’s rail operations under a single agency.
Lieber didn’t seem too intrigued by the idea.
“I’m a dyed-in-the-wool-New Yorker,” he said. “I don’t have any regional aspirations at all. I’m not even sure I’m welcome on Staten Island.”
NYC transportation news this week
Meet the man who fixes NYC’s subway mosaics. When the colorful, intricate tile mosaics featuring the names of subway stations like Columbus Circle or Cortlandt Street need to be replaced, the MTA relies on just one man to get the job done. Robert Shenfeld, 73, lives 250 miles north of the city in Syracuse. And he has a monopoly on restoring the MTA’s century-old tile mosaics. Read more about which stations he’s worked on here.
Horse carriages come to an end. Mayor Mamdani signed a bill into law banning the carriage horse industry in New York City by June 2028.
"The whole damn system" will finally get new subway signals. During the event at WNYC’s Greene Space, MTA Chair Janno Lieber shared that the agency plans to upgrade every mile of subway track with new signal technology by 2050.
The feds want to tackle street congestion. President Trump once declared congestion pricing would kill New York City, but his administration now wants to help other cities set up similar tolling programs for drivers as a way to reduce gridlock.
MTA looks to AI to spot people on subway tracks. The agency plans to spend up to $10 million to test a camera system on the front of a train car that alerts the operator to any hazard on the right of way as well as any erratic movement by passengers on the edge of subway platforms.
Brooklyn's Flatbush Avenue redesign gives bus riders priority. Two new bus lanes have been installed in the center of the road between Grand Army Plaza and Livingston Street, and passenger cars are now banned 24 hours a day.
MTA to pilot body-worn cameras on EAGLE teams. After two altercations with riders, the bus fare inspector teams will be retrained on de-escalation and emotional intelligence, and there will be a dedicated fare inspector customer incident hotline to report bad interactions.
MTA warns of major budget deficit without financial aid. The agency’s leaders proposed a balanced budget for next year, but the financial plan also projects a $585 million deficit in its operating budget for 2028, which could grow to a $979 million deficit in 2030 if the city, state and federal governments do not help balance the books.
Curious Commuter
Have a question for us? Use this form to submit yours and we may answer it in a future newsletter!
This week’s Curious Commuter question comes from an audience member at Tuesday’s event in The Greene Space, which has been edited for clarity:
"The MetroCard for years had a display on the turnstile that gave you the charge, whether you got a free transfer, how much you had left on the card. Now we've got this big OMNY paneI and I have no idea whether I've been charged a new fare, whether I got a free transfer, what's left on my card, whether my card is bad, whether it's out of money, whether it's low. Why? Any plans to improve that?"
Lieber's answer
“ I'm not going to make excuses. This is a system that has been designed for well more than 10 years. We’re going to make it deliver the features and the information that you want. It’s not a secret that we have struggled with this contractor who's responsible for all the software, including the features that you just enumerated so well. We have to give that kind of information. In the meantime, if you get online and do an OMNY account, you can confirm all the stuff that you said you want to know, but that's not good enough in the future. You're absolutely right. We have to have that type of information visible at the point of sale or transaction, at the turnstile, and on those validation machines. So point taken, and we're working on it. I can tell you it's coming. Probably another six months to a year before we start to see that kind of data be available as you tap.”

https://gothamist.com/news/rain-one-agai.title: Rain once again coming for NYC's idyllic fall — and maybe Thanksgiving, too
https://gothamist.com/news/rain-one-agai.author: Ryan Kost
https://gothamist.com/news/rain-one-agai.text:
New York City’s generational run of perfect fall days is about to wash out — and forecasters are already sizing up a second storm that could complicate Thanksgiving plans.
Sunday afternoon is set to get soggy when a low-pressure system moving up from the Southeast coast drops showers across the region, said Dominic Ramunni, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service's New York office. The rain will come and go throughout Sunday night and may even stick around for the Monday morning commute before things dry out.
Most of the New York City area will see about an inch or two of rain depending on how the storm tracks, Ramunni said, a significant amount for a short period.
“If it deviates just a little bit further east, the city itself could actually escape some of the steadier rain,” he said.
Once the storm has passed, temperatures are expected to drop from this weekend’s unseasonably warm weather to a more typical range in the 40s, and they’ll stay there throughout the week.
This Thanksgiving could be a blustery one. Ramunni said another coastal storm could swing north toward the region, bringing rain and gusty winds just as New Yorkers are getting their turkeys in the oven.
Still, that’s days away and Ramunni emphasized the forecast this far out is likely to change.
There’s “a lot of uncertainty as we go out that far at this point with a lot of different solutions still on the table,” he said. “But I would encourage anyone who is traveling anytime around Thursday to continue to monitor the forecast.”
Wind, of course, could be an issue for the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, which starts at 8:30 a.m. Thursday.
Under city guidelines, balloons cannot fly if winds consistently exceed 23 miles per hour or if gusts are stronger than 34 miles per hour. This dates back to an unfortunate “Cat in the Hat”-related incident in 1997, when wind blew the cat and his stove-pipe hat into a lampost on Central Park West. Part of the post fell into the crowd, and two people were hospitalized with head injuries.

https://gothamist.com/news/federal-judge.title: Federal judge in NY denies release of man shot by ICE in the Bronx
https://gothamist.com/news/federal-judge.author: Arya Sundaram
https://gothamist.com/news/federal-judge.text:
A federal judge ruled that Oscar Belgal, the man who was shot in the Bronx last month by federal immigration officers, will remain in custody as the Trump administration pursues his deportation case.
District Judge Hector Gonzalez of New York's Eastern District said U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement had the legal basis to arrest Belgal, whom ICE agents were trying to capture in October when police say federal agents fired seven rounds at Belgal’s SUV, wounding him in the neck.
Gonzalez found that ICE had an independent, credible basis for its arrest warrant, including biometric confirmation of Belgal's identity, prior criminal history, and federal records indicating he lacked legal immigration status, according to the order issued Friday.
Legal Aid lawyers argued that ICE did not properly evaluate whether Belgal should be detained before taking him into custody.
Judge Gonzalez disagreed, citing his prior arrest on a first-degree robbery charge and a conviction for fourth-degree grand larceny, among other things. While ICE officials were late to file proper documents formally initiating immigration removal proceedings for Belgal, Gonzalez ruled the tardiness did not lead to prejudice or legal harm.
Belgal, a citizen of the Dominican Republic, has said that he didn’t know that the men who ambushed and shot him were ICE agents until he later woke up in the hospital. According to an NYPD account, Belgal accelerated his SUV forward as plainclothes federal officers approached him with their guns drawn. His 5-year-old son was nearby when ICE agents opened fire, according to his attorneys and police accounts.
Lawyers had argued that the agents’ use of deadly force violated Belgal’s constitutional rights and agency policies, but the judge said the habeas petition filed by Belgal only covers whether someone’s custody is unlawful or not; it doesn’t extend to alleged police misconduct during an arrest.
Gonzalez did write, however, that Belgal could pursue an excessive-force claim through a separate legal action.
The Legal Aid Society said it was “deeply disappointed” in the ruling in an unsigned statement.
Belgal is currently detained in the Metropolitan Detention Center in Sunset Park, Brooklyn.

https://gothamist.com/news/new-york-appr.title: New York approves National Grid rate freeze, but customers could see higher bills soon
https://gothamist.com/news/new-york-appr.author: Rosemary Misdary
https://gothamist.com/news/new-york-appr.text:
The Public Service Commission approved National Grid’s rate freeze for nearly 2 million natural gas customers in New York City and on Long Island this week, but utility customers will still be on the hook for what the company spends during that period for capital improvements and other expenses.
The state’s largest natural gas provider said it proposed the yearlong freeze, which will extend from this March through March 2028, in an effort to address affordability concerns.
But utility advocates called it a sneaky way to pass costs on to ratepayers without having to go through the arduous process of a traditional rate hike case.
According to National Grid’s own filings, the utility estimated roughly $1.7 billion in capital investments during the freeze that it would seek to recover from customers after the rate freeze concludes. The move was unusual because utility firms typically ask for rate increases through a public process to pay for expenditures such as new infrastructure and taxes.
“ The proposal is reasonable as it will allow the companies to continue to make safety and reliability investments to their natural gas systems without creating an immediate rate impact for customers,” said Aric Rider, deputy director at the New York State Department of Public Service, at the commission’s meeting on Thursday.
National Grid did not respond to questions about whether its proposal is circumventing the rate hike process.
"We're pleased the Public Service Commission has approved our rate stabilization proposal that will provide immediate meaningful financial relief into 2028 for more than 1.9 million customers in New York City and on Long Island,” National Grid New York president, Matt Barnett, said in a statement. “This decision, along with the recent improved winter heating supply cost forecast, means customers can expect stable costs for the safe and reliable delivery of energy that heats their homes and powers businesses.”
The rate freeze case received hundreds of public comments, most of which argued that the proposal did not actually offer a true rate freeze.
Typically, companies request increases through an extensive and open public process. Utility companies are responsible for providing details on why they need to raise rates and how they will use the money. The state weighs testimony from regular customers, unions, interest groups and city leaders.
Advocates say the National Grid proposal lacks transparency, clarity and could leave customers vulnerable to hefty future increases.
“The commission is asking us to take it on faith that the companies have justified the investments they make with New Yorkers’ money,” said Hillary Aidun, senior attorney at Earth Justice. “The public has the right to participate, ask questions and hire experts to achieve an outcome that's best for ratepayers and we were deprived of that process here.”
A review of the utility's proposal by Synapse Energy Economics, a research consultant, revealed that the surcharge could add more than $50 to customers’ annual bills, capped at 2.5% of operating revenue, after the freeze ends. The surcharge would be on top of any rate hikes the commission approves in the future, the report said.
“What about next winter and the winter after that?” said Kim Fraczek, director of the advocacy group Sane Energy. “Nothing more than a fake headline for a fake rate freeze. This is all a windfall for National Grid.”

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/shaikh-marxi.title: Anwar Shaikh Renewed Marx’s Economic Theory for Our Time
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/shaikh-marxi.author: Riccardo Bellofiore
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/shaikh-marxi.text:
Anwar Shaikh Renewed Marx’s Economic Theory for Our Time
Anwar Shaikh was one of the most original economists of the last half-century. Few did as much to rescue the Marxian critique of political economy from its theoretical difficulties and develop it into a rigorous analysis of contemporary capitalism.
Anwar Shaikh, who died on October 6, 2026, was one of the most original economists of the last half-century. Few did as much to rescue the Marxian critique of political economy from its theoretical difficulties and develop it into a rigorous, empirically grounded analysis of contemporary capitalism.
Shaikh’s ambition was extraordinary. He reconstructed classical political economy as an alternative to the neoclassical mainstream, understanding capitalism not as a system tending toward harmonious equilibrium but as a turbulent social order whose normal functioning generates competition, conflict, structural change, and crisis.
I owe Anwar an immense intellectual debt. For more than fifty years, his writings were a source of inspiration and critical engagement. While our perspectives were never identical, his influence was deeply rooted in my thinking.
When Marx Was Supposed to Be Dead
I first encountered Anwar’s writings in the mid-1970s. In Italy, where I had studied with Claudio Napoleoni and wrote my dissertation on Rosa Luxemburg, the debate centered on Karl Marx’s theory of value and Piero Sraffa’s criticism of neoclassical economics. The demonstration that prices of production could be determined independently of labor values seemed to many economists to render Marx’s theory redundant. Others retreated into a primarily philosophical defense of Marx, preserving the critique of alienation and fetishism while abandoning much of its economic explanatory content.
Anwar refused this alternative. In the 1970s and early ’80s, his writings were decisive in restoring Marx as a scientific analyst of capitalism. His contributions on the transformation problem, technological change, international trade, competition, and crisis challenged both the claim that Marx had been superseded by Sraffa and the tendency to reconstruct Marxian political economy using categories borrowed from orthodoxy.
His celebrated 1974 article, “The Humbug Production Function,” exposed how apparently impressive empirical results could arise from algebraic identities rather than the neoclassical theory they supposedly confirmed. Mathematics, Anwar insisted, could not substitute for an explanation of the social relations underlying economic phenomena.
His two articles on foreign trade challenged David Ricardo’s understanding of comparative advantage, demonstrating that international competition could reproduce persistent inequalities between nations without requiring monopoly or imperfect competition. His intervention in the transformation controversy showed that Marx’s procedure could be interpreted as the first step in an iterative process leading to prices of production.
The essential issue was not simply mathematical consistency. Marx was investigating the historically specific relations of capitalist production, the exploitation of workers, and the processes through which accumulation transforms itself. What mattered was to recover and develop this distinctive object of inquiry.
Anwar’s essays on Maurice Dobb and on the history of crisis theories, both published in 1978, were equally important. He showed that capitalist crises were not accidental departures from equilibrium, because they belonged to the system’s normal movement. To understand capitalist reproduction was simultaneously to understand its interruptions.
For a generation that had witnessed the collapse of the postwar boom, these arguments were more than academic interventions. They restored confidence that Marxian theory could develop as a living research program rather than survive as a defensive orthodoxy.
The Turbulence of Capital
Anwar’s reconstruction of real competition was perhaps his most enduring theoretical contribution. From this perspective, competition was neither the harmonious mechanism imagined by neoclassical economics nor something abolished by the concentration of capital. It was a relentless struggle among capitals for profitability and survival.
As part of this struggle, firms introduced machinery to reduce costs, undercut competitors, and obtain temporary advantages. Successful innovations spread, transforming productive conditions and undermining the advantages that initially motivated them. Decisions that were rational for individual capitalists could have contradictory consequences for capital as a whole. Mechanization, driven by the pursuit of extra profits, could contribute to a declining general rate of profit.
As Vivek Chibber has reminded us, this view of competition also posed a challenge to the influential monopoly capital tradition associated with Paul Baran and Paul Sweezy. Anwar argued that its claim that concentration had superseded competition rested, paradoxically, on accepting the neoclassical identification of competition with perfect competition.
This conception was central to my own interpretation of Luxemburg. In my dissertation, completed in 1976, I had explored how technological change emerged from both the antagonism between capital and labor within production and competition among capitals for extra surplus value. These processes could generate problems of realization and insufficient investment, without supporting a theory of capitalism’s inevitable collapse.
Anwar gave me indispensable analytical tools for developing these insights. Probably, my subsequent reading of his work was more Schumpeterian than he would have accepted. I saw capitalist innovation as a dynamic of endogenous structural transformation that repeatedly displaced existing productive configurations. Anwar was more skeptical of Joseph Schumpeter, whose account he considered insufficiently emancipated from equilibrium thinking.
My 1985 article on Schumpeter’s monetary theory of development and my 1989 essay, “A Monetary Labor Theory of Value,” developed this difference further. My intellectual formation owed much to Napoleoni as well as Augusto Graziani, Meghnad Desai, and Duncan Foley. For me, Marx’s theory of value was a theory of exploitation within the monetary circuit of capital, not primarily a theory of relative prices.
I distinguished labor-power from living labor, arriving at the category of living labor-power: the capacity to work inseparable from the human beings who bear it. Its actual expenditure as living labor depends on capitalist command, cooperation, conflict, and resistance.
Capital cannot purchase a predetermined quantity of living labor as an ordinary commodity. The extraction of surplus labor is contested; new value originates in this process and acquires its social expression in money. Anwar understood exploitation and capitalist command, but our approaches diverged over the connection between labor, value, prices, and money.
The difference was especially over money. Anwar’s account of real competition and prices of production retained the classical notion of moving centers of gravity and treated money primarily in relation to exchange, prices, and profitability. I drew instead on Schumpeter’s bank-created purchasing power, Graziani’s monetary circuit, and Hyman Minsky’s financing of an uncertain future.
For me, money is constitutive of capitalist production from the outset: bank finance gives firms command over labor-power before production begins, while sales subsequently validate the value produced. Money as initial finance is not merely money as universal equivalent, nor is financing production identical to financing investment. This did not make Anwar indifferent to credit or finance; it marked a different theoretical starting point.
Different Crises of Different Capitalisms
Our views of capitalist crises were different, but also complementary. Anwar’s distinctive contribution was his theory of profitability crises. Capitalist accumulation, he argued, follows recurrent long rhythms, in which phases of expansion eventually give way to prolonged downturns.
Beneath shorter business cycles lies the movement of profitability, shaped by real competition, capital-intensive technical change, and the struggle over wages and working conditions. Particular historical shocks operate within these longer movements. For Anwar, the crucial incentive to accumulation was the rate of profit-of-enterprise, the difference between the general rate of profit and the interest rate.
This distinction was central to his interpretation of the Great Recession, which he called the first great depression of the twenty-first century. The financial collapse of 2007–8 was the trigger, not the underlying cause. But he did not argue that the general rate of profit had simply continued to fall throughout the neoliberal era. On the contrary, he insisted that the attack on labor from the 1980s onward had restrained the decline in profitability, while the dramatic fall in interest rates had raised net profitability and sustained a substantial economic expansion.
Against this backdrop, cheap credit simultaneously encouraged growing indebtedness and financial speculation. The recovery after the end of the postwar boom in the 1970s was real, but the conditions sustaining it could not be prolonged indefinitely. In his mature reconstruction, Anwar distinguished the normal maximum rate of profit, persistently eroded by capital-intensive technical change, from the normal rate of profit, whose decline could be counteracted by a rising profit share. His account of the neoliberal boom thus gave an essential place to countertendencies, without relinquishing the underlying logic of profitability-driven accumulation.
I read Marx’s falling rate of profit as a metatheory of crisis, not a law generating identical outcomes in every period. Countertendencies can prevail yet generate new contradictions: rising exploitation may sustain profitability while aggravating realization problems, and struggles over living labor can challenge capitalist command directly.
My reconstruction suggested a further historical distinction: the nineteenth-century Long Depression and the crisis of the 1970s were both crises of profitability, though arising from different mechanisms; the Great Crash of 1929 and the Great Recession beginning in 2007 revealed instead how the conditions sustaining capitalist expansion could generate crises of realization and financial breakdown.
Anwar recognized the distinctive historical forms of these crises but sought their underlying unity primarily in the recurrent movements of profitability and accumulation. The crisis of the 1970s was for me not merely a wage squeeze but a crisis of the capital-labor relation itself: a difficulty in extracting the quantity and quality of living labor required by capital.
The subsequent neoliberal restructuring transformed both production and finance, developing what I called privatized Keynesianism, sustained by asset inflation, private indebtedness, and politically managed monetary policy. Finance did not simply conceal the contradictions of a stagnant capitalism. It helped sustain accumulation and reorganize the conditions under which labor was employed and exploited.
These were not arguments against Anwar’s theory of competition and profitability. They were attempts to develop a complementary account of how capitalist contradictions take different historical forms.
Anwar engaged seriously with effective demand, credit, and debt, especially in his writings on Marx, John Maynard Keynes, and Michał Kalecki. Our disagreement was not about profitability versus demand but about how monetary finance, class struggle, and accumulation should be connected in a critique of changing capitalist forms.
An Expanding Critique of Political Economy
Over time, Anwar’s project expanded from the reconstruction and defense of Marxian political economy into an ambitious alternative framework grounded in classical political economy. Marx remained central, but the wider constellation included Adam Smith, Ricardo, Keynes, Sraffa, Roy Harrod, and Joan Robinson.
In an autobiographical essay published in 2014, Anwar explicitly characterized his approach to growth as following a “classical-Keynesian-Robinsonian path.” This broadening of his intellectual horizons did not mean abandoning Marx, still less weakening his criticism of capitalism. It expressed his conviction that the classical tradition could provide the foundations for a modern science of capitalist society.
Empirical investigation had been integral to Anwar’s work from the beginning. With E. Ahmet Tonak, he developed a Marxian reconstruction of national income accounts, distinguishing productive and unproductive activities and challenging the seemingly neutral categories of conventional statistics. His research on exchange rates, international inequalities, value-price relations, and profitability similarly connected theoretical arguments with systematic investigation of economic reality.
Anwar participated in the international conference I organized at Bergamo in 1994, marking the centenary of Friedrich Engels’s publication of the third volume of Capital. His contribution, subsequently published in a volume I edited, Marxian Economics: A Reappraisal, investigated the empirical strength of the labor theory of value, drawing also on the work of Luigi L. Pasinetti.
It illustrated a crucial aspect of his intellectual trajectory: Marx’s theory was not merely to be rescued through conceptual reconstruction. Its explanatory propositions had to confront empirical evidence. His association with the Levy Economics Institute, beginning in 1990, further enlarged his research. He engaged with macroeconomic modeling and with approaches related to Wynne Godley’s work without abandoning his classical foundations.
All this culminated in his monumental Capitalism: Competition, Conflict, Crises, a synthesis of decades of research. Few economists have attempted anything comparable. Anwar brought together competition, prices, wages, profitability, investment, effective demand, finance, international trade, and crisis into an integrated alternative to mainstream economic theory.
Capitalism as he understood it was regulated through turbulence, not by the imaginary perfection of equilibrium markets. His intellectual curiosity remained undiminished: his later research ranged from international trade and exchange rates to econophysics, income distributions, and the measurement of inequality.
Perhaps We Are Closer Than We Appear
We met again at a conference in İzmir in October 2014 devoted to the causes of the global crisis. Our discussion returned to a question that had accompanied us for decades: How could Marx’s critique of political economy be developed to account for the transformations of capitalism, drawing on Keynes, Kalecki, and Minsky without losing its theoretical foundations?
On this occasion, Anwar argued that our differences concerned primarily the movement from abstract categories to concrete capitalist reality. Marx had left his theoretical project unfinished, and subsequent economists had chosen different points at which to depart from it. Money, effective demand, and financial instability required further theoretical development but could not simply be added to Marx from outside.
Anwar suggested that Keynes, Kalecki, and Minsky could be integrated into an account of accumulation driven by profitability, provided their contributions were critically transformed. He then concluded: “Perhaps we’re much closer than we appear to be.”
I replied that I agreed with him word for word. My project was not an eclectic combination of Marx and later economists. At the beginning of my presentation, I had insisted on a distinction fundamental to my understanding of Marx: critique is not mere criticism.
Marx did not simply reject Ricardo’s political economy as false. He appropriated its scientific insights, exposed their limitations, and transformed them within a different theoretical framework.
The same task confronted us in engaging with subsequent theories and the changing realities of capitalism. This may also explain why, in his later work, Anwar became increasingly comfortable with a classical-Keynesian characterization of his theoretical project.
An Unfinished Conversation
Anwar’s intellectual independence was inseparable from his political commitments. He belonged to a generation for whom radical political economy emerged from struggles against war, racism, imperialism, and capitalist exploitation. He rejected both the false neutrality of mainstream economics and the reduction of critical theory to political slogans.
As E. Ahmet Tonak has movingly recalled, he was also an extraordinary teacher. My MA students in Bergamo organized a reading group on his book, concluding with a video discussion with Anwar. He explained that a theory of capitalism could not emerge merely by adjusting orthodox assumptions: it required different questions and foundations.
His generosity extended beyond academic life. I remember spending New Year’s Eve with him in 2017, shortly before a difficult period in my life. Our friendship mattered no less than our theoretical projects. We continued to exchange ideas in later years. In 2021, we discussed Sraffa, Marx, and money at considerable length, defending different interpretations while remaining attentive to each other’s arguments.
At the conclusion of one exchange, Anwar wrote: “No doubt there are other issues on which we differ, but the mutual respect and affection remains. I raise a glass to our meeting again under better conditions.” Unfortunately, it will never happen.
To me, Anwar’s legacy is not a closed theoretical system. It is an extraordinary example of how the criticism of capitalism can combine scientific rigor, historical understanding, empirical research, intellectual independence, and political commitment.
For those of us who encountered his work in the 1970s, he helped make it possible to remain faithful to Marx without treating Marxism as an orthodoxy. For younger generations, he demonstrated that an alternative political economy could be developed rather than merely proclaimed.
I will miss his friendship, his intellectual generosity, and his determination to pursue an idea wherever it led. Our intellectual dialogue will continue, at least in my mind. After more than fifty years of reading his work, I can think of no better way of honoring his memory.

https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-charges-.title: NYPD charges homeless man with murder after woman, 62, was killed at Chinatown apartment
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-charges-.author: Liam Quigley
https://gothamist.com/news/nypd-charges-.text:
Police say they charged a homeless man with murder after woman was found dead at her apartment in the Chinatown area Friday night.
The NYPD said officers responded to an emergency call at 27 Catherine St. at around 3:30 p.m. Friday. They found an unconscious and unresponsive woman at the scene, with signs of trauma to her neck.
Police charged Alexander Florentino, 25, with murder in connection with the attack. They said a 66-year-old man was also found bleeding from a wound to his face after he was struck with a broken bottle.
NYPD officials said Florentino, whom they described as "undomiciled," was taken into custody near the scene Friday evening, but they didn’t formally charge him until Saturday.
In addition to murder, he's also facing charges of attempted murder, two counts of strangulation, assault, attempted assault and burglary.
Police haven’t shared the identity of the victim and said the medical examiner’s office was still determining the exact cause of her death Saturday.

https://gothamist.com/news/fdny-grapples.title: FDNY grapples with lithium-ion danger,  EMS shortages and a building collapse
https://gothamist.com/news/fdny-grapples.author: Tiffany Hanssen, Jill Webb, Elizabeth Shwe
https://gothamist.com/news/fdny-grapples.text:
It has been a busy year for the FDNY. Hundreds of firefighters responded to a building collapse in Flatbush that killed eight people this month. Fire deaths across the city have nearly doubled since last year, with lithium-ion batteries driving many of them. And a recent city comptroller report showed that chronically underfunded and low paid EMS teams are taking longer to get to people in distress as life-threatening emergencies spike.
FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore and First Deputy Commissioner Daniel Flynn joined WNYC’s Tiffany Hanssen this week to discuss some of these challenges and the department’s response.
The following transcript has been lightly edited for clarity.
Tiffany Hanssen: Commissioner Bonsignore, you are the first EMS member to lead the FDNY in its history. EMS response times for life-threatening calls are still at a record high. Last month, Councilmember Joann Ariola, the chair of the Council's Committee on Fire and Emergency Management, told us that low pay is a big reason the FDNY struggles to retain its EMS workers; some making as little as $18 an hour. Do you think the councilmember is right? And what changes are you making to address the problem?
FDNY Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore: Yes, I actually really appreciate Chair Ariola's advocacy for EMS. She is definitely somebody who understands where some of the trouble lies. In this circumstance, she is correct that EMS are some of the lowest paid first responders, and that is making it somewhat difficult to recruit and retain talent. It is a very difficult job that requires a high level of medical training. And, you know, after COVID, I think some of the first responders really who were exposed to this were impacted very significantly by this event. You know, they were front and center in taking care of a lot of people. They were exposed to a lot of fatalities and overall, across the nation, it's been more and more difficult to recruit people who want to work for EMS.
With a shortage of EMS workers, I'm curious how you decide which neighborhoods might lose coverage or where to respond on a given day, how those decisions are made.
Bonsignore: It's very dynamic. We keep a close eye on response throughout the five boroughs, and if we have to redeploy and move resources around, we do. We also prioritize the calls that are coming in. Some are very, very serious and life-threatening, and some aren't. We focus our energy a lot on making sure we have a lower response time to those calls that are more serious. It is a constant monitoring of the system.
I want to switch gears here and talk a little bit about these lithium-ion batteries. The city has spent years educating people about lithium-ion batteries, encouraging them not to charge them indoors because of the risk of fires. Some progress has been made, but concerns over battery-fueled fires are back. So for folks who are charging and storing these batteries, what warning signs should they be aware of?
First Deputy Commissioner Daniel Flynn: Well, I think they definitely need to heed our safety warnings, which you can find at fdnysmart.org. That covers a lot of the messaging that we've done in the past. You certainly don't want to put one of these devices between you and your primary means of egress of your apartment. Make sure that you have a plan to get out. When possible, always keep these outside, store them outside, charge them outside. I think it's unfortunate that this has come back into the public eye 'cause I don't think it should have ever left. This isn't a problem that has ever gone away since we've been reporting on this. Since 2021 our numbers have continued to rise. This year we're at 423 fires so far this year.That is compared to year-to-date last year at 256. So we have a significant increase, but I will say that our informational campaign has been effective. Structural fires this year are at 161, whereas last year they were 149, so not a big change, although the total number of fires has changed. So people are listening to us. People are keeping them outside. Unfortunately, this year we have nine fatalities related to these devices. Last year we only had one. Also, one thing you didn't mention is legislation. We are working to craft legislation and support legislation on the federal level as well to prohibit these bad devices from being imported into our country. We think we've made a lot of progress. We've been down to DC several times to support some of these bills. We think we're close to getting some federal rules in place that would prohibit dangerous devices from being imported to our country in the first place, and I think that'll make a big change. We have passed some good legislation here in the city that prohibits the sale of non-certified batteries. That means batteries that have not gone through the testing process with a nationally recognized testing laboratory. And we go out and conduct enforcement with our partners in [the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection] every single day to make sure the shops within the city are not selling dangerous products.
Speaking of that, I'm wondering if you think that has something to do with the rise in the number of cases that we've seen of fires involving these batteries?
A lot of the rise has to do with some better reporting processes and by us raising the attention. I think everybody in the city now at some point has heard our message and is aware of these devices and the fires that they can cause. As I mentioned, our non-structural number has gone up very, very significantly, and we think that has a lot to do with maybe the improper disposal of these devices. We're seeing a lot of fires garbage truck hoppers. So we wanna make sure also that people understand how best to dispose of these devices. You can go to the sanitation's website for information on where to find a disposal site. Do not throw these in the garbage. Do not put them down your compactor chute.
I'd like to pivot now to talking about the building collapse in Flatbush. First Deputy Commissioner Flynn, I'm wondering what you think the department has learned from that tragedy.
Flynn: That our training works and our coordination within this department and with the other agencies cannot be any better. You know, we are able to communicate effectively with the NYPD and other rescue agencies in the city. [New York City's emergency management office] was out there coordinating our efforts. The mayor's office was on scene immediately.
Bonsignore: I think it's important also for the public to know that if you feel nervous or you feel like the place where you are is in jeopardy, you should make that known. You know, you can call 311, put a complaint in if it's non-emergent. If it's something that you feel is an emergency, you can call 911 and somebody will get out there to assess that situation. I know some people are very nervous now about could this possibly happen again. There are people there that will answer those questions for you if you just reach out.

https://gothamist.com/news/adopt-a-storm.title: Adopt a storm drain? NYC proposal aims to enlist residents in flood prevention.
https://gothamist.com/news/adopt-a-storm.author: Giulia Heyward
https://gothamist.com/news/adopt-a-storm.text:
New Yorkers could soon be able to adopt a storm drain on their block and help keep their streets from flooding.
The City Council is considering a bill that would allow residents to volunteer to clear leaves, litter and other debris from storm drain grates, also known as catch basins, that can become clogged during heavy rainfall.
The proposal comes as New York City faces growing flood risks from climate change and an aging sewer system. It would establish a citywide volunteer program to help keep storm drains clear, building on an effort the city's Department of Environmental Protection has already piloted in Greenpoint, Brooklyn.
Total precipitation in the city is expected to increase by as much as 11% by the 2050s, with climate experts warning that heavier rainfall could cause more infrastructure damage and pose safety risks to residents.
City Councilmember Nantasha Williams said concerns from residents in her Southeast Queens district spurred the bill.
“Flooding has been a major concern in our community, and our office receives so many complaints about clogged catch basins, standing water, and streets flooding whenever we experience heavy rainfall,” Williams said. “We hear from residents who are frustrated because these are issues they continue to deal with, sometimes on the same blocks, over and over again.”
Under the proposed legislation, the Department of Environmental Protection would be required to create an application process for volunteers and report annually on the program's effectiveness.
Volunteers would agree to clear leaves and litter from storm drain grates at least once a month and when needed before or after rainstorms. They would not be responsible for cleaning inside the drains.
William Scarborough, a longtime Queens resident who heads the Southeast Queens Residents Environmental Justice Coalition, said he welcomed the proposal.
He said volunteers participated in a similar effort to clean catch basins in the area over the summer, but he wants to see the city step up its own maintenance efforts as well.
“I will say that I think what's needed in addition to that is a regular maintenance schedule to actually clean the catch basins,” he said.
Scarborough noted that volunteers can only clear debris from the tops of catch basins, not clean inside them.
Williams acknowledged that the legislation would not address all of the city's flooding problems but said residents want to be part of the solution.
“We know that flooding is a much larger infrastructure issue, and this legislation alone will not solve it, but keeping catch basins clear of leaves, litter, and other debris is one practical step that can make a difference,” she said.
The city's Department of Environmental Protection launched its own Adopt-a-Catch-Basin pilot program last year in Greenpoint, another neighborhood prone to street flooding.
A DEP spokesperson said the agency was already exploring ways to expand the program to other neighborhoods.
“As climate change continues to increase the frequency and intensity of heavy rainfall, DEP is exploring expansion of the pilot program citywide,” said DEP spokesperson Deja Stewart. “We look forward to supporting the stewards, volunteers, and community groups helping to keep catch basins clear in neighborhoods across the five boroughs.”

https://gothamist.com/news/a-rush-to-ren.title: A rush to rent control in Jersey City ends in a setback for DSA council members
https://gothamist.com/news/a-rush-to-ren.author: Michael Sol Warren
https://gothamist.com/news/a-rush-to-ren.text:
A fight over rent control rules erupted in Jersey City this month, after progressive city council members pushed legislation to protect tenants of a downtown development from a rent hike — a move that ended with the bill getting tossed before it could be formally introduced.
The battle started when the owner of a waterfront high-rise paid off the building’s mortgage early, causing existing affordable housing protections for hundreds of units to expire. The protections came in exchange for state financing of the building decades ago. Tenants were warned that rents would spike to market rate, sparking outcry and spurring the councilmembers to introduce an ordinance they said would protect people on the verge of being priced out of their homes.
But the measure proposed by Councilmember Jake Ephros, a democratic socialist who took office in January, was financially unsound, according to critics and other officials. With only Ephros and fellow democratic socialist Joel Brooks supporting, the nine-member council declined to entertain the bill. Now pro-development groups are claiming a win against rent control in a city that is rapidly gentrifying.
An early payoff and a warning
It’s been 40 years since ground broke on Newport, a master-planned community developed by the LeFrak Organization and the Simon Property Group. The neighborhood sprawls over hundreds of acres on Jersey City’s waterfront, right above the Holland Tunnel. It’s land that was a derelict railyard bolstered by landfill. Today there’s a mall, a row of high-rise hotels and office buildings, restaurants, parks and even a heliport.
The Presidential Plaza towers were the first residential buildings at Newport, and they were financed through a New Jersey Housing and Mortgage Finance Agency program that required a portion of the units be affordable to low-income and moderate-income tenants. That protection was in place for the life of the loan so when LeFrak decided to pay off the debt early, it was no longer bound by the income restrictions.
“ This year, we were in a position where we could prepay the mortgage. We wanted to refinance it so that we could pay for and finance building renovations,” said Charles Burton, LeFrak’s head of government and community relations.
After paying off the mortgage, LeFrak informed tenants in September that below-market rents would only be available for one more lease. Rents would rise to market rate in subsequent leases.
The move was something LeFrak had warned city officials in recent years was coming. The developer had offered to extend the affordable housing protections on the towers last year as part of a new tax abatement deal, but the city council overwhelmingly rejected the proposal.
Newport tenants said they feared being priced out of their homes and they called on city leaders to help them.
The ordinance
Ephros, a political newcomer who ran for council last year as a democratic socialist, responded to the Newport situation with an ordinance that would change Jersey City’s rent control law to eliminate a lifetime exemption for developments built in a designated redevelopment area.
“This is about more than Newport,” he said. “This is about tackling skyrocketing housing costs and moving just a step closer to winning housing as a human right.”
There are dozens of redevelopment areas across Jersey City, all designated by the Jersey City Redevelopment Agency, that are places where builders are incentivized to invest in struggling neighborhoods. Newport is built in one of those areas, but has long since ceased to be an area in need of investment.
About 100 municipalities across New Jersey have some form of rent control. The state law that allows for rent control exempts new construction for 30 years. Jersey City’s local rules give new construction in redevelopment areas a lifetime exemption.
“ The deal was that if developers come in and build housing, they would in return get the ability to have rent control exemption indefinitely,” said Ben LoPiccolo, the CEO of the development firm BLDG-UP and the president of the Jersey City Apartment Owners Association. “That was what gave them the incentive to take the risk to invest the money in a city like Jersey City.”
Nicholas Kikis, the vice president of legislative and regulatory affairs for the New Jersey Apartment Association, said the lifetime exemption was critical for allowing developers to recover the costs of high-rise construction.
“ When you're talking about redevelopment projects, they are significant projects, often significantly vertical,” Kikis said. “We're talking about luxury towers, and this is not the type of project that recovers its entire cost basis in a thirty-year time period.”
Mayor James Solomon said he was skeptical that the ordinance was financially sound. He worried about potentially discouraging development at a time when Jersey City faces a deep fiscal crisis.
“ We're not at a place right now as a city where we can afford tens of millions of dollars of loss to our tax base, particularly from some of the biggest developers in the city,” Solomon said.
But Ephros noted that other cities and towns which don’t offer the lifetime exemption have been able to sustain their own redevelopment efforts.
“ We have had decades and decades, 40-plus years of rent control in New Jersey, and we have not seen evidence of a collapse in property taxes or a collapse in property values that leads to this massive shift in the burden of property taxes,” Ephros said. “We just haven't seen that.”
Ephros’s ordinance was not the first time the redevelopment area exemption was targeted. A similar measure was introduced by the city council in 2019, but never received a final vote.
The new measure, at least in its current form, won't ever get a vote. Councilmember Eleana Little, who represents Newport and often aligns with Ephros and Brooks, abstained despite previously voicing support.
The council members who voted against advancing the measure said they sympathized with the Newport tenants, but didn't have enough information about the potential effects of ending the exemption.
Thomas Zuppa, the member representing Journal Square, called the measure a potential “monumental shift” in city policy.
“ I live in a redevelopment zone in Journal Square with a landlord who raised my rent,” Zuppa said. “I have to set aside my own personal interest for the betterment of the city. Journal Square's had some lean years there for about four decades, and we're finally seeing some growth and development infrastructure built. So I wouldn't want to put us in a position where we're hampering that at this point without the appropriate studies.”
A new deal for Newport Towers
Though the proposal that would place the Newport towers under rent control is stalled, new affordable housing protections for tenants at the properties could be on the way.
Solomon announced Thursday that city hall had reached a deal with LeFrak for a new payment-in-lieu-of-taxes (PILOT) agreement. As part of the deal, LeFrak would increase the number of affordable units in the Newport towers from 272 to 299, with some offering rents at $1,000 a month.
The new tax abatements would last for 30 years. But LeFrak will have the option to cancel the affordable housing agreement after 10 years.
“ We want to protect our residents. We want to keep them in our homes,” Burton said. “They're very much a great part of our community, but affordable housing is a public-private partnership, and we just hope that the city government works with us to accomplish this goal for everyone.”
Burton said LeFrak and the Solomon administration began negotiating the deal in October, the same time that Newport tenants were pressuring city leaders for help.
“Families at Newport were told this fall that their rents were going to market rate,” Solomon said. “Many of them had no idea where they would go. Because of these agreements, they get to stay, and get to stay at affordable monthly rents.”
The new proposal must be approved by the city council. The pair of ordinances being considered are on the agenda to be introduced at next week’s meeting.
“ It gives me no joy to offer LeFrak a tax abatement,” Ephros said. “But my duty is to protect these tenants who are fighting for their homes. And if this is the only way because we are not able to, this time, bring the building under rent control, I'm willing to entertain it if the deal is right.”
LeFrak had been on the verge of a similar deal with the city last year, after negotiations with former Mayor Steve Fulop. But the city council rejected it by a large majority.
The future of rent control
Ephros and Brooks said they intend to bring back the proposal to end the redevelopment area exemption as expanding rent control remains a core part of the democratic socialist platform. It’s unclear when, or how it might be amended to win over skeptical council members.
Developers pledged to fight any future version of the ordinance.
“ I don't think there's anything you can change about the proposal to make me feel comfortable,” LoPiccolo said. “I think that when you really dig deep into any proposal that eliminates the rent control exemptions and you truly do an impact study on what will happen if that happens, it will really create a disaster for real estate here in Jersey City.”
Ephros cast the ordinance’s defeat as a learning lesson. He noted the recent win for rent control advocates in Elizabeth came after years of organizing and campaigning in that city.
“ I see this as a first step,” Ephros said. “We understand a lot more of the terrain that we're going to have to deal with.”

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/23/t.title: ‘Taking Your Life In Your Hands’: Residents Outraged At Slow Redesign Of Dangerous Chinatown Crossing
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/23/t.author: Sam Brule
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/23/t.text:
Child's play? The city places crossing guards around the chaotic Chatham Square to protect pedestrians. Photo: Sam Brule
How long must Chinatown residents wait for safety?
In the wake of yet another crash that critically injured a senior, residents of the Lower Manhattan neighborhood are outraged that the city’s redesign of Chatham Square is expected by 2030 at the earliest — a delay orchestrated by car-focused residents who think the project would make the area worse for drivers.
The proposed redesign would move the intersection’s centerpiece — Kimlau Square — from the east side of the Bowery to the west and rework the intersection to prioritize pedestrians.
But until it happens, Chatham Square remains a confusing jumble full of cars and long crosswalks, with pedestrians and drivers constantly in conflict, as DOT noted in a September 2025 presentation. It’s no wonder that there have been 64 reported crashes and 24 injuries in Chatham Square since January 2022, including the most recent: An SUV driver struck and critically injured a 74-year-old man crossing the street on Nov. 10.
“You’re taking your life into your own hands as you’re trying to get your dim sum,” said Lydia Polgreen, who lives near Chatham Square. “It’s really awful.”
Those substandard conditions persist even though pedestrians compose 80 percent of the people using the square, but only get about one-third of the space, according to the city Department of Transportation. The proposed redesign would give walkers a little over half of the space.
Residents and passing pedestrians agreed that the dangerous area needs to be fixed.
“Something has to change,” said Polgreen, the noted New York Times opinion columnist. “They should at least start with changing some of the patterns around the intersection to make it safer for those of us who live and work there.”
For Polgreen, even an interim safety update to fix signal timing would help calm the violent mess of intersections.
“At best, it’s confusing and frustrating,” added her neighbor, Felix Salmon.
The long-overdue, $56-million redesign was introduced by then-Mayor Eric Adams in February 2024, with construction expected to run from 2027 to 2029. DOT now estimates it will be complete by 2030, according to a city presentation that called the crossings “long and dangerous.”
The project mirrors a redesign pushed in 2008 by the Bloomberg administration that Community Board 3 rejected. The panel — seven of whose members are still on the board — argued that three years of construction would be unfair for a neighborhood that, the board claimed, had been already hurt by the post-9/11 ban on cars on Park Row.
The city put the project on hold, and the Lower Manhattan Development Corporation later redirected $30 million that it had set aside for the project.
The current project has been facing similar opposition, especially from car owners who claim without evidence that Chinatown has experienced an economic downturn since the closure of Park Row to most traffic after the Sept. 11 attacks. The redesign plan is seen by such people as a way to make the closure of Park Row permanent, which is likely true, and would cause more congestion, which is likely not.
The Chinatown Core Block Association — a coalition of neighborhood residents and one of the forces fighting on the frontline of the opposition — has focused a lot of energy on reopening Park Row to motor vehicles.
But that’s a non-starter, thanks to a DOT study that found reopening Park Row to cars would increase evening rush traffic in the square by 45 percent and reduce safe pedestrian crossings from 61 percent to 35 percent. Plus, reopening the roadway to cars isn’t popular: In a Park Row Alliance survey of the two co-op buildings on Park Row, 76 percent of residents wanted to keep the street closed to public traffic.
Still, Council Member Chris Marte, who represents the area, has pushed to reopen Park Row since taking office in 2022. Though a frequent supporter of livable streets issues, Marte has complained that Park Row’s closure reduced foot traffic and affected the local economy.
Other residents of the neighborhood have taken aim at other aspects of the redesign.
One such qualm is that buses will not be able to turn safely in the new layout, a concern raised in 2008, but debunked by the MTA in 2009. “The 60-foot articulated buses, although longer than the 40-foot standard buses, have a shorter turning radius than the standard-sized buses which allow them to make tight turns more easily,” the MTA said in a statement at the time.
Another objection is that the redesign would create traffic bottlenecks, but DOT’s traffic model shows that 76 percent of vehicle trips through the square would get faster as a result of the redesign, while only 16 percent would get slower.
The opposition centers around the alleged impact on car owners. “A lot of people who speak out tend to be vehicle owners,” said Jason Lee, a resident of the area. He didn’t derogate members of the opposition, but merely said that car drivers might simply not be “aware of the complexity and the difficulty the situation is currently presenting.”
But what is clear, is that there is still strong support for a safer Chatham Square. Among residents, Marte also welcomed the redesign when it launched — despite wanting Park Row open to motor vehicles — calling the square “the chaos corner” and saying the plan would reduce bumper-to-bumper traffic. His top priority was improved safety for the chronically messy and dangerous area.
“The intersection is just too big and too complex,” Polgreen said. “Rethinking intersections like this one really needs to be priority.”
But until construction ends, the nearly 10,000 pedestrians who pass through the square at peak hours will have to wait a bit longer for that safety.
Streetsblog reached out to DOT for comment and the agency said that the stretched-out time reflects refinement of the design of the project as well as considerations for complex underground work there.
“Planning and community engagement for the capital redesign of Kimlau Square are well underway and we’re excited to bring world class public space and safety upgrades to this intersection,” said agency spokesperson Will Livingston. “We’re working closely across city agencies to deliver this transformative project, and others like it, faster than ever, so New Yorkers can enjoy public spaces that are thoughtfully designed to improve their quality of life and keep them safe.”
Sam Brule is a senior at The New School. He’s previously worked at the New School Free Press, the Sopris Sun in Colorado, and most recently amNY. When he’s not writing, he works as a bike messenger.
"It is pretty shocking that no one seems to know why the program has been discontinued. It’s really unacceptable to be honest," said Menin, after asking the panel about the pilot.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/do.title: Dora Maar’s Paris Apartment Is For Sale, Picasso Wall Drawings and All
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/do.author: Devorah Lauter
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/do.text:
In this quiet, 17th-century Parisian apartment on rue de Savoie in the 6th arrondissement, strange-looking insects appear to be climbing up the middle of the living room wall near the chimney. But these 15 or so critters—spiders, ants, and cockroaches—are actually drawn and carefully protected by glass coverings.
That’s because they were made by none other than Pablo Picasso, once a regular visitor to this home, where his lover, the artist Dora Maar, lived from 1946 until she died in 1997. The abode, along with the Picasso drawings on the wall, is now for sale, listed for the lump sum of €2.85 million (about $3.1 million), reports Le Parisien. How’s that for a dinner party icebreaker?
Picasso used to call Maar “ma puce,” which literally means “my flea” and is used as an endearing term in French for “my sweetheart.” It is believed Picasso’s drawings were a playful pun on his nickname for Maar, per the apartment’s current owner, identified only as Ida. “They give it a history,” she added.
All the wall artworks have been officially recognized by the Picasso Administration, which manages the artist’s estate, and oversees a committee that catalogs his works.
Many may know Maar (1907–97) as the famous figure Picasso depicted in many paintings over the course of their seven-year relationship, including his “Weeping Woman” series, and another portrait of her from 1943 that sold for $37 million in 2025, quadrupling its estimate. Yet Maar herself has been belatedly recognized for her own paintings and photographs that contributed to the Surrealist movement’s heyday in Paris from the 1920s to the 1940s.
The 1,600-square-foot apartment’s well-lit rooms, large windows, and high ceilings do fit an artistic sensibility, said the owner. With two bedrooms, an office, kitchen, and the famous Picasso-drawn living room, the Maar’s former home also boasts 13th-century petrified wooden beams from a former mansion that was converted into the apartment building.
Future owners of Maar’s apartment will also be able to hop over to the Louvre and the Centre Pompidou, right across the Seine River. Then again, if the urge to see art by a modern master strikes them, they won’t even need to leave their living room.

https://taz.de/Berliner-Linke-hat-entsch.title: Berliner Linke hat entschieden: Emde muss aus Linksfraktion raus
https://taz.de/Berliner-Linke-hat-entsch.author: Stefan Alberti
https://taz.de/Berliner-Linke-hat-entsch.text:
Berliner Linke hat entschieden: Emde muss aus Linksfraktion raus
Die Linke im Berliner Abgeordnetenhaus hat Vanessa Emde aus der Fraktion ausgeschlossen. Drei Abgeordnete mehr als nötig stimmten dafür.
Die Linksfraktion im Abgeordnetenhaus hat ihr umstrittenes Fraktionsmitglied Vanessa Emde ausgeschlossen. Am späten Dienstagnachmittag stimmten 33 von 43 anwesenden Fraktionsmitgliedern für einen Ausschluss. 6 votierten dagegen, 4 enthielten sich. Für die laut Satzung nötige Zweidrittelmehrheit waren 30 Ja-Stimmen erforderlich.
„Wir haben uns das nicht leicht gemacht“, sagte Fraktionschef Tobias Schulze in einer anschließenden kurzen Pressekonferenz. Man habe am Ende keine Möglichkeit mehr zur Zusammenarbeit mit Vanessa Emde gesehen. Es hatte laut Schulze in der Fraktion einhellige Kritik an Emdes Verhalten gegeben. Emde hatte sich Mitte Oktober in einer Videobotschaft von einem gemeinsam mit den Grünen und der SPD in einer Vorsondierung formulierten Papier distanziert, dass das Existenzrecht Israels bestätigt.
Der Ausschluss beziehe sich auf das fehlende Vertrauensverhältnis in der Fraktion, sagte Schulze. „Er bezieht sich explizit nicht darauf, dass jemand von außen diesen Ausschluss gefordert hätte.“ Grüne und SPD hatten zuvor in unterschiedlicher Stärke klargemacht, dass sie keine Koalition mit der Linkspartei bilden würden, wenn Emde Fraktionsmitglied bleibt.
„Wer für uns antritt, der übernimmt Verantwortung für das, was wir erreichen wollen“, ergänzte die Landesvorsitzende Kerstin Wolter, die auch der Fraktion angehört. Sie betonte, dass der Ausschluss Emdes nichts an der Position der Fraktion zu Palästina ändern soll.
Schulzes Co-Fraktionsvorsitzende Elif Eralp, die in der angestrebten rot-grün-roten Koalition Regierende Bürgermeisterin werden will, nahm an der Pressekonferenz nicht teil. Laut Wolter leitete sie parallel die nach Ausschluss Emdes als Tagesordnungspunkt 1 fortgesetzte Fraktionssitzung.
Als Emde den Sitzungssaal 311 verließ, gab es Juchzer und Applaus von Unterstützern. Eine Frau umarmte sie und führte sie in einen Flur. Unterstützer blockierten den Zugang zum Parlamentsflur.
Hannah Bruns, zentrale Stimme in der Landesarbeitsgemeinschaft (LAG) Palästinasolidarität, gegen die ein Parteiausschlussverfahren im Gange ist, kritisierte den Ausschluss. Die Positionen, für die Emde in den vergangenen zwei Monaten kritisiert wurde, sah sie in einem Fernsehinterview durch Positionen der Linkspartei gedeckt.
Die Fraktionsspitze hatte bereits vor einer Woche beantragt, Emde auszuschließen. Laut Satzung musste bis zur Abstimmung eine Woche vergehen und Emde in der Fraktionssitzung Gelegenheit zur Stellungnahme haben.
Der Neuköllner Bezirksverband der Linkspartei kritisierte die Entscheidung der Fraktion hart. „Der Ausschluss von Vanessa Vedi Emde ist ein schwerer politischer Fehler“, äußerte sich der Verband in einer Pressemitteilung. „Ihr Ausschluss folgt auf eine wochenlange Kampagne, in der falsche Antisemitismusvorwürfe instrumentalisiert wurden.“

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120411.title: Berlin nach den Wahlen | Berlin: Emde muss Linksfraktion verlassen
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120411.author: Marten Brehmer
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120411.text:
- Berlin
- Berlin nach den Wahlen
Berlin: Emde muss Linksfraktion verlassen
Mehr als zwei Drittel der Berliner Linke-Abgeordneten stimmen für den Ausschluss der propalästinensischen Abgeordneten Vanessa Emde. Das Ende des Konflikts dürfte das nicht sein.
Die umstrittene Abgeordnete Vanessa Emde muss die Linksfraktion im Abgeordnetenhaus verlassen. 33 Linke-Abgeordnete stimmten für einen Ausschlussantrag des Fraktionsvorstands, sechs Abgeordnete stimmten mit Nein. Vier enthielten sich, ein Stimmzettel war ungültig. Das erfuhr »nd« aus Fraktionskreisen.
Für einen erfolgreichen Ausschluss war notwendig, dass zwei Drittel der Mitglieder der Linksfraktion für Emdes Ausschluss stimmten. Bei 44 Abgeordneten – die Abgeordnete Aysa Şenyüz wurde wegen eines längeren krankheitsbedingten Ausfalls bislang nicht in die Fraktion aufgenommen – entspricht das 30 Stimmen. Dieses Quorum wurde erreicht. Damit ist Emde nun fraktionslose Abgeordnete, aber Mitglied der Partei.
Die Abgeordneten hatten zuvor etwa zwei Stunden lang über den Ausschlussantrag debattiert. Eingereicht worden war er in der vergangenen Woche. Schon vor zwei Wochen hatte der Fraktionsvorstand angekündigt, Emde ausschließen zu wollen. Es gebe »keine gemeinsame Arbeitsgrundlage« mehr, hieß es zur Begründung.
Der Streit um Emde beschäftigt die Linkspartei seit dem Wahlabend am 20. September. Da zeigte sich die frisch gewählte Abgeordnete auf der Wahlparty der Linken in Neukölln auf Fotos mit dem Aktivisten Ibrahim Ibrahim. Der nannte sich selbst 2019 einen »Unterstützer« der militanten Palästinensergruppe PFLP. Auf der arabischsprachigen Webseite der Gruppe wird er sogar als ihr deutscher Vertreter bezeichnet. Die PFLP ist für zahlreiche Terroranschläge gegen Zivilisten in Israel verantwortlich und beteiligte sich auch am Massaker am 7. Oktober 2023. Hinzu kamen ältere Aussagen, die Emde bei einer Demonstration im Sommer 2026 getroffen hatte. »Staaten haben kein Existenzrecht, Menschen haben ein Recht zu existieren«, sagte sie dort – und sprach Israel so wenig verklausuliert das Existenzrecht ab.
Mit den Beschlüssen der Linkspartei ist das nicht vereinbar. Gleich mehrfach bekannte sich die Partei auf Bundes- und Landesebene zur Zweistaatenlösung. Zunächst wirkte es so, dass Emde einlenken würde. Sie unterschrieb wie alle anderen Abgeordneten der Linksfraktion eine Erklärung, die das Bekenntnis zum israelischen Existenzrecht bekräftigte. Doch nur zwei Tage später veröffentlichte sie ein Video auf Instagram, mit dem sie ihre Unterschrift zurückzuziehen schien. »Ich stehe zu meinen Aussagen, und ich nehme keine einzige davon zurück«, sagte Emde in dem Video.
Damit brachte Emde auch jene Linke-Funktionäre gegen sich auf, die ihren politischen Positionen durchaus nahestehen. Es half wenig, dass Emde sich an einer Gegendemonstration zum Landesparteitag am 31. Oktober beteiligte, statt am Parteitag als Delegierte teilzunehmen. »Komplizenschaft mit Völkermördern« warf sie ihrer Partei in einer Rede vor, die pünktlich zur Mittagspause des Parteitags begann, als zahlreiche Delegierte und Journalisten den Saal verließen.
Das Verhalten Emdes verdrängte schon bald die Kritik an ihren Positionen, wenn die Fraktions- und Parteispitze ihren Ausschluss begründeten. »Sie hat sich wiederholt und bewusst über unsere gemeinsamen Beschlüsse hinweggesetzt«, sagte die Landesvorsitzende Kerstin Wolter vor zwei Wochen. Durchaus bemerkenswert äußerte sich die Bundesvorsitzende Ines Schwerdtner: »Diese jetzt oft geäußerte Kritik an Emdes Palästina-Position, diese sei antisemitisch, teilen wir nicht«, sagte sie gegenüber »T-Online«. Der Grund für den Ausschluss sei vielmehr Emdes »permanente Provokation« und ihre »Verweigerung, zusammenzuarbeiten«.
Emde selbst bezeichnete das Ausschlussverfahren in einem Interview mit dem »Freitag« als »Schmierentheater«. Sie verurteile Kriegsverbrechen und Angriffe auf Zivilisten. »Ich lasse mich nicht verbiegen, entmutigen und ich bleibe«, so Emde. Ihr geplanter Ausschluss verfolge das Ziel, die Forderungen der Koalitionspartner zu erfüllen und die Palästina-Solidarität zu schwächen.
Ganz falsch ist das nicht. Vor allem die SPD unter Landeschef Steffen Krach hatte in den sogenannten Vorsondierungen darauf gedrängt, dass Emde aus der Linksfraktion ausgeschlossen werden sollte. Zuletzt bekräftigte die Grüne-Bundesvorsitzende Franziska Brantner gegenüber der »Frankfurter Allgemeinen Zeitung« die Erwartung der möglichen Koalitionspartner der Linken: »Wenn das scheitert, kann ich allen nur abraten, in eine Regierung mit einer politischen Führung zu gehen, die in der eigenen Fraktion keine Macht hat.«
Während Emde in Berlin außerhalb des Jugendverbands Solid kaum noch Verbündete hat, kam ihr zuletzt bundesweit Unterstützung zu. Am vergangenen Wochenende hielt sie beim Landesparteitag der Linken in Hessen via Videoschalte ein Grußwort – unter dem Jubel der Delegierten. Der bayerische Landesverband sicherte ihr mit einem Instagram-Post seine Unterstützung zu. Beiden Verbänden ist gemein, dass sie nicht nur von einer Regierungsbeteiligung, sondern auch von einer parlamentarischen Repräsentation meilenweit entfernt sind.
Auch im Bundesvorstand und in der Bundestagsfraktion kann Emde auf Unterstützer setzen. Unter anderem die stellvertretende Bundesvorsitzende Özlem Demirel und die stellvertretende Fraktionsvorsitzende Clara Bünger sprachen sich in einem offenen Brief gegen den Ausschluss Emdes aus. Am Wochenende ist eine bundesweit aktive Gruppe hinzugekommen. Bei der Gründung der »Sozialistischen Vernetzung« im hessischen Kassel sollte Emde ein Grußwort halten, das sie allerdings absagte. In den Vorstand der Gruppe, die eine Anerkennung als Bundesarbeitsgemeinschaft anstrebt, wurde auch Hannah Bruns gewählt, eine enge Verbündete Emdes. Gegen sie läuft ein Parteiausschlussverfahren. In einem Beitrag hatte Bruns geschrieben: »Ich stehe uneingeschränkt hinter dem Recht der Palästinenser*innen auf bewaffneten Widerstand gegen Besatzung und Völkermord.«
Mit dem Ausschluss dürfte die Debatte über propalästinensische Positionen in der Linkspartei kaum beendet sein. Schon für den Dienstagabend ist Emde als Rednerin bei einer Veranstaltung der Linksjugend in Neukölln unter dem Titel »Palästinasolidarität ist kein Verbrechen! Raus aus der Defensive!« angekündigt. Der Konflikt könnte weit über die Linkspartei hinausweisende Konsequenzen haben. Nach dem geplanten Abschluss der Koalitionsverhandlungen wollen alle drei Parteien ihre Basis über den Koalitionsvertrag abstimmen lassen – ein möglicher rot-grün-roter Senat könnte daran noch scheitern.
In den vergangenen zwei Jahren hat sich die Anzahl der Linke-Mitglieder in Berlin fast verdreifacht – von 7000 auf etwa 20.000. Viele Neumitglieder sind ausgesprochen jung. Ob sie Emdes Positionen unterstützen, weiß allerdings niemand. In der Führung der Berliner Linkspartei ist die Hoffnung groß, dass Verhandlungserfolge in den Koalitionsgesprächen bis dahin die Emde-Frage im Bewusstsein der Mitglieder verdrängt haben.
Die Wähler der Linkspartei sind mehrheitlich nicht auf Emdes Seite: 52 Prozent der Anhänger der Partei befürworten laut einer Umfrage von »Civey« den Ausschluss aus der Fraktion. Unter allen Berlinern unterstützen 65 Prozent der Befragten den Rauswurf. Befragt wurden in der vergangenen Woche 5000 Menschen.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.
