Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Back in January 2024, just weeks into Israel's onslaught in Gaza, the World Court found a "plausible risk" that Palestinians there were being subjected to genocide.
It also imposed a series of provisional measures on Israel to ensure its military did not commit genocidal acts, that aid was allowed in, that all incitement stopped, and that the destruction of evidence was prevented. Israel ignored all of these obligations.
Intent on show
First, the ICJ ruling against Myanmar has set a legal precedent. It is the first time the court has found a state guilty of genocide. It clears a path for the United Nations court to make the same finding, based on even more damning evidence, against Israel.
The bar for establishing genocide has always been higher than for proving war crimes or crimes against humanity because, critically, it requires demonstrating intent by the state under investigation.
In ruling against Myanmar, the court noted that the regime had encouraged anti-Rohingya hate speech, portraying the minority as "sub-human" and posing a "violent threat". This rhetoric, in the view of the judges, exposed the deeper reasoning behind Myanmar's "clearance operations".
In Israel's case, it should be easier to establish intent than it was with Myanmar. Nine pages of South Africa's 84-page submission (59-67) to the ICJ were quotes from Israeli leaders, from the prime minister down, expressing genocidal intent towards Gaza's civilian population.
As is often pointed out, this was the most publicly confessed crime in history.
Israel could carry out operations to eradicate Hamas, or disarm it, and still be committing genocide
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu compared Gaza's Palestinians to Amalek. In the Bible, the Israelites are ordered by God to kill every last Amalek man, woman and child, leaving no one alive. In other words, to commit a genocide.
Former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant called the people of Gaza "human animals" and insisted they be denied all food, water and fuel.
President Isaac Herzog declared no one in Gaza, not even its children, to be innocent: "It is an entire nation out there that is responsible. It is not true this rhetoric about civilians not aware, not involved. It's absolutely not true."
The record of genocidal incitement by Israel's leadership is indisputable.
Second, the ICJ rejected Myanmar's defence that its violence was a justifiable response - that it was counterterrorism - following violent attacks by fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army.
The judges ruled that the junta could be pursuing more than one strategy at the same time, and that its military actions to kill rebel fighters could run in parallel to a wider policy of targeting the civilian population.
This is precisely where Israel's narrative is likely to come unstuck.
Israel and its apologists prefer to start the clock with Hamas's one-day breakout on 7 October 2023 from long-besieged Gaza - effectively a concentration camp for Palestinians engineered by Israel over the preceding decades.
Hamas's short, bloody attack inside Israel did not initiate the violence. As the ICJ found in a separate advisory opinion in 2024, Israel has committed crimes systematically against the Palestinian people for decades - and long before October 2023.
That includes an illegal and brutal military occupation, the forced transfer of Palestinians from their homes so Jewish settlers can colonise their land, the prolonged siege of Gaza, and a violent regime of apartheid rule against Palestinians.
More specifically, Israel has claimed its carpet-bombing of Gaza, and its destruction of essential civilian infrastructure - homes, hospitals, schools, government offices, bakeries, agricultural land - is warranted by its efforts to "eradicate Hamas".
In the Myanmar ruling, the ICJ showed it is likely to give short shrift to such rationalisations.
Israel could carry out operations to eradicate Hamas, or disarm it, and still be committing genocide. In fact, it could do so precisely to remove the possibility of resistance to its war crimes and make the task of committing genocide easier.
Cover story
Third, Myanmar argued that, if its goal was genocide, it could have killed far more Rohingya than it actually did. Estimates are that the junta's actions most likely killed between 1 and 2 percent of the Rohingya people.
The ICJ found, in accordance with the 1948 Genocide Convention, that genocide is not a numbers game. Once intent to destroy a people in whole or part is established, other practices - such as preventing births, forcibly displacing the population, and making their lands uninhabitable - also qualify as genocide.
Israel and its apologists have wilfully sought to mislead about the convention's definition, treating the Holocaust as the only model of what a genocide looks like.
Their argument rests heavily on the false idea that genocide is indeed about numbers, and that Israel would have wiped out everyone in Gaza were it actually bent on genocide.
Netanyahu has regularly articulated this sentiment. In August 2025, for example, he told a press conference: "If we had wanted to commit genocide, it would have taken exactly one afternoon."
Again, the ICJ is unlikely to entertain this as a defence.
Netanyahu's logic intentionally obscures the obvious fact that, in an age of international law, states like Myanmar and Israel have a vested interest in concealing their genocidal intent both by carrying out their crimes incrementally and by offering military rationales as a cover story.
Based on the Rohingya ruling, the number of dead in Gaza is sufficient to qualify as genocidal violence. The known death toll, at nearly 75,000, is more than 3 percent of Gaza's population - and double the percentage of known Rohingya fatalities at the hands of Myanmar's junta.
The Gaza estimates, however, are likely to be a severe undercount, given that many Palestinians were buried under rubble or vaporised by US-supplied 2,000lb bombs. It is also a count of those killed by Israeli weaponry, not those who have died as a result of the dire conditions Israel has engineered in the enclave.
The Israeli military's own assessments are also damning. According to their tally, revealed in August 2025, more than four in five of the dead were civilians, not Palestinian fighters.
Genetic harm
Fourth, the ICJ found that Myanmar had committed genocide in three of the convention's five categories: the mass killing; causing serious bodily and mental harm through torture, physical injuries and sexual violence; and preventing births within the group by targeting children and reproductive organs.
Israel has clearly committed crimes on a significant scale in these same three categories, plus it has violated an additional, fourth category of the convention.
As noted earlier, both numerically and proportionally, Israel has killed more Palestinians than Myanmar killed Rohingya. UN bodies have repeatedly found that Israel has caused serious bodily and mental harm to the people of Gaza.
Nearly one in ten Palestinians there are known to have been maimed by Israel's attacks, and nearly everyone has been left with deep mental scars from Israel's relentless bombing campaigns, the equivalent of unleashing at least six Hiroshimas over the tiny enclave.
In addition, thousands of Palestinians - men, women and children - have been seized from Gaza and held in detention camps where torture and sexual violence are reported to be rife. Inmates often emerge severely malnourished.
In June, a UN commission of inquiry concluded that Israel was deliberately targeting children in Gaza. It said these acts "form part of a deliberate strategy to destroy the future of the Palestinians in Gaza by targeting their children".
Independent witnesses, such as international doctors volunteering in Gaza, have testified that soldiers appear to be playing horrifying games in which they compete with each other to show off their prowess as snipers.
Each day, according to the doctors, the soldiers target a different body part: the neck, the abdomen, the testicles.
The ICJ also has plenty of evidence to find against Israel in an additional category in the Genocide Convention, that of creating conditions destructive to life.
In Myanmar's case, the ICJ ruled that evidence the Rohingya had been confined in internment camps where they were denied basic healthcare was not sufficient to meet this fourth category.
In Israel's case, by contrast, Palestinians have not only been denied access to health services. Israel has systematically gone about destroying the entire healthcare system and blocking the entry of medicines and medical equipment.
It has subjected the people of Gaza to sustained starvation, creating widespread malnutrition that scientists warn will cause lasting genetic harm.
It has blocked the entry of equipment to repair water and sewage systems Israel has destroyed, exposing the people to contaminated groundwater and the spread of disease. It has also blocked tents, blankets and mattresses desperately needed as winter sets in.
As Oxfam and the Conflict and Environment Observatory reported on 23 November, by reducing Gaza's buildings to rubble through the use of many tens of thousands of tonnes of explosives, Israel has created a "toxic wasteland", one that will expose the enclave's inhabitants to grave health dangers for "generations to come".
On these and many other grounds, the ICJ can find Israel has violated the Genocide Convention even more comprehensively than Myanmar.
Journalists killed
Fifth, as part of the genocide finding against Myanmar, the World Court factored in a wider context of systematic discrimination by Buddhist majority against the Rohingya that reinforced suspicions of genocidal intent.
These discriminatory policies included eroding the Rohingya's human rights through restrictions on movement and the blocking of humanitarian aid, and limiting married couples to two children.
Other matters served similarly as circumstantial evidence, especially the concealment and destruction of evidence, a failure to prevent civilians from committing atrocities alongside security forces, and a reluctance to prosecute perpetrators.
As noted earlier, the ICJ has already found Israel guilty of operating a decades-old system of apartheid against Palestinians. That included blockading Gaza by land, sea and air for nearly two decades, strictly controlling who could go in or out of the enclave.
Israel has repeatedly been caught in lies designed to cover up its atrocities
Israel was also forced to admit in 2012 that it had imposed a near-starvation diet on the people of Gaza starting four years earlier. In the words of a close adviser to the prime minister of the time, Ehud Olmert, the goal was "to put the Palestinians on a diet, but not to make them die of hunger".
In 2015, the UN warned that Gaza, under Israel's severe restrictions, would soon become "uninhabitable", that Israel had sought to de-develop the enclave, and that the enclave's aquifers were quickly becoming contaminated by seawater, posing a threat to the health of the population.
Israel has sought to conceal its crimes in Gaza by refusing to allow entry to foreign journalists to report on what is happening there. Meanwhile, it has killed local Palestinian journalists in unprecedented numbers in an attempt to stop them from documenting its crimes.
Israel has repeatedly been caught in lies designed to cover up its atrocities and has sought to destroy incriminating evidence, including by secretly burying Palestinian victims of its violence in mass graves.
The UN found in March 2025, for example, that the Israeli military had buried in a mass grave 15 emergency workers who it had picked off "one by one" after ambushing their vehicles.
The crews had been coming to the aid of another team attacked by the Israeli army earlier that day in Rafah. The UN noted that Israeli bulldozers had crushed the ambulances and then covered them with sand.
Similarly, Israel attacked and seized two large hospitals in Gaza, Nasser and al-Shifa, in early 2024. After its forces pulled out, large mass graves were found close by both.
At Nasser Hospital, three mass graves contained 392 bodies, including those of women, children, the elderly and injured people. Evidence was found of "field executions" and mutilations of some of the dead.
As with Myanmar, such atrocities by Israeli soldiers go uninvestigated and unpunished. Even after a video showed five reservists anally raping a Palestinian prisoner with a baton, causing him severe internal injuries, the Israeli military dropped all charges.
Also like Myanmar, Israel has let civilian groups from its Jewish population collude in its genocidal violence without punishment. Far-right groups have regularly been allowed to mass at crossing points to block the delivery of critically needed food. On repeated occasions, they have looted the aid.
In summer 2024, at the height of these blockades, it was found that three of the groups were being rewarded by Israel and the US with special tax-deductible status for donations.
Hypocrites to the end
In these and all other cases of suspected atrocities, Israel has refused access to outside investigators, just as it has journalists. It has continued that policy even after agreeing to a ceasefire in October 2025 - a ceasefire it has entirely ignored.
More than 1,670 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza during the ceasefire period.
Israel's aversion to transparency is likely to incriminate it further in the eyes of the ICJ's judges, just as it did for Myanmar.
The court has shown in its latest ruling that it is ready to fill evidential gaps, even if it means drawing on arm's-length investigations by UN agencies and international and local human rights bodies. There is a wealth of damning evidence already.
The ICJ is also likely to accept the growing body of confessions made by Israeli soldiers of their involvement in atrocities and the systematic use of violence against the people of Gaza through AI, as set out by whistleblowing intelligence officers in a recent documentary, NAZA.
It is not just Israel, however, that has reasons to be fearful of the Myanmar judgment.
Several western states, including Britain, Canada, France and Germany, backed the genocide case against Myanmar at the ICJ initiated by The Gambia. Separately, the US assessed in 2022 that Myanmar had committed genocide against the Rohingya.
On 19 November, Ed Miliband, the UK foreign secretary, welcomed the ICJ ruling, ordered the expulsion of Myanmar's defence attache and threatened "further action". Four days later, Britain formally recognised the genocide and sanctioned five Myanmar generals.
The US noted that it had been the "leading donor for the Rohingya refugee humanitarian response", and that it shared "grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights" of the Rohingya.
Western states' hypocrisy is fully on show. They have failed in their duty to prevent an even more obvious genocide in Gaza than the one in Myanmar, despite the World Court warning them of the "plausible risk" in January 2024.
Not only that, but the genocide in Gaza would have been impossible without active help from the US, Britain and Germany in supplying the weapons used to kill Palestinians en masse, providing intelligence to Israel and offering diplomatic cover.
The case against Myanmar took seven years to reach its conclusion after The Gambia brought it to the ICJ. If a similar timeline is followed in Gaza's case, Israel may not be found guilty for another three or four years.
Israel can do a lot more damage to the enclave and its population in the meantime. The Myanmar case should prove to western states that they need to act now. It should galvanise a response.
Instead, hypocrites to the bitter end, western capitals will carry on backing the current genocide in Gaza as they lament the earlier one in Myanmar.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120412.title: Care-Arbeit und Frauen – Die Medienkolumne | Sorgearbeit macht Sorgen
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120412.author: Sheila Mysorekar
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120412.text:
- Kommentare
- Care-Arbeit und Frauen – Die Medienkolumne
Sorgearbeit macht Sorgen
Frauen werden bei den geplanten Sozialreformen massiv benachteiligt. Das scheint aber allen egal zu sein. Eine Kolumne.
Vorige Woche ging in den USA ein Video der Satiresendung Saturday Night Live viral, mit Millionen Klicks innerhalb weniger Tage. Der Titel lautete »Sister« und war eine Parodie auf Reklamevideos von Versicherungen für Senioren-Pflege: Mehrere Männer im Video sagten stolz, dass sie eine kostenlose und unkomplizierte Pflegeoption für ihre alten Eltern gefunden hätten. Nämlich ihre Schwester. Im Hintergrund war eine Frau zu sehen, die putzte, einen alten Mann fütterte und so weiter, und im Vordergrund stand der »Bruder« und sagte, es sei total einfach – man brauche nur an seine Schwester eine WhatsApp zu schicken mit den Worten »Vater ist gestürzt«, und schon habe man im Nu eine kostenlose Pflegerin engagiert, weil die Schwester sofort anreisen und die Pflege übernehmen würde. Am Ende des Videos sagten die Männer zufrieden lachend: »Und ich kann in Ruhe mein Leben weiterleben!«
Dieses Satirevideo traf offensichtlich einen Nerv in den USA, wo drei von fünf Menschen, die sich um pflegebedürftige Verwandte kümmern, Frauen sind – über 50 Millionen Frauen, die ihre eigenen Bedürfnisse und Berufspläne zurückstellen, um »sich um die Familie zu kümmern«. Erst die Kinder, dann die alten Eltern.
Die Zahlen sind ähnlich in Deutschland. Es gibt rund 5,7 Millionen Pflegebedürftige (2023). Vier von fünf werden zu Hause versorgt, davon 3,1 Millionen von Angehörigen. 64 Prozent dieser Hauptpflegepersonen sind Frauen.
Sheila Mysorekar ist Vorsitzende des postmigrantischen Netzwerks der Neuen Deutschen Organisationen.
Und jetzt wird mit den Sozialreformen die Hilfe dafür weiter gekürzt. Diese Kürzungen betreffen durchaus nicht alle Menschen gleichermaßen – Reiche sind beispielsweise gar nicht betroffen, Arme hingegen sehr. Und da trifft es vor allem Frauen. Die Kürzungen im Haushaltsentwurf für 2027 sind unter anderem beim Wohngeld, der Kitafinanzierung, beim Unterhaltsvorschuss für Alleinerziehende und den Kinderkrankentagen vorgesehen. Laut einer Studie des Thinktanks »Dezernat Zukunft« im Auftrag des Deutschen Frauenrats gehen 60 Prozent der geplanten Einsparungen zu Lasten von Frauen.
Unter anderem wird laut darüber nachgedacht, den Entlastungsbeitrag bei Pflegegrad 1 und die Verhinderungspflege zu streichen. Letzteres bedeutet, dass Menschen – also meist Frauen – die hilfsbedürftige Angehörige pflegen, nicht einmal für ein, zwei Wochen im Jahr eine Ersatzpflege bezahlt bekommen, damit sie in Urlaub fahren oder überhaupt mal eine Pause machen können.
»Schwarz-rote Kürzungspläne treffen vor allem Frauen«, schreibt die »taz« in aller Deutlichkeit. Die »Frankfurter Rundschau« und das ZDF griffen das Thema ebenfalls auf, aber nur, um über das Ergebnis der Studie zu berichten. Darüber hinaus gab es keinerlei öffentliche Diskussion, was diese Kürzungen für den weiblichen Teil der Bevölkerung bedeutet, und zwar vor allem für Alleinerziehende und arme Frauen sowie diejenigen, die sich um pflegebedürftige Angehörige kümmern.
Care-Arbeit ist nach wie vor unsichtbar, ob es um Kinderbetreuung, Haushalt oder Pflege geht. Frauen kümmern sich halt um Haushalt und Familie, soweit normal, soweit frauenfeindlich. Aber diese Situation ist nicht nur für die einzelne Frau eine Belastung und ein Armutsrisiko, sondern auch für die gesamte Gesellschaft, wie eine kürzlich veröffentlichte Analyse der Bertelsmann-Stiftung zeigt: »In knapp zwanzig Jahren werden 13,3 Prozent der Bevölkerung im Erwerbsalter Angehörige pflegen – besonders betroffen sind Frauen. Ohne bessere Pflegevereinbarkeit steigt der Verlust an Erwerbsvolumen damit um ein Viertel an«, so die Warnung. »Wenn Frauen Pflege übernehmen, reagieren sie häufiger und früher als Männer mit einer schrittweisen Reduzierung ihrer Arbeitszeit. Die Folgen für die Erwerbstätigkeit treffen Frauen damit besonders stark. Setzen sich diese Muster in den kommenden Jahren fort, könnten im Jahr 2045 rund 580.000 Frauen wegen ihrer Pflegeverantwortung weniger oder gar nicht erwerbstätig sein. Das entspricht drei Viertel des gesamten Verlusts an Erwerbsvolumen und einem Umfang von 173.000 Vollzeitäquivalenten.«
Wo sind die Schlagzeilen? Der WDR und die »Zeit« berichteten knapp darüber, aber das war schon das Ende vom Lied. Keine heftige mediale Debatte, keine Forderungen an die Bundesregierung, keinerlei Bedenken bei den Sozialreformen. Die Frauen werden es ja schon abfedern. Irgendwie.
Kein Milliardär im Rücken
Andere Medien haben Konzerne oder Milliardäre im Rücken. Wir haben die nd.Genossenschaft und Leser*innen wie dich. Das macht uns unabhängig und genau das wollen wir bleiben. Aber es heißt auch: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Du kannst direkt hier spenden, einmalig oder regelmäßig, damit nd bleibt.

Morning update
Good morning Middle East Eye readers,
Here are the latest developments:
- An Israeli attack on an apartment in Gaza City has killed a senior Palestinian security official alongside his wife and two daughters, aged 13 and 15. According to the interior ministry, the man was identified as the director of the Internal Security Service in northern Gaza, Muhammad Majid Abu al-Awf, 47. This marks the second killing of a security official in Gaza in less than 24 hours, with the previous attack killing director-general of the Internal Security Service, Naim Mohammed Abu Nahl.
- Iran's First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref said that Tehran is not concerned about the US naval blockade, the semi-official Tasnim news agency reported. He indicated the country's self-reliance with the increase of cargo clearance through its non-southern borders and added that reserves of strategic goods remain strong.
- Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy said that two "offending" oil tankers on the southern and eastern coasts of the Strait of Hormuz suffered explosions. "These tankers, believing they were secretly trying to pass through the fake Strait of Hormuz route, were prevented from passing by naval mines, causing a massive explosion and fire," it said in a statement.
- The Saudi-led coalition's spokesperson said in a post on X that it targeted "operational capabilities" at Yemen's Hodeidah port. Additionally, Turki al-Maliki added that a number of targets in northern Yemen's Saada and Amran governorates were destroyed.
- The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed four drones in Ras Tanura, located in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province. The coalition's spokesperson Turki al-Maliki indicated that a number of fragments had fallen as a result of the interception, with no casualties reported in the initial assessment.
- A US poll shows Trump's approval at 37 percent, with strong disapproval over his handling of the Iran war.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Who is Chen Jining, China’s latest Politburo member under investigation?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Who is Chen Jining, China’s latest Politburo member under investigation?
Chen is the fourth high-ranking Politburo member to be pushed out in two years.
The Chinese Communist Party has launched investigations into the party’s Shanghai secretary Chen Jining for alleged “serious violations of discipline and law” – usually code for corruption.
The anticorruption watchdog, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, announced the probe in a brief statement on Tuesday, according to Xinhua News Agency, but did not give more details.
It comes amid widespread purges in the Political Bureau, one of the top bodies of the CCP, as the party prepares for its next congress in the second half of 2027, where President Xi Jinping is expected to clinch his fourth five-year term.
Xi, who has pushed greater party discipline and anticorruption, has for years pursued a long, intense purge on a scale not seen since the rule of Mao Zedong, experts say.
Chen is the fourth high-ranking Politburo member to be pushed out in two years.
The Shanghai Communist Party’s leaders have backed the move, with its standing committee stating it firmly supported the decision to investigate Chen and that it showed Beijing’s determination to continue its anticorruption campaign.
“The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping’s anticorruption campaign has no limits,” Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, told The Associated Press news agency. “The pattern is unprecedented.” Here’s what we know:
Who is Chen Jining?
Chen, 62, joined the CCP as a 20-year-old environmental engineering student at the highly-rated Tsinghua University. After spending a decade researching in the United Kingdom, the scientist and academic returned to Tsinghua, where he was eventually appointed one of its youngest presidents in 2012.
He went on to serve as the Minister of Environmental Protection from 2015 to 2017, and led efforts to cut pollution in Beijing. He was later appointed Mayor of Beijing in 2018.
In 2022, he was appointed party secretary of Shanghai, the country’s financial hub, amid Xi’s push to install people with strong scientific backgrounds in key roles.
Chen was widely seen as Xi’s protege. His post is usually seen as a stepping stone to party leadership; President Xi previously held the position of Shanghai Party Secretary in 2007.
Chen hosted some of China’s most prominent diplomatic visitors, including former US Secretary of State Antony Blinken, former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.
He led the opening ceremony of the World AI Conference held earlier this year in Shanghai.
Who else has been targeted?
Other senior party officials have been purged in recent months, especially in the military.
- General Zhang Youxia, the senior vice chair of the powerful Central Military Commission (CMC), was investigated for the same “serious violations of discipline and law”, China’s Defence Ministry said in January. The commission is the top military body and is chaired by Xi, making Zhang the military’s number two. He was part of the informal “Shaanxi clique”, a network of political leaders who share ancestral ties to Shaanxi Province with Xi.
- Liu Zhenli, another CMC member who served as the chief of staff of its Joint Staff Department, was being investigated by the CCP, the Defence Ministry also said in January.
- He Weidong, the other vice chair of the military commission, was expelled last October on allegations of “serious misconduct” and violations involving “exceptionally large amounts of money”. Eight other senior military members were also dismissed. He was part of the “Fujian clique”, a tight circle of officials who have long been allied with President Xi since his time as Fujian governor from 1999.
- Miao Hua, former head of the political work department in the military commission and another member of the Fujian clique, was removed in June 2025.
- Ma Xingrui, former party secretary of Xinjiang, was charged with accepting “exceptionally large” bribes in November. Ma’s investigation was first announced in April.
Why is this happening?
The military shakeups and wider purge are part of Xi’s years-long anticorruption drive that has seen hundreds of senior and junior government officials investigated, prosecuted or dismissed since Xi first came to power in 2012.
Analysts believe the purges are designed to reform the military and to ensure unwavering loyalty to Xi.
Some military expulsions have been linked to suspicions of political divergence. Official sources, for example, described additional allegations against He Weidong, the former vice chairman of the military commission, as being a “loss of chastity,” a rare phrase which, in CCP speak, refers to political disloyalty and ideological collapse.
The takedowns reveal how Chinese politics often depends on shifting circumstances, with even officials possessing the qualifications Xi wants being vulnerable to removal, said Joseph Torigian, a professor at the Washington-based American University.
“On paper,” they appear to be “individuals Xi would appreciate,” Torigian told the AP. But afterwards, “we could easily come up with hypotheses for why he got rid of them”.

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/amerique-l.title: « Pour Fidel Castro, l’internationalisme constituait un principe fondateur de la Révolution » : entretien avec Ignacio Ramonet (2/2)
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/amerique-l.author: Luis Reygada
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/amerique-l.text:
Tout juste dix ans après la mort du leader historique de la Révolution cubaine, l’essayiste et universitaire franco-espagnol Ignacio Ramonet rappelle l’empreinte laissée par l’un des grands symboles la lutte pour l’émancipation des peuples du Sud.
Ancien directeur du Monde diplomatique (1990-2008) et spécialiste de géopolitique et des médias, Ignacio Ramonet revient pour l’Humanité sur plusieurs aspects de la pensée du dirigeant communiste, décédé le 25 novembre 2016 à La Havane.
Après avoir évoqué l’impact de son héritage théorique dans la première partie de notre entretien, le journaliste revient ici sur la capacité de résistance de Cuba, à l’heure où le processus révolutionnaire initié en 1959 subit l’hostilité sans limite de Washington, et se trouve « peut-être à un tournant décisif » de son histoire. Pour l’auteur d’une biographie de référence sur el Comandante1, « il faut distinguer la fin d’une époque de la fin d’une révolution ».
Outre son soutien aux luttes de libération, l’influence de Cuba dirigée par Fidel Castro au sein des pays du Sud s’explique aussi par un internationalisme qui a pris d’autres formes concrètes de solidarité, et de coopération…
Ignacio Ramonet
Journaliste, essayiste et universitaire franco-espagnol
Tout à fait, il ne faudrait pas réduire cet internationalisme à sa dimension militaire. Cuba a également envoyé des médecins, des enseignants, des ingénieurs et des techniciens dans de nombreux pays. Des milliers de jeunes Africains et d’autres régions du Sud ont pu étudier à Cuba. Cette coopération dans les domaines de la santé et de l’éducation a constitué une autre expression, durable, de la solidarité internationale.
Il y a enfin une dimension géopolitique fondamentale. Fidel fut l’un des dirigeants qui ont le plus contribué à affirmer l’existence politique du Sud global comme sujet...

- Wirtschaft und Umwelt
- Bangladesch
Beschäftigte in Textilfabriken erhalten 36 Prozent mehr Lohn
Die Kommission zur Lösung des Konflikts hat die Erhöhung des Mindestlohns angekündigt.
Dhaka. Die Beschäftigten in der Textilindustrie in Bangladesch haben nach wochenlangen Protesten eine Lohnerhöhung von 36 Prozent zugesagt bekommen. Die Kommission, die von der Regierung zur Lösung des Konflikts eingerichtet worden war, beschloss am Mittwoch eine Erhöhung des Mindestlohns von 12.500 auf 17.000 Taka (rund 125 Euro). Die Arbeiter hatten 30.000 Taka gefordert. Der neue Mindestlohn wird ab Januar gezahlt.
Noch am Mittwochmorgen errichteten hunderte Demonstranten im Industriegebiet von Gazipur am Rande der Hauptstadt Dhaka Barrikaden. Sie wurden von der Polizei mit Tränengas und Blendgranaten auseinandergetrieben, wie Augenzeugen der Nachrichtenagentur AFP schilderten. Ein Polizeivertreter sagte, die Beamten versuchten, »die Lage unter Kontrolle zu halten«. Arbeitnehmervertreter riefen die Beschäftigten dazu auf, an ihre Arbeitsplätze zurückzukehren.
»Auch wenn wir nicht ganz zufrieden sind, ist das Ergebnis doch auch nicht gänzlich schlecht«, sagte Babul Akhter, der Arbeitnehmervertreter in der Mindestlohnkommission. »Früher erhielten die Arbeitnehmer alle fünf Jahre eine Lohnanpassung, doch dieses Mal erhalten sie bereits nach drei Jahren eine neue Lohnfestsetzung.«
Die Proteste hatten im Oktober begonnen und beeinträchtigen die Produktion des für die Wirtschaft des Landes zentralen Sektors an mehreren Standorten. Der Verband der Bekleidungshersteller und -exporteure von Bangladesch (BGMEA) teilte am Sonntag mit, dass die Proteste der Branche Verluste in Höhe von schätzungsweise 428 Millionen Dollar (gut 391 Millionen Euro) verursacht hätten.
Bangladesch ist nach China weltweit zweitgrößter Exporteur von Kleidung, die Ausfuhren machen rund 80 Prozent der Exporteinnahmen des Landes aus. Wichtigste Abnehmer sind die USA und die EU. Etwa 4,5 Millionen Menschen schneidern und nähen in den Textilfabriken, die meisten von ihnen Frauen. AFP/nd
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.

More on Israeli strike targeting apartment in Gaza City
An Israeli attack on an apartment in Gaza City has killed a senior Palestinian security official alongside his wife and two daughters, aged 13 and 15.
According to the Interior Ministry, the man was identified as the director of the Internal Security Service in northern Gaza, Muhammad Majid Abu al-Awf, 47.
The ministry slammed the attack as a "horrific massacre" and called for "urgent and genuine action to restrain the occupation from committing further crimes against innocent civilians" in the Gaza Strip.
"The Ministry of Interior and National Security condemns this heinous crime against security personnel and affirms that it comes within the context of ongoing attempts to undermine the security apparatus in the Gaza Strip in an effort to spread chaos within Palestinian society."
Earlier, the director-general of the Internal Security Service, Naim Mohammed Abu Nahl, was assassinated in an Israeli strike west of Gaza City.

https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: Could Netanyahu take Israel into another war with Iran to cling to power?
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
Could Netanyahu take Israel into another war with Iran to cling to power?
As Israeli opposition leader Eisenkot moves to form a government, could war with Iran derail talks and save Netanyahu?
Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot is seeking to form a coalition government before an escalation in the US-Israel war on Iran works to interim Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s advantage.
Eisenkot’s bloc’s 48 seats still leave him 13 short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset needed to form a new government. But he could count on the support of the Arab parties and their 19 seats from outside the government, which could be enough to cross the line.
Netanyahu’s supporters are averse to an alliance with the Arab parties, while the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism (UTJ) alliance could support either side in the coalition talks.
The Netanyahu-led Likud party’s 46 recommendations from Knesset members following UTJ’s decision not to endorse either candidate could prove decisive ahead of the initial December 6 deadline for a government to be formed.
Negotiations between Eisenkot’s Yashar (“Straight”) party and Likud remain fractious. Eisenkot has already ruled out serving in any government led by Netanyahu, but has pressed for a unity government where he would share leadership roles with another party leader.
Netanyahu argues that Israel needs a government free from what he portrays as the “taint” of Arab-party participation and can respond to what he has argued is an imminent military threat from Iran.
Some analysts argue that renewed conflict with Iran could derail negotiations, forcing the rival blocs to fall in line behind Netanyahu.
But Eisenkot has told party members he has seen no imminent threat requiring military action before a new government is sworn in. His ally, Avigdor Liberman, recently appointed to the Knesset’s Foreign Affairs and Defence Committee and therefore privy to classified intelligence, also said he had seen no justifications for new Israeli strikes.
“If we end up seeing a strike right now, then we’ll know that it’s completely motivated by politics and not security concerns,” Liberman told Israeli media.
Israel’s military chief, Lieutenant General Eyal Zamir, and researchers within Mossad, the country’s foreign intelligence service, also reportedly see no case for an immediate attack on Iran.
Although defence officials have warned Netanyahu that new attacks on Iran could trigger a wider regional conflict, Mossad chief Roman Gofman has reportedly advocated for renewed military action.
So, how pressing is the case for war, and could it really override negotiations to form government?
Here’s what we know.
What have Netanyahu and his allies claimed?
In mid-November, US media reported that Netanyahu dispatched his longstanding ally Gofman to Washington, DC, to urge joint strikes on Iran, based on new intelligence Israel had reportedly uncovered indicating that Tehran was developing chemical weapons.
Several other Netanyahu appointees are also reported to support military action. On Tuesday, Netanyahu’s decades-old ally, Defence Minister Israel Katz, called for preemptive strikes against Iran before it could fully develop the chemical weapons programme he claimed was already under way.
Also reportedly backing new strikes on Iran is David Zini, head of the Shin Bet internal security agency, and two further Netanyahu appointees – National Security Council chair Shmuel Ben Ezra and Israel’s ambassador to the US, Yechiel Leiter.
US President Donald Trump appeared to echo many of Netanyahu’s claims in a November 19 interview Fox News on, although he stopped short of committing to military action before the end of the year.
“There is indication that Iran is looking at gases, looking at bio, because we’ve shut them out with the nuclear. Nuclear is much harder. And they’re looking at gas and… biological weapons, not nice, and other things,” he said, without providing evidence.
What have other countries claimed?
Gulf countries, which would likely be heavily affected by a renewed conflict with Iran, have reportedly urged Washington to maintain its economic pressure on Tehran rather than return to military action. According to the US news website Axios, some senior US officials are also highly sceptical of Israel’s claims, with one telling the outlet they appeared to be “driven by an agenda”.
Iran has also denied developing chemical weapons, and has compared claims that it is with the false claims that Iraq had weapons of mass destruction, used to justify the US-led invasion in 2003.
Writing on X, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei accused those making the allegations of expecting the world to suffer “a bout of collective amnesia”, likening the situation to Dory, the forgetful fish from the 2003 animated film Finding Nemo.
Could another war derail negotiations to form a government?
In the eyes of many, yes.
Many in Israel regard Iran as the ultimate regional threat. For years, Iranian propaganda and that of its regional allies, such as Hezbollah in Lebanon, have called for the destruction of Israel as a state. There have also been repeated claims by Netanyahu, dating back to at least the 1990s, that Iran is poised to develop a nuclear weapon that could be deployed against Israel without hesitation.
“If war started, even manufactured, everyone would rally around the flag, as this is what Israelis do in crisis,” Ahron Bregman, an Israeli security analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London, said.
“Netanyahu can go to war knowing that no political leader will oppose him the moment bombs started falling on Iran,” he said.
Would Netanyahu risk war rather than cede power?
Netanyahu has been frequently accused of prioritising his political survival over other pressing national issues, and some believe he could restart the war on Iran to save his career.
Alongside the multiple corruption charges for which he has been on trial since 2020 are allegations that he misled lawmakers about his administration’s failures ahead of the October 7 Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel, sparking Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, to stave off an inquiry.
There have also been widespread accusations, including from former US President Joe Biden, that Netanyahu has prolonged the genocide in Gaza for political reasons.
“I think it would be very easy for him,” Israeli political analyst Nimrod Flashenberg said.
“His own survival and what he sees as Israel’s are aligned. It’s not that he thinks of it purely in terms of attacking Iran to stay in office. He sees attacking Iran, as he always has, as necessary for Israel and a path that will also need him to stay in office.”

https://www.humanite.fr/monde/argentine/.title: En Argentine, la « tronçonneuse » de Javier Milei a sabré l’économie et le pays est désormais en récession
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/argentine/.author: La rédaction avec AFP
https://www.humanite.fr/monde/argentine/.text:
À moins d’un an de l’élection présidentielle, l’Argentine est entrée en récession, estiment des économistes. En tranchant dans les dépenses publiques, le président ultralibéral Javier Milei a mis un coup d’arrêt à l’activité économique.
Deux trimestres consécutifs de recul de l’activité, avec -1,8 % au troisième trimestre par rapport au trimestre précédent, après un repli de 0,6 % au deuxième trimestre : l’Argentine est techniquement entrée en récession selon les critères des économistes, après la publication mardi 24 novembre 2026 de projections officielles. Ces chiffres sont publiés alors que Javier Milei, au pouvoir depuis près de trois ans, prévoit de briguer un nouveau mandat en octobre 2027.
Anticipant la publication de ces données, le gouvernement argentin avait affirmé, plus tôt dans la journée, qu’il convient d’attendre les données relatives au PIB qui seront publiées le 16 décembre prochain – et non de se baser sur l’estimateur mensuel de l’activité économique de l’Indec, l’équivalent argentin de l’INSEE.
La dernière fois que l’Argentine est entrée en récession remonte à 2024, période des premiers mois au pouvoir de Javier Milei dont la « tronçonneuse permanente » – nom qu’il donne à son vaste programme de réduction des dépenses publiques – a permis cette année-là le premier excédent budgétaire du pays en 14 ans, ainsi que de ramener une inflation à trois chiffres à près de 30 % sur un an.
Mais à quel prix ? La drastique austérité budgétaire du président libertarien, récemment reçu à l’Élysée, et nostalgique de la dictature, a eu un lourd impact sur l’emploi – avec plus de 300 000 emplois perdus entre privé et public, quelque 30 000 entreprises ayant mis la clé sous la porte – ainsi que sur la consommation et l’activité. La pauvreté a rebondi de quatre points au premier semestre 2026, rompant avec une tendance à la baisse. Elle touche désormais près d’un Argentin sur trois.
Oui, on s’en doute : vous en avez assez
Voir ces messages d’appel au don, ça peut être pénible. Nous le savons. Et on doit bien vous avouer que nous préférerions ne pas avoir à les écrire…
Mais voilà : c’est crucial pour l’Humanité. Si ce titre existe toujours aujourd’hui, c’est grâce au financement régulier de nos lectrices et lecteurs.
- C’est grâce à votre soutien que nous pouvons exercer notre métier avec passion. Nous ne dépendons ni des intérêts d’un propriétaire milliardaire, ni de pressions politiques : personne ne nous dicte ce que nous devons dire ou taire.
- Votre engagement nous libère aussi de la course aux clics et à l’audience. Plutôt que de chercher à capter l’attention à tout prix, nous choisissons de traiter les sujets que notre rédaction juge essentiels : parce qu’ils méritent d’être lus, compris, partagés. Parce que nous estimons qu’ils vous seront utiles
À l’heure actuelle, moins d’un quart des lectrices et lecteurs qui viennent plus de 3 fois sur le site par semaine nous aident à financer notre travail, par leur abonnement ou par leurs dons. Si vous voulez protéger le journalisme indépendant, s’il vous plaît, rejoignez-les.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120411.text:
- Politik
- US-Abschiebepolitik
Fall Abrego Garcia: US-Ministerium verkündet »Selbstabschiebung«
Kilmar Abrego Garcia wurde zum Symbol für Donald Trumps radikale Abschiebepolitik – und ihr Scheitern vor Gericht. Nun soll er ausgereist sein.
Washington. Einer der bekanntesten Betroffenen der Abschiebepolitik von US-Präsident Donald Trump hat die Vereinigten Staaten nach Angaben des Heimatschutzministeriums in Richtung Spanien verlassen. Das Ministerium äußerte sich in einer Mitteilung »entzückt darüber«, dass »der kriminelle illegale Ausländer« Kilmar Abrego Garcia »sich selbst abgeschoben hat«. Der Salvadorianer habe das Land infolge einer Ausweisungsanordnung verlassen, seinen Flug selbst gezahlt und werde nie mehr in die USA zurückkehren dürfen, verkündete die Behörde auf der Plattform X. Unabhängig bestätigt wurden die Angaben zunächst nicht.
Abrego Garcias Fall steht exemplarisch für eine größere Debatte über die radikale Abschiebepolitik der US-Regierung in Trumps zweiter Amtszeit. Im Kern steht die Frage, ob Betroffene vor ihrer erzwungenen Ausreise ausreichend rechtliches Gehör erhalten.
Abrego Garcia war im Frühjahr 2025 im Bundesstaat Maryland festgenommen worden. Ihm wurde unter anderem vorgeworfen, bei einer Verkehrskontrolle Migranten ohne gültige Aufenthaltspapiere transportiert zu haben. Kurz nach der Festnahme wurde er unrechtmäßig in sein Heimatland El Salvador abgeschoben, wo er in einem berüchtigten Hochsicherheitsgefängnis landete. Nach längerem juristischem Tauziehen – die US-Regierung sprach von einem »administrativen Fehler« – kehrte er im Juni 2025 zurück in die USA, woraufhin die Regierung weitere Ermittlungen gegen ihn anstrengte. Ein mit angeblichem Menschenschmuggel begründetes Strafverfahren scheiterte im Mai 2026.
In der Mitteilung wiederholte das Ministerium nun seine Vorwürfe, Garcia habe Menschenhandel betrieben und sei Mitglied der berüchtigten Bande MS-13 aus El Salvador, was Garcia bestreitet. dpa/nd
Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf
Bei uns muss niemand zahlen, um informiert zu sein. Klingt nach einem schlechten Geschäftsmodell? Ist es auch. Aber uns sind unabhängiger Journalismus und Teilhabe für alle wichtiger als Profit. Journalismus kostet trotzdem Geld: Recherche, Druck und all die Menschen, die ihn machen. Deshalb sind wir auf dich angewiesen. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro.
Spende einmalig oder regelmäßig, jeder Betrag zählt. Damit nd bleibt.

https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/ameriqu.title: Fidel Castro ou la conquête de la dignité
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/ameriqu.author: Tribunes
https://www.humanite.fr/en-debat/ameriqu.text:
Dix ans après sa disparition, Fidel Castro reste une figure majeure de l’histoire du XXe siècle. De la révolution de 1959 à son engagement pour la souveraineté des pays du Sud, son héritage continue de marquer les luttes politiques et sociales à travers le monde. Et de symboliser la résistance à l’impérialisme ainsi que la « solidarité internationaliste qui a tendu la main généreuse de l’île aux peuples en lutte pour leur dignité », rappellent la poétesse et militante afro-américaine Alice Walker et le chercheur Salim Lamrani.
Figure controversée en Occident, Fidel Castro est en revanche plébiscité dans le reste du monde, où il est perçu comme le vecteur d’un message universel d’émancipation. Défenseur de l’aspiration des peuples à la souveraineté nationale, à la justice sociale et à la dignité humaine, le leader de la Révolution cubaine est considéré comme l’archétype de l’anti-impérialisme du XXe siècle.
Entré de son vivant dans le Panthéon des grands libérateurs du continent latino-américain, Fidel Castro a vu son œuvre dépasser les frontières de l’île pour irriguer les forces progressistes du Sud global.
Depuis José Martí, aucune figure n’a symbolisé avec autant de force l’aspiration du peuple cubain à l’indépendance véritable. Arrière-cour des États-Unis pendant près de six décennies, Cuba était constamment humiliée par la domination du puissant voisin qui avait placé le pays sous sa tutelle, contrôlait la politique nationale et dictait la conduite à suivre aux présidents successifs.
Renonçant à ses privilèges de classe, Fidel Castro a pris les armes contre la dictature militaire de Fulgencio Batista soutenue par la Maison-Blanche, revendiquant le droit inaliénable de son peuple à l’autodétermination.
L’avènement de la Révolution cubaine en 1959 a marqué l’aboutissement d’une longue lutte pour l’affranchissement, engagée en 1868, ouvrant la voie à l’ère de l’indépendance véritable. En brisant les chaînes hégémoniques imposées par Washington, Fidel Castro a fait d’une petite île de la Caraïbe une puissance morale admirée par les peuples du Sud.
Revendiquant sa liberté de choisir sa propre voie, défiant l’impérialisme étasunien, Cuba est devenue un symbole de résistance à l’oppression et une source d’espoir pour les déshérités aspirant à une vie meilleure.
Malgré ses ressources extrêmement limitées et un état de siège économique implacable imposé dès les premiers instants, Fidel Castro a fait de Cuba un modèle pour les nations du Tiers-Monde en reprenant le contrôle des ressources naturelles, en procédant à une répartition plus équitable des richesses du pays et en universalisant l’accès à l’éducation, à la santé, à la culture, aux sports et aux loisirs.
Cuba révolutionnaire a ainsi démontré qu’il était possible de mettre en place un système de protection sociale performant pour l’ensemble de la population, y compris dans un contexte géopolitique d’extrême adversité.
En plus de revendiquer le droit de son peuple à vivre debout, Fidel Castro a fait de la solidarité internationaliste un pilier de la politique étrangère de Cuba, apportant son soutien aux grandes causes de l’émancipation humaine, en particulier aux luttes de libération des peuples africains, martyrisés par des siècles de colonialisme.
De l’Algérie à l’Afrique du Sud, en passant par l’Angola et la Guinée-Bissau, La Havane a joué un rôle déterminant dans la lutte pour la liberté du continent. L’inoubliable Nelson Mandela synthétisa cette générosité sans faille : « Quel autre pays peut se prévaloir d’avoir fait preuve d’un plus grand altruisme que Cuba dans ses relations avec l’Afrique ? »
Outre l’envoi de centaines de milliers de professionnels à travers le monde – médecins, ingénieurs, enseignants ou techniciens – pour contribuer au développement du Sud global, la Cuba de Fidel Castro a également formé des dizaines de milliers de cadres venus de tous les continents. Aujourd’hui encore, malgré le blocus médiéval imposé par les États-Unis, de nombreux médecins cubains continuent d’œuvrer dans les coins reculés de la planète, apportant des soins aux populations démunies, y compris en Europe occidentale.
Fidel Castro restera dans l’histoire comme l’architecte de la souveraineté nationale de Cuba ayant mis fin à la domination néocoloniale étasunienne ; le réformateur social ayant procédé à une distribution plus équitable des richesses du pays, créant ainsi l’une des sociétés les moins inégalitaires d’Amérique latine ; et l’internationaliste solidaire qui a tendu la main généreuse de Cuba aux peuples en lutte pour leur dignité.
Alice Walker, poétesse et militante afro-américaine, Salim Lamrani, historien et universitaire, spécialiste de Cuba et des relations cubano-américaines.

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.title: Pro-Palestine activist sought by US in extradition case: ‘I still have a right to my beliefs’
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.author: Timothy Pratt
https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text:
James “Fergie” Chambers, the wealthy leftwing activist and donor controversially sought in extradition by the US, has told the Guardian that he is “not asking anyone to endorse my ideas or not think I’m a jerk – but I still have a right to my beliefs and should not be unjustly accused because of them”.
Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.
The complaint also includes riot and conspiracy to riot charges stemming from 2023 protests against New England branches of Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit.
Chambers was speaking from his Madrid apartment in his first in-depth interview after a Spanish appeals court ordered his provisional release on bail on Friday. That release was due to issues with the legally required US translation of the extradition request’s core documents into Spanish, first reported by the Guardian.
“Support for my case doesn’t imply support of me, or my ideas,” Chambers said. “It’s about my right to have those ideas – and not be falsely accused of things.”
Chambers, whose case has gained attention across the world, had been detained since 10 July, when Spanish authorities arrested him in Ibiza.
The order granting Chambers’s provisional release asserted that the translation issues cause “a diminishment, at least for the time being, in the solidity or foundation of the extradition request”. Spanish judges had previously denied bail three times.
The wealthy heir to at least $250mn from his family’s business – Atlanta–based Cox Enterprises – was in the middle of his first visit without being separated by glass with his mother, Lauren Hamilton, when he was summoned to receive the “good news” on Friday, Chambers told the Guardian.
Minutes later, he returned to tell his mother he was being released. “She freaked out crying. We went nuts for about five minutes. Then we got to contacting my lawyer and getting my kids on a plane to Spain.”
On Monday, Chambers’s five-year-old son with actor and activist Stella Schnabel could be heard in the background. The tableau was in stark contrast to his months in prison.
“I tried to build a cocoon to deal with the immense unknown, the immense fear,” he said of his time in Aranjuez prison. “I would pray a lot. The only idea I could hold onto was, my home is the truth. The truth of who loves you. The truth of my own innocence. And the truth of what is happening in Palestine and all the things connected to what is happening in Palestine – other wars, gas prices. No one can take that away from you.”
Chambers has been supported by his mother throughout his case, and has reconnected with his father, James Cox Chambers – who owns an estimated 17% stake in Cox Enterprises but does not play an active role in the company – for the first time in five years.
“Speaking with my parents has provided emotional stability – and intelligent, adult minds to help make decisions,” Chambers said.
Although he has had political disagreements with his father, a donor to the Democratic party, Chambers said his father “sees this situation as totally unthinkable and out of step with anything resembling a just society”.
He also invoked his grandfather, the ACLU civil rights lawyer James Cox Hamilton, who died in 2014. “He would’ve turned in his grave over this,” Chambers said.
While locked up, Chambers, a US citizen, received hundreds of letters of support from friends, family and strangers, postmarked from Atlanta to Barcelona – including, he said, “from a guy who had been imprisoned under [Spanish dictator Francisco] Franco, who painted the ‘key of return’ [a symbol of homes lost in the 1948 Nakba] on the Palestinian flag”.
Chambers’s views and donations to progressive and humanitarian projects have been extensively profiled in US media, including his controversial public comments on Israel and Gaza. A week after the 7 October Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”
His release followed a separate decision on Thursday by a three-judge panel at Spain’s high court tasked with deciding on the extradition to pause the proceedings in order to evaluate the impact of the alterations the US made to the original, machine-made translation of the extradition request into Spanish.
The US admitted to making several of the changes, calling them “substantial [and] inadvertent”. These and dozens of other changes introduced prejudicial notions with specific legal implications that in turn wound up in the Spanish prosecutor’s report on the case, Aitor Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team, told the Guardian last week.
It was also recently revealed that there is no indictment behind the complaint, meaning the federal government has not had a grand jury evaluate evidence against Chambers, and instead is seeking his extradition based on the affidavit of a single FBI agent, the core of the sealed criminal complaint.
During his time in prison, Chambers also began the process of applying for political asylum in Spain. He cannot be extradited until the asylum case runs its course, and also cannot be extradited if he is granted asylum. His legal team has notified the government office evaluating his asylum petition of the altered translations.
Chambers was arrested 10 July as he and Schnabel pulled into the driveway of a school they were visiting to see about enrolling their five-year-old, part of plans to move to Spain. They had been staying in Ireland, where Schnabel was working on a film.
Although the arrest came as a surprise – “I was confused! Did I speed?” he thought – Chambers revealed to the Guardian that a car had been following him around Dublin only days before, and that someone had broken into their car parked outside their house at night, without taking anything of value.
“I noticed signs of surveillance,” he said. Months later, last Wednesday, Irish police raided the same house, acting on a request from US authorities.
With his immediate future uncertain, Chambers said he was “looking forward to sharing a couple of nice dinners with my family this week”.
As for the past, he said the millions he has donated to an estimated 100 projects in about 20 countries is “the most important thing I’ve done”.
“Somebody with the political orientation I have and with resources, no matter how good of an activist I am, it’s not gonna be as effective as medical aid or feeding children in Gaza, supporting independent media that wouldn’t otherwise exist, or paying people’s bail who have been arrested for protesting.
“I’m giving a lot of money to things that other people aren’t giving money to.”
Chambers also said he was “grateful for the way Spanish courts have dealt with this – just focusing on the facts. It shouldn’t matter that I’ve made some emotional statements.”

Frauen in Iran: Die Unbeugsame
Verisheh Moradi ist eine von mindestens neun Frauen, die in Iran auf der Todesliste stehen. Doch sie hat ihr Leben lang für Freiheit gekämpft – auch jetzt noch.
Verisheh Moradi hat gelernt, sich zu verteidigen. Als Jugendliche trainiert sie Kung-Fu, später wird sie Trainerin und Schiedsrichterin. Sie bringt Kindern in ihrer Heimatstadt Sanandaj im iranischen Kurdistan den Sport näher. Disziplin, Kraft, Körperbeherrschung. Fähigkeiten, die sie eines Tages brauchen wird im Kampf gegen den sogenannten Islamischen Staat.
2014 schließt sich Moradi den kurdischen Frauenkämpferinnen in Rojava an. In Kobane kämpft sie gegen die IS-Miliz. Sie erlebt, wie ihre Freundinnen sterben. Manche ihrer Leichen trägt sie selbst fort, damit die Dschihadisten ihre Körper nicht schänden können.
Nach der militärischen Niederlage des IS bleibt Moradi in Rojava. Sie will an einer Gesellschaft mitbauen, in der Frauen selbst über ihr Leben bestimmen. Doch die türkische Invasion und die Überwachung durch den türkischen Geheimdienst machen ihre Arbeit zunehmend gefährlich, weshalb sie im Sommer 2023 nach Iran zurückkehrt, um ihren Einsatz für Frauenrechte dort fortzusetzen.
Am 1. August 2023 wird sie in Sanandadsch von Geheimdienstmitarbeitern des Regimes festgenommen. Fünf Monate verbringt sie in Einzelhaft, wo sie schwer gefoltert wird. Später wird sie nach Teheran in das Evin-Gefängnis verlegt.
Im November 2024 wird Moradi wegen „bewaffneter Rebellion“ zum Tode verurteilt. Im Dezember 2025 hebt der oberste Gerichtshof das Urteil auf, nur damit im Oktober 2026 dasselbe Revolutionsgericht erneut die Todesstrafe verhängt. In einem Brief aus dem Gefängnis schreibt sie: „Ich wurde zum Tode verurteilt, weil ich eine Frau bin, weil ich Kurdin bin und weil ich ein freies Leben suche.“
Wieder Frauen auf der Todesliste
Das iranische Regime hat eine neue Eskalationsstufe erreicht; über ein Jahrzehnt wurden keine weiblichen politischen Gefangenen mehr hingerichtet. Die letzte bekannte Hinrichtung einer Frau aufgrund einer politischen Anklage war die Kurdin Shirin Alam Holi, die im Mai 2010 gemeinsam mit vier weiteren politischen Gefangenen im Evin-Gefängnis gehängt wurde. Nun greift die Führung wieder systematisch zu diesem Mittel.
Mit den Todesurteilen gegen Moradi und die kurdische Sozialarbeiterin Pakhshan Azizi tastete sich das Regime zunächst vor. Wie weit kann es gehen, ohne dass die Weltöffentlichkeit sich empört? Beide Frauen hatten sich für andere eingesetzt, beide waren Kurdinnen. Beiden wird „Rebellion“ vorgeworfen.
Es ist nicht schwer, darin auch eine gezielte Einschüchterung jener Frauen zu sehen, die seit der Protestbewegung „Frau, Leben, Freiheit“ nach dem Tod der Kurdin Jina Amini im Herbst 2022 die patriarchale Ordnung des Regimes herausfordern und die revolutionäre Bewegung anführen. Kurdinnen, deren Widerstand die Bewegung mitgeprägt hat, stehen unter besonderem Druck.
Nach den Protesten im Januar 2026 ist die Gefahr längst über diese Fälle hinausgewachsen. Auch Frauen, die während der Demonstrationen festgenommen wurden, erhalten Todesurteile. Die UN-Untersuchungskommission dokumentierte im September mindestens neun Frauen, die in diesem Zusammenhang zum Tode verurteilt wurden.
Moradi weigert sich, den Prozess als rechtmäßig anzuerkennen. Sie blieb den Gerichtsterminen fern und protestierte im Gefängnis gegen Hinrichtungen. Sie ist nicht die gehorsame Frau, die der Staat will. Sie ist nicht die schweigende Kurdin, nicht die Gefangene, die um Gnade bittet. Sie hat sich für ein anderes, freies Leben entschieden.
Dafür soll sie sterben.

Lebenserwartung in Kuba gesunken
Laut WHO hat sich die Säuglingssterblichkeit zwischen 2020 und 2025 mehr als verdoppelt. Zuletzt sank die Überlebensrate bei Kindern mit Krebs rasant.
Havanna. Die Lebenserwartung in Kuba ist nach Angaben der Weltgesundheitsorganisation (WHO) erstmals seit Beginn der Aufzeichnungen im Jahr 1950 gesunken. Sie ging zwischen 2020 und 2025 von 78,8 auf 74,4 Jahre zurück, sagte WHO-Chef Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus am Dienstag in Havanna. Das Gesundheitssystem des von einer schweren Wirtschaftskrise erschütterten Landes befinde sich in einem »kritischen« Zustand.
Die Säuglingssterblichkeit hat sich Tedros zufolge zwischen 2020 und 2025 mehr als verdoppelt: Sie stieg von vier auf 9,9 Todesfälle je 1000 Lebendgeburten. Diese Zahlen stammen noch aus der Zeit vor der Verhängung der US-Ölblockade zu Jahresbeginn, die Kubas Wirtschaftskrise weiter verschärft hat. Seit Beginn der Blockade sei die Überlebensrate bei Kindern mit Krebs von 85 auf 65 Prozent gesunken, sagte Tedros.
Der WHO-Chef kündigte Hilfen in Höhe von zwei Millionen Dollar für Impfkampagnen für Kinder und die Beschaffung dringend benötigter medizinischer Ausrüstung an. Tedros führte die Probleme im kubanischen Gesundheitswesen sowohl auf die US-Sanktionen als auch auf interne Schwierigkeiten zurück. Er begrüßte die von der kommunistischen Regierung angekündigten Wirtschaftsreformen, mit denen das Land stärker für die Marktwirtschaft geöffnet werden soll. AFP/nd

Lagebilder zur Gewalt gegen Frauen: Mehr Licht im Dunkelfeld
Das BKA stellte Lagebilder zur Gewalt gegen Frauen vor. Immer mehr Delikte werden angezeigt. Warum das wichtig ist, erklärten zwei Ministerinnen.
Die aktuellen Lagebilder des Bundeskriminalamts zu häuslicher Gewalt und zu Straftaten gegen Frauen zeigen ein düsteres Bild. Die Zahl der Delikte ist 2025 in allen Bereichen gestiegen – obwohl die Zahl der Gewalttaten insgesamt zuletzt rückläufig war.
Im vergangenen Jahr wurden 54.675 Frauen und Mädchen als Opfer einer Sexualstraftat registriert. Das entspricht einem Anstieg von 2,3 Prozent gegenüber dem Vorjahr. »Knapp die Hälfte war zum Tatzeitpunkt minderjährig«, sagte die zuständige Bundesfrauenministerin Karin Prien bei der Vorstellung der Lagebilder in Berlin.
Auch die Gewalt im Netz nimmt zu. Dazu zählen Nötigung, Bedrohung und Stalking. Die Zahl der weiblichen Opfer stieg um knapp 16 Prozent. Insgesamt wurden in diesem Bereich 31.221 Fälle registriert. Auch hier verwies Prien auf den hohen Anteil Minderjähriger: Etwa 30 Prozent der Betroffenen waren unter 18 Jahre alt.
Noch beklemmender sind die Statistiken zur häuslichen Gewalt. 292 Menschen starben im vergangenen Jahr an den Folgen von Gewalt in den eigenen vier Wänden. Das waren sechs Todesfälle mehr als im Vorjahr. 209 der Opfer waren Frauen und Mädchen. 130 von ihnen starben durch die Gewalt eines Partners oder Ex-Partners.
Die Zahl der polizeilich registrierten Opfer häuslicher Gewalt erreichte mit 280.129 Geschädigten einen Höchststand. Erfasst werden sowohl Gewalt in Partnerschaften als auch Gewalt innerhalb der Familie. Bei der Partnerschaftsgewalt sind fast 80 Prozent der Opfer weiblich. Bei der innerfamiliären Gewalt liegt der Anteil der betroffenen Frauen und Mädchen bei 70,6 Prozent.
»Die Zahlen der Lagebilder zeigen auf alarmierende Art und Weise, wie alltäglich Gewalt gegen Frauen in Deutschland ist«, betonte Prien. »Hinter jeder Zahl steckt unermessliches Leid der Betroffenen.« Der Ministerin ist allerdings bewusst, dass die Lagebilder nur einen Teil des tatsächlichen Ausmaßes der Gewalt abbilden.
Anfang des Jahres beleuchtete erstmals eine Untersuchung das Ausmaß des Dunkelfelds. Die Studie »Lebenssituation, Sicherheit und Belastung im Alltag« zeigte, dass weniger als zehn Prozent der Straftaten angezeigt werden. Bei sexuellen Übergriffen erstatteten lediglich drei Prozent der betroffenen Frauen Anzeige.
Angesichts des verbreiteten Schweigens dankte Prien allen Betroffenen, die sich an die Polizei wandten und über ihre Erfahrungen berichteten. Dies trage dazu bei, das Thema stärker ins öffentliche Bewusstsein zu rücken und das Tabu bei dieser Form der Gewalt aufzubrechen.
»Häusliche Gewalt und Straftaten gegen Frauen verlangen eine klare Antwort des Rechtsstaats«, erklärte Bundesinnenminister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU). Der Handlungsauftrag sei angesichts der aktuellen Lagebilder eindeutig: Betroffene müssten besser geschützt, Täter konsequent zur Verantwortung gezogen und Gewalttaten frühzeitig verhindert werden.
Bundesjustizministerin Stefanie Hubig (SPD) erwägt eine Reihe von Maßnahmen, um Frauen besser vor Gewalt zu schützen. »Familiengerichte können künftig die elektronische Fußfessel anordnen, mehr Betroffene erhalten psychosoziale Prozessbegleitung, und K.o.-Tropfen-Täter werden härter bestraft.« Letztlich sei aber ein Umdenken in der Gesellschaft unerlässlich, erläuterte die Ministerin. Nötig sei eine »Abkehr von überkommenen Männlichkeitsbildern und patriarchalen Denkmustern«.
Auch Prien will eine »Veränderung in den Köpfen der Männer« erreichen. Einen Schwerpunkt legt sie auf die Prävention. Bereits Jugendliche möchte sie für das Thema sensibilisieren. Ihr Ministerium plant derzeit Modellprojekte zur Prävention häuslicher und geschlechtsspezifischer Gewalt. Diese sollen in Schulen, im digitalen Raum und in der Täterarbeit ansetzen.
Prien und Hubig verwiesen auch auf das Gewalthilfegesetz, das im Vorjahr beschlossen wurde. Schrittweise soll ein kostenloses Hilfesystem entstehen. Ab 2032 haben Frauen dann einen individuellen Rechtsanspruch auf Schutz und Beratung.
Doch bislang reicht das Angebot an Hilfen nicht aus. Für viele Frauenhäuser ist die Finanzierung weiterhin ungeklärt. Zudem fehlen bundesweit rund 12.000 Plätze. Viele akut bedrohte Frauen erhalten daher nicht den Schutz, den sie dringend bräuchten.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. ‘We need to be seen’: Over a third of UK Muslim students face Islamophobia
From being spat on and assaulted to suffering humiliation in lectures, Muslims on campus are increasingly vulnerable, says a new report.
London, United Kingdom – Haanyah Cassam, 23, was only a few weeks into her first year at the University of London’s School of Oriental and African Studies (SOAS) when a security guard walked into a hall where she and other students had gathered for a lecture.
Most of the group were Muslim.
According to Cassam, the guard told them they were behaving “like a pack of animals, especially those hijabis”. He then made a remark about “towel heads” and walked off.
Cassam, who chose to wear the hijab despite her family’s fears for her safety, told Al Jazeera, “It takes a lot of confidence and a lot of power to put something on your head that you know is going to make you a target.”
At the time, she felt “there was no one we could go to about this”, she said.
She later raised the issue with a professor, and was told their hands were tied by bureaucracy. The guard left the university at the end of that year.
Cassam, who studied global liberal arts and is now training as an English teacher at University College London (UCL), said that on another occasion, someone spat at her as she entered university.
Cassam’s experience reflects the findings of a report released on Wednesday by the Federation of Student Islamic Societies (FOSIS), which found that 38 percent of Muslim students in the United Kingdom have experienced Islamophobia at university.
The survey carried out this year of 715 students at 63 universities found women were more likely to be targeted than men, at 42 percent compared with 34 percent. The rate was highest at Russell Group universities, the UK’s leading research institutions, where 53 percent of Muslim women reported Islamophobia.
Back in 2005, about 25 percent said they experienced Islamophobia.
For Cassam, being spat on hurt less than what she heard in lectures.
She recalled a lecturer who, while teaching Mauritanian poetry and dance, told the class that Islam forbade Muslim women from expressing themselves artistically, calling it “savage” and “uncivilised”. When Cassam objected, she was told: “You’re just one Muslim.”
Her dissertation examined the emotional impact of Prevent, the UK government’s “counterterrorism” programme, on Muslim students. She said the academic meant to oversee it refused to help and told her she would not give it a mark of more than 50.
She did not take the matter further. “I was told it’s best not to rock the boat,” Cassam said. She found another tutor to supervise her, and was awarded a first-class honours mark of 76.
Wednesday’s survey painted a grim picture of abuse. In one example, a group of students had urine thrown at them while wearing the hijab, which the university in question would not classify as a hate crime.
Another student said that when they tried to report an incident, they were told to go home if they did not like being in the UK.
A separate student said they were locked out of a lab session after asking to attend Friday prayers.
Of those affected, 68 percent did not feel able to report it, and almost half of all respondents did not know how. Of those who did report, 45 percent felt their concerns were not dealt with properly.
Islamophobia on campus also had an effect on mental health, with 45 percent reporting a moderate to high impact.
Three in five said they felt afraid or intimidated to express their views on Palestine.
FOSIS is calling on universities and students’ unions to adopt a definition of Islamophobia, train staff and student leaders, and give it a category in reporting systems, with complaints against staff investigated outside the staff member’s department. It also wants Friday prayers protected in timetables, no exams on Eid, and the government to review Prevent.
“Too often [students] stay quiet because they do not expect anyone to be held accountable,” said Rahma Hegy, FOSIS vice president for student affairs. “That lack of accountability concerns us most.”
At the University of York, Aayan Hashmi, 20, a second-year law student and president of the Islamic Society, said his faculty and the students’ union were supportive.
But he has felt “alienated” at times.
Sports and social societies centre on pub crawls and bar crawls, and Muslim students who do not drink “could be the best player” and still never fully realise their potential, he said.
Last year, as he walked to his first-year house after Friday prayers, a driver rolled down his window and gave him the middle finger.
Students have also told him they feel forced “to choose between their faith and their studies” when Friday prayers clash with lectures.
The FOSIS survey found that 21 percent of students said their timetable was “not compatible at all” with daily and Friday prayers.
Muslim students at the university are currently pressing the university for a larger prayer space.
At the University of Cambridge, Syed Ali, 21, a final-year politics and international relations student, said that rather than slurs, prejudice is dressed in “academic” and “sophisticated” language to make it appear legitimate.
Ali said it can be hard to tell where racism ends and Islamophobia begins.
“It’s difficult to disentangle,” he said.
The FOSIS report found that half of respondents counted the racialisation of Muslims as Islamophobia. Several described racial slurs in a survey about religious hatred, and the report says Muslims’ faith and race are “often read together”.
“It has been a very frightening experience to start realising that the world does not love me as I love it,” Cassam said. She is now urging others to speak out.
“We need people to report,” she said. “Statistics are political, and we need to be seen in policy.”
Al Jazeera contacted SOAS, the University of York and the University of Cambridge for responses, but did not receive replies by the time of publication.
