https://apache.be/2026/11/16/deze-impact.title: Deze impact had Apache in oktober
https://apache.be/2026/11/16/deze-impact.author: Redactie Apache
https://apache.be/2026/11/16/deze-impact.text:
Van Reynders in steeds nauwere schoentjes tot privérusthuizen die subsidies wegsluizen. Onderzoeken van Apache rolden in oktober over de tongen. Zo woog Apache de voorbije maand op het debat en het beleid.
- Het op een schandaal zonder weerga afstevenende fraudeonderzoek naar Didier Reynders – met nu ook smoking gun-bewijzen dat de ex-Eurocommissaris zaken waarin zijn naam viel in de doofpot liet stoppen – waarbij een “geklasseerde” zaak uit 2014 heropend werd na onthullingen van Apache.
- De financiële doorlichting die uitwees dat drie op de tien private rusthuizen in Vlaanderen en Brussel niet kunnen uitleggen waar hun zorgsubsidies naartoe gaan. Die kwam er nadat Apache in 2020 beschreef hoe private zorggroepen dat geld met slinkse truken wegsluizen naar hun aandeelhouders.
- De zogezegd “onaanraakbare” bevroren Russische miljarden bij Euroclear die dan toch al bleken te zijn aangesproken, niet om Oekraïne te steunen maar om Europese investeerders wiens geld vastzit in Rusland te compenseren. Een onthulling waarmee Apache ook in Kyiv de krant haalde.
Het zijn maar drie van de meer in het oog springende vormen van impact die Apache in oktober had. Ze illustreren hoe onze journalistiek niet alleen bewustzijn creëert, maar ook het beleid achter de veren zit en het gerecht een handje toesteekt.
Wegen op het beleid
Wegen op het debat én het beleid: dat probeerden we in oktober ook te doen met stevige argumenten voor een stop op het bouwen van datacenters, of om de kerncentrales niet holderdebolder te nationaliseren. Maar ook met een gouden tip voor de regering-De Wever over 15 miljard euro die zomaar voor het oprapen ligt. En met harde cijfers over beroepsziekten veroorzaakt door pesticiden – waarvan België er in tegenstelling tot meerdere buurlanden niet één erkent.
Weg van Amerikaanse big tech
De impact van datacenters en big tech onder de loep nemen, dat kun je moeilijk zonder conclusies te trekken over je eigen technologiegebruik. Daarom ruilde Apache de diensten van een Amerikaanse bigtechreus in voor Europese opensource-oplossingen, voor onze digitale werkplek, onze cloudopslag en onze redactionele chat. Dat vergde enig aanpassingsvermogen en had een zekere impact op de geoliede machine die we doorgaans zijn, maar daar heb jij als lezer hopelijk niets van gemerkt. Niettemin kunnen we iedereen aanraden om zelf de switch te maken – ook de Vlaamse overheid.
Klacht ongegrond, toch op kosten gejaagd
Impact van het minder leuke soort creëert onze journalistiek helaas ook van tijd tot tijd. Zoals voor de rechtbank of de Raad voor de Journalistiek gedaagd worden. En ook als zo’n klacht ongegrond wordt verklaard – omdat je aan niets schuldig bent behalve aan waarheidsgetrouwe berichtgeving – word je op kosten gejaagd. Ook daarom is journalistiek zoals die van Apache niet goedkoop, en de steun van onze leden onbetaalbaar.
Meer directe en indirecte impact van ons werk, maar ook kanttekeningen van onze redactie bij de dagelijkse actualiteit, vind je voortaan in de nieuwe rubriek Opgepikt.
Niets van het bovenstaande hadden we kunnen uitzoeken of onder de aandacht brengen zonder financiële steun van onze betalende leden.
Ben jij nog niet aangesloten bij Apache? Neem dan vandaag nog een betalend lidmaatschap, en geef ons meer middelen om te schrijven wat iedereen moet weten. Om kritische vragen te blijven stellen – hoe hardnekkig sommige politici ze ook negeren.

https://inthesetimes.com/article/big-tec.title: Big Tech’s Millions Backfired in the Midterms
https://inthesetimes.com/article/big-tec.author: Maegan Llerena and Theo Oshiro
https://inthesetimes.com/article/big-tec.text:
Big Tech’s Millions Backfired in the Midterms
Big Tech companies and their executives poured hundreds of millions of dollars into the midterm elections to both Democrats and Republicans—and, in large part, they lost.
Maegan Llerena and Theo Oshiro
Big Tech billionaires tried to buy our elections — but the millions of dollars in political contributions they made largely backfired. In a number of high-stakes races, rejecting Big Tech money helped deliver wins to candidates that ran on an anti-Big Tech platform. Why? In the recent midterms we witnessed a popular uprising that cut across traditional political fault lines to build new political power that overcame Big Tech’s millions.
We’ve had a first hand look at how voters are coming together to reject Big Tech’s undue influence. At Make the Road Action, we knocked on hundreds of thousands of doors and have organized in some of the communities where popular rejection of Big Tech is at its highest — Lehigh Valley, PA, Lansing, Michigan and Reno, Nevada, to name a few. On the doors, we saw that voters — across party lines and demographic differences — consistently shared concern over skyrocketing utility bills, fears around job replacement, and the role of Big Tech surveillance firms in ICE enforcement.
For example, in Northeastern Pennsylvania, which is quickly becoming one of the epicenters of the data center boom, working class Latino voters in Reading and Hazleton — once strongholds for President Doanld Trump — expressed increasing concern about spikes in utility costs and the rise of data centers. More than 77% of voters we surveyed in the area told us they were worried about the growth of data centers, especially as it impacted their electric bills. Nationally, the Wall Street Journal reported that 56% of the voters they polled cited data centers as a key issue in determining who to vote for in Congress. Pennsylvania Republican Reps. Ryan MacKenzie and Rob Bresnahan — both of whom took large sums from Big Tech executives — lost re-election, in part due to their pro-data center, pro-AI stances.
Rejection of data centers and a broad based fight around AI also powered Will Lawrence’s long shot win in the deep purple 7th congressional district in Michigan. Voters we spoke with were deeply skeptical of his opponent, sitting Rep. Tom Barrett, a Republican who took substantial campaign contributions from Big Tech executives and voted to stop states from regulating AI. Lawrence flipped the seat on an AI accountability platform that spoke to the pocketbook concerns of voters as well as the more pervasive fears of AI job replacement and safety.
In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins, the top recipient of Palantir donations in Congress, lost her race, as did Republican Darline Graham in South Carolina, who lost despite substantial support from data center companies. Democrats that cozied up to Big Tech also lost: Jimmy Gomez, a California pro-tech Democrat lost to a progressive in an “AI proxy battle.”Our analysis shows that about half of all incumbents that took money from Palantir Technologies lost their races this year — six out of the top eight recipients of money from Palantir executives lost. And in a shocking twist, one of the largest AI Super PACs, Leading the Future, run by Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale and OpenAI CEO Greg Brockman, pulled back their investments just weeks before the midterms because of concern their support would hurt, not boost, candidates. 
Across the country, voters came out to demand a say in what happens in their neighborhoods and towns, and an America they can afford, where rights are respected, kids are safe, and local economies are thriving. Where technology makes life better, not worse. And where elected officials are not in the pockets of corporate giants.
As Democrats take back control of Congress, now is the time to set a vision and comprehensive plan for AI in our country. We are at a critical juncture. Democrats must use their investigatory powers to bring AI CEOs before Congress to demand answers on safety breaches, out of control surveillance, and the impact of AI on workers and families. 
Now is the time to advance a vision for AI safety and regulation that includes public oversight and real public enforcement, a jobs guarantee for workers who fear being left behind by automation, and a plan to tax AI companies so that working people can share in the increased productivity. 
Thank you for reading this story. At a time when corporate media is dominating the web and our airwaves, independent journalism is more important than ever, and that’s what we provide at In These Times. We offer some of the best reporting, investigations and analysis on the growing movements for justice in the U.S.—and our work is firmly pro-labor and anti-fascist. To continue producing it, we need your support.
If you believe in the power of an independent press, please make a donation to In These Times today. By becoming a sustaining member, you can ensure that our work reaches even more readers.
And if you become a sustainer right now, you'll get a free year-long print subscription and a special subscribers-only print from artist Molly Crabapple.
Thank you.
Maegan Llerena is Co-Executive Director at Make the Road Action.
Theo Oshiro is Co-Executive Director at Make the Road Action.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: Documenting Women Out of Their Cells
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Sara Bennett
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
Sara Bennett, a former public defender, spent more than a decade photographing women sentenced to life, mostly for homicide, in New York State’s prisons. A new book of her photographs, Looking Inside: Women With Life Sentences, traces their lives behind prison walls and, for those who have been released after decades behind bars, their reentry into the outside world. Most of the women in the book were released through parole. Others had their sentences reduced through New York’s Domestic Violence Survivors Justice Act, which allows people to petition the courts for resentencing if the crime they were convicted of was linked to abuse they had suffered. Meanwhile, in New York’s three women’s prisons, 174 people are serving life sentences. As of 2024, one in 11 incarcerated women, or more than 6,800 nationally, were serving life sentences. Reprinted here are some of Bennett’s photos of those women from Looking Inside.
—Victoria Law
Looking Inside was published by Kehrer Verlag in 2026. Bennett’s photos will be on display in 2027 at Baxter St at the Camera Club of New York in Manhattan.
To most people, the archive is just a portal on their computer. But it’s also a physical space made by a person who has never cared more about the preservation of digital history....

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Why Jensen Huang’s Downfall Is No Victory for Progressives
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Tobita Chow
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Why Jensen Huang’s Downfall Is No Victory for Progressives
The big winners are anti-China hawks in the national security establishment and OpenAI and Anthropic.
Last week, Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of chip giant Nvidia following a damaging news cycle focused on his affair with Alice Huang (no relation), widely referred to as an “alleged spy” for the Chinese government. It has since become unclear who exactly is alleging that Alice Huang is a spy or what exactly is meant by the word “spy”—but set that aside for now. What should progressives make of this?
It is understandable that some progressives have felt like cheering these developments. Jensen Huang is part of the AI oligarchy, and at long last one of them has been taken down a notch. But it would be a mistake to view Huang’s loss as a win for the people against the AI oligarchy as a whole. It is rather part of an intra-elite struggle that spans both Silicon Valley and Washington, DC. The major policy outcome is support from the Trump administration for tighter restrictions on the ability of Chinese AI firms to access Nvidia’s advanced chips. The big winners are anti-China hawks in the national security establishment and the frontier AI labs, OpenAI and Anthropic.
At issue is a growing convergence between the national security establishment and the AI industry. National security leaders hope that the US lead in advanced semiconductors and in frontier AI can yield an advantage in the arms race against China, helping to counter China’s edge in manufacturing capacity, while also boosting overall US economic growth, which can indirectly translate into military power. In turn, the national security establishment has much to offer the AI industry in the face of the latter’s increasingly pressing challenges: protection from rival Chinese AI firms on the grounds that their cheaper models are a national security threat, a potential source of bailouts through the Pentagon in the event that the AI boom turns to bust, and an ally against growing populist opposition within the United States.
Jensen Huang has been a leading obstacle to this convergence between AI and national security. This is because Huang’s position in US-China AI competition is uniquely contradictory: Nvidia’s profits come mainly from the US AI industry, which is entirely dependent on Nvidia’s advanced chips, but Nvidia also has the potential to earn major profits from AI companies in China. Indeed, if Nvidia were to gain the ability to sell directly in the Chinese market, it would be able to do so at premium prices. For OpenAI and Anthropic, in contrast, China’s AI firms pose a one-sided competitive threat.
Thus OpenAI and Anthropic have for the most part supported chip restrictions against China, while Nvidia’s Huang vigorously lobbied Trump to weaken those restrictions. Trump, who is independently interested in maintaining warm relations with Xi Jinping, was very responsive to Huang’s lobbying. As a result, the Trump administration allowed Nvidia both to continue supplying chips to data centers in third countries that service Chinese firms and to sell its (second-rate) H200 chips directly to China—although, ironically, China blocked imports of the H200 chips in order to protect demand for competing chips produced by Chinese firms.
Huang, for his part, argued that if Nvidia maintains a customer base in China, that is in the US national interest. For example, this would perpetuate Chinese dependence on US chip technology, which is a form of leverage, and Nvidia could invest profits from the Chinese market into further innovation, which would help maintain the lead of US technology over China’s. Whatever merit these arguments may have had, the national security establishment overwhelmingly rejected them.
National security leaders were accordingly frustrated that Trump listened to Huang and weakened anti-China chip restrictions. This is in turn part of a broader set of grievances that Trump has “caged the China hawks” in his administration. Marco Rubio, one of these hawks within the administration, is reported to have set the “alleged spy” scandal in motion. National security hawks across the political spectrum then successfully used the scandal as an opportunity to increase support for their desired chip restrictions, particularly within the administration, and to remove Huang as the leading obstacle to their agenda within Silicon Valley. At a time when national security arguments about the necessity of confrontation with China are declining in popular appeal, Huang was an exceptionally convenient target as an extraordinarily wealthy leader in the unpopular AI industry.
It is too little understood how damaging the US chip restrictions have been to the stability of US-China relations. Leaders in China (as in the United States) see advanced chips and AI as key to future economic development. During the Biden administration (which initiated the chip restrictions), the Chinese government denounced the chip restrictions in increasingly strident terms, culminating in the accusation that the United States is “containing China’s hi-tech development and depriving China of its legitimate right to development” and the statement that China’s “right to development” is one of its “four red lines,” alongside issues whose sensitivity is much better understood in the US, such as the “Taiwan question.” (The formulation of these “four red lines” has subsequently continued under Trump 2.)
The danger of the chip restrictions lies in the escalatory cycle they kicked off. China reacted by developing its own export controls on rare earth elements. This tool was activated following the intense escalation in the US-China trade war in 2025, leading to the October 2025 trade truce that Trump and Xi have sustained to this day. This Trump-Xi truce, however, is not a long-term solution to US-China tensions. The potential for China to cut off access to rare earths poses an existential threat to a few US industries, including arms manufacturers, which has of course further aggravated tensions on the US side. And this cycle of economic warfare creates new risks of US-China military conflict.
Seen in this context, there is little in Jensen Huang’s downfall, and the re-escalation in the chip war that it has enabled, for progressives to celebrate. But it doesn’t follow from this that progressive goals or the interests of the 99 percent can be won by siding with Huang. Rather, we need a way out of the intra-elite struggles between Silicon Valley and the national security establishment that brought down Huang. The real solution is to build a new US economy that isn’t dependent on AI as the sole source of growth, and a new approach to US security that provides an alternative to zero-sum tech-military-industrial competition against China.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Make America Function Again!
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Elie Mystal
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Make America Function Again!
Who is going to fix all the things the Republicans, corporations, and tech titans broke?
The thing about bills is that they always come due. Americans are starting to see the true price of years of Republican malfeasance, corporate greed, and rushed reliance on unproven artificial intelligence systems. That price looks like e-mail outages. It looks like nationwide flight ground stops. It looks like data breaches, malware attacks, and the enshittification of every product, good, or service available for purchase.
America is not a failed state—not yet at least. In the scholarship, a “failed state” is one that has lost its monopoly on the legitimate use of force, and one that cannot provide basic public services. We’re not there yet; our extrajudicial murder force, ICE, still technically acts under the color of government authority. And the government, at the federal as well as state and local levels, still has the ability to provide services: We can maintain the electrical grid, support a transportation network, and (mostly) deliver clean drinking water to those lucky enough to have homes and not live in Michigan. We just screw up the delivery of those services with increasing and alarming frequency.
The United States is not failed, but it’s far from functional. We’re a nation held together by duct tape and super glue. Everybody can see the cracks forming, and people are starting to realize that there is nobody minding the store. There are a few heroic individuals holding their fingers in the dam, and we’re all just hoping the dam doesn’t break today.
Everyone knows the broad contours of how we got here. Republicans run for office on the claim that government cannot work, and then spend their time in power destroying government just to prove that they were right. Neoliberals help Republicans by ceding critical government functions to the private sector, which in turn ignores the public good in an all-consuming chase for greater margins and profits. Occasionally things get so bad that the people elect leaders who are modestly responsible—who fix things just enough that the next guy (and it’s pretty much always a guy) can come in and complain about taxes and Black people and get elected to wreck the government again.
The latest version of this cycle has been especially damaging because the second Trump administration was captured by people who had a plan to destroy the government (Project 2025), and Trump then went ahead and empowered Elon Musk as the chainsaw-wielding destructor. With a truly breathtaking lack of knowledge or care, Musk did serious harm to the functioning of the government by firing career professionals who actually understood how everything worked. Everybody can complain about the incompetent rogue’s gallery of cabinet secretaries Trump has appointed, but it is the loss of these institutional experts that has done the most damage to the United States’s ability to work properly. The grounding of every plane in the country is just one of the more obvious consequences of Musk and his DOGE initiative, but there are many others.
Musk is also the bridge between the dysfunction of our government and the dysfunction of our society more generally, because he is one of the eight to 10 oligarchs who have amassed power at an unbelievable scale. We live in a world where if one of these guys (and once again, they’re all guys) has a bad day, everybody has a bad day. If one of them decides to bump chips with a spy, entire industries can be manipulated. If one of them changes the algorithm, our whole perception of reality can be warped. We have global “key man risk.”
And then there’s the tech these oligarches have helped create. The problem is not that we’re reliant on technology; humans have always relied on technology, whether that technology was a spearpoint or a fish hook or Uber Eats. The problem is that the tech is no longer made to be reliable. The tech is made to make money. Everything is designed either to break or become obsolete so we have to buy a new thing.
Then that nondurable tech is integrated into a bunch of other nondurable tech so that if one thing breaks it can cause a cascade of failures. Somebody introduces a bug into a hardware system, and suddenly we cannot access our bank accounts. Somebody installs a new router, and suddenly the airplanes cannot fly. Somebody hacks into a software program and suddenly all the refrigerators in the supermarket stop working.
Oh, and just in case you think I am merely listing petty inconveniences, the National Security Agency’s internal communication system went down while I was writing this.
The monopolies controlled by the oligarchs and the integration of their tech into everything we use combine to destroy our system resiliency. If one system fails, entire systems fail. The tech bros always claim to have various contingencies, but because of conglomeration, we don’t have backups for when those contingencies fail.
On top of all of this, these same oligarchs are pushing to incorporate artificial intelligence into everything. This is a technology that few people understand, and worse, the ones who do understand it are warning us that they can’t control it. We’re also using the AI to replace human workers, so when the AI breaks, our only choice is to ask the AI how to fix it. Wonderful world we’re building here.
All of this political, corporate, and technological dysfunction has a natural endpoint: People will get hurt; people will suffer. Some might eventually die. Hell, we have managed to bring back measles. There is no clearer indication that things no longer work the way they should than people getting sick from a disease previous generations worked hard to eradicate.
What naturally follows from this gross incompetence is social unrest. Once people can’t reliably go about their daily lives without hassle, the pitchforks and torches come out. We’re seeing a little of this already. In the midterm elections, people who were willing to suffer Trump’s racism, misogyny, thievery, buffonery, incompetence, and incontinence decided to vote for Democrats for the first time in their lives because they couldn’t afford gas and eggs.
The affordability crisis is a symptom of the deeper rot in our society. Things don’t work. Things are expensive and still don’t work. Things that worked yesterday might not work tomorrow—and the update you’ve been forced to download to make it work might brick your whole system.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
A political leader could rise by running on a platform restoring functionality to our daily lives. I’d hope that such a leader would be a progressive, but I’ll remind readers that fascists and authoritarians have earned a lot of supporters over the course of history simply by making things, like trains, work. Running on an agenda of making things work properly is usually very popular, and it gets more popular the crappier things are.
I also want to be clear that I’m not talking about an institutionalist platform—I have lived through the Joe Biden era of restoring competency to government and found it lacking. I’m talking about a radical, populist platform that improves people’s daily lives and kneecaps the kleptocrats running the joint. Everybody’s flights didn’t get canceled because Sean Duffy is an incompetent boob (though he is an incompetent boob). Everybody’s flights got canceled because there was some stupid problem caused by our long failure to invest in our infrastructure—and when there was a problem, rich people were able to opt out of the entire system and charter their way home. Markwayne Mullen was literally able to fly to a football game (football teams also saw their travel prioritized, for honestly no good reason) while regular people were still sleeping in airports with their children.
Making America functional again means prioritizing the needs of people over the needs of investors. It means paying more attention to purchasing power than to quarterly profits. It means valuing durability over planned obsolescence. It means busting monopolies and restoring consumer protections. It means testing experimental technologies before they are approved for wide-scale use instead of treating every American as a beta tester or lab rat. It means being able to fill a prescription provided by your doctor without having to spend two hours on hold with your insurance company. And, for the love of humanity, it means regulating AI.
It’s one thing for stuff to break. Entropy is undefeated, but enshittification is a choice. Things are breaking because a small cadre of people have decided it’s more profitable for things to break than it is for things to last. We’re not suffering because of the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune. We’re suffering because we are paying for the fortunes of others. My computer is more expensive because AI is buying up all the RAM. My water is more expensive because AI is sucking up all the water. And all the while my e-mail sometimes doesn’t work, probably because of some AI assistant I never even asked for.
You know how most zombie movies depict “the day” the zombie plague becomes active and society is destroyed? There are always planes falling out of the sky and car crashes and fires, and the hero ends up surviving because they were functionally off the grid that day by some happenstance? The problem with these movies is that societies don’t collapse in a day (well, maybe Pompeii, but that’s an exception). They fall apart over a long period of time. Things stop working; people adjust and make workarounds, and soon enough nobody can remember what it was like when that thing worked. And within a generation or two, you go from reading a scroll in a Roman library to using the paper with the weird markings on them for kindling.
We need to make America functional again—before nobody remembers how to fix it.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/trum.title: Trump Intel Pick Calls $1 Million Bribe for a Pardon a “Complicated Legal Question”
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/trum.author: Matt Sledge
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/trum.text:
Asked at a Wednesday confirmation hearing whether the law allowed people to give the president a $1 million bribe in exchange for a pardon, a White House attorney up for a major intelligence job said it was a “complicated legal question.”
Gary Lawkowski, who advised President Donald Trump in office and on the campaign trail, faced tough questioning from Democrats during his Wednesday hearing to serve as general counsel to the Office of Director of National Intelligence.
The hearing came as Senate Intelligence Committee Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark., sought to rush Lawkowski’s confirmation to the top intelligence posting before the end of the year, when Democrats take over Congress.
Although Lawkowski drew no hostile questions from Republicans, Democratic senators were concerned about Lawkowski’s role in Trump’s pardon spree, as well as his involvement in controversial executive orders that directed federal law enforcement to crack down on the left and designate antifa as a domestic terror organization.
“We’re looking for judgment here,” said Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., vice chair of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence. “And I understand: You were just the lawyer. But so many times, ‘I was just the lawyer’ kind of becomes the default answer.”
Lawkowski’s current position is deputy assistant and deputy counsel to the president. He was little known outside the White House before Trump nominated him earlier this month to serve at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, a Cabinet-level department where he would coordinate legal advice for the 18 different agencies making up the intelligence community.
According to a questionnaire, Lawkowski has not held jobs at intelligence agencies before. His prior national security experience involves advising Trump on classified matters over the past two years.
He also has a long-standing relationship with Trump. During Trump’s time out of the White House, he helped provided legal advice to the president’s reelection campaign and defended him from lawsuits brought by people harmed during the January 6 insurrection.
Questioning His Record
During the Senate hearing, Warner criticized Trump’s pardons for January 6 rioters and for crypto mogul Changpeng Zhao. The crypto tycoon’s company Binance was involved in a transaction that benefited one of the Trump family’s crypto ventures.
Lawkowski suggested that prior reporting in the New York Times had exaggerated his role in the pardon process.
“My main focus was litigation and policy,” he said. “I’m actually not our primary pardon counsel. I have worked on some pardon issues.”
Sen. Angus King, an independent from Maine who caucuses with the Democrats, pressed Lawkowski on whether it would be illegal for someone to walk into the Oval Office and hand the president a $1 million bribe for a pardon.
“That’s OK?” King said.
“Well, bribery itself would be a separate statutory crime. How that would interact with presidential immunity would be a complicated legal question that I think the court kind of reserved in that case,” he said, referring to a 2024 Supreme Court decision that granted the president broad immunity from prosecution for official acts.
Another senator zeroed in on Lawkowski’s role in crafting National Security Presidential Memorandum-7, commonly known as NSPM-7, the executive order directing federal law enforcement agencies to target “antifa” and other boogeymen of the far right.
In the written questionnaire, Lawkowski said he was involved in “communications” regarding that order and another that purported to designate antifa — the loose-knit anti-fascist movement — as a domestic terror group. He declined to explain further, citing the confidentiality of his legal conversations with the president.
“There is no basis in law to designate a domestic terrorist organization, but you have claimed the president can just do it anyways based on some magical constitutional authority,” said Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore. “Once he’s operating outside the law, are there any limits to how Donald Trump can persecute Americans?”
“I don’t agree with the premise that the president is acting outside of the law,” Lawkowski said. “Of course, the president is constrained by the limits of the Constitution.”

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.title: Chicago’s City Council Orders Independent Review of Finances as Scrutiny Intensifies
https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.author: Heather Cherone
https://www.propublica.org/article/chica.text:
The debate over Chicago’s financial struggles — out in the open as never before — took a new turn on Wednesday as the City Council added to the scrutiny.
The City Council voted 45-5 in a special meeting to give a leading alderperson the authority to hire an outside firm to independently review Chicago’s finances.
It’s unclear if an audit would be complete in time for the City Council to consider its findings before the Dec. 29 deadline mandated by state law to pass a 2027 budget, in what likely will be contentious negotiations with Mayor Brandon Johnson. Later in the day came another sign of distress: S&P Global put the city on credit watch with a warning that the budget wrangling is likely to result in a credit downgrade within 90 days.
The intense council debate over the city’s financial future comes in the wake of a package of stories published Monday by WTTW News and ProPublica that examined how a $55 billion debt burden, decades in the making, was hampering efforts to service Chicagoans and how the Johnson administration was turning to more borrowing to plug holes, such as large police settlements.
Alderperson Pat Dowell had called for the outside review after former Chief Financial Officer Ashlee Gabrysch abruptly resigned Friday over what she described as a political environment that forced her to downplay certain facts about the city’s financial situation. Gabrysch argued that her integrity would be compromised if she stayed on.
Just as Gabrysch had once been a trusted part of Johnson’s team, Dowell was once thought to be a mayoral ally. Johnson tapped Dowell, who endorsed him during the 2023 mayoral election, to lead the City Council’s Finance Committee soon after he took office.
But since then Dowell has proven to be a thorn in the mayor’s side, refusing last year to support his proposal to impose a $25 per month per employee tax on most firms that have more than 125 employees and hike the city’s personal property lease tax. (Johnson continues to push for that idea.)
The ordinance gives Dowell the authority to spend whatever is necessary “to determine whether any material or intentional misstatements of the city’s financial condition to investors, the City Council and the public have been made in any public document, presentation, offering or financial reporting within the prior three years.”
The firm, or firms, hired to conduct the review will have access to all city documents and records, and all city officials must cooperate with the probe, according to the ordinance.
“We must ensure that our math is correct,” Dowell said, vowing to act quickly. “The discrepancies over the past few weeks have been particularly disturbing to me. As my mother used to say, where there’s smoke, there’s fire.”
Johnson said he welcomed the review and will not veto the ordinance.
Justin Marlowe, a professor at the University of Chicago’s Harris School of Public Policy and the director of the Center for Municipal Finance, said he wasn’t certain an audit was warranted while acknowledging its importance in another way. He noted that the audit vote coupled with the inability of the council and the mayor to agree on a budget plan already may have done damage with credit rating agencies.
“The way cities make their budgets matter,” Marlowe said. “It matters that for the third year in a row that there are disagreements over basic facts.”
In short, Marlowe said, “Investors don’t like uncertainty, and this is creating a lot of uncertainty.”
Alderperson Matt Martin said Wednesday that the analysis by ProPublica and WTTW was “sobering.” He is questioning some of Johnson’s borrowing strategies.
Over the years, Chicago alderpersons have generally acquiesced to mayoral directives on finances. But that has changed under Johnson, in part due to his preference for a head tax but also because of the growing realization that the city’s finances have been undermined by a series of decisions from previous mayors.
Similarly, top administration officials generally choose to leave City Hall either quietly or with words of praise for the current mayor. That’s not how Gabrysch handled her exit.
The statement she released Friday made it clear she had severe doubts about the way Johnson was portraying the city’s debt problem. And she reiterated those concerns in a commentary in the Chicago Tribune over the weekend that also laid out her suggestions for how the city can more responsibly handle its budgeting (for example, “Don’t borrow to pay everyday bills, even if we’ve done so in the past”).
Then, in a brief interview with the Chicago Sun-Times on Monday, she said she supported calls for a financial audit.
“If this makes it easier for residents to see that Chicago actually is in a fairly dire fiscal situation where hard decisions … and shared sacrifices have to be made, that can be helpful,” Gabrysch said. “Shining some light on the city’s finances — whether or not they discover wrongdoing, but rather showing the nuances of how dire some things have become — could be worthwhile.”
Chicago’s credit rating has been plummeting, adding to the cost of borrowing and leaving the city just two or three levels above junk status among leading Wall Street rating agencies. Gabrysch had been hired just three months ago from Fitch Ratings, with an eye toward shoring up the city’s reputation.
S&P Global, one of a handful of major ratings agencies, released a statement on Wednesday about its “CreditWatch” for Chicago. It cited the intense battle over the budget and an increased likelihood that “the city will resort to significant one-time measures to balance the fiscal 2027 budget.”
That means analysts see at least a 1-in-2 chance of issuing a rating cut in the next three months.
Johnson’s administration has sought to portray Gabrysch as someone who fell short in her duties and mismanaged a major transfer of funds — characterizations she has disputed.
Read More
The mayor has dismissed the conflict that led to Gabrysch’s resignation as a “technical dispute.” When he unveiled his 2027 budget, Johnson and administration officials said 76% of the budget gap would be closed with “structural fixes” — long-term or permanent solutions — that would bring expenses in line with revenues. That could help the city avoid another credit downgrade.
But Gabrysch told the City Council on Oct. 26 that the decision to borrow $481 million to cover the cost of resolving police misconduct lawsuits in 2027 and 2028 changed that calculation, reducing the amount the gap closed with revenue the city can count on in future years to just 56%.
As recently as September, Johnson told reporters the city would not borrow to cover those costs.
If the City Council approves Johnson’s proposal to borrow $481 million, the city’s massive debt burden — which now tops $55 billion — is set to grow for the second straight year to cover the cost of running the city, a sign of financial trouble.
That distress, Johnson has argued, is largely due to the decisions of previous administrations. “It’s no secret: Our city finds itself in a precarious financial situation due to decades of mismanagement,” he said Tuesday.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/greg.title: Greg Abbott Tried to Destroy Muslim Group By Calling Them Terrorists. Texas Voters Balked.
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/greg.author: Sanya Mansoor
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/18/greg.text:
As Texas Republicans pursued their crusade against the Council on American-Islamic Relations, they ran into an unexpected obstacle: voters.
Republicans Gov. Greg Abbott and Attorney General Ken Paxton had carried out their crackdown on the largest Muslim civil rights group in the U.S., hoping to ban CAIR’s operations in the state and label it a terrorist organization. That agenda suffered a crippling blow in the midterm elections, when Democratic candidates beat Abbott and Paxton in stunning upsets — with both their current offices set to be led by Democrats.
Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa promised to reverse Abbott’s designation of CAIR as a foreign terrorist organization. She told the Washington Post last week, “We have to use public safety measures for public safety” — decrying Abbott’s designation as “nonsense.” Paxton, who lost a bid for an open U.S. Senate seat, dropped a lawsuit, filed in February, that would have banned CAIR from operating in Texas.
“Don’t underestimate the power of the vote to create the administration that creates and enforces these laws,” said Chelsea Glover, a lawyer with the Muslim Legal Fund of America, who is representing CAIR Texas in litigation challenging Abbott’s designation. “Lots of times we don’t think it’s possible but, as Texas has shown, anything is possible.”
The Muslim Legal Fund of America said the lawsuit is ongoing and will be until Abbott’s terror designation is formally withdrawn by Hinojosa.
CAIR’s suit was necessary, said Glover, but acknowledged that the ballot box can be a faster way to shut down bigotry than drawn out court cases.
CAIR welcomed Hinojosa’s promise to walk back Abbott’s proclamation, which CAIR called a “baseless, unconstitutional order.”
The proclamation classified CAIR and its Texas chapter, as well as the Muslim Brotherhood, as foreign terrorist groups; it also banned designated groups from buying or acquiring land in the state.
“When you get the right person in power, who is going to follow the Constitution, it’s like — poof, the designation is gone almost overnight,” said Imran Ghani, director of digital communications for CAIR Texas and operations director for the Houston branch.
Ghani said CAIR Texas noticed a chilling effect after Abbott’s proclamation last November. Some donors stopped giving money, and a few mosques became hesitant to platform CAIR. He said the organization quickly rebuilt trust and also won over new supporters who were invigorated by the state’s targeting of CAIR and wanted to help.
“I tend to look at it rather positively,” Ghani said. “The designation gave CAIR more publicity than we have ever received.”
CAIR Texas officials pointed out that Republican candidates leaned heavily into fabricated fears about Muslims taking over Texas and enforcing sharia law.
“We had to send a strong message,” said Shaimaa Zayan, Austin director for CAIR Texas. “If we allow them to say all of that and stay home that would be a green light for them to continue harassing our community.”
CAIR Texas says the organization scaled up its engagement around the elections this year by showing up weekly to dozens of mosques in Houston, Austin, and Dallas, from August until early October, during Friday prayers, to encourage voter registration.
CAIR Action, the group’s political wing, reported historic turnout for Texas Muslims voting early in a general election—marking a 78.6 percent increase since 2018.
State-Level Bigotry
Republican candidates’ anti-Muslim rhetoric came alongside the state education board approving an anti-Islamic rewrite of Texas social studies lessons and exclusions on a voucher program for K-12 Islamic schools.
Islamophobia has also led to violence against Texas’s Muslim population in recent years. In 2024, the Justice Department sentenced a Dallas man to 37 years in prison after he killed one person and tried to kill four others during a mass shooting at a Muslim-owned business; the FBI said he intentionally targeted Muslims.
While designating terrorist organizations is normally a power reserved for the federal government, Texas and Florida have taken unprecedented actions to allow state officials to apply those labels.
CAIR and its Florida chapter suspended operations in Florida earlier this month after Gov. Ron DeSantis and four state officials designated the groups as domestic terror organizations under a new, unprecedented administrative process approved by the legislature this summer.
The American Civil Liberties Union and CAIR sued DeSantis, alleging free speech and due process violations. The civil rights groups also argued that the debilitating penalties associated with the designations effectively force targeted groups to shut down.
On Monday, DeSantis commented on X about news of Hinojosa’s promised reversal and said, “This would be a huge contrast with Florida, where CAIR has disbanded.”
“Elections have consequences,” said Shirin Sinnar, a law professor at Stanford University.
She pointed out that the different outcomes in Florida and Texas “show the power of electoral consequences on the same issue.”
“A Loaded Gun”
Sinnar cautioned that the federal government may have plans of its own to crack down on nonprofits.
The Wall Street Journal reported on November 6 that the Trump administration is considering an executive order that would list some nonprofits as being tied to terrorists, effectively shutting down their operations.
Sinnar said that while Texas may be backing off from the executive order and lawsuit against CAIR, there’s more work to be done at the state level.
“It’s a good moment for civil rights advocates and communities to push the legislature to repeal the laws that enabled these designations,” she said. “Otherwise, they’re a loaded gun available to be used in the future against CAIR or another disfavored target.”
Those laws include measures that created the category of Texas foreign terrorist organizations and authorized state and local officials, as well as private residents, the ability to bring civil suits against them without having to prove any personal injury.
Youssef Chouhoud, a research scientist for the Texas-based nonprofit Yaqeen Institute for Islamic Research, which focuses on issues related to Muslims, said Republicans in the state will likely continue engaging in Islamophobic rhetoric and policies. Attacking the Muslim community was “very much a winning strategy” in the Republican primaries, he said.
Though 95 percent of Republican primary voters said they supported a ballot proposition asking if “Texas should prohibit sharia law,” critics pointed out that the state’s anti-Muslim hysteria has led to an overblown focus on Muslim religious law.
Ghani, in Houston, had left a corporate job for more meaningful work and joined CAIR only about two months before Abbott’s terror designation. He took solace in his five daily prayers and hoped the past would become precedent.
“History has shown this is the path of many civil rights groups,” Ghani said of the persecution — and perseverance — of other civil rights groups like the NAACP in the 1950s and 60s, and the ACLU itself during the McCarthy era.
“It’s a badge of honor,” Ghani said, “to be targeted by extremists in the government.”

https://www.propublica.org/article/calif.title: This Counselor Faces Trial for Sexually Abusing 15 Students. California Has Been Warned About Him for Years.
https://www.propublica.org/article/calif.author: Holly McDede
https://www.propublica.org/article/calif.text:
Reporting Highlights
- Licensed Until Charged: Three educators who were reported to the state for alleged misconduct were allowed to keep working — and to draw new complaints — until they were criminally charged.
- Incomplete Investigation: One was reported for allegedly touching children inappropriately in 2019. California didn’t suspend his credentials until his 2024 arrest.
- Lack of Guidelines: California’s educator licensing agency provides no guidelines to the volunteers who review teacher misconduct cases for determining when and how to mete out punishment.
These highlights were written by the reporters and editors who worked on this story.
Five years before police arrested former elementary school counselor David Braff for allegedly sexually abusing students, complaints had already been sent to the state of California: that Braff had sat students on his lap, rubbed their legs and touched them near their vaginas.
But California’s educator licensing agency failed to conduct a thorough investigation after his school district reported Braff to the state in 2019. And the agency allowed Braff to continue working with children. It wasn’t until his 2024 arrest that the agency suspended his credentials. By then, he’d gotten jobs at three more Southern California schools. At one of them, prosecutors allege, another student complained the guidance counselor had touched him, too.
The state Commission on Teacher Credentialing also delayed revoking the credentials of two other teachers who were later convicted of sexually abusing students. As with Braff, schools had reported those educators to the agency that determines who can work in California’s public schools. And as with Braff, the commission allowed those teachers to keep teaching — and draw new complaints — until after they were criminally charged, an investigation by KQED and ProPublica found. That includes a middle school math teacher who sent his student a video showing a boy’s genitals and an elementary teacher who touched students’ butts and vaginal areas and placed their hands on his crotch, according to court records.
In each of the cases, state investigators did not interview some of the students who had alleged abuse, according to the students, parents and attorneys who spoke to KQED and ProPublica. Several former agency staffers, including investigators, told the news outlets that, at times, the volunteer panel tasked with assessing teacher accusations overlooked evidence of wrongdoing. That perspective from staff members was backed up by two former members of the panel and two people who served on the state commission that ultimately decides teacher discipline.
After police arrested Braff in 2024, a parent emailed Jeffrey Weinstein, superintendent at Santa Paula Unified School District, where Braff was first accused of sexually abusing students. “Who dropped the ball and allowed this monster to still be around kids?” the parent wrote, according to public records obtained by the news outlets. (Weinstein was not working at Santa Paula at the time students accused Braff.)
In his emailed response, Weinstein blamed the state’s teacher licensing agency. He told the parent that the district had conducted its own investigation and reported the guidance counselor to the state as well as to police. He also said he had reviewed the district’s investigative file and “vehemently disagreed” with the agency’s decision not to revoke Braff’s credentials.
“We sent all the evidence we had gathered,” Weinstein said. “The district did everything in its legal capacity it could.”
Braff is soon to stand trial for sexually abusing 15 students, including 13 from Santa Paula. He has been in jail since November 2024. He has pleaded not guilty and did not respond to a request for comment sent through the Ventura County Sheriff’s Office’s electronic messaging system. His attorney declined to comment.
Braff had previously told Santa Paula Unified administrators that he did not touch students near their private parts or have them sit on his lap — and that he only gave students side hugs, high-fives, fist bumps and taps on the knee, according to the district’s 2019 report to the state.
“Mr. Braff described keeping an office environment where kids can move around; and he would not be closer than arm’s length,” the report said, summarizing the district’s interview with Braff. “It was not his intent to make them afraid but rather feel that there was someone in their corner; someone to talk to.”
Anita Fitzhugh, a spokesperson for the Commission on Teacher Credentialing, said the state automatically revokes teachers’ credentials when they are convicted of sexual criminal offenses. But she wrote in a statement that “unless the applicant or educator is convicted of a mandatory criminal offense, there are no written criteria that set the level of adverse action for educator discipline matters.” She did not answer questions about specific cases or details of the investigative process.
Fitzhugh said the state does not provide any guidelines for those reviewing teacher misconduct cases about when discipline is warranted or the type of punishment that should be meted out. And she said it was the commission’s role to balance “protecting students as well as the legal rights of educators who have been accused but not convicted.”
California’s system of disciplining educators dates to the 1970s, Fitzhugh said, and “a deep and comprehensive review of the educator discipline system, prioritizing student safety in the schools, is in order.”
“We expect the Commission to take this up in the near future,” she said.
Students Not Interviewed
In the summer of 2019, California’s Commission on Teacher Credentialing received a detailed report from the Santa Paula school district about Braff’s alleged misconduct at McKevett Elementary School. The state requires districts to report educators when they resign or are fired after allegations of misconduct. Braff, who had been a guidance counselor at the school for four years, had resigned in the midst of the district’s investigation into complaints by at least seven students that he had touched them inappropriately.
The district told the state agency that it had contemplated but did not initiate any discipline against Braff before accepting his resignation. The district said it appeared, based on student interviews, that Braff “had engaged in at least inappropriate conduct.” Its report to the state, submitted two months after he resigned, included a 20-page summary of the principal’s interviews with at least seven accusers and two witnesses. It also included Braff’s defense and noted multiple inconsistencies in his account of what had occurred.
One fifth grade girl said that during a visit to his office, Braff had locked the door, grabbed her by her hips and forced her to sit on his lap, according to the district’s report to the state of its investigation. She said she did not like being touched and cried every time she had to see him for counseling. The girl requested to transfer to another school, district investigators said, because she wanted to “be away from” Braff.
Two other girls alleged Braff touched them near their “privates,” the district reported to the state. Neither girl was aware of the other’s claim.
One of them, a fourth grader, told the principal that she had been meeting regularly with Braff for counseling since second grade. During those visits, he would make her sit on his lap. She told the principal that Braff tapped her on the leg with his hand “in a way to try to make her feel like she was doing a good job,” but she said the tapping hurt. After two school years of regular counseling, she alleged he started tapping her higher on the thigh, close to her “private.” In contrast, she said a different teacher pats students on the head when they do a good job, according to the district’s report to the state.
The girl, who is now 18, spoke to KQED and ProPublica with her mother and attorney present on the condition that only her first initial, J., be used to protect her privacy. J. said Braff had told her that whatever happened in his office was a secret. She said she had few friends at the school and was terrified of getting in trouble when she reported the person she confided in.
The district’s report to the state included notes from an interview with J.’s former principal, Lydia Olivo, who had left the school before J. and other students complained about Braff. Olivo told Santa Paula investigators that J. was “not always honest,” the report said. Olivo described Braff as a reliable employee who had strong relationships with parents, staff and students. She “seemed surprised that any of this could have occurred while she had been Principal at McKevett,” the district’s report said. Olivo did not respond to calls, emails and texts seeking comment.
During the district’s investigation, Braff acknowledged touching students on the knee. “He explained if someone is crying, he taps on the knee to say they are doing a good job to get the sad feelings out,” according to the district’s report to the state. “When asked to demonstrate, Mr. Braff showed a slap on his own knee.”
Nonetheless, the educator licensing agency appears not to have attempted to reconcile the very different accounts of Braff’s behavior. Informed of Olivo’s characterization of her complaint, J. and her mother told KQED and ProPublica that no one at the state agency had called to ask them about it or sought to verify any details, even though the district’s report to the state included J.’s contact information along with that of the other students.
“If a little girl comes up to you and says something, maybe you should not say that they’re a liar,” J. said.
“They should interview students themselves and not just rely on the school district. Do a legit investigation,” said J.’s mother, who did not know that the state had decided not to discipline Braff until the news outlets alerted her.
Fitzhugh, the spokesperson for the teacher credentialing agency, did not answer questions as to why J. was not interviewed or whether anyone else was. The case was assigned to a staffer whose job description did not include interviewing victims.
At least one other student who had reported Braff for touching her inappropriately also told KQED and ProPublica that no one from the state contacted her about her allegations.
A former agency investigator, who reviewed the district’s report to the state at the request of the news outlets, said she believed the students’ accusations because the district’s investigation described multiple children making similar claims. She also noted the contradictions in Braff’s responses. Cases involving allegations of inappropriately touching students should always be assigned to investigators trained to interview victims, she said.
“Any claim of sexual misconduct should go to somebody who’s going to be making phone calls,” said the investigator, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to protect her current job. “This man is grooming these children. There’s no other way to look at it to me. Their stories are credible.”
Per state law, the agency staff assigned to look into Braff’s case did not make recommendations about whether or how to discipline him. That recommendation is left up to a little-known group of volunteers who meet monthly at the agency’s Sacramento headquarters to weigh reports from state investigators, school districts, police and others. That volunteer panel sends its recommendations to the 19 commissioners of the credentialing body, most of whom are appointed by the governor.
If the panel does recommend discipline, the commissioners have the final say. However, if the panel decides that no punishment is warranted, the commissioners do not review that case.
Two former investigators at the state agency told the news organizations that the panel’s recommendations did not always align with the evidence they found. “Sometimes, as investigators, we’ll see the recommendations, and we’ll be like, ‘What the hell happened here?’” one former investigator said.
“I Was Consistently Shocked”
Over three days in December 2020, during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, members of the volunteer panel, known as the Committee of Credentials, dialed into their monthly phone meeting to address 198 cases of educators accused of misconduct. Among them was Braff, who by then was working in another school.
The volunteers included a retired law enforcement officer, a school board member, a school administrator, an education consultant and several teachers. They had been selected by the commissioners for two-year terms.
State regulations give the volunteer committee broad latitude when assessing allegations of teacher misconduct and recommending discipline to the commission. Unlike jurors in a criminal trial, who need to believe a case is proven beyond a reasonable doubt in order to convict, the committee only needs to find “probable cause” before recommending a reprimand, a far lower standard.
“It’s where a normal and reasonable person would feel that there’s a chance that this person did this,” said Steve Thorpe, the former law enforcement officer who served on the committee when Braff’s case was reviewed. “It’s a low threshold. You know it when you see it.” He declined to comment on Braff’s case.
The fact that Braff’s case was not forwarded to the commissioners, former committee members said, meant the majority of the seven-member panel did not see enough evidence in the district’s investigation and the state’s report to discipline Braff.
One former committee member, who spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of repercussions from the teacher licensing agency, said she tends to scrutinize district investigations because administrators can misrepresent the facts or ask children leading questions.
Another former committee member who served during the Braff case said that they were generally alarmed to hear some fellow members dismiss children as unreliable sources. The person, who declined to comment on Braff’s case, spoke on the condition of anonymity because they feared professional repercussions.
“I was consistently shocked,” they said. “To have committee members discuss serious allegations as, ‘Well, you know how girls can be. They say all kinds of things they don’t mean,’ is an unacceptable, antiquated point of view. What if we get this wrong? Who are we allowing in the classroom?”
By the time the committee decided against recommending punishment for Braff, he had already been working as a counselor at a different elementary school in Los Angeles for more than a year. (A former student at that charter school would tell police after Braff’s 2024 arrest that the counselor had touched the boy’s thigh near his groin when the two met in his office, according to a court transcript from his criminal case.)
In 2022, nearly two years after the state closed Braff’s case, a school administrator reported to the district that one of the girls who had accused Braff of abuse continued to suffer severe anxiety and could not be in rooms alone with men. Another had attempted suicide multiple times and spent a year in residential treatment, she wrote in an email obtained by KQED and ProPublica.
In his response, an assistant superintendent informed the administrator that the district had previously filed with the state to have Braff’s credential revoked or suspended but the agency chose not to do so. “At this point, I think pursing this matter legally is the best way to address these issues,” he wrote, referring to following up with Santa Paula police.
Santa Paula administrators did not respond to requests for comment.
Two Additional Cases
KQED and ProPublica identified at least two other educators who, like Braff, were reported by their school districts to the state for sexual misconduct but were allowed to keep teaching until they were criminally charged. Each would draw additional allegations of sexual abuse.
As in the Braff case, the volunteer committee in these two cases evaluated much of the same evidence as police, including complaints detailing students’ experiences. And in both cases, investigators with the teacher credentialing agency did not interview some victims.
In one, a Southern California school district shared with the state agency screenshots of messages that middle school math teacher Brashawn Washington had sent to his 11-year-old student, who he regularly contacted through the video game Fortnite. Those messages included a TikTok video showing another boy’s penis. (At his trial, Washington told jurors that he did not send the video to his student.)
The Romoland School District also shared with the state screenshots of Washington’s Google Hangouts chats asking the student if he worked out, calling him “guapo,” or handsome, and sending him kissing emojis.
The boy’s mother had provided the screenshots from her son’s phone to the school in May 2020, according to public records obtained from Romoland. The school district promptly alerted police and began its own investigation, filing a report to the teacher credentialing agency that summer, district records show.
The district included in its report the mother’s contact information, records show. But neither the student nor his mother were interviewed, the mother told KQED and ProPublica. Fitzhugh, the credentialing agency spokesperson, did not answer questions about how state investigators decided who, if anyone, to interview.
A Romoland administrator who said the district shared the screenshots with the state as part of its report did not answer questions about the state’s response.
Washington resigned during the school’s investigation and soon got hired at Pasadena High School starting in the fall of 2020. Washington, teaching virtually at first during the pandemic, continued messaging students over Fortnite despite district policy prohibiting personal contact with students. He had been teaching there for seven months when the volunteer committee recommended a 21-day suspension in March. (Commissioners did not approve the suspension until after school let out.)
State law did not require Washington to notify the Pasadena school district of the recommended suspension. Nor did the teacher licensing agency have to alert his new employer of any discipline if it did not know where he was employed.
Just as his suspension was set to begin in July 2021, Washington was arrested — and the state suspended his credentials indefinitely.
The next year, while out on bail, Washington sent a Pasadena High student images of himself having oral sex with another man, among other messages, according to court records. At Washington’s 2024 criminal trial, that student testified that the teacher had also asked him to share naked pictures of himself when he was 16. Washington told jurors that he did not know the student was a minor. He was sentenced to eight years and eight months in prison for multiple sex offenses, including “annoying or molesting” the Romoland student by sending him the video, as well as producing and possessing child sex abuse material related to minors who were not his students.
A spokesperson for Pasadena Unified did not respond to questions regarding Washington’s hiring or the state’s recommended discipline, but said in a written statement that the district conducts background checks during the hiring process.
Both Washington and his former attorney declined to comment.
A similar pattern unfolded with a San Francisco Bay Area elementary teacher, Matthew Shelton, who was convicted of sexually abusing four students last month.
Shelton had first been arrested in 2007 on charges of sexually abusing students in Napa Valley. Three third-graders had told police he touched their butts or crotches, or made them touch his penis during class.
Shelton was acquitted in that case, but the state’s licensing body did investigate the claims. At the time, Shelton told state investigators that the students had made up the allegations and that he passed a polygraph test, which he had obtained himself. Two of those former students told KQED and ProPublica that state investigators never interviewed them. The agency did not respond to questions about why the students were not interviewed.
In 2008, the licensing agency issued Shelton a confidential written warning, which was expunged after three years, according to trial testimony. That decision meant Shelton was able to keep teaching for the long term; he had already begun a new job in nearby Benicia.
Years later, in 2022, students began accusing Shelton of touching them inappropriately. The Benicia school district and a student’s parents reported him to the state commission in 2023. More students came forward and told police that Shelton had touched their crotch or butt over their clothing; one student said he made her touch his penis when she was in first grade during a school field trip.
Shelton resigned but quickly got a job at another school. As with the other cases, the new school said it had no information about the ongoing investigation. It also had no knowledge of his earlier warning, which had been expunged more than a decade earlier.
This time around, however, things unfolded differently: While the state did not alert the new school about any problems, a parent did. In September, just weeks into the school year, Shelton’s new employer learned from a Benicia parent about the active police investigation as well as the earlier issues in Napa.
Shelton was immediately put on leave. In February 2024, prosecutors charged him, requiring the state licensing agency to automatically suspend his credentials. Unlike in Napa, the agency revoked his license in July 2024 without waiting for a conviction.
Shelton did not respond to requests for comment, and his attorney declined to comment. He is due to be sentenced in December. Benicia Superintendent Chris Calabrese declined to comment on Shelton’s hiring.
There are significant repercussions when the state fails to take disciplinary action. For one thing, it means that other schools receive no indication of a problem. A red flag typically appears next to an educator’s name in a public database when they are punished by the Commission on Teacher Credentialing. But no such warning appears when a teacher is fired or forced to resign without state discipline, leaving their potential future employers in the dark. Nor would a confidential warning letter like the one Shelton received result in a red flag. California lawmakers have tried to address the gap, but their efforts failed.
Student victims, too, suffer long-lasting damage.
One of the students who accused Shelton in Napa told KQED and ProPublica that for years she wished she hadn’t reported him to anyone because she and her classmates were characterized as liars after “we poured out so much.”
“It could’ve been stopped with us, but it wasn’t,” she said. “They didn’t believe us.”
In Braff’s case, the Santa Paula Unified students who had accused him of abuse continued to struggle in school as their former counselor kept getting new jobs in education.
J. told KQED and ProPublica that for years she avoided acknowledging what Braff did to her. “I couldn’t place where all these emotions were coming from. I was blaming everything else except the actual problem,” J. said, referring to the abuse by Braff. “I didn’t want to live anymore.”
J., now a high school senior, has been homeschooled by her mother for almost three years. She said she still has nightmares in which Braff yells at her for “telling on him.”
And she has long faced doubts from others about her account of what happened to her in elementary school. A few years ago, she recalled, a former classmate told her: “Why would they let him go work somewhere else if he did that to you?”
