“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
The Trump administration has already tried to apply the immigration-related restrictions of the 1996 welfare reform law to other programs, most notably Head Start. Last year, a handful of federal agencies issued guidance saying they would classify the same group of immigrants as ineligible for Head Start enrollment, as well as for access to things like mental health services, domestic violence shelters, adult education programs, and federally funded health centers, deeming these things to also be “public benefits.” The effort has been permanently blocked by the courts nationwide, in part because the judge said the agencies violated procedure in issuing the guidance. But the judge left open the possibility of agencies’ issuing rules similar to what the IRS has proposed for tax credits in an attempt to do it in a more lawful way. “It would not be surprising,” D’Avanzo said, if the agencies try again through rulemaking.
In November, the administration did the same thing to a variety of programs at the Department of Housing and Urban Development, many of which fund affordable housing and homelessness services. The administration has also finalized a rule that prohibits entire families with mixed immigration status—where one or more family members don’t have a qualifying immigration status, even if others do—from living in federally subsidized housing, including both public housing and private apartments that receive rental assistance. Nearly 80,000 people could lose their rental assistance, including 52,500 citizens.
The administration has also finalized a harsh so-called “public charge” rule that will allow immigration officials to deny people’s green-card applications. It gives these officials wide latitude to take an immigrant’s use of nearly any public benefit into account and deem that it’s a negative factor in their quest for legal status. Most of the immigrants who go through that process are not undocumented and have a pathway toward lawful permanent status, but now they will face the choice between keeping benefits that allow them and their families to eat and survive or giving them up for a shot at a green card. Between 1.4 million and 4.1 million people could end up deciding to disenroll from Medicaid and CHIP, including their 1.7 million children who are US citizens. When the Trump administration issued a similar rule during his first term, which was later blocked by the courts, it still led 31 percent of adults in families with at least one family member who did not yet have a green card to forgo benefits. It’s “another way of scaring people who remain eligible for benefit programs from accessing them,” Gonzales said.
On top of all of that, early in Trump’s second administration he rescinded a Biden-era rule that allowed DACA recipients to get health coverage on the Affordable Care Act exchanges, instead blocking them from that option.
This is “a very coordinated effort to take away eligibility for benefit programs,” Gonzales noted. And that is meant to make life as uncomfortable as possible for immigrants in this country, with and without legal status. The Trump administration is using “every lever of the federal government for making immigrants feel unwelcome and unsafe living in the United States,” D’Avanzo said. “The overarching goal is to make it as hard as possible to be an immigrant in the United States.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Emily Carr and E.J. Hughes lead the way at Heffel's $10m autumn auctions
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Larry Humber
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Heffel Fine Art Auction House held its marquee autumn evening sales on Wednesday (18 November) in Toronto, attracting a packed house of bidders and spectators to the city’s swank Yorkville district and generating C$14.4m ($10m) in sales, works by Canadian masters taking top dollar. As things got underway, a Heffel representative noted that any US tariffs were “the responsibility of the buyer”, a reflection of these often-testy times.
“At a time of strong national pride, it is especially meaningful to see collectors celebrating Canada’s artistic achievements and our distinct national culture,” David Heffel, the auction house’s president, said at the end of the evening.
The back-to-back sales (41 lots of post-war and contemporary art followed by 47 works of Canadian, Impressionist and modern art) got off to a flying start when a watercolour by the Vancouver-born artist E.J. Hughes hammered for C$475,000 ($331,700)—nearly 12 times its high estimate. Titled Wharves at Chemainus (2000) and depicting the titular logging community on Vancouver Island, the painting is modest in size at 20in by 24in; with fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900).
Hughes had made waves at Heffel’s auctions last spring, when his Coastal Boats Near Sidney, BC realised a whoppingC$5.7m ($4.1m), including fees. Several more Hughes works were up for sale Wednesday night including two that significantly outperformer their estimates: The Hope River at Chilliwack, BC (1961), which took in C$253,250 ($176,800) with fees; and The Freighter “World Ares” at Crofton (1980), which hauled in C$229,250 ($160,000) including fees.
The second sale’s cover lot, Emily Carr’s luminous canvas Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure) (around 1912), brought C$1.3m ($922,000) including fees, comfortably within its estimate. It was the only seven-figure result of the night. Some of the proceeds from its sale will benefit the Audain Art Museum in Whistler, British Columbia, where it was shown in the context of a major traveling exhibition of Carr’s work in 2019-20.
A work on paper by the Carr, Music in the Trees (around 1935), topped its high estimate to achieve an impressive C$421,250 ($294,100) with fees. In all, six works by the Victoria-born artist were sold at Heffel on Wednesday night, fetching a combined, fee-inclusive total of C$2.5m ($1.7m).
A handful of works by Jean Paul Riopelle were on offer during the post-war and contemporary portion of the night, generating around C$1.3m ($907,800) in sales. His large-scale, wintry abstraction Herbeuse (1967),proved particularly appealing. Swift bidding pushed it to around double its high estimate. With fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900). It was shown in the Carnegie International the year Riopelle painted it, and later in Paris, where the Montréal-born artist, a master of the palette knife, spent decades. The work with the highest estimate in the post-war and contemporary sale, Riopelle’s Brumaire (1953), was expected to bring between C$1.5m and C$2m, but failed to sell.
Among the night’s other big-ticket items was Paul-Émile Borduas’s oil painting Empâtement (1957), from the artist’s black-and-white period—and punctuated with splashes of red. It realised C$841,250 with fees ($587,400), easily topping its high estimate of C$500,000. It had been acquired directly from the artist by London’s Arthur Tooth & Sons gallery in 1957 and, more recently, was in the collection of Québecois lyricist and songwriter Luc Plamondon.
J.E.H. MacDonald’s oil sketch Magnetawan River Rapids (1912), a preparatory work for a major canvas that is in the collection of the Art Gallery of Hamilton, achieved C$451,250 with fees ($315,000), tripling its high estimate of C$150,000.
Arguably the surprise of the night was Ivan Eyre (1935-2022), who was long a professor at the University of Manitoba and is best known for his prairie landscapes. His intensely autumnal acrylic-on-canvas landscape Golden Rod (1981) realised C$391,250 with fees ($273,200), more than tripling its high estimate of C$120,000 while setting a new auction record for the artist. That record was smashed in turn just one lot later, when Eyre’s Yellow Wood (around 1995) realised C$481,250 with fees ($336,000), five times its high estimate of C$90,000.
The beloved William Kurelek, who was raised on a farm near Winnipeg, also made a splash.His snowy landscape painting I Knew How the Clouds Arise (1969), which was featured on the cover of the catalogue for the artist’s first retrospective in 1970, realised C$313,250 including fees ($218,700), just over its high estimate, while the evocative campfire scene Wiener Roast on My Father’s Farm (1974), exceeded expectations to sell for C$265,250 with fees ($185,200).

https://citylimits.org/like-a-child-agai.title: ‘Like a Child Again’: How Late Night Soccer Gives Busy New Yorkers Time to Play
https://citylimits.org/like-a-child-agai.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/like-a-child-agai.text:
Share This Article
At five public parks, free soccer games continue until 2 a.m., giving workers, students and residents a place to exercise and build friendships. “You forget about life for a good hour or two,” one player said. “You kick a ball around with some of your buddies, feel like a child again.”
At Calvert Vaux Park in Brooklyn, the night doesn’t begin with a referee’s whistle. Players arrive in groups, laughing and passing the ball around as they wait for their games to begin.
For some, it’s an opportunity to exercise after a long day. For others, it’s a chance to reconnect with friends whose busy schedules rarely allow them to meet.
Juan Gomez, a 20-year-old Brooklyn resident, knows that feeling well.
Between school, work and Brazilian jiu jitsu, Gomez said he rarely has time for soccer before late evening. His classes and training can keep him occupied until around 9:30 p.m., leaving little room for another activity.
“A lot of friends that I really don’t have the time, or I don’t really have the chance to see, actually come out and play, and it’s kind of like a big reunion,” Gomez said.
That reunion is made possible by NYC Open Play, a city initiative that keeps soccer fields open until 2 a.m. at five public parks, one in each borough.
Introduced during the 2026 FIFA World Cup, the program returned on Oct. 5 after a summer pilot recorded 4,531 player check-ins across 696 field bookings. It offers free pickup games for adults from 10 p.m. to 2 a.m. every night through the end of the month (and will resume in the spring after a winter hiatus).
“The World Cup may be over, but our commitment to a city where every New Yorker can find joy for free continues,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said last month when announcing the program’s extension.
For Gomez, the program provides an affordable alternative to private soccer facilities. Without the late night games, he said he would consider playing at Soccer Roof in Sunset Park, Brooklyn, though the cost can make it less appealing.
“It’s not a bad place to play. It’s just sometimes you know, it’s kind of pricey,” he said.
A familiar field, a different time
For Angel Yax, a 24-year-old electrician from Brooklyn, Calvert Vaux Park is more than a convenient place to play.
“This park brings a lot of memories to me because when I was younger, I used to come here a lot with my boys and my friends, and we used to hang out all the time,” Yax said.
Now, as a working adult, he returns to the same field after spending much of his day on electrical projects. His work sometimes requires him to stay beyond his scheduled hours, leaving evenings as one of his few opportunities to exercise.
Tim Brown, a field host at Calvert Vaux Park who also worked with NYC Open Play during its summer pilot, said he has witnessed players forming relationships through the program.
“I’ve seen a lot of people make friends,” Brown said. “I’ve seen a lot of really cool connections come together in real time just from having the field lights on.”
Finding community after hours in Queens
Across the city at Astoria Park, players described a similar atmosphere, where soccer provides an escape from daily responsibilities and a chance to spend time with others.
Eric G., a 29-year-old Mexican-American resident of Astoria, balances work, college and fatherhood. He said late night soccer fits into a schedule that otherwise leaves him with little time for recreation.
But what keeps him coming back isn’t simply the opportunity to exercise. It’s also the moments he shares with other players.
Eric recalled watching a friend score a bicycle kick, known in Spanish as a chilena, during a game the previous night. “I’ll probably remember that moment maybe in 20 years from now,” he said.
For Anthony Vayeko, 25, those shared experiences have turned regular games into friendships.
Vayeko drives from Elmhurst, Queens, after finishing his workday, usually around 5 or 5:30 p.m. Once home, he showers, eats and prepares to head to Astoria.
He said the late night sessions provide an opportunity that can be difficult to find during the day, when public soccer fields are often crowded or reserved.
“Given how limited the permits are, you know, fields are packed in the mornings and the afternoons,” Vayeko said. “So these late night games definitely give us an opportunity to get some exercise in.”
Over time, the familiar faces at the park have become part of his routine.
“You learn their names, you see each other week in and week out,” he said. “Making friends outside of work, outside of school.”
Playing late can mean getting fewer hours of sleep and feeling sore the following morning. Still, Vayeko said the experience gives him a break from the responsibilities waiting for him outside the field.
“You forget about life for a good hour or two,” he said. “You kick a ball around with some of your buddies, feel like a child again.”
Where the late night games draw the biggest crowds
Calvert Vaux Park in Brooklyn and Astoria Park in Queens have emerged as the two busiest locations during NYC Open Play’s fall season, according to Tarek Pertew, co-founder and CEO of NYC Footy, which coordinates the games.
Between Oct. 5 and Oct. 24, Calvert Vaux recorded approximately 720 of the 1,800 player check-ins across all five parks. Astoria Park ranked second and had been the busiest during the program’s opening week.
Pertew said many participants are workers whose schedules make daytime recreation difficult, including restaurant and hospitality employees, delivery workers and people finishing evening shifts.
It also makes it easier for individuals to participate without organizing a team beforehand. “Most players show up on their own. That’s the point of the program,” Pertew said.
Field hosts organize pickup games as participants arrive, divide them into teams and rotate players so everyone gets time on the field.
For some participants, convenience is another factor. Pertew said transportation after 2 a.m. has not emerged as a significant concern among players so far, noting that many live near the participating parks and that the locations have overnight transit connections.
Still, the program currently operates at just one park in each borough, leaving questions about how easily residents farther from those locations can participate.
Five parks, five boroughs
NYC Open Play operates at five participating parks:
- Bronx: Soundview Park
- Brooklyn: Calvert Vaux Park
- Manhattan: Harlem River Park
- Queens: Astoria Park
- Staten Island: Fairview Park
Each location provides space for seven-on-seven pickup soccer between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m. The program is free for adults ages 18 and older. Players can participate individually or reserve a time slot with a team.
To join, participants must visit nycopenplay.com and complete an online waiver before arriving at the field. Individual players do not need to make a reservation. After signing the waiver, they can arrive at a participating park, check in with an onsite field host and join an available game.
Teams can reserve a time slot online, but every player must complete an individual waiver. Team captains or representatives are instructed to arrive at least 20 minutes before their reservation to check in.
NYC Footy coordinates the games onsite, while NYC Parks manages field permits and lighting. Parks Enforcement Patrol officers also maintain a presence at participating locations.
Keeping the connections going
The fall season is scheduled to end in November, with NYC Open Play returning from April through September 2027.
Pertew said NYC Footy is working with NYC Parks to explore additional opportunities for recreational field access across the city. One recent development is a pilot involving temporary lighting at Robert Moses Playground in Kips Bay, which Pertew said followed three years of advocacy for expanded playing hours.
For players at Calvert Vaux and Astoria Park, the program has already provided more than a place to exercise. It has become an opportunity to reconnect with childhood friends, meet new people and make room for recreation in otherwise demanding schedules.
At Astoria Park, field host Dewan Gurung said the program gives New Yorkers a chance to stay active after their daytime responsibilities.
“I think it’s a wonderful program. It needs to keep on running,” Gurung said.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/elon.title: Elon Musk Thinks You’re an Idiot
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/elon.author: Katherine Krueger
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/elon.text:
After the cresting of a blue wave in the midterm elections earlier this month, it’s officially about-face season, and Elon Musk is the latest major figure to predict which way the wind is blowing. During the New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday — which also featured appearances by the war profiteer Palmer Luckey, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, and Hailey Bieber, I guess — the chief of Tesla and SpaceX appeared by video to recast himself as a political moderate.
“I’m not MAGA,” Musk told columnist Andrew Ross Sorkin. “I’m not sure what MAGA means, but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that. I think there are positives and negatives in both parties.”
This “both parties” lip service is deeply revisionist recent history for the man who became the largest individual political donor in U.S. history in the midterms by spending almost $450 million on Republican candidates, particularly in Texas. Reflecting on that complete and utter waste of unfathomable resources, Musk said he feels “pretty foolish” in retrospect.
“Republicans were routed, and the money I spent — I feel pretty foolish having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” he said. “If I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.”
Musk went on to say the Democrats winning the governor and Senate races in Texas is no crisis for the world’s richest man, who infamously moved Tesla from California to Texas to dodge taxes, regulations, and woke. He also expressed his optimism that Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa would actually be “quite moderate” in office.
This reversal is a telling, but not novel, approach as the rats flee the sinking ship of Donald Trump’s presidency and the Make America Great Again ideology made in his image. Just one day after Republicans were shellacked on Election Day, Vice President JD Vance planted his 2028 flag by distancing himself from the administration he’s still part of to declare that the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran was “the reason we lost.” (Trump is reportedly not pleased with Vance throwing him under the bus.) Other Republicans who previously cheered the country into war have also picked up the scent, and now we seem to be left with a war that absolutely no one claims to have wanted in the first place, apparently save for Trump, who said the war was worth losing the midterms.
As with Vance, cozying up to Trump paid extraordinary dividends for Musk, until it became a political liability. Musk knew exactly what MAGA was when it was lavishly benefiting his bottom line, and infamously declared himself “not just MAGA, but dark MAGA” while tipping his custom black-on-black Make America Great Again hat at a Trump campaign rally.
As a special government employee in the Trump administration, the Tesla CEO launched the Department of Government Efficiency, better known by its epic meme acronym DOGE, which took a “slash and burn” approach to the federal government under the banners of increasing “efficiency” and eliminating “fraud and abuse.” Musk empowered a merry band of half-smart racists to lay off federal employees en masse; handed down devastating cuts to foreign aid, killing hundreds of thousands of people around the world; eliminated jobs that undergird the social promises that the things we eat and the medicines we take should be safe; and set scientific research back untold years.
Musk did all this as part of a project to extract even more wealth from the government — he and his businesses have benefited from a staggering $38 billion in public loans, subsidies, contracts, and tax credits over the years — with minimal oversight, and to reshape the work of a functioning federal government into a right wing political project.
The South African businessman, who became the world’s first trillionaire this summer, is deeply invested in eugenics-based causes like the pronatalist movement, which encourages the right kind of Americans to have more kids so “humanity” doesn’t die out. He has pushed the notion that “white genocide” is well underway. When he launched his AI chatbot’s competitor to Wikipedia’s “propaganda,” Grokipedia dubbed itself “MechaHitler,” praised Adolf Hitler, and listed which races it deemed “good.”
This is who Elon Musk is, and he hopes Americans have the memory of a fruit fly when it comes to everything he’s said and done in public. But like the public rejected his campaign to convince us he was cool, we can’t allow this cynical rebrand to proceed as planned.
Musk is an extremist staring down the barrel of years of courtrooms and congressional hearings who knows the Trumpism he once boosted is a spent political force. He’s experienced no dark night of the soul that’s caused him to meaningfully break from the president or from the far right wing, and no serious person should allow him to deploy that fantasy.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Voters Just Rejected Data Centers and Big Tech. Congress Is Moving Fast to Undermine Them.
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Basav Sen
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Voters Just Rejected Data Centers and Big Tech. Congress Is Moving Fast to Undermine Them.
A look at the forces driving the rush for “permitting reform” before a new Congress starts its term.
Despite a populist midterm wave driven by outrage over corruption and inequality, the lame-duck Senate has rushed to advance a bipartisan “permitting reform” bill perpetuating much of what voters just rejected. Instead of waiting for new members to be sworn in, the bill’s bipartisan backers have opted to skip even a committee hearing, rushing it straight to the floor.
Officially called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), the bill will deregulate environmental permitting laws to ease the construction of energy projects. Among other changes, it will restrict states from imposing more rigorous standards than the federal government under the Clean Water Act and make it easier for developers to sue the government if their permits are denied for environmental reasons.
This massive giveaway to the polluting fossil fuel and data center industries is bad policy. It will lock in new fossil fuel infrastructure at a time when we need to be cutting back. It will facilitate the buildout of data centers. And it will not reduce energy bills—and may even raise them instead.
Data centers are widely hated nationwide and across partisan lines. Local initiatives to put serious regulatory restrictions on data centers, or outright ban them, passed with wide margins almost everywhere they were on the ballot this November.
Indigenous tribes, environmental justice communities, immigration justice advocates, and historic preservationists are all part of the broad civil society coalition that has formed in opposition to this disastrous bill.
So why are elected officials pushing this bad, unpopular policy? Money is part of the answer, but not the whole thing.
Three of the four senators sponsoring the bill—Senator Shelley Moore Capito (R-WV), Mike Lee (R-UT), and Martin Heinrich (D-NM)—receive large campaign contributions from the oil and gas and utility industries. The fourth, Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), does not, but he and his wife have large holdings of stock in Big Tech companies behind the data center boom.
But there are factors at play as well. The idea that our environmental permitting system is failing to do its job by blocking or delaying too many projects appears to have become conventional wisdom among influential sections of the political, policy, and media elite.
But rigorous, peer-reviewed evidence does not support this conclusion. The available evidence suggests that the primary reasons for permitting delays are understaffing or communication errors, not stringent regulations. Instead, it appears that a kind of mass hysteria has gripped our elites.
Another factor behind the support for BAAJA is deference to corporate agendas. Being “pro-business” is a default ideological position for many US politicians. The American Petroleum Institute, the American Coal Council, and other polluting industry lobby groups support this bill.
So does the tech industry, in spite of strenuous efforts by some to deny it. BAAJA facilitates the buildout of fracked gas infrastructure that the tech industry needs to power its energy-hungry data centers. It also facilitates the buildout of data centers on federal lands, which triggers federal environmental review.
An industry-aligned consulting firm points to provisions in BAAJA that require data centers to pay for their share of the costs of increasing grid capacity. Similarly, an industry-aligned think tank is claiming that BAAJA will protect utility ratepayers from rising bills attributable to data centers.
But this is misleading. It doesn’t account for the fact that many data center developers are already bypassing grid connections altogether and building their own captive gas power plants. The purported ratepayer protection provisions in BAAJA incentivize more off-grid gas-powered generation for data centers, and the permitting deregulation provisions make it easier to build the ancillary gas infrastructure.
Even if they aren’t connected to the grid, these projects can still increase utility bills by driving up demand for natural gas—a potent greenhouse pollutant often obtained by fracking.
It’s noteworthy that the data center industry is not vociferously arguing against BAAJA provisions requiring data centers to pay for the grid updates they need. On the contrary, tech industry interests and business associations with tech industry membership have come out in favor of the bill, giving the game away.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
No self-interested, powerful corporation would push for legislation that actively harms their self-interest. The reasonable conclusion is that BAAJA is backed by—and serves the interests of—Big Tech.
Finally, there’s one more constituency pushing for BAAJA: the far right.
The bill faithfully implements the Project 2025 deregulation agenda developed by the Heritage Foundation. It is part of the far-right agenda to gut landmark environmental laws such as the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act.
Unsurprisingly, President Trump and his newly elevated extremist chief of staff Stephen Miller are both pushing for the bill’s passage. They obviously support making it easier for their Big Oil and Big Tech friends to ram through polluting pipelines, LNG export terminals, and data centers. They may also recognize that BAAJA will make it harder to block construction of the ICE concentration camps they want to build.
For Democrats to be supporting a bill that benefits Big Oil and Big Tech, silences impacted communities, expedites detention center construction, promotes the Project 2025 deregulatory agenda, and aligns with Trump’s goals—immediately after voters resoundingly rejected Trump and Big Tech in a landslide—is nothing short of a betrayal.
It’s now up to us to stop BAAJA from ever becoming law. If your senator was among the 73 who voted to advance the bill, please call them to voice your displeasure and urge them to oppose it in the next vote. And tell your representative in the House to pledge to oppose the bill, should it be passed by the Senate and go on to the House.

https://inthesetimes.com/article/boiling.title: Boiling Point: The road to war and Ukraine’s uncertain future
https://inthesetimes.com/article/boiling.author: John P. Ruehl
https://inthesetimes.com/article/boiling.text:
Boiling Point: The road to war and Ukraine’s uncertain future
In his new book, Boiling Point, journalist and historian Stephen Kinzer traces decades of US involvement in Ukraine, which helped start one of the deadliest and most consequential conflicts in the 21st century.
John P. Ruehl
This article was originally published by the Independent Media Institute on Nov. 02, 2026. It is shared here with permission.
The narrative surrounding the Ukraine war often marks its beginning on February 24, 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion. But the rivalries and political decisions that brought the two countries into conflict stretch back centuries. The start of the Cold War, meanwhile, was the beginning of sustained US efforts to further antagonize Ukraine’s relationship with Moscow.
In his new book, Boiling Point: How America Brought War to Ukraine, author Stephen Kinzer presents an account of how successive US administrations sought to cultivate Ukrainian nationalism and challenge Moscow, helping set the stage for conflict. Instead of viewing the invasion in isolation, Kinzer details Washington’s involvement over decades, from covert CIA operations in Soviet Ukraine during the early Cold War to Ukrainian independence and the post-Cold War tensions with Russia over NATO expansion, which all culminated in the outbreak of war.
Kinzer provides an extensive, detailed account of the history of US foreign policy in the region, without losing sight of the larger geopolitical forces at play. By challenging the conventional narrative of the war’s origins, Kinzer offers a deeply researched perspective largely absent from mainstream discussions.
Understanding the decades of geopolitical competition and political motives that preceded the war is essential to seeing why it began and where it might lead. Any eventual peace settlement will pose difficult questions about territory and security guarantees, as well as Ukraine’s reconstruction and place between Europe and Russia. The war will likely end without resolving Ukrainian and Russian divisions that, as Kinzer describes in his book, US policy helped deepen, leaving both countries and the wider region to contend with the consequences for years to come.
As a journalist, author, and historian, Kinzer has spent decades examining American foreign policy, interventionism, and the consequences of US involvement abroad. His work has appeared in The New York Times and other major publications, and he’s written several books exploring America’s role in shaping international affairs. I spoke with him about the history behind Boiling Point, the choices that might have prevented the war, and what he believes lies ahead for Ukraine.
John P. Ruehl: Your new book, Boiling Point, examines the history of US policy toward Ukraine and Russia, tracing Washington’s efforts since the end of World War II to cultivate Ukrainian nationalism and challenge Moscow’s influence. It looks at how those efforts contributed to the tensions that ultimately erupted into the ongoing war in Ukraine.
To start, could you tell us a little about the book, its central argument, and the history you believe readers need to understand to make sense of the war today?
Stephen Kinzer: One of the points that I hope people will take away from this book is that much of what we have been told about the Ukraine war is wrong. And, in particular, there’s one word we constantly hear about the Russian invasion, and it was that word, really, that set me off after about the 200th time I heard it, and that word, of course, is unprovoked. We always read about that not just the February invasion, or the Russian invasion, or the military invasion, but the unprovoked invasion. Now, you can say a lot of things about this invasion, for example, that it was illegal under international law, just like many American operations have been, but it was definitely not unprovoked. How do I justify that statement? That’s my book.
The book traces 75 years of uninterrupted American plans to turn Ukraine into a battering ram against Russia. This began with the dropping of armed commandos into Ukraine back in the late 1940s, and it continued through a whole series of covert actions leading up to Ukrainian independence in 1991; then the project went into overdrive. [The US] spent huge amounts of money promoting anti-government groups in Ukraine and groups that would support the idea of confrontation with Russia.
That finally exploded. You might make an argument that we did the right thing to provoke Russia and to promote all this nationalist feeling in Ukraine. And I’m okay with that. But before you make any judgment on the justice or nature of the Ukraine war, you should know what happened before.
If you look at a snapshot of… February 24, 2022, you will see what happened. Russia invaded a peaceful country, Ukraine. But that picture should really be seen as just one frame in a very long movie that unfolded over 75 years. My book is an attempt to show you the real background of the Ukraine war.
JPR: Do you think Washington still has a bipartisan commitment to supporting Ukraine, or has it largely achieved what it set out to accomplish and now is unsure about how to proceed, amid the Trump administration’s efforts to negotiate peace?
SK: I think most people in Washington still think the Ukraine war is a great idea. It comes out of a deep-seated hatred for Russia, a belief that Russian expansion or anything good for Russia is bad for the world. I actually think that many Americans consider this war a success. The reason is, we’ve killed a lot of Russians. The fact that tens of thousands of Ukrainians have been killed and their country has been devastated doesn’t really register in Washington.
Most of the people in Washington who are most eagerly promoting this war can hardly find Ukraine on a map. They are not interested in Ukraine. All they’re interested in is Russia. … The result is that Ukraine has gotten wrecked, but for Americans, and I think for some Europeans as well, it seems like a win because it has wounded Russia.
JPR: You write about the CIA’s espionage and covert operations in Soviet territory within Ukraine’s modern borders, particularly during the early Cold War, which created massive tensions. The NATO expansion after the Cold War has been another major source of tension with Russia.
Now, NATO appears less central to US policy under Trump. If NATO’s role diminishes, what other institutions or government agencies might take the lead in sustaining pressure on Russia?
SK: The whole NATO argument is really one of the saddest pieces of this whole story. If Joe Biden had simply stood up and said five words: “Ukraine will not join NATO,” the war would have been avoided. He refused to say that. But the worst part of it is that in private, American leaders all admitted that Ukraine was never gonna join NATO; it’s not nearly ready, and there were all kinds of problems that would take decades [to resolve]. But nobody wanted to say this in public because it would seem like we were responding to Russia, we were intimidated by Russia, and we were doing what Russia wanted. The fear of seeming to grant any credibility to Russia was so great that we refused to do that.
There were many off-ramps for this war, and simply declaring that NATO would not accept Ukraine as a member would have stopped it. What you really need from Ukraine is essentially a peace accord, which was hammered out in Istanbul a month after the war began. Henry Kissinger used to say the same thing — Ukraine needs to be a bridge between east and west. It shouldn’t be a territory that the two sides fight over.
A great model would be Austria. After World War II, to ensure the withdrawal of occupying forces, Austria signed a treaty and inserted, in its constitution, a pledge that it would never join a military alliance and would never have foreign troops on its soil. That has worked great. That should be a model for Ukraine, but Americans don’t like that because it doesn’t smell like victory.
JPR: You dedicate the book to the Ukrainian people and argue that they didn’t really understand the consequences of the policies pursued by the United States and NATO toward Russia.
How do you respond to those who would argue that opposing the United States and NATO policy toward Ukraine amounts to supporting Russian aggression? Beyond reading your book, what evidence or arguments do you find most persuasive in that view, and what convinces people to reconsider the United States’ and the West’s role in the conflict?
SK: I don’t think Russia is seeking to capture Ukraine, much less further territories, but Russia has a fear that is understandable, and that is, they don’t want a nuclear-armed military alliance that they are not a member of right on their border. I pose this analogy: suppose China decided with Mexico that it would open a military base in Veracruz, or suppose Russia would open an air base in Quebec. Would the United States say, “Well, every country has a right to choose its own security partners, so I guess there’s nothing we could do about it.” Of course, we wouldn’t do that. We would bomb those bases. We would never tolerate that. So we’re now expecting Russia to accept something we would never accept.
There is room for negotiation, but only if the United States and the Europeans, who are now really taking on the extreme burden of the war, accept that they have to recognize Russia’s security interests. This is a horrific idea in some European capitals. But in the end, the only way there is ever going to be peace and stability in Europe is if there is a security architecture that takes into account the security interests of all countries, including Russia.
JPR: You discuss Kosovo and the Western effort to separate it from Serbia. Was there ever a realistic possibility of peacefully accommodating separatist sentiment in eastern and southeastern Ukraine after the 2013 – 2014 Maidan Revolution? Or were Ukrainian nationalist forces, Western interests, and Russian influence too deeply entrenched? And what alternative policies might have prevented the current conflict after the end of the Cold War?
SK: The most important off-ramp we had was at the beginning of the post-Cold War period, so around 1990 and the early 90s. Our president then, George H.W. Bush, fully understood this, and he promised Mikhail Gorbachev that he would not promote any eastward expansion of NATO. Soon, of course, Bush was gone; Clinton came in. There was a completely different approach. But there is a perfectly reasonable argument for a neutral Ukraine.
And I’ll tell you, one of the reasons that I got so passionate about this project, I realized later on, well, part of my experience way back in the 1980s, I was the reporter covering the Contra War in Nicaragua. And one thing I took away from that experience is that the war had nothing to do with Nicaragua. It was a conflict between two great powers that chose that poor country as the stage on which they fought. And, of course, [most of] the dead people were just the locals.
The same thing is happening in Ukraine. This war is not about Ukraine. It’s Ukraine that is suffering, and the big powers are holding its fate in their hands. Now, you talk about obstacles to peace. You’re absolutely right about the difference between eastern Ukraine and western Ukraine. Really, they are two countries that got stuck inside the same border by accidents of history. And one of the real sticking points, one of the real difficulties in reaching some kind of a national accord, is that for non-Russian-speaking Ukrainians, those in the western part of Ukraine, being anti-Russian, hating Russia, is a fundamental part of the national patriotic Ukrainian identity. And as long as there are millions of Russians in the country, these other Ukrainians feel they are a fifth column; they’re always going to be promoting enemy interests.
So, any Ukrainian leader who signs a peace treaty runs an immense danger, not only from history, but also from far-right militias that are going to attack them. The cleavage between the two parts of the country is so deep that it’s hard to imagine how they would ever come together, at least without some kind of federalized structure, if not by moving those eastern provinces directly under Russian control.
JPR: Could Ukraine’s postwar frontline resemble the situation between Russia and Georgia after their 2008 war, with an unstable standoff and Russia gradually altering the boundaries? Or do you expect a different outcome in Ukraine?
SK: I think the Russians won’t stop until they’ve consolidated their power over [the] four eastern provinces that they claim. After that, I do think there is a possibility that it could settle into a kind of frozen conflict. That would avoid forcing some Ukrainians to sign an agreement under which part of their territory is surrendered, but it could also end combat. It’s not an ideal solution. I would compare it to what’s happening in Korea. But at least that might be one way to end the conflict without putting people on either side in an untenable position.
JPR: What do you see as Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s political future after the war? Wartime leaders can struggle to retain public support in peacetime. Or do you think he will remain a central figure in Ukrainian politics?
SK: Zelenskyy is really an odd figure who emerged; I have a whole section in my book about how he did this. He was a TV personality. He was a fictional character who led a political party that was against corruption. And then this oligarch who owned the TV station said to him, “You know, we’re going to make that fake party. We’re gonna make it into a real party, and I’m gonna make you run for president.” So, he was about the most unlikely character you could imagine for that job.
And I don’t think he’s gonna wind up being a major figure in the future of Ukraine. Poor Zelenskyy, I think, is in a really difficult position now. Here’s what I think is going through his mind: “So the Americans are yelling at me because I didn’t make a deal. I didn’t accept a compromise with Russia. But when I tried to make a compromise with Russia, just a month after the war started, they stopped me! They told me not to do it. So now I’m being punished for doing what you told me to do.” And I can understand and sympathize with Zelenskyy’s frustration.
JPR: There have been reports of Ukrainian involvement in training militants in Mali against Russian interests, while Ukraine has also continued striking Russian oil infrastructure, despite pressure from Washington to stop. And Ukraine now has a large battle-tested military, even if the country itself is severely weakened. What consequences could this have for Europe and the United States, particularly if the Ukrainians come to feel that the West and the United States have betrayed them?
SK: The situation you’re describing is somewhat analogous to what’s happening in the Middle East; a war that was supposed to be localized has metastasized and is turning up in different incarnations in different places, even far from the nations that were supposed to be the target.
So, I do think we’re gonna wind up with a highly militarized Ukraine. The worst part is that many of the strongest military units are not the actual regular army, but are far-right militias, which proudly use Nazi insignia and proclaim their loyalty to Ukrainians who fought alongside the Nazis and helped participate in the Holocaust. That is going to be a project that Europe’s going to have to deal with.
But I don’t even think Europe is thinking about a postwar yet. I feel like Europe is in a complete delusion. They have the idea that if we just keep pouring weapons into Ukraine and pouring money into Ukraine, somehow the tide will turn. Meanwhile, inside those European countries, there’s tremendous political turmoil. Much of it is based on frustration that the government isn’t using its money to provide schools and other services people want. One reason is that so much money is going to Ukraine.
So, I think you might see resentment [toward] Ukraine growing, and depending on the way the war finally ends or freezes, people will become generally sympathetic to Ukraine, or very hostile to Ukraine. It’s another example of how wars like this set in motion processes that can’t be stopped and can affect international relations for decades to come. It’s really an object lesson in how you should stop and think about long-term consequences before launching foreign interventions.
JPR: What will or what can the EU do if Washington pulls away from Ukraine?
SK: The EU then has two choices. One is to continue its policy, which is ever more war, ever more arms for Ukraine, ever more money, or Ukraine could go back to the agreement that was tentatively reached a month after the war began and accept Ukrainian neutrality. This would be very wise for Europe. It’s foolish for the United States to be promoting war in Ukraine; it’s even more foolish for the Europeans. They are going to face real crossroads, and I fear the rise of radical political parties in Europe will create an even more difficult situation.
So that’s another reason I dedicated Boiling Point to the people of Ukraine; it’s my sympathy for them as victims of a great-power rivalry they don’t want anything to do with.
JPR: What was one of the biggest revelations you had while writing and researching for the book?
SK: The biggest revelation, by far, was my realization of how completely American foreign policy toward Russia and Eastern Europe has been shaped by officials with family backgrounds in the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe. We had [former] Secretary of State Madeleine Albright. We had [former] National Security Adviser Zbigniew Brzezinski. We had a [former] ambassador to NATO, Victoria Nuland. There’s a whole list of these [names] in my book.
So, what you had was a group of children and grandchildren of emigres from Eastern Europe and what became the Soviet Union. These people grew up with bitter, anti-Russian hatred, and that’s quite understandable, frankly, when you look at the history of what Russia has done to those countries. But when those grandchildren and children of emigres decided they wanted to affect American politics and foreign policy, they found themselves unwelcome in the Republican Party, which was then not interested in ideological crusades. So, they became Democrats. And all these people filled the Biden administration, the Obama administration, and the Clinton administration. It’s the only example in the entire history of American foreign policy where all major policies toward one part of the world were shaped by people with family background in that region. They turned the United States into the instrument of their vengeance against Russia, and thereby greatly distorted American foreign policy.
Those diplomats were quite capable. They should have been made ambassador to Brazil, or assistant secretary of state for Asia or something like that. But to place them in these positions where they were able to wreak havoc against Russia in accordance with the long instincts that had been bred into them from childhood is unique, and it greatly distorted American foreign policy. That was really the greatest single revelation I had.
JPR: And that’s a dynamic we really don’t see regarding China and Taiwan.
SK: Absolutely. You don’t see Chinese, let’s say, the children of Chinese immigrants, or the grandchildren, trying to get into the State Department so they can shape the US policy toward China. That would be the equivalent, but that has never happened in US policy toward any other part of the world, and it’s the piece of the story that I don’t think has been told, and I hope it’s one of the pieces of Boiling Point that turns out to be a major revelation and point of discussion.
JPR: With much of Ukraine’s industrial base, energy infrastructure, and population severely diminished by the war and emigration, what realistic prospects does the country have for rebuilding?
SK: Rebuilding prospects are very difficult to imagine. First of all, you have to have an end to active fighting. Now, in the Russian-speaking regions, there’s been a tremendous amount of destruction. But if you look at what Russia did in Chechnya, where the capital city essentially was completely destroyed, you get the idea that they do know how to rebuild things, because Grozny is now a thriving city. What about the rest of Ukraine, the western part? I think Ukrainians would be very justified in turning to the Europeans and saying, “You’re the ones who pushed us into this war; how about helping us resolve some of the damage?”
JPR: Finally, is this the end of NATO expansion, or is there room in the Balkans for more?
SK: I don’t believe there’s gonna be any expansion of NATO anytime soon. But what I would really like is that since everybody in Washington realizes this, they would say it. Instead, they try to keep it vague to pressure Russia. Announcing that would be a way to lower global tensions, but in some circles that is seen as a concession to Russia, and maintaining tensions is actually thought to be in our interest. I don’t believe that’s true, and until that mindset fades, it’s difficult to see a prosperous future for Ukraine.
John P. Ruehl is an Australian-American journalist living in Washington, DC, and a world affairs correspondent for the Independent Media Institute. He is a contributor to several foreign affairs publications, and his book, Budget Superpower: How Russia Challenges the West With an Economy Smaller Than Texas’, was published in December 2022. Follow him on X @john_ruehl.

https://citylimits.org/opinion-its-time-.title: Opinion: It’s Time for Stricter Enforcement of Unpaid Building Fines
https://citylimits.org/opinion-its-time-.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/opinion-its-time-.text:
Share This Article
“When he was running for mayor, Mr. Mamdani said he’d work on collecting fines the city was owed as part of finding funding for policy proposals like universal childcare. The time is here.”
Many times over many years, I have pointed out—to mayors, the City Council, state elected officials, at Charter Commission and city agency hearings, community board and Civic Association meetings, even in letters to editors—that there are hundreds of millions in unpaid Department of Buildings and Environmental Control Board (DOB/ECB) fines. I found this out via freedom of information requests to the City’s Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings (OATH) several years ago. Nothing has been done.
With the recent, tragic building collapse on Brooklyn’s major Flatbush Avenue attracting so much attention, perhaps it’s finally time to wake up.
In fact, there is this clause in NYC’s Charter chapter 45A, re. “Environmental Control Board” section 1049-a(d) (1)(i): “A judgment entered pursuant to this paragraph shall remain in full force and effect for eight years.” I have argued for its repeal—finding that many officials are unaware of it.
I have not been able to find out exactly when, how and why this sentence came to be in the City Charter. Keep in mind that real estate developers are prime donors to campaigns for candidates running for city and state office. Indeed, imagine a candidate for, say City Council, asking developers for campaign contributions one day and the next introducing a bill to collect on their long-overdue violations?
If you check the city’s Buildings Information Systems site and enter the address of a building with a history of violations, you are bound to come across the phase “written off” for fines levied more than eight years ago, even where a dangerous condition existed.
While recognizing that real estate development is an important sector, and does contribute to the economy in many ways, I submit that it should not hold so much influence that it is able to control elected officials in order to get whatever it wants—or ignore “Stop Work Orders” at construction sites.
While more affordable housing clearly is needed, I have seen Brooklyn neighborhoods become unaffordable with the creation of high-end condos and “starter castles” (a term borrowed from former City Councilman Tony Avella when he visited us).
Whether it’s former Mayors Bill de Blasio’s Mandatory Inclusionary Housing (MIH) and Zoning for Quality and Affordability (ZQA) or Eric Adams’ “City of Yes” initiatives, they actually are developer dreams. Ask homeowners and you’d learn that the initiatives do nothing for preserving the character and safety of neighborhoods.
So, now my question: will the attention to and investigation of this Flatbush building collapse force Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the City Council, along with NY State Assembly and Senate oversight committees, to finally push the City’s Department of Finance to stop making excuses and aggressively pursue owed fines, and the Department of Buildings to assure that accompanying violations are fully addressed?
Furthermore, besides—very importantly—trying to prevent more avoidable tragedies like this building collapse, imagine adding nearly hundreds of millions to the city’s budget?
After all, when he was running for mayor, Mr. Mamdani said he’d work on collecting fines the city was owed as part of finding funding for policy proposals like universal childcare. The time is here.
Ed Jaworski is president of the Madison-Marine-Homecrest Civic Association and co-founder of the Brooklyn Neighborhood Congress.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/iowa.title: Just Rinse It Off, Army Says Before Blowing Up Five Tons of Lead Compound
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/iowa.author: Austin Campbell
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/19/iowa.text:
When the U.S. Army blows up nearly five tons of unstable lead azide in southeastern Iowa on Friday, blanketing communities in lead-containing particles up to 100 miles away, it has a simple solution for concerned Iowans: Just rinse it off.
“The good thing is, if people have concerns about it being on their property, all they have to do is hose that off, and it’s gone,” Army spokesperson Justine Barati told Radio Iowa earlier this week.
This won’t be sufficient to mitigate the harm of the toxic plume the Army plans to release, environmental health experts based in Iowa told The Intercept. And, while the Army’s publicly released dispersion modeling shows that airborne lead particles could travel northeast from the detonation site near Burlington, Iowa, as far as Maquoketa, the experts found the Army’s modeling incomplete.
Burlington is in southeastern Iowa, just west of the Mississippi River and the Illinois border. Because the Army’s plume modeling is a prediction based on anticipated weather conditions, changes in wind speed or direction could carry lead-containing particles into neighboring Illinois, even if the published projection does not show that path.
“They put out this plume model, which is basically a colored blob, so to speak, on a map,” said Patrick O’Shaughnessy, a professor of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa. “What they didn’t show was the projected or estimated concentration of settled dust within that plume.”
That settled dust will come from lead azide, a highly sensitive explosive commonly used in detonators. The Army has been storing the material at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in a water-and-ethanol solution intended to keep it stable, but dangerous crystals formed during storage, according to an Army environmental assessment The Intercept found using the military’s Digital Visual Information Distribution System. Army officials determined that the resulting instability made the material too hazardous to move or transport, leaving an in-place detonation as their best option for disposal.
Now, the Army is warning residents and workers within the areas identified on its projected airborne exposure map to remain indoors, close windows and doors, and adjust air conditioning systems to prevent outside air from entering their homes “until the plume passes.” Children and pregnant individuals are among those specifically warned to avoid outdoor exposure.
O’Shaughnessy said the airborne plume could dissipate within hours, potentially ending the immediate inhalation hazard by Friday evening. But residents may not know how long they need to take precautions.
“Should I stay indoors all weekend? You know, the public doesn’t know, and no fault of theirs,” he said.
The Army environmental assessment shows that military officials considered several alternatives to Friday’s detonation, including chemically neutralizing the explosives or transporting them to an existing demolition facility, both of which were rejected as too dangerous. The Army also warned that leaving the explosives in storage could leave them to blow up by accident — and indefinitely disrupt the installation’s ability to make new ammunition.
The assessment does not establish how long the explosives had been stored, whether their deterioration was detected before March, or whether earlier intervention could have prevented them from becoming too dangerous to handle.
The Environmental Protection Agency, which issued an emergency permit authorizing the detonation, said the risk of an accidental explosion presented an “imminent and substantial threat to human health and the environment.”
“The Army, which has unparalleled expertise in matters concerning explosives safety, concluded that this material cannot safely be handled or moved and therefore, cannot be treated by any method other than in-place detonation,” an EPA spokesperson told The Intercept.
The permit requires the Army to notify potentially affected communities, conduct environmental sampling before and after the detonation, clean up contaminated areas, and report its findings to the EPA. At the University of Iowa, which is 60 miles away and not in the predicted pathway, researchers hadn’t gotten details about how that monitoring would be conducted, O’Shaughnessy said.
“We don’t know where it’s going to be conducted. We don’t know what instrumentation they’re going to use or how they’re going to report the information,” he said. Researchers there are preparing to assess the consequences independently, including by measuring potential lead contamination and conducting their own plume modeling.
The Army’s environmental assessment also acknowledges that contaminants from the detonation could enter waterways through stormwater runoff or seep into groundwater.
It’s clear, said Peter S. Thorne, professor emeritus of occupational and environmental health at the University of Iowa, that washing away lead dust would not eliminate the contamination.
“Hosing lead dust off of cars and other surfaces will indeed move it to the soil or into surface water,” he told The Intercept. “This could lead to human and animal exposure beyond inhalation of the generated lead dust plume.”
Asked what scientific evidence supported the advice to hose lead dust off residential property, the Army did not provide any studies or technical analysis. Instead, it said the EPA had provided cleanup guidelines as a condition of the emergency permit.
In an environmental handout prepared for an Oct. 15 community open house, the Army acknowledged that the detonation could damage nearby homes and contaminate surrounding property. The military said it would conduct environmental sampling on private property with homeowners’ permission and clean up lead contamination exceeding regulatory thresholds. It also acknowledged that cleanup operations could temporarily disrupt agricultural leases.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has found that no safe blood lead level in children has been identified. Even low levels of exposure can harm children’s brain development and ability to learn.
Asked what concentrations of airborne lead it expected in surrounding communities, the Army did not provide specific projections. Instead, it pointed to naturally occurring lead in soil and contamination associated with leaded gasoline, lead-based paint, and hazardous waste sites. Asked about plans to monitor potential long-term health effects, Barati, the Army spokesperson, said only: “We do not anticipate long-term health impacts.”
O’Shaughnessy recommended testing surfaces in communities affected by the plume, including playground equipment, every three or four days for approximately a month to determine whether lead contamination persists after airborne particles have settled. “You can’t just sugarcoat this,” he said.
The Army’s assurances come against a documented history of lead contamination at military installations, including cases in which officials failed to address known hazards.
A 2018 Reuters investigation found that children living in Army housing had been exposed to hazardous lead paint, with military medical records documenting more than 1,000 elevated blood lead tests among young children processed by one Army medical center between 2011 and 2016. The investigation also found failures to report some test results to state health authorities.
Additionally, a 2024 investigation by The Intercept found that the Army National Guard had failed to adequately remediate lead contamination at armories used by soldiers and civilians, including children. A 2020 Army audit obtained by The Intercept found that 73 of 83 indoor firing ranges examined in New Jersey, North Carolina, and Ohio had not undergone thorough remediation or the required evaluations of lead hazards.
At New Jersey armories, officials had used high-pressure washing to remove lead contamination, despite a 2020 Army audit warning that the method was prohibited because it could embed lead throughout facilities and generate hazardous waste.
Asked whether earlier intervention could have prevented the explosives from deteriorating to the point that detonation became the safest available option, the Army did not answer directly. Instead, it referred The Intercept to previously published information about the operation.
“It strikes me that this is a case of neglect leading to only bad choices available to avoid a catastrophe,” Thorne said.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Chris Lehmann
