https://inthesetimes.com/article/the-sup.title: The Superintelligence Racket
https://inthesetimes.com/article/the-sup.author: Alberto Toscano
https://inthesetimes.com/article/the-sup.text:
The Superintelligence Racket
In the face of rising opposition to data centers, the AI industry is holding us for ransom.
Alberto Toscano
In the largest initial public offering (IPO) in history, Anthropic, the company behind the AI chatbot Claude, opened on the Nasdaq on Nov. 19 at a valuation of about $2 trillion.
Its 335-page prospectus, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on Oct. 26, devotes 93 pages to risk factors and declares that AI systems could “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” especially if “misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy.”
Sociologist Charles Tilly once defined a racketeer as someone who “produces a danger and, at a price, the shield against it.” By that definition, the AI industry is operating like a racket. And we are being asked to accept U.S. imperialism as the shield against its dangers.
On the face of it, the AI industry’s warnings of possible human extinction seem a bizarre departure from how companies should do marketing. And yet it makes sense.
The industry holds populations, governments and even markets hostage, while warning that failure to risk everything for the “superintelligence” project — even geopolitical stability — could spell “p(doom)” for us all.
After former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned and made the media rounds, Anthropic alignment science lead Evan Hubinger personally put the odds of AI triggering human extinction within a decade at greater than 10%. The company’s public filing does not refute that. On the contrary, estimating the odds of an irreversible, AI-driven cataclysm — “p(doom)” in industry shorthand — is so routine that the depiction of Coxon as a whistleblower is hard to sell.
Scratch under the surface of the apocalyptic tone frequently used when discussing AI, and you will find eminently economic and political concerns, such as speculation on tech stocks and big spending on data centers and semiconductor chips. These have been the primary drivers of U.S. economic growth and a buoyant stock market.
Advanced AI models, like those built by Anthropic and OpenAI, require colossal cloud-computing infrastructure, and that buildout has put the companies driving it at the core of today’s capitalist economy. They include both “hyperscalers,” such as Amazon, Alphabet (Google), Meta (Facebook) and Microsoft and chip designers and producers, like Nvidia, TSMC and Broadcom. Speculation about AI’s impact on the future of humanity is now inextricable from their bottom lines. Their warnings of catastrophe and their pursuit of profit have become one and the same enterprise. This is the superintelligence racket. 
In the wake of Coxon’s revelations of the end, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called on the industry to “pace the frontier.” Critics quickly labeled this a ploy to promote “regulatory capture” — rules shaped to favor the firms already on top — using the specter of catastrophic risk to dig a “moat” against competitors.
As the journalist Steve Howell put it, Amodei’s strategy was “to form a cartel with the other major players so that they work at the same pace, while disadvantaging emerging rivals through regulation.”
Big Tech companies, while competitors in some respects (the hyperscalers have rival AI arms), are profoundly interlocked — from their financial structures to their supply chains to the political strategies they pursue in Washington. Anthropic’s IPO makes this plain.
Amazon, Google and Microsoft are at once Anthropic’s investors, customers, cloud providers, distributors and competitors, according to its filing. Anthropic has committed to pay Google at least $121.3 billion, Amazon $110 billion and Microsoft $44.9 billion for computing power through the mid-2030s. It carries about $161.2 billion in equipment leases tied to the chip designer Broadcom.
The IPO, meanwhile, is a windfall for the same giants: Google’s $33 billion investment is now worth more than $140 billion, and Amazon’s $18 billion in early financing has ballooned to more than $250 billion, the New York Times reported. The company has also turned to special purpose vehicles (financial devices that played a key role in the 2008 financial crisis) to keep “massive hardware deployments entirely off its corporate balance sheet,” as Yahoo Finance previously reported.
In the frenzy to build the data centers required to run ever more demanding AI models, the companies that control the hardware — that design and fabricate the chips, build and manage the data centers — hold an important advantage. Industry commentators have called them “compute landlords,” stressing their outsize power over the sector.
Chip designer Nvidia sits high on the list of global companies ranked by market capitalization and has accordingly been described as the AI boom’s “bank.” (Nvidia’s stock fell sharply after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO amid a scandal over his affair with an executive of a Singapore-based company, who U.S. officials reportedly believe was passing information to China. But it remains the second most highly valued company after Apple.)
Those who discern the lineaments of a bubble point to Nvidia’s “circular financing.” Typically, Nvidia has invested billions in data infrastructure built by companies like OpenAI, and, in turn, these companies have populated their servers with Nvidia chips. But this tells us little or nothing about the customer demand or productivity gains that would justify the trillion-dollar valuations of AI companies.
Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI has demonstrated an ability to reliably turn a profit. Yet the perceived centrality of AI to U.S. economic dominance and military primacy has been touted by the White House. As President Donald Trump wrote in September:
In the wake of Coxon’s apocalyptic declarations, Trump dismissed demands to regulate AI — a product subject to fewer rules than milk or washing machines, according to the president of Microsoft. Instead, he summoned Big Tech executives, including Amodei, Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Huang and OpenAI president Greg Brockman, to a White House lunch to sign a “constitution” aimed at coordinating federal policy and corporate strategy, and a few days later announced the creation of a “Superintelligence Task Force” to help ensure U.S. leadership in AI development. Trump then proceeded to promote AI’s new designation of superintelligence, or “SI”: From now on, use of the term artificial intelligence would be treasonous, as he implied on Truth Social: 
Trump’s semantic preference likely owes less to the philosopher Nick Bostrom, whose book Superintelligence helped shape the industry’s doom talk, than to the idea that saying AI “makes it sound fake.”
For Trump and his entourage, AI is crucial to U.S. dominance. (“WHOEVER WINS AI, WINS!” Trump declared on Truth Social.)
This dream of unchecked primacy is shared even by Big Tech companies outside of MAGA’s far-right inner circle. As the diplomat and historian Julian Gewirtz noted, Amodei believes that, in Gewirtz’s words, “getting ahead now could allow the U.S. to prevent anyone from ever catching up.”
Amodei calls this an “eternal 1991”: the West’s moment of triumph after the Cold War prolonged indefinitely by AI. This is the Faustian bargain tech oligarchs champion. The possibility of human extinction must be countenanced. After all, eternal domination is at hand.
The AI oligopoly is animated by its pact with unending U.S. global dominance. This pact has even led some oligarchs, like Palantir CEO Alex Karp, to envisage a “nationalization” of the industry, in which the federal state assumes the technology’s “unlimited risks.”
The industry’s turn to the state, even to fantasies of state capitalism, is entirely unsurprising. How could this industry — which feeds on gargantuan investments in fixed capital infrastructure and skyrocketing quantities of energy and water — not turn to the concentrated power of the state as its ultimate guarantor?
As tech analyst Paris Marx has observed, the AI industry is “incentivized to make most clients’ business more computationally intensive to guarantee revenue.” It is this imperative that makes it such a threat to local communities and collective survival. As OpenAI CEO Sam Altman fantasized: “I do guess that a lot of the world gets covered in data centers over time.”
As Anthropic’s SEC prospectus makes clear, it is not the obliteration of mankind that keeps AI moguls up at night. That would be the questionable viability of their business model, which is predicated on lack of regulation and suppression of dissent. In other words, it is not human, but corporate extinction that they fear.
More so than firms with more diverse revenue streams, Anthropic is vulnerable to regulatory changes — especially when it comes to its infrastructure. As the prospectus notes, the company’s “collective data center infrastructure is currently concentrated primarily in the United States, which exposes us to risks associated with regional regulatory changes, power grid constraints or failures, disruptions to network connectivity between facilities, natural disasters, physical attacks — including those motivated by geopolitical events, opposition to AI and opposition to data center development.” 
Popular discontent with data center buildout and its disastrous effects on the planet is a critical risk AI firms are strategizing against. Their alliance with an administration that is ratcheting up its repression of dissidence is no mystery.
Already, federal security agencies have identified “anti-tech violent extremism” as a counterterrorism threat. The warning signs of what may lie ahead are flashing. As protests of AI’s social, economic and ecological effects, and its signal contribution to war and genocide, continue, opposition is being framed as a threat to U.S. national security and the viability of a leading sector of U.S. capital.
The Anthropic prospectus can be understood as, among other things, a planning document for a preemptive struggle against social opposition to AI primacy. This opposition was incontrovertibly felt in the “blue wave” of the November midterms. A Democrat won a U.S. Senate seat in Texas, arguably the nucleus of the data center boom, for the first time since 1988. Democrats also took over the Texas House of Representatives. This was after public pressure had caused outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott to institute a moratorium on new data centers. And across the country, ballot measures curtailing or forbidding data center buildout prevailed in 46 out of 47 cases, mostly with ample margins.
While we can’t quite say that data factories are sites of class struggle, the intimate link between AI capital and the growing movement against it shows that the industry has a class consciousness of its own.
Wall Street clearly isn’t flinching yet, but Anthropic’s own prospectus lists opposition to data center development among the risks to its business. AI capitalists know that movement could collapse their model, and they’re using warnings of extinction to postpone their own demise. The superintelligence racket is one we all need to protect ourselves from.
ALBERTO TOSCANO is the author of Late Fascism: Race, Capitalism and the Politics of Crisis (Verso) and Terms of Disorder: Keywords for an Interregnum (Seagull). He lives in Vancouver.

https://inthesetimes.com/article/whats-n.title: This Better Not Be What’s Next for the Democrats
https://inthesetimes.com/article/whats-n.author: Hamilton Nolan
https://inthesetimes.com/article/whats-n.text:
This Better Not Be What's Next for the Democrats
After a historic midterms, let’s go inside the great battle for the Democratic Party’s future.
Hamilton Nolan
DENVER—The Democrats! Like migratory birds they descend upon this swagless Western city, seeking warmth among the microbreweries. After years of dark political winter they are emerging into the light, peeking out of their Uber Black Escalades, giddy with the scent of opportunity. They have come to Set the Agenda, to Write the Narrative, to revel in their sudden ascendance. But like all gathering flocks, they are conscious that they must, before anything else, establish their new pecking order.
Their confidence drips from their strange and audacious plumage! This species, native to the sterile government buildings and imperial nighttime restaurants of Washington, D.C. has its own uniform — repugnant to outsiders, but a sign of beauty in their isolated culture. For these men, there is nothing more suave than neatly pressed blue jeans, a blazer, and sneakers. Sneakers! With a blazer? This is the devil-may-care rakishness they bring to their serious work, a way to allow their complex personalities to shine through during their dreary days of policymaking.
The rascals! Those blazers are not just blue. Some are checked. Some carry even more exotic and abhorrent patterns. Most men undo one or even two of the buttons on their shirts, exuding a studied casualness. And around their necks? Nothing at all! With their bold lack of ties, the modern Democrat strikes a blow against conformity. They retain the barest form of the business suit while remixing it with all of the cutting-edge style that D.C. is known for. This is a party of Regular Folks, not stuffed suits. Like all regular folks, they wear sneakers and blazers and lanyards and think about kitchen table issues like working hard to support their families as was promised to them by the American Dream.
Here we all were, in Denver, at the Mission Ballroom, for What’s Next, an event that brought together the professional spine of the Democratic Party to try to lay down exactly what should and will be happening for the next two years. The wi-fi password was “NineDaysLater,” a nod to the midterm wipeout that had the hearts of all the attendees throbbing like a big shot of cocaine. The surface-level theme of the event was unity, coming together as one big tent, but make no mistake: This was the first organized effort to establish exactly which faction will control this party for the next term. The smiles and lack of ties and complimentary Brandi Carlisle concert did not mean that this event was not, in its essence, cutthroat.
The event was put on by Majority Democrats, a moderate-ish group that seeks to build a majority caucus inside the party. It explicitly distinguishes itself from those three apocalyptic horsemen, “The Gerontocratic Establishment,” the “Activist Left,” and “The Maga Right.” Majority Democrats is funded by a hedge fund billionaire, and you could really tell in the event’s production values. Get a bunch of the Activist Left together and you’re looking at janky PA systems and unruly stacks of fliers. But here at What’s Next, there was unlimited free snacks and professional execution and a wondrous lighting display on stage that looked like a sculpture of huge lamps of all colors turned on their side, hypnotizing and soothing the crowd as some Congressman drones on. If I were a billionaire dark money funder I would take a hard look at how much of my political money is being spent on lighting. I guess they can afford it, though.
The money also bought graphic design, and it was an atrocity. Any normal human would step back and clutch their chest in agony at the sight of the posters that adorned the hallways. They were all done up in the style of classic concert posters, like something you might see hanging on a telephone pole to advertise a Grateful Dead or Bob Marley show, except they featured the most aggressively uncool politicians in the United States. There was Hakeem Jeffries, wearing shades; there was an ad for Cory Booker & The Revolution; there was a four-peat of Josh Shapiro’s head in four different colors; there was a hand drawn picture of CIA agent-turned-governor Abigail Spanberger as a hippie with flowing blond hair holding a batch of flowers.
Prowling the hallways between these posters were Majority Democrats staffers wearing custom-made Dickies jackets with “Majority Democrats” in yellow cursive and a sewn-on name tag like a genuine working class person somewhere might wear. (Or so they’ve heard.) Wherever you turned you would be faced with this sort of visual assault, physical manifestations of the way that culture is ingested and destroyed by capital. Like the cheeky blazers and the Adidases worn with suits, you can be sure that the people involved in this would wink and say that they were in on the joke, without knowing that their comedy is actually a horror film.
The public believes that politics is about politicians, and movements believe that politics is about people, but What’s Next was an event centered on the real heroes: the consultant class. This vision of politics is one in which good political decisions emanate from a small group of ultra-smart nerds immersed in data, who tell the party what it should be doing. Deviations from this path — whether to the right or (more likely) the left — are treated as verifiable errors, juvenile indulgences, refusals to face facts about what voters really want.
Thus, the consultants that took the stage in Denver delivered lectures to the assembled functionaries about What Voters Are Thinking. And what they are thinking is: Affordability. Affordability, affordability, affordability. The economy, stupid. Prices of things. They’re high, and they should be lower, for the sake of affordability. “I hope you’re very excited to hear someone repeat the phrase ‘cost of living’ for seven minutes and 45 seconds,” joked Charlotte Swasey, director of analytics for the Searchlight Institute. Searchlight is a sort of companion think tank for the Majority Democrats project, funded by the same billionaires, whose schtick is “we serve up centrism but from a guy with long hair.” That guy is Adam Jentleson, the bearded and man-bunned former Harry Reid and John Fetterman staffer who has now found himself a secure perch in the lucrative Telling The Left To Shut Up industry.
Jentleson is a fascinating figure. Besides his personal appearance, which is that of a bartender at a craft cocktail speakeasy in 2007, it is unclear to me what makes him so alluring to the political establishment. His ideas are standard, rehashed Clintonism. He’s not much of writer. He’s a workmanlike speaker. He glanced down at his notes continually while instructing the crowd about the “messy” political beliefs of Americans. “They want a stronger safety net, but also want fiscal discipline,” he revealed. “They think private enterprise is good, but also want to raise taxes on the wealthy.”
Gadzooks! Stop the presses! It is very hard to conclude that Adam Jentleson’s position of power is not due in large part to his haircut. It is exactly the sort of thing — like, say, a concert-style poster of Pete Buttigieg — that a billionaire might imagine would lend a rock-n-roll frisson to the project of producing a stable regulatory environment conducive to capital growth. Searchlight sponsored a welcome reception in an adjacent bar the first day of the event, and adorned the tables with QR codes that would allow you to take a quiz to determine your own “Political Neighborhood.” The first question was about how you feel about trans people in bathrooms. I clicked off at that point. There were free Searchlight-branded tote bags and hats that said “tax-and-spend liberal” available, but I left them there. Couldn’t think of anyone who would get the irony of the souvenir.
Amid all of the lectures from pollsters and consultants, two anecdotes stood out to me. The first was a remark from Sarah Longwell, a political strategist and former Republican who grew disgusted with Trump and founded The Bulwark, the center-right anti-MAGA news outlet. Longwell is very much a DC creature. (Earlier this year, she stopped the Bulwark from publishing an in-depth investigative story critical of Democratic fundraising practices because she couldn’t imagine what was wrong with fundraising spam.) She spoke enthusiastically of her desire to “Burn MAGA to the ground and salt the earth.” But as her speech unfolded, it became clear that all of her conclusions, all of her recommendations, all of her insights into What Voters Want, came from listening to focus groups. “I listen in the shower, and I listen on the treadmill, and I listen when I’m walking places,” she said of focus group recordings. “I have voters in my ear all the time, and the disconnect between what we talk about in rooms like this and the way they sound is enormous.”
This was disconcerting. Here was a person who was paid to be an expert on what regular people want, and was invited to instruct the Democratic Party on what regular people want, whose own alleged expertise on what regular people want was not drawn from actually knowing any regular people. Not at all! Regular people were convened to sit in rooms and be questioned and recorded by professionals, and this woman listened to those recordings while on the treadmill, and from these data events she is now prepared to declare herself an expert on the will of regular people. Equally disconcerting is the fact that when this group, the “Majority” Democrats, went to seek out an expert on regular people for its big event, it did not to think to invite any regular people, nor even anyone who personally associates with regular people, but rather a political consultant who listens to a lot of focus groups that are presumably made up of regular people.
The second, and related, remark that struck me came from Daniel Squadron, an intellectual liberal consultant who gave an interesting talk on the long, pernicious influence of right wing thinkers like Ayn Rand and Carl Schmitt. He was making the point to the audience that Democrats will need more than a catchy slogan to succeed. “You can’t ask what your slogan is until you ask a different question: What do you believe?” he said. “Why are you doing this? It’s a question that I bet many of you have never been asked in a real way.”
Squadron, a man who has spent his entire career in Democratic politics, was speaking to a room full of professional Democratic functionaries, and he casually voiced that it was his working assumption that these people — the people who were there to determine the future of progressive politics — have never been asked the question, “What do you believe?” This smart and experienced man, a man intimately familiar with this milieu, took it for granted that this audience of thousands had probably never encountered a question so tawdry, so elementary, as “What do you believe?” For the hardnosed, data-driven consultants in the room, such a question would, I guess, be a waste of time.
Remarks like these are a little unnerving, because if you are a more or less regular person who holds unforgivably childish ideas like “I believe we must help the working class break the power of capital,” you start to realize that you are in a big tent that is owned and controlled by a whole other set of people who don’t have time to think about stuff like that because they are too busy listening to recordings of focus groups of people like you saying cute things like “my rent is too expensive.” You are supposed to take your marching orders on political action from these people. These are the majority Democrats. What that makes all the rest of us, I do not know.
Spending some time in this setting will help you understand why the Democratic Party is so perpetually frustrating. In this consultant-centered model, the politicians themselves become little more than actors, sent out to convincingly perform the script that the consultants have devised. The best politicians are not the ones who have their own ideas but rather the ones who can sound winning and likable while repeating back to voters the things that voters themselves have said in various focus groups just a short time ago. Listening to the parade of national politicians take the stage at What’s Next, it was hard not to notice that most of them — the brightest stars of the non-left wing of the Democratic Party — did, if you paid attention to their actual words rather than their charming faces and aw-shucks jokes, seem to be doing exactly this.
“We must bridge the divide between us,” said James Talarico, in jeans, a blazer, and no tie. “We must repair the ties that bind us.”
“Working hard every day. Building a home, starting a family, sending their kids to a good public school,” said Colorado Congressman Joe Neguse, in a blue suit and no tie. “That type of opportunity is what makes me believe in America. It’s why I refuse to abandon my bone-deep commitment to expanding opportunity.”
“I tell people the political system is broken, because it is,” said Iowa governor-elect Rob Sand, sporting the impassive face of the male model he used to be. “I tell them, too often it feels like two private clubs who are more interested in beating up on each other than they are in solving anyone’s problems.”
“For too long, we’ve been afraid to talk like normal people,” said burly Arizona Senator Ruben Gallego. “Big-ass truck politics is what unites Democrats like never before.”
“Affordability. That’s what we ran on,” said New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill.
“Affordability,” said Colorado governor-elect Phil Weiser.
“Affordability,” said Virginia’s Abigail Spanberger.
“Affordability is front and center,” argued Alaska governor-elect Jonathan Kriess-Tomkins, by contrast.
Presented in this rapid-fire manner, the impression that all of the elected officials are just reading their lines is unavoidable. Nobody embodies that robotic discipline like Hakeem Jeffries, the man that leftists in the party fear is about to become Speaker of the House. Jeffries has the gift of moving his mouth without moving any other portion of his face, which gives him a flinty, imperturbable air that serves him well amid chaos. When he sat down for a chat on stage with Fox News token Democrat Jessica Tarlov, he was quickly interrupted by not one, not two, but three protesters, each of whom stood up and started shouting at him as soon as the one before had been escorted out by police. They yelled that he didn’t listen to young people, that he had aided genocide in Gaza, that we need a Green New Deal. Jeffries sat still, totally unmoved, for a few seconds of this, and then proceeded to just carry on with his applause line about the Knicks winning the championship (the very same line that he used in a video clip played during his introduction).
The final protester, as he was being pulled past me, burst out in frustration, “Fuck you all!”
“Fuck you too, bitch!” hollered an older black man who was sitting in front of me, purely out of reflex. On stage, Jeffries continued talking about how he enjoyed seeing himself portrayed on Saturday Night Live recently. Tarlov, on the other hand, was flustered. “I’m nervous, compared to like, The Five,” she sputtered.
Jeffries immediately began talking about the need to get permitting reform done. This is his power. He may be corrupt, and an obstacle to true progress, but he has achieved total unflappability. He cannot be disturbed, and he also cannot be made to answer a question with truth or clarity, two qualities which are effectively superpowers for a man in his position. He would say things like, “We have to get dark money out of politics,” without defining it in a way that might get him into trouble. When asked something he didn’t want to answer at all, like whether he supports term limits, he would say, “It’s the right conversation to have.” He would say things that are vaguely reassuring to people of all political persuasions, like, “We’re going to be guided by the Constitution.” If you didn’t press hard, he can leave you thinking he agrees with you on everything. If you do press hard, he slips out to the side, like trying to snatch a quick fish underwater. Even if you don’t like him, you must admit that he is a perfect leader for the Democratic Party: a human bowl of Jell-O, capable of holding a shape for a while, but always ready to ooze into any new container as necessary.
The one firm claim that everyone at What’s Next hastened to make was that the Democratic Party is not divided. Is this billionaire-backed convention of centrists somehow a sign that there is a divide between the left and the centrists in the party? Not at all! Nothing could be further from the truth, the officials invited to this gathering proclaimed.
“This isn’t about middle, left, or right. It’s about up versus down,” said former New Orleans mayor Mitch Landrieu. “Insiders who take everything, and leave everybody else out.”
“There is no so-called moderate Democratic Party. There is no so-called progressive Democratic Party,” said former attorney general Eric Holder. “There is one Democratic Party.”
“We need to think bigger now,” said New Jersey Senator Cory Booker, channeling a preacher. “We need to call left and right together to show them that the lines that divide us are not nearly as strong as the ties that bind us.”
“The new generation is not gonna be defined by progressive versus moderate,” said Michigan Senator Elissa Slotkin. “That new generation is, quite simply, are you on team fight, or team flight?”
Notably, the one genuine left winger who spoke on stage, Congressman Ro Khanna, struck a different tone. He knew he was in the minority here. Unlike almost every other speech, his contained actual policy prescriptions. He called for Medicare for All (not to be confused with “universal health care,” a term that sounds kind of like Medicare for All but is not the same, and which was in widespread use among newly elected Democrats here). He called for a wealth tax. He called for a $25 minimum wage. He called for an end to aid for Israel, and no more foreign wars. These are all common things to hear when you are at leftist events. But among the Majority Democrats, Khanna’s directness only served to highlight the absence of real policy positions from most of the other speakers.
Let me try to be fair. Let me try not to piss on the parade. Democrats just won their biggest midterm victory in decades and they seem to agree that they need an agenda that they can act on, which is certainly better than no agenda. By listening to the moderates here and combining it with what we know the left wants, you can begin to see the outline of some agreed-upon things: Building more housing, ending gerrymandering, some modest expansion of Medicare to either the young or the old, a ban on stock trading for members of Congress, more green energy, some sort of AI regulation, aggressive investigations of Trump administration crimes. These things have broad appeal, and could well get passed quickly. They would be good. Sure. They would be an improvement from what we have now. They would live up to the underlying tone of the Majority Democrats’ oxymoronic platform: Big, Bold, and Moderate.
The truth is, though, that no matter how big a tent you put over the Democratic Party, it will still be divided. Why? Because that is the nature of politics. Factions are not inherently bad. They exist because people genuinely disagree on substantial things. You can say “let’s all come together in unity,” but when we propose a wealth tax and you say no, there is no unity there. There is just a fight. When we ask for Medicare for All and you say no, there is not common ground. There is a fight.
Policy differences matter. Party unity is important in general elections, but when it comes to governing, it is more instructive to think of politics as a battle. The left has more common ground with the moderates in Denver than it has with the fascists in Trumplandia, yes. But what the moderates and the fascists have in common is that they are both trying to ensure that the left does not gain power. The hand of friendship that centrists extend to the newly ascendant left wing of their party comes with a tacit agreement that the left will remain the minority partner in this coalition. If you are on the left and you actually want to change the structural problems that brought us to this point, the holes in the big tent are easy to spot.
The morning of the last day of What’s Next, about 20 protesters gathered a couple of blocks outside of the venue, holding signs for a Green New Deal and chanting about dumping Chuck Schumer. In response to this small crew, the Denver police deployed dozens of riot cops in full tactical gear, helmets, and body armor. They even sent an armored SWAT team vehicle that would have looked far more appropriate navigating the IED-strewn streets of Fallujah than parked on the curb just down from the Chubby Unicorn Cantina. The whole scene would have been laughable, were it not for the presence of so many heavily armed men. Majority Democrats staffers stood out there looking worried, thanking the police for their work. I spoke to one older man holding an Indivisible sign who had come to protest. He was jealous of my press pass. “I wish I was in the press,” he said. “Getting into that event costs five thousand bucks.”
That afternoon, Georgia Senator and rumored presidential hopeful Raphael Warnock took the stage. He is a real live preacher, a gifted speaker, a man who knows how to call forth the spirit of the civil rights movement. He told a story about watching his grandmother chop the head off of a snake in her garden when he was a child. “As I witnessed the traumatic and menacing movements and convulsions after she decapitated it, I thought we were really in trouble. What I didn’t understand as a six year-old kid is that that snake was moving not because it was living, but because it was dying,” he said. “This is now the last gasp of an old order that knows it is on its way out!”
It is a neat metaphor — the snake, as evil, writhing in its death throes. Yet the other quality of snakes is that they shed their skin. They change their outer appearance and are reborn. Sometimes, they slither right inside of your big tent, curl up beside you, and try to make friends.

https://hellgatenyc.com/mamdani-gets-ser.title: Mayor Mamdani Gets Serious About Closing Rikers
https://hellgatenyc.com/mamdani-gets-ser.author: Nick Pinto
https://hellgatenyc.com/mamdani-gets-ser.text:
Almost 10 years after New York City first committed to close the fetid, crumbling, unconstitutionally violent and cruel jail complex on Rikers Island, Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled a plan on Friday morning to finally get the job done.
After languishing under Mayor Eric Adams, who evinced no enthusiasm for closing Rikers, the process for shuttering the island dungeon is years behind schedule, and the City will unavoidably blow through its legally mandated deadline to shutter the island jails by next August. Mamdani is hoping to negotiate an extension of the deadline with City Council, to the end of 2032.
But while begging an extension to keep Rikers open for five more years, even as people continue to suffer and die on the island, is incredibly discouraging, the mayor's plan is detailed, specific, and contains enough incremental benchmarks to suggest that New York finally has a government serious about the task, and that Mamdani isn't just kicking the can down the road.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: National Gallery of Canada receives major gift of modern and contemporary glass art
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Annabel Keenan
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The National Gallery of Canada (NGC) in Ottawa is embarking on a new chapter in its collecting history with a promised gift of 56 modern and contemporary glass works from Canadian American businessman and philanthropist Charles Bronfman and his late wife, Andrea Bronfman. Accompanied by an endowment to establish the institution’s first curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design, the donation will help broaden the museum’s collection and increase its scholarly contributions.
“This is the gallery’s first gift of modern and 20th-century glass,” Jean-François Bélisle, director and chief executive of the NGC, tells The Art Newspaper. “It significantly expands our understanding of art history, bringing together artistic expression and material and technical innovation.”
The gifted Bronfman Collection spans more than a century of glass experimentation, with works by 29 artists from Canada, Europe, the United States and Asia. The collection traces the medium’s evolution from the sinuous forms of Art Nouveau and Arts and Crafts to the streamlined aesthetics of Art Deco and Modernism. Early 20th-century examples by Tiffany Studios, Émile Gallé and the renowned studio Daum demonstrate how artists pushed glass beyond traditional decorative applications.
The works also chart the emergence of studio glass as an independent discipline in the post-war period. Additional artists with works in the donation include Dale Chihuly, whose gravity-defying installations are in museums worldwide, as well as the studio glass pioneer Toots Zynsky and the well-known Canadian American artist Laura Donefer.
A selection of pieces from the collection is currently on view in the NGC’s European galleries (until 30 April 2027). Highlights of the installation include Edward Hald’s The Fireworks Bowl (around 1921), alongside architectural works by Tiffany and Frank Lloyd Wright.
“Harvey Littleton’s Red Crossed Form (1990) is another notable work that reflects the development of studio glass as an independent artistic medium,” says Anabelle Kienle Ponka, the NGC’s senior curator of European, American and Asian Art. “The presentation brings together very different approaches to glass, from the decorative traditions of the early 20th century to the formal and technical experimentation of contemporary artists.”
The international scope of the donation highlights the exchange of technical traditions, particularly the influence of Venetian glassmaking on successive generations of artists, Kienle Ponka says. Together, the works demonstrate the medium’s versatility across sculpture, architecture and ornamentation.
Equally significant for the NGC is the accompanying endowment, which will fund the museum’s first curatorial position dedicated to decorative arts and design. The NGC has not shared the sum of the endowment, but notes that the post will support research, exhibitions and future acquisitions, establishing a foundation for sustained institutional engagement with the field.
“[The donation’s] significance extends well beyond this gift,” Bélisle says. “The position will allow us to pursue further acquisitions, develop exhibitions and scholarship, and build relationships with artists and institutions.”
The donation builds on a long history of the Bronfman family’s philanthropy in Canada's cultural sector. “My late wife Andy and I were admirers of the art of glass making and wanted to share this love with other Canadians,” Charles Bronfman said in a statement. “With the planned celebrations marking the upcoming 100th birthday of my sister, Phyllis Lambert, founder of the Canadian Centre for Architecture, and the 50th anniversary of the Canada Council for the Arts’ Saidye Bronfman Award, named after my mother, I am truly delighted to be contributing in this meaningful way to the national collections.”
The NGC has received other transformative gifts in recent years, including a 2025 donation of 61 contemporary works valued at C$22.8m ($16.8m) from collector Bob Rennie and his family. “The Bronfman gift is significant in a different way,” Bélisle says. “Its importance lies not only in the quality and range of the works, but also in the accompanying endowment, which will provide the expertise and resources to develop decorative arts and design as a sustained area of collecting and scholarship.”

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/20/fisa.title: Establishment Dems Want to Renew Trump’s Domestic Spy Powers Before New Congress
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/20/fisa.author: Matt Sledge
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/20/fisa.text:
With huge changes looming in Congress, the fate of a controversial warrantless surveillance law underlying many of former National Security Agency contractor Edward Snowden’s disclosures is up for debate.
And, instead of waiting for an influx of progressives in the next Congress to shake up the conversation, establishment Democrats are pushing to renew the law before the Republican-dominated Senate and House flip over.
The might, however, run into the same foes who have held up the renewal of Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act — chief among them Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore.
Wyden and other privacy advocates said they are opposed to passing the law during the lame-duck period without major reforms. One long-sought-after goal is a warrant requirement.
Wyden told The Intercept this week that he has never felt so close to achieving real reform.
“I would very much like to see a FISA program that would ensure both liberty and security,” Wyden said. “I have been through this for quite some time. I think we’ve now got a huge following on both sides of the aisle.”
The surveillance law has long sparked complicated maneuvering in Congress, where the warrant question scrambles traditional partisan divides. The law, which allows the NSA to collect communications of Americans made from or to recipients abroad, expired in June. Existing court orders, however, meant that the NSA and other agencies can continue to collect reams of intelligence from foreign communications until March 17, 2027.
President Donald Trump inflamed the debate over renewal this spring by tapping a loyalist mortgage official, Bill Pulte, to briefly lead the Office of the Director of National Intelligence.
The result was a collapse in Democratic support for the law — but not a permanent one.
Top Democratic members on the House and Senate intelligence committees, Rep. Jim Himes of Connecticut and Sen. Mark Warner of Virginia, want a renewal this year.
Warner acknowledged in comments to reporters this week that the only way the controversial law can pass is if it’s tacked on to a larger piece of “must-pass” legislation.
“We need FISA,” he said. “I think the only way to get it done is if it gets attached to something, at this point. But none of this gets easier in a new Congress.”
“Take It or Leave It”
The few pieces legislation considered by broad swaths of Congress to be “must-pass” bills this year include the National Defense Authorization Act and a bill to replace the current government funding law, which expires December 11.
Both bills will already involve fraught negotiations over funding for the Iran war. The ranking Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee told Punchbowl News that he opposes adding FISA to the defense law.
Senate Judiciary Committee ranking member Dick Durbin, D-Ill., told The Intercept that he is doubtful a renewal can pass this year.
“I don’t think that’s realistic,” said Durbin, whose committee has dual jurisdiction over the law. “I think it’s time to sit down and make some meaningful changes to FISA.”
The Democrats joining Trump loyalists in favor of renewal before a new Congress is sworn in were bolstered by testimony from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton at a Tuesday hearing. Clayton, who said the lapse of the authorization hadn’t caused a substantial decline in the number of foreign communications collected, argued that the law needs to be renewed soon to prevent internet communication companies from refusing to comply with the law.
The push from Democrats such as Himes and Warner has outraged progressive groups who favor adding a warrant requirement. They argue that voting on the law now before the next Congress would represent a betrayal of the voters.
“Even with the rejection of the status quo that we saw at the ballot box earlier this month, the leadership, possibly of both parties, seem to be pulling the same tactics, possibly leaving members with a ‘take it or leave it’ proposition,” said Hajar Hammado, a senior policy adviser at the group Demand Progress.
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., have not said whether they support passing a renewal of the law this year.
Jeffries said Tuesday that there were open discussions between Himes and House Judiciary Committee ranking member Jamie Raskin, who favors stricter limits on the spying program.
One representative-elect who campaigned on reform, Brad Lander, told The Intercept last week that he is agnostic on the timing of FISA renewal — as long as a warrant requirement is included.
“We should add a warrant requirement,” Lander said. “If that can happen now, great, but if it’s not going to happen now, we should wait and do it in the new Congress.”
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://citylimits.org/nycha-to-use-fede.title: NYCHA to Use Federal Program to Help Public Housing Residents Buy Their Homes
https://citylimits.org/nycha-to-use-fede.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/nycha-to-use-fede.text:
Share This Article
The properties are among more than 700 Federal Housing Administration (FHA) homes, which were transferred to NYCHA from the federal government between the 1960s and early 1980s for use as public housing.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani is rolling out a plan for residents of 91 public housing units to buy their longtime homes.
The initiative marks the first time the New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) is using a federal program called Section 32, which allows public housing residents to buy their homes while maintaining strict affordability requirements.
“Homeownership should not be a privilege for the wealthy few,” Mayor Mamdani said in a statement Thursday. “Through this program, we’re investing in the homes public housing residents already know and building the future they dream of, whether they rent or own.”
According to the plans, the housing authority will onboard a developer, general contractor and resident support team to rehabilitate the 91 units. Once renovations are complete, the same partners will facilitate the homeownership process for eligible residents who meet income and other program criteria.
Most of the houses are located in Southeast Queens, with others in Brooklyn and the Bronx. They include 75 single-family homes, 11 two-family homes, three three-family homes, and two four-family homes.
The properties are among more than 700 Federal Housing Administration (FHA) Homes, which were transferred to NYCHA from the federal government between the 1960s and early 1980s. The housing authority has used them as additional public housing, where tenants typically pay a third of their income in rent.
“Residents of the FHA Homes are excited about the opportunity to finally purchase the home they have lived in for decades,” said Doreen Goggans, the tenant association president of FHA Homes, in a statement. “We are looking forward to these properties getting the investment they deserve.”
On Thursday, the housing authority released a formal request for submissions, called a Request for Expressions of Interest (RFEI), from partner teams interested in taking on renovations and facilitating the homeownership process for eligible residents. The housing authority will host a virtual pre-submission conference for potential applicants on Dec. 8, and will accept submissions from Nov. 19 through Feb. 18, 2027.
The housing authority expects the selected partner team to work with families that aren’t eligible for the homeownership program to identify alternative ways to carry out repairs, like using Community Land Trust models.
“As we begin the search for a partner, we are committed to selecting a team with the expertise and the ability to build relationships with the community to make homeownership a reality for as many of these families as possible,” said Heather Beck, NYCHA’s executive vice president.

https://www.propublica.org/article/texas.title: A Texas Police Department Got $100K After a Single Immigration Arrest. It Stands to Earn Much More.
https://www.propublica.org/article/texas.author: Josh Hinkle, David Barer, Arezow Doost, Grace Reader, Dalton Huey, Matt Grant
https://www.propublica.org/article/texas.text:
Last spring, the police chief in a tiny North Texas suburb called Pantego went before his town council with what might have sounded like an audacious pitch to bring in more money for policing.
His department could accept the federal government’s offer to get into the business of immigration enforcement.
“I won’t say there’s unlimited funding, but there’s quite a bit of money in the fund,” Pantego Police Chief Robert Rife said during the April meeting in which council members approved an agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
He was right. After a single immigration arrest this past June, Pantego received $100,000.
It stands to earn much more.
Rife predicted in his presentation to the council that federal grants could bring in an additional $720,000 for the 2,500-resident town a few miles east of Fort Worth. For perspective, combined with the money it had already received, that’s roughly equivalent to 40% of the town’s $2.1 million police budget last year.
Pantego is one of 429 law enforcement agencies in the state as of mid-September that have entered into agreements with ICE as part of President Donald Trump’s efforts to accelerate deportations. Texas leads the nation in these partnerships, known as 287(g) agreements, which authorize local officers to make immigration arrests during their normal course of duty. A key incentive for local governments across the country has long been the funding that comes with participation.
The federal program funnels millions of dollars to local law enforcement while requiring few measurable results and little tracking of how the money is spent. KXAN reviewed minutes from nine local government meetings and found that, over and over again, Texas law enforcement officials sold the program to their local elected leaders as a boon for their cash-strapped departments.
The same month Pantego decided to join the program, for example, the police chief in the small suburb of Hollywood Park near San Antonio made a similar pitch to his city council. The city “actively profits on payroll for the time spent,” he said.
And in Smith County in East Texas, Sheriff Larry Smith told county commissioners that “equipment, use of fuel, mileage and things of that nature” could all be reimbursed, plus there would be $100,000 for two new vehicles and money for overtime.
“How often do the feds offer us money for anything?” Smith County Commissioner John Moore asked.
“Not very often,” the sheriff responded. He declined to speak with KXAN.
Austin-based immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch worries that local law enforcement will become dependent on the financial incentives, making it difficult to pull away from the program in the future.
“I’m concerned about what this money is going to be doing to the mindset of these small police departments,” she said.
In the Texas Panhandle, Hartley County Sheriff Chanze Fowler said nearly all the federal funding his department receives supports its regular operations, in addition to immigration work.
The sheriff’s office recorded 54 arrests under 287(g) authority from January to early July, most for minor traffic and vehicle violations, according to records obtained by KXAN. It received more than $205,000 during that time. By this past summer, it had spent about $30,000 on things like wages, extra pay for officers who became 287(g) certified, payroll taxes, retirement funds and “fleet purchases.”
Almost all of the 287(g)-related funds “go towards items needed for our everyday job,” Fowler said.
Other local city and law enforcement officials said the additional funds help officers protect their communities and carry out core duties. ICE did not respond to a request for an interview for this story but instead provided a statement that explained the program. Its website says the program targets dangerous criminal offenders.
Pantego officials have declined to answer KXAN’s questions about the department’s involvement with the program since August, despite repeated attempts to reach the mayor, town council, city manager and police chief by phone, email and in person.
“We are not interested in interviewing at this time,” said City Manager Leslie Galloway, the only official to respond.
Ammon Blair, a senior fellow for the Texas Public Policy Foundation, a conservative think tank that supports the program, acknowledged the money can help departments operating on thin budgets, including helping to pay for overtime. But he said there should be more oversight of how the federal money is spent.
KXAN obtained service agreements between ICE and the Smith County Sheriff’s Office and the police department in Bullard, Texas, a town of about 5,300 people in East Texas. The agreements allow either party to terminate with 60 days’ notice. None indicate that the federal government can reclaim funding if an agreement is terminated.
That was one of the selling points in Pantego. The department could get federal funding and eventually drop out of the program without penalty and keep the equipment already purchased, the police chief told town council members. All it had to do was make at least one immigration arrest.
Between the end of April and mid-June, it made two.
“Are You a U.S. Citizen?”
Local law enforcement agencies that join forces with ICE can choose among three models, two of which focus on identifying people already in jail who may be subject to deportation.
Trump revived the third kind, called the task force model, at the beginning of his second term. Task force agreements often worry civil and immigrants’ rights groups because of the model’s problematic track record: ICE started phasing them out in 2012, after Department of Justice investigations revealed that sheriff’s offices participating in the model had committed civil rights violations.
But task force agreements can also be lucrative.
Agencies can receive federal reimbursement for salaries, overtime and benefits for “conducting purposeful and intentional” immigration enforcement activities once the contract starts, according to a service agreement obtained by KXAN.
They can also get recurring quarterly incentive payments and one-time stipends for equipment, technology and vehicles, though federal memoranda and agreements obtained by KXAN don’t specify what agencies can purchase.
The Department of Homeland Security stopped renewing task force model agreements during the Obama administration after federal investigations revealed civil rights violations involving sheriffs’ offices in Arizona and North Carolina.
Since Trump’s return to office, the model has become the most common of the three agreement types. At least 241 task force model agreements were signed in Texas in 2026 alone, compared to just 30 combined for the other models in that time period, according to ICE participation data from September.
Smith County was among the first in Texas to sign on after the president reinstated the task force model in early 2025.
Moore, the only member of Smith County’s Commissioners Court who agreed to speak with KXAN, explained why he thought the commissioners wanted to partner.
His first word: “budgetary.”
“Any kind of training that any of our departments need to have, or are required to have, costs money, and it’s rare that we get an opportunity to get funding for training from outside county taxes,” Moore said. “Any time we can save the taxpayers money, I’m all for it.”
Smith County got more money than any other of the 93 Texas law enforcement agencies whose funding KXAN reviewed. The sheriff’s office received nearly $2.2 million in federal 287(g) funding from January 2025 to June 2026, according to records obtained by KXAN. That’s equivalent to about 12% of its budget for fiscal year 2025.
Smith, the sheriff, told the Commissioners Court last November that although vehicles purchased with that money would be used for the 287(g) program, “that doesn’t mean, if we’re out here, we won’t run to another call or take another call that comes across the radio. We will do that. We try not to separate 287(g) from our other law enforcement duties. We do it all together.”
About 120 of 198 licensed officers in the Smith County Sheriff’s Office participated in the program. Together, they conducted 124 immigration enforcement actions between October 2025 and July. KXAN requested a list of 287(g) stops from the department, in addition to any associated charge. Smith County listed no associated criminal charge for more than 100 of these stops.
Jose Rodriguez and his 23-year-old son, Pablo Rodriguez, were among those affected.
One afternoon in late June, the pair cruised along Loop 323, a circular segment of highway in Tyler, a city of 113,000 people in East Texas. They’d spent hours working in the summer heat at a construction job and were headed to Chick-fil-A to pick up lunch for their family.
Then red and blue lights appeared behind them. The law enforcement agent said that he’d pulled their black extended-cab work truck over because of a missing license plate on the trailer attached to the pickup and a missing dual-wheel mud flap.
Body and vehicle camera footage showed the detective requesting that Jose Rodriguez get out of the truck. “Any English at all?” the detective later asked. Jose Rodriguez raised his right hand, holding his thumb and index finger close together.
“Un poquito?” the detective asked, followed by, “Are you a U.S. citizen?”
The man shook his head and answered. “No.”
Seconds later, the detective pulled Jose Rodriguez’s hands behind his back and put him in handcuffs.
He was eventually taken from the Smith County jail to an ICE detention facility, about two hours west of Tyler. His son, who is a U.S. citizen, said Jose Rodriguez was detained for about three months before being deported to Mexico.
KXAN could find no criminal convictions or arrests on his record when the Smith County detective took him into custody in June.
“Just like that, he’s gone,” Pablo Rodriguez later told KXAN. “My dad’s gone.”
Law enforcement officers, Pablo Rodriguez said, “portray us as criminals, rapists, violent people. We’re not that. We’re just regular people trying to find a better life. The only difference is our skin. That’s pretty much it.”
The Future of the Program in Texas
Elections earlier this month have left the 287(g) program’s future uncertain, at least in Texas.
While the Trump administration has reached agreements with local law enforcement to work with immigration officials, Congress has broader oversight authority. That includes decisions about funding. In January, Democrats will take over both chambers of Congress and many, including freshman Texas Sen. James Talarico, have criticized ICE tactics. It’s unclear, however, how much of their focus will be on immigration enforcement and specifically on the 287(g) program.
More locally, state Sen. Charles Schwertner, the Republican lawmaker who authored a measure in 2025 that required most Texas sheriff’s offices to participate in the program, wants to expand the mandate during the coming legislative session to include other law enforcement agencies, like police departments. So does the conservative think tank where Blair works.
But support for such legislation may be harder to get after November’s midterm election.
Schwertner retained his state Senate seat, and Republicans maintained their majority in that chamber, but Democrats took control of the governor’s mansion and the state House of Representatives for the first time in a generation. Any new bills would require legislative approval from both chambers and the governor’s signature, or enough legislative support to override a veto.
In a press release well before the election, Democrat Gina Hinojosa called on Gov. Greg Abbott to “demand accountability from the Trump administration and stop enabling ICE operations that are terrorizing communities and violating the law.” The release did not mention the 287(g) program by name. Hinojosa beat Abbott in this month’s election and will take over as governor in January. She did not respond to a request for comment for this story.
The state program could also be affected by this month’s election of Democrats Nathan Johnson, who won the race for state attorney general, and Sarah Eckhardt, who won her bid to become state comptroller.
Johnson, as a state senator, opposed the mandate that sheriffs’ offices participate in the program. He will inherit responsibility for enforcing the law, which requires most sheriffs to seek agreements with ICE by Dec. 1. Johnson said he will use his discretion in deciding whether to sue sheriffs who fail to comply if they have “legitimate law enforcement reasons for not having a 287(g) agreement.”
He also questioned the state attorney general’s continued participation in the program. Current Attorney General Ken Paxton signed a 287(g) task force model agreement in February 2025.
“The attorney general’s office has tremendous, vast responsibilities,” Johnson said. “Never included among them since the creation of this state was outsourcing your employees to a federal agency for a purpose in which we’re not trained or qualified and which distracts me from the mission of my office.”
Johnson didn’t entirely rule out working with ICE in some capacity if it allowed his office to investigate crimes committed by ICE agents in Texas.
Eckhardt, meanwhile, will take over oversight of a $20 million grant program that state lawmakers created two years ago to help sheriff’s offices cover any costs of participation in the 287(g) program not reimbursed by the federal government. By late September, the comptroller’s office had awarded more than $6.5 million to 78 sheriff’s offices, according to figures obtained by KXAN.
During her campaign, Eckhardt warned that expenses for the program could eventually fall on local taxpayers, calling it “unsustainable.” After winning her seat, she said she would “do a 287(g) audit to show how that expense is driving up property taxes.”
Even if state leaders don’t expand the participation requirement or remove the current mandate, departments can choose to keep collecting federal money to enforce immigration law.
In Fayette County southeast of Austin, Sheriff’s Lt. David Beyer told KXAN that the 287(g) funding his office had already received totaled about $800,000, which helps purchase equipment it can also use for ordinary police work.
“If they want to pay us extra to do that job,” Beyer said, “we’re more than happily going to accept those funds, because that saves our taxpayers money.”

https://hellgatenyc.com/maga-landlord-br.title: MAGA-Loving Landlord Lives It Up at Mar-a-Lago While Bronx Tenants Freeze
https://hellgatenyc.com/maga-landlord-br.author: Jessy Edwards
https://hellgatenyc.com/maga-landlord-br.text:
It's been a warm week, but on Tuesday, Eric Rivera's two-bedroom apartment was an ice box. 
Since November 11, the 69-year-old fashion designer has been without heat or hot water—along with the rest of the tenants in the Bronx building where he's lived for 20 years—and the chill has settled in.
"I'm very depressed, because I love the apartment and everything, but it's freezing," he told Hell Gate. "And because I have my condition and I work from home, I have to warm the apartment. And now I'm waiting for the bill."
Rivera lives with several health issues, including HIV. Since his Allerton building lost utilities, he's bathed by heating a pan of water on his stove and carrying it to his bathroom in a bucket. His bedroom is the coldest room in the apartment. At night, he burrows under three heavy blankets just to get to sleep. 
But while Rivera and the other tenants of 2265 Olinville Avenue live without basics like heat and hot water, their landlord has been projecting images of wealth and luxury on his social media account. The rent-stabilized building is owned by Dardani Investment Group LLC, with Connecticut-based landlord Gjok Paloka at the helm. His son Zef Paloka, 24, acts as the building manager.
The Palokas are Trump enthusiasts, according to the elder Paloka's public Instagram account, where he posts pictures of the high life. One day, it's hanging out with President Donald Trump at Mar-a-Lago. The next, it's riding in a helicopter over Dhërmi, a picturesque village on the Albanian Riviera. Cruising on a pleasurecraft. Having a laugh with former NYC Mayor Rudy Giuliani. Or advocating for a handful of former Kosovo politicians who were recently convicted of war crimes (Paloka is a proud Albanian American with close ties to Kosovo). 
For example, the same week in January that tenants at 2265 Olinville filed more than 40 complaints reporting leaks and a lack of heat and hot water in their apartments, Paloka and his son, Zef, were hobnobbing with the Trumps in Palm Beach.
"They're acting like they're the mafia," said Rivera. "They come in with different beautiful cars all the time—Mercedes, Range Rovers, big cars, fancy cars—and I say to myself, 'What the hell? How can these people afford this and not fix the building?'"
