https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Van Eyck’s genius, New York auctions, Cosimo de Medici’s wine cooler—podcast
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Ben Luke, Alexander Morrison, David Clack
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
One of the year’s most hotly anticipated exhibitions, Van Eyck: The Portraits, opens at the National Gallery in London this weekend after a rapturous response from the critics. Uniting all 10 of the Flemish master’s surviving portraits, including the one miraculous drawing attributed to him, it is truly a once-in-a-lifetime experience. Ben Luke takes a tour of the show with its co-curator, Emma Capron.
It is auction week in New York, with hundreds of millions of dollars of art coming under the hammer. Ben asks Melanie Gerlis, an art market columnist for the Financial Times and The Art Newspaper, about the week’s results so far.
And this episode’s Work of the Week is a maiolica wine cooler, made in 1574 by the workshop of Flaminio Fontana, in Urbino. It was made for Cosimo I de Medici, who is the subject of a small exhibition that opened this week at the Wallace Collection in London. Ben speaks to the curator of the display, Julia Van Zandvoort, about this remarkable piece.
- Van Eyck: The Portraits, National Gallery, London, 21 November-11 April 2027
- Cosimo I de’ Medici: Art and Dynasty, Wallace Collection, London, until 21 March 2027

https://www.propublica.org/article/snap-.title: How SNAP Theft Happens — and What to Do if It Happens to You
https://www.propublica.org/article/snap-.author: Cassandra Garibay, Eli Hager
https://www.propublica.org/article/snap-.text:
When Kelly Joly swiped her electronic benefits transfer card at a Kroger in Beaumont, Texas, this August, she was trying to buy groceries for herself and her teenage son. Joly had worked for decades as a waitress. The day before her grocery run, she’d received her monthly $530 in Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or food stamp, benefits, she said. But now, her EBT card was being declined. She tried swiping again and began to cry. The cashier told her that this had been happening a lot recently and suggested she report the issue. Joly stepped to the side and called Texas Health and Human Services as her food sat bagged up on the belt.
The representative at the agency that oversees SNAP in Texas told her there was nothing they could do to replace the funds, Joly recalled. Her benefits were gone, likely stolen by fraudsters. Joly said her account showed transactions from the day before at stores in Illinois, Minnesota and California.
“I don’t understand why they wouldn’t replace [our food assistance] if they can see that it was fraud,” she said. “And on top of that, how am I going to feed me and my son this month?”
Read More
If you receive SNAP benefits, Joly’s experience may sound all too familiar. Last year alone, more than $470 million was stolen from SNAP recipients by card scammers, affecting about 990,000 households.
ProPublica recently published an investigation into why Congress and the Trump administration have failed to crack down on SNAP theft despite promises to tackle fraud and waste in safety-net programs. As part of this reporting, we gathered detailed accounts from more than 50 people across 18 states who’ve had their benefits stolen in the past five years and reviewed dozens more messages, comments and social media posts from people who said they were targeted.
Many of the victims we heard from had similar questions: How did this happen? How can I prevent it from happening again? Why am I not being reimbursed? And why does it seem like little is being done to prevent these crimes in the first place?
We spoke with dozens of federal prosecutors, Secret Service agents, U.S. Department of Agriculture officials, caseworkers, food security advocates and other experts to help answer these questions for you.
How does SNAP theft happen?
Much of this crime is the work of low-level street operatives for transnational criminal organizations who install “skimming” devices on card readers at local grocery stores and bodegas. When you swipe your card, these devices capture your data off the magnetic strip on the back, as well as your PIN. That data is either picked up later or transmitted via Bluetooth to thieves waiting nearby.
Skimming is largely preventable via microchips and tap-to-pay technology, which have been greatly successful in reducing fraud in credit and debit card transactions for over a decade. But efforts to install these chips in EBT cards have moved much more slowly.
In recent years, criminals have also used random number generators, phishing calls and spam texts to steal people’s card information, and they will call state hotlines to try to check your SNAP balance and deposit date. In other instances, corner store owners themselves are in cahoots with these scammers, ringing up fake grocery purchases in exchange for cash. And in at least one prominent case, a federal SNAP employee gave sensitive data to criminals for them to be able to steal benefits.
What can I do to protect my benefits?
Unfortunately, due to the government’s inaction, the burden of protecting benefits from being stolen has largely been left up to you, the individual SNAP recipient. And the options are less than ideal.
Phone apps, like ebtEdge or Propel, allow you to keep careful track of your card balance, monitor your transaction history for any suspicious purchases and lock your card when it isn’t in use. These apps may also allow you to change your PIN and block out-of-state or online transactions.
But these aren’t always practical solutions, many victims told us. Remembering new PINs all the time, for example, isn’t easy, especially for older beneficiaries.
Cynthia Clark, a 63-year-old retired special education teacher in Jackson, Tennessee, said she has several health conditions that affect the dexterity of her hands, her vision and at times her speech. After her SNAP benefits were stolen in May, she was advised to lock her card every time she wasn’t using it. But she said her disabilities make using a cellphone incredibly difficult. On more than one occasion, she has locked herself out of her SNAP account trying to access her benefits.
“I was simply unable to do whatever the steps were, no matter how hard I tried,” she said.
Besides card locking and changing PINs, the Secret Service has suggested that people may be able to spot evidence of tampering with card readers at grocery stores. For example, if you look closely at the reader and see a noticeable gap between the keypad and the rest of the device, or if you see that something is blocking the light from under the keys, there may be a skimming device there.
What can I do after my benefits have been stolen?
If you’ve had your SNAP benefits stolen, you can report the theft to your state or local social services office — the agency where you applied for SNAP — or to the EBT card customer service line on the back of your card to receive a new card and change your PIN so thieves can’t continue to access your benefits.
You can also report the crime to local law enforcement and to the agency within your state in charge of investigating SNAP fraud — for example, in Texas, SNAP theft victims are advised to report it to the Texas Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General. (This map shows where to report SNAP fraud for each state).
A representative for Texas Health and Human Services said, “HHSC takes the security of our client’s benefits very seriously. SNAP card skimming has been a persistent problem across the country, including Texas.”
While there have been some large-scale investigations into SNAP theft, individual reports don’t often lead to an arrest. More than 40 of the victims we heard from said that they had reported their stolen benefits to a SNAP office, the EBT card customer service line, the police or all of the above. A handful also called the stores where they’d noticed unrecognized transactions on their card history, and two said they contacted the FBI. Most were told nothing could be done.
“I was told that I will receive another card in the mail and that I will not get the money back,” one person wrote us. “They took my statement but said they couldn’t help,” wrote another. “No one ever followed up,” said a third.
The main benefit of reporting these thefts is that doing so keeps the issue on the radar of SNAP officials. Many program administrators and caseworkers told us that they feel the urgency of this crisis precisely because so many people have been calling in about it.
Will my stolen benefits be replaced?
In all but two states (California and Maryland), your benefits will not be reimbursed.
The federal government had been reinstating stolen SNAP funds in all 50 states starting in late 2022. However, at the end of 2024, an effort to extend that reimbursement system was quashed after Elon Musk posted more than a hundred social media messages opposing legislation that included it, as the Department of Government Efficiency era began. (Musk did not reply to a previous request for comment.)
Democrats in Congress have proposed legislation to restart the reimbursement program. Following the recent midterm elections, they will take power in January.
How does law enforcement investigate SNAP theft?
As ProPublica has reported, the Secret Service devotes a lot of investigative resources to this issue, with teams going store to store around the country to manually check card readers for skimming devices. But that’s not a very efficient approach — it’s a little like playing whack-a-mole, multiple Secret Service agents told us.
Local cops and state prosecutors, meanwhile, are often overmatched, having neither the jurisdiction nor the technical chops to catch scammers who are constantly crossing county, state and international lines. And the feds, who do have the capacity to bring interstate conspiracy charges, haven’t always shown an interest in doing so, given that these are considered relatively low-level cases compared with the other types of crime that federal prosecutors work on.
As for caseworkers, most can’t offer concrete help. Several said that all they can do is provide a list of local food banks.
Will chip cards help prevent theft?
If your benefits were stolen, there’s a good chance they were skimmed. And the best solution to skimming appears to be tap-to-pay EBT cards with microchips.
In California, where chip cards were implemented independent of federal efforts, reported theft of SNAP and other benefits decreased by more than 80% within two years.
Following ProPublica’s reporting in October, the federal Department of Agriculture, which oversees SNAP, announced plans to require all 50 states to adopt more secure card technology. But overhauling the SNAP payment system could take years, as well as additional funding from Congress.
The chip card transition comes at a time when social benefits are being drastically cut and more of the financial weight of SNAP is being shifted to the states. Issuing these new cards is likely to cost states millions, involving complicated negotiations with EBT card companies like FIS and Conduent, which are essentially the Visa and Mastercard of SNAP. Grocery stores, bodegas and any places that accept EBT will also need to update their card reader systems. It will be mostly up to states to notify local stores about this and help them with it, which some, like California, Alabama and Oklahoma, have already tried to do.
Do You Administer SNAP or Medicaid Benefits? Help ProPublica Report on America’s Safety Net.
While ProPublica is no longer gathering information about people’s experiences with SNAP theft, we are still interested in learning more about America’s changing safety net. If you work to administer SNAP or Medicaid, we want to know how the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill is shaping your work and what you are seeing and hearing from the communities you serve.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Finding, acquiring and showing off: how rich buyers use social media to build art collections
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Aimee Dawson
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
How do major collectors use social media to help them navigate the art world? The latest Art Basel & UBS Survey of Global Collecting 2026 report, which surveyed 3,100 high net-worth individuals (HNWIs) who collect art, shows that social media platforms—and Instagram in particular—are an increasingly important tool for discovering art and artists, buying works and promoting collections. Here is how online platforms are being used and what the art world can learn from it.
Starting
While the most common routes into collecting according to the report were the influence of family (28% of respondents) and cultural exposure through visits to museums, galleries, and fairs (22%), a surprising 13% discovered art collecting independently through online channels or social media. Interestingly, online channels were a less common route into collecting for Gen Z collectors (10%) than for Gen X (16%), “running against any assumption that younger collectors might be more likely to find their way to collecting through digital channels”, the report says.
The data also shows that those who started their art collecting journey online had higher levels of engagement with in-person exhibitions and events, both locally and overseas. “While being introduced to art through family or cultural exposure may reflect a more passive route into collecting, those who started out online were typically more active in seeking out art content,” the report says. “This suggests a more deliberate, self-directed collecting journey that carries forward into greater engagement with events later on.”
Learning
When it comes to collecting, 58% of respondents said they had used digital resources for advice with 32% of collectors citing either Instagram or X (formerly Twitter) as sources when it came to making purchases. Nineteen percent used recommendations from Instagram (up 2% year-on-year), including 22% of Gen Z respondents, and women were more likely to use them than men. The platform X—which has seen decreased usage in recent years due to controversies around its ownership and usage—was used by 18% of the sample, and this was again highest among Gen Z (23%).
A collectors’ likeliness to use social media recommendations for collecting also depended greatly on where a person was from: collectors in Hong Kong, the US and the UK were most likely to use social media for advice while those in Mainland China were less likely, undoubtedly due to the restrictions of social media platforms in the country.
Contrary to popular belief around the slow uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) in the art world, the study also showed that collectors trusted AI tools for art recommendations twice as much as those from social media and influencers, and also slightly more than in-store advisors and editorial content.
Buying
The importance of online and social media platforms in reaching collectors is growing. According to the survey, 27% of HNWIs’ total expenditure was made through such external platforms, up by 5 percentage points year-on-year and from 17% in 2024. The share of collectors buying directly from artists also grew to 69%, with 38% of works bought via Instagram, highlighting the benefits of a strong, independent social media presence for artists. It is also interesting to note that artist-direct spending through Instagram was higher among new collectors than more experienced ones: 8% for those in the market for two years or less, versus just 2% for those collecting for 20 years or more.
But can seeing a work online really seal the deal? Apparently so—among the 75% of respondents who had purchased a work directly from a dealer in 2025/2026, 53% had bought via Instagram without viewing the work in person, up from 43% in 2024.
Sharing
The report interestingly states that the youngest generation of collectors—Gen Z—are not the ones using social media the most in their collecting journeys. “The generation raised on social media is, it turns out, the one most inclined to keep its collecting close,” the report says. While the data showed that Gen Z were the highest-spending generation surveyed and had the most wide-ranging collecting habits, their awareness of digital footprints leads them to seek greater control and privacy over their "personal and cultural identities".
“Anonymous accounts and smaller, niche social networking platforms allow them to communicate in ways that feel less pressurised and performative,” the report states. “With social media feeds heavily controlled and populated by algorithms rather than personal networks, Gen Z consumers are increasingly interested in taking back control over who sees their personal content by sharing it with smaller, vetted and carefully chosen audiences.”
When it came to sharing information about their collections with the wider public, only 25% Gen Z shared their own content publicly, compared with 36% of millennials and around one third of other older collectors.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Van Gogh’s record-breaking ‘Blossoming Chestnut Trees’: the $190m sale and the restitution claim that nearly upended it
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Martin Bailey
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees sold at Sotheby's New York on Wednesday night (18 November) for $190.4m, including fees. Auctioneer Oliver Barker began the sale by stating that “the work is being offered for sale pursuant to an agreement between the seller and the heirs of the Hedwig and Samuel Fischer family”. The Fischer family had sold the painting in 1936.
The auction of the Van Gogh opened at $135m, two telephone bidders coming in. A third bidder, in the saleroom, won the contest after less than four minutes, at a hammer price of $165m. He is the New York dealer William Acquavella, presumably acting for an unidentified client.
Before the auction, Sotheby’s had not announced a formal estimate range, but instead suggested that the painting should fetch a hammer price of around $180m (before fees). This may have been slightly optimistic, since it was far more than any Van Gogh has ever made. Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (May 1890) is a fine landscape, although not among his very best. And the other 11 pictures in last night’s auction of the Blaquier-Arrieta collection generally sold for around, or even below, their lower estimates.
The uncertainty last weekend over a possible Nazi-era claim for the Van Gogh may have discouraged some potential bidders, but the $190m (including fees) was nonetheless an astonishing result. This was for an artist who had failed to sell during his own lifetime. Van Gogh completed nearly a thousand paintings in his career, with only a single recorded sale: The Red Vineyard (November 1888, Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, Moscow).
Only three artworks have ever sold for more at auction: Leonardo’s Salvator Mundi (around 1500, $450m, Christie’s, 2017), Gustav Klimt’s Portrait of Elisabeth Lederer (1916, $236m, Sotheby’s, 2025) and Andy Warhol’s Shot Sage Blue Marilyn (1964, $195m, Christie’s, 2022).
The previous record price for a Van Gogh was $117m (including fees) for Orchard with Cypresses (April 1888), which Christie’s sold in 2022. The Blossoming Chestnut Trees price was 62% more.
Nazi-era shadow
Sotheby’s has been open about Blossoming Chestnut Trees’s Nazi-era (1933-45) provenance. Following our inquiries, we reported in our 2 October blog post: “It was purchased four years later [in 1926] by the Berlin-based publisher Samuel Fischer, and on his death in 1934 it passed to his daughter Brigitte. Although the family was persecuted because of their Jewish heritage, a Sotheby’s spokesperson confirmed to us that, based on recent research, the family was free at all times to dispose of the painting.”
News of a possible Nazi-era claim emerged only five weeks later. Berlin-based Gunnar Schnabel, who describes himself as a “looted art researcher” specialising in the Nazi period, told the New York Times that he first heard about the sale on 7 November, when he was “lying on a sofa in his vacation home”. His letter to Sotheby’s calling for the sale to be delayed was sent on 12 November, just six days before the auction. Obviously this put Sotheby’s in a very awkward situation: should the sale be postponed or go ahead?
In response, Sotheby’s stated: “We are aware of the persecution experienced by the Fischer family. After the Anschluss in 1938, the family fled Austria, and the Gestapo confiscated their Vienna home, library and remaining art collection. But the circumstances around this transaction were different”. The auction house also added that after the war, no claim was ever made for the Van Gogh.
Urgent negotiations were held with the representatives of the Fischer family. The key question at stake was whether their ancestors had been the victim of a forced sale at a lower than market value. By June 1936, when the Van Gogh was sold, the family had just moved to Vienna. They had consigned the painting to the Cassirer gallery in Amsterdam several years earlier, in 1932-33. The price eventually paid in 1936 by the buyer, Paris-based collectors Henriette and Marcel Kapferer, was $22,000.
Comparisons with other Van Gogh sales around the time are telling. In 1935, the year before the Fischer sale, Orchard with Cypresses had sold for $15,000 at the New York auction house Parke Bernet (this was the painting which later fetched a record Van Gogh price in 2022). That makes the $22,000 seem reasonable.
Then there is the Sunflowers (August 1888), which had been sold to London's National Gallery in 1924 for the equivalent of $5,800. Although this sale took place 12 years before Blossoming Chestnut Trees and Jo Bonger, Vincent’s sister-in-law, probably reduced the price for a major museum, it is now regarded as Van Gogh’s greatest masterpiece. This again suggests that the Fischers received a reasonable sum for their picture.
Following yesterday’s Sotheby’s auction, Schnabel told The Art Newspaper that the Fischers had also been supported by the Commission for Looted Art in Europe's co-chair Anne Webber. He added that the family is delighted that Blossoming Chestnut Trees “which hung in the Berlin home of Samuel and Hedwig Fischer for a quarter of a century, has now found a new owner”. They hope this case “may offer some encouragement to other families who have faced persecution during the Nazi era, and that they, too, may find a path toward the recognition of their rightful claims.”
The terms of the 17 November settlement between the heirs of the Fischer family and the Blaquier-Arrieta family remain confidential. Presumably some sort of financial compensation has been paid. The agreement opens the door for the Fischer heirs to make claims for further paintings which had once been in their family if they come onto the market in the future.
As a postscript on the 1930s story of Blossoming Chestnut Trees, soon after the Kapferers bought the picture they lent it to an exhibition in London, Artists who Died Young at the Leicester Galleries in 1938. A year after the London exhibition, war broke out. Blossoming Chestnut Trees had been sent to the United States a few months earlier to New York dealers Wildenstein & Co and, after passing through two American private collections, it went to Argentina in 1975, to the Blaquier-Arrieta family. Following the Sotheby’s sale, it remains a mystery where the Van Gogh will ultimately reside.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Five Ethiopian artefacts restituted in London ceremony
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Martin Bailey
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Five historic Christian artefacts were restituted to the Ethiopian Heritage Authority in a ceremony at the country’s London embassy on Wednesday (18 November). The process was part of a wider initiative by the American collector Robert McCarthy and the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio that is expected to see many more objects returned to Ethiopia.
McCarthy, an American financier who used to live in London and now resides in East Asia, has long been a serious collector of European medieval art. He broadened his collection in the 1990s to include Ethiopian art, at a time when there was less concern about provenance. In 2023-24 he lent objects to the exhibition Ethiopia at the Crossroads, which was presented in venues in Baltimore, Salem in Massachusetts and Toledo. It was at Toledo that he began discussions with Sophie Ong, assistant director of strategic initiatives, about the future of his collection.
This eventually led to the new, complex arrangement. Toledo will acquire McCarthy’s 375 Ethiopian objects, one of the largest such private collections. Two thirds will be donated and the remainder bought. Some of this material will be exhibited when the museum’s galleries reopen in autumn 2027 after a major reinstallation of its permanent collection.
The museum then intends to return much of the collection to Ethiopia, in tranches over the next 20 years. Any items deemed to have left Ethiopia illegally or inappropriately will be restituted. Details have not been released, but it is assumed that this will include looted material seized by British troops at the 1869 battle of Maqdala and which later came onto the international art market.
Objects judged to have been exported properly will remain at the Toledo museum. Stewardship of items with an indeterminate status will be decided jointly by the Toledo museum and Ethiopian officials. It is thought that ultimately half of McCarthy’s 375 items may be returned.
The unusual tripartite arrangement between McCarthy, the Toledo museum and the Ethiopia authorities could prove to be a template for dealing with restitution claims by other African countries. At the handover, Alula Pankhurst, speaking on behalf of the Ethiopian Heritage Authority, described it as “a new model of partnership”.
Five historic artefacts
This week’s restitution of five objects to the government’s Ethiopian Heritage Authority is slightly different, in that they have been directly returned by McCarthy. The Toledo museum was unwilling to accession them because of records suggesting that they had left Ethiopia after the 1970 Unesco convention.
The items are two 15th-century illuminated manuscripts and three processional crosses. All are believed to have been improperly removed from Ethiopian churches.
The earliest of the two manuscripts is a Book of Revelation with a Horologium (daily cycle of prayers). It includes seven full-page illuminations, dating from around 1400. The volume was recorded in the late 20th century as being in the Saqqā Madḫānē Ālam Church in Šawā Province.
The other manuscript is a large mid-15th century Gospels, which includes full-page images of the Four Evangelists. The scholar Diana Spencer noted in a 1974 article that she saw it at the church of Emmaus Giyor near Wafa Yasus.
The three brass processional crosses being returned date variously from the late-18th to early-20th centuries. Each has incised inscriptions which may make it possible to determine which church they came from.
The five returned objects are now being sent from London to the National Museum of Ethiopia in Addis Ababa, where a new display of restituted material is scheduled to open in December. Most of the rest of the display will be material which had been looted at Maqdala.
However, the forthcoming Addis Ababa display may feed into a debate over whether religious items that can be identified with a particular location should be retained in the National Museum or returned to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.

Ten countries in the European Union have urged the European Commission to keep Russia out of Venice’s 2027 architecture biennale. The effort is led by Poland and includes Austria, Croatia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, and Sweden. The countries say that allowing Russia to participate normalizes its actions in Ukraine.
Russia participated in this year’s Venice Biennale for the first time since 2022, despite financial pressure from the European Commission and protests from several EU countries and activist groups like Pussy Riot and FEMEN. The EU terminated a €2 million grant to the Biennale because of Russia’s involvement. The Biennale said in a statement at the time that it “rejects any form of exclusion or censorship of culture and art.”
The EU is preparing its twenty-second package of sanctions against Russia, expected before the end of the year. EU foreign ministers have called for it to include even tighter visa restrictions for Russians and a ban on Russian athletes competing in sporting events in the EU. The group of ten countries wrote a diplomatic note laying out its concerns ahead of a November 19 meeting of EU culture ministers.
“In light of the current geopolitical realities… there should be no room for ‘normalization’ of Russia’s participation in international sporting and cultural events, as long as there is no just and lasting peace in Ukraine,” the countries said in the note. The architecture biennale will take place from May to November of next year. The Venice Biennale has not yet said whether Russia is expected to participate.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Russian strikes damage historic buildings in Kyiv and Odesa, including World Heritage sites
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Sophia Kishkovsky
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Multiple heritage sites in Ukraine were damaged by Russian strikes on 19 and 20 November, including the Unesco-listed St Michael’s Golden-Domed Cathedral and Monastery complex and St Volodymyr’s Cathedral in Kyiv, known for its frescoes, as well as 12 cultural heritage sites in Odesa, the strategic port city on the Black Sea, which was hit a day earlier. The entire historic centre of Odesa was added to Unesco’s list of endangered World Heritage sites in 2023.
At least nine people were killed in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine during the hours-long attack on 20 November.
“Today, Russian drones damaged one of the most famous monuments of our country, the Volodymyr Cathedral,” Tetyana Berezhna, Ukraine’s deputy prime minister for humanitarian policy and minister of culture, wrote in a Facebook post on 19 November after the cathedral in Kyiv was hit, breaking windows and frames and causing “some damage to the paintings and structural elements”.
The neo-Byzantine St Volodymyr Cathedral, built in the 19th century, is under the jurisdiction of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (OCU), which broke with the Moscow Patriarchate and was granted autocephaly by Constantinople in 2018. Three of Russia’s most famous artists of the 19th century and early 20th century—Viktor Vasnetsov, Mikhail Vrubel and Mikhail Nesterov—created religious art for St Volodymyr’s, as did the Ukrainian artist Mykola Pymomenko, a teacher of Kazimir Malevich.
The Austrian embassy, located next-door to St Volodymyr's Cathedral, was also damaged. Kyiv's municipal cultural heritage department published an inventory of damage from the attack, which also includes the embassy of the Netherlands.
A Russian drone was shot down over St Michael’s, which is the headquarters of the OCU, on 19 November.
Berezhna’s post cites the cumulative damage from Russia’s accelerating attacks: “Since the beginning of this year, the number of monuments damaged by Russia has increased by more than a third, and by the end of October it was almost 2,200. Almost 2,700 cultural institutions were also affected.”
The minister was in Lutsk, a historic city in northwestern Ukraine, this week to plan for a conference marking the 600th anniversary in 2029 of the Congress of Lutsk, which brought together the regional monarchies of the time. A Russian strike on Lutsk in October damaged Ukraine’s largest painting, Cosmogony, a 2,000 sq. m work by the contemporary artist Petro Antyp.
Unesco has condemned the latest attacks, especially on Odesa, “which hit the centre of the city, within the boundaries of the World Heritage property ‘The Historic Centre of Odesa’” and “reportedly caused damage to several heritage buildings, including the Kalio Palace, a monument of national importance,” according to a statement released by the organisation. The Kalio Palace, built in 1834, is attributed to the Swiss Italian architect Giorgio Torricelli.
The strikes came amid escalating tensions and a diplomatic chasm that appears to be widening. The Russian President Vladimir Putin said this week that the Kremlin would not negotiate any partial ceasefire or deal with Ukraine after it struck and incapacitated the Kerch Bridge linking mainland Russia to Crimea, a symbol of Russia’s annexation of the Black Sea peninsula in 2014, on 16 and 17 November. At the same time, US President Donald Trump claimed that peace, largely on Russia’s terms, is within reach and reportedly urged European leaders to stop funding weapons for Ukraine. Trump, Putin and the Chinese President Xi Jinping signed a “peace declaration” on 20 November at a trilateral summit hosted by Xi in Shenzhen, China.
A petition to “safeguard Ukraine’s cultural heritage and artistic integrity” was launched last month by the curator Konstantin Akinsha and Bjorn Geldof, the artistic director at Kyiv’s PinchukArtCentre. It calls “for immediate sanctions and the suspension of Russian state participation in international cultural events”. Rapporteur, a Brussels-based policy publication, reported this week that ten European countries are seeking to keep Russia out of the 2027 Architecture Biennale. Russia’s participation in the 2026 Venice Biennale set off a series of protests.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Mamdani Officials Defend Response to Deadly Lithium-Ion Battery Fires
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Claudia Irizarry Aponte
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
The City Council is once again debating a slate of bills to step up safety and rein in the sale and distribution of uncertified lithium-ion batteries commonly used for powering e-bikes that have led to a surge in deadly fires across the city.
The Council has already approved a raft of reforms granting the Fire Department greater power to crack down on illegal battery sales and to speed up inspections. On Thursday night, the U.S. Senate unanimously approved a bill sponsored by New York Sens. Chuck Schumer and Kristen Gillibrand to stem the sale of unsafe e-bike batteries.
But the rate of fires has continued a steady climb across the five boroughs since 2022 in spite of local reforms. At the hearing on Friday, officials from the Fire Department defended its record to the palpable frustration of Julie Menin, the Council speaker.
“I asked for an emergency hearing because we are in an emergency. The numbers in terms of fatalities, injuries are just completely unacceptable. This is a crisis of epic proportions,” said Menin. “The Council has passed bill after bill after bill and yet the problem is getting worse, not better.”
Calls for Public Education
Fire Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said that without curbing illegal sales, there is little officials can do to prevent fires without greater education for the public about how to safely vet, charge and store lithium-ion batteries.
“We do understand how big a problem this is, but this is a technology that more people are now starting to engage with,” said Bonsignore. “So I think we have to accept that this is a changing technology and it’s putting us in a very difficult place as it emerges and standards start to become something that will make it safer. But education is by far, I think, one of the most important things we can do — and we need to do this in every language.”
Fire officials testified alongside representatives from the housing and buildings departments. While previous hearings on the issue of lithium-ion battery safety have attracted large crowds eager to speak directly to lawmakers, on Friday only about two dozen members of the public were in attendance at the Council’s main chambers in City Hall, a handful of app-based delivery workers among them.
Faulty lithium-ion batteries have ignited 408 fires resulting in nine deaths so far this year, including a fire at a South Bronx public housing development that killed four people and another weeks later at a Sunset Park home that killed six. The cause of the latter fire has not yet officially been determined, but fire officials confirmed at the time that two charred e-bikes were removed from the burnt structure.
The Council heard seven bills on Friday to restrict the sale, distribution and possession of lithium-ion batteries that do not meet existing federal standards and to step-up the Fire Department’s investigation and reporting capabilities.
The only bill that fire officials explicitly endorsed on Friday, sponsored by Brooklyn Councilmember Susan Zhuang, lowers the threshold for the city’s consumer watchdog agency to shut down stores that sell the illegal batteries. The Department of Consumer and Worker Protection currently shut down stores after three violations; Zhuang’s bill would reduce that threshold to two strikes.
Stores that sell, store, and maintain e-bikes and related equipment cater mostly to the city’s vast community of app-based delivery workers, many of whom are immigrants living in the outer boroughs. The main group representing these workers, Los Deliveristas Unidos, have long said their own members are the ones most at-risk by the technology, a reality that fire officials have long acknowledged.
The fire department and worker groups have long taken pains to address proper safety measures for storing and maintaining e-bikes and e-bike batteries — including by hosting training sessions, battery swaps, and lessons on how to identify UL-certified equipment.
On Thursday, Councilmember Shaun Abreu introduced a bill, with the mayor’s support, that would make companies like UberEats and DoorDash responsible for ensuring workers use safe equipment.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: Dmitri Kasterine obituary
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Greg Whitmore
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
In 1963, the photographer Dmitri Kasterine heard that Stanley Kubrick was in London filming Dr Strangelove. Kasterine was a fan, so he approached the editor of Queen magazine and successfully pitched a feature on the director at work. Kubrick noticed him on set and said: “Would you like to come and work for me? You stand in the right place.”
Kasterine worked for Kubrick from 1963 to 1971, taking the stills on Dr Strangelove, 2001: A Space Odyssey and A Clockwork Orange. Kubrick taught the photographer the importance of courage, patience and perseverance.
These lessons supplemented his photographic craft, honed since the beginning of the 1960s, creating a style that led to Kasterine, who has died aged 94, becoming one of the most significant portrait photographers of the 70s and 80s. He photographed James Baldwin, Michael Caine, Patricia Highsmith, Martin and Kingsley Amis, Tom Stoppard and Queen Elizabeth II for Harpers & Queen, Vogue, the BBC’s Radio Times and the Daily Telegraph magazine.
In his work, Kasterine wanted to “avoid the conventional” and prevent the sitter from “putting on a polite face”. He utilised his gentlemanly charm and elegance, putting the subject at ease before turning away, pretending to adjust his equipment, ignoring the sitter – attempting to catch them off guard, thus revealing something of themselves. This approach unveiled vulnerability in Dirk Bogarde, discomfort in Samuel Beckett and boredom in Muriel Spark.
In an interview with the reporter Bradley Towle, Kasterine said: “I look for something that gives me a shock. I look for something that has unusual elements. It could be what they’re wearing; it could be the background. It could be just an expression. I don’t really look for it, it comes to me.”
As well as his acclaimed portraits of the literati, he took great pride in a personal project undertaken between 1996 and 2018 in his adopted home of New York state. He had become fascinated with the city of Newburgh on the Hudson River, which, from being awarded the title of All American City by Look magazine in 1952, had become, by the 1990s, blighted by recession, corruption and racism. He set about to capture the decaying splendour of the city and, more importantly, the dignity of the overlooked, predominantly Black community that called it home.
In the introduction to his 2012 book, Newburgh: Portrait of a City, Kasterine wrote: “This is a record of uncelebrated and ignored people … But in the ruins of the buildings and in the faces of the people I see warmth and beauty, and in some of the faces a determination to change things.” Three years later, Kasterine filmed a documentary, Newburgh: Beauty and Tragedy. The city embraced his work, and 44 of his Newburgh portraits were mounted on the exterior of its Ritz theatre, from 2012 to 2026.
His photographs are held by the Royal Collection Trust and the National Portrait Gallery in London, and the Smithsonian Institution’s National Portrait Gallery in Washington DC.
Dmitri’s father, Nicolas Kasterine, had served in the Russian Imperial Guard and was the aide-de-camp to the Grand Duke Dmitri Pavlovich, who was involved in the assassination of Grigori Rasputin. Having fought the Bolsheviks in the 1917 revolution, Nicolas escaped Russia via Finland, bringing with him a large, uncut diamond, which, when in London, he sold to buy a suit and a sports car. There, Nicolas married Katherine White, the daughter of an insurance broker, and the young couple socialised with other Russian émigrés in Paris, Monte Carlo (where Dmitri’s elder sister, Irina, was born), and London.
The young family then settled in the village of Kemsing, near Sevenoaks, Kent, where Dmitri was born, named after his godfather, the grand duke. Kasterine’s parents divorced in 1935, and Katherine took her two children to live outside the village of Westerham, also in Kent. Nicolas died in a car crash the following year.
The second world war was a frightening experience for the sensitive Dmitri. Being close to Biggin Hill aerodrome, Westerham was frequently bombed by the Luftwaffe, and on his eighth birthday, bombs fell so close that the house was badly damaged.
When the air raids stopped, Katherine put up a bird table outside the kitchen window. Dmitri wanted to photograph the birds, so his mother bought him a camera. He built a dark room and excitedly developed the film. When he saw that the birds were pinpricks in the frame, he burst into tears. Undeterred, he moved on to cows in the fields, with excellent results.
After the war, Dmitri was sent to board at Radley college in Oxfordshire, where he remained until 1950. It was while at school that he learned of his mother’s death in a riding accident in 1948. He was just 15.
After leaving Radley and working briefly as a wine merchant and then for Lloyd’s of London, Kasterine, who had inherited a love of fast cars from his father, took up motor racing. In 1956, he suffered a life-threatening injury when the Lotus-Bristol racing car he was driving at the Aintree International meeting overturned and crashed through the safety barrier. A friend visited while he was recovering in hospital and suggested he take up flying. He did, and for a while he worked as a commercial pilot flying to Australia.
On a stopover in Karachi, Kasterine photographed the breaking-in of a young thoroughbred. Pleased with the result, and frightened of flying, Kasterine decided to take up photography professionally.
In London from 1961, Kasterine shared a studio with the photographer Michael Wallis, who mentored both Kasterine and their dark-room assistant, Patrick Lichfield. Dmitri hustled for work from magazines and sought out public figures to request a sitting, and his career took off.
In 1981 his first book, England and the English, was published. This gentle collection of portraits, daily life and landscapes was a swansong to the bucolic ideal of his native land. He needed a new challenge.
He had been to the US once, to photograph Mick Jagger in Los Angeles in 1975, and had visited New York City on the way home. He liked it, and moved there in 1984. There, he shot celebrated portraits of art-world luminaries such as Jean-Michel Basquiat, Roy Lichtenstein and Cindy Sherman, and commissions for the Sunday New York Times.
In his later years Kasterine moved to Garrison, in the wilds of New York state, with his second wife, Caroline (nee Cristofalo), whom he had married in 1988. There he took pictures of farmers and people who loved horses, and in 2021 he published a collection of his work, Who How When Where. After seven decades taking photographs, he was, he told Towle, still “… always on the lookout … It’s very difficult to explain exactly why and wherefore I take a picture, but it’s a silence; it’s a tap on the shoulder.”
He is survived by Caroline and their son, Nicholas; his children, Alexander and Cathy, from his 1963 marriage to Elizabeth Dickson, which ended in divorce, a daughter, Lucie, from a relationship with Frances Pemberton, and six grandchildren.

https://citylimits.org/advocates-sue-ove.title: Advocates Sue Over Federal Rule Threatening Aid for Mixed-Status Immigrant Families, And What Else Happened This Week in Housing
https://citylimits.org/advocates-sue-ove.author: Jeanmarie Evelly
https://citylimits.org/advocates-sue-ove.text:
Share This Article
A NYCHA residents’ association is among the plaintiffs challenging the federal rule, which advocates say could force thousands of families to separate or lose their housing assistance.
A coalition of public housing residents and immigrant advocates filed a federal class action lawsuit Thursday challenging a Trump administration rule that could force thousands of families with mixed immigration status to choose between staying together and keeping their federally subsidized homes.
The lawsuit, filed Thursday in U.S. District Court in Massachusetts, seeks to block a new U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) rule scheduled to take effect Dec. 14. The plaintiffs argue that the regulation violates federal housing law and constitutional protections.
Plaintiffs include the Alfred E. Smith Houses Resident Association, representing tenants at a New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) development in Lower Manhattan. According to the complaint, 16 of the development’s 1,876 households have mixed immigration statuses and could face displacement under the rule.
The legal challenge follows HUD’s announcement of the final regulation on Nov. 10, which would require members of households that receive federal housing assistance through programs like Section 8 and Section 9 to verify their U.S. citizenship or eligible immigration status.
Under existing law, mixed status households can receive reduced federal rental assistance based on the number of eligible family members. Those who do not qualify for subsidies can still live with eligible relatives, including children who are U.S. citizens.
The new rule would end the longstanding arrangement allowing mixed status families to receive prorated assistance indefinitely, potentially forcing households to separate or give up their rental aid. As City Limits previously reported, approximately 2,500 New York households could be affected by the changes.
Among those challenging the rule is a Honduran woman identified in the complaint as Jane Doe #2, who has lived in the United States since 2009. She resides in New York City with her husband, a lawful permanent resident, and their three U.S. born daughters.
The family has lived in a federally subsidized Section 8 apartment for nine years. Although the woman has been authorized to live and work in the country since receiving U nonimmigrant status in 2022, it does not qualify her for federal housing assistance under the law cited in the complaint.
According to the lawsuit, the family cannot afford market rate housing in New York City. The plaintiffs argue that the rule could force the woman to leave the apartment or cause the entire family to lose their home.
The lawsuit also challenges new documentation requirements that would apply to recipients of federal housing assistance, not just mixed status households. The plaintiffs argue that the requirements could disrupt benefits for eligible tenants, particularly elderly and disabled residents who may have difficulty obtaining the necessary records.
Nationwide, roughly 80,000 people, including approximately 36,000 eligible children, could face displacement under the regulation, according to estimates cited in the complaint.
In a statement provided to City Limits, HUD Secretary Scott Turner defended the change saying it fully implements the Housing and Community Development Act of 1980.
“This rule guarantees ONLY AMERICAN citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD funded housing,” Turner said.
He added that the change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million in housing assistance to eligible Americans currently on waiting lists.
The plaintiffs dispute HUD’s interpretation of federal law, arguing that Congress explicitly authorized reduced subsidies for mixed status households. They are seeking a court order declaring the rule unlawful and preventing its implementation next month.
Housing lawyers who spoke to City Limits earlier this week urged households potentially impacted by the change to stay put.
“People need to know that until it goes into effect, nothing has changed,” said Lucy Newman, the supervising attorney of Legal Aid Society’s public housing unit. “They should not move, or evict out of fear.”
Here’s what else happened this week in housing—
ICYMI, from City Limits:
- For the first time, NYCHA is using a federal program called Section 32 to repair 91 single-family to four-family houses—opening a path for public housing residents to buy their homes.
- A career training program for the city’s public housing residents is getting $1 million from an unusual source: Kalshi, the prediction market company recently sued by New York State for allegedly operating as an illegal and unlicensed gambling platform.
- All but one building in a portfolio of properties that recently went to foreclosure auction failed to receive any bids, raising alarm about the health of the city’s rent-stabilized housing. Tenants, and the mayor’s office, hope to steer the buildings to a buyer they say will work to preserve them.
ICYMI, from other local newsrooms:
- The city is suing a landlord for evading fines and failing to make building repairs under a local fraud law, what City Hall described as a novel tactic to hold bad property owners accountable, according to Gothamist.
- Astoria residents are opposing proposals for three new apartment buildings on Steinway Street, the Queens Eagle reports.
- The city is billing 7,500 households under the new pied-à-terre tax on expensive second homes, what officials say will raise $500 million, according to The City Reporter.
- The Mamdani administration shuttered its last remaining migrant shelter in the Bronx this week, potentially stymying a a subpoena from the Trump administration demanding the city disclose the names of undocumented immigrants with criminal records who lived there, the New York Times reports.

https://inthesetimes.com/article/midterm.title: After a Midterm Feat, the Left Now Faces a Staggering Test
https://inthesetimes.com/article/midterm.author: Branko Marcetic
https://inthesetimes.com/article/midterm.text:
After a Midterm Feat, the Left Now Faces a Staggering Test
Swept into power by November’s midterm elections, progressives and socialists are tasked with pushing a reluctant Democratic Party establishment to enact real change—or risk squandering a historic victory
Branko Marcetic
Two days after President Donald Trump and the GOP’s historic drubbing in the midterms, Corbin Trent, in the midst of a post-election media blitz, admits, “I feel terrified.”
It’s not the reaction you’d expect from someone like Trent, a campaign staffer on both of Sen. Bernie Sanders’ (I-Vt.) presidential runs and a co-founder of Justice Democrats, the progressive group that saw eight of its candidates swept into Congress on the blue wave that crashed across the United States on Nov. 3.
And yet for Trent and many on the Left, winning the election was the easy part. Trump and his authoritarian administration are still in the White House, and the Left now needs to prove that Democrats can deliver for the working class.
In the week following the midterms, the historic scale of Democrats’ rout of Republicans came into sharper focus: the largest Congressional majority in nearly two decades, secured by the widest popular-vote margin in 50 years and the biggest single-election flip in the Senate in nearly 70 years.
And at the state level, more than 500 legislative seats flipped to give the party six additional trifectas and a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010. Roughly 75% of U.S. residents will have Democratic governors, including residents of Texas, where a 24-year Republican trifecta has come to an end.
Democrats will now control the U.S. House of Representatives and the Senate, and the party plans to make use of its newfound electoral power.
It’s a loss for the U.S. Right that has left the movement and the Republican Party shell-shocked. After the presidential election two years ago, Republicans believed they had forged a new, lasting working-class majority after big swings toward Trump from nearly every demographic group, even those the party had previously struggled with: youth, Latinos and Black voters.
Two years later, those voters swung back. Other than white evangelicals, every single voter group saw a major shift towards the Democrats, nearly all of them by double digits — including Trump’s stalwart base of white voters without a college degree, who swung 14 points towards the Democrats, a trend seen across nearly every state. The Republican politicians ousted by the blue wave included decades-long incumbents, such as Ohio Rep. Mike Turner, who had been in office for 24 years, and GOP leaders including National Republican Congressional Committee chair Rep. Richard Hudson (R-N.C.).
The outcome wasn’t just good for Democrats — it was the best electoral result for the U.S. Left in more than a century. Eight years after Congress gave Trump a standing ovation for saying the United States “will never be a socialist country,” the House will include eight members of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), along with at least 12 other progressives who ran on agendas and campaigns in the style of “the Squad” — the Sanders-inspired progressive bloc. The Democrats’ Senate majority will feature one socialist in Sanders, 18 others who co-sponsored his Medicare for All bill, and three incoming, Sanders-backed progressives who campaigned on universal, single-payer healthcare.
Progressive organizations like the Working Families Party (WFP), whose candidate endorsements often overlapped with those of DSA, saw their best-ever results, with the WFP claiming 16 new members of Congress and two senators, as well as more than a hundred new state legislators, 38 of whom flipped GOP-held districts. By contrast, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) fell flat on its face, blowing 66% of the estimated $84 million it spent in the midterms on losing races.
“Breaking from Israel was way out of the mainstream of political discourse just a few years ago,” says Joe Dinkin, WFP’s national campaigns director.
The Left may have finally put to bed the perennial charge made by its critics: that progressives and socialists can only win in deeply blue states and even bluer districts, and are a risk to run anywhere else.
Instead, progressives won in red and purple areas across the country. Two separate union leaders and firefighters endorsed by Sanders flipped red districts: Bob Brooks in Pennsylvania’s 7th District, and Sam Forstag in Montana’s solidly red 1st District, who will now be the first Democrat to represent the state in the U.S. House in more than 30 years. Another Sanders endorsee, Rebecca Cooke, a waitress with a background as a Democratic consultant, flipped Wisconsin’s mostly rural, Trump-voting 3rd District. They are just three of what will be a contingent of at least 21 Democrats in the next Congress with working-class backgrounds, ten of whom won their elections for the first time this cycle.
After California redistricting turned the 22nd District from deeply red to a toss-up, Sanders-endorsed candidate Randy Villegas knocked out a six-term incumbent by more than 35 points in a race that focused on Trump’s Medicaid cuts. With next to no national help, badly outspent DSA member Angie Nixon came within three points of taking a Senate seat in Florida, outperforming her Republican opponent in Miami-Dade County — an assumed anti-socialist stronghold in a state known for its hostility to left-wing candidates.
And progressive epidemiologist Abdul El-Sayed won his Senate race in the battleground state of Michigan by seven points, the same state where Sunrise Movement co-founder Will Lawrence flipped what former Michigan Rep. Andy Levin calls “the purplest district in a super important purple state.”
“Quit this line that you have to have a centrist to win,” Levin tells In These Times. “People don’t care about left and right, they care about top and bottom.”
Despite the historic results, there is a reason that some on the Left, such as Corbin Trent, aren’t celebrating just yet. Over the last 20 years, the U.S. voting public has ricocheted from one party to the other in a desperate search for fundamental political change. Progressives are keenly aware that they could just as easily be thrown out in a few years’ time.
“If the new crop of Democrats who just got elected and others don’t understand that this was a rebuke of the status quo, and not an embrace of the Democratic Party,” Trent tells In These Times, “then we’re not going to be able to take advantage of what I think is a generational opportunity.”
Moving left
It’s not just that more progressives are entering Congress. It’s that the Democratic Party as a whole has become more progressive across the board. Perhaps nothing illustrates this shift better than Texas, where four-term state representative and Presbyterian minister-in-training James Talarico became the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in 38 years.
Talarico, a progressive viewed by nearly half of all Texas voters as “very liberal,” ran a campaign railing against billionaires, vowing to end the “reckless war” in Iran, framing America’s true divide as “top versus bottom,” and touting a public health insurance option and universal pre-K. He won by 12 points. 
Talarico’s messaging wasn’t unique. This year, the two issues Democrats spent the most on— $732 million, or 47% of the party’s ad spending — were affordability and healthcare.
In red state after red state, winning candidates publicly refused corporate PAC money and framed their races around rhetoric that once saw Sanders condemned by Congressional Democrats for waging “class warfare.”
In Iowa, Democrat Josh Turek won a Senate seat after repeatedly linking his opponent to “billionaires and large corporations.” In Mississippi, Scott Colom, the first Democrat to win a Senate race in the state since 1982, pilloried his opponent for voting to strip Mississippians of health insurance in order to send money to the “millionaires and billionaires.” In South Carolina, Senate winner Annie Andrews promised she would “not sell out to big money or take any corporate PAC money.” And in Ohio, populist Sherrod Brown won his Senate seat by leaning into rhetoric around “workers” versus “billionaires,” and running multiple ads hitting his opponent for taking money from one of convicted sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein’s ultrarich associates.
Five different Democrats have failed to unseat “moderate” Maine Republican Senator Susan Collins over the past three decades, including the former Maine House speaker Sara Gideon, who outraised Collins more than two-to-one, only to lose to her by nine points in 2020. The Democrat who finally beat her was Troy Jackson, a fifth-generation logger who ran ads highlighting his modest, working-class roots and attacked Collins over her alleged corruption and support for both Trump and the Iran war. Collins, meanwhile, garnered backlash for a personal attack on Jackson’s family and for running an ill-advised ad suggesting his background as a woodworker meant he wasn’t up to the job of senator.
But arguably no race had bigger stakes than the mini intraparty civil war that played out in Michigan, a key swing state in the Trump era, where El-Sayed became the first left-wing candidate to win a statewide general election with a purple electorate.
Sanders’ upset win in Michigan’s 2016 primary was written off by many pundits as simply a product of anti-Hillary Clinton sentiment, a narrative pushed by establishment voices who insisted it was too risky to nominate progressives and socialists outside of coastal, deep-blue strongholds. “The factor that actually explains 2016,” moderate commentator Jonathan Chait wrote in 2020, pointing to the Michigan result, “was Hillary Clinton’s idiosyncratic personal unpopularity.”
Every Michigan election that followed seemed to bear that belief out: El-Sayed’s own first, failed 2018 gubernatorial run; Sanders’ dramatic underperformance in the 2020 primary; and CIA analyst Elissa Slotkin’s knife’s-edge, 0.3-point win over former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers in the state’s 2024 Senate race. 
El-Sayed’s 2026 race against Rogers didn’t just seek to keep the Trump loyalist out of the Senate a second time; it was also a challenge to the narrative about what kind of Democrat could win. And it came at a time when the Israeli government’s genocide in Gaza had transformed the politics of U.S.-Israeli relations nationwide, particularly within the Democratic Party.
“Being able to call it what it is, and to have the moral courage to stand up for that, was a litmus test for people,” Adam Hamawy, a doctor who served in Gaza and saw the horrors of U.S. weapons first-hand, tells In These Times. Hamawy won a heated Democratic primary for a New Jersey House seat in June, and went on to win the general election on Nov. 3.
In addition to campaigning on Medicare for All and taxing the rich, El-Sayed ran as an outspoken critic of Israel. As a result, his campaign served as a test case for AIPAC’s claim that unconditional U.S. support for Israel was politically necessary.
“I don’t think anyone has ever run as a major party nominee for the U.S. Senate and said, ‘Not only am I against offensive aid to Israel, I’m against defensive aid like Iron Dome and related programs,’” says Levin.
With so much on the line, the forces traditionally arrayed against the Left went into overdrive to sink El-Sayed. First, he had to overcome $32 million of AIPAC spending in the primary. Once he won the primary in a squeaker and moved on to the general election, Rogers ran a smear campaign focusing on El-Sayed’s background and identity.
“The fearmongering that you heard wasn’t, ‘Oh my god, he’s going to give healthcare to everyone,’” Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.), who entered Congress on an earlier wave of Left insurgency in 2022, tells In These Times. “It was the fact that he was Muslim. They used bigotry against him.”
With public support for Medicare for All now standing as high as 65%, the Trump camp made El-Sayed’s faith and Arab ethnicity the overwhelming target of their attacks. They were joined in the effort by a small but vocal group of Democratic saboteurs, including his defeated primary opponent, Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), and her backers. One of those supporters openly admitted he aimed to sink the Democratic nominee to “show that anti-Israel candidates like El-Sayed can’t win, thus bringing the Democratic Party back to its more traditional and pro-Israel stance” and preventing the party’s “hostile takeover” by left-wing forces come 2028.
Bend the Arc, a progressive Jewish organization that deployed to Michigan to talk to voters about antisemitism, encountered Jewish residents both excited to be represented by a Muslim senator and genuinely conflicted over El-Sayed’s views on Israel. “We tried to frame the conversation around our priorities,” says Bend the Arc CEO Jamie Beran.
“We were asking them to consider what would actually protect Jewish safety, and what empowering Christian nationalism would mean for Jews,” Beran tells In These Times.
In the end, it wasn’t even close. El-Sayed outperformed Kamala Harris in several key counties, decisively won back the Arab-majority city of Dearborn that Trump had poached in 2024, won young men back from the president with a 55-point swing, and won 92% of the vote in Detroit, deflating claims made, in the wake of the primary, that he struggled with Black voters.
Most strikingly, despite fearmongering about the supposed danger El-Sayed’s candidacy posed for Jewish residents, both exit polls and analysis of county- and municipality-level voting patterns showed that, at worst, he had lost roughly a fifth of Jewish voters while still comfortably winning the vast majority of them.
For most Jewish voters, “the most important issue in voting is not Israel-Palestine,” says Levin. “Overwhelmingly, they care a lot about reproductive rights, immigrant rights, LGBTQ rights, economic justice and racial justice. Abdul lines up with them on every issue.”
DSA on the rise
The midterm wins for the Left and its policy positions also solidified a major trend of this election cycle: what Politico has described as “DSA’s improbable rise to a power center in the Democratic Party.”
In the space of a decade, DSA has transformed from an obscure organization of some 6,000 members, with barely a footprint on the nation’s political landscape, to one of more than 130,000 members — making it the largest socialist organization in U.S. history. And, when the winners of these midterms are inaugurated, more than 400 DSA endorsees will serve as elected officials at virtually every level of government across the country, according to DSA press coordinator Rachel Monk.
One of the most high-profile members to take office is Zohran Mamdani, who last year upset disgraced former governor and Democratic establishment choice Andrew Cuomo to become mayor of New York City.
That upset was just the first spark of a chain reaction that saw New York City-DSA candidates achieve a near-total sweep in June primary elections, knocking out powerful and years-long incumbents.
“Over the years, we’ve been building a political operation, political machinery” in the city, says Claire Valdez, a Mamdani ally elected to represent New York’s 7th Congressional District after winning her primary in June. “That came to a head last year in the mayoral election, and that sense of optimism and the belief in the political power of the working class carried over into this year as well.”
During this year’s primaries, DSA candidates took out more incumbents than the Tea Party did during its famous 2010 wave of victories. Across the country, DSA recorded more than three times as many wins than last year, for a total of 158. Even in races where DSA didn’t endorse a candidate, it still played a role.
For instance, while El-Sayed doesn’t identify as a socialist, he openly welcomed DSA members into his coalition and benefited from the organization’s local ground game. Likewise, while no DSA chapters formally endorsed Talarico, his campaign benefited from the volunteer power of Texas DSA members in the state’s large metro areas.
In Maine, Troy Jackson had the backing of the state’s DSA chapter when he ran for governor earlier this year. When the Democratic Party was left scrambling this summer to find a replacement for former Senate nominee Graham Platner, who dropped out in July following sexual assault allegations, socialists quickly coalesced around Jackson for a second time.
DSA candidates, meanwhile, continued the organization’s patient build-up of power downballot, expanding the political pipeline that has helped elect a record number of socialists to the next Congress. As of the time of this writing, DSA candidates notched 79 state, county and municipal wins, including the mayorships of Washington, D.C., Los Angeles, and Providence, Rhode Island.
“It’s not surprising that all these wins for mayors and federal candidates came from DSA chapters who were already building the bench and developing the experience to not just elect people, but to work with them once they were in office,” Ashik Siddique, DSA National Co-Chair, tells In These Times. “That took many years of work.”
Many of those wins came in surprising places.
“Until this year, the narrative has often been, ‘DSA is winning all these races, but they’re mostly in already blue districts and all mostly in a Democratic city. Talk to us when you win a swing seat,’” says Siddique. “That’s actually happening now.”
One such surprise was DSA member Ashley Herrmann flipping a swing Florida county in Tampa to become the second socialist ever elected to office at any level in the state. Another is David Chappell, who cinched Utah’s State House District 62, beating a six-term Republican incumbent. Kentucky and Georgia, where Trump won in 2024, now have their first and second socialist state legislators in the modern era, respectively, albeit elected in blue areas.
As DSA and its political fortunes have transformed, so have the public’s attitudes toward socialism. Associated less today with long-extinct Soviet authoritarianism than with popular figures like Mamdani, Sanders, and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), socialism is now viewed more positively than ever by U.S. residents, especially non-white voters and those earning less than six figures.
Increasingly, U.S. voters themselves are identifying as democratic socialists — with the largest share in states like Hawai‘i, Oregon, and California, where exit polls show they made up roughly a quarter of all midterm voters. Yet even in Texas, nearly a fifth of voters call themselves democratic socialists. In Denver, where DSA member Melat Kiros unseated a 15-term incumbent in her June primary, a greater share of voters describe themselves as socialists than Republicans, and hold a more favorable view of socialism than capitalism.
“I think it was really powerful for our campaign that I wasn’t identifying the incumbent or any person as a problem, but rather the systematic way we’ve organized our economy and government around protecting the interests of the ultrawealthy,” Kiros tells In These Times. “We were able to pull in a lot of voters who weren’t necessarily regular Democratic voters: we had a lot of unaffiliated supporters, we had a lot of new voters and young voters.”
You don’t have to be a socialist to recognize the organization’s growing clout. In New York, Gov. Kathy Hochul has embraced the socialist mayor of her largest city and provided support to his agenda. Ocasio-Cortez, meanwhile, was in high demand this election season, transferring money to, and barnstorming on behalf of, battleground candidates in the final stretch, with even some Republican operatives begrudgingly acknowledging her popular appeal. This midterm blitz and her “race-changing endorsements” of a host of progressives were conspicuously detailed in a post-election memo by her team, as the congresswoman weighs a possible 2028 run for president.
“A responsibility to deliver”
Following this Democratic romp, the next battle will be deciding what the party will do with its majority.
Already, divisions are emerging in the Democratic camp. The agenda laid out before the election by House Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) primarily consisted of reversing recent Trump policies rather than pursuing more aggressive plans. Sen. Brian Schatz (D-HI), for his part, has urged Democrats not to pass bills that Trump is likely to veto, and to save the “more aspirational” and “bold policy changes” for 2028. Even once the enormous scale of Democrats’ victory became clear, centrists such as centrist Blue Dog Coalition leader Rep. Adam Gray warned progressive colleagues not to “yell and scream about your ideas that aren’t gonna get done.”
That’s not how everyone sees it.
“We have a responsibility to deliver,” says Kiros.
While many Democrats are breathing a sigh of relief, progressives are experiencing flashbacks to 2008, when hopes of a permanent Democratic majority curdled thanks to promises that were either broken or fell short, culminating in a Democratic wipeout at the state and federal levels two years later.
“Absent really tangible results, I think people are going to feel like they were duped,” Valdez tells In These Times.
“We have to ensure that we can prove to them that their vote mattered,” says Ramirez.
In a post-election statement posted on X, Rep. Greg Casar, who chairs the Congressional Progressive Caucus and just won his third term to a Texas House seat, cautioned Democrats not to spend the next two years being “the party of nervous lawyers who just tinker around the edges.” Other high-profile progressives such as Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.), have similarly advocated an ambitious approach, daring Trump to veto popular ideas like Medicare for All or cutting off weapons to Israel.
“Fuck the press when they say, ‘These are show bills, the president’s going to veto them, this is all just messaging,’” says Levin. “I don’t care. Let Trump veto them all, and say to the American people, ‘Okay, so if you get a Democratic president and Congress, this is what you’ll get.’”
WFP’s Dinkin agrees, adding, “If that means Trump vetoes healthcare for all, that would actually be advantageous.”
Those sentiments may be more widely shared within the party. Longtime Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) echoed progressives on the eve of the election when she said Democrats “have to deliver” when they win and not simply “look like Republicans.”
Sanders himself has proposed lowering the eligibility age of Medicare to 55; adding dental, vision, and hearing to its coverage; and ensuring it covers all kids. These are measures partly resurrected from negotiations over the never-passed Build Back Better bill during Joe Biden’s presidency, which had overwhelming approval from both the public and the party caucus. Even moderate, pro-Israel Democrats who flipped red districts have publicly signaled an openness to restricting weapons to Israel, including Eileen Laubacher, an alumn of Biden’s National Security Council and retired Navy rear admiral who defeated far-right Rep. Lauren Boebert (R-Colo.). Another issue that ties together progressives and other Democrats is restrictions on data center construction, a hugely popular demand that made for potent campaign fodder.
Progressives don’t seem phased by arguments that the massive size of the Democratic majority has eroded their leverage.
“I actually make the argument that it’s the opposite,” says Ramirez. “Most of my frontline colleagues just won by major numbers. So if, in fact, all we need is 218 votes for Medicare for All, then we just gave Hakeem Jeffries a very big gift. He can lose eight or 10 people, maybe, and the majority of us can center ourselves around the American people and get this stuff done.
“There’s always strength in numbers,” says Hamawy, who believes that the number of elected Democrats who back Medicare for All is larger than publicly known. “We have more candidates now who are standing up for issues that people want.”
They’ll be assisted by left-wing political groups like DSA and WFP that have seen their own ranks grow alongside progressives in Congress, and who view their task as continuing to organize long past the election season.
“Once people are in office, they have a big membership group like DSA to work with, to have an outside-inside strategy,” says Siddique. “While they’re haggling over bills and taking votes, we’re doing stuff on the outside to make things even more possible.”
With the Democratic electorate spoiling for a fight with the Trump administration (and to some extent hostile to its own existing party leadership), progressives and socialists aren’t worried they’ll end up in the vulnerable position that left insurgents found themselves in during the Biden era. At the time, former Sanders ally Nina Turner was defeated in her Ohio House race after facing accusations of party disloyalty over her criticism of the Democratic establishment, while “Squad” members found themselves fending off charges of sabotaging Biden’s agenda by withholding their votes to secure progressive concessions.
“Any appetite for that kind of narrative among the American people is entirely gone,” says Kiros. “I look at what Summer Lee and Ro Khanna and Thomas Massie did to make sure the Epstein files were finally released, and that annoyed a lot of people in the way they were doing it, but the American people were pleased to see it. During the government shutdown, we held the line for quite awhile until Chuck Schumer and a handful of senators decided to concede. Voters want to see us fight for the betterment of the American people.”
Valdez, who previously served in the New York State Assembly, says that working in Albany has shown her the power of “operating as a bloc that can withstand a lot of attacks.”
“When we can move together, we give each other protection, we can take bigger swings, bigger risks,” she says.
The stakes are unimaginably high. If the Democratic failures of the Obama era helped lead to Trump’s presidencies, the onus may now fall on progressives and socialists in power to bring about a political transformation.
“People are desperate for systematic, long-lasting change,” says Trent. “Until that’s delivered, voters are going to continue swaying back and forth desperately.”
“This is the most hopeful political time I’ve ever had in my life,” Trent says. “But the problem with hope is that any conditions that make transformational change possible for the better are the ones that make it possible for the worse — that make it possible to take a darker, more sinister turn.”

Branko Marcetic is a staff writer at Jacobin magazine and the author of Yesterday’s Man: The Case Against Joe Biden.
