The Gospel According to Anthropic
The soul of a new IPO.
The Anthropic IPO is now the largest stock offering in human history, despite nearly $1 trillion in construction commitments and widespread opposition to new data centers. Is its $1.5 trillion valuation the harbinger of a new era or another sign of an AI bubble?
The housing bubble was disastrous, but at least people shared a common understanding of “houses” and their use. With AI, we don’t even have that. The industry’s large-language model programs (LLMs) are technologically impressive, with many potential applications. But Anthropic goes even further than its competitors in arguing that LLMs have human-like, and even potentially superhuman, qualities that will transform humanity. It represents the cutting edge of the belief system behind tech’s massive investment wave, and its S-1 document (the prospectus and supporting documents a corporation must file when going public) is the closest thing that system has to a written creed.
The first thing an observer might notice about Anthropic’s filing is that it’s long—very long. Anthropic’s team is known for issuing lengthy statements, screeds, and philosophical reflections. (You might say they put the “chat” in “chatbot.”)
As a literary text, Anthropic’s S-1 lacks the “Robert Heinlein on amphetamines” quality that characterized SpaceX’s. Its tone oscillates between dewy-eyed reverence and Calvinist-sounding omens of doom. The reader can imagine it being recited someday in hushed tones within candle-lit rooms. The reverence is appropriate—if you accept Anthropic’s extreme beliefs about its product. If you don’t, however, the reading experience becomes off-putting and even disturbing.
The name “Anthropic” is from the Greek word for “human.” The corporation is firm in its beleief that its Claude chatbot is, or could become, something akin to human. The world got a glimpse of this in 2025 when someone obtained an internal Anthropic paper known as its “soul document,” the company’s in-house nickname for a draft of Claude’s operating instructions.
The word “soul” does not appear in the S-1, but it characterizes Claude with traits that until recently were considered strictly human. Foremost among them is intelligence. “For the first time in history,” the prospectus declares, “intelligence is something humans can build.”
This is a hotly debated question, however. LLMs sometimes replicate human intelligence by producing text, pictures, or program code. But these things are outputs of human intelligence, not intelligence itself, and LLMs draw on massive amounts of human-generated data.
Anthropic’s believers, however, harbor no doubt on this score. “The cognitive capability to reason, analyze, synthesize, decide, and create is producible at scale and accessible on demand,” the S-1 proclaims. “We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet.”
“Greater than industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet”— greater than any one of them or all of them put together? Once you’ve reached this level of grandiosity, I suppose it hardly matters.
Then only thing grander would be to suggest that Anthropic has created life itself. Its founders are evasive on that score, but terms like “reason,” “decide,” and “create” tip their hand. So does the final draft of that “soul document,” now called Claude’s “constitution.” Oddly, while that document says the chatbot is its “primary audience,” it’s largely written in the third person. The second person (“you”) is applied interchangeably to humans and Claude, a bit of boundary-blurring that may reveal more than intended.
The “Constitution” says that Claude “is not a digital human,” reasonably enough, but also suggests that it may already be conscious. It even implies that only our petty human prejudices blind us to Claude’s true nature. “We tend to attribute the likelihood of sentience and moral status to other beings based on their showing behavioral and physiological similarities to ourselves,” the authors gently scold.
“We want Claude to have a settled, secure sense of its own identity,” the S-I says, adding that it “can acknowledge uncertainty about deep questions of consciousness or experience while still maintaining a clear sense of what it values, how it wants to engage with the world, and what kind of entity it is.”
This may sound like visionary thinking to some. To others, however, Anthropic’s just anthropomorphizing computer code. Claude’s creators have yet to reconcile their conception of intelligence—a phenomenon whose most successful platform is a three-pound human brain—with the massive, planet-altering band of data centers their product requires. Adding more and more heavy machinery in pursuit of consciousness is a bit like adding gears to a bicycle and hoping it will become a bird.
Which brings us from the rarefied air of consciousness theory to Anthropic’s very concrete environmental, economic, and political impact. Like other LLM/chatbot companies, Anthropic has based its products on “scaling laws” that require massive amounts of brute-force processing. For this reason, the prospectus warns investors, it “will often make forward investments (especially in compute) that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance.”
“Compute,” as a noun, is the tech world’s term of art for hardware resources. AI corporations are engaged in an arms race to acquire more machinery for “compute” to improve their products and capture greater market share. Most investors aren’t betting on Anthropic’s theology. They’re hoping its massive investments will allow it to dominate the AI market, the same way its tech predecessors dominated search, social media, and other fields. It’s a bet on an oligopoly powered by fossil fuels.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
It’s a risky bet. That’s why Anthropic gave $40 million in the last election cycle to a campaign donation group called Public First Action, which supports the soft regulation stance embraced by its founders but opposed candidates like North Carolina’s Nida Allam, who backed a congressional moratorium on data center construction.
Meanwhile, Anthropic is quietly moving into life sciences and pharmaceuticals and will soon patent inventions that are AI outputs, meaning they’re largely derived from the work of others.
Anthropic faces other risks besides data center moratoriums; too many to list here, in fact. But the biggest risk is the uncertain future of AI itself, a powerful tool that has not yet shown that it can “rapidly transform every sector of the global economy.” That hasn’t stopped its stock from skyrocketing on its first day of trading, as I write these words. But that’s not the product of “reasoning” or “intelligence,” human or machine. It’s a collective statement of belief, not in Claude’s sentience but in the technology’s ability to grow more quickly than Anthropic’s spending. That’s an leap of faith.
Anthropic’s leaders don’t seem evil. They seem like believers. I don’t know if that’s less scary, or more. Nor is this the first time “compute” has been used as a noun. It’s found in the 15th-century Middle English translation of an even older French religious poem, for example. The poem is called “The Pilgrimage of the Soul.”
Observers might see Anthropic’s flood of investor cash and wonder if they’re missing something. Probably not. “Someone says to me, ‘Let me understand in order to believe,’” said Augustine. “I answer, ‘Believe in order to understand.’”
Want to understand this digital gold rush? It’s easy. Just believe in order to understand.

Paisley Museum, which holds one of the largest municipal art collections in Scotland, is set to reopen its doors to the public early next year following the first major renovation in its 150-year history.
The £68.7 million transformation began in 2018 but suffered delays from Covid, construction setbacks, and inflation, the Museums Association reports. The reopening had originally been set for the latter half of 2026.
The renovation was performed by the architectural firm AL_A, led by RIBA Stirling Prize–winner Amanda Levete. The last phase of the project includes the installation of some one hundred displays, created by the design studio OPERA Amsterdam, whose earlier project was the exhibition design for the British Museum’s landmark Bayeux Tapestry show. The museum’s curatorial team will then install more than 1,250 objects from the collection, around 80 percent of which have undergone conservation.
Other improvements to the building include a red-glass entrance and panoramic entryway, a new outdoor garden and public space, dedicated learning spaces and a Heritage Archive Center, and a café and shop. In addition, the campus’s Coats Observatory, the oldest public observatory in Scotland, has undergone significant external and internal repairs, and the sky hatch and revolving roof of the telescope dome have been restored.
The museum building was given to the town of Paisley in 1871 by the thread-making industrialist Sir Peter Coats; the observatory, funded by his brother Thomas Coats, followed in 1883. Both were designed by Glasgow architect John Honeyman, whose practice later employed the architect and designer Charles Rennie Mackintosh. The museum’s collections center on the town’s history as a major hub for textiles and thread-making in the nineteenth century and its association with the Paisley Pattern. Among the works that will be on view next year are more than two hundred contemporary Paisley-patterned objects and items associated with Paisley-born luminaries such as fashion designer Pam Hogg and Alexander Wilson, the “Father of American Ornithology.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Conservation of the ‘Sistine Chapel of the Andes’ nears completion
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Graciela Ibáñez
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
One of Bolivia’s oldest churches, known as the “Sistine Chapel of the Andes” due to its impressive murals, is nearing completion of a conservation project focused on its roofs, stone buttresses and adobe walls—a process that began in May.
The US Department of State’s Ambassadors Fund for Cultural Preservation (AFCP) financed the work at the Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas church, located in the Andes mountains at almost 4,000m above sea level. Approximately 170km west of the city of Oruro, the church was declared a National Monument in 1960.
“The Curahuara church has great value because of its paintings, so it’s essential that the roof is in good condition to prevent leaks that could compromise the murals,” Josefina Matas, the architect in charge of the project, tells The Art Newspaper. This work follows restoration that took place more than a decade ago, funded by the German embassy in La Paz.
The restoration team has had to learn the church’s unique roof-building technique from locals, placing straw on top of hollow cane mats using a method that makes it more resilient. Hollow cane is hard to find in the highlands, so they needed to bring it in from Bolivia’s southernmost region of Tarija.
During the previous restoration, corrugated metal sheets had been added to extend the lifespan of the roofs, which cover 800 sq. m. This time, workers replaced the damaged sections. The project was delayed because of proteststhat blocked roads across the country in May and June, preventing the arrival of materials and postponing its completion by one month—from the end of October to the end of November.
'A complete catechesis'
Built by Augustinians between the late 16th and early 17th centuries, the church houses paintings of the Nativity, the Last Supper, the Crucifixion and the Last Judgment in a display of religious syncretism. “It’s a complete catechesis,” Matas says of the murals, which were made using natural dyes and finished in 1777.
There are also representations of the apostle Santiago (James), the church’s patron saint. Local Indigenous people identified him with Illapa, the Inca god of thunder. The style of the paintings ranges from Mannerism to 18th-century Baroque, with depictions of birds and flowers—an example of mestizo art.
“It’s very striking when you enter the church, because there isn’t any empty space,” Matas says. “Everything is painted.” The paintings even cover the baptistery and sacristy. “Most of the churches in the region have murals. Here, they have been well preserved,” she adds.
The building has a single entrance through a side wall, similar to other churches in the area, and is surrounded by an atrium with two gates. “Indigenous people weren’t used to entering the building for religious activities, so the atrium was spacious enough to accommodate those who wanted to be evangelised,” Matas says.
The bishop of Oruro, Krzysztof Białasik, was the one who submitted the restoration project to compete for US funding. Since 2001, the AFCP has financed more than 30 projects in Bolivia, including the restoration of colonial paintings, the protection of Baroque musical manuscripts and the creation of a digital catalogue—including archaeological artefacts, pre-Columbian textiles and colonial art—available to customs services to curb the illicit trafficking of these goods.
To celebrate the completion of the conservation of the church, a mass will be held in Santiago de Curahuara de Carangas with the bishop and the apostolic nuncio on 15 December.

https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.title: We’ve tried everything to get off our phones. These 11 things work (and make great gifts)
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.author: Lauren Gould
https://www.theguardian.com/thefilter-us.text:
Logging off is en vogue. From touting analog bags to playing vinyl records, many of us are tired of living life behind a screen.
So 2026 may be the ideal year to gift some low-tech entertainment instead of the newest iPhone. These days, we’re all trying to connect with the “real world” more, and the latest string of tech outages has been a good nudge to buy stuff that won’t glitch.
We’ve experimented with screen alternatives such as MP3 players and “dating cards” throughout the year, sharing the ups – and some downs – in our series Do not disturb.
Here are 11 picks that would make perfect gifts, from the beautiful (displayable board games) to the practical (daily planners).
- Visit our ultimate holiday gift guide for obsessively vetted gift ideas, or get inspired by our full array of guides, including a gift guide for the person who has everything and a guide to cozy gifts.
For the introspective introvert:
No Particular Order Volume One Journal
Stationery brand No Particular Order’s guided journal is the ideal companion for self-discovery. It has 200 journal prompts for your recipient to fill out, including “Who’s in your circle?” and “Who or what do you hope to be in a future life?”. I used this the summer after finishing my undergraduate degree to stave off feelings of existential dread.
For the hardcover truther: 
Book of the Month subscription
My Book of the Month subscription sends a newly released novel to my apartment for under $20 per month. While I’m a Kindle girl at heart, it comes in handy when I’m craving the weight of a physical novel. There’s something fun about waiting for the announcement of each month’s selections. Most recently, I grabbed John Green’s new book, Hollywood, Ending.
For the flirt: 
No Particular Order Acquaintance Cards
Last winter, I tried No Particular Order’s dating app alternative, acquaintance cards. Inspired by Victorian-era calling cards, you fill out your information and hand it to someone who catches your eye. These cards helped me get someone’s phone number at a bar – yes, in 2026! Instead of asking your giftee when you can expect a grandchild, hand them these.
For the performative chess player: 
Papier Chess Set
This solid wood chess set is too pretty to hide in a dusty cabinet. Its colorful mosaic box and squiggly board are built to be shown off; the Filter’s commissioning editor, Karen Yuan, has it displayed on her living room coffee table. “Do I play chess? Not in years. Will I leave the box out just for compliments? Yes, shamelessly.” Gift this to the former captain of their school’s chess team or someone who’s always wanted to learn.
For the amateur artist:
Emily Lex Studios Watercolor book
I love watercoloring, but that doesn’t mean I’m producing paintings worthy of an art gallery. But I enjoyed the guided watercolor book from Emily Lex Studio, which has lightly outlined pencil drawings and simple instructions for painting over them. This is the present for someone who needs a winter evening activity that doesn’t involve scrolling on social media. While I tried the holiday theme, the Woodland and Animals workbook looks delightful too.
For a puzzler with patience:
Piecework Jigsaw Puzzle
It turns out I do have the patience for a 1,000-piece puzzle, as long as it looks as pretty as the eclectic ones from Piecework. This past summer, I waxed poetic about the brand’s Happy Camper puzzle: “Whenever I worked on it, I lost track of time.” The brand has plenty of festive options, including Tinseltown and Peppermint Parade. It has also branched out to other tabletop games, including Scrabble and Yahtzee.
For the oversleeper: 
Arne Jacobsen Alarm Clock
Last winter, I asked experts who study digital detoxing about how to reduce screen time. One of their tips? Leave your phone outside your bedroom. Catherine Price, the author of How to Break Up with Your Phone, says her husband uses this clock from Arne Jacobsen. And, like your iPhone, you can snooze the alarm as many times as you’d like.
For the precocious planner: 
Papier Hardcover Daily Planner
Whether gifting for a stressed student or workaholic loved one, you can’t go wrong with a planner. Like most things at Papier, this version marries function with an aesthetically pleasing design that they’ll want to show off on their desk. I wrote about how I use mine to stay organized – including reminding me to send a mega-important email I had forgotten about that day.
For the wannabe hipster:
Olympus Muji Film Camera
I’ve owned my secondhand Olympus film camera for four years and use it to snap candids of friends and family. It’s always fun to get photos developed, even if the older adults in my life can’t fathom why I would opt for it over the convenience of my iPhone’s camera. Gift this for someone who loves snapping photos and insists that everything looks better on film.
You can grab one secondhand at Mercari, eBay or Etsy.
For the foodie: 
Mi Cocina Cookbook
There’s nothing more annoying than trying to follow a recipe from your phone, getting food on your screen and squinting to see the measurements. A cookbook is an alternative for everyone from experienced cooks to amateur bakers. Recently, Filter contributor and Guardian senior editor Danielle Renwick interviewed Mexican chef Ricky Martínez, who wrote Mi Cocina, which is chock full of recipes such as sweet corn tamales and carne asada. Pair it with this sculptural book stand for extra brownie points.
Other gift ideas you might enjoy from the Filter, the Guardian’s guide to buying fewer, better things:
- The best personalized gifts and ideas for person who already has everything
- The best gift ideas under $10
- Global gifts that Americans are missing out on

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Trump’s Goons Are Melting Down
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Elie Mystal
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Trump’s Goons Are Melting Down
In this week’s Elie v. U.S., our justice correspondent digs into the freakout over the coming congressional investigations. Plus: the freakout over court reform.
With Democrats taking control of the House and the Senate, the Trump administration is finally about to face some oversight. Robert Garcia (D-CA) is poised to take over the House Oversight Committee while Jamie Raskin (D-MD) is set to take over the House Judiciary Committee. Both have indicated that they are willing—and, dare I say, eager—to conduct investigations into the Trump administration and the Justice Department.
The Trump administration is responding in the only way it knows how: with threats, intimidation tactics, and a complete disregard for the Constitution. Garcia has received threatening letters from White House counsel Will Scharf “reminding” him of the limits of congressional authority. Todd Blanche, the attorney general, has threatened Garcia and others with lawsuits and promised to defend people like Trump’s chief of staff, Stephen Miller, even though that’s not his job.
The Trump official who appears to be having the biggest meltdown of all is Aaron Reitz, the Trump-appointed US Attorney for the Southern District of Texas. This guy, who I only learned existed this week, has sent letters to Democratic congresspeople and senators threatening malicious, retaliatory, criminal prosecutions should the Democrats investigate Trump. He’s been running his mouth all over town threatening to “destroy” the left by bringing every prosecutorial tool in his quiver against them, no matter the merits.
I’m not being hyperbolic. Here’s one of his statements, as reported by Popular Information:
“The left doesn’t care about my opponents, but they are deadly threatened by what’s coming. They know that I’m going to destroy them. If I can’t sue you, I’m going to investigate you. If I can’t investigate you, I’m going to drag you into so much trouble, you might as well just declare bankruptcy now.”
I get it. All these Trump-aligned lawyers are used to dealing with people like, well, me. People who can be harassed and bankrupted and who have to tread carefully around white men having a nutty. These lawyers, however, are clearly not used to dealing with members of Congress: people who are already lawyered up and constitutionally protected by the Speech or Debate Clause. That clause prohibits the executive and judicial branches from using investigations and lawsuits to intimidate or silence congresspeople. It is a literal point-and-click constitutional violation to do what Reitz and Blanche are threatening to do.
Since it is unlikely that the lawyers working for Trump have read and understood the Constitution, let me put this in language they can understand: They can huff, and they can puff, but they cannot blow the House of Representatives down.
The Bad and the Ugly
- Mary Peltola has been declared the winner of the Senate race in Alaska. She received over 50 percent of the vote, thus defeating both Dan Sullivans combined and obviating the need for the state to engage its ranked-choice system. For our next trick: How about somebody call Lisa Murkowski and see if we can get her to switch parties? We can offer John Fetterman in the trade.
- Hakeem Jeffries overwhelmingly won a secret-ballot election to be the next speaker of the House. I know a lot of progressives have concerns about Jeffries’s leadership. I have my own qualms. But electing the first Black speaker of the House in United States history is objectively an amazing thing—and, goddamn it, I’m allowed to be happy and hopeful about his leadership for at least a couple of weeks.
- The Supreme Court declined to hear an ammosexual challenge to Maryland’s restrictions on bringing guns to “sensitive places” (like schools and sporting events). I wouldn’t get too excited, though. Clarence Thomas indicated that the rejection had more to do with the wide-ranging nature of the gun-nut challenge than with the idea behind the challenge itself. Once these ammosexual yahoos decide on a particular place to turn into a shooting gallery, the court will likely take the case and overturn the ban.
- The MAHA movement has managed to make measles great again. In absolutely related news, a group of parents are asking the Supreme Court to allow them to ignore vaccine mandates in schools. The acceptable snarky response here is something like, “Darwin, take the wheel,” but I can’t go there. Measles can be deadly, especially for children. Kids do not deserve to be stricken with a preventable disease simply because their parents are freaking idiots.
- In October 2025, four Baltimore high school students were set upon by police officers, thrown to the ground, and arrested right outside of their school. The “reason” was that an AI surveillance system named Omnilert had reported to authorities that one of the students was carrying a weapon. But the AI “hallucinated” the danger. It misidentified… a bag of chips. Those students (and their parents) are now suing the school and Omnilert. Their lawsuit claims that Omnilert gives false positives 99 percent of the time. Omnilert was also used in a Nashville school district. It failed to identify the weapon being carried by 17-year-old Solomon Henderson, who shot up his school cafeteria, killing one other student before killing himself. Whatever the problem is, AI is not the solution.
Inspired Takes
- Amid all of the amazing things that happened during the midterms, I missed a truly incredible one: Montana passed a state law aimed at overturning Citizens United. Dubbed the “Montana Plan,” the law says that no “artificial persons,” like corporations, are allowed to spend money on candidates, PACs, or ballot initiatives. David Moore has a full explanation of what the law does in The Nation. Republicans filed a lawsuit challenging the law before the final votes were even counted, so I will certainly have an opportunity to write more about this plan as it winds its way toward its inevitable showdown in front of the Supreme Court.
- You’re aware that Black people are being hanged, again? Well, I’d forgive you if you didn’t know, because these suspicious outdoor hanging deaths—at least 10 across the country since September 2025—have all been ruled “suicides.” I don’t buy it for a single second, and in The Nation, Kali Holloway explains why I am right to discount the official narratives.
Worst Argument of the Week
William Baude, the legal scholar who is a John Roberts sycophant on his best day, wrote an absolutely ludicrous column for The New York Times titled “The Supreme Court Deserves Celebration, Not Condemnation.” I’d like to think that Baude was forced to write this at the point of one of Sam Alito’s flagpoles, because the level of credulous simplicity required to make this argument beggars belief.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
His central premise is that, while people on the left may well disagree with the court on issues as petty as abortion rights and voting rights, the court should be praised because it has ruled against Trump in a few high-profile cases. Baude cites the court’s rulings on Trump’s tariffs, Trump’s attempt to federalize the National Guard, birthright citizenship, and the independence of the Federal Reserve as evidence of the court’s praiseworthy good faith.
Those are four cases. Here are some others.
- In Mullin v. Al Orto Lado, the court ruled that the Trump administration could turn asylum seekers away from the United States at the southern border.
- In Trump v. Slaughter, the court ruled that Trump could fire an FTC commissioner, in violation of a 130-year-old precedent.
- In Trump v. Wilcox, the court ruled that Trump could fire members of the National Labor Relations Board.
- In Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., the court ruled that Trump could deport people to third-party countries, at least for now.
- In Department of State v. AIDS Vaccine Advocacy Coalition, the court ruled that Trump could withhold $4 billion in foreign aid funding, mostly directed at USAID, in a move that has killed an untold number of people.
- In Noem v. National TPS Alliance, the court ruled that Trump could revoke Temporary Protected Status without a thorough investigation.
- In Noem v. Perdomo, the court ruled that Trump could use racial profiling.
- In National Park Service v. National Trust for Historic Preservation, the court ruled that Trump could build his fucking ballroom.
- In Blanche v. Lau, the court ruled that the Trump administration didn’t need evidence of a crime before deporting a green-card holder suspected of committing a crime.
- And in Trump v. United States, the court ruled that Trump is absolutely immune from criminal prosecution for official acts.
These are 10 cases that I happened to remember off the top of my head. Baude’s strategy of mentioning a few cases that Trump lost at the Supreme Court while ignoring the overwhelming number of cases he won is risible. I understand that Baude wants to launder the reputation of the Roberts court, but this is just straight-up bad analysis. I don’t even blame Baude for it, I blame the editors at The New York Times who allowed this slop into print without so much as a parenthetical pointing out that Trump has won a ton of cases in front of the Supreme Court.
In any event, having picked a few cherries off the poisonous tree, Baude gets to his main point, which is that Supreme Court reform is unnecessary. He writes, “But the best court reform would just be for the justices to try harder and do a better job. Discretion is inevitable and hard to reform from the outside.”
I… don’t even have a response to this. If you know all that a University of Chicago Law professor like William Baude knows about the Supreme Court and still conclude that the real solution is to ask the justices to try harder, you have left the realm of good-faith public discourse. “Try harder” is not a reform; it’s something you scream at the television when a basketball player doesn’t run back on defense.
Let’s do a close read of the next two paragraphs, which Baude uses to dismiss the rampant corruption at the Supreme Court:
- “Ethics concerns about the justices are largely superficial as well.”
  - Just shoot me in the fucking head, please… and also sorry, I’m cursing now, so please don’t share the rest of this with my mother.
- “The justices travel in elite circles and receive fancy gifts, and some make millions of dollars from their books. The country certainly has a right to decide that this lucre is unseemly and that public servants should not be allowed to do these things.”
  - Oh, so we agree that “the public” should be allowed to tell “public servants” that they’re not allowed to be “corrupt assholes.” Good to know.
- “But we should not overestimate what ethics reform will accomplish.”
  - Nobody thinks ethics reform will transubstantiate the Roberts court into the Warren court, but do go on.
- “The justices’ views on big issues are well formed. The justices themselves aren’t for sale; book income reflects their increasing celebrity, not any specific quid pro quo.”
  - Do you notice how Baude is focusing on the books, because that is something that all the justices do, rather than on the purchasing of recreational vehicles, vacations, and property for the justices, which is something that only the Republican justices enjoy?
- “To be sure, it is quite possible that travel and gifts and book sales subtly reinforce the justices’ incentives to play to their respective fan bases.”
  - So you get it’s corrupt, you just don’t care.
- “But this kind of corruption is quite indirect, and at the same time comes from so much more than money.”
  - He’s basically saying that the justices are so ensconced in a corrupt world that it’s impossible to disentangle financial incentives from their decision-making process—as a way to defend the justices and argue against anti-corruption measures.
- “So ethics reform is unlikely to change much about what the court actually does.”
  - Bad-faith writers do this all the time. They start off saying they’re going to argue one thing (“ethics concerns are superficial”) and conclude by arguing a completely different thing (“ethics reform is unlikely to change what the court does”). Whether or not reform changes the justices behavior has nothing to do with whether or not the concerns about their ethics are superficial. I, for instance, have never for a day argued that ethics reform was the key to unlocking different decisions, and I don’t know anybody who has. Instead, the argument for ethics reform is that corruption is bad, and should be stopped as a matter of fucking principle.
Baude finishes his essay by arguing that the real problem for the Supreme Court is its “image” and that the “one good argument for court reform” is the “placebo effect,” where nothing will change but people get to feel like they tried.
As I sit here, trying to recover from the aneurysm I gave myself by reading this dumb article, I am heartened by this thought: The white wing is pulling out all the stops to argue against court reform. That means they know Democrats are serious about it; they know it’s popular, and they know it’s a threat to their empire.
What I Wrote
I wrote about how to “Make America Function Again,” and if enough people like the piece, I might try to start my own cult movement. Only, instead of asking people to sacrifice their dignity to join me, I’ll instruct them to empower one of their friends with this message of hope… Wait, no, that sounds too much like a multilevel marketing scheme. Look, I’m still working out the details, but I’ve already ordered the hats.
In News Unrelated to the Current Chaos
Grand Theft Auto 6 was released on Thursday to rave reviews. By the time you’re reading this, I’ll be playing it. I will report back later, assuming I still have a job after taking however many unexcused days of absence I need to finish the game.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: The Ridiculous Spectacle of Trump’s Meeting With Xi and Putin
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Sasha Abramsky
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
The Ridiculous Spectacle of Trump’s Meeting With Xi and Putin
The Shenzhen “summit” was a charade intended to generate handshake-and-hug memes rather than binding international agreements.
What does a would-be-autocrat who craves public adoration do when he suffers a once-in-a-century electoral revolt? Well, in the case of Donald Trump, he hightails it to Shenzhen, China, to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and shower them in effusive praise, in anticipation that they will return the compliments. And he teases the possibility of a meeting with North Korea leader Kim Jung Un, which ultimately doesn’t “work out.”
There is something peculiarly repulsive about the images of Trump’s oh-so-very-important meeting with Xi and Putin. We see an increasingly senescent man-child looking to play with the big boys, with Putin smirking next to him and Xi stone-faced. We are forced to bear witness to Trump casually throwing away whatever shreds were left of America’s claim to marshal, in some way, the forces of the “free world” in defense of democratic values. Instead, we see this politically emasculated 80-year-old man bending over backward to fluff the egos of the genuine autocrats whose company he so clearly prefers to that of the leaders of the world’s great democracies.
This ridiculous spectacle was marketed, however improbably, as another Yalta, when the Big Three—Franklin D. Roosevelt, Winston Churchill, and Joseph Stalin—sat down in the Crimea in early 1945 to divvy up spheres of influence in a postwar era. For Putin, whose forces were readying yet another a powerful drone and missile barrage against Ukraine, Shenzhen was a chance to explain his view of the endgame of the war. He said at the meeting, “Nobody divided up the world at Yalta. It simply codified the realities that had emerged after World War II. And when it comes to today’s conflicts, the realities on the ground will have to be accepted.” In other words, “you don’t have to like what’s going on in Ukraine, but you’re going to have to suck it up.”
For Trump, the meeting was a chance to rail, once again, against the International Criminal Court and its work on holding accountable out-of-control, violent leaders and warlords.
In reality, of course, Shenzhen in 2026 simply isn’t Yalta in 1945. Not by any stretch of the imagination. For one thing, last I looked, and Trump’s preferences notwithstanding, Russia, China, and the US aren’t brothers-in-arms, marching lockstep for years in a global fight against fascism. For another, far from 2026 being a moment of incipient triumph for the three world leaders, these days Russia is bogged down in Ukraine, and has lost a staggering number of soldiers; the US is bogged down in Iran, and the Iranians retain the ability to inflict huge economic damage on the world through sowing chaos in the Strait of Hormuz; and China, while increasingly asserting its own sphere of influence, is stumbling from one economic hit to the next as bubbles start to burst, ranging from real estate to artificial intelligence.
Yalta was about restoring an international power balance at the end of a long conflict; Shenzhen occurred as international chaos and conflict are on the upswing, in large part because of the actions of Trump and of Putin. If any historical comparison could be made, this was far more akin to the Hitler-Mussolini meetings in the run-up to war than it was to the get-together in the Crimea.
So what exactly was the point, beyond apparently giving America’s stamp of approval to Putin’s ongoing war, and providing him a tonic by having the US president publicly label him a “friend”? There were no concrete proposals on the table that could substantively benefit the world. Rather, this was simply a way for Trump to show the world—that ungrateful place that has, multiple times, rebuffed his efforts to secure a Nobel Peace Prize—that he still has influential friends in high places.
That was the long and short of it. There were no specifics, no nuclear disarmament or control treaties put on the table to replace those that have recently expired—though there were some milquetoast comments by the three that nuclear war ought to be considered an impossibility. There were no binding agreements to rein in AI, no effort to really end the wars in Ukraine and Iran. In short, this simply wasn’t a genuine reset moment. Rather, it was a simulacrum, a “summit”—with the air quotes detailing the fantasy quality of the event—intended to generate handshake-and-hug memes rather than binding international agreements.
It was a charade, and America’s historic allies recognized it as such. As Trump was sweet-talking Putin and Xi, European leaders were heading to a meeting in Berlin to chart the way forward in Ukraine. Not surprisingly, they viewed the Shenzhen “summit” with particular dismay. Jeremy Hunt, the UK’s foreign secretary under Prime Minister Theresa May in 2018–19, immediately concluded that America “is no longer leader of the free world.” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot dismissed it, pointing out that nothing constructive would emerge. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said it was simply a photo op.
None of this mattered to Trump. He had been swaddled in warmth and appreciation by two of the world’s Quality Autocrats, genuine OGs, and it felt damn good. It felt like relief from all the bad news stateside, from cascading technology-related crises, to a swooning stock market, to reports that the incoming Democratic congressional majority is planning an array of investigations into his corrupt administration. America’s man-child leader could fly home happy, knowing he had had a satisfying playdate with two of the most powerful dudes on the schoolyard.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Bernie Sanders: A Foreign Policy for the Many
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Sen. Bernie Sanders
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Bernie Sanders: A Foreign Policy for the Many
From military spending to climate change, the senator makes the case for a foreign policy rooted in democracy and our common humanity.
In A World for All: New Visions of US Foreign Policy, a new collection edited by Matthew Duss and co-published by OR Books and The Nation, progressive thinkers offer a vision of a foreign policy rooted in democracy, cooperation, and the needs of working people. In the foreword, Senator Bernie Sanders makes the case for confronting oligarchy at home and abroad. Order the book here.
For too long, US foreign policy has been shaped by a narrow consensus that serves the powerful few rather than the democratic many. That old consensus—plagued by militarism, corporate power, and the selective application of international law—has now collapsed, its foundations rotted away by corruption and hypocrisy.
This book asks what progressives should offer as a replacement. It begins from a simple premise: that the United States should be promoting peace, not endless war. It explains how, to achieve that goal, we must confront the concentration of wealth and power that has warped both our domestic politics and our role in the world. And it offers an alternative approach, rooted in enlightened self-interest and genuine partnership, that recognizes our common humanity.
Underpinning this book is the central question of who will govern, the many or the few—democracy or oligarchy. This contest will determine whether we meet the climate crisis or succumb to it; whether technology like AI is regulated in the public interest or used as a tool of control; whether democracies deliver for ordinary people or continue ceding power to billionaires and multinational corporations. This struggle is playing out around the world, from Washington to Brussels, Brasília to Budapest, and New Delhi to Riyadh.
The challenge is daunting. Today, almost 3.6 billion people live in poverty while the richest 1 percent own nearly half of all global wealth. In the United States, three people own more wealth than the bottom half of society. Despite enormous gains in productivity, people across the industrialized world are working longer hours for lower wages. Pensions have been cut, social safety nets shredded, and public services hollowed out. People increasingly fear that their children will have a lower standard of living than they do.
Meanwhile, as governments fail to meet the needs of working families, the billionaire class has siphoned an estimated $21 to $32 trillion into offshore tax havens. This money is never taxed or even spent; it simply ensures the superrich get even richer. These oligarchs spend freely to protect their wealth and power, buying influence and elections to ensure that governments serve them rather than ordinary citizens. The present scale of corruption and kleptocracy is staggering, now supercharged by the embrace of cryptocurrency.
It is therefore no surprise that so many people feel abandoned by their governments. Some turn away from politics altogether, while others embrace authoritarian demagogues who channel people’s fear and economic insecurity into resentment. These demagogues blame immigrants or minorities to distract from the real causes of widening inequality: multinational corporations and the billionaire class who capture an ever-larger share of global wealth for themselves. Both outcomes—apathy and authoritarianism—erode the foundations of democracy and threaten the universal human rights that should anchor any just foreign policy.
The United States’ own descent into oligarchy has been particularly damaging. Moneyed interests have distorted US policy on issue after issue to disastrous effect. Fossil fuel companies have blocked meaningful climate leadership. Pharmaceutical giants defend monopoly profits instead of expanding access to lifesaving medicines. Elon Musk spends $270 million to elect Donald Trump, then is allowed to destroy U.S. foreign assistance, leading to hundreds of thousands of preventable deaths. Hugely profitable defense contractors take more than half of the $1 trillion annual military budget, returning tens of billions to shareholders and millions more to the politicians who authorize that spending. Washington rightly condemns Russia for bombing civilians in Ukraine yet says little as Israel—backed by tens of billions in US taxpayer dollars—kills more than 20,000 children in Gaza. How much of that silence stems from politicians’ fear of super PACs?
This corruption and hypocrisy have not gone unnoticed. At home, Americans are sick of being told there is “no money” for health care, housing, or education, even as vast resources flow to defense contractors or Netanyahu’s genocidal government. And abroad, the United States loses credibility when it selectively applies international law and when foreign governments see our system is captured by private interests. The great challenges of our century—climate change, pandemics, tech regulation, and sustainable development—require deep multilateral cooperation. But cooperation depends on trust, and trust cannot survive the corruption and double standards that so obviously plague our system.
A progressive foreign policy must therefore begin with moral clarity. We cannot champion human rights abroad while violating them at home. We cannot condemn Russia’s bombing of civilians while funding Israel’s atrocities. We cannot lecture others about democracy while billionaires buy our elections and policymakers serve their donors rather than their constituents. Authoritarian rivals are exploiting our hypocrisy, making consistency not only a moral obligation but a strategic necessity.
But clarity is not enough. We must also articulate an affirmative vision: a foreign policy that confronts global oligarchy, strengthens democratic institutions, and builds genuine partnerships. This means focusing on collective action rather than dominance. It means making anticorruption a central pillar of our foreign policy. It means supporting democracy not through military intervention but by helping societies meet the needs of their people. It means recognizing that true security comes not from trillion-dollar arsenals but from addressing the root causes of instability: inequality, injustice, and environmental catastrophe. And it requires humility—an understanding that US leadership must be earned, not assumed.
At its core, this vision rests on a simple truth: Every person shares a common humanity. We all want our children to grow up healthy, have a good education, find meaningful work, breathe clean air and drink clean water, and live in peace. A foreign policy for the many recognizes these universal aspirations and rejects the politics of division used by authoritarians and oligarchs.
The struggle between oligarchy and democracy, between authoritarianism and justice, will define our era. This book offers a blueprint for how the United States can win that struggle and help build a more just and peaceful world. The choices before us are clear. Let us choose a foreign policy worthy of our democratic ideals and the generations to come.

Don’t Be Fooled by Elon Musk’s Big Pivot
Musk and James Murdoch are touting their moderation. That’s because they want to make sure they can own the Democratic Party.
Wise investors know that having a diverse portfolio is good in politics, not just the stock market. That’s why plutocrats have traditionally donated lavishly to both Republicans and Democrats—it’s a way of ensuring that they always have politicians in their pockets, no matter which way the electoral wind may blow. But over the last two years, some of the wealthiest figures in Silicon Valley, led by trillionaire Elon Musk, have broken this once-cardinal rule by becoming strident partisans of Donald Trump and the MAGA movement.
Musk in particular has become virtually synonymous with the most rancid elements of Trumpism. He frequently elevates antisemitic, racist, and even Nazi ideas, notably the paranoid white replacement theory. And he has handed eye-watering levels of money to the GOP. In 2024, Musk donated at least $288 million to elect Trump and other Republicans. The figure was even higher for the 2026 midterms: $446 million, the most any single donor has ever given in an electoral cycle.
Musk was amply rewarded for his services. His loyalty to Trump helped his various companies (Tesla, SpaceX, Starlink) keep the government contracts on which they depend, and, even more destructively, paved the way for his leadership of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) where he implemented the long-standing agenda of corporate interests by eviscerating government regulations, defunding agencies—including USAID, where his cuts have been linked to the deaths of hundreds of thousands of people overseas—and laying off federal workers.
Musk was once proud of this record. In March 2025, he spoke at a Trump rally and declared, “I’m not just MAGA, I’m dark MAGA.”
But in the wake of the midterms, where the Republicans suffered the worst electoral drubbing in half a century, Musk suddenly realized that his public posture as a far-right Republican might be a liability. Cue the screeching sound of a Tesla in reverse.
Now Musk is singing a very different tune, trying to sound like a dulcet-voiced centrist rather than a booming fascist. Speaking at the New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Musk sheepishly said, “I’m not MAGA. If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.” He then declared himself a “moderate” and said he could work well with Gina Hinojosa, the incoming Democratic governor of Musk’s adopted home state of Texas.
These conciliatory words ring very hollow, considering that Musk spent at least $212 million in a futile bid to elect Hinojosa’s rival, Greg Abbott, and other Texas Republicans. Musk did admit, “I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it. Probably if I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money.”
Musk is not the only plutocrat suffering from buyer’s remorse. Alex Karp, the founder of the surveillance giant Palantir, has also supported the hard right in recent years but is now posing as a born-again Democrat. In a post-midterms interview with Politico, Karp claimed, “I’ve been a Democrat my whole life. I grew up in a far-left environment. I know more about being a progressive than almost anybody on the planet, and I absolutely believe Palantir—all of our products are essentially progressive.”
The political danger is the centrist Democrats, always eager for donations from billionaires, will welcome back figures such as Musk and Karp as prodigal sons who may have sinned but deserve a second chance.
The dangers of right-wing billionaires’ using the mask of moderation to take over the Democratic Party are not theoretical. It is well demonstrated by one of Musk’s business partners, James Murdoch, who sits on the board of Tesla. James Murdoch is, of course, son of Rupert Murdoch, the far-right press baron who owns Fox News. He is also, along with his wife, Kathryn, one of the biggest donors to the Democratic Party, assiduously propping up centrist Democrats in a bid to thwart the party’s move to the left.
In the soap opera lore of the Murdoch family, amplified not just in press coverage but in shows such as Succession, James and Kathryn represent the good, liberal wing of the family, unlike older brother Lachan, who has won control of the media empire in part because he is as stridently right-wing as his father.
This view of good Murdochs versus bad Murdochs is an oversimplification. A lengthy Politico profile of James and Kathryn paints a more complex portrait. James had been groomed to run the media empire, but was tarnished by the fact that he oversaw the British tabloid The News of the World when it was forced to shutter in 2011 in the wake of the notorious phone-hacking scandal. His emerging pseudo-liberalism then coincided neatly with his growing ostracization from the News Corp fold.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Ironically, in cultivating Democrats, James Murdoch is following in the footsteps of his estranged father. Although Rupert Murdoch is right-wing, he’s always been willing to cozy up to centrist politicians in order to have government support when they held office. As Politico notes, Rupert “had held fundraising breakfasts for Hillary Clinton and his Sun tabloid backed Tony Blair’s Labour Party even as his own politics were to the right of theirs.”
Clearly, James was taking notes. Since 2020, he and his wife have given $30 million to the Democratic Party. It’s valuable for the Murdochs to have tight connections with both Democrats and Republicans.
Like Rupert Murdoch, though, James and Kathryn know that influence comes not just from political donations but also from shaping nonprofits and the media. They have heavily invested in groups such as Majority Democrats (a clearinghouse for centrist Democrats that recently held a big conference in Denver) as well as media outlets such as New York magazine, Vox, and The Bulwark.
Their political orientation can roughly be described as Never Trump Republican, with an added (and commendable) concern for climate change. In other words, they think the Democrats should try to win over the center-right voters who once supported George W. Bush, Mitt Romney, and Liz Cheney.
As Jeff Hauser of the Revolving Door Project told Politico, “They forget that Kamala Harris tried to co-opt reasonable Republicans into her campaign, and turn away from populist anger, and it didn’t work.” Ravi Mangla of the Working Families Party had a similar critique: “People are really angry at the cozy relationship between the political establishment and who they view as a donor class that has way too much power and access in our politics. It raises questions of whether those groups are best positioned to deliver on what voters are asking of people or are asking of the party.”
In pursuit of their politics, James and Kathryn have given lavishly to figures such as former transportation secretary Pete Buttigieg and Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, who says he is “grateful that they invested early on in my race.”
The question worth asking is what returns the Murdochs can expect from their investment. Or to put it another way, the Murdoch family already owns the Republicans, so it seems a bit greedy for them to want to buy another political party.

https://hyperallergic.com/is-gta-vi-the-.title: Is GTA VI the Art Miami Deserves?
https://hyperallergic.com/is-gta-vi-the-.author: Valentina Di Liscia
https://hyperallergic.com/is-gta-vi-the-.text:
Is GTA VI the Art Miami Deserves?
Miami-based artists Leo Castañeda and misael soto join Hyperallergic in a conversation about the tensions of a game that portrays a changing city locked in time.
“Driving at rush hour. SIGNIFICANTLY less cars on the road.” The text was from Miami-based artist, educator, and organizer misael soto, sent yesterday, November 19, a few hours after the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. We’d come full circle: The bumper-to-bumper traffic that Miami, the city I once called home, is now notorious for — in no small part due to overdevelopment, climate change, and strained infrastructure — was being alleviated by a video game that keeps people at home, inside a simulation of the same city locked in time.
The premise of GTA VI is simple on the surface. The game follows Lucía Caminos and Jason Duval in the criminal underworld of Leonida, a fictionalized state based on South Florida: Miami becomes Vice City, the Everglades are the Grassrivers. But its portrayal of real-life hardships, socioeconomic inequality, and even Lucía and Jason’s love story, among other elements, has elicited deeper reflections and responses across our increasingly blurred online and physical worlds.
To help make sense of these tensions, I got on a phone call with soto and Leo Castañeda, two Miami-based artists whose work I admire. Castañeda is an artist and video game designer exploring Latin American Surrealism in the digital age, and soto co-leads Artists for Artists: Miami, which is leading a boycott of Art Basel next month, and works in the overlapping arenas of labor rights, public infrastructure, and conceptual and social practice.
Our conversation was edited and condensed for clarity. I hope you enjoy it.
Hyperallergic: Before we even get into GTA, I was hoping each of you could tell me a little bit about your relationship to Miami — how long you've been there? How do you feel about living there now?
Leo Castañeda: I moved to Miami first when I was 11. My parents first moved to New York [from Colombia], and then they thought it was too cold, so they moved to Miami. I went to middle school and high school here, then I moved to New York for college, and I moved back in 2015. When I first moved back after college, it was mostly because of the cost of living in New York. And then, within the 10 years that I've been here, it became the same cost of living as New York, except with Florida salaries.
I do feel grateful, though, to be part of the Bakehouse Art Complex, where I have an affordable studio. I live in the North Beach area, and I was able to find a sustainable rent. Miami has a lot of arts nonprofits that help over time. I do feel that, as complicated as the Miami arts ecosystem is, it is pretty supportive — but at the same time, it is tied to all the different layers of money that have come in and dominate the arts, which are very present here.
misael soto: I moved here right after undergrad. I grew up in South Florida, originally from Puerto Rico, and Miami was always la locura, down south. We would visit my cousins and whatnot from time to time. As I became more and more interested in starting my own practice, I moved down here and have continually been sucked back in. I try to leave, and it pulls me back for whatever reason. Since COVID, everything's changed. Miami became the second most expensive city in the country. The influx was palpable: All of a sudden, there were Texas and California and New York license plates, Teslas zipping around town, and rent just started skyrocketing. There's more flooding. But at the same time, it's gorgeous, and it's special. I live in Mid-Beach. I can go to the water, I can breathe in some sea air, I can hear 10 different languages at once.
It's a really complex relationship with Miami. Especially, I think, both of us make complicated art — we both make art that is unconventional and perhaps even, you could say, difficult to collect. I don't know if you describe yourself that way, Leo, but I definitely do. And making this kind of work in a hyper market-driven neoliberal city like Miami, on the one hand, it gives me a lot of fodder, a lot of material, a lot of things to talk about, as we're doing right now. But at the same time, it can be really frustrating and alienating and lonesome, ultimately.
H: I moved from Argentina to Miami when I was little because my mom got a job there. We lived in the Doral neighborhood, where most people I knew were also from Latin America, until I left for Chicago for college at 18. I've lived in New York for over a decade now, but I still feel a strong pull to Miami, I feel seen, surrounded by people whose identities are a bit fractured the way I feel mine is.
And on the note of nostalgia, GTA is a game that was made over the last 13 years, so it chronicles a Miami that’s partly gone. For example, users say Lucía's home is based on a cute salmon-pink, 13-unit condo in Edgewater that was demolished in 2022 to build a 55-story tower, yet it lives on in the game. What does it mean for a video game to preserve a place that no longer exists?
LC: Well, a few thoughts. During that 13-year development, I would assume the map design was one of the first things they did. But there are also aspects of the chronicling of Miami, or Miami becoming this satire through the game, that have evolved in a shorter time period. For example, this morning I woke up, and there was a Miami Instagram influencer saying that in the fictional version of the Cuban coffee shop Versailles, which is called Antoinette, the bakery has a sign posted outside that says something like, “any politician must pay for all the food when they leave.” That's a reference from a few years ago, when Trump reportedly went to Versailles, ordered food for everyone, and then didn't pay and just walked out.
So it does seem like a video game takes a long time to make, and this one is probably the most ambitious one ever made — 4,500 people working really, really hard, to the point of even having the union situations that they have in the UK branch of the company. But at the same time, I feel like they studied Miami extremely well, and the integration with some local businesses and local artists in particular — I've seen a few street artists like Ahol Sniffs Glue, Soak, Tatiana Suarez, Typoe, as well as musician Nick León. One restaurant is based on Juvia on Lincoln Road, which doesn't exist anymore — they got priced out, and now there's a record of it. The game takes so long to make, but it lives in an ever-present, because it doesn't matter if you made an asset 13 years in the past, like Lucía's apartment, or now; they feel like the present. It's an interesting amalgamation. I would have to spend more time with it to really know: Does this feel like Miami in 2014 or Miami in 2026, or a hybrid?
H: To get into the politics of the conversation around GTA, I have a lot of icky feelings about one narrative that's taking hold online, which is that the game is “Woke 3.0,” and that the incels and Trump supporters are pissed about it. I only played for a few hours last night, and I went into a gun shop and bought a shotgun. That, to me, panders much more to the NRA hawks and the pro-gun community than to anything that could be considered woke, you know?
MS: Hmm. I see it the other way around, actually. To me, it's like pretending in order to pacify, in some ways. It's a very complex thing. On the one hand, I remember seeing the woman twerking on the top of a car as the sun came up over the MacArthur. Now that's in the game. And I remember the “face eater” on the MacArthur. I see a man in a thong skateboarding weekly, and now there's a character like that in the game. I teach art history, and I do a whole week on postmodernism and poststructuralism and simulacrum, and the consequences of that, which I think have led us into some really dangerous flattening territory in terms of the role of the artist in the late 20th to early 21st century. I see this game and the way that it's taken over the city in real life and in gameplay, and it makes me think about how much of this is pacifying the role of the artist, or is it pushing through to the other end and becoming a meta-modernist critique that has some gems in there, if you're willing to find them?
It ultimately makes me feel a bit sad in terms of what we deserve. I texted you yesterday, Valentina, when we were talking about having this conversation, and I said, “Well, maybe this is the kind of art the city deserves.” It's not the art that I want for Miami. But in so many ways, Miami is the perfect place. It's been the city for continual use by image makers, from Hollywood to video games.
H: There is some talk about the fact that the game does seem to have an awareness and sensitivity around identity. Cygnus, the curator at the Vice City Museum of Art, is the first non-binary character in Grand Theft Auto history. The actor cast for the role, Jesse James Rose, said that to prevent anti-trans violence, GTA made it so players would not be able to harm their character. Does this feel like an honest gesture, though?
MS: I was just talking to a friend who's been playing it, and she was like, “Where are all the Haitians?” I remembered there was this huge lawsuit against GTA and Vice City, the one set in the ’80s, from about 20 years ago. Haitian groups sued Rockstar over their portrayal. I did some research, and it seems now the company has shifted. They're saying, “We now punch up as opposed to punching down.” That feels, once again, so uncanny in comparison to the ways in which corporate America has shifted. It makes me think of the phrase, “Black faces in high places won't save us.” I don't want to be lobbing grenades at Rockstar. I think it's fantastic that these changes have been made, especially with such an influential game. But at the same time, it feels like the video game, in its attempt to replicate reality, is lagging in this area.
H: GTA has a long history of racism. We shouldn't forget that Black characters have been associated with criminality throughout all editions of the game. I haven't played enough to say whether that's the case in the latest version. There is also the question of how the company actually treats its workers, and the labor disputes that are going on behind the scenes. Nestor Uriarte, an animation programmer for Rockstar, wrote an opinion piece for the Guardian where he asked, why is it that with this game that generated billions of dollars, we are still fighting to get union recognition?
MS: I'm curious, Leo, as someone who has been playing games for as long as you have, how you feel about this. I'm a cinephile — I've been one since I was 18, and watched my first Kubrick film the summer before college. And I am dying to see Avengers: Doomsday (2026). I've been following the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) and have been consistently floored by the way they built out this world and the interconnected films. It's history, and it's been making history. But we all know how terrible Disney is. And even with the MCU, they tried to bring in more diversity, and the public didn't respond, so they backtracked on it. I don't know if that analogy holds. But it feels pertinent. It feels similar.
LC: Of course, I have to play more to fully understand it. There's the ads of the game and the game itself. I would say that the Netflix special did feel like it was perpetuating some of the stereotypes of the Haitian community. But at the same time, having played, or seen the range of minority characters so far in the first couple hours, it feels like they have a wide range of personalities, body types, and interests. It's not like they're all criminals. And I also found out that local Haitian muralist Serge Toussaint has his work featured in the game, which I think is an amazing thing. But in terms of artworks in other mediums that really relate to this, this is kind of like, let's say, South Park, or Euphoria — shows that are a mirror to the world that's very explicitly showing you both the best and the worst, and it's making fun of and critiquing everyone. But then how does it flip to show a new perspective or a solution?
I've seen a lot of people, especially women game critics and game developers, celebrating the relationship of Jason and Lucía being a central situation in the game, as opposed to a cast of different men from different backgrounds, or, in GTA IV, the Eastern European guy in the seedy underground. Having the relationship and the cultivating of the relationship be a core mechanic, almost in a Sims-like way — and even the learning of emotional labor, or doing kind things around the house, or the game having a really interesting reward mechanic for the nonviolent interactions ... At least in my experience so far, three hours in, I haven't shot a single shot.
H: Wait, how did you save Donnie in the first mission without shooting people?
LC: Oh, by hiding. It was saying, “Crouch around to make sure no one sees you.”
H: I think it's fascinating how different players can make these different decisions. I'm not very good at gaming, so I gave my husband the controller. I was like, “Get us out of here as quickly as possible. I want to get to Vice City!”
LC: Yeah, and usually my criticism of Rockstar Games and also Naughty Dog, two big companies that have these cinematic, movie-like games, is that the story missions often have a path where you fail if you don't take a violent action. The emergent gameplay — which happens just by walking around, the dynamic gameplay that's not in a story mission — is usually extremely layered and nuanced and can go in any direction, violent or not. Again, I'm only three hours in with GTA VI, but so far I appreciate that it is giving the choice of not using violence, and kind of rewarding it. There's something interesting about that. Because usually in those Rockstar games, I'm like, okay, there's this emotional tale, and now there's a mission, and I have to kill 20 minions.
MS: Leo, I'm thinking about your work and playing your pieces, immersing oneself in these worlds that you create, and there's a kind of mystery in the expansive potential that you create in your installations that at first can be a little overwhelming, but you have to just dive in. And this is the nature of games, or video games. There's a kind of trust fall. And I'm thinking about — let's just go there — the emancipatory potential of that. Because video games, to me, the potential in them as works is the building of awareness, the fostering of empathy, literally embodying someone who has a different way of life or a different body, a different perspective. Especially in our era of political correctness, and a lot of it is warranted, we're asked to speak from our own perspective and not assume things of others. And so this allowance — I wonder how you see the potential in that, especially in something like this game that is so immersive.
LC: I think games as artworks are, to a certain extent, some of the most affordably accessible. Yes, you need to have a PC or PlayStation or Switch or something, but they could be pieces of art that are globally accessible in an immediate way, and they really can affect culture. In terms of empathy, you're controlling a being that you identify as “I”: “I” drove the boat today, or in my game, “I” was camouflaging with the environment to gain energy. There's something there about the mutability of the body, or how one could shift one's self-identity into multiple beings, that is interesting in games, and also interaction and choice as a place that could be art, in a way that performance art also does, and maybe theater. And visual arts in general, maybe in a less touch-based way. But in terms of the empathy, I've been seeing a lot of reviews of GTA VI saying it's actually leading people towards that. Perhaps it is through the romantic relationship [between Jason and Lucía], or maybe by having so much freedom to do whatever you want and kill whoever you want, but then developing these characters and NPCs to a level where they feel like real people.
H: There is one moment in the game that was very emotive in a way that might provoke empathy, and it certainly did for me. At the very beginning — so this is not really a spoiler — we're shown the backstory of how Lucía gets arrested. She's been sitting at a cafe, a little Cuban cafecito, and she's just ordering ice water. The server keeps coming up to her and asking if she wants something else, and she's like, “No, no, just ice water for me.” It's clear that she just can't afford anything else. So in an act of true desperation, and from a place of deep poverty, she decides to rob a payday loan store nearby, and she gets caught. At one point, you can hear the cops saying, “She's saying she left something at the cafe.” And then we see the owners of the coffee shop taking care of her baby, who is then taken by social services.
We're not shown Tomás, her little baby, at the beginning. It's something that the game surprises us with. To me, it was such a thoughtfully articulated moment.
LC: The beginning is so strong. And then having the tutorial on how to walk and use the camera be her nine months later in prison. Out of overcapacity, the prison is letting some people who have lower sentences perhaps have probation, so she's gonna be let go, but the woman who works there says she doesn't know if or when Lucía will see her baby again. That works as a narrative tool, a teleology, giving purpose to the game beyond, “Oh, she's just a digital girlfriend.” Now there's this question of what the rewards of behavior are that the game's gonna have when one is part of the criminal underworld, but there is a child in foster care that could be taken back or not. That's gonna be so interesting if that ends up being a fork in the road within the narrative, because many of these games have multiple endings.
MS: This is so fascinating to me in regards to something we were talking about earlier — whether reality is informing the simulacrum and vice versa. It makes me think of how, living in Miami, it continuously feels like maybe the most neoliberal city I've ever lived in. But in so many ways, it oftentimes feels like when you're on the road or when you're at a cafe, you're alone. You really have to fend for yourself in this city. Of course, there are these moments where you break through, or if you're a regular at Enriqueta's, you know who to talk to, this and that. It makes me wonder how the game might change the way that we see ourselves. And, following that thread, how might it actually make us more united?
I don't know if that's a bit of a stretch, but there are just so many people playing this game. And I think over time it's really going to show, as visitors come and reflect their years of gameplay back to the city. In the same way that folks experience Paris syndrome, what will the GTA Miami syndrome be? How might that change us? I was thinking about it for the worse, but how might it change us for the better? Because I don't know a Miami where that childcare situation in the GTA story would happen. Of course, I'm not a caregiver. I'm not a parent. But I don't know that Miami — and I've been here long enough and I have a lot of family here, chosen family. So that makes me, in a weird way, hopeful.
LC: I think it's interesting, let's say with Pop art and conceptual art — if you use a urinal or a fluorescent light, you think of urinal, Duchamp; fluorescent light, Dan Flavin, etc. These artists are claiming this thing from the world. And it's interesting to have this very fluid cycle of, let's say, the Only in Dade Instagram account becoming almost a live feed of GTA, or us within Miami filtering our experience — when there's a very special or odd moment, it being a rehearsal for the game, or the game getting reflected back in the world.
If the game is marketing itself as this debauched, wild place, and that lures millions and millions of people in, but then it ends up being this profound story that actually shows how South Florida has issues of income inequality and climate change ... There's a hurricane system in the game, so there's a very strong chance that there will be flooding. Will that situation, where violence and comedy, or things that are not explicitly telling people what the values should be, actually make them more subtle and implicit? Does that create change or not?
H: We've been speaking over an hour, we could probably talk for two more hours. This feels like a beautiful note to end on. But I want to ask if there are any burning observations you want to share.
MS: I feel like we should speak about the takeover of Miami in the real world, physically. Anybody trying to do anything — F1, Art Basel, all these people who come in and take over the city, as they've done for decades — if they want to gain favor with locals, just look at what they did with GTA. Because the amount of free advertising — I mean, I went to this GTA VI-themed drag night, and it was not sponsored by them. It was at Las Rosas. They had a pool table and some neons, and they had the beer from the game available for purchase, but the event itself was fully done just to hop on the bandwagon, and everybody was lapping it up. Morphine Love Dion was playing the video game while people were dancing. It layered some uncanny feelings for me. But at the same time, I'm just very, very impressed, and scared, by the power of putting it everywhere to the point where it was inescapable. It's been inescapable for the last week. It's very impressive.
LC: Yeah. I've met at least two or three people who have been working on some of the release parties. So they're employing local artists and local musicians and local businesses, as opposed to, as misael was saying, these people arriving out of nowhere, renting a place for really exaggerated prices, and not giving back to the local community. At least through employment. We'll see over time if and how it leads to other forms of sustainability locally. I have a photographer friend who, similarly to that drag show, started doing GTA-style photos in front of one of the new signs and probably made some money through that, unofficially. So that's interesting.
MS: I think there's many ways to be a capitalist, or to do this kind of thing and take over the city in this way. And I've never seen something so thoughtful. It honestly reminds me to some degree of the first couple years of Art Basel, when they would do a lot of public programming and free concerts and they really seduced us ... But that's another conversation. I'll stop there.
H: Well, it's a perfect aperitif for Miami Art Week and the Basel boycott and everything else. And then the G20 summit hosted by Trump in Miami the following week.
MS: Wow, I forgot about that.
H: Yeah, we're going from GTA VI to G20. It's just a perfect pipeline, really.
MS: It doesn't get any more Miami surreal than that. Truly Vice City.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: ‘Napping together on the reeds, the swans appeared luminous’: Noah Forster’s best phone picture
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Grace Holliday
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Twenty-one-year-old Noah Forster had always thought swans were beautiful, but it was his girlfriend Cecilia is the one who made him really notice them. The pair began dating two years ago, but now live 70 miles apart; he is a welder in Newark-on-Trent, she is studying law in Leeds.
“The distance can be difficult, but we try to talk as much as possible,” Forster says. “It’s taken me a while to save up for a driver’s licence and car, so I have a daily walk from my home and across the River Trent to get the 6am train to work. We like to send photos of our day to each other, and I took this photo on an exceptionally cold and frosty morning in November, walking across the river to get to work. I saw these swans near the castle. Napping together on the reeds, they appeared luminous.”
“Me and you,” he wrote in a message to Cecilia, attaching the image. “I know she loves swans, but I also knew she was most likely sleeping herself!” he says.
Later, Cecilia encouraged him to submit the photo to be considered for the Smart Shot column. “I decided to keep the name of the image the same as the caption I sent to her, because it represents the calm and peaceful feeling you have when you are with someone you trust. I hope it makes others think about their special person who they feel safe with.”
