https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-dinki.title: David Dinkins Wasn’t Loud Enough for New York City
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-dinki.author: David Duhalde
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/review-dinki.text:
David Dinkins Wasn’t Loud Enough for New York City
David Dinkins, New York’s first black mayor and a Democratic Socialists of America member, practiced a quiet, dignified form of municipal leadership — so hushed that he was easily drowned out by more reactionary and demagogic forces in the city.
In the past few weeks, New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani has proposed breaking up the Strategic Response Group and closing Rikers by 2032, the former established by progressive Mayor Bill de Blasio, who also revived a plan to dismantle the latter by 2027. But unfulfilled promises of police and carceral reform efforts go back to the 1990s. How much should the failures of previous mayoral administrations weigh on the decisions of Mamdani and his allies in regard to public safety and police?
This question has no easy answer. But a new book by James Barney on the tenure of New York City’s first black mayor, David Dinkins, offers insights on his efforts to rein in police excesses based on new research, especially in the local press of the era — and critically how those attempts failed, despite Mayor Dinkins’s desires and promises.
In A Fragile Alliance: David Dinkins, Coalition Politics, and the Struggle to Govern a City in Crisis, Barney, while sympathetic to Dinkins, argues that both Dinkins’s quiet leadership style and inability to create a narrative uniting his own multiracial coalition, much less the majority of the city, proved to be his undoing, dooming his reelection prospects and much of his agenda.
Barney, critical of identity politics throughout his history book, sums up his reservations here:
. . . in particular, Dinkins’s reliance on the mosaic metaphor betrayed a worldview that privileged difference. While Dinkins repeatedly noted that New York City was a “gorgeous mosaic,” in a “mosaic” each of the pieces is different. They only produce any meaning by being part of a larger piece of art. But this type of thinking was at the heart of Dinkins’s problems as a leader because it emphasized differences rather than commonalities.
Barney’s reservations about celebrating difference are at times too determinative. For instance, I doubt Dinkins could have done much to stop the disintegration of the New Deal/Great Society coalition that voted Democratic as white ethnics left the party across the country. But Barney’s concerns about the communication failures of Dinkins’s tenure were real and went beyond narrative to style.
While noble at times, the mayor’s quiet leadership style prevented New Yorkers — especially in a time without social media to get news rapidly and easily outside major media like Mamdani enjoys and uses today — from seeing their mayor’s interventions that created more peace than was seen elsewhere in America at the time, for example Los Angeles, which experienced a much deadlier upheaval triggered by the lack of convictions for the police who senselessly beat Rodney King, as well as the killing of teenager Latasha Harlins by a Korean American storeowner. This failure provided an opening to power for demagogues such as Rudy Giuliani to paint a darker picture around crime and disorder than actually existed.
While New York City’s political landscape has changed in many ways — the Staten Island secession movement, for example, is almost forgotten today — one thing Barney covers remains very much the same. The New York Police Department (NYPD) and institutions around it enjoy strong independence from civilian control that makes it difficult for any mayor to shape policy and personnel decisions commensurate with other major city agencies.
A famous instance of this was when the Sergeants Benevolent Association (SBA) tweeted out personal data of then-Mayor de Blasio’s daughter’s arrest related to the George Floyd uprising. Former SBA head Ed Mullins eventually faced disciplinary charges over this, though by then it was overshadowed by his federal indictment and conviction of stealing from his members. It is difficult to think of any other agency and its unions who would feel so emboldened to reject democratic oversight.
Dinkins, unlike most of today’s socialists and progressives, ran on a tough-on-crime agenda. He promised to hire thousands more police officers. The issue of crime polled high across racial and gender categories of voters. But Dinkins targeted his law-and-order proposals to include increasing policing in communities of color with officers of similar backgrounds. A major critic of this policy was Giuliani, who claimed this public safety policy would take police away from white neighborhoods. Giuliani’s racialized law-and-order rhetoric helped sink Dinkins.
Progressive mayors following Dinkins, such as de Blasio and Mamdani, have reckoned with the political reality that a public safety reform agenda is territory that isn’t worth attempting battle upon. And losing puts their whole left-wing agenda, not just public safety, at risk. Case in point: after Dinkins’s defeat, New York saw two decades of fiscal conservative and anti-police-reform mayors.
Crown Heights as a Turning Point
Two chapters of the book that expand on how such demagoguery on policing helped cost Dinkins his mayoralty focus on the Crown Heights riots and Patrolmen’s Benevolent Association (PBA) riots, respectively. These chapters also go beyond those two episodes of public violence to discuss how other instances of excessive police force neither led to uprisings nor successful efforts to advance civilian control of law enforcement. Barney’s research uses these events to help us understand how perceived disorder would be viewed as a key reason Dinkins lost, even though the crime rates were falling, and how his relationship with the police leadership and rank and file did not recover despite his own law-and-order narrative.
Dinkins won a surprise primary victory against three-term incumbent and bombastic erstwhile liberal Ed Koch in 1989. Barney credits Dinkins’s win through efforts to build a black-led, multiracial coalition out of the efforts in and around Jesse Jackson’s 1988 presidential campaign and subsequent Rainbow Coalition. Voter registration and mobilization, especially of black voters, to back Jackson were then used to elect Dinkins.
Those new voters proved fruitful for Dinkins’s own Rainbow Coalition. Dinkins won over half the vote in the multicandidate Democratic primary against Koch. But his candidacy against the Republican in the general was unusually closer. In New York, the Democratic Party primary more often than not is the de facto election. Not for Dinkins. He faced Giuliani, famous at the time for his federal prosecution of the mafia in New York’s Southern District, in 1989 and 1993. Each time, the victor only bested his opponent by around 2 points.
Not only were the margins similar, but Barney argues that themes in each election centered around crime, racial tension, and divisive ethnic politics. What made the difference was how a slim number of voters (turnout was roughly the same, 1.9 million in both mayoral races) eventually shifted toward a harsher response to perceptions of disorder, even as crime rates were declining.
Dinkins lost ground partly because of both the Crown Heights riot and PBA riot. Each contributed to the public perception of an ineffective Dinkins, which undermined his promises to create a safer city and less brutal policing methods.
The Crown Heights riot story officially begins on August 19, 1991, when a vehicle in a motorcade following the chief Lubavitcher (a sect of Jewish Hasidim) rabbi hit two Guyanese American children. The immediate lack of medical attention for the children by emergency medial technicians, explained by the Jewish volunteer service that initially responded to the accident lacking professional skills needed to treat the young people’s injuries, led to a retaliatory stabbing of a rabbinical student days later. The following unrest, in which 150 people were arrested and one hundred police injured, led the media to publicly question Dinkins’s ability to heal the racial and ethnic divide in the city and portray him as a weak leader.
But the conflict in Crown Heights went further back than these two incidents. The riot itself reflected the tension between the religious Jewish enclave and their black neighbors, largely of West Indian descent. In a city where fights over resources can feel zero-sum, the well-organized and self-isolating Lubavitcher community appeared to gain at others’ expense. Their leadership, politically well-connected as a result of their well-organized followers voting as a bloc, primarily looked after their own. Barney notes, for example, that the police protection for the Lubavitcher headquarters was seen as taking officers away from the crack epidemic, fostering further estrangement from their black gentile neighbors.
Dinkins, viewing this as a battle of “good and evil,” according to Barney, responded to the restive state of Crown Heights by sending in a thousand police officers to quell the violence. Black civil rights leaders and organizers such as the Reverend Al Sharpton and Sonny Carson, at times previously allied with the mayor, turned on him. Sharpton even characterized Dinkins’s action as setting up an “apartheid state.”
But a second, seemingly contradictory viewpoint sprung up from Giuliani and his allies that Dinkins actually held the police back from acting. This narrative fit well with voters that Barney says wanted to lump Dinkins, Carson, and Sharpton together. Dinkins couldn’t win.
To make things worse, Dinkins publicly stated — repeating doctors’ misdiagnosis — that the stabbed rabbinical student would recover. But his wounds were fatal. The Jewish man died a few hours after Dinkins’s remarks. The death made Dinkins look, even if unfairly, incompetent.
Barney credits much of the success the mayor did achieve in facilitating conservations between different Crown Heights faith leaders. These dialogues between Christian and Jewish leaders were rarely reported in the press. To Barney, this was just another example of Dinkins’s “quiet leadership” that, while noble, undermined public perception of governance.
Ultimately, a 1993 internal city investigation called the Girgenti Report vindicated Dinkins from the viewpoint that he had not, in fact, held back the police nor abetted the prosecution of the rabbinical student’s killing. But the report’s timing was poor for the incumbent. Barney concludes it did more to remind voters in an election year of the chaos of two years earlier than absolving Dinkins in their eyes: “For a mayor who longed to unify, Crown Heights became the moment when broad segments of the public lost confidence in Dinkins and when his vision of a gorgeous mosaic, while laudable, was found insufficient to meet New York City’s realities.”
The narrative that Dinkins held the NYPD back in Crown Heights was one of many that undermined his relationship with the police department and its officers. Another was that the overwhelming white police force felt the mayor was giving preferential treatment to people of color and criminals.
The Police Riot as a Point of No Return
In 1992, a police officer shot a Dominican immigrant in Washington Heights, which sparked a series of events that led to a police riot by September. The Washington Heights shooting seemed to be heading toward similar unrest — this time, sparked by young people who felt overpoliced. Dinkins was able to de-escalate the situation well, such that even his critics like Cardinal John O’Connor gave the mayor credit for his handling of the shooting’s aftermath.
The mayor’s initial success and efforts included allies he recruited. Dinkins had an ally in Lee P. Brown, an African American criminologist and former police chief of Houston, Texas, that took the same role under Dinkins. As commissioner, Brown supported community policing, which brought more officers who looked like the people of the neighborhoods they patrolled. Again, this policy was not favored by some white people who felt it took resources from their residential areas.
But this balance between reform and political reality in policing became unstable for both Dinkins’s coalition and the NYPD brass. At the time, the police practiced stop and frisk, an invasive and violating search practice that nearly exclusively targeted young men of color. Dinkins would come to regret this policy. Beyond the ethics, stop and frisk also fostered a schism in his coalition between the young people who felt brutalized and the older residents who wanted more police. Roscoe C. Brown Jr, a Tuskegee airman veteran quoted by Barney, summed up this division in the simple fact that black people had been victims of both crime and racist policing. Solving one requires tackling the other.
But doing so for Dinkins became impossible. Brown resigned as commissioner in 1992, because, according to Barney, even this reformer did not want to go as far as Dinkins in empowering the police watchdog city agency, the Civil Complaint Review Board. Dinkins, unlike Brown, determined the NYPD was unable to hold itself accountable. Still, Brown’s departure was from the worst rebuke Dinkins would experience by the NYPD.
On September 16, 1992, organized by the police union (PBA), nearly ten thousand off-duty officers rallied outside city hall. Fueled by alcohol and rhetoric from Giuliani and PBA union leaders saying Dinkins favored criminals over cops, some police wore anti-Dinkins shirts, and others overturned barricades.
While the media and some allies like Sharpton returned to Dinkins’s camp after this because of the racist slurs hurled at Dinkins and noxious nature of the police riot, the damage was done with enough of the public. The perception that Dinkins had lost the police overrode the actual declining crime rates with a sufficient number of voters to eventually swing the election toward Giuliani the next year. This would end a progressive holding the mayor’s office until 2014 with the election of Bill de Blasio.
NYPD Reform Returns
Today not only is the mayor a progressive but, like Dinkins, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA). Zohran Mamdani also shares the challenges of balancing the wishes of his coalition and campaign promises with those of political reality. Policing is no different.
Recently, Mamdani has pledged to disband the Special Response Group (SRG), a controversial police unit with both counterterrorism and protest control duties, and also backed socialist councilmember Chi Ossé’s CURB Act, which would limit tactics employed by SRG. As the SRG’s responsibilities will be reassigned to other police units, a move reportedly supported by NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch, limiting existing practices that police reform advocates say they are most against is critical to the success of reform.
Unlike Commissioner Lee with Dinkins, Tisch was not the incumbent mayor’s appointment but a holdover from the previous mayor. Mamdani has resisted calls from parts of his coalition to fire her; these allies identify her support of Zionism and a strong carceral state as incompatible with a socialist vision. Except for not hiring nearly six hundred more police officers after pushback from NYC-DSA and others, the recent moves against SRG nearly a year into his term are a first real push to tackle unaccountable and abusive police power.
While New York City crime stands at record lows, the experience of Dinkins should serve as a warning that statistical realities such as declining rates are sometimes no match for scare tactics. The police still have soft and unchecked power, with council allies allegedly quietly opposing the CURB Act.
Hidden opposition can become public, and allies can return. But sometimes it is too late, as Dinkins experienced after the police riot. As the title of Barney’s book reminds us, holding power can be fragile. It will take a balance of principle and strategic planning to successfully rein in the police. Or else we will set back again.
A lesson the current mayor can also learn from Dinkins is in a communication style to avoid. Instead, he should continue to present an accessible vision and visible actions so voters and other members of the public can easily understand and repeat his policy priorities.
Had Dinkins been able to enjoy the social media platforms and fluency that Mamdani does to get around mainstream gatekeepers and parochial local press, he might have been able to overcome the idea he was ineffective. But even with such tools, it requires a willingness to be public, even boastful, which people adverse to demagoguery understandably avoid.
But good intentions can be fatal. Quiet leadership, while noble, may be silent even to your supporters. And it can be used against you by your enemies. The base needs to know what you’re doing to counter the inevitable lies and distortions thrown at left-wing politicians by their reactionary political opponents.
The success of a progressive and socialist public safety agenda depends on winning the majority. That requires a tremendous amount of organizing from the grassroots, but also political leaders who can help echo a narrative that can cut through the noise trying to maintain the status quo or reserve the gains made by reformers so far.
A Fragile Alliance is worth reading for anyone trying to comprehend how the past can weigh on today’s New York. It is a valuable resource in seeing how old attack frames, especially around identity, which seem outdated but once worked against Dinkins, could return against Mamdani. But more critically, how previous efforts of mayors around police reform failed and succeeded. Learning from that history can better prepare activists to push those in power, even our allied electeds, in a more strategic direction.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/inflation-au.title: Inflation Is About Resources — and Power
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/inflation-au.author: Oskar Brandt
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/inflation-au.text:
Inflation Is About Resources — and Power
Inflation policy is a fight over real resources: who controls them, who gets access to them, and who pays when prices rise.
After prices began rising and rising in the wake of COVID-19 and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, some blamed welfare and public spending for the inflation. Yet in many economies, weak demand and falling public investment after 2008 held back investment and productive capacity. Austerity can also weaken productivity and future growth. In the United States, changes to trade policy during Donald Trump’s first presidency added to uncertainty about the economic situation. Trade policy uncertainty between 2017 and 2018 may have lowered investment by 1 to 2 percent. During the pandemic, automakers canceled orders and halted production. Demand returned before factories, suppliers, and transport networks could restart. The Cleveland Fed documented how factory shutdowns, parts shortages, and shipping delays during the pandemic disrupted supply chains. The oil crisis of 1973 is a reminder of how a real supply shock can also become a lasting case for austerity.
Joe Biden’s American Rescue Plan expanded the child tax credit. Child poverty fell from 9.7 percent in 2020 to 5.2 percent in 2021, then rose to 12.4 percent in 2022 after Congress let the expansion expire. From 2019 to 2023, low-wage workers’ real pay grew by 13.2 percent. Real manufacturing-construction spending rose by 85 percent from January 2021 to a six-decade high in part as a result of new investment laws. These gains helped poor families, workers, and industry, though they cannot all be attributed to Biden’s policies.
US inflation also fell earlier than in the eurozone. Consumer price index (CPI) inflation peaked at 9.1 percent in June 2022 and fell to 3 percent by June 2023, while eurozone inflation was still 5.5 percent. Global supply pressures eased, energy prices fell, and the Federal Reserve raised rates sharply. Still, stronger wages and public investment can coincide with falling inflation. The gains for poor families, however, can disappear when that policy ends.
Sweden brings the question into focus in 2026. In its March 2026 forecast, the Swedish Agency for Financial and Public Management projected a general government deficit of SEK180 billion for the year. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) describes the fiscal policy as expansionary but expects headline inflation to remain below target. Inflation can rise when spending meets shortages of labor or natural resources, limited production, or firms with the power to raise prices. But spending and higher purchasing power do not cause inflation by themselves. The result depends on resources, production, prices, and import dependence. The deficit forecast and the IMF’s outlook show why.
Production Is Power
Imagine a low-paid worker with rent due and a child to feed two weeks until payday. A pay raise may help, but it cannot create affordable homes or medicine. When the costs of essentials rise faster than incomes, people with little room in their budgets absorb the shock first. Inflation policy decides who loses purchasing power, whose costs get protected, and whose prices remain beyond public control.
A government that issues its own floating currency creates money as it spends and withdraws money from the private economy through taxes. But it still faces real limits: labor, technology, materials, energy, and ecological capacity. Reliance on imports, foreign-currency debt, and exchange rate pressure can tighten those limits. If spending exceeds what producers can supply, prices may rise. A deficit alone cannot tell us where that point lies. An economy with available workers and room to raise productivity can absorb spending without necessarily generating inflation.
Banks create money when they lend. Each loan creates a matching deposit; as the loan is repaid, that deposit money disappears. But money cannot summon nurses, electricity, medicines, homes, or skilled workers. Private credit can sustain demand when wages and public spending lag, but households and firms cannot increase debt indefinitely. When borrowers repay loans more quickly than banks issue new ones, this bank-created money contracts. Austerity can exacerbate this fall in demand. If households and businesses try to pay down debt at the same time, a financial crisis can ensue.
Globalization gave rich countries access to abundant goods and helped keep some prices down, but it tied factories to long shipping routes and distant suppliers. Military power can protect routes, resources, and property rights, but it also depends on domestic industrial capacity and state support for its industries. Japan, South Korea, and China built technical capacity through public investment, industrial policy, directed credit, protection, and managed trade, while many Western economies have become dependent on finance, services, and imported goods. This has weakened the West’s ability to sustain the military power that keeps globalization in place.
Globalization also exposed the costs of weakening domestic industry. Trade shocks left factory workers with lasting job losses and lower incomes. Research has linked layoffs to far-right support, unequal exposure to economic shocks to racial animus and right-wing voting in the United States, and local trade shocks to authoritarian values.
A company that dominates its market sector can raise prices with less fear of losing customers. Across industries in fifteen European economies, the average market share of the four largest firms rose from 26 percent in 2000 to 32 percent in 2019; average markups rose about 7 percent. A US manufacturing study found that mergers were associated with higher markups and little evidence of higher plant productivity. Firms can also use monopsony power to hold down wages and hiring. In a study of French labor markets, a 10 percent increase in labor market concentration was associated with nearly 0.9 percent lower wages for new hires and 12.4 percent fewer hires.
Shocks Give Price-Setters Cover
COVID caused real supply problems. Lockdowns disrupted production. Households saved more, while spending shifted from services to goods. Auto demand plummeted in 2020, causing carmakers to cut their chip orders. In turn, chipmakers shifted production to other customers, and when auto demand returned, they could not quickly meet carmakers’ renewed need. Shortages can make it easier for powerful firms to raise prices. When rivals face the same shock and customers expect increases, price hikes can spread even without a cartel.
In 2022, profits rose faster than production across the eurozone and accounted for the largest share of price increases. Real cost shocks, like those associated with the recent US wars of 2025–26, can nonetheless coexist with wider margins. In food markets, financial speculation and stockpiling can drive price rises beyond what shortages alone would explain, especially when war creates expectations of shortages.
When COVID arrived, manufacturers expected a prolonged recession and cut production, capacity, and orders. Demand and employment recovered faster than expected, leaving shortages of semiconductors, lumber, and other inputs. Fiscal expansion did not invent these bottlenecks; it revealed them. Repeated periods of weak demand can close factories, disperse skilled workers, and delay investment, making supply slower to recover.
In the 1960s, large industrial firms had built capacity but struggled to sell everything they produced. Some responded by buying unrelated businesses, selling off or outsourcing production, and relying more on short-term finance. This shift away from production gave financial markets greater influence over industrial decisions. In the decades that followed, private debt could temporarily sustain productive capacity despite weak wage growth, but when borrowing slowed, spending and sales fell. Debt-led crises also enabled investors to buy distressed property, companies, and assets from poor households cheaply, at a high social cost.
Debt and Austerity
Some Mesopotamian rulers in antiquity periodically canceled debts, freed people from debt bondage, and restored property, in part to check mass indebtedness and land concentration. These measures were episodic, not part of a regular, universal system. Debt was contested in Ancient Greece too, as seen in Solon’s reforms. Rome faced recurring credit crises and public-land conflict. Debt crises and land struggles shaped the politics of the late Roman Republic.
The two world wars showed that markets could be governed. During World War I, the US War Industries Board coordinated production. After the war, advocates of austerity in Britain and Italy promoted balanced budgets and hard-money policies and accepted high unemployment as ways to restore economic hierarchies at labor’s expense. During World War II, the United States used price ceilings, rationing, taxes, wage policies, credit controls, and resource allocation to restrain inflation, raise revenue, and direct production toward the war effort.
One historical estimate put the price level more than 30 percent below where it would have been without general price controls. Controls did not abolish scarcity. Many goods were rationed or simply unavailable, but alongside public management of demand and physical resources, the controls worked. World War II was one of the few times that the US came close to full productive capacity. During the war, labor shortages and stronger unions also improved many workers’ bargaining position.
A study of 166 elections in 16 OECD countries from 1980 to 2016 found austerity associated with increased electoral abstention and support for nonmainstream parties. Austerity weakens workers’ bargaining power and public services, reduces demand and investment, and can undermine social stability.
The late 1990s surpluses, combined with the trade deficit, pushed the US private sector into record deficits. Household debt grew much faster than income as Washington paid down public debt. Levy researchers later linked private sector deficits to the global crisis of 2008. Post-COVID inflation had different causes, including supply bottlenecks, a shift toward goods, and energy shocks.
Lessons From Past Shocks
Inflation was already rising in the United States before the 1973 oil shock. The US chose to escalate the Vietnam War. The war diverted workers, fuel, and materials from civilian production and sent dollars abroad. In 1971, Richard Nixon ended the dollar’s convertibility into gold. The dollar continued to serve as a major world currency without a promise of redemption in gold. Fiat money still faces real limits: the availability of oil, labor, materials, and productive capacity.
During the Yom Kippur War, Arab oil states imposed an embargo and cut production. Separately, the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) raised prices. Iran’s shah, a US ally, pushed for higher oil revenues to finance the country’s military buildup. Nixon had promised to sell him the arms he wanted. A contemporary account argued that Washington encouraged Middle Eastern producers to raise prices from 1971; Washington had earlier accommodated the shah’s push for higher prices, but during the crisis it opposed the Arab embargo and resisted OPEC’s proposed 100 percent price hike.
The United States did not create the whole crisis. But US leaders accepted higher oil revenues for a strategic ally. Meanwhile, oil companies, banks, and arms firms gained from the new flows of money, while workers and households paid higher prices. Leaders later used the crisis to attack welfare and full employment, even though the oil shock did not prove that public spending caused inflation.
The shift toward policies that tolerated high unemployment, wage restraint, and public spending cuts was a political choice, not an automatic result of the oil shock. Naomi Klein has traced disaster capitalism to Milton Friedman’s argument that crises can open the way for sweeping economic change. She shows how leaders and businesses have used this approach repeatedly, from Chile and post-Soviet Russia to the Iraq occupation and Hurricane Katrina, to push privatization and expand corporate control.
This selfsame policy choice — the choice between using inflation to justify austerity, or addressing its causes and effects — is reflected in Sweden’s response to the latest energy shock.
The Swedish Case
The war in the Middle East disrupted shipments through the Strait of Hormuz this past year, raising Swedish motor fuel prices by 25 percent. Yet Eurostat’s November release put Swedish inflation at just 0.6 percent, compared with 4 percent in the eurozone. On the Riksbank’s target measure, which holds mortgage interest rates fixed, Swedish inflation rose from 0.7 percent in August to 1.5 percent in September before easing to 1.1 percent in October. Excluding energy, it was just 0.1 percent in October.
Some measures that widened Sweden’s deficit also lowered prices. The November budget projected a 2026 deficit of SEK158 billion, or 2.3 percent of GDP. After Sweden halved the value-added tax (VAT) on groceries in April, food prices fell 5.5 percent that month; a government review found that retailers passed on most of the cut. The government also subsidized half-price monthly transit passes from July through December. The Riksbank estimates that without the temporary measures’ direct effects on prices, September inflation would have been 3.0 percent, twice the actual rate.
Growth continued alongside low inflation. Real GDP grew 1.6 percent, and the European Commission raised its forecast for 2026 growth to 2.8 percent. Household spending, investment, and net exports also lifted growth. The available figures give no separate estimate of how much the relief measures added to output or productivity.
The labor market recovery has been slower. A labor force survey put trend unemployment at 8.7 percent in the third quarter, even as employment rose. Sweden has also cut support for people in employment programs for more than 300 days. The government expects the cuts to speed up the return to work. But when households on tight budgets cut their spending, local businesses lose sales; and if financial pressure pushes people into jobs that make poor use of their skills, productivity could suffer. Sweden’s 2026 figures do not yet tell us how large these effects are.
The Riksbank expects inflation to exceed 2 percent in 2027 as the recovery strengthens and higher energy and import costs feed through. The government forecasts 2.8 percent in 2028 when the grocery VAT is due to return to 12 percent. Further disruption in Hormuz, the war in Ukraine, and new trade barriers could also raise costs and weaken demand for Swedish exports.
Sweden can issue kronor, but what it can buy depends on the fuel, labor, and equipment available. Higher interest rates can slow spending and hiring, but they won’t bring another tanker through Hormuz. Cheaper fares leave commuters with more money in their pockets today, and better public transport gives them a way to use less imported fuel tomorrow.
A state cannot buy resources that do not exist. But concentrated firms may raise prices before resources run out, while austerity can destroy demand and productive capacity. Inflation reflects pressure on real resources, but power determines who controls them and who pays when prices rise.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/democratic-s.title: Under Capitalism, Socialism Will Never Disappear
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/democratic-s.author: Alex McCarron
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/democratic-s.text:
Under Capitalism, Socialism Will Never Disappear
The Left won the midterms not by inventing a new politics but by reopening old fights the Right thought it had won. As long as capitalism exists, socialism can’t be consigned to the past.
If socialists and progressives had a good night on November 3, it wasn’t so much because they brought new ideas to the election, but because it was a chance to relitigate fights the Right thought it had won years ago: universal health care, Palestinian solidarity, and the expansion of the labor movement. We even got a rematch between George W. Bush–era Islamophobia and two of the Muslim Americans who had to live in its shadow, Adam Hamawy and Abdul El-Sayed.
Many have lauded Zohran Mamdani’s novel use of the term “affordability” for the recent shift in political common sense. But while his branding is new, his politics are not. Mamdani has never styled himself as a new kind of politician. He seems to be constantly locating himself in history, comparing himself to Milwaukee’s sewer socialists and New Dealers like Fiorello La Guardia. This makes sense when you consider that his policies represent decades of struggle: the project of expanding democracy into the workplace dates to the late nineteenth century, and the fight to guarantee health care as a right dates to the early twentieth.
Critics often ask why socialists are bringing a nineteenth-century ideology to bear on twenty-first century problems. The simple answer is that it seems to be what’s working. Since the turn of the twenty-first century, a series of global social movements have sought a new kind of political orientation, one that would allow for a break with the politics of the last century and the historical culs-de-sac they crashed into. Every few years brings a new form of right, center, and left politics: Occupy, Abundance, the Yellow Vests, the Movement of Squares, prison abolitionism. These movements all respond to real problems, but what’s new about them is mostly just branding. Few offer genuinely new critiques or build lasting political constituencies or institutions. Their strength is being novel enough to draw a crowd, drive a news cycle, or launch an academic career. Such innovations move to the same rhythm as capitalism’s own churning drive to simulate invention, revolution, and disruption across the economy.
At the same time, one sees the appeal. We can’t exactly blame radicals for wanting a disruption of their current institutions. Everywhere you look, leftists are trying to overcome the NGOization of the Left and searching for a common ground between their alienated, specialized critiques. Ecologists want to talk about the environmental catastrophe of the genocide in Gaza, while anti-racists want to connect their work to the extreme weather events that disproportionally effect the Global South. This is the basic drive of left-wing politics: to establish continuities between spheres of knowledge and to build connections between people.
The 20th Century Never Died
To find that meeting place in socialism is to recognize that what is happening to you has been happening to you for a very long time. Embracing the old language means realizing that you’re settling unfinished business rather than facing a new foe. Comparing the capitalist class to the aristocracy that came before it enables a person to see how arbitrary and contingent ruling-class power really is. One can understand why Bernie Sanders traded loaded terms like “bourgeoisie” and “proletariat” for the “1 percent” and “99 percent.” But it was just as important that he held onto “democratic socialism.” The term signaled that he was continuing a struggle and adding to an existing tradition of critique rather than declaring a year zero for left politics.
We are likely to be haunted for years by how dynamic, inventive, and exciting the twentieth century was. Every decade brought a new way of dressing, a new style of painting, and new stage in the maturation of cinema and popular music. Our hunger for political novelty is not just a reflection of market forces. It’s also a long shadow of that era of continuous revolution in politics and culture.
Look closely, though, and you’ll find many of the twentieth-century movements that sought a break with tradition did so while grabbing hold of another tradition buried even deeper in history. Le Corbusier claimed his form of architecture would clear “the charnel house of past ages” that our homes had become, but he did so by marrying the mathematical proportions of the Parthenon to the logic of mass production. As much as Henri Matisse and Pablo Picasso wanted to carry Paul Cézanne’s project into the future, they were also looking for a way to reconnect Western painting to the animism of African sculpture. The French New Wave paid an equally backhanded compliment to the “naive” genre films of Americans like Raoul Walsh and Sam Fuller, whose primitivism could liberate French filmmakers from their own pretensions and refinement.
As Long as There’s Capitalism, There Will Be Socialists
Even Karl Marx had this moment of paradox. In The Eighteenth Brumaire of Louis Bonaparte, he writes that “the social revolution of the nineteenth century cannot take its poetry from the past but only from the future.” A few lines later, he quotes the Gospel of Luke 9:60: “Let the dead bury their dead.” Marx was inveighing against the tendency of revolutionaries to reach for the words and costumes of past eras when faced with the task of changing the world: Rome for the French Revolution, the Old Testament for the English Civil War. This awkward LARPing is what turns history’s repetitions into farce. Yet Marx’s famous line about history occurring “first as tragedy, the second time as farce” is itself framed as an amendment to Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. Even the poetry of the future has a few allusions in it.
The difference between the French revolutionaries’ idealized Rome and today’s democratic socialism is that socialism is no more a thing of the past than capitalism is. Capitalism constantly calls the concept back into existence, raising its own gravediggers out of the grave, over and over again. As long as capitalism exists, it will exploit workers and destroy the planet, and the masses will find a way to fight back. Our present sits on a much longer timeline than the twenty-four-hour news cycle has accustomed us to. One day we’ll have new words and new costumes, but those belong to a new world, and we’re not there yet.

https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.title: Tyson Fury looks back: ‘Once the Anthony Joshua fight is over, what will I do next? Walking the dog ain’t gonna cut it’
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.author: Harriet Gibsone
https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle.text:
Born in Manchester in 1988, Tyson Fury – known as the Gypsy King – is a former unified heavyweight world champion. He turned professional in 2008 and in 2015 defeated the long-reigning champion, Wladimir Klitschko, to claim the WBA, IBF, WBO and Ring magazine heavyweight titles. He made a comeback in 2020, and his long-awaited final fight is on 11 December against Anthony Joshua. He appears with his wife, Paris, and seven children in the docuseries At Home With the Furys. A documentary charting his life, Fury, is out on Netflix on 27 November.
This was taken when I was nine, back when I was cute, shy and poorly dressed. The jumper would have been knitted by my grandma. The hairstyle isn’t great but a lot better than what I have now. I loved boxing and I loved singing.
I come from a travelling background, but we never moved anywhere. We lived in a house in a village outside Manchester called Wilmslow that had a farm. Me and my three brothers would ride quads, build treehouses and make dens. Roaming around the countryside was a dream life for a young boy. Nobody knew where we were or what we were doing – there were times we could have died – but there were no worries about perverts getting us or anything like that.
Growing up, masculinity meant showing no emotion. We never discussed feelings or love. My dad was a big influence on me. I inherited his ability to talk, his size and aggression. But I was soft, too. I inherited that from my mother – a gentle, kind nature. I remember the first time I felt anxiety. I was six and hiding in the wardrobe. I had this awful feeling something bad was about to happen. I didn’t tell anyone and have no idea what triggered it.
I started going to the gym when I was six, just to mess around. By the time I was 14, I was taking it more seriously. I was always confident in boxing, but over time, I realised that it is not just raw aggression and violence, it’s an art form.
My family were not as enthusiastic about my ambitions as I was. Dad was a professional and bare-knuckle boxer. He tried to encourage me to get a normal job – to have a stable existence instead. Mum was the same. I didn’t listen. There was no other option for me.
All I did was box and train – so in many ways I was the world’s best kid. I didn’t go out partying, didn’t have any idiot friends. When I met Paris I knew she was the one straight away. She was 15. I was 16. We were children, really, but I told her: “I’m going to marry you.” She went: “What? I don’t even know you.” I replied: “I’m going to make you fall in love with me. I’m going to be world champion and we’re going to have all these kids.” I was right. I signed my first professional contract on the first day of our honeymoon. We were meant to have two weeks away. We left four days later as I had to come back to fight.
From as far back as I can remember, Wladimir Klitschko was the guy I wanted to beat. He was the world heavyweight champion when I was a kid. He was my target, but when I told people I would win, everyone laughed at me, as they always did. In 2015, I finally got my chance to prove them wrong. There was a lot going on in my life at the time – we’d had a miscarriage and a very close uncle had died. I was grieving, but I tried to push it to the back of my mind so I could focus on Wlad.
Then the fight came, and I beat him. That’s when the problems started. Almost immediately, I felt like I was spiralling out of control. I had no purpose. I didn’t want to be at the press conference, or celebrating. Me and the family went on holiday. “Enjoy this,” I said to Paris, “because it’s downhill from here.”
For that whole period I was screaming out for help, but everyone around me wanted to put me in a rematch. It was like I was a demon possessed and I needed a hospital rather than a ring. I was hearing voices – horrible, scary voices. At night my head was full of terrifying screams, to the extent I thought someone was in the room. Alcohol and drugs played a part, and I was also comfort eating – mainly sugar. It gave me joy, a short term sensation of happiness. But it wasn’t real. I was hurling myself into oblivion. If I left the house for more than an hour, Paris would call everyone we knew, as she thought I had gone to kill myself.
Two years later, everything changed. It was Halloween and I was dressed as a 400lb skeleton. I was drunk. But I had a moment of clarity. I watched these young people at the bar – kids at the beginning of their lives. I thought: “What am I doing here? I’ve been offered everything a person could want, and I’ve blown it all.”
Back at home, I took off the costume, got on my knees and started praying to God. I thought: “If I can get better, then I’ll be happy. I’d rather have nothing, live in a tent and be on benefits than go back to how I feel right now.” It seemed like I was on my knees for an eternity, but it was probably only 10 minutes, when suddenly I felt a change. I screamed out to Paris – she thought I was drunk – saying: “I’m going to make a comeback in the morning.” She’d heard it all before, but I was serious this time.
That was the start of the return mission. I went to a leading specialist and was diagnosed with schizophrenia and bipolar. I learned that you can never truly get away from mental health. You can only learn to manage and maintain. I started training with Ben Davison and working with promoter Frank Warren. Within a few months, I was back in the ring. Now I’m gearing up for the final hurrah. I’m 38 years old, at the end of my boxing life. What better way to go out with a bang, putting on a fight that people have been waiting a decade for?
Once that fight is over I have to decide: what will I do next? I need to find a job. Waking up in the morning and doing normal stuff ain’t going to cut it. Walking the dog or taking the kids to school is fantastic, but it’s not enough of a purpose to get up for. Once the kids are done with school, then what? It does play on my mind, but I can’t think about it as I have to focus on the fight.
Sometimes I forget the long distance I’ve travelled and everything I’ve had to overcome. That nine-year-old boy was just a nobody – an unknown person from wherever. But he knew he could be a boxer. That I would become a world champion is one thing, but to transcend the sport and do TV shows, publish bestselling books, sing with Robbie Williams, is another level. I am truly blessed – not only with the ability to work hard, but to keep the faith all the way.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/dsa-la-elect.title: Los Angeles Socialists Won Big in the Blue Electoral Wave
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/dsa-la-elect.author: Chris Kutalik
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/dsa-la-elect.text:
Los Angeles Socialists Won Big in the Blue Electoral Wave
A key but occasionally overlooked site of socialist resurgence in the United States: Los Angeles, where members of the Democratic Socialists of America won local races, the mayoralty, and a seat in Congress.
The midterm elections were truly seismic. Like many places across the country, Los Angeles made good on its protean potential from the 2026 blowout with a stronger socialist movement and a larger share of political power. Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) members won up and down the ballot. Nithya Raman won the mayor’s office of the country’s second-largest city in an upset victory. Marissa Roy has won the city attorney’s office, and Angela Gonzales-Torres is headed to Congress.
Together their victories put democratic socialists in two of Los Angeles’s most powerful citywide offices and sent a DSA-LA member to Congress for the very first time in a race that few expected a year ago would even be a close challenge. The formerly conservative, sleepy suburb of Burbank has elected a DSA council majority, one of the first on the West Coast.
Behind those wins is DSA’s second-largest chapter. In the last year alone, the LA chapter doubled its membership to over six thousand members, launched a citywide Shake Up LA slate, and knocked more than 110,000 doors. And it did so alongside a realignment of the city’s left-labor coalition, especially that of the powerful hotel workers union UNITE HERE Local 11, which cross-endorsed most of DSA-LA’s Shake Up City Hall slate from Nithya down to Burbank City Council, and whose thousands of members knocked doors for her.
National Earthquake
This didn’t happen in a vacuum. Nationally, Democratic candidates of all stripes won control of both chambers of Congress, while Republicans lost ground in a shocking 99 percent of roughly 2,100 counties where most ballots had been counted by the morning after the election, according to Reuters. The electorate shifted left nearly everywhere, all at once.
Within that national revolt, Los Angeles voters were also shifting left. Gonzales-Torres decisively defeated Democratic incumbent Jimmy Gomez, winning over 62 percent of the vote while running openly as a DSA member, supporting a free Palestine and the abolition of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and rejecting corporate money. Her victory gives DSA-LA its first foothold in Congress with a candidate that took clear positions against corporate power and state violence and for Palestine and the Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS) movement while building a winning electoral coalition.
Roy’s victory carries a historic mandate as well. With more than 695,000 votes and roughly 68 percent support, she received the largest vote total ever won in a Los Angeles city election at any time, according to her campaign. She campaigned uphill, against the Democratic establishment and real estate lobby’s support of the incumbent, on turning the City Attorney’s Office into LA’s largest public-interest law office: pursuing abusive corporate landlords, enforcing workers’ rights, holding polluters accountable, and challenging the Trump administration in court.
Raman’s mayoral victory expands that opening considerably. Her 2020 city council victory helped establish DSA-LA as a force in city politics. Six years later, she has defeated incumbent (and onetime New Leftist) Karen Bass to become Los Angeles’s first democratic socialist (and immigrant) mayor.
Her victory gives the socialist movement a new scale of power to advance housing, tenant protections, and public services across Los Angeles. An ongoing tension will be between her independence as an elected and the co-governance and criticism of both the LA chapter and DSA’s national leadership about her level of support for the BDS movement and other issues she may not be in lockstep with the chapter on.
The chapter has also consolidated its existing beachhead on the LA City Council. City Council Members Eunisses Hernandez and Hugo Soto-Martínez and Los Angeles Unified School District Board Member Rocío Rivas all won reelection. In the Inglewood area, Estefany Castañeda retained her seat on the Centinela Valley Union High School District board, while Yaritza Gonzalez won election to the Inglewood Unified School District board.
Red Burbank
The chapter’s reach also expanded beyond Los Angeles. In Burbank, victories for Mike Van Gorder and Nolan Southerland created a democratic socialist council majority alongside Konstantine Anthony, while Stephen Post won in West Hollywood. Estuardo Mazariegos’s race in Los Angeles’s Ninth Council District remained unresolved, with Mazariegos trailing by a mere eighty-seven votes after taking on an opponent backed by major corporate and police union spending.
Los Angeles is also part of a national advance forward by socialists. DSA reported at least eight members elected to the next House: Gonzales-Torres, Chris Rabb, Darializa Avila-Chevalier, Melat Kiros, Claire Valdez, and Donavan McKinney, alongside Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Rashida Tlaib. Its election coverage also recorded state legislative wins in Florida and Tennessee. These wins give the socialist movement more opportunities to connect local organizing with struggles over national policy.
The scale of the work behind these campaigns matters. In its largest electoral effort to date, DSA-LA endorsed thirteen candidates and mobilized more than 1,700 volunteers to fill over 4,000 canvassing shifts. Its members knocked more than 110,000 doors in chapter-led canvasses. Over the same period since the 2024 election cycle, membership grew from nearly 3,000 to more than 6,000 and has added several hundred new members since Election Day alone.
The Long Arc
The chapter’s program places this strategy in a longer history of multiracial working-class struggle, from Justice for Janitors in the 1990s to the immigrant rights marches of 2006 and the teachers’ strike of 2019. Those movements demonstrated how organized workers could reshape Los Angeles’s politics and advance demands benefiting the wider public.
Combining electoral work, movement activism (from anti-ICE mobilizations to mass transit organizing to Palestine solidarity work), and member growth points toward a way to build durable socialist organization and power. An endorsement backed by thousands of volunteer shifts creates opportunities to develop new organizers and leaders, forge relationships with neighbors, and bring people into a member-run organization.
Keeping that capacity alive takes work. New members need meaningful roles and on-ramps to activity, political education, and a voice in deciding what comes next. Campaign volunteers need opportunities to remain active after their candidate wins or loses.
There is a wide constituency for that work. Gallup’s September report found that 43 percent of Americans viewed socialism positively, the highest share in its series. In Los Angeles, late October University of California, Berkeley Institute for Governmental Studies polling put democratic socialist identification at roughly a third of likely city voters. “The democratic socialist constituency is real, and it is growing,” said DSA-LA Cochairs Leslie Chang and Sean Wakasa.
The Promise
The election results alone cannot settle every argument about which message or strategy worked best. They do, however, create an opening for a Left that offers more victories, confronts concentrated wealth, and refuses to sacrifice solidarity for supposed electoral advantage.
The next test will be whether these victories open up more struggles and, most of all, change people’s lives. Roy’s promised enforcement agenda, a stronger socialist presence on city council, and Raman’s incoming mayoral administration create opportunities. Those gains, as always, will require organized pressure, alliances with unions and community groups, and members willing to remain involved in the difficult work of governing. They will also take sustained and coordinated pushing and accountability from movements and DSA locally.
The promise of the democratic road to socialism is that working people can collectively govern the institutions that shape their lives. In Los Angeles, that promise now has more members, more organizers, and more elected socialists behind it.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/21/trum.title: An Air Force Major Is Being Held in Solitary Confinement for Criticizing Trump on CNN
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/21/trum.author: Seth Stern
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/21/trum.text:
Seth Stern is the director of advocacy for Freedom of the Press Foundation.
Government lawyers on Tuesday played a video in court of a CNN interview where an American citizen called for President Donald Trump’s impeachment, arguing that the video alone proves the interviewee must remain in solitary confinement until his February trial.
“Not only is [Trump] a failure as president, he is flagrantly violating the Constitution, breaking the law, engaged in rampant corruption, and is killing Americans,” the now-defendant told CNN host Erin Burnett in August. “I believe we can defeat this government if we just take a stand.”
This view of the current presidential administration is hardly controversial, as this month’s midterm elections proved, let alone criminal.
The catch is that the interviewee is an Air Force officer, Maj. Jason Watson. In July, he was arrested during a protest on the steps of the U.S. Capitol where he wore his military uniform and held a sign calling for Trump to be impeached and removed from office.
He was subsequently charged under the Uniform Code of Military Justice over the protest and the CNN and other media interviews, including for “contemptuous words” against the president, failing to obey orders or regulations, and conduct unbecoming of an officer.
The military, unfortunately, has been afforded significantly greater leeway by the judiciary to punish speech than civilian courts.
But not that much leeway. As we’ve seen before, when the law gives the Trump administration an inch, it takes a mile. Watson’s case is the latest example of the administration plucking low-hanging fruit to suppress — and harshly punish — dissent.
The administration took advantage of purported ambiguities in immigration law to try to deport noncitizens for protesting and writing op-eds and posting on social media. It believes its broad authority to fight terrorism empowers it to make up a domestic terror organization, antifa, and prosecute and convict protesters — or people who merely read radical literature — as conspirators. It has used the archaic Espionage Act to harass journalists and their sources for exposing its incompetence.
Now, it’s weaponizing military law to retaliate against soldiers who talk to journalists.
The Trump administration is far from the first to try to justify punishing whistleblowers, and like its predecessors, it claims, based on flimsy or no evidence, that leaks of newsworthy classified documents threaten national security. But like the noncitizens the administration targets for their political speech, Watson leaked nothing. He simply spoke his mind, and for that he’s being held in extreme isolation for 24 hours a day, as if his freedom poses a danger to Americans.
The conditions of Watson’s confinement are further proof of the government’s vengeful motives. The charges against him cite the July 1 protest and his anti-Trump comments to a Substack blog in June in addition to the CNN interview, but he was placed in pretrial solitary confinement after the cable news appearance, where he’s been ever since. That interview was also used to justify his conditions at the recent hearing.
The Air Force says the CNN interview establishes probable cause of “continued misconduct.” But “continued misconduct” implies an initial misconduct, and according to military defense attorney Cody Harnish, who has followed the case closely, the order that Watson reportedly violated by talking to Burnett had expired weeks earlier.
But what kind of “continued misconduct” does the military fear enough that warrants keeping a decorated officer in conditions the United Nations considers torture? Is the prospect that he might give further interviews (despite his attorneys offering assurances he won’t pending trial) so terrifying that Watson must be caged for months?
Even those who agree that the military should be able to punish political expression in ways that civilian courts cannot should be alarmed by this escalation.
Watson has been convicted of no crime. Military law says a service member awaiting trial cannot be punished, and confinement may not be any more rigorous than the circumstances require.
According to Watson’s legal team, the government’s own witnesses testified Watson is not a flight risk. The military has not argued he is dangerous to anyone. Watson offered to resign in lieu of being court-martialed, an offer his attorney said in court that the government declined within a day.
Watson’s attorney, Christopher Mutimer, says Watson is the first major in the history of the military to be charged for “contemptuous words.” Harnish counts only three modern “contemptuous words” cases against service members of any rank. He has noted the offense is aimed at personal attacks, not advocating for legal processes like impeachment.
Yet the government is so committed to keeping Watson in solitary confinement that it’s willing to spend additional taxpayer funds to do so. Watson sits in a Maryland civilian jail because Joint Base Anacostia–Bolling, where he is stationed, has no confinement facility of its own. That means the government is contracting to hold Watson in jail, at your expense, for speaking his mind about the current presidential administration.
The government has claimed Watson is allowed to leave his cell for recreation and library visits. But the defining characteristic of solitary confinement, under the U.N. Nelson Mandela Rules, is solitude rather than space constraints.
His lawyers say he spends 20 to 22 hours a day alone in a small cell, where the lights are on around the clock. But as Mutimer told CNN, “Even if he gets an hour to eat or to exercise, he’s alone.”
Conditions are only getting worse. With the weather getting colder, he reportedly has to wear thermal underwear in his cell to keep warm. Guards have suggested jumping jacks to keep his body temperature up. That will, presumably, be less effective come January.
Mutimer told NPR that even soldiers who have been arrested for sexual assault and other violent crimes are not held in solitary confinement.
Watson’s case is selective enforcement at best and lawless retaliation at worst. Americans — whether they’re military or civilian, immigrant or citizen — should not be held in torturous conditions for months at a time, without having even been convicted of a crime, merely because they criticized the president or his policies.
A ruling in Watson’s case should come down soon, but even if he succeeds in being freed from solitary confinement, the administration will have succeeded in making an example of him.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/tech-enshitt.author: Jatinder Hayre
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/tech-enshitt.text:
The Enshittification of Everyday Life
The apps promising easier access across health care, insurance, and telecomms have been a giant bait-and-switch. Digital convenience turns out to be little more than the degradation of institutional capacity and the transfer of work onto customers.
Have you tried to speak to a human being lately? Perhaps you wanted to question an energy bill, rearrange a hospital appointment, claim a benefit, or discover why your insurer had refused treatment your doctor said you needed. You will probably have been invited to download an app, create an account, and remember a password. The most recent demand is that you must interrogate a chatbot. And then, as a final act of administrative penance, you can telephone a call center, where a recorded voice assures you that your call is terribly important. Somewhere along the way, a strange inversion occurred: the institution still takes your money, increasingly so, but you perform more and more of the labor.
This sort of scenario is usually called decline, but I think that is too generous. Decline suggests something tired, neglected, perhaps capable of rescue with another budget, or, more rarely, a sufficiently earnest politician. What we have instead is a deliberate paradigm shift.
Cory Doctorow has a gloriously apt vulgarity for this: enshittification. Digital platforms court users with convenience, become indispensable, then worsen the bargain once leaving becomes harder than staying. You can delete Facebook. Try deleting your need for health care.
Privatization and austerity have produced a miserable chimera: monopoly capitalism married to managerial bureaucracy. Government commissions, contractors deliver, regulators regulate, consultants advise, managers manage. Together they form the processariat: everybody owns a part of the process; nobody quite owns the responsibility. The exhausted receptionist absorbs the anger, while staffing and spending decisions are made in the ivory tower. Meanwhile, you are still on hold.
This is “socialized inconvenience.” Once, institutions encountered complexity and employed people to deal with it; now they email the complexity to you. We photograph the meter, chase the referral, upload the evidence, and pursue which department has lost the form. Nevertheless, this is recorded as efficiency. Even the language has been enshittified: a closed desk becomes “digital transformation” and work transferred from salaried staff to unpaid customers becomes “empowerment.” Still, enshittification is subtler than collapse: things keep functioning, but with enough friction to render using them a second occupation.
Your Call Is Important to Us
As a practicing doctor, I see the more dangerous version. Being ill is work nobody pays you for: ringing at the right hour, decoding the letter, affording the fare, losing a day’s wages, explaining yourself again to somebody new. Patients increasingly become project managers of their own illnesses. The sicker the patient, the more administrative competence we seem to demand of them. The sickest people are often required to become the most capable bureaucrats.
I remember one of my own patients who underwent a biopsy of a neck lump and was found to have cancer. The biopsy was performed, the pathology was reported and the result entered the system. Yet no appointment followed, no clinician called and nobody appeared to take responsibility for what happened next. My patient simply waited, assuming that somebody, somewhere, was dealing with it. Of course, cancer does not wait to consider mitigating circumstances. On paper, each step had occurred. In reality, the one thing that mattered had not: the patient had not been followed up with. Every part of the process can function while the person at the center of it is still failed.
The American version comes with insurance paperwork. In a survey of 4,155 insured adults ages eighteen to sixty-four, 24.4 percent reported delaying or forgoing care because of administrative tasks. Respondents with disabilities reported greater burdens; those with higher incomes, fewer. They already had insurance.
The affluent can often buy their way out of the processariat altogether: a private consultation instead of the appointment queue, a taxi instead of the disrupted train, a tutor instead of navigating a struggling school, an accountant or assistant instead of another afternoon lost to forms and hold music. Those without that option remain trapped inside the machinery and pay in the resource institutions almost never count: time. Forty minutes on hold is an irritation to somebody answering emails from home — to a care worker on an unpaid lunch break, it can mean abandoning the problem altogether. Money increasingly buys something subtler than luxury — an exit from process. In 2024, across twenty-eight OECD countries, the poorest fifth were, on average, 2.5 times more likely than the richest fifth to report unmet medical needs because of cost, distance, or waiting times.
Chasing down a child’s appointment or a parent’s prescription requires human effort. The International Labour Organization’s 2018 report, drawing on sixty-four countries, estimated 16.4 billion hours of unpaid care work daily. Women performed 76.2 percent. Institutions shedding work rely on households already doing plenty.
We empirically tested whether the effort and resources an intervention requires affect who benefits from it. Income support, housing measures and regulation produced the most consistent equity gains. Programs demanding sustained personal effort, without support, often widened health inequality. Giving everybody the same instructions does not give everybody the same capacity to act on them. When people give up asking, that can look like reduced demand, although the need has gone nowhere.
Please Rate Your Health From One to Ten
Arkansas made Medicaid coverage conditional on work and reporting requirements. By the time a judge halted the policy, eighteen thousand adults had lost coverage. Researchers found no employment increase over eighteen months. In Jharkhand, India, reforms introducing biometric identification for subsidized food reduced corruption, but an estimated 1.5 to 2 million legitimate beneficiaries lost access at some point during the reforms. The researchers traced much of the harm to how the transition was managed.
Public ownership must mean enough staff with the authority to resolve problems. Universal entitlements must be obtainable without a second occupation spent pursuing them. The worker answering from another country has no more power over the staffing budget than the patient waiting. Both have an interest in changing who controls the service. And an institution claiming an efficiency saving should have to account for the work transferred to the public.
Perhaps the most corrosive achievement of enshittification is our own habituation. We budget for the delay, expect the missed call and quietly absorb another piece of work the institution once did for us. What begins as irritation becomes adaptation. What once looked like failure is the new baseline. The processariat wins twice: first by making the service worse and then by persuading us that expecting better is somehow unreasonable.
As we wait, chase, upload, appeal and telephone, the processariat can point to its dashboards and insist that the machinery is working. Broken institutions would at least have the decency to stop. Enshittified institutions keep going, largely because we have been conscripted into keeping them going ourselves. But at what cost?
