https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ea-tech-ai-s.title: Effective Altruism Is Increasingly Just Funding Itself
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ea-tech-ai-s.author: Jacob Davis
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/ea-tech-ai-s.text:
Effective Altruism Is Increasingly Just Funding Itself
Effective altruists say they want to widen the circle of moral concern to include distant strangers. Follow the money, and the circle increasingly ends at other effective altruists.
The basic pitch for effective altruism (EA) is simple: charitable giving is an investment, whose return is in others’ well-being rather than your financial betterment. Given that it’s an investment, it makes sense to look for a strong, measurable return from wherever you choose to donate. After all, if you really care about others being well-off, you should be at leastas conscientious about these investments as you are about your retirement savings.
This is, to say the least, a controversial approach to charity. It has many detractors: those who argue that the approach flattens value to numbers in a spreadsheet, or that it ignores the place of solidarity and political organizing. But the ethic also has its undeniable appeal. Among effective altruists, the standard example of effective giving is usually the Against Malaria Foundation (AMF), which distributes insecticide-laced bed nets in sub-Saharan Africa to combat mosquito-borne illness. It is hard to argue that AMF is not a better place to give your money than many competing organizations, like various sketchy “voluntourism” outfits or microloan creditors.
Where many critiques of EA miss the mark is in taking this pitch at face value. In reality, as measured by volume of money flow, EA is more a means of cultivating a self-selecting, insular subculture based around the tech industry. The biggest objection that can be laid against it is not that its founding principles are misguided, but that they have come to play third or fourth fiddle to building a playground and safety net for a small, privileged portion of the global population.
Short-Term vs. Long-Term EA
Within EA, a distinction is sometimes drawn between “long-term” and “short-term” effective altruism. Classic poster children like AMF almost all fall on the “short-term” side of the split: concrete, clearly specifiable interventions to promote measurable goods in the present or near future. “Long-term” cause areas are generally more nebulous or speculative: preparations for future pandemics, the eventual curtailment of wild animal suffering, or (above all) artificial intelligence safety.
Long-term cause areas generally, and AI safety specifically, have come to dominate EA organizing. One measure of this is the recent spending decisions of Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy), the dominant EA grant-making body. In 2025, nearly $490 million of Coefficient Giving’s roughly $840 million in grants were dedicated to “long-term and existential risk,” overwhelmingly in AI safety. This is in contrast to the approximately $150 million spent on global health and development, the classic “short-term” general cause area.
This spending strategy is puzzling, under traditional EA principles. As Coefficient Giving states on its funding page, effective altruists deliberately focus on funding for problems that are important, neglected, and tractable. Without prejudice to the issue’s importance, there is a growing consensus among concerned parties that AI safety is not currently tractable: there is widespread recognition that no robust technical road map to safe AI has been, or will likely soon be, forthcoming. And leading AI safety organization Anthropic just opened its initial public offering (IPO) at around $1.5 trillion — prompting disillusionment even within EA. Rarely in human history has any problem been less economically neglected.
Anthropic, like OpenAI before it, highlights the double-edged nature of much technical AI safety research. In the eyes of most effective altruists, developing AI capabilities is directly opposed to the goal of AI safety. And yet most avenues of technical safety research go hand-in-hand with capabilities development; indeed, this is a criticism lobbed against AI safety initiatives by many effective altruists. Research projects on interpretability, reinforcement learning with human feedback, and thinking traces have all failed to realize the elusive dream of AI “alignment” but have provided considerable returns to sheer performance levels.
What AI safety funding does offer is an opportunity to spread money around a self-selecting community of EA researchers and activists. A dizzying number of conferences, think tanks, and fellowships have sprung up to study the topic, backed by funders like Coefficient Giving. Much as a liberal-interventionist foreign policy makes for “a full-employment strategy for the foreign policy establishment,” so the focus on AI safety provides the AI safety community abundant opportunity for remunerative work and stimulating play.
Effective Altruism for Profit
Perhaps no organization better illustrates these tendencies than Manifund, a San Francisco–based fundraising body closely tied to the EA community. Whereas Coefficient Giving has historically acted mainly as a channel for the philanthropy of billionaire couple Dustin Moskovitz and Cari Tuna, Manifund is designed to invite funding from a range of interested onlookers. Much of this fundraising is conducted through Manifund’s “impact certificate ecosystem,” which they describe as “like Kickstarter meets the stock market.” The organization also subscribes to a principle of full transparency, making its grant-making process unusually accessible.
Many of its grant choices are atypical, to say the least. In a recent blog post, for example, Manifund CEO and cofounder Austin Chen explains a number of routes the organization uses to funnel donor money into for-profit ventures — in spite of Manifund’s status as a 501(c)3 tax-exempt non-profit. These range from the relatively innocuous (commissions for specific services) to the legal but abnormal (outright investment).
Manifund has adopted more indirect means of supporting for-profit entities, as well. For example, it is responsible for funding and running Mox, an EA workspace and community hub in Downtown San Francisco. In addition to offering work space for individual paying members, Mox — which shares Chen as head — plays host to several EA-affiliated small businesses. And this summer, Mox and Manifund co-organized Surplus, a software start-up incubator offering generous seed funding and pitch opportunities to successful applicants.
Similarly unorthodox have been the charity’s recent hiring decisions. Against considerable uproar, Manifund recently hired effective altruist and convicted fraudster Caroline Ellison to serve on its administrative staff. In 2024, Ellison was sentenced to two years’ incarceration in connection with her roles at cryptocurrency trading firm Alameda Research and sister company FTX. She has since July played a major role alongside Chen in approving and directing grant decisions at Manifund, as well as contributing to the charity’s Substack.
This decision prompted considerable backlash from the EA community. Complaints stemmed partly from concerns about optics, given the extremely negative attention Ellison had already attracted to EA. But there were also more direct concerns about her trustworthiness and competence, especially in a financially responsible role, as well as resentment from victims of fraud connected to FTX and Alameda Research.
Chen defended the decision in the September blog post announcing the hire, offering among other reasons a sense of indebtedness to FTX:
I felt a keen debt to the FTX Future Fund. They provided seed funding for Manifold. They funded the retreat which drew me into the EA community, and the conference where I met my wife. Much of Manifund’s work today is directly inspired by the Future Fund’s approach.
The Future Fund was the philanthropic wing of FTX, which at the time was linked to fraudulently acquired funds siphoned from the exchange’s account holders. In addition to Manifund, the Future Fund supported a number of EA-related causes, primarily related to AI safety and pandemic prevention.
The Transfer of Wealth
In all of these capacities, Manifund has consistently deprioritized “short-term” EA work of the sort exemplified by AMF. Often, this has been in favour of recognizable “long-term” cause areas, like AI safety. But sometimes its beneficiaries have not even clearly fit this more extensive mold and instead have been connected to EA more through cultural and ideological affinity.
An easy indication of this is the official breakdown of Manifund grants by cause area. Best-funded is “Technical AI Safety” at over $8 million, coming out ahead of similarly AI-dominated causes like “AI Governance” ($5.2 million) and “Global Catastrophic Risks” ($4.7 million). All of these come out ahead of “Global Health and Development,” which clocks in at a comparatively meagre $436,000. (Cause areas are not mutually exclusive, so some of these funding amounts overlap.)
The immediate net effect of this outsize investment in technical AI safety is a transfer of wealth to the EA-dominated AI safety research community. Existing technical AI safety initiatives are effectively all research- or education-oriented: given the lack of any widely recognized way of implementing AI safety, the main place for funding to go is to researchers either currently trying to develop strategies for AI safety or learning what is needed to do the same. EA-affiliated AI governance initiatives, in turn, are carried out in close coordination with technical researchers and draw from a similar subcultural pool.
Many non-AI projects with heavy support from Manifund similarly circulate the EA cash pool among other effective altruists. For example, Manifund has raised $132,000 in funding for “human intelligence amplification @ Berkeley Genomics Project” — an attempt to breed a new generation of hyperintelligent humans through genomic engineering, in the hopes that they may be better suited to design safe AI systems. Setting aside any ethical considerations, the project is unlikely to generate immediate fruit. Rather, the main immediate impact is the opportunity to conduct highly speculative bioengineering research much in vogue among effective altruists.
The same tendency is even more directly on display in the “EA Community” category ($1.6 million). Best-funded of all projects in the category, after Mox, is Lightcone Infrastructure — the common funding and governing body of LessWrong and the EA hotel turned event venue Lighthaven. Lighthaven, acquired by Lightcone in 2022 (reportedly with the substantial financial assistance of FTX), has subsequently hosted a number of conferences, programs, and parties associated with the EA community in the Bay Area.
More indirect support from Manifund, such as through Mox, continues this trend. Some of the start-ups using Mox’s office space, for example, are only very dubiously philanthropic ventures. They include The Relationship Company (a dating app “making AI systems that understand who you are and find people you’d genuinely connect with”) and Stardrift (an AI-based travel agency).
Expanding the Circle
A common metaphor used to explain EA to outsiders is the “circle of concern.” Moral progress, in this story, is largely a matter of expanding this “circle:” the range of people, animals, and things about which one cares. At the center of your circle is you, whom you will care about even if you are maximally greedy and selfish. Beyond that lie family, neighbors, countrymen, humanity writ large, and the animal kingdom, at ever wider removes. Effective altruism, at its best, is about maintaining a wide circle of concern, in a self-consciously rational way.
The irony in this tale is that EA has often had the opposite effect. Where charitable donations might otherwise have gone to distant victims of poverty, illness, and disaster, many EA organizations have instead channeled them primarily to one another. Rather than expanding its devotees’ circle of concern, effective altruism has come to consist largely in narrowing that circle to effective altruists.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
The journal of a punk photographer from Wollongong to London and back – in pictures
Katelyn Slyer’s book, The Middle, records a generation of young people negotiating their identity while caught between the intimacy of the analog era and new digital world from 2004 to 2010. Her photographs explore the ideas of becoming and connection in Australian and English punk scenes
Katelyn Slyer feeds ‘Boris’ the possum (who had been misgendered) with her baby in the kitchen. Boris would sneak into her bedroom and eat the Iced Vovos stashed under the bed. Photograph: Katelyn Slyer
My friend Jemima arriving at our home in Austinmer on the New South Wales south coast after pulling an all-nighter from Sydney. The house was nicknamed The Love Shack – a half-condemned house with million-dollar views that overlooked the rock pools between the water and the escarpment. A lot of the photos from The Middle were taken during the time we lived there. Lorikeets used to perch on our Hills Hoist, flying over to our hands, which we would cover in honey
After living in London for a while I ran out of money and was couch-surfing/squatting with friends. I knew Katie from Wollongong. We moved in similar circles back home, but we became close while I was living in England. When I had nowhere to stay, she let me stay at her place, even when her housemates were reluctant. We got up to all sorts of mischief. This portrait is of Katie and Alberto, an Italian punk who I met in Camden
Landscape of the Port Kembla stack in 2005. It dominated the Wollongong skyline for nearly half a century before it came down in 2014. I always appreciate a gritty industrial landscape
In the early 2000s, whenever the Melbourne crew would visit, we would take them on adventures to local spots around Wollongong. We loved hanging out in the old tunnels under Hill 60, a second world war underground military fort. It was a bit creepy and fun to explore, and had rad views. This image is Dan and Sikk Mikk admiring Five Islands off the coast of Port Kembla
Christopher Zero mucking around in London with souvenirs after hours, when the tourists had gone home and the markets were being closed down for the night. I like this image as it encapsulates a snapshot of the time, showcasing royal memorabilia of that era
Before Austinmer, I used to live in Coniston, a suburb of Wollongong. During that time, I met Shane and Emma, who lived up the road from me. They always had wild and memorable parties with all the local skate crew, punks, hippies and everybody in between. They also had a massive skate ramp in their back yard
Az and Lulu were a well-known couple growing up in the Wollongong punk scene. Here they lie in MacCabe Park next to the youth centre one late afternoon. People grow and change but these images remind me of my past and make me nostalgic for moments that would otherwise be forgotten with the erosion of time and brain rot
Patto, from the Footscray crew, did himself some mischief and ended up on crutches. I appreciate his attention to detail, styling the crutches to suit his aesthetic. And the fact that it matched the couch at the pub perfectly. When I took the photo it was a happy snap. What I appreciate most about it now is the smaller details of his surroundings. The textures and the decor
An impromptu portrait of Rachelle in Sydney. I transitioned from a point-and-shoot film camera and started experimenting with my first digital camera. Rach is one of my beautiful mates who has allowed me to practise and hone my artistic skills and techniques. Any time we hung out she would be up for anything I threw her way
Hannah, my favourite Welsh gal. This image was taken at a gig in Soho at the 12 Bar, one of the local haunts that always had great bands playing. Hannah didn’t take herself too seriously and would always crack me up with her wit and intellect. I liked loitering out the front shooting the goings on between there and the Intrepid Fox
Once our friends started to have kids, we would find wholesome activities to do so we could keep hanging out. The Punk Cricket team was created and we would play at Conno school on the weekends. This is a portrait of my mate Lowki getting amped for the game. Lowki has a great voice, charisma and awesome stage presence. He was lead vocalist in Wollongong punk band Run 4 Cover and 3KD
When the Wollongong crew would visit the Melbourne crew, we would stay in Footscray and get up to all types of shenanigans. This boozy shot of Dan was taken on the way back from the annual Melbourne Punx pub crawl that happens to fall on AFL grand final day
Little Barry Jr and Bruiser. Baz was always a character with many cool stories and yarns to tell of a life well lived. When I came back from London, I lived with him for a while when the girls moved out. Eventually, I too moved and he became the custodian of The Love Shack until it was sold and demolished
When I was a teenager my family moved from Sydney to Wollongong. It was a big change for me at 16, leaving my friends and starting in a new town. One of the first friends I made was Erin. She was a couple of years older, super creative, made her own clothes, and had good taste in music. She was also my first friend who got pregnant and became a mother. This image is of her at the Austinmer rock pools with her two daughters, Zoe and Ella. Looking back, we were so lucky to have this spot to grow up and have fun in our back yard. The Middle was a formative time in my life. Not only was I growing and exploring individual identity, I was able to grow with them and witness their childhood close up
Back in 2009, I took a trip with my partner, Stevie, around Europe. Tucked away in a fjord near Molde in Norway was his mate Pauli’s back yard skate ramp
This was taken in Wombarra, in northern Wollongong, at a friend’s house at night. Dogs and goats hanging out together. I don’t remember their names, or much of this evening
DeeDee and Jemima. This image epitomises Aussie barbecue vibes. We had an old red Weber my folks had given me. We would cook up a barbecue and have jelly-wrestling parties in a blow-up pool in our yard

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Abu Dhabi markets itself to global elites—can its public art biennial reach local communities?
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Kabir Jhala
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The arrival of Frieze furthers Abu Dhabi’s ambitions to become a premier events destination for global elites. Beyond the fair (which runs until 22 November), the coming weeks will see the jetset descend on the emirate to bid on Picassos at Sotheby’s, sit front row at the Grand Prix and Abu Dhabi Open tournaments, and rub shoulders with celebrities and chief executives at the Global Cultural Forum and the Milken Institute's Middle East and Africa Summit.
But a glittering trail of franchised events is unlikely to leave a lasting impact on the local communities that have built Abu Dhabi and will continue to sustain it. Focusing efforts on attracting the itinerant super-rich might also prove short-sighted for a country surrounded by well-armed and hostile neighbours. So, how to engage those who will remain when regional conflicts escalate or the markets turn?
Public art appears to be one strategy, so proposes the second edition of Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial (until 15 February 2027). Organised by the Department of Culture and Tourism (DCT), the exhibition Home: A Glossary for a Communal Sense of Place has brought 18 works—most of them new commissions—to public sites across the city, with a further four situated in the nearby oasis desert town of Al Ain.
“Everyday life is central” to this biennial “both as backdrop and method”, writes its artistic director, Elvira Dyangani Ose, in the accompanying guide. Out in the desert, Iron Age irrigation systems still used today form the basis of Ascunción Molinos Gordo’s rammed earth sculpture Bil Hana wa Al Afia (2026), installed among working farms during the biennial’s run. Back in the city, the ubiquitous infrastructure of cooling vents is brought to the fore by Shama Al Hamed’s installation of fluorescent aluminium ducting, which spill out like entrails from the observation deck of the former industrial port.
Key to a public art biennial concerned with the quotidian is appealing to non-art specialist audiences. This means considering the “many publics” that exist in Abu Dhabi, Dyangani Ose says. Visitors at sunset will see families jumping on Ivan Argote’s see-saw installation and zooming down its animal-shaped slides.
Despite the temporary nature of an exhibition, each edition of the biennial achieves permanence through its acquisition structure. Last edition, 15 works—around half—were acquired by Public Art Abu Dhabi and are now on display across the city. They include a crescent of silver oyster sculptures by the Emirati artist Farah Al Qasimi, referencing the Arabian Gulf’s once-booming pearl diving industry.
The director of Public Art Abu Dhabi, Clémence Bergal, says a similar acquisition round will take place at the end of this edition. “With so many of the biennial’s works being new commissions, it is a great way to collect work that feels deeply connected and responsive to Abu Dhabi,” she says.
The biennial is not only a tool for engaging Abu Dhabi’s various communities, but for considering how they live with each other. The theme of this year is the unstable and contested definition of “home”, and Dyangani Ose writes in the catalogue that she is interested in how a “communal sense of place” is formed and negotiated by various groups, sometimes of vastly different cultures and material conditions. “Abu Dhabi is a city in which that distinction matters enormously,” she writes. “Communities from across the world share its streets, its coastline, its daily rhythms without sharing the same histories, the same rights or the same relationship to the land.”
The curatorial statement provides a potent line of inquiry in a country where only a small portion of the population—estimated to be around 12%—has citizenship, and in which the working and living conditions of migrant labourers has been criticised by leading human rights organisations.
These issues appear to be broached obliquely in the multiple references to migration and labour throughout the biennial, including in a striking coastline installation by the Ghanaian artist Serge Attukwei Clottey, composed of thousands of interlocking yellow plastic pieces made from Kuffuor gallons—containers that are ubiquitous in Accra and used to transport cooking oil, water and fuel. These Kuffuor installations are Clottey’s signature, and he has spoken widely about how they refer, in part, to the imbalanced relations of labour and resource extraction between African nations and their trading partners. The UAE is Ghana’s third-most important importer, chiefly purchasing gold. Immigrants from Ghana and other West African nations represent an increasingly large portion of the UAE's manual labour force, chiefly working in construction, hospitality and security services.
Unsurprisingly considering the emirate's strict censorship laws, little in the show could be openly perceived as critical, at least of the UAE. Dyangani Ose tells The Art Newspaper that there are certain “limits presented by the framework” of a publicly funded exhibition in Abu Dhabi. She adds that "as global subjects", we are all bound within certain limits.
To its credit, the biennial's public setting provides opportunities for conversations that many art institutions in other parts of the world might shy away from. For instance, Yinka Shonibare’s towering metal plume, painted in both his signature Dutch wax patterns and those of Bedouin textiles, serves as a welcome shade structure for outdoor labourers working in the harsh midday sun. "These publics are just as important to take into account as any other," Dyangani Ose says.
Indeed, providing a platform for a diverse and unexpected set of interactions is a vital part of how Dyangani Ose conceives of a communal sense of place, as “making meaning, despite differences, in public”. For the biennial, this might be its greatest impact of all.
- Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial, until 15 February 2027, various locations, Abu Dhabi and Al Ain

https://hyperallergic.com/orthodox-cleri.title: Orthodox Cleric Wanted in Connection With International Forgery Scheme
https://hyperallergic.com/orthodox-cleri.author: Rhea Nayyar
https://hyperallergic.com/orthodox-cleri.text:
Orthodox Cleric Wanted in Connection With International Forgery Scheme
Greek police has arrested one man in the $1.85 million art trafficking case.
A 44-year-old man was arrested during an undercover operation into an art forgery scheme in Athens, Greece, on Saturday, November 21, exposing an international network allegedly overseen by a Florida-based Orthodox priest. The arrest subsequently yielded the discovery of 35 forged paintings falsely attributed to prominent Greek and international artists, among other valuables.
The man, who remains unidentified to the public, was arrested on his way to make a sale to an undercover cop who posed as a client online. He had six paintings that he was going to sell to the undercover agents for €5,150 ($5,613). The investigation began in early October, when an art specialist tipped off authorities after encountering an online listing of two paintings attributed to famous 20th-century Greek expressionist George Bouzianis with counterfeit certificates of authenticity for sale.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: Matchbooks are on fire at NYC restaurants
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: Hannah Frishberg
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
Cigarette smoking is on the decline, disposable lighters are cheap and easily available, and vapes are self-contained, and yet the humble matchbook has lit a fire in New York’s fine dining scene. Indeed, the retro collectible has made a full-fledged return as a restaurant giveaway and as an opulent piece of pocket-sized art.
At Manhattan’s buzzy small chain Dante, where the large format matchbooks boast gold leaf inlay, custom interior artwork and cost approximately $4 each to make, they had to stop handing them out at the front door. “ It was financially becoming quite burdensome,” said the restaurant’s co-founder Linden Pride. The matchbooks are now only available as a free add-on with purchase of their Negroni fragrance candle.
In addition to their classic appeal as miniature memorabilia from a nice meal, modern diners also find them attractive as tangible objects in an increasingly digitally-based world.
“I think in the digital age where, like, everything is online, people really want something to hold onto physically,” said Connor Pacharis, who late last year founded the website Matchbook Directory so he and his fellow phillumenists could have a place to congregate and swap sticks.
On social media and within the directory’s now nearly 900-user strong community share and trade matchbooks, which are prized for their aesthetic appeal and as compact reminders of real world experiences.
Indeed, most directory users are looking to acquire matchbooks from places they’ve visited but failed to nab a book from, or to determine which restaurants have matchbooks, so they can dine there.
“ I can go on my camera roll and I have 10,000 photos from one vacation,” said Pacharis, a San Diego-based product manager who recently visited New York, by far the most popular location in the directory. “But when I think about my New York trip, I don't really think about the photos I took. I think about my New York matchbook collection, and what a good time I had.”
City restaurateurs are aware of this burgeoning market of significantly young people, and have entered something of an aesthetic design race to keep up and stay competitive in a tough business.
When 19-year New York City restaurateur Joshua Boissy opened now-shuttered Greenpoint eatery Sauvage in 2016, they made multiple matchbooks, a choice which was “was totally psychotic, but, like, a really fun thing to do at the time; it was very unusual,” despite it not being the most cost effective. Although he’s yet to see anyone else do the multiple style shtick, luxury matchbooks are now far less of a surprising marketing stunt.
“The matchbook game has evolved a lot. We've been doing it for a while at each of our places, and I remember, you know, from 2011 when we opened Maison, matchbooks were not treated this way. They were all kind of very similar,” said Boissy, co-founder of the Lower East Side’s swanky cocktail lounge Tigre.
But in New York City fine dining “there’s always an upping of the game,” and others have since gotten in on the luxury matchbook craze, he said.
In addition to being a trendy and in-demand piece of branded merchandise, the fact that they are physical reminders of a good meal long after the bill has been paid makes them quite ideal from a marketing perspective.
"They serve as a lasting extension of our branding,” said KwangHo Lee, owner of fine-dining institutions One Bryant Park and Momoya, both of which boast delicately gilded books carefully tailored to evoke the same upscale aesthetic as their corresponding restaurants.
“In a digital world, having a physical keepsake to say ‘Hey’ with makes a lasting impression and keeps us top of mind,” added Jacob Hadjigeorgis, owner of the Upper West Side Southern food establishment Jacob’s Pickles, which boasts matchbooks inspired “by a little nostalgia for a time when restaurants had more personality in the small details.”

Art Basel Hong Kong has revealed its 232 exhibitors for its 2027 edition. The fair will take place at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre from March 25-27, with VIP previews from March 23-24.
Exhibitors at next year’s fair hail from over 40 countries and are spread out across nine sections: Galleries; Insights; Discoveries; Echoes; Film; Kabinett; Encounters; Magazines; and Zero 10. 31 exhibitors are showing at the fair for the first time.
The most significant change comes in the form of a new floor layout, similar to the upcoming edition of Art Basel Miami Beach. Discoveries, Insights, Echoes and Zero 10 will shift to Level 3 of the convention center. Art Basel Hong Kong Director Angelle Siyang-Le described this as a “reimagined visitor journey designed to foster discovery and deeper engagement.”
The Galleries sector has 171 participants, 11 fewer than the 2026 fair. “Blue chip” galleries participating in the fair include Gagosian, Hauser & Wirth, David Zwirner, Pace Gallery, and White Cube, among others.
More than half of the participating galleries have spaces in the Asia-Pacific region, with 27 of them operating in Hong Kong, including Alisan Fine Arts, Blindspot Gallery, Empty Gallery, gdm, Kiang Malingue, and Rossi & Rossi. Siyang-Le noted that this edition “reflects Asia’s creative vitality and growing influence while reaffirming Hong Kong’s unique position as a meeting point for global cultural exchange.”
Discoveries, the section which showcases upcoming talent, has stayed steady with 25 exhibitors, of which 14 are first-time participants. Insights, which is dedicated to Asia-Pacific artists, and Echoes, centered on recent work from the last five years, have 18 exhibitors apiece.
Zero 10, a section dedicated to digital art, will be curated by Sunny Cheung, a former curator of design and architecture at M+, Hong Kong, who is now working independently. The fair will also incorporate a city-wide public program alongside its Conversations and Film sections, the latter of which will be curated by renowned media artist and curator Ellen Pau.
The full list of exhibitors is available here.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/malraux-lesp.title: Man’s Hope Is a Masterful Tableau of Spain’s Civil War
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/malraux-lesp.author: Jeff Fuller
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/malraux-lesp.text:
Man’s Hope Is a Masterful Tableau of Spain’s Civil War
French writer André Malraux died 50 years ago today. Based on a rich cast of characters, his 1937 novel, Man’s Hope, brilliantly portrayed the conflicts facing the Left during the Spanish Civil War.
Fifty years ago today, André Malraux died in a hospital bed in Créteil, a southeastern suburb of Paris, just after his seventy-fifth birthday. His remains would be moved to the Panthéon twenty years later, where he is honored among illustrious scientists, statesmen, and military leaders as well as more proximate figures such as Victor Hugo and Antoine de Saint-Exupéry. Malraux’s intellectual achievements are hardly in dispute in France; he left behind a diverse body of work, including essays, imposingly large theoretical works on art, memoirs, one feature film, and several highly regarded novels.
More than that, Malraux’s reputation rests upon his status as a consummate man of action. He was an agitator for decolonization in then French Indochina in the 1920s; a republican fighter in the Spanish Civil War and, soon after, in the French Resistance; and finally a minister, first of information (1945–46) and then of culture (1959–69), in Charles de Gaulle’s governments.
The above résumé may also give a sense of why, for a left-wing audience, it is difficult to be anything other than ambivalent about Malraux. There are entries in the ledger that will displease just about everyone. He had much to say on the topic of revolution, but he never really embraced Marxism, being a far greater admirer of Friedrich Nietzsche. In the late 1920s and early ’30s, he had cordial relations with Leon Trotsky, who admired his novels set in China — 1928’s Les Conquérants (The Conquerors) and 1933’s Prix Goncourt–winning La Condition humaine (translated into English as Man’s Fate) — and found in them support for the Left Opposition’s perspectives on the Stalinist Comintern’s miscalculations (or perhaps misdeeds) there.
In the latter half of the 1930s, Malraux was a committed antifascist and fellow traveler who held to a Stalinist line, particularly during the Spanish war, keeping his silence during the Moscow trials to Trotsky’s bitter disappointment. He was a vocal anti-communist from World War II onward, though in typical Gaullist fashion, cool and distant toward American civilization.
My purpose here is not, however, to draw up a neat balance sheet of a complicated life with a view to rendering a political judgment. Rather, the anniversary offers an occasion to point toward what is most worthy of reconsideration, in this case Malraux’s literary masterpiece, the 1937 novel L’Espoir (translated as Man’s Hope or, alternatively, as Days of Hope).
Malraux’s Hopes
L’Espoir remains, in my view, one of the truly great novels in a century populated with many good ones. Pieces of it began coming out in November 1937, while Malraux was still very active in the war effort, and when it was not yet absurd to speak of hope in Spain. Sadly, in today’s anglophone world it enjoys nothing like the reputation of English-language literature of the Spanish war, such as Ernest Hemingway’s For Whom the Bell Tolls or George Orwell’s Homage to Catalonia: the last American edition of L’Espoir, from the Modern Library, came out some forty-two years ago, which would be unthinkable in the case of Hemingway or Orwell. Whatever the many merits of their two books, neither matches the scope and vitality of Malraux’s novel.
L’Espoir gives a sweeping account of the war from the initial chaos of the July 1936 nationalist uprising to the republican victory at Guadalajara in March the following year, passing through various advances, such as the successful defense of Madrid, and setbacks, such as the fall of Toledo to Francisco Franco’s forces, along the way.
Like Hemingway and Orwell and many other left-wing intellectuals besides, Malraux was in Spain during the war. Unlike them, he had a quite broad experience of the war and many roles within it. The nationalist uprising that sparked the war began on July 17, 1936, and Malraux, who was following events closely from France, was in Madrid by July 24. Back in Paris soon after, and with the complicity of some figures in France’s Popular Front government, notably Air Minister Pierre Cot, he helped organize operations to smuggle arms and planes into Spain as well as recruiting men to fly them. By mid-August, the plucky, makeshift air squadron that Malraux was instrumental in organizing was flying reconnaissance and combat missions, many of which he participated in directly, though he was not himself a pilot.
Once the squadron was disbanded in early February 1937 and its volunteers incorporated into the regular army, he went on a two-month tour of North America to raise funds and agitate against the Western democracies’ policy of nonintervention. It was around this time he began preparing his novel. Throughout the war, he maintained close relationships with many important figures in Spain, particularly but not only among the Communists. He was in and out of the country for various reasons for the remainder of the war, notably the shooting of his film, Espoir: Sierra de Teruel, which prominently features episodes from L’Espoir, and whose production was disrupted by the fall of Barcelona in January 1939, at which point Malraux left Spain definitively.
The novel is not the most formally daring work in an age of modernist and avant-garde experimentation. If it has a convention-defying quality, it resides in forgoing the anchoring formal element of the traditional novel, namely the individual protagonist, instead opting for an expansive cast of characters, both Spanish and international — officers, soldiers, political commissars, journalists, artists, and so on. They are geographically dispersed and ideologically disparate, thrown together by a common threat but internally riven by the question of how to respond.
This latter circumstance lends Malraux’s novel greater coherence, as a novel, than other, more panoramic literature of its time, for example John Dos Passos’s U.S.A. trilogy. Whatever the heterogeneity of Malraux’s characters, they function within a fairly traditional narrative structure much like a single protagonist. As Georg Lukács writes in his classic Theory of the Novel: “the content of the novel is the story of the soul that goes to find itself, that seeks adventures in order to be proved and tested by them, and, by proving itself, to find its own essence.” The protagonist of a novel is by nature a figure whose inner life is in some way out of joint with the external world, “the arena and substratum of its actions.” For Malraux’s collective protagonist, the object of the novelistic quest is the means through which a spontaneous, ecstatic rising of the Spanish masses against the forces of reaction — what Malraux calls the “Apocalypse” — can become a disciplined, fraternal force capable not just of heroic sacrifice but of victory: “Our humble task,” says Garcia, an intelligence officer, “is to organize the Apocalypse.”
The conflicts that drive Malraux’s narrative forward are, at bottom, the same political questions that created dividing lines on the international left faced with the Spanish war, both in terms of analysis of the situation and the political perspectives that resulted. Were the events of July 1936 simply a defense of the democratically elected Popular Front government, however wild and unorganized or, on the contrary, did they set in motion the first genuine social revolution since the one in the Russian Empire two decades before? The Communist position at the time held very firmly to the former outlook. For example, here is how Arthur Koestler, at the time still very much in the Communist camp, characterized the politics of the Spanish left in 1937:
The truth is that the Spanish Popular Front was not striving towards a Soviet State or a Bakunian Utopia, but towards one goal alone: the raising of the Spanish State, which had never yet succeeded in emerging from the clerical, feudal stage, to the constitutional, material and spiritual level of the great European democracies.
Others, such as Franz Borkenau, were nonplussed by this line of thinking:
I hinted at the fact that the workers were armed, that the administration had fallen into the hands of revolutionary committees, that people were being executed without trial by the thousands, that both factories and estates were being expropriated and managed by their former hands. What was revolution if it was not that? I was told that I was mistaken. . . . I wonder how it is that communists, who, all over the world, for fifteen years have discovered revolutionary situations where there were none, and done tremendous mischief by it, now do not recognize revolution when, for the first time in Europe since the Russian Revolution of 1917, it is really there.
Finally, Orwell laid out the consequences of the Communist position:
The workers could always be brought to heel by an argument that is almost too obvious to need stating: “Unless you do this, that, and the other we shall lose the war.” In every case, needless to say, it appeared that the thing demanded by military necessity was the surrender of something that the workers had won for themselves in 1936. But the argument could hardly fail, because to lose the war was the last thing that the revolutionary parties wanted.
Malraux’s novel is, among other things, a defense and illustration of the Communist position: that socially revolutionary measures, particularly in the Spanish countryside, were at best a distraction and at worst courting defeat; that the popular militias that sprang up following the nationalist uprising urgently needed to be disbanded and their forces placed under the control of the government; in a more abstract vein, that the concrete instantiation of revolutionary or otherwise antifascist values could be summed up by two watchwords, efficacity and discipline.
“Doomed to change . . . or to perish,” as Malraux’s Soviet journalist Golovkin — possibly modeled on Ilya Ehrenburg — puts it. The composition of the left wing of the republican camp was hardly conducive to this conservatizing project: pace Koestler, a great many in Spain absolutely were striving for a Soviet state or a Bakuninist utopia. Spain’s own radical traditions skewed decidedly toward the latter, and many internationals fighting there had for some years looked with envy to the revolutionary East. The war had an appeal of its own: for the many Hungarians, Germans, and Italians, here was finally a chance to counterattack, following years of defeat and humiliation at the hands of the Right. For Spanish workers and peasants, it would have been more like centuries. The point is that there is a clear romantic aspect to Malraux’s “Apocalypse,” and cautioning patience and modesty of ambition is perhaps not as easy to sell as Orwell claims in the passage above.
The Communists’ more cautious position ultimately won out within the republican camp, but this was far from just about having the most compelling argument. For one thing, Soviet support for the war effort, especially in terms of providing matériel and organizing the International Brigades, gave the Communists influence quite out of proportion to their numbers in Spain. Just as important, the instances of repression of dissident elements in the republican camp are well known. Sticking to the literary works already named, Orwell recounts the May Days in Barcelona, in which the anarchists were disempowered, and the Catalan-centered, anti-Stalinist Marxist Partit Obrer d’Unificació Marxista (POUM) was outright suppressed by force of arms. Its leader, Andreu Nin, was arrested and never heard from again. And For Whom the Bell Tolls contains a rather unflattering portrait of André Marty, the chief political commissar of the International Brigades, whom Hemingway depicts as a bloody-minded and paranoid heresy-hunter. (For what it’s worth, the depiction was highly controversial among veterans of the brigades.)
Malraux’s gaze does not linger on these darker corners of the tableau. And there is no particular reason that it should. If the Spanish war remains a key reference point for the international left, whatever its grubbier aspects and however total the Left’s failure, it is precisely because it seems, from a more global perspective, a transcendent moment in what was otherwise, in W. H. Auden’s memorable phrasing, a “low dishonest decade.”
Malraux would have been particularly sensitive to its grandeur, having risked life and limb and lost comrades on air missions that he either joined or helped plan. But this grandeur is of a particular sort. I said above that Malraux doesn’t linger on the most sinister or demoralizing aspects of the war, yet the picture is hardly rosy. His characters all tend to comport themselves much as one imagines that Malraux himself would, as hardened men of action and at the same time intellectuals whose action is reflected upon, in an often metaphysical vein and to an almost obsessional degree. War and politics — as an old cliché has it, two modalities of the same thing — are excellent grist for philosophizing, abounding in moral quandaries and tragic choices.
For instance, one later chapter recounts the aftermath of a battle in which a court-martial is called and some republican deserters are sentenced to death. From their knees, the condemned men plead with their commander, Manuel, to countermand the decision, but he does not:
Manuel felt inclined to say: “The court-martial’s nothing to do with me.” But he was ashamed of such a disavowal. He could think of nothing to say, and he knew he could only shake off the second condemned man by pushing him away with his foot. And the idea of that revolted him. . . . Manuel wondered what he could say to them. The argument for their defence was something inexpressible in words; it was in that streaming face, that open mouth, which had made Manuel aware that here was the everlasting visage of the man who pays.
The pathos of the episode does not end here. Manuel will become aware that that face, “of the man who pays,” is no less his own than that of the pleading, condemned man. In a subsequent conversation, he is told by Heinrich, a Communist commander of a section of the International Brigades:
“We are, both of us, engaged in changing the conditions of this war,” Heinrich said. “Surely you don’t believe you can change things without being changed yourself? From the day you take a commission in the army of the proletariat, your soul is no longer your own.”
. . . .
“What do you, as a Marxist, mean by ‘lose your soul?’” Manuel asked, a little stiffly.
Heinrich watched the pine-trees scudding by in the melancholy light.
“All victories involve losses,” he said; “and not only on the battlefield.”
Unlike Hemingway’s novel, Malraux’s has little time or patience for the heroic death, the unspoken desire for which is often imputed to anarchists and other characters with a negative exemplary quality. As Garcia says on the subject of one such character, Hernandez: “What’s most dangerous about these semi-Christians is their angle on self-sacrifice: they’ll indulge in the worst follies provided they pay for them with their lives.” War and revolution are not means for realizing one’s own “moral aspirations,” and one does not serve by subtracting one’s self from the struggle.
The true loss, or heroic sacrifice, for Malraux — what Heinrich the Marxist means by “soul” — is that of the integral, human individual. The near-dissolution of this individual into a collective imbued with a single overriding purpose is, in L’Espoir, the concrete manifestation of a value claimed by revolutionaries from 1789 up to the present: fraternity, which in Malraux’s 1930s work is given its broadest metaphysical amplitude (much more than either liberty or equality). For Malraux, who like many of his generation held to a view of life that emphasized anguish and a sense of the absurd faced with the omnipresent knowledge of human existence’s ultimate horizon (i.e., nonexistence), fraternal revolutionary action was the twentieth century’s single best antidote to despair.
The action of L’Espoir breaks off at a climactic moment in the war, when republican forces rout the Fascist-led Italian Corps of Volunteer Troops at the town of Guadalajara, preventing the encirclement of Madrid by the nationalists. Many of the novel’s characters, who have yet to intersect in the several hundred pages preceding, are involved in the effort. In terms of narrative structure, the protagonist’s apprenticeship seems to be complete; a disciplined force capable of taking the offensive has successfully been molded out of the raw material of workers’ and peasants’ militias.
Writing for the Present
What would it mean for a novel to hope? It would first and foremost have to reject the retrospective gaze. This is part of what Jean-Paul Sartre had in mind when, at the end of World War II, he began calling for a “committed” literature (littérature engagée) with the imperative to “write for one’s epoch.” Above all, one must not write as if the chips are down, as if things can only be interpreted in various ways, because they no longer can be changed. Sartre could very well have been thinking of L’Espoir, with its lack of a firm resolution to the conflict that sets its narrative into motion — though I know from reading his journal that, in reality, he found the book to be a bore. I cannot agree; a left-wing anglophone readership could today find much that is both intellectually stimulating and highly moving in Malraux’s work, and I do hope more will seek it out.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: As Thanksgiving Approaches, Will Hochul  Replace Stolen SNAP Benefits?
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Rosa Goldensohn
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Last holiday season was not a happy memory for Oybek, 19, and his family in Bensonhurst.
“The whole month sucked,” he said.
His mother, a home care attendant, tried to pay for groceries at the supermarket — only to find that the family’s food assistance for the month had been stolen. They were among the thousands of New Yorkers who rely on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program to eat and who’ve been swindled by a now-common form of fraud that targets benefit cards.
That meant a food squeeze for the whole family: no more apples or bananas, a pared-down celebration for their big holiday, New Years. The soup they ate often that month required few ingredients, he noticed — half a carrot, a potato, barely any meat and a whole lot of water.
“I’d just, like, open the fridge, looking for some snacks, and yeah, just go for water at the end,” he said.
The CUNY student and his parents tried to keep things as normal as they could for his kid sister.
“All of us had to like, keep it up, because my sister is still six, and no one wants a kid to know that their parents are financially struggling,” he said.
The family thought the stolen benefits might be replaced. But Congress in 2024 stopped refunding SNAP for users who lose it to theft — and neither the city nor state have moved to fill the gap.
The Trump administration has chipped away at SNAP from all sides, restricting eligibility, tightening work requirements and shifting the funding burden further onto states in last year’s H.R.1, the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.” In New York City, enrollment dropped by nearly 175,000 between July 2025 and August 2026, despite high food prices and steady reported need. A new proposed federal rule would kick millions more people off nationwide.
In a letter to Gov. Kathy Hochul this month, more than 150 groups called on the state to create a compensation fund to repay families whose SNAP is stolen in its upcoming budget, among other interventions. The Food Bank for New York City, New York State American Academy of Pediatrics, United Way of New York City and YMCA of Greater New York were among those who joined that call, as did many city service providers who have been pressing for reimbursements in Albany — as yet, to no avail.
Asked whether the state would take up such a fund and what families who lose benefits should do in the meantime, the governor’s office indicated that it would look to Washington for solutions. “EBT skimming is a national problem, and we look forward to working with the incoming Democratic majority in Congress to ensure New Yorkers get the assistance they deserve,” spokesperson Jonah Allon said in a statement.
The Chinese-American Planning Council, which organized the letter along with the advocacy group Hunger Solutions New York and where Oybek is now an intern, said the state needs to step in to counter federal changes.
“EBT skimming is a national problem, but with H.R.1 cutting SNAP, New York is best positioned to protect its own residents,” said Wayne Ho, the group’s president and CEO. While the governor deserved credit for moving the state to chip cards this year, Ho said, “New York should pair that prevention with a fund that makes families whole whenever their benefits are stolen.”
California, under state law, does reimburse benefits lost to theft, and has already instituted credit card industry-standard chip-and-tap EBT cards that prevent fraud in the first place, along with algorithmic fraud detection. But even with those improvements, some fraud persists. Chip cards are supposed to roll out in New York some time in the first quarter of next year, the governor’s office announced this summer.
Queens Assemblymember Jessica González-Rojas tried for a state-backed compensation fund in the last legislative session, but neither the Assembly nor the governor made it a priority. She plans to try again in the next session, which starts in January, when she will become a state senator.
“Families in the past two years have not been made whole, and you know, that’s real loss, that’s literally food that’s not on their table,” González-Rojas said in an interview.
“It’s a policy failure that we’re still dealing with this, and they should have acted much quicker.”
New York City no longer collects reports of stolen SNAP benefits, but when the federal government did reimburse the claims and the city had that data, the refunds totaled on average $2.6 million a month. Earlier this year, in a survey of 827 city SNAP recipients conducted by the nonprofit Community Service Society, 31% of respondents said they had been a victim of such fraud in the past three years. The Department of Social Services received an average of 7,000 claims a month in 2024.
A new report from the city’s Robin Hood foundation also recommends the fund. Asked if Robin Hood could itself step in and fill the gap, director of policy research and initiatives Chloe Sarnoff said it was a job for government. “We cannot backfill the social safety net,” she said.
At a press conference earlier this month, asked whether the city would consider refunding the lost food money, Mayor Zohran Mamdani demurred. “That’s something we’re going to continue to work with the state on, to ensure that we’re protecting New Yorkers to the best of our ability,” he said.
Robin Hood and Columbia University’s Center on Poverty and Social Policy found in their new report that nearly a third of city residents experienced food hardship last year, meaning they “sometimes or often ran out of food or worried it would run out before they had money to buy more.” About 15%, nearly 1.3 million people, turned to free food providers like food pantries, the report said.
At a grocery store on Myrtle Avenue in Brooklyn, cashier Kim braced for one of the least festive parts of her holiday season: assisting customers who try to check out — only to find that their SNAP benefits have been pilfered.
Just last month, she said, she helped a man check his $300 balance, and by the time he had finished shopping, all but $9 was gone.
It seems a more frequent occurrence than ever, Kim told The City Reporter, and “it’s heartbreaking.”
“And now, they don’t want to return the money,” she said. “Before, when it first started, they would return the money.”
Ron Roberg, 72, of Pelham Parkway in The Bronx, was at the checkout at Key Food when he found his full $306 food benefit had been stolen. “The cashier told me, ‘Ron, you got 13 cents,’” he recalled.
Roberg was already unsure about Thanksgiving plans this year. After his wife’s death a year and a half ago, holidays are in flux.
But at least, if nothing else panned out, the retired electrician and lifelong New Yorker could cook himself a special dinner. And he still will, he resolves, even though he’s not sure how the rest of the month will go.
“It leaves me constricted,” he said. “I was hoping that there would be some way of getting recompensated, considering it was stolen.”

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: Dapper Liam and Noel, experimental Björk, and Bowie ‘cuddling himself’: Rankin reveals his never-before-seen shots of the stars
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Graeme Green
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
“I hate AI,” says Rankin. “A lot of people think I’m an evangelical twat about it, and I’m not. I think it’s disgusting. I think the people who run it are disgusting. They’ve made a massive gamble with humanity and society and culture.”
His contempt may surprise anyone who’s familiar with Rankin’s substantial AI output. Ever since the artist Damien Hirst introduced him to the possibilities of generative AI in 2021, the British photographer has been going further down the rabbit hole. “I’m not somebody who likes to be critical about something without actually knowing about it,” he explains. “I’ve gone deep into trying to work it out.”
That culminated in nine months of work for his scathing AI conceptual art project and magazine Faik (thefaik.com), made up of artificially generated images, from a skateboarding granny to Rankin-style magazine covers of the likes of Elvis, Frida Kahlo, Nelson Mandela and even God, as well as billboards with bleak warnings: “The people who control AI will control history itself”; “When anyone can generate art in seconds, who will pay for it?”
Rather than falling head-over-heels for the alluring new tech’s “limitless” possibilities, Rankin’s exploration of AI sent him running back into the arms of his first love – photography, as made by real humans in an actual time and place – and inspired his new book, Contact. “Trying to figure out what this new technology means for the craft and the thing I love reaffirmed how important the exchange between people is,” he says.
The hefty 500-plus-word page tome contains an ocean-size collection of images (bands, actors, writers, models) that Rankin took between 1987 and 2006: Oasis, Blur, Tony Blair, Kylie, Kate Moss, André 3000, Hugh Grant … Rather than presenting just the standout shot selected for a magazine cover or lead, Rankin presents contact sheets of thumbnail images, which bring to life the encounter between photographer and subject – the double meaning of the book title’s referencing the importance of human contact. “It’s about how much you kind of fall in love with people each time – platonically, of course, unless it’s my wife,” Rankin says. “I’m always going for connection. You rarely see a picture of mine where the person isn’t looking in through the camera. I tell them: ‘Forget about me – connect through the lens.’”
Born in Glasgow in 1966, Rankin, or John Rankin Waddell, grew up in St Albans, initially training in accountancy before photography consumed him. In 1991, he and Jefferson Hack co-founded the influential arts, culture and fashion magazine Dazed & Confused, Rankin’s exuberant images dominating the covers. He went on to photograph everyone from the Rolling Stones to Queen Elizabeth II. In 2011, he also founded Hunger magazine.
His next major project will be a sequel to his 2006 book Tuulitastic, dedicated to the model Tuuli Shipster, his wife of 17 years. He’s also planning to immerse himself in wet-plate photography, a slow 19th-century process that also feels like an antidote to AI.
Rankin doesn’t believe AI will replace people wanting to take or have “proper photos” taken. But he does expect it to transform the medium and devastate the industry, predicting it will be replacing jobs within less than a year, from image-retouching agencies to hair, makeup and styling. “AI is like Photoshop on crack,” he says.
While he’s not working on any AI-focused projects currently, he hasn’t finished with it entirely. “I’m quite sick of it,” he says. “But I do feel I’ve got more to explore. I’m looking at what you can create with it that you’ve never created before. People really hate it and I can’t stand it. But I’m still inquisitive about what it will become.”
Contact by Rankin is published by Hunger (£30), with a Contact exhibition also at Rankin’s Annroy Gallery, London, 2 December to3 February.
Top Rankin: six photos from his new book
Liam and Noel Gallagher, 2002, Q, issue 190 (main image)
 
“I always loved photographing Liam and Noel. Liam was like a panther – you never knew if he’d scratch you or purr. And Noel had brilliant one-liners. I’d set up a studio. Keith Drummond, the art director, and I were obsessed with David Bailey’s Lennon and McCartney shoot, so that inspired us. They looked so dapper, like real rock stars, and they played up the sibling rivalry for us.”
Björk, 1994, Dazed & Confused, issue 9
  
“Björk is the best person in the world to photograph; she’s so experimental. I was trying to do a version of another photographer’s image. She knew the photo and said: ‘Don’t do that – be yourself.’ I must’ve taken 200 rolls of film with her.”
David Bowie, 1995, Dazed & Confused, issue 14 
  
“I expected to meet the dude from The Man Who Fell to Earth film: a spaceman who was cold, serious and unemotional. Instead, I met Tigger,” says Rankin. “Bowie was so excited. I sometimes say to people: ‘Cuddle yourself’ – it’s a self-love thing. David Bowie was one of the first people I tried it on. You can see he’s cuddling himself, but then there’s a performance there.”
Vivienne Westwood, 2002, POP magazine
  
“Vivienne was so funny – no ego. She was such a laugh to shoot. The editor who commissioned me for this hated editing my shoots, but you can see her mark on this one. Most people would think they look ugly in that picture but Vivienne loved it so much that picture ended up being her poster for her V&A exhibition.”
Goldie, 1999, Dazed & Confused and INCredible Supplement
  
“What’s great about Goldie is that he always performs to the camera. You never fail to get a good picture with Goldie. I like this one, as it’s a bit less like Goldie – it’s more subtle. He’s often in-your-face, which is lovely, but I feel that there’s a bit more of the softer Goldie in this photo.”

https://www.thenation.com/article/enviro.title: As Wildfires Worsen, a New Generation Is Joining the Fire Service
https://www.thenation.com/article/enviro.author: Yong-Yu Huang
https://www.thenation.com/article/enviro.text:
As Wildfires Worsen, a New Generation Is Joining the Fire Service
Young firefighters in Washington cite environmental concerns, workplace culture, and economic stability as draws to the profession.
When he was growing up in Nine Mile Falls, it wasn’t unusual for Gabriel Sossaman’s late summer sports practices to be canceled because of poor air quality. His community—straddling the Spokane River and packed with evergreen trees—is no stranger to wildfire smoke. On multiple occasions as a child, Sossaman witnessed first responders descending upon his neighborhood to save it from flames..
By the time the Gray Fire swept over the region in August 2023—destroying more than 200 homes, including those of some friends—the now-23-year-old had seen enough. He decided to ditch his business degree at Eastern Washington University and become a firefighter. Soon thereafter, he enrolled in an EMT class cosponsored by the Cheney Fire Department. Today, he is a firefighter with Spokane County Fire District 3.
While overall fire service applications have gone down in recent years, Sossaman is just one of the many young people who have taken an interest in the fire service. At the top of their minds: climate change.
This summer, Sossaman and his family were forced out of their home during the Spokane Complex fires. In early August, the disaster forced more than 65,000 people to evacuate and destroyed more than 700 structures. Although an alleged arsonist set one of the three fires comprising the blaze, a combination of high temperatures, low humidity, and strong winds fanned the flames.
As of early September, more than 900,000 acres had burned across Washington in 2026 alone—one of the worst years on record. According to research led by the University of California, Los Angeles, wildfires in the Western United States have worsened significantly in the last few decades. Researchers say that climate change, along with forest management concerns, is a key factor.
“[Climate change] is a motivator for sure in the younger generation coming up now,” said Ryan Rodruck, a spokesperson for the Washington State Department of Natural Resources. “It’s getting hotter. That’s happening earlier in the season, and it’s going longer in the season.”
Haley Nonnemacher-Stiles, a 22-year-old volunteer with the same fire district as Sossaman, doesn’t think weather conditions will improve anytime soon. “We are not on top of climate change. All the way to October, it was 80 degrees,” said Nonnemacher-Stiles. “That’s insane.” According to a 2024 study, Washington’s average temperature climbed nearly two degrees Fahrenheit from 1900 to 2024, prolonging and intensifying the wildfire season.
Indeed, this past wildfire season was Washington’s most destructive on record, with around 1,000 structures or homes lost to flames. Nonnemacher-Stiles was working as a wildland firefighter for the first time this past summer and found herself combating the Spokane Complex fires. “It was crazy,” she said. “I just got thrown into the mix, and I was like, ‘OK, now I’m stuck here for 35 hours.”
Despite Nonnemacher-Stiles’s intense first experience on the job, she intends to apply to be a firefighter after she completes her associate’s degree in fire science from Spokane Community College.
Justin de Ruyter, who works for the Spokane Fire Department, has been in the fire service since 1997—first in Washington’s Cowlitz County, then in Portland. He said city departments like his were not built for wildfire, but now, metropolitan areas “all over the West” are grappling with wildfire threats.
“We’ve been seeing that in Washington, and we’ve seen it in Hawaii and several times in California,” de Ruyter said. “Communities that never really had wildfires are now experiencing them.”
But even though environmental concerns are driving young people into fire service, many are also turning to it for the flexible schedules and departmental culture. To Sossaman, the freedom outside of work and the prospect of forming “another family” were appealing aspects of the career. “It provided a home for me,” Sossaman said. “I’m part of something bigger than myself.”
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
Tyler Lehnertz, 24, joined Portland Fire & Rescue in January for similar reasons. While many of the places he grew up hiking, hunting and fishing have burned in recent years, Lehnertz, whose father has worked for Portland Fire and Rescue for 30 years, said that it was the workplace culture that was the biggest draw for him.
Working 24- or 48-hour shifts and living together at the station, along with experiencing potentially traumatic experiences together, he explained, helps firefighters bond in a way that other professions do not. “Those are your roommates,” Lehnertz said. “Those are your people that you eat, sleep, and suffer with.”
As remote work has grown in popularity since the Covid-19 pandemic, concerns about social isolation have followed, leading many who came of age during the coronavirus to seek more human interaction in their careers.
Meanwhile, for those entering the workforce for the first time, firefighting offers a level of financial and job stability that are increasingly difficult to attain. According to Washington’s career board, the state’s firefighters’ “typical hourly rate is $53 per hour with a typical salary of $137,900 per year.”
“You get a lot of bang for your buck. You find a lot of meaning and you find family. At a time where I think people feel very isolated, your crew just becomes your people,” Tina Grubb, a 32-year-old Portland Fire & Rescue academy instructor, said.
Grubb said she has witnessed departmental shifts with the influx of young firefighters. The fire service has traditionally leaned more conservative, which Grubb said, might have made discussing topics like climate change or diversity and equity difficult. However, she has noticed the culture shifting.
Younger firefighters openly discuss seeing a therapist at the firehouse kitchen table, something she said was once unheard of. “They show up in a very subtle way,” Grubb explained. “They say: ‘Diversity and equity is important. Climate change is important. I care about what kind of foam we use at fire scenes. I care about what kind of materials are burning because I care about the planet.’” Today, Grubb sees the fire service transformed by “a different generation with different values.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Chile’s first Anglican church to host a new museum
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Graciela Ibáñez
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
One of the most famous churches in Valparaiso, Chile—a meeting point for seamen, merchants, shipbuilders, musicians, artists and engineers during the 19th and early 20th centuries—will soon host a museum celebrating the influence of British immigration on the port city.
St Paul’s Cathedral was the first Anglican church built in Chile, as well as on the west coast of South America. It was one of the first buildings on the hill where British and German immigrants settled after the country’s independence from Spain in 1818.
The cathedral’s neighbour, Destino Valparaíso (which houses the Immigrant Museum), will oversee the church’s management, restoration and conservation as part of a 50-year lease agreement with the Anglican Episcopal Church Corporation of Valparaíso. The agreement will take effect on 30 November. St Paul’s will undergo restoration of its roof, floors, pews and stained-glass windows—a project expected to last at least a year.
“The church was deteriorating and, as a historic monument, was in poor condition,” Eduardo Dib Maluk, the executive director at Destino Valparaíso, tells The Art Newspaper. “We felt the need to restore it and develop a business model like the one we have at Destino Valparaíso.”
The Dib family bought the building that now houses Destino Valparaíso in 2016. The former German School of Valparaíso, also a historic monument, was built by the local immigrant community. The school operated from 1870 until 1985, when an earthquake damaged the building and classes were moved to the German school in the neighbouring city of Viña del Mar. The Dib family renovated the building, transforming most of its space into a museum that tells the stories of British, German, Italian, Spanish, French and Arab immigrants who arrived in Valparaíso after Chile’s independence.
Since the Immigrant Museum’s opening last year, it has been the most visited place in an area that Unesco declared a World Heritage Site in 2003. The museum recently opened a space dedicated to the history of sports that immigrants brought to Chile—including rugby, cricket, football, polo, tennis and cycling.
Dib plans to incorporate technology and design into the new museum spaces at St Paul’s Cathedral, as he has in the old German School building. “It won't be an extension of the Immigrant Museum," he says. “It will highlight the milestones achieved by the British, who shaped the Valparaíso that was known until the 20th century.” The city was a technological centre driving the country’s development in the 19th century; it was home to Chile’s first bank, observatory and stock exchange.
St Paul’s was built by the English engineer William Henry Lloyd, who had come to Chile to work on the construction of the Valparaíso-Santiago railway. The church was inaugurated in 1858, at a time of Catholic restrictions on other religions in the country. As a result, the church was built in a discrete style with small windows and without a main door, spire, cross or bell tower. With a single nave and an adjacent hall, the Neo-Gothic style building occupies a whole city block.
Inside, Lloyd used laminated Oregon pine beams attached with nails and screws to form the cathedral’s ceiling arches, an advanced technique at the time. Its stained-glass windows, representative of the British Gothic Revival, include one by Morris & Co. The church’s organ, made by Forster and Andrews in England, arrived in Valparaíso in 1902. An earthquake in 1906 damaged the massive instrument, which was repaired four years later. (The Queen Victoria Memorial Organ, as it is known, has kept the space active, with concerts every Sunday for the past 35 years.)
Over time the city's British community largely migrated to Viña del Mar or Santiago, reducing St Paul’s sources of funding. “This church requires a lot of maintenance and repairs because of the earthquakes,” says Lynn Gray, a member of the board that manages the cathedral. “It's very reassuring to be able to keep its heritage alive.”
As part of the agreement with Destino Valparaíso, St Paul’s will maintain services such as the ordination of pastors, weddings for members of the British community and the Remembrance Service in November.

https://hyperallergic.com/joni-mitchell-.title: Joni Mitchell Has Some News
https://hyperallergic.com/joni-mitchell-.author: Nereya Otieno
https://hyperallergic.com/joni-mitchell-.text:
Joni Mitchell Has Some News
In a collection of political paintings, the famed musician and artist lambastes MAGA, the Epstein class, and Trump's attacks on immigrants.
In her song “A Case of You,” Joni Mitchell described herself as “a lonely painter / I live in a box of paints.” She has never been a particularly shy one. The famously elusive artist, who has pronounced painting her "first love" before music, makes plain statements in NEWS, a collection of political paintings.
Conceived and designed by Mitchell, the book unfurls a scathing rebuke of recent Republican administrations in the United States. Twenty-three paintings are presented chronologically, with a handful created between 2001 and 2004 and the majority made in the last 18 months. Works from the Bush years show the Twin Towers aflame with a sinister face in the smoke or a bare-chested blonde woman who sits astride Osama Bin Laden’s shoulders.
More recent works feature Adolf Hitler with the letters "MGGA" ("Make Germany Great Again"), former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem on horseback labeled “grifter,” and a triptych of Jeffrey Epstein, Ghislaine Maxwell, and President Trump as disgraced royalty playing cards. A spread of all the works becomes a Thunderdome-like arena of modern US politics — ending with a self-portrait of Mitchell receiving a Kennedy Center Honor. As if the answer to all that chaos is elevating impactful art.

https://gothamist.com/news/attorney-gene.title: NYC, state sue Trump administration over ‘mixed-status’ federal housing assistance rule
https://gothamist.com/news/attorney-gene.author: Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/attorney-gene.text:
New York Attorney General Letitia James and the city of New York sued the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development Monday over a new rule that would strip federal housing assistance for families with mixed immigration status.
The state lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts alongside a coalition of 21 other attorneys general across the country, argued that the proposed rule change — which could strip assistance for 20,000 mixed-status families or around 78,100 people, many of whom are children — exceeds HUD’s authority and violates the Administrative Procedure Act.
The city lawsuit included a coalition of more than a dozen local governments and housing agencies.
The existing rule allowed families to live together in “HUD-assisted” housing if at least one family member is a U.S. citizen or an eligible non-citizen, such as a visa holder. The new rule states that every family member in that household must be a U.S. citizen or eligible non-citizen and each member must demonstrate their eligibility or risk losing their housing.
James said the new rule means that HUD will require people in federal housing programs to prove their citizenship through an “unreliable” process or even risk eviction.
“Everyone deserves a safe place to call home. Denying a child that security because who they live with is cruel and indefensible,” James said in a statement. “With our country already in the throes of a housing crisis, it is outrageous that the federal government would push even more families out of their homes. This rule runs counter to our nation’s values and the very purpose of these housing programs.”
The state's lawsuit also argues that the federal rule change harms the states that signed on as plaintiffs in at least three ways: an increase in administrative costs for state agencies that report to HUD, increased spending on state social safety nets like right-to-shelter programs, and a reduction in income for state-financed housing developments that host tenants with federal subsidies.
The city lawsuit argued that tens of thousands of people would be removed from the program, including public housing and Section 8.
And as a result of removing people from their homes supported by federal assistance, the lawsuit argued the new rule would increase homelessness and shift much of these costs to house people to local governments.
In a statement, HUD Secretary Scott Turner said the rule change “ends the exploitation of taxpayer dollars.”
“This rule guarantees only American citizens and certain eligible noncitizens will reside in HUD-funded housing. This change represents a reallocation of up to $218 million which will now go to eligible Americans that are currently on a waitlist,” Turner said.
The existing rule, called “proration,” was written into law by Congress in 1997, which helped reduce a family’s subsidy so it only covered the payment for eligible household members. The law explicitly specified that families “shall not” lose their benefits if an eligible family member lives in the same household.
James also said the rule would make it harder for millions of U.S. citizens to keep the housing they already qualify for because they’d have to provide their Social Security number and authorize a citizenship status check through a database.
