https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Efforts to save I.M. Pei’s Dallas City Hall likely headed to referendum
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: James M. Russell
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
When the mayor of Dallas, Erik Jonsson, inaugurated I.M. Pei’s city hall in 1978, he called it “a monument to the city’s pride, a symbol of a first-class city that’s reaching for greatness”. The seven-storey inverted pyramid slopes over a large plaza with site-specific sculptures like Henry Moore’s Vertebra in Three Pieces (1978, also known as The Dallas Piece) and Marta Pan’s Floating Sculpture (1973), which sits in a reflecting pool.
Since early 2025, the current Dallas mayor Eric Johnson and city manager Kimberly Bizor Tolbert have pushed to abandon and sell Pei’s city hall to private developers. They have cited the prohibitive costs of renovating the building, which ballooned within a matter of months from $81m according to an initial estimate for a basic infrastructure upgrade to $1.4bn for massive upgrades over two decades.
In recent interviews, Johnson has sounded far different from his predecessor. He has called the building “obsolete”. Architecturally significant or not, moving the municipal headquarters “would make this location available for development, which I would also support. I believe that will be a very, very big part of the future of downtown and its revitalisation.” Spokespersons for the city did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s questions.
The current mayor is in alignment with the “Say Yes to Downtown” campaign group led by former mayor Mike Rawlings. With developers and other former leaders, the campaign argues that city hall must be demolished to create an entertainment district, including a new arena for two of the city’s professional sports teams, the Dallas Mavericks basketball team and the Stars hockey team. When the teams announced plans to move out of the city’s core, both considered relocating to the city hall site. They ultimately chose other locations.
Amid the uproar over the possible demolition of Pei’s modernist complex, few have questioned the fate of Pan’s and Moore’s sculptures. Both were gifted to the city and are part of the municipal public art collection. But the future of Moore’s, which has required previous renovation, in part with help from the artist’s London-based estate and foundation, is a particular concern. The large grouping of organic forms was meant to complement Pei’s rigidly angular structure. It was also a gift to the city from the philanthropist W.R. Hawn in memory of his wife Mildred Hawn, whose favourite sculptor was Moore. Both sculptures are part of the preservation plan for the building; representatives for Moore and Pan’s estates did not respond to The Art Newspaper’s inquiries.
The non-profit Save Dallas City Hall, an ideologically diverse grassroots coalition, has been among the loudest voices opposed to moving the facility. It is led by president Bruce Richardson, a musician, artist and former political candidate, and vice-president Zaida Basora, an architect and former city employee who oversaw maintenance of properties, including city hall, and currently serves as the executive director of the American Institute of Architects Dallas.
Basora and her colleagues have proposed a ten-year phased plan that, even factoring in inflation, is estimated to cost between $70m and $100m, and would not require municipal staff to move. The cost of simply demolishing the building—to say nothing of the expense of building something in its place—has been estimated at $60m.
Deferred maintenance and a looming referendum
The Dallas city council gave Tolbert a deadline of 26 August to present relocation options for city hall, which she missed. Inflation has also increased the cost of relocating. The same month, Save Dallas City Hall sued the city, arguing that it was committing “demolition by neglect”.
“Dallas city hall has at least one failed generator, active parking garage leaks and is due for roof maintenance,” Richardson said in a statement. “Instead of tackling these problems with millions in available funds, the city halted repairs, wasting money and time to explore a move.”
On 2 October, the Save Dallas City Hall coalition started an effort to gather signatures to create a ballot referendum on the fate of city hall, which would be put to residents for a vote in May 2027. In early November, the group announced it had gathered around 25,000 signatures—well over the minimum 20,000 signatures needed for a ballot referendum. If the group’s proposed amendment to the city charter passes next spring, the municipal government will be required to continue operating from Pei’s city hall.
During elections earlier this month, 56% of Dallas voters opposed a $443m bond package. That package had included funding to move emergency operations out of city hall, which, according to advocates of preserving Pei’s building, would have been a first step toward abandoning it.
For the local activist Stephanie Drenka, a co-founder of the Dallas Asian American Historical Society who has spoken at nearly every public hearing since she learned of the building’s significance, preserving city hall is essential to recognising Pei’s contribution to Asian American history.
“The stakes are beyond our city alone,” she says. Less than 1% of historic markers in the US acknowledge the contributions of Asian Americans, according to the national non-profit Asian & Pacific Islander Americans in Historic Preservation.
“This also makes demolition of city hall an issue of further erasure of Asian Americans in history,” Drenka says. “It’s not just Pei’s legacy, but we’re defending ourselves. Everything in our community is embodied in this building.” She adds: “If we can’t save city hall then what threat can we stop?”

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/24/t.title: Tuesday’s Headlines: Another City Bike Edition
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/24/t.author: Gersh Kuntzman
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/24/t.text:
Som Ray and David Krawcyzk of Clip show off their new product, the Neon (theirs are well-worn; yours will be sparkling clean). Photo: Gersh Kuntzman
For a minute, it looked like I’d picked the wrong day to check out the latest bike accessory that promises to “turn-your-regular-bike-into-an-e-bike.” After all, hours earlier on Monday, Mayor Mamdani announced that the price of a 45-minute electric Citi Bike ride would be capped at $3.65.
The price cap seemed like a game-changer to me … until I realized that it wasn’t: Sure, $3.65 is a decent price for a 45-minute electric bike ride, but it still means that a Citi Bike member who likes to commute on Lyft’s white bikes would pay about $2,000 a year (including the annual $239 membership). And it’s likely going to mean slightly worse service for all of us, as more people sign up to use the same finite supply of bikes and docks (docks that are often full when you want to drop off, or empty when you need a bike after work).
Full disclosure: I’m a Citi Bike annual member, but I haven’t used the electric bikes because they are just too damn expensive. But as my age rises in indirect proportion to my muscle tone, I confess that I’m jealous of the electric horsemen who get a little boost to get over the East River and up the hill that the name “Park Slope” doesn’t do justice.
So that’s how I ended up in the Brooklyn Navy Yard on Monday talking to Som Ray and David Krawczyk, the CEO and chief of product, respectively, of Clip, the e-bike accessory company. You may have read about the company’s first product, the Clip, (in these pages, even), but now Ray and Krawczyk are hawking an entirely new e-bike concept that threatens to take some wind out of Mamdani’s Citi Bike announcement:
It’s called Neon — and it comes in two options:
- For $365 (once), you get a new front wheel with a hub motor built in that’s easy to install on your existing bike, plus the 3.5-pound Neon battery pack that clips on and off for easy portability. The electric boost is controlled via Bluetooth from a small button that clips to your handlebars (no wires). The UL-certified battery pack isn’t going to take you to White Plains and back, but it’ll get you to work, where you’ll recharge it for the ride home.
- For $49 a month, you can lease a new bike with the Neon wheel and battery, aka “Neon Fleet.” Repairs and replacement batteries are covered. There’s no per-minute charge. That’s about $600 per year for all the e-bike rides you want.
Either option ends up less than commuting on Citi Bike e-bikes, even once the price is capped (which was covered extensively on Monday in The Times, in Streetsblog, in the mostly negative New York Post, mostly positively in Hell Gate, and in Gothamist).
Now, look, I have no financial interest in Clip and no personal relationship with anyone who works there (though they seem nice). As a newsman who bikes, I just wanted to share info about a different way to get around (plus I thought it would be fun to test the Neon — which I did, and it was). The Neon provides more than enough boost to get you up hills, but it only adds about five pounds to the weight of your regular bike, so your bike rides normally when you don’t need the boost. And the battery clips off easily, so you can toss it in your backpack when your ride is over.
And best of all: No empty docks when you need an e-bike and no full docks when you want to return one.
In other news:
- Speaking of e-bikes, the Pope looks like he’s violating at least two of the seven deadly sins as he lusts after this gorgeous two-wheeler:
- They finally un-paved paradise! Gov. Hochul announced a plan to turn the parking lot next to Tavern on the Green (reminder: it’s inside Central Park!) into a soccer field. (Westside Rag)
- No one has covered the Council’s battle with Amazon better than our own Sophia Lebowitz (archives here), but more and more outlets are noticing what oligarchy looks like. (Jacobin)
- Great minds think alike: Streetsblog USA and the NY Times both looked at the Trump administration’s latest attempt to gut public transit.
- We enjoyed the Daily News’s editorial about lithium-ion batteries (including a link to our coverage), but it also raised one thought: Is there no accountability for Sen. Ted Cruz? The Texas Republican blocked — for like two years! — a federal bill to set up battery standards only to finally yield before the bill passed unanimously. So does anyone ever go back and say, “Yo, Cruz, what was that bullshit all about anyway?” Interested, Greg B. Smith?
- And, finally, how about a map of all the detours on all the bike lanes? (Two Pedals)
Tabloid legend Gersh Kuntzman has been with New York newspapers since 1989, including stints at the New York Daily News, the Post, the Brooklyn Paper and even a cup of coffee with the Times. He's also the writer and producer of "Murder at the Food Coop" (NYC Fringe Festival, 2016) and “SUV: The Musical” (Fringe, 2007). On Jan. 1, 2027, he will step down as editor in chief of Streetsblog and remain as senior editor. His Cycle of Rage column is archived here.

Days before the Venice Biennale opened, the Golden Lion jury resigned amid calls to exclude Israel from the festival. Dozens of artists and pavilions took themselves out of the running in solidarity. Now, as the exhibition draws to a close, the Biennale is ready to present its visitors’ choice awards — a “poisoned chalice,” in the words of the Art Not Genocide Alliance (ANGA), that “few want to win.” ANGA reflects on a historic year of organizing against attempts to artwash Israel’s assault on Palestine in an opinion piece today.
As gamers everywhere pore over Grand Theft Auto VI, Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia sits down with Miami-based artists misael soto and Leo Castañeda to make sense of the game’s many tensions and complexities, while Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar tracks down its various art references. In another form of uncanny valley, Associate Editor Phillip Pyle wanders through empty corporate offices in Midtown Manhattan, transformed by artists who dismantle the systems of technocracy from the inside out. More to start your week below.
—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books
The Venice Biennale’s Sham Awards Cannot Artwash Genocide
Stripped of the silver and gold they wore in previous iterations of the Biennale, the new Lions have been thrown to the tourists; “Best Artist” and “Best National Pavilion” will be decided by a popularity contest. Why this surprising democratic turn? The expert jury initially appointed to give these honors resigned en masse in April of this year. These resignations were, in part, the result of the Art Not Genocide Alliance’s (ANGA) nearly three years of campaigning to exclude the Israel pavilion from the art world’s most important biennial. | Art Not Genocide Alliance

https://gothamist.com/news/former-nypd-d.title: Former NYPD detective ordered held in jail in fatal George Washington Bridge shooting
https://gothamist.com/news/former-nypd-d.author: Ben Feuerherd
https://gothamist.com/news/former-nypd-d.text:
A New York City judge on Monday ordered a former NYPD detective to be held in jail until his trial in the killing of a man during an apparent road rage incident on the George Washington Bridge.
A Manhattan grand jury indicted Victor Romero on a second-degree murder charge for the Oct. 20 killing, according to the district attorney’s office.
Dozens of people came to court to support the man who was killed, Koran Irvine. They marched through the hallways outside the courtroom before the court appearance, and cheered after the judge ordered Romero held in jail.
Romero, 62, who was an NYPD detective before he retired in 2001, has pleaded not guilty. His attorney, Joel Cohen, declined to comment Monday.
Prosecutors said Romero fired at Irvine’s car on the George Washington Bridge after their vehicles nearly collided as they both approached the upper-level onramp.
After the shooting, prosecutors say, Romero may have tried to obstruct the investigation into the killing by wiping down the driver’s side of his car at a gas station and by cleaning the inside center console of the car.
Prosecutors said Romero gave police a revolver after the shooting, saying that was the gun he usually carried with him. However they say the murder weapon was a different gun: a 9mm pistol they found in Romero’s home.

A nine-month restoration of El Greco’s The Martyrdom of Saint Maurice and the Theban Legion (1580–82) has removed more than four hundred years’ worth of varnish, dirt, and repainting and revealed the composition’s vivid colors and striking details.
Housed in the Royal Monastery of San Lorenzo de El Escorial near Madrid, the monumental painting was restored at Madrid’s Royal Collections Gallery by Rafael Alonso, an eighty-one-year-old former Prado Museum restorer, according to Artnews. Alonso, who has worked on El Greco’s paintings for decades, originally projected a four-month timeline, but quickly found that the damage and neglect accumulated over 444 years would require a much longer process.
“When I put the cotton to the painting, my heart sank,” Alonso told El País. Varnish and overpainting dulled El Greco’s colors and flattened the overall composition. After removing reinterpretations made over damaged areas in the nineteenth century, Alonso and his team restored areas where the original paint had been lost using soluble materials that could be removed later.
King Philip II of Spain commissioned the altarpiece from El Greco, but when he saw the completed painting in 1583, he was dissatisfied. It depicts Maurice in a bright blue breastplate over a red tunic surrounded by his officers and legion of soldiers. Philip wanted the execution of Maurice and his Christian soldiers to be foremost in the painting as a statement of Catholic faith, but El Greco set the martyrdom in the background, anticipated by a host of angels above.
Commissioned for the king’s monastery and palace outside Madrid, the painting was instead relegated to another room, and El Greco did not receive the permanent position as a court painter that he had hoped for. The Martyrdom of Saint Maurice and the Theban Legion remained at its original site until 1999, when it was transported to Madrid for an exhibition.

https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.title: Henry Kissinger’s Reputational Management
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.author: Peter Kornbluh
https://www.thenation.com/article/politi.text:
Henry Kissinger’s Reputational Management
Barbara J. Keys’s new book, Super K, reveals Kissinger’s ceaseless efforts to burnish his bloody legacy.
Henry Kissinger’s Reputational Management
Barbara J. Keys’s new book, “Super K,” reveals Kissinger’s ceaseless efforts to burnish his bloody legacy.
On November 7, 2002, I attended a lunch meeting with Henry Kissinger’s personal lawyer, William D. Rogers, at a tony Spanish restaurant in downtown Washington, DC. Rogers was concerned about my forthcoming book, The Pinochet File—what it would reveal about Kissinger’s documented roles as chief architect of US efforts to undermine Chile’s democratically elected president, Salvador Allende, as well as lead enabler of Gen. Augusto Pinochet’s consolidation of his vicious dictatorship. Based on advance access to my manuscript, a year earlier 60 Minutes had broadcast a hard-hitting segment that tied Kissinger to the CIA’s violent plot to neutralize Chile’s commander in chief of the armed forces, Gen. René Schneider, who had opposed a preemptive coup to prevent Allende’s inauguration. On Henry’s behalf, Rogers had cause for concern.
Nevertheless, our conversation was civil; we discussed our differences on key points of the dark history of US intervention in Chile and agreed that we would debate each other in a special event when the book was published on the 30th anniversary of the Chilean coup.
Somewhat naïvely, I agreed to give him an advance galley of the book so he could prepare.
Rogers’s mission, as he reported to Kissinger via e-mail, was “to head off [Kornbluh’s] book or diffuse it.” I later learned that he had a team of associates pick apart the galleys to refute the evidence the book would present. Rogers drafted a 14-page rebuttal to share with those in the media who could counter my arguments. When he received a tip that I planned to write an opinion piece in The Washington Post on the 30th anniversary of the coup, he pressed editors there for “equal time and ink” and advised Kissinger to reach out to his friend senior associate editor Lally Graham Weymouth. In what became the biggest “project” to countermand the book, Rogers enlisted conservative academic Mark Falcoff to write a major article on what Rogers called “the powerful and pernicious myth” of US involvement in Chile. “Mark and I met yesterday for some extensive editing of his paper,” Rogers reported to Kissinger in mid-August 2003, as the anniversary of the coup approached. “I told him I would not—unless I heard otherwise from you—be sending you the draft beforehand. Thus, we can all say that the appropriate niceties of authorial independence were strictly observed.”
Their plan was to publish Falcoff’s attack article in Foreign Affairs, the prestigious journal of the Council on Foreign Relations (CFR), where Kissinger wielded tremendous influence by bringing in big donors to support the “Henry A. Kissinger Chair for U.S. Foreign Policy.” But that plan fell through when the editor James Hoge rejected the Falcoff article as “too narrow a defense of Kissinger.” Instead, the CFR’s Latin America specialist, Kenneth Maxwell, wrote a lengthy and moderately favorable review of The Pinochet File, sending Kissinger into a complete meltdown.
For Kissinger, “being attacked in Foreign Affairs was like being mugged in his own living room,” writes historian Barbara J. Keys in her compelling and damning new book, Super K: The Making, Breaking, and Remaking of Henry Kissinger’s Legacy. As Kissinger told his colleagues, Foreign Affairs had been used “to smear a former secretary of state closely associated with the Council for fifty years in a manner comparable to those of the most radical journals.” In addition to trying to get the entire Foreign Affairs issue pulled from circulation and threatening to resign from the Council and take the endowed chair along with its wealthy donors with him, Keys recounts, Kissinger “briefly contemplated a libel lawsuit before launching into a monthslong campaign to discredit the review.”
As a target (along with Ken Maxwell) of Henry Kissinger’s wrath, one of the great rewards of reading Super K was to learn that mine was not a special case. When William Shawcross published his meticulously documented Sideshow: Kissinger, Nixon, and the Destruction of Cambodia, Kissinger fired off a long letter to The Economist (reprinted in The New York Times) denouncing the book as “based on omissions, inaccuracies and inventions.” He tasked his assistant, Peter Rodman, with drafting a 17-page “independent examination” to be distributed to journalists and editors attacking the book as “a compendium of errors,” “shoddy,” and “deceitful.” Keys describes how Kissinger also halted the prepublication process of his forthcoming memoir, already in galleys, to rewrite the chapter on Cambodia; he added complete falsehoods about the secret bombing campaign in a damage-control effort against Shawcross’s book, which, as Keys points out, “tether[ed] Kissinger to one of the twentieth century’s worst genocides.”
In the case of investigative reporter Seymour Hersh’s The Price of Power: Kissinger in the Nixon White House, Kissinger launched his counteroffensive even before the book was published. He tracked Hersh’s interviews with former colleagues to ascertain whom he was talking to, what issues he was researching, and what evidence he was seeking. “His lawyers used the Freedom of Information Act to get copies of Hersh’s own FOIA requests,” Keys reports. They also sent prepublication letters of intimidation to Hersh’s publisher, Simon & Schuster, threatening libel lawsuits. Kissinger’s office developed a “dirt file” on Hersh to challenge his integrity as a reporter. When The New York Times gave The Price of Power a positive review, Kissinger sent a bitter 22-page letter to the executive editor, A. M. Rosenthal, excoriating Hersh and claiming that books like his would deter “people who value their reputations” from pursuing public office, thus doing damage to US national security. In a damning episode that Super K describes in detail, Kissinger collaborated with one of his most influential mainstream media buddies, Ted Koppel, to use his popular ABC News program, Nightline, as a platform to trash Hersh and the best-selling book he had written.
And when then–Nation magazine columnist Christopher Hitchens published The Trial of Henry Kissinger in 2001, Kissinger did his best to attack him as well. In her chapter titled “War Criminal,” Keys recounts how the history-changing arrest of Gen. Augusto Pinochet in London in October 1998 for human rights crimes offered a legal foundation on which Hitchens built his case for prosecuting Kissinger. If the international legal community could breach Pinochet’s immunity, it could do the same with Kissinger and hold him accountable for the thousands of human lives lost to his immoral foreign policies.
“Not since Hersh’s The Price of Power in 1983 had a book so enraged and provoked Kissinger,” Keys notes. Hitchens’s was “a far smaller book,” thinly researched with no new revelations. “Yet thanks to a propitious climate it inflicted more damage to Kissinger’s reputation,” not to mention threatened his very freedom.
Kissinger understood that Pinochet’s predicament could quickly become his own. He enlisted his media mogul friends in Britain, Conrad Black and Rupert Murdoch, to use their news outlets to demand the release of the former Chilean dictator. He began researching the powers of the International Criminal Court and wrote an article in Foreign Affairs condemning universal jurisdiction—the legal concept used to detain Pinochet—not mentioning that he himself was likely to become a target.
Nevertheless, the Pinochet precedent would haunt him. Not long after The Trial of Henry Kissinger was published, French policemen showed up at the Ritz hotel in Paris, where Kissinger was staying, with a summons for him to testify on his knowledge of Pinochet’s human rights crimes. Soon thereafter, judges in Chile and Argentina sought him for questioning. As Kissinger prepared to travel to Brazil to receive a prestigious award, a special prosecutor announced a plan to interrogate him; he promptly canceled his trip.
To attack Hitchens, Kissinger’s office compiled a 1,000-page rebuttal to his 160-page book. Kissinger hired a defamation lawyer in London to sue The Guardian, which had published excerpts. In the end, however, the suit did not move forward. “A lawsuit would have played into Hitchens’s hands, allowing the critic to subpoena documents and witnesses, from Kissinger and third parties, that might bring new, damning material to light,” Keys writes. “More documents would expose more issues and invite new lines of inquiry, without any guarantee of interpretive control—exactly what Kissinger wanted to avoid.”
Kissinger’s aggressive quest for guaranteed “interpretive control” of his legacy after he left government service is the central subject of Super K. The title is drawn from the many “mythologizing monikers” bestowed on Kissinger during his time in office—in this case, the June 1974 cover of Newsweek magazine, which depicted a soaring secretary of state with six-pack abs, red cape flapping in the wind, under the banner “It’s Super K!” The Superman image encapsulated the way Kissinger saw himself—and wanted to be seen. “Like the comic book superhero, in this telling, he possessed special powers: a strategic mind that grasped what eluded others and diplomatic skills that could unlock any impasse,” as Keys writes in her ultra-engaging introduction. “He was, it seemed, indispensable.”
Kissinger’s Super K persona was, of course, a myth—one that he assiduously cultivated through constant “reputation management.” When he left government, he built a self-promotion machine to protect and burnish his image, as Super K reveals, and “he spent the next forty-seven years of his life defending, explaining, and justifying his record.”
Sometimes Kissinger’s aggressive efforts backfired spectacularly. In the case of my book, as Super K recounts, Kissinger’s campaign to discredit the review in Foreign Affairs led to Ken Maxwell’s high-profile resignation—and his publication of a 30-page exposé of how Kissinger had bullied top officials at the Council on Foreign Relations to censor honest discourse on his own role in Chile. The scandal inside America’s preeminent foreign policy institution generated significant publicity: The Nation published a substantive article; The New York Times published two articles; and The Washington Post ran a three-page spread (with a half-page photo of a smiling Kissinger shaking Pinochet’s hand). The media coverage was negative for Kissinger’s reputation but positive for book sales.
But often Kissinger’s efforts to cast himself as the indispensable statesman and savior of humankind proved quite effective. His master manipulation of the media kept him in the public eye on his own terms; his close friendships with celebrity reporters such as Koppel and Barbara Walters, and top officials at The Washington Post, Time magazine, NBC, and ABC News, among other major outlets, provided a steady supply of positive press and ready channels for Kissinger’s self-promotional information warfare when needed.
But to truly secure his eternal legacy, Kissinger needed a like-minded, kindred-spirit biographer. In the final chapter of her book, “Kissinger’s Last Battle,” Keys tells the story of how he recruited a young, fiercely conservative British historian named Niall Ferguson to write the definitive, authorized history of Henry Alfred Kissinger.

“Kissinger sought to bind his biographer with ties of friendship and intimacy,” Keys reports, plying Ferguson with access to “the rarefied world of power and money that Kissinger inhabited.” This courtship of hospitality succeeded. “I’m in Henry Kissinger’s swimming pool talking about his meeting with Mao Tse-tung, thinking I must be dreaming,” Ferguson exclaimed. The first of his two-volume biography, Kissinger: 1923–1968: The Idealist, was published in 2015, covering Kissinger’s pre-government life. The second volume, which will address Kissinger’s years in the Nixon and Ford administrations, is reportedly finished but yet to be released.
Keys, however, seems to have obtained an advance sneak peek. “He will say that Kissinger made the entire globe more stable, and that the suffering of millions unlucky enough to live outside strategically vital regions was the necessary price for this stability,” she reports. “In the end, much of what Hersh and Hitchens wrote about is trivial,” Ferguson told Keys dismissively. Three years after his death at age 100, it seems, Kissinger’s efforts at reputation management continue from the grave.
But regardless of what Kissinger’s handpicked biographer publishes in the future, the man that Newsweek dubbed “Super K” will forever be vulnerable to the kryptonite of history. As Keys’s book reminds us, the historical record haunted Kissinger’s many attempts to spin, falsify, or simply fabricate the true history of his role on the world stage when he was alive. And that historical record will continue to offset efforts to rewrite the past since his death.
William Shawcross used the Freedom of Information Act to obtain declassified Pentagon records that exposed Kissinger’s mendacity on Cambodia; Sy Hersh obtained troves of TOP SECRET records from various secret sources to write The Price of Power. Super K features my late (and great) colleague at the National Security Archive, William Burr, who was the first to obtain the declassified memoranda of conversations Kissinger held with leaders of the Soviet Union and China and publish them in The Kissinger Transcripts. And through legal efforts that Keys describes, the National Security Archive was able to force Kissinger to return some 30,000 pages of telephone transcripts that he illicitly took with him when he left office, precisely so he could control the historical narrative as he fostered his legacy.
Super K itself is evidence of how the effort to excavate the historical record on Kissinger’s true legacy continues. To write the untold history of how Kissinger sought to salvage and shape his enduring reputation, Keys has obtained access to many of his private papers, including letters and communications he himself wrote after he left office.
As her important book demonstrates, those records provide a powerful indictment of Kissinger’s insidious efforts to create a false legacy and cover up the true history of his rampant abuses of power. In the end, it is not just historians and reporters who have exposed the myth of Super K. It is his own words.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: First Frieze Abu Dhabi proves successful for the region's dealers, despite geopolitical jitters
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Melissa Gronlund
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The inaugural Frieze Abu Dhabi (19-22 November) opened to a promising start. Strong sales were reported across many galleries, and the fair had an energy that spread from the stands to the garden outside at the Manarat Al Saadiyat, where guests lingered for hours over the unlikely combination of pizza and champagne.
“They’re looking after us very well here,” one established Dubai collector said. “Unlike at other fairs, where we feel pressured to buy, here we can take a breather and reflect on things. The art world is very collegiate in this region and the collectors are here to support.”
Like its name, Frieze Abu Dhabi was a mix of two halves. The successor to the long-standing Abu Dhabi Art fair that has been operating, under various names, in the UAE capital since 2007, the fair is co-run by Frieze Fairs and the UAE government’s Department of Culture and Tourism (DCT). Accordingly, the event blended elements of Abu Dhabi Art’s programme with those more familiar to Frieze's flagship event in Regent’s Park.
Chief among these is the Ladies’ Day—the day before the public opening that is reserved for Abu Dhabi’s sheikhas—and the pre-bound book of available works that is sent around to the city’s royals.
Meanwhile Frieze brought its art fair expertise, giving the fair a better layout and an improved allover experience. “The fair still has its Abu Dhabi Art soul but feels a lot tighter in terms of the number of galleries and the selection,” said Taymour Grahne, whose eponymous gallery moved from New York to London and has now settled in Dubai. Grahne was showing a series of mosaics by the Palestinian artist Ala Younis, which by the opening day had mostly sold.
Most of the galleries’ presentations were rooted in the Wanasa (West Asia, North Africa and South Asia) region. Standout booths included that of the Cairo gallery Art Talks/Kanafani's solo presentation of the Egyptian surrealist Samir Rafi, and the Dubai gallery Ayyam’s booth of the Dutch-Iraqi artist Sadik Kwaish Alfraiji. By the opening day, the Rafi works were about half sold.
Other Dubai galleries, who had a strong showing at the fair, equally did well, with Lawrie Shabibi selling out its marble inlay works by Hamra Abbas by the opening day for $50,000 each; Zawyeh Gallery selling about half of its collages by the Gazan artist Mohammed Joha, which had attracted much attention this year at the Venice Biennale; and Tabari Artspace, which showed two early works by another artist born in Gaza, Hazem Harb, amidst a group show, also reported selling half their booth. Most artworks were priced in the region of ten-thousands to mid-hundred thousand dollars.
A mix of blue-chip Western galleries were also in attendance. Pace were offering their fresh-to-market, large-scale paintings by the indigenous Australian artist Emily Kame Kngwarreye for between $80,000 to $750,000, although confirmed sales for these works appeared to be slow.
And in the small Frieze Masters section, a 2,000-year-old funerary stele made out of luminous alabaster, taken by a British official from what is now Yemen, was sold by the Mayfair gallerist David Aaron for "seven figures".
There were also a substantial number of new visitors to the fair, including a few starry faces like the tennis star Venus Williams. A smattering of museum heads and curators from the US, Asia and Europe also flew in, such as Michael Govan of Lacma (who was speaking at the fair), Eugene Tan of the Singapore Art Museum, and the Aspen Art Museum’s Nicola Lees, one of a number who brought along a patrons group.
And though the fair also had a number of South Asian galleries, Indian and Pakistani collectors were less present than expected, partly because the fair came right on the heels of Art Mumbai.
Perhaps as importantly, most galleries reported selling to these new collectors—both to collectors who had flown in as well as new collectors living in Abu Dhabi. The city’s population has swelled recently, particularly in the finance and tech sectors, in addition to the surge of Russians who moved to the UAE after the 2022 restrictions imposed on their country.
But the larger context of regional instability could not be ignored. Though it was hard to say how many people had stayed away because of fears of a resumption in Iran’s attacks on the UAE, it is undeniable that the frothy hype of a year ago, when the Art Basel/Doha and DCT/Abu Dhabi partnerships were announced, has settled for now. There was some sense of the fair’s energy being a product of solidarity—one collector from Beirut noted that Art Basel Paris closed early because of threats of riots, whereas the Arab art scene was pulling together under keener threats. But it would be more accurate to say that most people felt the need to get on with things rather than waiting for some far-off resolution.
This applies too for the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi, which is scheduled to open next month after twenty years in the making. While the imminent opening partly detracted from the fair—some VIPs saw a choice between attending the fair and the early December festivities—the finished building and the buoyant museum team contributed to a sense of anticipation and substance within Abu Dhabi’s art scene.
High-level VIP tours got a preview of the building, The Art Newspaper understands, while the general VIP program was padded out with tours of the recently opened Public Art Abu Dhabi biennial, the Nomad art fair, and shows at the Cultural Foundation, the Bassam Freiha Art Foundation, and 421, as well as a number of private collections in the city—an itinerary that the city could not have supported even five years ago.
What was less visible on the trip, however, was commercial galleries. These remain almost exclusively in Dubai and fostering an independent commercial scene is a key reason for DCT’s partnership with Frieze, and also animates the city’s development of two new cultural districts, Noma on Saadiyat, led by the developer Aldar, and MiZa in Mina Zayed, led by the Sheikha Salama Foundation.
Both of these areas promise infrastructure to support artists and creative freelancers, such as studios, galleries, and co-working spaces.
These offerings will entail a loosening of control over the cultural programme in the city and—as is the case with Frieze—partnerships with private enterprise. For many who have followed the scene for a long time, this transition towards multiple stakeholders will be a key test for the capital.
“What Abu Dhabi has been doing over the last two decades is building an ecosystem, and one that is not solely institutional, but which also includes academia and smaller art spaces like 421,” says Aaron Cesar, the director of London’s Delfina Foundation. “There is now a clear path for the development of patrons and collectors—still in the making but a real possibility now, with MiZa and Noma to help complete the process. But Abu Dhabi can only do this through partnerships between public/private—that is, if they allow the voices of artists, designers, writers, and curators to come to the table with those who have money and power.”

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/23/m.title: Mamdani Won’t Guarantee More Citi Bike Service As Lyft Commits to Fare Cap
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/23/m.author: Kevin Duggan
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/23/m.text:
Citi Bike e-bikes will become cheaper, but will the system be able to hold up? File photo
Mayor Mamdani would not commit to increasing Citi Bike service as part of his new plan to slash the cost of a ride — even as experts warned lower costs would increase demand and add strain to the already strained system.
On Monday, the city and bike share operator Lyft agreed to immediately freeze Citi Bike’s annual subscription at $239 and cap e-bike rides for members at $3.65 for the first 45 minutes starting on Jan. 19.
The announcement garnered praise from lawmakers and advocates who have amped up their fight in recent months for more affordable fares from the largest docked bike system in the Western hemisphere.
The deal will be in force until the current bike share contract expires in 2029, but the price cuts could strand riders as more and more New Yorkers choose to ride — but only if officials don’t push the tech company behind Citi Bike to deliver more service as well, according to a former city transportation leader.
“There’s tunnel vision on price, and not on operation or quality of experience,” said Jon Orcutt, director of policy at DOT during the Bloomberg and de Blasio administrations, who spearheaded the launch of Citi Bike in 2013. “It could create some more stresses on the system if more people use it.”
Mamdani said the city recently completed an expansion of the network to 3,700 stations in parts of Brooklyn, Queens and the Bronx — but that work dates back to an Adams-era plan from nearly two years ago.
The mayor added that the Department of Transportation will work with utilities to make it easier for Lyft to electrify 130 docking locations next year, though officials did not share a specific plan. Dock electrification reduces the necessity of manually swapping out batteries, a process that requires workers to drive vans around the city.
“We have been working with Lyft on increasing supply across the network,” Mamdani told Streetsblog at a press conference in Prospect Lefferts Gardens. “And in early 2027, we’re going to be delivering new charging stations that will also help to keep [up] with growing demand.”
Hizzoner said the price cap will also allow riders more time to search for open docks without incurring extra charges. “I also think it will reduce in anxiety… for New Yorkers who have ended their ride, and yet are then looking for a place to dock it, and know that the price is going up,” he said. “Now you have through 45 minutes to find that dock.”
Orcutt disagreed. “That’s still not helpful to someone who’s missing a doctor’s appointment they waited six months to get,” he said.
Citi Bike ridership surpasses 200,000 daily trips during the warmer months — on par with the PATH train — but both completely full and completely empty docks continue to plague New Yorkers. This problem is particularly acute in high-demand areas, such as Downtown Manhattan, and the edge of the system in neighborhoods such as Red Hook in Brooklyn. Moving bikes around to ensure availability — a process known as “rebalancing” — plummeted after Lyft took over the bike share contract in 2018.
One rider told Streetsblog that he often has trouble finding a bike for his commutes between Brooklyn and Lower Manhattan, and urged officials address those shortages before they open the floodgates to more users.
“I think they have a logistical issue,” said Morgan, who declined to give his last name, at a dock at Broadway and Reade Street in Tribeca “There’s hardly any open docks when I need a bike in Brooklyn.”
Rebalancing will always cost time and money, Orcutt said, but the city should also pressure Lyft to station more valet attendants to handle overflow bikes. “That’s the answer, really, is staffing a set of key nodes where you know those tidal flows are really bad,” Orcutt said. “That costs money, so that’s one of the questions that’s always gonna be out there with bike share operations in a big city.”
Lyft representatives attend, but did not speak at, Monday’s press conference. Company spokesperson CJ Macklin said the company is working with DOT to “add incremental docks” to hotspots like Midtown, where many of its valet-staffed stations operate, and that they will evaluate demand patterns monthly.
Both Lyft and Mamdani touted the addition of 130 charging docks starting next year, which will be installed by early 2028, according to the company. But Lyft already committed to hooking up at least 160 docks back in August, which is about that same number of supposedly new docks on top of the existing 33 in operation.
Those docks will still account for only 4 percent of the network. Lyft previously told Streetsblog that it would need to electrify between 10 and 20 percent of its busiest stations to “materially reduce” its costs.
Indeed, DOT officials and Lyft set a 20-percent electrification target in a 2023 amendment to its current contract. That would amount to around 740 stations in today’s network. The city said at the time it would engage in “good faith negotiations” to reach that goal and discuss possible public subsidies, but that never happened. The city has not published any updated contract amendments relating to Mamdani’s latest announcement.
Unlike other cities, New York City’s bike share runs without a public subsidy, and Lyft’s largest expense is field operations, which includes fleet maintenance, charging, redistribution, and renting space, which made up $87 million out of its $203 million in total expenses last year.
To make up for lost income, the Mamdani administration agreed to ditch an annual $1 million reimbursement fee the city has charged bike share operators for lost parking meter money, and allowed Lyft to keep more of its earnings under its revenue sharing agreement.
“When it comes to revenue share, we’re saying that the city will be paid whatever exceeds $5.25 million a year, and that threshold will be modified annually according to the consumer price index,” Mamdani explained at the Monday press conference.
The price cap came with other changes. Lyft will no longer provide 60 free e-bike minutes to members who renew their membership. The city will also allow Lyft to install more advertisements on docks and bikes.
“We’re likely going to make less [money] on this system. Hopefully volumes increase to make up for it, but who knows. It’s worth a try,” Lyft CEO David Risher shared on X.
Bike share experts had previously warned that Lyft was gaining enough leverage to dictate the terms of its 2029 contract renewal. The San Fransisco-based rideshare giant absorbed the company that builds the Citi Bike fleet and has amassed more bikeshare systems across the globe.
The company’s rep noted the new agreement will deliver good service and system growth, despite the lower fares.
“Reliable service is what makes an affordable fare worth having, and we’re investing to keep up with demand as more New Yorkers ride,” Macklin told Streetsblog in a statement. “Charging at the dock keeps more ebikes available, especially at the busiest stations and during peak commutes, and means fewer vans on city streets. Citi Bike also operates without taxpayer funding, so this agreement was designed so the system can deliver lower fares while continuing to grow and improve.”
Kevin Duggan joined Streetsblog in October, 2022, after covering transportation for amNY. Duggan has been reporting on New York since 2018, starting at Vince DiMiceli’s Brooklyn Paper, where he covered southern Brooklyn neighborhoods and, later, Brownstone Brooklyn. He is on Bluesky at @kevinduggan.bsky.social and his email address is kevin@streetsblog.org.

https://hyperallergic.com/inside-edward-.title: Inside Edward Said’s World
https://hyperallergic.com/inside-edward-.author: Hyperallergic
https://hyperallergic.com/inside-edward-.text:
‘Tis the season for great documentaries. Twenty years after the death of Palestinian literary critic and theorist Edward Said, a new film revisits his life and legacy. Moustafa Bayoumi, a student of Said himself, posits that it offers a new generation a glimpse of Said’s indomitable energy and inexhaustible fight.
The lovely Eileen G’Sell takes a look at Trisha Ziff’s latest documentary, Frida: The Girl That Just Doesn’t Go Away, which screened recently at DOC NYC. The film considers the commercial afterlife of Frida Kahlo, asking how the artist’s personal history has been whitewashed even as her image circulates endlessly through retail culture. What happens when an artist’s legacy becomes as much a consumer product as a creative one?
And finally, if you haven’t seen Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything, what are you waiting for? It may be the best film I’ve seen all year, full of unexpected twists, turns, and glorious awkward pauses. Though billed as a documentary, the film raises what I think is a more intriguing question: Is Fielder a performance artist playing a documentarian? Not to toot my own horn, but I explore that possibility and more in my recent review, though be warned: spoilers abound.
—Rebecca Schiffman, associate editor
Nathan Fielder Is a Performance Artist in Disguise
As an art historian, it’s hard not to relate what you see in everyday life to history — not in the sense that every lily pad recalls Monet or snowballs bring David Hammons to mind, but in the sense that sometimes art really does imitate life. This happened to me recently, maybe 10 minutes into Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything. I watched Fielder hold painful, prolonged eye contact with Elizabeth Holmes, the convicted fraudster whose eerily large blue eyes seem to enact their own kind of performance. Naturally, I thought of Marina Abramović’s “The Artist is Present” (2010). Perhaps it’s an obvious, pretentious comparison. But hear me out: Is Fielder a documentarian, or is he a performance artist playing one? | Rebecca Schiffman

https://gothamist.com/news/these-new-yor.title: These New Yorkers ditched their smartphones for a month. No, seriously.
https://gothamist.com/news/these-new-yor.author: Willow Higgins
https://gothamist.com/news/these-new-yor.text:
In an event space atop a warehouse in East Williamsburg, people lined up to check their phones at the door.
Being phone-free for the night was a requirement for those who wanted to party with the roughly 100 New Yorkers who had just given up their smartphones for a month. Friends and families were invited to celebrate along with them — and see a showcase of hobbies and art projects that were picked up during the month instead of screens.
In one corner of the dimly lit room, people practiced their yo-yo skills. Someone else passed out bowls of homemade chicken soup. Others, lubricated by Modelos and boxed wine, made artsy stickers formed from pictures of a black and white cat. But the main attraction was the dance floor, which thudded to the beat of a DJ, who spun actual vinyl.
“Free your phone and ur a-- will follow,” the party invite advertised.
The participants, mostly in their 20s and 30s, are part of a growing group of New Yorkers who have declared that they’re unsatisfied with their relationships with their smartphones and are looking to set new boundaries with technology. The Month Offline organizers host weekly meetups where participants find community IRL (in real life) rather than online.
The group challenge, which started last year in Washington, D.C, took off quickly in New York, according to Lydia Peabody, one of the organizers. Seemingly overnight, the waitlist to participate in New York’s Month Offline became hundreds of names long, she said.
Peabody said she was initially surprised that demand was so high in a city as plugged in as New York. But, it makes sense, she later concluded: Being on your phone all the time is isolating.
“People need this space to not feel alone,” she said.
During the October effort, phone-free crews met weekly in small groups, or pods, based on where they live. The idea, Peabody explained, is that as New Yorkers detox from their smartphones, they can lean on their neighbors and get to know each other in the process.
Groups congregated across boroughs, in neighborhoods like the East Village, Astoria and Fort Greene.
“It's kinda like Alcoholics Anonymous for smartphones and social media,” said Axel Berlin, who participated in the Month Offline challenge in Chelsea.
‘People do feel overwhelmed’
Caitlin Begg studies movements like these for a living.
The sociologist and founder of Authentic Social, a research lab that focuses on the intersection of sociology and technology, said more and more people are looking to change their relationships with their phones.
According to survey results Begg recently presented at a Princeton University TEDx Talk, the average person uses eight different methods of communication daily, including social media, Slack and other apps. More than 90% of respondents reported checking their smartphones within 15 minutes of waking up.
“People do feel overwhelmed,” Begg said. “That’s just a lot.”
Taking a break from your phone in hyperlocal groups, Begg said, makes particular sense in a city like New York.
“ We live in such an incredibly vibrant city,” Begg said, “and because of work constraints or just being in the routine of life, sometimes people are just going from place to place… you know, a slop bowl place and back to their apartment.”
She added, getting off your phone is “about pushing people past their comfort zone, and I think pods really encourage that pro-social behavior.”
Joining the the 'flipside' scene
On a balmy evening earlier this fall, dozens of New Yorkers congregated in the plaza of Tompkins Square Park to kick off their detoxes.
The organizers, using a megaphone, encouraged those in the audience — plus passersby who stopped to listen — to join what they called “the flipside,” by switching to low-tech flip phones that could be borrowed for free during the challenge.
(The phones are provided by dumb.co, a flip phone company that some of the Month Offline organizers started after the Month Offline challenge took off. For those looking for a permanent switch, the $20 phone is also available for purchase – and advertised on flyers across New York City.)
The leaders of the group told Gothamist that this isn’t just a trend — it’s an act of resistance to big tech, Silicon Valley and a social life increasingly organized around group chats and other digital platforms. It’s time to go back to analog, they told Gothamist.
“Building the capacity for technological resistance on literally the neighborhood level, I think is the most important place to build it,” said Damian Thomas, who led the Astoria pod and is the director of the Unplatform Project, a tech literacy initiative to get people to divest from big tech.
In Tompkins Square, under the park’s street lights, the facilitators of each neighborhood pod met with those who signed up to participate. Throughout the course of October, the leaders would host pods in their living rooms, bookstores or other neighborhood hangouts.
The Month Offline organization is working to democratize their program, so people across the world can start their own pod. The group published a DIY guide equipped with a curriculum for weekly meetups, including exercises on communication, memory and navigating urban space without GPS.
But pod facilitators told Gothamist that the weekly meetings are run with their own flair.
Thomas, whose group met weekly at the Museum of the Moving Image in Astoria, said at one meeting that he assigned his group to find a new movie, show or book without recommendations from social media. During another week, everyone had to find a new spot in their neighborhood without the help of Google Maps.
Quinn Winters, who helped lead the Greenpoint pod, said he realized that New York seems smaller when you’re not staring down at a screen all the time.
“Now I'm seeing the same people over and over again, and I'm actually able to wave and say hi,” Winters said.
But being without a smartphone is a unique challenge in a city that runs on apps like Google Maps, Apple Pay and DoorDash.
“Someone pointed out very reasonably like, ‘Oh, I use the Citi Bike to get around all the time, and I realized that I didn't have a smartphone on me, so I couldn't check one out,’” Thomas said.
He added, “People rely on the Citi Bike system to get around. That's a way that our public infrastructure now is locking people into the usage of these devices.”
Some people who signed up for the challenge didn’t complete it.
Facilitators of several pods told Gothamist that attendance to the weekly meetings was lower than they hoped — if there were 10 people in a pod, sometimes only six would show up.
Berlin, from the Chelsea pod, told Gothamist that, frankly, unplugging is hard.
“I think it's very likely that people, people got dragged back into their smartphone lifestyle,” he said.
Begg, the researcher, said giving up your smartphone isn’t for everyone; being able to do so is a privilege in modern society, and not everyone’s life allows the break.
“[Throwing] your phone in the river … from an economic standpoint, it's just not realistic for most people,” Begg said. “They have to support their families. There's childcare and things and other things that are wrapped up in the smartphone.”
Short of ditching their phone altogether, Begg said, there are other things people can do to set boundaries with their devices, like sleeping with their phones outside of their bedrooms or switching back to landlines at home.
Some participants said flip phones have everything they need, especially because they now come equipped with basic navigation systems. Others told Gothamist that being without smartphones isn’t sustainable long term, but they want to have new boundaries, like only taking them out to FaceTime with family.
At the East Williamsburg party, the white brick walls were decorated with an alternative to doom scrolling on social media: actual scrolls, made from butcher paper, with musings and reflections from each pod scribbled in crayon and markers.
On a neighboring wall, the group’s constitution, written boldly in Sharpie, was on display.
“We the participants of [Month Offline] declare that we ought to be free and independent human beings, that we are absolved of all dependence on big tech and other attention grabbing algorithms,” the butcher paper read. “Here is to boredom, wrong turns, to fruitful friction, to life beyond the screen.”
Winters, from the Greenpoint pod, stood beside an art installation where people wrote their secrets on slips of paper that would later be set on fire.
He said being off his phone frees up a part of his brain. Some people write books during their phone-free month, he said. Others simply choose to spend more time with their friends and families — or, in this case, their neighbors.
“More and more, I'm realizing the isolating part of New York is really a choice,” Winters said. “You can isolate yourself, but you can also choose to engage with the people nearby you."
Winters said taking a break from his phone has changed the way he moves through a city — even as those around him are glued to their screens.
“Every time that someone else is pulling out their phone to check their emails, I'm looking around and seeing what's in the sky,” he said.
This story was updated with additional details regarding the flip phones used by some Month Offline participants.

https://cartoonmovement.substack.com/p/f.title: Fight AI slop with art!
https://cartoonmovement.substack.com/p/f.author: Cartoon Movement

Artists are continuing to speak out against the soulless flood of AI slop that’s appearing in our timelines (and in various other places) these days. And not only artists; even a lot of non-creatives are complaining about the emptiness they feel when looking at a computer-generated image that’s trying to pass itself off as art.
As most of you (hopefully) know, here at Cartoon Movement we do our best to keep everything as AI-free as possible. Why? Because AI-generated visuals are based on the biggest art theft in history, the environmental impact of the wide-spread use of AI is enormous, and the people running the AI companies are the sort of greedy evil bastards that motivated most of us to become political cartoonists in the first place, so we could use our art to fight back with satire.
One cartoonist that has decided to fight back is CM-member Piet from France. Using the most powerful tool he has at his disposal, his pencil, Piet has created a series of stickers for people to publicly show what they think about AI ‘art’. Better yet, the stickers are free to download and can be used freely (under a Creative Commons license).
They are available in English and French; to download them, click the big red button:
And if you’d rather like to have ready-made stickers, you can purchase them in Piet’s Redbubble shop.
We hope we’ll see Piet’s stickers in a lot of places! If you decide to download/order them and use them, please send us some photos so we can share them on our socials and get even more people to use these stickers!

https://gothamist.com/news/th.title: Rain on the parade: Expect a wet and windy Thanksgiving Day in NYC
https://gothamist.com/news/th.author: Ramsey Khalifeh
https://gothamist.com/news/th.text:
The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day parade may be a wet and windy ordeal.
New York City is expecting rainfall, heavy winds and coastal flooding this Thursday, as families across the five boroughs prepare their Thanksgiving meals, according to the National Weather Service forecasts.
As is tradition, thousands will flock to Manhattan’s 6th Avenue to watch the Macy’s parade hoist up several-hundred-pound balloons. But NWS meteorologist Dave Radell warned of rain and wind that could shake up the festivities.
“The wind gusts are going to be ramping up really during the parade … If we start getting sustained winds certainly above 20, 30, 35 miles an hour, that is certainly going to have an impact on the parade itself,” Radell said.
The weather service also forecasts 1 to 2 inches of rainfall starting late Wednesday evening and continuing throughout Thursday. In parts of the city’s south shore, including beach areas of South Brooklyn and Queens, as well as Suffolk and Nassau counties, Radell said there could be a “couple of high tide cycles” that may create moderate coastal flooding.
“So for folks going to the parade, expect a windy and wet experience,” he added.
While Thursday’s storm will be particularly wet, it shouldn't top off any historical Thanksgiving records. The wettest Thanksgiving in terms of rainfall on record was in 2006, with 1.72 inches. Before that, 1985 tied with 1935 at 1.5 inches of rain.
As for the warmest Thanksgiving, in both 2007 and 1933, the temperature reached the upper 60s and almost 70 degrees. This Thursday’s forecast is much cooler, with highs in the 50s.
