https://www.propublica.org/article/ectop.author: Agnel Philip
https://www.propublica.org/article/ectop.text:
For years, ProPublica has examined maternal health and the ongoing impacts of abortion bans since the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. Data analysis has been central to that effort, offering a quantitative view into an area that has long been underresearched, especially as studying the impact of abortion bans has become politicized and federal agencies have been gutted under the Trump administration.
For example, last year my colleagues uncovered a dramatic rise in sepsis rates since Texas instituted its abortion ban, which carries the strictest penalties for healthcare providers. The number of blood transfusions during emergency room visits for first-trimester miscarriage spiked in the state as well.
Most recently, my colleagues Andrea Suozzo, Sophie Chou, Kavitha Surana and I examined pregnancy-related deaths on a national level. We turned our attention to Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data. The agency collects information from death certificates and publishes totals based on variables like location, demographics and cause of death. It’s a commonly used resource for journalists and academics who want to learn more about trends in mortality.
Pretty soon a trend leaped off the page: Almost 200 women died after ectopic pregnancies between 2020 and 2025, nearly twice the number of deaths compared with the previous six-year period.
The increase was particularly stark in states that had banned abortion.
This was a significant and serious finding. And as far as we could tell, the fact that the number of women who died from ectopic pregnancies nearly doubled after abortion bans came into effect hadn’t been reported before.
A death from an ectopic pregnancy should be a “never event,” according to Dr. Alice Abernathy, an OB-GYN in Philadelphia. And yet, as we later confirmed, more than a dozen leaders in the field of maternal health were unaware of the spike. Neither state governments nor the federal government, whose own dataset we were using, had publicly identified this trend.
How could it be that seemingly no one was aware of this but us?
The answer, as it turns out, is multifold and begins with the nature of the condition itself. Ectopic pregnancies occur when an embryo fails to properly implant in the uterus and begins to develop elsewhere, most commonly inside a fallopian tube. The pregnancy grows until it causes the organ to rupture, triggering catastrophic bleeding.
It is a rare condition, estimated to impact up to 2% of pregnancies, but it is incredibly dangerous.
“I genuinely thought I was going to die,” said Kyleigh Thurman, whose right fallopian tube ruptured after she struggled to get ectopic care in Texas in 2023.
“There were a few times I asked my husband if I was going to die,” Leitaea Lowrimore of Oklahoma said in an ongoing lawsuit challenging an abortion ban, after being denied treatment for an ectopic pregnancy at multiple hospitals in February. “I kept thinking about our kids.”
Even before ectopic pregnancy deaths began rising, the condition was noted as the leading cause of death in the first trimester of pregnancy. Yet it has received little research attention. For example, the CDC doesn’t track how many ectopic pregnancies occur a year and doesn’t require healthcare providers to report them. The most recent nationwide study we could find examined data only through 2013.
The U.S. doesn’t conduct national maternal mortality reviews in the same way as countries like the United Kingdom, which responded to a similar spike in the years after the COVID-19 pandemic by instituting changes to emergency services and promoting awareness of ectopic pregnancy symptoms. Instead, in our country, much of the work of investigating pregnancy-related deaths is left to state committees.
This creates a large potential knowledge gap. In individual states, the number of ectopic deaths is small and subject to a lot of variation, making it harder to spot a trend. After our story was published, we reached out to maternal mortality review committees in states with abortions bans; many of them responded that they didn’t identify an increase in ectopic deaths and that, despite the findings of our reporting, they had no plans to examine this issue further.
We realized the fact that nearly double the number of women are dying from ectopic pregnancies is visible at only the national level.
It is unclear why the CDC and other federal agencies across two administrations have failed to publicly respond to the increase in deaths despite having access to the same information ProPublica analyzed. We reached out to the CDC to ask what the agency has done to investigate or address this trend. It has epidemiologists who review death and birth records and has in the past done its own investigations and analyses. A spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the CDC, didn’t provide a direct answer to that question but said the agency continues to track maternal mortality trends, investigate their causes and provide funding for research.
Maternal experts agree that the government’s capacity to respond to this trend has been significantly reduced as a result of the staffing cuts initiated by the Trump administration since the beginning of last year. The CDC’s Division of Reproductive Health, for example, lost most of its 100 employees, according to a lawsuit filed by more than a dozen states’ attorneys general last year.
This lack of awareness surrounding ectopic pregnancy deaths is imperiling women’s lives.
We asked several experts why death rates were going up, but there was no consensus. And while our analysis can’t establish whether there is a causal link between abortion bans and the worse outcomes in the states that have them, there is no evidence that officials are stepping up to examine this question or offer solutions. Even professional organizations, such as the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, have yet to provide specific guidance to doctors about how to adequately treat women with suspected ectopic pregnancies in states with abortion bans.
But experts say the trend we uncovered is unacceptable and requires a response. As Courtney Schreiber, a professor of obstetrics and gynecology, told us, our work “raises concern that young women are dying from a preventable cause at an increasing rate. That is not what we should be seeing in the United States of America.”
We hope you’ll read our recent investigation, which includes more details on potential explanations for this trend and stories from women in states with abortion bans who faced delays in care. We plan to continue reporting on maternal health and the impact of abortion bans for the foreseeable future.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: State Probes Alleged Amazon Safety Violations at Staten Island Warehouse
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Claudia Irizarry Aponte
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
The state Labor Department is investigating a sprawling Amazon distribution center on Staten Island known as JFK8, The City Reporter has learned, over allegations that the megaretailer is ignoring rules that mandate transparent productivity quotas and ergonomic training for employees.
Amazon employs approximately 6,000 people at the 855,000 square-foot facility. In 2022, JFK8 became the first Amazon shop to unionize anywhere in the United States, and its workers have since voted to affiliate with the International Brotherhood of Teamsters, which also represents a number of drivers around the country who deliver packages for Amazon.
Sherri Raponi, a top official at the Labor Department’s occupational safety division, sent the Teamsters and other groups who submitted complaints on behalf of workers a letter on Nov. 3 informing them that it was launching an official probe of potential violations of a law known as the Warehouse Worker Protection Act at JFK8.
MORE: Exploitation or Opportunity? The Fight Over Amazon’s New York Drivers
“Please be advised the Safety and Health and Essential Rights (SHER) program of the Division of Occupational Safety and Health (DOSH) has received the complaints you referenced in your letter,” wrote Raponi. “Please be assured SHER has opened an investigation of this facility regarding compliance with the above provisions of the New York State Labor Law.”
Though the letter does not go into detail over what exact claims the agency is following up on, workers have sent numerous written complaints to the agency over Amazon’s alleged refusal to comply with rules governing the warehouse logistics sector.
According to the complaints, Amazon has not submitted ergonomic safety plans known as “worksite evaluations” or provided workers with productivity quotas in writing, while refusing to work on safety issues with the union.
“We comply with all laws and legal requirements, including the Warehouse Worker Protection Act, and we don’t use fixed quotas,” Amazon spokesperson Sam Stephenson said.
Warehouse Laws
The claims stem from a patchwork of laws — the Warehouse Worker Protection Act, the Warehouse Worker Injury Reduction Program and the New York HERO Act — all approved by lawmakers in the years since the COVID pandemic. The most recent of those laws, the WWIRP, went into effect last summer.
That law requires managers to create and implement injury reduction programs to identify and minimize the risk of ergonomic on-the-job injuries, which JFK8 workers claim the company has not done.
When staff presented a proposed safety plan this summer, managers refused to meet with them and did not respond to written requests for a meeting, according to several complaints reviewed by The City Reporter.
“I have had supervisors tell me I need to maintain a rate of 150 units per hour in shipdock, but I have seen in internal communication and managers that 250 units per hour is the ‘new normal,’’” one worker wrote. “None of this is ever explicitly communicated with us in writing.”
“In June 2026, JFK8 workers requested several documents from Amazon that the company must provide including the written evaluation of the on-site medical program and summary of treatment protocols,” wrote another employee. “To date, Amazon has NOT given us these documents…”
Department of Labor spokesperson Jack Lamson confirmed the Raponi letter’s accuracy and declined to comment further, saying the agency “does not comment on open investigations.”
State Sen. Jessica Ramos (D-Queens), the labor committee chair, was the lead senate sponsor on both the WWPA and the WWIRP, and she made warehouse worker safety a signature issue. Ramos, who was the subject of a recent New York Times investigation into complaints of alleged campaign finance violations related to her doomed 2025 mayoral campaign, could not be reached for comment on Tuesday.
The slate of laws regulating depots like JFK8 were meant to address the kind of injuries that are most common in warehouses — sprains, fractures and aches resulting from repetitive movement, heavy lifting and a fast-paced environment with high productivity quotas.
First Test of New Labor Rules
“No matter what your strength is, your size, your gender, no matter what your physical makeup is — if you are working at full speed, doing the same task day in and day out, you are going to have some kind of physical ramifications for doing so,” said Charlene Obernauer, executive director of the New York Committee for Occupational Safety and Health.
The Labor Department probe is the first major test for the relatively new rules governing warehouse worker safety, said Obernauer.
There are no federal standards governing ergonomic safety and warehouse injury prevention, said Debbie Berkowitz, a former policy chief at the Occupational Safety and Health Administration during the Obama administration. Rather, states are left to come up with their own rules. The law in New York was the subject of fierce debate before lawmakers ultimately approved the WWPA in 2023, and the Warehouse Worker Injury Reduction Program two years later.
Berkowitz, a worker safety and health policy fellow at Georgetown University, applauded the Labor Department’s decision to investigate safety concerns at JFK8. “This is exactly how things should work,” she said.
The law is far from perfect, advocates say. Some point to the relatively low penalties — the WWPA tops penalties at $3,000 for each repeat violation — which they say won’t deter companies like Amazon, which is valued at $2.7 trillion.
“As we test these laws, one of the questions that’s going to come up is the penalties, and whether they are enough to prevent the employer from breaking the law,” said Obernauer. “And if they are not enough, then what would be enough — is it the court of public opinion? Is it issuing press releases?”
MORE: Teamsters Hit Amazon Over Delivery Worker Layoffs, With Millions at Stake
JFK8 workers who spoke with The City Reporter said they had not received on-the-job injury prevention training at all.
Whenever workers walk in to seek treatment for stress injuries and other ailments they are, at most, given an over-the-counter pain medication like ibuprofen and allowed a few minutes to lie down, JFK8 employees said.
But most troublingly, workers say, is what they describe as Amazon’s apparent failure to provide a safety plan as required by the 2025 law. Anthony Sparrow, the union’s grievance director at JFK8, said management has “not acknowledged” the union’s requests for a written safety plan.
Sparrow and Xavier Villaroel, a shop steward, have said that when workers experience sprains, strains or other stress fractures, they are told to “walk it off.”
Villaroel said staff are told to stretch for a few minutes at the beginning of each shift, which helps prevent injuries — but workers routinely get hurt on the job anyway. Amazon and the JFK8 facility have been in the crosshairs of workplace safety watchdogs and federal regulators for years.
A 2022 study commissioned by the Teamsters and other groups found the Staten Island facility ranked among the workplaces with the highest number of injuries in the state, and federal prosecutors in Manhattan are investigating “potential fraud” related to claims that Amazon keeps its injury data artificially low.
A 2024 investigation by the U.S. Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee, then chaired by Independent Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, found that nationally Amazon discouraged workers from seeking medical care.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: ‘As much joy as I could find’: a splash of colour – in pictures
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Sarah King
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
‘As much joy as I could find’: a splash of colour – in pictures
From bright green kebab shops to a flash of red stocking, photographer Niall McDiarmid is constantly on the hunt for antidotes to our muted beige and monochrome world
Scottish photographer Niall McDiarmid’s work is a joyful antidote to the greyscale tones predominant across architecture, interiors, fashion and cars. Of this image he says: ‘I’m sure interior design for kebab shops is a niche profession but I salute whoever led this project. The addition of replica coloured Jacobsen dining chairs is genius. If only Christine Keeler had sat for that famous Jacobsen chair portrait in a green kebab shop in south Wimbledon.’ Niall McDiarmid’s Colour is available via RRB Photobooks. All quotes: Niall McDiarmid
For over 15 years, McDiarmid has been documenting the inherent colour of life as he finds it. ‘I was drawn into this kaleidoscope of colourful commuters,’ he says. ‘I suspect with over 2,000 trains passing through Clapham Junction every day these random colour moments happen regularly. But waiting around never seems to work for me in photography. I have to keep moving’
‘I set out with the project to photograph as much colour as I could. Frames that were full of colour from edge to edge, from corner to corner. I was looking for vibrancy, saturation, brightness, joy – and as much of it as I could find. The images were an antidote to the overwhelmingly diﬃcult times that our family were going through at that time. In some ways finding colour helped me get through those days. This shot was taken in an ice-cream shop in Covent Garden on a late September afternoon’
‘The entrance to Liberty’s department store is always awash with flowers and colours. Green and purple seems like a perfect combination here. I have a strong aﬀection for Liberty’s. As a family we came down to London for our first visit from our home in Highland Perthshire in the late 1970s. We lost my younger brother Calum in a lift mix-up in the store. He was about six. Panic ensued. He showed up pretty quickly but every time I walk by the building I remember the episode and chuckle’
‘Red stockings have been a constant inspiration for photographers. They are so vibrant and distinctive. Fred Herzog, who documented the streets of Vancouver, and French fashion photographer Guy Bourdin both had memorable shots that featured red tights. This shot was taken at the entrance to the Royal Academy on Piccadilly’
‘A woman in a yellow dress, reading a blue book, drinking orange juice, with a red rose on the table, all against a pink wall. Sometimes the gods of serendipity, luck, chance – call it what you like – just come good for you. This was shot in a coﬀee shop just oﬀ the Strand in London’
‘Although most of the images in the book were from London I did a number of trips to other towns in search of colour. This was taken in Folkestone, which has a burgeoning artistic scene. Luckily this enthusiastic fellow carrying a bright red box walked into the frame as I headed up to the town centre’
‘One of the earlier shots in the book, this was taken on a bright Sunday afternoon in February. I drifted into town from my home in south-west London with no particular mission in mind. I ended up wandering along the South Bank and came across this girl with wonderful hair browsing the secondhand book stalls. Six or seven shots taken on this day started a portrait odyssey that firstly took me all across London and then across the whole of Britain resulting in several books and exhibitions’
‘Bring up Tooting, the south London neighbourhood, and the most common response usually leads back to Wolfie Smith and his Popular Front [in BBC sitcom Citizen Smith]. “Freedom for Tooting!” But I’ve never watched the programme and I never have an adequate response. Tooting has always been a vibrant and exciting place to photograph for me and I’ve visited many times over the years. This was taken in the busy indoor market, now a big draw for street cuisine’Photograph: Niall McDiarmid
‘Like many photographers I’m drawn to greasy spoon cafes. Combine some warm evening light with Formica table tops and faded lampshades and the desire to drop in and photograph is irresistible. But then again, maybe that’s just an excuse for a full English breakfast at four in the afternoon’
‘A bright yellow umbrella will punch colour through even the wettest of days. This is the most recent shot in the book, taken early this year in Hoxton in the pouring rain’
‘Chris Oﬃli’s memorial to the victims of Grenfell Tower dominates the west stairwell in Tate Britain. In particular it commemorates the photographer and artist Khadija Saye whose career was cut short by this tragedy. I caught this yellow-clad visitor as he headed into the main gallery with the mural behind through the frosted glass’

Jacobin Is Hiring a Video Producer
Jacobin is seeking a full-time senior video producer to make video about socialist politics and ideas.
Location: Hybrid. New York metro area candidates; at least two days a week in our Brooklyn office
Salary: From $68,150.03 per year
Reports to: Director of Communications
Position: Full-time
Start date: As soon as possible, no later than January 7, 2027
Jacobin is seeking a Senior Video Producer to make thoughtful, engaging video about socialist politics and ideas, with a focus on YouTube and long-form work.
The producer will develop, produce, and edit videos; commission projects in consultation with the Director of Communications; work with contributors and freelancers; and coordinate video coverage of Jacobin events. They will collaborate with the Editor and incorporate feedback into their projects.
We’re looking for someone with experience producing and editing video, strong editorial judgment, familiarity with YouTube, and the ability to manage projects independently. Experience with livestreaming and event production is a plus. A commitment to democratic socialist politics is important to success in the position.
During the interview process, applicants will be asked about their familiarity with the theory and practice of socialism, including the thought of historical and contemporary Marxist thinkers.
Jacobin offers extensive health and dental benefits, a retirement plan with an employer match, generous leave, and a creative, collaborative working environment.
To apply, send a résumé, a short cover letter, and links to your portfolio to [email protected] with the subject line “Senior Video Producer application.”
Jacobin is an equal opportunity employer. We consider applicants without unlawful discrimination based on any protected status and provide reasonable accommodations during the hiring process. This position is covered by the collective-bargaining agreement between Jacobin and the NewsGuild of N.Y., CWA Local 31003, AFL-CIO.

https://www.artforum.com/news/thelma-gol.author: Polly Watson
https://www.artforum.com/news/thelma-gol.text:

The Studio Museum in Harlem, New York, has announced that longtime leader Thelma Golden will depart the institution in late 2027. Golden, who has served as the museum’s director and chief curator for twenty-one years, is practically synonymous with the institution, which she helped shape into an international force showcasing work by artists of African descent. Most recently, she spearheaded the construction of the museum’s first purpose-built home, which opened last year to great fanfare. Golden has left an indelible impact as leader of the Studio Museum, developing the institution’s collection, exhibition history, and storied artist-in-residence program.
“For more than twenty years, Thelma Golden has defined the vision and identity of the Studio Museum in Harlem,” said Kathryn C. Chennault, board chair of the Studio Museum in a statement. “She has elevated and strengthened this institution in every way, helped move Black artists into the center of the cultural landscape, and mentored countless Black museum professionals across the country. She is now passing on the leadership of the museum she helped build, entrusting it to a new generation she helped foster.”
Golden, a native of Queens, interned at New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art as a teenager. She first arrived at the Studio Museum as an intern, while studying at Smith College, before returning after graduation as a curatorial fellow. She began her career as a curatorial assistant at the Whitney Museum of American Art in 1988, rising to associate curator in 1993. That same year, Golden co-curated an iteration of the Whitney Biennial that proved controversial for its focus on diversity and inclusion. In 1994, she curated the landmark show “Black Male: Representations of Masculinity in American Art” at the Whitney. Golden returned to the Studio Museum in 2000 as deputy director for exhibitions and programs before being appointed to her current roles in 2005.
Chennault revealed that the board has begun the search for Golden’s replacement, and that Golden would remain onboard until that person was in place, assisting with the transition.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Toddlers are not just little people. Their culture deserves respect | Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Arwa Mahdawi
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
Nobody can be good at everything, can they? Take me, for example. While I excel at remembering useless facts, going down online rabbit holes and getting toothpaste on my shirt, my singing is so bad it makes small children cry. This is not hyperbole: my five-year-old has wailed on many occasions throughout her short life because I’ve had the temerity to sing along to various TV show jingles or songs.
As it turns out, however, it may not just be the fact that I can’t hold a tune that’s upsetting her. I’m not saying that everything I know about parenting I learned from viral posts on the internet, but there was an illuminating tweet doing the rounds last week that said: “Today I learned if you try to sing along with a toddler when you have not been invited to do so, it is a sign of great disrespect in their culture.” I immediately went down an online rabbit hole and discovered various other people have made similar jokes. It’s a common issue.
And it’s not just unsolicited singing: a lot of weird things are a sign of great disrespect in small-child culture. When they are clearly exhausted, for example, you must not, under any circumstances, say: “You are clearly exhausted.” This is considered rude and uncalled for. When they tell the postman about your bowel movements, you must smile politely rather than shush them. And when they find a decaying leaf on the filthy pavement and hand it to you, you must not say: “Yuck, that probably has dog pee on it.” Instead, you must marvel over how beautiful it is, and guard it with your life until they forget about it and it has crumbled to pieces in your pocket.
While I could do without my singing being critiqued, I do enjoy being given little street treasures. One of the greatest joys of parenthood is watching your child marvel over the mundane. To bastardise William Blake, little kids really are able to “see a world in a grain of sand / And a heaven in a wild flower”. As Blake also wrote in Auguries of Innocence (a real banger): “He who respects the infant’s faith / Triumphs over Hell and Death.” So, until she grows out of it, I shall be respecting my child’s faith. Next time my five-year-old screams when I attempt to sing along to Frozen, I’m not going to take it personally – I’m just going to let it go.

https://taz.de/Ermittlungen-gegen-Terror.title: Ermittlungen gegen „Terror 18“: Bundesanwaltschaft knüpft sich nächste Jungnazi-Gruppe vor
https://taz.de/Ermittlungen-gegen-Terror.author: Konrad Litschko
https://taz.de/Ermittlungen-gegen-Terror.text:
Ermittlungen gegen „Terror 18“: Bundesanwaltschaft knüpft sich nächste Jungnazi-Gruppe vor
Sie drohten in Chats mit Gewalt, wollten Brandanschläge verüben. Nun geht die Bundesanwaltschaft gegen die Neonazis von „Terror 18“ vor.
Sie sind sehr jung, posierten mit Hitlergruß, prahlten mit Gewalt. Nun ist die Jungnazi-Gruppe „Terror 18“, erst vor wenigen Wochen gegründet, ein Fall für die Bundesanwaltschaft. Die oberste Ermittlungsbehörde veranlasste am Mittwoch bundesweit mehrere Durchsuchungen und nahm drei Gruppenmitglieder fest; drei weitere befanden sich bereits in Haft. Der Vorwurf: Bildung einer terroristischen Vereinigung.
Die Gruppe hatte sich über eine geschlossene WhatsApp‑Gruppe zusammengefunden. Vor allem Teenager aus Mecklenburg-Vorpommern und Schleswig-Holstein, aber auch aus anderen Bundesländern versammelten sich dort. Gut 40 Mitglieder sollen es gewesen sein. Das Gruppenlogo war mit SS-Totenkopf oder Sturmgewehr versehen, in Chats wurde zu „Antifa jagen“ aufgerufen oder zu Gewalt gegen Geflüchtete.
„Lass mal was anzünden (…) dann verbrennen die alle und das ist sogar viel besser, dann müssen wir sie nicht schlagen“, schrieb ein Mitglied. Es müsse „wenigstens einen toten K*naken geben“. Verabredet wurde sich auch zum „Pedo Hunting“, zur Jagd auf vermeintliche Pädophile.
Und es blieb nicht bei Worten. Ende Oktober war ein 15-jähriges Mitglied, Marcello P., in Wahlstedt in Schleswig-Holstein mit einem Benzinkanister losgezogen – zuvor hatte er in der Chatgruppe einen Anschlag auf eine lokale Geflüchtetenunterkunft angekündigt, wie die Antifa-Recherchegruppe Exif öffentlich machte. Antifaschisten stoppten den Jugendlichen nahe seines Wohnhauses, die Polizei nahm ihn fest. Auch das Bundesamt für Verfassungsschutz soll in der Chatgruppe mitgelesen und die Polizei gewarnt haben.
Anschlag in Schwerin verhindert
Wenig später wurden zwei weitere „Terror 18“-Mitstreiter festgenommen: zunächst der mutmaßliche Gruppengründer Dwayne S., ein 18-Jähriger aus der Nähe von Schwerin, später dann Jarik Fabian W. aus Winsen in Niedersachsen, der Marcello P. mit angestachelt und bei sich vor Ort ebenso eine Unterkunft mit einem Stein beworfen haben soll. Die Gruppe hatte auf Social-Media-Kanälen auch danach getönt, man werde weitermachen.
Die taz hatte schon Anfang November berichtet, dass die Gruppe noch mindestens einen weiteren Brandanschlag plante: auf das linke Wohnprojekt Komplex in Schwerin. Die Polizei hatte die Tat zwar verhindert, die Bewohner*innen aber beklagten, sie seien nicht über den Tatplan informiert worden.
Die Bundesanwaltschaft geht nun von noch weiteren geplanten Brandanschlägen aus und von Gewalttaten „bis hin zu gezielten Tötungen von Ausländern und politischen Gegnern“.
Festgenommen wurden am Mittwoch deshalb Kalle K., Lasse G. und Shawn Z. in Brandenburg, Niedersachsen und Schleswig-Holstein, allesamt Teenager. Sie sollten anschließend Haftrichtern vorgeführt werden. Ob diese tatsächlich in allen Fällen Haftbefehle in Vollzug setzen, war wegen des jungen Alters der Beschuldigten ungewiss.
Zusätzliche Durchsuchungen gab es in insgesamt zehn Orten in Brandenburg, Niedersachsen, Bayern, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern und Sachsen. Ermittelt wird hier gegen vier weitere Beschuldigte, die die Gruppe unterstützt oder geplante Straftaten nicht angezeigt haben sollen. Durchsucht wurde dabei nach taz-Informationen auch ein 13-Jähriger, der noch nicht strafmündig ist. Im Einsatz waren rund 70 Polizeibeamte.
Die Bundesanwaltschaft war zuletzt schon gegen die Jungnazi-Gruppe „Letzte Verteidigungswelle“ vorgegangen, die bereits mit Anschlägen auftrat. Auch hier lautete der Vorwurf: Terror. Das Oberlandesgericht Hamburg verhängte im August gegen acht Beschuldigte Jugendstrafen von bis zu fünf Jahren Haft.
Unter den „Terror 18“-Mitgliedern war nun auch mindestens ein bekennender AfD-Fan. Fotos zeigen den Schweriner Amon G. auf zwei Kundgebungen der Partei im August und September in Schwerin, auch bei einem Aufmarsch der AfD‑Jugend. Die Partei hatte dazu eine taz-Anfrage unbeantwortet gelassen.

https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/25/h.title: How The MTA Plans To Build Up America’s Bus Manufacturing Base
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/25/h.author: Dave Colon
https://nyc.streetsblog.org/2026/11/25/h.text:
The MTA wants to buy a small number of buses from international bus manufacturers in order to encourage them to set up shop in America — an ambitious “try before you buy” strategy that could give the agency more options when it acquires thousands of buses in the near future.
Earlier this year, the MTA explained its struggle to find reliable zero emissions buses built in the United States, and paused an order for almost 500 electric buses from New Flyer until the manufacturer could ensure the company’s buses could consistently complete a day’s service. But instead of twiddling their fingers, agency executives are recruiting international firms in an attempt to develop a more competitive manufacturing environment while still taking advantage of federal help for bus purchases.
“Buy America” rules incentivize American transit agencies to purchases buses made in the United States, because the federal government will subsidize 80 percent of their cost. According to a recent study by the Eno Center for Transportation, the average price tag of an American zero-emissions bus is approximately $1 million.
The same Eno study found American bus manufacturing has dwindled to only two main firms: Gillig and New Flyer. Gillig does not bid on requests for proposals from large transit agencies, which means the MTA has little choice but to continue buying New Flyer buses even as transit companies around the country reported similar problems with its electric buses.
Now, in order to better understand the global bus market, the MTA will purchase a small number of buses from overseas manufacturers without any federal subsidy. It will then stress-test those buses by running them on city streets. By doing so, the agency hopes to learn more about the rolling stock from new companies and how they work in the Big Apple.
The pilot will place a major emphasis on electric buses, which are popular and widely used in Europe but have yet to gain traction in the United States.
Transit officials are currently racing to replenish the MTA’s bus fleet with new buses so and take older, less reliable buses off the road. Last month, the MTA published a request-for-proposals for 650 new buses that run on compressed natural gas.
But the scale of the entire bus replacement program goes far beyond last month’s RFP. According to an outside engineering firm that monitors the MTA capital plan, the agency must purchase 500 new buses per year, and MTA executives say the agency needs to order 4,500 buses over the next few years.
The agency hopes the pilot, and the knowledge it gains from stress-testing, will help it lure non-American manufacturers who make buses that satisfy the agency’s needs. The idea is to provide the chosen firms with the promise of immediate business, to accomplish the monumental task of keeping the MTA’s bus fleet in a state of good repair. It’s plenty of desirable work for the right firm, but also so big that the MTA is skeptical a single new entrant to the American market will suffice.
“The size of our orders are very interesting to these companies that are making service and delivering a great product in Europe and Asia,” said Jessie Lazarus, the MTA’s head of rolling stock procurement. “But they’re deterred a bit by the scale, which is sort of the irony around it. We need so many buses, so we obviously need to think really broadly about who those partners can be, or cast a really wide net as we’re doing that market outreach because we can’t rely on just one new partner. We need to think about bringing in a few more. But I think for any new manufacturing relationship, we need to de-risk this for both sides.”
In this case, Lazarus explained that the small orders take the risk out of both sides of the relationship: the MTA doesn’t over-commit to a single company, and can learn about new bus designs used around the world, while bus manufacturers don’t need to navigate the process of establishing factories in America without the certainty of future business.
“We are going to run several pilot fleets,” Lazarus said. “Think of the fleet size as five to 10 buses. We’re going to run those buses for 52 weeks. We’re gonna put them into service and at depots, we are gonna give those manufacturing partners an opportunity to learn more about the New York City operating environment, and we’re going to give our teams an opportunity to learn more about a design that is unfamiliar to us but not unfamiliar to bus service globally.”
European and Asian manufacturers bring certain challenges: some are unaccustomed to placing the operator booth on the left side of the chassis, while others and may not be suitable for dense urban environments. But Lazarus noted that the MTA’s fact-finding mission is receptive to designs that differ from the expectations of the MTA and its bus passengers, if the design is still familiar enough to drive in America.
“If we get close on those dimensions, then we look really closely at [the manufacturer’s] technical specifications, what does this bus look like,” she said. “And if it’s pretty different than what we have, but it’s working really well in a lot of urban areas with varied weather conditions, we think it it would be a good fit to to at least try it in New York.”
MTA leadership has struggled to reconcile two important and seemingly competing goals: completing the transition to a fully zero-emissions bus fleet by 2040, and also ensuring the buses the agency owns are able to stay on the road.
Although those goals are not in natural competition, the central roadblock to the MTA’s effort to acquire more zero-emission buses is New Flyer — the only manufacturer from which the MTA can buy electric buses and still enjoy federal matching funds that cover 80 percent of the cost of new buses under the Buy America program. As a result, the MTA owns a handful of New Flyer electric buses that continue to suffer from major problems with battery charging and equipment failure. That makes it impossible for these buses to complete their runs without breaking down.
Understandably, the MTA has held off on acquiring more rolling stock from New Flyer. But that also means the agency is running hundreds of buses that are more than 12 years old — the effective lifespan of a bus before breakdowns become more frequent.
Another difficulty stems from the companies that make parts for electric buses, such as batteries, seats, doors and HVAC systems. These firms have experienced the very same kind of consolidation and industry shrinkage that destroyed American bus manufacturers. Lazarus said the MTA hopes that overseas companies who make bus components will follow bus manufacturers to the states.
“The constraints on low and no emissions busses in the U.S. have been in part on the [original equipment manager] side, but also on the supplier side,” she said. “Buses have lots and lots and lots of subsystem components, and unfortunately, the story in the subsystem supplier market is pretty similar to that in the [original equipment manufacturer] side, which is a ton of consolidation and not a lot of competition.”
Lazarus continued: “My hope here is that our work to bring in new bus manufacturers will also demonstrate to their suppliers, that if we’re able to prove that those components work for our operating folks and work in our operations, and we generally like our relationships with the the bus manufacturers, we might also be able to encourage some of their subsystem suppliers to come to New York State also and hang a shingle.”
The MTA’s not-so-secret weapon: a well-funded capital plan
The MTA’s plan to engage foreign manufacturers and put their buses on the road is a decidedly non-traditional strategy that its peer agencies in other cities and states would likely struggle to pull off. But the MTA has a not-so-secret weapon to lure manufacturers here: its fully-funded and very large capital plan, which sets aside a big chunk of money for rolling stock.
“Having a funded capital program with $12 billion set aside for rolling stock and very specific commitments on bus replacement and bus purchase is the biggest tool that we have, and the one and the biggest tool that we would need,” Lazarus said.
“We looked initially in the United States for how to spend this money and how to get these buses as quickly as we need them,” she added. “We don’t have the the option to to do that, and so we’re investing these dollars in relationships with new manufacturers that we can bring to the United States and to New York State, hopefully specifically.”
A bus manufacturing company won’t show up in America out of the goodness of its executives’ hearts, and it certainly won’t do so if there’s any chance the MTA will decide its products don’t work in the five boroughs. The pilot fleets allow the MTA and the bus builders to avoid that initial risk.
Tariffs pose another challenge. President Trump has repeatedly applied the import taxes as an unpredictable cudgel. MTA Chairman and CEO Janno Lieber has bemoaned how they have forced the MTA to scrounge up an additional one billion dollars for rolling stock, because the federal government doesn’t exempt parts purchased overseas even if firms used them to build trains and buses in America.
Lazarus echoed her boss’s concern but also suggested the Republicans’ recent midterm losses could relieve the situation.
“The major elephant in the room for all of these companies selling to North America and setting up shop here right now is the tariff environment,” she said. “The biggest obstacle that I’m talking to folks about. We can overcome a lot, but we can’t really overcome the current volatility of the tariff environment. That’s a major deterrent, and I hope we’ll start to see something change on that.”
Environmental advocates praised the MTA’s new strategy.
“Cities around the world successfully run transit bus fleets that are majority electric,” said Rachel Spector, the deputy managing attorney of Earthjustice’s northeast office. “New York City shouldn’t be left behind, and it’s great that MTA is pursuing new vendors. Electric buses can work for New York City and are critical to cleaner air and meeting our climate targets. Especially in light of surging diesel prices, it’s never been clearer that electrification and defending healthy transit budgets go hand in hand.”
Lazarus hopes the pilot will benefit other American transit agencies who need reliable buses, and potentially revive the country’s bus manufacturing sector.
“If we’re able to issue a request for proposals for hundreds or thousands of new buses, that plus the collective demand from other public transit agencies will be attractive enough for [manufacturers] to set up shop in North America,” she explained. “This is really aimed at how can the MTA put these dollars to work to support the health and diversity of the bus ecosystem in North America. We don’t want to be buying from abroad once we solve the problem, we’re trying to solve the problem so we don’t have to do that.”
Dave Colon is a reporter from Long Beach, a barrier island off of the coast of Long Island that you can bike to from the city. It’s a real nice ride. He’s previously been the editor of Brokelyn, a reporter at Gothamist, a freelance reporter and delivered freshly baked bread by bike.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: MTA Seeks ‘Millions and Millions’ Over Bungled OMNY Rollout
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Jose Martinez
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
The MTA is pumping the brakes on doling out “millions and millions” of dollars to the tech giant overseeing the troubled rollout of the MetroCard’s replacement.
Nearly a decade after awarding a $573 million contract to Cubic Transportation Systems to develop OMNY, the tap-and-go technology that pays for subway and bus trips, the country’s largest mass transportation authority has paused some payments to the company for repeatedly failing to meet its marks.
Saying “we have a problem with our software developer,” MTA chief Janno Lieber last week confirmed that the authority is following through on threats made at the authority’s October board meeting to withhold money over OMNY software shortcomings.
“We have to keep working with Cubic,” Lieber said. “But they have been a disappointment in many respects and we are holding them aggressively to their contract obligations and withholding payment of millions of dollars to make sure they make good on these commitments.”
An MTA spokesperson declined to specify how much Cubic is being docked on a contract that has ballooned to more than $700 million since it was first awarded. The penalties come as the company is facing financial woes that include getting downgraded by credit rating agencies, with the latest coming last week — and after the MTA officials had hoped OMNY would be “good to go” by the time the MetroCard reached the end of the line at the end of 2025.
According to the MTA, more than 5 billion trips have been via OMNY since it was introduced in 2019 as the MetroCard’s eventual replacement. The fare-payment system pays for rides via mobile devices, contactless credit and cards and MTA-issued fare cards.
But its rollout has been plagued by technical glitches and repeated rider complaints about delays in processing bank card payments, getting double-charged for transfers and having to go online for information on trip history and card balances.
Eileen Robbins, 80, said she has been frustrated for months after her OMNY account stopped automatically replenishing via a credit card once it dipped below $10.
“I found out the hard way,” she said. “But the bus driver let me on.”
After multiple calls to OMNY’s customer-service line, Robbins said she was frustrated enough to take Access-A-Ride from her home in Astoria to an MTA board meeting in Lower Manhattan to complain.
“They seem to be throwing good money after bad, even though they’re withholding some of it,” Robbins told The City Reporter. “In the meantime, they are infuriating their customers, whether it’s the students with their cards or the Access-A-Ride users or the general public.”
Lieber acknowledged the long-running rider frustrations.
“All of those features that people want from OMNY, they’re right,” he said. “We want to deliver those features where there’s more transparency and predictability and people can be confident that they’re getting those transfers and so on.”
MetroCard sales ended at the end of 2025, with the MTA saying almost all paid transit trips are now processed via OMNY.
“The underlying issues from a technology standpoint have made the rollout extremely problematic,” said Brian Fritsch, associate director of the Permanent Citizens Advisory Committee to the MTA. “From my understanding, the system architecture has not been where it needed to handle the number of transactions and the speed at which they need to be computed at the scale that New York City Transit requires.”
Riders who have been caught up in OMNY’s issues said they have been flustered by issues with the new fare-payment system.
Frederic Klein complained to the MTA board that in the last six months, the OMNY card that he has used since 2023 no longer automatically reloads $50 at a time.
“They’ve been paying them a lot of money for, what, nine years now?” the 35-year-old Washington Heights man told The City Reporter. “I think it’s disappointing that it’s taken so long for the MTA and its board to get on the same page with where riders are at and the frustrations with the system, but I am glad that they are finally taking notice and are starting to withhold money.”
Eric Schmidt, said his own problems with OMNY — which centered around being repeatedly double-charged a few years back for transfers — drove him back to using the MetroCard until its retirement.
“It’s wild,” said Schmidt, 41, of the Upper West Side. “OMNY is obviously more convenient because you can tap your card or your phone instead of loading money on a MetroCard, but in almost every other way, it’s worse.”
Cory Shields, a spokesperson for Cubic, told The City Reporter that the company is “committed to working closely with the MTA” to boost the OMNY experience for commuters.
“We take feedback seriously, and that input helps guide our joint efforts to strengthen the system, enhance reliability and incorporate the latest advances in fare-payment technology,” Shields said in a statement.
Fritsch of the PCAC — which last year issued recommendations on how to improve OMNY — said Cubic’s financial struggles compound its problems with the MTA.
Just last month, the company named Lee Sander, a former MTA CEO and executive director, as its new chief executive.
“Cubic can’t really afford serious financial penalties from the MTA,” Fritsch said. “Hopefully, that means they will do everything in their power to make good on their end of the contract in short order.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: We’re in a flaking epidemic. No wonder no one wants to host gatherings | Chelsea Flagan
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Chelsea Fagan
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
You might have heard by now, but Americans are quite lonely, especially if they’re young.
The kind of low-effort, high-frequency hanging out we used to rely on – dropping by for dinner, meeting up at the park, watching each other’s kids – has all but evaporated from our lives, leaving us unmoored from the social fabric that underpins our most basic wellbeing. (For reference, chronic loneliness has a comparable impact on long-term health to smoking.)
And if you’re looking for a culprit, there are many to blame: the dissolution of third spaces and encroachment of car culture, the declining participation in social networks such as churches and unions, and the harsh economic conditions that have people working longer hours for less money with each passing year.
And data shows that sheer disposable income is not as strongly correlated with social life as one might think: we are often completely eschewing the budget-friendly forms of contact that used to be standard in favor of being alone and scrolling on our phones.
But, as someone who literally wrote the book on getting together, and doing so across all income and age brackets, I would like to posit another reason why the American social fabric has so rapidly dissolved.
It’s not just that phones make it more appealing to scroll aimlessly than to have a conversation – it’s that they’ve made us more selfish, less community-minded people. Nearly every time I post a video about hosting, for example, my comments are filled with the same refrain: What’s the point of spending all this time and effort if no one actually shows up?
And the concern that you might go through all the trouble of planning a party just to sit in an empty room surrounded by food and decorations is not irrational.
When I posted this recent video about the psychic damage inflicted on a host by no-showing on an RSVP, it quickly racked up thousands of commenters sharing their experiences with the phenomenon. I am tagged daily in videos of people who did what I firmly believe we all should do: they took the risk of trying to get people together in real life, and they were left feeling humiliated by the realization that their party was simply an inconvenience that could be tossed overboard at the last minute.
And with social media and party apps making it easier than ever to invite anyone you’ve ever met, and to perpetually “maybe” your entire calendar so you can make a game-time call as to what invitation you deem worthy (as this excellent Substack explores), we have entered a dual crisis. Fewer people than ever are willing to host, and when they do, it’s a massive gamble: who will actually show up?
While there are, very occasionally, legitimate reasons to bail on a gathering at the last minute, we’ve also gotten very good at leveraging the language of mental health to lean into our most selfish impulses.
We speak in terms of boundaries and self-care about actions that don’t just devastate the person on the other side of our unreliability, but also sap at our own mental health, as community is arguably more important to it than our own immediate comfort.
The truth is, whether it’s exercising, spending time outside, showing up to a social commitment, or opting for more nutritious food over some quick takeout, it is often in doing the less immediately comfortable or enjoyable thing that we are truly caring for ourselves and those around us.
And when it comes to gathering, the social isolation factor is very real: making and keeping platonic bonds is a skill, and the longer you are out of practice, the harder and more scary it becomes to start again. People are losing friends, and the process can accelerate until the entire concept of socializing feels like a threat.
It has never been easier in those moments to get under a blanket, make up a thin excuse for not showing up to a commitment, and reassure yourself that you have engaged in a powerful, therapeutic exercise by choosing to watch a screen again instead of literally anything else.
We increasingly speak of gathering in terms of self-sacrifice and effort, but, as this meme deftly satirizes, the thing we’re talking about – making friends and then hanging out with them – is supposed to be the fun part. It’s supposed to be the reward for all the work we do, both professionally and in our daily lives.
Instead, the act has slipped so far from our cultural routines in just two generations that we no longer understand it as a leisure activity. (The performance of ultra-perfect hosting and homemaking on social media doesn’t help, but that’s a subject for another day.)
Simply put, we have so radically devalued not just what it means to spend time with people we love, but to show respect for the people who facilitate it, that we have enabled a full-blown flake epidemic. And while I’m not willing to say that being a chronic flaker makes you a bad person, I am willing to say that it should not be acceptable – to you, or to anyone else.
There are so many problems to fully address our hosting and loneliness crises, but none are more immediately solvable on a personal level than holding ourselves accountable. If we say we are going to do something, it is our responsibility to actually show up.
No, it doesn’t matter that you don’t really feel like it, or that it’s raining outside: grab an umbrella, put on a smile (and maybe pick up a nice little hostess gift on the way), and go be a part of the community we all desperately need to rebuild.
- Chelsea Fagan is an author and the co-founder of The Financial Diet

https://taz.de/Umweltschutz-und-Landwirt.title: Umweltschutz und Landwirtschaft: Pestizidrecht schützt Böden Studie zufolge zu wenig
https://taz.de/Umweltschutz-und-Landwirt.author: Jost Maurin
https://taz.de/Umweltschutz-und-Landwirt.text:
Umweltschutz und Landwirtschaft: Pestizidrecht schützt Böden Studie zufolge zu wenig
Forscher:innen stellen Defizite beim Schutz der Böden vor Pestiziden fest. Die Regeln seien veraltet und bei Verstößen gebe es kaum Konsequenzen.
Die deutschen Gesetze schützen Böden einer neuen Studie zufolge nur unzureichend vor Pestiziden. Die Vorschriften zur Anwendung der Mittel hätten eine „sehr begrenzte Steuerungswirkung“, schreiben Katharine Heyl, Jessica Stubenrauch und Felix Klickermann vom Helmholtz-Zentrum für Umweltforschung (UFZ) in der Fachzeitschrift Environmental Management. Sie seien zu ungenau und kaum durchsetzbar.
Der Einsatz von Pestiziden ist eine von mehreren Methoden, mit denen Landwirt:innen ihre Pflanzen vor Schädlingen schützen können. Die Chemikalien tragen aber dazu bei, dass Pflanzen- und Tierarten aussterben. Zudem haben sich manche Mittel im Nachhinein als gesundheitsschädlich erwiesen.
Als Beispiel für mangelhafte Regulierung nennen die Forscher:innen die im Pflanzenschutzgesetz vorgeschriebene „gute fachliche Praxis“, die unter anderem einen möglichst umweltschonenden Pestizideinsatz sicherstellen soll. Die Grundsätze seien seit 2010 nicht aktualisiert worden, neuere Erkenntnisse über die Belastung der Böden fehlten deshalb. Verstöße gegen die gute fachliche Praxis seien zudem nicht unmittelbar sanktionierbar. „Kontrolle und Durchsetzung sind daher praktisch unmöglich“, schreiben die Autor:innen, solange eine Behörde keine konkreten Maßnahmen angeordnet habe.
Wie selten kontrolliert wird, zeigen Zahlen des Bundesamts für Verbraucherschutz und Lebensmittelsicherheit, auf die sich die Studie stützt: 2023 wurden demnach nur 1,5 Prozent der Betriebe überprüft, bei 21 Prozent dieser Kontrollen gab es Verstöße gegen Vorschriften zur Pestizidanwendung. Bei einer Kontrollserie 2025 verstieß rund ein Drittel der überprüften Betriebe (230 von 687) gegen Gewässerabstände oder produktspezifische Anwendungsbestimmungen.
Bundesagrarministerium „prüft“ die Studie
Auch das Bundesbodenschutzgesetz bietet nach Einschätzung der Wissenschaftler keinen ausreichenden Schutz. Auf Agrarflächen gingen die spezielleren Regeln des Pflanzenschutzrechts vor. Das führe zu einer „bedauerlichen Situation“, schreiben die Autor:innen: Der Vorrang des Spezialrechts gelte selbst dann, „wenn die Bodenschutzmaßnahmen in den Spezialgesetzen hinter dem Standard des Bundesbodenschutzgesetzes zurückbleiben“.
Ähnlich fällt die Kritik am Bundesnaturschutzgesetz aus. Nach einem Urteil des Bundesverwaltungsgerichts von 2016 enthalten die Vorgaben für eine naturverträgliche Landwirtschaft nur unverbindliche Leitlinien. Die UFZ-Forscher schließen sich dieser Bewertung an. Außerhalb von Natura-2000-Gebieten leiste das deutsche Naturschutzrecht deshalb keinen ausreichenden Beitrag zur Verringerung der Pestizidrisiken, schreiben sie. In und in der Nähe dieser EU-Schutzgebiete müssen die Mitgliedstaaten dagegen nach europäischem Recht schädlichen Pestizideinsatz zumindest einschränken, sofern keine rechtlich zulässige Ausnahme greift.
In nationalen Naturschutzgebieten ist der Einsatz zwar grundsätzlich verboten. Doch Ausnahmen, etwa zur Abwehr erheblicher wirtschaftlicher Schäden oder zur Sicherung von Bahnstrecken, schwächten die Verbote und erschwerten ihre Durchsetzung.
Die Forscher empfehlen, die gute fachliche Praxis zu aktualisieren und verbindlich zu machen, mit überprüfbaren Anforderungen sowie Kontroll- und Sanktionsmöglichkeiten für die Behörden. Außerdem schlagen sie Pufferzonen zwischen Naturschutzgebieten und Agrarflächen vor. Zusätzlich halten sie eine Pestizidsteuer für nötig, deren Höhe sich nach der Umweltgefährlichkeit der Wirkstoffe richtet. Eine pauschale Abgabe hingegen könnte dazu führen, dass Landwirte weniger, aber giftigere Mittel einsetzen, so die Wissenschaftler. Die Einnahmen könnten Umweltleistungen der Landwirtschaft finanzieren.
Das von dem CSU-Politiker Alois Rainer geleitete Bundesagrarministerium teilte der taz in einer Stellungnahme zu der Kritik nur mit: „Die genannte Studie ist dem Bundesministerium für Landwirtschaft, Ernährung und Heimat (BMLEH) bekannt. Sie wird derzeit im BMLEH geprüft.“

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: Our ‘Paris manifesto’ proposes how to deal with extreme wealth in the AI age | Open letter
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Open letter
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
The explosion of extreme wealth in the world is the defining social fact of our times.
When Forbes magazine began ranking the world’s largest fortunes in 1987, the wealth of the richest 0.0001% of our planet’s population equaled 3% of global GDP. Since that time, the wealth held by this tiny group of people – just 3,000 households – has ballooned and now reaches 17% of global GDP.
This extreme wealth explosion has upended the balance of power, leaving choices that affect all of humanity to a few billionaires at the helm of a handful of corporations. The economic power of the ultra-wealthy is being used to consolidate their political power, creating a dynamic that is threatening democracy.
This dynamic of wealth and power is nothing new (the word “oligarchy” comes from ancient Greek), but its velocity and the scale of its cross-border impacts are unprecedented. A single decision made by the controlling shareholder of a multinational firm can wipe away jobs, deplete resources, or determine the course of a war.
Choices made by the ultra-rich ignore national borders as they disrupt work and home lives, inject their ideas into the public discourse, bend public policy to fit their desires, siphon revenue away from states, and damage our earth.
The power dynamic of this international oligarchy must be countered with a transnational coalition to defend democracy. To this end, we affirm three principles.
1 Fair taxation
The ultra-rich should pay taxes in proportion to their resources. As studies in many countries have shown, this is currently not the case. Myriad loopholes allow the wealthiest in the world to pay little or no income tax.
A tax floor, expressed as a percentage of personal wealth, would put an end to this situation. This idea was first developed in a report commissioned by the G20 in 2024, under the presidency of Brazil, which proposed setting an individual tax floor equal to 2% of wealth for all fortunes more than $100m.
Such an initiative would ensure that the ultra-rich would pay at least as large a share of their income in tax as the middle class – the bare minimum required to ensure that fiscal law complies with the principle of tax fairness.
This annual tax floor should be accompanied by a one-time “catch-up” tax on the wealth of the super-rich to settle the outstanding tax inequalities that have fueled the explosion of extreme wealth. If this exceptional levy took into account any taxes paid during the time period covered by the catch-up, only those ultra-rich individuals who had avoided meeting their fiscal obligations would be affected.
2 Media independence and pluralism
Information is not just another commodity, and access to it forms the bedrock of our democracies. The power of oligarchs to control information must be curtailed.
The purchase of media outlets and social platforms is one of the most glaring ways in which the ultra-rich capture power, ensuring themselves control over what is said, heard, learned and read. It is crucial to provide stronger support for public media and implement anti-concentration policies. In the age of big digital platforms, these anti-concentration policies should be designed on an international scale.
3 Decisions to develop and deploy artificial intelligence technologies must be democratized
Knowledge, artistic creation, and works of imagination assembled over centuries are being captured, processed and repackaged (often without permission!) by a handful of corporations to be resold as artificial intelligence to the very humanity that produced them. There is still time to refuse that hijacking.
Technologies associated with artificial intelligence come with astronomically high risks: the possibility of cyberattacks with lethal consequences, rapid and profound transformations of the labor market, the emergence of new forms of manipulation and disinformation, even the risk of human extinction. It would be folly to leave decisions about the deployment of these technologies in the hands of a few Silicon Valley billionaires.
In the field of information technology, the non-profit model has a proven track record. Some of the most popular applications and websites in the world, such as Wikipedia, Signal or Firefox, were developed by non-profit organizations. To build AI without oligarchs, companies working in this field should consider adopting the model of the non-profit foundation, with decisions piloted by those who understand them best: their own workers – the same people who, week after week, have been stepping down from their posts to warn us of the looming risk.
Today, around the world, voices are being raised to protect our democracies from the threats of oligarchy. We are calling for a transnational coalition to defend democracy because, as history has shown, our voices are most powerful when we raise them together, as interconnected citizens. It is possible for democracy to reverse the dynamic of oligarchy. It is possible to work for a world that is no longer defined by exploding inequality. Now is the time to reorient our trajectory. We hope you will join us.
