https://taz.de/Gen-Z-Proteste-und-Gewalt.title: Gen-Z-Proteste und Gewalt: Karneval der Freiheit
https://taz.de/Gen-Z-Proteste-und-Gewalt.author: Robert Misik
https://taz.de/Gen-Z-Proteste-und-Gewalt.text:
Gen-Z-Proteste und Gewalt: Karneval der Freiheit
Ja, der Typus des übermotivierten Engagierten kann nerven. Doch brauchen Bewegungen ihre Energie, um die Ohnmacht der Vereinzelung zu überwinden.
D ie Protestler wurden als ungewaschene Langhaarige geschmäht, die konservative Presse und andere mediale Leitkulturen konnten sich gar nicht mehr einkriegen: „Rote Unruhestifter“, „Politgammler“, „Volksfeinde“ machte die Bild-Zeitung aus. Gegenstand des bürgerlichen Nervenzusammenbruchs waren Hippies, die 68er-Bewegung und natürlich deren Frontleute wie Rudi Dutschke und Daniel Cohn-Bendit. Sechzig Jahre ist das jetzt her. Heute lachen wir über die autoritären Leitartikler von damals.
Jetzt protestiert die Jugend unserer Tage auch wieder. Und die alten Feindmuster sind wiedergekehrt. Nur dass die Jugend nicht mehr als langhaarig und ungewaschen diffamiert wird, sondern als gewalttätige Plünderer, Chaoten, als Antisemiten und – natürlich – als testosterongetriebene „migrantische Milieus“. Grotesker Treppenwitz der Geschichte: Es soll vorkommen, dass nicht wenige derer, die vor sechzig Jahren selbst als „Politgammler“ diffamiert wurden, jetzt bei der Elitenpanik mitmachen. Man hat sich in der Altbauwohnung schön eingerichtet.
Die Sozialfigur des migrantischen männlichen Jugendlichen erinnert als soziale Wahnvorstellung manchmal an die Angstfantasie der gesetzten bürgerlichen Milieus des 19. Jahrhunderts: Die gruselten sich über jene, die man seinerzeit die „gefährlichen Klassen“ nannte.
„Der Begriff der gefährlichen Klassen (französisch: classes dangereuses) stammt aus dem 19. Jahrhundert und bezeichnete im Zuge der Industrialisierung die schnell wachsende, eigentumslose Armuts- und Unterschicht in den Großstädten“, weiß schon die KI. Prägend für die Diskurse ist „bürgerliche Angst“. Denn: „Die bürgerliche Oberschicht und der Staat fürchteten, dass sich Teile der verelendeten Bevölkerung der staatlichen Kontrolle entziehen, kriminell werden oder soziale Unruhen und Revolutionen anzetteln.“
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Die Phase der (post-)pubertären Unsicherheit reicht heute weit hinein ins Lebensalter zwischen dreißig und vierzig. Einstieg ins Berufsleben? Holprig. Wohnungen? Faktisch nicht zu bekommen und sowieso unleistbar. Das Leben selbst? Unleistbar. Prekäre Jobs reichen vielleicht für ein Zimmer, jeder Jobsverlust bedroht die Existenz. Früher konnte man für kleines Geld ein Bohemeleben führen. Heute kommt man mit weniger als 1.500 Euro kaum durch den Monat. Ein bisschen rumlungern und sich ausprobieren? Das ging früher, wenn der Wohnraum gerade mal 200 D-Mark kostete.
Was glaubt die heutige Mehrheitsgesellschaft eigentlich: Dass man die Leben der Jungen ruinieren kann, das Weltklima zerstören, die Lebenshaltungskosten in die Höhe treiben kann, dass man die Idee von einem eigenen Wohnraum in eine irreale Fantasie verwandeln kann? Dass man alle auf Dauer mit der Peitsche der Prekarität gefügig halten kann und sie schön den Rücken krümmen und einen Knicks machen? Glaubt sie das wirklich?
Die Revolte ist nicht ein Aufstand gegen die moralische Ordnung, sondern umgekehrt ein Aufstand dagegen, dass die moralische Ordnung gebrochen worden ist. Die wahren Plünderer ziehen nicht mit Kapuzenpulli durch die Straßenzüge. Nicht die Proteste sind radikal, sondern die Verhältnisse, gegen die sie sich wenden. Radikal ist die skrupellose Schurkerei, mit der die Wichtigtuer, Gutvernetzten, die Tech-Oligarchen und die besonders gut organisierte Kriminalität der Geldsäcke die Welt ruinieren und den Jungen die Zukunft stehlen.
Trivial ist der Vorhalt, dass Proteste auch Halbstarke anziehen können, bei denen der Erlebnishunger die politische Strategie überwiegt. Radikalinski-Getue und Spinnertum gehen gelegentlich Hand in Hand, und kaum ein gesellschaftlicher Fortschritt wurde je erkämpft ohne ein paar nervige Narren am Rand.
Der Sozialwissenschaftler Tareq Sydiq hat vor kurzem das Buch „Die neue Protestkultur“ herausgebracht. Proteste haben es schwer, sie werden niedergeschlagen, sie werden ignoriert, sie verlieren mit der Zeit ihren Elan – warum haben sie „trotz allem regelmäßig Erfolg?“, fragt Sydiq. Protestbewegungen sind dann erfolgreich, „wenn sie es schaffen, heterogene Gruppen zu mobilisieren, weil sie damit unterschiedliche Milieus ansprechen“, so Sydiq.
Und wer einmal an Protesten teilgenommen hat, wird auch künftig leichter mobilisierbar sein. So entstehen politisch aktive Milieus mit langfristiger Wirkung. Besonders wirksam sind sie, wenn Verbände entstehen, die die Aktivitäten verstetigen, und wenn damit ein „Marsch durch die Institutionen“ gelingt. Sind sie friedlich, nützen sie dem Anliegen, werden sie gewalttätig, stoßen sie auch Verbündete ab. Sie können Parteien treiben und anstacheln. Nicht immer können Regierende den Protest aussitzen.
Ausbruch aus Demütigung
Dabei ist noch die Randale – als Sprache der Sprachlosen, als Ausnahmezustand von unten – nicht nur Spektakel, von Lust am Exzess getrieben, sondern immer auch eine Art Karneval der Freiheit. Was den einen als sinnlose Zerstörung erscheint, ist manchmal auch temporärer Ausbruch aus Demütigung, Kommandiert-Werden und der Erfahrung chronischer Respektlosigkeit.
Bewegungen haben auch etwas Ansteckendes. Sie überwinden die Ohnmacht der Vereinzelung, geben Schwung und Gemeinschaftsgefühl, können den Nebel der Depression vertreiben. Politische Bewegungen sind Erfahrungsräume des Politischen, und das unmittelbarer als die Ortsverbände von Parteien. In ihnen lernt man Dinge, die kein Lehrbuch vermitteln kann und die die Engagierten prägen.
Bevor sie die Welt verändern, verändern sie die Aktiven. Im besten Fall ist solches Engagement Einübung in Lebenskunst. Der Typus des übermotivierten Engagierten kann einem zweifelsohne oft ordentlich auf die Nerven gehen: Gern gilt ihm der, welcher nicht alles exakt genauso erregt sieht wie er selbst, nicht als potenzieller Verbündeter, sondern als Gegner.
Der übermotivierte Engagierte hat nicht immer automatisch recht, aber das elitäre Naserümpfen über das Engagement hat immer unrecht.

https://taz.de/Ungarns-Magyar-besucht-di.title: Ungarns Magyar besucht die Ukraine: Volleyball statt Eiszeit
https://taz.de/Ungarns-Magyar-besucht-di.author: Florian Bayer
https://taz.de/Ungarns-Magyar-besucht-di.text:
Ungarns Magyar besucht die Ukraine: Volleyball statt Eiszeit
Ungarns Regierungschef Peter Magyar trifft den ukrainischen Präsidenten Wolodymyr Selenskyj in Transkarpatien. Die Beziehungen tauen zumindest ein bisschen auf.
Ungarns Regierungschef Péter Magyar hat am Dienstag das westukrainische Transkarpatien besucht und dort den ukrainischen Präsidenten Wolodymyr Selenskyj getroffen. Mit dabei war Außenministerin Anita Orbán (nicht verwandt mit dem früheren Premier). Magyar sprach von einem historischen Tag und einer großen Chance, ein neues Kapitel aufzuschlagen, „das gute Nachbarn brauchen“. Selenskyj erklärte, die Ukraine sei bereit, „einen konstruktiven Dialog und eine Beziehung“ mit Ungarn aufzubauen.
Unter Magyars Vorgänger Viktor Orbán hatten sich die Nachbarländer stark entfremdet, nun nähern sie sich wieder an. Es ist der erste Besuch eines ungarischen Ministerpräsidenten in Transkarpatien seit 2015. Selenskyj kritisierte die frühere Führung in Budapest. In der politischen Elite habe es keinen Respekt gegeben, man habe die Menschen „aufgehetzt“.
Der Tag begann in der Gebietshauptstadt Uschhorod an der slowakischen Grenze. Auf dem Kalvarienfriedhof legten beide Staatschefs Kränze für gefallene Soldaten nieder. Hauptort war aber Berehowe, ungarisch Beregszász, das Zentrum der ungarischen Minderheit. Dort besuchten Magyar und Selenskyj ein mit ungarischem Geld renoviertes Krankenhaus und das ungarischsprachige Kossuth-Lyzeum, wo sie die Anzüge ablegten und mit Schülern Volleyball spielten. Am Abend traf Magyar Vertreter der ungarischen Gemeinschaft.
In Transkarpatien lebten bei der Volkszählung 2001 gut 150.000 ethnische Ungarn. Durch Abwanderung, vor allem seit Kriegsbeginn, dürften es heute weniger als 100.000 sein. Orbán nutzte die Minderheit immer wieder politisch. Auch Magyar macht ihre Rechte zur Bedingung für Ungarns Zustimmung zum EU-Beitritt der Ukraine. Dass das ukrainische Parlament im Oktober ein Minderheitengesetz beschloss, habe das Vertrauen gestärkt, so Magyar. Zugleich dämpfte er die Erwartungen. Ein beschleunigtes Beitrittsverfahren „gibt es nicht“, Ungarns eigener Beitritt habe 13 Jahre gedauert. Selenskyj nannte den EU-Weg seines Landes „unumkehrbar“.
Weiterhin keine Waffen aus Ungarn an die Ukraine
Magyar betonte die Unterstützung des von Russland überfallenen Landes. „Das ungarische Volk verurteilt entschieden die schreckliche russische Aggression, die seit fast fünf Jahren gegen Zivilisten und Soldaten tobt“, sagte er. Für einen Frieden brauche die Ukraine internationale Sicherheitsgarantien. Er erinnerte an das Budapester Memorandum von 1994, mit dem Kyjiw seine Atomwaffen abgab.
Seit Orbáns Abwahl im April hat sich Ungarn der Ukraine wieder angenähert. Im Juni und im Oktober gab Budapest sein Veto gegen weitere Beitrittskapitel auf, vier von sechs Verhandlungsclustern sind nun geöffnet. Ungarn will zudem die humanitäre Hilfe ausbauen: Magyar brachte Medizintechnik, Medikamente, Generatoren und Fahrzeuge im Wert von einer Milliarde Forint mit, rund 2,7 Millionen Euro. Auch kündigte Magyar einen neuen Sozialfonds für die Ungarn in Transkarpatien an. Waffen will Ungarn weiterhin nicht liefern.
Besprochen wurde zudem Zusammenarbeit bei Energie und Handel. Selenskyj sprach von großem Bedarf an Diesel und bot Mais an. Nach der Dürre fehlen Ungarn rund zwei Millionen Tonnen, weswegen die Agrarminister beider Länder nun über befristete Einfuhren verhandeln. Die Grenzübergänge sollen zudem erneuert und um neue ergänzt, die Bahnstrecke Kyjiw-Budapest ausgebaut und elektrifiziert werden. Beim Wiederaufbau sieht Magyar Ungarn logistisch in einer Schlüsselrolle.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.title: AI's shock-and-awe raid on maths looks like pride before a fall | Rafael Behr
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.author: Rafael Behr
https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text:
In most walks of life, trying something 12,363,153,437,138 times and getting the same result is reason enough to assume it works every time. Not in maths, where a conjecture that holds up more than 12tn times looks very probably true but doesn’t qualify as proven.
That was the status of the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous mathematical conundrums in existence, until last week. Then Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, said he and his collaborator, Claude AI, had crossed the line from conjecture to proof.
I don’t pretend to understand much of what Bernhard Riemann proposed in 1859. I know it relates to primes – whole integers greater than 1 that are divisible only by 1 and themselves – and the pattern of their distribution along the infinite number line. But you don’t need to know what a zeta function is to recognise that the solution to a near-170-year-old problem is a big deal in maths, or that the role of AI in completing the quest is a big deal for humanity.
Around two years ago, large language models that mesmerised users with their verbal dexterity sucked at maths. They made basic arithmetic errors. Now they resolve unfathomably hard problems with ease. In Alpöge’s breathless account of the process, Claude “flew, and danced, and sparkled” towards its conclusion. It left him “in awe”.
Other mathematicians whose discipline is being eaten by machines report more complex feelings. In October, OpenAI published hundreds of AI-generated papers containing proofs to unsolved problems, stunning faculties that had been toiling over the relevant questions for years. Some called it the “mathocalypse”.
There is still a long process of verification to run. Humans have to check that the machines haven’t taken rogue shortcuts, but early indications back the AI. Researchers are witnessing intricate edifices of abstract cognition, their life’s work, crushed under silicon bulldozers.
Many are upset, angry. Some are excited by the future possibilities, some more sceptical or feeling a combination of emotions that an LLM can describe and imitate but not, as far as we know, experience.
Mathematicians are not the first people to worry that a rising technological tide will wash away their livelihood. But their position is unusual in ways that go beyond the conventional fear of obsolescence.
Maths describes fundamental laws of the universe. Nothing is truer than a mathematically proven truth. The limit of what advanced mathematicians know delineates the frontier of human knowledge – or it has done until now. The soaring rate of computational capability raises the prospect of machines exploring dimensions that humans cannot comprehend, generating proofs that have to be taken on trust. What kind of knowledge even is it if no organic mind knows how it came to be known?
In the past, when great mysteries have been solved, the method has been as thrilling as the result. Andrew Wiles cracked Fermat’s Last Theorem by building bridges between previously disconnected realms of maths, opening new vistas of theoretical space for further exploration. It was an arduous ascent to higher truth. AI-generated proofs are windowless lifts that hoist you to the summit with little sense of how you got there.
They are also weird, according to people who can decrypt them. Hannah Fry, Cambridge maths professor, broadcaster, author and one of the world’s best communicators of hard concepts to a lay audience, called one of the recent OpenAI proofs “almost hilariously ugly”.
That might sound like a marginal quibble if the underlying logic is sound, but the aesthetic of an answer is not a minor consideration in maths. The human mind is gratified by the elegance of a solution. It is hard to celebrate an insight extracted by tens of thousands of AI agents torturing equations day and night, burning tens of millions of dollars of computing power, just so a tech company with an eye on its prospective stock market valuation can say it got to the answer before any human.
To that objection, AI evangelists say the mathematicians are being precious. If an LLM found a safe treatment for a previously incurable disease, doctors would prescribe it even if they didn’t understand how it worked. Does it matter if humans get left behind as the frontiers of knowledge are pushed forwards?
The answer depends on who controls the pace of advance and their motives. Tech boosters talk about godlike intelligence emerging when autonomous AI models start coding their successors on a trajectory of exponential self-improvement. The mathematical breakthroughs of recent weeks don’t tip us over that threshold but they bring it into view.
That a scenario is conceivable doesn’t make it inevitable. But it would be complacent to assume that soaraway superintelligence won’t happen just because it sounds far-fetched, or because tech bros are given to hyperbole, or because their businesses are perched on a Jenga tower of debt.
It can be true that AI investment is a bubble and also that the technology is capable of superseding humanity. When the first dotcom boom turned to bust at the turn of the millennium, it didn’t reveal the internet to be all worthless hype. Railways were a transformative technology for the US despite cycles of irrational exuberance, track laid to nowhere and spectacular bankruptcies.
The precedent of past industrial revolutions suggests today’s AI pioneers will be a coalition of canny entrepreneurs, philanthropic idealists, suckers, charlatans and sociopaths. Their product will offer benefits and harms; economic gains and toxic contamination. The industry will resist regulatory constraints. Resistance will take the form of increasingly blatant corruption. It will be overcome only when scandals generate a backlash of sufficient force.
In an optimistic reading of the current moment, the feeling of vertiginous peril indicates proximity to the top of the cycle. We are at the apex of hubris, when the people who are profiting most from the absence of restraint insist that laws of economic and political gravity no longer apply, shortly before discovering that they do.
This is why brute-forcing famous mathematical conundrums matters so much to the AI labs. Proving that the machines can transcend every conceivable human achievement is a way to sustain the idea that this time is different, that an AI-powered Icarus can soar beyond the sun. And this is the ugliness that despondent mathematicians discern in those proofs. It is the difference between exploration to advance knowledge and a land grab in pursuit of power.
- Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

https://taz.de/Menschenrechtspreis/!6232.title: Menschenrechtspreis: Palästinensischer Anwalt für Kinderrechte wird geehrt
https://taz.de/Menschenrechtspreis/!6232.author: Serena Bilanceri
https://taz.de/Menschenrechtspreis/!6232.text:
Menschenrechtspreis: Palästinensischer Anwalt für Kinderrechte wird geehrt
Amnesty International hat den Anwalt Khaled Quzmar für seinen Einsatz für Kinder in Haft ausgezeichnet. Die israelische Regierung bringt seinen Verein mit Terror in Verbindung.
Seit fast vier Jahrzehnten beschäftigt sich Khaled Quzmar mit einem besonders schwierigen, ja fast grausamen Thema: Kindern in Haft. Jetzt erhält er für seine Arbeit den Menschenrechtspreis der Organisation Amnesty International.
Quzmar ist Anwalt, spezialisiert auf die Verteidigung von Minderjährigen, die vor Gericht landen. Fast sein ganzes Leben lang vertritt er im von Israel besetzten Westjordanland Palästinenser:innen, die sich vor Militärgerichten verantworten müssen. Denn im Westjordanland gilt für sie, anders als für israelische Siedler:innen, das Militärrecht. Etwa 350 Kinder befinden sich derzeit in Haft. Und die Verwaltungshaft erlaubt es den israelischen Behörden, Menschen ohne Anklage jahrelang in Gewahrsam zu halten. Unter ihnen befanden sich laut Daten von Unicef, die sich auf Angaben des israelischen Gefängnisdienstes stützen, im September 2026 mindestens 164 Minderjährige.
Auch für sie setzt sich Quzmar ein. Immer wieder berichten seine jungen Klienten von Schlägen und Misshandlungen im Gefängnis. An die Erzählungen hat sich der Anwalt selbst nach 40 Jahren nicht gewöhnt. „Das sind Kinder, sie haben diese Brutalität nicht verdient“, sagt er.
Er selbst hat sich für den Beruf des Juristen entschieden, als sein eigener Bruder festgenommen wurde. Damals war Quzmar 13 Jahre alt und lebte noch in einem kleinen Dorf im westlichen Westjordanland. Während des Besuchs im Gefängnis durfte er den Bruder nicht in die Arme schließen, sondern lediglich seine Hand durch das Drahtgitter berühren. Seinen Anwalt ließen die Sicherheitskräfte hingegen hinein.
Also ließ er sich nach dem Schulabschluss an der algerischen Universität in Oran für Rechtswissenschaften einschreiben, denn eine juristische Fakultät gab es damals im Westjordanland nicht. Er kehrte dann in den 80er Jahren zurück und bildete sich später in Irland weiter. Zunächst engagierte er sich im Verein Defense for Children International-Palestine. Seit Juni 2026 ist er Geschäftsführer des Palestinian Centre for Child Rights.
Quzmar, der auf Bildern immer einen nachdenklichen Blick unter den markanten Augenbrauen hat, ist eine kontroverse Figur: In den palästinensischen Gebieten wird er gefeiert, in Israel harsch kritisiert. Die israelische Armee führte 2021 eine Razzia im Büro von Defense for Children International durch, die Regierung bezeichnete sie kurze Zeit später als „Terrororganisation“.
Sie soll Verbindungen zur verbotenen Volksfront zur Befreiung Palästinas gehabt haben, was Quzmar bestreitet. Überzeugende Beweise legte Israel nicht vor, so weigerten sich Deutschland und acht weitere EU-Länder, die NGO als Terrororganisation einzustufen. Ein Jahr später bestellte der israelische Inlandsgeheimdienst Schin Beth den Anwalt auf eine Militärbasis, in der er zwei Stunden lang verhört wurde. Anschließend kam er wieder frei.
Seit dem Hamas-Massaker am 7. Oktober und dem Krieg in Gaza ist Quzmars Arbeit noch schwieriger geworden. „Um Informationen über inhaftierte Kinder zu bekommen, muss ich Briefe an die Gefängnisse in Israel schreiben und monatelang auf eine Antwort warten“, erzählt er. Insgesamt, das belegen Berichte von Menschenrechtsorganisationen sowie eine Recherche der taz, haben sich die Haftbedingungen palästinensischer Insassen deutlich verschlechtert – auch die von Minderjährigen. Trotz der Schwierigkeiten lässt sich Quzmar nicht entmutigen. „Du musst in die Kinder investieren, damit sie in Zukunft führen können“, sagt er.

https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.author: Adrian Horton
https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/no.text:
The film-maker Beth de Araújo likens the personal experience that inspired Josephine, her disquieting second feature, to a slow-acting poison. Early one Saturday morning when she was eight years old, Araújo and her father were playing soccer in Golden Gate Park, near their home in San Francisco, when they heard a woman scream. Her father, a former Olympic runner for Brazil, told her to stay and bolted to help; Araújo, scared and alone, ran after him, and instead found the woman in a clearing, naked from the waist down. Araújo was too young to understand what had happened, but she knew something was wrong.
So, too, does an eight-year-old Josephine, played by the remarkable newcomer Mason Reeves, in the one scene crafted exactly to Araújo’s memory: Josephine, confused and restless, observes as the woman tucks her hands under her legs to keep them from shaking. She is further confused when her father, Damien, played by the aspirationally everyman actor Channing Tatum, seems extra keen to return to their soccer game afterwards, one of many echoes of Araújo’s memory in this taut drama. In real life, Araújo’s father “put on a face, put on energy and made it seem fun,” she recalled. “And I was like: ‘This is so weird. Why is my dad being so extra fun right now?’”
The two never discussed the incident. In the meantime, Araújo developed a sense of hyperawareness for potentially fragile safety, often double-checking the locks of her family’s home. Occasionally, she overheard her parents talk about the morning in the park, or the subsequent rape trial, or the fact that the perpetrator was released from prison when Araújo was 15. She often struggled to sleep. Then, in 2014, another incident – a stranger groped her in a theater – tipped her “functional hypervigilance” into a dark spiral. After 20 years, she finally asked her father about what they had both witnessed; she learned, for the first time, that the perpetrator had pulled a knife on her father, who tracked him at a distance until police arrived. “I asked him why he didn’t explain it to me on the day, when I asked what was going on, and he said he didn’t want to scare me,” she recalled. “But with his best intentions, of exactly how he wanted to protect me and love me, the exact opposite occurred. I became much more scared.”
In the days after that phone call, Araújo wrote a “vomit draft” in a near-literal sense, a regurgitation of that long-ago poison. “I needed to purge it out of me,” she said. The result was Josephine, which arrives, more than a decade and many revisions later, in theaters this month after a heralded festival fun; the film won both the grand jury prize and audience award at Sundance, where it left me stunned – by its refusal to blur what Josephine sees, by its bravura performances and by its precise evocation of a child’s mind ruptured by darkness she can’t yet comprehend. Like Araújo, Josephine learns the word “rape” from the incident (and then sneaking her mom’s phone to search “raip”). Writing from Josephine’s perspective became a question of: “Can I transport the audience back to being de-assimilated, to a time before they knew what sexual violence was?” Araújo said. “I learned about it in a very specific and very harsh way, but everyone learned it at some point. And so how did it then inform how we moved our bodies through the world, how we thought about our own safety?”
The film is “fictionalized, but factual”, tracing a different arc of aftermath to Araújo’s, one contained to Josephine’s immediate fear and confusion – in the days after the incident, Josephine begins to view all boys or displays of adult intimacy with hostility – and her parents’ fumbling attempts to help her. Both Gemma Chan, as her mother, Claire, and especially Tatum are superb as parents whose own coping mechanisms for male violence – calm dissociation on the one hand, fighting back on the other – cloud their well-meaning but inadequate responses to their daughter. Damien insists, without merit, that something like that will never happen to Josephine. Like Araújo’s own father, he enrolls her in self-defense classes. Claire attempts therapy, then gently tries to distract.
Damien and Claire’s counterproductive efforts “are not because they don’t love their daughter”, said Araújo. “Channing and I talked about this extensively, because he has a daughter himself – how do you talk to your daughter about sexual assault?” The inability to confront such a verboten topic from either side – the loving parent, the innocent child – forms the backbone of the film. For parents, “the lack of control must feel horrifying, because you love this person so much and yet you can’t control them starting to learn and experience the darkness of this world.” Neither parent can conceive that at night, Josephine imagines the perpetrator from the park in an aqua polo (Philip Ettinger) lurking about her room.
Viewers know the perpetrator from the film’s shattering first scene, which breaks with recent cinematic convention to elide the horror of sexual assault, allowing the viewer to fill in the blanks (see: Women Talking, She Said and Sorry, Baby), with a graphic account of just what Josephine witnesses from the bushes. It’s every film-maker’s choice, how they want to portray it,” said Araújo of the decision to stage a rape in full (the scene was shot so that Reeves, of course, sees nothing). “I just felt like if we didn’t fully see what Josephine sees, the audience would lose connection to her fear, and where she goes for the rest of the film.”
The decision was also partly informed by Araújo’s time training as a witness advocate in San Francisco, focusing on accompanying victims to obtain rape kits at a hospital within 72 hours of an assault, and her time working shifts for the LA Rape and Battering Hotline. “So many times, I heard from people that they wish they had fought back more, that they wish that they had done something differently, that if they had done this, maybe they could have stopped it.” As a witness advocate, Araújo says: “We are trained to remind survivors that their first goal was to keep themselves alive. So often when survivors fight back, it does get more violent. And I really wanted to honor that experience, because sexual violence is violent.”
Thanks to the help of screenwriters’ grants, Araújo shadowed multiple sexual assault cases through the San Francisco Hall of Justice, which informed the film’s second half, in which Josephine is called upon as the sole witness for the perpetrator’s rape trial. Two judges, two public defenders and two prosecutors read over the script to ensure accuracy to the California legal system, including the fact that female public defenders are often assigned to defend men charged with rape; in the film, the perpetrator’s lawyer attempts to undermine Josephine’s confidence and suggests that she witnessed consensual role-playing. “I’ve had such a challenging time throughout my life trying to wrap my head around him pleading not guilty,” said Araújo. “I never testified in court, and I think part of why I wrote that in was to say what I know is true.”
Araújo is resistant to discuss Josephine in terms of healing or progress. “I don’t think that anyone ever fully heals or has this big, beautiful catharsis from anything having to do with sexual violence,” she said. “I think you become a different person, and that person can continue.” But it’s “no surprise” that the film’s release, after years of development and revision, funding secured and pulled and resecured with the help of Tatum’s star wattage, coincides with a release of some fear. “This year, I’m sleeping through the night,” she said. “That’s very meaningful in my life.”
- Josephine is out in US and UK cinemas now and in Australia on 18 February

https://gothamist.com/news/community-boa.title: Community board votes to replace iconic Tompkins Square Park pull-up bars
https://gothamist.com/news/community-boa.author: Willow Higgins
https://gothamist.com/news/community-boa.text:
The calisthenics-enthusiasts fighting to preserve the beloved, '90s-era pull-up bars in Tompkins Square Park lost a battle last night.
The Manhattan community board that represents the East Village voted to support the New York City parks department's plan to demolish the pull-up bars and other calisthenics equipment and replace them with new materials. The nearly $10 million renovation project also includes reconstructing the adjacent basketball courts and improving the miniature, kids-only swimming pool.
The vote comes after regular users of the outdoor fitness area pleaded with the parks department for months to repair the aging equipment, rather than demolish it. Some fans told Gothamist that they moved to New York solely to be near the Tompkins Square Park pull-up bars and the community of people who use them.
“We think that those bars, the way they've been built…somehow we struck gold with this equipment of how versatile, how sturdy, how open-ended they are,” said Salo Coslovsky, an associate professor of urban planning at NYU who is at the forefront of the preservation fight and fears the new equipment won’t be the same.
The plan the community board approved was designed as a compromise for the pull-up bar advocates’ request to preserve the existing equipment and to keep the park open during any necessary construction. The pull-up bars and calisthenics equipment will be replaced with new, high-quality material, according to the parks department's plan, and will be reconfigured in the exact same way as it is now, barring changes that will make the equipment more accessible for all users.
Construction will follow a phased schedule that, according to the community board’s resolution, will keep the outdoor fitness area open while the pool and basketball court are under construction, which is expected to take 15 months.
The resolution states that the fitness area will be closed for an anticipated nine-month construction period, but that the parks department will wait until the nearby East River Park fitness area – which is currently under construction – is reopened, so that locals have an alternative space for exercise.
“We at Parks have a long-standing tradition of soliciting and honoring community input and remain committed to creating an inclusive, fully accessible exercise area at Tompkins Square Park while minimizing disruptions to the fitness community,” Parks Commissioner Tricia Shimamura said in a statement. “We look forward to moving this project forward and working with our partners to enhance this beloved public space.”
Members of Manhattan Community Board 3 did not respond to requests for comment in time for the publication of this article.
The fight over Tompkins Square Park is far from over. The preservationists told Gothamist they are now thinking of creative ways to help the city understand why the pull-up bars and the community that surrounds them are so special.
That includes inviting Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who recently tore his Achilles tendon, to come out to the park for physical therapy.
Accessibility concerns were of top concern for the community board and the parks department when advancing the proposal.
The community board “believes that compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act and other applicable accessibility standards is a baseline, not the limit of public investment, and that NYC should strive to exceed minimum requirements,” the resolution states. “NYC Parks has identified deficiencies involving accessible routes and maneuvering space, overlapping equipment activity and fall zones, signage and maintenance.”
But Coslovsky said that he and other people fighting to preserve the bars agree that the area needs to be made more accessible.
“ That's not only a legal mandate, but a moral imperative. So we are on the same page,” Coslovsky said.
Still, accessibility concerns are being used as an excuse to demolish the existing equipment, he said.
The community board’s approval is just one of many backstops required before the city can begin construction on the park. Those fighting for its preservation said they have no plans to give up.
“ There’s a procedural kind of sequence that Parks has to go through,” Coslovsky said. “Wherever they go, we’re going to be there.”

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/sh.title: Shahzia Sikander Sculpture in St. Louis Generates Protests and Counterprotests
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/sh.author: Andy Battaglia
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/sh.text:
Activists against women’s right to choose in relation to their reproductive rights protested a sculpture by Shahzia Sikander in St. Louis this week, calling for the removal of the 18-foot-tall work titled Witness (2023).
As reported by St. Louis’s First Alert 4, protesters associating the sculpture with pro-choice abortion rights gathered outside the home base of Rung for Women, a nonprofit devoted to women’s career development that hosts it. As the organization describes itself on its website, “Too many women are unfulfilled, unhappy, and underpaid in their jobs, but afraid to take the leap into the unknown. We designed a program to guide motivated women through a process to start working in exciting careers and get paid what they’re worth.”
First Alert 4 quoted an activist with a group called Students for Life America associating Sikander’s sculpture with the overturning of Roe v. Wade in 2022. “Her skirt spells Hava, which is Eve, the first female rebel, to breathe life,” said Reagan Barklage, who related the work to the late US Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg. “It’s just, you do not need to kill your children in order to breathe life. That’s actually the exact opposite of what that means.”
She continued: “We’re alarmed that this is what they’re choosing to use to represent our city. We do not stand for these pro-abortion rights. And we’re trying to stand for women and true empowerment.”
A counterprotester thought otherwise. “We’re here because this organization that’s located on this block has every right to display whatever artwork they want on their own property,” said Leslie Zacks, who spoke of the protest in the context of a recently failed amendment that would have reinstated a near-total abortion ban. “The reality of the situation is that the people in Missouri have twice had the opportunity to voice their preferences with regards to the abortion issue and have made it very, very clear with increasing majority where their preferences are.”
Rung for Women issued a statement saying the organization “respects the right of individuals to express their views about art, including those that differ from our own. We recognize that Witness has prompted strong reactions and respect the sincerely held beliefs of those who have expressed concern. We remain proud to host this work by Shahzia Sikander at Rung for Women.”
The same sculpture by Sikander was the subject of heated protest in Texas in 2024, when it was decried by a group that called it “satanic” before it was to go on view at the University of Houston. After an opening and artist talk related to the work were subsequently canceled, Sikander said, “Art should be about discourse and not censorship. Shame on those that silence artists.”
An attempt by ARTnews to reach the artist was not immediately successful.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Justiça do Trabalho mantém condenação da Volkswagen por escravizar trabalhador em fazenda no Pará
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Diego Junqueira
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
A Volkswagen do Brasil foi condenada nesta terça-feira (24) pela Justiça do Trabalho no Pará, em segunda instância, por submeter o trabalhador Raul Batista de Souza a condições análogas à escravidão na Fazenda Vale do Rio Cristalino, propriedade mantida pela montadora no Sul do Pará nas décadas de 1970 e 1980. A empresa pode recorrer.
A 3ª Turma do TRT-8 (Tribunal Regional do Trabalho da 8ª Região) manteve, por 2 votos a 1, a condenação da montadora em primeira instância, que fixou indenização de R$ 2 milhões por danos morais e existencial. Nos próximos dias, o tribunal vai analisar recursos da empresa em outras duas ações semelhantes, nas quais a companhia também foi condenada em primeira instância.
Entre as décadas de 1970 e 1980, a montadora alemã era a principal sócia da Companhia Vale do Rio Cristalino (CVRC), empresa responsável por uma fazenda de 139 mil hectares comprada com apoio do governo militar, que investiu cerca de R$ 500 milhões em recursos públicos (em valores atuais). Conhecida como Fazenda Volkswagen, a propriedade era dedicada à extração de madeira e à criação de gado.
As ações defendem que a submissão a trabalho escravo é um crime imprescritível, segundo a jurisprudência do TST (Tribunal Superior do Trabalho) e da Corte Interamericana de Direitos Humanos. As ações requerem indenização de R$ 2 milhões por trabalhador.
Nesta terça, o desembargador Marcus Augusto Losada Maia, relator da ação, afirmou que violações como as sofridas pelo trabalhador Raul Batista de Souza não podem ser esquecidas.
“Esse tipo de conduta não pode nem deve ser esquecida, e estará sempre submetido ao crivo da avaliação de cada um sobre o que é humanidade, sobre o que é respeitar a pessoa humana, o que é respeitar o trabalhador e a trabalhadora”, disse. O desembargador também afirmou que cada empresa é responsável pelo que acontece dentro de seus estabelecimentos.
“Dar esse tipo de tratamento a uma pessoa humana é afastar por completo esse sentimento de civilidade”, acrescentou.
Maia votou pela manutenção da condenação da empresa, sendo acompanhado pela desembargadora Ida Selene. O voto divergente foi da desembargadora Mary Anne Acatauassú Camelier Medrado.
“Estou sentindo que a justiça foi feita”, afirmou Raul Batista de Souza à Repórter Brasil em junho, após a decisão de primeira instância. “Espero que fique tudo bem, para tirar um pouco do peso de cima da gente”, disse o ex-trabalhador, que atuou na Fazenda Volkswagen em 1986, quando tinha 17 anos.
Procurada pela Repórter Brasil, a empresa disse que não comenta ações em andamento, mas declarou que atua há 73 anos no Brasil, com “respeito absoluto” às leis brasileiras e aos direitos humanos. “A empresa repudia qualquer forma de trabalho forçado, degradante ou análogo à escravidão e reitera sua dedicação histórica à promoção de um ambiente laboral digno”, diz o posicionamento (leia o texto na íntegra ao final da reportagem).
Essa é a segunda vez que a Volkswagen do Brasil é condenada em segunda instância pelos episódios ocorridos na Fazenda Volkswagen. Em fevereiro, o TRT-8 condenou a montadora em ação civil pública movida pelo MPT (Ministério Público do Trabalho), determinando pagamento de R$ 165 milhões por danos morais coletivos. A condenação se refere à exploração sistemática de centenas de trabalhadores na mesma propriedade rural durante as décadas de 1970 e 1980.
Tanto na ação coletiva quanto nos processos individuais, a Justiça rejeitou os argumentos da montadora de que os crimes estariam prescritos ou de que a empresa seria apenas acionista minoritária.
Entenda o julgamento sobre a Fazenda Volkswagen
Entre as décadas de 1970 e 1980, a montadora alemã foi sócia e administradora da Companhia Vale do Rio Cristalino (CVRC), responsável por uma fazenda de 139 mil hectares no sul do Pará, comprada com apoio do governo militar. A propriedade, na qual foram investidos cerca de R$ 500 milhões em recursos públicos (em valores atuais), era dedicada à extração de madeira e à criação de gado.
Nas ações, os trabalhadores afirmam ter sido submetidos a um sistema de servidão por dívida, no qual eram aliciados por intermediários em outros estados, com promessas de bons salários, para atuarem no Pará com derrubada de mata, montagem do pasto e obras internas.
Ao chegarem à propriedade, os trabalhadores dizem ter sido informados de que o custo da viagem e um suposto adiantamento haviam se convertido em dívidas. Tudo o que consumiam — de alimentos a ferramentas e roupas de trabalho — precisaria ser comprado a preços abusivos na cantina controlada pelos próprios aliciadores, o que fazia a dívida aumentar.
Os trabalhadores alegam nas ações que eram impedidos de sair da fazenda por conta das dívidas crescentes, mesmo quando enfrentavam problemas de saúde, como a malária. Também afirmam terem sido vigiados constantemente por pistoleiros a serviço dos “gatos”, como são conhecidos os intermediários responsáveis pelo recrutamento de mão de obra.
Na decisão de primeira instância, o magistrado rejeitou os argumentos da Volkswagen de prescrição das acusações, em razão de se tratar de “violações gravíssimas aos direitos humanos e à dignidade da pessoa humana”. A decisão reconhece, nos casos, a servidão por dívida, a jornada exaustiva, a restrição da liberdade de locomoção e as condições degradantes de trabalho e alojamento.
No processo, a Volkswagen alegou que não teria responsabilidade sobre os episódios, pois seria apenas acionista da empresa, e não sua controladora, e também porque os acordos dos trabalhadores eram com os intermediários, que eram contratados para atuarem na derrubada de floresta e na abertura de pastos.
Para o juiz, contudo, documentos internos da empresa acessados durante o processo confirmaram que a Volkswagen do Brasil era não apenas acionária da fazenda, como sua gestora. “A própria ata de instalação registra a posse de dirigentes diretamente vinculados à Volkswagen nos principais cargos executivos da CVRC”, diz a sentença.
“Mais do que simples aporte financeiro, a documentação evidencia efetiva participação da reclamada na constituição, administração e direção do empreendimento agropecuário”, escreveu o magistrado. Segundo a decisão de primeira instância, a empresa teria se beneficiado economicamente da exploração dos trabalhadores.
Ainda de acordo com o magistrado, “a robustez da prova oral produzida nestes autos é reforçada por expressivo conjunto de registros documentais históricos contemporâneos aos fatos”, incluindo “radiotelegramas e comunicações oficiais encaminhados por agentes públicos a autoridades do Estado brasileiro, noticiando a existência de trabalho escravo, retenção de trabalhadores e servidão por dívida na Fazenda Vale do Rio Cristalino.”
Posicionamento da Volkswagen do Brasil:
“A Volkswagen do Brasil não se manifestará sobre discussões judiciais em andamento. Adicionalmente, a empresa ressalta que, com um legado de 73 anos, a Volkswagen do Brasil reafirma seu compromisso permanente com o respeito absoluto à Constituição Federal, às leis brasileiras e aos princípios internacionais de direitos humanos, que orientam sua atuação como uma das maiores empregadoras do país. A empresa repudia qualquer forma de trabalho forçado, degradante ou análogo à escravidão e reitera sua dedicação histórica à promoção de um ambiente laboral digno, ético e responsável.”

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Judge Tosses Lawsuit Against Mamdani’s Signature NYC Rent Freeze
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Samantha Maldonado
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
Rent freezes for stabilized tenants across roughly 1 million New York City apartments will remain in place after a Manhattan judge on Wednesday dismissed a lawsuit brought by landlords challenging the policy.
The decision marks a major win for Mayor Zohran Mamdani, one of whose signature campaign promises was to freeze rents for stabilized units as an affordability measure. Neither City Hall nor a spokesperson for the plaintiffs immediately responded to requests for comment. It was not clear if the plaintiffs will appeal.
In his ruling, Manhattan Supreme Court Judge Brendan Lantry called Mamdani’s campaign pledge to freeze rents “reckless and irresponsible” because the mayor cannot unilaterally do so. But Lantry wrote that the plaintiffs failed to establish the freeze enacted by the city’s Rent Guidelines Board in June was “unreasonable, arbitrary or capricious.”
The judge said the freeze, which affects one- and two-year stabilized leases and took effect on Oct. 1, “has a rational basis and must therefore be upheld as valid.” Still, he warned the policy could negatively affect the residential real estate industry.
A group of several landlords, who are represented by former Mayor Eric Adams’ first deputy Randy Mastro, sued in July to try to overturn the freeze. Pointing to Mamdani’s campaign pledge, they alleged the Rent Guidelines Board, which sets allowable rent increases for stabilized units, “ran a sham process with a predetermined outcome.” 
Throughout the lawsuit, the board maintained its independence from City Hall and said it voted to freeze rents after examining official data. Three previous rent freezes were in place under Mayor Bill de Blasio.
While Mamdani could not direct a freeze, he appointed six of the board’s nine members when he took office. Adams appointed three of the members, including one who resigned just hours before the board voted on how much stabilized landlords could raise rents.
Tenants and some housing advocates have long said many stabilized tenants cannot afford to keep up with rent increases.
Landlords and housing analysts have argued rents must increase so owners can keep up with rising operating costs, including for insurance and fuel.
Sumathy Kumar, director of the advocacy group New York State Tenant Bloc, celebrated the judge’s decision.
“Today’s decision affirms that tenants won the rent freeze fairly and secures relief for millions of tenants,” she said in a statement.

https://www.propublica.org/article/fda-p.title: FDA to Expand Prescription Drug Testing After ProPublica Revealed Safety Concerns
https://www.propublica.org/article/fda-p.author: Naisha Roy
https://www.propublica.org/article/fda-p.text:
The Food and Drug Administration will test more prescription drugs for impurities and other dangerous quality lapses under an expanded program described by safety experts as a critical step to better protecting America’s drug supply.
About 90% of prescriptions in the United States are for generic drugs, many manufactured thousands of miles away in countries that include India and China. Until now, the FDA has only periodically tested a sampling of those drugs to see if they were safe or worked as effectively as the brand-name medications they are meant to replicate.
Last week, the FDA announced it will test more often and identify poorly performing drugs for further study.
The agency said it will buy the medications from retail pharmacies and wholesale distributors, but it did not say how many drugs it plans to test or how frequently. A spokesperson did not answer questions about how the FDA would select drugs for testing or how it would hold manufacturers accountable for inferior products, beyond posting the results on its website. Still, drug-safety experts said the expansion helps address long-standing concerns that some suppliers sacrifice quality to keep costs low — and that the FDA has for years looked the other way.
“All drugs, regardless of where they are manufactured, must meet the same FDA standards for safety, effectiveness and quality,” the FDA spokesperson told ProPublica.
A ProPublica investigation last year found the agency routinely relied on the drug companies themselves to do their own testing even as doctors, researchers and the Department of Defense warned that essential medications were contaminated or ineffective. On its website, the FDA said it has relied on a “more targeted, risk-based” approach to testing since 2018, choosing samples of drugs that have safety, effectiveness or quality concerns. The agency publicly reports the results on its website and notes that a majority of the tested drugs meet its standards.
ProPublica, however, found the agency for years failed to regularly test both the generics that have worried outside experts and drugs coming from factories that amassed so many serious quality and safety violations they were ultimately banned from the U.S. market. ProPublica later used FDA data to create Rx Inspector, a first-of-its-kind tool that allows consumers and doctors to look up the inspection records of the factories where more than 40,000 generic drugs are made.
Researchers have repeatedly urged the FDA to test more often. In fiscal year 2025, the FDA reported testing 46 different drugs, and for 29 of those drugs, the agency only tested one manufacturer. All but one passed every test.
The FDA’s new testing regime is “a huge validation of the research that we’ve been doing raising concerns about the quality of generic drugs,” Dr. Kevin Schulman, a professor of medicine and health policy at Stanford University, said of the FDA’s new testing program. “This is a great effort on their part.”
In February, senators also introduced a bill targeting transparency in the drug supply chain process, in part because of similar public concerns.
In response to questions about how it would decide which drugs to sample and how results would drive future enforcement, the FDA spokesperson said the initiative will “help the FDA identify potential drug quality issues faster and will provide more information the agency can use to decide if further action is needed.”
Experts say they ultimately hope the FDA’s program will work alongside independent testers to shift the generic drug market to be competitive on quality rather than price. While the agency can focus on weeding out the worst actors, independent labs can test manufacturers against one another to find the most effective products, said retired Col. Vic Suarez, a former medical supply-chain commander. A similar system is already used at the Department of Defense.
“It’s an important thing because they will probably catch extreme violators of regulatory standards, so that’s a good thing,” Suarez said. “But you also need to have a complementary system where you’re actually raising the bar.”
ProPublica previously engaged an independent lab, Valisure, to test several generic versions of three of the most prescribed drugs in the United States and in two cases identified irregularities that experts said could compromise their effectiveness.
“I think, high level, the idea that we should be doing more testing is fantastic,” said David Light, the co-founder of Valisure. “I think there’s so much growing energy behind that.”

https://taz.de/Bill-Kaulitz-stellt-Sachb.title: Bill Kaulitz vs. Ordnungsamt Leipzig: Eine Entschuldigung wäre angebracht
https://taz.de/Bill-Kaulitz-stellt-Sachb.author: Carolina Schwarz
https://taz.de/Bill-Kaulitz-stellt-Sachb.text:
Bill Kaulitz vs. Ordnungsamt Leipzig : Eine Entschuldigung wäre angebracht
Es ist das Markenzeichen der Kaulitz-Brüder, arrogant und abgehoben und doch irgendwie charmant zu sein. Aber der Vorfall in Leipzig war eins drüber.
A ls Bill Kaulitz einmal gefragt wurde, ob er nicht Lust hätte bei der Datingshow „The Bachelor“ mitzumachen, verneinte er. Die ausgefallenen Dates mit Helikopterflügen seien vielleicht für die Kandidaten etwas Besonderes, aber für ihn sei das Alltag, erklärte er sinngemäß. Ein anderes Mal sagt er im Podcast „Kaulitz Hills“ zu seinem Bruder Tom, dass er es ekelig fände, wenn jemand nicht konsequent jede Woche seine Bettwäsche wechsele. Dass die meisten Menschen aber keine Haushaltshilfe haben, die das mal eben übernimmt, schien er in dem Moment nicht mitzudenken.
Bill Kaulitz ist arrogant und abgehoben. Und genau das macht seinen Charme aus. Während man es anderen Superreichen missgönnt, wenn sie im Überfluss leben, freuen sich die Fans für den Tokio-Hotel-Sänger. Der fliegt im Heli durch die Welt, badet mit Champagnerglas im neu angelegten Pool in Los Angeles und lässt sich von Assistent Daniel die Hermès-Taschen durch die Stadt schleppen. Mit Bodenständigkeit hat das nichts mehr zu tun.
Seine Fangemeinde stört das nicht – im Gegenteil. Vielleicht, weil man den Kaulitz-Brüdern, die in finanziell schwierigeren Verhältnissen in einem Dorf in Sachsen-Anhalt aufgewachsen sind, den Reichtum gönnt. Vielleicht, weil sie nicht wie Kanzler Merz so tun, als seien sie Teil der Mittelschicht, sondern einfach zugeben können, dass sie reich sind und verdammt gerne Geld ausgeben. Oder vielleicht macht es einfach Spaß, ihnen im Podcast, ihrer Netflix-Show und bei Instagram dabei zuzusehen, wie sie ein abgedrehtes Leben führen.
Sicherlich ist die Antwort eine Mischung aus allen drei Vermutungen. Feststeht: Bill und Tom Kaulitz wissen, wie man unterhält. Dass es wichtig ist, sich über andere lustig zu machen und noch wichtiger, dass man über sich selbst lachen kann. Im Regelfall funktioniert die Gratwanderung des guten Geschmacks bei den Brüdern gut, sie stellen nur die in die Öffentlichkeit, die eh schon da sind. Bis jetzt – bei der Tokio-Hotel-Arena-Tour durch Europa haben sie einen Menschen an den Pranger gestellt, der es nicht verdient hat und keine Person des öffentlichen Lebens ist.
Wer ist hier der Spielverderber
Es war beim Konzert in Leipzig als Bill Kaulitz einen Sachbearbeiter des Ordnungsamtes namentlich genannt und ausbuhen lassen hat. Er machte ihn dafür verantwortlich, dass die Band einen Teil ihrer Pyrotechnik nicht abbrennen lassen durfte. Schon okay, sich darüber zu ärgern, wenn Special Effekts, wie eine sprühende Feuerwerksfontäne aus Tom Kaulitz Gitarre, verboten sind.
Weniger verständlich ist es, dass der Frontsänger vor 10.000 Fans einen Sachbearbeiter in die Öffentlichkeit zieht, ihm unterstellt er habe ein Scheißleben und solle besser seinen Job verlieren. So viel Verständnis für die Lebensrealität der anderen erwartet man dann auch von einem Superstar. Dass er anerkennt, was es für Konsequenzen für einen einzelnen Menschen haben kann, wenn sein Job und sein Ruf öffentlich angegriffen werden.
Die Stadt Leipzig reagierte prompt, Bürgermeister Burkhard Jung verurteilte die „Grenzverletzung“ durch Bill Kaulitz stark und forderte mehr Rückhalt für Beschäftigte im öffentlichen Dienst. Die Stadt kündigte eine umfassende juristische Prüfung an. Und auch in den Medien ist die Empörung groß.
Manches wird dabei etwas aufgebauscht. Bislang hat die Stadt Leipzig weder wie angekündigt Kontakt zum Management von Tokio Hotel aufgenommen noch Anzeige erstattet. Und auch über einen Shitstorm gegen den Sachbearbeiter, wie manch einer es suggeriert, ist nichts bekannt. Das sagte die Stadt der taz auf Anfrage.
Ernsthafte Konsequenzen wird Bill Kaulitz Auftritt wohl also nicht haben. Eine echte Entschuldigung wäre trotz allem angebracht. Bislang passiert eher das Gegenteil. In der aktuellen Podcast-Folge von „Kaulitz Hills“ treten die Brüder nach und ziehen noch einmal namentlich über den Sachbearbeiter her. Vielleicht warten sie mit ihrer Entschuldigung aber auf die ganz große Bühne: Als Moderatorenduo bei „Wetten, dass..“ nächste Woche. Wie man einen großen Auftritt hinlegt, wissen die beiden ja.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/gta-rockstar.title: Grand Theft Auto Grew Up. America Didn’t.
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/gta-rockstar.author: Ryan Zickgraf
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/gta-rockstar.text:
Grand Theft Auto Grew Up. America Didn’t.
The United States under Donald Trump has turned into a parody of itself, descending further and further into juvenilia. Grand Theft Auto VI, meanwhile, has turned more darkly serious and morally complex.
Early in Grand Theft Auto VI, you and your girlfriend drive to the local branch of Fleeca bank on an errand that, by the franchise’s standards, is something of a novelty. Your job is not to rob a bank but to open an account at one.
Lucia Caminos, fresh out of prison, needs somewhere to deposit her check from her mandatory reentry job, and since her boyfriend, Jason Duval, has made it this far in life without a checking account, they’d like to open one. But after a quick financial review, the manager wonders whether they’ve considered maybe downloading an app instead, and you leave empty-handed.
There are any number of teenagers who could, with a few shakes of a PlayStation 5 controller, get these two out of a police pursuit and across three counties of South Florida without putting a scratch on the car. None, however, can get Jason approved for a checking account. As in real life, the credit score — not brute force or cunning — is the god of this universe.
It’s a telling moment, because the Grand Theft Auto (GTA) that I grew up with was two things at once. It was an adolescent male power fantasy, a sandbox where you could steal a sports car, mow down a crowd, and outrun the police with no lasting consequence beyond a few hundred dollars docked from your wallet. And it was a South Park–style satire of American life, all fake radio ads for penis pills and televangelists and talk-radio cranks. The jokes were broad, and the violence was cartoonish, and the upshot was that nothing meant anything, so everything was permitted. GTA III let you hire a prostitute and beat her to get your money back. GTA V let you torture a man with a car battery and then play golf. It all had a weightless quality.
Yet in the thirteen years since Grand Theft Auto V came out, something peculiar has happened: Rockstar, the studio that produces the game, and its subject have switched places. The United States has turned into a parody of itself, while GTA VI has turned more darkly serious. It plays less like a theme park and more like prestige television, something like HBO’s The Wire or Task crossed with It’s Florida, Man.
In VI, you alternate between the two leads: Jason Duval, an Army veteran doing errands for drug runners, and Lucia Caminos, his girlfriend and partner in crime, recently out of prison. Their relationship is the spine of the game, and a score is kept. If Jason behaves like a sociopath, Lucia notices. Push it far enough, and the game will decide you are, in its own words, “Irredeemable,” and you will be saddled with the suboptimal happy-never-after ending.
Protagonists for the 2020s
Perhaps even the idea of a happy ending is laughable. Jason and Lucia are not mafia dons or retired bank robbers in shiny new Miami mansions; they are among South Florida’s ever-growing lumpenproletariat, Karl Marx’s term for the drifting, disorganized underclass that sits below the working class and outside its institutions. They’re the deinstitutionalized, dealigned masses who hold no union card, no pension, no political loyalty, and often no permanent address. Together they must navigate the gig-work and shadow economy with one hand on their guns and one eye over their shoulders for a probation officer who could help take their young son away from them forever into the foster care system.
So, yes, you can still be a monster, and there are plenty of mindless action sequences and shoot-outs. But they’re tempered by real-world obligations (your son’s crib isn’t going to build itself) and the moral weight of your misdeeds.
Likewise, the world of Leonida, Rockstar’s faux Florida, is much more than a virtual crime laboratory. For twenty-five years, GTA’s pedestrians were furniture with legs. They walked, they screamed, they died. In GTA VI, if you accidentally bump into a man outside a gas station, he’ll square up and may throw a punch. Cut someone off on the highway, and they’ll chase you down in their own bout of road rage. Try to make small talk with a stranger, and there’s a decent chance she’ll tell you to go to hell — or worse — because in a place like this, hardly anyone talks to strangers.
The city is no longer a collection of victims waiting for you to beat up or exploit them. It’s a collection of people with their own short fuses, and many of them are as broke, as frightened, and as intoxicated as you are.
Because the city seems to have a soul, however shrunken, it’s striking what isn’t in Leonida. There are no churches, an observation by British critic Peter Hitchens, who once called GTA the Devil’s Bible. There are also no schools, no community centers, no food pantries, no nonprofits. To be fair to Rockstar, there were never caring institutions of any kind in Grand Theft Auto; the series has always been a portrait of America with the heart surgically removed. But in the older games, the absence read as a joke, a deliberate cartoon of a godless consumer wasteland.
Here, in a world rendered with photographic fidelity, that absence feels like a statement. Every building you can enter exists to extract something from you — your money, your labor, your time. Pawnshops, payday lenders, strip clubs, car washes that launder cash. The only god in Leonida is the market, and you are a free agent navigating its moods, which are capricious and rarely in your favor.
For half a century, Florida has been where America goes to see its own fever dreams, from glamorous to gonzo. In the 1980s, it was cocaine-cowboy Miami: Scarface and Miami Vice, pastels and shoulder holsters, an image so seductive that Rockstar lifted it wholesale for Vice City in 2002. Later came Carl Hiaasen’s crooked developers and his hit man with a Weed Eater for a hand, Tom Wolfe’s Back to Blood, Harmony Korine’s Spring Breakers, the “Florida Man” headline construction, and Tiger King. From high culture to low, it all seemed insane and fun.
Not here. There were stretches early on when GTA VI made me queasy. Rockstar doesn’t open with the postcard Florida of South Beach sunsets or champagne-soaked nightlife, but with the ugly, uncinematic Florida: trash-strewn trailer parks, run-down motels with hourly rates, drug dealers too strung out to count their own money, and skeezy strip club owners who talk to Lucia like she could be part of the inventory. It’s Sean Baker’s The Florida Project, minus the Magic Kingdom glowing on the horizon. I’ve played every GTA since the series went 3D, and this is the first one in which I occasionally wanted a shower, as if the scum from the swamps I was wading through had rubbed off on me.
We’re at a strange moment in the culture wars. In 2026, the people defending Grand Theft Auto VI’s honor are largely progressives — even though one of its leads is a violent white man devoted to his straight, monogamous relationship — while it’s MAGA types who seem to want more anarchy and amorality in their games.
For a quarter-century, hating on Grand Theft Auto was one of the few things Washington could agree on. In 2005, Hillary Clinton demanded a federal investigation after the Hot Coffee scandal in GTA: San Andreas. After Sandy Hook, Joe Biden called video game executives in for a meeting. In 2018, after Parkland, Donald Trump held his own meeting: “The video games, the movies, the internet stuff is so violent. It’s so incredible,” he said. A year later, after El Paso, he blamed “gruesome and grisly video games” for glorifying violence.
Blaming Rockstar Games was once the bipartisan comfort food of American politics: cheap, filling, and nobody ever had to touch a gun law.
So you’d expect Grand Theft Auto VI, the biggest entertainment launch of the decade, to set off the mother of all moral panics. The timing could hardly be better: Republicans were just routed in the midterms and lost both chambers of Congress. Why not change the subject to a video game where you can rob a liquor store in a neon-soaked Florida?
Instead, we’ve mostly heard crickets, with a couple of notable outliers. Tennessee Congressman Tim Burchett told TMZ the game is “more of a how-to video” for stealing cars and shooting cops and said those who let their kids play it are bad parents. But he immediately added, “We’re not going to legislate it.” On Fox & Friends Weekend, Rachel Campos-Duffy said she was “gonna push back a little,” because she didn’t think the game was good for our culture and asked whether Lucia, one of the coprotagonists, was “the hooker.” (Surprise: sex workers are gone from this version.) Fox News Digital’s big GTA story last week was about the dangers of sleep deprivation from playing games all night.
Liberals? They gave up the video game hate beat years ago. Since the Gamergate wars of the 2010s, progressive game criticism has mostly asked who gets to be the hero and how women are depicted. How many cops you can run over hasn’t been the question, and a game with a Latina colead has largely inoculated itself on that front.
So why has the Right gone soft? Perhaps because the Trump White House is like a parody that Rockstar’s writers’ room would have rejected in 2013 for being too on the nose.
The day before GTA VI launched, the official White House account posted a montage of Donald Trump striding past fighter jets, rendered in the game’s signature font, set to Dire Straits’ “Money for Nothing” and captioned “WELCOME TO MAGA CITY XLVII.” This wasn’t shocking, because for more than a year the White House’s social media team has embraced a strategy of appealing to gamer bros.
Consider the back catalog. In September 2025, the account cut footage of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrests to the Pokémon cartoon’s opening theme, then closed on fake trading cards bearing detainees’ faces under the tagline “Gotta Catch ’Em All.” When the bombs started falling on Iran in March, the White House opened its war montage with a Call of Duty killstreak animation, as if the strikes were a reward for thirty kills without dying. Then, in September this year, came Arcade.gov, a set of retro browser games in which you can build the wall and deport people.
The Pokémon Company objected; Halo’s cocreator said a Halo-themed ICE recruitment post made him sick. The White House’s response? More or less its mission statement: “Nowhere in the Constitution does it say we can’t post banger memes.”
That line tracks with an administration that has governed as if life were a nihilistic M-rated game, with the president living out an adolescent male power fantasy: parading young blonde female aides on his arms, staging an Ultimate Fighting Championship fight card on the South Lawn for his eightieth birthday, and floating Nicki Minaj as press secretary after the previous one lasted five days in the job. Alligator Alcatraz might sound like a sick joke from GTA, but indeed, it was all too real: a dehumanizing makeshift immigration detention center in the Florida Everglades, complete with Florida Republicans selling branded merch to chuds.
Even outside of Mar-a-Lago, there are signs everywhere that America has hit a midlife crisis, descending into juvenilia — or, worse yet, psychosis. Grown men trade cartoon apes or dogs on the blockchain and lose their savings, while Hunter Biden gets in on the action with a $LAPTOP coin; bets on Jesus Christ returning for the Rapture in 2026 on Polymarket turn out to be a better wager. Even Las Vegas is dying, because everywhere in America is becoming like Las Vegas, a casino and a vape pen in every pocket.
One of our nation’s biggest young celebrities, sadly, is Clavicular, a twenty-year-old famous for smashing his own face with a hammer to “improve” his bone structure. Out on bail for rape charges, which he denies, stemming from an alleged assault shortly after a live stream, he’s complained about GTA VI being too “cucked” because it wants you to be kind to your virtual girlfriend.
The politicians and pundits worried about GTA corrupting America have it the wrong way around. These days, the game is the one that should worry about being corrupted by us.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Preserving Henry Ford’s failed Amazonian empire
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Gabriella Angeleti
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Deep in the Amazon Rainforest, in the Brazilian state of Pará, lies the dilapidated settlement of Fordlândia. A once bustling—albeit highly exploitative—village, it was established by the US industrialist Henry Ford in the 1920s. Fordlândia’s sole purpose was to serve as a rubber-tapping enterprise that would provide materials for the Ford Motor Company. But less than a decade after its founding, the rubber crops failed. With the development of synthetic rubber following close behind, Ford abandoned the project in 1945, and the village along the Tapajós River fell into severe disrepair.
Earlier this year, almost a century after Fordlândia was built, a federal court ruled that it must be protected as a heritage site under the Brazilian constitution. Local and national authorities have until the end of this month to come up with a conservation plan.
Ford’s company originally acquired the land for what would become Fordlândia in 1927. He envisioned building a Midwestern-style village as a hub for latex extraction, supplying materials for his factories in Michigan. Ford hoped to upend the dominance of British-controlled rubber plantations in Southeast Asia, which had left US manufacturers dependent on foreign suppliers.
Fordlândia, beyond giving the Ford Motor Company control over its supply of raw materials, was imagined as a self-sufficient settlement for around 10,000 people in the Amazon. Ford himself viewed Fordlândia as a sociological experiment intended to “Americanise” the local population, although the tycoon never visited his dystopian village. Workers there, many of them Indigenous people and migrants from northeastern Brazil, endured cultural subjugation and often faced dangerous conditions—including having to work through the hottest part of the day. Hundreds of people died during the short-lived project.
Workers organised a mutiny in 1930 after unreasonable restrictions were imposed in Fordlândia, including the prohibition of alcohol and tobacco, as well as the requirement of US customs like square dancing and a diet of wholewheat bread, brown rice, oatmeal and canned peaches. Shortly afterwards there was a full-scale riot, in which workers chased their American managers and the village cook into the jungle. The Brazilian army was brought in to restore order. The company subsequently fired a number of workers and appointed a new manager to complete Fordlândia’s infrastructure. (An agreement on serving different food to the workers was also reached.)
Ford’s social experiment unfolded alongside agricultural problems. Without the consultation of local experts, the rubber trees had been planted too close together. This made them vulnerable to disease and pests, and the growing conditions along the river were unsuitable. In 1933, at the recommendation of the American plant pathologist James Robert Weir, a second plantation was established downstream at Belterra, where conditions were more appropriate. Although it fared better than Fordlândia, production remained costly and it never became commercially viable.
No usable latex was ever produced in Fordlândia. After investing millions of dollars with no return, Ford sold the land back to the Brazilian government. The population dropped by more than 90% in the following years, but squatters and families moved back into the decaying structures in the 2000s. Around 3,000 people live in Fordlândia today, even as the village remains unconnected to paved roads.
A unique historical moment
The federal process for the designation of Fordlândia as a heritage site has been unresolved since the 1990s, when the move was first suggested by local advocates. In 2015, Brazil’s federal public prosecutor’s office filed a lawsuit stating that the site had “unquestionable” cultural value. In 2024, the National Institute of Historic and Artistic Heritage (Iphan) countered that Fordlândia lacked the criteria required for federal heritage listing, pointing to the loss of its original characteristics and the site’s deteriorated condition.
But in May 2026 a federal court ruled that, even without formal heritage status, the site should be protected. This decision was based on a 1988 constitutional article that mandates the conservation of both material and immaterial assets connected to Brazilian communities. The court added that uncertainty over ownership of the site had been used repeatedly as justification for inaction, and that the state of Pará and the municipality of Aveiro (which administers Fordlândia) had previously signed an agreement to begin conservation measures that never materialised. It also alleged that some interventions had been carried out without authorisation.
The court ruled that Iphan must now work with the state and municipality to deliver a plan by the end of November 2026, outlining the responsibilities of each government entity and the needs of each site in Fordlândia—including emergency measures for structures at imminent risk. Once approved, conservation work must begin within 30 days. If deadlines are not met, the court will impose a daily fine of $2,000 (10,000 reais) on the federal government and Iphan, and a $1,000 (5,000 reais) fine on the state and municipality. Iphan must also begin the administrative process to recognise Fordlândia as a heritage site.
In a statement to The Art Newspaper, a spokesperson for Iphan says the agency does not comment on ongoing legal proceedings. It remains unclear if Iphan plans to counter the court’s decision. “In May 2024, Iphan’s cultural-heritage advisory council denied Fordlândia’s designation as Brazilian cultural heritage,” the spokesperson says. “Iphan reiterates that it remains committed to the preservation of Brazilian cultural heritage, as mandated by the constitution.”
The sites to be reviewed include the former Fordlândia Hospital, designed by the Detroit architect Albert Kahn; the long-abandoned industrial and port warehouses; the houses of the American Village, where the company’s American managers lived; the workers’ village; the Henry Ford School; the Cine Patinha, a cinema whose roof has recently collapsed; and a convent on a cliff overlooking the Tapajós River, built in the post-Ford era and active until the early 2010s. All these structures have been exposed to the Amazon’s heat, humidity and heavy rainfall for years.
TripAdvisor-approved
Fordlândia remains highly remote, receiving few outside visitors and requiring a minimum six-hour trip to reach via high-speed boat. Still, there is evidence that intrepid travellers have made the journey. A company specialising in tours of the Amazon is currently offering a five-day visit to the region, including a stop in Fordlândia, for approximately $3,000 (16,000 reais) per person. Reviews for “Fordlândia Ghost Town” on TripAdvisor average 4.7 out of 5 stars, with one reviewer in 2016 calling the site “historical, magical and melancholic”, and another saying it tells a story of “hubris, determination, paternalism and ultimately failure”.
Although Fordlândia is unlikely to be commercialised as a tourist destination, the village’s surviving infrastructure has come to represent an unusual and failed attempt to Americanise and industrialise the Amazon. The remnants of the settlement also tell the story of the Brazilian workers who lived there, and those who have continued to inhabit it. The Brazilian government maintains that Fordlândia has “unquestionable historical, cultural and architectural value”, and that it represents “an American attempt to break the British monopoly on rubber and bring modern infrastructure to the middle of the Amazon”.
