Das deutsche Biathlon-Team will die Handbremse lösen
Beim Saison-Auftakt in Kontiolahti wollen die deutschen Biathletinnen mit ihrer neuen Bundestrainerin den langen Weg zurück zu alter Stärke antreten.
Neue Damen-Bundestrainerin, neuer Sportdirektor, neues Glück? Das deutsche Biathlon wagt nach der schlechtesten Olympia-Bilanz seit 50 Jahren mit nur einer Medaille im Februar in Antholz den Neuanfang. Sportdirektor Bernd Eisenbichler, der die Nachfolge des zum Biathlon-Weltverband IBU abgewanderten Felix Bitterling als Sportdirektor angetreten hat, möchte vor der am Donnerstag im finnischen Kontiolahti beginnenden Weltcup-Saison keine großen Zielvorgaben machen: »Am Anfang geht es darum, wieder Selbstverständnis und Selbstvertrauen nach der letzten Saison zu entwickeln.« Aber natürlich sei es der Anspruch, vor allem im Nationencup und den Staffeln ums Podium mitzulaufen.
Ein Selbstläufer wird das nicht. Die Männer stecken unter Regie des auch erst seit Februar 2025 amtierenden Cheftrainers Tobias Reiter mitten im Generationswechsel. Führungsfigur Philipp Nawrath wird bald 34, auch Philipp Horn ist bereits 32 Jahre alt. Nach einigen Jahren mit latenten Nachwuchsproblemen gibt es inzwischen aber wieder einige verheißungsvolle Talente im deutschen Team: Mit Fabian Kaskel (22) und Elias Seidl (22) messen sich zwei davon beim Weltcup-Auftakt ab Donnerstag mit der Weltelite.
Flungers schwierige Mission
Bei den deutschen Frauen hat mit der inzwischen schwangeren Franziska Preuß die Führungsfigur der vergangenen Jahre ihre Karriere beendet. Sie studiert Architektur in Rosenheim und erwartet mit ihrem Lebenspartner, dem einstigen Top-Biathleten Simon Schempp, ein Kind. Nur drei Podestplätze holten die deutschen Frauen im vergangenen Winter – mit diesem schwierigen Erbe hat Sandra Flunger ihre Mission im deutschen Biathlon-Team angetreten. Die 44 Jahre alte Österreicherin soll die deutschen Frauen als Nachfolgerin von Kristian Mehringer auf dem Bundestrainerposten zurück zu alter Stärke führen. Eine schwierige Aufgabe, schließlich sind die Zeiten deutscher Seriensiegerinnen wie Magdalena Neuner und Laura Dahlmeier längst vergangen.
Einen Vorteil hat die schwierige Gemengelage vor dem Weltcup-Auftakt in Finnland für Flunger: Die Erwartungen sind moderat. Genau wie Sportdirektor Eisenbichler versucht auch Flunger, die Latte für ihre deutschen Frauen möglichst niedrig zu legen. »Ich glaube, es wäre falsch, jetzt etwas Großes auszurufen«, sagt die Frau, die vor allem durch ihre achtjährige erfolgreiche Arbeit in der Schweiz in den Fokus des deutschen Teams gerückt ist. Zum Schluss war sie im Nachbarland Cheftrainerin für Männer und Frauen. Als deutsche Bundestrainerin wartet nun in einer der auch wirtschaftlich wichtigsten Biathlon-Nationen eine Aufgabe in einer viel größeren Dimension auf sie. Finanzielle Möglichkeiten, öffentliche Aufmerksamkeit und die Zahl der Athletinnen sind hier viel größer, als sie es zuvor in der Schweiz erlebt hat.
Keine Angst vor Fehlern
Die 44-Jährige ist die Aufgabe mit der ihr eigenen Zurückhaltung, aber auch Konsequenz angegangen. Als eines der Hauptziele hatte sie mit Blick auf die latenten Probleme am Schießstand angegeben, die »Handbremse« bei ihren Frauen lösen zu wollen. Die neue Cheftrainerin forderte mehr Mut und Geschwindigkeit beim Schießen ein: »Angst vor Fehlern zu haben, ist nicht der richtige Weg.« Als neue Führungsfigur in ihrem Team nach dem Abschied von Franziska Preuß kristallisiert sich die erfahrene Janina Hettich-Walz heraus, die bei den Deutschen Meisterschaften gleich dreimal Gold gewann.
Flunger bewundert, wie die 30-jährige Hettich-Walz ihre Mutterrolle mit dem Sport verbindet. Die zweite routinierte Athletin Vanessa Voigt (29) bereitete sich auf eigenen Wunsch abseits der Mannschaft auf die Weltcup-Saison vor. Beide Leistungsträgerinnen loben den Weg, den Flunger im Team eingeschlagen hat. Voigt findet es gut, dass eine Frau an der Spitze des Teams stehe, die eine andere Ansprache als ihr Vorgänger habe. Hettich-Walz glaubt, dass Flunger die großen Potenziale im deutschen Team hervorheben könne.
Ein prominenter Name fehlt
An Talenten mangelt es bei den deutschen Frauen tatsächlich nicht. In Flungers erstem Weltcup-Aufgebot sind vier der sechs Athletinnen um die fünfmalige Junioren-Weltmeisterin Julia Tannheimer Jahrgang 2002 oder jünger. Allerdings fehlt im Youngster-Quartett ein prominenter Name: Die 22 Jahre alte Selina Grotian, die bereits einen Weltcup und zwei WM-Medaillen gewonnen hat, darf nur im zweitklassigen IBU-Cup starten. Ein Zeichen, dass bei der schwierigen Mission der neuen Cheftrainerin nur Leistung und keine alten Verdienste zählen.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.title: There’s Nothing “Crazy” About Wanting to Abolish Prisons
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.author: Dave Zirin
https://www.thenation.com/article/societ.text:
There’s Nothing “Crazy” About Wanting to Abolish Prisons
A recent New York Times article argued that “wokeness,” including calls for prison abolition, is a political liability. That’s simply not the case.
There’s Nothing “Crazy” About Wanting to Abolish Prisons
A recent “New York Times” article argued that “wokeness,” including calls for prison abolition, is a political liability. That’s simply not the case.
In a recent op-ed for The New York Times, Jacobin editor Meagan Day offered a pointed critique of the ways that identity politics can be weaponized to muzzle dissent. On its face, this could have been a valuable contribution to larger conversations about how the powerful co-opt anti-oppression language to silence and discipline their critics. Instead, Day punches down.
In his indispensable 2022 book Elite Capture: How the Powerful Took Over Identity Politics (And Everything Else), Olúfẹ́mi O. Táíwò explains how those in power deploy the politics of identity to entrench their own class or managerial positions, a method we have seen utilized in breathtakingly cynical fashion with the recent push to secure the speaker of the House position for Representative Hakeem Jeffries. According to Al Sharpton, Van Jones, and Jeffries himself—not to mention centrist fossils like Paul Begala and James Carville—opposing Jeffries is “racism of the left,” an accusation that undercuts any principled objections to his centrist politics, his commitment to funding the war on Iran, and his fealty to Israel and AIPAC.
It would be extremely valuable to introduce the concept of “elite capture” to a New York Times audience. But that’s not the op-ed Day wrote. Instead, starting with a headline that could comfortably appear as a chyron on Newsmax—“Woke 1 Was Crazy—and It’s Still Here”—the article rehashes what I’m sure Day would agree has been a well-trod argument across the political spectrum: that the “wokeness” of the “crazy” left is pushing people away from progressive politics. (Before reckoning with Day’s argument, it’s worth saying that her pejorative use of the word “woke”—a linguistic attack coined by the nationalist right to mock the phrase “stay woke” in the Black community—is an unfortunate choice.)
In the op-ed, Day argues that for democratic socialists to move forward, they must reject “wokeness,” which she argues has devolved into a “crusade against personal transgressions” built on the performance of empty absurdities. She explains the “crazy” of “wokeness” by telling the story of an almost-two-decade old experience she had in 2009 at Oberlin College, involving confusion over whether a frat was throwing a racist party and the ensuing uproar. What her disdain for these overzealous, painfully earnest college students (and don’t we want our college students to be overzealous and painfully earnest?) has to do with the actual titanic challenge plaguing the left—namely, how to organize this generational thirst for socialist politics—is left unclear.
In its last paragraphs, the op-ed gets at what seems to be its real intent. Here, Day calls for the “woke” brigade to stop attacking those in the DSA who say that the only way to build a mass party is to accept some degree of law-and-order politics—an idea that Day and other DSA thought leaders are calling “carceral minimalism.”
“Carceral minimalism” is a pithy label for a socialist position that makes strategic peace with the prison-industrial complex. Instead of advancing the century-old socialist principle of calling to abolish this country’s system of mass incarceration, they argue that such a demand is “not a viable road to social justice.” Police and prisons effectively reduce crime, they argue (although criminologists differ on this point), making them a necessary part of society, one that actually “protects the weakest.” Instead of abolishing this system, they argue that we should focus on jailing fewer people.
But the proponents of “carceral minimalism” never say how many human beings have to be locked away to meet their criteria. Currently, the United States has the largest prison population on earth, with 2 million people behind bars. Would 1.5 million incarcerated be the goal? That certainly would be better than our current nightmare. And decarceration reforms—like eliminating prison terms for nonviolent offenses or drug abuse and bail reform—have long been demands of the prison abolitionist movement. But this country would still be jailing more people per capita than anywhere on earth. Statistically, we know who would continue to get locked away: overwhelmingly the poor, some wrongly accused, few with decent legal representation, and disproportionately Black and Latino. Calling for “carceral minimalism” amounts to playing a racialized lottery with people’s lives. It’s about as far as a person can venture from the tradition of socialist prison abolitionists like Angela Davis and Howard Zinn. It is also a rebuke of the great socialist leader Eugene Debs’s thunderous declaration: “While there is a criminal element I am of it. While there is a soul in prison I am not free.”
Day and her cohort advance these politics in order to separate themselves from the “crazy” identitarian dead-enders and, in their telling, fully seize the power and opportunities that come with DSA’s unprecedented presence within the Democratic Party. This could come, however, with the price of unnecessarily dividing or pushing away the many in DSA who are joining in droves in order to build a multiracial organization that can effect radical change. There are no easy answers for how to accomplish this mammoth task, but history tells us that the organizations that did the most successful work in building multiracial coalitions—like the Communist Party in the 1930s or the Student Non-Violent Coordinating Committee in the early 1960s—were able to do so because they threw themselves into explicitly anti-racist work.
To abandon that and support, even tactically, our racialized prison-industrial complex doesn’t seem like a feasible path to that goal. If anything, it recalls the early-20th-century Socialist Party’s terrible position on race, summed up best in Debs’s regrettable assertion, “We have nothing special to offer the Negro, and we cannot make separate appeals to all the races.”
Debs’s position, in addition to undercutting the Socialist Party’s ability to build in Black communities, also gave cover to the party’s outwardly racist, hyper-nationalist right wing, led by Representative Victor Berger. The Wisconsin congressman supported the Chinese Exclusion Act, promoted white-supremacist race science, and was not a fan of organizing Black and white workers together. As W.E.B. Du Bois wrote in 1911: “So long as the Socialist movement can put a ban upon any race because of its color, whether that color be yellow or black, the negro will not feel at home in it.”
Berger’s views changed for the better in subsequent decades, but the harm caused by a Socialist leader taking those positions caused irreparable damage to the reputation of socialism—one that lingers. It also played a role in the eventual split and near-total destruction of their organization, as socialists inspired by the 1917 Russian Revolution and those who became disgusted by the right of the Socialist Party split off to build the Communist Party of the United States.
Today, some thought leaders on the right of DSA have been publishing a great deal in praise of Victor Berger—his later years, of course—as a model for socialist organizers today. That the praise for Berger is happening alongside arguments for “carceral minimalism” feels more like a concerted branding rollout than a coincidence.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
What a time, in a moment so bursting with possibility, to choose to stand with the political establishment and join their exhausting “war on woke.” But even more harmful, what a time to introduce “carceral minimalism” to a mass New York Times audience as an aim of the socialist movement. This only serves to undermine those trying to organize in the best traditions of the movement and not its most regrettable.
Decades ago, Howard Zinn made it plain: “I am convinced that imprisonment is a way of pretending to solve the problem of crime. It does nothing for the victims of crime, but perpetuates the idea of retribution, thus maintaining the endless cycle of violence in cruel and useless substitute for the elimination of those conditions—poverty, unemployment, homelessness, desperation, racism, greed—which are at the root of most punished crime. The crimes of the rich and powerful go mostly unpunished.”
Is it “crazy woke” to want to tear down the prison-industrial complex? If so, it beats dreaming that the path to socialism is paved with the discarded remains of anti-oppression principles in the name of electoral expediency.

Sotheby’s withdrew a painting by Wade Guyton valued at $1 million from its Contemporary Day Auction in New York on November 17 after a collector notified the auction house that it might be a fake. Guyton confirmed that the work was not his, according to Artnet.
The untitled painting, dated 2006, was on view in a presale exhibition, where it was spotted by the collector, who noted its similarity to a work by Guyton in their private collection. The artist and his gallery, Matthew Marks, were contacted and arrived to inspect the work. They concluded that the work was not authentic, and it was withdrawn from the show.
The work in question was listed as an Epson ultrachrome inkjet on linen measuring 89 ½ by 53 inches. The canvas depicts two uneven columns of black with flames at the bottom of each and a red U shape in the right column that echoes the shape of the flames at left. An untitled work by Guyton sold at Sotheby’s in 2014 for nearly $6 million, a record for the artist.
The Contemporary Day Auction included postwar, Abstract Expressionism, Minimalist, and contemporary art by artists such as Helen Frankenthaler, Mark Rothko, Alice Neel, Wayne Thiebaud, Faith Ringgold, and Christopher Wool. Some works arrived from private collections, but it is not yet clear where the fake Guyton originated.

https://theintercept.com/2026/11/25/sena.title: It’s Time to Ditch Kirsten Gillibrand
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/25/sena.author: Eoin Higgins
https://theintercept.com/2026/11/25/sena.text:
Eoin Higgins is the author of “Owned: How Tech Billionaires on the Right Bought the Loudest Voice on the Left.”
The stakes in 2028 couldn’t be higher for Democrats. Americans see the party as likely to win the White House after another two years of Donald Trump, especially given his historic unpopularity, and Democratic leadership will look to further expand their majorities in Congress.
How the Democratic Party selects candidates and develops strategy is going to have an outsized effect on the overall results — and the direction of the country.
After Senate Democrats elect their leader for the next two years on December 1, Chuck Schumer or Chris Van Hollen will have the opportunity to name the next head of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. It’s a powerful role: Whoever’s chosen will have an outsized voice in what kind of candidates run in 2028 and how much support they get.
New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, a close ally of Schumer and a loyal member of the party’s pro-business wing, is making her case to remain DSCC chair for a second two-year term. On the face of it, she has a lot to commend her record: nine flipped seats in the 2026 midterms and a new majority that is likely to extend to 2030. It’s inarguable that under her leadership, the DSCC saw major gains.
Yet Gillibrand’s political instincts have, at times, threatened electoral success. Her tenure at DSCC has been marked by pushing ideological preferences, and candidate choice from her and Schumer has been a mixed bag.
While Gillibrand and the DSCC can point to real success stories like James Talarico in Texas and Mary Peltola in Alaska, they also backed Haley Stevens in Michigan, a charisma void who turned on the Democratic nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, in the last days of the race allegedly over his views on Israel.
In Maine, the DSCC and establishment Democrats recruited Gov. Janet Mills, a 78-year-old with little interest in running, whose campaign against progressive upstart Graham Platner failed to launch. That was true even despite the many glaring deficiencies that ultimately doomed Platner’s candidacy and saw him replaced with ultimate general election winner Troy Jackson (whom Mills declined to endorse outright).
Even in cases when her instincts are right, Gillibrand struggled to exercise her influence for material effect. In Florida, left-wing Democratic Socialists of America member Angie Nixon came within 2 percentage points of winning the state’s Senate seat. Gillibrand, alongside Schumer, donated $5,000 each from their own leadership PACs and urged other senators to do the same — but couldn’t get the party overall to commit cash when it could have mattered.
The Democratic Party is not a monolith bringing together moderates and progressives into a general left-of-center umbrella. There are, necessarily, compromises for those in the tent, as Third Way Democrats are in coalition with DSA members.
After a blue-wave election, it’s important for party leaders to keep both sides happy as much as possible — within reason. The current push and pull and jockeying for position is leading to some dubious assertions of success metrics that the next DSCC chair will need to keep a clear head about.
Polling decisively showed Americans want action on the economy, healthcare, and the war with Iran. Over and over again, the public has made its priorities clear about accountability: Many voters in Texas were motivated this year because of the brutality of the administration’s immigration crackdown; voters also named “corruption” as a top concern.
Given those concerns, a role in leadership for someone like Gillibrand raises questions. The senator’s coziness with the crypto industry has drawn criticism as sector heavy-hitters poured over $196,000 in campaign donations to her in 2026 alone, by far the most for a candidate or officeholder in New York state.
This summer, Gillibrand’s son, Theo, started a financial exchange at age 22. He quickly took on investments from powerful financial operatives like crypto billionaire Chris Larsen and Palmer Luckey, founder of Anduril Industries, among others.
Gillibrand has legislated in lockstep with industry interests and repeatedly publicly defended crypto —even, in 2022, analyzing the feasibility of investing retirement plans in the currency market. As The Intercept reported in July, she was a lead negotiator in the crypto industry-favored legislation known as the Clarity Act, which would have allowed Wall Street to directly invest in the currency. The bill stalled out in the Senate in September despite her best efforts.
It’s hard to see a context in which it makes sense to send the message that corruption will continue, just as long as it’s our team doing it. But with Gillibrand at the head of the DSCC, that’s exactly what voters will hear in the next election cycle. The New York senator simply isn’t the right leader for the moment.
DSCC vice chairs Adam Schiff, Lisa Blunt Rochester, and Mark Kelly seem to be the three most likely alternatives, and all bring with them their own baggage. But they can plausibly claim a break with the existing do-nothing-Dem approach aimed more at personal enrichment and out-of-touch ideological commitments than Gillibrand can.
Newly elected Democrats understand the need for change and have almost uniformly rejected calls to continue the status quo by backing stale leadership in the Senate. Whether their efforts to change the face of the party in the chamber succeed or not, first-term Democrats are going to be more attuned to the concerns and priorities of the voters who sent them to Washington.
Senate leaders should listen to them. Democrats have an opportunity to show the public they heard the change message on Election Day.
Sticking with Gillibrand won’t help get that across to voters.
IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.
What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.
This is not hyperbole.
Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.
Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”
The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?
IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.
We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.
In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.
That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
We’re independent of corporate interests. Will you help us?

The driver accused of fatally mowing down a nurse as she crossed a notoriously deadly Brooklyn roadway in August has been arrested, police said, and records show his vehicle was repeatedly cited for speeding on the day of the hit-and-run.
Staten Island resident Justin Mercado allegedly blew a red light on Aug. 29 and plowed into 28-year-old nurse Jiayi Zheng as he flew down Third Avenue at 55 mph, more than double the speed limit, authorities said. Officials said that Zheng, who had just finished a shift at nearby NYU Langone Hospital, was rushed back to the same hospital, where she died.
Authorities said Zheng was walking in a marked crosswalk when she was hit. In 2020, another nurse, Clara Kang, was killed by a motorcyclist while riding her bike home on the same stretch after an overnight shift.
City transportation department data shows there have been 17 deaths on the roadway in the past decade.
The NYPD said Mercado turned himself in on Wednesday after detectives identified him through surveillance footage.
He pleaded not guilty to manslaughter, criminally negligent homicide, leaving the scene of a crash, assault and reckless endangerment.
Mercado’s 2014 Cadillac, which had Pennsylvania plates, was captured flying through Brooklyn on the day of the crash. On the morning of her death, the sedan was clocked speeding through a school zone in Lower Manhattan just 30 minutes before he plowed into Zheng, data shows.
The Cadillac was cited for another speed camera violation on Third Avenue minutes after the crash. The car received two more school zone speeding violations in Brooklyn eight minutes after the crash.
Weeks before the crash, the car received a school zone speeding violation on Staten Island.
Mayor Zohran Mamdani restarted plans to make Third Avenue safer following Zheng’s death. Traffic lanes in both directions will be replaced over a 2.1-mile stretch beneath the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway with bike lanes, and the street’s pedestrian crossings will be shortened.
A call to Mercado’s lawyer was not immediately returned.

https://www.humanite.fr/politique/associ.title: « L’objectif est de museler les contre-pouvoirs » : derrière les menaces aux associations, le projet autoritaire de Marine Le Pen
https://www.humanite.fr/politique/associ.author: Florent Le Du
https://www.humanite.fr/politique/associ.text:
En menaçant les associations de supprimer leurs subventions publiques arbitrairement, au prétexte flou d’une « politisation », la candidate du Rassemblement national assume sa volonté de mettre au pas les contre-pouvoirs pour basculer dans une démocratie illibérale. Syndicats, agences, collectivités, médias, justice sont également dans le viseur.
Un « ramassis de gauchistes » ? Sur LCI, le 16 novembre, c’est par cette expression que Marine Le Pen a qualifié la Ligue des droits de l’homme (LDH) pour justifier son intention de supprimer les subventions attribuées à l’organisation née durant l’affaire Dreyfus et interdite par Vichy.
Mais, en réalité, c’est potentiellement l’ensemble des associations que comptent le pays et leurs 13 millions de bénévoles que la candidate d’extrême droite place sous la menace, dans son projet plus global de s’attaquer à l’ensemble des contre-pouvoirs, pour faire glisser la démocratie française vers l’illibéralisme.
La candidate du Rassemblement national (RN) entend couper les subventions de l’État aux « associations politisées », dénomination suffisamment large pour procéder à des retraits arbitraires. En premier chef, cela devrait concerner les organisations dont les projets entrent en opposition au programme du RN, comme l’aide aux migrants.
Dans une tribune au Figaro, Marine Le Pen déverse son mépris envers les associations qui selon elle « prennent soin de se présenter avec des objets mâtinés d’angélisme et des dénominations parées d’un habillage moral ». Comme défendre les droits de l’homme, l’environnement, aider des personnes dans le besoin, des femmes victimes de violences, des personnes LGBT isolées, etc. Des actes trop politiques, trop...

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/de.title: Dead Man Is Accused of Stealing Art from Michigan Museums
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/de.author: Anne Doran
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/de.text:
The FBI is seeking a warrant to search electronic devices belonging to a Grand Rapids man accused of stealing art from two Michigan art museums. The news was reported by multiple outlets, including MLive.
According to a federal affidavit, Mikolai Augustine Stasiulewicz, 27, allegedly stole a color lithograph by artist Ellsworth Kelly, from Western Michigan University’s (WMU) Richmond Center for the Visual Arts on June 23. A worker notified WMU police that the work was missing, and Stasiulewicz, who was caught on surveillance video carrying the framed print, was identified through facial-recognition analysis by Michigan State Police.
Stasiulewicz is also alleged to have stolen a 16th-century Albrecht Dürer print from the Grand Rapids Art Museum (GRAM) on July 2. According to the FBI, he had been seen at the museum on June 17, “in what appeared to be a pre-theft surveillance visit.” Between the two thefts, he is accused of entering nonpublic areas at the Muskegon Museum of Art on June 25; however, Muskegon police said he didn’t take anything.
The FBI, which eventually took over the case, learned during its investigations that Stasiulewicz had met with a man on July 8 at the Gun Lake Casino Resort in Wayland, Michigan. Surveillance video shows him leaving with an unknown amount of cash.
Stasiulewicz was found dead in his home on July 30. According to the Kent County Medical Examiner’s Office, he died of a morphine overdose on July 26. Although the office’s autopsy report rules the death an accident, it also notes that “the decedent is currently under investigation by the FBI for involvement in an art gallery theft,” and that a brother had told police that may have played a part in his death.
Four artworks, including the Kelly, valued at $10,000 and the Dürer, valued at $10,000–$20,000, were found at the home the next day.
On Monday, November 23, the FBI sought a warrant to search Stasiulewicz’s cellphone and laptop computer to determine if any others were involved in the thefts. “In my training and experience, and that of the Art Crime Team, phones and computers like the devices will often be used to communicate with co-conspirators,” FBI Special Agent Evan Alkema wrote in the federal affidavit. “They may contain evidence of communications about what art pieces to steal, negotiations for sale prices, and arrangements to transfer and ‘fence’ the stolen works.”
Since its inception in 2004, the FBI’s Art Crime Team, which handles cases involving the theft, forgery, and trafficking of art and cultural artifacts, has recovered more than 20,000 objects valued at $1 billion.
Stasiulewicz was an amateur artist who studied at the Interlochen Center of the Arts, the FBI said.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Cruz com suástica no Amapá mobiliza missão de direitos humanos e busca de reparação histórica por presença nazista na Amazônia
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Uma missão de direitos humanos realiza, entre esta quarta-feira (25) e sexta-feira (27), em Laranjal do Jari, no sul do Amapá, uma audiência pública e reuniões com o poder público para debater a reparação histórica pela presença nazista na Amazônia. A iniciativa do Conselho Nacional dos Direitos Humanos (CNDH) e do Observatório Brasileiro sobre Discurso de Ódio, Extremismo e Neonazismo (Oben) busca aprofundar a discussão sobre o reconhecimento formal das responsabilidades dos Estados alemão e brasileiro por esse passado.
O símbolo mais visível desse capítulo é uma cruz de madeira de quase três metros de altura, marcada com uma suástica, que identifica o túmulo de Joseph Greiner, integrante de uma expedição alemã realizada durante o regime de Adolf Hitler.
A missão é desenvolvida no âmbito da Relatoria Especial de Enfrentamento ao Discurso de Ódio, Extremismo e Neonazismo do CNDH, em parceria com o Instituto Brasileiro de Análises Sociais e Econômicas (Ibase). Participam o relator especial do CNDH, Carlos Nicodemos, e Maria Fernanda Fernandes, consultora da relatoria e coordenadora-geral do Oben.
“A missão em Laranjal do Jari representa uma ampliação da atuação da Relatoria Especial de Enfrentamento ao Discurso de Ódio, ao Extremismo e ao Neonazismo e de seu mecanismo, o Oben, a partir da perspectiva de incidência em um território que carrega, em sua memória, a influência direta do nazismo. A iniciativa atuará especialmente nas frentes da educação, da cultura e da memória em direitos humanos, contribuindo para o reconhecimento dessas violações e para a reparação histórica”, explica Maria Fernanda Fernandes.
A audiência pública deve reunir lideranças da região, representantes de comunidades locais e movimentos sociais para discutir o significado histórico da cruz, a memória da expedição e os caminhos para a reparação. Nas reuniões com a prefeitura e representantes do poder público, estão em pauta a queda do monumento em 2022, sua reinstalação e as responsabilidades institucionais pela preservação da memória local.
Para a presidenta do CNDH, Ivana Cláudia Leal de Souza, a discussão diz respeito também ao presente. “Não há democracia plena sem verdade, memória e justiça. Para o CNDH, falar em reparação histórica na Amazônia é tirar essas violações da invisibilidade e reafirmar o dever do Estado de combater qualquer resquício de ideologias supremacistas ou antidemocráticas no Brasil de hoje”, afirma.
Expedição nazista
A cruz fica em um pequeno cemitério às margens do Rio Jari, próximo à cachoeira de Santo Antônio, a cerca de uma hora de barco de Laranjal do Jari, município a 287 quilômetros de Macapá. Em alemão, a inscrição diz: “Joseph Greiner morreu aqui de febre em 2 de janeiro de 1936 a serviço da pesquisa alemã”. Depois do sepultamento, a área passou a ser usada como cemitério pelas comunidades do território.
Greiner integrava a chamada Expedição Jari, liderada por Otto Schulz-Kampfhenkel, que percorreu a região entre 1935 e 1937. Oficialmente, a missão fazia pesquisas sobre a fauna, a flora e a geografia amazônica, mas estudos apontam interesses estratégicos da Alemanha nazista na região. Segundo historiadores, o objetivo era reunir informações para a implantação de uma colônia alemã na América do Sul, com vistas a uma possível invasão da Guiana Francesa.
O plano nunca foi levado adiante. Ao longo da expedição, os alemães levantaram dados ambientais e sobre a cultura indígena. Registros da época mostram a relação do grupo com o povo Aparai. Doenças como malária e difteria atingiram os integrantes da comitiva. Greiner, que, segundo historiadores, vivia no Brasil desde a adolescência e foi recrutado como capataz para facilitar a comunicação, morreu de uma febre não especificada.
Em 2022, a cruz foi encontrada caída após uma cheia do Rio Jari. A prefeitura levou o monumento para a sede do município, onde ele foi restaurado por um escultor, e em 2023 o reinstalou no local de origem, sobre uma nova base, como registro histórico do município.

https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.title: Rikers Monitor Details 14-Hour Delay in Finding Overdose Victim, Slams Slow Pace of Reforms
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.author: Reuven Blau
https://www.thecityreporter.nyc/2026/11/.text:
The body of a Rikers Island detainee who overdosed wasn’t found for about 14 hours, according to a report by a court-appointed monitor overseeing the Department of Correction, as wider long-delayed jail reforms move at a “glacial pace.”
“The glacial pace of reform has been frustrating to all stakeholders and is far less than the urgency of the situation demands,” said monitor Steve Martin, noting violence is still far above levels the jail system reported in 2016, when he was first appointed.
“The high risk of harm is ongoing and pervasive,” the 432-page report said.
The report is the most recent oversight document detailing negligence and excessive use of force by corrections officers amid efforts to close Rikers and build new jails closer to courts.
The status update comes a week after Mayor Zohran Mamdani detailed the city’s latest plan to shut down Rikers, which will begin gradually as the first new jail in Brooklyn is expected to be complete in about three years and extend until 2032. The report did note some positive developments. Martin, who is based in Texas, said the Correction Department and the federally appointed remediation manager, Nicholas Deml, and his team “have made some important forward progress.”
Martin credited them with establishing a reliable baseline of staffing practices for the first time in more than a decade, reorganizing the Correction Department’s deeply flawed investigations division, and winning court approval for a comprehensive action plan to guide reforms.
Jail staff appear to have curtailed some of the most extreme uses of force, the report said. But Martin described that as a baseline expectation, not proof of compliance, and wrote that the city’s jails reflect “a system that is generating avoidable force events and then responding to them.”
The report, which covers January to June 2026 (and all the deaths since), is Martin’s 23rd status update. It echoes many prior failed efforts to improve conditions for detainees and staff, including a deeply flawed disciplinary system, officers too quick to use force, and hundreds of broken cell doors.
Conflict Over Solitary Confinement
The monitor also raised new concerns about a City Council law sharply restricting the use of solitary confinement, arguing that the legislation — currently on pause due to mayoral override — could make an already volatile jail system more dangerous if implemented before the Department of Correction addresses its underlying problems.
Martin and Deml said the city’s jails lack the operational foundation needed to safely implement key provisions of what is known as Local Law 42.
They warned that eliminating managerial discretion in certain situations could increase the risk of harm. Martin also flagged potential conflicts between the law’s requirements and existing court orders governing jail operations.
Still, the city and the monitoring team are continuing to develop a pilot program for restrictive housing where detainees who act out would be placed as an alternative to solitary. That includes finding a location, the right staff, security protocols and rehabilitative programming.
Martin and Deml’s concerns come after city lawmakers spent years crafting the new rules following the death of Layleen Polanco. The 27-year-old transgender woman was in the ninth day of a 20-day solitary confinement sentence when she was found lifeless inside her Rikers cell. She was being held in lieu of a $500 bond for misdemeanor sex work and drug possession charges.
Overall, Martin’s review used almost identical language from his prior report, in January, to describe the slow pace of meaningful changes.
“The reform effort continues to progress at a glacial pace,” he said, citing entrenched resistance and “pervasive poor practices.”
Martin and his team, led by Anna Friedberg, a lawyer with no previous jail experience, have billed the city $22 million since 2024, the latest year of available data. Martin rarely visits Rikers himself and primarily relies on Friedberg and some city jail staffers assigned to assist.
For all the damning findings in his reports, Martin has seldom pressed U.S. District Judge Laura Swain, who oversees the case, for immediate action. Instead, he has repeatedly chided jail officials for ignoring his advice and dragging their feet.
The review was made public late Tuesday night before the Thanksgiving holiday weekend. Several of Martin’s prior reports have also been published right before holiday stretches when the public is less focused on news.
Violence and Mayhem
In the latest report, Martin cites one eight-day stretch, Oct. 1 to 8, as an illustration of the ongoing danger. Over those days, the Correction Department reported 148 uses of force by correction officers, six stabbings and slashings (including two attempts), seven fires, 42 incidents of detainees hurting themselves, and 35 assaults on staff. There were also 16 serious-injury reports from fights or reported assaults, seven incidents in which Narcan was administered, 38 discoveries of contraband, and 28 emergency lock-ins.
The report also describes two incidents in a two-week span in late August and early September when staff at the Otis Bantum Correctional Center used pepper spray on men who had tied sheets around their necks and attached them to holding pens.
In both cases, staff hit the men, who were trying to take their own lives, with pepper spray.
Martin called the incidents “especially troubling” because the department’s own directive expressly prohibits using chemical agents on someone trying to hang themselves. The department revised that directive in 2025, but Martin wrote that his team “continues to identify incidents” in which staff use pepper spray in those dire mental health crises.
In one July 5 incident at the West Facility on Rikers, the report says an officer grabbed a detainee by the neck, pulled his hair, kneed him in the head and struck him with a chemical-agent canister. The officer then sprayed him while he was restrained and also used racially charged language during the violent encounter, according to the report.
A captain had to order the officer to step away. He was suspended for 30 days and resigned in September while facing formal charges.
The 14-Hour Delay
As for deaths in custody, nine people have died behind bars this year so far.
That includes Barry Cozart, 39, who was found unresponsive inside the George R. Vierno Center on March 25.
Cozart had a history of substance abuse and was seen on surveillance video looking intoxicated the night before his death, according to the report.
Staff repeatedly failed to conduct proper tours, left their posts unsupervised for extended periods, and a logbook entry falsely recorded that a tour-tracking device was working. Cozart’s body wasn’t found until roughly 14 hours after he was last seen moving, the report said.
The Medical Examiner said the cause of death was acute intoxication from the combined effects of methadone and gabapentin.
The area captain and floor officer were each suspended without pay for one month.
Another detainee, John Price, 49, suffered from clear signs of medical distress as he waited for roughly 3 ½ hours in a clinic holding pen without being seen because jail officers didn’t tell medical staff he was having a medical emergency inside the Eric M. Taylor Center on March 28.
No jail or medical staff have been disciplined but the investigation is ongoing, Martin said.
“The deaths of people in DOC custody are tragic and continue to expose the serious consequences that occur when basic security, supervision, and correctional health practices break down,” Martin wrote.
Martin urged better communication between DOC and Correctional Health Services, which oversees medical care, “to improve prompt identification of people in distress, and improve emergency response times.”
The Correction Department did not respond to an email seeking comment.
The Legal Aid Society, which brought the class action case that has led to the monitor and remediation manager, said the report showed how little progress had been made despite a decade of court oversight.
“The conditions at Rikers Island remain dangerous and unacceptable,” said Mary Lynne Werlwas, director of the group’s Prisoners’ Rights Project, and Debbie Greenberger, a partner at the law firm Emery Celli, who issued a joint statement.

https://www.propublica.org/article/smith.title: Democrats Vow to Shield Smithsonian From Any Trump Overhaul
https://www.propublica.org/article/smith.author: Andy Kroll
https://www.propublica.org/article/smith.text:
A top congressional Democrat announced she will investigate the Trump White House’s potential overhaul of the leadership and curatorial decisions at the Smithsonian Institution, the independent agency that oversees 21 national museums.
In a letter sent on Tuesday to the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents, Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-Maine, cited ProPublica’s recent story on the draft plans by a White House staffer targeting one of the Smithsonian’s most prominent museums, calling the reporting “extremely concerning.”
Read More
Pingree, who is slated to lead the subcommittee that controls the Smithsonian’s funding in the next Congress, said the plans revealed in the ProPublica story align with the administration’s broader efforts to interfere with the Smithsonian, which receives federal funding but is governed by a 17-person Board of Regents whose members include the chief justice of the United States, members of Congress, the vice president and private citizens.
In an interview with ProPublica, Pingree said that she intended her letter to put the Smithsonian governing board on notice that the incoming Democratic majority in Congress is monitoring the institution to make sure the board upholds its responsibility to keep the agency independent from political pressure.
“No White House employee riding on the Metro gets to design a plan for what future exhibits look like or gets to veto staffers or exhibits at the Smithsonian,” Pingree said. “That’s not how it works.”
Pingree told ProPublica that she plans to use her powers as chair in the next Congress to aggressively look into what she called the Trump administration’s meddling with the Smithsonian and to expose those efforts to the broader American public.
“We fully intend to dig deeper than has been done in the past,” she said.
Pingree’s letter comes in response to ProPublica reporting on a 25-item list of possible changes that, taken together, would amount to an unprecedented attempt by the White House to control the content and personnel of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, which attracts nearly 2 million people a year.
Those reforms include firing many of the museum’s top officials; rolling out a new permanent exhibit called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance”; introducing new K-12 learning materials such as a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage”; and unveiling a new “Colossus Statue” of George Washington for the museum’s entrance.
The draft plans were visible on the laptop and in handwritten notes of a White House staffer who was riding a D.C.-area Metro train in late October. A nearby commuter took pictures of the materials and sent them to ProPublica reporters, who in turn verified the information. It’s unclear what kind of reception the plans have received inside the Trump White House. The staffer and White House did not respond to requests for comment for the story.
Also on Tuesday, Lonnie Bunch, the Smithsonian Institution’s outgoing leader, responded to ProPublica’s reporting in a message sent to employees. “The intended use of this list is unclear,” Bunch wrote in his letter. “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programs.”
Pingree was not the only member of Congress who responded to ProPublica’s reporting with a pledge to defend the Smithsonian’s independence.
Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., said on social media that if he becomes chair of the Senate Rules Committee — which has jurisdiction over the Smithsonian — in the next Congress, “we will protect it from Trump’s interference and overreach.”
“The Smithsonian is NOT a federal agency, it is an independent, nonpartisan organization overseen by Congress – not the White House,” Padilla wrote.
Incoming Congressman Fred Wellman, a Democrat elected this month to represent the suburbs of St. Louis, responded even more forcefully to ProPublica’s reporting on social media.
“Over my dead body,” he wrote.

https://taz.de/Flixtrain-Tickets-bei-der.title: Deutsche Bahn und Flixbus: Nur ein erster Schritt
https://taz.de/Flixtrain-Tickets-bei-der.author: Wolfgang Mulke
https://taz.de/Flixtrain-Tickets-bei-der.text:
Deutsche Bahn und Flixbus : Nur ein erster Schritt
Bei der Bahn kann man künftig auch Tickets von Flixtrain buchen – gut so. Doch für echte Kundenfreundlichkeit muss noch viel getan werden.
L ange hat sich die Deutsche Bahn hartnäckig an ihren exklusiven Ticketvertrieb geklammert. Tickets der inländischen Konkurrenz wollte der Konzern partout nicht verkaufen. Damit ist nun zumindest teilweise Schluss. Demnach kann die Buchung von Fahrten der Konkurrenz oder auch eine Kombination von Reisen demnächst auf den DB-Portalen in einem Schritt erledigt werden. Für die Reisenden ist das eine gute Nachricht. Die verkauft die DB zwar als besseren Kundenservice – doch ganz freiwillig kam die Einigung mit dem Wettbewerber Flixtrain wohl nicht zustande.
So drängte das Verkehrsministerium schon länger auf ein einheitliches Ticketing. Eigentlich wollte der frühere CDU-Verkehrsminister Patrick Schnieder die Vertriebsplattform Navigator sogar an die gemeinwohlorientierte Netzsparte der DB übertragen. Das konnte der Konzern noch verhindern.
Auch die Bundesnetzagentur ist der Bahn in die Parade gefahren und warf der DB den Missbrauch ihrer Marktmacht gegenüber konkurrierenden Mobilitätsplattformen vor. Es war nicht das erste Mal, dass die Behörde die Vertriebsstrategie der DB kritisierte. Der nun erzielte Fortschritt dürfte auch diesem Druck aus Politik und Netzagentur geschuldet sein.
taz debatte
Die taz ist eine unabhängige, linke und meinungsstarke Tageszeitung. In unseren Kommentaren, Essays und Debattentexten streiten wir seit der Gründung der taz im Jahr 1979. Oft können und wollen wir uns nicht auf eine Meinung einigen. Deshalb finden sich hier teils komplett gegenläufige Positionen – allesamt Teil des sehr breiten linken Meinungsspektrums.
Weiterhin fehlen kundenfreundliche Regelungen
Es sollte nur ein Zwischenschritt sein. Denn spätestens ab 2028 wird sich der Wettbewerb im Fernverkehr enorm verstärken. Dann will auch das italienische Unternehmen Italo in Deutschland Fuß fassen. Für die Bahnreisenden ist das bisher nur zum Teil eine positive Aussicht: Erfahrungen aus anderen Ländern legen zwar nahe, dass die Konkurrenz für sinkende Preise und eine bessere Qualität sorgt.
Doch es fehlen noch kundenfreundliche Regelungen, etwa für die Nutzung von Zügen anderer Unternehmen bei Verspätungen oder Ausfällen. Auch gilt die beschlossene Kooperation ja nur für die beiden beteiligten Unternehmen, nicht für Tickets neuer Wettbewerber. Es gibt also noch viel zu tun, um den Kunden Bahnreisen so leicht und angenehm wie möglich zu machen.

Generally I don't mess around with food pop-ups and limited drops and such. I don't think there's anything wrong with them ethically or, like, strategically, but unless you're my personal friend (for whom I will go anywhere and do anything!), the irreplicable nature and inherent scarcity of the model usually requires jumping through more hoops, and causes more anxiety, than I care to handle.  
Sometimes though, I'm happy to make an exception, especially on a lovely day weather-wise, at a location that's an enjoyable bike ride from my apartment, and most importantly, for something that's rarely offered anywhere else and when prepared well, hits me exactly right. Which is why I was delighted to spend last Saturday morning with Mikey Deegan and his partner Susie Thomas as they hurriedly prepared their weekends-only, holiday-season takeover of the Screen Door in Greenpoint. https://jacobin.com/2026/11/koch-economi.title: Charles Koch Has a Dystopian Plan for How to Control Workers
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/koch-economi.author: Henry Snow
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/koch-economi.text:
Charles Koch Has a Dystopian Plan for How to Control Workers
Ultraconservative billionaire Charles Koch likes to style himself as a champion of individual liberty. But his phony science of workplace management created an atmosphere that Koch’s workers compared to living in a totalitarian state.
At a conference in Orlando, Florida, in 2005, the American billionaire Charles Koch gave a speech explaining how he and his audience could protect “freedom and prosperity in the world.” While accepting an award named after potato chip magnate Herman Lay, Koch explained that he had conceived a “science of liberty,” which he described as “the study and practice of sustainably advancing liberty to create prosperity and social progress.”
The solution lay, Koch said, in economic analysis — treating every interaction between people as a market exchange. He claimed this “Market Process Analysis” helped him build not only his fortune but also his family life and interpersonal interactions.
Out of it, he created what he called Market-Based Management (MBM), a theory for managing workers and his business. The science of liberty he outlined in Orlando applied those same principles to government — in America and around the world.
Playing God
Workers at Charles Koch’s web of companies felt differently. One anonymous Koch employee in Wichita wrote that their colleagues were “walking around like they are in the George Orwell book, ‘1984,’” terrified of the Koch family, the “only major employer in the area,” who used their power “to control the employees and their movement within the other Koch entities.”
Another, in Atlanta, called Koch’s extensive training in MBM “brainwashing.” The atmosphere, others reported, was “cult-like,” and employees were “noticeably unhappy,” with fifty-hour workweeks as well as mandatory overtime and weekend work. A software engineer in Bangalore wrote that at Koch’s companies “managers are GOD. . . . They can play with anyone’s life.”
Some of these disgruntled employees, hoping to convince management to change their ways, insisted they were not “practicing what they preached” — that MBM’s values were good and simply being misapplied. But Charles Koch had worked on the system for decades.
He personally cultivated its materials, and his company forced employees to study them for upward of five hours a week, according to one review. Some of the values in Koch’s system of MBM were simply anodyne — “respect” is its ninth “guiding principle.” But the underlying purpose of the philosophy was to extract maximum profit from employees.
Science of Control
The science of liberty seemed more like a science of control. Koch’s “science” relied on four connected claims about human behavior that structure economic and political life across the globe today.
First, that we should analyze society as merely a collection of individuals, an idea known as methodological individualism. Second, the claim that individuals are motivated only by self-interest, generally though not exclusively in the form of material incentives — or psychological egoism.
Third, an insistence that deliberate planning cannot be trusted: humans are too selfish, and too limited, to make or execute grand plans for society. We should trust the competitive evolution of markets over the cooperative intention of democracy.
And fourth, the belief that everything is — and should be — a market. The world consists of competing individuals, and social science exists to figure out how to structure that competition so prosperity arises out of it. This paradigm is known as market fundamentalism.
Proponents of these ideas present them as inescapable truths about the world, like gravity. If we know how human beings will act, there is no need to speak of how they should act. Thus, “there is no alternative,” as the Victorian philosopher Herbert Spencer put it, to these cruel calculations: they are an inescapable truth about human action.
Political Visions
But these ideas are not scientific truths that experts have discovered. They are political visions that ideologues have created. There are other ways we can live and work, and generally most people prefer those alternatives when asked and frequently pursue them when we are not.
From Samuel Bentham’s program of mechanized and precarious shipbuilding labor to Frederick Winslow Taylor’s floundering efforts to optimize pig iron loading, supposedly optimal methods for manipulating workers have generally failed — until their architects relied on political and economic force to impose their ideas anyway.
Four hundred years of elite scheming have failed to produce either the technocratic control that utilitarians like the Benthams wanted or the pure competition advocated by market radicals like Ludwig von Mises. Every country in the world, even those with little or no political freedom, has major movements that demand better. Those movements do not always win. But every victory builds a foundation for the next.
Today we have labor rights, voting power, and political freedoms — where we have them — because of the hard work of those who came before us. Building on their legacy, we can continue to make a better world now and to create conditions for yet more advances after we are gone.
Control science is not “human nature.” It is not “how the world works.” It is not just orthodox economics or economic common sense or advanced political discourse. Identifying the different intertwining strands that give control science its strength and naming the total result, helps us take it on. Labeling control science — and labeling it accurately as a matter of control — is all the more important because of how it works.
Rule Without Rulers
The irony of control science is that it is ultimately not a theory of control by anyone at all. Control science respects no kings, no presidents, and no gods but what one of Herbert Spencer’s followers called “that awful One to whom it is profanity to pray.” This is an ideology for control by no one, of everyone. Its advocates call this freedom.
The science of control is an attempt at rule without rulers, an abstract authoritarianism, an art of excuses: centuries of elites finding themselves in positions of power and scrambling to justify that power to themselves and the world. This vast program of institutionalized apathy has been developed through, and always relies on, the forceful control of workers themselves.
Identifying this program does two things for us. First, it makes clear that cynical claims about “human nature” are social and political constructions, not an objective truth discovered by capitalists. Second, then, this intellectual history of economic thought reveals how much it has always been about control of us, not by us. We can rally against it accordingly: control science is fake, and it is wrong.
Ideas alone will not be enough, of course. Control science has succeeded by embedding itself in the legal, political, and economic structures of the world around us. It does not describe actual human nature, but it does describe how many people do, and must, act, precisely because of the way capitalists have made the world.
Selfishness is embedded in the real material relations we have with each other: the most responsible strategies for investing, for example, may include investments in oil companies. The cheapest products are produced under the worst labor conditions. Buying better or investing differently as an individual will accomplish little, and it is difficult to build collective movements around doing something that makes us, temporarily, worse off, in a world of economic scarcity and against constant competition by the preachers of selfishness.
We cannot defeat control science as individual consumers. But we can as workers, as voters, and as full human beings. Over the last four centuries, many of the greatest victories for justice, equality, and freedom have relied on mass movements of working people, from the revolutions of the eighteenth century to the New Deal and decolonization in the twentieth century.
Workers’ Control
The twenty-first century has been, in much of the world, a period of defeat and retreat for working-class left-wing politics. But it does not have to be that way. The science of control was made in the workplace. It can be unmade there as well. Labor organizing forces idealistic progressives to ground our projects in material incentives: better wages, improved working conditions, more free time.
This is particularly necessary in the cynical world control science has made. We have been told that everyone is selfish and that an alternative world is impossible. This makes it all the more difficult to believe rousing appeals to empathy and ethics alone. Organizing within workplaces must become part of a broader movement for democracy and equality at work — control by workers, not of them.
Most of us recoil at the idea of an absolute monarch or a dictator. Yet we spend a good portion of our days, and our lives, doing the bidding of bosses over whom we have little power. We should abhor authoritarian company “presidents” and company boards the way we do dictatorship and monarchy. Working people should wield power through robust and assertive democratic unions to force our bosses to take our needs and desires and dreams into account.
A powerful labor movement alone will not end the science of control. And an economy of competing democratic cooperatives would still be one driven by markets and competition. Thus, we also need to aim for democratic control of the economy writ large. Human needs and collective desires, not the movement of markets, should determine what we make and do.
A market is a forever skewed democracy: your voting power is proportional to your wealth, and the most exploitative actors are therefore the most powerful. We should find this an offense against democracy, and we should act accordingly. Rule by market rules has only succeeded in leading us to a world that satisfies no one.
Mass working-class movements, wielding the power of democracy, can build an intentional and deliberate world that reflects our most meaningful and deeply held collective wants, democratically aggregated, rather than our individual purchasing choices, scaled by our wealth. We can build our moral principles and our material needs into the legal structure, social fabric, and collective ideals of our societies so that acting in the common good, instead of against it, becomes easier and more obvious every day.
A Collective Program
We know collective effort can outcompete nihilist competition, because it has done so before: an imperfect fraction of this program of economic democracy saved the world from fascism. Imagine what a full-fledged collective program could do for living standards, economic growth, and climate change.
Through public housing authorities, we can determine where housing is built and how much it costs based on our need for comfortable homes, instead of the political demand to keep housing prices up for those already locked into an expensive mortgage. With utility nationalization, we can replace hated telecommunications monopolies with less expensive, more functional infrastructure that we control.
All of this requires no promises of or belief in a socialist utopia (though it will help us move toward one). Right now, it is right-wing economics that is in the way of lower rent, higher wages, shorter hours, full employment, and economic dignity, for all of us. If we take control of our work and our lives, we can secure a better life together.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: Artist Nick Cave and India pavilion win Venice Biennale prizes following controversy
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: James Imam
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
The Venice Biennale has named the American artist Nick Cave and India’s national pavilion as the winners of its top art prizes this year, following a controversy that saw the competition’s jury resign and several artists and pavilions withdraw from the running.
In previous editions of the Biennale, an international jury has selected the artist and national pavilion to receive the prizes, traditionally known as Golden Lions. This year, however, the awards were renamed Visitors’ Lions and awarded on the basis of votes cast by visitors to the exhibition.
The new voting system was introduced following a dispute over the inclusion of Russia and Israel in the 2026 Biennale. In a statement in April, the five-person jury announced that it would not award prizes to national pavilions or artists from countries whose leaders were charged with crimes against humanity by the International Criminal Court (ICC).
The International Criminal Court had issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin, Russia's president, in 2023, and for Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's prime minister, the following year.
The jurors resigned days later, saying they were doing so “in acknowledgement” of their previous statement.
Dozens of artists then ruled themselves out of the contest in solidarity with the jury, though they remained on the ballot. The Biennale clarified that votes for withdrawn entries would not be considered.
It is unclear whether Cave and the India pavilion received the most votes of all entries on the ballot, including withdrawn entries. The Biennale declined to provide The Art Newspaper with a breakdown of the results.
“The Venice Biennale does not publish rankings or detailed voting results, as the regulations do not provide for this,” a Biennale spokesperson tells The Art Newspaper. “This applies to the Visitors’ Lions, just as it has always applied to the decisions of the international juries.”
Cave is best known for work that combines fashion, sculpture and performance. His exhibition at Venice’s Arsenal includes seven works, among them Amalgam (Origin) (2024), a monumental bronze sculpture of a figure with branches growing out of its body and birds nestling among twigs. Each of the seven works address a stage of grief.
"On the eve of Thanksgiving, I feel an even deeper sense of gratitude, for the friendship that bound me with Koyo Kouoh, and for the fact that she decided to include my work in the In Minor Keys exhibition," Cave said in a statement. "This project is a synthesis of my wider artistic research: it recognises the history of violence and oppression that Black people have endured and continue to endure in the United States, and it pays tribute to the beauty created by that very community, expressing the possibility of growth towards a different future."
India's exhibition, titled Geographies of Distance, features works by five artists including clay sculptures, dried flowers and plants hung from the ceiling, and a demolished family home reconstructed in white thread. Curated by Amin Jaffer, the exhibition reflects on the rapid expansion of cities in India, according to the Biennale's website.
On Wednesday, when this year's winners were announced, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco, the Biennale’s president, praised the new voting system.
He said in a statement: “The public of the Exhibition embraced this recognition—the Visitors’ Award—as an opportunity to bring Pablo Picasso’s practice to life: a painting only comes to life through the person who looks at it".

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120414.title: Krankenhausfinanzierung | Kreisklinik wagt den Klageweg
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120414.author: Ulrike Henning
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120414.text:
- Wirtschaft und Umwelt
- Krankenhausfinanzierung
Kreisklinik wagt den Klageweg
Die Kreisklinik Groß-Gerau verklagte die Bundesregierung auf Schadensersatz wegen Unterfinanzierung. In der ersten Instanz wurde die Klage abgewiesen.
Eine Klage der Kreisklinik Groß-Gerau auf Schadensersatz vom Bund wegen Krankenhaus-Finanzierungen ist vom Landgericht Darmstadt am Mittwoch abgewiesen worden. In dem Zivilverfahren sagte der Richter in seinem Urteil, dass die Klage inhaltlich unbegründet sei. Es gebe keinen Anspruch auf Zahlung von rund 1,2 Millionen Euro. Auch das EU-Recht gebe hier keinen individuellen Anspruch. Gegen das Urteil kann Berufung eingelegt werden – genau das wird die Klägerin vermutlich nach Prüfung der Urteilsbegründung tun.
In dem Verfahren ging es formal um eine Schadensersatzklage der Kreisklinik wegen aus ihrer Sicht struktureller Krankenhausunterfinanzierung. Die Klägerin, vertreten durch Geschäftsführerin Erika Raab, sah vor diesem Urteil hier ein grundsätzliches Verfahren mit Pilotcharakter. Für sie stellt sich die Frage, wie die Verantwortung des Gesetzgebers für seine Gesetze aussieht.
Die wirtschaftliche Lage des Kreisklinikums Groß-Gerau in Hessen entspricht in etwa dem, was jedes Jahr neu im Krankenhaus-Rating-Report verkündet und zuvor errechnet wurde: Die Lage ist weiterhin angespannt, ab 2027 droht sogar wieder eine deutliche Verschärfung. Und schon 2024 – aus diesem Jahr stammt die Klage des Kreisklinikums – schrieb rund die Hälfte der deutschen Krankenhäuser einen Jahresverlust. Insgesamt lag das durchschnittliche Jahresergebnis deutschlandweit damals bei minus 0,6 Prozent der Erlöse.
In Groß-Gerau hatte man sich entschlossen, den Finanzierungsproblemen an einer heiklen Stelle auf den Zahn zu fühlen und zu handeln. Dabei geht es um die Auswirkungen politischer Entscheidungen auf die wirtschaftliche Stabilität von Krankenhäusern. Das Klinikum hatte 2024 eine Klage gegen die Bundesrepublik Deutschland eingereicht. Die Politik habe zu einer systematischen Unterfinanzierung der Krankenhäuser und auch zu immer mehr Schließungen geführt. Konkret ging es um Schadensersatz von 1,7 Millionen Euro für 2023.
Die Klinikleitung setzt hier auf europäisches Recht, wonach ein hohes Niveau der Daseinsvorsorge im Gesundheitswesen zu sichern sei. Dementsprechend müsste der Staat die vollständige Finanzierung von Leistungen in diesem Zusammenhang sicherstellen. Das Problem im deutschen System: Hier wurde Privatisierung über Jahrzehnte erwünscht, zugelassen und vorangetrieben – und damit die Gewinnerzielung zur zentralen Triebkraft. Dazu und in diesem Sinne wirkt das System der Fallpauschalen in der deutschen Version.
Konkret soll eine grundsätzliche Klärung durch den Europäischen Gerichtshof (EuGH) erreicht werden. Im Mittelpunkt steht dabei die Frage, ob sich aus Artikel 14 des Vertrags über die Arbeitsweise der Europäischen Union ein Ansatz für den Schadenshaftungsanspruch ableiten lässt.
Deutsche Politik könne hier nicht haftbar gemacht werden, so die Gegenthese. Auch im Prozess von den Vertretern der Bundesrepublik eingebracht, laufen Gegenargumente darauf hinaus, dass die Ursachen für wirtschaftliche Verluste in schlechter eigener Qualität, in mangelndem Bedarf und in miserabler Krankenhausführung liegen – oder liegen könnten. Vielen Dank, werden viele Klinikleitungen sagen. Aber schwer vorstellbar, dass innerbetriebliche Faktoren bei dem großen Anteil der Krankenhäuser, die existenzbedroht waren und sind, die alleinige oder wesentliche Ursache für die Defizite waren.
Das Bündnis Klinikrettung bedauert die Ablehnung, begrüßt jedoch, dass eine Berufung möglich ist. Eine grundsätzliche Klärung der Verantwortung Deutschlands für eine ausreichende Finanzierung der Krankenhäuser sei überfällig. »Mit seiner Klage kann das Krankenhaus Groß-Gerau beweisen, dass sein Defizit nicht selbstverschuldet ist, sondern auf die geltenden Berechnungsmechanismen im Fallpauschalensystem zurückzuführen ist. Die Unterfinanzierung ist also politisch gewollt und, weil die Bundesregierung dies nicht ändern will, hofft die Klägerin auf eine positive Entscheidung des Europäischen Gerichtshofs«, kommentiert Herbert Storn die Entscheidung vom Mittwoch. Er war für das Bündnis Klinikrettung vor Ort.
Auch Bündnis-Sprecherin Laura Valentukeviciute hat noch Hoffnungen: »Wenn Groß-Gerau gewinnt, gewinnen auch alle anderen Krankenhäuser bundesweit, die aufgrund der Fallpauschalenberechnung Defizite erleiden. Die Bundesregierung will die Zahl der Krankenhäuser drastisch reduzieren, die systematische Unterfinanzierung ist für sie dabei ein Mittel zum Zweck.« Es sei überfällig, dass die Unterfinanzierung gerichtlich unterbunden werde, aber: »Einfacher wäre es, wenn die Regierung die Fallpauschalen abschafft und die Selbstkostendeckung einführt.«
Zumal auch die absehbaren Wirkungen weiterer Gesetze die Krankenhäuser belasten werden. Ab 2027 gibt es Erlöseinbußen durch das Gesetz zur Beitragsstabilisierung bei den gesetzlichen Krankenversicherungen. Bis 2030 könnten bis zu 70 Prozent der Krankenhäuser rote Zahlen schreiben. Rund 400 Standorte gelten mittelfristig als wirtschaftlich gefährdet, darunter besonders ländliche und öffentliche-rechtliche Kliniken – genau solche wie das 220-Betten-Haus in Trägerschaft des Kreises Groß-Gerau in Hessen.
