https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.title: Trump Wants to Quiet Quit the Iran War—but the War Won’t Let Him
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.author: David Faris
https://www.thenation.com/article/world/.text:
Trump Wants to Quiet Quit the Iran War—but the War Won’t Let Him
The president’s senseless war of choice has left him without any good choices.
Despite the GOP’s historic drubbing in November’s midterm elections based at least in part on the fallout from America’s disastrous war of choice in Iran, President Donald Trump seems to have no new ideas about how to end the conflict, apart from randomly declaring that it’s already over. He likewise is at a loss to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and return the global economy—upended by the war’s shocks to the supply chains for oil, fertilizer, and other essentials—to normalcy.
If anything, Trump appears determined to “quiet quit” the war, simply by declaring the status quo to his liking and pushing new attacks into the next calendar year. This move stands athwart his repeated vows during the midterm campaign to renew an aggressive bombing campaign in Iran after the election. But Trump won’t be able simply to walk away from his war of his choice, because no amount of flimflam and media manipulation can make this problem go away.
A diminished Trump, just back from his embarrassing hang-out session with the brutal autocratic leaders of Russia and China, shuffled slowly to the podium at the White House last Friday and mumbled that he would “absolutely” launch the war again. “Well. I’ll talk to you about it after the beginning of the year,” he said about the possibility of new hostilities, as if the war is a work project to be circled back to when it’s convenient. You can’t send a war home for the holidays.
This latest effort to kick the can down the road is very much of a piece with the countless ultimatums Trump has issued and then walked back in the weeks and months since this pointless and ill-conceived war failed to achieve its objectives. The president finds himself mired in an open-ended standoff that not only strengthened the Iranian regime and its resolve but has also sent catastrophic ripple effects through the global economy. And with both sides seemingly eager for a pretext to move on to the next, and potentially much more destructive, round of fighting, the Iranian stalemate has become a catastrophic setback in a year already overstuffed with them.
For months, the United States has been leading an end-run around the Strait of Hormuz, escorting mostly Saudi and Emirati tankers to safety. This policy has succeeded in the short-term goal of bringing prices down somewhat—but its costs are staggering. There are now three aircraft-carrier battle groups in the Persian Gulf, along with dozens of support vessels, all working around the clock to sustain the expensive illusion that oil exports are back to prewar levels. Operating a carrier group runs about $8–9 million a day, which means that keeping three of them in the region is running taxpayers upwards of $27 million a day, to say nothing of the munitions and opportunity costs. The United States may be spending as much as $42 million a day on naval operations in and around the Strait of Hormuz alone.
Yet it is hard to know exactly how well this gambit is going even on its own logistical terms, because the Pentagon has descended into Vietnam-era degrees of lying and misdirection, even allowing for the impressive levels of mendacity reached by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and his minions. Classified briefings are provided only to Trump’s Republican quislings, while tallies of killed and wounded have been altered and updated without explanation. And cost estimates are almost certainly fanciful.
What is actually happening in and around the Strait of Hormuz is likely much uglier than what we have thus far been told. On Monday, for example, two tankers reportedly hit Iranian mines in the strait and caught fire. Last week, New York Times columnist Thomas Friedman, a longtime enthusiast of the Gulf monarchies, went to the Gulf to perform his decades-old shtick of mixing metaphors and quoting cab drivers. But this time, Friedman may have inadvertently relayed the truth about what’s really happening.
From an unnamed “senior Emirati oil official,” Friedman claimed that, far from carrying out the perfectly calibrated petroleum-exfiltration scheme detailed in credulous news reports, the escort convoys are subjected to relentless Iranian ballistic missile and drone attacks. These salvos, Friedman wrote, result in a “bull’s-eye every time,” disabling tankers and forcing them to be towed back to port. This is “happening every day” according to Friedman’s source. If this is even remotely true, American war planners will eventually run out of ships to carry oil in and out of the Gulf and possibly people willing to operate them. Are people dying in these attacks? We certainly won’t be getting this kind of information out of the Pentagon anytime soon.
Hegseth’s strategy of deception and diversion simply won’t work in the long run. Remember that it wasn’t a string of dramatic sinkings of tankers that forced the Strait of Hormuz to close in the first place—it was shipowners and maritime insurance underwriters who found the threat of catastrophe to be far too high and effectively halted operations in the area. If the mighty American military, working day and night with its closest regional partners, cannot avert nightly precision strikes that disable countless tankers or permanently eliminate Iran’s capacity to harass shipping, then the forces of economic gravity will once more overtake the rhetoric of Trump administration jingoists.
Even if American political leaders were willing to continue to indefinitely foot the bill for this fool’s errand, it won’t return oil markets to the prewar status quo or ease the pain of diesel prices that are still close to $6 a gallon. And if there is no deal in place, the whole edifice will collapse in five minutes when the United States pulls the plug, just as it did when America jettisoned its occupations in Afghanistan and Iraq after 20 years.
So what’s the plan here? Iran has spent decades in an economic straitjacket imposed by the United States and its allies, and yet the regime persists. Neither economic isolation nor months of punishing attacks from the US and Israel have made them crack. Still, even though Tehran is willing to impose almost limitless hardships on its citizens so that its authoritarian system may endure, it’s unlikely to sit back and let America choke off its oil exports forever. This dangerous moment is made potentially more combustible by both a radicalized Iranian leadership and an American president who habitually threatens war crimes and escalation as a negotiating tactic.
A reckoning may come sooner rather than later. The Institute for the Study of War warned on Sunday that Iran “will likely attempt to run the US naval blockade in the coming days” in an effort to break it. Tehran has reportedly positioned 14 tankers around the export hub of Kharg Island and intends to use them to test US resolve—perhaps by setting China as a destination and daring the United States to stop them.
Popular
“swipe left below to view more authors”Swipe →
If the United States moves to interdict or disable the tankers, Iran may choose to retaliate by hitting targets it has thus far deemed off limits, including vital Gulf energy infrastructure or the multitude of unhardened civilian targets across the region. This threat is why, almost nine months into the war, America has chosen not to strike vital facilities of the Iranian oil industry or critical civilian infrastructure, despite Trump’s continued threats to do so.
Last week, CNN reported that Iran may be planning to target Trump administration officials with a so-called dirty bomb attack in Washington DC. Based on unnamed sources, the report reeked of the kind of media manipulation and errant fearmongering that led to the Iraq War more than 23 years ago. Zeteo’s Asawin Suebsaeng asked his own intelligence sources about the threat, which they deemed “total horseshit.” Both the contents of the report as well as its timing are disturbing—in the same way that alarmist accounts of new terrorist plots fed pro-war sentiment prior to the invasion of Iraq.
Meanwhile, as Tehran and Washington signal their intent to renew widespread hostilities, Iranian leaders are openly contemplating reversing their long-standing claim that the country’s nuclear program is for civilian purposes only. This would, of course, reverse the ostensible rationale for Trump’s war—and confirm the many warnings from regional experts that a military confrontation with Iran presents Tehran with a powerful incentive to build up its military nuclear capacity. It’s a problem Trump has been on a collision course with since his rash 2018 decision to pull out of the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action that stemmed the development of nuclear weapons in Iran.
American intelligence sources claim that they’ve pinpointed the location of Iran’s highly enriched uranium stockpile beneath a bomb site in Isfahan—but officials from the International Atomic Energy Agency say they can’t confirm these claims. For all we know, there are centrifuges spinning day and night deep inside Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain as the emboldened junta of Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps leaders who seem to be making the day-to-day decisions in Iran race toward a nuclear weapon.
Trump is, therefore, stuck exactly where he has been for months—desperate to be finished with a war that is far from finished with him, with the worst seemingly yet to come.

https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.title: Fishing in Goa before tourism made taxi-drivers of everyone: Karan Kapoor’s best photograph
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.author: Interview by Charlotte Jansen
https://www.theguardian.com/artanddesign.text:
I was born in India in 1962, the year after Goa was liberated from Portuguese rule. My mother was English and my father was Indian. My maternal grandparents worked in a theatre company and toured the east doing Shakespeare plays. My father, Shashi Kapoor, was an actor who worked for my grandparents’ theatre company and met my mother – Jennifer Kendal – there when he was 18. He then became a very successful movie star in India. They had a remarkable, unusual life. I thought it was normal.
In 1970, my parents decided to take a family holiday in Panjim in Goa. We stayed at the Mandovi hotel, an amazing place. I remember it vividly. We discovered a restaurant on the beach in a village called Saunta Vaddo, run by a seafarer, Anthony, who made incredible food. We fell in love with Saunta Vaddo. There was no electricity or running water back then. We went out exploring every day – there was always something to do. We swam, went fishing and read a lot. We rented a house called the Love House, because of the white heart painted on the roof – a shack on the beach that was previously inhabited by hippies and was full of books.
From then on, we spent every holiday there – Diwali, Christmas, Easter. Back then, if you took a ship to Goa from Mumbai it took 24 hours, and there were often no cabins left so you slept out on deck. But sometimes we drove and once my grandfather, who was a very bad driver, took us there. You couldn’t use headlights because of the war in the east, so we used torches from the backseat to light the road. The whole family would come at Christmas, and my dad would appear with a turkey on Christmas Eve, and fried fish and prawns from Anthony’s.
We became part of the village and we knew everyone. Eventually I started to record and photograph the people around me – our friends, weddings, ceremonies – characters I had known since I was eight. Then I started travelling to other parts of Goa with my brother, first on bikes, then motorbikes.
For me, this image of a big boat is very symbolic of everything that was amazing about Saunta Vaddo at that time. The whole village was involved, all the men were launching the boats out to sea to catch mackerel. A scout would look out for the schools, millions of them would come down the coast. There was a lot of excitement and shouting because, if they missed the catch, the next village further down would get them, so it was all a bit competitive.
As a child it was the most exciting thing, screaming and pushing this massive boat out, held together by tar and rope, and made the same way boats were made a century ago. The villagers would sing songs and drink feni, a local liquor; it was a way of life we had that doesn’t exist any more. In many ways, that boat held the whole village and the old slow Goan way of life together. Then tourism hit and the fishers became taxi drivers and waiters – they could make a better living that way. Things changed.
I continued photographing Goa until about 1996. You can’t recognise these places now, they’re so built-up. I’ve made a book of the photographs as a tribute to my parents, and will exhibit them in Panjim next month. I like to romanticise that the picture shows the last time they fished like that.
I went around on my Royal Enfield motorcycle with my Nikon FM and Hasselblad, stopping in tavernas to have a beer and some fried fish. I was drawn to the Portuguese influence in Goa, a legacy of more than 450 years of colonial rule. I photographed religious festivals, tiatr (musical theatre) and dhirio (a traditional bullfighting sport native to the state). I do remember the hippy era in the 1960s and 70s in Goa very well but it never interested me. I never photographed it.
Music was always a very big part of life in Goa: serenading, singing, playing instruments – and drinking. And the amazing fish curry rice is the best. I still go there every year, but I don’t go back to Saunta Vaddo – it’s been devastated. At first it made me sad but now I just feel fortunate to have had this experience, to have lived like that and known what it was like. It was incredible. I’m still looking for places like it.
My Goa 1976-1996: Photographs by Karan Kapoor is at Serendipity arts festival in Panjim, Goa, 13-20 December.
Karan Kapoor’s CV
Born: Mumbai, 1962
 
High point: I am just grateful that I have been able to have a successful career that provided for me and my family, doing what I love most
 
Top tip: Work with what is most personal and closest to your heart

https://gothamist.com/food/inside-the-th.title: Inside the Thanksgiving pie rush at the Brooklyn bakery Four & Twenty Blackbirds
https://gothamist.com/food/inside-the-th.author: Sonia Rao
https://gothamist.com/food/inside-the-th.text:
At the Brooklyn pie shop Four & Twenty Blackbirds, Thanksgiving prep begins in August. That’s when Ben Heemskerk, director of operations, said he starts to think about the massive amount of dough needed to fulfill an influx of orders for meticulously baked desserts. In September, he puts a team together to make that dough, which is kept frozen until much closer to the holiday.
“It’s like a roller-coaster where you’re just gradually going up,” Heemskerk said. “You feel the ch-ch-ch-ch-ch-ch and you know the time is coming. You know November is on its way.”
When November hits, the roller-coaster drops. Because everything other than the pie dough at Four & Twenty is made fresh for Thanksgiving orders, Heemskerk said the two weeks leading up to that Thursday are full of confectionery madness. Tensions rise with the oven temperatures as staff members work around the clock to bake pies for pickup and delivery orders, along with larger batches for wholesale shipments to places like Butterfield Market, Union Market and the Park Slope Food Coop. This year, according to Heemskerk, Four & Twenty will have produced something like 30,000 pies in the run-up to Thanksgiving.
“I’m really proud of [that] fact,” he said. “This year is actually the biggest year yet.”
Four & Twenty co-founders Melissa and Emily Elsen (they’re sisters from South Dakota) started custom-baking pies in their Crown Heights apartment in 2009. They opened a brick-and-mortar location on Third Avenue in Gowanus in 2010 and, within a couple years, had started to bake out of a nearby facility on Sackett Street as well. I swung by that roughly 3,000-square-foot facility earlier this week, hoping to catch a glimpse of the Thanksgiving sugar rush.
Melissa had warned me ahead of time that some employees might be stressed out, given the demands of baking this many handmade desserts: “When we’re only making a few hundred or even a thousand [pies], it’s doable,” she said. “When we scale up to this volume, you realize that it’s slow. Making things by hand takes a lot of time.”
But the facility turned out to be a pretty calm environment. By mid-Tuesday morning, all of the wholesale orders were out the door, and the bakers vibed to pop music while whisking custards and carefully folding pie crusts for local pickup and delivery orders. A warm buttery scent greeted me upon entering the space.
Four & Twenty hired several seasonal employees to join a dozen (or so) staff bakers during the Thanksgiving scramble. One of those staff members, Rufus Read, told me Tuesday that he had worked 12-hour shifts three days in a row. During that time, he oversaw the production of custard fillings for three of the four pies Four & Twenty offered customers for Thanksgiving orders: bittersweet chocolate pecan, salty honey and brown butter pumpkin. (The fourth and most popular pie of the bunch, the salted caramel apple, doesn’t involve custard.)
“We try to keep morale up,” he said. “It’s a long shift, but it could be way worse.”
Read estimated that he had made close to 50 rounds of pumpkin pie filling by the time I talked to him. “There’s 6,000 grams per batch, so you guys do the math,” he said. This would explain the massive stack of Libby’s canned pumpkin I saw resting against a wire storage rack.
Heemskerk talked me through some other Thanksgiving purchase orders, many of which were negotiated with suppliers over the summer. Four & Twenty ordered six pallets of 40-pound apple bushels from the Hudson Valley; three 1,700-pound pallets of medium-sized Georgia pecans; about 1,200 pounds of flour; and “lots and lots of butter” (specifically, Cabot’s European-style butter with 83% butterfat).
I walked around the facility to observe these ingredients in action. The bakers seemed to have reached a flow state, each one bouncing between different stages of the process. Rica Borich, a former Four & Twenty kitchen manager who returned to help with the Thanksgiving rush, told me she was working on a brown butter butterscotch for the pumpkin pie while also helping a colleague make chocolate ganache to spread across the bottom of the pecan pie.
The Four & Twenty employees working on the packaging side of things were a little more frantic, given that the unparalleled logistics of Thanksgiving pie delivery remains a headache. The completed wholesale orders had included 3-inch and 8-inch pies, which required a separate packaging process. Now, at least, all the pies were the traditional 10-inch size. (Thanksgiving orders have closed, but the same pies will be available afterward.)
McKale Goodwin, a fulfillment lead working his fifth Thanksgiving with Four & Twenty, said he had worked eight days in a row “trying to keep things going as smoothly as possible.” His job is to make sure the pies are packaged correctly and sent to the right destinations, lest someone not receive what they paid good money for (the 10-inch pies run $46 each). On Tuesday, Goodwin flitted about the facility to make sure his team had removed pies from the racks quickly enough for everyone in the kitchen to replenish the supply.
Four & Twenty scaled up operations as its client list grew over the past couple years. The company now works with Baldor, a food distribution service that Heemskerk said stretched the pie delivery zone from Maine to Washington, D.C. He told me about an email he received that morning from a loyal customer in Virginia who worried that her Thanksgiving would be ruined if she didn’t receive her Four & Twenty order in time. (She had nothing to be worried about, per Heemskerk.)
“People get really stressed out about their Thanksgiving dinners, and they want to be amazing hosts,” he said. “Whether you buy 5,000 pies for your company or one apple pie for your dinner table, it’s the same importance. It’s the same priority for those two customers.”
Heemskerk has a far more relaxed attitude toward his own Thanksgiving celebration. He said he planned to take a Four & Twenty pie to the house of friends who are hosting his family.
I asked which flavor he would bring. “Good question,” he answered. “At that point, it might just be whatever’s left. Don’t tell my hosts that.” (Sorry, hosts, if you’re reading this.)
Read, the custard czar, assumed he would end up in the kitchen on Thanksgiving, as per usual, but noted that there’s a lot less pressure when you’re cooking at home and can “wave my drink around and say hi to everyone and make some food.” Maybe someone else will bring the pie.
“That’s what I’ll be doing at some point on Thursday,” he said. “Might have to sleep in first.”
That rest is well deserved. Heemskerk said he encourages his staff to take the work seriously, given how much these pies mean to their customers — especially those like the woman in Virginia, who said that she’s ordered Four & Twenty pies for the past 10 Thanksgivings.
But Heemskerk also acknowledged that these aren’t life or death matters.
“I love my job,” he said. “It’s an important thing … but it’s just pie, right?”

Le Conseil supérieur de l’Éducation doit valider prochainement un projet de décret prévoyant de permettre aux Dasen, les représentants directs du ministre dans les départements, de convoquer et superviser les conseils de discipline.
La dérive répressive se poursuit dans l’Éducation nationale. Alors qu’environ 3 000 élèves sont passés en conseil de discipline entre septembre et début novembre dans le cadre du mouvement lycéen, un projet de décret prévoit de modifier le cadre juridique de la procédure disciplinaire applicable dans les établissements scolaires publics du second degré.
Il doit être présenté d’ici au 2 décembre lors d’une réunion du Conseil supérieur de l’éducation, et permettrait aux Dasen (directeur académique des services de l’Éducation nationale), les représentants directs du ministre à l’échelle départementale, de convoquer et de conduire ces instances. https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.title: US Army declares Iowa lead azide detonation ‘tremendously successful’
https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/2.text:
US Army declares Iowa lead azide detonation ‘tremendously successful’
Army hails Iowa’s lead azide detonation, claiming no traces of airborne lead have been detected so far.
United States Army officials have hailed Wednesday’s mission to destroy 68 drums of volatile lead azide — a sensitive munitions explosive — at a military base in Iowa as a success, saying it had “wildly exceeded their expectations”.
Speaking at a news conference in Middletown, a southeastern rural city adjacent to the ammunition plant where the operation was carried out, Major General Eric Shirley, the Army official in charge of the disposal effort, said overhead footage showed that “all of the lead azide barrels were definitively removed”.
The controlled detonation at 10:15am (16:15 GMT) destroyed approximately 4,500kg (10,000lb) of deteriorating lead azide — an explosive that has been used in military munitions since World War I.
“There was no secondary explosions. There was no kick-out. There was no infrastructure damage in or around our installation,” Shirley said, adding that the operation was “tremendously successful”.
Officials also said that extensive mitigation measures, including earthworks, foam barriers and gel blocks, had helped to absorb the shockwaves and toxic fallout.
However, Democratic Illinois House Representative Mike Quigley voiced dissatisfaction over how military leaders handled the operation, calling the holiday-eve scheduling and lack of communication “unconscionable”.
In a statement on X, the congressman wrote: “It is unfair that our military leaders are releasing 9,500 pounds of unstable lead azide on our friends in Iowa the day before Thanksgiving.”
‘Zero detection of airborne lead’
Following days of heightened alarm over lead dust contamination and its environmental repercussions, federal officials announced that preliminary data from Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) sensors had detected no airborne lead particles.
Ongoing monitoring efforts continue in the immediately affected blast zone.
A post on the agency’s social media account shortly after the operation said that “ALL EPA real-time air monitors are reporting ZERO detection of airborne lead throughout the region”.
Chemists have noted that lead, as a nonbiodegradable element, cannot be chemically decomposed or destroyed. It persists in the environment, with airborne particles capable of travelling considerable distances before settling on soil and potentially leaching into groundwater.
Detonating large stores of the unstable explosive would decompose the compound into its basic elements – nitrogen gas and metallic lead.
Lead is a potent neurotoxin that poses its sharpest threat to children and pregnant women, with links to learning disabilities, impaired neurological function, mental health challenges, reproductive harm, hearing loss and other impairments.
“The EPA can do millions of tests, but they [must also] test for the breakdown products and the stabilisers and plasticisers [containing] lead azide [which] are endocrine disruptors; some are cancer-causing chemicals,” said Scott Smith, an independent environmental testing expert who was heavily involved in air testing after the 2023 East Palestine, Ohio train derailment and industrial incidents.
The Army Sustainment Command said it would release a final breakdown of the affected area — including lead-dust dispersion and surface-deposition maps — after the operation.
“I believe absolutely that we reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanely possible the risk to the health and the safety of the people in Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” said Shirley.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/je.title: The Critic as Artist (And Vice Versa): A Fireside Chat with Jerry Saltz
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/je.author: Sarah Douglas
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/news/je.text:
During Art Week NYC, a citywide festival organized by ARTnews, Artforum, and Art in America, I had the great pleasure of doing a fireside chat with New York magazine senior art critic Jerry Saltz.
Like many of us, Jerry has been skeptical of AI, so I started the conversation by reading him a description of his approach to criticism produced by an AI that was based on a talk he gave a couple years ago. After chewing on that for a few minutes, we went on to speak about how he became a critic, how he became famous on social media, what he thinks about art being produced today, his strong feelings about auctions (he despises them), and what advice he would give creative people.
We also touched on the recent documentary made about Jerry and his wife, the former New York Times chief art critic Roberta Smith. And of course, it wouldn’t be a conversation with Jerry without plenty of engagement with the audience.
Despite its myriad challenges, Jerry still believes in New York City as a center for artists, and as a place with a vital community. You can watch the full talk, which took place on Saturday, November 14 at the PMC Studio in Midtown Manhattan, via the video here.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: ‘Emergência climática é realidade entre nós’: sobe para seis o número de mortos após tempestades no PR
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Murilo Bernardon
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
Os temporais que atingem o Paraná desde segunda-feira (23) deixaram seis mortos e afetaram mais de 10 mil pessoas em 50 municípios, segundo balanços divulgados pela Defesa Civil estadual nesta quarta-feira (25). A região Sudoeste concentra os maiores estragos, com famílias ilhadas, resgates por embarcações, desalojados e desabrigados. Segundo o climatologista e professor da Universidade Federal do Paraná (UFPR), Francisco Mendonça, “o fato é resultante das mudanças climáticas globais na fase da emergência climática”.
Segundo o Sistema de Tecnologia e Monitoramento Ambiental do Paraná (Simepar) e o Instituto Água e Terra (IAT), cidades paranaenses chegaram a registrar mais de 100 mm de chuva em 24h. Os maiores volumes de chuva acumulados incluíram Francisco Beltrão (PR), com 106,8 mm; Pato Branco (PR), 87,6 mm; Bom Sucesso do Sul (PR), 74 mm; Capanema (PR), 60,2 mm; e Toledo (PR), 55,6 mm. Ao todo, seis pessoas morreram em decorrência de afogamentos e enxurradas: duas em Campo Largo (PR), duas em Nova Esperança do Sudoeste (PR), uma em Verê (PR) e uma em Mato Rico (PR).
Segundo a Defesa Civil, mais de 10 mil pessoas foram atingidas direta ou indiretamente pelas chuvas em até 50 municípios paranaenses, com registros de 1.655 imóveis danificados e 13 casas destruídas. 216 pessoas estão desabrigadas e precisaram de abrigos públicos, e 511 estão desalojadas e foram para casas de parentes ou amigos. O órgão ainda está contabilizando novas informações sobre os afetados pelas chuvas intensas.
Segundo Mendonça, a frequência de chuvas intensas, que se estendem há meses no Paraná, saturou o solo de umidade, o que facilita a ocorrência de alagamentos. Aliado a esse fenômeno, o desmatamento intenso e histórico no estado e a impermeabilização urbana têm diminuído a capacidade de absorção da terra. O geógrafo, que também coordena a rede de pesquisa NAPI-Emergência Climática, afirma que “o que está acontecendo agora, a ciência tem já mostrado, e a situação tende a piorar em dezembro”.
Ele defende que é necessário agir antecipadamente, com articulação entre pesquisadores, Defesa Civil, sistemas de políticas públicas, secretarias de Estado, o que não vem sendo feito.
Um balanço da Companhia Paranaense de Energia (Copel) apontou cerca de 110 mil unidades consumidoras sem luz no estado na manhã desta quarta-feira. As regiões mais atingidas são Oeste (31 mil), Centro-Sul (26 mil) e Sudoeste (21 mil). A Companhia de Saneamento do Paraná (Sanepar) registrou danos em aproximadamente 100 unidades operacionais, afetando o fornecimento de água em 56 cidades. Municípios do Sudoeste, como Ampére, Salgado Filho, Enéas Marques e Nova Esperança do Sudoeste, tiveram tubulações arrancadas e poços alagados.
“O que aparece como primeiro sinal, como sintoma dessa doença no planeta Terra que a gente está vivendo? Eventos climáticos extremos mais fortes, mais intensos, mais repetitivos. Este ano de 2026 é essa junção de evento climático extremo, que já está cenarizado nas mudanças climáticas, com o El Niño”, analisa.
Mendonça afirma que é preciso criar estratégias de enfrentamento e que haja “uma mudança fundamental na estrutura do sistema econômico-político mundial”, com urgência. “Entre 1997, em Kyoto, e a COP 21, em Paris, em 2015, quase nada foi feito no planeta para reduzir as emissões, para reduzir o desmatamento, consumo, poluição, quase nada foi feito”, afirma.
O Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (Inmet) mantém aviso de perigo para tempestades nesta quarta-feira (25), com previsão de chuvas intensas (até 100 mm/dia), queda de granizo e ventos de 60 a 100 km/h. O Simepar indica que a instabilidade continua na quinta-feira (26), com maior intensidade na metade Oeste do estado. A Defesa Civil orienta a população a não atravessar áreas alagadas e acompanhar os alertas via SMS (40199).

https://www.propublica.org/article/orego.author: Rob Davis
https://www.propublica.org/article/orego.text:
When Oregon’s Housing Stability Council met by Zoom in early October, the state’s top housing official told the oversight board that she wanted to address a story ProPublica published that morning.
The story revealed that the official, Andrea Bell, hadn’t clearly disclosed her husband’s work for a small consulting firm that helps housing authorities develop apartments, sometimes with money from Bell’s agency. Nor had she notified Gov. Tina Kotek about it, something Oregon law requires of a governor’s appointee when an actual or potential conflict arises.
Council members, who award hundreds of millions of dollars in housing subsidies, affirmed their support for Bell, who told them she wanted to be clear: “None of the projects that are coming from the council impact my household income.”
Newly obtained records, however, show a clear financial connection between the council’s decisions and her husband’s employer. The records also show that Bell was personally involved in meetings and internal discussions about state funding of a large apartment project, Aloha 209th, which her husband’s employer is helping to develop.
Backers of the Aloha 209th project in Portland’s suburbs are seeking $17.5 million from the housing council, which receives funding recommendations from Bell’s agency.
JH Brawner, the consulting firm that employs Bell’s husband, Joshua Crites, will earn a $2 million fee from the housing authority in Washington County if the transaction closes. If not, JH Brawner gets nothing.
A separate project outside Portland, the Park Place apartments in Clackamas County, already received money through Oregon’s housing agency. Five months after Oregon awarded $36 million to the project in May 2025, Clackamas County’s housing authority paid JH Brawner a $2.4 million consulting fee, the new records show.
Like the Washington County contract, the one with Clackamas County says that if funding fell through for any reason and the project didn’t move forward, “no fee shall be due” to the firm.
JH Brawner said Crites, the firm’s director of strategic initiatives, has not worked on the Aloha 209th project but was one of five staffers assigned to Park Place. JH Brawner pays employees, including Crites, a fixed salary that is not tied to any project closing, according to managing director Zak de Gorgue.
Bell, executive director of Oregon Housing and Community Services, said in a statement that she is “committed to transparency, accountability, and compliance with state law.”
“At no point in my tenure as executive director have I used my position to influence or benefit myself or anyone related to me,” she said. “To be clear, I made no efforts to influence funding, and the Aloha 209 project has not received funding from OHCS and remains on the waitlist.”
Bell’s public agency sits in the middle of the state’s effort to combat a homelessness problem that is among the nation’s worst. Kotek, the governor, has made building more housing a pillar of her time in office. Oregon Housing and Community Services has distributed billions of state and federal dollars to subsidize the construction of apartments intended to have affordable rents.
Norman Williams, a law professor at Willamette University College of Law who teaches about government ethics, said Bell should have reported to the governor that she had a possible conflict and stayed out of any discussions about the projects her husband’s employer helped develop.
“It may all be an innocent mistake on her part,” Williams said, “but she knows who her husband is working for and she doesn’t report that. It makes it look like she’s trying to conceal this.”
De Gorgue said in a statement that the Aloha 209th project is still in development and the company had “no knowledge of Andrea Bell taking any action to move the project forward, nor has JH Brawner & Company engaged in any advocacy to secure funding approval” from Bell’s agency. Funding applications were submitted by the local housing authorities, not by JH Brawner.
“We have no indication, nor any reason to believe, that any project on which we have consulted has been the beneficiary of inappropriate influence,” de Gorgue said.
Separately, he said Clackamas and Washington counties chose JH Brawner as a consultant years before the company hired Crites in 2023.
Crites did not respond to an emailed request for comment.
After ProPublica asked Bell about her husband’s employment in September, she amended three years of ethics disclosure forms, explicitly naming JH Brawner as his employer. (The one time her state filings alluded to Crites’ job before that was in 2025, with a misspelling: “Spouse serves in an advisory role for a developmen.” It showed only the company’s street address, misspelled, and not its name.)
Bell also asked the Oregon Government Ethics Commission for a formal opinion about her potential conflict at the direction of Kotek’s staff. That evaluation was paused after the commission opened a preliminary review in response to a citizen complaint about her lack of disclosure. The preliminary review is ongoing.
ProPublica obtained the new details about Bell’s involvement through county contracts and emails to and from Bell, which were released under Oregon’s public records law. Bell’s agency initially said the emails would cost $612.50 to produce but eventually provided them for free. Washington County charged $364.25 for contracts, invoices and other documents.
Though backers say the Aloha 209th housing development is ready to be built, it’s on a waitlist to receive money from the state. Its turn is not likely to come until at least late 2028. By then, local officials worry that the delay will jeopardize its other funding sources and the project may need an even larger subsidy.
ProPublica previously reported that Molly Rogers, head of the county housing agency seeking money for Aloha 209th, spoke publicly about contacting Bell and said the state agency director was receptive to talking further.
The new records contain Bell’s recollections of the phone conversation she had with Rogers. The same morning the two spoke, in June, Bell told another department official by email that Aloha 209th had “a unique dimension of urgency and angst” because it was one of the last projects funded by a 2018 voter-approved housing bond administered by the Portland area’s Metro regional government.
Natasha Detweiler-Daby, who leads the state housing agency’s affordable rental housing division, responded to Bell that it could be “responsive and logical” to have lawmakers “add nuance” next year by dedicating some portion of funding for housing authority projects on Oregon’s waitlist. Detweiler-Daby did not respond to an email from ProPublica seeking comment.
Behind the Aloha 209th discussion was the way that Oregon awards its housing subsidies. Since 2024, Oregon has given the money on a first-come, first-served basis. When funding runs out, Bell’s agency places applications on a waitlist in the order received.
Bell spoke with Washington County officials about Aloha 209th during a 45-minute Zoom meeting in August, records show. Internal notes summarizing the conversation say that the county would send an updated report to the state agency to “inform movement of 209.” The summary said the groups involved would have a follow-up conversation about the project.
Bell went on to discuss the project with regional government officials in early September. About two weeks before the meeting, she emailed her deputy with two possible ways to get the project funded: a legislative “carve-out” or Metro consolidating its subsidies so it could fully pay for the project. “I want to do everything we can to help the metro projects be successful and the resources, like ours, are nearly depleted,” Bell wrote. She acknowledged that Metro might not find the solution appealing.
Bell told ProPublica that she met with Metro and Washington County at the other agencies’ request. She said her agency “does not have and is not pursuing a ‘legislative carve out’ for any project.”
“My approach is to listen to partners’ concerns and explain our funding process,” she said in an email. “I have no role in deciding whether projects should receive funding as part of this process, and I do not advocate for individual projects. Characterizing these routine discussions and legitimate concerns as something improper fundamentally misrepresents their purpose and context.”
A spokesperson for Washington County’s housing authority told ProPublica that Bell did not make any commitment to alter the prioritization of Aloha 209th. Another Washington County spokesperson said the August meeting with Bell was mainly focused on the housing authority’s desire for “clearer criteria” for how projects on the state’s waitlist get funded.
A Metro spokesperson said the regional agency requested the September meeting with a goal “for the two agencies to strengthen our working relationship and coordination.”
“Metro does not, and did not, advocate for any specific project,” the spokesperson said. “We clearly indicated this at the meeting and in writing ahead of the meeting.” The agency has advocated for a group of remaining projects, including Aloha 209th, to get money so Metro can fulfill commitments made as part of its affordable housing bond, the spokesperson said.
Oregon’s Government Ethics Commission has until early December to complete its preliminary review of the complaint over Bell’s financial disclosure, which will help the agency decide whether to open a full investigation.
Bell said she will “continue to remain responsive to the Ethics Commission” as it completes its examination.
Kotek’s office, provided with a list of ProPublica’s latest findings, said in a statement that the governor “holds all agency leadership to consistent and high ethical standards” and that her office “is closely following” the ethics panel’s review.

https://taz.de/EU-Gipfel-zum-Westbalkan/.title: EU-Gipfel zum Westbalkan: Jetzt oder vielleicht nie
https://taz.de/EU-Gipfel-zum-Westbalkan/.author: Mathias Brüggmann
https://taz.de/EU-Gipfel-zum-Westbalkan/.text:
EU-Gipfel zum Westbalkan: Jetzt oder vielleicht nie
Nach dem Machtwechsel in Serbien will die EU die Annäherung der Region beschleunigen. Das Zeitfenster für Beitritte schließt sich aber.
Nach dem Erdrutschsieg der Opposition in Serbien am 25. Oktober beschleunigt die EU ihre Bemühungen, den Westbalkan in die Union zu holen. Die Niederlage von Aleksandar Vučićs prorussischer Regierungspartei und der Erfolg der auf Rechtsstaatlichkeit pochenden Studierendenliste im bevölkerungsreichsten Westbalkanstaat eröffnen Brüssel eine Chance. Zugleich steigt mit Blick auf einen möglichen Sieg der Rechtspopulistin Marine Le Pen bei der französischen Präsidentschaftswahl 2027 der Zeitdruck.
„Die Zukunft des Westbalkans liegt in der Europäischen Union. Ihr Beitritt ist unsere Priorität, unser gemeinsames Ziel und eine entscheidende geopolitische Investition in diesen herausfordernden Zeiten“, erklärte EU-Ratspräsident António Costa kurz vor dem Westbalkangipfel in Brüssel. Auf diesem wollten die Staats- und Regierungschefs der EU und der sechs Staaten des westlichen Balkans am Mittwochabend über eine weitere Annäherung beraten.
Fünf Länder des Westbalkans – Albanien, Bosnien und Herzegowina, Montenegro, Nordmazedonien und Serbien – gelten als EU-Kandidaten. Das sechste, die Republik Kosovo, hat zwar einen Beitrittsantrag gestellt, doch fünf EU-Staaten – Griechenland, Rumänien, Slowakei, Spanien und Zypern – erkennen es nicht an, weshalb es keinen Kandidatenstatus besitzt. Montenegro gilt unterdessen als einer der am weitesten fortgeschrittenen Beitrittskandidaten. Das Land mit rund 625.000 Einwohnerinnen und Einwohnern könnte bereits 2028 der Union beitreten. Allerdings bestehen zwischen Montenegro und dem benachbarten EU-Mitglied Kroatien noch ungelöste Streitigkeiten.
„Serbien hat die Chance auf einen Neuanfang“, machte Erweiterungskommissarin Marta Kos Hoffnung auf ein Ende der zuletzt angespannten Beziehungen zwischen Brüssel und Belgrad. Doch viele Fragen bleiben offen: Das außenpolitische Programm der Studierendenliste, die nun mit absoluter Mehrheit bis Jahresende eine Regierung bildet, bleibt unklar.
Wie die neue serbische Regierung aussehen wird, womit sie sich beschäftigen und wie sie arbeiten wird, ist eine Frage, die derzeit sowohl in Serbien als auch darüber hinaus gestellt wird. „Antworten gibt es bislang nicht“, sagte der Berliner Analyst Adi Cerimagic vom Thinktank European Stability Initiative (ESI) der Deutschen Welle.
Eine Hoffnung ist, dass Vučićs bisherige Doppelstrategie – Annäherung an die EU und zugleich engere Kooperation mit Russland und China – endet. Dass Russland und China ihren Einfluss auf dem Balkan ausweiten, beunruhigt Brüssel.
Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz und andere EU-Regierungschefs denken über eine engere Anbindung der Westbalkanstaaten nach, auch ohne sofortigen Beitritt – etwa durch eine schrittweise Integration in den EU-Binnenmarkt. Doch schon der 2023 entwickelte Westbalkan-Wachstumsplan, der Beitrittskandidaten nach konkreten Reformen finanziell unterstützen soll, stößt auf Probleme. Bisher flossen erst 673,6 Millionen der bis 2027 vorgesehenen 6 Milliarden Euro. Zudem blieb bis zuletzt offen, wer Belgrad auf dem Gipfel vertritt und wer das innenpolitisch fragile Kosovo repräsentiert.

https://jacobin.com/2026/11/lawsuit-amaz.title: Pregnant Workers Say Amazon Is Violating Their Rights
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/lawsuit-amaz.author: Jenny Brown
https://jacobin.com/2026/11/lawsuit-amaz.text:
Pregnant Workers Say Amazon Is Violating Their Rights
Amazon now faces a class-action lawsuit on behalf of its pregnant workers, many of whom say their rights to accommodation have been violated. They describe a pattern of being refused chairs, additional bathroom breaks, and relief from strenuous work.
Willamina Barclay was working as a picker at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Rochester, New York, when she felt lightheaded again. “She pleaded with a manager for a seat. . . . He refused: ‘No, because you don’t have a [pregnancy] accommodation. If I give you a chair, I have to give everybody else a chair,’” he said, according to a recent lawsuit.
But Barclay, who learned she was pregnant in March 2025, had already asked managers many times for accommodations — a seat, extra breaks to drink, eat, pee (or throw up) in the bathroom, no ladder-climbing or squatting, and no heavy lifting.
Amazon — a company known for fast delivery — had failed to answer for weeks, demanding medical documentation. Even after Barclay provided it, Amazon still refused most accommodations, permitting her four breaks a day but no chair. She was moved to a different position but still required to lift heavy packages.
Amazon counted her new breaks against her unpaid time off (UPT), a leave bank that workers accumulate at five minutes per hour and that maxes out at eighty hours. She went to Human Resources several times to try to rectify the situation but stopped, because they were also counting those visits as UPT, the lawsuit says.
The heavy lifting led to sharp pains. At one point she left the warehouse in a wheelchair headed for the hospital. Amazon also counted that time against her unpaid leave bank. On another occasion, she had to leave due to uncontrolled vomiting. Despite a doctor’s note, that was also counted against her. Her UPT thus used up; Amazon fired her.
Under the law, workers cannot be penalized for taking pregnancy-related leave.
Barclay’s ordeal is detailed in a lawsuit filed September 8 by A Better Balance, a nonprofit focused on work policies affecting families. It’s a proposed class action on behalf of all US workers whose rights under the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA) have been violated by Amazon.
Systematic Violations
Barclay’s harrowing experience is common, said Sultana Hossain, recording secretary of the Amazon Labor Union (ALU) on Staten Island: Under the law, “pregnant workers don’t have to give in paperwork,” she said. “They only have to verbally say, ‘I’m pregnant and I need to be accommodated.’ But we’re seeing Amazon systemically violate that.
“Even if workers get an accommodation eventually, it can take several weeks,” said Hossain. “So people really don’t have any choice but to keep working in their regular role, which is really dangerous if they actually need an accommodation.”
Key’Asia, a worker at Amazon’s fulfillment center near Wilmington, Delaware, said that Amazon management twice rejected a note from her doctor, once because it had an e-signature, and then again when she got an ink signature. (For privacy to discuss medical matters, some workers asked that last names not be used.)
Managers said the signature looked fraudulent and still refused to accommodate her pregnancy, Key’Asia said. “They are making you do the things that your doctor told you that you’re not supposed to be doing,” she told attendees at an online Jobs With Justice event in October. “They’re making you do things that are putting yourself and your baby at risk.” She said Amazon fired her twice, both times when she was pregnant.
Pattern of Illegality
Workers have noticed a pattern: When they request accommodations, Amazon managers ask if they are “safe to work.” If they say yes, they are forced to continue to work without accommodations. If they say no, Amazon puts them on unpaid leave, which rapidly runs out.
Marissa, who worked at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Rossford, Ohio, said that after her accommodations were denied, she was forced out on unpaid leave, and she ended up losing her apartment. “I was out $1,700. . . . I couldn’t pay for my vehicle. I couldn’t afford to eat.
“Amazon doesn’t care about whether or not you’re in pain,” she said. “They care about whether or not you can get their packages out on time.”
Hossain said it was typical for workers to get fired for “job abandonment” because “they ran out of time-off options because they were just not given the accommodation.” (A Better Balance has also sued Amazon for this practice on behalf of a disabled worker.)
Tragic Results
Hayat Bzezi was working at Amazon’s Staten Island JFK8 warehouse during the busy holiday season of 2024, when all workers were required to take an additional weekly ten-hour shift. She had asked for lighter duty, and management said she could use a chair, but then she was denied it.
She was “lifting heavy products, climbing up and down the stairs, despite having a high-risk pregnancy,” said her husband Wajdy, an elected ALU trustee who works at the same warehouse.
Hayat worked through pain, but it got worse and finally she had to go to the hospital, where she miscarried. It was the second time she had miscarried while working at Amazon. After that the couple decided to speak out. Since then, she has stopped working at Amazon and has been able to bear a child.
Law Reduces Miscarriages
When the PWFA went into effect in 2023, a study found that it reduced miscarriages by 9.6 percent. This suggests that many more miscarriages could be avoided if Amazon, the country’s second-largest private employer, started following the law.
But there is every indication that Amazon is ignoring it. Last year, New Jersey’s attorney general filed a lawsuit against Amazon after reviewing thousands of worker requests for accommodations. Amazon is New Jersey’s largest private employer, with around fifty thousand workers.
“When Amazon’s pregnant workers and workers with disabilities request accommodations, Amazon stonewalls them,” the suit charges. “It forces them through a byzantine accommodations process, imposing rigid and unnecessary paperwork requirements and subjecting workers to unexplained weeks-long delays.”
Rosa, a worker at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Akron, Ohio, said she asked for pregnancy accommodations because she was working in Ship Dock, a role that requires heavy lifting, pushing, and pulling. She was hospitalized for dehydration four times, but managers still kept her in that role, she said.
“Eventually my symptoms became so severe that I had to take an unpaid leave of absence,” she said. “I found out afterwards that I could have done paid short-term disability leave, but these options weren’t told to me.”
Amazon denies this. “The suggestion that we routinely deny or don’t support pregnancy accommodations is simply untrue,” said Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel. She said “99.9 percent” of pregnancy accommodation requests this year had been approved.
But New Jersey investigators found that Amazon regularly fired workers for requesting accommodations, in violation of New Jersey’s Law Against Discrimination and the PWFA. New York State has also sued Amazon for this.
Hossain said the medical forms that Amazon requires for pregnancy, injury, and disability accommodations are so comprehensive and invasive that doctors have objected that they violate medical privacy laws.
Amazon wants such detailed medical documentation, Hossain said, because “they want to claim that if workers ever get injured, it’s because of conditions they came to work with, and it’s not workplace injuries.” Asked about this, an Amazon public relations representative declined to respond.
Pace Drives Injuries
The worker justice group Warehouse Life has been tracking and protesting Amazon’s health and safety record since 2023, and helping injured workers who have to “fight through a lot of misinformation and lies that they received from [Amazon] managers about workers’ comp,” said Chloe Sigal, campaign manager for the group.
Sigal said Amazon’s rate system, along with “time off task” (TOT) policies, make the work unsafe: “Amazon is pushing people to work as fast, as hard as humanly possible — or really outside what is humanly possible. That’s what’s driving this injury epidemic.”
In 2021 the California legislature found that injuries in Amazon warehouses were driven by its rate system. Workers were forced to work faster and faster because if they fell into the lowest 25 percent they could experience discipline, and the bottom 5 percent risked termination.
California passed a law requiring warehouses to publish stable quotas and not constantly accelerate them. In 2024 the state fined Amazon $6 million for violating it.
Workers also accumulate TOT when surveillance detects a pause in their package scanning. Fear of too much TOT pushes workers to cut short their breaks, skip bathroom breaks (and reduce liquid consumption to match), and push on through pain. Dehydration is particularly risky during a pregnancy. “The reason that people are miscarrying at Amazon is because of this rate system,” said Sigal.
Doctors agree. Jenny Fish is a Santa Rosa, California, physician who provides prenatal care. “Prolonged standing, going the whole shift without water, lifting more than 15 to 20 pounds, working night shifts regularly,” she said, “all of this has been irrefutably linked to higher risk of miscarriage, preeclampsia, increased maternal fatigue, preterm delivery, low birth weight, and just in general adverse birth outcomes.” Preeclampsia is potentially fatal.
Is There a Policy?
Sigal said that soon after Warehouse Life started, several Amazon workers came to the group reporting pregnancy issues. But when the group put out a call on social media for experiences working at Amazon while pregnant, it was flooded with stories. Two thousand women from forty states responded, and eighty-one described loss of a pregnancy. (Get more info on Warehouse Life here.)
Now some of these workers are leading the charge to get changes at the company. They have put pressure on New York City’s Mount Sinai Health System to terminate Amazon board of directors member Edith Cooper as a hospital trustee, given Amazon’s dismal safety record.
Warehouse Life members have also met with Amazon management. Sigal said that during those meetings Amazon claimed to have a policy on pregnancy that was only available to workers. But no workers were able to access it. “Nobody has it. We’ve heard from managers that they don’t have it either, that they don’t receive training on what to do,” Sigal said.
When Labor Notes asked Amazon for its pregnancy policy and any training materials, no documents were forthcoming. Warehouse Life counters that the company’s real pregnancy policy is “Delay. Deny. Discipline.”
March on HR
The Amazon Labor Union organized on Staten Island in 2022, and in 2024 affiliated with the Teamsters. But Amazon refuses to negotiate with the union at the five-thousand-worker warehouse, despite being ordered to do so by the National Labor Relations Board in April.
The union can still help, though. “Just a few weeks ago a pregnant worker came to our union hall saying she wanted help getting an accommodation at work,” said ALU’s Hossain. The worker had already told her manager that she was pregnant.
The union sent several workers to accompany her to HR, saying “that should be enough, and Amazon needs to start the process of accommodating her,” Hossain said. “And they actually did listen, but only because a group of workers accompanied her.” A contract could provide additional protections.
The union isn’t waiting for workers to seek it out. Union activists distribute fliers with a QR code to a reporting form that goes to the union. Half of the reports “are unfair discipline, the other half is workers who are dealing with injuries or the accommodation process or need workers’ comp or whatever,” said Hossain. “It’s such a big issue.”
“It really does feel like we’re all just numbers,” said Rosa in Akron. “I want them to take more accountability. They make it so hard when it comes to a life-changing thing.”

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: What is at stake for Spain’s art sector as snap election approaches?
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Alexandra F. Coego
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Spain’s snap elections, due to take place on 29 November, have left several long-awaited new measures and legislation for art and culture hanging in the balance. These include regulations on AI, intellectual property and artist welfare. With a coalition between the conservative Partido Popular (PP) and the far-right Vox party looking increasingly likely, here is what the vote could mean for the country’s art and culture sector.
Reduced budget and censorship fears
The future of the ministry of culture has been a subject of debate in the lead-up to the election. PP has argued in favour of maintaining it, albeit merged with other portfolios, but Vox will only support the ministry’s existence if cultural powers currently held by Spain’s autonomous communities are transferred to the central government.
The prospect of such a transfer has raised concerns over censorship, particularly in the light of a wave of cancelled art festivals and plays in PP-Vox-led regions since the 2023 regional elections. At a party meeting on 22 November, Vox’s secretary general, Ignacio Garriga, stated that they will support cultural professionals who “create quality national products” and “highlight the value of the country's culture”.
Even if the ministry of culture continues, the sector expects budget cuts under a PP-Vox coalition. The PP has pledged to quickly pass a new patronage law with tax and legal incentives to encourage private businesses and individuals to fund cultural projects, arguing that healthcare and defence spending will leave culture underfunded by the state. The PP's proposals for culture also include auditing working conditions, exhibition standards and security protocols across national museums.
Long-awaited legislation up in the air
The Status of the Artist bill, a welfare package designed to improve working conditions of those in the cultural sector, will enter into force in 2027 regardless of the election results, after being approved by the Council of Ministers in July. However, the inclusion of visual artists—who, unlike other types of artists, were entirely left out of the bill and continue to face prohibitive self-employment quotas—remains up in the air.
Earlier this year, the Union of Contemporary Artists of Spain launched a campaign to push for their inclusion with the support of the ministry of culture, but the decision stalled in the ministries of social security and finance. Gloria Reguero, the president of the union, says that they have been waiting since 2018 for painters, sculptors and photographers to be recognised as artists. “Just when it seemed we were going to start negotiating our terms, the elections came along, and with them, another setback,” she tells The Art Newspaper.
Meanwhile, a separate draft bill regulating the use of generative AI in the arts is not getting off the ground at all. The legislation was put out for public consultation in late September and it marked the government’s third attempt to regulate AI in the arts following two failed royal decrees. The draft bill sought to prohibit the use of generative AI to exploit an artist’s image, voice or work without their express consent and specific remuneration and, like the Status of the Artist, it left out the visual arts.
Major museum projects in the balance
Both PP and Vox have strongly opposed plans by Ernest Urtasun, the current Spanish culture minister, to review state museum collections—specifically the Museum of the Americas and the National Museum of Anthropology—to “move past a colonial framework”. When the initiative was first announced in early 2024, the PP dismissed the push for decolonisation, in a statement, as “a false debate, imposed and manufactured to create division among Spaniards”.
In November 2025, the ministry formally presented a €13.6m project to overhaul the permanent exhibitions and narratives of both institutions through an “anti-racist and gender perspective”.
Ahead of the elections, the project has reached different stages: while the National Museum of Anthropology has already moved through its public tendering process for the remodelling of its permanent exhibition, the Museum of the Americas remains at an earlier stage, with major works still pending. If a new government takes office, the initiative’s long-term completion, scheduled for 2028, faces significant uncertainty—with a risk that yet-to-be-contracted tenders may be halted or that curatorial direction may be revised. A spokesperson for the Museum of the Americas declined to respond to The Art Newspaper's request for comment, “especially now that we’re on the eve of the elections and everything is so uncertain”, they say.

https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120415.title: Berlin-Wahl | Konflikt um Vanessa Emde: Die Linke wird erwachsen
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120415.author: Marten Brehmer
https://www.nd-aktuell.de/artikel/120415.text:
- Kommentare
- Berlin-Wahl
Konflikt um Vanessa Emde: Die Linke wird erwachsen
Mit dem Ausschluss von Vanessa Emde zeigt die Berliner Linksfraktion rote Linien auf. Um eine inhaltliche Auseinandersetzung stiehlt man sich aber herum. Ein Kommentar
Ob die Neuköllner Abgeordnete Vanessa Emde aus der Linksfraktion im Berliner Abgeordnetenhaus ausgeschlossen wird, war bis zur letzten Minute unsicher. Vorhersehbar waren dagegen die Reaktionen ihrer Unterstützer, als am Dienstagabend bekannt wurde, dass Emde tatsächlich die Fraktion verlassen muss. »Die Berliner Parteispitze lässt sich von SPD, Grünen und bürgerlicher Presse vor sich hertreiben, statt selbstbewusst linke Opposition zu organisieren«, schreibt die Landesarbeitsgemeinschaft Palästinasolidarität in einem Beitrag auf Instagram. Man brauche keine »angepasste Regierungspartei«, heißt es weiter. Die Partei dürfe sich nicht »von Regierungsambitionen, Posten und wirtschaftlichen Interessen« leiten lassen.
Die Engstirnigkeit, die aus solchen Sätzen spricht, begleitet die politische Linke schon seit Jahrhunderten. Lenin nannte die Weigerung, im Dienste einer ideologischen Reinheit Verantwortung zu übernehmen, einst eine »Kinderkrankheit« sozialistischer Parteien. Seine Polemik aus dem Jahr 1920 richtete sich gegen die Theoretiker des Rätekommunismus – eine bis heute verbreitete semianarchistische Irrlehre. Gültig ist sie aber ebenso für den selbst ernannten linken Flügel der Linkspartei.
Dass Die Linke nun erstmals eine Grenze zum radikalen Teil der Palästina-Unterstützer zieht, ist ein wichtiger Schritt. Er zeigt, dass sie gewillt ist, auch innerparteiliche Konflikte zu riskieren, um ihre Kernforderungen durchzusetzen. Enteignung großer Wohnungskonzerne, Bezahlbarkeit angesichts galoppierender Inflation, Schutz vor Abschiebungen – für all das wurde sie gewählt, nicht für eine kompromisslose Haltung in der Nahost-Frage.
Ernüchternd ist allerdings, dass die Parteispitze nicht den Mut gefunden hat, den Konflikt inhaltlich auszutragen. Stattdessen zog man sich darauf zurück, dass Emdes Verhalten in diesem Streit eine Zusammenarbeit unmöglich gemacht habe. Angesichts der Dreistigkeit, mit der Emde alle Beschlüsse ihrer Partei ignorierte, ist es wenig überraschend, dass man das als den Weg des geringsten Widerstands ansah. Dass Emde sich an einer Gegendemonstration zum Landesparteitag am 31. Oktober beteiligte, dürfte auch ihren engsten Geschwistern im Geiste unmöglich gemacht haben, sie weiter zu unterstützen.
Der Konflikt bleibt so jedoch, auch wenn Emde vorerst nicht mehr daran beteiligt sein wird. Denn die Anhänger ihrer Positionen sind nach wie vor zahlreich, auch wenn sie nur eine kleine Minderheit der 20.000 Linke-Mitglieder in Berlin ausmachen.
Es ist nur eine Frage der Zeit, bis der nächste Skandal um den ewigen Zankapfel Nahost die Linkspartei erschüttert. Zwischen den radikalen Palästina-Aktivisten und der bürgerlichen Presse hat sich längst ein symbiotisches Verhältnis etabliert. Die eine Seite provoziert immer wieder mit gezielten Grenzüberschreitungen – und die andere Seite greift das bereitwillig auf und münzt es zu pauschalen Zweifeln an der Regierungsfähigkeit der Linken um. Ironischerweise teilen die Aktivisten mit Springer und Co. das Ziel, einen Senat unter Linke-Führung zu verhindern. Deprimierend ist die Erkenntnis, dass beidseitig das Leid der Menschen in Nahost am Ende nur Mittel zum Zweck ist.
Dabei hätte der Streit um Emde der Linken die Chance geboten, eine klare rote Linie zu ziehen. Gebetsmühlenartig wiederholte Emde immer wieder einen Satz: »Staaten haben kein Existenzrecht, Menschen haben ein Recht zu existieren.« Gemeint ist damit offenbar, dass Israel im Rahmen einer »demokratischen Einstaatenlösung« durch einen gemeinsamen Staat für Juden, Muslime, Christen und alle anderen Bewohner zwischen Jordan und Meer ersetzt werden solle.
Man mag das als utopische Hippie-Träumerei abtun. In Wahrheit hat diese Forderung aber einen perfiden Hintergrund. Der Verweis auf das harmonische Zusammenleben in ferner Zukunft dient als moralischer Freibrief dafür, all jene bedingungslos zu unterstützen, die militant gegen den Status quo vorgehen. Dabei brauchte es nicht erst das Massaker am 7. Oktober 2023, um zu verstehen, was passiert, wenn die Hamas freie Hand bekommt. Den Massenmord an den jüdischen Bewohnern Israels nehmen die Unterstützer der Einstaatenlösung implizit in Kauf – ob nun aus Naivität oder Kalkül.
Ihr komplementäres Äquivalent findet diese Haltung in der kaum weniger menschenverachtenden bedingungslosen Unterstützung für das barbarische Vorgehen der israelischen Kriegsmaschinerie in Gaza. Der Schutz, den Israel Juden bietet, wird auch in der Linken von nicht wenigen in einer Weise fetischisiert, die den Blick für den real geschehenen Massenmord in Gaza zwischen 2024 und 2025 verstellt.
Frieden statt Sieg muss die gemeinsame Position der Linken sein, wenn sie unter den herrschenden Verhältnissen humanistisch bleiben will. Der Streit um Emde hätte ein Anlass sein können, das offensiv hervorzuheben – und sich zugleich aus dem Klammergriff innerparteilicher Konflikte zu befreien. So bleibt der Streit nur beruhigt, aber nicht beigelegt.
Wir haben nachgerechnet
Dieser Artikel hat dich nichts gekostet. Uns schon: Recherche, Produktion und Technik. Wir haben bei der Büromiete sowie bei Druck und Vertrieb gespart. Und wir haben auf Gehalt verzichtet. Trotzdem gilt: Ohne dich geht die Rechnung nicht auf. Bis Ende des Jahres brauchen wir 300.000 Euro. Du zahlst, was du kannst, dafür schreiben wir weiter.
Keine Paywall, kein Kleingedrucktes, nur ein Ziel: dass nd bleibt.

https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.title: Steelers reportedly cut Rodgers after QB accuses coach McCarthy of sleeping during meetings
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.author: Tom Lutz
https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/n.text:
Aaron Rodgers launched an extraordinary attack on his head coach, Mike McCarthy, on Wednesday after the Pittsburgh Steelers benched him in favor of backup quarterback Mason Rudolph.
ESPN have reported that the Steelers have released Rodgers after his outburst. If no other team claim Rodgers on waivers, he will become an unrestricted free agent. Several teams, including the Indianapolis Colts and New England Patriots, are in need of a starting quarterback at the moment.
McCarthy, who was also Rodgers’ coach with the Green Bay Packers, had said on Monday that the 42-year-old was still the team’s starter despite recent struggles. On Tuesday night, the Steelers changed course and said Rodgers, one of the greatest players in NFL history, would be deactivated for Friday’s game against the Denver Broncos.
On Wednesday, Rodgers appeared on The Pat McAfee Show and set fire to whatever remained of his relationship with the coach. Rodgers first said he would not return to the Steelers, stating: “That ship has sailed”. He then accused McCarthy of falling asleep during meetings.
“Last Wednesday, we were in a quarterback meeting. Mike came in late, sat down, and within 10 minutes began snoring. Woke himself up, was rattling his papers,” Rodgers said. “We all looked around. Five minutes later, you hear the snoring again. And less than five minutes after that, he walks out of the room like nothing happened.”
Rodgers added that he only found out about McCarthy’s decision when his teammate Pat Freiermuth told him. Rodgers said Freiermuth had called him and said “I can’t believe they’re doing this.” To which Rodgers replied: “Doing what?”
Rodgers, who said this summer that he will retire at the end of the season, also alleged that McCarthy appeared to think he was still coaching the Packers during Sunday’s defeat to the Philadelphia Eagles. “The nail in the coffin for so many of us was at halftime, towards the end of it, we’re kind of on the offense on one side of defense on the other side,” said Rodgers. “And there’s some rambling or something [from McCarthy] and without even a heads up, he says, ‘All right, one, two, three Packers.’ That’s what he broke it down on in the locker room … [We] looked around going, ‘What the fuck? What is going on? Where’s his head at at this point?’” ESPN reported that multiple sources agreed with Rodgers’ version of events.
Rodgers said he had spoken regularly to McCarthy over the last few days, and the coach had not mentioned the possibility of being benched. He did, however, say they had discussed McCarthy sleeping during meetings. “[I told McCarthy], we can’t even have an honest conversation. I’m telling you, you snored in the meeting twice, in a quarterback meeting, that’s unacceptable,” Rodgers said. “And you’re telling me you’ve never slept at a facility before. And I’m telling you, I have a hundred witnesses and collaborating people who would support what I’m saying. I’m not saying that to fucking bury you.
“I’m saying that because this behavior and these habits are not healthy and they’re not becoming of someone intimately involved in the game plan. And that’s my whole point. And so, I left it with him that if you try and bench me or don’t change the play call, then you should just release me because I feel like at this point, I’m doing what’s right for the organization”. Rodgers said after his comments to McCarthy that the coach decided he was “getting rid of me”.
The Steelers (6-4) have lost their last two games but are still clinging on to the final playoff place in the AFC. NFL Next Gen Stats gives them a 62% chance of making the postseason, although the model does not take into account players flambéing their own team’s coach on live television.
Rodgers is considered one of the greatest quarterbacks of all time, someone whose single Super Bowl win does not match his natural talent. He is all but guaranteed to be a first-ballot Hall of Famer. His NFL records include highest passer rating for a quarterback with a minimum of 1,500 attempts (102.5), highest passer rating in a single season (122.5 in 2011) and lowest interception in a season (0.3% in 2018).
This season, however, has arguably been the worst of Rodgers’ career. His QBR of 45.6 ranks him 26th out of 30 qualified quarterbacks, ahead of only Deshaun Watson, Baker Mayfield, Justin Herbert and Daniel Jones. His completion rate of 60.9% is the second-lowest for any season of his career in which he has started more than one game and he leads the league in yards lost in sacks.

https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.title: A new NYC Thanksgiving tradition: Stocking up at the legal weed dispensary
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.author: James Ramsay
https://gothamist.com/arts-entertainment.text:
This column originally appeared in the Looped In NYC newsletter. Sign up here.
For many Americans, Thanksgiving promises two things: a feast on the table and an extended cast of relatives seated around it.
And for some, there’s one substance that can enhance the experience of both.
“I can't be around my family sober,” said Campbell Saverein, who was picking up weed at the SoHo dispensary Mighty Lucky before heading to Long Island for the holiday.
“It really helps me, personally,” she said. “ We get into political arguments — someone's mad at some skirt being too short on Instagram.”
The “cousins walk” — wherein the young people (or any other down-to-clown relatives) go outside before dinner and smoke weed — is a long-standing Thanksgiving tradition. But now, four years into New York’s rollout of legal cannabis dispensaries, the once illicit pastime is not only less stigmatized — it’s also marketable. (Enter: “Green Wednesday” sales.) So we stopped by Mighty Lucky on Bowery to see how the shop, and its customers, were gearing up for the big day.
“As somebody who's been selling cannabis illegally, then legally, Thanksgiving specifically was the biggest sales holiday for me in the entire year — bigger than 4/20,” said Beau Allulli, the store’s co-owner.
Veteran stoners, we learned, know their way around a Thanksgiving high. Pre-rolls. Edibles. Volcanoes. Dabs. A lemony bud that one customer said pairs well with her mashed potatoes.
“I have a recipe where I make it kind of like patatas bravas style, so lemony and spicy,” said Stephanie Villavicencio, who popped into the store while visiting from Miami, where recreational weed is illegal. (“I carry it in smell-proof things.”)
William Diaz, who celebrates Thanksgiving with his family in the Bronx, said there’s no need for a sneaky walk at this point — all the adults, ranging in age from 23 to 75, take part.
“We smoke first, before the turkey. And then pray. And then eat,” he said.
Hmac, an artist and weed delivery driver, said she’s “definitely getting high on Thanksgiving,” but the party starts even before the walk.
“The morning of any holiday in our family, we have killer-dillers and cinnamon rolls,” she said.
A killer-diller?
“It's like Orange Julius mixed with vodka,” she explained. “It's, like, game over. Starts your day off right. We get goofy, for sure.”
Getting goofy, if you can handle it, sounds fantastic. But say you’re an uninitiated cannabis user — surely you’d want to avoid paranoia, drowsiness or absently staring into the bowl of cranberry sauce. Is there a way into this for the uninitiated?
“If I was going to curate something for you, you'd start out with probably a low-dose sativa,” Allulli said, walking me through a case of products.
“And then maybe, right before dinner, go for a little bit of a CBG-combined edible. That will increase the appetite,” he said. “ And then, after dinner, for me, it would be smoking some sort of fat indica. Really something that's gonna just sort of, like, totally mellow me out.”

https://www.humanite.fr/feminisme/associ.title: « Les attaques du RN contre le Planning familial ne sont pas qu’un positionnement, c’est un projet de société », alerte la présidente de l’association Sarah Durocher
https://www.humanite.fr/feminisme/associ.author: Kareen Janselme
https://www.humanite.fr/feminisme/associ.text:
Le Planning familial fête ce samedi 28 novembre ses 70 ans d’existence, à Paris, à la Bellevilloise. Malgré ses sept décennies d’existence et d’expertise sur le terrain, l’association engagée pour les droits et la santé des femmes et l’éducation à la sexualité n’a cessé d’être attaquée par le RN. Entretien avec sa présidente Sarah Durocher.
Comment réagissez-vous face aux attaques du RN, et notamment à la menace de Marine Le Pen, formulée récemment sur l’antenne de France Inter, de couper les subventions au Planning familial si elle accédait au pouvoir ?
Sarah Durocher
Présidente du Planning familial
Il n’y a rien de nouveau. Le projet politique de la droite conservatrice a toujours été contre le Planning familial et contre les droits des femmes, plus particulièrement contre les droits sexuels et reproductifs. Ces paroles n’ont donc rien d’étonnant.
Nous alertons depuis très longtemps, avec des exemples précis. Ainsi, à Carpentras, la première décision du maire, à son arrivée, a été d’enlever les financements au Planning familial. Ces menaces-là existaient donc déjà....
