https://www.artnews.com/art-news/sponsor.title: Warhol’s Watches
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/sponsor.author: John Yan
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/sponsor.text:
Piaget’s second collaboration with The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts translates the pop artist’s 1986 Camouflage self-portraits into dials made of gemstone marquetry.
Long before luxury watches were as sought after as they are today, Andy Warhol coveted and collected them. Over the course of the 1960s, ’70s, and ’80s, the Pop Art pioneer amassed more than 300 timepieces that reflected his high-low tastes. He collected watches the way he collected everything, with an appetite that blurred connoisseurship and compulsion. When Sotheby’s sold his estate in 1988, the sale featured timepieces by Cartier, Bulgari, and Patek Philippe alongside cookie jars and Art Deco furniture. Warhol is often said to have worn watches less to tell time than to be seen in them. For an artist who made a career of elevating the ordinary, a watch was a portable piece of pop culture, a status symbol he could wear and treasure.
One brand, however, stood out. Warhol owned at least seven wristwatches by the Swiss maison, Piaget. Founded in 1874 in La Côte-aux-Fées, a village in the heart of Switzerland’s Jura mountain range, the house was renowned in the latter half of the 20th century for its creative selection of timepieces in unusual shapes, many featuring dials made of exotic ornamental stones. One of those watches, a quartz-powered reference 15102 model that Warhol purchased from the brand in 1973, now forms the foundation for a Piaget collection bound to appeal to lovers of art in general and fans of Warhol’s revolutionary oeuvre in particular.
Housed in an 18-karat gold, 45 mm cushion-shaped case designed by Jean-Claude Gueit, Piaget’s then artistic director, the striking piece, which was part of a limited series manufactured between 1972 and 1977, featured a black onyx dial. Fittingly, it was called the Black Tie. In 1988, Piaget purchased Warhol’s watch at Sotheby’s landmark sale.
The artist’s choice of Piaget was no accident. In the 1950s and ’60s, the house had built its reputation on extreme thinness, introducing ultra-thin movements that transformed the watches into slim, supple pieces of jewelry. By the 1960s, Piaget had paired that technical prowess with a bolder sensibility: gold bracelets, vivid hardstone dials, and silhouettes that owed more to the jeweler’s bench than to the watchmaker’s. The result was a crossover brand that suited the decade’s appetite for spectacle. For Warhol, who drew no line between commerce and art, a watch that doubled as a gem-set object was irresistible. The Black Tie’s onyx dial, as sleek and dark as a lacquered cigarette case, could not have been better suited to the man who documented the era’s elite so closely.
Twenty-six years after Piaget purchased the Black Tie, the brand used the occasion of its 140th anniversary in 2014 to create a revival collection called Black Tie Vintage. The line caused such a stir among Piaget’s clientele that in 2024, for its sesquicentennial, the maison decided to up the ante. Thanks to a collaboration with The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, Piaget was given the rights to rename the Black Tie Vintage watch after Warhol himself.
From Collage to Camouflage
The first collaborative watch to emerge from Piaget’s work with the foundation was the 2025 Collage, a limited edition of 50 pieces featuring an artful composition of ornamental stones—yellow Namibian serpentine, pink opal, and green chrysoprase—inspired by Warhol’s Polaroids. This month, Piaget has introduced a second piece, which also uses ornamental stone marquetry, this time to pay tribute to the Camouflage self-portraits that Warhol created in 1986.
“When you buy it, you don’t only buy a watch, you buy a whole story and heritage,” Jean-Bernard Forot, Piaget’s head of patrimony, tells ARTnews. “You can, of course, talk about the material, what it does for you. But at the same time, you have to talk about Warhol, you have to talk about Piaget, you have to talk about art.”
Limited to 86 pieces, after the year in which Warhol created the eight-print Camouflage series, the watch, whose dial combines the ornamental stones sodalite and turquoise with satin-finished yellow gold and polished rose gold, faithfully interprets the artist’s work without blindly mimicking it.
“Camouflage is very difficult to work on, even in design, because we don’t just copy and paste the artwork—we have to find another way to express camouflage,” Forot says.
Among the final serial group of paintings Warhol completed before his untimely death in 1987, the works paid homage to the military-inspired camouflage pattern, originally intended to help soldiers blend in with their surroundings. In Warhol’s hands, they became a comment on Abstract Expressionism, not to mention a deeply personal statement on his lifelong effort to conceal his true self beneath wigs, makeup, and a carefully constructed facade.
Printed in acid brights across enormous canvases, the swirling forms feature in self-portraits overlayed with Warhol’s face, framed by his signature shock of hair. For an artist who spent his life hiding in plain sight, the Camouflage series is arguably his most meta work.
In order to capture the essence of the paintings on the face of a watch, Piaget’s artisans took some liberties with color. Rather than emphasizing Warhol’s use of yellow, for example, they highlighted the brand’s use of turquoise, Forot says.
“Once the team finished the drawing, which was validated by The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, then they started working with the gem material,” he says. “We have to try to remain true to both the design itself as well as the techniques.”
Mad About Hue
Study the dial of the watch and you’ll see something of an optical illusion: a sense of depth and texture that isn’t quite there. “When you look at the Piaget Camouflage, you have the feeling that you have four layers,” Forot says. “But in fact, it’s an illusion because they are all flat and on the same level. Even if you have the feeling that the turquoise is above the gold, in fact, it’s at the same level.”
The careful craftsmanship required to make the watch—each dial features 27 pieces of gold and ornamental stone marquetry and takes more than 100 hours of labor to design, research, and craft—is a testament to Piaget’s decades of expertise in the esoteric world of gem-setting. Since the maison introduced gold and color into its watches in the 1960s, it has worked with some 50 different ornamental stones, including lapis lazuli, jade, coral, onyx, and tiger’s eye.
The maison’s legitimacy in the realm of color is unassailable—and enduring. Piaget designated 2026 its “Year of Color,” based on its Colours of Extraleganza collection, representing the third and final chapter of a high jewelry trilogy that began with the maison’s 150th anniversary in 2024. “Piaget is really coming back to visibility in color and gold,” Forot says.
While the blend of hues on the dial of the Camouflage watch lends the piece its name and raison d’être, don’t overlook its iconic gold frame nor the movement that ticks within. The cushion-shaped case features three rows of textured grooves known as gadroons, a Piaget signature. It houses a self-winding manufacture movement, the 501 P1. And let’s not forget the caseback, where Andy Warhol’s signature appears alongside the number of timepieces in the limited series.
Like Minds
Best of all, the Camouflage limited edition, like the Collage that came before it, is steeped in the lore that swirls around Warhol’s personal history with Piaget.
“Warhol was a real collector—of everything,” Forot says. “But even if he owned many watches from many brands—including Patek Philippe, Cartier, Bulgari, and so on—there is only one picture with him and the founder of a watchmaking company. And it’s Yves Piaget.”
The legendary chairman of the maison, Yves Piaget is the fourth generation of his family to be involved in the business, which was founded by Georges-Édouard Piaget in 1874 and acquired by the Swiss luxury group Richemont in 1988. In the 1970s, at the height of the brand’s 20th-century popularity, Yves and Warhol became friends.
A photo of the men dated 1979 offers proof that they found common ground in their shared love of timepieces. At the time, Yves presided over the Piaget Society, a glamorous social circle centered on the brand and its community of jet-setting movers and shakers. And Warhol, of course, had the Factory, his studio in Manhattan, a hub of art, filmmaking, and creativity.
“They weren’t exactly the same, but they were both surrounded by artists, extravagant personalities—they were social long before The Social Network,” Forot says. “In a sense, they had the same philosophy.”
High Society
Yves’ recollections of Warhol during that time paint the artist as a quiet figure, whose later fame didn’t square with his penchant for careful observation.
Nevertheless, the two hit it off. Yves invited Warhol to Palm Beach to attend the world cup of polo, a sport that the maison made famous through its 1979 Polo timepiece, an emblem of the rich and famous. And he continued to send Warhol gifts, including boxes of chocolate, that the artist, a true magpie, kept as part of his time capsules. Stored in cardboard boxes, the objects, ephemera, letters, and gifts Warhol collected included personal relics from his multiyear friendship with Yves, although Forot jokes that the box of chocolate, while part of the collection housed by The Andy Warhol Museum in Pittsburgh, is, thankfully, empty.
Warhol’s attraction to the brand was hardly anomalous. Piaget’s clientele included more than its fair share of the rich and famous, including Jackie O, Elizabeth Taylor, and Halston. Even Salvador Dalí was a longtime collaborator. In 1967 the surrealist teamed with Piaget on a collaborative collection of gold watches and jewelry, long before such partnerships became commonplace. Featuring gold coins, dubbed Dali D’Or, emblazoned with profile portraits of himself and his wife, Gala, the watches and jewels that emerged from the partnership offer yet another testament to Piaget’s high-flying reputation as the watch for those in the know and a symbol of wealth, taste, and extravagance, all qualities that continue to define the brand today.
Michael Dayton Hermann, managing director of strategic initiatives at The Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts, says that the collaboration with Piaget “is an expression of how the artist’s vision remains as relevant and compelling today as ever.”
“This unique ongoing project is especially meaningful given Warhol’s personal friendship with Yves Piaget and his passion for the maison’s watches, which he collected during his lifetime,” Hermann tells ARTnews. “It also embodies Warhol’s belief in the creative possibilities of art and commerce, generating proceeds that support the foundation’s philanthropic mission, which has awarded more than $300 million in grants to advance contemporary visual art.”
Just as the collaboration celebrates Warhol’s singular take on the role art plays in commerce, it equally underscores Piaget’s decades-old legitimacy in the world of art. Watches may not be the first things that come to mind when recalling Warhol and his legacy, but he collected them, wore them, and, in the case of Piaget, befriended the man who made them. Think of the Camouflage limited edition less as a commercial arrangement and more as the next chapter of a decades-long conversation started by Warhol and carried on in gold and gems.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Governo da Venezuela lança plano econômico até 2036, com raio-x inédito de inflação e dívida externa
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Leonardo Fernandes
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
As autoridades econômicas da Venezuela apresentaram na terça-feira (24) o Plano Venezuela Renasce, um programa nacional estruturado para orientar a recuperação econômica e social do país. Os números chegam após anos sem divulgar os dados oficiais da macroeconomia e mais de uma década do país submetido a sanções internacionais, asfixia econômica e desequilíbrios estruturais, agravados pelo impacto dos severos sismos ocorridos em 24 de junho de 2026, que deixaram mais de 23 mil pessoas desabrigadas e provocaram danos físicos significativos.
O programa foi elaborado com base em dados oficiais do Ministério do Poder Popular de Economia e Finanças e do Banco Central da Venezuela. Durante a divulgação do plano, a presidenta em exercício, Delcy Rodríguez, ressaltou o caráter rigoroso da proposta para a reconstrução do país.
“É um programa baseado em métodos científicos. Não é um improviso, não é mágica que tira um coelho da cartola; é um método científico para dizer ao país: ‘Temos um plano econômico’”, declarou a mandatária.
Por sua vez, o vice-presidente setorial de economia, Calixto Ortega Sánchez, destacou o nível inédito de detalhamento do documento, após anos de forte nebulosidade sobre os dados oficiais da economia do país. “Este plano é colocado à disposição do país com o maior detalhamento possível. Contém números, projeções, mecanismos de implementação e objetivos concretos. A Venezuela não tinha um plano com esse nível de precisão há muitos anos”, disse Sánchez.
Panorama macroeconômico e projeções de crescimento
O documento divulgado pelo governo venezuelano apresenta um diagnóstico transparente sobre o estado recente da economia, ao mesmo tempo em que traça metas de expansão para curto, médio e longo prazo até o ano de 2036.
Em 2025, o Produto Interno Bruto (PIB) nominal do país situou-se em US$ 98,1 bilhões, valor que representa apenas 36% do nível real registrado em 2012. Para o encerramento de 2026, a equipe econômica prevê um crescimento do PIB entre 5% e 6,5%.
As projeções oficiais apontam que, durante a próxima década, a economia venezuelana registrará uma expansão média de 6,3% ao ano. Esse ritmo permitirá duplicar o tamanho do PIB em cinco anos, alcançando US$ 200,9 bilhões em 2031 e chegando a US$ 290,6 bilhões em 2036.
Em relação à inflação, após o indicador encerrar o ano de 2025 em 475,3% e atingir 534,2% no acumulado em 12 meses até agosto de 2026, a meta do plano é promover a convergência para dois dígitos no curto prazo, por meio do ordenamento das contas públicas e da unificação do mercado cambial.
O vice-presidente de Economia, Calixto Ortega Sánchez, sintetizou os pilares centrais dessa estratégia. “O Plano Venezuela Renasce estabelece objetivos claros e mensuráveis: restabelecer a estabilidade macroeconômica, acelerar o crescimento, resolver a situação da dívida pública e reinserir a Venezuela na economia mundial. Tudo isso com o objetivo central de melhorar a renda de todos os trabalhadores”, pontou.
Raio-x da dívida pública
Um dos pontos mais detalhados pelas autoridades econômicas foi a situação da dívida pública, classificada pelo relatório como insustentável e em inadimplência desde o ano de 2017 devido ao acúmulo de sanções, à queda das receitas petroleiras e aos desequilíbrios históricos. Ao final de 2025, os passivos totais do setor público venezuelano atingiram US$ 237,5 bilhões, o equivalente a 242% do PIB do país.
Esse montante se divide em US$ 116,5 bilhões de dívida comercial, composta por US$ 110,1 bilhões em eurobônus e US$ 6,4 bilhões em empréstimos bancários; US$ 67,3 bilhões em obrigações não financeiras da Petróleos de Venezuela S.A. (PDVSA), US$ 26,3 bilhões em resoluções arbitrais; e US$ 4,2 bilhões em dívidas multilaterais com instituições como o Banco Interamericano de Desenvolvimento (BID), que detém US$ 2,735 bilhões, e o Banco de Desenvolvimento da América Latina e Caribe (Corporação Andina de Fomento em castelhano, ou CAF), com US$ 1,423 bilhão.
No que diz respeito à dívida bilateral, que soma US$ 23,3 bilhões, a China figura como a maior credora individual da Venezuela, somando US$ 16,866 bilhões por meio do Banco de Desenvolvimento da China e do Banco de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social de Venezuela (BANDES) no âmbito do Fundo Chinês. Esse valor representa 72,5% de toda a dívida bilateral venezuelana.
A dívida bilateral com a Rússia é a segunda maior, com US$ 5,080 bilhões, por meio do banco estatal russo Vnesheconombank. Por sua vez, com o Brasil, o saldo devedor atinge US$ 1,128 bilhão, correspondente a financiamentos do Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES).
Para resolver o impasse dos passivos externos, o governo venezuelano estabeleceu uma reestruturação baseada em quatro princípios orientadores: sustentabilidade, integralidade, boa-fé e transparência, e rapidez.
O plano ressalta que a Venezuela já normalizou sua representação junto a organismos financeiros multilaterais e avança em negociações para regularizar pagamentos em atraso e obter assistência técnica sob condução soberana.
Impulso petrolífero, investimentos e reconstrução social
A riqueza energética permanece como o principal motor da recuperação venezuelana. O país possui reservas comprovadas superiores a 300 bilhões de barris de petróleo e 190 trilhões de pés cúbicos de gás natural.
O plano projeta elevar a produção de petróleo de cerca de 1,21 milhão de barris diários em 2026 para 2,27 milhões em 2031 e 2,91 milhões em 2036. Essa expansão está apoiada na reforma da Lei Orgânica de Hidrocarbonetos, realizada em janeiro de 2026, e nos Convênios de Participação Produtiva, esquema contratual que permite que investidores internacionais assumam a maior parte dos US$ 160 bilhões em investimentos petrolíferos previstos até 2036.
A projeção do governo venezuelano indica que esses investimentos gerarão uma média de 323 mil empregos anuais entre 2026 e 2031, além de movimentar US$ 3,5 bilhões anuais em compras junto a fornecedores nacionais.
Além disso, no âmbito social, o plano destina US$ 10 bilhões em investimentos públicos plurianuais entre 2026 e 2030 para a reconstrução das comunidades afetadas pelos terremotos de junho de 2026 e para garantir o acesso à primeira moradia.
A presidenta Delcy Rodríguez ressaltou a preservação do investimento em políticas sociais como prioridade do orçamento público.
“Está previsto um financiamento multilateral de mais de 10 bilhões de dólares, ou valor equivalente, tanto para o setor público quanto para o setor privado, destinado à construção de moradias. A iniciativa abrange não apenas as pessoas que perderam suas casas após o terremoto, mas toda a população venezuelana, permitindo a recuperação dos serviços públicos, incluindo o sistema elétrico e o abastecimento de água, bem como a restauração de escolas e hospitais”, disse a presidenta, que voltou a prometer um aumento sustentado e responsável dos salários.
Cronograma de implementação e as três fases da recuperação
A execução do Plano Venezuela Renasce está organizada em três fases sequenciais para garantir a estabilização gradual e a sustentabilidade das reformas no longo prazo.
A fase 1, denominada “normalização”, compreende o período de zero a 12 meses. O objetivo central dessa etapa é restabelecer a estabilidade macroeconômica por meio de uma âncora fiscal crível, regras fiscais e a reestruturação da dívida. Inclui a adoção de um regime cambial unificado com o Banco Central da Venezuela, o fortalecimento da administração tributária e os primeiros passos para atração de investimentos privados em serviços públicos e energia.
A fase 2, chamada “recuperação”, é projetada para um horizonte de um a três anos. Nessa etapa, a expansão da produção de petróleo e gás passa a atuar como motor primário do crescimento. O plano prevê o apoio às pequenas e médias empresas, investimentos em conectividade, modernização da rede elétrica com autogeração em modo ilha nos campos petrolíferos e a recuperação progressiva do poder de compra.
“Os salários dos trabalhadores continuarão subindo, assim como o orçamento destinado ao pagamento das pensões, de maneira responsável e sustentada”, disse o vice-presidente de Economia durante a apresentação do plano.
Finalmente, a fase 3, denominada “diversificação”, está prevista para um prazo superior a três anos. O foco dessa etapa é consolidar uma economia diversificada e resiliente, apoiada em um “setor privado dinâmico” e na indústria de maior valor agregado.
A política monetária passará a operar sob um regime de metas de inflação e será criado um Fundo Soberano de Riqueza para gerir as receitas extraordinárias dos recursos naturais, garantindo a estabilidade diante de futuros choques externos.
Sindicatos chavistas e opositores protestam
No mesmo dia da divulgação do documento pela Vice-Presidência setorial de Economia, trabalhadores, aposentados, pensionistas, profissionais da saúde e professores universitários fizeram uma manifestação em Caracas para exigir melhorias salariais e um incremento na gratificação de fim de ano — equivalente ao 13º salário no Brasil.
O grupo, convocado por sindicatos opositores, tentou furar o bloqueio policial para chegar às imediações do Palácio de Miraflores, no centro da capital. Houve tumulto e pelo menos três pessoas ficaram feridas, incluindo um agente de segurança.
Em outro ponto da cidade, outro grupo de sindicatos se mobilizou em comemoração aos 15 anos de fundação da Central Bolivariana Socialista de Trabalhadores (CBST). O ato reuniu representantes das 17 federações que compõem a organização nos 24 estados do país.
Durante a atividade, os sindicalistas denunciaram as mais de mil medidas coercitivas contra o Estado venezuelano. Segundo os dirigentes, essas sanções promoveram uma enorme defasagem dos salários dos trabalhadores, obrigando o governo a adotar um sistema de compensação por meio de bônus extras que não são contabilizados para efeitos de cálculo de prestações sociais.
“Não nos deixamos estigmatizar pelo sindicalismo que hoje pretende tomar bandeiras que historicamente nunca teve. Porque, com a moral elevada, com o comandante [Hugo] Chávez, resgatamos os direitos trabalhistas e as prestações sociais dos trabalhadores, resgatamos os direitos dos trabalhadores e consagramos uma Constituição com um capítulo completo das lutas históricas dos trabalhadores e das trabalhadoras. Bastante orgulho temos de ser bolivarianos, de ser chavistas e de ser revolucionários e revolucionárias”, disse o dirigente da CBST Wills Rangel durante o ato.
Os sindicalistas também denunciaram o sequestro ilegal do presidente Nicolás Maduro e de sua companheira, a deputada Cilia Flores. Ambos foram levados à força aos Estados Unidos após a operação militar contra a Venezuela no dia 3 de janeiro, que resultou em mais de cem mortos.

Les cookies et technologies similaires que nous utilisons sur Mediapart sont de différentes natures et nous permettent de poursuivre différentes finalités. 
Certains sont nécessaires au fonctionnement du site et de l’application mobile (vous ne pouvez pas les refuser). D’autres sont optionnels mais contribuent à faciliter votre expérience de lecteur ou de lectrice et d’une certaine façon à soutenir Mediapart. Vous pouvez les refuser ou les accepter ci-dessous, selon leurs finalités. 
Acceptez-vous que Mediapart utilise des cookies ou technologies similaires pour les finalités suivantes ? 
Vous pouvez faire votre choix, pour chaque catégorie, en activant ou désactivant le bouton interrupteur.
                    
                            
                                Nécessaires au fonctionnement
du site ou de l’application
                            Connexion des abonné·es, mesure d’audience anonymisée, envoi des notifications push, suivi des pannes, mise en avant de nos services : ces outils sont nécessaires au suivi de l’activité de nos services et à leur bon fonctionnement.
                                    Voici les différents cookies et technologies similaires compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Cookies d’authentification : connexion des abonné·es.
- Batch (uniquement sur l’application) : envoi de notifications push et de messages in-app.
- Affichage de contenus éditoriaux multimédias : vidéos (YouTube, Dailymotion, Vimeo, INA), réseaux sociaux (Facebook, Instagram, Pinterest, Twitter), documents (Scribd, Document Cloud, Slideshare), sons (SoundCloud, Spotify, Deezer), cartes (Google Maps, Mapbox, CartoDB, uMap), infographies (Highcharts, GitHub, Datawrapper, Flourish, Infogram, ThingLink, jQuery, Google Fonts, Bootstrap), live blogs (24liveblog, CoverItLive), aide à l’intégration de média dans les publications Journal et Club (Embedly).
- Datadog (uniquement sur le site web) : indicateurs techniques et équilibrage de charge.
- Firebase Cloud Messaging (uniquement sur l’application) : nécessaire au fonctionnement des notifications push sur Android.
- Microsoft App Center (uniquement sur l’application) : système de mise à jour et de suivi des pannes de l’application.
- Piano : mesure d’audience anonymisée
- Selligent (uniquement sur le site web) : communication avec l’abonné·e, mise en avant des services, offres et avantages.
- Typeform : questionnaires facultatifs pour recueillir les avis des lecteurs sur nos produits numériques.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Ces outils nous permettent de recueillir des statistiques de fréquentation du site et de l’application mobile pour comprendre les usages, détecter d’éventuels problèmes et optimiser l’ergonomie de nos produits.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Batch (uniquement sur le site web) : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- CrazyEggs (uniquement sur le site web) : analyse de parcours client.
- Nonli (uniquement sur le site web) : permet à notre équipe des réseaux sociaux de publier les contenus Mediapart sur les réseaux sociaux.
- Piano : mesure d’audience reliée à l’identifiant d’abonné·e.
- Qiota (uniquement sur le site web) : gestion du système de datawall.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                            Il n’y a pas de publicité sur Mediapart. Mais nous faisons la promotion de nos contenus et services sur d’autres sites et réseaux sociaux. Pour cela, nous utilisons les technologies mises à disposition par certains acteurs publicitaires.
                                    Voici les outils tiers compris dans cette catégorie :
                                                                                    - Facebook (uniquement sur le site web) : ciblage d’audience sur les réseaux sociaux pour faire la promotion de Mediapart.
                                                    
                                            
                            
                                Gestion de l’accès aux contenus
                            Nous utilisons le service Qiota d’Opper Marketing Suite pour configurer l’activation d’un datawall sur certains de nos contenus (uniquement sur le site web). Ce dispositif destiné aux utilisateur·ices non abonné·es requiert la saisie d’une adresse email pour accéder aux contenus concernés. En fournissant cette information, l’utilisateur consent à sa collecte, son stockage et son utilisation à des fins statistiques. Conformément à la réglementation en vigueur, les utilisateurs disposent d’un droit d’accès, de rectification et de suppression de leurs données, qu’ils peuvent exercer en contactant dpo@opper.io.

https://taz.de/Podcast-des-Frauenhauses-.text:
Podcast des Frauenhauses Oberhausen: Geschichten der Gewalt
Das Frauenhaus Oberhausen lässt Betroffene von häuslicher Gewalt ihre eigenen Geschichten erzählen. So detailliert hört man das selten.
Dieser Podcast hat es in sich. In sechs Folgen konfrontiert einen „Baby No More Time“ mit sechs Geschichten häuslicher Gewalt. Jede Folge ist der Geschichte einer Frau gewidmet. Im Fokus stehen dabei verschiedene Formen der Gewalt. In der ersten geht es um psychische, in der zweiten um körperliche Gewalt. Später wird es noch um sexualisierte, digitale, finanzielle und soziale Gewalt gehen.
„Baby No More Time“ ist ein Podcast des Frauenhauses Oberhausen. Das merkt man. Alle Beteiligten sind auf der Seite der Betroffenen, Täterkonfrontationen gibt es nicht. Für Fans von epischen Storytelling-Produktionen oder True-Crime-Thrillern ist die Serie kaum geeignet. Die Moderator*innen Suna Tanış, die zugleich das Frauenhaus leitet, und Eike Weinreich, der Schauspieler ist, führen nüchtern durch das Grauen.
Doch das ist gerade die Stärke des Podcasts. Ohne das Frauenhaus mit seiner Parteilichkeit und dessen Zugängen zu Betroffenen, die Schlimmes erlebt haben, könnte der Podcast nicht die Geschichten erzählen, die er erzählt. Die sind so eindringlich, dass zusätzliches Dramatisieren boulevardesk und unpassend wirken würde.
„Baby No More Time“ zwängt die betroffenen Frauen nicht in ein dramaturgisches Korsett. Die meiste Zeit hört man ihnen einfach zu. Sie erzählen ihre Geschichte selbst, nur unterbrochen durch gelegentliche vorsichtige Nachfragen von Tanış oder Weinreich. Zusätzlich kommen Expert*innen zu Wort, die das Gesagte einordnen. Dadurch doppeln sich die Inhalte manchmal – doch die Geschichten der Frauen lassen einen dran bleiben.
„Manchmal holen mich die Schatten wieder ein“
Die Struktur ist dabei in den bisher erschienen ersten zwei Folgen identisch. Die Frauen geben wieder, wie sie den Täter kennengelernt haben. Wie die ersten Monate und Jahre waren. Wann es anfing, zu bröckeln. Und wie schlimm es geworden ist, bevor sie geflohen sind. Dazu nur so viel: Die Triggerwarnungen sind zu Recht am Anfang der Folgen.
Eine Gewaltform tritt dabei selten allein auf. Daher erfährt man in jeder Folge auch etwas über andere Formen. Und zusätzlich streift der Podcast auch weitere Themen rund um geschlechtsspezifische Gewalt. Es geht um Probleme beim Sorgerecht, um Lesbenfeindlichkeit, die mangelnde Finanzierung von Frauenhausplätzen, um Gewaltspiralen in Familien, um Kinder, die mit betroffen sind.
der podcast
„Baby No More Time“
vom Frauenhaus Oberhausen
bisher zwei Folgen
überall, wo es Podcasts gibt
Die Folgen enden mit der Stimme der Frauen: „Ich habe immer wieder Flashbacks gehabt, schlaflose Nächte, ich bin schweißnass aufgewacht. Ich reibe bis heute meine Füße aneinander, damit der Stress weggeht. Wenn irgendein anderer neben mir liegt, mache ich kein Auge zu. Es sei denn, es ist mein Hund.“ Oder: „Es ist nicht einfach. Es ist auch gleichzeitig Trauer. Trauer über die ganzen Jahre, die ich verloren habe. Trauer über die Familie, die nicht so war, wie sie hätte sein sollen. Manchmal bin ich auch wütend, wütend, wieso das alles passieren musste. Manchmal fühle ich mich frei. Und manchmal holen mich die Schatten wieder ein.“
Einen so tiefen Einblick in die Dynamiken rund um häusliche Gewalt bekommt man medial selten. Betroffenen zuhören – diese Forderung gibt es oft. Wer das ernst meint, sollte diesen Podcast hören.

https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.title: A brush with... Zanele Muholi—podcast
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.author: Ben Luke, David Clack, Aimee Dawson
https://www.theartnewspaper.com/2026/11/.text:
Content warning: this episode has some discussion of sexual and homophobic violence.
Muholi was born in 1972 in Umlazi, Durban, South Africa and lives today in Cape Town. They are a self-described visual activist, who, since the mid-2000s, have used photography to document the lives of LGBTQ+ people, initially in South Africa, where they were born.
They have since expanded their project around the world and work in discrete, often ongoing series that have a common aim: to respond to violence and discrimination against queer and trans communities, to reflect their defiance and resistance, and to expand their visibility in visual culture in South Africa in particular but also far beyond.
The people they depict have, since the start, been far more than sitters or subjects; they are collaborators, participants who help define the way they are represented. A crucial factor is that Muholi turns the lens onto themself. “When I position myself in my own frame,” they have said. “I do so on my own terms attempting to articulate my own way of seeing and wanting to be seen.”
And whether it is their unflinching and tender portraits of their collaborators or their imaginative and improvised self-portraits Muholi’s photographs are always beautiful objects, with a fastidious attention to the properties and possibilities of their medium.
They discuss the influence of their mother, who was a maker herself, and was a profound influence on one of their most notable works, Somnyama Ngonyama (2012). They reflect on the enormous impact of photographers including Rotimi Fani-Kayode, Lola Flash and Joan E. Biren, writers including Audre Lorde, and musicians including Brenda Fassie. Plus, they answer our usual questions, giving insight into their daily practices and the rhythms of their work, and reflecting on the ultimate question: what is art for?
- Faces and Phases: Zanele Muholi, MACK, $80, £65
This podcast is sponsored by Bloomberg Connects, the arts and culture platform.
Bloomberg Connects offers access to a vast range of international cultural organisations through a single click, with new guides being added regularly. They includeseveral guides to institutions that have shown and collected Zanele Muholi’s work, including SFMOMA in San Francisco, Tate in the UK, the Center for Visual Arts in Denver in the US, and MEP, the Maison Européenne de la Photographie in Paris. On the guide to the MEP, you will find features on its current exhibitions. They include Penn and Fashion, exploring the photographer Irving Penn’s long association with the fashion world, in which his stripped-back style has had a lasting influence on generations of photographers. You can hear audio features on all the sections of the exhibition, from his early years at Vogue magazine in the 1940s to the photographs made when Penn was in his 90s of Karl Lagerfeld, John Galliano and Christian Lacroix. You can also explore the related exhibition in La Petite Galerie, called Everyday Clothing, which allows young visitors and families to explore the creative process through works from the MEP’s collections.

Anwalt der Kinder
Der diesjährige Menschenrechtspreis von Amnesty International in Deutschland geht an den palästinensischen Rechtsanwalt Khaled Quzmar.
Khaled Quzmar ist ein typischer Alltagsheld: Was er tut, sieht man meist nicht, doch ist seine Arbeit fundamental für die, die davon profitieren. Seit Jahrzehnten setzt er sich für die Belange von Kindern in den von Israel besetzten palästinensischen Gebieten ein, streitet als Rechtsanwalt für deren Rechte gegen ein übermächtiges Besatzungsregime, das auch bei Kindern und Jugendlichen vor Gefängnis, Schikanen und Folter nicht zurückschreckt.
Und seine Aktivität ärgert die Besatzer offenbar so sehr, dass der israelische Geheimdienst ihn vorladen ließ, mit Gefängnis drohte. An den Druck und die Diffamierungen ist der in Ramallah ansässige Quzmar zwar gewöhnt, doch aufgrund der anhaltenden Repressionen musste er im Frühjahr dieses Jahres die von ihm geleitete NGO Defense For Children International – Palestine (DCI-P) nach über 35 Jahren auflösen. Seit Juni 2026 fungiert er als Geschäftsführender Direktor der Organisation Palestinian Center for Child Rights. Für sein langjähriges Engagement als Menschenrechtsanwalt erhält er in diesem Jahr den Menschenrechtspreis der internationalen NGO Amnesty International in Deutschland.
»Khaled Quzmar gibt seit fast 40 Jahren unermüdlich und allen Widerständen zum Trotz der vulnerabelsten Bevölkerungsgruppe Palästinas eine Stimme: den Kindern. Ihre erschütternde Lebenssituation ist die direkte Folge systematischer Menschenrechtsverletzungen und Unterdrückung, die sich in den letzten Jahren noch einmal deutlich verschärft hat«, erklärte in einer Pressemitteilung Julia Duchrow, Generalsekretärin von Amnesty International in Deutschland.
Aus den Erzählungen von Khaled Quzmars meist minderjährigen Mandanten lässt sich verstehen, was diese in israelischen Gefängnissen durchmachen müssen. So beschreibt ein heute 18-Jähriger in einer Reportage des Amnesty-Journals nach seiner Haftentlassung, was er im Knast erlebt hat: »Im Gefängnis gab es jeden Tag Schläge. Die Wärter kamen in unsere Zelle, ordneten an, uns bis auf die Unterhose zu entkleiden und auf den Fußboden zu legen. Dann schlugen sie uns mit einem Stromkabel.«
Khaled Quzmar hat ihn als Anwalt gegen gravierende Anschuldigungen verteidigt: Der bei der Festnahme noch Minderjährige soll Bomben fabriziert haben. Beweise gab es demnach keine, trotzdem musste er mit einer Gefängnisstrafe von zehn Jahren rechnen. Nach Quzmars Aussagen sei es gelungen, »das Gericht milde zu stimmen«, sodass er »nur« 13 Monate habe absitzen müssen. »Das sind Kinder, sie haben diese Brutalität nicht verdient«, sagt Quzmar. Die Militärgerichte, vor denen Jugendliche im Westjordanland regelmäßig angeklagt werden, würden sich nicht darum scheren, ob ein Anwalt bei der Verhandlung dabei sei. Und vor einem Militärgericht müsse der Angeklagte den Beweis führen, dass er KEIN Terrorist sei.
Nach Angaben von Amnesty International sind derzeit mindestens 350 Minderjährige in israelischen Gefängnissen teils für viele Jahre inhaftiert, nicht selten verurteilt aufgrund von erzwungenen »Geständnissen«, die unter Druck, Gewalt und ohne rechtlichen Beistand abgegeben werden. Ein besonders perfides Mittel der israelischen Justiz ist die sogenannte Administrativhaft, von der mehr als die Hälfte der inhaftierten Minderjährigen betroffen sein soll. Das heißt, sie können ohne Anklage auf unbestimmte Zeit festgehalten werden.
Khaled Quzmars Wunsch, den Rechtsanwaltsberuf zu ergreifen, hat mit der Verhaftung seines Bruders zu tun. Als er diesen im Gefängnis besuchte, durfte er ihn nicht umarmen, ein Anwalt dagegen wurde zu ihm durchgelassen. Damit stand Quzmars Berufswunsch fest: Das Jura-Studium absolvierte er in Algerien, da es in Palästina seinerzeit keine juristische Fakultät gab. Ab 1987 arbeitete er dann als Rechtsanwalt, genau in dem Jahr, als im Westjordanland die erste Intifada begann: Bald hatte er pro Tag 30 bis 40 Fälle, auch viele Kinder und Jugendliche, die Steine auf Panzer geworfen hatten. Er lernte Hebräisch, um mit Richtern und Staatsanwälten verhandeln zu können, und sattelte noch einen Master-Studiengang in Internationalem Recht drauf – in Irland.
Der 62-jährige Quzmar hat zwei Töchter sowie zwei Söhne, von denen einer ebenfalls als Rechtsanwalt arbeitet. In Ramallah lebt die Familie nahe einer israelischen Siedlung. Früher habe es keine Probleme mit den Siedlern gegeben, sagte er in der Reportage des Amnesty-Journals. »Aber seit dem 7. Oktober 2023 leben wir in Angst.«

https://www.thenation.com/article/econom.author: Dylan Gyauch-Lewis, Matthew Scherer
https://www.thenation.com/article/econom.text:
How Congress’s Permitting Bill Doubles as an AI Bailout
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is loaded up with giveaways to the AI sector—part of the Trump White House’s broader plan to shield AI from economic reality.
Bailouts come in many forms. For the financiers and tech moguls who’ve been inflating the AI bubble, the seeds of a federal rescue are sown in the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA). The massive bill, which the Senate approved last week and is now before the House, needs to be understood as part of a multifront deregulatory push to embed the AI industry’s policy preferences into law. There’s no explicit language in BAAJA charging taxpayers to bail out AI companies—but there doesn’t really need to be.
After the 1980s savings-and-loan crisis, law professor Cheryl Block offered a taxonomy of modern government bailouts, dividing them into two classes: overt and covert. The overt bailout is the more familiar: direct cash infusions, credit guarantees, and so on. Covert bailouts also prop up distressed businesses, but are structured so as to mask their purpose and beneficiaries. Instead of directing public funds to failing companies, a covert bailout typically assists them through subtler measures such as looser regulations, tax relief, or protection from competition.
Tech lords and financiers, through their Trumpist cronies, have already sought to obtain covert bailout protections in piecemeal fashion, from promoting favorable legislation on transmission line siting to diluting SEC oversight of corporate accounting to shield AI platforms from basic consumer liability. BAAJA represents their crowning bid to secure deeper and more durable protection before a new Democratic majority is seated in Congress next January.
BAAJA would codify many of the industry’s preferred energy policies while also abetting the massive buildout of AI data centers. If it wins passage in the House, the bill would help place AI development beyond the basic forces of market discipline, and set the stage for indemnifying the corrupt and cronyist tech sector from any meaningful responsibility for promoting the largest investment bubble in human history. Without pledging taxpayer funds outright, BAAJA bears all the hallmarks of a covert bailout.
This de facto mandate stands out in especially high relief if you examine the manic push to pass BAAJA in the context of the Trump White House’s other flagrant giveaways to the AI sector. Some involve the use of taxpayer funds, such as the many government contracts that the Trump administration has doled out to the industry. The growing role of the public sector in financing the bubble similarly serves as a slow-roll cash injection that would buffer AI concerns from the impact of a full market collapse.
But most of the Trump administration’s AI giveaways have come through policy changes at federal agencies. This summer, the SEC signaled that it was effectively exempting certain data center debt from key regulatory requirements—a key concession that makes it easier for risky AI-linked debt to be packaged and sold throughout the financial system. The regulatory carve-outs kicked into high gear this month as investors began to flee AI stocks. On November 12, the White House urged federal agencies to place limits on liability for cybersecurity incidents—a measure disingenuously presented as an overdue initiative to update “aging” cyber liability regulations. In reality, the new rule serves to protect AI model developers from damages arising from high-profile hacks like the notorious release of AI bots in the Hugging Face incident. In fact, Trump assured AI moguls and their backers that his administration would continue shilling on their behalf, sternly announcing that his administration wouldn’t “allow” any “robust regulation” of AI, a statement that serves as a nice capsule summary of the Trump administration’s AI policy.
The most recent and starkest example of the Trump administration’s alignment with AI billionaires was, of course, the unprecedented pressure campaign from Trump and Vice President JD Vance to get Nvidia’s corporate board to restore Jensen Huang as the company’s CEO after he resigned in disgrace for conducting an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. That effort had the desired effect on Monday, when tech stocks soared on the announcement that Nvidia had brought Huang back—though Nvidia’s subsequent performance on Wall Street suggests that these gains may not amount to much more than a dead cat bounce.
The bailout that AI interests are on the verge of procuring in BAAJA, which the White House also strongly backs, is somewhat better disguised. The bill’s headline provisions seem at first glance as though they’re designed to benefit ordinary people and their communities. BAAJA’s new rules on “ratepayer protection,” for example, are advertised as guarantees that data-center developers cover the cost of building out new infrastructure for energy generation, grid transmission upgrades, or other commitments that utilities face in providing power and other services to data centers.
But the devil is in the details. BAAJA does not require data center developers to pay upfront for the infrastructure and transmission costs they impose on utilities. Instead, the bill only stipulates that utilities obtain “reasonable financial assurances” that they would be able to “recover” those costs from the data center’s “owner” or “operator.”
We know from bitter experience how such riders play out in reality. When the dot-com bubble burst in the early aughts, many companies that devoted themselves to building Internet and mobile telecoms infrastructure, such as Global Crossing and Worldcom, went bankrupt. If that pattern repeats when the AI bubble bursts, many utilities—together, in all likelihood, with the households and small businesses they continue to serve—would find themselves saddled with the full cost of infrastructure improvements. What’s more, the owners and operators of record for AI data centers typically are not the megacorporations behind the projects but shell companies set up in part to shield those megacorporations from liability.
These are questions of grave concern, given how the financial house of cards underpinning AI capital expenditures has been teetering. Revenues for AI companies have utterly failed to keep pace with the massive investments in new data centers—and in a financial crisis, that means much of the industry’s vast economic power could vanish. (For another early-aughts cautionary tale, see the fate of the massively overleveraged accounting firm Enron, which also brought many energy companies and utilities to the brink of oblivion.) The Trump administration’s blind support for the data center building spree is a ploy that essentially triples down on the bet that AI will spur a historic productivity boom and result in an infusion of real cash to replace the circular financing network that’s currently propping up the industry. But that productivity boom has not yet appeared, and until and unless it does, the AI sector will continue to more closely resemble a Ponzi scheme than a sustainable industry.
It’s true that BAAJA’s permitting provisions would extend to most energy infrastructure projects—yet their benefits will flow disproportionately to the companies racing to build AI data centers. The AI Now Institute, a nonprofit research organization, warned as the Senate was preparing to consider the bill that “BAAJA weakens or removes essential environmental protections and democratic levers that preserve clean air and water and allow communities, states, and Tribes to decide whether and on what terms data centers are built in their communities.” The language of the bill also helps to preemptively open up federal lands for data centers. The Southern Environmental Law Center notes further that BAAJA will likely spur the continued siting of on-site or “behind-the-meter” power sources, like the roughly three dozen methane gas turbines that Elon Musk’s xAI was operating largely without oversight in Memphis.
What makes BAAJA a bailout rather than just another good-old-fashioned corporate giveaway is the plainly distressed condition of the AI industry. AI companies are collectively spending more than a trillion dollars this year alone on infrastructure to train and run generative AI models, but those models are only bringing in a small fraction of that amount in sales of generative AI products and services. Despite their enormous revenues, the cash flows of Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft—the biggest spenders on AI infrastructure—are all either already negative or soon will be. As a result, the AI industry has been forced to accumulate a staggering amount of debt over the past year, most of it hidden from public companies’ balance sheets.
Lenders are starting to heed these distress signals. Many “neoclouds”—newer companies that focus on leasing data centers and access to AI chips to model developers—have to pay double-digit interest rates when they borrow. Even bonds tied to tech giants like Microsoft and Meta now often carry high interest rates closer to those of junk bonds than those of typical blue-chip companies.
Interest rates across the rest of the economy, in turn, are rising in no small part because of the pressures that the AI buildout exerts on supply chains and bond markets. Additional rate hikes are expected in the coming months—another indicator, as was the case in the dot-com bust, that the bubble is poised to burst.

These pressures make implementation of BAAJA and the Trump administration’s recent slew of covert bailouts an urgent priority for AI companies so that data center construction and model development can continue to race ahead. Delayed or canceled data centers can’t produce the revenues that AI companies need to pay down the trillions of dollars in debt they have accumulated.And potential liability for cyberhacking incidents could make the industry’s eventual market reckoning worse. Dismantling industry regulations and protecting AI companies from lawsuits might seem like wonky and technical fare, but they represent enormous boons for Silicon Valley and Wall Street.
More bailout proposals are no doubt in the works. In its IPO S-1 filing, Anthropic hinted that AI might need to be exempted from standard consumer product safety and even criminal liability, writing, “Any determination that we are liable under such theories, or any judicial or regulatory expansion of tort, product liability, or consumer protection law, or criminal liability” would unfairly “require us to change how we design and offer our models, platform, and applications”—and, yet again, pose an unthinkable risk to the business. The company’s pitch to essentially operate above the law came as watchdog groups and state attorneys general had begun to sue for major public harm. Meanwhile, the financing mechanics of the AI boom threaten to embed a covert bailout in the bubble itself. The private credit firms doing the lion’s share of lending to AI infrastructure are deeply intertwined in life insurance markets—a position that could open the door to state government insurance guaranty funds serving as a backstop to company failures. This would be a kind of institutionalized bailout that both increases the risk of contagion and socializes the cost of reckless AI lending.
Anthropic has also pushed for Silicon Valley model developers to be protected from global competition by pressing Washington to ban or restrict (mostly Chinese) open-weights models, which are priced far lower than Anthropic’s offerings.
While none of the steps taken so far have been as dramatic or financially costly as the overt bailouts of airlines, banks, and Silicon Valley billionaires over the past quarter century, they reveal a pattern of assistance that has accelerated as the strain on the AI industry has continued to mount. Moreover, covert bailouts have often set the stage for far larger overt bailouts. When the savings-and-loan sector began teetering in the early 1980s, the federal government first responded by loosening regulations. That spurred years of reckless lending by emboldened S&Ls, all but guaranteeing the much bigger S&L crisis that hit when defaults started to pile up on S&Ls’ risky loans. Eventually, Congress stepped in with a $160 billion taxpayer-funded bailout ($380 billion in today’s dollars).
BAAJA, alongside the Trump White House’s supine regulatory posture toward the industry, would produce much the same effect, allowing the speculative frenzy behind the AI buildout to continue building in defiance of both political oversight and a market that was finally showing signs of restraint. These covert bailouts bespeak a shocking disregard for the will of voters, who loudly expressed their opposition to data centers in this year’s elections, while also ignoring the interests of the communities sure to be saddled with stranded and underwater assets in an AI collapse.
To begin steering a viable path toward the regulation of AI in the public interest, Congress needs to completely jettison the Trump White House’s model of appeasing the sector at all costs. A necessary first step in that direction is ensuring the defeat of BAAJA—an overdue signal that we need to stop bailing out the AI sector and the lords of Big Tech, and start acquainting them with real accountability for their reckless actions.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.title: Lululemon founder stuns Canadian women’s leadership conference with sexist comments
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.author: Leyland Cecco in Toronto
https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/n.text:
The controversial founder of Lululemon suggested women in Canada are having too few children and this could lead some men to bring in brides from Thailand, in remarks that stunned audience members at a women’s leadership conference.
Chip Wilson, who built the Vancouver yoga-wear startup into a global athleisure empire, was a featured speaker at the Leadership Forum in Calgary earlier this week, an event organized by Axis Connects to advance women in leadership. The organization says it aims to create space for “candid conversations about the barriers women face both in business and society”.
Wilson’s talk on 23 November, titled “Little Black Stretchy Pants” after his memoir, was billed as an “intimate, fireside chat” offering insight into the “mind and instincts of the man himself”. It was moderated by Nuvyn Peters, CEO of Axis Connects.
There is no publicly available video of the event, but the Guardian spoke with people who attended it and reviewed social media posts from those present. Outrage over the event was first reported by the Globe and Mail.
According to people who were there, Wilson told the audience that companies would be reluctant to hire a 22-year-old woman because she might become pregnant at 23 and take maternity leave. He went on to suggest that women were waiting too long to have children, prompting men to import brides from Thailand.
“There were audible gasps in the room and everyone was clearly uncomfortable. It was a mix of disengaging, walking out and also just complete shock of what was being said on stage,” one person said.
“I am floored that Axis gave this man a platform. We all were saying before the event it was surprising he was there – and it’s clear that [Wilson] runs in the organizer’s circles after she opened with the fact that they go on walks [at a Vancouver mountain] together.”
The event, which was supposed to run for an hour, was cut short at 45 minutes.
The remarks are not the first time Wilson has attracted criticism for his comments about women and their bodies. He stepped down as chair of Lululemon’s board in 2013 after the company’s signature black yoga pants were criticized for being see-through and Wilson blamed the problem on the body types of some customers.
On Monday, he reportedly told the group that those prior comments about body types had been “misconstrued” and said he was referring to women who wear sizes that are too small.
Wilson, who is believed to be worth more than C$6bn, has not had a leadership role at Lululemon for several years but remains a major shareholder.
He also reportedly told the audience that poverty had largely been eradicated, and that he was looking forward to going to space with Elon Musk.
Audience members also said Wilson suggested that men were better suited to helm clothing companies that catered to women, because they knew what looked good on women’s bodies. He said the same was true of women who lead companies focused on men’s fashion.
“We recognize that several comments made by Chip Wilson at the Leadership Forum were offensive and inconsistent with the values and mission of Axis Connects,” Peters said in a statement. “We understand why those remarks caused concern and disappointment among members of our community. His comments also underscore an uncomfortable reality: attitudes and assumptions that hold women back in the workplace and in leadership have not disappeared. Challenging those attitudes is central to the work and ethos of Axis Connects.”
Wilson’s spokesperson pointed to the work the Lululemon founder has done to mentor and “empower” women in leadership roles over the years and said his efforts “speak for themselves”. A number of women who were early employees of the company and worked closely with Wilson became millionaires when the company went public, he has previously noted in his memoir, and have gone on to found their own businesses.
More than 700 women attended the conference, many representing organizations they worked for. One person said the experience left her “irate”, adding that it was also indicative of what women continued to tolerate.
“It’s just sad that this is what women still have to deal with, in a forum literally for women.”

https://gothamist.com/news/thanksgiving-.title: Thanksgiving Day forecast upgraded to a high wind warning ahead of parade
https://gothamist.com/news/thanksgiving-.author: Rosemary Misdary
https://gothamist.com/news/thanksgiving-.text:
Tie your turkey bonnets tight; the National Weather Service has upgraded its forecast to a high wind warning for Thanksgiving Day, and that spells trouble for balloon enthusiasts.
High winds will begin to pick up in the late evening Wednesday and continue to increase throughout Thanksgiving morning before peaking in the afternoon. Meteorologists forecast a very rainy parade with up to 2 inches of precipitation and coastal flooding. If weather conditions manifest as predicted, the Macy’s Centennial Thanksgiving Day Parade will likely still go on but without its more than 100 iconic inflatables.
“They should be concerned,” said Joe Pollina, a National Weather Service meteorologist. “Overall, it’s going to be a very windy day tomorrow.”
Mayor Zohran Mamdani and NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch are expected to give a parade update on Wednesday evening.
Winds will begin to pick up at sunrise on Thanksgiving Day, with speeds up to 20 mph and gusts that can reach 30 mph, forecasters say. The high wind warning goes into effect at 10 a.m. just as the parade is in full swing, with forecasted wind speeds of nearly 30 mph and gusts that could exceed 40 mph.
During these windy conditions, the National Weather Service highly recommends securing or bringing in any loose outdoor objects, such as holiday decorations, which could become dangerous projectiles. The gusts could bring down power lines and tree limbs. The service also warns paradegoers to stay clear of trees.
“ When we issue a high wind warning like this, that means we have an 80% confidence level at least that these conditions will occur,” Pollina said. “Don't go outside during the peak of the storm, which is during the afternoon tomorrow.”
While the floats, dancers, and performers could still take to the streets, the giant character balloons such as Mickey Mouse and his gal pal Minnie may have to be grounded. As a safety rule, if winds exceed 23 mph or wind gusts surpass 34 mph, giant balloons are grounded or ordered to fly lower than usual.
Pollina said New York City wind is unpredictable and this is a concern for giant inflatables hovering in the canyon of streets. Because of the city’s vertical geometry, there could be spots of higher wind.
“You could have higher winds around a certain corner,” Pollina said. “It's very much a microclimate.”
In addition to the gales, weather predictions include moderate to heavy rain with widespread flooding that could be major at some of the city’s typical flood-prone spots.

https://www.artnews.com/art-news/artists.title: What Is Internet Cinema?
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/artists.author: Tessa Solomon
https://www.artnews.com/art-news/artists.text:
Editor’s note: This story is an edition of Link Rot, a column by Shanti Escalante-De Mattei that explores the intersections of art, technology, and the internet.
During last June’s heat wave, I found myself standing outside an unassuming office building in Crown Heights, Brooklyn, baking in the sun’s glare. The Gallery, a nomadic curatorial platform, had set up an exhibition, titled “WeWork (oralmoral)”, in one of the building’s vacant office spaces. In celebration of the show’s closing the curators were screening films, some of which fall into the category of what is being called “internet cinema,” a burgeoning movement, or method, that has been in the making since late 2020.
Once inside, I wandered around the cool, unlit space, laughing at funny paintings and sculptures until it was time to find a spot on the floor for the screening. Someone in front of me was hastily scrawling the lineup of the screenings on paper with a black marker and passing them around as fast as he produced them. One passed back to me. The first film on the list was Zarina Nares’ I am going to die (this is my sign) (2025). The projector was fiddled with and a rectangle of white with a buffer symbol appeared on the blank wall in front of the seated crowd.
	A chorus of female voices rose up, all in some general distress, and while I couldn’t see these women, by the tone, I could tell they were speaking into a front-facing camera. The chorus cut out to a single voice, which spoke over dashcam footage of a car crash: “You’re having problems at work, your boyfriend broke up with you, your parents are mad at you, everything is going wrong, your car broke down – that is a good sign. Like, that is the very best sign.”
What followed was a montage of TikTok videos featuring motivational advice. One video bled into another, linked by the formulaic hooks used by podcast bros, emotional car seat influencers, clips of celebrities’ acceptance speeches, athletes in interviews, or passionate pastors, all of which was set to music. One after another these TikToks reveal ‘the one thing that you need to learn’ in a high-speed carousel of intense emotion that feels increasingly forced as it becomes clear how many of these impassioned speeches are copies of one another.
“Internet cinema isn’t necessarily about the internet or its aesthetic but about its logic, how it functions and how it makes us feel,” Zarina Nares said in a phone call. On the process of making I am going to die, she added that “Clearly, I watched enough advice videos for too long that I kept getting more. Once you watch so many you see the formula behind them, whether it’s a certain cadence of speaking or certain music.”
Internet cinema was first defined in a 2007 paper by Chuck Tryon titled “New Media Studies and the New Internet Cinema.” The technologies and formats that concerned Tryon —iPods and camera phones, software like Final Cut Pro, and home movies—are far dated, but his paper was prescient, having tapped into impulses and concerns that reflect contemporary internet cinema: a do-it-yourself ethos that blurs the line between amateur and artist; the popularization of “niche exhibition;” and a “self-reflexive style” that works “to call attention to the narrative codes and technological specs that shape cultural productions.”
Contemporary internet cinema has its roots in the COVID-era, which saw an explosion of participation in internet culture and production, that often bled out into one particular place: Dimes Square, a patch of Manhattan where Chinatown and the Lower East Side meet.
	One of the most memorable dramas that played out at the time was puppeteered by a then-anonymous internet figure who went by the name Angelicism01. This figure posted creeds about extinction on Substack, and gained infamy for growing a cult-like following among young women in New York (who had never met him). With the help of various film makers, he made a three-hour long movie called Film01 which includes fast paced montages of memes, tweets, videos of natural disasters and terrorist attacks, alongside long scenes featuring the ‘it-girls’ he had recruited. Writer Madeline Cash described Film01 in the art publication Spike as “an unsophisticated collage of localized content that mimics, rather than intervenes or questions, our digital conditions,” which ultimately did nothing more than tap “into the scene’s libidinal narcissism.”
Yet, with some distance, Film01 has proven to be a productive experiment. One of Angelicism01’s collaborators, the filmmaker Dana Dawud, found internet footage to splice into the film, created short edits that became a part of the larger film, and remotely directed certain sequences. Dawud would go on to launch Open Secret, an international screening series of internet cinema that has since played a large part in consolidating disconnected artists and practices under the term.
At the same time that young women were running around Dimes Square at Angelicism01’s request, people were locked away at home with TikTok. More than ever, people around the world were subjecting themselves to hours and hours of scrolling on this relatively new video content platform.
“When you’re doom scrolling, there is, technically speaking, no specific author to this montage that you’re watching. So, it’s as if you’re exposed to radical experimental cinema all the time by a completely cynical industrial apparatus,” said 0nty, the co-author of “Dialogues on CoreCore & the Contemporary Online Avant-Garde” during a Zoom interview also attended by his co-author Mischa Dols. “The question is, how do you even begin to think about this problem? And I think internet cinema is an answer,” 0nty said.
0nty and Dols describe internet cinema as a method, rather than a genre or an aesthetic, which seeks to expose or comment on the way that the internet functions through editing found footage.
It’s worth noting that some works under the umbrella of internet cinema do feature the production of new images. Dahlia Bloomstone’s 20,000 Tokens (2025) is a screen recording of the artist chatting with men and exposing herself on the webcam site Chaturbate (the video is spliced with a glitching 3D-rendering of a blonde avatar in a black void). For The Sight is a Wound (2024), Parham Ghalamdar filmed himself burning his own paintings, as a statement on how tthe seemingly endless documentation of the genocide of Palestinians in Gaza has made images useless. Yet the particular process of editing found footage is usually highlighted in definitions of internet cinema because this method represents the folk practice that preceded internet cinema: corecore.
	
	Core, or rather, -core, is a suffix that denotes some kind of bundle of aesthetics and moods. Cottagecore, for example, is a reference to an image universe of milkmaid tops, galoshes, a straw basket full of wildflowers, a shingled cottage, butter made with wooden tools, but also, beyond images, a wish for simple, optimistic, pastoral life. But corecore emerged not as a specific aesthetic but as a way of making video content through editing together music, clips from movies, podcasts, and other TikToks.
These videos are often melancholic ruminations of the deep and unrecognized suffering of young men, the terrible sublimity of being alone with your screen, an alienated awareness of hurtling towards extinction while scrolling on your parents’ sofa. Watching compilations of corecore I reminded me intensely of my time on Tumblr as a teenager.
On Tumblr, the practice of posting and reblogging images, fragments of text, and GIFs under an “aesthetic” was a way of cultivating and nurturing a feeling: a world of images that created a visual language for all that we thought life could be. Painful, dramatic love; intensity chased by the doom of its own ephemerality; cold, beautiful suffering. In the pivot to video platforms, corecore takes that tendency to collect images and feelings and turns it into a form much more contained and shareable than a blog: the film.
	Removed from the usual logics of personal branding and sponsorship deals, it became an exciting trend for those who take internet-based cultural production seriously. Corecore, as a mass movement of people making films on the same devices they watch them on, represented the realization of an old dream of experimental cinema: film as a truly collective practice.
“Authorship gets really muddy, you have content creators and video artists making films on the same platforms. Dana [Dawud] has compared internet cinema to the way that SoundCloud functions, where people can steal your edit, steal your beat, steal a sample, and then it gets lost who put it online first, and that’s okay,” said Edison Niebla Rodriguez, a curator who also creates video art with his wife, Dayana Matasheva, under the name Demon Lovers Inc. “Obviously, it’s kind of at odds with video art which is very hard for people to see because of the way that the art market functions.”
That said, video art has been a major inspiration for artists working in internet cinema. Arthur Jafa’s Love Is the Message, the Message Is Death (2016) in particular is often cited as a kind of totem of legitimacy for internet cinema. The film is a montage of civil rights–era footage and grainy videos of Black Americans circulated online: reaction memes, women twerking, women getting slammed to the ground by police, men getting shot by police, arms raised in the air. It’s profound love and profound despair, but also a comment on how images of Black people circulate online. When I first saw it, I was struck by how internet it felt: the video was playing on a laptop, which had been filmed by a phone camera. Of course, it turned out I’d been watching a bootleg, and that extra frame wasn’t part of the original.
	Dawud’s film Palcorecore (2024) can be read in Jafa’s lineage. Like Jafa, Dawud cuts together found footage in an act of memory, love, and grief. The footage shows Palestinians flying kites, breakdancing, rapping, riding horses, and playing by the sea. Children surround a tank; a mute man desperately mimes a murder he witnessed. “The internet exists to document its own martyrdom,” a computerized voice says, playing on the fact that the Arabic word for martyr comes from the root meaning “to witness.” “We are martyrs together,” the voice says: we are witnesses together.
“What interests me about internet cinema is that it creates a history of internet artists, the thoughts and languages they develop online, and the possibility of establishing a continuity between what they produce on the internet and how it can be given a temporal form through cinema,” wrote Dawud in an email. “Internet cinema doesn’t merely document an existing culture; it participates in the creation of its history. It is a way for the internet to historicize itself.”
Ultimately, internet cinema is less a practice than a name: one that gives form to a whole range of ways of making online that are often lost in the tumult of the internet’s incessant production. If there is one thing that separates the art world from online cultural production, it is that the art world is nothing if not a form of memory. In its obsession with provenance, catalogues, and archives, it is a network of stewardship. Internet cinema is a means of making an object of what is so fleeting online, by turning the internet into a film.

https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.title: Selo ‘Não é Não’ certifica bar e mobiliza rede de proteção às mulheres na Paraíba
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.author: Redação
https://www.brasildefato.com.br/2026/11/.text:
O Bar do Baiano, em João Pessoa, será referência em uma iniciativa de prevenção à violência contra as mulheres. Na sexta-feira (27), às 18h30, o estabelecimento, no bairro dos Bancários, receberá o “Selo Não é Não – Mulheres Seguras”, após participar de uma capacitação voltada ao acolhimento e à proteção de mulheres em situações de assédio e violência. A ação é promovida pelo Ministério das Mulheres e pela ONU Mulheres, por meio do Projeto das Articuladoras Territoriais na Paraíba, representado por Patrícia Oliveira, coordenadora, e Marcella Arbia, especialista, em parceria com movimentos sociais do estado.
Segundo Arbia, o Protocolo Não é Não vai para além dos grandes eventos, envolvendo diretamente os proprietários de bares e os trabalhadores do setor de entretenimento
“Aqui na Paraíba, neste ano, o Ministério das Mulheres lançou novamente a iniciativa do Protocolo Não é Não. Para que o protocolo seja aplicado, é necessário que os estabelecimentos participem da capacitação para receber o Selo Não é Não. O selo é concedido após um treinamento realizado por uma pessoa indicada pelo próprio estabelecimento, que aprende como prevenir situações de violência contra as mulheres e como agir diante desses casos”, explicou.
Para Patrícia Oliveira, a iniciativa é importante para garantir que bares, casas de shows e boates adotem protocolos de segurança para proteger mulheres vítimas de violência e saibam como acionar a rede de proteção diante dessas situações.
“A importância reside exatamente no cumprimento, pelos estabelecimentos, sejam bares, casas de shows ou boates, da instituição de um protocolo de segurança para as mulheres vítimas de violência. É fundamental que esses espaços estejam preparados para acolher e proteger as mulheres. Sobretudo, precisam saber como acionar a rede de proteção quando uma mulher passar por esse tipo de situação”, destacou.
Capacitação e rede de proteção
De acordo com Arbia, um representante do estabelecimento participou de um curso on-line de 36 horas. Além do certificado, o bar recebe um cartaz identificando o espaço como seguro para mulheres.
“É importante que as mulheres saibam que estão em um ambiente mais seguro, onde os funcionários fizeram o curso e sabem como agir diante de uma situação de violência. Eles precisam saber a quem recorrer e quais procedimentos adotar para proteger a mulher. Queremos que o Bar do Baiano seja um exemplo para que outros estabelecimentos também adotem o protocolo”, comentou ela.
A entrega reunirá instituições da rede de proteção, incluindo a Delegacia Especializada no Atendimento à Mulher (Deam), a Patrulha Maria da Penha, o Procon – órgão responsável pela aplicação do protocolo – as secretarias de mulheres estadual e municipal e conselhos. Bares interessados poderão procurar os movimentos de mulheres, as secretarias ou as articuladoras territoriais. O curso também pode ser acessado pelo portal do Ministério das Mulheres.
O que prevê a lei federal
A Lei Federal nº 14.786/2023 estabelece medidas de prevenção ao constrangimento e à violência em casas noturnas, boates, shows e espetáculos musicais em locais fechados com venda de bebidas alcoólicas. Entre as medidas estão acolhimento da vítima, afastamento do agressor e capacitação de funcionários.
Na Paraíba, a Lei nº 12.724/2023, de autoria da deputada Silvia Benjamin (Republicanos), determina a divulgação da campanha “Não é Não” em shows, festas e eventos realizados ou patrocinados pelo governo da Paraíba, incluindo campanhas educativas e presença de órgãos para receber denúncias.
Contexto nacional
Segundo o Ministério das Mulheres, a iniciativa integra uma mobilização nacional prevista para 27 de novembro de 2026, com a certificação de bares nas capitais brasileiras por meio do Selo “Não é Não”. A ação busca incentivar a adesão de estabelecimentos ao protocolo federal, ampliar a capacitação de funcionários e fortalecer a prevenção ao assédio e à violência contra as mulheres em ambientes de lazer.
